text: Matteo Renzi came to power in February 2014 with a promise of widespread reform, at the head of Italy's powerful centre-left Democratic Party (PD). Prior to his relocation to Rome's Chigi Palace at the age of 39, his principal political experience comprised serving as Florence's mayor. He had never held parliamentary membership. Nevertheless, it was scarcely two months following his assumption of party leadership in December 2013 that he precipitated the fall of his Prime Minister and party adversary Enrico Letta and assumed office. His entrance into national politics was proclaimed as an indication of essential generational transformation in a nation governed for years by ageing men. Even prior to becoming prime minister he was recognised as Il Rottamatore (The Scrapper) - an allusion to his appeal to dismantle Italy's political establishment, extensively considered as discredited, corrupted by scandal, and as having disappointed the nation repeatedly across decades. Whilst he guided the party to victory in European elections several months following his appointment as prime minister, his party's electoral share in local contests in May 2015 fell beneath 24% and he has yet to face a general election. Mr Renzi developed his political skills as Florence's mayor, earning extensive acclaim for his promotion of the city and his management of a significant pedestrianisation scheme. However, he was not without detractors. One former Florentine councillor protested he was more concerned with his Facebook posts than monitoring the city's finances. And opposition councillor Ornella De Zordo protested he excelled at making pledges rather than fulfilling them. He has employed the motto 'Said, Done!' repeatedly, she stated. I would declare 'Said, But Not Done!' because Matteo Renzi is exceptionally skilled at a communicational level - at making declarations. However, when one examines his achievements, matters are considerably different. He markets himself exceptionally well. Matteo Renzi assumed power believing politics could be conducted differently, and once advocated dismantling the old guard. Citizens are exhausted and disillusioned, he declared. They no longer believe. I believe, and that is why I pursue politics - because I continue to believe. Some observed parallels with the early period of former British leader Tony Blair, and his seizure of the left-wing Labour Party during the mid-1990s. Like Mr Blair, the reformist Mr Renzi attempted to draw the PD towards the centre ground, and appeal to voters typically more comfortable on the right. In his own terms enormously ambitious, he pledged all the courage, dedication, vigour and enthusiasm of which I am capable. Radiating limitless energy, he appears as composed on television and in parliament, and swift and articulate in his presentation. Whilst his governmental success will probably be determined by the outcomes of his reform campaign, his tenure in office has been dominated by Italy's Mediterranean migrant crisis. An estimated 45,000 migrants have reached Italy since January and more than 1,830 individuals attempting to traverse the Mediterranean have perished. Mr Renzi has charged other European nations with ignoring the tragedy developing near Italy's coastline, and the matter has benefited his right-wing anti-immigration adversaries, the Northern League. His position has been assisted by Federica Mogherini, a party colleague who was designated EU foreign affairs chief following the 2014 European elections. In his pursuit of reform, he provoked fury from his party's left by conducting a prominent meeting at PD headquarters with Silvio Berlusconi, the former centre-right prime minister expelled from parliament but still controlling the opposition Forza Italia (FI) movement. However, Mr Renzi remained defiant. It constitutes a contradiction in terms to declare 'You should have consulted FI but not Berlusconi'. Should I have consulted [Berlusconi's fiancée's dog] Dudu? Within weeks, Mr Renzi had progressed towards a party coup. Following a dinner with President Giorgio Napolitano, the young challenger was reported as stating the government's batteries were depleting and a decision was required on whether they needed recharging - or replacement. Following his visit to Mr Letta, he thanked the prime minister but declared the country was at a crossroads: there was an urgent requirement for a new phase with a new executive. Shortly thereafter, Mr Letta announced he would resign. However, administering the magnificent Renaissance city of Florence and removing traffic from its central squares and streets differs considerably from governing Italy and reforming its politics. He has succeeded in restructuring the electoral system, establishing a form of proportional representation that ensures a substantial majority to the victorious party, following a protracted struggle that estranged some of his own party's MPs. However, he confronts additional battles ahead, as he attempts to advance changes designed to elevate standards in Italy's schools. He has already commenced work on restructuring the labour market to enhance job creation, but he intends to accomplish more and confronts opposition from trade unions and from within his own party.

text: Being in a wheelchair doesn't mean that I can't do it or anyone else can't do it - we're just as capable as any other models. Gemma Flanagan propelled herself along the catwalk for the first time at a London fashion event on Wednesday. It was so incredible to do it and not fall off. My greatest concern was I'd roll off the end or the side, she stated. Prior to an illness that left her unable to walk, she worked as a flight attendant and part-time model. I surprisingly felt just as confident as I have done previously which, considering it was the first one in my chair, I wasn't certain how I'd manage with. When you're walking you can sort of have a little strut and do your thing. That's what I was concerned about - not being able to show the clothes off as effectively. The designer's just so delighted with how I showcased their items and at the end of the day that's what modelling's about. The fashion show was organised by the group Models of Diversity which campaigns for the fashion and beauty industries to represent diversity, and occurred at the Ideal Home Show in London's Olympia. Gemma, who is celebrating her 32nd birthday this week, wants using disabled models to be the standard. The more people that are willing to using models with disabilities then the more people will see it as normal. We've all been in campaigns that have been a one-off for companies and many of them aren't paid either. It would be good to use models with disabilities just as models, not as one-offs - we're better than that, she states. As for her future, she states: I've got a hair show in May and a couple of shoots lined up with local photographers. I want to do a lot more using my chair. I'm in it nearly all of the time now. Part of me doing this show was to embrace myself and embrace the fact that the chair isn't the enemy anymore. It's basically seeing past the metal and the wheels and just saying, 'that's a gorgeous model' rather than 'a girl in a chair'. In 2011 Gemma was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, a serious condition which affects the nervous system. She spent seven months in rehabilitation trying to learn to speak, write and walk again. Recently though she states she's found it harder to walk with crutches and has become increasingly reliant on her wheelchair. When I got ill they were hoping I'd make a full recovery, she stated. But I've started getting worse again and the consultant thinks this may be the best I'm ever going to be. I've been a bit up and down, but now I feel OK mostly. I want to show other people they don't need to be defined by their disabilities. Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube

text: Fireworks scratched colours into the slate grey sky after being unleashed from the top of Tower Bridge as the historic royal flotilla finished gliding along the Thames. This marked the conclusion of the Diamond Jubilee pageant in London, though other events failed to survive the wet conditions - specifically the cannons prepared to discharge confetti and a helicopter flyover, which was abandoned due to poor visibility. The gentle yet persistent rainfall showed no compassion for the drenched performers who courageously performed the national anthem during the final moments. These occasions represented the final remnants of a day that had witnessed entertainment, refreshments, festivities, fancy dress and multiple performances of the national anthem, alongside a demonstration against the monarchy - all determinedly executed despite the precipitation. Earlier in the day, certain revellers travelling to the capital experienced disrupted plans due to overcrowding on the railway system, with accounts of passengers abandoned on platforms because coaches were packed. Others remained at home to commemorate, with nearly 9,500 roads closed throughout England and Wales for gatherings. Those in the capital immersed themselves in the festivities, particularly those who participated in the Big Jubilee Lunch in Piccadilly, comprising an extended row of tables along this typically congested thoroughfare. Ms Symonds stated: I genuinely appreciate the Royal Family and the heritage it embodies. I attended the royal wedding as well and that was magnificent. We wished to dress formally for the Jubilee and participate in the ambience to feel included in the commemorations. It transformed into an even more magnificent occasion when the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall appeared, proceeding along the row of tables and even pausing to settle onto a potentially damp chair to converse with some of those consuming their meals. Street gatherings proved particularly fashionable on the day, especially in Bristol, which received more requests for road closures than any other city beyond London. Celebrants there assembled in a red, white and blue-decorated Millennium Square, which featured its own create your own corgi display. Motivated by the Thames pageant, Andrew Southerden, a publican in Kibworth, Leicestershire, converted his establishment into HMS Coach & Horses, attaching portholes, lifeboats, chimneys and a prow to the structure. Attendees in Richmond Park, Gainsborough, Lincolnshire, could purchase refreshments at 1950s costs. Hot dogs cost 7p, bacon rolls 9p and a cup of tea merely 2p. In Belfast, Samuel and Margaret Sloan, 80, were marking their 60th wedding anniversary alongside the Jubilee at a tea gathering hosted by the city's Lord Mayor. It represents a tremendous privilege, stated Mr Sloan, a retired automotive engineer. She remains a most dignified Queen and she genuinely cares for her subjects. Over 300 official street gatherings occurred throughout Wales. Cardiff's St Mary's Street accommodated a Big Lunch celebration whilst hundreds participated in a comparable occasion in Swansea. A seaside gathering was cancelled due to rain in Rhosneigr, near the Anglesey residence of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, though the celebration proceeded nevertheless - a picnic was conducted in the village hall alternatively, attended by hundreds of individuals. Ten street gatherings occurred in Edinburgh, with the Scottish capital believed to have submitted one-third of Scotland's street gathering applications. However, not everyone participating endorsed the royal family's constitutional position. Abigail Burnyeat, who participated in a street gathering in Edinburgh's Stockbridge, informed the BBC she enjoyed herself but did not regard the occasion as approval of the monarchy. It represents a celebration of community, she stated, adding: I would not scrutinise it excessively. As the Diamond Jubilee pageant commenced, its 1,000 craft were welcomed along the course by 1.2 million onlookers, according to the organisers. Crowds gathered along the Thames banks, some ascending onto window sills of adjacent buildings to attempt securing a superior view, all grateful that presently the skies were retaining their moisture. On Lambeth Bridge, a carefully regulated number of the public were permitted access, each selecting a side to occupy, to either observe the pageant arrive or witness it depart into the distance. As it drew near, the smaller craft preceding the larger ones, tremendous cheers erupted, alongside the rustling of plastic flags. That sound reached its peak when the royal vessel approached, prompting numerous hands to lift mobile telephones and cameras, resembling electronic meerkats eager for a glimpse. Among those on the bridge was Marilyn Griffiths, 59, from Ledbury, Herefordshire, adorned in a union jack hat, earrings and carrying a flag. She characterised the pageant as magnificent, adding: I simply adore the Royal Family and respect them all for their contributions. They all labour tremendously. I wished to attend here to demonstrate my support. By the pageant's conclusion the rainfall had become nearly torrential, with everyone thoroughly soaked. Nevertheless the crowd's cheerful disposition endured, with one gentleman even savouring a rather waterlogged ice cream. The final steam vessels sailed past sounding their horns collectively and attracting cheers from the flag-bearers along Tower Bridge. I observed the Queen, exclaimed one small child to his mother. text: Labour MP Simon Danczuk has been suspended by the party after newspaper allegations about his private life. These are external links and will open in a new window The Sun claimed he exchanged explicit messages with a 17-year-old girl. On Twitter, the Rochdale MP stated the story was not entirely accurate but referenced an extremely low point in his life. He stated he apologised unreservedly for his inappropriate conduct, adding: I was stupid [and] there's no fool like an old fool. A Labour Party spokesman stated: The general secretary of the Labour Party has today suspended Simon Danczuk's membership of the party, pending an investigation into allegations published in the media today. A full investigation will now take place under the authority of the National Executive Committee, which will be responsible for determining any further action. Mr Danczuk, who separated from his wife earlier this year, has served as the MP for Rochdale since 2010. The backbencher has been a strong critic of Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and his predecessor Ed Miliband, and has conducted a high-profile campaign to expose historical child abuse. In his statement on Twitter, he added: I'm more saddened that this episode could overshadow the important work we're doing to help Rochdale [and] that's where my focus lies. The Rochdale MP possesses a reputation as an outspoken backbencher. He has been a thorn in Jeremy Corbyn's side and has described his predecessor Ed Miliband as one of the worst Labour Party leaders in history. The 49-year-old is perhaps best known for his campaigning work on historical child sex abuse, having co-authored a book on alleged abuse by former Rochdale MP Cyril Smith and called for action over a missing 1980s dossier about alleged paedophiles at Westminster. In July, he stated he was stepping back from his child abuse campaigning work to seek help for depression, adding that he was in no doubt it had taken its toll on his marriage. As a consequence of his suspension, Mr Danczuk has had the Labour whip withdrawn, meaning he will sit as an independent MP. Although the girl featured in The Sun was above the age of consent, BBC political correspondent Chris Mason stated the allegations were particularly embarrassing for an MP who had devoted much of his time in recent years to campaigning about child protection. In interviews, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and shadow chancellor John McDonnell both emphasised the independence of the National Executive Committee (NEC) investigation. Corbyn ally and NEC member Ken Livingstone told the BBC people should not jump to conclusions based on Mr Danczuk's suspension. We won't be rushing to any judgement, he stated. The party clearly had to investigate the allegations, he stated, adding: The simple fact is that it might not be illegal but a lot of people are going to disapprove of that sort of age gap and that sort of texting, particularly given this is an MP who made the exposure of child abuse a key part of his political career.

text: Manchester City earned their first Premier League home win in almost three months as they battled past Watford at Etihad Stadium. The fourth-placed Blues, seeking to prevent a third consecutive top-flight defeat, took the lead when an unmarked Pablo Zabaleta calmly side-footed home Kevin de Bruyne's deep cross. Raheem Sterling struck the Watford crossbar after the interval, before Odion Ighalo poked wide the visitors' finest opportunity. And the Hornets, who slip to 11th, were punished when David Silva slotted home a late second on his 200th league appearance following a rapid City counter-attack. However, the sole negative for Blues manager Pep Guardiola was Germany midfielder Ilkay Gundogan sustaining a serious knee injury that the Spaniard stated will sideline him for several months. Cast your mind back to late September. Manchester City had secured their first 10 matches under Pep Guardiola, including their opening six Premier League fixtures to establish a four-point advantage at the summit. Fast forward to mid-December and the situation appears less promising. Guardiola's team have subsequently fallen from the top, losing ground on their title competitors after securing just four victories from their previous 15 matches before Watford's arrival. Questions have been posed regarding the acclaimed Spanish manager's approach, which delivered him such tremendous success at Barcelona and Bayern Munich. The Blues had not secured a top-flight victory before their own supporters since that 10th consecutive triumph - a 4-0 success against Bournemouth on 17 September. And whilst their display lacked the energy and flair of those early days under Guardiola, the Blues will certainly be more than satisfied with a determined performance that maintains them in fourth place. It has been a considerable time without a victory playing at home, it has been peculiar, stated Zabaleta. City remain seven points behind leaders Chelsea, now one point behind Liverpool and Arsenal - with the Gunners visiting the Etihad on Sunday. Where City's difficulties have originated from in recent weeks is quite evident - their porous defence. The Blues had maintained just one clean sheet in their 17 previous fixtures and, following Saturday's humiliating 4-2 defeat at champions Leicester City, Guardiola altered his defence in both personnel and formation. England centre-back John Stones was the notable omission, relegated to the bench as his manager switched from three centre-backs to a four-man defence. Consequently, they appeared more organised and resolute than at any other time in the past two months. It was not the most attractive match tonight but we possessed determination to secure the victory. We achieved the clean sheet we've been discussing and were solid defensively, added Zabaleta. Nevertheless, they were still nearly punished when striker Ighalo escaped Zabaleta - but he directed Nordin Amrabat's right-wing cross over the crossbar. The Blues were also indebted to goalkeeper Claudio Bravo, who has received some criticism from City supporters, for a sharp save from Hornets midfielder Etienne Capoue. It is not straightforward to join a new club and a new country, stated Guardiola about the Chile international, who arrived from Barcelona in the summer. I understand what people say about him, but he possesses good experience. When moments arise he must be brave. Today he was excellent. Media playback is not supported on this device. Watford have displayed two aspects to their character under Italian manager Walter Mazzarri - one which is capable enough to defeat Manchester United and Everton to climb as high as seventh, plus the one which collapsed in a 6-1 demolition by Liverpool earlier in the campaign and lost three in four before defeating the Toffees at the weekend. This Hornets display was somewhere in between. They demonstrated resilience in not permitting City to slice them open, but opportunities at the other end were restricted. Despite netting three against Everton at the weekend, Mazzarri's side have not found goals straightforward to come by all season. text: A Carmarthen school at the centre of a police investigation into claims of historical abuse has been criticised by care inspectors in a new report. The Care and Social Services Inspectorate Wales stated that the residential facility at Rhydygors school, Carmarthen, was not meeting minimum standards. The institution was additionally criticised by educational inspectors, Estyn, in September last year. The governing body stated they were developing the advancement already achieved in tackling issues highlighted in the Estyn assessment. This month, Dyfed Powys Police announced they had detained six former employees under Operation Almond, which examines allegations of mistreatment at the institution between 1976 and 1986. Rhydygors School, located in Johnstown, delivers specialist education for students with social, emotional and behavioural challenges. The CSSIW assessment stated: In general, we determined that young people and their advocates cannot be assured that proper care and consideration has been given to the national minimum standards for residential special schools during the time since our previous inspection, as the service has not completely satisfied these standards. The institution is now receiving monthly inspections from Carmarthenshire council to oversee the standard of care students receive. The assessment stated its interim headteacher, Margaret Davies, and the governing body ought to be more conscious of national minimum standards. The document also stated 80% of care personnel should possess a relevant qualification but the residential facility had not achieved that objective. The service additionally failed to conduct an annual assessment of the school's welfare arrangements for residential students. Educational inspectors Estyn characterised the school's performance as satisfactory but stated its potential for improvement was inadequate. The body stated: The school's procedures for protecting pupils broadly satisfy requirements but several areas present a cause for concern. The school's governing body chairman Matthew Harries stated: Rhydygors underwent inspection by Estyn in September 2014 and, as the incoming chair of governors, I shall be seeking to develop the advancement that has been achieved to tackle the recommendations of the assessment. Furthermore, we are satisfied that advancement has been achieved in numerous of these areas as acknowledged in the more recent CSSIW assessment. A CSSIW representative stated: We do not hold any major concerns regarding Rhydygors School. Operation Almond is additionally examining allegations of mistreatment at Cartref-y-Gelli children's facility in Carmarthen between 1986 and 1990.

text: The spacecraft which made a spectacular landing on a comet last year has discovered a rich array of carbon compounds. A prominent scientist has described the chemicals as frozen primordial soup. This reinforces the hypothesis that comets might have provided the early Earth with life's essential components. The discoveries emerged following the lander, designated Philae, making contact with comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko 67P in November. The European Space Agency's Rosetta mothership deployed it during the culminating phase of a decade-long mission. Findings from the lander's seven instruments appear in a special compilation of studies in the journal Science. A team operating an instrument called COSAC identified sixteen organic compounds, four of which were previously unknown on comets. Professor Ian Wright from the Open University, who directs another instrument, Ptolemy, described the findings as genuinely fascinating. I regard this cometary material we are examining as frozen primordial soup. It represents the type of substance that, if available and heated somehow, and placed in suitable surroundings, with appropriate conditions, might ultimately produce life. What we could be observing here is our abiological ancestral matter - this material contributed to the mixture that generated life. In numerous respects it is rather humbling work, because this represents life before life occurred. Among Ptolemy's most important findings is a compound called polyoxymethylene, a chain of comparatively simple molecules forming a formaldehyde polymer. Professor Wright stated: This polymer's basic unit comprises one carbon, two hydrogens and one oxygen, which then repeats. That identical elemental ratio appears in carbohydrates and sugars, making it extremely interesting and implicated in Earth's biological processes. In another study, Fred Goesmann and colleagues detail the sixteen compounds discovered by their COSAC instrument, and their potential significance for life's emergence. Hydroxyethanal represents an effective catalyst in the prebiotic creation of sugars, they report. Methanenitrile constitutes a crucial molecule in the prebiotic synthesis of amino acids and nucleobases and provides an elegant route to sugars. The researchers conclude that the comet's chemical complexity, and the presence of nitrogen-containing organics, suggest that early solar system chemistry promotes prebiotic material formation in substantial concentrations. None of the studies indicates more advanced compounds such as amino acids exist - although additional analysis might reveal these. Professor Charles Cockell, director of the UK Astrobiology Centre, who was not part of the mission, told the BBC the results were extremely important. Discovering basic organic compounds on a comet in space, demonstrating they could have reached the early Earth during our planet's early history, is enormously thrilling. It provides improved understanding of how those life components might have developed and their possible origins. It establishes that organic chemistry exists throughout the universe, that carbon-based compounds, some highly complex, might be forming on comets within our solar system. Professor Mark McCaughrean, the European Space Agency's senior scientific adviser, told BBC News: Consider wanting to construct a house and visiting a forest containing trees, mud and rocks. You might build a house from these materials, but it would require considerable effort. We have now found the comet resembles a hardware store - numerous ready-made components, including door frames, bricks and similar items. It provides an advantage. One major question remains: was this material created on the comet? Or was it first produced in space then incorporated into the comet? We lack that answer currently. Today's published data was collected during Philae's turbulent comet landing. Ptolemy was programmed to activate ten minutes following touchdown. Professor Wright informed the BBC: The plan involved a brief atmospheric sample - there was no compelling reason for this, it was to verify the instrument survived landing, a precautionary measure to obtain immediate data. Events unfolded differently as Philae failed to secure itself at its intended landing site but rebounded, meaning Ptolemy's 'sample' occurred whilst the spacecraft was airborne. Nevertheless, the instrument successfully obtained readings of material that had entered its intake tube. We captured a glimpse of dust particles present during landing but obtained highly significant data, Professor Wright stated. Following extended silence, the Philae lander established contact last month, though communication has been sporadic and the spacecraft's condition remains uncertain. One hypothesis suggests it might have been displaced or overturned by gas jets emerging from underlying rocks. Gas jets are intensifying as the comet nears the Sun - with its closest approach, termed perihelion, occurring imminently on 13th August. Another possibility is that because Philae is thought to rest at a cliff base, it might have been struck by falling debris, loosened as the surface heats. However, mission participants remain determined to stay positive that the lander has survived and will restore communication. Even without further contact, multiple datasets, gathered and transmitted during Philae's initial 60 hours on the comet, continue undergoing analysis and await publication.

text: Nigeria's main opposition party has condemned a weekend raid of its Lagos offices by state security agents. We demand an independent commission of inquiry to determine the reasons why armed officers raided our office, All Progressive Congress (APC) deputy chairman Lawal Shuaibu informed the BBC. The party stated that computers were destroyed and documents confiscated during the raid. The State Security Service declared it was investigating alleged cloning of voter cards, prior to elections in February. The petition claimed that those behind the activities were cloning Inec [Independent Electoral Commission] permanent voters cards, with the intention of hacking into [the] Inec database, corrupting it and replacing them with their own data, the SSS stated. Based on this information, the Service placed the building under surveillance and having been convinced that some unwholesome activities were occurring in the building, it undertook a raid of the premises. It stated its agents had removed a server, three hard drives and 31 bags of documents on Saturday. However, the APC declared the incident was another one in the string of attacks and illegal actions of the administration. It stated more than a dozen computers had been destroyed, a server had been vandalised and 28 people detained. Nigerians have been witnessing the way and manner the government have been using force in oppressing us, Mr Shuaibu informed the BBC Hausa service. This is to be condemned and we have been restraining ourselves from taking actions based on the provocations by the government and the security personnel. APC spokesman Lai Mohammed likened the raid to the Watergate scandal in the United States, which led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974. Just like the Watergate scandal in the USA, the state-sponsored security operatives apparently acting at the behest of the ruling PDP [People's Democratic Party] government turned the office upside down, and pulled out and vandalised everything in sight, he informed the AFP news agency. The APC has stated the office was operating as a data centre to process registration of party memberships and was a legitimate operation. The APC was established in a merger of four opposition parties in 2013. It declared there was an urgent need to challenge President Goodluck Jonathan whose party, the PDP, has won every election in Nigeria since the end of military rule in 1999. The International Crisis Group recently warned that February's election may be volatile and vicious. If this violent trend continues, and particularly if the vote is close, marred or followed by widespread violence, it would deepen Nigeria's already grave security and governance crises, the think tank stated. The government, its agencies and all other national figures must work urgently to ensure that the vote is not conducted in an explosive situation as this could further destabilise the country.

text: Writer and humourist Shovon Chowdhury gives his perspective on a recent advert featuring lesbians in India, arguing that we shouldn't be surprised, given India's ancient liberal tradition, which accepted all forms of sexuality and sexual expression. They created an advertisement about lesbians! declared a companion. I heard librarians, so initially I was perplexed. It appeared to be a positive development. I frequently fret about reading practices in this nation. However, he subsequently showed me. It is an advertisement for a brand of women's apparel, and it depicts two women in love. I considered it very well directed and performed and irritatingly challenging to ridicule. Was this a monumental step? It appeared to be one, until I recalled Parveen Babi. Parveen Babi was an actress who illuminated our youth. She also brought the country pride by featuring on the cover of Time magazine. This entire lesbian matter is not as novel as people are portraying it to be. In the film Razia Sultan, released in 1983, she and Hema Malini recline on a sumptuous boat in carefree abandon, Hema Malini half-asleep, Parveen Babi gazing at her intently, singing a lullaby. At one moment, Hema Malini awakens and they kiss. The kiss itself is concealed behind some feathers. This was the standard for any sort of kiss at that period. Feathers, flowers and dupattas were the favoured methods of maintaining discretion. What this television commercial offers us is a more contemporary setting, with fewer feathers. It renders the whole matter more relatable. That girl could be my cousin, you consider, or my best friend's sister. However, cinema was there initially. In general, cinema has been a powerful force for social transformation in this country. The post-independence filmmakers felt the warmth of freedom upon their faces, and they were unashamed about incorporating positive social messages in their films. It was part of nation building. Until the 1990s, when we discovered a vital fact about television. You need not leave the house. This has resulted in a decline in the significance of cinema. More television has meant more advertising, and this is where economics assumes a role. Most producers of television serials are notoriously economical, as a consequence of which people speak very slowly, and an arrow fired in one episode reaches its target several episodes later. Television writers are poorly compensated. Advertising personnel are paid considerably more. Consequently, the advertisements are often superior to the programmes. Some of the copywriters do wish to accomplish good things, and sometimes, clients support them. So there have been quite a few positive social messages in Indian advertising. We have witnessed three broad phases. We are a very impoverished country, and some products have had to establish their markets from the ground up. Early on, in the 1970s and the 1980s, advertising taught us simple matters, like the benefits of bathing, the virtues of brushing teeth, and why you should be kind to your wife. This was the phase during which I saw a woman in a bikini for the first time, in an advertisement for Liril soap. It marked me permanently, and I can still recall her name. As society developed, so did the lessons. In the subsequent phase, women continued to assume a significant role. Advertising demonstrated to us that women can actually accomplish things, such as purchase clothes, possess credit cards, and drive stylish convertibles. In phase three, which is presently, socially conscious advertisers are addressing stuttering, cancer survivors and partition [the 1947 partition that made Pakistan a separate state]. And also lesbians. However, why all this commotion about lesbians, you may enquire. Is it a conspiracy against women? Is it prohibited in the Kama Sutra? Has Indian society traditionally disapproved of gay people? Not particularly. For instance, in the Laws of Manu, which are more than 2,000 years old, and establish rules for everything, the prescribed punishment for homosexuality is taking a bath with your clothes on, after which you are purified. In case you consider this is extreme, consider that the prescribed punishment for forcible intercourse was the immediate removal of two fingers. Kautilya's Artha Shastra, an economic and political treatise, takes a more economic view of the matter, and suggests a small fine. The Kama Sutra provides detailed instructions for homosexual acts, as it does for everything else. The Sushruta Samhita was a medical treatise written around 600 BC by Sushruta, one of the greatest medical men in history. He determined how to reconstruct noses, amongst other things. He defines types of homosexual behaviour, and states clearly that sexual orientation is something that is determined at birth. He drew a distinction between transgenders and homosexuals. Transgenders themselves have not always had the simplest of times in India, but they have a place in our society. They have presented television shows. We have voted for them in elections, sometimes to show other leaders what we think of them. The temples of Khajuraho, constructed around 1000 AD, feature a wide variety of people getting fortunate, in every possible combination, including some that are quite implausible. So what went awry, you may enquire? When did we become such prudes? The primary cause was a small, plumpish white woman. It would be unjust to place all the blame on Queen Victoria, though. We also had a role to perform. Unable to perceive the benefits of British rule, we revolted in 1857. Once the revolt was suppressed, a new Indian Penal Code (IPC) was developed, which came into force in 1861. It was designed to ensure that the natives would never raise their heads again. The creators of this document also took into account the wishes of their sovereign. Queen Victoria disapproved of sex, and the IPC of 1861 acknowledges this. It criminalises almost any kind of sexual activity, excluding the missionary position. Nearly 75 years after independence, it appears that the natives still cannot be trusted, which is why the IPC remains in force. This means that this film that millions of people have appreciated on YouTube is more than merely a film. It is an act of civil disobedience. It depicts a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison, under Section 377. I do not know what the punishment for directors is, but if the police do their job, as mandated by her majesty, we ought to be discovering soon. text: There has been a 65% increase in children recorded as home educated in the UK over six years. Parents provided reasons including their lifestyle, dissatisfaction or disputes with local schools, special needs, bullying and religion. Responses to Freedom of Information requests from 190 local authorities revealed 36,609 home educated children. text: General Motors chief executive Mary Barra has apologised for an ignition switch fault in some cars linked to at least a dozen deaths in road crashes. During a United States congressional hearing on Tuesday, she also stated she was disturbed by the corporation's earlier remarks regarding the substantial expense of replacing the faulty components. General Motors (GM) has thus far recalled 2.6 million vehicles due to the defect. However, it has faced criticism for taking excessive time to do so. Problems with ignition switches in certain GM models, including the Chevrolet Cobalt and Saturn Ion, were initially reported over a decade ago. Yet the corporation only commenced recalling vehicles in February this year, one month after Ms Barra assumed the role of chief executive. I cannot explain why it required years for a safety defect to be announced... but I can assure you that we shall discover the answer, stated Ms Barra, giving evidence before a United States House of Representatives panel investigating the matter. As soon as I became aware of the problem, we acted without delay. We informed the world we had a problem requiring resolution. We did so because whatever errors were committed previously, we shall not avoid our responsibilities now and in the future. Today's GM will act appropriately. That commences with my heartfelt apologies to everyone who has been affected by this recall, particularly to the families and friends of those who perished or sustained injuries. I am profoundly sorry. Ms Barra said she found it disturbing that cost considerations might have discouraged an immediate replacement of the defective switches. The chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, Republican Fred Upton, told Ms Barra: With a two-tonne piece of high-velocity machinery, there exists zero margin for error; product safety represents a life or death matter. But regrettably, vehicle safety has proved inadequate. text: A law has come into force in France which makes it an offence for a Muslim woman to conceal her face behind a veil when in public. It represents the first European nation to publicly prohibit a form of attire that certain Muslims consider a religious obligation. Readers of the BBC News website in France have been submitting their responses to this story. Here is a selection of their observations. In my view, the legislation seems to oppose individual freedoms. I am a Muslim but I do not wear a headscarf as I believe it contradicts my principles. Nevertheless, this prohibition will undoubtedly stigmatise Islam. This practice affects a small number of Muslim women in France and in this manner it seems extreme and unjust, because these women will be inclined to remain confined at home for most of the time. The outcomes will be socially catastrophic. Through this legislation one can observe that Islam in France is viewed as a threat to French values and society. Sabrina, Lille, France As a Muslim residing in Paris, I am so pleased that this new legislation is present, for there has been an increasing problem for some time now in Paris, with the radicalisation of young Muslims. Some of the more extreme Muslims have started to employ dress as a symbol or statement against French society. I believe that the extreme example of the Muslim faith operates against all that Muslims in France represent. That is, that we can exist in harmony alongside other religions and faiths. Jean Paul Baptiste, Paris, France Finally a law that safeguards the dignity and the human rights of women. This is not a racist law, it is a courageous and progressive law that seeks to end the scandalous persecution of women in the Muslim community. I am not Sarkozy's greatest supporter and I wish someone else was governing my country, but I endorse this law completely as the suffering of women having to wear this garment around the world truly saddens me. Rachel Sword, Aix en Provence, France I support this law. The women who move around in public in the burqa, provoke feelings of both fear, and pity. I have frequently heard that these women complain of being completely ignored by those around them - hardly surprising, really. Concealing your identity causes others to become wary and suspicious. Fiona Ricard, Gailhan, France Despite being a human rights barrister, I have mixed feelings about the law. Freedom of religion dictates that people should be able to express their faith how they wish, though it can be restricted by the state if there are strong reasons and it is proportionate. I think it should not be prohibited outright and that it is excessive, but it should perhaps be restricted in the case of employment or other areas of society. Whilst the state has to respect the diverse values of its population, immigrants also have to respect the values of the society they have chosen to live in - and France is a secular state. Andy, Strasbourg, France Enacting a law to prohibit face covering veils in France is taking an approach that will polarise and entrench opinions. Very few Muslim women wish to wear face veils, but telling them they cannot will make them want to do so to protect what they see as an attack on their identity. Why take a line that will push Muslims (the majority of whom are not conservative) into a more polarised stance (unless of course it is to win a few votes)? Naveen Webber, Gex, France I have been residing in France for about six months now and the relative absence of political correctness is a refreshing change from the UK. The veil ban is not a major issue here, more like a gentle re-assertion of French equality values. It certainly has nothing to do with a personal crusade by Sarkozy to win votes. Robin Marshall, Avignon, France

text: The museum at Cuba's most famous beach, the Bay of Pigs, is under renovation. Within, employees are diligently fitting fresh multimedia displays whilst outside a construction crew is pouring the concrete terrace and decorating the museum entrance. The ceremonial reopening is scheduled for April, which commemorates the 55th anniversary of the arrival upon the coastline at Playa Giron of hundreds of CIA-trained Cuban exiles in a failed bid to topple Fidel Castro and his socialist revolution. The unsuccessful invasion represented a nadir in US-Cuba relations, only exceeded by the Cuban missile crisis twelve months subsequently, and continues as a byword for Washington's clandestine interference in Latin America. Numerous original Cuban combatants - both militia and regular army personnel - remain living today. However in Playa Giron itself merely a few survive, and several of these are in declining health. Eighty-three-year-old Dolores Vic Hernandez may not have battled the invading troops, but she can remember in sharp detail having to flee from them, abandoning her residence in the small coastal settlement for the surrounding highlands with her sister-in-law and their offspring. We possessed only the garments we were donning and the infants were in nappies. We gathered our companion who had six offspring and whose spouse was in Havana and we brought her with us to the mountains. Dolores cannot move as readily as she formerly could and her vision is deteriorating, but it remains easy to envisage how resolute she must have been as a young mother attempting to shield her family from the intensifying conflict. I am a person who has never been frightened of anything, she declares with determination as she recounts entering an empty dwelling to obtain a little coffee and sugar, some biscuits for the offspring for their expedition. Eventually naturally, Fidel Castro assumed command of the revolutionary troops at Giron and orchestrated a celebrated triumph, one which would humiliate Washington for decades. Obama-Castro summit caps thaw in US-Cuba relations What is behind the US-Cuba thaw? How does Obama get along with Latin America? Scenes from a warming Cuba-US relationship Would Che Guevara oppose warmer US-Cuba relations? Since the rapprochement with the US was declared, Fidel Castro - the elder statesman of the Cuban Revolution - has only issued the briefest of statements regarding the fresh relationship: I do not trust in the United States' policy nor have I exchanged a word with them, he penned in an editorial in the state-controlled newspaper, Granma, published slightly over twelve months ago. His absence of trust is unsurprising, considering he survived dozens of assassination attempts by the CIA during his period in office. He proceeded to state that the president, his brother Raul, was taking the appropriate steps in accordance with his prerogatives and the powers granted to him by the National Assembly and the Cuban Communist Party. To certain readers, it failed to sound like a wholehearted endorsement. However Cuban academic, Esteban Morales disagrees: That did not mean to suggest he does not support the process, contends Dr Morales who has written extensively regarding Cuba's relationship with the United States. I believe Fidel is someone who is wise enough to recognise that this is the sole possible route. What is the alternative? Stand against the US cannons firing across the bow like we did previously? No. That is why Fidel intellectually comprehends that this is a moment to progress. Rather, Dr Morales believes that Castro was warning the Cuban people to Washington's genuine motives: Fidel knows perfectly well that international relations is a broad battlefield. We do not expect the United States to transform into our closest friends or allies overnight, not by any means. But perhaps in time they might become trusted neighbours. However it is not solely Fidel who harbours his doubts. There are Cubans who are anxious about (the opening), states Jon Lee Anderson of the New Yorker and author of the definitive biography of Che Guevara. They appear to be people who were already of a certain age when the revolution arrived and this has been their existence, the true believers in Fidel Castro's lengthy project of socialism. Their concerns for Cuba are as much social and cultural as economic and political, he contends. They worry about what will occur to their way of life. They worry about 'will the Miami Cubans arrive and purchase everything and exclude them?' And they worry about the influence of capitalism in undermining their values. However they may already be too late in that respect: Most people in Cuba are aware that in the 25 years since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the changes that already commenced in Cuba, that erosion began some time previously. Whilst it might appear unlikely to many of Fidel's generation that the relationship with the US could advance so far so rapidly, the overwhelming majority of young people in Cuba are impatient for even swifter change. There can be little superior expression of that change than President Obama walking the streets of Old Havana with his family. He is also anticipated to speak to private business owners, meet dissidents and deliver a major address during his trip, in which he intends to emphasise the importance of young people in shaping Cuba's future. Earlier this month in Havana, tens of thousands of young people gathered on the Malecon for a concert by the American dance music group, Major Lazer - intended to promote 'Musicabana', a landmark electronic music festival in Cuba later this year. This is the first international music band to arrive in Cuba at the peak of their success, states Fabien Pisani, the concert organiser and director of 'Musicabana'. What is fascinating here is that this is the music that every child who is 12 through to 17 is listening to presently. So you can observe the degree of excitement here, to be able to touch that and dance and sing together. The concert was conducted just metres from the US embassy, in the 'Anti-Imperialist Plaza', a site previously associated with government-organised demonstrations against US policy. On this occasion, an estimated 150,000-200,000 people gathered in the square, not to protest but to dance in the late afternoon sunshine. I never thought that in my lifetime a US president would come to Cuba.

text: A teachers' union is warning that schools are increasingly likely to use unqualified teaching staff. Parents no longer possess the certainty when they dispatch their child to school that they shall be taught by qualified teachers, states NASUWT leader Chris Keates. Labour's Tristram Hunt declares this is nothing short of a scandal. However, the Conservatives maintain there are fewer teachers in school without qualified status than in 2010. The NASUWT teachers' union, conducting its annual conference in Cardiff, will receive claims that more teachers without qualified teacher status are being employed in schools. The union has questioned its members regarding their experiences. Amongst the 4,600 who replied, 61% stated they were working alongside unqualified staff, with 66% asserting the situation was deteriorating due to funding difficulties. This is endangering the educational progress of children, declared Ms Keates who criticised the use of unqualified staff as a crude cost-cutting measure. Teachers replying to the union's survey included observations such as: They lack any training in classroom management and discipline and I feel that parents are being misled by the quality of teaching within the school. The employment of unqualified teachers has become a general election matter. Labour has campaigned against permitting academies and free schools to employ teachers who do not possess qualified teacher status or who are training towards becoming qualified. The increasing number of unqualified teachers in our schools demonstrates yet again that the Tory plan is threatening standards and failing children and working families, stated shadow education secretary Tristram Hunt. David Cameron has eliminated the requirement for teachers to be qualified, and consequently over 400,000 children are now being taught by unqualified teachers without receiving training in skills essential to the profession such as classroom discipline, safeguarding and how to deliver effective teaching for all children. The Liberal Democrats also wish to require teachers to possess qualified status. text: Shaun Johnson scored a winning drop-goal as New Zealand beat England in a tense and physical Four Nations match at a sell-out Huddersfield. Media playback is not supported on this device Man of the match Johnson, who netted a final-moment try to defeat England in the 2013 World Cup semi-final, placed the Kiwis 17-16 in front with 14 minutes remaining. His side then maintained their position for valuable two points that propels them significantly towards the final on 20 November. Gareth Widdop had converted two penalties whilst England had consistently threatened the Kiwi line as the home side controlled the initial 20 minutes. However, New Zealand subsequently assumed command, registering a Jordan Kahu penalty and a try from Jordan Rapana in the right corner as David Kidwell's team carried a 6-4 advantage into the interval. They promptly doubled their lead when Johnson intercepted a Widdop pass for an 80-yard score that Kahu converted. England responded, with Huddersfield Giants winger Jermaine McGillvary crossing in the corner as the hosts closed to within two points. Another try from winger Rapana - following a superb Manu Ma'u offload - was negated by a converted Ryan Hall touchdown beside the corner flag created by an exquisite flicked pass from Widdop. This left the score 16-16 before Johnson struck from directly in front of the posts. Media playback is not supported on this device New Zealand captain Jesse Bromwich stated before the match that the round-robin format of the Four Nations gave Saturday's Test the atmosphere of a semi-final. With both sides yet to encounter favourites Australia, alongside minnows Scotland, the significance of victory at Huddersfield was apparent. England face Scotland in Coventry next Saturday but will likely need to overcome the Kangaroos in London on 13 November if they are to reach the final at Anfield. This leaves Wayne Bennett's gifted team with a challenging task as they seek to end their lengthy wait for a major tournament triumph - a sequence that extends back to Great Britain's World Cup success in 1972. The match was forward Sam Burgess's first for England since his return from rugby union and his debut as captain, whilst it was also the first occasion Australian Wayne Bennett had coached England in a meaningful fixture after last Saturday's warm-up victory over France in Avignon. It appeared extremely encouraging for them as England commenced with a purpose and determination that the Kiwis seemed unable to equal. Canberra hooker Josh Hodgson directed the team excellently and England were deserving of their 4-0 lead. Nevertheless, they were unable to register a try and, by the interval, had been compelled to defend numerous repeat sets as the Kiwis assumed control. Although England refused to surrender after the influential Johnson's intercept try, they were constantly pursuing the game during an increasingly disjointed second half as the Kiwis demonstrated why they are regarded as the world's number one side in the manner they concluded the game. The prospect that this might be the beginning of a promising new era for an England team with a history of disappointing in crucial contests was rapidly extinguished, and many of the players collapsed to the ground at the end of what was ultimately a very disappointing afternoon. England defeated New Zealand 2-1 in a Test series last year whilst the Kiwis had won only two of their past 10 away games against Great Britain or England. It has not been straightforward for new coach Kidwell in 2016, his team managing only two line breaks and one try in their previous two matches this year, both of which saw them comprehensively beaten by Australia. However, with a massive forward pack providing a platform for versatile, aggressive hooker Issac Luke, as well as the unpredictable Johnson, the Kiwis secured a much-needed victory ahead of their match against the Kangaroos in Coventry next weekend. They defended resolutely early in the match and built pressure excellently as they seized the initiative away from their opponents - and with it valuable two points. text: George the Poet, a spoken word performer and rapper who wants to use his voice as a force for change in society, has come fifth on the BBC Sound Of 2015 list, which showcases emerging artists for the coming 12 months. These are external links and will open in a new window George Mpanga draws inspiration from the injustice he witnessed whilst growing up on the Stonebridge Park estate in north-west London. Following his studies in politics, psychology and sociology at Cambridge University and conducting poetry workshops for children in London, he is now preparing to release his debut album on Island Records and publish his first poetry collection. The 23-year-old states he wishes to inspire others to achieve greater things. I want people to be aware of their power, he states. He is the first artist to be announced from the BBC Sound Of 2015 top five. One act from the top five is being revealed every day this week, leading up to the announcement of the winner on Friday. The list was compiled by asking 139 DJs, critics and broadcasters to name their favourite new acts. Are you a poet or a rapper first? Chronologically I was a rapper first, but at this point in time I'm primarily a poet. When did you discover the power of words? I was always into music and my mother used to talk me through a lot of lyrics. I remember her sitting me down and talking to me about the Bob Marley song Buffalo Soldier. Dreadlock Rasta/Taken from Africa/Brought to America/Fighting on arrival/Fighting for survival. It made a big impression. At the same time, I grew up in church and again my mother used to read the Bible with me. And then I saw the pastor commanding an audience, and thought, I want to do that. I remember watching the film of Malcolm X and seeing what he did with words and thinking, I really want to do that. When did you move from rap to poetry? I believe rap to be a specialist form of poetry - specialist only in that it is very strict on time metre, which you can find in traditional forms of poetry. In William Blake's poem London, you find a lot of very regimented thought. I would argue that I did start off writing in a traditional poetry form but the extension of that was I was performing them. But if you took the music away, the essence was exactly the same as what William Blake was offering. You say you draw on your early life in the inner city. How does that inform what you do? It made a profound impact on me. I was exposed to quite a range of life. I saw people lose loved ones, I saw people make a lot of money, make a lot of change. When I was in year six - I must have been 10, 11 - I took a shine to these children who were in my primary school. They were lovely children. Sunshine every time they opened their mouths. I remember them casually mentioning that the night before, their father was beating up their mother and their big sister had to fight him off with a baseball bat. They didn't understand the gravity of what they were saying. But this disturbed me. I remember trying to fight everything, trying to save everyone from every calamity. At some point I realised that I'm not going to be able to save everyone, but that when I do have the platform I will do everything to enact structural change... A lot of my frustrations stem from the fact that I cannot share my blessings with my family and friends, my community. There are structural things that keep them in place, whether that's the disintegration of their family or their inability to organise themselves financially and sustain their communities financially, or the lack of political influence on the things that affect them. All of these things make it harder for me to move forward professionally with everyone I grew up with. That needs to change. How can you make a difference? I need to be an example of what I think needs to happen. So for example I'm self-employed. I have an enterprising mind. I demonstrate these things and I think it will be beneficial if everyone has a degree of enterprise. I need to be an example, but at the same time there's the content. My EP, The Chicken and the Egg, is about premature parenthood. Discussing that helps. For one thing, you're giving visibility to the issue. Secondly, you're providing some sort of catharsis for anyone who can relate. Do you write about yourself or do you create fictional characters? I draw partially from personal experience and I also draw from observation. Did the premature parenthood thing happen to you? No. It didn't happen to me. It happened all around me. Why try to bring about structural change through entertainment and not politics? Because the political space is too regulated. And it's already exclusive. Entertainment isn't as exclusive. If I'm known for making sounds that people want to hear, it's much harder to justify stymieing that process. Is it possible to enact structural change through music and poetry? Yes. Apart from the fact that anything's possible, it's very obvious. I speak. You listen. You come to my gig. All we need to do is make decisions. That's it. Job done. Where do you see yourself in five years time? I see the manifestation of everything I'm talking about now. I see myself providing the structures for people to enact and demonstrate of all the things I'm talking about - autonomy, taking control, owning the entertainment space. If what I'm saying sounds too lofty for you, demonstration's the highest form of argument. First I'm going to show you how to do it, then I'm going to invite you to do it.

text: Welsh cyclist Elinor Barker believes there is less pressure on GB's women's Olympic pursuit team in Rio because they are not clear favourites to win. Team GB secured gold at London 2012 but managed only third place at the 2016 World Championships. The United States and Canada will pose threats to the British squad of Barker, Laura Trott, Ciara Horne and Joanna Rowsell Shand. There is perhaps less pressure now because it is not necessarily ours to lose, the 21-year-old Barker stated. It remains ours to win, but there is not a dominant force in women's team pursuit now which there had been for many, many years. I believe it makes it much more exciting but it also means no one is watching any one team. We are all watching each other, we are all interested in what everyone is going to do and there are probably about five teams who could quite easily win it if it goes well for them on the day which makes it pretty exciting. Barker was a 17-year-old watching on television when the GB squad of Trott, Rowsell Shand and Danielle King defeated the USA in the pursuit final at the 2012 Games. She stated it was difficult to believe that four years later she will be competing at Rio. Probably a combination of luck and very hard work has brought me here, added Barker. I would not be here if I had not worked very hard and been very specific in my training but I have also been very lucky in the opportunities I have been given. Barker, from Cardiff, was in the squad that claimed a bronze medal in the World Championships this year, when a poor performance in an early round ended their chances of reaching the final. Discover how to get into cycling with our special guide. After years of dominating the event, the result attracted criticism though Barker believes there is much that the GB squad have learned from that setback. It just goes to show people make mistakes all the time but it does not mean that we are not a good team, she added. We came back from it [to take bronze] with exactly the same line-up so it shows it was that ride rather than us - it was a bad race and it does not define us as a team.

text: An adventurer is to spend Christmas Day alone in the Antarctic as he bids to become the first Scot to undertake a solo, unassisted and unsupported expedition to the South Pole. Luke Robertson, 30, aspires to become the youngest Briton to accomplish the achievement, in support of the charity Marie Curie. He is spending 40 days in isolation, hauling 130kg of gear across 730 miles of ice. Mr Robertson hails from Aberdeenshire but currently resides in Edinburgh. He will consume more than 10,000 calories daily whilst enduring temperatures of -50C and 100mph winds. He has already covered nearly 300 miles since departing from Hercules Inlet on Antarctica's edge on 5 December. The explorer was motivated to undertake the challenge following recovery from a series of medical conditions, including an operation to remove a suspected brain tumour a year ago, which proved to be a large and rare cyst. He also received a pacemaker at the age of 23 after experiencing a complete heart block. Mr Robertson chose to contribute the funds raised from the Due South 2015 expedition to Marie Curie after observing first-hand the remarkable work of the charity's nurses. He stated: I have been overwhelmed by the support and generosity I have received thus far in my fundraising endeavours and know the endless encouragement will enable me to push myself further and keep me smiling when I spend Christmas Day alone. I've witnessed first-hand the strength of human character and hope that through undertaking this extreme endurance expedition I can inspire others and demonstrate the capacity to overcome even the most challenging situations. Dr Jane Collins, chief executive of Marie Curie, stated: Luke's story is extraordinarily inspiring and I would like to thank him on behalf of everyone at Marie Curie for undertaking this remarkable personal challenge. He is a genuine inspiration to others and we know that his Antarctic adventure will make a real difference to people living with a terminal illness and their families. The expedition has garnered high-profile support from explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes and cyclist Mark Beaumont.

Among those who have criticised him is Assembly Member Simon Thomas, who said that Plaid Cymru's group on Conwy Council did not want Mr Jones to accept the position in the first place. What is the rule as far as working with Labour is concerned which poses as much threat as the Conservatives? he asked. I cannot understand Plaid Cymru's strategy - there is nothing in the constitution which refers to any party... but suddenly this business... we do not work with the Conservatives but there is collaboration with the Conservatives in several places across Wales, including the National Assembly. He added that his intention in establishing a coalition was to govern openly. Conwy's cabinet includes two members from Plaid Cymru - including Mr Jones - five Conservatives, and one independent councillor. Labour councillors refused a request to join. There were two other Plaid Cymru members part of Mr Jones's original plans, but they are not in the final cabinet. Mr Jones said the decision to leave was a difficult one, but there was no choice of course because I must respect the decision made by the national working group. Gareth Jones's proposals were put before the party's National Executive Committee and rejected in a democratic vote. Plaid Cymru will therefore not become part of the coalition proposed in Conwy Council.

text: Pokemon Go was released to most parts of the world this month, and in a matter of days has become a global phenomenon. The augmented reality game has been downloaded by millions of players, who are encouraged to venture into real-world locations to hunt down virtual creatures. However, the game has proved controversial - with some users disregarding safety warnings, resulting in car crashes, muggings, injury and even death. Saudi Arabian clerics have declared the game un-Islamic. Indonesia has prohibited its military from playing the game, and a Cossack leader has stated it smacks of Satanism. Police worldwide have issued warnings to players in the hope of preventing further incidents. So what do we know of the incidents thus far? On 20th July, Jerson Lopez de Leon, 18, and his cousin Daniel Moises Picen, 17, were ambushed whilst playing the game south-east of Guatemala City. Mr Lopez de Leon was killed and his cousin was seriously injured. Police discovered nearly 20 bullet casings at the scene but are uncertain of the motive behind the killing. On 18th July, a man crashed into a parked police car in Baltimore, US, continued driving, and finally stopped at the end of the road after the police pursued him. Police say he admitted he was playing Pokemon Go at the time. Baltimore Police say there were two other Pokemon Go related incidents just this week. On 19th July, a group of 20 teenagers stole a boat in efforts to catch Pokemon characters on a lake in Liverpool, UK. The group abandoned the boat in the middle of the lake after the coastguard was called to investigate. The rescue team said users should take care not to put themselves and rescue services at risk. A woman in New Jersey, US, had to be rescued by firemen after becoming stuck in a cemetery tree whilst playing the game. The fire chief issued a public safety warning, but spared the woman further embarrassment by not releasing her name. On 14th July, two men in California, US, fell up to 33m (108 ft) off a cliff after ignoring no trespassing signs whilst playing Pokemon Go. Firefighters rescued the men and took them to a nearby hospital. They have not been charged with trespassing.

text: Tom Watson, who has been elected as Labour's deputy leader, has been an MP since 2001. The 48-year-old held ministerial office in the Labour administration and enjoyed a period as the party's deputy chairman, acquiring a reputation - which he disputes - as a formidable political enforcer. The MP for West Bromwich East is equally recognised as an activist, notably on historical child abuse and a recent legal challenge to the government's surveillance legislation. However, his most celebrated campaign concerned phone hacking. He assumed one of the leading roles in the examination of Rupert and James Murdoch in 2011, as a member of the Commons culture select committee. His persistent investigation earned acclaim, and he co-authored an account of his hacking endeavour - Dial M for Murdoch - and became a recognisable figure on rolling news channels. He has subsequently campaigned for stricter press regulation and for the recommendations of the Leveson Inquiry to be implemented completely. Following his select committee questioning of the Murdochs, he was recruited into Labour leader Ed Miliband's senior team as the individual tasked with organising the forces to secure an outright majority at the subsequent general election. Mr Watson's record as campaign leader was varied - the party notably lost safe Bradford West to a resurgent George Galloway but achieved other by-election successes during this period. His downfall occurred following a dispute over trade union influence over Labour candidate selection. After Labour's general election defeat, he presented himself for the position of deputy leader, promising to rebuild the party throughout the UK. A former trade union official himself, who previously shared accommodation with Unite leader Len McCluskey, Mr Watson entered Parliament in 2001 as MP for West Bromwich. Following an initial period in the whips' office, he was assigned to the Ministry of Defence, where he was credited with helping secure pardons for soldiers executed for cowardice during World War One. However, in 2006, he resigned as a defence minister, demanding Tony Blair to quit in the interest of the Labour Party and the country - a move that accelerated the then prime minister's departure from office. He was accused of plotting against Mr Blair with Gordon Brown when it emerged he had visited the then chancellor at his residence in North Queensferry, Fife, shortly before stepping down. Both men denied any conspiracy, but many - within and beyond Labour - did not believe them. When Gordon Brown assumed leadership and became prime minister in 2007, Mr Watson was brought back into government as a whip, and in 2008 was appointed minister for digital engagement. In that position, he discovered a speciality. Recognised as an early adopter of social media, he was the first MP to maintain a blog and has described himself as an apprentice nerd for his enthusiasm for all things technological. However, during this period Mr Watson was accused of being implicated in the scandal surrounding a plot by Gordon Brown's spin doctor Damian McBride to spread smears about senior Tories. The Mail on Sunday accused him of encouraging Mr McBride whilst the Sun published a cartoon of him beneath the headline Mad dog was trained to maul. Mr Watson subsequently secured substantial libel damages from both newspapers in the High Court, which ruled the stories linking him to the plot were untrue. He resigned from his ministerial position following the McBride controversy for family reasons, he maintained - he wished to withdraw from front-line politics and concentrate on his wife and children. Hoping for what he termed a productive life as a backbencher, he decided to join the culture select committee to pursue his interests in sport and the arts. However, just two days after joining, the Guardian newspaper returned phone hacking to the agenda and the committee decided to investigate it - once again propelling Mr Watson into the spotlight. The first thing News International did was attempt to have me removed from the committee, he claimed in 2011. I realised then that these people were never departing. Something had clearly gone wrong with newspapers and somebody had to discover the truth. There weren't many MPs who were prepared to do that for fear of being targeted, so I decided I had to do it. People then started approaching me - whistleblowers and victims - and I felt I had a responsibility towards them. I couldn't walk away. A prolific Twitter user about politics, as well as his latest discoveries in music, film and video games, he managed to include a mention of little-known blues-rock band, Drenge, in his resignation letter from the position of general election co-ordinator in 2013. In the letter, Mr Watson, the son of a union official and a social worker, who has two children with estranged wife Siobhan, said it was preferable for the future unity of the Labour Party that he departed. His resignation was triggered by a dispute over the Falkirk seat being vacated by Labour's Eric Joyce - the Unite union was accused of hijacking the process to select a new candidate to replace him, and Mr Watson's office manager was the union's preferred candidate. In his letter to Mr Miliband, Mr Watson said he was not resigning because of unattributed shadow cabinet briefings around the mess in Falkirk... though they don't help. He said some within the party had still not forgiven him for resigning as defence minister in 2006, but added: I fully accept the consequences of that decision and genuinely hope my departure allows the party to progress. As deputy leader, he is now at the forefront of the party's attempts to progress, this time from its general election defeat.

After a short time in the office of the whips, he was appointed to the Ministry of Defense, where he is credited with having obtained pardons for the soldiers who had been executed for cowardice in World War I. After the defeat of the election, he offered himself as a candidate for the deputy chairmanship of the party. Both denied any plot, but many people in and out of the party did not believe them. However, in June of that year he resigned from the Ministry of Defense and called for Tony Blair to step down in the interests of the country and the party. When Mr. Brown became Prime Minister in 2007, Mr. Watson was once again a ministerial whip and in 2008 was made Minister for Digital Engagement. In this capacity, he developed a particular interest in new media. He was one of the first members of Parliament to have a blog and has described himself as a “geek apprentice” because of his enthusiasm for technology. As a result of what he called his ‘productive’ life as a backbencher, he joined the Select Committee on Culture, Media and Sport, in which he could pursue his interests in the arts and sport. Meanwhile, Mr. Watson was accused of having encouraged Damian McBride’s attempts to smear senior Conservatives; the Mail on Sunday accused him of having tamed him, while The Sun printed a cartoon of him with the caption: ‘A mad dog bred to bite.’ Mr. Watson later won substantial damages from both papers in the High Court, which found that the libel was untrue. After the scandal over the leaking of information on the death of the Princess of Wales, he had resigned from the cabinet, saying that he was withdrawing from the front of the political battle in order to be able to concentrate on his family.
