text: Police are too sensitive about asking victims of crime if they are disabled, an inspection has found. Disability hate crime remains overlooked and under-reported, according to a joint inspectorate review examining police, probation and the Crown Prosecution Service in England and Wales. The review recommends establishing a new common definition of the crime to ensure effective and swift handling. Senior police officers stated they had worked diligently to improve its management. Police in England and Wales recorded more than 1,700 disability hate crimes during 2011-12. The joint review of disability hate crime was triggered by the Fiona Pilkington case, who took her own life and that of her disabled daughter Francecca Hardwick in 2007 following repeated complaints to police regarding harassment by youths. The review cautioned that a similar case could occur again without urgent changes. Inspectors interviewed staff of different seniority levels at six police forces and the corresponding CPS and probation trust offices located in Cleveland, Cumbria, Derbyshire, Hertfordshire, Greater Manchester and West Midlands. They also observed seven court proceedings and consulted disabled victims, representatives from witness care units, the witness service, victim support and several independent disability advocates. Disabled individuals informed inspectors that police officers and control-room operators had become overly sensitive about causing offence, and consequently, they were hesitant to ask victims whether they were disabled. Additional findings by the inspectors included: Steve Ashley, programme director at HM Inspectorate Constabulary (HMIC), stated: There exists a lack of willingness amongst police officers and police staff in control rooms to ask the appropriate questions to establish whether it constitutes a crime, whether it represents anti-social behaviour and what impact disability is having on that individual regarding the crime's effect. Mr Ashley noted there was also confusion regarding how to define disability hate crime. It is not as straightforward as identifying a religiously-motivated attack or a racially-motivated attack. Police officers dislike asking people 'Are you disabled?', he stated. When asked whether the Pilkington case could recur given the review's findings, Mr Ashley responded: Yes, it could. Disability charity Mencap reported its own research indicated that nine out of 10 people with a learning disability had experienced hate crime victimisation. Emma Harrison, assistant director at the charity, stated the review demonstrated that victims of disability hate crime continue to be failed at every stage of the criminal justice system. She said Mencap welcomed the review's recommendation that police, probation and CPS must collaborate to address these serious and ongoing failings. Amongst its recommendations, the review stated a single, clear and uncomplicated definition of disability hate crime was necessary to reduce confusion. It suggested the three agencies should consider how their front-line staff engage in disability hate crime training. It also urged police to encourage victims of the crime to come forward to prevent under-reporting remaining a significant concern. The review stated it would recommend that the Law Commission, the body responsible for law reform, examine creating a stand-alone offence for addressing disability hate crime. Speaking for all three agencies, CPS chief inspector Michael Fuller stated: This report determines that in many respects disability hate crime is the hate crime that has been overlooked. The criminal justice system must therefore change to provide an enhanced service for those with disabilities. Javed Khan, chief executive of charity Victim Support, stated police must ensure they begin delivering enhanced services to disabled victims of hate crime. The Association of Chief Police Officers stated the police service had worked diligently to improve its handling of disability hate crime by consulting with disabled people to understand the types of harassment they encounter and the barriers preventing them from reporting it, then working with the community and other agencies to help remove those barriers. Meanwhile, a Home Office spokeswoman stated: The Home Office has enhanced the way police forces collect and record data on hate crimes, including those against disabled people, and we will continue working with disability groups to ensure victims have the confidence to come forward.

text: A dog owner whose pet was the latest victim to die from from Alabama Rot says more needs to be done to inform owners of the risks. Steve Kirwan, from Lyndhurst, Hampshire, suspects his Labrador-collie cross developed symptoms following a walk in the Whitefield Moor area of the New Forest. Bodhi, aged three, died from kidney failure in February, a fortnight after falling ill. The cause of the condition, which has claimed 24 dogs' lives in the UK since 2012, remains unidentified. Between November 2012 and March last year there were 12 confirmed cases - five in the New Forest - and two unconfirmed cases, the Forestry Commission reports. Since December last year there have been a further 12 cases. Six of these occurred in the New Forest. Tests continue on an additional 22 suspected cases of the condition. Also termed cutaneous and renal glomerular vasculopathy (CRGV). First recognised in the US during the 1980s. Initial symptoms may, but do not invariably, include lesions or wounds on legs, paws and faces. Within the subsequent two to seven days dogs develop clinical signs of kidney failure, which may include vomiting, reduced appetite and fatigue. Does not appear to transmit from dog to dog. Source: Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists The cases outside Hampshire occurred in Northamptonshire, Yorkshire, Monmouthshire, Dorset, Shropshire, Surrey, Cornwall, Worcestershire and County Durham. The Forestry Commission has initiated a poster campaign in 29 of the New Forest's car parks warning dog owners to remain vigilant. However, Mr Kirwan stated: I do not think it is sufficient. There are numerous car parks in the New Forest, considerably more than 29. I believe the coverage requires extension right across the forest, because there is a genuine concentration in the New Forest as [part of the] national picture. Mr Kirwan said Bodhi never exhibited any lesions, but was dragging his rear legs. From his other symptoms veterinarians suspected it was Alabama Rot but he did not respond to treatment and required euthanasia. The investigation into the precise cause is being conducted by Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists, in Hursley, near Winchester, who are collaborating with the Forestry Commission, Environment Agency, Suffolk-based Animal Health Trust and local veterinarians. David Walker, from Anderson Moores, said: There are enormous amounts of research ongoing, multiple different avenues, but at this stage we are no nearer to knowing what the trigger is. Research will continue but there is the possibility that we could research this disease for five, ten years and not discover the underlying cause. But that does not mean we are not going to continue looking.

text: A £5 note engraved with a tiny portrait of Jane Austen and said to be worth up to £50,000 has been found in a Christmas card. The second of four special £5 notes featuring artwork by specialist micro-engraver Graham Short emerged on Thursday in Scotland. The first was discovered in change from a café in south Wales earlier this month. Two additional special £5 notes, circulated in England and Northern Ireland, remain in general circulation. See more stories from across Birmingham and the Black Country here The two banknotes carry the serial numbers AM32 885552 and AM32 885554. Anyone discovering one of the notes has been advised to contact the Tony Huggins-Haig Gallery in Kelso, in the Scottish Borders, which initiated the project. Mr Huggins-Haig told BBC WM the recipient of the latest note, who had examined the note on the off chance, wished to remain anonymous. When somebody opened their Christmas card from a loved one, it was contained within that Christmas card, he said. The person who placed it in did not necessarily know what they were doing. That's two down and there are still two out there. Keep checking your change. The banknotes carry the following serial numbers and quotes: Mr Short, from Birmingham, conceived the idea of engraving a 5mm portrait of Jane Austen on the transparent section of the new plastic Bank of England £5 notes to mark the 200th anniversary of her death next year. He has incorporated a different quote around each one ensuring that each note is unique. Both recipients have thus far stated they intend to retain the notes rather than sell them. Mr Short said: I do not know whether I am disappointed that they have not wanted to sell them because I wanted them to have some money for Christmas, but the fact that they are so happy to keep them, that is nice as well. And he admitted he is also checking his change and said he was terrified of discovering one. He said: When someone gives me a £5 note in my change now I always check. Would it not be awful if it came back to me? People would say it was a fix.

text: The family of a 20-year-old woman from Glasgow who has travelled to Syria and married an Islamic State (IS) fighter have said that she has betrayed them. Khalida Mahmood and Muzaffar Mahmood stated they were appalled to discover their daughter Aqsa had been radicalised. They spoke following remarks attributed to their daughter on Twitter which urged people in Britain to replicate terrorist attacks witnessed in Woolwich and America. Mr and Mrs Mahmood declared they loved their daughter and desired her return home. In a statement, the pair said: We continue to love you, Aqsa, but we must now prioritise your family, your brother and sisters as you have betrayed us, our community and the people of Scotland when you took this action. You have ripped the heart from our family and altered our lives permanently. Please return home. They cautioned: If our daughter, who possessed all the opportunities and liberty in life, could become a bedroom radical, then it is conceivable for this to occur to any family. Privately-educated Aqsa is understood to have promoted terrorist acts through a Twitter account under the name Umm Layth. The account has subsequently been removed. She journeyed through Turkey to Aleppo in Syria during November and was reported missing to police. Before vanishing she attended Craigholme School, then university and was well integrated into society, her parents stated. They said she was raised with love and affection in a contented home. text: Home Secretary Theresa May's internet monitoring plans need significant work, a committee has ruled. The proposed Investigatory Powers Bill will compel internet service providers to retain all web activity for twelve months. The legislation will additionally authorise the mass collection of personal information and the hacking of mobile phones by British intelligence services. Government ministers state the amendments will assist in apprehending terrorists and combating organised crime by modernising laws to match new technology employed by criminals. However, civil rights campaigners contend the provisions within it constitute mass surveillance of British citizens - and that the committee's findings meant the Home Secretary required to return to the drawing board. Shami Chakrabarti, Liberty's director, stated: This report demonstrates precisely how much preparation the government must undertake on this significant legislation. Labour's shadow Home Secretary Andy Burnham has corresponded with Mrs May stating that whilst Labour endorses the bill's overall objective - to provide police and security services necessary powers - the government must now allow time to reconsider its proposals to ensure they achieve the proper balance for our security and privacy. Mrs May declared the government would thoroughly consider the findings of three committees which have examined the Bill before presenting its final recommendations. This constitutes essential legislation, and we remain absolutely committed to achieving success. Our proposed Bill followed three independent reviews on investigatory powers, whose contributors were united that new legislation was essential. We maintain clarity that we must introduce legislation which addresses the threats we confront in the digital era, safeguards both public privacy and security, and delivers world-leading oversight and protections. All parties acknowledge new legislation governing surveillance powers is essential but the challenge lies in the specifics, as multiple parliamentary reports have demonstrated. The current law, all concur, remains complex and lacks transparency but all indications suggest the new legislation has not yet resolved this issue completely. The question now concerns how extensively the Home Office incorporates some criticisms and whether sufficient time exists to achieve this - a final bill is scheduled for introduction shortly so it can be debated and enacted before year's end. Read more from Gordon. The Joint Committee on the Draft Investigatory Powers Bill stated in a 194-page report it was convinced the worth of so-called Internet Connection Records to law enforcement agencies could exceed the intrusiveness involved in gathering and utilising them. However, it reflected concerns from technology companies regarding the practicality of protecting users' privacy in the manner Mrs May has pledged, by solely collecting website names visited, rather than individual web pages. The committee was informed this might not be technically feasible, but it stated the Home Office was collaborating with the industry to identify a solution. Ministers must additionally clarify their encryption plans to ensure they will not compel technology firms to provide a back door for intelligence services, the parliamentary committee declared. And the Home Office must also supply greater justification for collecting emails and other internet traffic passing through Britain by the security services, as disclosed by American whistleblower Edward Snowden, and other so-called bulk data collection operations. Committee chairman Lord Murphy of Torfaen stated the Home Office possessed a substantial amount of additional work to complete before Parliament can be assured that the provisions have been thoroughly considered. The bill was condemned as a dragnet approach and excessive by former Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg, who prevented Mrs May's earlier attempt to enact surveillance legislation, termed the snooper's charter by critics, whilst he served in government. The Liberal Democrat MP informed BBC Radio 4's Today programme the Home Office sought to gather everything on everyone to locate information on suspected terrorists or criminals they are pursuing. Suggesting that everyone may be culpable when millions of innocent people are simply conducting their daily business free of any wrongdoing whatsoever is... something which does not align with long-established British traditions, Mr Clegg stated. He questioned whether it was proportionate in a liberal democracy to preserve information on everything from the music you download on Spotify, to the application that you open, to the supermarket website that you visit, to pursue the criminals? He stated he supported a more focused approach to data retention, and that other nations concentrate on collecting data on those individuals who appear on the radar screen of security services initially. Much of the extensive bill is dedicated to the activities of Britain's intelligence agencies, and focuses on clarifying the legal foundation under which they operate, following Edward Snowden's disclosures. It proposes equipment interference warrants, permitting spies to hack into suspects' mobile phones and computers and extract data from them, either within Britain or overseas. Other warrants will encompass the downloading of bulk databases of personal information, which could include medical records, and the collection of internet traffic passing through Britain for future analysis by GCHQ. text: Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said the inconclusive election result means no party can govern alone. His party, the AKP, is convening to attempt forming a government following the loss of its majority in a general election for the first time in 13 years. It obtained 41%, a steep decline from 2011, and must establish a coalition or face entering minority government. Mr Erdogan has urged all parties to maintain the atmosphere of stability in Turkey. I believe the results, which do not provide the opportunity for any party to establish a single-party government, will be evaluated sensibly and realistically by every party, Mr Erdogan stated. The AKP is now expected to attempt forming a coalition, though no party has yet signalled it is prepared to unite with it. Opposition parties may still attempt to establish a coalition against the AKP. However, Numan Kurtulmus, one of Turkey's four deputy prime ministers, stated there would be no government without AKP representation. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu is meeting AKP cabinet members and officials to evaluate the election results in Ankara. Following the official final result declaration, he will have 45 days to establish a government. Mr Kurtulmus stated another election was possible. This is potentially a fresh political era in Turkey. The AKP still secured this election, with over 40% of the vote - a proportion of the vote that parties in any democracy would desire. It still possesses a substantial power base, primarily of the more religious, conservative Turks, who feel liberated by the party and the president. However, the AKP's dominance, the one-man political show that has unfolded in Turkey for 13 years and polarised this nation, has just received a very significant blow. Turkey: Bloody nose for Erdogan Profile: Recep Tayyip Erdogan The result represents a setback to Mr Erdogan's plans to enhance his office's powers. He had been pursuing a two-thirds majority to transform Turkey into a presidential republic. The pro-Kurdish HDP surpassed the 10% threshold, obtaining seats in parliament for the first time. The discussion of executive presidency and dictatorship have concluded in Turkey with these elections, stated HDP leader Selahattin Demirtas. Kurds, women, gays put faith in upstart Turkish party On Monday morning, the Turkish currency declined to near-record lows against the dollar, and shares fell by more than 8% shortly after the Istanbul stock exchange opened. The central bank moved swiftly to support the lira by reducing the interest rate on foreign currency deposits. Are you in Turkey? What is your reaction to the election result? text: Overall crime in England and Wales fell by 15% in 2013, official figures show. The Crime Survey for England and Wales recorded 7.5 million offences against households and adults during that period, representing the lowest figure since the survey commenced in 1981. Distinct police statistics demonstrated a 2% decline in crime for 2013, whilst noting increases in certain areas including fraud (25%) and a 17% rise in recorded sexual offences following the Jimmy Savile affair. Government ministers described the statistics as encouraging news and indicated that reforms were proving effective. The CSEW report, issued by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), calculates crime levels based upon the number of individuals reporting victimisation. The survey indicated that offences against households and adults in the year concluding December 2013 had decreased by 15% when compared with the preceding year. By Danny Shaw, Home affairs correspondent, BBC News These statistics are unsurprising - crime has declined almost consistently since the mid-1990s. What proves unexpected, nevertheless, is the magnitude of the decrease: the 15% reduction represents the largest percentage decline since the survey commenced 33 years ago. The 22% reduction in violence also exceeds substantially that of previous years - supporting recent conclusions from Cardiff University's research into individuals treated for crime-related injuries. The sole statistics presenting a contrasting narrative are those compiled by police forces. However, these require treatment with considerable caution - not merely due to concerns regarding manipulation of figures but also because they depend upon whether victims report offences to police. Mark Easton: The reality behind the increase in sexual crimes The ONS stated the measured crime reduction resulted from declining offences - including domestic theft, which decreased 25%, and overall violence, which dropped 22%. text: About one-third of workers in Clackmannanshire and Dumfries and Galloway will benefit from the national living wage, according to research. The Resolution Foundation analysis demonstrates the impact of the national living wage will differ substantially across Scotland. A national living wage of £7.20 per hour for workers aged 25 and above will be implemented in April. The UK government stated millions of people will receive a pay increase. The study indicated 500,000 employees in Scotland will be affected in total. Whilst one-third of employees in Clackmannanshire and Dumfries and Galloway will be affected, merely 16% of employees working in Aberdeen are expected to benefit. Edinburgh (17%), Dundee (18%) and Glasgow (19%) are also considerably lower. Whilst strongly endorsing the new wage floor, the Foundation observes that implementing it will present a greater challenge in lower-paying regions. It urges the Scottish government, the Fair Work Convention, local leaders and businesses throughout the country to collaborate to minimise any job losses and ensure large groups of workers do not become trapped earning only the legal minimum. The Foundation also urges employers to concentrate on enhancing productivity in retail, hospitality, cleaning and care to ensure the national living wage is affordable for them. The organisation states the UK government's new pay structure is not genuinely a living wage, and calls for an extension to the voluntary living wage of £8.25 throughout the country. Conor D'Arcy, policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation, stated: The welcome new national living wage will have a substantial impact on low pay, particularly towards 2020 as it approaches £9 per hour. Whilst our analysis suggests the pay rise should be affordable for most firms, implementing the new wage floor will be challenging for some employers. That is particularly true in areas where wages tend to be lower. Politicians must work closely with employers to ensure that the national living wage is a success, particularly in low-paying sectors. A UK government spokesperson stated: The government is ensuring Britain receives a pay rise and that businesses have the skills they need to succeed. We are already witnessing record employment rates and real wages growing to levels not seen since the recession. As the report itself highlights, workers in some cities will see even greater benefits, reinforcing our drive to rebalance the economy through the northern powerhouse and the devolution of powers to local government and cities.

text: Algerian militant Mokhtar Belmokhtar is reported to have masterminded the two suicide bombings in Niger on Thursday. A spokesman for the Signed-in-Blood Battalion informed Mauritanian news agency Alakhbar that he had overseen the assaults, conducted alongside another organisation, Mujao. The attackers struck a military installation in Agadez and the French-operated uranium facility in Arlit, resulting in 21 fatalities. On Friday, French special forces and Niger troops killed two militants who had taken refuge within the Agadez base. Niger's Defence Minister, Kardijo Mahamadou, stated they had fortified themselves inside a dormitory alongside two soldiers, who were liberated during the operation. Our military forces and French special forces stormed [the building] and the hostages - totalling two individuals - were liberated, he informed the Associated Press. There were two captors who were concealed in the military dormitory, and both were eliminated. The operation has now concluded. Mr Mahamadou separately informed RFI radio that eight Islamist militants had been eliminated in the Agadez operation and two additional ones in Arlit, stating: All of them were wearing explosive-laden belts. France's Defence Minister, Jean-Yves Le Drian, informed BFM television that its forces had intervened following a request from Niger President Mahamadou Issoufou and that the situation had stabilised. A French defence ministry official also informed AP that the two soldiers held captive by the militants had been liberated in the assault. Previously, local and military sources informed the BBC that they had been eliminated. Thursday's bombing at the military compound in Agadez resulted in 19 deaths, including 18 soldiers. Four assailants also perished whilst a fifth was subdued by security forces. The assault on the Somair facility, in the town of Arlit, resulted in one death and injured 14 others, its operator Areva stated. Alakhbar quoted El-Hassen Ould Khalil, a spokesman for al-Muwaqqioun bi-Dima (Signed-in-Blood Battalion), as stating: It was Belmokhtar who personally oversaw the operational planning of attacks. The assaults targeted elite French forces who were providing security at the uranium facility that is majority-owned by Areva, he stated. An online statement, purportedly signed by Mokhtar Belmokhtar, declared: This represents the first of our responses to the statement of the president of Niger - from his masters in Paris - that he eliminated jihad and the mujahideen militarily. Previously, the Movement for Unity and Jihad in West Africa (Mujao) also claimed it had executed the two attacks. However, Mr Khalil's statement to Alakhbar indicated the Signed-in-Blood Battalion had jointly directed the attacks with Mujao. Mujao spokesman Abu Walid Sahraoui stated on Thursday that its militants had targeted the enemies of Islam in Niger, according to the AFP news agency. We struck France, and Niger due to its cooperation with France, in the war against Sharia [Islamic law], he stated, believed to reference French and Niger involvement in expelling Mujao and two other Islamist organisations from northern Mali earlier this year. In the statement threatening additional attacks, Mokhtar Belmokhtar's organisation warned against Western intervention in the region. Columns of commandos and those seeking martyrdom are prepared and awaiting their targets, it declared. We shall have additional operations, by the strength and power of Allah, and not only that, but we shall move the battle to the interior of his country if he (the president of Niger) does not withdraw his mercenary army, another statement to Mauritania's ANI news agency declared. On Thursday, French President Francois Hollande pledged to protect French interests and cooperate with Niger in its fight against terrorism. Mokhtar Belmokhtar was believed responsible for the deadly assault on an internationally operated Algerian gas facility in January in which 37 hostages and 29 insurgents were killed. He separated from al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) last year and established a new jihadist organisation, known variously as the Signed-in-Blood Battalion, the Masked Men Brigade and the Khaled Abu al-Abbas Brigade. Armed forces in Chad stated he perished in a raid in northern Mali on 2 March, although there was no confirmation and his death has been reported numerous times previously. Mujao (the Movement for Unity and Jihad in West Africa) is a breakaway faction of AQIM which operates primarily in northern Mali. It states its objective is to extend jihad to West Africa rather than restrict itself to the Sahel and Maghreb regions - the principal focus of AQIM.

text: A judge in Argentina has been told to reopen a criminal investigation into former Top Gear host Jeremy Clarkson's infamous drive through the country. Production of a Top Gear programme was halted last year following demonstrations concerning a number plate on a Porsche which Clarkson was operating. The plate - which seemed to allude to the 1982 Falklands conflict - was substituted. This year, a local magistrate determined the Top Gear team had not operated in bad faith when changing the plates. However, a tribunal has now determined the inquiry be resumed, stating the crew exchanged the plates knowing it was unlawful. The programme sparked outrage in 2014 amongst residents by employing the registration number H982 FKL - interpreted by some as an allusion to the Falklands. The Top Gear team were compelled to depart South America during furious demonstrations. The programme's vehicles had to be left beside the road and the crew accompanied to the airport after being struck with stones. Andy Wilman, the programme's executive producer, supported the programme contending the plate number had not been intentionally selected and it was most definitely not a publicity stunt. A collection of Falklands conflict veterans challenged the closure of the matter and it has now been resumed by the appeals tribunal in the Tierra del Fuego province. The prosecution charges Mr Clarkson with falsifying, modifying or concealing the number of a lawfully registered object. We believe that the Top Gear team altered the plates with complete awareness of the fact that it was unlawful, spokesman Osvaldo Hillard of the Centre for Malvinas Veterans stated. The matter will now be resumed at Tierra del Fuego's High Court and it could require years to be resolved. Falsifying, modifying or concealing the number of a plate in Argentina can be penalised with sentences of between six months and three years in gaol. Wilman stated at the time: Top Gear production acquired three vehicles for a forthcoming programme; to suggest that this vehicle was either selected for its number plate, or that an alternative number plate was replaced for the original is entirely false. Clarkson was dismissed from the programme this year after assaulting a Top Gear producer. Colleagues James May and Richard Hammond also departed the programme, alongside Wilman, to begin a new motoring programme for Amazon TV.

Offensive chants were audible during Liverpool's 2-0 victory at Anfield in the opening leg of their last-16 encounter. text: Apple has just turned 40 years old - a timely reason to track down a man who helped start the firm and then walked away. Travel one hour from Las Vegas into the Nevada desert. Upon reaching what appears to be civilisation's edge, continue onwards. There lies Pahrump. Within Pahrump resides the co-founder of Earth's most valuable, arguably most influential corporation. Ronald G Wayne is aged 81. At 41, he was employed at Atari. There he encountered a young, impressionable Steve Jobs who frequently sought Wayne's counsel on various matters. Jobs enquired whether he should establish a slot machine manufacturing enterprise. Wayne advised against it. Jobs asked whether he should travel to India for self-discovery. Wayne responded: if necessary, proceed cautiously. Eventually, Jobs posed the question that altered history: Could you assist me in reasoning with Steve Wozniak? Bring him to my residence, Wayne replied. We shall sit and discuss matters. The charismatic, endearing Wozniak - known as Woz - had been collaborating with Jobs on dismantling business computers and transforming them into more personal devices. The duo regularly attended the now legendary Homebrew Computer Club, a gathering where enthusiasts dissected circuitry and reconstructed it innovatively with the same enthusiasm as an imaginative six-year-old confronting Lego blocks. Woz excelled above others. His circuit board design would become the foundation for the Apple 1, the firm's inaugural computer - which sold at auction in 2015 for $365,000 (£254,300). Jobs desired Woz's expertise exclusively for Apple. Woz refused entirely. Thus they convened at Wayne's apartment in Mountain View, California, to resolve the matter. Jobs believed I possessed greater diplomatic skills than himself, Wayne remembers. He felt extremely eager to proceed with Steve Wozniak towards production. However, Wozniak, being the whimsical individual he was, approached everything purely for enjoyment. Woz lacked business understanding or knowledge of commercial principles. During approximately 45 minutes, Wayne reversed the situation. He accepted the proposal. He comprehended, Wayne states. At that moment Steve Jobs declared: 'We shall establish a company. It will be called the Apple Computer Company.' Wayne immediately typed the documentation using an IBM typewriter, amusing Woz, who marvelled at Wayne's ability to produce four pages of legal language from memory. Dividing the Apple ownership proved straightforward: Jobs and Wozniak received 45% each, whilst Wayne obtained 10% and responsibility for mediating disputes. Twelve days subsequently, Wayne withdrew from the agreement. For excellent reasons that remain valid today, he stated, four decades and a $600bn market capitalisation later. Jobs, the accomplished salesman, had secured Apple's first major contract. A small computer retailer, the Byte Shop, required 50 machines. Apple needed to borrow $15,000 for funding. However, Wayne had learned - from an unremembered source - that the Byte Shop possessed a poor reputation for settling accounts. Should the company fail, we bear individual liability for debts, Wayne explained. Jobs and Wozniak possessed no financial resources. I owned a house, bank account, and automobile... I was accessible! Wayne informed the Steves he would assist where possible, but could no longer maintain official company membership. One enduring contribution involved designing the company's initial logo - an ink drawing depicting Newton beneath a tree, with an apple suspended overhead. Wayne signed the image, but Jobs noticed. Remove that! Wayne recalls him demanding. He complied. Months after formally severing Apple ties, Wayne received correspondence. The letter stated I need only relinquish every possible interest in the Apple Computer Company, and the payment would be mine, he explains. He received $1,500 in return. I considered it 'discovered money'. Therefore I proceeded and signed. Pahrump lies 500 miles (800km) and an entire universe from Cupertino, Apple's current headquarters. Wayne's residence is both modest and cherished. Artefacts from a curious engineer and collector's life are scattered throughout. Near the entrance stands an antique silver slot machine. Against one wall, a functioning 1930s radio housed in exquisite mahogany. He described creating a scale replica, both interior and exterior, of the Nautilus - the enormous submarine from 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea. Without blueprints, he studied film freeze-frames instead. Upon completion, he donated it to a museum. Currently, a 10% Apple shareholding would be valued at nearly $60bn. If Wayne regrets his decision, he conceals it masterfully. I would have managed a substantial documentation department at the building's rear, handling paperwork for the subsequent 20 years. That was not my envisioned future. If money were my sole objective, numerous alternatives existed. However, pursuing personal interests held greater importance. My counsel to young people remains constant - discover something you enjoy sufficiently to perform without payment... and you shall never labour a single day. Wayne stores fan mail in a small study corner box. It contains autograph requests, advice appeals, and general admiration messages. One letter from Jason, a fan, jokes about the notoriously self-assured and confrontational Steve Jobs accepting constructive criticism that Wayne could deliver. He was a remarkable individual, Wayne reflects. Who created Apple's success? Obviously, Jobs. Was Jobs pleasant? In many respects, no. However, that is irrelevant. Wayne considered himself the adult supervision for Jobs's vision, even providing early encouragement. Jobs said: 'I'm reconsidering this. Other pursuits interest me'. I replied: 'Steve, whatever your desires, money facilitates achievement. Earn the money first, then pursue your goals. Simply remember your original motivation'. He forgot. I believe he became so absorbed in Apple's operational mechanics that nothing else held significance. Whilst feeling no remorse about abandoning his Apple role, Wayne harbours one regret: selling his original signed contract copy for $500. In 2011, that identical document achieved $1.6m at auction. Another what if for consideration. Examining Wayne's home reveals no Apple products. He prefers constructing and customising personal technology - it provides greater enjoyment, he explained. In 2011, someone presented him with an iPad 2. Like much else in his life, Wayne donated it. Follow Dave Lee on Twitter @DaveLeeBBC and Facebook.

Tesco stated it would raise hourly pay in three phases: to £8.02 in November 2017, then to £8.18 in July 2018 and to £8.42 in November 2018. This reward package represents our largest investment in store pay for a decade, and provides colleagues a sustainable pay agreement that rewards them for everything they do, whilst allowing us to also attract new talent, stated Tesco UK chief executive, Matt Davies. This is designed to meet the government legislative requirement regarding the minimum wage. text: With the #OscarsSoWhite controversy and calls for the Brit Awards to be more truly representative, there has never been more discussion about diversity in the arts. Upon the stage, recent major productions of Hamlet and King Lear featured predominantly black, Asian and ethnic minority (BAME) casts, yet according to some within the industry, you can walk onto a construction site and see more diversity than in the typical theatre. Paapa Essiedu, who is presently the Royal Shakespeare Company's Hamlet, states theatre is caught between two worlds at the moment. There exists considerable positivity about how we perceive our present and future and that is all positive, but I still do not see or feel that impact. What is needed is for people to be more bold and more adventurous in what they support. In Manchester, the Royal Exchange's King Lear witnessed veteran actor Don Warrington assume the lead, something which he states should not be in any way startling. Yet numerous reviews drew attention to his race, which Warrington states is an indictment of where we are. He states whilst conditions have improved since he commenced his acting career almost 50 years ago, that anyone wishes to discuss his casting demonstrates there remains a problem. There exists higher visibility, but the question concerns the quality of that visibility and the quality of the parts. I do not think that is where it should be. Hamida Ali, the acting union Equity's equalities and diversity organiser, shares Warrington's unease. One of the matters we remain concerned about is how surprised we might be when we observe a black actor in a lead role, not just in Shakespeare, but generally. It states something in itself that that remains something of note. She states there is definitely a consensus that there exists a problem, but what the cause is, who is responsible and what the solutions are is perhaps more in debate. The production of Lear was staged with Talawa, a theatre company established in the 1980s in direct response to the lack of creative opportunities for actors from minority ethnic backgrounds. Artistic director Michael Buffong states three decades on, there remains a rapid need for change. What we require is different people to reflect different aspects of the same world, otherwise we have this very narrow viewpoint. Essiedu agrees theatre needs to be more diverse about the stories we are telling and the people that are telling them. By doing that, there will be more opportunity for a more diverse group of actors. We are in 2016 in an international, multicultural, integrated society and we have a responsibility as artists to reflect that in the work that we create. Matthew Xia, an associate artistic director at the Royal Exchange, states far from improving, theatre has gone backwards in so many ways. It is not just about the art, it is also about the organisational structure. In the majority of organisations, the moment you reach the leadership, it drops right down with regards to proportionate representation of the cities that they are working in. It is beyond me, because you can walk onto a construction site and see more diversity than you can see in what is meant to be the liberal end of the work spectrum. Buffong states, as a result, there exists a need to change the gatekeepers, because that is where the power is. You can cast two black actors in a play and go 'wow, we have got two black actors' but that is not really the same as having a story from a particular point of view. Just because there is a black actor on the stage does not necessarily mean it is your story. Dawn Walton, the founder of Sheffield's Eclipse - which uses the Black British experience to create new work that will enrich the canon of British theatre - agrees. There exists a belief in theatre that what is on stage is what needs to be diverse, so cross-casting is always where people go - casting a black whatever - but if that solved it, we would have beaten this in the 1970s. She states theatre boards need to change because they are very much into doing the same thing over and over again... but the country has shifted. The institution is becoming less and less relevant because it does not represent what goes on right outside its doors. Xia states theatre is still at a place where actors of colour are expected to play peripheral characters unless the play is explicitly dealing with race, which is ridiculous. The human experience is so much broader than that. I have heard quite scary things said by directors which shows a lack of understanding about roles and who can play what. Ultimately, people are always going to represent their world on stage, so if their world has been monocultural, it is highly likely that is how the work will be rendered. The diversity of theatre generally is an issue, according to Arts Council England's director of theatre, Neil Darlison. I think theatres are aware of it and if they are not, they should be, because ultimately it is going to affect their business. However, he states there are some positive signs, particularly in metropolitan centres, where the diversity of people working in organisations and running them is better than it was. They are starting to reflect the stories of the inhabitants of the city. Warrington believes direct action is needed to effect change. We have to wake up our consciences and we can do that by having a deliberate policy, so that it becomes part of everyday life. It has to become something we do. Buffong adds that he is in favour of anything that gets an instant result. Targets, quotas, ringfencing money - I am in favour of making it happen now. The idea of more initiatives and training is so over. There exists a wealth of people who just need the opportunity to work. Ali states those opportunities may be hampered by the law, which in some ways supports equality, but also has grey areas. There are exemptions from the duty not to discriminate where appropriate and casting is one of those. If you are casting for realism purposes or because of the way a character is written, that is permitted, so you could argue that exemption has worked against progress. I understand that we are talking about an artistic process, but we must recognise it is an industrial one, and decisions made have an impact disproportionately on working opportunities. It is a difficult and thorny question because there are pros and cons on both sides. Essiedu believes the answer may be a simple one. We mimic what we see, so we need to put that in front of people to get that machine started. I had never seen a black actor performing the lead in a Shakespeare play until I was 18 and I saw Chiwetel Ejiofor doing Othello in the Donmar Warehouse. Because I had not seen it, I did not think it was possible and I did not explore that avenue. People from whatever background are only going to be inspired to write or perform if they see it. If you have got an artistic director who is willing to try and fail, then you are going to get a wider palette of works. Some of it will probably be terrible, but some of it will be unbelievably brilliant. Hamlet is in cinemas from 8 June and at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon 13 August.

There is greater visibility, but the question is about the quality of that visibility and the quality of the parts. I don’t think it’s where it should be. Hamida Ali, Equal Opportunities and Diversity Manager for the actors’ union, shares Warrington’s concern. “One of the things we have to think about is how surprised we are to see a black actor in a leading role, not only in Shakespeare but in general. That in itself is a statement, that this is still the case.” There is, she says, a general agreement that there is a problem, but what causes it, who is to blame, and how to resolve it are matters of debate. The production of Lear was staged by Talawa, a theatre company founded in the 1980s in direct response to the lack of creative opportunities for ethnic minorities. As artistic director Michael Buffong says, three decades later, a need for change still exists. Essiedu believes that theatre must be more diverse in the stories it tells and in the people who tell them. You need people to represent different aspects of the same world, otherwise you get a very narrow perspective. And that would lead to a more diverse group of actors as well. It’s not just the art, it’s also the organization. Matthew Xia, associate artistic director of the Royal Exchange, said that in some ways the theatre was going backwards. We live in 2016, a society that is international, multi-cultural and cosmopolitan, and as artists we have the responsibility to reflect this in our work. It is strange, for I see more variety in the population of a building-site than in what is supposed to be the liberal end of the labour market. Buffong, therefore, insists on the necessity of changing the gatekeepers, because there is the power. In the majority of institutions, as soon as you reach the top of the hierarchy, the proportions of the local population decrease. She says that theatre boards must change because they are very much into doing the same thing over and over again, whereas the country has moved on. Dawn Walton, founder of the Eclipse Theatre Company, which creates work based on the black British experience, and which aims to enrich the canon of British theatre, agrees. “Just because there are two black actors in a play, and people go, ‘Oh, look, it’s got two black actors in it’, doesn’t mean it’s your story. Xia says that the theatre still only uses people of colour as the comic relief unless the play has a very strong ethnic overtone, which is absurd. The theatre is becoming less and less relevant because it does not reflect society outside its doors. There is a tendency in the theatre to see the need for diversity in terms of what is on stage, so the first thing is to cross-cast, to put a black person in a part, but if that were the solution we would have done it in the seventies. The issue of diversity in theatre is a problem, says the Theatre Director for the English Arts Council, Neil Darlison. “I’ve heard some very frightening things from directors about the roles and who can play them. The human experience is far more varied than that.” Warrington thinks direct action is needed to bring about a change. Yet he does find some signs of hope, especially in cities where the diversity of those who work in and manage organizations is greater than it was. In the end, people will always represent their world on the stage, and if their world has been a mono-cultural one, so too will they. Buffong adds that he's for anything that has an immediate effect. We must arouse consciences, and that's why we need a clear policy that makes it part of daily life. It has to be done. They're beginning to reflect the social composition of the city. Targets, quotas, money set aside - I'm for that. The idea of more initiatives and more training is so old. There are so many people who only need the opportunity to work. In Ali’s opinion, such opportunities may be curbed by the law, which in many ways supports equality, but which also has its ambiguous points. Casting for the sake of realism, or because a character is written as such, is allowed, so one can argue that this exception has worked against progress. There are exceptions to the prohibition of discrimination in appropriate cases, and one of them is casting. This is a difficult and thorny question, for both arguments for and against are extremely weighty. Essiedu believes the solution is quite simple. I understand that we are talking about artistic work, but we must also admit that it is also an industrial process, and the choices we make have a disproportionate influence on the number of work opportunities that are created. We imitate what we see, so we have to put it in front of us so that it becomes the engine. I had never seen a black actor play a leading role in a Shakespeare play until I was eighteen and went to the Donmar to see Chiwetel Ejiofor as Othello. Because I had never seen it, I didn't think it was possible and didn't explore it. If an artistic director is willing to risk and fail, you will get a much wider palette of works. You won’t inspire people of any background to write or perform if they don’t see it. Some of it will be terrible, but some of it will be unbelievably good. June 8 and August 13 in the cinema, and from August 13 in the theatre.

text: Edinburgh Capitals captain Jacob Johnston was delighted as his team ended their losing run of games - but was then left to rue another defeat. The Capitals concluded a seven-match winless streak with a 3-2 home triumph against Dundee Stars on Saturday before suffering a 6-0 defeat on Tayside in Sunday's return fixture. This left Johnston with mixed feelings following a weekend that had offered considerable promise after their Murrayfield success. Saturday's victory felt extremely positive, Johnston stated. We have experienced some setbacks and confronted adversity during recent weeks, so breaking that losing sequence was excellent. We were genuinely seeking those points on Sunday and failed to secure them. It represented a fine opportunity to achieve a four-point weekend since they remain close to us in the table. We approached it in that manner, but in every match we enter, we must anticipate victory. We cannot expect to defeat particular teams and must begin securing wins if we wish to start ascending. The contrasting weekend left the Capitals still three points behind second-bottom Dundee following both matches, though they possess two games in hand over Marc LeFebvre's team. That losing sequence, during which they conceded a staggering 47 goals, concluded as they defeated the Stars 3-2 at Murrayfield on Saturday. Ian Schultz and Matt Tipoff scored to frame the opening period as Edinburgh commenced the match in ideal fashion, with Mason Wilgosh adding a third early in the second session. Stars responded through Matt White and Kevin Bruijsten, but could not locate an equaliser to extend their dismal form to 13 defeats in their previous 14 encounters. The fixture returned to Tayside on Sunday as Dundee hosted, but the Stars ended their own sequence of seven consecutive losses with a 6-0 shutout victory over Michal Dobron's side. Dundee established a four-goal advantage during the second period when Mikael Lidhammar, Brett Switzer and two from Matt White positioned them comfortably. Two additional strikes from Justin Faryna in the third supplemented what proved a successful evening for the Stars ultimately. Fife Flyers collected two outstanding points away at Manchester Storm on Saturday to commence their double-header, prevailing 4-2 in a contest that remained scoreless for the initial 35 minutes. Ryan Dingle finally broke the deadlock before Taylor Dickin equalised as both sides entered the interval locked at 1-1 after two periods. Dingle restored the advantage then Sebastien Thinel extended it before Matt Bissonnette reduced the deficit for the hosts. Flyers debutant Bryan Cameron added a fourth to secure victory. In Sunday's return encounter in Kirkcaldy, they achieved two victories from two and four points with a 3-1 triumph on home ice. Paul Phillips gave the visitors the lead late in the opening period, but the Flyers reversed the situation as Brendan Brooks and Dingle each scored, with Justin Fox adding a late empty-net goal. Braehead Clan began their weekend at in-form Nottingham Panthers and despite missing five players, still claimed a point in a 4-3 overtime defeat. Lee Baldwin opened the scoring for Clan, but Panthers reversed the match through Brian McGrattan and Matt Carter before Mike Hammond equalised for the Glasgow side. Jeff Brown and Alex Leavitt exchanged goals for respective teams, taking the encounter into the additional period where Robert Farmer clinched victory with the overtime strike. Clan returned to Glasgow to host league leaders Cardiff Devils and despite further heroics from the depleted squad, concluded with a penalty-shots defeat following a 2-2 draw. Daniel Åhsberg's opener was cancelled by Joey Hadded, before Bari McKenzie put Braehead ahead in the second period, which was equalised through Andrew Hotham. The Devils prevailed on penalty shots with their goalkeeper Ben Bowns saving Åhsberg's decisive attempt to secure the points for the Welsh side. text: Sinn Féin has dismissed a proposal to stand independent anti-Brexit candidates as part of a general election pact in Northern Ireland. These are external links and will open in a new window The SDLP had proposed that parties which backed a Remain vote in last year's EU referendum should forge an agreement on candidates for the 8 June poll. The party's leader Colum Eastwood stated that putting forward agreed candidates with no party affiliation was a possibility. However, Sinn Féin's John O'Dowd declared this was not a credible offer. Several parties opposed to Brexit have conducted discussions about forming what Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill termed a progressive alliance in certain constituencies for the Westminster election. The objective was to capture seats from parties that support the UK's withdrawal from the EU. The Democratic Unionist Party and the Ulster Unionists, which both voted in the House of Commons to trigger the Brexit process, have also conducted discussions about the prospects of agreeing to field a single unionist unity candidate in certain areas. It is understood that Mr Eastwood's proposal for independent anti-Brexit candidates was to encompass the East Londonderry, Fermanagh and South Tyrone and North Belfast constituencies. However, Mr O'Dowd stated it would not receive backing from Sinn Féin and any pact would be focused on political party representation. We do not believe that's an acceptable way forward, declared the Upper Bann MLA. It is political parties that will drive forward change in this society. We view that as a proposal from Colum to stymie Sinn Féin and bolster the SDLP - that's not what progressive political alliances should be about. He added that his party remained prepared to speak to others about a possible deal. Mr Eastwood acknowledged that there is probably no chance now of his proposal becoming a reality. If Sinn Féin have ruled that out, I think it's very, very difficult, he stated. We have always declared that we would not do a pact with Sinn Féin alone. We wanted this to be broad; we wanted this to be non-nationalist; we wanted to go right across the political spectrum. On Tuesday, the Green Party declared it would not unite with parties that did not share its vision for a progressive society. Its leader Steven Agnew stated the SDLP's decision to select incumbent MP Alasdair McDonnell as its South Belfast candidate for the snap election ended chances of an agreement in the constituency.

text: Police Scotland has said that it does not collate or hold specific figures on child sexual exploitation. Through a series of Freedom of Information requests, BBC Scotland enquired how many cases, concerns and complaints of child exploitation, and child sexual exploitation were recorded in the previous four years. However, the force stated the figures were not maintained on a single system. Scotland's Children's Commissioner described the revelation as disturbing. This emerges on the day that officers launched a new unit to assist with what police recognise is the complex problem of child abuse and neglect across Scotland. It will provide expertise to enable local teams to thoroughly investigate cases, including child sexual exploitation, online offences and other forms of abuse. In its response to the BBC's FOI requests, Police Scotland stated: Child exploitation encompasses a broad range of criminal activity and does not correlate to a specific offence, but rather can involve a range of differing offences...The level of data you have requested is not maintained on a single system. This follows the publication last summer of the Jay report into sexual exploitation in Rotherham in South Yorkshire. It disclosed that more than 1,400 children were subjected to appalling sexual abuse. Last year Glasgow City Council stated 97 children in the city were victims, or at risk of, sexual exploitation. The Association of Chief Police Officers stated most forces in England and Wales now place a marker on such offences in their records, but senior officers here state that it is not straightforward to do. Children's Commissioner Tam Baillie stated: I am disturbed that we do not yet collect police figures on children who are the subject of sexual exploitation. This was a recommendation of the Scottish Parliament and features in the Scottish government action plan on child sexual exploitation. The reason this is so important is that unless we know the scope of the problem we are attempting to address, then we will not have the appropriate or proportionate response. Assistant Chief Constable Malcolm Graham, from Police Scotland, stated the nature of child sexual exploitation made it highly unlikely that young people would come forward to report being abused. Our priority is to be focusing on identifying as many victims as we can and identifying perpetrators who have the intent to commit these devastating crimes so we can prevent the abuse from occurring, he stated. Scotland is at the forefront of approaches to child sexual exploitation. Sexual exploitation is a form of abuse and it is not a specific crime type recorded as such. Children and young people may be victim of repeated rapes, physical assaults or grooming offences and we categorise all of these in crime recording. He added: But what is most important here is our focus on identifying who these victims are. Our focus is always on where there are child protection issues, and on keeping children safe. Martin Crewe, director of Barnardo's Scotland, stated: Rotherham was a real wake-up call and led to the Scottish government's national action plan last year but we could and should be doing more. Our concern is that we do not know the full extent of the problem. We welcome the work of the police. Since the publication of the Barnardo's Scotland petition in 2011 we have been pushing for a better understanding of child sexual exploitation in Scotland. In January 2013, Aileen Campbell, Minister for Children and Young People, responded to the Public Petitions Committee inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation in Scotland, and announced four points including, action to improve the way child sexual exploitation is identified by Scotland's new single police force to make this form of abuse more visible. However, sexual exploitation per se is still not recorded or centrally collated. The Scottish government stated figures are available on the wider problem of child abuse. A spokeswoman stated: The safety of our children is a key priority for the government and an issue we take extremely seriously. The launch of the National Child Abuse Investigation Unit will help to target and bring to justice those who seek to harm our young people. The unit has been established to tackle all forms of child abuse, and child sexual exploitation is one aspect of this. We have robust legislation in place to cover a wide range of these offences, including online abuse and are working to strengthen the law even further. She added: The extent of the problem is often difficult to assess because abuse by its very nature is concealed. That is why prevention and swift action to safeguard children are a significant part of our strategy to tackle these terrible crimes. This includes robust National Child Protection guidance, action to tackle emerging forms of child abuse including child sexual exploitation, a national public awareness campaign and guidance for night-time workers such as taxi drivers and hotel staff who may come into contact with those at risk.

text: The range and quality of research at Scotland's universities has been praised in a new UK-wide survey. The majority of Scottish universities have sustained or enhanced their position in the league table. Edinburgh University secured 4th place overall whilst Glasgow University achieved 13th position. More than 85% of university research in Scotland was deemed to have an outstanding or very significant impact in the broader society and economy. This percentage exceeded the UK average. The assessment, compiled by Research Fortnight, was founded on the outcomes of the 2014 Research Excellence Framework (REF 2014). This constituted a comprehensive exercise which examined the standard of research in various subjects at universities throughout the UK. Expert panels evaluated the work of more than 52,000 academics from 154 UK universities. Edinburgh and Glasgow Universities both advanced one position in the table compared to the previous one in 2008. St Andrews, Strathclyde, Aberdeen, Dundee, Heriot-Watt and Stirling also achieved places in the top 50. Strathclyde's physics department was designated as the finest in the UK - surpassing Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial College. Aberdeen and Dundee both declined slightly in the overall rankings, whilst the others advanced. Generally speaking, the data indicated Scottish universities have sustained or even enhanced their research rankings since tuition fees for Scottish students were eliminated. International rankings also indicate the general position of Scottish universities is being sustained. Each of Scotland's 18 higher education institutions conducts research deemed to be of world-leading standard whilst Scotland performs more strongly than the UK average when evaluated on the impact of its research. For the first time, REF 2014 also evaluated the impact the research has had on the economy, society, public policy, culture and the quality of life. Laurence Howells, chief executive of the Scottish Funding Council, stated: Today we have received confirmation that our universities' research is world-leading and impacts upon almost every aspect of daily life, from the manner we treat patients in hospital, to the way we communicate with smartphones. By maximising our investments in research, Scotland's universities are rightfully on the podium with the finest in the world. It is particularly gratifying that Scotland's pioneering approach to collaboration through research pooling has helped to deliver this success in the REF. Each of the University of Edinburgh's three colleges possessed at least one research area ranked first in the UK. Edinburgh research in Sociology, in Earth Systems and Environmental Sciences and in Computer Science and Informatics was rated the finest in the UK, based on breadth and quality of research. The principal, Prof Sir Timothy O'Shea, stated: Research at the University of Edinburgh is continuously expanding the depth of human knowledge and making an impact on the broader world - whether it be improving the effectiveness of youth justice policy and practice, or shaping the technologies employed to manage the world's data. Our outstanding researchers enable us to establish links with charities, businesses, policy makers and other universities, so that together we can address long-standing challenges at home and abroad. The University of Glasgow stated its achievements included pioneering research in medicine with new drugs and treatments; software revolutionising the design of electric motors; new methods of controlling animal diseases including TB in cattle and rabies; a positive impact on knife crime policy; and assisting the transformation of Stirling Castle into one of the UK's leading heritage sites. Principal and vice-chancellor Prof Anton Muscatelli stated: It is particularly gratifying that, in accordance with the aspirations of the university set out in the university's 2020 Global Vision, 31% of our output was judged to be of 'world-leading' quality. This success lies at the very heart of our contribution to the UK's economy and, in particular, Scotland's economy. The report was welcomed by Education Secretary Angela Constance, who stated Scotland was globally recognised for pioneering research, with four universities in the world's top 200. This was more per head of population than any other country except Switzerland, she stated. Ms Constance added: The 2014 Research Excellence Framework has now demonstrated that all of our institutions are producing world-class research in a variety of areas. Research is also fundamental to our economic growth and prosperity. Figures published earlier this year demonstrated that our £124m investment in eight innovation centres has the potential to generate up to £1.5bn and around 5,000 jobs for the economy, through sectors such as energy, aquaculture and construction. However, the University and College Union cautioned that world-leading research was too often being conducted by people on zero-hours contracts. It also cautioned institutions against using any perceived low scores as an excuse to consider reducing staff numbers. The union added that much research not included or rated highly in the REF still made a hugely important contribution. UCU Scotland official Mary Senior stated: Our universities must be free to continue pushing the boundaries in their cutting-edge work. We must also acknowledge that much research not included or rated highly in the REF is still incredibly important. Too often our world-leading research is being conducted by people with little or no job security. Universities must avoid any knee-jerk reactions to the results or use perceived low scores to attempt to make unnecessary cuts. We are not alone in criticising what we regard as a flawed process when it comes to the REF and have outlined the need for a fundamental overhaul of the research system. We want to see better funding that expands our research base, covering more institutions and more diverse areas of research.

text: The mother of an RAF airman who went missing more than three weeks ago has said she absolutely believes her son is still alive. Corrie Mckeague, 23, a gunner stationed at RAF Honington in Suffolk, disappeared following an evening out in Bury St Edmunds during the early hours of 24 September. His mother Nicola Urquhart informed the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme: Nobody can simply vanish. She stated it would be characteristic of Mr Mckeague to get into a stranger's vehicle. Mr Mckeague, originally from Dunfermline in Fife, was last seen on CCTV walking alone and consuming takeaway food in Bury St Edmunds at 03:20 BST. A trace on his mobile telephone showed it was in Bury St Edmunds early on 24 September but subsequently moved to the Barton Mills area. For further updates on this story, visit BBC Suffolk Live Ms Urquhart said the telephone data indicates this journey took 28 minutes, which is how long it would take to drive [between the two locations]. It remains unknown whether the telephone was in Mr Mckeague's possession at the time of the journey, but Ms Urquhart said that entering a stranger's vehicle was genuinely something Corrie would do. She said he was the sort of person that, if he saw someone walking down the road and he was in a car, he would stop and give that complete stranger a lift. Police have located neither Mr Mckeague nor his telephone. However Ms Urquhart said there were many possibilities as to why the telephone's signal was no longer being detected - that it could have run out of battery or been damaged. She said that police - who are continuing to search for the missing airman - have got so much CCTV they've still not been able to watch it all. She added: They've widened the parameter to look further out. They've got [access to] private CCTV. But not a single [new] image of Corrie [has been discovered]. Ms Urquhart said she believes somebody does know something about the events surrounding her son's disappearance, but added that the public have been desperate to help. But nothing, not one person [has been able to] give us anything - and that simply doesn't make sense, she added. If you have any information which might be relevant, please telephone the Suffolk Police incident room on 01473 782019. The Victoria Derbyshire programme is broadcast on weekdays between 09:00 and 11:00 on BBC Two and the BBC News Channel.

text: UN human rights chief Zeid Raad Al Hussein has described the Syrian city of Aleppo as a slaughterhouse. During an address, he declared that the siege and bombardment of Aleppo's rebel-controlled eastern sector constituted amongst the crimes of historic proportions occurring in Syria. Nearly 500 individuals have perished and 2,000 sustained injuries since governmental forces, supported by Russian aerial strikes, commenced an offensive on the east one month previously. Syria's administration has stated that civilians are enduring hardship due to terrorists. Concurrently, the United Nations reported that insufficient security assurances had compelled it to postpone arrangements to conduct medical evacuations from Aleppo on Friday during the second 11-hour humanitarian pause announced unilaterally by the government and its partner, Russia. Russia has declared it will additionally halt air strikes between 08:00 and 19:00 local time (05:00-16:00 GMT) on Saturday to permit civilians and rebels to depart the city through safe passages. Nevertheless, remarkably few individuals have allegedly utilised the proposal, with rebel groups maintaining that it would constitute forced displacement and capitulation. Aleppo, formerly Syria's most populous city and the nation's commercial and industrial centre, has been ravaged by conflict since 2012. It has remained divided approximately in half, with President Bashar al-Assad's forces commanding the west and rebels the east. At September's commencement, troops and Iranian-supported militiamen cut the rebels' final route into the east and imposed siege upon its 275,000 inhabitants. A fortnight subsequently, following the breakdown of a nationwide ceasefire negotiated by the United States and Russia, the government initiated a ground campaign to secure complete control of the city, accompanied by an aerial bombardment of unparalleled scale and ferocity. The historic city of Aleppo, a location of ancient civility and magnificence, is presently a slaughterhouse - a horrific centre of suffering and terror, where the lifeless remains of young children lie trapped beneath streets of debris and expectant mothers are deliberately targeted, he stated. Mr Zeid noted that his personnel had recorded breaches of international humanitarian law by all parties in Aleppo. Armed opposition factions continue to launch mortars and other munitions into civilian districts of western Aleppo, but indiscriminate aerial attacks throughout the eastern section of the city by governmental forces and their allies are accountable for the vast majority of civilian fatalities. These breaches constitute war crimes. And if deliberately committed as part of a widespread or systematic assault directed against civilians, they constitute crimes against humanity. text: UK astronaut Tim Peake has begun his life in space with tea and a bacon sandwich. He reached the International Space Station on Tuesday following his launch from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan aboard a Soyuz rocket. In social media posts, he stated he was loving every minute of the initial days of his mission. On Friday afternoon he will respond to questions from reporters in a live connection with the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany. Mr Peake is amongst six crew members residing and operating in space. These include American station commander Scott Kelly, who is completing a year aboard the ISS. In a social media post, referencing the NASA astronaut, the 43-year-old from Chichester in Sussex wrote: What makes a good leader? @StationCDRKelly having a hot bacon sarnie waiting as my 1st meal on #ISS. Boy that tasted good! #Principia. He subsequently added: 1st 48hrs on ISS - busy but incredible. Amazing how fast the body adapts to new environment. Found my tea ... life is good! The former Army pilot and helicopter test aviator also received messages of encouragement from the Queen and Sir Elton John following the successful launch and docking on Tuesday. He posted to singer Sir Elton John from space, citing his renowned song Rocket Man, in reply to a good fortune message. He also posted to the Queen from space after Buckingham Palace's social media account published a good luck letter from the monarch. On Friday afternoon, Mr Peake will address members of the media through a live connection to the European Astronaut Centre near Cologne in Germany. The question and answer session will be broadcast live on the European space agency website. It will provide a brief respite from a demanding schedule. According to the European Space Agency, he has numerous duties to complete, including unpacking cargo, spending an hour on an exercise bicycle and participating in an experiment examining the effects of microgravity on the bone marrow. text: All living flowers ultimately derive from a single ancestor that lived about 140 million years ago, a study suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window Researchers combined evolutionary models of flowers with the most comprehensive dataset of characteristics from contemporary flowers ever compiled. From this, the research team was able to deduce the appearance of the ancestral flower. The flower possessed numerous concentric cycles of petal-like structures in groups of three, organised in whorls, and was hermaphroditic. Hervé Sauquet, from Université Paris-Sud, France, one of the study's authors published this week in Nature Communications stated: No living flower appears exactly like the ancestral specimen - and why would there be? This represents a flower that existed at least 140 million years ago and has had substantial time to evolve into the remarkable diversity of flowers that exist today. We are all acquainted with the beauty of flowers - the reproductive organs produced by approximately 90 per cent of all living terrestrial plants. However, their origin and early evolution remains a mystery. This is primarily due to the absence of fossilised flowers from the time period when the ancestor of living flowers is believed to have existed. Dr Jason Hilton from the University of Birmingham, UK, who was not involved in the research, stated: The structure and organisation of the ancestral flower has remained enigmatic. For example, we do not know whether the earliest flowers were unisexual or bisexual, or whether they were pollinated by wind or insects. To reconstruct the appearance of the first flower, the researchers recorded the characteristics - such as the petals and sepals - of the flowers from 792 living species. They mapped the distribution of these characteristics onto the evolutionary tree of flowering plants, enabling them to construct a picture of what flowers appeared like at crucial points in their history - including the last common ancestor of all living flowers.
