text: The Solar Impulse plane has broken the record for the longest non-stop solo flight without refuelling. The milestone was reached 76 hours into the current stage of its bid to circumnavigate the globe. Pilot Andre Borschberg is making steady progress as he attempts the first solar-powered crossing of the Pacific. Following his departure from Nagoya, Japan, early on Monday (local time), he has now passed Midway Island and is proceeding towards his destination of Kalaeloa, Hawaii. At 76 hours into the flight, he surpassed the record for the longest ever non-stop solo flight without refuelling. The previous record was established by the American Steve Fossett in 2006. His jet-powered Virgin GlobalFlyer aircraft completed a full circumnavigation of the world in that duration, covering more than 41,000km. By comparison, Mr Borschberg's Solar Impulse aircraft, which carries no fuel whatsoever, had travelled merely some 5,500km in its 76 hours of flight. Wednesday witnessed the Swiss pilot fly a holding pattern to time his encounter with an approaching cold front to the optimum. This will take place on Thursday, and Mr Borschberg requires good sun conditions to get his aircraft up and over the weather system so that he can navigate the final stretch into Kalaeloa on Friday. Exactly when this historic landing will take place is somewhat uncertain. Solar Impulse has some quite strict constraints to ensure the 72m-wingspan aircraft can put its wheels down safely. These include a maximum cross wind of no more than four knots and a maximum overall wind speed of no more than 10 knots. If it is too windy at ground level, Mr Borschberg will be instructed to circle overhead until the conditions calm down. By then, he will probably have spent more than 120 hours in the air. Thus far, he has coped remarkably well on very little sleep, and on Wednesday even found time to joke around in his cockpit by donning a wig and fake beard. When he reaches Hawaii, he will be met by fellow adventurer and business partner, Bertrand Piccard. The pair have shared the flying duties in the single-seater aircraft's round-the-world quest, which commenced in Abu Dhabi, UAE, back in March. It is Mr Piccard – who famously made the first non-stop, global circumnavigation in a balloon – who will fly the next stage from Kalaeloa to Phoenix, Arizona. That is not quite as far as the current stint, but it still likely to take four days and nights. From Phoenix, Solar Impulse will head for New York and an Atlantic crossing that would eventually see the aircraft return to Abu Dhabi. Borschberg and Piccard have used the various stopovers on their round-the-world journey to carry a campaigning message to local people on the topic of clean technologies. Their Solar Impulse aircraft is not intended to be a vision of the future of aviation. Rather, it is supposed to be a demonstration of the current capabilities of solar power in general. The aircraft is covered in 17,000 photovoltaic cells. These either power the aircraft's electric motors directly, or charge its lithium-ion batteries, which sustain the aircraft during the night hours. LEG 1: 9 March. A Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) spokesman said the profiteering was simply not fair. High-profile artists such as Adele and Ed Sheeran have previously criticised the touts and requested their fans not to purchase tickets from secondary sites. Last month, resale site Viagogo was accused of moral repugnance for selling tickets to an Ed Sheeran Teenage Cancer Trust concert for up to £5,000. And an £85 ticket to see Adele at the O2 in London last year was reportedly being sold for £24,840. As part of the touting crackdown, ministers will accept in full the recommendations of a review by Professor Michael Waterson. Ed Sheeran angry after his tour tickets end up on secondary sites The government said it wants the major companies in the secondary ticket market to do more to identify ticket touts and differentiate them from individual fans who wish to sell tickets for events they can no longer attend. Heavy metal fans Brian and Jane O'Donoghue aim to attend a concert once a month but say that touts make purchasing tickets incredibly frustrating. It was the only way, says Brian, 51, from Hereford. We weighed up going to see Metallica in Copenhagen instead, which including flights and hotel was not much more. Jo Dipple, chief executive of music industry representatives UK Music, welcomed the move. Massive profit is made by people who are taking value out of the music industry and putting tickets out of the reach of music fans, she said. Banning bots is a step towards ensuring the ticketing market for live events works more fairly for concert-goers. Minister of State for Digital and Culture, Matt Hancock, said: It is unacceptable that touts are misusing technology to bypass security measures and purchase vast numbers of tickets before real fans get the chance, only to sell them on at rip-off prices. text: A petition calling for jousting to be made an Olympic sport has been launched by English Heritage. The charity's jousting specialist Dominic Sewell informed BBC Radio 5 Live that the mediaeval pursuit represented a global phenomenon that merits recognition. Approximately 20 individuals in Britain joust competitively, though the charity stated tournaments occurred worldwide. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) declared it remained unaware of any formal application for recognition. For a discipline to gain inclusion in the Olympic Games programme, it must be administered by an international federation, practised extensively across the globe, and satisfy various additional criteria before consideration by the IOC's executive board. English Heritage confirmed it had made preliminary contact with the IOC and the Federation Equestre Internationale (FEI) - which oversees all Olympic equestrian disciplines - as an initial step towards jousting's Olympic aspirations. Jousting would require FEI recognition before Olympic consideration by the IOC, English Heritage confirmed. Mr Sewell, who competes in jousting, stated: Like the Olympic British equestrian squad, we ride magnificent horses to an outstanding standard. He declared jousting demanded considerable skill and daily training, adding one must be resilient, not merely physically but mentally, enabling fearless positioning in the saddle, confronting opponents, and presenting oneself as a target. Mr Sewell, formerly a furniture assembler in manufacturing, stated: This has evolved from hobby to sport and profession. He informed BBC Radio 4's Today programme his initial interest stemmed from attending historical re-enactments, though added: I am a sportsman, not a performer. Mr Sewell continued: Upon mounting a horse everything transformed and I realised: this is my calling, I wish to excel at this. English Heritage acknowledged the path to Olympic recognition for jousting could prove lengthy, though noted positive indicators. Tournaments were gaining popularity, the charity reported, now occurring in nations including Belgium, Brazil and New Zealand. In America, where jousting has served as Maryland's official state sport since 1962, competitors have initiated comparable Olympic campaigns. Contemporary jousting represents quite a secure sport for participation, Mr Sewell maintains. The regulations essentially establish single combat within a designated area, a pitch - or 'tilt-yard' - containing a tilt rail. The competitors charge along the rail towards each other with points allocated for style and impact strength. Wearing armour weighing approximately 20kg, the athletes grip a 12ft lance in one hand and their horse's reins in the other, whilst riding towards opponents at maximum gallop - reaching speeds of 30mph. Currently injuries are infrequent... though occasional dismounting might cause minor bruising, Mr Sewell states. The IOC confirmed its programme was under review within Olympic Agenda 2020, the organisation's strategic framework for Olympic futures. A spokesperson declared: One proposal involved making the Olympic programme more adaptable by shifting from sport-based to event-based programming. This month, the IOC endorsed proposals adding karate, skateboarding, sports climbing, surfing and baseball/softball to Tokyo 2020's programme. If approved, the additions would contribute 18 events and 474 athletes to the Olympic Games. Jousting, originating in Ancient Greece as military preparation, emerged in England during the 10th Century as knightly training for equestrian and lance proficiency. England's first jousting tournament was reportedly organised by Frenchman Godfrey de Preuilly in 1066. The tournaments achieved such popularity that during the 12th Century, King Henry II prohibited the sport, considering it hazardous to assemble numerous skilled knights simultaneously. The prohibition was rescinded under King Richard I and the sport maintained popularity, particularly throughout the Tudor period, before declining following French King Henry I's death during a 1559 joust. Jousting experienced revival during 19th Century romanticism, with authors including Lord Byron, Percy Shelley and Sir Walter Scott romanticising chivalric ideals through tales of knights and maidens.

text: Two 15-year-olds have been given life sentences with 20-year minimum terms for the murder of a mother and daughter in Lincolnshire in April. School meals assistant Elizabeth Edwards, 49, and Katie, 13, were suffocated and stabbed whilst sleeping at their residence in Spalding. During sentencing, the judge declared it was a dreadful crime which has few equivalents in contemporary criminal history. The perpetrators were aged 14 at the time, seemingly making them Britain's youngest dual murderers. The judge at Nottingham Crown Court, Mr Justice Haddon-Cave, stated the case possessed defining and exceptionally chilling characteristics, and denounced the killers' behaviour as grotesque. Jurors were told that the killers proceeded to share a bath, engage in sexual intercourse, and view four Twilight vampire films following the murders in Dawson Avenue, Spalding, on 13 April. For additional coverage on this and other Lincolnshire news Speaking to the teenagers, the judge informed them: There exists clear intent to kill both victims - both defendants acknowledged wanting to murder them. There was extraordinary premeditation and planning - it was, by any measure, substantial, meticulous and repeated. He continued: The killings were savage in the manner of executions, and both victims, particularly Elizabeth Edwards, must have endured terribly in the final moments of their lives. Mrs Edwards and her daughter were repeatedly stabbed by the couple, who were characterised in court as maintaining a Bonnie and Clyde-style relationship. Mrs Edwards was stabbed by the boy eight times, twice in the throat, in a calculated attempt to ensure her daughter was not awakened by screams or pleas for assistance. Katie was stabbed twice in the neck with considerable force before she was suffocated by the boy. Throughout his sentencing observations, the judge said both teenagers were equally culpable for the murders and had delighted in what you accomplished. I perceive no reason to differentiate between you in any manner, he said. Had you been adults you might have been confronting the entirety of your lives in prison for this double murder. Outside court, Karen Thompson, deputy chief crown prosecutor for the East Midlands, said: This represents one of the most distressing and disturbing cases that I have ever encountered. Our profound sympathies are now with the extended family and friends of Elizabeth and Katie Edwards as they attempt to come to terms with this horrific crime. Det Ch Insp Martin Holvey, of Lincolnshire Police, said it had been a rare and unprecedented case. The planning that preceded these brutal murders of Elizabeth and Katie, as they slept in their own beds, was cold, ruthless and chilling - as was the absence of remorse demonstrated by the two juveniles afterwards. In court Peter Joyce QC, prosecuting, detailed for the first time the account provided by the boy shortly after he was arrested. He said the pair had met and both agreed to kill Mrs Edwards and her daughter after the girl had requested him to kill both of the victims as she did not like the smell of blood. He proceeded to describe the killing of the mother, Elizabeth, and said that during the attack she had struggled and scratched his face, back and buttocks, Mr Joyce told the court. After approximately three minutes she had ceased struggling and had gone limp. He had got off the bed and removed his trainers since they had made the floorboards creak. The boy then entered Katie's room, bent down and pushed the knife through her throat before using a pillow to suffocate her, the court heard. Defending the boy, Simon Myerson QC said the two children became ensnared in a fantasy of their own creation. Andrew Stubbs QC, representing the girl, said the pair were in a toxic relationship and were almost playing chicken with each other as they encouraged each other to commit the killings. The pair pleaded guilty to manslaughter at a hearing in September but subsequently the boy admitted to murder before the trial commenced. His girlfriend maintained her innocence to murder but was found guilty of two counts.

text: Steven Wilson is often dubbed the hardest working musician in the world of progressive rock. The versatile musician secured three awards at this month's Progressive Music Awards in London, including album of the year for Hand. Cannot. Erase. The Guardian's five-star critique described it as a smart, soulful and immersive work of art. Since the 1980s, Wilson has served as the creative force behind numerous musical ventures, the most renowned being the rock group Porcupine Tree. Currently, before two sold-out performances at the Royal Albert Hall, Wilson is issuing a vinyl-exclusive double LP, Transience, to highlight the more accessible aspect of his solo catalogue. He discusses with the BBC his passion for vinyl, his demanding timetable and reveals how comedy performer Matt Berry became his supporting artist. What significance does vinyl hold for you? I matured during the final period of the vinyl age, and at that time, I recall, we eagerly anticipated CD's arrival because vinyl proved so vexing. You would purchase the album, bring it home, and it would contain a scratch, requiring you to return it once more. I adore CDs, and for certain types of music - classical for instance - it surpasses vinyl. However, the difficulty with CD and digital downloads is that there exists nothing you can genuinely cherish or value. Possessing vinyl resembles having a magnificent painting displayed in your lounge. It represents something you can grasp, examine the lyrics and lose yourself in the artwork. I believed it was merely a sentimental matter, but it cannot be if youngsters too young to recall vinyl are relishing that type of experience. Do you possess a piece of vinyl that you value? The reality is I disposed of 100% of my vinyl during the 90s. All the vinyl I own has been repurchased. I began from the standpoint that I wished to reconstruct the collection I possessed when I was 15, but it has exceeded that. The initial record which I convinced my parents to purchase for me was Electric Light Orchestra's Out of the Blue. If I still possessed my original copy, it would hold sentimental worth, but, regrettably, it sits in a charity shop somewhere. Why issue your new compilation Transience on vinyl? It was initially conceived as a concept for Record Store Day, but we missed the opportunity for that. My record label had proposed I compile some of my briefer, more accessible compositions. I became somewhat fixated by the notion to create something like an introduction to Steven Wilson, and I was dedicated to it being a vinyl-exclusive release. Anyone who purchases the vinyl also receives a high-resolution download. Do you harbour concerns that the album will not represent your work authentically? No - because whilst I do concentrate on more extended musical pieces, there exists one element I have consistently valued above all else: melody. There exists considerable progressive rock which concentrates on the technical intricacy of the composition rather than the melodic aspect. Pink Floyd, the most commercially successful progressive rock band in history, have endured because the emphasis remained consistently on melody and atmosphere. What do you have planned for your Albert Hall performances? I prefer not to reveal too much. The repertoire shall be entirely different each evening. The opening night will present a version of the Hand. Cannot. Erase. performance I have been presenting this year - but enhanced - with several guests. The second evening will offer more of a journey through my past, which targets more the supporters who have followed me for years. How did it occur that Matt Berry serves as the supporting act on the second evening? Myself and everyone aboard the tour coach are enormous admirers of [Channel 4 comedy programme] Toast of London to the extent that we quote it continuously. I considered that I should investigate Matt's music, so I obtained a copy of his Music for Insomniacs. I spoke with him regarding our appreciation of Mike Oldfield and invited him to perform at the Royal Albert Hall. I shall be extraordinarily star-struck by my opening performer. You have been remixing albums by artists such as XTC, Tears for Fears and Yes. How significantly does that influence your personal work? I do not deliberately draw from that, but, unavoidably, if you are deconstructing these classic albums they truly penetrate your mind. My previous solo album, The Raven That Refused to Sing, was undoubtedly the most traditional progressive album I have ever produced. I do not believe it was coincidental that I had been remixing King Crimson, Jethro Tull and Yes almost exclusively for the preceding year. The present album, Hand. Cannot. Erase., expanded considerably because I had been working on Tears for Fears and XTC. You are frequently characterised as progressive rock's most industrious musician. Is that how it appears? You can eliminate the word progressive. I believe I am probably amongst the most work-obsessed individuals in the music industry today, and I do not state that with any sense of pride because believe me it constitutes a curse. I believe I inherit it from my father, who also possessed an exceptionally strong work ethic. If I accomplish nothing for an entire day, I begin to experience this encroaching guilt. That explains why the remix work has proved such a blessing to me because it means I need not be creating my own music constantly. The music industry represents a difficult place to earn a living for oneself. I would not recommend it to anyone as a career now. I work daily, and I am not wealthy, but I earn a decent living. I love what I do, it constitutes a privilege, but if I were idle about it, I do not think I would be able to survive. Transience is released in the UK on 25 September. Steven Wilson performs at the Royal Albert Hall on 28 and 29 September as part of his 2015-16 European tour.

text: Food bank use in Scotland has increased to record levels, with more than 60,000 referrals over a six-month period, according to a charity. These are external links and will open in a new window The Trussell Trust stated that on average individuals required 1.7 referrals, indicating 35,000 people received assistance. Between April and September its food banks distributed 60,458 three-day emergency supplies, an increase of 17% from the previous year. Delays in receiving benefits was the most frequently cited reason for financial hardship. Approximately 28% of recipients stated this was the cause of their difficulties, the same proportion as the previous year. The percentage of referrals attributed to benefit changes fell from 18% to 16%. The proportion of those referred owing to low income rose from 18% to 21%. The trust's Scotland network manager Ewan Gurr stated he was concerned low income would become a greater problem in forthcoming months. He stated: Difficulties relating to welfare benefits are still driving the majority of individuals to our Scottish food banks but now one in five of those referred is on a low income. Within that number is a growing body of individuals in low paid employment who are simply unable to make the pay cheque stretch far enough when crisis strikes. The increasing instability of the oil, gas and steel industries has already resulted in significant numbers of individuals being made redundant and figures revealed in the past week also demonstrate that unemployment has risen in Scotland whilst decreasing in the remainder of the UK. The trust stated it also feared a repetition of the previous year when low income referrals increased sharply in December as fuel costs became an additional drain on household finances. Responding to the figures, SNP MSP Kevin Stewart described them as alarming. He added: The figures also demonstrate that UK government benefit changes and delays continue to be the most common reason for individuals seeking emergency food aid. Whilst Tory ministers have their head in the sand on the issue, the Scottish government recognises this connection and is spending almost £300m over three years to mitigate Tory social security cuts. That any government would consider further cuts to the incomes of the poorest families in our society in the face of such clear evidence of rising poverty is appalling - yet George Osborne is set to plough ahead with £12bn more social security cuts. A UK government spokesman stated: Our reforms have secured record employment, a near record number of job vacancies and a growing economy. We maintain a strong social safety net and continue to spend around £80bn on working age benefits. We know that the reasons for food bank use are complex and overlapping and it is spurious to claim that it is driven by changes to welfare. Work remains the best route out of poverty and thanks to this government's long term economic plan thousands of individuals are experiencing the dignity of a job, the security of a wage and the peace of mind that comes from supporting your family, many for the first time. In terms of food donated, the figures revealed Scotland was second only to the north west of England. When populations were compared, the statistics also indicated that a disproportionately high number of individuals were being referred to food banks in Scotland compared to other parts of the UK, the trust stated. Scottish Labour's equality spokesman Neil Findlay stated: In a country as wealthy as Scotland it is unacceptable that more than 60,000 individuals had to rely on food banks over the past six months. text: Skier Dave Ryding matched Britain's best ever alpine World Cup result when he finished second in the Kitzbuhel slalom in Austria. He was leading following the opening run but was defeated by local favourite Marcel Hirscher to secure his maiden career podium finish. It represented the finest result for slightly more than 35 years, since Konrad Bartelski finished second in a downhill in Italy in 1981. The 30-year-old had already placed sixth and seventh this season. He informed BBC Sport: The opening run was simply incredible. I knew I had skied it cleanly, but could not believe it when I crossed the finishing line. Between runs I attempted not to raise the heart rate or become stressed. I was trying to convince myself I was not the final one to go but it was difficult. It was a psychological battle with myself but I won the psychological battle. Hirscher skied so brilliantly, so finishing second almost felt like a triumph. It is extraordinary. I am simply extremely proud of what I have accomplished. The Lancashire native competes without UK Sport funding after it was removed from the alpine programme in 2010 but does receive alternative sponsorship. Ryding, who learned to ski on a dry slope at Pendle Ski Club, has been a British ski team member since 2006 and participated in the 2010 and 2014 Winter Olympics, placing 17th. He held a 0.29 seconds advantage over Italy's Stefano Gross entering the second run with Hirscher 1.02 seconds behind. However the Austrian, who claimed the race in 2013 and has secured the overall slalom title three times, produced a magnificent second run to advance from seventh to first, with Ryding finishing 0.76 seconds behind. More than 60,000 spectators were present and Ryding stated the noise was overwhelming. Kitzbuhel is like the FA Cup final in England. The downhill race is the premier event but the slalom is also enormous. The supporters are remarkable. The alpine ski World Cup was established in 1967 and, in 50 years of competition, Ryding and Bartelski are the sole British men to finish on the podium whilst Gina Hathorn (1967) and Divina Galica (1968) achieved top three finishes on the women's circuit. When Bartelski accomplished it in Val Gardena, Italy, it prompted a French commentator to declare: This is not possible, he is English! In the pre-World Cup period, Britain's Gordon Cleaver claimed the combined race on Kitzbuhel's Hahnenkamm course in 1931. Whilst the alpine team are no longer supported by UK Sport, the Great British freestyle ski and snowboard team are. Following Jenny Jones' historic slopestyle bronze in Sochi, they will obtain £4.9m for the four-year cycle leading to the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea. They have achieved numerous World Cup victories with Katie Ormerod becoming the first snowboarder to claim a World Cup big air, whilst cousin Jamie Nicholls has triumphed in slopestyle, Lesley McKenna and Rowan Cheshire in halfpipe and Zoe Gillings-Brier in snowboardcross. Skier James Woods has claimed three World Cup slopestyle events. Meanwhile in cross-country skiing, Briton Andrew Musgrave achieved his finest World Cup result, when he finished sixth in a 15km race in Sweden on Saturday.

text: An archive of sketchbooks, drawings and letters belonging to artist Lucian Freud has been acquired by the nation through the acceptance in lieu scheme. The archive contains studies for many of the artist's major works alongside a collection of 162 childhood drawings depicting family life. They were created whilst Freud was residing in Germany, before his family escaped to England in 1933 as Hitler rose to power, and preserved and dated by his mother. text: Three years ago thousands of Tunisians protested on the streets, demanding, among other things, more economic opportunity. The demonstrations resulted in the exit of the nation's previous leader, President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, and triggered the broader Arab Spring throughout North Africa and the Middle East. Nevertheless, despite President Ben Ali's removal, economic reforms in Tunisia since 2011 have stagnated owing to persistent political instability, which continued until the conclusion of last year. Still, with a moderate, transitional government of independent personalities appointed in December, and the nation's new constitution being finalised in January, there is now fresh optimism that pro-business modifications will be introduced, to allow entrepreneurship and small enterprises to prosper. The feeling of confidence has been reinforced by support from the World Bank, which last month granted Tunisia loans totalling $1.2bn (£719m) to help drive economic and political reform. The World Bank stated that this sum included $750m in support of government reforms to level the economic playing field and promote growth and job creation, and $100m to increase lending to small and medium-sized enterprises. For most Tunisian entrepreneurs, reforms to make their work easier cannot arrive quickly enough. Ramzi el Fekih, 46, states the key to helping new enterprises launch and expand in Tunisia is an improved judicial system. Mr el Fekih is chief executive of Viamobile, a mobile telephone banking and payments application. He established the enterprise in Tunisia in 2009 after returning to the nation following 25 years working overseas, including 20 years in the mobile telephone technology sector in California. The greatest difference between working here and in California is the absence of trust, states Mr el Fekih. People attempt to protect themselves, because they have been deceived before, but it becomes very restrictive. There is such control, that we cannot move, but what we require is a judicial system that punishes people who do not follow the law. Mr el Fekih states he would also like to see considerably less regulation and bureaucracy, complaining that it took him two years to get Viamobile approved by the nation's central bank. However, despite his frustrations, he states he has no regrets about returning to his homeland. I genuinely believe that there is enormous potential in Tunisia and Tunisian entrepreneurs, he states. Mr el Fekih is hoping that now, with the new constitution in place, the Tunisian state will move swiftly on reforms. His comparison is borrowed from the world of mobile technology. What politicians can do is design an easy and accessible operating system, so entrepreneurs can follow and create applications, he states. Now is the time. For fellow entrepreneur Zied Jallouli, 29, the major problem for start-ups in Tunisia is securing financial backing. Raising funds here for a significant idea is really, really difficult, states Mr Jallouli, shaking his head. He and his business partner have developed a smartphone application called Disrupt CK, which they claim can help people to purchase clothes or other consumer goods similar to those they see in a film or television programme. Mr Jallouli states you simply point your smartphone at the television, press the application button, and it will produce a list of suggested items. Whilst Mr Jallouli could not get a Tunisian bank or wealthy Tunisian investor to back him, he was ultimately able to secure investment from a Swedish expatriate. The Swede in question is Thomas Adner, a former executive for Swedish packaging giant Tetra Pak, who had been working in North Africa for eight years. Mr Adner is so impressed with Mr Jallouli's product that he has even joined the company as its chief marketing officer. There are some excellent business opportunities in Tunisia, states Mr Adner, who points out the low cost of hiring well-trained web developers and programmers. You can run quite a few miles with the cash that you have, he states. However, Mr Adner still sees numerous obstacles to doing business in Tunisia that need removing. Back home [in Sweden] it takes about 30 minutes to register a new business, and in two days all the paperwork is completed, he states. Tunisian authorities make it not only very difficult to start a company, it takes months if not longer. There is so much red tape here, for anyone who wants to start a business. The government really needs to make it easier to start a company. Laurent Gonnet, the World Bank's financial sector specialist in Tunisia, also agrees that much work needs to be done in the country to help businesses. He states the nation's commercial banks are extremely cautious and risk averse, particularly when it comes to technology companies. He adds that Tunisia is also one of the last countries that lack a private credit rating system, making it even harder for entrepreneurs to convince banks to lend them money to back a business idea. Fortunately, the nation's politicians now seem committed to pro-business reform, no doubt encouraged by the World Bank, and a challenging economic backdrop, with unemployment at 16%. The hope is that this commitment will not be curtailed by general elections due at the end of this year. We are reviewing the investment code in order to reduce red tape, states Dhamir Mannai, an assembly member from the CPR party of current President Moncef Marzouki. Meanwhile, Moncef Cheikhrouhou, a member of the opposition Democratic Alliance, and the deputy chairman of the parliament's finance, planning and development committee, states that entrepreneurship is most needed to create wealth. We are treating this as an urgent matter, and are looking for input from entrepreneurs as well, he states.

These are external links and will open in a new window Baroness Hilary Armstrong informed the BBC that Mr Corbyn was the greatest rebel ever whilst serving as a backbencher, though Mr Blair was hesitant to discipline him. She stated the then prime minister believed that Labour was a broad church. Amidst allegations Mr Corbyn's opponents might be forced out, Baroness Armstrong declared he must demonstrate he is tolerant. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's The Westminster Hour, Baroness Armstrong expressed satisfaction that Labour party chairman Ian Lavery had stated de-selection was not the appropriate path forward. However, she continued: I know MPs where essentially there exists a process of harassment, where at every meeting they face criticism, they encounter challenges, they receive instruction that they do not represent the people in the room. Baroness Armstrong continued: Jeremy has the opportunity over the summer and at party conference to make it absolutely clear that he will not lead a narrow sectarian faction, he will lead a broad church that is tolerant. Mr Corbyn voted against his own government more than 500 times and Baroness Armstrong stated at the time there was upset amongst party members in his Islington North constituency. text: Formula 1 is the most technologically advanced sport on the planet, and the latest radical rule changes have imposed a whole new set of challenges on the teams. Special Report: The Technology of Business Hey you, get on to my cloud Domain shift sends cyber world dotty How to cash in with off-the-peg apps Taj Mahal comes to your living room Sochi 2014: Hi-tech Winter Games The BBC visited the Lotus F1 Team at Enstone, Oxfordshire, to observe how it is preparing for the 2014 racing season, scheduled to commence in Melbourne, Australia, on 16 March. With a budget less than half that of the leading F1 teams and other challenges to address, Lotus requires all the assistance technology can provide. It is managing the recent departure of its team principal, Eric Boullier, to McLaren and a new chief executive attempting to address last year's £140m deficit in the company's finances that resulted in the departure of star driver Kimi Raikkonen to Ferrari. As every tenth of a second matters in F1 racing, the manner in which technology is optimised can ultimately create tens of millions of pounds' difference to a team's annual revenue, states chief executive Matthew Carter, brought in by owners Genii Capital to attempt to stabilise the business. We are working on half the budget of some of the major teams, so we must consider different methods of making that function and being competitive, he states. That requires making superior use of technology in every aspect of the business. The recent rule modifications - involving a smaller turbo-charged engine with a more powerful electric battery and energy recovery system, as well as a narrower front wing and lower chassis to reduce downforce - have required thousands of new drawings, components and tests. They're the most significant rule changes I've witnessed in 20 years of working in the sport, states Nick Chester, chief technical director for Lotus F1 Team. We had to begin developing this car two and a half years ago. To assist in improving efficiency, the team has abandoned its piecemeal approach to software - different packages performing different tasks - and entered into a £4m, four-year contract to utilise Microsoft's Dynamics enterprise resource planning (ERP) software across the entire organisation, states Mr Chester. The nature of the Microsoft partnership - whilst not exclusive to Lotus - permits the team to customise the software to suit its requirements and gain access to the technology giant's research and development team in Redmond, Washington, he states. The ERP assists in planning and managing the highly complex process by which computer-aided designs, informed by computational fluid dynamics, eventually become wind-tunnel-refined carbon-fibre speed machines racing round a circuit. It assisted us in coping with an increase from 12,000 to 14,000 drawings that the new car required, he states. It also enables us to operate parallel design programmes and allocate resources accordingly. During a season, a car might receive 200 to 250 aerodynamic and mechanical upgrades, he states, requiring an additional 6,000 drawings, all of which need to be planned for, resourced and delivered to the circuits on schedule. Development costs have been reduced by the introduction of laser 3D printing, which can transform designs into prototype components far more quickly and cheaply than previously. Superior technology also assists in reducing time wasted on basic administration by automating common processes, according to IT director Michael Taylor. If you can liberate an aerodynamicist's time by just one minute a day, over the course of the year that represents a significant amount of time. And if you can extend the design lifecycle, in theory, you create a superior design, he states. And when a component fails, the team needs to identify precisely what caused the problem and at what stage the weakness occurred, from the moment the purchase order for the materials was placed right up to the second it broke. We require a single source of truth, states Mr Taylor. Data represents a huge part of the sport - the car's on-board computer and the many sensors that wirelessly communicate with the team will generate up to 50 gigabytes of data per race, all of which requires immediate analysis. Whilst the car is racing round the track at up to 200mph in Abu Dhabi, for example, the team back in Enstone is monitoring the real-time data flow remotely using VMware's virtual desktop technology. All this commercially sensitive data is stored in two concrete bunkers at the Oxfordshire site - external cloud storage services are not yet trusted sufficiently, although Mr Taylor does envisage such a move in the future. Top-secret files are shared securely between partners, such as engine provider Renault, using EMC's Syncplicity software. It's like a commercial version of Dropbox, he states. IT enables everything within this business. And the ultimate goal of our IT strategy is to provide us with a competitive edge, states Mr Taylor. In-season testing on track, in wind tunnels and simulators has been restricted by the sport's governing body, the FIA, in an attempt to reduce costs and allow the smaller teams to survive. Whilst these restrictions were absolutely essential, according to chief executive Matthew Carter, it places far greater emphasis on IT to fill the gap. The lack of testing in F1 means we must do an enormous amount of work back here, ensuring there's a really good correlation between the information we obtain from the simulator and wind-tunnel testing and what happens on the track, so that we can continue punching above our weight, he states. If you cease investing in technology and stand still, others overtake you very rapidly in this sport.

When the car is racing at 320 kilometers per hour in Abu Dhabi, for example, the team at Enstone can monitor the real-time data stream remotely with the help of VMware virtual desktops. Confidential documents are transferred between partners such as engine manufacturer Renault with EMC's synchronization service. During the season, the governing FIA has restricted track testing, wind tunnels, and simulators, to reduce costs and help smaller teams to survive. Such restrictions were essential, says Matthew Carter, FIA chief executive, but they have also increased the importance of information technology. “It’s a bit like a commercial version of Dropbox,” he says. “The main aim of our IT strategy is to give us an advantage,” said Taylor. “If you stop developing technology, you're done for. Other teams will overtake you.” “We have to do an enormous amount of work here in order to get a very close correlation between what we do in the simulator and in the wind tunnel and what we do on the track,” he said.

text: A financial scam was committed once every 15 seconds in the first half of the year, prompting a new campaign to highlight the risks. These are external links and will open in a new window More than one million instances of card, cheque, telephone or online fraud were recorded from January to June, Financial Fraud Action (FFA) stated. That represented a 53% increase on the same period last year. The FFA, which receives funding from banks and payment card companies, is promoting advice to help prevent fraud. Losses are frequently refunded by banks, but not in every instance. Many individuals are too embarrassed to acknowledge they have been caught out. The Take Five campaign, supported by police, the banking industry and consumer groups, is designed to ensure busy lives do not make people easy targets. We are asking people to take five - to take that moment - to pause and think before they respond to any financial requests and share any personal or financial details, stated Katy Worobec, director of FFA. Home Office Security Minister Ben Wallace, said: The impact of financial fraud can be devastating on victims, with fraudsters using increasingly cunning and convincing tactics. They prey on people who are trying to get on with their lives but in a moment where they are busy or distracted become vulnerable. At the same time, the government is working closely with law enforcement and the banking sector through the Joint Fraud Taskforce to take action to stop the organised criminals behind financial fraud. Banks maintain they are preventing £7 of every £10 in potential fraud losses, but millions of pounds are still being lost to fraudsters. Last year, financial fraud losses reached £755m - a 26% increase on the previous year. You can probably add to that a significant sum that goes unreported every year. Email deception, as well as telephone and text-based scams, are now common tools in the modern-day bank robber's trade - reflected in official crime figures which now include fraud data. Fraud and cyber crime account for nearly half of all offences, according to the British Crime Survey. Police experts state that consumers are aware of the dangers of giving out personal details, but can still be caught out. A survey by FFA suggested that this was most commonly because victims felt the caller was genuine, with nearly four in 10 being caught out as they felt pressurised, with a similar proportion letting their guard down when they were busy. How to avoid falling victim to a scam A separate survey commissioned by a comparison website suggested that more than four in 10 people have needed to cancel credit or debit cards after falling victim to fraud in the last year. Jody Baker, head of money at comparethemarket.com, said: Most of the transactions we make now are digital and our research suggests that over a quarter of people carry as little as £10 in cash. With so many of us shopping and banking on the internet, combined with a rise in contactless payments, it is more important than ever to be vigilant when managing your money. More: The Met Police Little Book of Big Scams

text: Families of football fans who died in the Hillsborough disaster are pursuing High Court misconduct action against the South Yorkshire and West Midlands police forces, lawyers have said. The inquests jury determined victims were unlawfully killed and there were police failings. Families have submitted claims of misfeasance in public office, stated Saunders Law Solicitors. Legal proceedings commenced in 2015 but were suspended awaiting the conclusions. Both forces have been approached for comment. Following a 27-year campaign by victims' families, the inquests jury determined match commander Ch Supt David Duckenfield was responsible for manslaughter by gross negligence owing to a breach of his duty of care. Police mistakes contributed to a dangerous situation at the FA Cup semi-final at which 96 supporters died, jurors determined on Tuesday. Five myths rejected by the jury Hillsborough: What's next? Police chief's role in the disaster The 96 who died Misfeasance in public office is a civil proceeding against the holder of a public office, alleging that the office-holder has misused or abused his or her authority. The proceeding relates to the events on 15 April 1989 and the aftermath. Families are pursuing the claim in an effort to secure accountability, solicitors stated. South Yorkshire Police was responsible for planning and operational duties on the day of the disaster. West Midlands Police was brought in to conduct the original investigation into the conduct of officers. A statement on behalf of Saunders Legal team stated there was evidence of the systematic cover-up intended to transfer the blame for what happened from South Yorkshire Police to the innocent, by spreading lies, doctoring evidence, pressurising witnesses and suppressing the truth. The evidence points to abuse on an industrial scale by both South Yorkshire and West Midlands Police, beyond any one bad apple analysis, it added. It stated the evidence suggested institutional misfeasance by the two forces against supporters. South Yorkshire Police's current chief constable David Crompton was suspended on Wednesday because of the approach the force adopted to the inquest. In 2012, Mr Crompton acknowledged grave errors were made during the Hillsborough disaster and has apologised profoundly. On Tuesday after the inquests conclusions were delivered, he acknowledged the policing of the match was catastrophically wrong and unequivocally accepted the findings. Hillsborough families have expressed anger after retired South Yorkshire police officers were told to be proud of their work, despite the inquests' conclusions. A message on a website for the force's retired officers stated they had served dedicated and courageous careers. Families of those who died have called for criminal prosecutions to follow the hearings. The CPS stated it would formally consider whether any criminal charges should be brought against any individual or corporate body based upon all the available evidence. Two ongoing investigations into the disaster and its aftermath could conclude by the end of this year. A police inquiry, Operation Resolve, is examining the lead-up to the crush on the day of the match, whilst a separate inquiry by the IPCC is investigating allegations of a cover-up.

text: The botched Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scheme was set up to encourage uptake of eco-friendly heat systems over the use of fossil fuels. These are external links and will open in a new window However its excessively generous provision of fuel subsidies meant it could cost taxpayers an additional £490m. The fallout has now caused the collapse of the power-sharing Northern Ireland Executive. BBC News NI examines those who have found themselves in the spotlight over the scandal. Northern Ireland's former first minister, Arlene Foster, led the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Investment (Deti) when the RHI scheme was designed. Essential controls to limit the scheme's cost were not introduced, something she has since described as her deepest political regret. However the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader fiercely contested claims by Jonathan Bell - her party colleague and successor as enterprise minister - that she ordered him to keep the scheme open. Following his allegations, Mrs Foster faced calls to step aside to allow a judge-led public inquiry into the scheme. Mrs Foster restated in January that she would not be standing down over the issue, adding that some calls for her to do so were misogynistic. In the end, her time as first minister was brought to an abrupt end when the Deputy First Minister, Martin McGuinness, resigned, forcing an election. Jonathan Bell was the minister at Deti during the period that the RHI scheme did the most damage to the public purse. A total of £485m was committed when applications suddenly flooded the department in October and November 2015. However in an explosive interview with the BBC's Stephen Nolan earlier this month, Mr Bell said he tried to close it down before that point, only to be thwarted by DUP advisers. He also accused the advisers of attempting to alter documents without my knowledge, without my consent. The DUP MLA has called for a public inquiry into the scandal, and has since been suspended by his party. Although he shies away from the public eye, Timothy Johnston (above left, with former DUP leader Peter Robinson) has long been regarded as perhaps the most powerful official behind the scenes at the DUP. In the days when the party opposed David Trimble's Ulster Unionists, Mr Johnston was its communications director, working particularly closely with Peter Robinson. He was involved in the negotiations around the St Andrews Agreement that led to the restoration of devolution in 2007, and has been an adviser at Stormont Castle for Ian Paisley, Peter Robinson and now Arlene Foster. The Paisley family publicly blamed Mr Johnston for compiling a critical survey about Dr Paisley's leadership before the party founder resigned, a claim he said was regrettable and inaccurate. He is one of two DUP advisers that Jonathan Bell has claimed would not allow the RHI scheme to close in early-autumn 2015, but he has rejected that allegation. As an adviser to Arlene Foster, he is paid the maximum salary allowed for a special adviser - £91,809 A son of a farmer from Beragh in County Tyrone, Dr Andrew Crawford is a former employee of the Ulster Farmers' Union. He was an assistant to the former DUP MEP Jim Allister before the North Antrim politician quit to form the Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV). Dr Crawford was an adviser to Arlene Foster when she was enterprise minister during the time the RHI scheme was created, and followed her to the Department of Finance and Personnel last year. Jonathan Bell accused him of preventing the closure of the scheme, but Dr Crawford has denied that claim. He was also named by senior civil servant Andrew McCormick, in a PAC hearing, as the adviser who exerted influence to keep the scheme open - although Dr McCormick said he had no evidence for his claim. These days, he advises another DUP minister, Michelle McIlveen in the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs. Dr Crawford's poultry-farmer brother is a claimant of the RHI scheme. A qualified barrister, Richard Bullick is one of the DUP's most important policy advisers and has been deeply involved in various political negotiations down through the years. Last year, he gave evidence to a Stormont committee about contacts between ministers and bidders involved in the controversial Nama property deal. In the more distant past, he was a junior barrister to Jim Allister and was involved in the DUP's decision to lure Mr Allister back from the legal world to replace Ian Paisley as an MEP. However the DUP's leadership came to regret that move later, when Mr Allister rejected its deal with Sinn Féin and set up his own party, the TUV. Mr Bullick now works as an adviser to Arlene Foster in the Executive Office, and is paid the maximum allowed for a special adviser - £91,809 Jonathan Bell said Mr Bullick was present for his hostile meeting with the first minister, but the adviser has said he was not there. One of the more recognisable of the DUP's advisers over the years, Stephen Brimstone is no stranger to controversy. He was an aide to the former social development minister Nelson McCausland, during which time he became entangled in the Red Sky housing maintenance scandal, and his treatment of then DUP councillor Jenny Palmer over that affair led to her whistleblowing on a BBC Spotlight programme. Mr Brimstone was later promoted to advise the first minister but resigned from his role in November. According to Jonathan Bell, Mr Brimstone was one of three advisers who witnessed a tense and angry exchange between him and Arlene Foster over the proposed closure of the scheme in early 2016, but he, like Mr Bullick, said that was not the case. He has confirmed that he is a claimant on the RHI scheme, but Arlene Foster has said his link to it was not a factor in his decision to quit his £91,809-a-year job. His brother, Aaron, is also a beneficiary of the green energy initiative, the Irish News reported in December. Timothy Cairns was Jonathan Bell's adviser at Deti, and offered advice to the minister about the controversial RHI scheme. However he has said that the ultimate decisions about it were for the minister to make. Mr Bell said his adviser told him that other DUP advisers were preventing the closure of the scheme. Timothy Cairns previously worked as an aide to Peter Robinson when he was first minister, but is no longer employed as a DUP adviser. As the permanent secretary at the Department for the Economy, formerly Deti, Dr Andrew McCormick is the man who has to clear up much of the mess of the RHI scheme. He arrived at the department in 2014, long after the scheme was conceived, and drew Jonathan Bell's attention to major concerns over its operation in the summer of 2015. In an email in January 2016, Dr McCormick said there was some initial reluctance to limit the generous tariff offered by the scheme shortly before a crucial spike in applications that led to a spending commitment of almost half-a-billion pounds. And appearing before Stormont's Public Accounts Committee in November, he said a whistleblower flagged concerns with the scheme two years before its closure, but she was not believed by officials. A former permanent secretary at Deti, David Sterling has denied attempting to duck responsibility for his role in the RHI scheme's set-up. I'm not seeking to pass the buck, he told Stormont's Public Accounts Committee. I accept responsibility for failures which occurred during my time. However he told the committee's inquiry on the RHI fiasco that he had no satisfactory answer for why a planned review of the initiative in January 2014 did not happen. Mr Sterling moved to the top civil service post in the Department of Finance and Personnel in July 2014. Jonathan Bell claimed that Chris Stewart, his deputy permanent secretary at Deti, sought a one-to-one meeting to blow the whistle on an attempt by DUP advisers to remove references to Arlene Foster from official documents about the RHI scheme. The former minister said Mr Stewart was willing to back his claims in a public inquiry, but three days later the civil servant disputed Mr Bell's version of events. He said he did not seek a meeting as a whistleblower. He did acknowledge that a DUP adviser changed wording of a Deti document, but added that Mr Bell later advised that he had dealt with the matter to his satisfaction. Up until June 2016, John Robinson was the DUP's director of communications, a role he relinquished when he was appointed as a special adviser to the Department for the Economy. Jonathan Bell named Mr Robinson on the Assembly floor as one of two DUP advisers - the other was Timothy Johnston - with extensive interests in the poultry industry. At the time, Mr Robinson said his family farm has chicken houses which are not part of the RHI scheme but did not mention his in-laws had benefitted from the green energy subsidy. The party described Mr Bell's comments as nothing short of mud-slinging. When the Press Association revealed his father-in-law's involvement in the scheme, Mr Robinson issued a statement explaining that, before he got married, his father-in-law purchased two 36kw boilers for his poultry business in May 2015 and applied to the scheme on 3rd August 2015. He said he did not discuss RHI with his father-in-law and that neither he, nor his wife, had any role or benefit in his in-laws' farming business.

text: Developing post-Brexit trade with the Gulf region will be the focus of a two-day trip to Bahrain by Theresa May. She shall become the first British prime minister and female politician to attend the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council. Mrs May stated some would contend the United Kingdom should not seek to strengthen relations with the states owing to their contentious human rights records. However, we do not uphold our values and human rights by turning our back on this matter, she maintained. The prime minister shall attend a dinner with the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman on Tuesday evening, before addressing the plenary session on Wednesday morning. She shall announce a space technology partnership with Abu Dhabi and a new multiple five-year visa entry scheme for British firms conducting business in Saudi Arabia. There is so much we can accomplish together - whether it is assisting one another to prevent terrorist attacks, Gulf investment regenerating cities across Britain or British businesses helping Gulf countries to achieve their long-term vision of reform, Mrs May stated. Therefore I hope my visit will herald the beginning of a new chapter in relations between the United Kingdom and the Gulf. During a series of bilateral meetings, Downing Street stated it anticipated the situations in Syria and Yemen and relations with Iran to be discussed. Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson stated on Sunday he had repeatedly expressed concerns to his Saudi Arabian counterpart regarding its involvement in the Yemeni civil war amid allegations that civilians had been targeted during bombing campaigns against Houthi rebels fighting the government. However he stated he did not believe a threshold has been crossed requiring the suspension of British arms sales to Saudi Arabia. Mrs May shall meet young people in Bahrain to discuss progress on political and social reforms since the widespread unrest in the Gulf nation in 2011, which prompted a much-criticised crackdown by the authorities. Undoubtedly there will be some people in Britain who say we shouldn't seek stronger trade and security ties with these countries because of their record on human rights, she stated. [However] we achieve far more by stepping up, engaging with these countries and working with them to encourage and support their plans for reform. That is how Britain can be a force for good in the world as well as helping to keep our people safe and create new opportunities for business. The government states it has identified £30bn of high-value opportunities for British businesses across 15 different sectors in the region over the next five years.

The hearings were postponed at a preliminary stage last November amid uncertainty over the attorney general's authority to authorise them. At the time the coroner, appointed chief legal adviser to the Stormont Executive in 2010, cited potential national security concerns. The dispute focused on whether the cases should instead have been examined and directed by the advocate general for Northern Ireland. The coroner's decision sparked outrage amongst relatives of those whose deaths were to be examined. Lawyers for several of the families launched legal challenges, alleging the decision was unlawful and procedurally unfair. The deaths that were due to be examined include 11-year-old Francis Rowntree, who was struck by a rubber bullet fired by a soldier in west Belfast in 1972. Another case concerns Gerard Slane, a 27-year-old father of three shot dead by the Ulster Defence Association at his home in the city in 1988. His killing prompted claims of collusion between loyalist paramilitaries and the security forces. Proceedings were also initiated on behalf of relatives of Gerard Casey, murdered by the Ulster Freedom Fighters in Rasharkin, County Antrim in 1989; Danny Doherty and William Fleming, shot dead by the SAS in Londonderry in 1984; and Francis Bradley, killed by the SAS near Castledawson, County Londonderry in 1986. A full hearing of the families' judicial review challenge was scheduled to take place next week. On Monday relatives of the victims appeared in court in Belfast, where the High Court ruled that Mr. Leckey had exceeded his powers. The decision of the coroner caused anger among the relatives of those whose deaths were to be investigated. At the time the coroner, who was appointed in 2010 to the position of chief legal adviser to the Stormont Executive, cited national security concerns. Among these deaths were those of eleven-year-old Francis Rowntree, who was struck by a rubber bullet fired by a soldier in West Belfast in 1972. Another case involved the murder in his home of Gerard Slane, a father of three, by the Ulster Defence Association in the city in 1988. Lawyers for some of them pleaded the case in court and declared the decision unlawful and arbitrary. They also included relatives of Gerard Casey, killed by the Ulster Freedom Fighters in Rasharkin, County Antrim, in 1989, of Danny Doherty and William Fleming, killed by the Special Air Service in Derry in 1984, and of Francis Bradley, killed by the Special Air Service near Castledawson, County Londonderry in 1986. Outside the court, Mr. Paul Pierce, who represented Mrs. Slane, said: “We welcome the coroner’s decision to lift the suspension on these inquests. We need answers.” The full hearing of the families’ judicial review is scheduled for next week.

text: There is a new class of planet out there that astronomers are calling the mega-Earth. It is an object with a solid surface like our own world but much, much larger. The requirement for the new designation follows the discovery of a planet which possesses a mass some 17 times that of Earth. Known as Kepler-10c, it orbits a star approximately 560 light-years away. Scientists described its characteristics at an American Astronomical Society meeting in Boston. They acknowledge it is something of a head-scratcher. Theorists had always believed that any planet that large would attract so much hydrogen onto itself that it would appear more like a Neptune or a Jupiter. The proper way to call it is something larger than a 'super-Earth', so how about 'mega-Earth', Prof Dimitar Sasselov, of the Harvard-Smithsonian Centre for Astrophysics (CfA), told reporters. He also used the phrase, the Godzilla of Earths!. Kepler-10c, as the name suggests, was detected by the US space agency's Kepler telescope. This finds new worlds by looking for the tiny dip in light as they pass in front of their parent stars. The technique provides a diameter - in this case, 29,000km, or just over two times the width of Earth - but not a mass. For that, astronomers observed 10c with the Harps-North instrument on the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo in the Canary Islands. It extracts a mass measurement by examining the gravitational interaction between the planet and its host star. Combined with the diameter, the mass figure showed that Kepler-10c cannot be a gaseous world but must comprise very dense material. It's 17 - in fact, it's more than 17 - Earth masses, and that brings the density to 7.5 grammes per cubic centimetre, which is a lot more than what we know of rock here on Earth (5.5g/cm3), said Prof Sasselov. But remember, this is a very massive planet, which means those same minerals are highly compressed. So, what you see in the density is mostly due to compression rather than different composition. The composition comes out as being a combination of rocks and some volatiles, probably 5-15% at most of water. The discovery adds to our understanding of the mix of planet types we now know are out there, and tells us something new about when rocky worlds might transition to gaseous planets in their formative years. Interestingly, the age of the host star is about 11 billion years old, which is early in the evolution of the Universe when generations of exploding stars have not had long to make the heavy elements needed to construct rocky planets. So, Kepler-10c's properties suggest rocky planets may have formed earlier in cosmic history than many thought possible, and that very old star systems should not be ignored in the search for life beyond Earth. It is [on] solid planets that is the place, as far as we know - and we know very little about the origins of life - where we think the chemistry is capable of building those molecules that lead to the emergence of life from geochemistry, says Prof Sasselov. text: Terror attacks can be difficult for adults to understand - so how should we talk to children about terrorism? These are external links and will open in a new window Last year an NSPCC report disclosed that children are becoming progressively anxious about global issues. Many of those who contacted Childline informed counsellors they were worried about the EU referendum, the US presidential election and conflicts in the Middle East. Is it feasible to discuss distressing news stories with children without increasing their concerns? Psychologist Emma Kenny and Nicky Cox, the editor of children's newspaper First News, discussed the matter on BBC Radio Scotland. Even if children are protected from distressing news stories at home, they are likely to hear about it from friends in the playground or on social media. In fact, parents who believe they are protecting their offspring may be doing them a disservice, according to Nicky Cox. The editor stated: If you think as a parent you've done a really good job in protecting your child, you're doing them a disservice because they're going to go into school, they're going to be discussing it in the playground, in the lunch hall, and they're going to be receiving information second, third and fourth hand. It's so crucial that parents do not think that they are in control of how their children access information because they are not. They need to be certain that they ensure that children receive accurate information and they are empowered to know the truth when they are speaking to their friends. As editor-in-chief of First News, Nicky Cox said her team of reporters are careful to present the facts to their readership. She said it was vital children are taught how to identify reliable news sources over so-called fake news. We tell the truth, she added. I think there's absolutely no reason not to tell them the truth because they are going to hear all sorts of misinformation if they're on the internet or they're just talking at school. There is so much fake news out there, there is so much misinformation out there and it is crucial that they are educated to recognise where to go to get proper information. I think children are more savvy than most adults give them credit for. Psychologist Emma Kenny said very young children are likely to be put at ease with reassurance from their parents. But older children may not tell their parents they have heard about a distressing news story or seen graphic images on social media. Ms Kenny said it was vital that parents initiate an open conversation. Ask them if they've heard the news and allow them to have that conversation, she said. That's how they can start to ask you the questions that really most people want to ask each other. Ms Kenny told BBC Radio Scotland that her eldest son told her he didn't really want to return to London, following the Westminster attack. I said to him, we're going to London in April because the reality is you're more likely to die by falling out of bed than in a terrorist attack, she said. She told him that the few bad or sick people were in the minority and the UK is full of good people. When you look at what happened yesterday, it was full of people running towards that attack to help, not people running away to save themselves, she added. She advised parents to use their children's experiences as props for their conversation, then use statistical analysis to give them some reassurance. Ask your child, in all the years you've been here, how many times has that occurred for you, how many times have you been involved in it?

text: London Underground office staff have voted for industrial action in a row over ticket office closures. Approximately 68% of Transport Salaried Staffs' Association members supported strike action on a 44% participation rate. The union has stated its members have endured unprecedented levels of harassment following ticket office closures. A TSSA survey revealed most personnel felt less secure after relocating from offices onto station platforms. Tom Edwards, BBC London Transport Correspondent The ticket office closures represented one of the most significant transformations on the underground for decades. With the emergence of automated payment systems including the Oyster card and contactless technology, the concept was to move personnel from behind glass barriers onto the ticket barrier areas. However, the trade unions have consistently resisted this and maintain the redeployment has resulted in increased solitary working and personnel deficits. The TSSA, which represents station personnel, states it will determine, likely tomorrow, what industrial measures it will implement in the disagreement. Strike action is not being excluded, though it might be an overtime prohibition. Additional forms of industrial measures received support by nine to one. The union stated personnel were being confronted by exasperated passengers when ticket machines malfunction. TSSA general secretary Manuel Cortes stated the ballot concerned our members being willing to participate in strike action to inform the world that the Underground they are utilising is not suitable for safe operation. Our customer service representatives are predominantly attempting to alert the public that the Underground they use is not secure. We no longer possess sufficient personnel, he stated. Steve Griffiths, London Underground's chief operating officer, stated: We encourage the TSSA leadership to collaborate with us constructively on the matters they have highlighted rather than threaten to disrupt our passengers with strikes. The ticket offices were shut as part of the Fit for the Future initiative implemented by former London mayor Boris Johnson. His successor Sadiq Khan has commissioned a review of the scheme. Underground drivers are to conduct 24-hour strikes on 6 and 7 December, coinciding with a walkout by Southern Rail guards.

text: The new Harry Potter play in London has removed the use of live owls from the production. The decision follows an incident during Tuesday's opening performance when an owl escaped into the auditorium. The bird had failed to return to its handler after completing a brief flight during a scene. Previews of the two-part production, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, commenced this week. At Thursday's performance of part two, a notice at the Palace Theatre informed the audience that there were no real birds in the production. A statement released on behalf of the producers said: The production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is currently in its preview phase, with the process designed to allow the creative team time to rehearse changes or explore specific scenes further before the play's official opening. As part of this process earlier this week the decision was taken not to feature live owls in any aspect of the production moving forward. The owls that were associated with the production were expertly cared for by a team of certified trainers and an on-site specialist veterinary surgeon (Steve Smith, MRCVS) who ensured the owls' welfare and enrichment needs were safeguarded at all times. This was of utmost importance to the production. Fan excitement for JK Rowling Animal charity Peta (People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals) welcomed the announcement. Peta commends the production team for coming to its senses and recognising that treating owls like props goes against every message of respect and kindness that JK Rowling's wonderful books taught us, director Mimi Bekhechi said. Harry Potter can now join the ranks of innovative stage productions like War Horse, The Lion King and Running Wild which prove that animals need not be exploited for the theatre - and that the possibilities of prop design are limited only by our own creativity. Shortly before the second half of Thursday's performance began, JK Rowling was spotted in a box stage right, causing screams of excitement from the audience with hundreds craning their necks attempting to catch a glimpse of her. The production does not have its official opening until 30 July. Based on an original story by Rowling, writer Jack Thorne and director John Tiffany, the production is set 19 years after the events of the seventh and final book in the series, the Deathly Hallows. It portrays a grown-up Harry (Jamie Parker) as an employee at the Ministry of Magic, whilst his youngest son Albus (Sam Clemmett) has to deal with the heavy burden of the Potter family legacy. The production runs in the West End to May 2017.

A traumatic accident such as the one Mr Mureta endured is often challenging to discuss, but he is content to share details. It becomes even more strange when you realize that the person who says this, Chad Mureta, is the prototype of the tech millionaire. In many respects, however, he is not your typical technology entrepreneur. His applications, which include Emoji, an application that helps users spice up their messages with an enlarged variety of funny images, and a security application called Fingerprint Scanner Pro, have been downloaded more than 50 million times, and his company App Empire has a turnover of between 3 and 5 million pounds per year. In the year 2009, he was returning from a game of basket-ball. He was not fortunate in circumstances. It took a near-death experience to guide him on the right path. As he drove along the highway, a deer came onto the road in front of him. He had sold things on eBay, sold time-shares, and ran a nightclub. He was a real estate agent at that time, very unhappy and not knowing what he wanted to do with his life. He swerved to avoid him. His car hit the barrier of the aqueduct. It overturned end over end, rolling four times, and finally came to a stop. In front of him were six painful months in the hospital, and another six months in a rehabilitation center, with a hundred thousand dollar bill at the end of it all. It is a well-known fact that the United States demands payment from patients for medical care. The doctor almost amputated Mr. Mureta's left arm. I was in such a desperate situation, he says. I suffered such terrible pain, I didn’t think I could go on. Extremely depressed, unable to sleep, on enormous quantities of drugs—and actually quite suicidal. One of the few objects that survived the collision was his smart phone. It was brand new the day of the accident, but despite its damage, it somehow survived a little unused, and still had 12% of its battery. What happened next is the sort of thing that even the most daring screenwriters in Hollywood would find it hard to believe, and yet Mr. Mureta insists that it happened. He was still being given powerful medication, and his thoughts were occupied with something else. But then a friend visiting him presented him with an article about a new telephone application. As he lay on his hospital bed, he saw the doctors casually flicking through the phone book, and he thought how useful it would be to have some means of enhancing security on the phone. “I simply experienced that 'eureka' moment when I declared: "God, I'm going to pursue this," says Mr. Mureta. I was there, connected to all these injections, morphine, and I looked around, and I finally saw the whole picture. This happened during the early years of application development, when a handful of programmers from lofts transformed the world. I’ll never forget that feeling—it’s beyond words. That was the moment when it was so clear to me: here’s your solution and you’re stupid to think about anything else. I considered a different future. As stated, this was easier said than done. At the time, the resources for developing applications were not so widely available as they are now, and Mr Mureta had no experience in coding. But he had one valuable asset, and it was time. I remained there examining all these applications, he tells us. I was asking myself, “Why does the customer prefer this application?” Moreover, one of the physicians had a relative in India, who told Mr. Mureta that he had just started a business of development of mobile applications. He took the risk and borrowed $ 1,800 from his stepfather, overcoming the language and technical obstacles and launching his first product. That was the winning combination to make it work. Nevertheless, it was irrelevant. Two months later Fingerprint Security Pro was in the app store.
