text: If this secret left-wing plan to take over the Labour Party comes to pass, our electoral existence is in peril. These are external links and will open in a new window. Tom Watson did not mince his words when he spoke to me on Monday morning. However, was he genuinely more concerned about his party's future - or his union's future, the now-inappropriately named Unite? Both are, indeed, presently inextricably linked. Mr Watson had been personally close to the union's general secretary Len McCluskey - they are former flatmates. However, relations deteriorated when Labour's deputy leader failed to convince Mr McCluskey to persuade Jeremy Corbyn to agree a date when he would stand down as party leader last summer, after eight out of 10 of his MPs declared no confidence in him. Therefore, there is now political and personal animosity. Mr McCluskey is up for re-election at the end of next month and those close to Mr Watson see an opportunity to weaken both him and the current party leader. Mr McCluskey's main opponent is the West Midlands organiser Gerard Coyne, who is politically to his right. Mr Watson is backing the challenger partly because Unite, under its current leadership, has generously funded Mr Corbyn's two leadership campaigns - and a change at the top might put a block on cheques to any aspiring left-wing replacement. Mr Coyne's initial pitch was that the union was too focused on Westminster politics under Mr McCluskey and not enough on members' interests. However, some of Mr Corbyn's critics at Westminster argued that the Coyne campaign had had too subtle a message to gain prominent media coverage - and the contest should be recast as a proxy battle for Labour's future. Therefore, this weekend Mr Watson was gifted strong ammunition to launch a campaign of shock and awe to get party and union members to sit up and take notice. Jon Lansman established Momentum to maintain the spirit of the first Corbyn leadership campaign, harnessing the energies of those who came into Labour to change both the party and the country. However, the recording of his remarks to a local group in Richmond, obtained by the Observer, suggested that he was rather more interested in changing Labour than changing the government - he talked of how an early election would disrupt our plans but what we need to do next is a number of things to change the nature of the Labour Party. Even better for Mr Watson was the suggestion that the link forged between the current Unite general secretary and Momentum was going to become stronger and tighter. Mr Lansman opined that assuming Len McCluskey wins the general secretaryship...Unite will affiliate to Momentum and will fully participate in Momentum. Mr Watson has suggested that Mr McCluskey would rather fund a left-wing faction inside Labour than the party itself. He believes this revelation might encourage more moderate members of Unite to turn out and vote to change their general secretary. The acting Unite leader Gail Cartmail told me that there were no plans to affiliate to Momentum and Mr Watson had not checked his story before going public. However, with or without union funding, just what is the hard-left plot that Mr Watson believes will destroy Labour? First, Momentum wants to see Labour's leadership rules changed. Currently a candidate for the leadership requires the support of 15% of MPs and MEPs before the wider, left-wing membership gets a chance to vote for them. Mr Corbyn only succeeded in getting on to the ballot in 2015 because some of those to his right 'lent' support to broaden the debate. Those MPs who regarded their actions subsequently as a huge mistake will not make the same one twice. Mr Lansman is heard emphasising how crucial it is that the 15% threshold is reduced should Mr Corbyn stand down. At this September's Labour conference, it is almost certain delegates will be given the option to reduce that threshold from 15% to only 5% - a much smaller hurdle for a left-wing candidate to overcome. Mr Lansman is recorded saying we really need to win that vote and we have to work to get delegates to that conference. However, internal groups such as Labour First and Progress - put simply, Brownites and Blairites and those who were once called modernisers - are working together in many local constituencies to select delegates sympathetic to them. Like Mr Watson, their view is that if Mr Corbyn was simply replaced by someone with similar politics, Labour would have missed an opportunity to appeal to a wider electorate who believe the party is now too left wing. The only way to stop the changes is to get more anti-Corbyn delegates to Labour's conference this autumn than those who support the leadership. Therefore, Mr Watson's apocalyptic warnings are, in part, aimed to sound a klaxon that the longer-standing but demoralised moderate party members will hear. Equally, perhaps the reason that Mr Lansman was so honest about Momentum's intentions was to encourage left-wing, newer Labour members who would prefer to be on demonstrations to attend the rather tedious party meetings that nominate conference delegates. Secondly, Mr Watson believes that Momentum will seek to depose MPs and councillors who it regards as hostile or right wing or both. Momentum says that it is entitled to put forward its views and it is up to local members to decide who they would like to represent them. And far from hatching secret plans, Mr Lansman made his remarks at a meeting that was open to the wider public. It is perfectly possible, of course, that Mr McCluskey wins the union leadership contest and Momentum members fail to get the leadership changes it wants. Therefore, the armed impasse between Corbyn supporters and opponents could continue, very possibly, to the party's electoral detriment. Already sources close to the leadership are warning that Mr Watson's intervention means we are really worried about our local election prospects in the spring because he has highlighted divisions. They were going to be tough enough to begin with but this stuff from Watson put the elections in real jeopardy, they say. Therefore, if there are poor results, the anti-Corbyn camp would use this as further evidence of the leadership's failures. However, leadership supporters are getting their retaliation in first by trying to shift the blame to the deputy leader's door. At the end of a shadow cabinet away day on Monday afternoon, Messrs Corbyn and Watson issued a statement saying they had had robust and constructive discussions. However, there may have been more of the former - and a bit less of the latter.

text: The daily commute to work is something to be put up with rather than enjoyed, yet how we get there and how long it takes has an impact on how we feel. Such findings are scarcely unexpected when one considers that the typical British worker spends 54 minutes commuting daily. This significant and continuously growing portion of the working week carries costs - and these extend beyond merely financial implications. The Office for National Statistics reports that feelings of happiness, life satisfaction and the perception that one's activities are worthwhile all diminish with each additional minute of workplace travel. These elements comprise personal wellbeing and, generally speaking, the lengthier the commute the greater its reduction. Extended commutes, lasting between one hour and ninety minutes, produce the most adverse impact on personal wellbeing, the ONS research determined, whilst bus travel to work on journeys exceeding 30 minutes represented the commuting method most likely to cause irritation. I reside in Porthcawl, Wales, and journey at least five days weekly to Watford. My alarm sounds at 03:30 daily and my travel requires two-and-a-half to three hours. My working day may extend to 12 hours. I subsequently travel home when considerably more traffic exists than during morning hours, with an average of three to three-and-a-half hours being typical for this single journey. Tales from readers regarding extreme commuting The 2011 census reveals that 7.2% of working individuals in England and Wales travel by bus or coach to work, compared with 5% by rail and 3.8% by underground or tram. The vast majority, 59%, drive or receive lifts in cars or vans. In perfect circumstances, commuting ought not to influence psychological health since it represents a choice. Commuting journeys lengthen because individuals relocate from towns and cities to secure superior housing, additional green space and enhanced living standards. Professor Jenny Roberts, from Sheffield University, has examined how wellbeing is influenced by alterations in commuting duration by monitoring 7,000 men and 7,000 women across 13 years. By comparison, the ONS report derives from a single survey of over 60,000 employed individuals between 2012 and 2013. She found, in her paper published in the Journal of Health Economics, that women suffered adversely from commuting, whilst men did not, despite women generally commuting less and working fewer hours. This occurred after considering income, job satisfaction and housing quality. Therefore why do women demonstrate greater sensitivity to commuting time? The sole explanation we could identify was trip-chaining, Professor Roberts clarifies. Women typically make additional intermediate stops during their journey, through the nursery or school or shops, therefore they possess reduced flexibility and undertake more multiple activities. This increases commuting stress. Commuting influences wellbeing due to the established connection between stress and mental health. The stress results from insufficient control during commuting, caused by delayed trains, traffic congestion and unpredictable weather conditions, for instance. Research additionally demonstrates that boredom and social isolation amongst commuters may lead to unhappiness. Nevertheless, certain commuters do discover advantages in daily commuting since it provides time to work and read or simply relax. 'Extreme commuting' is becoming increasingly common and the ONS research indicates that commute times of three hours or more often constitute a more pleasant experience than briefer journeys. This may occur because these exceptionally long journeys represent positive lifestyle decisions for extreme commuters, who typically possess higher average incomes, and can consequently utilise their travel time more productively. Those who cycle or walk to work benefit from knowing that physical activity enhances wellbeing, but the ONS research states that cycling to work may also prove stressful. This particularly applies if commuters cycle due to lacking alternative options or on routes through heavy traffic. Ultimately, the psychological health of commuters matters because everyone commutes, yet we often hesitate to examine how we accomplish it, states Professor Rogers. Do individuals truly make that calculation when relocating to suburban housing regarding how much time, how much income it will cost and how it will affect their mental health?

text: In a football match, it is not usual to start 3-0 down. However, in economic terms, that is essentially where the government finds itself as it approaches the Autumn Statement at the month's end. The former Chancellor, George Osborne, established three rules the government would follow, an effort to demonstrate to a sceptical public that it was tackling the nation's deficit (the sum a country expends on public services against the amount a country generates through tax receipts) and being stringent on debt accumulation (the total sum a government owes). All three have been breached or discarded - the limit on welfare expenditure, the commitment to reduce debt as a share of national income and the vow to balance the accounts (thus ending the deficit) by 2020. The final target was abandoned following the referendum result which brought forth a series of economic downgrades for the UK economy which - should they materialise - will result in a decline in government revenue and make eliminating the deficit more challenging without additional tax increases and public sector reductions. That is the unhelpfully fragmented pitch upon which the current Chancellor, Philip Hammond, is operating ahead of his first significant economic appearance, the Autumn Statement in a fortnight's time. Today's report from the Institute for Fiscal Studies exposes the challenges ahead. It indicates that given the slowdown forecast in the economy the chancellor will be confronting a public finances outlook £25bn worse than anticipated in the Budget last March. With no policy alterations - and that represents a significant assumption given that Mr Hammond is (a) a new chancellor and (b) has already discussed a fiscal reset - the IFS states tax revenues will be £31bn lower. That will be partly offset, the IFS states, by the £6bn the government might recover by terminating its contributions to the EU budget. However, again, that constitutes a rather significant assumption. Numerous government sources I have consulted believe that to facilitate the transition to a free trade agreement with the EU (particularly if there is no accord on freedom of movement) the government might need to maintain certain budget payments. Naturally, in public finance terms, it is not entirely one-way traffic regarding Brexit. The Bank of England's decision to reduce interest rates to 0.25% decreases the cost of servicing the government's debt. The decline in sterling's value (which increases import prices) also makes Britain's trade deficit smaller as it enhances export performance. And the rise in dollar earnings and profits for global companies headquartered in the UK will also benefit the government's tax receipts. These are all considerably more marginal than the overall adverse effect of the predicted economic slowdown. Some believe those pessimistic predictions will prove overly gloomy - just as the predictions of a potential recession this year proved to be. And, should they be, all the public finances estimates will require revision, once more. Such is the difficulty and unpredictability of economic forecasting. This near to the Autumn Statement, the Office for Budget Responsibility - the official economic watchdog - will be providing the Treasury with weekly updates on its predictions for the public finances' future. The OBR is likely to downgrade its growth forecasts for the UK economy - following the Bank of England's lead. That means government receipts will be projected to be lower. The government could respond by reducing spending further (unpalatable), increasing taxes (unpalatable) or relaxing the deficit reduction target (probable). Should economic growth indeed slow, Mr Hammond's scope for manoeuvre to regain some of those lost objectives will be constrained.

text: Motorists trying to access a new system for hiring a car have been experiencing problems with the DVLA website. Several individuals stated the system - which does not apply to Northern Ireland motorists - was not functioning correctly, whilst certain car rental companies had to manage queues. The modifications, which involve the elimination of the paper counterpart, become effective on Monday 8 June. However, the DVLA stated that more than 20,000 motorists had succeeded in accessing the site without problems. From this point forward, drivers hiring a vehicle may need to provide a special temporary code as proof of their convictions. The DVLA stated it had been developing the new system for months. As a consequence of the elimination of the paper counterpart, all evidence of driving endorsements and convictions will be stored online exclusively. Drivers are being requested to log onto the DVLA website, and obtain a code, which they may be required to provide when they go to hire a vehicle, either in the UK or overseas. Nevertheless, the code is only valid for three days, creating the possibility that those going on holiday may need to locate internet access. Several customers complained to the BBC that they had been unable to access sections of the website on Monday. One car rental company in Bristol stated it had a queue of 20 people waiting, as personnel struggled to access their details online. The DVLA system has crashed a dozen times this morning, stated Richard Stock from U-drive. Another operator nearby had a queue of customers extending out of the door. The DVLA informed the BBC that there had been exceptionally high demand on its website, and it was urgently investigating the matter. The car rental industry has accused the DVLA of implementing the system too rapidly. The project is being rushed through. It is not brilliant, stated Gerry Keaney, the chief executive of the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA). The RAC has previously cautioned that many people were unaware of the new regulations. A more recent survey by the website money.co.uk indicated that 73% of drivers did not know they had to provide a code when hiring a vehicle. And the AA has recommended motorists to take their paper counterpart with them, even though it is no longer valid. But the DVLA rejected that using the system is complicated. It is very straightforward to view and share your driving record. Simply go to gov.uk and search for 'view driving licence', stated Oliver Morley, the DVLA's chief executive. He stated that motorists could also save their driving records as a PDF file, which they could store on a mobile device. The DVLA has produced a step-by-step guide to assist motorists through the process. For those who forget to obtain a code, a telephone number is also available, but only between the hours of 8am and 7pm on weekdays, and 8am and 2pm on Saturdays. In many instances, motorists hiring a vehicle are not asked for evidence of convictions. Nevertheless drivers are being advised to contact their rental company before they travel, to determine which documents they need to bring with them. Smaller rental companies, particularly based overseas, may be unaware of the changes. As many as eight million old-style paper licences - which carry endorsements on them - will remain valid. However endorsements will no longer be added to them by the courts. The government has defended the new system, stating it will save millions of pounds, and reduce bureaucracy. Last year, the DVLA had to replace 445,000 paper counterparts. Motorists who lost them were charged £20 for replacements. However, the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association stated it would be much better if there were an online IT system which rental companies could use to check convictions themselves. It, too, has produced guidance for motorists. The new arrangements are valid in Britain only. Northern Ireland has a separate licence scheme.

text: The makers of the Raspberry Pi computer have created a version of its graphical front end that can run on ordinary desktop computers. These are external links and will open in a new window. The Pixel desktop has been reworked so it operates on PCs and Apple Mac computers, stated the Foundation. Individuals who utilise it on a Raspberry Pi and other devices will now receive the same familiar software across both. The Pi Foundation stated the release also supported its plan to deliver the finest desktop computing experience. Raspberry Pi co-founder Eben Upton stated the software should assist schoolchildren who employ the credit-card sized Pi in lessons or for their own projects but must continue their work on PCs or Macs. The Pi edition of Pixel and the version adapted for larger machines employs precisely the same productivity software and programming tools, in precisely the same desktop environment, he wrote. There is no learning curve, and no requirement to adjust... schoolwork to operate on two subtly different operating systems, he stated. Additionally, he stated, developing such a version of Pixel kept the Raspberry Pi foundation honest as it would assist the organisation's programmers work out which parts of the user interface required work. Mr Upton stated that because the core software underlying Pixel was founded on a relatively old computer architecture, it should operate on vintage computers. He cautioned that the software remained experimental so might contain bugs or other minor problems that might mean it does not operate well on some computers. Pixel was initially released in September this year and overhauled the main graphical interface owners observe and utilise when working with their Pi. It is founded on a version of the open source Linux software called Debian. The desktop version lacks two programmes - Minecraft and Mathematica - because the Pi organisation has not licensed those applications on any computers other than its own. In April last year, the Raspberry Pi officially became the most popular British computer ever manufactured. More than 10 million have now been sold. The computer was initially released in 2012 and is widely employed as an educational tool for programming.

text: Doctor Who's Peter Capaldi has passed on his sonic screwdriver to Jodie Whittaker who becomes the 13th doctor and first woman to take on the role of television's famous Time Lord. These are external links and will open in a new window She follows a distinguished succession of theatrical (male) talent that extends all the way back to the science-fiction favourite's inaugural episode in 1963. William Hartnell was the first actor to portray the Doctor, featuring in the BBC programme from 1963 to 1966. Hartnell, who passed away in 1975, had previously featured in television's The Army Game and Carry On Sergeant, the inaugural Carry On film, in 1958. When poor health compelled Hartnell to abandon the role, the Doctor regenerated - for the first time - into Patrick Troughton. Notably dishevelled and eccentric, Troughton spent three years traversing time and space before departing in 1969. When the rakish Jon Pertwee became the third Doctor, he also became the first to be witnessed on television in colour. His period, which extended from 1970 to 1974, witnessed the Time Lord banished to Earth and collaborating with Unit, otherwise known as the United Nations Intelligence Taskforce. Pertwee's period with the programme also witnessed the first of the popular ensemble narratives in which previous Doctors feature alongside the current one. Transmitted over December 1972 and January 1973, The Three Doctors witnessed him accompanied by Patrick Troughton and William Hartnell in what would be the latter's final acting commitment. When Pertwee departed in 1974, Tom Baker arrived - and would become the longest-serving Doctor to date. Deep-voiced, curly-haired and perpetually long of scarf, his seven years in the Tardis secured him legions of admirers who were delighted anew in 2013 when he appeared at the conclusion of a 50th anniversary special. When Baker finally departed from the role in 1981, his position was filled by the fresh-faced Peter Davison. The youthful actor spent three years as the Fifth Doctor before taking his departure at the conclusion of the programme's 21st series. Davison's period coincided with Doctor Who's 20th anniversary, celebrated by a feature-length special that witnessed him accompanied by Jon Pertwee and Patrick Troughton. The First Doctor also made an appearance, with Richard Hurndall substituting for the late William Hartnell. Tom Baker chose not to return for The Five Doctors, which concealed his absence by incorporating material from one of the actor's unbroadcast adventures. Similar deception was required for this 1983 photograph session, which witnessed Hurndall, Davison, Pertwee and Troughton accompanied by an unconvincing Baker mannequin. Davison's departure opened the opportunity for another Baker to take command of the Doctor's time-travelling police box in 1984. Colin Baker (no relation of Tom's) spent fewer than three years in the role, with his appearances limited further by an 18-month suspension in production. Though Baker had limited time to enjoy the Tardis, he did receive the opportunity to meet one of his predecessors when Patrick Troughton returned - for the third time - in 1985. The Two Doctors marked Troughton's final reprise of his signature role. Some years later, his sons David and Michael would both make Doctor Who appearances. Scottish actor Sylvester McCoy assumed control from Colin Baker in 1987 and portrayed the Doctor until the programme's cancellation in 1989. Michael Grade - the controller of BBC One at the time - was no admirer of the programme, which was appearing increasingly threadbare and cheap-looking in the face of glossier cinema offerings. Some believe, though, that this period in the programme's evolution has been harshly assessed. An attempt was made to revive Doctor Who in 1996 with a television film that witnessed McCoy regenerate into Paul McGann on American territory. It was hoped the special would generate a television series but it never materialised, making McGann's tenure the shortest of all the Doctors. In 2005 Doctor Who regenerated into the ambitious, well-funded property it is today. It also introduced a new Doctor in the form of Christopher Eccleston. To the disappointment of many, the Salford-born actor chose to make only one series of the rebooted programme. His departure was confirmed only days after his debut episode was transmitted. Eccleston's exit witnessed David Tennant join the programme, with his first full episode - The Christmas Invasion - shown on BBC One on Christmas Day 2005. Tennant's affable style and enthusiasm made him a popular choice for the role, which he finally relinquished on the first day of 2010. The sequence of junior Doctors continued with the casting of Matt Smith, who was just 27 when he made his debut as the Time Lord's 11th incarnation. His four years in the role, which coincided with Doctor Who's 50th anniversary, witnessed the programme both maintain and strengthen its renewed popularity. Doctor Who's 50th anniversary in 2013 was marked by The Day of the Doctor, a feature-length special in which Matt Smith's Time Lord was accompanied by David Tennant's version of the character. The Day of the Doctor also introduced a previously unknown incarnation of the Doctor, known as The War Doctor and portrayed by Sir John Hurt. Peter Capaldi was no stranger to the Doctor Who universe when he was cast as the Doctor in 2013. A lifelong enthusiast of the programme, he featured in an episode of the programme in 2008 and also had a role in its spin-off Torchwood. His hawkish features brought a new intensity, and maturity, to the Tardis from the moment his first full episode was transmitted in August 2014. Capaldi's most recent adventure witnessed him briefly accompanied by the original Doctor, portrayed on this occasion by David Bradley. Bradley will return in this year's Doctor Who Christmas special. Bradley's appearance was a pleasing one for Whovians after his role as William Hartnell in An Adventure in Space and Time, a 2013 dramatisation of the programme's early years. Jodie Whittaker has been named as the 13th Doctor and the first ever woman to portray the role. She will make her debut on the science-fiction programme this Christmas when Capaldi regenerates. text: Celtic reached an important milestone by beating Aberdeen in the League Cup final, says manager Brendan Rodgers. Media playback is not supported on this device The 3-0 victory - courtesy of strikes from Tom Rogic, James Forrest and Moussa Dembele - delivered Celtic their 100th major trophy, and Rodgers his maiden triumph as manager. The Northern Irishman stated his players had been truly impressive but they must now capitalise on their achievement. It's a victorious club, that's what the heritage of this club has been founded upon, declared the former Liverpool manager. It signifies a milestone, the century of trophies and we must commence the next century of trophies. That will be crucial for us and the club. Celtic, undefeated domestically this campaign, dominated most of the match, netting twice in the opening half through Rogic and Forrest. Aberdeen responded just after the break, but their challenge concluded when Anthony O'Connor surrendered a penalty that Dembele dispatched. It's a magnificent evening for the Celtic supporters to celebrate and we strive for the next one, stated Rodgers. It's six months and a week since I arrived and we discussed what we wished to accomplish and how we intended to do it and we're progressing well towards that. We're attempting to enhance standards on and off the pitch. We're developing the team to perform in a particular style and that's proceeding very well. There are matters we'll examine, what can we do better, how can we advance. Ultimately, the objective was to claim the cup and fortunately we've secured it. Rather than lingering on his inaugural trophy, Rodgers concentrated instead on the endeavours of his players. He commended the performance and, particularly, the authority of Scott Brown in midfield. I've an enormous task to undertake here in terms of developing it and maintaining it, he stated. It's a tremendous achievement. For the players, it's something to demonstrate for the excellent work they've been producing. It's wonderful for the confidence and it prepares us for the remainder of the season. If I'm to comment on obtaining my own first trophy as Celtic manager, having Scott as the captain is a tremendous honour. He truly controlled the match and collectively he draws the team together on the pitch. text: A team of UK scientists hopes to shed light on the mysteries of bleeding canker, a disease that is threatening the nation's horse chestnut trees. The researchers have sequenced the genome of a bacterial strain that causes the virulent infection. A survey conducted in 2007 revealed that bleeding canker had spread rapidly, with nearly half of the two million horse chestnuts exhibiting symptoms of the disease. The findings have been published in the journal PLoS One. A visible symptom of the disease is a lesion upon the bark, which exudes a resin onto the trunk or occasionally the branches. The bark beneath the canker is killed, and if cankers succeed in encircling the entire trunk then the horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) will perish because it severs the food supply. The researchers sequenced the genome of the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pathovar aesuli (Pae) from three specimens collected from different locations across the UK. They compared these with specimens from the only other recorded case, obtained from an Indian horse chestnut in India during the 1960s. What we discovered was that the three British specimens were all identical, stated co-author Dr David Studholme, presently at the University of Exeter but who was based at The Sainsbury Laboratory, Norwich, during the study. This indicates that they all probably descended from a single introduction, he informed BBC News. Nevertheless, he added that additional work was required before they could determine whether or not the bacterium originated from India, where the pathovar (a bacterial strain that only affects certain plants, in this case horse chestnuts) was initially recorded. The Indian [specimen] has only ever been known to cause a leaf spot; there is no evidence of it causing cankers. Dr Studholme's fellow co-author was Sarah Green, a plant pathologist at Forest Research, the research division of the UK Forestry Commission. She stated Pae was very mobile, very aggressive and that it certainly required study. There were some interesting genes that we discovered that may well be assisting it to be so aggressive, she explained. It affects the woody portion of the trees, whilst other bacterial diseases attack the soft tissues (such as leaves). However, she added that considerably more work was required before it would be possible to understand how the bacterial strain interacted with the trees and how it was transmitted. Since Pae was first recorded in 2002, it has become present throughout the UK and more than 70% of horse chestnuts in certain areas are displaying symptoms of being infected. Roddie Burgess, head of plant health at the Forestry Commission, stated he hoped the research would assist in developing a strategy to address the problem. It always takes you by surprise when you investigate a previously unknown disease and discover that almost half of your tree population may already be infected, he informed BBC News. He stated that several thousand trees were known to have been felled by local authorities amid concerns that infected trees would pose a risk to the public. Quite a substantial number were felled before we realised that the trees sometimes enter remission and may recover. Our advice for now is not to go rushing in with a chainsaw. He added that further research was underway to determine if the disease had the potential to kill the trees in ways other than severing the supply of nutrients. These are the sorts of matters we need to understand before we even begin to consider how best to manage infected trees.

text: Head teachers warning that they face financial meltdown are furious that the government has been pledging funds to create grammar schools in England. Ministers were disclosed on Wednesday to have invited grammar school leaders to submit applications for £150m across three years for new selective school places. School leaders have additionally demanded the restoration of £384m, originally pledged to convert schools into academies. The Department for Education states that school funding stands at record levels. School leaders have been incensed that whilst they have been cautioning about insufficient basic funding, the government has been capable of pledging hundreds of millions for initiatives such as expanding grammars and converting schools to academy status. Head teachers in West Sussex have been campaigning against what they assert are severe budget shortfalls. They have written to local MPs to convey their incredulity at the funding that appears to be accessible for grammars. They are additionally calling upon political leaders to account for their expenditure decisions. The Grammar School Heads' Association held a private meeting with the education secretary and schools minister in which they discussed proposals to expand selective places and to establish new grammar schools for 2020. The meeting notes, published by the grammar heads, include particulars of how to contact the department for £50m annually for new selective places. The heads in West Sussex have called for emergency funding of £20m and have cautioned that without this schools may have to reduce hours, enlarge class sizes or cease teaching certain subjects. They have informed MPs that throughout our campaign school leaders have sought to be 'relentlessly reasonable'; now we are simply furious. They describe local schools as scrabbling around for any form of cash like a desperate person checking down the side of their sofa for the odd pound coin or two. Earlier this week, finance directors and school business managers from Barnet wrote to the Department for Education warning of an approaching financial crisis. They called upon the government to restore the £384m pledged to fund a plan to convert all of England's schools into academies. When that was overturned by a backbench rebellion, it was disclosed that the funding was reclaimed by the Treasury. School leaders have contended that a redistribution of how schools are funded, in a new funding formula, could prevent having any losers if this money, once announced for schools, could be restored. Grammar school head teachers have also been complaining about funding shortages - and have cautioned that they may have to begin requesting payments from parents. The National Union of Teachers has criticised the government for pledging funds for new grammar places when schools are already crying out for sufficient funding. The union's general secretary Kevin Courtney accused the education secretary of fiddling around with secret plans for a return to a two-tier education system which would be of no benefit to 90% of children. A Department for Education spokeswoman stated schools in West Sussex would benefit from changes in the funding formula - with an additional £145 per pupil annually. We have protected the core schools budget in real terms since 2010, with school funding at its highest level on record at more than £40bn in 2016-17, stated the DFE spokeswoman.

text: Double Olympic champion Alistair Brownlee says he may not return to triathlon for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. Media playback is not supported on this device The World Triathlon Series commences in Abu Dhabi on Friday but Brownlee, 28, is not competing as he prepares to progress to the longer half-Ironman distance. The Yorkshire athlete secured triathlon gold at Rio 2016, defending his title from London 2012. There exists a possibility I might never be at an Olympic Games again but to state I'll never do it is impossible, he said. The Olympic Games are simply fantastic and I would definitely love to be there but the course in Tokyo is going to play a significant part in terms of whether I feel I can go there and win. It is going to be a case of sitting down at the end of 2018 and weighing it up - am I enjoying the long distance stuff? Am I still able to be competitive enough to win a medal in Tokyo? Brownlee will defend his World Series title in Leeds on 11 June, but that remains his only confirmed race so far this season, whilst brother and Rio silver medallist Jonny begins his campaign from the second race in the Gold Coast on 8 April. For the remainder of the year, Alistair Brownlee will combine standard Olympic length events - 1.5km swim, 40km on the bike and 10km run - with half Ironman distance competitions, also known as Ironman 70.3 in reference to the total number of miles covered. He added that the Ironman 70.3 World Championship in September is an obvious target as he builds up to the full Ironman distance, which he says has always been on his bucket list. Ironman has got to be one of those things you always want to do - it's like the London or Boston marathon of triathlon, he added. The two-time gold medallist added that his Rio 2016 victory was slightly marred by the absence of long-term rival and London 2012 silver medallist Javier Gomez, who withdrew from the Games after breaking his elbow in a cycling accident. It definitely took a bit away from my gold in Rio that Gomez wasn't there, said Brownlee. You want to be there in your best shape and race the best athletes in their best shape - we were fortunate to have that in London and it would have been fantastic to have had that in Rio as well but what happened happened. But on that day, on that course, I'm fairly confident I would have had him anyway. With Gomez, 33, back from that injury, Brownlee expects the Spaniard to challenge for the World Series title, alongside compatriot and current champion Mario Mola, 27. And the older Brownlee expects Jonny, 26, to complete the podium and says his brother could claim the title with a bit of luck and a fair wind behind him. Alistair Brownlee says he may have been bored returning to World Series racing, having experienced the same kind of racing against basically the same people for the last 10 years. However, he adds that he is motivated by his new goals, which could include competing in 10,000m running races and the marathon. I now have an opportunity to try these other things without hurting my chances if I do decide I want to compete in four years in Tokyo, he said. I thought about a lot of things after Rio. I definitely want to run a marathon and that might be in the not too distant future. The other obvious thing is cycling and trying to make a wholehearted jump into being a professional cyclist but although that's possible, I'm very aware that in that arena and in running, I can be good and get to a level where I could be professional, but never to a level where I can win stuff. I still feel like I want to be the best at what I'm doing so that's why I'm choosing things I feel like I can win.

text: A Venezuelan teenager taking part in an anti-government protest has been killed in Caracas, the chief prosecutor's office has confirmed. These are external links and will open in a new window Fabián Urbina, 17, was shot when security forces and demonstrators clashed in the Altamira district. Interior Minister Néstor Reverol spoke of a potential improper and disproportionate use of force by the security forces. He stated that several officers were under investigation. Mr Reverol also condemned the violence and the calls for an uprising made by the Venezuelan opposition. Rights ombudsman Tarek William Saab tweeted [in Spanish] that two National Guard members had been detained over the undue use of a firearm. There have been almost daily anti-government protests in Venezuela for the past 80 days as the nation's economic and political crisis has deteriorated. Many of the demonstrations have ended in violence as protesters hurled petrol bombs and stones and police discharged tear gas. More than 70 people have died in protest-related violence since 1 April, according to figures issued by the chief prosecutor's office. A list published by the information ministry places that figure higher and suggests most of those killed were participating in anti-government demonstrations. But amongst the dead are also security force members, people caught up in the violence, and a group of men who were electrocuted when a bakery was looted. Monday's opposition demonstration was called to denounce government plans to convene a citizens' assembly to draft a new constitution. Opposition activists say the constituent assembly is an attempt by President Nicolás Maduro to consolidate his power and circumvent the opposition-controlled National Assembly. The president contends that the aim of the new constitution is to safeguard social programmes created by his socialist government and that of his predecessor in office, Hugo Chávez. Whilst anti-government protesters clashed with the security forces in Altamira, government supporters participated in an anti-imperialist march in support of the constituent assembly in the city centre. The aim of that demonstration was to send a message to members of the Organization of American States (OAS) meeting in Mexico not to interfere in Venezuelan affairs. Foreign ministers of OAS member states have again discussed the political and economic crisis in Venezuela, but failed to agree on a resolution criticising the Venezuelan government. The draft resolution which called on President Maduro to abandon his plans for the constitutional assembly was supported by 20 countries, opposed by five and eight abstained. Twenty-three votes were required to adopt the resolution.

text: On 2 May 2011, Barack Obama announced that al-Qaeda leader Osama Bin Laden had been killed by US forces in Pakistan. These are external links and will open in a new window He was shot dead at a compound near the capital, Islamabad. And once again, Pakistan was in the headlines for all the wrong reasons. A country accustomed to bad news - both politically and economically - it has long been regarded as the basket case economy of South Asia due to its declining foreign reserves, weak currency and absence of foreign direct investment. It was probably one of the last places on Earth that a foreign investor would consider putting their money. But not Mattias Martinsson. Six months later, in October 2011, he launched Pakistan's first ever foreign equity fund. Initially he could not get anyone to back the fund, so he invested $1m (£780,000) of his own cash and that of his partners. Today, that fund is worth $100m. It was a difficult sell at the time, chuckles the soft-spoken Swede on the telephone from Stockholm. That is an understatement. At one point - shortly after the Bin Laden killing - things became so bad that furious investors stoned the exchange because of the falling share prices. Then the US military bombed a Pakistani military base, and Pakistan initiated a blockade of the routes for Nato supplies. The market fell 10%, Mr Martinsson says. But he remained in the stock market and in 2012 things began to turn around, with a tax amnesty the government launched to encourage the Pakistani diaspora to repatriate money. The market rose and we raised $50m in three months, he recalls. It also marked the first time in decades that more money was entering Pakistan than leaving. Almost a decade later, Mr Martinsson feels vindicated. That is because on 1 June 2017, Pakistan enters the MSCI Emerging Markets Index - a sign that things are turning around. And investors are already beginning to pour in. The MSCI Emerging Markets Index is composed of 23 high-growth economies including India, China and Brazil. Pakistan's main index, the KSE 100 has consistently outperformed the index. If you had invested $100 into the KSE in January last year, it would now be worth $164. If you had put it into the MSCI, it would only be worth $137. That is a success that helped make the case for it to be included. Being in the Emerging Markets Index is a reputational reassurance to investors about the growth prospects and transparency of companies in that country. Pakistan used to be part of the index, but was downgraded to frontier market because of the exchange's decision to shut down for four months in late 2008 after prices dropped dramatically. That meant foreign investors could not get their money out. We were kicked out in 2008 after the financial crisis because of measures Pakistan took at the time to stop foreign funds from fleeing the country. Obviously foreign investors received a rude shock, says Nadeem Naqvi, the Karachi Stock Exchange's managing director. We did considerable lobbying and reforms to get re-included again into this index, he tells me from Karachi. And he assures me and investors, that the KSE will be a liquid market. Parliament passed the Pakistan Stock Exchanges Act in 2012, which has improved corporate governance and reforms to prevent a reoccurrence of what happened in 2008, he says. Pakistan's gross domestic product (GDP) has also soared over the last few years, much of that is thanks to the growth in the middle classes, in part fuelled by the Chinese investment boom that is part of Beijing's One Belt One Road initiative. China is spending $46bn building roads, ports and highways in Pakistan as part of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). It is just starting, says Mr Naqvi. You will see the real impact in the next 12 to 24 months. That will be an added impetus to the growth rate. Chinese investors have also bought into the Pakistan Stock Exchange, and they now own 40% of it. All of this is going to add to the confidence of the middle class to spend more, and add to domestic demand, Mr Naqvi says. In five to six years the growth rate should average out to above 6%. Having said that, though, there have already been signs of trouble on the CPEC routes. text: Five disabled social housing tenants have lost their Court of Appeal bid to have benefit cuts for those deemed to have spare bedrooms ruled unlawful. Judges declared the court could not intervene in the government's controversial housing benefit modifications - termed a bedroom tax by opponents. Solicitors for the group had contended the regulations applying in England, Wales and Scotland failed to reflect the accommodation requirements of disabled people. They stated they intended to continue fighting. The court also ruled against two single parents who claimed the government's cap on the total benefits paid to families breached human rights laws and common law due to its impact on vulnerable families. Lord Dyson, Master of the Rolls, stated the legal challenges were to two of the government's most controversial measures concerning state benefits. He declared the court could intervene only if the measures were manifestly without reasonable foundation and he ruled that stringent test was not met and both challenges must fail. However Ugo Hayter, who represents two of those challenging the changes, said they were baffled by the Court of Appeal's findings and were considering taking the case to the Supreme Court. The court acknowledged that our clients and thousands of disabled people across the UK had a need for accommodation not provided for by the new housing benefit rules, however the court decided that disabled tenants should not have their housing needs met on an equivalent basis to their able-bodied counterparts, just because they are disabled. By Jayson CarmichaelAppellant I hope we can appeal it in the Supreme Court. It must be the worst High Court decision that's ever been made, I'm very angry about it. We're going to continue to fight for justice, because we haven't really got a spare bedroom because of my wife's severe disabilities and to say that disabled people are justifiably discriminated against can't be right for Britain in 2014. We have to fight loads of medical issues; I'm a 24/7 carer and I do overnight care for her and everything, and on top of the fight in this case it's just put me in a state of exhaustion. We have had some help with some discretionary housing payments but we've been promised no more for this year, so we might fall behind with our rent like other disabled tenants now. We're hoping to stay. We haven't got much room as it is; with medical equipment there's not really a lot of space in a two-bedroom housing association flat. Instead disabled tenants are being compelled to rely on short-term and discretionary payments. And Anne McMurdie, whose firm represents three of the appellants, said: Disabled tenants are not requesting extra funds - they are requesting for housing benefit to be paid at a level which meets their needs - for the same right as others. Discretionary payments are not the solution. Jayson Carmichael, from Southport, Merseyside, who was one of the appellants, said he was devastated by the ruling. He stated: It's ludicrous because human rights laws have been implemented by tribunal judges up and down the country. I think we're just being made an example of because of our high profile in this group case. Richard Kramer, deputy chief executive of national deaf-blind charity Sense, said it was extremely disappointed with the outcome. Although this decision concerns the cases of five individuals, the impact of this policy has been devastating for many disabled people, he stated. National Housing Federation head of policy Kevin Williamson said the court action demonstrated how desperate people had become. He stated: Disabled people across the country are being compelled to cut back on food and heating to pay the bedroom tax. Richard Hawkes, chief executive of disability charity Scope, described the ruling as a setback for the campaigners and a major blow for the 400,000 disabled people who are experiencing the impact of this policy. The Department for Work and Pensions, which was a defendant in both cases, welcomed the rulings. Reform of housing benefit in the social sector is essential to ensure the long-term sustainability of the benefit. But we have ensured extra discretionary housing support is available for vulnerable people, a spokesman stated. Referring to the benefit cap, the spokesman added: We are pleased that the courts have ruled again that the benefit cap complies with the European Convention on Human Rights. The benefit cap sets a fair limit to what people can expect to receive from the welfare system - so that claimants cannot receive more than £500 a week, the average household earnings. Since April last year, people deemed to have one spare bedroom have had their housing benefit reduced by 14% whilst those with two or more spare bedrooms have seen reductions of 25%. The challenge to the change originally concerned 10 families but five cases involving disabled children are no longer being pursued because they have since become subject to an exemption from the benefit cut. The group includes wheelchair user Richard Rourke, 46, from Bakestone Moor, Derbyshire, who states he needs an additional bedroom to store mobility equipment. Among the others involved in the case is Mr Carmichael's wife Charlotte who states her spina bifida means she is unable to share a bedroom with her husband, who is also her full-time carer.

text: Argentina's economy minister Axel Kicillof has returned to the negotiating table in a last-ditch attempt to prevent the country defaulting on its bonds. Mr Kicillof's discussions with hold-out investors concluded late on Tuesday evening in New York without reaching agreement. They are demanding complete payment of $1.3bn (£766m) on the bonds they possess. A US judge has determined that the hold-outs must receive payment by Wednesday evening if no deal is reached. However, thousands of miles distant in Buenos Aires, many remain doubtful that any agreement can be achieved. The government's position has been unambiguous. The hold-outs are US hedge funds that purchased debt at reduced prices during Argentina's most difficult period and never consented to restructuring. President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner labels them vultures, alleging they are exploiting Argentina's debt difficulties to secure substantial profit. What exacerbates the problem is that if the hold-outs succeed, other bondholders who accepted reductions of up to 70% in what they are owed might also seek full repayment. Ask citizens on the street regarding their opinion on Argentina's debt troubles and most acknowledge it is too complex for them to comprehend. However, the two words they do recognise are fondos buitres - vulture funds in Spanish. Despite the defiant stance of the government, many people appear resigned. Argentina has defaulted previously and it will do so again. I encountered Carina Etchegaray, the mother of two children aged 14 and 16. When Argentina last defaulted at the conclusion of 2001, she lost substantial amounts of savings. She had wished to purchase a house for her young family. However, at the end of 2001, the government implemented what was termed the corralito. It literally signifies a small enclosure in Spanish, but refers to when the government partially froze bank accounts and people were prevented from withdrawing money. When we finally possessed the money, because of devaluation, we could only purchase a car for the same amount of money we had for a house, she states. However, she is also pragmatic. We live with this shadow of crisis. You must continue with your life because you have children and must work. You must adapt - in this country, it's the manner of life. And that is what entrepreneur Federico Dumas is doing as well - but not in the manner that Argentina would wish. He operates a software company, but states he is not investing as he would prefer to. I'm fearful of everything and my customers are not prepared to invest, so that will impact my business, he states, adding that he is optimistic Argentina's problems will be resolved reasonably. However, if the country enters default, I'm extremely concerned about what's going to occur to my business and my employees. Default or not, when I met Guillermo Nielsen, the man who directed the negotiations when the country was restructuring its debts in 2005, he stated what is occurring in Argentina is something he had never anticipated. I never envisaged this - not in my wildest dreams, he states. People, although they were dissatisfied and they were very difficult negotiations, they understood that Argentina was not capable of paying, so that's a very significant difference. Today, Argentina possesses the money - back then, we didn't possess the money. In my own view, I believe the forthcoming negotiations are going to be much more difficult than the ones we had to endure. His concern is that if the country defaults, it could activate what is termed an acceleration clause. It would mean creditors could compel Argentina to repay bonds within a much shorter timeframe than previously established. That, he states, is a genuine concern. However, all this is speculation. With just a few hours remaining, no decisions have been taken and it is all still discussion. The detail of what has been discussed remains unclear. As people here state, the Argentine manner of conducting business will mean talks until the 11th hour. The vultures will continue circling until then.

text: Military landing craft have been suggested as a possible solution to a breakdown of Lochaber's Corran Ferry. These are external links and will open in a new window A report to Highland councillors following a problem that affected the ferry last month stated that requesting assistance from the Royal Navy has been proposed. Nevertheless, council officers stated that due to the number of vehicles that are transported more than one landing craft would be required. Additionally, the ferry's slipways are not appropriate for the military vessels. Last month, the Corran Ferry, which Highland Council operates on Loch Linnhe in Lochaber, was out of service for several days following a mechanical failure. The vessel had drifted and struck rocks near a slipway. The usual reserve ferry, the Maid of Glencoul, was unavailable because it was undergoing a refit. The Corran Ferry was able to resume service following repairs and an inspection. The council officers' report on the incident stated it cost the local authority £39,000 owing to loss of revenue and the cost of the repairs and inspection, which involved a remotely operated vehicle. The report to Tuesday's Lochaber Committee also commended the meticulous and diligent work of the ferry's staff in maintaining incidence of breakdowns on the ferry at a low level. Highland Council faced criticism at the time for having to suspend the service. There were allegations of a lack of information regarding the status of the service and contingency plans. At the time, Highland Council stated it had done everything possible to restore the service, and had placed information on its website and on Twitter. It also requested Traffic Scotland to warn people of the problems with the ferry with messages on its electronic signs on the A82 trunk road. However, road works and warnings of heavy rain had to be given priority. The Corran Ferry permits access to and from the communities of Ardgour, Morvern and Ardnamurchan via a narrow stretch of Loch Linnhe. It is also utilised by people and businesses on Mull, who first travel to the mainland on the Fishnish-Lochaline ferry. The Corran Ferry and Fishnish-Lochaline services also provide tourists an alternative to the Oban to Mull ferry.

text: William Hague is standing down as an MP after an illustrious 25 year career in the House of Commons. These are external links and will open in a new window Reflecting upon his political career, in an interview with the BBC's Norman Smith, the former foreign secretary and Conservative Party leader stated he harboured few regrets, apart from losing the 2001 general election. I am not one for harbouring numerous regrets but I do regret that we failed to reunite the Conservative Party more swiftly, he added. However, Mr Hague is hardly alone in pursuing a fresh role, distant from the renowned green benches, following 7 May's general election. A total of 86 MPs have declared their intention to step down, according to BBC Analysis and Research. It may appear substantial, from 650 MPs, but it falls considerably short of the 2010 total, when 149 MPs departed in the largest Commons exodus in history, following the expenses scandal. A total of 17 former cabinet ministers - 12 Labour and five Conservative - are stepping down at this election. The exit of Mr Hague, Sir George Young and Stephen Dorrell reduces the number of John Major cabinet survivors to three: Ken Clarke, Peter Lilley, (who both served under Margaret Thatcher as well) and John Redwood. Three female Conservative MPs, all elected in 2010, have declared they will retire. This represents 6% of female Tory MPs. In total, seven of the 2010 Tory intake will step down after a single term. Prominent Tory retirees include former health secretary Andrew Lansley, Sir George Young and Sir Peter Tapsell, the Father of the House, who was first elected to the Commons in 1959. He has accumulated 54 years on the green benches, with a two-year break from the Commons in the mid-1960s, making him amongst the longest-serving MPs in British history. Former Foreign Secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind, who now sits as an independent after having the Tory Whip withdrawn, is also stepping down. The retirements on the Labour side leave only three members of Tony Blair's first cabinet - Nick Brown, Margaret Beckett and Harriet Harman - in the Commons, assuming they succeed in retaining their seats. Prominent Labour retirees include former Prime Minister Gordon Brown and ex-cabinet ministers Alistair Darling, David Blunkett and Dame Tessa Jowell. Former Foreign Secretary Jack Straw, who has had the Labour whip suspended, and who now sits as an independent, is also stepping down. Eleven women, 16% of Labour's female MPs are stepping down, although in contrast to the Conservatives, they are all long-serving MPs. text: The Irish government arranged for a doctor to visit Ibrahim Halawa in jail in Egypt following concerns about the health of the 21-year-old Dubliner. These are external links and will open in a new window. He has conducted a series of hunger strikes in protest at being detained without trial for more than three years. Last month, his solicitor said he was so frail that prison staff employed a wheelchair to transport him to family visits. Upon the doctor's recommendation, the Irish government urged Egypt to release him for additional medical examinations. Before the visit, Taoiseach [Irish Prime Minister] Enda Kenny said he was troubled by reports that Mr Halawa was requiring a wheelchair and wanted his health to be evaluated from an Irish medical perspective. In a statement on Monday, Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs, Charlie Flanagan confirmed that the prison assessment occurred last week, at his government's request. It has long been the government's expressed wish to see Mr Halawa returned to Ireland and we have made direct appeals to the Egyptian government on numerous occasions, Mr Flanagan added. He said that after receiving the doctor's report, Mr Kenny wrote to the Egyptian president, requesting Mr Halawa's release to enable further examinations. The foreign minister added that he discussed the case with the Secretary General of the League of Arab States, Abou El Gheit, on Monday. I also once more raised the case with the EU's High Representative, Vice President Federica Mogherini, who has taken a personal interest in the case, Mr Flanagan added. He said the case was continuing to receive unprecedented attention and resources in Dublin and in Cairo. Nevertheless, the Halawa family have said that the Irish government must do more and have previously urged Mr Kenny to bring international legal action against the Egyptian government. Mr Halawa is the son of the most senior Muslim cleric in the Republic of Ireland. He was 17 when he was arrested with three of his sisters during a siege at the Al-Fath mosque in Cairo in 2013. The women were freed after three months, but their younger brother remained in prison and his court case has been postponed 20 times. For several years, Mr Halawa was informed he would face the death penalty if he was convicted at a mass trial. However, in January the Egyptian president told a delegation of Irish politicians that he will offer a pardon to Mr Halawa once his trial is concluded. The Egyptian parliament has previously opposed calls from the Irish parliament to release the Dubliner, saying the request would interfere in the affairs of the Egyptian judiciary.

text: The board of Rangers discussed putting the club into administration months before it was bought by businessman Craig Whyte. These are external links and will open in a new window. According to former financial director Donald McIntyre, the scale of the club's financial liabilities meant it would have been negligent not to do so. Mr Whyte stands accused of a fraudulent acquisition of Rangers. The 46-year-old denies two charges relating to the purchase - one of fraud and another under the Companies Act. Speaking from the witness box where he was providing evidence for a second day, Mr McIntyre discussed the financial obligations faced by Rangers in the months preceding the sale of the club to Mr Whyte in May 2011. He said Rangers faced a potential bill from HMRC of approximately £50m, which had been described as the Big Tax Case. Defence QC Donald Findlay called the debt a nuclear missile that was heading directly for Rangers. He said it was like an exocet, nothing could be done to stop it. Mr McIntyre said Rangers board members had hoped to challenge the amount owed and that counsel at the time had suggested they had an excellent chance in the case. However, Mr Findlay put it to the witness that the tax bill was a potentially terminal event for the club. The advocate asked when Mr McIntyre first knew the board was discussing the possibility of administration for Rangers. Mr McIntyre said he could not be specific of a date but that the subject would have arisen in 2010. The court went on to hear about a meeting of Rangers directors in March 2011. They discussed the money owed to HMRC and the possible impact for the club. Mr Findlay put it to Mr McIntyre: Rangers could not contemplate paying up that size of debt? Mr McIntyre agreed. Later the jury was told that Rangers did go into administration much later but that it was nothing to do with the Big Tax Case. The trial also heard the claim that Rangers former owner Sir David Murray, who purchased the club in 1988, had described Mr Whyte's bid for the club as the only show in town. Mr Findlay put to Mr McIntyre: Did it become abundantly clear that Murray would do virtually anything to secure the deal with Mr Whyte? Mr McIntyre responded: I would not put it like that. I do not think a deal would have been done under any circumstance. The defence advocate went on: A deal was done under any circumstance...Rangers was bought for a pound. Mr McIntyre added: With commitments and obligations. Mr Whyte is accused of pretending to former Rangers owner Sir David Murray, and others, that funds were available to make all required payments to acquire a controlling and majority stake in the club. The funds included clearing the £18m bank debt, £2.8m for the small tax case liability, a £1.7m health-and-safety liability and £5m for the playing squad. The Crown alleges Mr Whyte had only £4m available from two sources at the time but took out the £24m loan from Ticketus which was held subject to an agreement or agreements being entered into between the club and Ticketus after said acquisition. The second charge under the Companies Act centres on the £18m payment between Mr Whyte's Wavetower company and Rangers to clear a bank debt. The trial before eight men and seven women continues.

text: Huddersfield Giants climbed off the bottom of the Super League table to leave Hull Kingston Rovers as the only winless side in the top flight. The Giants held a 12-0 advantage at half-time following tries from loan debutant full-back Jordan Tansey and Michael Lawrence. Rovers subsequently reduced the margin with Thomas Minns' converted try. However, Aaron Murphy's touchdown restored the 12-point lead and the Giants extended their advantage through Jermaine McGilvary, Larne Patrick and Ukuma Ta'ai. Danny Brough, who troubled the visitors with his tactical kicking, converted all six attempts, one following England winger McGilvary's 100th Super League try, plus a penalty for a personal 14-point tally. Huddersfield had suffered defeat in their opening four Super League fixtures, but the victory allowed them to move above Rovers, who have collected just one point from their initial six matches, following last month's draw with Castleford. In his inaugural match as interim head coach until the season's conclusion, former Rovers captain James Webster's team were outclassed throughout, despite being strengthened by the injury return of former Huddersfield forwards Shaun Lunt and Graeme Horne, whilst James Green and John Boudebza returned from suspension. However, captain Terry Campese lasted merely 42 minutes before departing with a hamstring injury on his return from a nine-month absence following knee reconstruction. Giants coach Paul Anderson confirmed that prop Daniel Smith will not feature again this season after undergoing foot surgery but anticipates fellow front rower Craig Huby to be the next player returning from injury at Easter. Huddersfield coach Paul Anderson: Victory is certainly preferable to defeat. It does ease some pressure, the players are pleased in there. There was no genuine sense of panic but we cannot rest on that. We have an opportunity to begin reducing some points. For 40 to 50 minutes you could observe both teams were slightly nervous but we settled quicker and created numerous opportunities. We remained patient and produced some excellent sets. We simply need to get people back on the field and training consistently. We have not lost anyone else today which is positive. All the people who returned developed into the match and Jordan Tansey made an impact and can only improve as he learns our structures. Hull KR interim coach James Webster told BBC Radio Humberside: Media playback is not supported on this device We were not adequate with the ball at the beginning. We were second best at the ruck and they ran somewhat harder than us. We performed a really good job to remain within 12 points at half-time. We appeared to address several of the issues we discussed at half-time but the fatigue factor really damaged us towards the conclusion. It will be difficult work but we are a confident club and we believe we can reverse it. When Terry Campese was on the ground with his hand raised in the air, you think 'has he injured his knee?' but it is the hamstring in his other leg. Whilst we are obviously disappointed, it is positive that it is not his knee. text: The search for two climbers missing on Ben Nevis has been suspended because conditions were too dangerous. Tim Newton, aged 27, and Rachel Slater, aged 24, both from Bradford, had been mountaineering on the peak during the weekend. The alert was triggered when they were reported overdue from their climbing expedition on Monday. Lochaber Mountain Rescue Team stated that 36 personnel participated in search operations on Tuesday, with two team members becoming caught in an avalanche. It is understood the pair had been camping in a green tent situated behind the Charles Inglis Clark (CIC) memorial hut on the mountain's northern face. A motor vehicle belonging to Ms Slater has been retrieved. Rescue personnel described the weather conditions as challenging, with wind gusts reaching 80/90mph. A statement published on the Lochaber MRT Facebook page declared: Following five hours of searching, it was determined that conditions were too hazardous to continue the search which concentrated on Coire na Ciste and South Trident Buttress area after a potential sighting of two individuals matching their description climbing in this location early Sunday afternoon. The statement continued: Two rescue team members were avalanched whilst traversing beneath No 3 Gully Buttress. Anyone possessing information regarding the missing pair has been requested to contact police in Fort William. Police Scotland issued a photograph of the couple and stated they would have been dressed in climbing equipment similar to that displayed in the image. Ms Slater is a seasoned, well-travelled mountaineer. In a web-based blog, she documented: I've been surrounded by rocks throughout my life as my parents are extremely enthusiastic climbers - the majority of my childhood was spent scrambling about at the cliff base with the occasional straightforward top rope. She is presently working as a mineral, waste and environmental consultant near Bradford. Mr Newton, originally from Leicester, also resides in Bradford and has pursued physics studies at Manchester and Leeds universities, according to his Facebook profile. Logbook records for Ms Slater on UKClimbing.com indicate she has undertaken numerous climbs alongside Mr Newton. Multiple messages have been published on social media platforms from individuals sharing information and expressing hope that the couple will be located safely. On the Lochaber MRT Facebook page, Tony Walker posted: The missing individuals are Rachel Slater (my niece) and her partner Tim Newton. Both highly experienced climbers. Most probably they are dressed in the same attire as shown in the photograph. Any information greatly appreciated. On a climbing forum, Patrick Roman stated he observed the pair during the weekend. He commented: I was outside the CIC on Saturday morning. There were two individuals matching the appearance in the photograph. He was dressed in a red jacket and she in a green and turquoise jacket.

text: A 14-year-old boy who stabbed a supply teacher before bragging about the racially-motivated attack on Facebook has been handed an 11-year sentence. The youth stabbed Vincent Uzomah, 50, in a classroom at Dixons Kings Academy, Bradford, on 11 June. There was clear evidence he assaulted Mr Uzomah because he was black, the city's crown court was told. He received an 11-year extended sentence, comprising six years' detention and five years on licence. The youth, who pleaded guilty to causing grievous bodily harm with intent but denied attempted murder, was informed he could serve half of the six years in custody. He racially abused Mr Uzomah before stabbing him in the abdomen with a kitchen knife he had brought to school, the court was told. Jonathan Sharp, prosecuting, stated the youth had discussed the assault with a friend beforehand, and subsequently made sick boasts about his actions on Facebook. Approximately 20 minutes after the assault, the youth, who was not arrested until six hours later, posted a status update containing the line I stick a blade straight in his tummy. The post received 69 likes, something the judge described as an appalling reflection of a small microcosm of our society. Mr Sharp told the court the youth had taken a dislike to Mr Uzomah in the seven weeks he had worked at the school. The defendant disliked him, claiming he could not teach, and freely referred to him by the epithet beginning with the letter n, including saying it in anger just before he attacked him, he stated. He said the youth attacked Mr Uzomah following a row over his mobile telephone. The teenager was described by witnesses as getting angry, red in the face, Mr Sharp stated. He approached Mr Uzomah and reached into his pocket, but at that point he took out the knife and stabbed Mr Uzomah in the abdomen. Mr Uzomah thought he was going to die. Sentencing the youth, who cannot be named because of his age, Judge Durham Hall QC described him as out of control and a bully who could not tolerate being told off. Speaking outside court, Mr Uzomah stated: As a Christian, I have forgiven this youth who has inflicted this trauma and pain upon me and my family. It was, however, important for the law to run its course and for a strong message to be sent out, especially to children of similar tendencies, that violence is never acceptable. Our prayer for him is that he will make use of the opportunities and support that will be provided to him, to become a changed person who will make a positive contribution to society. Detective Superintendent Simon Atkinson, from West Yorkshire Police, stated: This was a shocking and very serious assault on a man doing a job he loved, and he was fortunate that the consequences were not more serious. His attacker showed no concern by fleeing the scene...he worryingly showed a further lack of remorse towards his victim by boasting about it on social media. Outside court, Mr Sharp stated it was truly remarkable that Mr Uzomah had forgiven his attacker. He stated: The victim has suffered serious physical and psychological injuries, has had to put his career plans on hold and is uncertain when, or if, he will feel able to return to teaching - a profession he loved. It was also profoundly distressing to Mr Uzomah - and shocking - that the youth posted a Facebook update boasting of what he had done. This subsequently received 69 'likes' from his circle of acquaintances. In the circumstances it is remarkable that Mr Uzomah has expressed his desire to forgive the attacker, whilst wishing to see justice done as a deterrent to others. In a statement posted on the Dixons Kings Academy website, the school stated: This was a very shocking crime, and today a young man has had to face the consequences of his actions. We are pleased that Mr Uzomah is making a good recovery, and our school community will continue to do what we can to support Vincent and his family.

text: Ashley Giles has left Lancashire to rejoin Warwickshire as sport director. Former England spinner Giles, aged 43, previously served as director of cricket at Edgbaston and will supervise both the men's and women's sides, alongside the club's academy, in his new position. Dougie Brown departed Warwickshire by mutual agreement in October following four seasons in command. Giles served as Lancashire's cricket director and head coach for two years but was eager to relocate nearer to his family. He represented Warwickshire's preferred candidate to succeed Brown and, having secured an arrangement with the Bears, Lancashire have freed him from his Old Trafford contract, which was scheduled to conclude in 2018. Recently appointed first-team coach Jim Troughton will answer to Giles, who departed Warwickshire in 2012 to assume England's one-day coaching position after the Bears' seventh County Championship victory. The new position at Edgbaston represents an excellent opportunity and I am thrilled to return to Warwickshire, stated Giles, who spent 14 years as a Warwickshire player and appeared in 54 Tests for England. Whilst I possess considerable history with the Bears and have previously experienced success as a player and a coach, this represents a completely new challenge and I anticipate meeting all the players and the new management team in January. Giles guided Lancashire to promotion into County Championship Division One and a first T20 Blast title in 2015, before they narrowly escaped relegation by finishing seventh in the Championship in 2016. He continued: I completely enjoyed my period at Lancashire and I wish to thank chairman Michael Cairns and the board for the opportunity to serve as director of cricket at such an outstanding club. I remain extremely grateful for their understanding and for consenting to release me from my contract so that I may accept this new position with Warwickshire and return to the Midlands, where my family have stayed. Lancashire have appointed Glen Chapple in charge as interim head coach, with another former captain Mark Chilton as interim assistant coach.
