text: Listening to new music is rewarding for the brain, a study suggests. Employing MRI scans, a Canadian team of researchers discovered that regions within the brain's reward centre became activated when individuals heard a song for the first time. The greater the listener's enjoyment of what they were hearing, the stronger the connections proved in the brain region termed the nucleus accumbens. The research is published in the journal Science. Dr Valorie Salimpoor, from the Rotman Research Institute in Toronto, informed the BBC's Science in Action programme: We understand that the nucleus accumbens is associated with reward. However, music is abstract: It is not as though you are genuinely hungry and you are about to receive a piece of food and you are truly excited about it because you are going to consume it - or the same principle applies to sex or money - that is when you would typically observe activity in the nucleus accumbens. But what is fascinating is that you are anticipating and becoming excited over something completely abstract - and that is the next sound that is approaching. Fresh melodies To conduct the research, which occurred at the Montreal Neurological Institute at McGill University, the researchers played 19 volunteers 60 excerpts of fresh music, based upon their musical preferences. Whilst they were listening to the 30-second-long tracks, they had the opportunity to purchase the ones they favoured in a simulated online music store. All of this was undertaken whilst the participants were positioned in an MRI machine. Test yourself with 'How Musical Are You?' Can the tone deaf learn to sing? Through analysing the scans, the researchers discovered that the nucleus accumbens was illuminating and depending upon the level of activity, the scientists could predict whether the participant was likely to purchase a song. Dr Salimpoor stated: As they are listening to this music, we can examine their brain activity and determine how they are appreciating or enjoying this music before they even inform us anything. And that is part of this new direction that neuroscience is pursuing - attempting to understand what people are thinking, and inferring their thoughts and motivations and ultimately their behaviour through their brain activity. The scientists found that the nucleus accumbens was also interacting with another region of the brain termed the auditory cortical stores. This is an area that stores sound information based upon music that people have been exposed to previously. This part of the brain will be unique for each individual, because we have all heard different music in the past, explained Dr Salimpoor. The scientists now wish to discover how this drives our musical tastes, and whether our brain activity can explain why people are attracted to different styles of music. text: Former soap-actress Tracy Brabin has been selected as Labour's candidate for the Batley and Spen by-election prompted by the killing of Jo Cox. The Coronation Street, EastEnders and Emmerdale actress was selected as the party's candidate ahead of fellow contender Jane Thomas. Mrs Cox, who served as MP for Batley and Spen, was shot and stabbed in Birstall, West Yorkshire, on 16 June. The by-election shall be held on 20 October. Ms Brabin was born in Batley and collaborated with Mrs Cox on her campaign to preserve the town's library. She portrayed Tricia Armstrong in Coronation Street during the 1990s before featuring as Roxy Drake in EastEnders and Carole in Emmerdale, and has additionally written for programmes including Family Affairs, Tracy Beaker and Hollyoaks. Ms Brabin, who was selected at a hustings event on Friday, stated she was humbled and privileged to have the opportunity to succeed Mrs Cox. Jo was my inspiration. I intend to do her proud, she stated. Obviously nobody wanted this, but I'm the only person on the ballot paper that can stand up for everyone in Batley and Spen. I'm hoping people will put party politics to one side and we can work together. Meanwhile, the husband of Mrs Cox has held a meeting with US President Barack Obama at the White House in Washington DC. Brendan Cox, who brought his two children, wrote on Twitter that he and the president had talked about Jo and fighting extremism. He praised President Obama as being excellent with the kids, adding that the kids gave him their best drawings. text: Parents who restrict their children to a vegan diet could face a jail term if a controversial bill is passed by the Italian parliament. Such parents, the draft legislation contends, are enforcing a diet lacking essential elements for [children's] healthy and balanced development. The proposal has been put forward by Elvira Savino of the centre-right Forza Italia party. The measure follows several prominent Italian cases in which malnourished children have been placed in care. During four instances over the past 18 months, undernourished children were admitted to hospital in Italy following consumption of a vegan diet. Nevertheless, nutritionists including the American Dietetic Association state that vegan diets are appropriate for children but recommend that attention must be paid to ensure children receive the complete spectrum of necessary nutrients - particularly vitamin B12. Medical professionals suggested in certain cases that the carers of the hospitalised children may not have comprehended how to supplement a vegan diet to render it safe for children. A vegan diet excludes anything which derives from animals: The emergence of the part-time vegans Is it more challenging for vegans to drive themselves to physical extremes? Ms Savino's proposed legislation will be examined by parliamentary committees before proceeding to the chamber for discussion - likely later this year, Reuters news agency reports. Concurrently, three competing bills are under consideration - all seeking to make vegan and vegetarian choices more widespread in Italian canteens. In the introduction of Ms Savino's bill (in Italian), she emphasises the growing conviction in Italy of substantial health benefits offered by a vegetarian or vegan diet. There is no opposition if the individual making this decision is an informed adult. The difficulty emerges when children are concerned... The vegetarian or vegan diet is, indeed, lacking in zinc, iron, vitamin D, vitamin B12 and omega-3. Her draft legislation seeks to condemn the reckless and perilous eating conduct imposed by parents who adopt a vegan diet, to the detriment of minors. Offenders would face up to one year in prison - increasing to a maximum of four years where the child experiences illness or permanent harm and six years in the event of death. Whilst some nutrition specialists have questioned the validity of the bill, other observers have warned that its imprecise language means it could be employed to penalise a far broader range of parents than vegans or vegetarians - for example, the parents of obese children. Some suggest improved public health education rather than punitive measures would be more effective at enhancing children's nutrition.

text: Is Facebook a media company? This abstract question may appear to be the domain of Palo Alto aspirants, Lower East Side podcasters, and media commentators nearer to home. In reality the response, whilst complex, addresses the fundamental nature of democracy in our era. And one cannot comprehend Thursday's announcement from the corporation, regarding its crackdown on false news, without addressing the preceding question above. The measures Facebook is implementing - which span from facilitating the flagging of false news to damaging the finances of false news producers - whilst welcome, fall short of what certain critics would prefer to witness. The transformation in media signifies that platforms such as Facebook are progressively performing what publishers perform. As Tony Haile contended in a recent instalment of the Wall Street Journal's excellent Media Mix podcast, Publishers accomplish five tasks: they create, post, curate, distribute and monetise content. Facebook now accomplishes four of those five... [But] they do not create. I believe even this assertion is questionable. It is accurate that Facebook does not commission original content, or journalism. However the introduction of Facebook Live brings them remarkably close to accomplishing this. When Lavish Reynolds employed that tool to produce an extraordinary broadcast of the moments following her boyfriend Philando Castile being shot by a Minnesota Police officer, she was clearly transmitting live news. Naturally Facebook did not request her to; but through Facebook Live, as through the social network's Instant Articles feature, Facebook enables original journalism, much as Amazon assisted entrepreneurs with its Web Services technology. Financed by advertising; assisting to create enormous quantities of stories; the primary source of news for millions across the globe. That resembles a media company, does it not? And yet Facebook does not perceive it that way, in one crucial respect. It does not wish to use human judgement to arbitrate between truth and falsehood. On Wednesday I spoke extensively to Adam Mosseri, Vice President of Product for News Feed at Facebook. He briefed me on Facebook's latest efforts to clamp down on the false news which, some contend, assisted Donald Trump to enter the White House. Mark Zuckerberg initially described such a claim as crazy, but has since attempted to demonstrate he takes the issue seriously. Hence the announcement that Facebook will accomplish four tasks: Together, these measures will make a difference. As Zuckerberg has contended, and Mosseri reiterated, false news is a very small fraction of the material shared by the Facebook community, and eliminating it completely is impracticable. But there is one, fascinating, crucial respect in which Facebook will not accomplish what its critics desire. It will not ask staff to make a judgement on what is true or false. In other words, it will not employ editors. As Mosseri said to me in relation to the above, this effort to clamp down on false news is algorithmic - Facebook will rely on algorithms, and the judgement of its community of users, to flag potential false news. It will not make those decisions for itself, using its own staff. Years ago, Zuckerberg described Facebook as a utility company. Then some intelligent people pointed out that utilities operate in a regulatory environment. So the emphasis changed to it being a technology company. Just this August, Zuckerberg said we are a tech company, not a media company in Rome. But Facebook's impact on the media industry has been revolutionary, consuming advertising and attracting vast new audiences. Every day there are several pieces lamenting the duopoly that Facebook and Google allegedly possess over the media industry. Those complaints unite the New York Times with The Sun. So whilst Facebook claims not to be a media company, the impact that it has on other media companies, together with its role in disseminating false information, will mean that publishers continue to condemn it. They argue that Facebook may be one of the world's greatest companies, but it is avoiding a crucial public duty - namely, to be arbiters of truth. The world's largest platform, increasingly, has the role once fulfilled by news publishers, without the legal restrictions and social obligations. In short, Facebook is a media company - even though it does not wish to be.

text: The plays of William Shakespeare have endured for centuries, and so have many of the names he created for his characters. Several of those names remain currently popular, whilst even a few of the more unusual ones continue to survive today. For the anniversary of the Bard's death, we spoke to a Hero, a Lysander, a Macbeth and a William Shakespeare to discover how their Shakespearean name has influenced their lives. My parents never truly explained why they wished to call me William, but I suspect it was because of my father. My father was also named William, though he was the first William of whom I am aware in the family. I have not followed that family tradition, my son is named Peter and my daughter Susan. I do not recall people remarking on my name when I was growing up. It was during the War, so I suppose people had other matters on their minds. I have wished to know more about the name and whether our family is linked to the other William Shakespeare. I examined the family tree and we believe there might be a connection, but we are not certain how legitimate it is. I have been reading about William Shakespeare, but I do not have any other links to him. I did visit Stratford upon Avon once. I was in a bookshop there and did offer to sit in a corner and sign some books for visiting tourists - I do not think the shop owner understood the joke. William Shakespeare, London I have always been surrounded by a multitude of cultures and histories, people and experiences, but the one thing that always remains the same, regardless of where I am, is the fact that everybody remembers my Shakespearean middle name. My lecturers and fellow students appear to enjoy my name, probably because we study literature and it seems as though I was destined for this field of study. When I commenced studying for my bachelor's degree, in England, there was no question that I would not study English (and German) literature - I am presently studying for my master's in Sweden. I collect Shakespeare works in various editions and in both English and German, because I am interested in how the works are translated and republished. Shakespeare is an important part of my studies, because his works are constantly referenced or alluded to in new works about post-colonialism and world literature. All in all, I adore my name and it is very precious to me. I love the amusing reactions I receive and the fact that I usually only need to introduce myself once. I have never had a truly bad reaction towards it, unless you count being associated with bad luck because of your name. Me and my two sisters all share the middle name Macbeth and are, therefore, often referred to as the three little witches by the rest of my family. My friends however tend to call me Lady Macbeth when I become angry or say something snobbish (usually about food). So, even if it has just been on a light-hearted and amusing level, my Shakespearean name has always accompanied me around. Shuna Macbeth Blankenhaus, Sweden My parents obviously adore Shakespeare. Ariel was my father's favourite name and he was always fascinated by the shape-shifting sprite seeking freedom, and Ophelia was my great grandmother's name. The Shakespearean connection was not lost on my mother, who was a theatre major at university. It is certainly an icebreaker, and I instantly recognise a Shakespeare enthusiast when introduced if they say: Ariel, as in The Tempest? instead of: Ariel, as in The Little Mermaid? It does amuse people to discover I have a Shakespearean middle name as well, and I am quite sure it always put me on the right foot with my English teachers and literature professors over the years. The name certainly gave me a connection to Shakespeare at an early age, and I have taken considerable interest in his work throughout my life. When I was very young, around the age of five, my parents took me to Shakespeare in the Park in Savannah, Georgia, US. I remember very vividly A Midsummer Night's Dream - I enjoyed it so much that we attended several times. I remember being so delighted by the fairies, the mischievous Puck and the humour of it all. It was magical to me and remains one of my fondest childhood memories. Later in secondary school, I recited Ophelia's monologue from Hamlet for an English class. I still enjoy seeing the occasional play or watching my favourite film adaptations. Naturally, I have reflected on these two characters. Both were restricted in life: Ariel a slave and Ophelia a young woman in a nobleman's world. Life overcame the latter, but she was loved by all and revered in death. Ariel was determined to succeed and won his freedom in the end. Both characters have taught me something about strength and kindness. Ariel Ophelia Meadows, New Zealand My mother and father attended to see A Midsummer Night's Dream, and, afterwards, my mother told my father she wished to call her next child after Lysander. There was no discussion, they both adored the name. Sometimes, when people have only read my name without meeting me in person, they think I am a girl, as my name appears a little bit like Lisanne, which is a common name in Belgium. Fortunately, this has not happened too often. When I introduce myself to new people I often have to repeat my name several times before they realise they have not heard it before. Although it is from A Midsummer Night's Dream, one of the better known plays, it is not well known among average Belgians. But after I explain that it is from a play by Shakespeare, they are impressed and they tell me it is a wonderful name to have. A special name like this is always a good conversation starter, and I have the feeling that it triggered my interest for Shakespeare and other literature and cultural activities. Lysander Fockaert, Belgium My parents apparently named me partly after the character in Much Ado About Nothing and partly after the Greek myth of Hero and Leander. My mother adored Shakespeare. I used to be teased as a child, which was not pleasant, they used to say things like: Why are you not called Heroine as you are a girl? I did not like my name then, but I do like it now. My name is a topic of conversation upon first meeting and is rarely forgotten, which can be embarrassing because I am terrible at remembering names. I notice that Hero is becoming more common as a name. When I was a child, it was extremely rare, (I am mid-50s now). One of [radio presenter] Myleene Klass's children is called Hero, and I saw a writer from a newspaper mentioned she named her daughter Hero. Also, my niece is called Hero, and my brother's friend's daughter is called Hero. My job requires me to email many customers, and they are very often surprised when we then speak on the telephone and they discover I am a woman - a bit disconcerting but amusing. Hero Selwood, Cornwall When I was young, I did not like my name because I got bullied considerably by my classmates. The name Puck was a very strange name at that time. Usually, dogs were named Puck. That is why I always thought I was named after an acquaintance's dog. When I became a little older, I learnt that my parents named me after one of Shakespeare's characters. I felt much better until I discovered that Puck was this mean, male goblin from Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream. Personally, I do not have a particular interest in Shakespeare - but my parents do. My name has affected my life in negative and positive ways. Children my age bullied me, but older people always said to me that they think Puck is a wonderful name to have. Despite the fact I did not like my name when I was younger, I have truly grown to love it. I now like the fact that I have a connection to Shakespeare, and I am honoured to have this unique yet famous name. Puck Creemer, Holland My name certainly receives considerable attention, but people mispronounce it all the time. I was named Portia after the heroine in The Merchant of Venice. However, most people do not know that and ask what it means. They assume I was named after the car, when I first tell them my name. Also, they find it difficult to pronounce when they read it, so I receive many Pour-tia. My parents heard the name when linked with [US talk show host] Ellen DeGeneres, whose wife is the actress Portia de Rossi. But they later discovered more and thought it was classy. I know the story by Shakespeare, and I do like Portia's character - she stands up for what she believes in. I think it is a unique name. Portia Miller, Berkshire My husband is from Stratford upon Avon, and we live in Belfast. We lived in Stratford together for a while some years ago and lived on Arden Street in the centre of town. When we discovered we were having a baby girl, we wished to name her something meaningful but unique. We love to visit the Forest of Arden and generally love all things Shakespearean, so we thought Arden would be a perfect choice of name for our little girl. Fortunately, when she arrived, she suited the name and still does now. Everyone always comments on how beautiful a name it is, and we love it as it is a lovely reminder of Stratford. Lynsey Richards (mother of Arden), Northern Ireland Compiled by Andree Massiah

The Government has pledged to invest £1.4bn to transform young people's mental health services. Statistics reveal one in 50 children under 18 are in contact with specialist mental health services in England. Dr Vautrey stated: This is an emergency. NHS Digital began collecting statistics about under-19s in contact with mental health services in January, and in June the figure stood at 235,189. The information also reveals wide geographical variations in how long young people wait for treatment. text: A dog which went missing on a mountain, sparking a social media campaign by more than 6,000 people to find him, has been rescued. Border Collie Jasper disappeared whilst on a walk up Scafell Pike in the Lake District with his owner Adam Nolan. A mountain rescue team, helicopter, police and dog enthusiasts searched for him and he was discovered on Thursday. A JustGiving page established by Mr Nolan to raise funds for the rescue team had collected more than £25,000 by 19:00 GMT. Jasper was last observed at approximately 14:00 on Sunday at Cam Spout Crag beneath Scafell Pike. The day out was nothing out of the ordinary and Jasper was accustomed to walking and running on the fells, his owner stated. Devastated by his disappearance, Mr Nolan, from Cleator Moor, turned to social media for assistance to locate his four-legged companion, with the #FindJasper campaign becoming viral. On Wednesday, following a possible sighting in Seascale, Mr Nolan pledged he would not cease searching until Jasper was home and in front of the fire. The local community supported the search for Jasper and Wasdale Mountain Rescue located him in the early hours of Thursday. Mr Nolan stated on Facebook: I'm over the moon to announce the safe return of my best friend Jasper. This morning Geoff Horky [from the rescue team] climbed Scafell Pike in response to the information received yesterday regarding the sighting of Jasper near the Scafell Pike summit. Geoff discovered Jasper at 2.00am in very good condition. The Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team were then alerted and commenced the rescue operation. Upon hearing the news I followed the Wasdale Mountain Rescue team to Lingmell Col where I was reunited with Jasper. Naturally, there are numerous individuals whom I would like to thank, but at the moment I would say a huge thank you to Geoff and the Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team for their heroic efforts this morning. A spokesman for Wasdale Mountain Rescue stated: The team are pleased to announce that we have been involved in the successful rescue of Jasper. The team responded and recovered Jasper back to the valley to meet Adam.

text: Sprinter Sacre beat favourite Un De Sceaux to win the coveted Queen Mother Champion Chase for a second time at the Cheltenham Festival. Longshot Special Tiara (16-1) claimed third position for trainer Henry de Bromhead. Another previous champion, the Gary Moore-trained 10-year-old Sire De Grugy finished eighth on this occasion. Its'afreebee persevered courageously for third, seven lengths further behind. Walsh remained competitive aboard Roi Des Francs in the RSA Chase but ultimately weakened to sixth as the Nigel Twiston-Davies-trained Blaklion, (8-1) partnered by 22-year-old Ryan Hatch, succeeded in a thrilling battle with Shaneshill to triumph by half a length. Market leader More Of That, ridden by Barry Geraghty, finished third, another eight lengths adrift. Gordon Elliott's eight-year-old Diamond King, (12-1) with Davy Russell aboard, charged through on the outside to secure victory by one length and a quarter. text: Peterhead boss Jim McInally hailed his League Two side after they stunned Hearts in the League Cup. I believed we merited it, McInally stated after Rory McAllister's late penalty defeated the Premiership side 2-1 at Balmoor Stadium. For 70 minutes we were arguably the superior team and we received the fortune at the conclusion, McInally informed BBC's Sportsound. Hearts head coach Ian Cathro stated: We're disappointed and we ought to be performing better in these circumstances. Jason Brown nodded the League Two side into an early advantage in their Group B fixture, with Kyle Lafferty equalising with his fourth strike in three matches. With the League Cup tie seeming headed for a penalty shoot-out and a battle for a bonus point, McAllister's penalty ensured a memorable victory. Paradoxically, we netted or obtained our penalty when we had genuinely fatigued in the final 10 minutes and [were] clinging on, stated McInally. I'm tremendously pleased for the players because they focused for the entire match and distributed it effectively when they required to. [Playing] twice in four days is challenging for part-timers. Many of these lads have just travelled up from Glasgow today. Willie Gibson and Greg Fleming, the goalkeeper, [have travelled] from Dumfries. Hearts were up here last evening resting. Therefore, it makes it even superior and the significant thing is we have an opportunity of progressing now if we can triumph on Saturday [against Elgin City]. Cathro, whilst disappointed with the outcome, considers his players are still bonding. We anticipated a challenging match, he stated. And it's invariably the situation, particularly at the beginning of these matches when you compete against teams from the lower divisions. We're disappointed and we ought to be performing better in these circumstances but we're at a phase where new players are present and we're developing some aspects and matters are a work in progress. We began to establish ourselves ahead in the match, we possessed some energy and competed with slightly more urgency as matters developed. However we didn't convert our opportunities and perhaps some of our choices in the final third weren't entirely correct. We endured because of that but, as I mentioned, there are numerous new partnerships within the team and there's considerable positive developments building across all three [League Cup] matches and we'll continue to work to prepare ourselves and improve. We're disappointed with the outcome and maintain expectations which are higher than that - we advance very swiftly and concentrate on Saturday [against Dunfermline at Tynecastle].

text: The EU's latest Earth observer has returned its first pictures. Sentinel-3a, which launched a fortnight ago, shall maintain a particular emphasis on the oceans, measuring the colour, temperature and height of sea surfaces. The data will prove invaluable to weather forecasters, and to marine biologists attempting to comprehend the health of global waters. The initial images display the Strait of Gibraltar, the Californian coastline, and an ice-covered Svalbard archipelago. They were captured by the spacecraft's Ocean and Land Colour Instrument, OLCI. As the designation indicates, this sensor is not exclusively dedicated to ocean work, and shall collect data about land surfaces as well, monitoring the condition of vegetation across the planet, for instance. We received the initial images on 29 February, but we have had to spend considerable time working on them to achieve the correct calibration, stated Volker Liebig, the director of Earth observation at the European Space Agency (Esa). We are not prepared with everything aboard the satellite yet, that is evident; but we considered it important to release the pictures, he informed BBC News. Several months of testing still remain ahead before the spacecraft commences routine observations. Sentinel-3a represents one in a series of satellites being acquired for the European Union's Copernicus programme. The data from this multi-billion-euro project is anticipated to drive numerous applications, ranging from air quality updates to crop-performance monitoring, from water-resource management to transport infrastructure planning. Esa serves as the technical agent, defining the design of the satellites and then commissioning industry to construct them. For Sentinel-3, all the subsequent models - b, c and d - have already been contracted, ensuring there should be operational continuity in orbit extending through to at least 2030. Besides OLCI, the new satellite possesses a radiometer to measure the temperature of ocean and land surfaces, and an altimeter to measure ocean height. Together, these two instruments shall prove useful for tracking phenomena such as El Nino, which witnesses warm waters bulge in the eastern Pacific every few years. The current event - one of the largest on record - has triggered disruption in weather patterns worldwide. It comes as no surprise then that Europe's national meteorological agencies are particularly eager to obtain Sentinel-3 data, to utilise in their numerical forecasting models. Indeed, Sentinel-3 is an ocean workhorse, but it is also a global workhorse, stated Esa senior scientist Dr Craig Donlon. The vegetation products we shall obtain from OLCI in 21 bands will be truly excellent, so there will be a substantial amount we shall derive from it simply examining land surfaces. And then there is all the work it will undertake measuring ice surfaces, and rivers and lakes using its altimeter, he informed BBC News. Sentinel-3a joins two other series satellites already in orbit. Sentinel-1a launched in 2014 and is equipped with a radar to measure the shape of the Earth's surface; Sentinel-2a, which ascended last year, possesses a colour camera to record how the land surface is being utilised and how that changes over time. Additional Sentinels are forthcoming, and the European Commission and Esa have even begun to consider extending the initial suite of sensors. There exists a desire for Europe to possess some form of space-borne carbon-monitoring capability - a tool to verify that countries are implementing policies to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. text: It didn't much look like a protest. Numerous casually attired, cheerful middle-class Germans - some accompanied by children, others with dogs, conversing enthusiastically in splendid parkland on Hamburg's periphery during a bright Sunday afternoon. However, this constituted a protest assembly, compiling a petition in a bid to prevent a new refugee facility being constructed on the green space. Residents were eager to stress that they harboured no anti-immigrant sentiment. Their primary objective, they stated, was safeguarding an area of natural splendour. Yet once conversation commenced, wider concerns quickly emerged. Birgit remarked that securing accommodation was sufficiently challenging for Germans. Hamburg experiences an acute housing shortage under normal circumstances. With the influx of tens of thousands of immigrants, the port city risked bursting at its limits. In desperation, officials have been converting shipping containers into refugee accommodation and requisitioning vacant commercial premises and open areas to construct new migrant facilities. I believe Angela Merkel has no comprehension of what she initiated, Birgit concluded. Hanno continued shaking his head whilst declaring, I simply believe Germany cannot integrate this quantity of people. It constitutes a genuine concern. A genuine concern. This represented no demonstration by Germany's minority anti-immigrant far right, so skilled at seizing headlines. These were Angela Merkel's principal supporters: the prosperous middle classes. Now afflicted by doubt and uncertainty. To clarify: most Germans do not question an obligation to assist those escaping war or human rights violations but they do find the enormous number of arrivals disturbing. Over one million refugees are anticipated here by year's end. Some specialists we consulted indicated the figure could reach 1.5 million. Like a football team's captain, Chancellor Merkel continues repeating: Wir schaffen es! (We can manage it!). It represents her version of Barack Obama's Yes We Can - but increasingly Germans are enquiring: How? Only one in three here state they support Mrs Merkel's migrant policy, according to the latest poll. And she is declining in popularity ratings. The jest used to be that she was a politician of 'small steps' who made decisions only after she had examined the opinion polls. But a summer of refugees drowning in the Mediterranean and desperate crowds gathering at Europe's gates appears to have altered all that. Mrs Merkel completely astonished her compatriots a month ago by unilaterally declaring all Syrian refugees welcome and refusing to establish an upper limit on how many Germany would accept. It appeared like a passionate outburst, a spontaneous abandonment of caution by a woman traditionally admired by Germans for her stable, strong and stoical character. All coveted qualities here. Florian Juerg, a branding consultant, questions whether Angela Merkel is now expressing her alternative self. Until now she has behaved like the sensible scientist that she is, he informed me (Mrs Merkel is a qualified physicist). But suddenly she has transformed back into the morally-driven pastor's daughter of her youth. Hamburg serves as the German centre for marketing and brand imaging. I enquired of Florian whether Brand Merkel would be damaged by the migrant crisis. Not in the long-term, he informed me. Establishing a brand requires considerable time and the past 10 years of Merkel as Chancellor have been beneficial for Germans. Hers is a robust brand. For now. But if her refugee policy fails, it will tarnish her political legacy. Mrs Merkel's nickname here is Mutti, or Mummy. Election after election, Germans have placed their confidence in her to determine what is best for them. She is regarded as crucial in making Germany the success story it is today. The manner she is managing the migrant crisis represents the greatest gamble of her political career. Brand Merkel may have helped make Brand Germany great but she could now inadvertently harm her country. The arrival of so many asylum seekers simultaneously will affect Germany's economy, its society and its politics. Already there are well-documented divisions within Mrs Merkel's own conservative bloc. We must achieve the correct balance, stated Lorenz Caffier, CDU Interior Minister of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The German constitution requires that we care for refugees but the benefits we provide them are too generous. Frankly, I am astonished at any migrant who does not choose to come to Germany. Our benefit system functions like a travel agency. We must prioritise the wellbeing of our own people first. German newspapers are filled with reports about the benefits refugees receive compared to German citizens on welfare, leading, in some quarters, to a sense of injustice. There is also a more widespread concern about pressures on the national health and education systems. Germany cannot accommodate everyone, Mr Caffier told me. Until now we had no choice. Angela Merkel did not open the door to the refugees. They were already at the door. What was she going to do - dispatch tanks to the Austrian border? Actually it is impossible to close borders. Any politician who suggests that is deceiving. He insisted emphatically that the rest of Europe play its part. We Germans cannot do this alone. Brussels must decide whether it will focus on the curvature of cucumbers and bananas or address European issues of importance. In the meantime, other European leaders are not queuing up to accept asylum seekers by the hundreds and thousands. Chancellor Merkel's leading role in the migrant crisis is as controversial in the rest of Europe as it is at home. The queen of consensus politics exists no more.

text: Former bouncer Levi Bellfield, 43, has been convicted of murdering three young women and trying to kill another in south-west London and Surrey. Here are profiles of the women he targeted during his campaign of violence. Amanda Dowler, known as Milly, was a pretty, popular and intelligent 13-year-old girl. To all intents and purposes she was an ordinary girl who was developing into a fine young woman, prosecutor Brian Altman informed the Old Bailey. Milly resided in Walton with her parents Bob and Sally and elder sister Gemma, to whom the court heard she was close. Gemma informed the court: We would retire to bed at the same time and lie in the room discussing our day. Milly and I had no secrets and she would tell me about boys at school she fancied. Milly admired Gareth Gates and had seen him at a Pop Idol concert several days before she died. She had been anticipating an upcoming school performance, where she was due to see a boy she liked. However, the court also heard there was another aspect to her, as poems and a goodbye letter were discovered after her death, indicating she was unhappy. Milly was in Year 9 at Heathside School in Weybridge, where her mother Sally taught mathematics. It was only by chance that she took the route home which saw her cross Bellfield's path - she would normally have alighted at another station but had gone to a café with friends. She was one of the most amusing people I had ever met. She was always attempting to make people laugh and smile, her friend Danielle Sykes said. Marsha McDonnell, 19, had completed her A-levels and was taking a gap year before commencing university when she died. Described in court as an attractive blonde, she was attacked by Bellfield just yards from the Hampton home she shared with her parents, Phil and Ute, her two sisters and younger brother. Ms McDonnell, who was employed in a gift shop in Kingston, had visited the cinema with friends on the night she was attacked. Her sister Nathalie said: She always considered other people. She was a free spirit. Speaking after the verdict, her uncle, Shane McDonnell, said: Five years have passed since the night our beloved Marsha was so cruelly taken from this world, a girl that only had love in her heart, brutally slain by a man who only has hatred in his. Her uncle described the family's loss as devastating. Marsha we miss you. Our world now is incomplete, like a rainbow with a colour missing. We thank you for the joy that you brought us in your brief life. Your goodness, sense of fun, spirit and passion for life remain with us, he said. Ms McDonnell was passionate about music and a music room at the local children's hospice is dedicated to her memory. Her uncle said: For her family, life will never quite be the same ever again. The pain and hurt that we carry will always be there. It is a sentence with no remission. Amelie Delagrange, 22, had a passion for the English language and had moved to Britain to further her studies. Ms Delagrange, from Amiens in France, had passed her baccalaureate examinations with ease, and spent six weeks residing in Manchester as part of a language course. She enjoyed and wished to return to the UK. She had been living in Twickenham for just three months when she was killed. Ms Delagrange was employed at a patisserie in Richmond, had a close circle of both English and French friends and was happy, the court heard. Her parents Jean Francois and Dominique Delagrange travelled from France to the Old Bailey to hear details of their daughter's death. She was a good student, sensible, and never gave her parents any problems, her mother informed the court. Her boyfriend, Olivier Lenfant, also described her as a sensible girl who thought she lived in a safe area. In a statement Ms Delgrange's parents Dominique and Jean-Francoise said: It is nearly four years since our lives and our family's lives were so seriously disrupted, descending into a horror - a living nightmare. They added: We would like to have heard from Bellfield a confession of sorts, some evidence of remorse. In this we were disappointed. A memorial tree and a bench dedicated to her memory were placed on Twickenham Green by the local community and her family. Kate Sheedy, was 18 and the head girl at her convent school in Isleworth when she was attacked in 2004. She had spent the evening bidding farewell to friends after her last day at Gumley House School and was walking home when she was struck down by a car. She missed her A-levels because of the attack but was granted her predicted grades by the examination board and went on to study history and drama at York University. The trial heard she remains mentally and physically scarred by the attack. In a statement, Ms Sheedy said: On the day I was attacked I was celebrating about moving onto a new and exciting time in my life. All that hope and excitement was taken from me and I thought my life had changed for ever. The attack meant she attended university a year later than she had hoped. I will never be able to forget what happened to me, the scars on my body and the memories I have, are something I will never be rid of, but hopefully I can move on. she said. On top of the physical and mental ordeal, Ms Sheedy said she had also suffered additional trauma and stress from the police investigation.

Former five-weight boxing world champion Mayweather shall face UFC lightweight title-holder McGregor across 12 rounds under boxing regulations in August. He referred to black people as 'monkeys', stated the American, 40, during a press conference at Wembley Arena on Friday. Subsequently, when the pair entered a boxing ring at the event for the official promotion, Mayweather addressed McGregor as: You punk. You faggot. You ho. The two men have undertaken a series of press conferences in recent days to promote the bout, with stops in Los Angeles and Toronto before the journeys to New York and London. The 29-year-old Irishman has drawn criticism for a series of remarks during those events and is alleged to have made racist statements during the third stop of the tour in New York on Thursday. He completely disrespected black women, added Mayweather. Then he spoke disrespectfully to my mother and he spoke disrespectfully to my daughter. The American added on Friday: Racism still exists. I shall not stoop that low and speak about his partner or speak about his child. I am pleased that he just had a healthy child and he has a beautiful family. Responding to Mayweather at the New York press conference on Thursday, McGregor said: I am a multicultural individual and I do not have any ill feelings towards anyone. I do not even see colour. Sexist and homophobic language was used continually. The hype and hoopla - what should have been a carnival of over the top bravado - sadly had a misogynistic and outdated overtone.

text: A new chair-based gymnastics exercise programme has significant benefits for people with dementia, says a report. Media playback is not supported on this device Over 150 individuals have participated in the Love to Move scheme operated by the British Gymnastics Foundation (BGF). Research conducted by Age UK discovered the scheme to possess demonstrable benefits in the physical, emotional and cognitive aspects of older people. The organisers now seek to train additional people to deliver the programme and make it more broadly accessible. This age and dementia-friendly programme is astounding people with its life-transforming benefits, stated BGF manager Patrick Bonner. So many individuals involved are witnessing their lives improving as a consequence and it is inconceivable that people are recovering functions which were believed to be lost through participating in the Love to Move classes. I believed the programme would, at most, simply be capable of slowing down the rate of dementia advancing, but I am discovering some participants seem to be recovering functions which were believed to be lost In South Korea and Japan, outcomes have been so encouraging the programme has been entirely state-funded and operates in every care facility across the two nations. Exercise in any form can provide a multitude of health benefits for those with mental and physical ailments. Dementia is no exception. When the BGF discovered a chair-based exercise programme was producing remarkable results throughout care facilities in Japan and South Korea, it was resolved to bring it to the UK. Based on outcomes published in 2016 from the original Japanese programme, it was evident to the BGF that these simple exercises - founded around cognitive stimulation, memory arousal and music - could have a tremendous impact on the lives of dementia sufferers. By taking the core principles of the Japanese scheme and adapting them to suit British culture, the BGF developed the Love to Move programme in a pilot scheme. Can you tap your head and rub your stomach simultaneously? Even if you can, it requires considerable concentration. By practising it, you are enhancing your ability for the right and left sides of your brain to process information independently of each other. The Love to Move programme is founded on the concept of bilaterally asymmetrical movement (performing different movements with the right and left sides of the body simultaneously). By increasing the capacity to perform bilateral movement, the brain increases the number of connections it creates between its neurons, resulting in an increase in cognitive ability. For individuals with dementia, the Love to Move programme has been proven to increase their capacity to process everyday tasks such as feeding themselves, doing crafts and playing bingo, as well as socialising with friends and family. Do you know a family member, a friend, a colleague, who has dementia? Chances are you do. Download the booklet here Whether they have just been diagnosed, or have had the illness for several years, those close to them would give anything to witness an improvement in their health. The BGF understands this and is eager to share its exercises with the public in the hope they can provide those affected, both now and in the future, with a practical and gentle way to improve their health. The BGF has created a downloadable booklet containing some of the key exercises for people to try with top tips from head coach Kim Hall. The guide seeks to give an insight into the structure and history of the programme, as well as showing some of the key coordination exercises. Over a period of two years in the Cambridgeshire region, the Love to Move programme has delivered sessions focusing on improving coordination, posture, movement and core strength. In conjunction with the pilot scheme, staff from one care facility were asked to complete feedback forms for a sample of residents who took part in the exercise classes. Two residents involved were keen not to go off with their visitors…they did not want to miss the class, so they got them to join in as well! Key results from pilot scheme feedback: Results from the pilot scheme indicate exercises such as hand rotations, finger and thumb tapping, drawing shapes in the air and nose and ear grabbing, are effective ways to enhance coordination, whereas exercises focusing on balance and core have better equipped participants to sit, unaided, in their chairs. Those with more severe cognitive decline were seen to develop a more positive emotional state. By joining the classes, it was visible to the care facility staff that participants were visibly enjoying themselves, appeared more relaxed and even remembered the class and looked forward to the next one. Social interaction is often difficult for those with dementia, especially for those who would not normally have the opportunity to mix with other residents in the same facility. The pilot scheme gave these residents the opportunity to build bonds with one another, provide encouragement to their fellow Love to Movers, and socialise after the session. As with any pilot scheme, the aim is to learn, adjust and expand; and this is what the BGF hopes for. I feel stronger. I have difficulty moving, but I have started to move more than I have before The findings from Age UK reveal sessions need to take place in a social, enjoyable environment, be led by confident, patient staff and include time for refreshment afterwards. The BGF aims to replicate Japan's success and offer the Love to Move programme to all care facilities up and down the country. They say a large amount of staff training is required, in addition to a nationwide awareness campaign and a group of trained coaches to deliver the sessions.

text: The doctor at the centre of the Nike Oregon Project (NOP) drugs investigation altered athletes' medical records before handing them to anti-doping authorities, according to new disclosures. Dr Jeffrey Brown, alongside controversial NOP coach Alberto Salazar, has been under investigation by the US Anti-Doping Agency (Usada), following allegations of doping and unethical practice at NOP made by the BBC's Panorama programme and ProPublica in 2015. The elite endurance camp receives funding from Nike and operates under Salazar's leadership, who has coached Britain's double Olympic champion Mo Farah since 2011. Both Salazar and Dr Brown categorically deny any wrongdoing. In February this year, an interim report by Usada investigators concerning the NOP allegations was leaked by the Russian hacking group Fancy Bears. Details of various alleged anti-doping rule violations outlined in the report were published by the Sunday Times, the BBC and the New York Times. Usada has not yet formally charged anyone in connection with its investigation. Now, fresh disclosures seen by the BBC and ProPublica further implicate Dr Brown, a Texas-based endocrinologist who has treated numerous Salazar athletes and has been previously accused of prescribing thyroid medication (which is not prohibited under World Anti-Doping Agency rules) to athletes to enhance performance. Dr Brown denies this. Dr Brown, who serves as Salazar's personal physician, provided to Usada the medical records of certain athletes, including Steve Magness, then also Salazar's assistant coach. However, Magness, a central contributor to the BBC/ProPublica investigation in 2015, claims his medical notes have been altered by Dr Brown. He states he requested a copy of his notes to be provided to him in August 2015, before he signed a release form to permit Usada to obtain them from his former physician. One note shows details of an infusion of a controversial but legal supplement L-carnitine performed by Dr Brown in his office in Texas, on the instructions of Salazar, in 2011. The note on the left is, according to Magness, his copy of the note of the infusion, a medical procedure that involved Dr Brown placing him on a drip for more than four hours. In the same note subsequently provided by Dr Brown's office to Usada, on the right, and seen in the Usada report, various additions appear to have been made. A number of ticks appear to have been added under 'EXAM' options, including 'General,' 'Lungs,' 'Thyroid,' 'CV' (cardiovascular), and 'Neuro,' suggesting a comprehensive health check has been conducted by Dr Brown on Magness. Magness, who departed NOP in 2012 and is now a coach at the University of Houston, states those checks were never performed. He states: I do not recall these being conducted. I was not even in a patient room, but instead in his office during this visit. I do not recall him going through his normal checks of my thyroid or [anything else]. My only speculation is that [those boxes were ticked] to make it appear like care for the patient had been provided. He might have realised after the fact that when you have a patient, your doctoral duty is to the health of that individual. And that without the proper checks, it might appear like he was prioritising a company, Nike, Salazar, that was paying him over the health of his patient. Dr Brown had been my physician since the age of 16. The Usada reports alleges Dr Brown committed at least four anti-doping violations. Dr Brown categorically denies breaking anti-doping rules. The Texas Medical Board is also investigating Dr Brown, but it declined to comment. The supplement, L Carnitine, is legal, and is produced naturally in the body and assists in converting fat to energy. Salazar had been excited by a study suggesting the benefits of L-carnitine and had been keen to trial it on his athletes. After testing it on Magness, Salazar wrote to Lance Armstrong, who was then training for a long-distance triathlon. He told the now disgraced former cyclist: Lance, call me asap! We have tested it and it's amazing. You are the only athlete I'm going to tell the actual numbers to other than Galen Rupp. It's too incredible. Magness states he had been a reluctant guinea pig. Wada rules stipulate that infusions of any kind must be of less than 50ml every six hours - but according to the Usada report infusions of this relatively tiny amount of L-carnitine would be largely ineffective for an athlete's performance. Analysing the available data from the notes, Usada experts have concluded the infusion levels must have been significantly greater than 50ml and therefore constitute a breach of doping rules. Usada believes similar protocols were used on up to six of Salazar's other US NOP athletes, including Dathan Ritzenhein. Usada also believes the medical notes relating to Ritzenhein provided by Dr Brown have also been altered surreptitiously to suggest the infusion was within the Wada limit of 50ml. In this case, an annotation of 40ml appears to have been added before submission to Usada. The Usada report concludes that Salazar and Dr Brown were aware that infusions administered to NOP athletes including Magness and Ritzenhein were above the legal limits and violated Wada rules. The report concludes: Usada has found that these potential anti-doping rule violations appear to have wholly or largely occurred in the context of a larger conspiracy between Nike Oregon Project coach Alberto Salazar and Houston endocrinologist Dr Jeffrey Brown to collude in order to employ risky and untested alternative and unconventional [and sometimes potentially unlawful] uses of medical procedures and prescription medications [including both substances and methods prohibited under the rules of sport…] to attempt to increase the testosterone, energy and blood levels of Nike Oregon Project athletes in order to boost athletic performance. The Usada report credits Magness, who became aware that rules had been violated, for withdrawing from future competitions because he felt he had been given an unfair advantage. Though Magness has contributed significantly to the Usada investigation as a whistleblower, he may also face a ban for his part in the L-carnitine experiment. Dr Brown's lawyer told the BBC and ProPublica the allegations against him were false. In a letter, lawyer Joan Bain stated the Usada report leak was unlawful and accused it of fake news. Ms Bain said patient confidentiality prevented Dr Brown from responding to specific enquiries. Ms Bain was also highly critical of Usada and its investigation, stating: Notwithstanding its name, you should understand that Usada is not an official government entity, but rather a private corporation which stands to gain financially through publicity, essentially using the press to spread its own 'fake news'. She wrote that this was the latest attempt by Usada to bait Dr Brown into breaking the law by 'leaking' false information to journalists in the hope that Dr Brown will cross the line whilst trying to defend himself. In reference to the allegations notes were altered, she said: No-one at Dr Brown's office has inappropriately changed medical records. All medical records provided to Usada were accurate and provided with the patient's consent. She added: Dr Brown did not break any Wada rules and is unaware of any violation of Wada rules by Alberto Salazar… Dr Brown did not infuse any active athlete with more than 50ml of an L-carnitine solution. L-carnitine is an FDA approved amino acid supplement. It is not a banned substance. Following the response from Ms Bain, Magness wrote to her and Dr Brown waiving confidentiality on the specific notes the BBC and ProPublica were enquiring about, but Ms Bain did not provide further comment. Alberto Salazar has always strenuously denied breaking Wada rules or putting the health of his athletes at risk, and in response to the BBC and ProPublica's investigation published a lengthy and detailed response. In 2014, Mo Farah received an injection of L-carnitine before a major race which UK Athletics (UKA) doctor Robin Chakraverty failed to record properly. Before the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee in April, Dr Chakraverty said the injection was 13.5mls, well within the legal limit of 50ml, though UKA chairman Ed Warner called his failure to record the treatment properly inexcusable. The use of the substance by Farah remains under investigation by Usada, according to the leaked report, to determine whether rules were violated. Farah states he has never broken any rules and has vowed to stand by Salazar unless he is proven to have cheated anti-doping rules.

text: In our series of letters from African journalists, Nigerian writer and novelist Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani looks at the clamour for assistance that accompanies a politician's rise to office. These are external links and will open in a new window The political party primaries in Nigeria have concluded and voters now possess a clearer understanding of whose opportunity it may be to apportion the national wealth following the elections in February 2015. However, the victorious candidates will not be the sole individuals claiming their portion of the nation's resources. In Nigeria, news of an individual's electoral success frequently travels at lightning speed, across rivers and mountains and beyond fields and forests, to his relatives in every corner of the world. Those without employment believe their period of joblessness is approaching its conclusion; those lacking education consider it will shortly present no obstacle to ascending the corporate hierarchy; those in distant territories commence plans to return home. Shortly, these relatives and associates begin their journey towards the successful candidate. They telephone him; they dispatch text messages; they arrive at his entrance. They volunteer to assist his campaign in whatever manner possible; they arrange prayer meetings for his triumph, typically late at night in his sitting room. A colleague of mine who resides in Lagos informed me last week that he was journeying to Benin city. His associate had recently secured a position in the House of Assembly there. Another individual he knew was destined for another senior role. He's a close associate of my elder brother in Florida, he stated. I've already informed my brother: 'You'd better travel down and exchange ideas with him and introduce us to him.' Another colleague whose spouse is a close ally of a victorious candidate in one of Nigeria's most desirable states told me her telephone did not cease ringing following his victory announcement. People had been telephoning to extend congratulations. Indeed, even I had telephoned for that precise purpose. In Nigeria, the tradition has consistently been that anyone who enters power, who suddenly discovers himself wielding a knife with which to slice the national wealth, must invite his clan to both cut and consume it alongside him. The most inexcusable transgression a politician can perpetrate is to overlook his people following his assumption of office. He must acknowledge his sisters, brothers, cousins, nieces, nephews, in-laws, associates, schoolmates, and others. Preferably through contracts, appointments and employment. Failure to act accordingly will result in mockery and exclusion and on the day his term concludes, he will discover himself entirely isolated. Long following his burial, the resentful voices will persist in their criticism. Local chronicles will permanently document him as having refused his relatives their opportunity. I have encountered several entertaining accounts regarding the arrival of people from the Niger Delta region into Abuja, the Nigerian capital, following their kinsman, Goodluck Jonathan's, presidential election in 2011. One of my preferred narratives was recounted by my British-Nigerian colleague who instructs in one of those Abuja institutions where the children pay enormous fees in dollars and ridicule their teachers' inexpensive mobile telephones. She was astonished when a particular student, during a science lesson, appeared to understand more about crustaceans than one would anticipate of a child his age in the city. This child stood before the class and explained in considerable detail how the creatures are captured, cleaned and prepared. At the conclusion, my colleague summoned the boy privately and enquired how he possessed such extensive knowledge of the subject. The child revealed that he had matured in the creeks, where his family conducted small-scale crustacean trading for survival. That explains why the news of a candidate's potential elevation into political office generates such elation. In numerous regions of the world, it demands years of consistent advancement for one's financial situation to fundamentally change. Here in Nigeria, all it requires is an election, and a fresh political appointment. Suddenly, a child progresses from catching crustaceans in the creeks to an elite school in Abuja. Insatiable relatives and associates constitute the primary driver behind Nigeria's corruption challenge. Consider the thousands queued with extended hands behind each political office bearer. Attempt informing them that you plan to reform the system now that it is finally their opportunity to benefit. If you would like to comment on Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani's column, please do so below.

text: Learning a foreign language should be made compulsory in primary schools here, a new report has said. These are external links and will open in a new window. In Northern Ireland, acquiring a second language is not a compulsory component of the primary school curriculum. In England and Scotland, by contrast, primary school students are required to study a foreign language. The examination of primary languages in Northern Ireland has been conducted by researchers from Stranmillis University College. The authors surveyed language instruction at more than 100 schools. They discovered that Spanish and French were most favoured in schools where languages were delivered. Some students also studied German or Mandarin. Nevertheless, not all primary schools provided an additional language. This prompted the authors to determine that there was a lack of equity in provision for children throughout the country. They also discovered little consistency in how frequently languages were delivered to students, and when they commenced learning a language. Some primary headteachers also voiced concerns about the level of support and resources available to their staff and students. Nevertheless, the majority of headteachers and teachers who took part in the study agreed that studying an additional language was important and valuable. However, they also stated teaching foreign languages was not a priority for schools as it was not assessed or measured. The report's authors stated that the development of language skills was vital for economic prosperity, social cohesion and the acceptance of diverse cultural identities. It is hoped that the findings of this study may encourage policy makers, business and educational providers to support the revision and improvement of current curriculum provision in additional language learning, the report stated. It also stated that language learning was conducive to economic growth and that can enhance the lives and future employability of children and young people. Across the European Union (EU) more than 80 per cent of primary students study an additional language. The research was commissioned by the Northern Ireland Languages Council. It is a body established by the Department of Education, and more than 20 organisations are represented on the council, from business, education and the community sector.

text: Lewis Hamilton collided with Mercedes team-mate Nico Rosberg on the last lap before passing him to win a thrilling Austrian Grand Prix. After having to endure a round of booing from the predominantly German-Austrian crowd, Hamilton added on the podium: He made an error into Turn One and I had an opportunity to go around the outside in Turn Two. Behind Rosberg at the finish was Red Bull's Daniel Ricciardo and McLaren's Jenson Button, who drove a strong race to convert his remarkable third place on the grid to a strong points finish. Then his engineers called him in for a first pit-stop to change to the more durable soft tires, while the Mercedes stayed out on the brittle super-soft. Rosberg, who had avoided the collision with Kimi Raikkonen fairly easily, managed to catch up to twenty-one seconds and finished fourth behind Kimi and his team-mate Sebastian Vettel when, on lap twenty-one, Hamilton stopped for the first time. This should have been enough to keep him in the lead, but he was delayed by a problem with his left rear wheel in the pits and came out behind Rosberg. After a mid-race safety car, it first appeared that Rosberg would change cars twice, and that Hamilton only once—which was indeed the Mercedes plan. The safety car was activated when Vettel’s right rear tire burst on lap 27 of the race, within the projected life span of the tires, as the tyre manufacturer had warned. It was unfortunate that Mercedes had to decide on a one-stop operation for Lewis, so that both cars would have to stop on the same lap, with the first stop for the Mercedes on lap 54. The tires fitted to the Mercedes were already used, while Rosberg was given new supersofts, which the world champion didn’t have. Behind Rosberg came the Red Bull of Daniel Ricciardo and the McLaren of Jenson Button, who had worked hard to convert a great start into a strong finish after his amazing third-place start. Vettel, ahead of Rosberg, was irritated at missing yet another opportunity, which, this season, has become a regular occurrence for Ferrari. He was right, and this is what led to the dramatic finale. Button, who had stayed second for seven laps, had been in the thick of a midfield battle, and he was pleased to have ended up ahead of the pack. "Suddenly the tyre blew," said Vettel, who was the last driver to experience a blown tyre during a race, when his tyre burst at a speed of 200 kph in last year's Belgian Grand Prix.

text: In our series of letters from African journalists, veteran Ghanaian journalist Elizabeth Ohene reflects on why in Ghana a person's age is not etched in stone. These are external links and will open in a new window Ghanaians do not particularly cherish numerical precision. We tend to be rather relaxed, particularly with figures relating to age. An individual's birth date or age is not deemed significant and very seldom appears in any account concerning that person. I understand that in numerous regions of the world, once you are born and you obtain a birth date, it remains with you. It is immutable and you perish with it. In Ghana, it is commonplace to observe announcements in newspapers declaring a modification in someone's birth date. This frequently occurs when an employed person's retirement date is approaching. Individuals then swear affidavits to alter their records from the 59-year-olds they are recognised to be, to the 55-year-olds that they wish to be so they can continue earning wages for several additional years. According to the constitution, the retirement age for most public servants is 60. Seven years younger Some individuals have been recognised to swear affidavits to modify their birth date that would place them in Primary Class One before they were born. The most striking Notice of Change of Date of Birth I have witnessed was one that decreased an official's age by seven years. I am addressing this topic because of a recent news item that I believed went far beyond the exceptional, even for Ghana. The news report stated that approximately 800 teachers had petitioned the Ghana Education Service to have their ages modified. Some desired their birth dates altered to make them younger and a few wanted their dates modified to make them older than what appeared on their documentation. The news story was received with considerable outrage and I remarked to myself: This must indicate Ghana is finally joining the remainder of the world in showing respect to birth dates. How can individuals desire their birth dates to be altered? was the incredulous response to the story I heard from numerous young people. However, the head of one of the teaching unions emerged to make a vigorous defence of his members. The teachers desired their birth dates modified only because, according to him, errors had been made at the time of their employment by the payroll departments in recording the dates. This phenomenon has been feasible because very few births are documented. Once upon a time it was illiterate parents that did not trouble to have the births of their children documented and with time the date became lost in the mists of memory. A birth certificate is supposed to be supplied before a child can be enrolled in school but somehow or other, many people are able to get their children into school without birth certificates. Elizabeth Ohene: This complete disregard for the sanctity of birth dates manifests in other ways that sometimes undermines all official records in Ghana. When in later life you require a birth certificate, you would appear before a commissioner of oaths and offer a date that would be stated to be based on the best guessestimate provided you by your parents or family member. In much later life, when you are approaching the compulsory retirement age of 60 and you desperately wish to continue to work several more years because you cannot survive on your pension, you return to the commissioner of oaths and swear that you have now discovered compelling evidence that the original date of your certificate was incorrect. For example, you were informed that you were born in the year the chief of the village was enstooled (inaugurated) and you have discovered he was enstooled in 1968 and not 1965. There probably does not exist any official record of the date of the enstoolment of this chief anyway, so why create a fuss about a difference of three years? This complete disregard for the sanctity of birth dates manifests in other ways that sometimes undermines all official records in Ghana. I have observed school children who cannot be more than 14 years old who possess voters registration cards. The law states you must be 18 to register to vote. The consequences might follow you through life unless you are prepared to continue paying visits to the commissioner of oaths to acquire new birth dates. Police recruitment advertisements have a cut-off date of 25 years. You are actually 21 but possess a voters' registration card that states you are 26 because you presented yourself as 18 when you were 14. Sometimes it has been football players who attempt to reduce several years from their ages so they can participate in age-restricted competitions. These days technology is being deployed to ensure the integrity of such competitions, making it difficult for 20-somethings to participate in under-17 competitions. Numerous attempts have been made to enforce the registration of births and deaths, and so far all these attempts have failed spectacularly. There already exists a regulation issued by the head of the civil service some years ago which states public officials are not permitted to change their birth dates during their time in government employment. In other words, you are fixed with whatever birth date you enter the service with, and you cannot become younger or older by swearing an affidavit. It was always going to be difficult to enforce this directive because there are many people here who believe their ages are confidential and should not be publicised. You could ask someone how old they were and receive a reply: Is it my official or real age that you want? One of the firm pledges made by the new government is that within its first year in office, a national identification system will be in place. In other words, all Ghanaians will possess identification cards with their unchangeable biometric data and none of us will be able to swear an affidavit to acquire a new birth date. We are all holding our breath. And whilst I await this dramatic change, I have been wondering if there are any advantages in the current situation where a person's age is a changeable and confidential figure? My mind went to a sentence I read in an online article in a British newspaper earlier this year. Those who follow tennis would recognise that this was part of a report during the Australian Open: A few hours after Serena Williams, 35, joined her 36-year-old sister, Venus, in the women's final by trouncing the 34-year-old Mirjana Lucic-Baroni, Federer, 35, somehow conjured some more retro magic to beat Stan Wawrinka, a mere 31, for the 19th time in 22 matches, the article in The Guardian stated. I fear that faced with the possibility of such prose in our newspapers, many people in Ghana are going to opt to keep birth dates a changeable and private event.
