But I worry that faced with the possibility of such writings in our newspapers, many Ghanaians will decide to keep their dates of birth secret and ambiguous. And while we wait for this radical change, I wonder if there is anything good about the current situation in which age is not a solid, definite number. The tennis fan would have realized that this was a report from the Australian Open, when a few hours after Serena Williams, then 35, had joined her sister Venus, 36, in the final by defeating Mirjana Lucic-Baroni, 34, the Swiss, then 35, had somehow managed to use a trick of the past to defeat Stan Wawrinka, 31, for the 19th time in 22 encounters.

text: A chronology of key events: These are external links and will open in a new window c. AD 250-900 Classical Maya city states flourish in the far south of present-day Mexico, as well as in neighbouring Guatemala and Belize, before experiencing a mysterious collapse. c. AD 0-500 - Major cultural and religious centre of Teotihuacan flourishes. Believed to have been one of the world's largest cities at the time, but little is known about its ethnic and political character. Aztec-era traditions are still being preserved Mexico City to teach Aztec language Festival highlights indigenous pride 6th-7th century - Influx of new peoples into central Mexico from the north, including speakers of Nahuatl. 800-1000 - High point of the Toltec culture, centred on the city of Tula, in present-day Hidalgo province. 10th-16th centuries - Revitalised Maya civilisation flourishes in the northern Yucatan peninsula, creating major cities such as Chichen Itza and Uxmal. 1428-1521 - The latest of a long line of indigenous civilisations, the Aztec Empire - an alliance of Nahuatl-speaking city states led by Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City) - establishes hegemony over much of central Mexico. 1519 - Small Spanish army led by Hernan Cortes lands at Veracruz, marking the beginning of Spain's conquest of Mexico. 1521 - Allied with native anti-Aztec forces, Cortes' men capture the capital Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City). The Spanish conquest took decades to complete BBC History: Story of the Conquistadors 1521-1820 - Mexico forms part of the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Independence 1810-21 - War of Independence ends with the creation of the short-lived Mexican Empire, which includes Central America to the southern border of present-day Costa Rica, as well as what is now the southwestern US. 1824 - Mexico becomes a federal republic after the removal and exile of Emperor Augustin de Iturbide. Central American provinces secede, becoming the countries of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. The new Mexican state is characterised by tension between the conservative Spanish-origin landowning elite and the largely indigenous landless minority, resulting in instability and frequent armed conflict. 1836 - Former province of Texas, by now increasingly populated by English-speaking Americans, secedes after a war, proceeding to join the United States nine years later. 1846-8 - Mexican-American War ends with Mexico being compelled to sell its northern provinces (including present-day California, Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah) to the US. 1855-72 - La Reforma period, characterised by liberal reforms limiting the power and landholdings of the Catholic Church. 1864-7 - Archduke Maximilian Habsburg of Austria is installed as Mexican emperor with support from Napoleon III of France and conservative landowners, but is overthrown and executed by Republican rebels. 1876-1911 - Porfirio Diaz's 35-year-long dictatorship - known as the Porfiriato - brings a lengthy period of stability, modernisation and economic growth, but at the cost of political repression and stagnation. 1910-1920 - Mexican Revolution ends the Porfirio Diaz dictatorship and leads to establishment of a constitutional republic. 1913-14 - Diaz' successor, the liberal Francisco Madero, introduces land reform and labour legislation before being assassinated. Victoriano Huerta seizes power. Political unrest continues with Zapata leading a peasant revolt in the south. Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky (l) arrives in Mexico, where he was tracked down and killed The ice pick assassination 1914 - Victoriano Huerta - viewed with suspicion by the United States for alleged pro-German sympathies - resigns, and is succeeded by Venustiano Carranza. 1916 - US forces cross the border in pursuit of the guerrilla leader Francisco Pancho Villa. 1917 - US forces withdraw, having failed to kill Villa. A new constitution is adopted, which is designed to ensure permanent democracy in Mexico. 1920 - President Venustiano Carranza is murdered. Civil war follows. 1929 - The National Revolutionary Party is formed. In 1946 it is renamed the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI. 1934 - President Lazaro Cardenas begins programme of oil nationalisation, land reform and industrial expansion. 1940 - Leon Trotsky murdered in Mexico. 1942 - Mexico declares war on Japan and Germany. 1960s - Unrest amongst peasants and labourers over unequal wealth distribution is suppressed. 1968 - Student demonstration in Tlatelolco, Mexico City, during the Olympic Games is fired upon by Mexican security forces. Hundreds of protesters are killed or wounded. The extent of the violence shocks the country. 1976 - Huge offshore oil reserves discovered; the Cantarell field becomes the mainstay of Mexico's oil production. 1985 - Earthquake in Mexico City kills thousands and renders many more homeless. 1993 - Mexican parliament ratifies the North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta) with the US and Canada. 1994 - A guerrilla rebellion in Chiapas by the Zapatista National Liberation Army is brutally suppressed by government troops. The rebels oppose Nafta and want greater recognition for Indian rights. The government recognises the Zapatista National Liberation Front (EZLN). 1994 August - Presidential elections won by PRI candidate Ernesto Zedillo Ponce de Leon, after the previous candidate, Luis Donaldo Colosio, was murdered. The stock market plunges in December, the peso loses a third of its value. 1995 - Former President Carlos Salinas goes into exile after his brother Raul Salinas is connected with Colosio's murder. 1995 November - The government and the EZLN reach an agreement on greater autonomy for the indigenous Mayans of Chiapas. 1996 - The insurgency in the south escalates as the leftist Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) attacks government troops. 1997 - The PRI suffers heavy losses in elections and loses its overall majority in the lower house of parliament for the first time since 1929. 1997 December - 45 Indians killed by paramilitary gunmen in a Chiapas village. The incident causes an international outcry, President Zedillo launches an investigation. 1998 January - Governor of Chiapas resigns. Peace talks with the rebels are reactivated, but break down at the end of the year. 2000 July - Vicente Fox of the opposition Alliance for Change wins presidential elections, the first opposition candidate ever to do so. Parliamentary elections see the Alliance for Change emerge as the strongest party, beating the PRI by just over 1%. 2000 December - Vicente Fox is sworn in as president. 2001 March - Zapatista guerrillas, led by Subcomandante Marcos, stage their Zapatour, a march from Chiapas to Mexico City to highlight their demands. 2001 April - Parliament passes a bill increasing the rights of indigenous people. A few days later, Subcomandante Marcos rejects the bill, saying it leaves the Indian population worse off than before. Marcos says the uprising in Chiapas will continue. 2001 November - President Fox appoints a prosecutor to investigate the disappearance of left-wing activists during the 1970s and 1980s. 2002 March - Roberto Madrazo wins the contest to lead the PRI, which governed for 71 years until 2000. 2002 June - Millions of secret security files are released, shedding light on the torture and killing by security forces of hundreds of political activists in the 1960s and 1970s. President Fox says his government is not afraid to pursue prosecutions. 2002 July - Former President Luis Echeverria is questioned about massacres of student protesters in 1968, when he was interior minister, and in 1971 when he was president. The ski-mask wearing sub-commandante Marcos was the public face of the popular rebellion In the footsteps of Zapata Profile: Zapatista's mysterious leader 2002 September - Three army officers are charged with first-degree murder over the killings of 134 leftists in the 1970s. 2004 July - Investigator deems 1971 shooting of student protesters by government forces to have been genocide; judge refuses to order arrest of former President Luis Echeverria on charges that he ordered attack. 2005 January - Six prison officers are murdered and top-security jails are put on high alert amid escalating tension between the authorities and drug gangs. 2005 April - Political furore as Mexico City mayor and presidential favourite Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador is stripped of his immunity from prosecution by Congress in a land dispute. The government eventually abandons the prosecution. 2006 February - A federal post of special prosecutor is created to tackle violent crime against women. Mexico had been criticised by the UN and rights groups over the unsolved murders of more than 300 women over 12 years in the border city of Ciudad Juarez. 2006 July - Conservative candidate Felipe Calderon is declared the winner of presidential elections with a razor-thin majority over his leftist rival, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who challenges the result with mass street protests. The Federal Electoral Tribunal confirms Mr Calderon's victory in September. 2006 October - US President George W Bush signs legislation to build 1,125km (700 miles) of fencing along the US-Mexico border. Mexico condemns plans for the barrier, which is intended to curb illegal immigration. 2006 December - A new federal police force is created to tackle drugs cartels; thousands of troops are deployed in the western state of Michoacan as part of a major anti-drug trafficking drive. Hundreds died or disappeared when Luis Echeverria was interior minister or president New warrant for ex-leader Mexicans dig for 'disappeared' 2007 February - New law obliging authorities to take tougher action against domestic violence comes into effect. 2007 July - A financial website says that Mexican telecoms tycoon Carlos Slim has overtaken Microsoft founder Bill Gates to become the world's richest person. Genocide trial against former president Luis Echeverria is suspended. 2007 October - Heavy rains flood nearly the entire southern state of Tabasco. Some 500,000 are made homeless in one of the country's worst natural disasters. 2008 Drug-related killings soar. Murders linked to organised crime leap to almost 1,400 in first five months of year. 2008 May - Attorney-general Eduardo Medina Mora says more than 4,000 people have been killed in 18 months since President Calderon took office and declared war on drugs cartels. About 450 of the dead are police, soldiers or prosecutors, and many of the killings have been concentrated along the US border. 2008 August - Hundreds of thousands join marches throughout Mexico to protest against continuing wave of drugs-related violence. 2008 October - Faced with drop in Mexican oil production, government passes series of energy reforms. Package includes controversial plans to allow private investment in state oil giant Pemex. 2009 January - Government unveils package of emergency measures worth nearly $150m (£100m) to protect economy from effects of US economic downturn. 2009 February - Reports say about 1,000 people died in a further upsurge in drug-related violence in the first six weeks of 2009. 2009 March - Army troops enter Ciudad Juarez, on the border with the US, as open warfare erupts between rival drug gangs. 2009 April - Authorities close schools and public buildings after dozens are confirmed to have been killed by the virulent new swine flu virus. 2009 July - Opposition Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) makes large gains in mid-term congressional elections, winning 48% of seats in the Chamber of Deputies. 2009 October - Murder rate in Ciudad Juarez on Mexico-US border reaches all-time high amid battles between rival drug cartels. 2009 December - One of Mexico's most-wanted drug lords, Arturo Beltran Leyva, is killed in a shoot-out with state security forces. The US has erected border fences to try keep out illegal migrants Mexico-US migration on the slide The authorities put the number of drug-related killings for 2009 at around 6,500, the worst year of bloodshed since President Felipe Calderon declared war on the drug cartels in late 2006. 2010 March - President Calderon calls on United States to share responsibility in battle against drug trafficking, after the murder of three people connected to US consulate in border city of Ciudad Juarez. 2010 August - US President Barack Obama signs into law a $600m bill to put more agents and equipment along the Mexican border to stem the flow of illegal immigrants. 2010 December - Wikileaks releases US diplomatic cables revealing that the US ambassador questioned the Mexican security forces' ability to tackle organised crime. In 2006, President Calderon launched a crackdown on Mexico's brutal drugs gangs Q&A: Mexico's drug-related violence Mexico's gruesome killings 2011 August - An attack on the Casino Royale in Monterrey kills 52 people, after gunmen douse the building with fuel and set it alight. 2012 May - The army arrests a drug cartel leader over the killing of 49 people whose mutilated bodies are dumped on a major road in Nuevo Leon state, in one of the worst atrocities committed in the ongoing drug war. 2012 July - The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) candidate Enrique Pena Nieto wins presidential election. 2013 July - Miguel Angel Trevino Morales, head of the brutal Zetas drugs cartel, is arrested in the highest-profile arrest since President Pena Nieto adopted a policy of targeting local bosses rather than big names. 2014 February - Vigilante groups launch an offensive against the Knights Templar drugs cartel in the state of Michoacan; they are granted temporary legal status as Rural Defence Corps. 2014 August - Mexico's Congress approves sweeping reforms to the country's energy sector that will open the market to foreign oil firms and strip state-owned energy group Pemex of the monopoly it has held since nationalisation in 1938. 2014 November - Plans are announced to bring regional government and police under federal control after mass protests over the disappearance in September of 43 trainee teachers in the southwestern state of Guerrero. 2015 January - Authorities issue arrest warrants for 45 suspects - including a former mayor - in the case of 43 missing students kidnapped and thought killed in Guerrero. 2015 May - Hundreds of gunmen overrun the city of Chilapa in Guerrero, abducting 15 young men in a suspected drug gang turf war. 2015 June - Governing Institutional Revolutionary Party and its allies lose seats but hold onto power as independents and the new leftwing party Morena make a strong showing in regional and local polls. 2015 July - Top drug lord Joaquin El Chapo Guzman escapes from high-security prison through a tunnel, in his second prison-break since 2001, and over a year-and-a-half since his recapture in January 2014. He is recaptured in January 2016. 2015 August - Inter-American Commission on Human Rights complains its investigation is not being given access to suspects in Guerrero missing students case. 2016 February - Visiting Pope Francis urges a stadium packed with members of the clergy not to give up in the face of violence, drug trafficking and corruption. 2016 March - Mexico says it will not pay for a wall to be built along the Mexican-US border in its first direct response to US presidential candidate Donald Trump's electoral pledge. 2016 May - President Enrique Pena Nieto has announced proposals to reform the constitution to allow same sex marriages across the country. 2017 January - Drug lord Joaquin Guzman, known as El Chapo, is extradited to the United States to be tried on charges of money laundering, drug-trafficking, kidnapping and murder.

text: The debate over flying the Confederate flag has reignited in the US, but the American South isn't the only place in the world you'll see the emblem - it's also proudly displayed in the rural Brazilian town of Santa Barbara D'Oeste. Each year, the descendants of approximately 10,000 Confederates who fled the United States to Brazil following the American Civil War hold a type of family gathering. They all participate in characteristically southern activities such as square dancing, consuming fried chicken and biscuits, and listening to George Strait, states Asher Levine, a São Paulo-based correspondent for Reuters. And numerous Confederate flags everywhere, throughout the entire venue. Despite being six or seven generations distant from their antebellum heritage, many local Brazilians continue to maintain strong connections to Southern culture, and proudly display the Confederate flag. However for them, Levine states, the flag represents much more of an ethnic symbol than a political one. They view themselves as ethnically American to some extent, he states. At an Italian festival, one would observe people displaying an Italian flag. Or on Saint Patrick's Day one sees people displaying the Irish flag. They perceive it in that manner. They possess no political association with it whatsoever. Over time, the Southern white population has intermingled with the Brazilians, producing people with a variety of different skin tones displaying the Confederate flag. Americans might be surprised by the resulting sight. Many people who are descendants of these confederates possess African heritage as well, so one will observe at the celebration people with dark skin displaying the Confederate flag. Levine states he spoke to an American at the festival who was completely astonished at witnessing a young girl singing Amazing Grace - frequently sung in black churches throughout the US - whilst standing upon a Confederate flag. The banner appears everywhere - children wave miniature flags and women wear Confederate flag dresses. You know, the symbolism is completely lost upon them, but for us it represents quite a contrast, Levine states. Despite being a very mixed-race nation, Levine states that the killings in Charleston are being perceived in Brazil as more of a gun safety matter than a racial matter. When they observe an incident like what occurred in South Carolina last week, they question whether it is truly so much safer in the United States, safety-wise. text: Portsmouth made history in staging the The America's Cup World Series, the city council leader has said, despite criticism from some spectators. Racing was cancelled and public viewing areas were evacuated owing to adverse weather conditions on Sunday. Criticism emerged on social media regarding spectator facilities and the refund policy for a cancelled concert. The leader of the city council, Donna Jones, stated there would be a detailed analysis of the event. The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge were amongst those left disappointed as racing was abandoned on Sunday. Organisers Team Origin announced that Fanzone Arena and Grandstand ticket holders would receive refunds. Numerous spectators used the organisers' Facebook page to voice complaints about pricing, viewing facilities, toilet provision and catering services. Paul Dornan characterised the £45 Fanzone entry fee as a lot for what you got. Seafront businesses, including the Blue Reef Aquarium, attributed a decline in trade to the event. Manager Lindsay Holloway stated there had been miscommunication and frankly poor management by the organisers. A spokesman for Team Origin Events said the Fanzone area was positioned directly in front of the racing and enabled access to the free waterfront festival arena and the specific kids area. He stated: We have set out from the start to engage with the existing seafront attractions to ensure that everyone benefited from this event. Local boat tours proprietor Mark Askey also reported takings were down 70% compared to the same week last year. It was a big deterrent for us and numerous other small businesses, he stated. Record-breaking yachtsman Sir Robin Knox-Johnston commented: It was the right decision to cancel racing - but the real tragedy is Portsmouth built up so hard, but it has lost out on this big event. On Friday, ticket holders for a cancelled South Coast proms concert were offered a refund plus complimentary entry to Saturday's pop concert, angering people who had paid up to £48 for tickets for Saturday's show. Organisers described the complimentary tickets as a gesture of goodwill. Ms Jones stated: We need to remember this is the first time since 1861 this cup has been back on British soil, so regardless of what happens in the future, we've created history this weekend.

text: The Labour Party has made legal checks to ensure its leadership contest is complying with the law and try to avoid challenges to the result. Fresh regulations permit members of the public to register as a registered supporter for £3 to cast their ballot. The competition has been beset by worries that members from other parties have attempted to influence the result. A spokesperson for interim leader Harriet Harman dismissed any suggestion of proposals to stop or suspend the election. The spokesperson stated: The party's emphasis is on ensuring that the 2014 regulations are fully observed. We have sought legal counsel to ensure that the regulations are being observed and that all possible due diligence was being conducted. However there were no proposals to stop or suspend the competition. We monitor the process closely. A Labour spokesperson confirmed a Conservative activist who had paid £1 to join the Labour Party - under a reduced rate for former members of the armed services - had been excluded and would not receive a vote in the leadership competition. Alan Pearmain, a parish councillor and deputy chairman of the South Ribble Conservative Association, informed the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme he had joined as a form of mischief-making. Meanwhile, Scotland's Daily Record has offered its support in the leadership race to left-winger Jeremy Corbyn. The newspaper's front-page endorsement arrives a week after its sister publication - the Daily Mirror - supported Andy Burnham. • Everything you need to know about the four candidates seeking to become the next Labour leader. Mr Corbyn stated: I'm clearly pleased to have the support of a publication that has such a lengthy tradition of backing for the Labour Party. I'm certain that, at least partially, this endorsement will have been made with Labour's future in Scotland in consideration, which is significant as Labour has a genuine need to reconnect with communities in Scotland if we are to succeed across the UK. Meanwhile, former Home Secretary David Blunkett - who is supporting Andy Burnham for the leadership - has added his voice to the other senior Labour figures cautioning about a Corbyn victory. He informed BBC Radio 4's Today programme: Jeremy Corbyn has not only been effective at opposition against the Tories, he's also been profoundly effective at opposition against my party. If you wish to continue being in opposition, vote for somebody who is effective at opposition, he added. Mr Blunkett stated he wanted somebody who can actually address the world of tomorrow rather than taking us back to Old Labour or, for that matter, New Labour in the 90s, because we are addressing an entirely different world. Sarah Brown, the wife of former Prime Minister Gordon, has meanwhile supported Yvette Cooper for the leadership, with Andy Burnham as her second preference. Opinion polls suggest Ms Cooper is engaged in a battle with Mr Burnham to emerge as the main challenger to Mr Corbyn, with Liz Kendall trailing in fourth position. Mr Burnham, Yvette Cooper and Liz Kendall are competing against Mr Corbyn in the competition. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband has faced demands to apologise for the voting system being used to elect his successor. The shift from an electoral college system, which gave equal weight to MPs, party members and trade unionists, to one member, one vote, with the public permitted to join as registered supporters for £3, was overwhelmingly supported by a special Labour conference last year. However critics, including backbench Labour MPs Simon Danczuk and Graham Stringer, say the fresh system was too vulnerable to abuse. The outcome of the election will be announced at a special conference on September 12.

text: Nearly 15 years ago, successful Nigerian businessman Anselm Okoukoni was one of the desperate African migrants prepared to do anything to get to Europe. As the eldest son of his widowed mother - a farmer - tradition required that responsibility for his six siblings would transfer to him upon his graduation from university. Well before he obtained his degree in statistics, he determined that he did not wish to join the ranks of unemployed university graduates in his country. However, the embassies of Italy, Germany, Spain, Austria, France, Belgium, the UK and the US all declined to grant him a visa. Nevertheless, circumstances began to improve when someone introduced him to someone who knew someone who could arrange a visa to Greece - for approximately 400,000 naira which, at that time, was equivalent to roughly $3,500 (£2,350). My uncle in America had already instructed me to inform him whenever I obtained a visa, Mr Okoukoni stated. He subsequently sent a total of $5,000 to cover the visa, air ticket and some travel allowance - a gift, not a loan - his contribution to his nephew's future. Aged 24, Mr Okoukoni departed Nigeria in December 2002, arriving in a country where he knew absolutely nobody and so he swiftly headed to Italy where he had friends. Anselm Okoukoni: I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. I was sending money home to Nigeria. When his visa expired several weeks later, he did what most of his friends had done and sought asylum. I cannot recall what story I told, he said, explaining that the thing to do was to select a topical story. Over the following two years, he struggled with learning to communicate in Italian and found it impossible to secure a decent job. He ended up street hawking, which is illegal in Italy, and on numerous occasions he was arrested and his goods confiscated. It was not the kind of life I wanted to live, he said, adding that his income was barely sufficient to pay for his siblings' school fees. Once again, fortune smiled upon Mr Okoukoni when someone introduced him to a man who possessed a genuine passport from a European country and who shared a strong facial resemblance to him. He agreed to permit him to use his passport to cross over to the UK in the summer of 2004. Safe in London at last, Mr Okoukoni was both shocked and thrilled by his first impressions of the city. I saw Africans driving buses and cabs, and working in McDonald's and in hospitals, he said. In Italy, you could scarcely see a black person doing those kinds of jobs. Most of the black people I saw were factory workers or farm workers or cleaners or prostitutes. His Nigerian friends in London assisted him with accommodation; found him employment as a parking attendant and organised the relevant documentation. He would work under someone else's identity. Within one year, I had job satisfaction, he said. I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. I was sending money home to Nigeria. Mr Okoukoni recalls being delighted with his salary of £8.50 per hour, but after seeing an advertisement for a community college open day, he decided it was time to further his education. Of all the vocational courses available, he chose to study plumbing. I remembered that I had never entered a house in Nigeria where the plumbing was done properly, he said. The one-day-per-week course was free for British citizens but not for foreigners - and he was required to show his passport displaying his leave to remain in the UK when he handed over his fee of £1,400. Fortunately, the woman who registered him believed his story that he had forgotten his passport at home. After a year of studying, he left his job and, using his student ID card, found new employment as an apprentice plumber with a construction company. The pay was even more than what I earned as a parking attendant - at £9.70 per hour, he said. Why visa rejections do not halt Nigerian migrants Over the following few years, Mr Okoukoni acquired another qualification in plumbing, one in heating and gas and a certificate in building services engineering. I paid for all these courses myself. Everything cost me roughly £10,000. Long before he had completed his studies in 2012, he had decided to return to Nigeria as he knew his skills would be invaluable in his home country. In 2013, he purchased a van and loaded it with all manner of tools of his trade, then shipped it off to Nigeria. Shortly afterwards, he left his £12-per-hour job in London, for a property development company in Lagos. He proved so efficient his boss was reluctant to let him go at the end of it. But I wanted to go and build my own business, Mr Okoukoni said. His plans to immediately build a website and advertise aggressively did not materialise, as he was soon overwhelmed with contracts that came simply by referral from satisfied clients. As he had envisaged, the shortage of quality workmen in Nigeria had made his plumbing, fire protection, air conditioning and ventilation services highly sought after. Right now, I shuttle between Port Harcourt and Lagos doing jobs, he said. In Nigeria, it is common to enter a magnificent building only to discover that the toilets do not flush properly, or that the wall sockets are askew, or that the door handles come off in your hand, or that the windows cannot shut, or that the interlocking tiles have spaces in between that can be injurious to the Gucci or Jimmy Choo heels of the owners. Many developers who aim for high quality have taken to importing artisans from nearby countries like Togo and Benin, who are reputed to be more skilled than their Nigerian counterparts. Mr Okoukoni blames the poor quality of work by Nigerian artisans on their primary focus on money. The time it takes to learn a skill is time not earning an income. So, once they can hang one door, they go away and tell everyone that they are a carpenter. They stop coming to work. They do not wait to learn everything they should. His company, Ansko Building Services Ltd, currently employs 12 plumbers and two apprentices. His plumbers initially presented themselves as experienced, but he had to train them afresh. However, he paid them whilst they were learning, and also pays his two apprentices a salary that is above the country's minimum wage. That way, they were motivated to stay on. Since the beginning of this year I have not touched any tool. They now do all the work whilst I supervise. Mr Okoukoni's future plans include opening a training centre for people in the building services industry, to show them in particular the range of tools they could use. Nobody has ever taken the time to teach them, he said. He is ashamed of all the illegal steps he took in the course of his life's journey to and through Europe, but he is pleased with the way things have turned out. He is now able to provide employment for other young Nigerians, take care of the wife he married after returning to Nigeria, look after his mother and pay for his brother's studies in the US. And his advice for those migrants in Europe or making their way there? When they get to Europe, they should obey the law and do the right thing. They should look for unique skills that they can develop and use to improve the society over there and also back home. If you go to Europe to simply look for money, you are wasting your time.

text: Planning permission for a controversial peace centre at Northern Ireland's former Maze prison has been granted. This follows years of political disagreement regarding what should be undertaken with the site near Lisburn which accommodated paramilitary prisoners during the Troubles from 1971 to 2000. Ten men perished at the prison during the 1981 republican hunger strikes. Unionists expressed concern it should not become a republican shrine. Whilst there have been demonstrations by some individuals who oppose the new centre, it is understood that planners received only a single formal objection to the application for the new building. It has been designed by architect Daniel Libeskind who is celebrated for his involvement in the plan for construction on the site of New York's Ground Zero. It is a standalone structure but sits between two other sets of buildings that have also been retained and include parts of the former prison such as a watch tower, prison hospital, compound and H Block. There are also a pair of World War II hangars that were part of the old Long Kesh RAF airfield. Announcing the decision, Northern Ireland Environment Minister Alex Attwood stated: There is learning to be taken from the conflict here. The centre can contribute to sharing this learning and perhaps to help inform the resolution of conflict in other places. I believe that good planning requires good design. That is certainly the case in the design of the centre created by Daniel Libeskind, a world leader in architecture and a friend of Northern Ireland. Most of the cost of the peace-building and conflict resolution centre will be covered by an £18m grant from the European Union. The 350 acre site of the former prison is being redeveloped at a cost of £300m. A large part of it has been designated for the Royal Ulster Agricultural Society (RUAS). Since the jail closed in 2000, there has been a constant debate regarding how the site should be utilised. It was earmarked for a new national sports stadium but the proposal was rejected after years of disagreement. In April, DUP MLA Edwin Poots said his party had made a corporate decision to support the redevelopment of the former Maze Prison site. Speaking on BBC NI's The View, the Lagan Valley MLA said the sooner the site was redeveloped, the better. He said it would not become a republican shrine. At the same time, a senior republican ex-prisoner said any new peace and reconciliation centre on the former prison site must reflect the stories of all involved. Seanna Walsh said this should include loyalists and the British Army.

text: Married couple Dilshad and Barinder Hothi are joint founders of the international training company, the Knowledge Academy, which they aim to turn into the Amazon of the education world. When a husband and wife team jointly operate a business, one cannot help wondering: who is truly in command? With the Hothis it is difficult to determine. In discussion they tumble over one another with shared enthusiasm, interrupt and complete each other's sentences. She is excited about what makes their company distinctive in the already extremely crowded market for professional training. The future concerns blending, she states. Our online learning courses are traditional, computer-based courses, as one would expect, but we have what we term walk-in clinics. So if someone wishes to discuss an issue, they can locate a locally-based instructor, drop in, pose questions, obtain the human interaction. Dilshad is expansive regarding the grand vision. Right from the beginning, he states, they observed what the internet was doing to the manner people purchased books, groceries and clothes, and thought: Why will it not do the same for training? I knew there was a phenomenal opportunity, he states. In the next decade we shall be a global household name, I firmly believe that - rather like Google or Facebook - we shall probably be as large, if not larger. That might sound like arrogance, but the Knowledge Academy has expanded rapidly in its first six years and is amongst the largest training companies in the world, measured by the number of courses it provides - over 5,000 - in the number of locations. By the end of this year they state they shall be able to provide training in 3,000 cities in 210 countries, from the US to Australia, Bhutan to Chile. It delivers courses in dozens of professional areas from project management and IT to social media, aviation and animation. And they have supplied training to companies including Rolls Royce, HSBC, PwC and Disney. But whilst their operations are global, they themselves originate from a very specific cultural alchemy, a combination of Indian and English influences. Barinder's parents, immigrants to Britain from the Punjab, operated a restaurant in Harrow, London. Neither of them spoke any English, she states, which meant she and her siblings were drawn into the business at an early age, assisting their parents at the bank and with customers. But as in many Asian immigrant families, the children's education was always a priority. I still can hear my mother now saying 'Study, because this is what shall help you in life,' states Barinder. But if Barinder's life in Britain was suffused with Indian values, Dilshad's schooldays were a mirror image. I was born and raised in India itself, he states. His father was in the Indian air force and his family chose for him the nearest they could find to a British public school experience. They placed me in Lawrence School, Sanawar, he states. It is the Eton equivalent of India. He became house captain, played cricket and absorbed the very British atmosphere of the former colonial military school, at the foot of the Himalayas. I think my school background was very important, being a house captain. We were very competitive and sports-driven. We had a cricket competition and field hockey and athletics and I used to build tactics and think how many medals I would pursue. When he arrived in the UK, at the age of 21, Dilshad met Barinder through his aunt. For several years he worked for a UK-based training company whilst she worked for Microsoft. They chose to launch their own company at what to many would have seemed an inauspicious moment - in 2009 as the global economy crashed. It was actually the best decision ever. Any other time would have been more challenging, states Barinder. The new business benefited from the large pool of people who had been made redundant and lacked formal qualifications to show to prospective employers. There were so few positions that you needed to have more badges on your CV to secure a job, states Dilshad. Now, he states, sites like LinkedIn have made formal qualifications even more important by making them constantly visible to everyone. There is now one risk on the horizon, though. That for Dilshad and Barinder the business shall consume their life together entirely. Although they barely spend ten minutes together during the working day from 8am to 6pm, once at home around the kitchen table or on walks at the weekend, they admit, the conversation almost always turns to work. Their daughter, aged nine, has already spent so many hours at their office she is a proficient operator of the franking machine and can recite the names of almost every member of staff. Quite often we have to tell each other to turn the iPads off, states Barinder. They have developed a pattern of working very hard for a few months then taking a luxury break, somewhere like Dubai, for a few days. Neither seems to resent the time and dedication required, though they do approach things differently. I am more conservative, states Barinder. Typically British. And if she were not there to put Dilshad in check? I would try to do ten things at once, he states, grinning. So who is in command? Barinder is in charge of the people. I am probably in charge of the strategy itself, he admits. Do they argue? Barinder has been very supportive, he states. If she is supportive then is he really in command? She laughs. But refuses to give any ground at all.

text: Pop stars have always been clothes horses for fashion designers - but more and more of them are turning to designing themselves. These are external links and will open in a new window During this year, Skepta has launched his inaugural fashion collection and Zayn Malik's Versace Versus range was revealed. They join a roster of musicians-turned-designers that already features names such as Victoria Beckham, Kanye West and Rihanna. However, how straightforward is it for a pop star to become a successful designer in a world where, traditionally, one had to serve an apprenticeship in the industry before one's designs would reach the catwalk? Bid farewell to the artist formerly known as Posh Spice, and instead welcome leading British fashion designer Victoria Beckham. The former Spice Girl launched her inaugural fashion collection in 2008, and it is reasonable to say there was some snickering and several raised eyebrows. However, her first collection - a modest one featuring just 10 dresses - proved tremendously successful with critics. Nicole Phelps wrote in Vogue: The woman formerly known as Posh Spice has launched a dress collection, and, believe it or not, it is one of the most sought-after things happening in New York this week. And since then, Mrs Beckham has progressed from strength to strength. With Victoria Beckham, everyone wished to despise her and dismiss her and she learned from the outset how to accomplish everything from the beginning - now, she might not be capable of pattern-cutting but does that truly matter? says Glamour's fashion director Natalie Hartley. Beckham is gaining respect because right from the start, she genuinely put her reputation on the line. I recall the early days when she would stage her shows in New York, she would guide you through the collections personally and she became very amicable with the editors. It was a very astute move. People felt as though they came to know her and she would remember you every season... she was actually very personable and I believe that won them over. VB has secured several prestigious awards including two best brand honours at the British Fashion Awards in 2011 and 2014. As well as her own collections, she has collaborated with US high street brand Target, which features clothes in larger sizes and is affordable for the majority of us who cannot afford designer prices. She once stated: I want a woman to look and feel like the finest version of herself. Kanye is merely one of several US music stars to have made the venture into fashion - honourable mentions also extend to Jay Z and Pharrell. Kim Kardashian's husband first tested the waters in the fashion world in 2009 with a Nike collaboration - enter the Air Yeezys - before additional shoe lines followed with designer labels including Luis Vuitton. To demonstrate he was taking fashion seriously, West completed an internship with Fendi the same year. An original pair of 2009 Air Yeezys is currently available on eBay for a staggering $1,349.99 (£1,055). In 2011, the rapper premiered DW Kanye West, his women's fashion label, at Paris Fashion Week. However, it is reasonable to say it did not fare particularly well with the fashion establishment. The Daily Telegraph's Lisa Armstrong summarised it as a stupendously vacuous enterprise. And the New York Times' Suzy Menkes wrote: His collection of sexpot low-bodice dresses and skintight trousers, adorned with heaps of ginger fur, did not inspire the fashion crowd to tell him to abandon his day job. Ouch. On the positive side, Style.com did blog that it was a work in progress. Ever the optimist, Kanye returned to the saddle quickly and his second line, launched in 2012, was largely well received. He has since proceeded to produce five seasons of his Yeezy clothing line plus a trainer collaboration with Adidas. I am actually an admirer of Kanye's Yeezy collections, Natalie Hartley says. I adore sportswear and think he has accomplished an excellent job creating simple, modern sportswear. He has also worked hard to learn the ropes, he is passionate about fashion, and who can criticise that? The No Doubt singer first entered the fashion arena with the launch of her label L.A.M.B in 2004. The name is an acronym of her debut solo album Love.Angel.Music.Baby. She has frequently presented her collections during New York Fashion Week and has attracted largely positive reviews. On the label's Facebook page, L.A.M.B is described as a playful juxtaposition between classic Hollywood movie star glamour and more modern and casual street influences. text: The UK is to spend £25m on building a prison in Jamaica so that foreign criminals in the UK can be sent home to serve sentences in the Caribbean. Prime Minister David Cameron announced the agreement as he commenced a visit to Jamaica. The project has been settled to resolve the impasse in discussions regarding a prisoner transfer agreement between the two nations. More than 600 Jamaican citizens are held in British prisons but cannot be expelled due to Jamaica's inadequate prison facilities. Government officials state the foreign aid-financed agreement could preserve taxpayers £10m annually when transfers commence in 2020. More than 300 current prisoners are anticipated to be returned under the Jamaican prison programme, which encompasses those sentenced to a minimum of four years who have 18 months or more remaining to serve in detention. Presently they cannot be transferred to Jamaica due to concerns that prison conditions in the nation would permit a successful legal challenge under human rights legislation. Jamaica ranks third highest on the list of foreign nations with citizens serving prison terms in Britain. Nearly 70% of the Jamaicans imprisoned in the UK are serving sentences for violent crimes and drug-related offences. Britain is providing approximately 40% of the expense of constructing the proposed prison, which would accommodate 1,500 individuals. Mr Cameron, who had been at the United Nations in New York for discussions on the campaign against the Islamic State organisation, stated: It is entirely proper that foreign criminals who violate our laws are appropriately punished but this should not be at the cost of the industrious British taxpayer, he declared. That is why this arrangement is so significant. It will ensure Jamaican criminals are returned home to serve their sentences, saving the British taxpayer millions of pounds whilst still guaranteeing justice is served. And it will assist Jamaica by helping to establish a new prison, reinforcing their criminal justice system. Mr Cameron, the first British prime minister to visit the island in 14 years, is also scheduled to announce £300m of aid funding for infrastructure projects throughout the Caribbean, including roads, bridges and ports. He stated the regional infrastructure fund, which will be implemented in partnership with the Caribbean Development Bank, would help promote economic development in the Caribbean. Mr Cameron was welcomed upon his arrival at Kingston Airport by an honour guard and national anthems before he visited RFA Lyme Bay, the British vessel currently conducting anti-drug smuggling and emergency relief operations in the Caribbean. He is scheduled to conclude the day by conducting discussions with Jamaican Prime Minister Portia Simpson-Miller and attending a reception. BBC political correspondent Carole Walker reports that the PM has stated he wishes to enhance a neglected relationship between Britain and Jamaica.

text: Australian politician Bob Katter has defended a video that depicts him killing his electoral rivals. Mr Katter is an independent rural politician from northern Queensland. In the advertisement, he is shown blowing on a wisp of smoke from a toy firearm with the corpses of two faceless men from the major parties lying deceased in the earth. Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull urged Mr Katter to retract the advertisements, which were in the poorest of taste. However, 71-year-old Mr Katter, who leads Katter's Australia Party and represents the constituency of Kennedy, stated he considered the advertisements brilliant and hilariously funny. The advertisement, produced with assistance from satirical website Betoota Advocate, commences with members of the Labor Party and the Liberal-National coalition hammering a placard into the soil that reads Australia for sale. Mr Katter throws the placard on the earth, and when it is replaced, employs a large black marker to modify the placard to Australia not for sale, before cutting to the sequence with the firearm. I believe most people will appreciate the humour. I found it very amusing, I must confess, he told the ABC. What's not amusing is the selling off of this nation. We despise it and we're stubbornly opposed to it. Queensland Senator Barry O'Sullivan described the advertisement abhorrent and Finance Minister Mathias Cormann stated it was regrettable. On the Sunrise breakfast television programme, presenter David Koch challenged Mr Katter on why he released the video so soon after a gunman murdered 49 people at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando, Florida. Mr Katter replied that there were similar advertisements that did not generate controversy and also claimed not to be aware of the shooting. If this represents the finest Australia has to offer in terms of political scandal, then we truly are witnessing the world's most tedious election campaign. Mr Katter's advertisement is characteristic of Australia's larrikin sense of humour - politically incorrect, jarring and perhaps not quite as amusing as it believes it is. But is it abhorrent or in the poorest of taste? Should it have been released in the wake of the shootings in Orlando? Australia is a considerable distance from Florida and many people in regional centres will share Mr Katter's bawdy sense of humour. Sometimes humour is crude or tasteless. Sometimes it doesn't strike the bull's eye. But if Katter's constituents don't appreciate his joke, they can dismiss him at the election on 2 July. Betoota Advocate editor Clancy Overell, who portrayed one of the shot men in the video, stated he was aware the video might wind people up but was not certain Mr Katter had the same understanding. Mr Overell defended the video's timing, telling the BBC that shootings occurred in the US every day. Australians cannot be prevented from making jokes about cowboys and western-style gunplay, he stated. A video from the 2012 Queensland state election featured Mr Katter line dancing with a group of young people. The same video depicted him spinning on his head, although it is probable a body double was used for the stunt.

text: Eye doctors are warning about bird-scaring explosives, called bangers, being modified and used as fireworks. Last year these devices caused five severe eye injuries when hurled into crowds at a Bonfire Night celebration in Sussex. The agricultural implements are manufactured to frighten wildlife - but medical professionals are concerned that the tendency to employ them in this manner could proliferate. They documented their concerns in correspondence to the British Medical Journal (BMJ). The bangers - also called rookies and deer scarers - possess a slow-burning rope fuse that detonates multiple explosives along the cord. When severed, the fuse and explosive can be ignited and hurled. They are marketed for use in frightening birds and deer from agricultural land. Edward Pringle, retinal fellow at Sussex Eye Hospital and one of the correspondence's authors, stated: These banger fireworks are simple to hurl into crowds, people observe them and debris fires into the eye. It resembles a hand grenade detonating - a flash before the eye, and then the sensation of a blunt trauma. Medical professionals typically observe these types of injuries in combat zones. We were witnessing them in a small market town - those hurling them and the individuals attending public events do not understand how hazardous they can be. Eight patients attended Sussex Eye Hospital on the evening of 5 November 2011 following participation in the Lewes bonfire event attended by more than 60,000 people - two were blinded and three now face the risk of lifelong glaucoma. • Position yourself beside the injured person and separate their eyelids - request they look right, left, up and down whilst examining the eye • If you can observe a foreign object, rinse it out by pouring clear water across the eye from the inner corner • If unsuccessful then attempt lifting the object off with the moist corner of a clean tissue • If you still cannot extract the object, seek medical assistance From St John Ambulance The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (Rospa) stated: It is concerning that some individuals feel it is suitable to throw extremely dangerous agricultural products around crowds of people. Deer scarers, and indeed genuine fireworks, are not playthings. They are explosives and the injuries they can inflict can be catastrophic, as this account sadly demonstrates. Attending a public fireworks display remains the safest choice, but clearly there remains work to be accomplished to convey the message that throwing fireworks and other explosives is dangerous and illegal. The BMJ correspondence calls for stricter firework regulations, with the authors stating: Numbers of blinding injuries have declined in nations with legislation that regulates the use and distribution of fireworks. The UK has legislation to restrict distribution, but deer scarers are exempted because they are not genuine fireworks. With slightly more than half of firework injuries occurring at public events, they also request better safety restrictions in place at managed displays, suggesting organisers actively engage their audience in the safer use of fireworks and encourage eye protection. On average eight eye injuries are recorded throughout the whole of the UK on Guy Fawkes day each year, data from the British Ophthalmic Surveillance Unit demonstrates. Of the people who are injured in the eye from a firework - half will require surgery, half will become blind and one in six will need their eye removed. Approximately one-third of firework eye injury patients are under 18.

text: More than half of overseas students in the UK say they have felt less welcome because of policies on migration, a survey suggests. A survey of more than 500 international students across 105 institutions revealed 52 per cent held a negative perception of efforts to reduce migration numbers. Nearly half of North American students in Britain shared this concern. Universities have lobbied to have students counted separately from headline migration statistics. Business Secretary Vince Cable recently stated that Britain's torrid immigration debate risked harming the economically valuable recruitment of international students. He cautioned about the public panic regarding migrant numbers and how it might adversely impact international students. The survey of international student attitudes in Britain, commissioned by Regent's University in London, presents a contrasting picture. Whilst students feel that migration targets have made them feel less welcome, they hold a positive view of their British experience. Approximately four in five students endorsed the quality of their courses and teaching and nearly nine in 10 would recommend studying in Britain. There exists also a distinction between the public campaign to reduce migrant numbers and their private experience of people in Britain, with nearly nine in 10 stating that they felt welcome. There was greater uncertainty about international students' relationship with other students and the broader university, with a quarter stating that they did not feel part of the university community. The survey discovered that 40 per cent of international students mainly spend time with other students from their country and approximately one in five admitted feeling isolated. Nearly a third of international students agreed with the suggestion that my university is only interested in the fees I pay. However, despite warnings that negative rhetoric about immigration might deter potential students, the application figures for this year demonstrate rising rather than declining interest in British universities. There have been decreases from individual countries, but the overall figures from the admissions service Ucas, published last month, demonstrate that applications from international students are higher than last year. Aldwyn Cooper, vice-chancellor of Regent's University, a private college that gained university status this year, stated: These findings demonstrate that British higher education is unmatched in its global reputation. However, there are concerning signs that the government's migration policy risks alienating international students in Britain. This is being compounded by the tendency in some institutions for international students to be left in de facto ghettos, rarely mixing outside their national groups. A spokeswoman for the Department for Business, Innovation and Skills stated that international students make a huge contribution to Britain and emphasised that there is no cap on the number of legitimate international students. But we need to ensure that the message gets through that they are fully welcome in Britain to study. Our universities are second only to the United States as the favoured destination for international students, and to maintain this strong appeal around the globe the government is developing an industrial strategy to ensure our universities stay ahead in the global race.

text: History is useful when trying to make sense of present tensions between Russia and the West. At the Defence Academy, situated near Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, there exists a warehouse where library shelves house an exceptional collection of military publications. Numerous volumes are written in Russian and other languages from the former Soviet bloc: carefully and systematically collected during the past fifty years, to better understand the adversary. Currently designated the Russian Military Studies Archive, it represents a valuable record of the Soviet Union's rise and decline, the Cold War and ongoing tensions between Russia and the West. Following the collapse of the USSR and Warsaw Pact and with the emergence of digital documentation, maintaining archives such as this has become increasingly challenging. Certain individuals have determined that during this period of financial restraint, libraries containing physical books constitute luxuries we may not be able to sustain. Fortunately, this military archive has avoided becoming waste material. During recent years, the concept of Russia as a security concern has regained prominence. Examining recent history could prove significant as we attempt to assess developments in Moscow and potential future events. Certain memorabilia recalls one of the most remarkable episodes of my professional life: the three days in Moscow during August 1991 when military, KGB and Communist leaders attempted to execute a coup d'état. Their objective was to stop and reverse Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika reforms, which they considered were directing their great nation towards destruction. That moment shall remain unforgettable. It appeared as though history balanced precariously, and the world might proceed in either direction. I recall leaving our BBC office in Moscow to discover a column of tanks positioned along the inner ring road, bewildered young soldiers emerging from the turrets to determine their location. The tanks appeared threatening. The young soldiers did not. Our cleaner, Masha, dressed in her customary headscarf and apron, hobbled forward to reproach them. What do you believe you are accomplishing here? Your mothers would feel ashamed of you, she reprimanded. Return yourselves to the barracks where you belong. The coup attempt collapsed because Russia's new President, Boris Yeltsin, declared their actions unlawful and encouraged the armed forces to disobey orders, and because he called upon Moscow's population to support him in forcing the coup leaders to withdraw. The reaction proved extraordinary and inspiring. Soviet citizens, who merely years before had been terrified of public expression, were now marching into the streets to challenge the Kremlin. Young mothers with prams, government workers carrying briefcases, musicians bearing guitars and violins, all gathering at the Russian parliament to demonstrate through sheer numbers that they would no longer be intimidated, and would not permit history to reverse. Within the collection are pamphlets from that period - some remaining muddy from being trampled - hastily produced and circulated throughout Moscow by Yeltsin's allies, attempting to counter the coup leaders' transmissions on state television and radio. I recall them posted throughout the underground system. The language proves forceful and pressing. Above Russia storm clouds are forming, clouds of dictatorship and terror... Soldiers! I trust at this tragic moment that you will choose correctly, states one plea. And, my sincere gratitude to you all for your bravery, declares another, directed from Yeltsin to Moscow's citizens. I have been contemplating 1991 considerably lately, and questioning whether many Russians might emerge onto the streets again, should the present economic decline deteriorate, for example, and desperation emerge. Or would they remain inconspicuous and concentrate grimly on survival? And do they perceive their country and leader entirely differently today, more supportive and more hesitant to risk upheaval? This remains what Russian opposition figures must constantly consider. And Vladimir Putin and his close associates as well. It may be significant to observe that the political climate in 1991 differed greatly from today. Then, Russians felt authorised to demonstrate, granted permission from leadership - both through Yeltsin's encouragement and because for six years they had been informed by the General Secretary of the Communist Party himself, Mikhail Gorbachev, that speaking out constituted their right. Arguably this authorisation from above also influenced events in 2011, when middle-class Muscovites again gathered in the streets in substantial numbers, to protest against electoral fraud. Possibly they too were responding to the more liberal atmosphere, which existed when Dmitry Medvedev served as president, before Mr Putin returned. Today, a different atmosphere prevails. The public sphere for expression has contracted. Grassroots movements, rather than being supported, are frequently regarded as threats. New legislation and the precedent of prominent opposition leaders being assassinated all combine to convince critics they should remain silent, or depart and emigrate. And the fresh surge of nationalism following the Russian annexation of Crimea in 2014 has strengthened a potent message from leadership: that Russia faces external threats (from both NATO and jihadists) and confronts challenging circumstances domestically. Therefore, now particularly, the message continues, the nation requires a strong leader to maintain unity, eliminate that fifth column of enemies and preserve Russia's security. And should there be a historical lesson, it concerns events nearly one hundred years ago, when the Bolshevik revolution devastated the country. The final thing Russia requires, according to President Putin's supporters, is additional revolution and violence. However, when I reflect upon my personal experience of Russia during the past thirty or forty years, I continue thinking that precisely when you believe the giant slumbers, it surprises you by awakening. I cannot avoid remembering those Moscow residents, young and elderly, who crowded the city centre in 1991 to prevent the Communists' return. Nobody, not even the protesters themselves most likely, anticipated such a street uprising. Therefore who can predict what fate awaits Russia? History provides numerous parallels, from which we all derive different conclusions. Perhaps what seems most probable is a new development, which will surprise us all.

text: More than 60% of Australia's major organised crime figures now deal in crystal meth, a new report has found. The Australian Crime Commission (ACC) report stated the drug - referred to as ice - presented the greatest risk to Australian communities of any illicit substance. It additionally discovered that the drug's purity had risen over recent years, rendering it considerably more hazardous. Methylamphetamine exists in various forms, with the crystalline ice variant being most prevalent in Australia. The cost of crystal methamphetamine in Australia ranks amongst the world's highest, the report discovered, prompting the nation's organised criminal gangs to trade progressively in the substance. The report indicated that gangs distributing the drug were also incorporating other illicit substances into crystal methamphetamine in efforts to enhance addiction rates. The ACC stated there had been a substantial increase in the quantity and mass of detections at the Australian frontier without any reduction in domestic manufacturing. It noted Mexican drug cartels were becoming progressively involved in supplying the substance internationally, collaborating with distribution networks in other nations including Australia. The precursor chemicals utilised by Australia's domestic manufacturers to produce the drug were being increasingly imported from India and China, it determined. Chris Dawson, chief executive of the ACC, stated the accessibility and addictive characteristics of crystal methamphetamine had generated fresh demand in urban, rural and disadvantaged communities. Ice is a destructive, insidious substance. It impacts everyone from users, their families, and their communities, and the authorities who handle the users, he stated. In November last year, New South Wales police confiscated more than 800 kilograms of methylamphetamine, alongside two tonnes of MDMA - worth a combined estimated street value of A$1.5bn (£800m; $1.2m). And earlier this month, police uncovered 230 kilograms of liquid methylamphetamine in a shipment of 20,000 bottles of flavoured water bound for a Sydney warehouse. The ACC report recommended a coordinated national response to address the drug's growing prevalence. Everyone has a role in the battle against illicit drugs - including governments, law enforcement, health, education, industry, non-government organisations and the community, Mr Dawson stated.

text: Video sites such as YouTube will be forced to pay more to musicians and record companies under plans to reform European copyright laws. The draft directive shall also require publishers and producers to inform performers or authors regarding the profits their works have generated. The music industry has long criticised YouTube for failing to remunerate adequately for content such as music. News publishers shall also be recognised as rights holders for the first time. Under the directive, portals such as Google News would be compelled to pay newspaper publishers a fee when utilising small extracts or snippets of news stories. Carlo Perrone, head of the European Newspaper Publishers' Association, stated that creating a copyright for news publishers in Europe was a significant and historic step. Jean-Claude Juncker, president of the European Commission, stated: I want journalists, publishers and authors to be remunerated fairly for their work, whether it is produced in studios or living rooms, whether it is disseminated offline or online, whether it is published via a copying machine or hyperlinked on the web. The Commission has not detailed how it would compel sites such as YouTube to pay more to artists. The plans also call for easier access to online content across all EU countries and to reform copyright rules for research and education. Andrus Ansip, vice-president for the digital single market, stated: Our proposal shall ensure that more content will be available, transforming Europe's copyright rules in light of a new digital reality. The proposals, which are likely to be challenged by lobbyists, must proceed to the European Parliament and EU states for approval - which could take years. A Google spokesperson stated: We believe there is a better way. Innovation and partnership - not subsidies and onerous restrictions - are the key to a successful, diverse and sustainable news sector in the EU. More than 1,000 artists, including Lady Gaga and Coldplay, signed a letter earlier this year calling upon the Commission to take steps to address the value gap. It stated that sites such as YouTube were unfairly siphoning value away from the music community and its artists and songwriters. YouTube, which carries videos as well as audio-only content, generates revenue by selling advertising and then divides profits amongst rights owners. Its business model differs from music streaming sites such as Spotify and Apple Music, which pay record companies a small sum each time a song is played. The body representing the UK recorded music business, the BPI, welcomed Brussels' recognition for the need for a level playing field for digital music. Geoff Taylor, BPI chief executive, stated it was unfair that platforms such as YouTube are building huge businesses using music and other content whilst paying only a fraction of the royalties paid to artists and labels by services such as Spotify and Apple Music. PRS for Music, which represents the rights of almost 120,000 songwriters, composers and music publishers in the UK, stated it welcomed the move to ensure that searchable sites such as YouTube require a licence from the rights holders. The European Commission's proposed new copyright directive provides the framework for this essential legal clarity, stated chief executive Robert Ashcroft. IFPI, which represents the international recording industry worldwide, stated the proposals were a good first step towards better and fairer licensing for content in Europe. Chief executive Frances Moore stated: Importantly, it confirms that user uploaded content services such as YouTube, which are the largest source of on-demand music, should not be able to operate outside normal licensing rules. However, there is much more to do to make this a workable proposal. UK Music, which represents the British music industry, stated this week that YouTube was still not paying artists sufficiently for their music. UK Music stated the Google-owned site was yet to deliver fair financial returns for rights owners and creators, artists, composers, songwriters and publishers. The band Two Door Cinema Club stated: I do not think things at the minute are fair. YouTube does not pay a fair royalty. Google states it has paid the music industry more than $3bn (£2.3bn) since 2007. However, the Commission's proposals did not go far enough to prevent geo-blocking of online content, the European Consumer Organisation, BEUC, stated. It also criticised plans to compel websites to automatically detect and remove videos that contain parts of copyrighted works. This would punish millions of consumers who share a self-made remix of a song, family videos or holiday pictures which contain parts of a music tune or video clip, BEUC stated. The Commission has also proposed an overhaul of EU telecoms rules to ensure much faster internet access across Europe. It wants schools, universities, hospitals, transport hubs and companies that rely on digital technologies to have extremely fast connectivity exceeding 1 gigabits a second. All homes - both rural and urban - should have broadband speed of at least 100 megabits a second. Finally, the Commission calls for all urban areas, as well as major roads and railways, to have 5G wireless mobile data coverage. Each EU country should have 5G in at least one major city by 2020.

text: Back in the heady days of May 2010, when the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats united in government, they set out a detailed set of policy proposals called the Coalition Agreement. One paragraph stated: We will... pursue a detailed agreement on limiting donations and reforming party funding in order to remove big money from politics. Following disagreement between the parties in the aftermath of the cash-for-honours scandal, this all appeared rather promising. Several weeks later, the independent Committee on Standards in Public Life considered the matter worthy of investigation and commenced an inquiry. The chairman, Sir Christopher Kelly, acknowledged that significant difficulties remain but he was encouraged to declare that there is sufficient will to reform the system to give us some hope that it ought to be possible to find a solution. In the vernacular of Whitehall, that represents bold, optimistic material. Sir Christopher's cup was not merely half full, it was positively overflowing with hope. Now, following a delay of many months, we have discovered the results of Sir Christopher's effort. He is proposing a £10,000 limit on individual donations to political parties. At the last general election, approximately 30 million of us troubled to vote. So the plan would theoretically provide a substantial £90m to be distributed amongst the parties over the course of a five-year parliament. That represents quite a lot of money. The public would also be able to give a large sum of money to a party without paying tax. The difficulty is that no one appears to agree with this. The Labour member, Margaret Beckett, has set out her opposition to the union reforms. The coalition agreement promised that the government would pursue reform. But it did not promise to achieve it.

These are external links and will open in a new window We shall be updating this page with additional questions: Kenya lacks an election campaign funding law. An effort by the electoral commission to establish one last year was rejected by MPs. The commission had proposed limits for different seats: The absence of the law means candidates are presently free to spend as much as they wish. According to the privately owned Daily Nation, most of the money is spent on logistics and advertisements but many candidates and parties also bribe voters. It reports that in the 2013 election, then opposition coalition Cord spent in excess of $50m (£40m) whilst the governing Jubilee Party spent more than $100m to run its presidential campaign. Politicians raise money from businessmen and some hold fundraisers. Opposition parties however accuse the ruling party of using state resources in its campaigns. Ken Opalo, from Georgetown University in the US, says that whilst there is likely to be some trouble, it will not be on the scale seen 10 years ago, which left more than 1,000 people dead and about 600,000 displaced from their homes. I am not too worried about the national elections. The real action will likely be at the county level, he said. There will most certainly be violence. But again, that will be more a reflection of what is at stake, rather than some descent into complete chaos and state failure. This is a view shared by Nic Cheeseman, professor of democracy at the UK's University of Birmingham and a commentator on Kenyan politics. He says disorderly party primaries are a reason to be concerned, but that they may not lead to greater conflict come election day. What chaotic primaries tell us about election Kenya has maintained steady economic growth rate in the past five years, averaging 5% per year. However, rising prices of basic goods like milk, bread and maize flour have pushed inflation up to 12%, and many Kenyan families say they are now struggling to get by. Kenyans have been using the hashtag #CostOfLivingKe to share the costs of basic items and how they are adjusting their lifestyles. Every election year, the economy also experiences a shrinkage and that's no different this year as investors wait out on the election period, Kwame Owino, CEO of the Institute of Economic Affairs told the BBC. Some companies are currently cutting down employment, but not in big numbers, and the informal sector remains the biggest employer, he added. Kenya got $1bn in new investments in 2014 following some reforms like reducing the costs of doing business and bureaucracy, investment in infrastructure and lowering visa costs which has encouraged tourism. The economy has however been strained by corruption, heightened political tension and state-controlled bank interest rates - a measure meant to reduce borrowing costs that has failed to deliver. The UN's development agency (UNDP) says Kenya has the highest unemployment rate in the region, with four out of 10 Kenyans out of work. Mr Owino says that dispassionate voters may be guided by who they think will best serve their economic interests. In its 2016 report Transparency International ranked Kenya at position 145 out of 176 countries. It blamed Kenya's low ranking on the incompetence and ineffectiveness of anti-corruption agencies, saying that the failure to punish individuals implicated in graft had been a major stumbling block. Anti-corruption campaigner John Githongo has called President Uhuru Kenyatta's administration the most corrupt in Kenya's history. Mr Kenyatta has, however, said his anti-corruption efforts were being undermined by the courts, who were slowing prosecutions and the anti-corruption agency, who he said were sluggish. Mr Githongo cites several reported scandals involving alleged inflation of costs of projects and payments to phantom companies. Opposition members have also been named in several scandals but some have accused the government of scapegoating. Constitutional bodies set up to fight corruption have been accused of being partisan and lacking independence. Kenyan political analyst Barrack Muluka blames ordinary Kenyans for the corruption problem, saying that they are blinded by their ethnicity: A government can steal as much as it wants and Kenyans will be happy as long as it's 'our thieves'. He points at the April party primaries where candidates of questionable integrity and those accused of being involved in corruption won their races. Mr Githongo, calls it normalisation of the absurdity. He says that theft has become normal: Those we used to call thieves are now hustlers, he says.
