text: New rules for moving livestock will be disastrous for small agricultural shows, the Farmers Union of Wales said. These are external links and will open in a new window Farmers stated the Welsh Government's new regulations on livestock movement are excessively strict and costly. From 10 June, farmers must register a quarantine unit (QU) on their farm to move livestock on and off, and circumvent six-day standstill regulations. The Welsh Government stated the system was developed in partnership with the farming industry. Presently, if farmers bring new stock onto their farm, the entire farm is subject to a six-day lockdown, where no animals can be moved off. However, there are exemptions for seasonal events such as agricultural shows. A field or shed separated from other livestock, known as an approved isolation unit, can be utilised to circumvent the regulations. However, these isolation units cannot be utilised after 10 June and farmers must apply and pay for the new quarantine units. There are 61 regulations as part of the new system, which include installing double gates and double fences, as well as wearing specialised clothing. The fee is £172.80 for one QU and £244.80 for two. Farmer Gwilym Jones, from Blaenau Ffestiniog, stated: It makes no sense to show, it's not worth it. The regulations are going backwards instead of forwards. And Geraint Jones, from Ystrad Meurig, stated: I will break the law, and if they want to put me in jail, they can - I've got nothing to lose. If they want to kill the countryside, they're doing the right thing. Sian Davies, who shows her texel sheep around the country, stated the new changes cost money, they're a nuisance and they increase paperwork. She stated the Welsh Government don't know what's going on. I called the office in Aberystwyth and they didn't know what I was referring to. Geraint Jones stated he had a similar experience with the offices in Cardiff and Carmarthen. The Welsh Government has not confirmed there are delays in the registration process. Brian Walters, vice-president of Farmers Union of Wales, stated: This is disastrous for smaller agricultural shows. We don't feel there is sufficient evidence to indicate that diseases are passed between livestock at agricultural shows to justify such draconian measures. In England the changes to the regulations have been delayed until the autumn, avoiding the show season. In a statement, the Welsh Government stated: The new QU system was designed to simplify the standstill regime and provide extra flexibility whilst maintaining disease movement curbs. It was developed in partnership with the farming industry. Although QUs can be used to manage movements to and from shows it is important to note they are intended to be used for all types of animal movement, not just for shows. The alternative arrangements to the six-day standstill were developed at the request of the industry (through the Working Smarter review) and in close collaboration with the industry through the LIDAG (Livestock Identification Advisory Group) over the past few years - not rushed, worked through systematically, and collaboratively, with the support of Independent Veterinary Risk Assessments. It stated the recommendations were published in January 2012 and the Welsh Government had written to everyone in the industry twice, in April and May 2017, in addition to an extensive communications campaign.

text: Supermarkets and other big businesses could face higher business rates under a Welsh Conservative government, with a tax cut for smaller companies. The Conservatives propose altering the method by which rates are calculated, forming part of a commitment to place small business requirements at the heart of the Welsh government. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies stated that small firms were essential to Wales and required assistance to develop and grow. Retailers cautioned against creating winners or losers or more complexity. The Conservatives would additionally appoint a team of officials within the Welsh government dedicated to small businesses and accountable to the assembly, should they secure power in May's assembly election. Additional measures, some previously announced, include abolishing the age limit on a job creation scheme and committing to make it simpler for businesses to borrow money from the Welsh government. Mr Davies stated: Wales is a nation of shopkeepers, and those small firms are the lifeblood of the Welsh economy; which is why they require support to develop and grow. Business rates are paid to local councils and are based upon property values. Discounts are already available to small businesses from the Welsh government, known as rate relief. For instance, businesses with property valued up to £6,000 pay no rates. The Conservatives say they would extend rate relief to additional businesses. However, they would also introduce different rates for large and small businesses, ensuring that bigger businesses pay more. England and Scotland already possess separate rates, but Wales does not. The Welsh Retail Consortium, which represents shop owners, called for fundamental reform of business rates for all, whether that be small, medium sized or larger businesses. A spokeswoman stated: The proposed small firms' relief is a welcome acknowledgement of the need to keep down costs, however many high street retailers will not benefit and we would be alarmed if this new rate for medium and larger sized commercial premises simply opened the door to even higher taxes, as has been proposed in Scotland.

text: A Chinese authority has banned the importation of brown crabs from Anglesey after claiming they contain a metallic contaminant. The Hong Kong-based Centre for Food Safety (CFS) declared an embargo on the marine creatures and cautioned people on Wednesday against consuming them. The CFS stated samples it had gathered from the island contained excessive cadmium. Defra stated all crabs sold in the UK must comply with EU regulations on the permitted cadmium level. It added it was collaborating with the Hong Kong authorities to identify a workable solution so trade could restart as soon as possible. Two crab samples that were prepared for export to China contained the metal at 15 and 22 parts per million (ppm) - surpassing a limit of 2ppm, the CFS stated. More than 220kg of meat from one of the exporters has been detained by Hong Kong officials, but 160kg has already been distributed, the CFS stated. Officials cautioned that, whilst occasional consumption of crabs with cadmium will not cause significant harm, prolonged intake may have adverse effects on people's kidneys. The CFS has informed the relevant authorities of the United Kingdom and the local trade and will continue to closely monitor the incident and take appropriate actions, including enhanced surveillance of aquatic products imported from the United Kingdom, the announcement stated. Anglesey council stated it had not heard from the Chinese authority but added it was aware of the situation and was making enquiries. Brown crab is known to accumulate cadmium in the hepatopancreas (a component of the brown meat) due to the detoxifying function of this organ, a spokesperson stated. The authority has not issued export certificates in relation to brown crab destined for China for some months, following advice from Defra that the Chinese had placed restrictions on the import of live crabs from the whole of the UK, due to excessive cadmium levels found on testing. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) in Wales stated cadmium concentrations in brown meat from crabs - as opposed to white crab meat, which comes from the legs and claws - vary widely. It stated the NHS advises regular fish-eaters to avoid eating brown crab meat too often. The FSA is continuing to work with the crab industry to examine ways of reducing cadmium levels in brown crab meat through different processing methods, an FSA spokesperson stated.

text: British reggae band UB40 have praised Jeremy Corbyn as an incorruptible politician who will put working people first as they backed his campaign to remain as Labour leader. The ensemble, which has sold 70 million records, stated that Mr Corbyn had inspired young people and provided a credible alternative to conventional politics. Mr Corbyn has received support from numerous celebrities, including actor Daniel Radcliffe. However, bestselling Harry Potter author JK Rowling has described him as an ineffective leader. Mr Corbyn faces a leadership challenge from Owen Smith. The outcome of the contest will be declared on 24 September. The Labour leader, who has stated his desire for the arts to be a priority for the next Labour administration, has secured several celebrity endorsements in recent weeks. Birmingham-based UB40, named after the government's unemployment benefit form at the time, were amongst the most successful British bands of the 1980s and 1990s, achieving 50 hit singles - including the chart-toppers Red Red Wine, Can't Help Falling in Love and I Got You Babe. Whilst three members of the original formation have departed in recent years, triggering a legal dispute regarding the use of the group's name, the remaining members headed by guitarist and vocalist Robin Campbell have endorsed Mr Corbyn. Jeremy has rekindled an interest in politics for people who no longer felt represented, and engaged and inspired a new generation of young voters who, for the first time, believe they have an incorruptible politician who genuinely represents them, Mr Campbell stated. Drummer Jimmy Brown said Mr Corbyn was the sole frontline politician prepared to speak up for working people who have been poorly treated by successive governments, including New Labour, in recent decades. Mr Corbyn, who faces opposition from the majority of his MPs and lost a confidence vote following the EU referendum, welcomed the band's support ahead of a planned joint appearance on Tuesday. UB40's story was and remains inspiring; people from different cultures and backgrounds coming together and combining their talents - at a time when prejudice was more widespread - and creativity to produce music that has endured across decades, he stated. As part of his arts manifesto published last month, Mr Corbyn promised that all primary schools in England would receive additional funding for arts activities and a single national programme for arts scholarships would be established. The Labour leader told the Guardian on Monday he would be pleased to meet JK Rowling to discuss their disagreements after she said he was taking the party in the wrong direction. Her suggestion that Mr Corbyn risked destroying Labour and that the poorest in society require an electable alternative to the Conservatives rather than mouthy, impotent socialism prompted an angry reaction from Corbyn supporters on social media.

Shortly before 23:30 local time, officers Matthew Harrity and Mohamed Noor responded to Damond's 911 emergency call regarding a suspected assault in an alleyway behind her residence. She resided at the property with her American fiancé whom she intended to marry in August. Wearing her pyjamas, Damond approached the patrol car, which had its lights switched off. A conversation ensued and Officer Noor, who was seated in the passenger seat, shot her through the driver's open window, Officer Harrity informed officials. text: Almost four million children in the UK do not own a book, according to a report by the National Literacy Trust. These are external links and will open in a new window The proportion of children without books is rising, the charity stated. It is now one in three, compared with one in 10 in 2005. Children with their own books were more likely to be above-average readers and perform better at school, the study of 18,000 children indicated. Poorer children and boys were less likely to possess books, it added. The survey was conducted in September with school-aged children from 111 schools across the UK. It indicated that a third (33.2%) did not possess books of their own. That equates to 3.8m children UK-wide. Better off children and young people were more likely to state they had books of their own, compared with those who received free school meals. Trust director Jonathan Douglas said the sharp rise in the number of children without their own books was of particular concern. He stated: We know there is a direct correlation between book ownership and children's reading abilities. With one in 6 in the UK struggling with literacy it is very concerning that many children could be missing out on opportunities to develop these essential skills. The trust stated that children who owned books were more likely than others to read every day, and that book ownership had a clear link with reading ability. Of the children and young people with books of their own, more than half read above the level expected for their age, with fewer than one in 10 reading below the level. By contrast, amongst those without books of their own, nearly a fifth were failing to meet the expected reading level, with only a third reading above that level. The trust launched the survey to coincide with an appeal for public donations towards books and reading support for disadvantaged children. A number of children's book illustrators have designed cards to support the trust's Christmas Gift of Reading campaign. The survey also revealed links between reading ability and receiving books as presents. About a fifth of children stated they had never been to a book shop or a library. But the survey also showed that reading any type of material, for example magazines, outside class at least once a month was also associated with greater reading attainment.

text: Conservative backbenchers are demanding radical changes to school funding in England within months. They state ministers confront a campaign from dozens of their own MPs unless they pledge swift reform. Educators will face redundancy and class sizes will expand without action, they state. One backbencher, Daniel Kawczynski, stated that huge numbers of Conservatives in the Commons were demanding change. He informed BBC Radio 4's the World at One: I think you would be fascinated how strong the feelings are on this issue and the sort of campaign that is going to be pursued in the course of this year Conservative former chairman of the education select committee Graham Stuart stated he believed dozens of Tories would want the earliest possible announcement, ideally in July's Budget. He stated: You are seeing schools confronting prospects of deficits unless they don't take significant action to reduce headcount. We will you know potentially be examining redundancies in order to cope with the funding pressures. Backbenchers state the way government money is allocated for local authorities to fund schools must change from next April. There are sharp variations across the nation, with the best funded areas receiving as much as £7,000 per pupil and the worst off getting just over £4,000. Ministers stated they intended to change the system since 2010, promised reform in 2013, and made a fresh commitment in the Conservative manifesto. They provided an additional £390m to the worst funded authorities at the end of the last Parliament, but have not rewritten the funding formula. The move would almost certainly see well funded inner city authorities lose money, whilst some rural areas would be winners. A Department for Education spokeswoman stated: The last government made considerable progress in reforming the school funding system. In 2014 an additional £390 million was allocated to boost 69 of the least fairly funded areas in the country in 2015-16 - the biggest step toward fairer schools funding in 10 years. But we recognise there is still work to which is why we have committed to looking at what more needs to be done to ensure that all local areas are funded justly.

text: Brightly coloured murals adorn the walls of the 'Little Hands' nursery. The classroom walls are concrete, the roof plastic sheeting. Outside, a group of four- and five-year-olds are singing and dancing. Disregard the dusty roads beyond the chicken wire fence and you could be in virtually any kindergarten in the world. However, this is the Zaatari camp in Jordan, where thousands of Syrians fleeing their homeland now reside. Many of the children we are witnessing here now were born in the camp. They have known no other existence, states Neil Mathers, the head of Save the Children in Scotland. The charity operates three nurseries in Zaatari, with 52 per cent of the camp's children. Mr Mathers states: There are 40,000 children who require this kind of support in Zaatari camp alone. Our kindergartens reach approximately 2,000 children so much more is required to handle just the children in this camp. Zaatari refugee camp is one of the locations the refugees to be granted admission to the UK will be selected from. A few miles south of Jordan's border with Syria, the camp extends across 8 sq km (3 sq miles) of desolate stony desert. It has grown from nothing to become effectively Jordan's fourth largest city. With a population exceeding 80,000, it is the world's second largest refugee camp. A mixture of tents, tin shacks and ramshackle huts are what the refugees now call home. In the summer, temperatures here exceed 50C and in winter, nights can drop to below freezing. It is tough, states Dominic Graham, Jordan country director for Edinburgh-based charity Mercy Corps. Life in the camps is tough. Mercy Corps is just one of a score of non-governmental organisations which have been working in Zaatari since it was established four years ago when refugees first began fleeing Syria's increasingly brutal civil war. Water, sanitation, shelter are all in place in Zaatari. Rudimentary commerce has developed - there is a market and small shacks selling everyday items. Zaatari is slowly developing an unwanted permanence. However, it is a bleak existence. Lives on hold, going nowhere. When the Syrian refugees first arrived most thought they would be returning to Syria very soon. They thought President Assad's regime was going to fall. The government and aid agencies thought so too. A crisis of months rather than years. No one thinks that now. Hassan arrived in Zaatari last year. Like many here, he does not want to give his full name for fear of consequences for relatives who have remained within Syria. He and his family have no savings and now want to return to Syria. He said: I will go back as soon as it is safe. However, he does not think that will be soon. Mr Graham, from Mercy Corps, states most of the refugees are desperate to return to their former lives in Syria but the prospects of that are getting thinner and thinner. Zaatari is just the tip of the refugee iceberg. Inside Syria, it is estimated there are nearly eight million internally displaced people. Those who escape to camps such as Zaatari are those who are able to. Some had geography on their side, living just over the border. Others made it here because they could afford to pay smugglers to help them cross the borders into Syria's neighbouring countries. Those who are left inside are often the most vulnerable, the poorest. Getting aid to them is vital, according to Steve Gordon, from Glasgow, who is Mercy Corps' security manager for the region. If you are assisting inside Syria and people are staying there and not coming out, they are not becoming a burden on the surrounding countries. The challenges are immense. Front lines are constantly shifting. Russia's intervention has altered the dynamics. Mercy Corps states it is seeing massive changes with populations shifting. Gordon states even as the situation becomes more dangerous the need to keep supplies flowing increases. If an area is going to be cut off you have to pre-position supplies in those areas to sustain those communities through what could be very hard times. In Zaatari children play in the spray of water being hosed from a tanker to dampen down the dusty streets of the camp. In the distance the hills of Syria are just visible through the haze. Whether these children will ever return to their homeland is impossible to know. However, what the future holds is increasingly driving the thinking of the refugees here. Should they stay or should they go. A battered silver bus waits near the camp's security checkpoint. Its destination is the Syrian border. For some, life in the refugee camps holds so little hope they are choosing to return. It is only a trickle, but memories of the dangers that drove people here fade. For some Europe and the prospect of a new life there has become their goal. Individuals and small family groups make the arduous and dangerous journey. If they succeed and successfully settle in Germany, France or Britain perhaps the rest of the family can follow. Billions of pounds are being spent trying to deal with the Syrian refugee crisis. The UK alone has spent just over £1bn across the region, with £330m in Jordan alone, since the start of the war in Syria. Jeff Tudor is head of the UK government's international development programme in Jordan. As a veteran of the humanitarian and development aid business, he knows there is no easy or quick answer to the refugee crisis. He states: We are hanging on in there, but ultimately we will need a political solution to what is happening in Syria. Even if we get a political solution tomorrow we are looking at at least a decade. The refugees will not go back overnight, the situation in Syria will not allow it.

text: Asian stocks opened higher after turmoil on financial markets saw European and US indexes tumble following another oil price fall. Thursday's advances nevertheless failed to recoup the losses financial markets have experienced during recent days. Investors continue to fret over tumbling oil prices and decelerating growth in China. On Wednesday, equities had plunged to their lowest points since May 2009, with British, French and Japanese shares dropping more than 20% beneath their 2015 peaks. Wall Street proved vulnerable as well. The Dow Jones finished 1.6% down following a turbulent trading session that had witnessed stocks decline by as much as 3%. Overnight markets in Europe and the US endured a dreadful day, where sentiment surrounding a 'drunk' Asia spread, market strategist Bernard Aw of IG noted in a briefing. Mainland China's principal market in Shanghai was marginally down by 0.3%, validating international anxieties regarding the world's second-largest economy. Hong Kong, however, succeeded in recovering somewhat from the previous day's record decline. The Hang Seng index regained 1.3% after shedding nearly 4% on Wednesday. Dealers state there is limited conviction supporting the recent rally, the BBC's Juliana Liu in Hong Kong reported. Indeed, the advances are quite modest and susceptible to any suggestion of adverse news. They believe this might even constitute a so-called dead cat bounce, a phrase created in the 1980s to characterise a brief recovery in an otherwise falling market. Earlier during the day, Australia was the first to reverse the share market decline, with the ASX/200 advancing 1.1%. The increase occurred despite Australia being especially reliant on China's economic performance as most of the commodities propelling the economy down under are shipped to China. Japan and South Korea were likewise higher with the Nikkei rising by 1.4% whilst the Kospi climbed by 0.5%. Markets are simply very uncertain regarding the deceleration in the Chinese economy, Stephen Koukoulas, chief strategist TD Securities, informed the BBC. We observed the official figures, but frankly not many individuals place substantial weight on the dependability of them and instead examine commodity prices as a gauge for how the Chinese economy is performing. Oil prices have dropped beneath $28 per barrel, whilst coal, iron ore and other metals are all likewise in a protracted decline. Numerous analysts have reduced their 2016 oil price projections, with Morgan Stanley analysts stating that oil in the $20s is feasible, should China devalue its currency further. Economists at the Royal Bank of Scotland suggest that oil could tumble to $16, whilst Standard Chartered forecasts that prices might reach merely $10 per barrel. Therefore, investors are especially anxious about the loss of impetus in China, Mr Koukoulas stated. The question remains: Is it merely an adjustment to some of the previous excesses or is this the beginning of something rather more unpleasant that will drag the economy to a considerably weaker growth trajectory? Some commentators believe that numerous markets were heading for a decline. Asset prices were inflated by ultra-low interest rates in the developed world and also by the central banks that have pursued quantitative easing, purchasing financial assets with newly created money. That occurred with shares, with bonds and with commodities. For commodities the boom has well and truly concluded, partly owing to the slowdown in China and in the case of oil chiefly owing to abundant supplies. Clearly there are some worrying developments and the IMF has issued a warning: If these key challenges are not successfully addressed, global growth could be derailed. That fundamentally is what the markets are concerned about. Read more from Andrew here Just how low can oil prices fall? China economic slowdown: Can it avoid a crash? text: Scotland's largest council has said the greater Glasgow area will suffer unless there is specific government action to mitigate the effects of Brexit. A fresh report from Glasgow City Council outlines challenges the region shall confront following the referendum outcome supporting Britain's departure from the European Union. The document states that specific policy decisions are required from the British and Scottish administrations to assist the city region. Amongst these requirements is for European Union-funded programmes to be assumed by both administrations. Glasgow City Council leader Frank McAveety stated that intervention was required from both administrations to prevent a potential crisis. I consider that Brexit shall present Glasgow with significant economic challenges, he stated. I equally consider these may be surmounted if particular intervention is undertaken by the Scottish and British administrations. Should that occur then the difficulties linked with Brexit may become an opportunity for economic expansion rather than a threat of crisis. The document, Brexit and the Glasgow Economy: Impacts, Actions and Asks, was prepared by the council, Glasgow Chamber of Commerce and Glasgow Economic Leadership board - a partnership organisation comprising the council, chamber of commerce, Scottish Enterprise and Skills Development Scotland. The council stated the document was compiled with assistance from more than 100 senior business, local authority and academic leaders. It shall now be presented to the first minister's Standing Committee on Europe, headed by Professor Anton Muscatelli, Principal of Glasgow University. The document presents six principal requests of the Scottish and British administrations to reduce the impacts of Brexit. These comprise: Professor Sir Jim McDonald, chairman of the Glasgow Economic Leadership board and Principal of Strathclyde University, stated: There exists no doubt that Brexit represents a fundamental system shock and one that presents challenges to us all. We shall now position our city to address the challenges of Brexit and exploit longer-term opportunities to expand our economy. Only through working together may we enhance our economic fundamentals: our skills, innovation and entrepreneurship. It is upon these foundations that our future shall and must be established. Stuart Patrick, chief executive of Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, stated swift intervention was required to address the challenges ahead. He stated: In order to capitalise upon the new world as it exists following the Brexit vote and to grasp the opportunities that shall be presented to us, a clear, collective, coherent and forward-looking approach from the City of Glasgow and from the Scottish and British administrations is necessary. We cannot accomplish this alone and whilst uncertainty persists regarding our future trading relationship with the European Union we must combine all our efforts now to secure investment and employment and to enhance trade.

text: The UK's home secretary has expressed concerns about plans to make it easier for Chinese tourists to get visas. Culture Secretary Jeremy Hunt had requested the system be simplified to help turbocharge tourism following the London 2012 Olympics. However, a letter viewed by the Daily Telegraph indicates Theresa May considers it would present a security threat. The letter, authored by Mrs May's private secretary, states she regards the proposal as unacceptable. On Tuesday, Mr Hunt outlined a strategy to boost UK tourism after London's Games and stated ministers were examining simplifying visa applications for non-EU nationals. The strategy concentrated on attracting visitors from China, where the government believes there exists potential to treble tourist numbers - generating over £500m in additional spending and creating more than 14,000 positions. Presently, visitors may apply for a single visa to visit much of Europe - however a separate one is needed to travel to the UK. Nations such as France and Germany prove far more successful at attracting Chinese visitors, and the UK could perform better if obtaining a visa was simpler, Mr Hunt has indicated. However, a letter from Mrs May's private secretary to the prime minister's private secretary stated the existing rules were a key tool in protecting the public against significant harm. There exist already 400 Chinese criminals awaiting deportation and 1,000 asylum applications from Chinese citizens last year, it stated. The proposal... is not acceptable to the home secretary for national security reasons, the letter stated. We also confront significant challenges with foreign national offenders and organised crime, including drugs, money laundering, fraud, criminal finances, intellectual property, immigration and cyber crime. However, Mark Tanzer, chief executive of the Association of British Travel Agents (Abta), stated: In the absence of concrete data regarding visa abuse, it remains impossible to determine whether the correct balance is being achieved between the UK's commercial interests and its security requirements. He contended that proper visa monitoring and reporting processes were required, and any abuses of the system could be addressed as they emerged. We must not overlook that visas are merely one of the factors that deter Chinese tourists from visiting us - lack of air routes and high aviation taxes also suppress demand, he added. Mr Tanzer has previously stated his organisation welcomed Mr Hunt's position as a step in the right direction. Meanwhile, Immigration Minister Damian Green revealed that a visa scheme had failed to attract as many of the most talented artists, musicians and scientists to come and work in the UK as the government had anticipated. We offer a thousand visas annually for the exceptionally talented, Mr Green stated. In its first year of operation it came nowhere near utilising them all. That indicates to me we need to fine tune the system to ensure that around the world, if you are a bright young artist or a gifted young scientist, you understand there is this route to come and work in Britain. We need to perform better on that. The minister added: If you are a current Nobel Prize winner, you will not find it very difficult to enter this country. But we want the next generation of Nobel Prize winners, so we have carved out a specific route in the immigration system.

The SNP confirmed on Saturday that all 54 of its sitting MPs would be endorsed as candidates. text: Lufthansa pilots have begun their eighth strike this year, forcing the cancellation of 1,511 flights over Monday and Tuesday. The industrial action was originally targeted at predominantly European services, but will be extended to international routes on Tuesday, affecting 200,000 passengers. Lufthansa stated that the strike, concerning alterations to retirement and pension conditions, would damage profits and its reputation. However, the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) union declared it wished to deliver a clear message. Last week, VC summoned its members at Lufthansa's low-cost carrier, Germanwings, for a 12-hour walkout. The union, which represents approximately 5,400 Lufthansa pilots, is urging the airline to reconsider its decision to increase the age at which they may retire from 55. The company has proposed to maintain the arrangement for current members but not to extend it to new recruits. VC stated Lufthansa was obstructing negotiations. Union board member Markus Wahl declared: We are prolonging the strike to send a clearer signal. Perhaps now, Lufthansa will finally relent. However, Simone Menne, Lufthansa's chief financial officer, stated in a declaration: The strikes are not only causing substantial financial damage but are also harming our reputation, the consequences of which are considerable and not yet apparent, The airline stated it hoped to operate one-third of its flights over the two days. The Lufthansa strike follows a walkout over the weekend by railway drivers. The train drivers' strike concerned demands by the GDL for a 5% pay rise for 20,000 drivers and a shorter working week. The head of the GDL union, Claus Weselsky, stated there would be a week-long pause before any further strikes. The German Industry Federation business lobby criticised the strikes, stating they damaged the entire economy by affecting logistics, tourism and business travel. Germany's economy has been decelerating recently. Nevertheless, the Economy Ministry stated although the strikes would certainly impact some sectors of the economy, there was no reason to alter the 2014 growth forecast which was reduced this month to 1.2%. Germany's government is expected to produce a draft law later this year designed to prevent small numbers of employees paralysing large parts of the country's infrastructure through strike action.

text: AMs have agreed that the National Assembly for Wales should change its name. These are external links and will open in a new window The assembly's presiding officer Elin Jones has informed AMs that several possible options exist. Welsh Parliament has been suggested previously but one AM stated the name Senedd should be examined. However UKIP AM Gareth Bennett declared some organisations with Welsh-only names were recognised solely in the Welsh-speaking colony of Pontcanna in Cardiff. First Minister Carwyn Jones stated some would consider his remarks offensive. No new name was agreed at an assembly debate to examine the matter on Tuesday, but the presiding officer and assembly commission will now assess the implications of such a change. AMs unanimously endorsed, without a vote, a motion which stated the assembly should change its name to reflect its constitutional status as a national parliament. The assembly will shortly receive the power under the Wales Bill, which is progressing through the UK parliament, to rename the National Assembly of Wales with agreement of two thirds of the chamber, with demands for the name change to reflect its expanding powers. The Welsh Government had planned a vote requesting for the assembly to be known as the Welsh Parliament unofficially before a legal change could be implemented, but the vote was withdrawn. Ms Jones stated the next step will be to consult soon on what the name should be. There are several possibilities and many associated terms which would arise from that choice, she stated. The name should continue to inspire confidence and pride amongst the people of Wales. She added she will inform the assembly of the next steps at the outset of the autumn term. Bethan Jenkins, Plaid Cymru AM for South Wales West, has suggested that the Welsh word Senedd, which is used to refer to the assembly building, is used to refer to the institution itself. Let us be self-confident enough to discard our mental baggage and take this opportunity to be unique by adopting an official Welsh name for our Senedd, she told the debate. She stated some AMs wish to retain the name National Assembly, but added Senedd is already used widely on the ground. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies, who suggested the Assembly was renamed to the Welsh Parliament back in 2012, stated: I couldn't see why we couldn't have Senedd and Parliament, because obviously for people there is a complete understanding of the word Parliament, in the way UK democracy works. Over time I think the word Senedd could be readily taken on board, he added. UKIP group leader Neil Hamilton wondered whether the public at large would regard the debate as pretentious navel gazing. As and when the Wales Bill passes and tax raising powers are devolved to this institution there is, of course, a serious argument for calling ourselves a Parliament, he stated. He stated he was personally attracted to the idea of the Senedd as a name. I wonder whether that would make us Senators, he added. But Gareth Bennett, UKIP AM for South Wales Central, called for the term Senedd to be kicked into the long grass and stated it would distance the assembly from the majority of the people of Wales. Bethan is from a Welsh speaking background, or a bilingual background, and in her social circle Senedd may be a well used term, Mr Bennett stated, to laughs and derision from Ms Jenkins. In the Wetherspoons pub in Canton few people would know what I was talking about if I started talking about the Senedd, and I can tell you that from experience. Referring to a list of organisations with Welsh-only names, including the Urdd and Chwarae Teg, that Ms Jenkins had read out Mr Bennett stated: The problem is most people outside the Welsh speaking colony of Pontcanna, most people in Cardiff don't know what these things are. First Minister Carwyn Jones stated: If someone stood up in this chamber and described people in Ceredigion or in Gwynedd who are English speakers as a colony there would be uproar. It makes it sound as if people in Wales who speak a certain language don't belong in our capital city, and that is a wholly wrong remark, he stated, adding it would be highly offensive to a number of people although he wasn't sure Mr Bennett meant it that way.

text: The stories of those visiting and working at the Royal Welsh Show are being told on social media by a PhD student for his thesis. Greg Thomas, originally from Builth Wells in Powys but studying at Aberystwyth University, Ceredigion, commenced by conducting surveys at the show - but realised they were merely providing him with figures. I did not want [the thesis] to be terribly dull, Mr Thomas, who is scheduled to submit his work in October, stated. I did not want it to be read by five bearded academics and that's it - I wanted it to be useful and everyone to gain something from it. So what about examining the people behind the figures? It's 100,000 words - but there's so much happening here and the show means so much to so many people, is that even sufficient? Mr Thomas decided to break up his doctorate - which considers the exchange between farmers and non-farmers, Welsh identity and politics - with photographs and quotes from farmers, visitors, stewards and organisers. In other words - the humans of the Royal Welsh show. Taking inspiration from the Humans of New York social media phenomenon, Mr Thomas arranged interviews during the show and also approaches people he spots along the way who may have an interesting story to tell. Even though Mr Thomas said his most popular posts are usually those about real people, rather than celebrities or politicians, rugby referee Nigel Owens was an exception to the rule. Mr Owens contributed bilingual posts, stating: I've been coming to the Royal Welsh for years really, coming from a farming community and working on a farm, that was the interest originally. But then over the last few years I've been president of Wales Young Farmers clubs, and most of the time I've been coming here to compete with the Young Farmers when I was a member and then coming to help out in the YFC office during the competitions. The last four or five years, I've been coming here to referee the final of the sevens tournament. A voice regularly booming across the showground belongs to chief announcer and commentator Nicola Davies. And Mr Thomas wanted to give that familiar voice a name - so he interviewed Ms Davies for his Facebook page. I've been coming here as a child with my family, exhibited Welsh cobs here for many, many years, she stated. But I was asked to commentate here on an equine display back between 10 and 15 years ago, and I caught the bug. I was part of the team, some say it was a promotion, some not. But I'm now chief commentator, so I'm in charge of the commentators at the main ring, horse ring, the sheep, the cattle and the pig section. text: The final leaders' debate gave the opposition parties what they wanted in throwing the focus of the campaign well and truly onto the NHS. The opening thirty minutes proved emotionally intense, packed with policy detail and vigorous exchanges. Compelling viewing. Carwyn Jones established the atmosphere in his initial remarks by concentrating exclusively on health services and the predictable reference to the absence of junior doctors' industrial action in Wales. The ongoing dispute in England has provided Labour with a valuable point of comparison when responding to criticism of the NHS, and this week's strike could not have been better scheduled for them as we near next week's polling date. There existed a notable difference from last week's leaders' debate, when the opposition parties devoted considerable time to collectively targeting Carwyn Jones. There existed a fragmented atmosphere to this encounter, with various disputes erupting between different leaders at separate moments. Nathan Gill and Kirsty Williams clashed over EU steel dumping whilst Andrew RT Davies criticised Kirsty Williams and Leanne Wood for striking agreements with the Labour government. A notable pattern emerged through the persistent criticism by Carwyn Jones of Leanne Wood regarding Plaid's proposals to restructure the NHS and their intentions to settle only the debts of students who remain in Wales. This occurred despite Labour consistently stating that this election represents a contest between themselves and the Conservatives. Eventually, a visibly irritated Leanne Wood reached her limit, and charged him with misrepresenting her policies. Subsequently, Plaid declared they regarded the criticism as praise, stating it clearly demonstrated Labour felt threatened by a Plaid challenge. Labour for their part believe there exist vulnerable Plaid votes available for capture in marginal constituencies such as the Vale of Glamorgan and the Vale of Clwyd, where they face the Conservatives. Meanwhile, Nathan Gill adopted a different approach. Throughout the assembly campaign he has been careful to avoid any discussion of the EU as the party attempts to demonstrate its serious commitment to devolution. That strategy appeared to conclude with repeated mentions of the EU during the debate. This seemed to me an attempt to mobilise their core supporters. A significant question remains whether UKIP voters, who are clearly motivated by the EU referendum, will be sufficiently motivated to vote next week. There exists no precedent for guidance so we must all await developments, but the influence of the UKIP figures, particularly in the marginal constituencies could prove enormous. One party official described a substantial UKIP vote in a close marginal as like a bomb detonating due to the effect it might have on the votes of the remaining parties and, consequently, the final outcome in numerous counts.

text: Timing is everything in politics if you want to have a chance of being heard. The outspoken Chief Inspector of Schools, Sir Michael Wilshaw, has strategically chosen his timing to deliver a judgement on serious weaknesses at seven of the poorest performing academy school chains in a scathing letter to the education secretary. He does not restrain himself regarding what he characterises as worrying findings. And merely days earlier the government took a further step towards eliminating local councils from school management. Draft proposals for a national funding formula will result in the vast bulk of government education funding flowing directly to schools by 2020. That will permit the cake to be divided differently, but it is also a preparatory measure for another major government ambition - to make councils operating schools in England a thing of the past. I understand the Treasury was eager for the funding formula announcement to be made this week, which suggests we may hear more in the Budget next week about the drive for more schools to become academies. Many parents in England scarcely notice whether their local school is operated by the council or by an academy trust. They are preoccupied with other fundamentals such as a sense of order and community and, naturally, examination results. But by and large people do care whether their taxes, their public money, is properly spent. So it is no surprise that Sir Michael directs some of his criticism not merely at poor results, but at high salaries and large bank reserves. In essence he is asking if these particular seven trusts represent value for money for the pupils, the parents and taxpayers. Is it a partial and distorted assessment as the government suggests? Certainly there are plenty of excellent academy schools too, which he acknowledges. Regarding council-run schools, only yesterday, schools minister Nick Gibb highlighted some of the worst performing local authorities in terms of GCSE results. So it cuts both ways. Labour wants the government to press the pause button so they can examine the system of holding academy trusts to account and ensure it is robust. That is not going to happen. Instead the government will continue to point to its network of eight regional schools commissioners whose job it is to do precisely that. If anything, all the signals are that the foot will be on the accelerator towards all schools in England becoming academies.

text: Sheffield United got their first win of the season as goals from Billy Sharp and James Wilson cancelled out a Kane Hemmings opener to give them victory over Oxford United. Oxford United seized the initiative through Hemmings in the 16th minute after United goalkeeper Simon Moore managed only to parry a long-range Liam Sercombe effort into the path of the advancing striker. United sought an equaliser and Kieron Freeman was unfortunate to witness his attempt deflect over the crossbar following a weaving run and pass from Mark Duffy. Matt Done subsequently saw a low strike from within the penalty area pushed clear by a firm Simon Eastwood save. In the 52nd minute, a first-time shot from John Lundstram from the box's edge was parried clear by Moore following an intelligent free-kick routine from the away side. United drew level in the 65th minute as Sharp converted a Matt Done delivery from close quarters. The hosts subsequently assumed the advantage as an in-swinging free-kick from Duffy was nodded home by Wilson with 17 minutes left. Report provided by the Press Association. text: Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara became the first player to score four successive one-day international centuries as his side beat Scotland at the World Cup. The 37-year-old struck 124 in a total of 363-9 in Hobart, to accompany his previous centuries in the tournament against Bangladesh, England and Australia. Sangakkara surpassed 500 ODI dismissals as Scotland were dismissed for 215. Captain Preston Mommsen and Freddie Coleman registered half centuries but Sri Lanka conclude with four victories in Pool A. They appear destined to meet South Africa in the first of the quarter-finals in Sydney on Wednesday. Despite posting their finest ever total batting second against a Test-playing nation, a fifth defeat means Scotland remain without a victory. They will meet co-hosts Australia in their final match on Saturday in Hobart. On a day of records at Bellerive Oval, left-hander Sangakkara registered his fifth World Cup century and is now one behind the record of six held by India's Sachin Tendulkar. He has now accumulated 14,189 ODI runs and only Tendulkar (18,426), who retired in 2013, has more runs for their country in the 50-over format. Sangakkara, who became the first ever player to register four centuries at a World Cup, has previously indicated he will retire from ODI cricket at the end of the tournament. The wicketkeeper has enjoyed a prolific period in the last 12-18 months, becoming the fastest player to reach 12,000 Test runs in January in the same match in which he registered his 11th double century, moving him one behind the record held by Australian great Don Bradman. I've been batting and keeping for a long time, it's becoming harder and the joints are creaking and aching, but I consider myself fortunate to be part of a great team, he said. No matter how hard you try, it's difficult to pinpoint why I'm playing so well. Perhaps I'm making better decisions at the crease, I don't know. Whatever it is, it's working for me at the moment. His 124 against Scotland in Hobart followed earlier scores of 105 not out against Bangladesh, 117 not out against England and 104 against Australia. Batting first, Sri Lanka's total owed much to a 195-run partnership for the second-wicket between Sangakkara and Tillakaratne Dilshan (104). They reached their respective centuries in consecutive balls before being dismissed in the space of two balls by Scotland seamer Josh Davey. Davey's figures of 3-63 moved him to the summit of the World Cup wicket-takers with 14, one ahead of New Zealand pair Trent Boult and Tim Southee. A 20-ball half century from Sri Lanka captain Angelo Mathews, which included four successive sixes off the bowling of Matt Machan had put them on course for a score of more than 400. But a flurry of late wickets and some impressive catching meant Scotland restricted their tail enders. Scotland's reply got off to the worst possible start when Kyle Coetzer presented a simple return catch to Lasith Malinga second ball of the innings. Captain Mommsen (60) and Coleman (70) ensured the chase had respectability with a 118-run partnership for the fourth wicket. But once they had departed, only all-rounder Richie Berrington (29) could make a score of any note. Listen to highlights from Test Match Special's and 5 live Sport's 2015 World Cup coverage.

text: Too many patients are locked into mental health rehabilitation wards far from home, a review of England's psychiatric services suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window The Care Quality Commission stated there were 3,500 beds in locked facilities throughout the nation, but it considers more individuals could and should receive care in residential settings near to home. The report stated safety on mental health wards was another significant concern. NHS England stated progress was being achieved with increased funding for care. Claire Murdoch, director of mental health for NHS England, stated that whilst there were grounds for optimism, improvements - in accordance with the priorities outlined by the NHS five-year plan - were required. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) examined all specialist mental health services throughout England - inspecting NHS care and NHS services delivered by the independent sector. It stated nearly all services were rated as good or outstanding for possessing caring and compassionate staff and that there were numerous examples of excellent care. However the report identified several areas of concern. CQC leaders stated particularly that locked rehabilitation wards (of which two thirds are operated by independent providers) did not deliver the appropriate model of care for the 21st Century. They stated some patients remained too long on these wards - with an average length of stay of 341 days. And this places patients at risk of being institutionalised, with the ultimate goal of being rehabilitated back into the community being overlooked, the report cautions. Dr Paul Lelliott, director for mental health at the CQC, stated: We were not expecting to discover this many [locked rehabilitation beds]. We cannot state precisely how many of the individuals on these wards do not require to be in locked facilities, but we do suspect that quite a substantial proportion of individuals in these services could, and should be, transferred back to be much nearer to home and be cared for in residential settings that deliver much greater independence, and also be supported by community services rather than being in hospital. Inspectors also stated approximately a third of services required improvement regarding safety. And one in 20 were considered inadequate for safety, meaning genuine and sometimes immediate concerns for patient safety, according to CQC leaders. Inspectors highlighted old and unsuitable buildings - for instance buildings with blind spots in corridors where patients at risk of self harm could not be monitored. Contributing to safety concerns were nurse shortages - with a 12% decline in mental health nursing staff between January 2010 and 2017. Commenting on the report, Brian Dow, from the charity Rethink Mental Illness, stated there was a substantial level of commitment from individuals in the sector to provide a high level of care but that there was an awfully long way to go. He stated: There is fairly large number of services that the CQC states require improvement and that raises significant questions about what is occurring in this system. Is there sufficient money in there? Do we possess the appropriate kind of individuals able to provide the care? Are individuals involved in their own care and are individuals supported and trained to provide the care? Meanwhile, Ms Murdoch informed the BBC she considered the report was a genuinely fair assessment of the state of the nation's mental health services. She stated: It outlines the fact that most providers of mental health care are now either progressing towards the good category or are good and progressing towards outstanding - so it is demonstrating improvement. But quite rightly it also examines what requires to improve next.

text: Safety inspections will be carried out at schools across Scotland following the collapse of a wall at an Edinburgh primary, BBC Scotland has learned. Four buildings required temporary closure in the capital following the discovery of defects in schools constructed by Miller Construction ten years previously. The fresh surveys focus upon schools constructed by the identical company in Glasgow, Fife and Inverclyde. The contractor stated inspections were a precautionary measure. Hundreds of bricks were dislodged from the wall of Oxgangs primary school during Storm Gertrude in January. A safety inspection disclosed issues with how the external wall was constructed when the school was erected in 2005, as part of the Public Private Partnership 1 project. Oxgangs formed part of a broader programme that witnessed 17 schools constructed or refurbished following an agreement between the council and a private finance consortium. When the wall collapsed, broader inspections disclosed similar problems at three additional schools in Edinburgh - St Peter's RC Primary, Firrhill High and Braidburn Special Schools. All were constructed around the identical time by Miller Construction - which was acquired by Galliford Try in 2014. The four schools were considered unsafe for pupils and temporarily closed. They are scheduled to reopen following the Easter holidays. A spokesperson for Galliford Try stated: The four schools temporarily closed in Edinburgh comprised the second phase of the PPP1 programme, which was completed by Miller Construction in 2005. We have already commenced remedial work at Oxgangs Primary School and are evaluating the requirement for work on the additional three schools. Any remedial work required will be undertaken as swiftly as possible allowing the children to return to their studies with the minimum disruption. Whilst we are not aware of any defects, as a precautionary measure, we have contacted the clients of the PPP school projects Miller Construction undertook in Glasgow, Fife and Inverclyde. Further investigations will be undertaken as appropriate. Signed in 2001, Edinburgh's Public Private Partnership agreement for schools was valued at £360m. In exchange for 30 years of fixed payments from the council, a private consortium designed, constructed and managed the schools. Miller Construction formed part of that consortium, and part of others constructing schools elsewhere in Scotland. A PPP1 agreement signed in Glasgow a year earlier was valued at three times as much as Edinburgh's, and involved 29 secondaries and one primary school across the country. Glasgow City Council stated its PPP contract would now undertake surveys on the handful of schools constructed by Miller Construction. Galliford Try stated it had also contacted the clients of schools constructed by the company in Inverclyde, and inspections are also being undertaken by the council in Fife. Shelagh McLean, head of education and children's services (equity and system improvement), stated: Fife Council has contacted both of our PPP Contractors, who are monitoring the situation in Edinburgh. They will be undertaking inspections in Fife during the school Easter holidays. Both contractors also undertake annual inspections of the building fabric and free standing walls as part of their ongoing maintenance. Oxgangs primary school and St Peter's are scheduled to reopen on 11 April.

text: The head of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Martin Wheatley, is to stand down from his post after just two years in charge. He will depart the City regulator in September, the FCA announced. Chancellor George Osborne thanked Mr Wheatley for his service, stating he had performed a brilliant job of launching the FCA in tough circumstances. He stated: The government believes that different leadership is required to build on those foundations. Mr Wheatley will be succeeded on an interim basis by his deputy, Tracey McDermott, whilst a search for his successor is launched. He said he was incredibly proud of what he and his team had accomplished together in establishing the FCA over the past four years. I know that the organisation will build on that strong start and work so that the financial services industry continues to thrive. Make no mistake about it, the Treasury was behind Martin Wheatley's surprise decision to step down as the head of the Financial Conduct Authority. I am informed that discussions were conducted with the head of the FCA in recent weeks where it was made clear that the Chancellor would not be requesting Mr Wheatley to remain when his contract came up for renewal in March 2016. With that sword suspended over his head, Mr Wheatley decided that he would depart early. The Treasury has always maintained a fractious relationship with Mr Wheatley who famously declared he would shoot first and ask questions later when he encountered wrongdoing in the financial services sector. The banking industry did not much appreciate such a gung-ho approach and Mr Wheatley was frequently the subject of venomous comments from senior banking executives. Read Kamal's blog in full Andrew Tyrie, chairman of the Treasury Committee, thanked Mr Wheatley for his work. He stated: Martin assumed control at an exceptionally difficult time. He was confronted with the challenge of changing the culture of both the regulated community and the regulator, given the exposure by the crisis of the shortcomings of the FSA. With the interests of millions of consumers to protect, tens of thousands of firms to regulate and the need to secure more competition in the financial services sector, it will be essential to find a high quality successor. Mr Wheatley joined the predecessor to the FCA, the Financial Services Authority (FSA), in September 2011 before proceeding to take over from Hector Sants as chief executive of the newly strengthened City regulator, which launched in April 2013. Mr Wheatley established a reputation as a tough regulator in a number of markets including Hong Kong and also at the Securities and Exchanges Commission in the US. It was understood at the time that it was for these reasons that he was appointed to the position of chief executive of the FCA. In the past month, Mr Wheatley has repeatedly attempted to reassure City grandees that the regulator was not seeking to put heads on sticks nor hunting for scalps under new rules designed to increase accountability in the banking sector. But the FCA has also imposed some of the largest regulatory fines witnessed in the City. The regulator, however, has not been scandal free, encountering trouble with the insurance industry last year when a story, leaked to the Daily Telegraph, warned the regulator was planning an investigation of 30 million pension policies, some of which had been sold as long ago as the 1970s. Billions of pounds were erased from the share prices of major insurance companies, prompting a parliamentary inquiry and four senior executives, including Mr Wheatley, forfeited their annual bonuses.

text: The amount of nursery and pre-school provision for children in special schools is to be reduced. The change will take effect in September and will impact all 39 special schools across Northern Ireland. It will mean pre-school pupils with moderate to severe learning difficulties will attend school for 2.5 hours rather than at least 4.5 hours daily. The reduction was disclosed by the Education Authority (EA) in correspondence to a parent. It confirms that from September 2016 all pre-school pupils will receive 2.5 hours in pre-school daily. The EA stated the change is intended to enhance the opportunity for pupils to access special school places, and will deliver greater regional consistency. Nevertheless, an organisation representing special school headteachers and governors stated the reduction will impede and limit the development of pupils with complex needs. In a submission to the Northern Ireland Assembly, the Strategic Leadership Forum for Special Schools (SLFSS) stated they completely disagree with the change. They stated it will have a range of consequences including: Francine Wilson's three-year-old son Aodhan, is scheduled to begin pre-school at a special school in September. Aodhan has Down's Syndrome and we were anticipating in September 2016 he would receive five hours of nursery placement, she stated. Receiving two and a half hours will, I believe, lead to delayed development in Aodhan, both educationally and socially. However, a spokesperson for the EA stated the reduction was in accordance with the Department of Education's 'Learning to Learn' policy. There has been a gradual shift towards part-time places across all sectors, the spokesperson stated. This policy acknowledges the research evidence that there is no discernible difference in pupils' development at the beginning of primary school between those who received part-time and full-time pre-school provision. This change is intended to enhance the opportunity for pupils to access special school places, preferably closer to their homes. The provision of enhanced access and greater regional consistency is a priority, they added.

text: Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions, Theresa May refused to say whether the Conservatives will keep the same protections for the state pension if they win the general election. These are external links and will open in a new window The claim: Pensioners would be £872 worse off if the triple-lock were removed. The triple-lock is a commitment to increase the basic state pension by average earnings, inflation or 2.5%, whichever is highest. Reality Check verdict: In the long-term, pensioners would be worse off without the triple-lock. How much worse off would depend upon what replaces it. Ian Blackford's figure is a forecast of what would occur if the state pension were only increased in line with inflation predictions for the next five years. He appears to have misspoken, because the research actually stated that pensioners would lose £817 over five years. Responding to a question from Angus Robertson, the SNP's leader in Westminster, she pledged that pensioners' incomes would continue to increase, but would not specify by how much. The government is currently committed to maintaining the pension triple-lock until 2020, which means it will increase the basic state pension by average earnings, inflation or 2.5%, whichever is highest. Labour, the Liberal Democrats and the SNP are all committed to maintaining the triple-lock. However, the Work and Pensions Committee has stated it should be scrapped on the grounds that it is unsustainable and unfair on younger families. It suggested that pensions should increase in line with earnings and be protected against inflation being higher than earnings, but with no minimum annual increase. John Cridland, who published a report on the future of state pensions last month, suggested that the triple-lock would also eventually need to be abandoned in favour of an earnings link. In the long-term, the triple-lock is a significant issue, with the number of people of pension age per person of working age forecast by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) to increase considerably over the next 50 years. Speaking on BBC Newsnight, Mr Blackford cited research from the House of Commons Library, which found that over a five-year period, pensioners would be £872 worse off if the triple lock were removed. Providing a bit more detail, the library was asked to take Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts for the next five years of inflation and average earnings figures. It then compared what would occur to pensions under different scenarios. It emerged that protecting it in line with earnings would make almost no difference, because average earnings are expected to be more than 2.5% throughout the period. Protecting only in line with inflation would cost a total of £642 over five years for a pensioner on the basic state pension and £817 over five years for someone on the new state pension. Mr Blackford presumably remembered that figure incorrectly when he stated it would cost £872. Clearly these figures are based on forecasts for what will occur in the future, which are uncertain. An alternative is to examine how much the triple-lock has cost in the past as the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has done. The triple-lock makes a particularly significant difference in periods of relatively low earnings growth and low inflation as the UK has experienced recently. It found that the triple-lock had cost about an extra £6bn a year compared with only protecting with earnings and £4bn a year compared with adjusting in line with inflation. The IFS produced this chart showing the difference in the percentage of national income spent on the state pension with or without the triple-lock, also based on OBR forecasts. The IFS suggested that the government should decide what proportion of earnings it wants the state pension to be and then adhere to that, rather than arbitrarily increasing it gradually through the triple-lock. What occurs to the triple-lock is highly significant because it has made such a difference in incomes for pensioners compared with workers. In-work benefits are protected less generously than state pensions. The Resolution Foundation published research recently suggesting that pensioner households on average are better off than working households after housing costs have been taken into account. Taking income after housing costs makes a substantial difference because pensioner households are more likely to own their own homes and to have relatively small or paid-off mortgages. Former pensions minister Baroness Altmann told Newsnight that the triple-lock was particularly unfair on younger families because it was putting pressure on the government to keep increasing the pension age to keep pension costs down, so the time when they could claim their own pensions was being delayed. text: Chris Coleman says the 2018 World Cup campaign will be his last as Wales manager. Following Wales's historic semi-final achievement at Euro 2016, Coleman's reputation has reached unprecedented heights. The 46-year-old manager remains under contract until the conclusion of the forthcoming World Cup, with his squad set to commence their opening qualifier at home against Moldova on 5 September. I am certain this shall be my final campaign regardless of whether we qualify, Coleman stated. That would represent six or seven years in the position, which constitutes a considerable period. Therefore I believe this shall be my final attempt, so I shall deliver my utmost effort, though I would not contemplate departing elsewhere. I wish to complete this journey. There exists success within this squad, I believe, because they are at an optimal age. However I shall certainly provide everything I possess in this forthcoming campaign. I shall ensure they do likewise. Coleman has supervised a remarkable transformation in Wales's - and his personal - circumstances since his appointment in January 2012. Five months previously, Wales had dropped to their lowest global ranking of 117th and, despite enduring the poorest start of any Wales manager with four losses from his opening four matches, Coleman now steers his nation through its most triumphant period. Euro 2016 marked Wales's inaugural appearance at a major tournament for 58 years, and their advancement to the semi-finals enabled them to surpass the previous finest performance at a major tournament - achieving the quarter-finals at the 1958 World Cup. Coleman received recognition for qualification with a fresh contract in May, which extends until after the 2018 tournament in Russia, and harbours no regrets regarding agreeing the arrangement before Wales's Euro 2016 triumph. If they [FAW] wished to discuss another contract with me I would be exploiting the situation somewhat, would I not? Similarly if I departed and transferred elsewhere because we had performed well at a tournament. I would not feel comfortable. I have signed a favourable contract and I anticipate the campaign. Wales have remained the outsiders throughout much of their history, though that might alter following their accomplishments at Euro 2016. Coleman's team have received a relatively favourable qualifying draw for the 2018 World Cup, competing in the identical group as Austria, Serbia, Republic of Ireland, Georgia and Moldova. The greatest challenge for us is that we shall be a prize now in this campaign due to what we have just achieved, Coleman said. Teams will perform differently against us and rather than us being the outsiders, which we excel at, we shall be anticipated to triumph. We have not been accustomed to dismantling teams. We have been accustomed to striking teams on the counter-attack because they have attacked us since they expect to gain something from us. We may need to examine how we approach it somewhat differently regarding what the opposition will do to us. Coleman employed a 5-3-2 formation at Euro 2016, having utilised the identical system throughout most of the qualifying campaign. The former Fulham manager has switched to a four-man defence previously - a goalless draw in Belgium in 2014 amongst its most successful implementations - and he is contemplating additional tactical modifications before the 2018 World Cup campaign. When you alter formation with an international team, occasionally you are on precarious ground, but you must be courageous and I shall, Coleman added. I would prefer that than do nothing. In my initial campaign, for substantial portions of it I did nothing. I maintained it unchanged. I would not repeat that identical error. You learn from that, you learn from failing and falling short. I was attempting to replicate everything that Speeds [the late Gary Speed, Coleman's predecessor] was implementing because I was advised it was functioning and not to change it. It did not work for me - it exploded in my face. I shall never repeat that mistake.

text: Rafael Nadal beat world number one Novak Djokovic in a pulsating four-set final to claim his second US Open title in New York. The Spaniard, aged 27, held on magnificently in the third set to proceed and claim a gripping contest 6-2 3-6 6-4 6-1 in three hours and 21 minutes. One extraordinary 54-shot rally - the longest in the tournament by 20 shots - epitomised a battle that enthralled the 23,000 spectators in Arthur Ashe Stadium. Nadal has now claimed 13 Grand Slam singles titles and moves within one of Pete Sampras in the all-time list, with Roger Federer leading on 17. And after missing last year's US Open during a seven-month absence with a knee injury, Nadal is now positioned to regain the number one ranking. Having this success is incredible, he said. I never anticipated it. That's life and I'm fortunate to have what I'm having. If he remains healthy, he can easily claim four or five more Slams. No question about it. To me, he's superior than ever. It's incredible how desperately he wants it. I've never witnessed anything like it. Let's hope he remains healthy because it will be excellent for our sport. I truly love the competition, I truly love the sport. All my career I dreamed to be involved in matches like today. I enjoy every moment. These things are not eternal. In a few years I won't have this opportunity. I try my best, I have passion and that's all I can do. Monday's final was a predictably electrifying, punishing contest as the pair met for the 37th time - taking them beyond the rivalry of John McEnroe and Ivan Lendl to establish a new record since the Open era began in 1968. It was their sixth Grand Slam final and third at Flushing Meadows, after the Spaniard prevailed in 2010 and Djokovic took revenge in 2011. Nadal, seeded second, had a 21-0 record on hard courts this year heading into the final, and had dropped serve just once whilst powering through the draw in New York. He began as many people's favourite and set about proving them correct as he dominated for the first hour, accelerating through his forehand to find a gear that Djokovic simply could not contain. Two breaks earned Nadal the first set in a relatively swift 42 minutes, but for the next 80 minutes it was all Djokovic as his forehand now began to dictate, whilst his returning ability increased the pressure. Nadal's seemingly impregnable serve was broken three times in succession, the first thanks to that lung-busting 54-shot rally that explored every inch of the court, and Djokovic raced through six of seven games to take a 2-0 lead in the third. Nadal was reeling, fending off another break point to avoid falling a double break behind, and it proved significant when the Djokovic storm abated and the errors crept back in game six. After two hours and 17 minutes, the world's top two players were level at 3-3 in the third set, and it appeared as though Djokovic had made the decisive move when he earned three break points at 4-4. The belief appeared to drain from Djokovic and, after saving an early break point in the fourth set with a net cord, Nadal left no room for misfortune when he crunched another forehand on his next opportunity. A titanic struggle came to a tame end as Djokovic sprayed two backhands into the tramlines to fall 5-1 behind, but there were plenty of emotions on display after Nadal saw the Serb find the net on match point. Playing against Novak is always a very special feeling and nobody brings my game to the limit like he does. At primary school, he adored debating. He was relaxed and amiable and he simply loved staging plays and performing in the shed for other children. And very scholarly, I suppose you would say. Nothing was excessive when it concerned caring for the young Lynton. When he gained entry to Adelaide University to study economics, his parents relocated to the city to remain close to him. The fact that he won the London elections for the Conservatives, while the Tories lost everywhere else, was, in a way, a stamp of approval. Labour and Liberal Democrats will now study his methods and try to defend themselves against his black magic. “And look closely at this one, because that’s what you’re up against.” I remember saying that to Ed Miliband during the election campaign.

text: The gaming industry needs to get behind a centre dedicated to videogames or risk losing it forever, Games Workshop founder Ian Livingstone has said. Mr Livingstone, alongside other developers, has assisted in establishing The National Videogame Foundation in support of Nottingham's National Videogame Arcade (NVA). He stated it ought to be to gaming what the National Gallery represents to art. The NVA came close to closure merely one year following its opening. Mr Livingstone, who assisted in launching the Lara Croft franchise, declared it was his and the gaming industry's obligation to support the NVA - the sole institute of its type in the UK. He stated it was only when it nearly shut that its profile was elevated. There were individuals [in the industry] who were unaware of it, he stated. They enquired 'what is it?', 'how might we assist?' Visitor responses were favourable, achieving an average of 4.5 out of 5 on Tripadvisor, but for various reasons, including funding delays, the enterprise exhausted its finances. The NVA's co-director, Iain Simons, stated the arcade's personnel accepted deferred payment to maintain the doors open. He also made an appeal to videogame developers for assistance with investment, with Mr Livingstone amongst the individuals who responded to the call. It was unsurprising that Ian Livingstone, the co-founder of games company Games Workshop, intervened to assist the NVA. He has been an enormous supporter and states the National Videogame Arcade ought to be to gaming what the National Gallery represents to fine art. He was present at its launch in March 2015 and spoke of how widespread gaming was - wherever you travel people of all ages are playing games on smartphones, on consoles. Mr Livingstone also enjoys reminding people how much the games industry is valued, a substantial $100bn. But he stated gaming was far more than entertainment, it represents a genuine art form and ought to be recognised as such. He stated the NVA ought not merely be a museum but explore the cultural impact of videogames. The National Videogame Foundation shall concentrate primarily on education. Mr Livingstone stated it was a call to action and a crucial moment for videogames' cultural confidence. The foundation shall deliver the GameCity Festival, conducted every October, and operate the arcade. Richard Wilson, CEO of TIGA, which represents the UK's games industry, stated the NVA was a great project and the largest videogame developers could have a greater role to play there. However, he stated smaller companies were struggling and could not always surrender time and resources. National Videogame Arcade timeline
