text: China's economy is slowing down. We are aware of that. Naturally, President Xi Jinping is also cognisant of this fact. It represents one of the principal issues - indeed shadows - looming over his visit to the United States. Following an average annual growth rate of 10% across three decades, that momentum has diminished considerably. Last year the figure stood at 7.4%. Numerous economists remain deeply sceptical regarding China's official statistics, believing the actual figure to be significantly lower. For the coming year the IMF projects 6.8%. Moreover, the deceleration was inevitable. The IMF characterised the transition occurring in China as progressing towards a 'new normal', distinguished by slower yet more secure and sustainable growth. A new normal is required because the drivers of China's former dynamism are diminishing. The ageing population means there exists a constraint on the contribution that an expanding workforce can provide to the economy. All that preceding robust growth means the technological divide compared with the remainder of the world has contracted. This consequently restricts the potential for swift advances from catching up. Investment represents another growth source, which enhances the productive capacity of the economy. However, China's investment level is already exceptionally elevated. Indeed IMF research indicated even in 2012 that it was excessive. Why excessive? Because it redirects resources from other economic sectors including household consumption, and if a nation over-invests an increasing proportion of projects are liable to be economically inefficient. The question that has been troubling financial markets sporadically over recent weeks has been - will the transition prove smooth, or will China experience what is termed a hard landing, namely an abrupt deceleration or even a recession? The response genuinely matters for the remainder of us. China is by one measurement the largest economy on Earth. It represents 17% of global economic activity. The US economy is nearly as substantial but is not expanding so rapidly. Circumstances are likely to remain thus for years or even decades after China has adjusted to a more sustainable growth rate. This means that China's influence on global growth is greater, and so is the potential contribution it can provide to increased demand for goods manufactured by other nations. Therefore hard or soft landing truly is significant. Which can we anticipate? Opinions amongst economists differ - when do they not? There is one particularly influential voice who has presented a rather pessimistic assessment, Willem Buiter, chief economist at the major financial firm Citigroup, formerly of the Bank of England and the London School of Economics. He states: We believe that there exists a high and increasing probability of a Chinese, emerging market and global recession scenario unfolding. Now there is a discussion to be conducted regarding what the term recession signifies, particularly when applied to emerging economies and even more so for the global economy. Mr Buiter's definition is founded on an economy's capacity to expand. He determines that growth of less than 2% for at least one year constitutes a global recession. The benchmark for China is 2.5%. He is amongst the sceptics concerning China's data, so his perspective is that the Chinese economy is already nearer to that than the official figures indicate. For the world economy he estimates there is a 40% probability of a moderate recession, with a 15% likelihood of a more severe downturn and a financial crisis. If it does occur, he states, it is most probable the world would be pulled into a recession by sluggish growth in several key emerging economies, particularly China: We consider China to be at high and rapidly increasing risk of a cyclical hard landing. Why? Many of the traditional warning indicators are evident, he states - surplus capacity in a growing number of industries, excessive borrowing and debt, and instances of irrational exuberance in asset markets, recently property and the stock market. He states: This is the traditional formula for a recession in capitalist market economies. If it does occur then it would certainly affect many others. And there are other emerging economies already in recession including two substantial ones in the form of Brazil and Russia. China is amongst the most significant export destinations for many nations - number one for South Korea (more than a quarter of exports), Saudi Arabia and Iran. For the largest economies, China ranks as the second biggest export market for Japan, fourth for the US, and for Germany it is second amongst markets outside the European Union. Even nations with minimal direct trade with China could readily experience the effects of a hard landing, if they are suppliers to countries that do sell directly to China, or if they export commodities whose price in international markets is influenced by weakened Chinese demand. Consider two key industrial commodities, crude oil and copper. The price of crude oil has declined by more than half since June last year. There are supply factors underlying that - shale oil in the US and the reluctance of Saudi Arabia and others to reduce production as they might have done previously. But weaker-than-anticipated growth in demand from China is another element in the price decline. Copper is a key raw material for the construction sector. It is used extensively in electrical installations, and China's building boom has been voracious for copper. Its price is also down by half, in this instance from 2011. China's slowdown is the principal factor. So that is the argument for being pessimistic. But there are some who are more optimistic about the prospects. In a recent note to clients, the London consultancy Capital Economics wrote: In contrast to the widespread doom and gloom regarding China's immediate economic outlook, we believe growth has already stabilised following a slowdown at the beginning of the year, and that there are sound reasons to expect stronger growth in the months ahead. Prior to his visit to the US, President Xi told the Wall Street Journal: The Chinese economy is still functioning within the appropriate range. His host, President Barack Obama, must be hoping he is correct and that it remains that way. He is not the only one.

Even countries that trade with China only a little might be affected by a hard landing, if they are suppliers to the countries that directly trade with China or if they export products whose prices on the world market are affected by a drop in Chinese demand. Since last June, the price of oil has fallen by more than half, and that is due to supply factors: shale oil in the United States and the refusal of Persian Gulf states to cut back production as they might have done in the past. For the world's biggest economies, China is the second largest export market for Japan, the fourth largest for the United States, and for Germany the second largest export market outside the European Union. Copper, on the other hand, is not so bad. Copper is a basic building material, it is used in electric wiring, and the Chinese building boom has been devouring it. But the growth of demand from China is also to blame for the decline. The decline in China is the main factor. Its price is also down by half, this time since 2011. This is the argument for being pessimistic. He is not the only one. President Xi Jinping, before his visit to the United States, told the Wall Street Journal that the Chinese economy was in a good position. There are, however, more optimistic voices. In a recent letter to its customers, the London consulting firm Capital Economics wrote: "Contrary to the general gloom and doom about the immediate outlook for the Chinese economy, we believe that growth has already stabilized after a slowdown at the beginning of the year and that there are sound reasons for a higher growth rate in the coming months." The master of the house, President Barack Obama, must hope he is right and remains right.

The United States Air Force stated that decommissioning a satellite from service had triggered a software malfunction. A BBC spokesperson verified that the retirement of a GPS satellite resulted in complications for listeners receiving digital radio transmissions. The BBC has subsequently discovered that the difficulty arose after a decommissioned satellite triggered software complications which impacted numerous additional satellites. DAB transmitters must transmit at precisely the same frequencies and, to synchronise, they lock onto GPS satellite transmissions. Nevertheless, on 26 January, one of the GPS satellites - designated SVN23 - orbiting the Earth was retired. This unexpectedly triggered difficulties for the entire network. The matter was resolved at 06:10 MST, nevertheless global users may have encountered GPS timing problems for several hours. Indeed, as a consequence of the difficulty, some GPS positioning would have been displaced by nearly 4km. The time discrepancy was detected by the Metsahovi Radio Observatory in Finland. text: Councils have warned they may be charging more for services despite some already increasing such revenue by more than 100% in three years. Official statistics reveal councils generated over £11bn through fees, charges and sales during 2014/2015. The total rise in fees and charges revenue has reached 3% since 2012/2013. The Local Government Association stated councils confronted a challenging balancing act whilst determining fees and charges. The levies encompass various services including car parking, adult social care, planning and country parks. Whilst certain authorities have witnessed their revenue from such sources grow by tens of millions of pounds, others have experienced their fees, charges and sales income decline. Six English authorities - Breckland, Devon, Hinckley and Bosworth, South Northamptonshire and Sedgmoor - have witnessed their revenue from fees, sales and charges increase by over 100% during the previous three years, whilst Derbyshire, Westminster, Bristol and Shropshire, represented the largest gainers in actual terms, securing tens of millions of pounds more annually. A representative for Derbyshire, which raised its fees, charges and sales revenue by £33m between 2013/2014 and 2015, stated: Like all authorities we are seeking to boost our revenue where possible as we must identify savings of £157m between 2013 and 2018. There are also numerous areas where we are levying more for our services than previously. These encompass raising co-funding contributions for adult social care, levying for home to school transport for pupils attending faith schools and charging for parking at certain of our countryside locations. Sharon Taylor, interim leader of the Local Government Association, stated: There exists a law of diminishing returns with council charges. If you raise prices it may result in reduced usage of services. It must be a reasonable rise; it represents a balancing act. Councils of any political persuasion recognise that household budgets are constrained and they do not wish to increase costs. Ultimately, fees and charges must be weighed against council tax increases. Cambridge City Council, where fees and charges income has increased from £20.5m to £23.1m during the past three financial years, requires any department seeking to raise fees above inflation rates must demonstrate the increase is necessary initially. Lewis Herbert, leader at the Labour-controlled council, stated: We are attempting to achieve balance between the costs of operating services and not burdening our residents. We are not attempting to raise false alarms and are not in as poor a situation as certain councils, but it truly is precarious for many of us because we must examine what lies within the specifics of the government's proposals for local government. We are more commercially-minded than certain councils so might construct a cafe at the crematorium or sell flowers or lease additional space in the Guildhall building - thus extending income by selling more rather than raising charges. The Department for Communities and Local Government failed to respond to a request for comment.

text: Brazil's President Michel Temer has nominated his justice minister to the Supreme Court as it prepares to rule on one the biggest corruption scandals in the country's history. The minister, Alexandre de Moraes, represents one of Mr Temer's most trusted allies. He succeeds Judge Teori Zavascki, who perished in an aircraft accident last month. Demands have emerged for a less politically charged appointment, given that numerous senior politicians face accusations in the corruption affair. Mr Temer stated he had selected Mr Moraes for his robust academic qualifications. The 49-year-old barrister belongs to the PSDB party, which forms part of Mr Temer's ruling coalition. He entered the cabinet in May, when Mr Temer succeeded President Dilma Rousseff, who was confronting impeachment proceedings. Earlier this year, Mr Moraes was required to address his gravest crisis since assuming office, when over 100 inmates were murdered by fellow prisoners in a sequence of jail uprisings. He unveiled a strategy to establish police intelligence divisions and enhance collaboration with adjacent nations to diminish the influence of the criminal organisations that dominate most Brazilian correctional facilities. Mr Moraes's appointment requires confirmation by the Senate. He requested a 30-day period of leave to prepare for the confirmation procedure. However, experts suggest the administration does not anticipate the appointment to be declined, given it possesses a substantial majority in the Senate. Later this month the Supreme Court is scheduled to commence deliberations on the comprehensive evidence compiled during an inquiry into corruption at the state petroleum company, Petrobras. Judge Zavascki had been supervising the investigation, designated as Operation Car Wash. He had compiled a register containing the identities of numerous politicians who purportedly accepted payments from Brazilian construction conglomerate Odebrecht to ensure the firm secured profitable contracts with Petrobras. Odebrecht has acknowledged disbursing $1bn (£800m) in corrupt payments to secure contracts across 12 separate nations. Mr Zavascki was a highly regarded judge and the Car Wash inquiry acquired considerable credibility when he was designated to supervise it in the Supreme Court, reports the BBC's Daniel Gallas. The aircraft he was aboard crashed into the ocean during severe rainfall near the municipality of Paraty on 19 January. The opposition declared it suspected criminal involvement and demanded a comprehensive inquiry. Following Judge Zavascki's death, the Supreme Court has been functioning with 10 judges. His position supervising the corruption investigation was assigned last week to Judge Edson Fachin. He was selected randomly from a shortlist of five Supreme Court judges.

text: Saudi King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz has died, royal officials have announced, weeks after he was admitted to hospital. Abdullah, who had reigned since 2005 and was reported to be approximately 90 years old, had been afflicted with a pulmonary infection. His 79-year-old half-brother, Salman, has been confirmed as the new monarch. Within hours of his ascension to the throne of the oil-wealthy kingdom, King Salman pledged to maintain identical policies to his predecessors. We shall continue adhering to the correct policies which Saudi Arabia has pursued since its founding, he declared in an address transmitted on state television. Abdullah had endured frequent episodes of poor health in recent years, and King Salman had lately assumed the ailing sovereign's duties. Before announcing Abdullah's death, Saudi television switched to Koranic verses, which frequently indicates the death of a senior royal. A statement declared Abdullah had died at 01:00 (22:00 GMT Thursday). Here in Saudi Arabia's second city, the streets remained quiet this morning as numerous people gathered at mosques for Friday prayers. There is a muted sorrow in the atmosphere as Saudis absorb the loss of their monarch. Citizens throughout the kingdom are grieving a man whom many regarded as a good sovereign. A Jedawi I interviewed said that whilst it was known that Abdullah was unwell, to awaken to news of the king's death was distressing. Another Jedawi described the loss as resembling a family member's passing. It is only after the king is subsequently laid to rest, that people here and in the kingdom generally can begin to adapt to his passing. Another of the late king's half-brothers, Muqrin, who is in his late 60s, has been designated the new crown prince, according to an official statement. King Salman summoned the royal family's Allegiance Council to recognise Muqrin as his heir. He promptly appointed Interior Minister Prince Mohammed bin Nayef as deputy crown prince, making him second in line to the throne, and named his own son, Mohammed bin Salman, as defence minister. Other ministers, including foreign, oil and finance were retained in position, state television reported. The new king's profile was updated on his official Twitter account, where he posted: I ask God to help me succeed in my service of the dear [Saudi] people. In accordance with traditions of Wahhabism - the ultra-conservative form of Sunni Islam practised by the kingdom - King Abdullah will be buried in an unmarked grave immediately following Friday prayers. The Saudi religious establishment regards every aspect of life and death as submission to God's supreme will, and protocol allows no official mourning period. Government offices remain open and flags stay at full mast. Saudi Arabia under King Salman confronts numerous challenges. The first is ensuring the succession proceeds smoothly without any divisive competition for power within the ruling family. Then there is the continuing threat from jihadists, both domestically and across its borders. Saudi Arabia is now positioned between an aggressive Islamic State (IS) to the north and al-Qaeda in Yemen to the south. In recent months Abdullah's age and declining health had led to increasing focus on the issue of the Saudi royal succession. The crown has traditionally passed between Ibn Saud's sons, but few remain alive. King Salman's appointment of Mohammed bin Nayef - a grandson of Ibn Saud - as deputy crown prince effectively smoothes the line of succession for years to come. He permitted mild criticism of his government in the press, and suggested that more women should be allowed to work. King Salman spent 48 years as governor of Riyadh Province before becoming crown prince and defence minister. text: A doctor who misled other medics about Pauline Cafferkey - a nurse who developed the Ebola virus - has been suspended from practising for a month. These are external links and will open in a new window Dr Hannah Ryan measured Ms Cafferkey's temperature at Heathrow Airport upon returning from West Africa where they had volunteered to assist. However, despite an elevated temperature - an indicator of the virus - Dr Ryan consented to a reduced value being documented. The Medical Practitioners Tribunal determined she was guilty of serious misconduct. Dr Ryan stated she was in a condition of disbelief, fear and panic at that moment. Ms Cafferkey was subsequently permitted to travel home to Scotland, transporting the virus and placing others at unwarranted risk the tribunal heard. The Scottish nurse became ill the following day and survived an extended period of illness with Ebola and its complications. Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey had been working in Sierra Leone with other volunteers to assist in treating Ebola patients in 2014. The outbreak of the highly infectious virus resulted in thousands of deaths in the region. Returning on 28 December, Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey had arrived at Heathrow, eager to be home for the Christmas holiday period, the tribunal heard. They queued to obtain clearance from Public Health England medics to be permitted to depart. Attempting to assist PHE staff with the procedure, Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey agreed to take and record their own temperatures. Dr Ryan had subsequently measured Ms Cafferkey's temperature and obtained a reading of 38.2C - above normal. However, a reduced temperature, 37.2C, was actually documented and Ms Cafferkey was then permitted to catch her connecting flight to Glasgow to return home. Subsequently when a consultant telephoned to investigate what had occurred at the airport, Dr Ryan provided a dishonest response regarding her involvement, the tribunal was informed. The tribunal determined that whilst there were extenuating circumstances for her actions at Heathrow, her behaviour five days later when she received the call, was deeply deplorable. Dr Ryan informed the hearing: Pauline Cafferkey was my friend and someone I cared about and was genuinely worried she might die. Dr Bernard Herdan, chairman of the tribunal, stated: Since the tribunal is satisfied the risk of repetition of your misconduct is low, and there is no risk to patient safety, it has concluded that a one-month suspension will be sufficient to mark the seriousness of your misconduct and to send a message to the profession that dishonesty by a doctor cannot be tolerated under any circumstances. In September 2016, the Nursing and Midwifery Council cleared Ms Cafferkey of misconduct over allegations she had concealed her infection, after a panel ruled that her judgement had been impaired by her illness. In November, another colleague, senior nurse Donna Wood, was suspended by the NMC for two months. The panel found Ms Wood suggested a reduced temperature be documented on Ms Cafferkey's screening form so they could pass through checks at passport control more swiftly.

text: A woman has told the Surjit Singh Chhokar murder trial she did not tell police who attacked her partner because she was distraught. Elizabeth Bryce initially provided officers with the name of only one of the three men she alleges conducted the attack, Andrew Coulter. She has subsequently identified the two others as Ronnie Coulter and David Montgomery. Ronnie Coulter, 48, denies the murder of Mr Chhokar, of Gowkthrapple, North Lanarkshire, and attributes responsibility to the other men. Ms Bryce, 56, was providing testimony on the second day of the murder trial. Ronnie Coulter's defence counsel Donald Findlay QC questioned her regarding why she failed to inform police who was responsible. She stated: I was distraught. At the time I was not thinking. I was distraught at my man lying dead at my feet. She informed Mr Findlay she knew the identity of all three men but named Andrew Coulter because she was angry at him. Ms Bryce had previously informed the court she had confronted him on the day of 32-year-old Mr Chhokar's death as her partner had mentioned a missing giro cheque. She stated that, following enquiries, he informed her he understood it had been cashed at the post office by Andrew Coulter. Mr Findlay accused her of tailoring her evidence and suggested to her she had altered her partner's final words. The court was told that in a police statement, taken the day following Mr Chhokar's death, Ms Bryce stated his last words were I've been stabbed. However in court she stated he actually informed her they stabbed me. Ms Bryce denied tailoring her evidence. When questioned by Mr Findlay, she stated she had probably told a few lies but not regarding what happened to Chhokar. She also acknowledged having a conviction for £13,000 benefit fraud, stating it was not relevant to this case. Mr Findlay challenged her assertion that she observed both Coulters and David Montgomery walking past her window twice that day. Providing evidence on Wednesday, she stated she seized a garden spade and ran outside her home in Garrion Street, Wishaw, to confront the Coulters and David Montgomery, who she claimed were dragging her partner across the street. She stated the blood just flew out of Mr Chhokar and he collapsed dead. Ronnie Coulter denies murdering Mr Chhokar by repeatedly attacking him with a knife or similar weapon and a further charge of forging Mr Chhokar's signature on a £100 giro cheque. He also denies breaking into Mr Chhokar's home at Caplaw Tower, Gowkthrapple, on the day of his death and stealing a cooker and attempting to defeat the ends of justice by destroying or disposing of a knife and clothing. The trial before Lord Matthews continues.

text: Ministers have said the growth of high-stakes roulette machines on the High Street is concerning and they do not rule out action to restrict them. Culture Secretary Helen Grant informed MPs their future remained unresolved and bookmakers must take immediate action to enhance protection for players. Individuals can stake £100 every 20 seconds on fixed-odds betting terminals. Labour declared they were an example of David Cameron's Britain and councils should receive new powers to restrict them. However following a Commons debate, Labour's call for local authorities to be granted new powers to limit the growth of the machines was defeated by 314 to 232 votes. There are more than 33,000 fixed-odds betting terminals across the UK. The previous Labour government relaxed the gambling laws, permitting bookmakers to begin installing them. However the party has accused the gambling industry of exploiting those changes to target poorer areas of the country. It states fixed-odds betting terminals are acting as a magnet for crime and anti-social behaviour and local authorities should be granted new powers to address clusters of shops opening together. They would also review the number of high-speed, high-stakes fixed-odds betting terminals permitted on bookmakers' premises and would take steps to make the machines less addictive by requiring pop-ups and breaks in play. Shadow culture secretary Clive Efford stated the previous government had always maintained the machines should be kept under review. The world had changed since they were first licensed, he stated, with the online gambling industry now worth more than £2bn. These machines are an example of Cameron's Britain - one rule for constituents and another for big business which operate the betting shops, he stated. Another Labour MP, Brian Donohue, stated fixed-odds betting terminals had been likened to cocaine as they were absolutely and totally addictive. Ministers maintain that local authorities can already reject applications for new gambling premises and review existing licences. However Ms Grant acknowledged the growth of the machines was concerning and she expected the industry to introduce voluntary player protection measures, such as suspensions in play and automatic alerts when stakes reach a certain level, by March. She stated the government was awaiting the findings of a study into how [the machines] are used and the real impact on players before deciding what further action may be required. There is no green light for these machines. Their future remains unresolved pending the research we have commenced, she informed MPs. Labour, she added, had liberalised gambling laws and accused them of rank hypocrisy, total cynicism and outright opportunism. Labour brought these machines into being and they have the audacity to bring forward a motion blaming the government for any harm caused, she stated. The gambling industry maintains it does not target deprived areas and has introduced a code of conduct for player protection and responsible gaming. Betting is a pursuit enjoyed by millions of working class people throughout Britain and we seek to reach the widest audience possible by being present on High Streets, the Association of British Bookmakers stated. We accept there are concerns about these gaming machines and are always open to a constructive dialogue with politicians about the appropriate powers for local authorities. It added: The claims of widespread problem gambling on machines is simply not supported by evidence. The industry continues to develop its approach to harm mitigation for the small number of gamblers who do experience problems. MPs have previously rejected calls from Labour to reduce the maximum stake from £100 to £2 and to cut the top prize from the current £500.

text: A top NFL official has acknowledged a link between head trauma in American football and the brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). This marks the first occasion a league executive has made such an admission. Jeff Miller, the NFL's vice president of health and safety, was questioned about CTE by American politicians. When asked whether there existed a connection between the sport and neurodegenerative diseases such as CTE, Miller responded: The answer to that question is certainly yes. In the lead-up to Super Bowl 50 earlier this year, neurosurgeon Mitch Berger, who heads the NFL's subcommittee on long-term brain injury, stated no connection between American football and CTE had been established. Jan Schakowsky, who represents Illinois, was critical of Berger's remarks, stating the league was peddling a false sense of security in minimising the dangers of head trauma. Football is a high-risk sport due to the routine hits, not merely diagnosable concussions, stated Schakowsky. What the American public requires now is honesty regarding the health risks and clearly more research. The NFL has previously acknowledged that head trauma, particularly concussion, presents a risk to the long-term health of players. Nevertheless, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell and other senior officials have not made definitive public statements on the matter. text: Stoke held Southampton to a goalless draw despite having Marko Arnautovic sent off in Mark Hughes' 400th match as a Premier League manager. The visiting team enjoyed considerable possession but found it difficult to fashion opportunities in a disappointing encounter, with Arnautovic receiving his marching orders for a studs-up tackle in the 23rd minute. Saints replacement Jay Rodriguez squandered the match's finest opportunity when he could not connect with Sofiane Boufal's second-half delivery across the penalty area. James Ward-Prowse had an opportunity to net the decisive goal from short distance following a Glen Johnson mistake, but his effort was diverted wide. The result lifts Southampton to ninth position, whilst Hughes' Stoke remain in 12th place. Following the dismissal, Southampton controlled possession but they could not capitalise on their numerical superiority. Claude Puel's team were composed in possession and there was some delightful approach play, but at the conclusion of every carefully-crafted attack the final ball was insufficient. Ryan Bertrand challenged Lee Grant with a fierce strike from the penalty area's edge in one of the rare occasions Southampton adopted a direct approach, but Rodriguez's failure proved the decisive moment. After Joe Allen was dispossessed by Steven Davis, Boufal's delivery required only a straightforward conversion, but the 27-year-old striker could not make contact, apparently uncertain over which foot to employ. Arnautovic's dismissal was met with disapproval from the home supporters, but his studs were raised high on Boufal's leg and his tackle was tardy. Hughes will contend that his team were handicapped by the expulsion, but Stoke posed no threat whatsoever after Allen's low attempt at the near post was turned away by Fraser Forster's boot within six minutes. Xherdan Shaqiri delivered a disappointing display and struck one of the seats in the Stoke technical area with his fist after being substituted by Mame Biram Diouf in the second period, having offered very little. In reality, Stoke were fortunate to survive, and the stalemate owed more to Southampton's inadequate finishing than their own defensive work. Johnson's poor control in his own penalty area should have been penalised with a superior finish from Ward-Prowse, and Allen's indecision created the match's sole genuine clear-cut chance. It was not a joyous occasion for Hughes on a milestone evening. The former Blackburn, Manchester City, Fulham and QPR manager's 400th fixture in command in the English top division will not endure long in the memory. Hughes' victory percentage stands at 36%. That places him alongside Alan Pardew but beneath Harry Redknapp (37%) and David Moyes (41%). Stoke manager Mark Hughes on Arnautovic's dismissal: It's regrettable because he obviously caught him high on the leg but the ball was bouncing about and it wasn't a malicious movement to eliminate the player. The referee wasn't excellent on the evening, he overlooked a number of decisions and clearly missed an elbow from Shane Long on Bruno Martins Indi - that requires examining again. Overall the referee placed us in a situation and we had to demonstrate genuine work ethic and comprehension of what was needed. Given the circumstances, the point we secured was magnificent. Southampton manager Claude Puel: We're disappointed. Eleven against ten you must perform better. In the first period we were too anxious, in the second period we were superior and created several possibilities, but it was insufficient. There were excellent crosses and good combinations, but our play was too sluggish and not effective in the final third. It was two points dropped and it's regrettable. On Arnautovic's dismissal: I believe it's a significant foul, it was extremely dangerous, he does not play the ball. Stoke next compete on Saturday at home to Leicester in a 15:00 GMT kick-off. text: Two black former Scottish top-flight footballers claim the colour of their skin is holding them back from making the transition to management. Russell Latapy and Kevin Harper, both former Hibernian players, contend the absence of diversity in Scottish dugouts validates their argument. Each states they have submitted applications for multiple coaching positions without achieving success. Scotland's football governing authorities and the managers' union all declare they operate to advance diversity. Former England and Liverpool winger John Barnes remains the sole black individual to have managed in Scotland, having overseen Celtic for a brief period in the late 1990s. Latapy, who was born in Trinidad and coached his national team, has served as a coach at Inverness Caledonian Thistle and Falkirk but states the route to management in the nation is proving more challenging. For whatever reason, young black managers are not receiving the same opportunities as young white managers, stated the 47-year-old. As players, we compete alongside one another and all we are requesting is the same opportunity. Since John Barnes, there has not been another black manager, but I must state this: I do not want a position because of the colour of my skin. I want a position based on what the chairman believes I can contribute to that football club. Harper, who is presently undertaking his A Licence coaching qualification, states he feels the same manner. I have applied for at least 10 positions in Scotland and I have received two responses, disclosed the 40-year-old. I am new to it but to only receive two responses and not even secure an interview, I believe there is a genuine issue. The most recent Scottish government statistics demonstrate that approximately 4% of the population is classified as non-white. Of the 10,000 registered Scottish FA coaches, just under 6% fall within that category. Former Scotland Under-21 forward Harper, however, believes the issue exists at a higher level. There might be 6% progressing through the coaching system, but there is 0% at the clubs, he stated. There is certainly an issue for sure. The head of the Scottish Coaches' and Managers' Association, Alex Smith, states he is surprised by the allegations. We do not recognise this as a problem, he stated. Colour, creed or sexual orientation is never a consideration when clubs appoint coaches or managers. The only consideration is ability. The Scottish Professional Football League added: We are absolutely confident that all of our member clubs assess each management and coaching application on its individual merit and appoint only the finest candidates, regardless of the colour of their skin. All of our member clubs fully support the Show Racism The Red Card campaign and undertake an abundance of work promoting diversity in their communities.

text: Sinn Féin and the SDLP have criticised the government's plan for Brexit, but a White Paper published on Thursday has been welcomed by unionists. The document outlines the government's 12 principles, which Prime Minister Theresa May recently set forth in a significant address in London. Brexit Secretary David Davis presented the plan to the House of Commons. The document concentrates on several themes, encompassing trade, immigration, devolution and the Irish border. DUP Deputy Leader Nigel Dodds stated the central emphasis of the plan was the opportunity Britain's departure from the EU provides to strengthen the union. This is why the DUP backed Brexit, and this is exactly what Brexit allows the UK to do, he stated. I am pleased that the government took the time to reaffirm the obvious - that Brexit would have no effect on the Common Travel Area, or the special relationship between British and Irish citizens. This long preceded EU membership and will successfully survive it. Nevertheless, the White Paper attracted a less positive response from Sinn Féin, which advocated for the UK to stay within the EU. Michelle O'Neill, Sinn Féin's leader north of the border, stated the government is operating in its own self-interest. It's evident the only viable approach is for the north to be granted a special status within, rather than outside of, the EU, she stated. The SDLP's Mark Durkan was equally severely critical of what he observed in it, stating it was filled out with platitudes and there was not much substantial content. The Foyle MP stated that the government was proceeding in the wrong direction and had established a path to Brexit with no sat-nav, map or compass. Both Sinn Féin and the SDLP desire Northern Ireland to receive special status following Brexit, but such a proposal has been rejected by Northern Ireland Secretary James Brokenshire, who considers it is the incorrect approach. The Ulster Unionist MP Danny Kinahan praised the publication of the White Paper, stating that clarity is what constituents and businesses require in order to best prepare for the future. He stated: Now that we understand the government's intentions, we will work relentlessly to hold them to their pledge to ensure a seamless border, safeguard the rights of UK citizens in EU member states and obtain the best trade agreement possible for Northern Ireland and the remainder of the UK. MPs endorsed the European Union Bill by 498 votes to 114 on Wednesday evening following two days of discussion. The DUP and the Ulster Unionists backed the bill, whilst the SDLP and independent unionist Lady Sylvia Hermon opposed it. MPs will examine the bill in greater detail next week, when it reaches the committee stage in the Commons, and the Labour Party has pledged to push through amendments.

text: A study confirming a link between atmospheric pollution and heart-attack risk strengthens the EU case for tougher clean-air targets, experts say. Research published in the BMJ examining long-term data for 100,000 individuals across five European nations discovered evidence of damage, even at permitted concentrations. Specialists emphasised that the danger to an individual remained relatively modest. Some contended the findings were not definitive as they failed to account for prior exposure to elevated levels. Additional factors, including smoking or elevated blood pressure, contribute more significantly to an individual's heart attack risk than contamination from vehicle emissions and industrial sources, they stated. However, sustained, prolonged exposure to air contamination - residing beside a congested road in an urban area, for instance - does exact its price, the research, encompassing a partnership of European universities and institutions, demonstrates. The BMJ investigation discovered that for every 5 µg/m3 rise in annual exposure to fine-particulate (PM 2.5) air contamination - considered the most harmful variety, as tinier particles can infiltrate deeply into the human body - there exists a 13% relative rise in heart attack occurrence, even after accounting for additional risk factors including smoking. Likewise, increasing concentrations of larger-particulate air contamination (PM 10) were similarly connected to heart-attack danger. These correlations persisted even when exposure concentrations fell beneath current European thresholds. The study's authors - representing the most extensive investigation ever examining pollution exposure's impact on European populations - state their findings strengthen the argument for reducing EU thresholds for particulate matter air contamination. Present EU legislation establishes the annual mean threshold on PM 2.5 at double that recommended by the World Health Organisation. Jon Ayres, professor of environmental and respiratory medicine at Birmingham University, stated: There exists no uncertainty that further reduction of PM concentrations would produce improvements in cardiac health across Europe. One can merely hope that our European politicians shall be convinced of these findings' significance and reconsider their stance on air contamination in Europe. Professor David Coggon, from Southampton University's Department of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, proved more cautious. This investigation contributes to evidence that particulate air contamination causes heart disease, yet it fails to establish that significant health dangers exist from exposure levels beneath current exposure thresholds, he stated. This occurs because the risk differences observed may represent a long-term consequence of past exposures when contamination levels were elevated. British estimates indicate nearly 30,000 individuals die prematurely annually as a direct consequence of air pollution exposure, which has been associated with asthma and additional lung conditions, including cancer, alongside cardiac complications. A recent Defra report on this matter states evidence indicates no safe threshold exists for PM 2.5 exposure, and this variety of artificial pollution reduces average life expectancy for UK residents by seven to eight months. A Defra spokesperson stated: Air quality has improved substantially in recent decades and Britain currently satisfies EU thresholds for this contamination type. We aim to continue improving air quality and diminish its potential impact on human health and the environment.

text: Restoration work has started on a World War I cemetery in Surrey built for Muslim soldiers killed in combat. The Horsell Common Preservation Society aims to complete the project in time for the centenary of the First World War's commencement on 4 August next year. The Grade II listed structure in Woking has deteriorated through the years and suffered vandalism. The first phase of work, which has received partial funding from English Heritage, is hoped to be completed by November. The preservation society also hopes to establish a memorial garden at the location. John Kingsbury, leader of Woking council, stated the heritage site held importance for local residents and for descendants of those who sacrificed their lives in the conflict. English Heritage senior designation adviser Paul Stamper stated: Its architectural significance and unique status as a site of remembrance for Muslims who perished fighting for Britain in two world wars is acknowledged in its national designation as a Grade II listed structure. David Robbins, chairman of the Horsell Common Preservation Society, expressed hope that the town would take pride in the unique war memorial upon completion of the work. Over one million troops from pre-independence India served Great Britain during the First World War. Injured soldiers were transported to hospitals in the South East. Hindu and Sikh soldiers were conveyed to crematoriums, whilst Muslim soldiers lacked a burial ground until 1915. Woking's site was finished in 1917. According to the preservation society, seventeen burials occurred at the site in 1917 and each was marked with a round arched headstone facing west, following Islamic tradition. A cadet from the Sandhurst military academy was interred there in 1920, before the War Graves Commission assumed responsibility for the ground's maintenance in 1921. During the Second World War, eight additional Muslim soldiers were buried at the site, including three from the Free French forces. In 1968, following a series of vandalism incidents, all the burials were relocated to Brookwood cemetery and the ground was deconsecrated. The structure remains a Registered War Memorial.

text: The final of this year's Britain's Got Talent drew the lowest audience in the show's 10-year history, according to overnight figures. An average of eight million viewers tuned in to watch the finale during its live broadcast, with a further 500,000 watching on ITV+1. Audiences peaked at 9.7 million when Army bandsman and magician Richard Jones was declared the winner. The previous record low occurred in 2014, when 10.7 million witnessed singing group Collabro's victory. Jones, a lance corporal with The Household Cavalry, captivated both judges and audiences with his military-themed performance. I cannot believe it, thank you so much to everyone who voted - it has been an incredible experience, it means everything to me, the 25-year-old stated. The first magician ever to claim victory in the talent competition, he secures a £250,000 prize and the chance to perform at the Royal Variety Performance. Live audiences represented a 39.7% share of total television viewing, though final consolidated figures - incorporating all on-demand and catch-up viewing - will not be available for seven days. An ITV spokesperson confirmed audiences peaked at 10.5 million viewers when ITV+1 figures were included. The finale aired simultaneously with the UEFA Champions League Final between Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, which was shown on subscription channel BT Sport and YouTube without charge. Last year's Britain's Got Talent final attracted an average of 11.7 million viewers, representing a 46.6% audience share. Over 17 million viewers watched the final at its peak in 2009, when dance troupe Diversity memorably defeated Susan Boyle. The final typically ranks amongst the year's most-watched programmes. Nevertheless, this year it seems unlikely to appear in the top 10. 'Brilliantly British' Dressed in his Household Cavalry uniform, Jones's performance featured a card trick recounting the story of Britain's oldest surviving magician, Fergus Anckorn, and how he employed magic to help endure imprisonment during wartime in Singapore. The act concluded by bringing the 97-year-old onto the stage. Earning a standing ovation from the judges, Alesha Dixon characterised the performance as poignant, noble and brilliantly British. Speaking on Britain's Got More Talent following the main programme, head judge Simon Cowell said he believed the public chose Jones as winner not solely due to his magical abilities. I think people supported him as an individual, he stated. His presentation, his entire performance was flawless - it was very patriotic and heart-warming and he merited victory. Fellow judge Amanda Holden commented: I am absolutely thrilled because when magic initially appeared on Britain's Got Talent it was dreadful and after 10 years he has accomplished such excellent work. The Army posted its congratulations to Jones, alongside a photograph of The Band of the Household Cavalry celebrating his triumph. Swing vocalist Wayne Woodward - who became the bookmakers' preferred candidate late on Saturday afternoon - concluded as runner-up with his interpretation of Nina Simone's Feeling Good. Boogie Storm, a troupe of disco-dancing Star Wars stormtroopers, were placed third. Also amongst the 12 finalists was sword swallower Alex Magala, whose act required pre-recording for safety considerations. It involved him sliding inverted down a pole, whilst handcuffed, halting centimetres above an operating chainsaw. Other finalists included schoolgirl vocalists Jasmine Elcock and Beau Dermott, mother and son partnership Mel and Jaime, 100 Voices of Gospel, dancers Shannon and Peter and Balance Unity, impressionist Craig Ball and dancing canine Trip Hazard. To commemorate the programme's 10 years, numerous past winners and memorable acts performed on stage as part of a special presentation. Choreographed by Diversity's Ashley Banjo, it featured six winning acts including 2008's George Sampson, 2010's Spelbound, 2012's dancing dog Pudsey and 2013 champions Attraction. Last year's runner-up, Jamie Raven, also performed, though last year's winner, Jules Dwyer and her dog Matisse, were conspicuously missing from the line-up. Dwyer became involved in controversy last year when it emerged a stunt dog was employed in the final performance rather than Matisse. Ofcom determined the public had been misled regarding the incident, but stated it did not believe ITV intended to deceive viewers.

Liberal Democrat Willie Rennie urged Ms Sturgeon to cancel another referendum, stating Scots were sick and fed up of the matter. They clashed on matters such as independence, Brexit, health and education, as well as benefit cuts and policing. The party leaders also answered questions from a studio audience on matters such as terrorism and security. At times the exchanges became angry in a special segment when the four were permitted to cross-examine each other. But it was the claim by Ms Sturgeon that the Scottish Labour leader had told her in a private conversation that Labour could no longer oppose Scottish independence after the Brexit vote almost a year ago that provoked the biggest political reaction. Ruth Davidson asked the SNP leader: Did you just tell people you had a private conversation with Kezia last June in which she had said she was going to drop Labour's opposition to independence? Ms Sturgeon replied: She said she thought Brexit changed everything and the Labour party could no longer go on opposing a second independence referendum. text: The BBC has argued the case for popular shows like Strictly Come Dancing and Sherlock in its response to the government's green paper on its future. The broadcaster stated the public desires and expects the BBC to provide entertainment, following claims it focuses excessively on audience figures. It also presented arguments for the popular music stations Radio 1 and 2, asserting they broadcast a wider variety of music than their commercial competitors. The response has been made available online. This follows the government's closure of a public consultation regarding the renewal of the BBC's charter, which posed several fundamental questions: When the green paper was published in July, culture secretary John Whittingdale stated that challenging questions would be posed about the scale and scope of the BBC and declared a determination was required on whether the corporation should attempt to do everything or become more focused. Over 80,000 individuals have contributed to the public consultation, Mr Whittingdale informed the Conservative Party Conference earlier this week. The BBC's response, which extends to more than 100 pages, acknowledges that the Government consultation is correct to demand that the BBC should be distinctive. Nevertheless, it states: Distinctiveness does not mean... withdrawing from popular content. The BBC produces quality popular programmes - if we retreated, audiences would possess fewer options. It challenges the proposition that the BBC should withdraw from audience-pleasing programmes, declaring: Competition on a Saturday evening has been part of the television environment for decades and enhances quality - with the viewer being the beneficiary. The response states the discussion about the BBC should begin with its purpose and examine the type of society we desire. Access to culture, media and information should constitute a fundamental human right, guaranteed irrespective of an individual's capacity to purchase it, declares the report, noting that it represents the BBC's mission to inform, educate and entertain. The document also reveals that 49% of Radio 1's playlist comprises artists without a top 10 single, whilst for Capital FM it stands at merely 12%; and that 27% of BBC One's primetime programming is factual, compared to 12% on ITV. The corporation has also detailed proposals for a comprehensive programme of reform; encompassing enhanced efficiency and an initiative to boost revenues from the BBC's commercial division, BBC Worldwide. It presents arguments for future-proofing the corporation by modernising it for the digital era, and requests policy-makers to assist ensuring public service broadcasting remains accessible on future as well as current platforms. Furthermore, it requests the government to delay 11 years, rather than 10, before reviewing the BBC's charter again - thereby removing discussions from the electoral cycle. The matter of financing the BBC is also addressed, with the report describing the licence fee as the optimal method. It states subscription funding - either independently or as a partial replacement to the licence fee - represents the incorrect model. It does concede that the licence fee requires modernisation, however, including eliminating the current exemption which renders watching catch-up programmes on the iPlayer online free from the fee.

text: The final Anfield memorial service to remember 96 football fans who died at Hillsborough will take place in April. Memorial services have been conducted at Liverpool's stadium most years since the tragedy on 15 April 1989. Hillsborough families have determined that this year's service - on the 27th anniversary - shall be the final one. The coroner at the inquests into the fatal crush at the Sheffield stadium shall begin summarising evidence later this month. The decision to conclude the Anfield services was taken by the Hillsborough Family Support Group (HFSG) following consultation with the relatives of those who perished. On Tuesday, Coroner Lord Justice Goldring adjourned the inquests, being conducted in Warrington, Cheshire, until 25 January when he anticipates summarising evidence for the jury. Margaret Aspinall, chairwoman of the HFSG, stated: The 96 shall never be forgotten. This final memorial service shall provide the families with some closure. Mrs Aspinall, whose 18-year-old son James perished in the tragedy, added: The HFSG would like to thank everyone for all the support the families have received over the past 27 years and all those people who have attended the service at Anfield each year. We hope that the public and supporters respect the decision of the HFSG and shall continue to remember the 96 in their own, perhaps more private, manner. In the days following the tragedy, Anfield became the focus of grief on Merseyside. A carpet of flowers was placed over the pitch and a chain of football scarves stretched from the stadium, across the city's Stanley Park and to Goodison Park, home of local rivals Everton. On the first anniversary the club unveiled its permanent memorial to those who perished - a 10-tonne granite block inscribed with the names of the victims alongside an eternal flame. Since then bereaved families, survivors, Liverpool players and managers have attended the annual service at the ground. The service has been a very public display of remembrance - but also of the support shown to those affected by the tragedy. More recently it has also helped maintain the bereaved families' campaign in the public eye. Mrs Aspinall has also requested people to cease pledging financial donations to HFSG. The families have received numerous donations over the years, including £96,000 pledged by former Liverpool manager Rafa Benitez. But Mrs Aspinall stated: The families do not need the money now. I would like to thank everybody, not just for their support, but the monetary aspect of it. BBC News: Profiles of all those who perished

text: The SNP leader has hit back at claims that too much cash comes over Hadrian's wall during the ITV leaders' debate. UKIP leader Nigel Farage had declared that taxpayers in England were cheesed off with the quantity of public funds that flows to Scotland. However, Nicola Sturgeon stated that Scots had contributed more tax per head of population each year for the previous 34 years. The debate featured the leaders of seven parties from throughout the UK. It was the sole occasion Prime Minister David Cameron and Labour leader Ed Miliband would appear together on television before the general election on 7 May. Mr Cameron stated the Conservatives' economic plan was functioning, adding: Let's not return to square one, Britain can achieve so much better than that. Mr Miliband repeatedly outlined what he would accomplish if I am prime minister, in increasing the minimum wage, prohibiting exploitative zero-hours contracts and rescuing our NHS Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg also participated in Thursday evening's debate, alongside Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood and the Green Party's Natalie Bennett. A YouGov poll of 1,100 people delivered a clear victory to Ms Sturgeon, with 28%, followed by Mr Farage on 20%, Mr Cameron on 18%, Mr Miliband on 15%, Mr Clegg on 10%, Ms Bennett on 5% and Ms Wood on 4%. However, a ComRes poll for ITV made it a dead heat between Mr Cameron, Mr Miliband, Mr Farage and Ms Sturgeon, though Mr Cameron emerged on top on the question of who was most capable of leading the country. Mr Miliband was judged best performer in an ICM poll for the Guardian, securing 25% of support, just ahead of Mr Cameron on 24%. Nigel Farage was on 19%, Nicola Sturgeon on 17%, Nick Clegg on 9%. A Survation poll for the Daily Mirror also placed the Tory and Labour leaders neck and neck on 25%, with Mr Farage on 24%, Ms Sturgeon 15%, Mr Clegg 6%, Ms Bennett 3% and Ms Wood 2%. Asked to award leaders marks out of 10 - by YouGov for the Times - the scores were: Ms Sturgeon 6.7, Mr Miliband and Mr Cameron 5.9, Mr Clegg and Mr Farage 5.5. Ms Sturgeon began by declaring the SNP - which polls have suggested is on course to return a record number of MPs to Westminster - would always stand up for Scotland, but wanted to offer friendship to the peoples of England, Wales and Northern Ireland and would help to bring about change for you too. Mr Farage, however, claimed canny Scots had negotiated a superior deal than other parts of the UK when the Barnett formula - which determines how public money is distributed - was created. He stated: This all has to be rebalanced because frankly English taxpayers are a bit cheesed off with so much of their money going over Hadrian's wall, giving people no prescription charges and no university tuition. Ms Sturgeon told him Scots had paid more tax per head of population in every single year for the last 34 years. In the television debate, Ms Sturgeon also struck out at the prime minister by arguing that the UK government could not cut its way out of a deficit, and insisted the NHS was the most precious public service the nation possessed. In an apparent attempt to present the election as a straight choice between himself and Mr Miliband, the prime minister told the debate audience: The choice at this election is sticking with a plan that is working or going back to the debt, taxes, borrowing and spending that got us in this mess in the first place. I say let's not go back to square one. Britain can do so much better than that. Mr Cameron added: The problem - and the real choice - is with Ed Miliband, who still thinks the last government didn't tax too much and borrow too much. But Mr Miliband accused Mr Cameron of wanting to discuss the past rather than the future and said: Some people will tell you that this is as good as it gets for Britain. I say Britain can do so much better than it has done over the last five years. There could have been no superior image of the changing political landscape of Britain. Whilst 50 years ago two parties took almost every vote between them, and just five years ago viewers of the TV debates might well have thought the era of three-party politics was permanent, this time there were seven politicians on stage. And three were women. The SNP's Nicola Sturgeon dressed boldly in red - perhaps to underline her determination to supplant Labour as the main party in Scotland. And she derided the old boys' network in SW1. The prime minister was introduced last and it appeared as though he found it difficult to maintain a smile on his face for the time it took to welcome his six opponents. He seemed to grow in confidence but was perhaps wondering initially why he was so insistent on broadening the field from the 2010 threesome. You could almost believe the women on the panel - Natalie Bennett from the Greens, and Leanne Wood from Plaid Cymru, as well as Ms Sturgeon - had consulted each other over launching an early attack on the austerity advocated by the main Westminster parties. Read more from Iain Mr Miliband said Mr Cameron had marginalised Britain in Europe, and added: I don't think our place lies outside the EU. I think that would be a disaster for jobs, a disaster for families and business. The Labour leader also attacked his Liberal Democrat counterpart Mr Clegg for betraying young people over tuition fees. In response, Mr Clegg attacked the Labour leader's pious stance and challenged Mr Miliband to apologise to the British public for crashing the economy. Mr Clegg directly challenged Mr Cameron over his decision not to ask the wealthiest to pay more towards deficit reduction, but instead to impose ideologically-driven cuts. Responding to Mr Cameron's casting of the election as a choice between competence and chaos, the Lib Dem leader urged him to imagine the chaos in people's lives caused by cuts in spending on health, schools and childcare. The SNP later said it had gained 1,200 new members during the two-hour debate programme. The party's deputy leader, Stewart Hosie MP, also said an average of the YouGov, ComRes and ICM polls which were released immediately after the debate suggested Ms Sturgeon had won, which Mr Hosie said showed how strong and persuasive she had been. Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy said the debate had made crystal clear the choice facing Scots at the general election. He said: In the debate there were seven passionate speakers but only two potential prime ministers. There are lots of ways to protest against David Cameron but only one way to replace him. UKIP's Scottish MEP David Coburn - in an interview with Radio Scotland's Good Morning Scotland programme - defended Mr Farage's comments from the television debate. He said: I think most reasonable Scots believe in the fair allocation of money. I think the SNP may make a big fuss about this but I think fair minded Scots like myself and everyone else believe we should give the English a reasonable deal too.

text: Restrictions put on terror suspects by the home secretary may be withering on the vine, a group of MPs and peers has warned. They stated the subsequent government in 2015 must urgently address the role and effectiveness of Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPims). The Joint Committee on Human Rights' report emphasised the risk of someone disappearing whilst under TPims. The Home Office stated the measures were the strongest the courts would permit. TPims involve restrictions including overnight residence at a specified address, GPS tagging, reporting requirements and restrictions on travel, movement, association, communication, finances, work and study. By Dominic Casciani Home affairs correspondent, BBC News By the end of this month six TPim suspects shall be free - meaning there is only one man still subject to the monitoring conditions. Given the secrecy surrounding the system, you can never be certain that there isn't another suspect we don't know about. Control orders - the more restrictive regime that preceded TPims - had many opponents who stated the house-arrest style conditions were unjust and oppressive. TPims inherited those critics and attracted more still, including security experts who stated the new regime was too lenient. What does appear to be working now is a strategy to intervene earlier by charging suspects with preparing acts of terrorism. This group may include suspects who, at one time, would have been considered for a TPim because of police concerns that they had substantial intelligence but no hard evidence to present to a jury. The measures were introduced in December 2011 as a replacement for the more restrictive regime of control orders, intended to prevent suspects from engaging in terrorist-related activity. The report stated there were eight TPim notices in force as of November last year, all of which were for British citizens. But seven of those shall have expired by the end of this month, according to the report. The committee stated TPims should be examined as part of a wider review of counter-terrorism powers. Its report urged the government to engage more transparently and substantively with recommendations of the independent reviewer of terrorism legislation. The report stated: We are left with the impression that in practice TPims may be withering on the vine as a counter-terrorism tool of practical utility. The committee concluded that the measures were not investigative in any real sense, and suggested they should be known as Terrorism Prevention Orders or something similar. It stated it agreed with the independent reviewer that the very nature of TPims carries an inherent risk of the subject absconding. And it recommended that more information about an internal review of TPims - launched after two subjects went missing - be made public. Mohammed Ahmed Mohamed - who has been linked to the Somali militant group al-Shabab - absconded in November after changing into a burka whilst visiting a west London mosque. His case followed that of Ibrahim Magag, who went missing in December 2012 in a black cab after ripping off his electronic tag. Committee chairman Hywel Francis stated: There is no evidence that they serve any investigative function and even as preventive measures they appear to be going out of favour with the agencies. Very few TPims are in operation and almost all of these are due shortly to lapse after their two-year duration. Mr Francis stated there is too little information known about the individuals on whom these measures have been imposed to make a proper judgement about whether the power to impose them is no longer required. The next government shall need to look again at these measures within the context of counter-terrorism powers more generally, he added. David Anderson, the independent reviewer of terror legislation, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme TPims were a necessary evil. One thing it shows is that police and prosecutors are doing their job, he stated. We've had a lot of convictions over the last couple of years, a lot of guilty pleas and a lot of heavy sentences. TPims don't present a long-term solution, he added. Home Secretary Theresa May stated TPims would also help the authorities gather material that would lead to prosecutions. But the committee stated it failed to find any evidence the measures had led to more suspects being charged. TPim restrictions have been or are about to be lifted from seven suspects, including men allegedly involved in planning terrorist attacks. The measures were imposed two years ago and cannot be renewed. A Home Office spokesman stated: TPims were introduced because control orders were not working and their powers were being struck down by the courts. They now provide some of the strongest possible protections that the courts shall allow.

text: The idea that party leaders are decisively important in the winning or losing of general elections is implicit in much political journalism and it is a belief that some political leaders themselves - Tony Blair, in particular - have been eager to propagate. Such circumstances are exceedingly rare. Only in an extraordinarily tight contest can the leader's character and the disparity between that leader's reputation and their primary rival's appeal determine the distinction between triumph and failure. It is not particularly unusual for the political party of the less favoured leader amongst the two principal parties to emerge victorious in the election. Therefore, for instance, whilst journalists continue to describe Margaret Thatcher's defeat of James Callaghan, the Labour leader maintained approximately 20 points over Mrs Thatcher on the evening before the Conservative triumph in the 1979 election. Thatcher did not vanquish Callaghan but rather the Conservative Party overcame Labour. A comprehensive examination of post-Second World War British elections determined that only one leader could have altered the outcome between his party establishing a government or remaining in opposition - Harold Wilson, on two instances - in October 1964 and February 1974. This occurred because those elections were exceptionally tight and Wilson commanded significantly greater popularity than the Conservative leader in both cases - Sir Alec Douglas-Home in 1964 and Edward Heath in 1974. Between these contests, the Conservatives had secured the 1970 election, despite the reality that Wilson remained more popular than Heath at that time. Given that all available data indicates the May 2015 election will likely prove a nail-biting affair, with a clear possibility that no single party will achieve an outright majority, does this suggest that journalists' disproportionate emphasis on the principal leader might finally be warranted? Almost certainly not. Both major political parties would be prudent to provide substantial interview opportunities to other frontbench members rather than overexpose David Cameron and Ed Miliband in what, owing to the fixed election date, will constitute an exceptionally lengthy campaign by British standards - four complete months. Nick Clegg might similarly limit his losses by sharing (initially with Vince Cable) whatever reduced spotlight the Liberal Democrats will obtain. Mr Clegg appears highly unlikely to replicate his 2010 campaign, when he was considered the exceptional performer, particularly in the televised debates, amongst the three party leaders. Even during that period, with unparalleled mass media attention and Cleggmania widespread, the party's national vote increased by merely 1%, and the Liberal Democrats concluded with five fewer MPs than in 2005. Nigel Farage will undoubtedly persist in commanding UKIP coverage, though the defection and subsequent election under the UKIP banner of two Conservative MPs renders him less of a solo act than previously. UKIP's ascendancy, however, stems not from possessing a leader of remarkable capability - he possesses eloquence but we cannot determine, and may never ascertain, whether he would prove an effective minister. Their by-election and polling success derives principally from the party representing the acceptable face of anti-immigration sentiment. During a period when the major parties avoided the matter, UKIP expressed widespread public anxiety regarding elevated immigration levels. Their opposition to British membership of the European Union constitutes a less prominent concern for most voters, except where it connects to immigration levels. The EU itself, and the sovereignty question, naturally matters enormously to numerous Conservative as well as UKIP activists. It would prove surprising if UKIP secured more than a small number of seats in the general election, yet they could still influence the result, drawing more votes from the Conservatives than from Labour. The crucial question concerns precisely how substantial the difference between Conservative and Labour defections to them will prove - potentially very considerable, and to Labour's electoral benefit, if it can persuade its core voters that the party has not become disconnected from them and its origins. The Green Party may or may not enhance the single House of Commons seat it currently holds, but it possesses the capacity to influence the result in numerous constituencies. It may be the mass media's leader-obsession that denies the Greens the attention their support level, particularly amongst young voters, deserves. How many individuals approached on the street could identify the current leader of the Green party? No, not Caroline Lucas - Natalie Bennett. The Greens' more collective leadership may have impeded them from securing their proportionate share of media coverage, but it has not prevented their surpassing the Liberal Democrats in popular support - 7% nationally compared to the Liberal Democrats' 6% in the final YouGov poll before Christmas. The Greens will certainly erode the Liberal Democrat vote in the May election, and they present a threat to Labour in certain marginal seats. Of all the parties besides Conservative and Labour, including the far from insignificant Northern Ireland parties, it is nevertheless the Scottish National Party which - uniquely for a British general election - may possess the key to the outcome. They constitute, by any objective assessment, a more credible party than UKIP and will likely secure considerably more seats. Unlike UKIP, to which they are occasionally, misleadingly, compared, they have proven they can govern and do so competently. Having maintained office as a minority government in Scotland from 2007 to 2011, they achieved an absolute majority in 2011, despite a highly proportional electoral system intended to ensure that no party (particularly not the SNP) would ever monopolise government positions. Until recently Scots have voted differently for the Westminster Parliament than for that in Edinburgh. Not only did Labour secure 41 out of 59 Scottish seats in the 2010 general election, it also enhanced its Scottish vote share by 2.5% whilst declining by 6.5% across the UK overall. Labour's prospects of an absolute majority in the House of Commons after 7 May must rely upon them retaining most of those seats. Presently this appears improbable. A December 2014 ICM poll of voting intentions for the general election placed the SNP 17 points ahead of Labour, with the remaining parties lagging considerably behind. Unless Labour can restore its former credibility north of the border, a majority of Scottish members of the House of Commons will be nationalists. The SNP's rise over the past two decades has frequently been attributed to the remarkable ability of its leader, Alex Salmond. His political talent is undeniable, but once again this represents a case of a specific leader being employed to explain excessive amounts. Following the smooth transition to Nicola Sturgeon's leadership - also, undoubtedly, a formidable politician - support for the party has merely continued expanding. The SNP have declared that under no circumstances will they support a Conservative government, but - for a price - they might sustain a Labour administration. This carries extremely far-reaching consequences. If it prompted the predictable English reaction, this would provide ammunition for the separatist party, but prove detrimental in the long term for Labour - and for the continued existence of the British state within its current boundaries.
