text: Swedish journalists Johan Persson and Martin Schibbye have been speaking to the BBC about their time in prison in Ethiopia. They were recently released following more than 400 days' imprisonment of an 11-year sentence. The duo were convicted of illegally entering the nation and assisting a rebel organisation, the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF). Their extended prison terms brought Ethiopia's treatment of journalists under international scrutiny. Martin Schibbye and Johan Persson were apprehended alongside ONLF insurgents in June 2011. They insisted they were merely performing their duties, and human rights organisation Amnesty International stated the journalists had been prosecuted for conducting legitimate work. However, Ethiopian government spokesman Bereket Simon had previously justified the decision to imprison the duo, claiming the journalists were caught red handed collaborating with terrorist organisations. Late Prime Minister Meles Zenawi allegedly pardoned the journalists prior to his death in August, resulting in their release. Johan Persson informed the BBC World Service programme Newsday that conditions in the detention facility where they were confined were appalling. It was 200% overcrowded. It was extremely hot. There was insufficient water. It was dusty. There were rodents, fleas and numerous people were ill with HIV or tuberculosis, he stated. However, he said the conditions were less significant than the other prisoners: What's noteworthy is whom they place in there: journalists and the political opposition. Whilst the pair acknowledge they entered Ethiopia illegally, they contend their trial was unjust. The trial was a farce, said Mr Persson. Meles Zenawi was declaring on national television, three or four weeks before the trial commenced, that we were guilty. They also consider the charge of moral support for terrorism, for which they were convicted, has been misapplied against other journalists in Ethiopia. For recent years Ethiopia has been utilising its anti-terror legislation to suppress the media and to suppress journalism, Mr Schibbye told Newsday. The freelance correspondents had been in the Ogaden, an ethnic Somali region in eastern Ethiopia, for four days before their arrest. The Ethiopian army observed us. Then they tracked our movements for three to four days. Then they ambushed us. We were assaulted by approximately 150 Ethiopian army soldiers who fired upon us. We were struck quite rapidly. I was hit in the shoulder and Johan was hit in the arm. Someone shouted, 'media, media, international press,' and we were detained, said Martin Schibbye. Following their arrest they claimed they were commanded at gunpoint to participate in a film purportedly documenting their association with the Ogaden National Liberation Front. Two civilians, whom we had never encountered before, were disguised as rebels. The soldiers provided them with weapons and positioned them before us, and they testified against us and claimed that we accompanied them from Somalia, says Mr Schibbye. The journalists allege that senior Ethiopian civilian officials supervised the filming. This was not being conducted by some rogue militia: the director was the vice president in the region, and in the evening the regional president telephoned us and said, 'We are not satisfied by your performances in the film,' said Mr Schibbye. Subsequently the film was employed against them in court. Ethiopia's eastern Ogaden region has been the centre of an insurgency by local ethnic Somalis. We were traversing villages where there had been people residing until recently, but now they had departed, forced out by the conflict. There was intense fighting and that was one of the reasons why we were spotted and tracked and ambushed by the Ethiopian army, Mr Persson said. Despite spending more than a year in prison, they say they harbour no regrets about their time in Ethiopia. For Martin Schibbye, the work of foreign correspondent is one that demands taking risks and refusing to accept there are areas forbidden to journalists. His colleague concurs: As long as governments create laws to protect themselves against journalists, our duty is to breach those laws. I would do the same again today.

text: A year into power, if there is one thing that becomes clearer about the Xi Jinping leadership of the Communist Party of China, it is that it understands the value of political symbolism. One of the initial locations Mr Xi visited following his appointment as party secretary last November was Shenzhen, sacred ground of the Reform and Opening Up Process since 1978, and among the earliest and most vibrant Special Economic Zones. The conference at which the ideological breakthroughs were achieved that enabled the acceptance of foreign investment and a marketplace in China occurred at Jingxi Hotel in Beijing during December 1978. More than three and a half decades afterwards, approximately 400 super-elite party members convened at the identical venue once more. This alone generated expectations that momentous developments were imminent. The communiqué from the Third Plenum of the 18th Party Congress released on 12 November following the three-day conference should dispel the idea that this leadership intends to undertake the same dramatic transformation that the 1978 gathering accomplished. Circumstances have changed. The straightforward reality is that an error now would prove far more expensive than previously, when the nation was emerging depleted from late Maoism and required radical action to revitalise its economy. Currently, China represents a global economy, and one with considerable potential in the forthcoming decades. Its challenge presently is merely to, in Premier Li Keqiang's words, unlock fresh sources of growth internally. There exists no question of it, presently at least, requiring fundamental course alteration. The mechanism for achieving growth shall be enhancing and refining the market, and liberalising fresh sectors where growth might emerge. That represents the most significant message from this plenum. Questioning the fundamental principles of the Reform and Opening Up period was never anticipated. The party's primacy is declared with absolute clarity in the plenum document. Its central role in society remains supreme. The requirement for internal unity and collective leadership remains as valued as during the Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao period. The goal remains, through the ideological instruments of Deng Xiaoping theory and Socialism with Chinese characteristics, to accomplish the primary stage of socialism. That shall require, according to the communiqué, numerous years. More explicit references exist to establishing a national security coordination body. This appears to be the Hu and Wen preoccupation with pro-stability measures in different form, with some effort to finally coordinate and streamline decision-making in this sphere, particularly as no one on the current Politburo Standing Committee holds specific responsibility for security matters as existed in the previous one. Q&A: China's Third Plenum Third Plenum: Key issues The priority this leadership assigns to stability remains elevated, and the vehicle explosion in Tiananmen during early November alongside the improvised bomb attack in Taiyuan simultaneously will only emphasise to this leadership that relaxing regarding this matter is not feasible. Politburo member Yu Zhengsheng mentioned before the plenum that deeper fresh reforms were approaching. It is evident now that this concerned introducing a more adaptable system whereby rural inhabitants can relocate to urban centres, secure employment there, establish residence there, access social welfare and, perhaps most crucially, educate their offspring. The government during recent months has emphasised heavily the necessity to accelerate urbanisation, and possessing a framework to enfranchise and provide incentives to rural dwellers enabling their relocation is significant. Implementation nevertheless remains crucial here, so whilst the statement of intention is sufficiently robust, the question shall be how to persuade provincial governments throughout China that they can bear the expenses of a fresh wave of citizens for whom they must somehow provide social services. No explicit reference exists regarding whether provinces shall therefore receive broader tax-raising powers, though this would appear a natural consequence of accommodating a fresh influx of residents. Concerning economic reform, the strongest theme involves developing a finance market. Here also we observe Li Keqiang's intellectual influence, the individual most closely connected with establishing in October a Free Trade Zone in Shanghai, a location where China's capital account might be liberalised and Chinese yuan trading accelerated. Finance shall be a crucial sector for this leadership, one of the principal means of delivering a substantial service component in the economy, and of creating a high value-added economy. This plenum provides a framework, which confirms several themes that have already emerged from this leadership. No rapid ideological or political transformation, a continuation of emphasising people's material welfare and attempting to achieve robust growth, with the principal drive being to accomplish elevated urbanisation before 2020. If one bold characteristic of this plan exists, it is that virtually everything is wagered on an urban China being one where the current difficulties of achieving growth, addressing some sustainability issues, and tackling inequality will become more manageable. This represents a substantial gamble, because the pace at which China evidently plans to become urban exceeds that attempted by any other society. Vast questions exist about how social cohesion shall be achieved, and what manner of social and political structures might ultimately emerge from this to accomplish the harmonious society that the previous leadership discussed extensively. Kerry Brown is professor of Chinese politics at the University of Sydney, team leader of the Europe China Research and Advice Network (ECRAN) funded by the European Union, and an Associate Fellow of the Asia Programme at Chatham House.

German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schäuble and his Spanish counterpart Luis de Guindos released a statement. Mr de Guindos will meet French Finance Minister Laurent Fabius on Wednesday. Spain's financial position continues to concern investors, with borrowing costs increasing and the Catalonia region stating it will require government funds. On Tuesday, Spain asserted Italy and France supported a plan for the immediate implementation of measures agreed last month. These encompass aid targeted at Spain's banks without adding to national debt. Spain stated there had been a worrying delay in executing the agreements hammered out at the eurozone leaders summit on 29 June. The principal provision would be to permit the future European bailout fund, the ESM, to channel money directly into troubled banks such as those in Spain, bypassing national governments. The establishment of the fund has been hindered by constitutional challenges in Germany which mean Berlin will not be able to ratify the agreement before 12 September. Dickens's British publishers would have charged as much as they could manage for copies of Bleak House. Impoverished literature enthusiasts simply had to do without. Yet these potential substantial profits encourage new ideas. It took Dickens considerable time to write Bleak House. If other British publishers could have copied it like the Americans, perhaps he would not have troubled himself. Therefore, intellectual property reflects an economic trade-off, a balancing act. If it is too generous to the creators, then good ideas will take too long to copy, adapt and spread. If it is too mean, then perhaps we shall not see the good ideas at all. This trade-off has always been influenced by politics. The British legal system strongly protected the rights of British authors and British inventors in the 1800s because the UK was then - as now - a powerful force in world culture and innovation. However, in Dickens's era, American literature and innovation were in their infancy. The US economy was in full-scale copying mode: they wanted the cheapest possible access to the finest ideas that Europe could provide. US newspapers filled their pages with shameless copying - alongside attacks on the meddling Mr Dickens. A few decades later, when American authors and inventors spoke with a more powerful voice, America's lawmakers began to take an increasingly favourable view of the idea of intellectual property. Newspapers, once opposed to copyright, now depend upon it. And we can expect to see a similar transition in developing countries today: the less they copy other ideas and the more they create their own, the more they protect ideas. There has been considerable recent movement: China did not have a copyright system at all until 1991. The modern form of intellectual property originated, like so many things, in 15th Century Venice. Venetian patents were explicitly designed to encourage innovation. The inventor would automatically receive a patent if their invention was useful. The patent was temporary, but could be sold, transferred or even inherited during its lifetime. It would be forfeited if it was not used, and invalidated if the invention proved to be closely based on a previous idea. These are all very modern ideas. And they soon created very modern problems. During the British industrial revolution, the great engineer James Watt worked out a superior way to design a steam engine. He spent months developing a prototype, but then put even more effort into securing a patent. His influential business partner, Matthew Boulton, even got the patent extended by lobbying Parliament. Boulton and Watt used it to extract licensing fees and crush rivals - for example, Jonathan Hornblower, who made an even better steam engine yet found himself ruined and imprisoned. The details may have been sordid, but surely Watt's famous invention was worth it? Well, perhaps not. The economists Michele Boldrin and David Levine argue that what truly unleashed steam-powered industry was the expiry of the patent, in 1800, as rival inventors revealed the ideas they had been sitting on for years. And what happened to Boulton and Watt, once they could no longer sue those rivals? They flourished anyway. They redirected their attention from litigation towards the challenge of producing the finest steam engines in the world. They kept their prices as high as ever, and their order books swelled. Far from incentivising improvements in the steam engine, the patent actually delayed them. Yet since the days of Boulton and Watt, intellectual property protection has grown more expansive, not less so. Copyright terms are growing ever longer. In the US, they were originally 14 years, renewable once. They now last 70 years after the death of the author - typically more than a century. Patents have become broader and are being granted on vague ideas - for example, Amazon's one-click US patent protects the not-entirely-revolutionary idea of buying a product on the internet by clicking only one button. The US intellectual property system now has a global reach, thanks to the inclusion of intellectual property rules in what tend to be described as trade agreements. text: How often do we really look into someone's eyes? We exchange brief glances with strangers on the street and gaze affectionately at friends and family, yet how frequently do we maintain their gaze for more than several seconds? Not frequently enough states Nuala McKeever, who describes herself as a happiness instructor. Nuala considers eye contact could assist us in reconnecting with one another in a profound and spiritual manner, and the 40-year-old understands a considerable amount about the human spirit. Following her departure from a high-pressure position in the financial services industry, Nuala embarked upon a journey of exploration which resulted in her becoming a 'laughter-yoga' instructor. Originally from Londonderry, she currently resides in Belfast and operates the Sunshine Project alongside friend Michelle Major. As part of their mission to promote peace and love, the duo organised an event near Victoria Square, Belfast, on Thursday during which they encouraged members of the public to share 60 seconds of eye contact with a volunteer. I attended to observe how it felt to share such an intimate moment with a stranger. The group established themselves at Belfast's Corn Market during lunchtime. Each volunteer gazer was positioned within a hula hoop, upon a cushion or upon a chair with an empty space before them. Members of the public were encouraged to attend and sit or stand before the volunteer and, without speaking, gaze into their eyes for 60 seconds. I was matched with Nuala, who explained to me that we should each gaze into the other's left eye; this would prevent us from breaking eye contact by shifting our gaze from one eye to the other. As our 60 seconds commenced I began to feel uncomfortable. Nuala conversely, with her head tilted slightly to the side, appeared the picture of calm. As the seconds passed I wished to examine her face or look down but our eyes were locked together. When I accepted this and gradually relaxed, I began to experience some of the positive effects of the practice. I felt extremely calm and everything in the background became out of focus. For a brief moment it was as if we were the only two people in the bustling city centre. When the session concluded, Nuala threw her arms around me, an act that would have felt considerably more bizarre if I had not spent the previous 60 seconds gazing at her. She informed me I had made her feel emotional but she was not certain why. She stated: I frequently see myself when I gaze into someone's eyes. Eye contact is how we connect as human beings and it is different every time, yet it always reminds me that I am part of something much larger than myself. When we look into each other's eyes we see beyond our differences, I cannot think of anywhere where this is more important than in Belfast. One of the participants, Marcela Vojacova, 44, explained why she became involved in the project. I wished to see what could be accomplished by gazing into another person's eyes and what I might see, she stated. When I participate I experience a sense of fulfilment, love and happiness - I hope the other people do too. Mark Graham, who stopped by the event to see if it would assist him in de-stressing, was surprised by his experience. I have a job interview approaching and sharing 60 seconds with Marcela truly helped me to relax, he stated. For the time we were sharing the experience it was as if no one else was present. I think many people would laugh at the idea of participating in something like this but it could be truly helpful for some.

There are places where free movement of labour is more of an advantage to companies than to people and communities.” It is not true. In the present circumstances, free movement of labour increases inequality. We have not admitted that, and that is why we appear ill-informed. He said that the renegotiation which David Cameron was negotiating with the European Union before the forthcoming in-or-out vote offered a chance to protect the workers. The forthcoming vote was an opportunity to change things. Economic power was increasing in the big cities, and that was a good thing. It is an opportunity to place Labor in the foreground and be in touch. Let's put forward a new vision of a social Europe. The Conservatives and the Ukip want to eliminate these protections. We welcome those who want to work here as we have always done, but let us make it work for everyone with new European rules against undercutting, protecting the minimum wage for skilled workers. Let us have the courage to counter their scapegoating propaganda, which won't pay the rent, feed anyone's children or protect anyone's job. A Europe that puts people before profit and transnational corporations; a floor for all workers. Mr. Burnham’s words, Ms. Collin said, were a desperate plea from a man who for years had ignored the plight of the working classes caused by mass migration.

text: Justin Timberlake has said he'll be performing at this year's Eurovision Song contest in Stockholm, Sweden. The 35-year-old will perform during the interval at the grand final on Saturday. Eurovision officials confirmed his performance would be in a non-competitive capacity. It marks the first occasion in the contest's history that an artist of international prominence has appeared on stage to perform independently. In a statement, Sven Stojanovic, one of the programme's producers said: This represents a fantastic opportunity, we are delighted and thrilled that Justin Timberlake will perform his new song alongside his band in our programme. It renders it particularly special that the Swedish songwriters Max Martin and Shellback have co-written and co-produced the song alongside Justin Timberlake. The nine-time Grammy award-winner will perform his latest song, Can't Stop the Feeling, which he composed for the Dreamworks animation, Trolls. BBC Radio 1 presenter Scott Mills and The Great British Bake Off's Mel Giedroyc will co-present BBC Four's live coverage of the two semi-finals on 10 and 12 May. Graham Norton will once again provide commentary for BBC One's live transmission of the final from the Globe Arena. Timberlake, who is on a promotional tour for his single, also presented the best drama series award at this year's Bafta TV awards, alongside actress Anna Kendrick. The award was presented to BBC Two's Wolf Hall. Timberlake's performance announcement follows Eurovision's announcement that Romania was being excluded from the competition for failing to pay their fees. It also follows days after Eurovision officials relaxed their flag regulations, meaning the UK entry could display a Welsh flag. It was initially included in a list of prohibited flags because its red dragon was deemed a political statement. Previously only flags of contest members and UN states were permitted due to the event's non-political character. The UK entry features Joe Woolford from Ruthin, Denbighshire who will be performing You're Not Alone with Jake Shakeshaft from Stoke-on-Trent. The Eurovision Song Contest is on BBC One from 2000 BST.

text: Pupils have been so violent or disruptive that on eight occasions last year teachers held ballots to refuse to teach them in their classes. These ballots, by members of the NASUWT teachers' union, encompassed instances where pupils had attacked teachers but had been permitted to remain in school. Following these votes, pupils were excluded or relocated. Schools minister Nick Gibb stated teachers had received the support they require to address poor behaviour. NASUWT leader Chris Keates maintains the trend demonstrates deteriorating behaviour issues. The number of these refusal to teach ballots, throughout the UK, has increased for the third consecutive year - rising from three in 2012, four in 2013 to eight in 2014. The teachers' union, conducting its annual conference in Cardiff, states there were additional instances where a ballot was threatened, but alternative provisions were arranged for disruptive pupils without the ballot proceeding. Amongst incidents prompting ballots were instances such as a 16-year-old pupil in western England who had attacked pupils, teachers, the head teacher and police when summoned to help. Following a ballot by teachers, the pupil was educated off-site. At a secondary school in north Wales a teenager with a record of disruption had threatened to slit the throat of another pupil. Following a ballot by teachers, the pupil was excluded. A teenager at a secondary school in the English midlands, whom the union states had attacked and threatened staff and pupils, remained in school but was prohibited from attending lessons taught by NASUWT members. In another instance, the union states a ballot followed a disagreement over how a group of teachers intervened with a pupil with a record of attacking others. When there were accusations that teachers had attacked this pupil there was a refusal to teach ballot, following which the pupil was removed from the school. Ms Keates states schools face a widespread and growing problem of pupil indiscipline. The union questioned its members about their experiences of pupil behaviour, receiving approximately 3,500 online responses. Nearly three quarters of respondents claimed there was a widespread behaviour problem in schools today - a greater proportion than in a comparable survey last year. This is not a representative sample, but amongst those responding, 82% stated they had faced verbal abuse from a pupil and 38% from a parent in the past year. Some 23% had been physically threatened by pupils and 16% attacked. According to those who responded, the greatest contributor to declining behaviour is an excessive focus on data-driven targets, identified by nearly two thirds of teachers. Ms Keates also blamed increasing class sizes and the absence of support for children with special needs in mainstream schools. The conference will debate pupil indiscipline on Saturday. It will hear claims behaviour standards are being undermined by a blame culture in schools that seeks to hold individual teachers accountable for poor pupil behaviour, whilst overlooking the crucial role that school leaders should play. The motion will also criticise a lack of consistency in how rules on behaviour are implemented. School reform minister Nick Gibb stated: The Conservative party is committed to providing schools the support they require to address poor behaviour. That is why we have made it easier to search pupils, brought back same-day detentions and clarified teachers' power to use reasonable force. We have also ensured that a head teacher's ability to exclude pupils is not undermined by external bodies. As a result, three quarters of teachers now rate behaviour in their school as good or better. A Liberal Democrat spokesman stated: It is essential that teachers have the resources they require to manage behaviour and support those children who need additional help. This is precisely why, in government, Liberal Democrats protected school budgets and introduced the pupil premium - additional money to support the children most likely to struggle in class.

text: Is banning a person from contesting for public office if he or she does not have a toilet at home a good idea? India's western state of Gujarat certainly holds this belief. Earlier this week, the state's legislators approved legislation which renders it compulsory for candidates to possess toilets in their residences to qualify for standing in elections to local municipalities and village councils. Current elected representatives must also declare within six months that they possess toilets at home, failing which they shall face disqualification. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who governed Gujarat for more than a decade before he achieved victory in Delhi in May, has rendered abolishing open defecation a principal priority of his administration. It represents a commendable objective, though critics consider it fails to connect what remains largely an individually-driven campaign to the appalling practice of manual scavenging. Clearly legislators from Mr Modi's governing BJP in Gujarat have enthusiastically supported their leader's appeal. Certainly, there remains nothing incorrect in that. Open defecation damages the lives of millions of Indians and constitutes an enduring health hazard. Nearly half of Indians persist in defecating in the open. Gujarat, amongst India's most prosperous states, remains in haste to construct more toilets; the state possesses a patchy record here. Its new Chief Minister Anandi Patel states she desires the state to become open defecation free within two years. A recent report indicated more than 70,000 people defecate in the open in the principal city of Ahmedabad alone. Strong economics does not invariably produce good sanitation. However, does the latest measure linking a democratic right to constructing a private utility represent such a sound idea? Some 40% of people in Gujarat reside in its 159 municipalities and eight municipal corporation areas in what constitutes amongst India's most urbanised states. There exist some 13,500 village councils in its more than 18,500 villages. Elections to these bodies remain critical to the health of Gujarat's democracy and development. The freedom to contest the polls also constitutes an inalienable right of every citizen residing in their cities and villages. That explains why critics like economist Hemant Shah consider that the legislation remains essentially undemocratic and discriminatory, and should be challenged in the courts. Tens of thousands of people in Gujarat's crowded cities reside in sprawling chawls - densely packed buildings containing more than a dozen tenements - where many families share a single toilet. Shall a chawl resident be prevented from contesting because he lacks his private toilet? What occurs to the political aspirations of a resident of a squalid shantytown home so small that his living space sometimes equals the non-existent toilet? The government should first provide space and money to construct toilets for the poor. The poor remain most affected by urban planning because it has consistently excluded them. Now they cannot dream of standing for public office simply because they lack the space or money to construct their own toilets? asks Professor Shah. It constitutes a valid question.

text: Scientists have discovered another eight pieces of genetic code linked to osteoarthritis, bringing the total number to 11. These are external links and will open in a new window Hereditary factors account for at least half of any individual's risk of developing this common condition that affects the joints, experts believe. And comprehending these factors could provide new treatments. The research in The Lancet compared the DNA of 7,400 UK osteoarthritis patients with that of 11,000 healthy volunteers. This enabled scientists to identify the most promising culprit regions of the genetic code to examine in greater detail. They repeated their work in another group of 7,500 people with osteoarthritis and approximately 43,000 individuals without the condition from Iceland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and the UK. The results confirmed the three previously reported gene variants and discovered a further eight linked to osteoarthritis. Additional work is now required to pinpoint the actual DNA changes within the genetic regions to establish precisely how these changes lead to osteoarthritis. The one with the strongest effect was located in the region of the GNL3 gene which produces a protein with an important role in cell maintenance. Three others were in DNA regions involved in the regulation of cartilage, bone development and body weight. One of the lead scientists, John Loughlin, who is professor of musculoskeletal research at Newcastle University, said: We know that osteoarthritis runs in families and that this is due to the genes that people pass on, rather than their shared environment. In this study we were able to say with a high degree of confidence which genetic regions are the major risk factors for developing osteoarthritis: the first time that this has been possible for this common yet complex disease. It's an important first step. Prof Alan Silman, medical director of Arthritis Research UK, the charity that funded the work, said: Until we understand the cause of this complex disease, we cannot hope to find a cure. This is a major breakthrough in our understanding of osteoarthritis, which we hope will help us to unlock the genetic basis of the disease.

text: The number of young men using steroids in London is rising on a regular basis a drugs charity has warned. The South Westminster Drug and Alcohol Service reported that a growing number of young male clients were requesting assistance for anabolic steroid use. Home Office statistics reveal 60,000 individuals used steroids in the United Kingdom in 2014. However, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence stated this was the tip of the iceberg and recommended gymnasiums provide sharps bins for needles. Roy Jones, from the South Westminster service, stated: Our numbers are rising on a regular basis. I have been working with steroid users for 16 years and when I initially started, the men taking them were bodybuilders in their 30s. Now the average age I observe is 23. According to Professor Gillian Leng, deputy chief executive of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), there exists a concerning trend of young professionals turning to the substances. She stated: It is fair to say it is becoming a much more normal thing to do amongst some groups of young men who are concerned about the way they appear...injecting steroids has become a solution. Although government statistics suggest 60,000 individuals used steroids in 2014, professional bodies believe the figure is considerably higher, as only those ending up in police custody are recorded in the data. What are anabolic steroids? Professor Leng stated: I think it is inevitable that the number is significantly higher. From the epidemiology (the data) we possess about the kind of individuals who use steroids - it is a group that is not all going to appear in custody so that figure is bound to be the tip of the iceberg - it might be three times that number. A 25-year-old, who works in the City of London and requested to remain anonymous, told BBC London he had taken steroids for two years. He stated he purchased them from a dealer at his local gymnasium and he knows many others who do the same. I began taking them because I felt I could not get any bigger training naturally, he stated. It was the next step for me. There is immense pressure to look good - it is part of the culture we live in, we all want that big figure. Easygym has installed sharps bins in all their gymnasiums, whilst Fitness First, Virgin Active and David Lloyd stated some of their clubs also have them. All the gymnasiums stated they had a zero tolerance approach to steroids and the bins were a health and safety measure for diabetic members and the disposal of razors. The Department of Health stated it had given local areas the power and the funding to tackle public health issues like this. Despite the increased awareness, Matthew Dear, 17, from Southend, died following an adverse reaction to steroids. His mother Tina, who runs the Matthew Dear Foundation, which was established to warn people about the dangers of steroid use, stated: When we lost Matthew six years ago, people thought it was a problem that was not going to boil over. text: England seem set to end the series in South Africa with a defeat after a horrible start to their second innings. They swiftly collapsed to 18-3 and one senses something extraordinary must occur from the overnight score of 52-3 to avoid a substantial defeat, with a victory target of 382 surely completely theoretical. South Africa's pace assault revealed some familiar frailties but also demonstrated that the Centurion surface is extremely challenging, particularly with the new ball. There was pressure applied; the light was poor; England could not win the match; they were batting to preserve the game - all the customary problems. One might consider that England ought to have performed somewhat better but the new ball is challenging. It is extremely awkward as a batsman when the ball pitches in the identical spot on different occasions and behaves entirely differently. Captain Alastair Cook received one that rolled along the surface and another that almost removed his armpit, and when one has approximately half a second to respond and in one's mind one is questioning what the pitch will do, that generates uncertainty. Leading batsmen must handle these circumstances but it is considerably easier said than accomplished. Alex Hales received one that stayed rather low but it was another disappointment. He has played four matches and accumulated 136 runs. My opinion has not altered: any opening bowler would consider Hales provides more opportunity than he ought as an opening batsman. It is conceivable they will persist with him. They discarded Adam Lyth following seven matches, and they are exhausting options regarding whom to select with eight opening batsmen attempted since Andrew Strauss retired in 2012. They could position Nick Compton there but he has scarcely set the world alight, either opening or at number three, and he executed a careless shot to become the third England wicket to fall within the opening 10 overs. They will need to consider it carefully, but they must resolve the opening position. In the early summer circumstances when England contest three Tests against Sri Lanka, Hales may well accumulate some runs and it might simply be that one score which launches his Test career. But he possesses these technical problems that have been discussed repeatedly. He has achieved one score of 60 but the other innings he has not progressed and it will be the nature of the dismissals that will disappoint him. But pressure causes one to behave strangely and Hales, Compton and James Taylor all understand their positions are under scrutiny. Discarded players such as Gary Ballance and Ian Bell will be considering that if they commence the domestic season well they could force their return into the team. All of these players will participate in county cricket and will have several matches early-season. They must venture out there and struggle to earn selection. It is not a negative thing in a sense; one wants competition for positions and one wants it to be demanding but I do not believe any of them will be sleeping particularly comfortably before the selection for the first Test match against the Sri Lankans at Headingley on 19 May. I would be astonished if they returned to Bell, however. It appears as though they have progressed after he was part of the 2-0 defeat against Pakistan in the United Arab Emirates late last year. Ballance has compiled four hundreds and six fifties in his 15 Tests and I believe they wish to restore him to the side again, but he must earn it. Having lost the series, South Africa are ironically now enjoying some players in outstanding form, so they possess considerable hope for the future. Hashim Amla batted magnificently again. It was a most courageous innings after being struck several times on the thumb and it was unfortunate he did not achieve his second hundred in the match. And the diminutive Temba Bavuma, who compiled that marvellous hundred in Cape Town, continues to impress everyone. He possesses an outstanding attitude, he moves his feet extremely well, technically he appears sound and he has been a revelation, as has the young fast bowler Kagiso Rabada. He claimed two more wickets to devastate the England top order in that brief session before the close. They both arrived with promise but have truly demonstrated they can enjoy genuinely successful Test careers. It is a significant day for Rabada, who requires one more wicket to become the youngest South African to claim 10 in a Test match. I questioned how he would operate having bowled 29 overs, securing his seven wickets in the first innings haul of 7-112, but he certainly appeared to be moving satisfactorily. He will achieve that I am certain, and he and Morne Morkel will be quite a challenge. Clearly South Africa will be overwhelming favourites to conclude it on the final day. I was somewhat surprised how long they batted on. I thought they would have reached a 270 lead and truly advance and play more shots. Had they declared earlier they could have had England batting before the storm arrived and tested them in some extremely dark conditions. AB de Villiers is a new captain and it is always difficult establishing declarations, but the general opinion is they could have declared an hour earlier. Nevertheless, they possess plenty of time remaining and they have the second new ball, which is perfectly timed after 60 overs on Tuesday to conclude it if they have not already done so. Jonathan Agnew was speaking to BBC Sport's Jamie Lillywhite.

text: Syrian forces are continuing their crackdown on protesters in the port city of Latakia for a third day, reportedly using tanks and gunboats. Campaigners claim no fewer than 30 individuals have perished since Saturday, and that inhabitants attempting to escape the city's Ramel district have come under fire from soldiers. The administration in Damascus states it is confronting armed terrorist groups. Over 1,700 individuals have allegedly perished in the six-month revolt against President Bashar al-Assad's rule. The Ramel neighbourhood and adjacent areas are reported to be experiencing continuous heavy gunfire on Monday as tanks and soldiers advance through the streets. The offensive commenced on Saturday, one day following mass anti-government demonstrations in the city. By Jim Muir BBC News, Beirut Latakia was amongst the cities to become embroiled in the rebellion shortly after it began in mid-March. Despite repeated efforts by the regime to suppress defiance, it continues emerging. It represents a sensitive city. Its population numbers approximately 600,000, and it possesses a Sunni Muslim majority, as does the nation, but there are also districts dominated by President Assad's minority Alawite community. The current retribution is being administered to predominantly Sunni districts, a circumstance that could further inflame sectarian tensions already heightened by the situation. On Sunday, campaigners stated Syrian warships had participated in the assault, launching shells upon the city. One Ramel inhabitant informed Associated Press news agency: We are receiving fire from the ground and the sea. The gunfire is severe. We cannot venture out. They are conducting raids and forcing entry into people's residences. He stated that no fewer than three gunboats were participating and mosques had been struck. A Syrian military official on Monday rejected as completely unfounded reports that gunboats had bombarded Latakia, Syria's official Sana news agency reported. A UK-based Anglican clergyman who is visiting his relatives in Latakia stated the atmosphere in the city was exceptionally tense. [On Sunday] you could detect considerable shooting and bombing from various parts of the city, the Reverend Nadim Nassar informed the BBC. The entire city is now closed... the fear is extremely high and people do not know what is happening and what comes next, he stated. The London-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported no fewer than one young child had been killed. State television rejected any shelling had occurred. It stated the security forces were battling armed groups who had erected barricades and were firing from rooftops. The government reported three security force members were killed and 40 injured in confrontations. It interviewed some of the city's inhabitants in other locations who appealed to the army to eliminate the terrorist groups. Campaigners reject that their movement is armed but stated no fewer than one officer and several soldiers had defected to join the revolt. International journalists encounter severe limitations in operating in Syria, and it is difficult to confirm reports. Meanwhile, newspapers in the region have voiced anger regarding Arab states' failure to respond to events in that nation. Latakia has witnessed numerous anti-government demonstrations in the past six months. Syria has faced increased diplomatic pressure in the past week to halt its suppression of the dissent. The US has imposed sanctions on Damascus and has stated these could be expanded, whilst appealing to other nations to follow. Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait have all withdrawn their ambassadors, whilst Turkish Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu has characterised the methods employed by the Syrian security forces as unacceptable. Mr Assad has repeated promises of political reform, whilst remaining insistent his government would continue pursuing the terrorist groups he has blamed for the unrest. Demonstrations have been targeted in Homs, Hama, Damascus, Deir al-Zour in the east, Deraa in the south and Aleppo and Idlib near Turkey's frontier. A physician in Hama informed the BBC that medical services there had been severely impacted by recent government assaults. He stated two hospitals were shut and one had been raided by troops, injuring many of the medical personnel.

text: Young people who went through pre-school education are much more likely to do well in international Pisa tests when they are teenagers, says the OECD. These are external links and will open in a new window However, the international think tank states that to maximise the advantages of early years education, places must be available for the most impoverished families. The OECD states that the UK maintains low levels of hours in pre-school education. Plans exist in England to double the quantity of free childcare to 30 hours, though only for working families. The OECD study states that significant economic and personal advantages arise from investing in early years education - and it endorses the move in England to expand access to pre-school places. Currently, the 15 hours of free childcare ranks amongst the lowest levels of provision of any OECD country, though it will increase to 30 hours in the autumn, for families with a working parent. Andreas Schleicher, the OECD's education director, states that he comprehends the argument for concentrating pre-school places on working families - enabling parents to afford going out to work. However, he states that such an approach may diminish the educational advantages of early years support, which proves greatest for those from the most disadvantaged families. The OECD study demonstrates that by international standards the UK maintains high proportions of children in workless families, particularly in lone-parent families. These may be excluded if access to early years places concentrates on working families. Mr Schleicher emphasised the significance of pre-school education in providing children a strong start. This extended beyond learning, with the study emphasising links between access to early years education and reduced levels of obesity. However, the report cautioned that spending on this sector might be patchy and that staff might be less well-paid than in the school system. Pre-school staff in the UK have witnessed their pay decline in real terms since 2010, states the OECD survey. Searching for good quality pre-school places might also prove much more difficult for parents, compared with the quantity of information available about schools. Mr Schleicher stated the variety of early years places might be very fragmented and hard to navigate. Neil Leitch, chief executive of the Pre-school Learning Alliance, stated: We have long contended that, given current limited resources, the government should concentrate its spending on where it is required most. As such, we remain at a loss as to why there has been no attempt to reconsider the current eligibility criteria for the 30-hour offer. text: A Spanish MP has provoked criticism by taking her baby into parliament and breastfeeding him during its first session since an inconclusive general election last month. These are external links and will open in a new window All attention was focused on Carolina Bescansa, who was standing as a candidate for speaker. Pablo Iglesias, leader of the anti-austerity Podemos party, was amongst those photographed embracing the small boy. Political leaders are still arguing over the formation of a government following the 20 December election. The conservative People's Party (PP) secured the most seats in parliament but fell short of a majority. Ms Bescansa, an MP with Podemos (We Can) which finished third in the election, had pledged to breastfeed in parliament during her campaign, according to reports. Speaking on Wednesday, she defended the right of every parent to raise their child in whatever manner they are able to or wish to, after some politicians suggested what she had done was unnecessary, Spanish news agency Efe reported. She said she had been privileged not to have been separated from her baby, Diego, since he was born. However, acting Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz, of the PP, criticised the move as lamentable, according to El Mundo. Socialist MP Carme Chacon said it was frankly unnecessary. Ms Bescansa reportedly requested photographers not to broadcast her baby's face. However, some critics accused her of attention-seeking and pointed to the existence of a nursery in the parliament building that was introduced in 2006 to help MPs manage childcare. She was unsuccessful in her attempt to become parliamentary speaker. Socialist MP Patxi Lopez won the vote to become the first ever speaker from a party that did not win most seats in an election. Ms Bescansa has previously brought her son into parliament for ceremonial events including her swearing-in as an MP. Iolanda Pineda, of the Socialists' Party of Catalonia (PSC), also brought her baby into Spain's upper house of parliament in 2012. Italian politician Licia Ronziulli was first photographed with her baby in the European parliament in September 2010 when the child was six weeks old. Since then, photographs of the MEP with her daughter have documented the little girl growing up. Last year a group of MPs in the UK called for a ban on new mothers breastfeeding their babies in the House of Commons chamber to be overturned. Spanish MPs were assembled for the first session of parliament on Wednesday but deadlock remains over the formation of a government. Mariano Rajoy's Popular Party is pushing for a coalition with the Socialists (PSOE) and the centre-right Ciudadanos (Citizens) party, which finished fourth in the election. However, the Socialists are seeking a deal with Citizens and Podemos. So far, Podemos has refused to drop a demand for a referendum on independence in Catalonia, which the two other parties reject. If the main parties fail to reach an agreement, King Felipe VI will ask a party leader to form a government and MPs will vote on his nomination. New elections might have to be held.

text: Newcastle Falcons survive a second-half fightback from Bristol at Kingston Park to earn their third win of the season. Juan Pablo Socino, Will Welch and Joel Hodgson's first-half tries had provided Newcastle with a 19-point advantage. However Bristol - who have yet to secure victory since returning to the Premiership - scored through John Fisher and Mitch Eadie to reduce the gap to five points. Falcons maintained their lead to triumph and impose a sixth defeat from six matches on Bristol, who remain at the foot of the table. Both sides concluded the contest with 14 players as Newcastle's Alex Rogers and Bristol's Gaston Cortez were each dispatched to the sin bin. The away team pressed forward late in a tense conclusion but were unable to complete an impressive fightback - though they did secure their second losing bonus point of the campaign to double their points total. Joel Hodgson and Mike Delany both failed with second-half penalties that could have provided Falcons with a greater cushion in the closing stages. However the home side's commanding first-half performance proved sufficient to secure the match, with Hodgson's polished score shortly before the interval proving crucial. Newcastle director of rugby Dean Richards: If you had asked me 15 minutes before kick-off would I accept a 19-14 victory the answer would have been yes, but I am sitting here now slightly frustrated and so is the team. We are in the top half of the Premiership with three victories and a couple of losing bonus points but we do have numerous injuries to key players and were somewhat frustrated rather than pleased. We performed so well in the first half and could have scored two or three additional tries and we could have utilised those in the second half because we eased off the accelerator. They had two opportunities and converted them both and our kicking deteriorated slightly and that was probably the fundamental cause of the difficulty. I never believed we would ever lose but we could well have squandered it away. Bristol director of rugby Andy Robinson: I believed we began reasonably well but we lost our discipline and it was somewhat of an own goal when Newcastle scored their first try and that provided them with the momentum. In the second half, we began to advance off the line, completed our tackles and gained momentum. We scored two excellent tries but unfortunately just could not maintain that momentum. That second half was encouraging in that it demonstrated we do possess the talent to succeed in the Premiership. We accomplished some positive things here today and in the opening match of the season, but we desired at least one victory from the first six matches of the season and we are frustrated we have not achieved that. Replacements: Sowrey, Rogers, Welsh, Witty, Temm, Takulua, Hodgson, Agulla. Bristol: J Williams; Edwards, Tovey, Hurrell, Lemi; Pisi, Cliff; Traynor, McMillan, Perenise, Glynn, Sorenson, Eadie, Lam (capt), Crane. Replacements: Crumpton, Bevington, Cortes, Phillips, Fisher, Williams, Jarvis, Wallace. For the latest rugby union news follow @bbcrugbyunion on Twitter.

text: On a warm Saturday afternoon in March a group of campaigners heads to the Golden Lane estate in central London. These are external links and will open in a new window Local council elections are merely days away but these volunteers are not seeking votes on behalf of councillors. The members of the campaign group We Can Win want to ensure that residents are aware of the unique way that their local authority is elected. It is an electoral system to which they object. The City of London Corporation covers the so-called Square Mile, which is London's financial centre, and is distinct from the Greater London Authority which covers the whole of the UK capital. The City has a residential population of fewer than 8,000 but around 450,000 people work there - and the City Corporation enables a proportion of those workers to vote for councillors too, taking the electorate to almost 19,000. I was under the impression, in its simplest form, democracy was about one person one vote, says campaign director Dan Firth. But in the City of London Corporation elections, businesses have almost double the votes of ordinary people and to me that feels like an injustice. We Can Win is targeting the City elections with two main aims: to oppose what it sees as votes for big business and to maximise the number of residents who turn out and vote. The City is divided into 25 wards with residents mainly concentrated in just four of them: Portsoken, Queenhithe, Aldersgate and Cripplegate, which includes Golden Lane. Each ward is represented by Common Councillors and an alderman. Elections for Common Councillors take place every four years, with the next election on 23 March, whilst aldermen are elected at least every six years as their terms expire. Some residents I spoke to were already aware of how the voting system worked, says campaigner Georgia O'Brien. But those who did not know were shocked. When I explained that workers had almost double the number of votes as residents, they just looked utterly defeated. Golden Lane resident Beverley Bytheway is active in the residents' association yet unaware that workers as well as residents get a vote. The road straddles the border with the London Borough of Islington and she thought that both councils were elected in the same way. She is not a fan of the Corporation: If they could offload the residents, they would... they are really not interested. Despite an apparent lack of awareness among some residents, the City of London Corporation is quite open about its system of elections and its website contains information on how to register to vote as a resident or as a worker. The City is a democratic institution, insisted a spokesman. All of its councillors are elected. For residents, it is one person, one vote but for businesses the number of votes depends on the number of employees. Sole traders and businesses with up to nine employees get one vote, whilst organisations with up to 50 staff can appoint one voter for every five people who work there. Organisations with more than 50 staff can appoint 10 voters and then one voter per 50 voters after that. The City's spokesman added: As the local authority we provide public services to both 7,400 residents and 450,000 City workers. Therefore to reflect the needs of the workers who come to the City each day, businesses located in the City can appoint people to vote in our local elections. The votes allocated to a business are proportional to their number of employees - the first 50 staff entitles a business to appoint 10 voters, but every additional 50 members of staff only entitle it to appoint an extra one voter, so the largest firms do not dominate the list of voters as they could do if it was a simple proportional representation of their workforce size. In its advice to firms wanting to sign up staff as voters, the Corporation says: It is important that people nominated to vote reflect the make-up of the organisation as a whole - from chief executive to entry-level employees and even regular contractors - so that the City Corporation represents the full range of the City's workforce. Voters nominated should reflect the whole diversity of an organisation's employees, including gender, ethnicity and seniority. Professional services giant Deloitte employs over 10,000 staff and has 260 voters across two wards. A spokesperson said: We value the votes we have in the City of London. The City does have an unusual electoral system due to its high number of workers and small residential population, but there are many local issues that Deloitte people care greatly about. For example, a thousand Deloitte people cycle into work every day. Their safety and the safety of all road users in our neighbourhood is important to us. The councillors provide a very valuable link between Deloitte and our neighbours - other businesses and local residents. Local government in the City of London can be traced back to medieval times. It is the oldest local authority in Britain and a contender for the oldest continuing authority in the world. Non-residential votes in other council areas were abolished in 1969 but the system continued for the City Corporation. The current electoral system dates from an act of Parliament in 2002, which extended voting rights to companies limited by guarantee and increased the business vote. Boundary changes followed, which reduced the number of councillors. The City is known for its financial institutions but bodies qualifying for a vote include shops, bars, restaurants, charities and even churches and hospital trusts. Tobacconist Mukesh Gaglani has been a registered voter in the City for 25 years. As a small business owner with two part-time employees, he gets one vote. You have a say in the progress of the City, he tells me, adding that he does not feel that big business dominates. As far as I am concerned, my vote is the same as anyone else's. You do not feel like you are in a minority. What is his response to proposals that only residents should be allowed to vote? I do not think it is appropriate. The City gets most of its revenue from commercial properties. So how does being elected by workers as well as residents affect the job of a councillor? Sophie Fernandes has served as one of four independent Common Councillors representing Coleman Street ward since 2009. I get queries about rubbish collection, I get queries about the ease with which people get to work, about infrastructure, she says, adding: The City of London is also a landlord. It owns a few buildings in my ward. I have complaints just like any other landlord has. When asked how many residents her ward has, she can think of just four, two of whom moved out temporarily as a consequence of work on London's Crossrail transport project. We try to break up the wards, depending on whether it is a business vote or a residential vote, so that we can concentrate on the needs of that particular ward, because the needs of residents and businesses are very different, she says. It is workers who have a vote, it is not businesses who have a vote, she says. She adds: I do not think every worker should have a vote because it would completely outweigh residents but in wards such as mine, it is heavily business orientated without residents, so how would you represent this ward otherwise? What does she make of the allegation of Golden Lane resident Beverley that the City Corporation would rather be rid of its residential population? That is totally untrue. The residents bring diversity to the City. To stand as a councillor you need to be a registered voter and a Freeman of the City of London. If you are voter in the City then you can get freedom without cost, so there is no barrier to standing, Ms Fernandes says. Like nearly all councillors at present, she sits as an independent and does not take a party whip. She is standing this time on a slate alongside fellow independents Michael Cassidy, Stuart Fraser and Andrew McMurtie and argues that being independent helps the City work with both a Conservative government and a Labour mayor of London. We do not want party politics, she says. I fail to see the benefit that party politics will bring when you can still argue your point of view from an independent platform. That view is being challenged by the Labour Party, which first ran candidates in 2009 and is contesting wards in 2017. Paul O'Brien, who is contesting Coleman Street for the party, claims that there is an urban myth of independents in the City. He argues that many councillors list party memberships in their declarations of interests but only Labour openly fields candidates. A resident of the City himself, Mr O'Brien nevertheless agrees with Sophie Fernandes on the need for worker representation. Clearly there are wards with no, or virtually no residents, so there needs to be a different system, he says. Both opponents and supporters of the voting system agree that the City of London is an unusual organisation with a reach stretching well beyond the Square Mile. It owns and maintains housing estates and open spaces across Greater London and beyond, including Hampstead Heath and Epping Forest, and provides money to London boroughs though its City Bridge Trust. text: All it takes to officially run for the Republican presidential nomination is a one-page form sent to the Federal Election Commission, the US government entity in charge of overseeing campaign laws. That constitutes the straightforward element. Thus far this year, 213 prospective commanders-in-chief have accomplished precisely that. The challenging element encompasses everything that follows subsequently. Declaring one's candidacy, and rendering it official through federal documentation, secures a name on precisely zero ballots in the state-level primaries and caucuses that represent the key to securing sufficient delegates to obtain the presidential nomination at the Republican National Convention in July. Qualifying for those ballots constitutes a state-by-state endeavour, with different rules and regulations for each. It requires time and money - and considerable amounts of it. Only the most organised, professional campaigns can accomplish the task. For example there exists a $1,000 (£600) price tag attached to securing ballot access in New Hampshire - the early-voting state that has created, and destroyed, many a candidacy. That represents nothing, however, compared with South Carolina, the third state in the nominee selection process and a battleground for Republican candidates seeking to build momentum as the Southern states conduct their votes. To possess a chance at winning there, Republicans by Wednesday had to write a cheque for $40,000 (£26,500) to the state's Republican Party - half of which is transferred to the state government for administrative costs. The other $20,000 goes directly to the party's coffers. It's extortion, states Richard Winger, editor of Ballot Access News. And it may not even be lawful. In 1972 the US Supreme Court unanimously ruled that a fee of up to $8,900 to stand for a local office in the Democratic Party primary was unconstitutional. Many potential office seekers lacking both personal wealth and affluent backers are, in every practical sense, prevented from seeking the nomination of their chosen party, no matter how qualified they might be and no matter how broad or enthusiastic their popular support, Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote. The case speaks directly to fees like the one in South Carolina, states Winger. I think it's unconstitutional. If all these states started doing this, pretty soon it would be up to a million dollars. And South Carolina and New Hampshire are merely the beginning. Eight other states have primaries with filing fees, mostly in the $1,000 range. Arkansas, which conducts a primary on 1 March, charges $25,000 - payable by 9 November. Want in on the caucuses in Kansas or Kentucky? Those will cost $15,000 each. Complicating all this is the fact that filing fees must come directly from the candidates or their campaign funds - which have maximum contribution limits and strict reporting requirements - not from friends, relatives or the allegedly independent Super PAC entities that can raise unlimited amounts of money from deep-pocketed donors to support candidates. South Carolina's prohibitive amount is said to have helped persuade former Texas Governor Rick Perry to end his cash-strapped quest for the presidency in mid-September. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker paid the fee only to withdraw the following month. His campaign was reportedly more than $750,000 in debt by the time it collapsed. Despite this high bar, no one has stepped forward to challenge the fee in court - and all 15 remaining Republican candidates paid up in South Carolina. Some, like New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, former New York Governor George Pataki and that longest of long-shots, former Virginia Governor Jim Gilmore, filed within days - or even hours - of the afternoon deadline. Everyone, it seems, is content to simply sign the cheque and not rock the political boat. Democrats have their share of fees too, of course, but they are generally much lower. In South Carolina, for instance, candidates like Hillary Clinton will have to pay $2,500 to the state party, which then is responsible for covering the remaining $20,000 to the state for election administration costs out of its own funds. Money is not the only obstacle, either. Many states require candidates to gather up to 5,000 signatures from in-state registered voters - a task that demands a strong national organisation with a motivated volunteer base or the funds to pay professional signature-gatherers to pound the pavement. In 2012 Virginia ballot-seekers had to hand over petitions with at least 10,000 names - and only two, eventual winner Mitt Romney and libertarian Ron Paul, managed to qualify. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and former Senator Rick Santorum - each with earlier primary wins under their belts - failed to make the cut. For the 1 March, 2016, balloting, Virginia has reduced that signatures amount to 5,000, due by 10 December, but at least 200 of those names must come from each of the state's 11 congressional districts. Many states have similar district-by-district requirements, where the failure to gather enough signatures in even one district will keep a name off the ballot. Some states give candidates a choice. To qualify for the 1 March primary in delegate-rich Texas, for instance, presidential aspirants must either pay a $5,000 filing fee or submit the signatures of 300 registered voters in at least 15 of the state's 36 congressional districts. Florida, not surprisingly, is somewhat unusual. Candidates can write a cheque for $25,000, gather at least 3,375 volunteer-obtained signatures from across Florida or commit to attending the Sunshine Summit - a presidential forum hosted in Orlando by the state Republican Party in November. That summit could be a significant money-maker for the party, which expects to sell 2,500 tickets to the event - and is charging $200 for a two-day pass and $1,000 for premium reserve seating (all major credit cards happily accepted). Then there is first-in-the-nation Iowa, which has no petition requirements, filing fees or, for that matter, ballots. Voters can support whomever they please in the caucuses, and if enough likeminded individuals show up to do the same, the candidate will be on his or her way to winning prized delegates. But then the state's caucus system presents challenges of its own. Getting Iowans to turn out on a cold February weekday and spend an evening singing the praises of their politician can be a logistical effort that makes South Carolina's $40,000 price of admission seem like small change. text: Venezuela has donated $500,000 to US President Donald Trump's inauguration, newly released records show. These are external links and will open in a new window. Citgo Petroleum, a United States-based subsidiary of the Venezuelan state-owned oil company, is identified in documents filed with the Federal Election Commission. The disclosure emerges as the Venezuelan economy appears to be devastated by food shortages, violent crime and inflation. Three individuals were killed in demonstrations on Wednesday as tens of thousands took to the streets to demand fresh elections. Other major corporations identified in the documents include Pepsi and Walmart, which contributed $250,000 and $150,000 respectively, whilst owners of NFL teams or their companies contributed more than $5m. Casino owner and billionaire Sheldon Adelson also contributed $5m. Venezuela is in the midst of a major economic crisis, which has the oil-rich nation flirting with hyperinflation. This Wednesday, street demonstrations demanding the resignation of President Nicolas Maduro resulted in at least two people shot dead. In this chaotic context, it is perhaps less surprising that Venezuelan media did not appear to dedicate much time to covering the news that their government gave, through a state-owned oil company, a US$500,000 contribution to Donald Trump's inauguration. Nevertheless, some analysts in Venezuela are expressing anger at the news. We have been experiencing four consecutive years of recession, we have the highest inflation in the world and are facing scarcity in many basic goods. It is scandalous that Venezuela, facing such a crisis, would make those donations to the inauguration of a US president, who at least in theory, is ideologically confronted with the revolution, Jose Manuel Puente, a professor of public policy at IESA university in Caracas, tells the BBC. The payment was reportedly made through Citgo, a US subsidiary of Venezuelan state-owned oil company PDVSA. It is not the first time Citgo has been involved in politically controversial activities in the US. President Maduro's predecessor, Hugo Chavez, used the company several years ago to provide subsidised fuel to low-income citizens in several major US cities. His critics said then it was a propaganda ploy designed to annoy his ideological rivals at the White House. But now the Maduro administration would appear to be in a less confrontational mode towards Washington. The Venezuelan president has recently been quoted saying that Trump has been the target of a brutal hate campaign and added that he won't be worse than Obama. The (Bolivarian) revolution is pragmatic, Puente tells the BBC. Eighteen years after the beginning of the revolution, the US is still their main trading partner. It is business as usual.

text: Derby County climbed into the Championship play-off zone for the first time under new boss Paul Clement as they proved too good for Wolves. Chris Martin's two first-half strikes - a 20-yard curler and a powerful header - arrived either side of Benik Afobe's well-struck response for Wolves. Martin subsequently had a penalty saved by Emiliano Martinez but Bradley Johnson's gentle strike made it 3-1 at the interval. Johnny Russell struck a fourth before Adam Le Fondre made it 4-2. Le Fondre's arcing volley, from substitute Sheyi Ojo's knockdown, crept in despite home goalkeeper Scott Carson getting his fingertips to it. It compensated for the penalty appeal Wolves did not receive before the interval when his goalbound shot was blocked by former Wolves defender Jason Shackell's elbow. Added to that, the home side's second goal could have been disallowed as Martin levered himself into the air off Kortney Hause's shoulders. And Johnson knew little about the third goal, which struck his outstretched left boot after Wolves failed to clear the Russell corner which resulted from Martinez saving Martin's penalty, awarded for Danny Batth's foul on Tom Ince. Kenny Jackett's men did produce a well-worked training ground move for their first goal when Afobe lashed in James Henry's corner to cancel out Martin's early strike. Media playback is not supported on this device But the visitors were generally second best, no more so than when sustained Derby pressure resulted in Russell toe poking in from 12 yards for the Rams' fourth. Le Fondre's goal gave the scoreline a fairer reflection but few would argue that Derby deserved all three points as they extended their current run to 16 points out of a possible 18 to climb to sixth. Wolves, who had won both their previous two matches 3-0 prior to the international break, have dropped a place to 11th this weekend, now five points adrift of the play-off places. Derby head coach Paul Clement told BBC Sport: Our finest performance of the season. We've had some good first halves and some good second halves, but this time we were solid throughout and were deserved victors. Chris Martin delivered the finest performance I've seen from a Championship centre forward from the matches I've seen this season. A great finish for the first, a brave header for the second and he led the line well. It was a shame he didn't finish off the penalty for what would have been a first-half hat-trick. But he was a well-deserved man of the match. Against a good side, it was also a great response from the team to come back and score the way we did following the penalty miss. We could have gone in at half-time on a low. But to make it 3-1 was a big moment. Wolves head coach Kenny Jackett told BBC Sport: Derby were strong and take some stopping, but our defending was poor. We didn't work hard enough to put in enough blocks and cut down things at source. There were too many key moments when we didn't defend well enough. They had too many shots and far too many of them we gifted them. Their penalty was the correct decision. I also thought we should have had one for the handball, but it would be hard to get those sort of decisions here. Our goalkeeper's held his hand up for the second goal. text: A fund to raise money for the families of the five Birmingham wall collapse victims has passed £20,000. The men perished when a 15-foot wall of concrete and scrap metal collapsed upon them whilst they laboured on Thursday at Hawkeswood Metal in Nechells. The editor of the Birmingham Mail, which launched the fund, stated the response had been overwhelming. Police confirmed the site remains sealed and post-mortem examinations would occur on Monday. Donations have been pouring in from throughout the country for the men, who were Spanish nationals originally from Gambia. All the bodies were retrieved from the debris by Friday. Mr Reeves stated: No money can ever fill the void left by a loved one, particularly in a tragedy of this nature. But at least if the families are relieved from the concerns of paying for funerals, travel for family members, and all the other immediate financial worries that obstruct grieving, then it is worthwhile to raise some money to assist. The response is overwhelming, and as well as the financial support, we hope this conveys a message to the families that Birmingham cares about them and feels their pain. The men have been identified locally as Bangaly Dukureh, Ousman Jabbie, Alimamo Jammeh, Mohammed Jangana and Saibo Sillah. All are believed to be married with children. Relatives have stated they want the bodies retrieved for burial as soon as possible, in accordance with Muslim custom. A sixth man, who escaped with a fractured leg, is also a Spanish national of Gambian heritage. Detectives have stated they have a reasonable idea about what occurred. Hawkeswood Metal Recycling Ltd, which employs approximately 50 people, was established more than 40 years ago and states it handles more than 500,000 tonnes of scrap metal each year at its Nechells site. In 2012 it was fined £50,000 when a worker got his arm trapped in machinery. It also pleaded guilty at Birmingham Crown Court to a breach of health and safety law. The plant was also the scene of a major fire in February this year, as 700 tonnes of scrap metal went up in flames.
