text: Women who wore pantsuits in support of Hillary Clinton on US election day are now being urged to donate them to poor and homeless women. The invitation-only Facebook group Pantsuit Nation, which boasts 3.7 million subscribers, is supporting the Pantsuit Drive initiated by Meena Harris. The software company policy manager stated she wished to help address the pay gap confronting women of colour. Libby Chamberlain, founder of Pantsuit Nation, is encouraging members to contribute. The page was named after Mrs Clinton's signature trouser suits, which she was observed wearing throughout her campaign. In an article for feminist newsletter Lenny Letter, Ms Harris stated that the concept was conceived as she collected her dry cleaning near her San Francisco residence. The former Facebook employee, who studied at Stanford and Harvard, stated she contemplated what an obvious privilege it is to even own a pantsuit, let alone to purchase a new one for a special occasion. She continued: In 2016, too many women still struggle to support their families. They are disproportionately minimum-wage workers who balance multiple jobs to make ends meet, and they still do not earn equal pay. The pay gap for women of colour is not just a gap, it is a canyon. Pantsuit Nation: The secret Clinton Facebook group She posted a photograph of herself, alongside her mother and young baby, wearing a blue pantsuit in tribute to the Democratic candidate's signature trouser suits on polling day. Ms Chamberlain cited a Pantsuit Nation member, now a Harvard Kennedy School graduate and communications and strategy consultant, who had been homeless at the age of 20. Tanene Allison stated she had been offered a job interview but could not afford the bus fare or any smart clothing. Job interviews can be difficult enough, but they are outright terrifying when you fear you will walk in looking like you live in a homeless shelter, she was cited as saying. A woman at the youth shelter where she was staying assisted her in assembling an outfit from donated clothing, and she ultimately secured the job. Last Friday, the American media conglomerate announced it would propose £10.75 per share for the 61% stake in Sky that it does not currently possess. The independent directors of both corporations have achieved a preliminary agreement regarding this valuation. However, Richard Marwood from Royal London Asset Management has requested additional information. Those independent directors have received counsel, and we believe they ought to share that with shareholders, to permit the remainder of us to determine whether £10.75 represents the correct valuation, so we are all operating from identical information, he stated to BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Since it forms part of the FTSE 100, the Sky shares that 21st Century Fox seeks to acquire are held by numerous City investment houses. The shares were trading at 982p on Wednesday amidst increasing demands for any offer to be referred by the government to the media regulator, Ofcom. Royal London ranks merely as the 68th largest shareholder in Sky with holdings of just 2.4 million shares, representing 0.14% of the total. Nevertheless, Royal London's remarks contribute to a mounting protest from certain shareholders that Sky's directors ought to clarify their reasoning and maintain their position for a superior price. Standard Life and Jupiter Asset Management have previously challenged the alleged independence of the Sky board, noting that Rupert Murdoch's son James serves as both Sky's chairman and Fox's chief executive. Chase Carey, a former Fox Television chief executive and co-chief operating officer of Rupert Murdoch's newspaper company, News Corporation, also sits on the Sky board. Another non-executive director at Sky, John Nallen, simultaneously serves as the chief financial officer of 21st Century Fox. Mr Marwood from Royal London stated there were several question marks regarding Sky's corporate governance. We held concerns when he [James Murdoch] was appointed as Sky's chairman, precisely for this circumstance, he stated. We believed if there were ever to be an offer, there would be a conflict, and our concerns have been confirmed with what has occurred. Mr Marwood continued: To a certain degree, Sky have attempted to ease investors' concerns by having these independent directors provide opinions on the offer. However, I believe greater transparency to provide us with confidence that genuine independence exists would be most beneficial.

text: Hungary has passed a law that critics say could undermine the independence of its central bank. The governing Fidesz party, which holds a two-thirds majority, has endorsed the constitutional amendment in parliament's final session this year. Credit rating agency Standard & Poor's relegated Hungary's debt to junk status last week, partially owing to the proposed constitutional modifications. EU and IMF representatives have curtailed assistance negotiations with Hungary regarding the legislation. Hungary had been pursuing a standby credit facility of 15-20bn euros ($19.5bn, £12.6bn) should it encounter difficulties issuing fresh debt. However, the International Monetary Fund and the European Commission have both expressed reservations about assistance due to the legislation. On Thursday, Hungary withdrew part of a scheduled bond sale when investors required a higher interest rate on the debt the nation intended to issue. Hungary's central bank chief, Andras Simor, has stated the bill constitutes a seizure of the central bank. The legislation has also faced criticism from the European Central Bank, which said it raised concern as to whether [it] could be used to influence the decision-making process, to the detriment of central bank independence. International pressure The administration seeks to maintain low interest rates to stimulate growth - however last week, Hungary's central bank raised rates for the second consecutive month, to 7% from 6.5%. Consumer price inflation in Hungary is presently at 4.25%, considerably above the official 3% target. Certain amendments have been implemented since the original draft was presented before the Christmas recess, but concerns persist that the law's essence remains unchanged, stated the BBC's Eastern Europe correspondent Nick Thorpe. The bank's reform would establish deputy governors and permit the government greater potential control over crucial monetary policy elements, including interest rate levels. Hungary received a 20bn-euro standby loan from the IMF in 2008 to prevent defaulting on its obligations. However, the newly-elected Prime Minister Viktor Orban chose not to renew the standby arrangement last year. Standard & Poor's has referenced increased risks to the nation's debt repayment capacity due to the deteriorating domestic and international economic environment. In our assessment, the predictability of Hungary's policy framework continues to diminish, damaging Hungary's medium-term growth prospects, S&P stated. Last month, fellow ratings agency Moody's similarly downgraded Hungary to junk status, citing the economy's substantial debt levels and poor growth prospects.

text: The OFT has made a move to try to help people access discounts when booking online, after closing an investigation into competition practice between three companies. The investigation examined online agents Booking.com, Expedia and hotel group InterContinental Hotels (IHG). The inquiry initially suspected these arrangements violated competition law by restricting price competition. However, it has now permitted such arrangements subject to specific conditions. The OFT has permitted online agents to reduce hotel room prices, encouraging more competitive pricing. Previously, these websites could not provide discounts. Under these conditions, the OFT stated consumers must initially register for a membership programme with a hotel, either agent, or another online agent. Customers must have also previously purchased one room at the standard rate with the online agent or hotel, to qualify for subsequent discounts, stated the OFT. Booking.com and Expedia represent two of Britain's largest online travel agents. The OFT commenced its investigation in 2010 to examine allegations that agreements and coordinated practices might result in fixed or minimum resale prices. Whether this development will increase competition and reduce prices remains subject to considerable debate. Gaucho Rasmussen, enforcement director at the OFT, stated he had examined the conditions very, very carefully. He stated: We conducted consumer research and a substantial number of people would compare prices and utilise smaller websites and new entrants. Mr Rasmussen said the OFT had undertaken two consultations and the decision represented the optimal outcome. He stated that as the market continued evolving, smaller websites could innovate and discover methods to maintain their advantage. Dorian Harris, founder of discount booking website Skoosh, said he did not believe the development would liberalise the market and reduce prices. He stated: I am bewildered by the outcome. Smaller companies, including Skoosh, could not afford to modify their marketing strategy and hotel contracts to meet the OFT's conditions, therefore would struggle to provide discounts, he stated. Mr Harris stated the conditions would deter new consumers from utilising smaller, unfamiliar websites rather than Booking.com or Expedia: The OFT has not comprehended the market. It represents a significant failure in assessment. He stated consumers would not wish to purchase a full-rate room, to qualify for discounted rooms, from a new website such as Skoosh. They would instead prefer to obtain the discount immediately from larger websites, such as Expedia, where customers would most likely have already purchased a premium-rate hotel room from, to qualify. He stated the conditions would strengthen Booking.com or Expedia's dominance, adding the OFT had catered to the interests of the two major companies. The OFT's Mr Rasmussen acknowledged there existed a possibility the arrangement could lead to further monopoly, but he stated the OFT would be monitoring developments in the market.

text: Supporters and opponents of Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych are to hold rival protests in Kiev, amid fears of possible clashes. Campaigners and opposition parties hope hundreds of thousands of individuals will participate in a Dignity Day demonstration in central Independence Square. Mr Yanukovych's supporters will assemble in the adjacent Mariinskyi Park. Demonstrations commenced last month following the president's eleventh-hour decision to withdraw from a significant agreement with the EU. Mr Yanukovych has stated he fears the association and trade pact will endanger numerous enterprises reliant on commerce with Russia. The president - who states he ultimately intends to sign the agreement - has also acknowledged being under substantial pressure from Moscow, which desires Kiev to join a Russian-led customs union alternatively. Several thousand pro-EU demonstrators remained overnight in Independence Square before their demonstration, which is anticipated to commence at 12:00 local time (10:00 GMT) on Sunday. Barriers around the perimeter of the principal protest camp in the centre of the capital have been reinforced following an attempt by special police to remove them earlier this week. Opposition leaders have urged demonstrators to remain alert, fearing provocateurs might trigger confrontations between rival protesters. The opposition has also alleged the authorities of transporting people into Kiev for the pro-government demonstration and supplying them with money and food. The authorities officially refute this, but numerous participants in the demonstration have stated they were compelled to participate. The two opposing factions held demonstrations near each other on Saturday. There were no reports of any confrontations. In a separate development, Mr Yanukovych suspended his deputy security chief and Kiev's mayor regarding the police violence against pro-EU protesters on 30 November. Prosecutors are investigating Volodymyr Syvkovych and Olexander Popov - alongside two other senior officials - on suspicion of abuse of office in the crackdown. This has galvanised the pro-EU demonstrators, who are demanding that all those involved in the suppression be dismissed and punished. They also want the government to resign. Whilst pro-EU protests have seized the capital and other cities in western and central Ukraine, President Yanukovych maintains support in the east and south. Nevertheless, that backing may be diminishing, correspondents state, and there have already been pro-EU demonstrations in the south-east. Demonstrators state Mr Yanukovych's reversal on the EU agreement triggered the mass demonstration, but they now want the complete reload of what they describe as a corrupt system of governance. They believe signing the EU agreement would eliminate corruption and make Ukraine's economy more open and transparent, citing as an example Ukraine's neighbours to the west who are now EU members. Nevertheless, the government and its supporters fear that economic liberalisation would damage the country's economy, particularly the industrial south-east which depends on trade with Russia. Moscow has already imposed economic pressure on Ukraine, with customs delays and a prohibition on Ukrainian chocolates, and there are concerns it could escalate such measures if Kiev moved closer to Brussels.

Mr Yanukovych’s supporters will gather in the nearby Mariinsky Park. The protests began last month after the president’s last-minute withdrawal from an important agreement with the European Union. The President said that he was worried that the association and trade agreement would undermine many of the companies dependent on Russian trade. Although the president has announced that he will sign the agreement in the end, he admits that he is under enormous pressure from Moscow, which wants Kiev to join the Russian-led customs union instead. Many pro-European protesters spent the night on Independence Square ahead of the rally, which is expected to begin at noon local time (12:00 UTC). The barricades that had been set up around the main camp in the center of the capital were reinforced, after special police officers had attempted to remove them earlier in the week. Opposition leaders called on their followers to remain vigilant, fearing that provocateurs might provoke a clash between the two rival protest camps. The opposition also accuses the government of transporting people to the rally in favor of the government and of supplying them with money and food. The two parties held demonstrations near each other on Saturday. There is no report of a clash, but many participants in the demonstration testify that they were forced to take part. - And another time, Yanukovych suspended his security minister and the mayor of Kiev for the November 30 police crackdown on the Europeans, and this awoke the protesters who demanded that everyone who participated in the crackdown should be dismissed and punished. The prosecutor's office is already investigating Volodymyr Syvkovich and Alexei Popov, together with two other high officials, for alleged official abuse in the crackdown. But correspondents are saying that support for the president is also weakening in the southeast and that there are also European rallies there. Pro-European demonstrations have taken over the capital and other cities in western and central Ukraine, but President Yanukovych still has support in the east and south, but this support is also ebbing, say the correspondents, and there are already European rallies in the southeast. The government also has to go. Meanwhile, the government and its supporters are afraid that economic liberalization will hurt the economy, especially industry in the south-east that depends on trade with Russia. The protesters say that the refusal of Yanukovych to sign the association agreement with the EU sparked the protests, but now they want the whole system of corrupt power to be overthrown. They believe that signing the agreement would eliminate corruption and open up the economy, citing the example of Ukraine’s western neighbors, who are now members of the European Union. Ukraine is already experiencing an economic squeeze on account of an increase in customs duties and a ban on chocolates, and Moscow is expected to increase these measures if Kiev moves closer to Brussels.

text: Swiss pilot Andre Borschberg has begun his bid to cross the Pacific, from China to Hawaii, in the zero-fuel Solar Impulse aeroplane. The experimental aircraft, which possesses a wingspan larger than a jumbo jet but weighs little more than a substantial car, departed Nanjing at 02:39 (18:39 GMT). It is expected to require Mr Borschberg five to six days of continuous flight to reach his central Pacific destination. He will attempt to remain awake for much of that period, taking only brief catnaps. His progress will be monitored throughout the journey from a control room in Monaco. Meteorologists and flight strategists will continuously update him on the optimal route to follow. The journey represents the seventh leg in the single-seat, propeller-driven aircraft's quest to circumnavigate the globe using solely the energy of the Sun. The project made steady progress after commencing from Abu Dhabi in March, but was delayed for more than a month on China's eastern coast awaiting the correct weather conditions over the ocean. Solar Impulse requires not only favourable winds to help propel it forward, but also clear skies to enable its 17,000 wing-mounted photovoltaic cells to achieve peak performance. These cells must have the vehicle's lithium-ion batteries fully charged at dusk to sustain flying through to dawn the following day. Mr Borschberg is a highly experienced pilot, and as a trained engineer is completely familiar with the aircraft's systems. Nevertheless, he is in no doubt how challenging the mission will be. It's more in the end about myself; it's going to be an inner-voyage, he told the BBC before departure. It's going to be a discovery about how I feel and how I sustain myself during these five or six days in the air. And Bertrand Piccard - who has flown Solar Impulse on other stages of the voyage - told the BBC: There's one pilot at a time, so the pilot needs to do everything on his own. And it's a very large aeroplane, big wingspans, sensitive to turbulence, flying quite slow. So sometimes it's difficult to handle when the air moves. But we have an auto-pilot, we have toilets on board, we have food for days, water reserves and everything, and we are well trained. The distance to Kalaeloa airport on Hawaii's O'ahu island is more than 8,000km (5,000 miles). If, early in the flight, the weather deteriorates or he encounters a major technical problem, Mr Borschberg can always choose to turn around and head back to China or Japan. But there will come a point where that option is denied to him, and Mr Borschberg and his support team have had to prepare for the possibility of ditching in the Pacific if something goes seriously wrong. The pilot himself would not go down with the aircraft because of the risk of electrocution once in the water. Instead, he would bail out with a dinghy and wait for a ship to come and collect him. If he succeeds in reaching Kalaeloa airport, he will set several aviation records - not least the longest-duration journey for a single-seater aircraft. The purpose of the Solar Impulse project is not really to showcase a particular kind of future for aviation, but rather to demonstrate the potential of clean technologies more generally. text: There is no obvious link between tough laws and levels of illegal drug use, a government report has found. Liberal Democrat Home Office minister Norman Baker stated the report, which compared the UK with other nations, should conclude mindless rhetoric regarding drugs policy. He accused the Conservatives of suppressing the findings for several months. Prime Minister David Cameron stated the research did not provide specific conclusions and declared he did not believe in decriminalising drugs. Drugs policy was discussed in the House of Commons earlier, with Green MP Caroline Lucas pressing the government to review failing drugs legislation. Under existing laws, offenders may be imprisoned for up to seven years for possessing Class A drugs, and may be imprisoned for life for producing or supplying drugs. The Home Office report compared the UK's approach to drug misuse with that of 13 other nations. Nine have authorised drug consumption rooms, including Canada, Denmark and Switzerland. Eight are testing the treatment of addicts with pure heroin rather than methadone, including Switzerland, the Netherlands and the UK. Four have special drug courts, where people pleading guilty to drug offences may opt for treatment rather than prison, including the US. One has established dissuasion commissions - Portugal. After examining a range of approaches, from zero-tolerance to decriminalisation, it concluded drug use was influenced by factors more complex and nuanced than legislation and enforcement alone. However, it found there had been a considerable improvement in the health of drug users in Portugal since the country made drug possession a health issue rather than a criminal one in 2001. The Home Office stated these outcomes could not be attributed to decriminalisation alone. However, Mr Baker believes treating drug use as a health matter would be more effective, rather than presuming locking people up is the answer. Alex, a recovering heroin and crack addict from London stated: The majority of my family either suffer from addiction or have died as a consequence of it. I have buried two friends this year. Addiction is a progressive illness. I started smoking cannabis when I was 18 or 19 at university. I was abstinent in the army, but used alcohol in cross-addiction for approximately six years. I served in Iraq and was blown up in Basra. Post-Iraq, I worked in contract security and would use when I returned to the UK. I'm 38. I got clean at 30 and attend 12-step fellowship meetings nearly every day. I don't believe for one moment that the current laws deter any addict from using, to assume they do makes the assumption that addicts have control and choice. The views of the Home Office are out of touch and most probably based in ignorance of what addiction is. No-one I know chose to become an addict. The fact the Home Office is responsible for drug policy, including treatment, is alarming and probably why the UK is blighted with addiction. Lib Dem leader Nick Clegg accused the Conservatives of a totally misplaced, outdated, backward-looking view. Whilst Mr Baker stated: We've had what I would call mindless rhetoric over the last 40 years which has tended to say there is only one solution and anyone who offers any alternative must by definition be 'soft on drugs'. He stated the Conservatives had suppressed publication of the report because of the inconvenient truths it contained. However, Tory MP Michael Ellis, a member of the Home Affairs Committee, stated the Lib Dems had hijacked it for political gain. Their frankly pro-drugs policy is dangerous and irresponsible, he added. Mr Cameron stated: Under this government drug use is falling and I think that's because we have followed an evidence-based approach. We have been focusing on education and prevention and treatment - that is the right approach to take. He stated the report was interesting, but added: It doesn't draw specific conclusions. I don't think anyone can read that report and say it definitely justifies this approach or that approach. Danny Shaw, BBC home affairs correspondent, reported: The divisions within the coalition could not be more sharply exposed. The official Home Office position is that its drug strategy is working. Norman Baker, the Liberal Democrat minister with responsibility for drugs, states 'radical' change is needed. Mr Baker's claims have been fuelled by his department's own report, which finds no link between how tough a country is on drugs and how many people use them. It's an important finding, but the study also makes clear that drug policy is highly complex - approaches which may work abroad can't necessarily be implanted into the UK. The report stated it would be inappropriate to compare the success of drug policies in different countries because data collection and many other factors differ between each one. However, it stated some observations can be made and it was not clear decriminalisation has an impact on levels of drug use. Looking across different countries, there is no apparent correlation between the 'toughness' of a country's approach and the prevalence of adult drug use, it stated. Nick Barton, of charity Action on Addiction, stated: Today's report once again highlights the need for addiction to be treated as a health condition, rather than a criminal justice one. He stated jailing drug users was rarely a solution. Danny Kushlick, the founder of the group Transform, which has been campaigning for the legal regulation of drugs in the UK for almost 20 years, stated the report was an important step. For the first time in over 40 years the Home Office has admitted that enforcing tough drug laws doesn't necessarily reduce levels of drug use, he stated. Matthew Price, Europe correspondent, BBC News, reported: Back in the 1990s Portugal was struggling with a heroin epidemic of almost epic proportions. One person in every 100 was a heroin addict. Not everyone agreed with the approach that was adopted to try and end the problem. In fact, many on the right wing of politics were appalled when prosecutions for people using drugs were ended. They didn't like the idea that addiction would be treated as a health issue, rather than a criminal one, that addicts would be given treatment and healthcare to help them overcome their addiction. Those voices have been silenced now. Fifteen years later, and the number of people hooked on heroin has been halved, and there have been good results in terms of Aids infection, hepatitis infection and the like. Back in the 1990s 'we feared that Portugal could turn into a paradise for drug users', states Dr Jaoa Goulao, Portugal's national co-ordinator on drugs and drug addiction. Thanks to the policy, that didn't happen, he states. A separate Home Office report has called for a blanket ban on all brain-altering drugs in a bid to tackle legal highs. Currently, when a legal high is made illegal, manufacturers are avoiding the law by tweaking the chemical compound and creating a new substance. The government will consider legislation introduced in Ireland four years ago that bans the sale of all psychoactive substances but exempts some, such as alcohol and tobacco.

text: Vital health services in England including stop smoking, obesity and sexual health clinics are at risk, experts are warning. Earlier this year the Chancellor revealed proposals to reduce the £2.8bn public health budget by £200m from January. The fund is managed by councils so is not encompassed by the government's pledge to safeguard the health service. However, doctors, nurses and other senior health officials state the money is essential to easing pressure on the broader NHS. A total of 11 organisations, including the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Royal College of Nursing, NHS Confederation and Faculty of Public Health, have added their names to a letter to George Osborne requesting him to reconsider the proposals. The letter cautioned that plundering the funds would simply generate greater ill-health and inequality in the population. It also noted that the case presented by NHS England chief executive Simon Stevens for additional money ahead of the election - he requested an extra £8bn annually in exchange for £22bn of efficiency savings by 2020 - included achieving gains from improvements in people's health. It stated: We urge you to consider very seriously the position we have outlined, to reverse these cuts in your forthcoming spending review and give a clear commitment that no further cuts will be made to public health budgets in future years. The Chancellor is expected to outline his spending plans for this Parliament in November. Prof John Ashton, of the Faculty of Public of Health, stated: The legacy of a decision to cut the public health grant will be major further burdens on the health service within the foreseeable future. Preventable ill health, heart disease, sexual health problems, unplanned pregnancies - these are the sort of things which are being affected by this irrational cut to funding. The cost of being unhealthy Read more from Nick Follow Nick on Twitter Rob Webster, chief executive of the NHS Confederation, concurred, stating: There is an unprecedented consensus that we can only address the problems facing the NHS if we invest in the future of our nation's health by helping people to stay well. Open any report from any director of public health in any part of the country and you can see health inequalities and poor health putting pressure on NHS services and blighting people's lives. We need the upcoming spending review to protect public health budgets. text: The RMT union is staging a day of protests in support of safer Scottish railways. The railway union is urging the Scottish government to establish an immediate schedule for Abellio to be deprived of its ScotRail franchise. It has stated that enhancing Scotland's railway safety can only be achieved through a publicly-owned service. ScotRail stated it had invested hundreds of millions of pounds in new trains and enhanced technology. Demonstrations are taking place at railway stations throughout the nation. The RMT alleges that Dutch company Abellio is extracting a £1m-a-month profit which Scotland's railways urgently require. A Scottish government spokesperson stated: Any suggestion excessive profits are extracted is simply a fallacy. Abellio received the ScotRail franchise in 2015 for 10 years but could be deprived of the contract after five years if punctuality drops below 84.3%. ScotRail stated the union's remarks bore no examination. It acknowledged that performance had declined, but maintained it remained around 90%. text: In just a few years, Wonga has become one of the country's biggest, and certainly fastest growing, money lenders. Since its launch in autumn 2007, it has provided four million small, short-term loans, totalling more than one billion pounds overall. The company has drawn considerable criticism, with suggestions it is scarcely better than a digital loan shark, preying upon the impoverished and vulnerable. In January the company was embroiled in controversy regarding advertisements encouraging students with employment to secure loans for purchases such as overseas holidays. In March supporters of several football clubs demanded the removal of the firm's advertisements from their clubs' websites. This week it garnered further attention by introducing a lending service targeted at businesses experiencing cash shortages. Errol Damelin, Wonga's founder, remains remarkably undisturbed by his critics. At a journalists' briefing this week, he appeared cheerful and optimistic about his business prospects, as well as the legitimacy of short-term money lending. According to him, Wonga represents the iTunes equivalent for the financial sector. Wonga is a platform for the future of financial services; the digital revolution has not yet commenced in financial services, he stated. Comparing his firm to companies such as Google, Amazon, PayPal and Netflix, he contended that utilising technology and customer data would prove crucial to success. Wonga is embarking on a multi-year and multi-decade mission to construct the future of financial services, employing data and technology to make objective and impartial decisions, Mr Damelin declared. Individuals borrow money from Wonga by submitting applications on its website. This provides a rapid decision and subsequently transfers funds into a bank account within 15 minutes. The company employs over 100 personnel solely to develop its technology and ensure the site functions correctly. Its principal feature combines information about prospective customers in an extensive in-house credit scoring operation. Errol Damelin stated his computers utilise artificial intelligence software to gather and process up to 8,000 different pieces of applicant information to determine loan eligibility. We have constructed the world's first completely straight-through processing system for credit, so when someone approaches Wonga as an individual or business owner and requests a cash advance, the entire process is fully automated, he explained. Therefore, no more donning a suit and tie and pleading with a bank manager for a loan or increased overdraft, at least for short-term cashflow difficulties. Wonga's technology excludes applicants deemed excessively risky, with approximately 66% currently rejected for lacking creditworthiness. For example, you must possess a regular income, bank account, functioning debit card, mobile telephone and satisfactory credit history. This filtering results in only approximately 7% of Wonga borrowers failing to repay thus far. This represents a lower default level than the 10% bad debt rate on credit card lending, which has caused banks to write off billions of pounds in recent years. The credit scoring process, however, proves more sophisticated than merely posing several simple questions. The firm's technology enables it to monitor how customers utilise the website itself, as this provides valuable insights. For instance, potential borrowers employ online sliders on computer screens to determine borrowing amounts and duration. The company has discovered that individuals who immediately push the slider to the maximum available amount, currently £400 for 30 days for first-time personal loan applicants, are more prone to default than others. The excellent aspect is that our decisions remain consistently objective; we are not subject to the same imperfections that traditional lenders possess, where different bank managers maintain different preferences and often prejudices which influence how people obtain credit access, Damelin contended. What regarding the cost? Wonga makes no attempt to disguise the fact that its APR, a standard interest cost measure, reaches a frankly astonishing 4,214% annually. This is clearly displayed on the front page. Borrowers are informed precisely how much they must repay, and when. However, Errol Damelin stated that for his target market, price is not the concern, nor should it be. Speed, convenience and transparency constitute what he is selling - alongside cash. We have dared to pose difficult questions, such as how we can make loans instantaneous, how we can provide money to people 24 hours daily, seven days weekly, how we can be completely transparent? he said. Therefore what we have created is a solution centred on speed and convenience, and assisting people by dealing with them when they wish to engage with us. Wonga dismisses criticisms of its business by highlighting that its users appear extremely satisfied. Using a customer satisfaction measure called the net-promoter score, it claims to achieve a score exceeding 90%. Essentially, most of its customers would gladly recommend its services to their friends and family. Conversely, most banks possess negative scores, and even highly-regarded banks such as First Direct score below 50%. Nevertheless, the regulated money lending industry maintains a poor reputation and faces renewed examination. The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) announced in February that it would re-examine the lending practices of numerous firms offering payday loans. Two years previously it concluded that they and other high-cost credit businesses - such as home-credit lenders and pawn brokers - should not have their interest rates capped. Now it is again concerned about poor selling practices, such as targeting loans at people who cannot afford them, and allowing their debts to roll over and increase. Wonga maintains it has no connection with the more disreputable end of the expanding payday lending business. For Errol Damelin, the objective now is to expand his business by lending to small companies suddenly experiencing cash shortages. Financial services represents a challenging environment for innovation, so we are responding where we can provide superior service, he states. Businesses have been demanding a solution that is accessible 24 hours daily, seven days weekly, to resolve relatively small, relatively short-term cashflow problems.

text: A senior Labour MP has called for its leadership contest to be paused over fears it has been infiltrated by supporters of other parties. Barry Sheerman stated that those registering to participate included members of the Socialist Workers Party, the Green Party, the Conservatives and UKIP. Labour dismisses allegations of hard left and Conservative supporters enrolling to support left-wing candidate Jeremy Corbyn. A Labour spokeswoman dismissed calls to halt the leadership contest. She stated there was a very robust system in place to prevent fraudulent and malicious applications and additional checks were being conducted to ensure the rules were followed. An exclusion list is being compiled of those who have stood against Labour previously or had assisted others to oppose the party. The BBC understands that up to 1,000 applications have been rejected. One of Mr Corbyn's supporters called Mr Sheerman's suggestion ridiculous. Backbench MP Diane Abbott said it was coming from people who believe their side will lose. She added: This election is being conducted under rules that were agreed by the entire party last year. Under the new rules, introduced by former leader Ed Miliband, people can register as supporters for £3 and participate in the vote. They are asked to confirm they support the aims and values of the Labour Party. The popularity of Mr Corbyn's campaign has prompted warnings from the other candidates, Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper and Liz Kendall, about the party shifting to the left. Mr Sheerman's comments follow similar views from two backbench MPs, Graham Stringer and John Mann, who called for the leadership contest to be suspended. The Huddersfield MP and former select committee chairman, first elected in 1979, told the BBC there were large numbers of people joining Labour to vote for the new leader and some of their motives were malign. Labour MPs were dumbfounded when they discovered how the contest was to be conducted and the process was now in real trouble, he said. At-a-glance profiles of the four contenders Labour's acting leader Harriet Harman has emailed the party's MPs with a list of new members in their constituencies asking them to identify any suspicious names. Mr Sheerman said although he might be able to identify some usual suspects, many others would not be detected. He denied his concerns were in any way motivated by his support for Liz Kendall, saying he had fought against entryism previously and believed the current process was flawed. Labour says the verification process is ongoing, and that ballot papers have not yet been distributed. Labour recently rejected an application from Conservative MP Tim Loughton, who said he attempted to become a registered supporter to highlight flaws in the system. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's the World at One, Ms Kendall said it was great that more people were registering with Labour and said she had not seen anything that concerned her. The important thing is that the checks are put in place, she added. The Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition, which stood in 135 constituencies in May's general election and includes the Socialist Workers Party, said reports of infiltration were due to Blairite manoeuvres against the Corbyn campaign. It said one of its members, former councillor Chris Flood, had been wrongly named in a report in the Times as having registered. Labour's former communications director, Alastair Campbell, said the party could be finished if Mr Corbyn wins. On his blog, he warned of a car crash scenario and urged supporters to back anyone but Corbyn, warning it would not be easy to replace him if he won and Labour was struggling in the polls.

text: Chelsea moved six points clear at the top of the Premier League as Cesc Fabregas' first-half goal beat a stubborn Sunderland at the Stadium of Light. Fabregas guided the ball into the far corner from the edge of the penalty area as the Blues secured a tenth successive league triumph. Sunderland goalkeeper Jordan Pickford made saves from former Black Cat Marcos Alonso and Willian to prevent Chelsea from securing victory by a greater margin. The home side, who had organised themselves to attempt to neutralise their opponents' attacking threat, created few opportunities although they might have claimed a point in stoppage time but Thibaut Courtois brilliantly thwarted Patrick van Aanholt. It proved a hard-earned and crucial victory for Chelsea following Arsenal's setback against Everton on Tuesday and ensures Antonio Conte's team will lead the table at Christmas. A crucial factor in Chelsea's sequence of recent triumphs has been stability with Conte having selected an unchanged team in eight of the nine matches before the journey to Sunderland. Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp had recently indicated that Chelsea's excellent form might stumble when either Eden Hazard or Diego Costa sustained an injury, and Wednesday's match offered a chance to discover whether that would prove accurate. Hazard did not make the trip after sustaining a knock in Chelsea's 1-0 triumph over West Brom at the weekend, so he was substituted by Willian. Conte also seized the chance to rest Nemanja Matic as Fabregas earned his first start since 3 December. At first, Chelsea seemed to lack Hazard's inventiveness as they found it difficult to discover a method to penetrate a congested Sunderland defence, but Fabregas demonstrated the Blues' squad depth. As Sunderland's seven-man defence thwarted the visitors, Fabregas somehow succeeded in locating the space to thread a shot into the far corner and eventually secure Chelsea's victory. text: On Saturday, Scotland's Paul Craig will complete a remarkable journey from the Hearts youth team to the Ultimate Fighting Championship. The Craigneuk-based mixed martial arts competitor will face Brazilian Luis Henrique Da Silva at the 18,000-capacity Golden 1 Center in Sacramento, becoming only the fourth Scotsman to advance to the UFC. The 29-year-old has secured a four-bout contract with what he terms the Champions League of MMA, a considerable distance from his time at Tynecastle. It represents a platform he had not even contemplated until he discovered he was reducing adversaries to tears. The reality was I lacked sufficient ability, Craig stated regarding his efforts to establish a football career. I recognised that myself so I moved into the position of coaching football. I was adequate, it was pleasant, but I genuinely missed the competitive element, I missed having some form of competition. I began experimenting with martial arts and discovered that I excelled at it. It was never a matter of 'I shall be in the UFC one day'. I was travelling up and down the entire length of Britain competing in various tournaments concerning jiu-jitsu. My trainer told me 'there's an opportunity, do you want it?' and it was at a show in Sunderland. I distinctly recall the man I fought was Gary Sivills, and he was the leading competitor in that region. He possessed a truly excellent record, he subsequently wished to compete for a British championship, and he was using me as some cannon fodder, a stepping stone. He was anticipated simply to walk through me. I had no pressure whatsoever, I was entering as underdog. I brought four or five companions down with me, and I defeated him in approximately one minute and 37 seconds. I went to speak to him afterwards and he was weeping profusely and I could not understand why. It was not until I subsequently defeated a man called Karl Moore as a professional in my initial bout in BAMMA (British Association of Mixed Martial Arts). The UFC is the summit, everyone wishes to compete there, Craig informed BBC Scotland. It is going to be a good, challenging opponent and I desired that. As you can imagine, me as an MMA competitor entering a boxing gymnasium, I am always going in as an underdog, but I am maintaining my position. I am sparring with the finest professional men in Scotland. It is advancing me further because the stand up was where I had the weaknesses and I do believe the stand up is where I am strong now, the strongest aspect of my game. I believe I can knock him out in the opening round. If not the opening round, definitely I am going to put him down in the second round and it is going to be finished. I am always regarded as the submission competitor, but this is the occasion I get to demonstrate my stand up, and because he is a stand up man it is going to be a good contest.

text: The UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, says he is appalled and shocked that rebels in Aleppo are targeting civilians in the city. The relentless and indiscriminate rocket assaults had claimed dozens of civilian lives in western Aleppo during the previous 48 hours, Mr de Mistura stated. Such assaults could constitute war crimes, he declared. On Friday, insurgents launched an offensive designed to break the government blockade of east Aleppo. Approximately 275,000 residents have been under siege in the city's eastern sector for months. Russian and Syrian government aircraft commenced bombing Aleppo in September. Over 2,700 individuals are reported to have been killed and wounded since that time. Russia halted its aerial campaign on 18 October to permit evacuations of ill and injured individuals but few have responded to the call to depart. On Sunday, state media in Syria reported that insurgents had employed chemical weapons against government-controlled areas of Aleppo. A representative for one insurgent group rejected the allegation, stating rebel factions did not possess such armaments, the Associated Press news agency reports. Sana news agency reported 35 individuals in the areas of Dahiyet al-Assad and Hamdaniya had experienced breathing difficulties and numbness. Over 40 civilians are reported to have perished in western Aleppo since the rebel assaults commenced, campaigners say. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights stated 16 were children. It noted that 55 soldiers had also perished - alongside 64 insurgents. There is no verification of these fatalities. Insurgents from beyond Aleppo are reported to be leading the fresh offensive, attacking Hamdaniya, which is presently controlled by forces of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. The rebel factions include Jabhat Fateh al-Sham, previously the al-Qaeda-affiliated Nusra Front, alongside fellow Islamists Ahrar al-Sham. It represents the insurgents' second effort to break the Aleppo blockade. In August they briefly established a passage between the east and west after the government completely surrounded them for the first time in July. The city, formerly Syria's commercial centre, has been split between the two factions since 2012.

text: Undercover journalist Mazher Mahmood plotted to change a witness statement in a case against pop singer Tulisa Contostavlos, the Old Bailey has heard. The journalist recognised as the Fake Sheikh and his chauffeur Alan Smith both refute conspiring jointly, with intent to pervert the course of justice. Miss Contostavlos had faced accusations of supplying cocaine but the proceedings against her collapsed in 2014. Prosecutors stated Mr Mahmood possessed a vested interest in her prosecution. The tribunal heard that Miss Contostavlos had been targeted by the self-proclaimed king of the sting, who masqueraded as an influential film producer seeking the singer to appear in a Hollywood blockbuster. The vocalist had purportedly arranged for Mr Mahmood to purchase half an ounce of cocaine from one of her associates for £800. The former N-Dubz performer and X Factor judge was subsequently arrested and charged with involvement in the supply of a class A substance, after Mr Mahmood provided evidence to police. Mr Mahmood, 53, of Purley, south London, and Mr Smith, 67, from Dereham, Norfolk, stand accused of conspiring to modify a written statement the latter had provided to police because it favoured Miss Contostavlos's defence. Commencing the trial against Mr Mahmood and Mr Smith, Sarah Forshaw QC informed the jury: In essence, the hearing in June 2014 placed Mr Mahmood and his journalistic methods on trial. He preferred to style himself the king of sting, he boasted in a volume he had authored of the number of convictions for which he personally bore responsibility. He understood that if it could be demonstrated that he had conducted himself improperly as an agent provocateur, inducing Miss Contostavlos to undertake something she would not otherwise attempt, his own credibility and reputation and the likelihood of conviction in the case might both suffer severe damage. Miss Forshaw continued: Miss Contostavlos had voiced her disapproval of hard drugs to his own chauffeur, that constituted the portion of the statement that was modified. Mr Smith had informed the police officer compiling the statement that he recalled that whilst driving Miss Contostavlos... that she had discussed someone in her family being dependent on cocaine. Mr Smith had informed a police officer she appeared genuinely negative about cocaine but, one day later, he advised police he wished to withdraw that section of his statement, the tribunal heard. It is alleged that during the intervening 24 hours Mr Smith had transmitted a copy of his interview to Mr Mahmood and they had exchanged numerous texts and telephone calls. During a pre-trial hearing at Southwark Crown Court in June 2014, Mr Mahmood stated under oath that he had not discussed with Mr Smith Miss Contostavlos's remarks. He deliberately misled the tribunal - not only had he discussed it but he had received a copy of the statement, Miss Forshaw stated. When subsequently providing evidence to the jury in the proceedings, Mr Mahmood acknowledged he had examined a copy of Mr Smith's statement and Miss Contostavlos's trial consequently collapsed, she added. Miss Forshaw informed the jury: There exists no doubt that Smith did alter his statement... The alteration would undoubtedly have disadvantaged Miss Contostavlos's case. It would have deprived her of corroborating evidence from Mahmood's own right-hand man that she made an anti-drugs remark at a time when uncontaminated by any influence or pressure. She stated the evidence in the proceedings was overwhelming, adding: Mr Mahmood may be the master of subterfuge and deception. But on this occasion it is he, together with his employee, who stand exposed. The jury also heard Miss Contostavlos describe how she was deceived by Mr Mahmood after encountering him at the Metropolitan Hotel in Park Lane, London, in May 2013. In a statement read to the tribunal, she stated she could not completely recall the events because she was intoxicated. Miss Contostavlos stated Mr Smith had subsequently driven her home and she had discussed an unnamed member of her family with a hard drug problem. Mr Mahmood and Mr Smith face charges of conspiring together to perform an act, namely that Mr Smith would alter a draft statement to police, with the intention to pervert the course of justice, between 22 June and 22 July 2014. Both deny the charges. The trial continues.

Share this on Email Facebook Messenger Messenger Twitter Copy this link These are external links and open in a new window Every school is placed in a colour category ranging from green, to yellow, orange and red. This is the third year that this system of grading schools has been employed. Last year, 333 primary and secondary schools succeeded in reaching the main category, the green category - an increase of 41% on the previous year. The number of schools in the red category, the schools that needed to demonstrate the most improvement, decreased from 81 to 58. The Welsh Government believes that the categorisation system helps to identify the schools that require the most assistance, and to offer support and guidance to them. The 2016 results will be published on the My Local School website. The latest figures come a week after the inspection body Estyn published their annual report. The report stated that seven out of every 10 primary schools were good or better but that the figure dropped to four out of every 10 for secondary schools. Teaching unions have generally given a cautious welcome to the system, provided that it is used as part of a broader framework for evaluating schools. Rob Williams from the headteachers' union NAHT Cymru said: We still believe that for the categorisation system to work optimally, it needs to be part of a broader coordinated system designed to improve schools. As Estyn highlighted in their recent report, performance variation continues to exist across Wales, and the additional focus on schools in the orange and red categories does not conceal the funding differences that exist between schools. We know that the Welsh Government listens to school leaders and their concerns about a system that uses such data in an isolated manner, without identifying the progress that individual pupils make whilst at school. The National System for Categorising Schools has been agreed jointly between the education authorities and the Welsh Government with the principle that the system's purpose is not to attach labels or create bare league tables.

text: Nurses and midwives who complete their training in hospitals outside Europe will now face shorter tests to check they are fit to work in the UK. The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) states its proposals encompass a computer-based examination and assessments in simulated clinical environments. The regulator indicates these measures will substitute the minimum three-month period of supervised practice presently mandated. However, nursing leaders caution they require additional information to verify that safeguards are sufficient. Currently, nurses and midwives who have received training abroad constitute approximately 10% of the workforce registered for employment in the UK. Roughly 1,000 nurses annually arrive to work in the UK from beyond the European Economic Area - the majority originating from Australia, India or the Philippines. The NMC states one rationale behind the modification to assessments is that the existing supervised placements - which may extend from three months to one year - are insufficiently rapid to satisfy demand. The regulator indicates the system is insufficiently flexible for employers who require swift recruitment. The specialists report that applicants have encountered difficulties securing positions on the programme, as they are in limited supply. The new assessments, scheduled to commence in the autumn, comprise two components: Comparable evaluations have already been implemented by other healthcare regulators, according to the NMC. The regulator states: This will ensure the hundreds of nurses and midwives who received training overseas and wish to practise in the UK are evaluated in a proportionate and rigorous manner, to safeguard the public. Jackie Smith, the NMC chief executive, stated: The new system will not substitute the requirement for employers to ensure that the personnel they recruit demonstrate the behaviours, skills and knowledge essential for the particular role to which they are appointed, and provide additional support and development as necessary. Janet Davies, executive director of nursing at the Royal College of Nursing stated: Healthcare in the UK depends on the diligent work and commitment of numerous nurses who received training overseas. These proposals may indeed constitute part of a more rigorous and consistent framework for ensuring that nurses who work in the UK are prepared to practise in the UK. Nevertheless, we require further information about how nurses will be assessed within this system before we can determine whether the system is sufficient. Whether nurses originate from the EU or the remainder of the world, it is essential that employers are recruiting them for appropriate reasons and supporting them upon their arrival. Too frequently, nurses are recruited from overseas to address short-term shortages and provided with insufficient support to care for patients effectively. Official statistics indicate some 67,000 nurses and midwives who completed training outside Europe presently maintain NMC registration. This supplements the current workforce of more than 600,000 nursing and midwifery personnel who have trained within Europe and obtained registration with the UK regulator.

text: Plans to help nearly 100,000 small businesses due to be hit by changes to rates next month are being considered by Communities Secretary Sajid Javid. Among these, approximately 25,000 companies confront a cliff edge under the fresh business rates revaluation, according to ratings firm CVS. It submitted several proposals to Mr Javid during Wednesday's meeting. The Treasury is attempting to devise additional assistance for small companies following business outcry. Ministers have stated that the revaluation - the first since 2010 - will result in three-quarters of companies seeing their rates remain unchanged or fall. However, Mr Javid and Chancellor Philip Hammond have faced pressure to intervene to assist businesses confronting substantial increases in areas where rental values have risen dramatically. Critics argue the situation benefits large retailers and online companies over high street establishments. CVS conducted discussions with Mr Javid on Wednesday, and the company presented proposals for a package valued at up to £150m. The government is anticipated to take measures to reduce the revaluation's impact in next week's Budget. CVS chief executive Mark Rigby stated: The Secretary of State was clearly in listening mode and it was apparent to me that he was acutely conscious of the potential impact that the revaluation will bring to some communities and the anger felt by small businesses, particularly the retail and leisure sectors. He was clear in his determination to find a meaningful, targeted solution to ease the financial burden for those most in need ahead of the April tax changes. Theresa May suggested at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday that Mr Hammond would address the situation in the Budget. She stated Mr Hammond and Mr Javid had been requested to ensure that the support that is provided is appropriate and is in place for the hardest cases, adding she would expect... the Chancellor to say more about this next week in the Budget. The government has already established a transitional relief system, worth £3.6bn, to introduce the increases gradually over five years. Additional potential mitigation measures could include implementing a package similar to the retail relief scheme which was valued at £1,500 to companies when it concluded in April last year, and the threshold for tapered relief could also be increased.

text: The publisher of GQ magazine has been found guilty of contempt of court over its coverage of the News of the World (NoW) phone-hacking trial. The High Court ruled that GQ had generated a substantial risk that the trial of Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson and others would be seriously impeded or prejudiced. The court was informed that a GQ article, published by Conde Naste Publications Ltd, might have indicated to jurors that NoW's proprietors directed or were aware of hacking activities. Mrs Brooks was acquitted of all charges. Mr Coulson was found guilty of conspiracy to hack phones and received an 18-month prison sentence. Lord Thomas, the Lord Chief Justice, stated that a subsequent hearing would determine the penalty for Conde Naste. The GQ article, authored by Michael Wolff, was published in the men's magazine during April 2014, whilst the Old Bailey trial had been proceeding for over three months. The Attorney General brought the case against Conde Naste, with representation by Andrew Caldecott QC. The essence of the piece was that [Rupert] Murdoch, proprietor of News International, was, or likely was, involved in voicemail interception and that he ought to have been prosecuted and in his absence the trial possessed an air of unreality about it, Mr Caldecott had informed the court during a July hearing. He stated that such implications had not been presented by the prosecution in court. He additionally stated that the article suggested defence lawyers possessed a hidden agenda of safeguarding Mr Murdoch's interests and concealing his involvement. Adrienne Page QC, representing Conde Naste, described the article as a highly subjective, personal and impressionistic sketch founded upon the experience of visiting the trial courtroom. However, Lord Thomas, sitting alongside Mrs Justice Nicola Davies, determined that the article was seriously prejudicial. Following the ruling, Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC stated: Whilst it is uncommon to bring proceedings against publishers, the GQ article contravened the most fundamental principle of our criminal justice system; specifically that everyone is entitled to a fair trial and it is not for the press to determine who is deserving of this protection.

text: On a small yet busy lane in central Bangalore is a three-storey white house with a bright orange gate. These are external links and will open in a new window. One might not observe the property when walking past, yet some of India's finest companies of the future may be conceived within. The southern Indian city of Bangalore serves as India's start-up capital. Entrepreneurs from throughout the country, and indeed some from across the globe, migrate to the city - which also functions as the hub of India's computer industry - seeking ideas, investors and office space. They require accommodation as well, but when one lives and breathes entrepreneurship around the clock, having to return to one's mundane hotel room or dormitory at day's end proves rather tedious. This is where the white house with its orange gate has provided salvation. Opening its doors in May this year, it claims to be India's first start-up hostel. Providing a home-from-home for aspiring entrepreneurs, the 20-bed property - the Construkt Start-up Hostel - allows them to reside with like-minded individuals, and exchange their business ideas continuously day and night. More than half the bunk beds in the hostel are occupied during my visit. Besides a kitchen and washing machine, it provides those most vital services for would-be entrepreneurs - wi-fi and a coffee-maker. One wall of the ground floor has been transformed into a blackboard. Upon it is a calendar grid drawn in chalk, listing all the start-up and technology events in the city throughout the coming month. Amongst them is a boot camp for start-ups, where they may pitch to prospective investors, and a conference on data analysis. The founders of Construkt state this exemplifies how they assist residents in connecting with the city's broader start-up ecosystem. Most of the hostel's occupants are men and women who have come to Bangalore attempting to identify the company they wish to establish. Others know what business they would like to start, but are in the city assessing the market. Construkt resident Krishna Elakara is working on developing a fitness training product. The 42-year-old is of Indian origin, but has resided abroad throughout his life, most recently in Australia. On the first floor of the hostel, in a cheerful small room that functions as a mini-library, he explains why he has come to Bangalore. All the elements one needs to assemble a start-up, they are here, he states. I am staying at this hostel because I wish to build my network in the city. Other hostels or hotels typically have tourists, whereas here one meets people with a similar mind-set. Downstairs in the semi-circular living room, a so-called open hack session is about to commence. The residents of the hostel gather together, and some of the entrepreneurs share their business ideas with the group. Krishna is the first to deliver a presentation. What is unique about your idea? and Who would you partner with? are some of the questions that are directed at him. Shashikiran Rao, 36, one of the founders of the hostel, says with a smile: We take the idea and tear it apart, and allow everyone to jump in and identify flaws in it. We are very proficient at it. The idea is to assist entrepreneurs in developing their plans. Aashna Kaur is the next presenter at the session. The 24-year-old holds a degree in business administration, and has been consulting with start-ups for more than a year. But now she wishes to establish her own company and she is considering two ideas - technology that assists solo female travellers, or products that encourage more Indian women to enter the workforce. Aashna has been at Construkt for more than a week. At around $14 (£10.70) per night and $220 monthly, I ask her if low cost is the reason she chose to stay there. She states she would obtain a cheap hotel at the same rate, or perhaps even lower, but it is the networking opportunities that made her choose the hostel. Currently, apart from aspiring entrepreneurs, Construkt is also attracting people who are still exploring their career options. Prerna Gautam remains at university, but has moved from Mumbai to Bangalore for the summer to work as an intern at Microsoft Accelerator, a division of the tech giant that assists entrepreneurs in bridging the gap from idea to execution. She remains uncertain of what she wishes to do when she completes her degree, but states that her time in Bangalore is drawing her towards a start-up life. With Construkt hoping to open a second start-up hostel in Bangalore, analyst Sudhir Singh of consultancy group PricewaterhouseCoopers states that whilst it is meeting a market need, he does not believe it will become a widespread phenomenon. There is definitely space for something like this, but I do not know if it will catch on like wildfire, he states. It is where I am sure many aspiring entrepreneurs would choose to stay to network, but I am not certain a well-established entrepreneur would live there unless there are some innovative programmes they are creating to attract such people to the place. But back at Construkt everyone appears very content. There are strains of music, and people have brought out food and drinks to share. Some are typing away at their laptops, whilst others are discussing business, technology and politics. Not very long ago, these men and women would have been called foolish. Establishing one's own company was seen as risky and impractical in India. Today, I am told, if one does not have a start-up idea upon graduation, one would almost be looked down upon. It is a life that comes with its own struggles - obtaining funding, hiring the right people and paying salaries, to name just a few. But right now, none of that is deterring India's youngsters.

Coaches working in age-group rugby inform me that weight training and supplements appear to be proceeding hand in hand. It was not easy for the players and coaches in the Bloodgate affair, or in the various eye-gouging allegations, nor for the other 60-odd rugby players caught by the IRB consuming drugs or tampering with their samples. text: Donald Trump's plan to erect a huge sea wall at his Irish golf course has been withdrawn in the light of stiff opposition. The initial application referenced increasing sea levels resulting from climate change as a principal justification for the protective barrier. However, environmental activists opposed the two-mile long development, stating it endangered a rare species of snail. A revised plan featuring a smaller wall is anticipated to be lodged shortly. The Trump International hotel and golf links at Doonbeg on the western coast of County Clare was purchased in 2014. Storms during that year caused substantial erosion of sand dunes at the course and the Trump organisation submitted proposals to Clare County Council to construct a two-mile (2.8km) limestone wall to reduce the impact of the seas. At 4m in height and 20m wide, the 200,000-tonne structure would have necessitated approximately 200,000 tonnes of rock for construction. The €10m wall would provide protection against the damaging impacts of the seas, the initial application stated. The documents proceeded to outline that the increasing sea levels and heightened storm frequency and wave energy linked with global warming can accelerate the rate of erosion. The wall would also benefit the community, the documents stated, through the coastal protection works. Whilst the plan was enthusiastically supported by numerous local residents and businesses, there was substantial opposition from environmental groups. There was concern that the wall would affect the tiny, EU protected whorl snail, Vertigo angustior. Six months ago, the local authority returned to the Trump group for additional information on how the structure would affect the Carrowmore dunes special area of conservation, but none was provided. We received notification from the applicant yesterday that they were withdrawing their application, a council spokesman informed BBC News. The Trump group indicated that they had withdrawn their plans because the planning process would have taken far too long. In a statement, they said that the resort contributed approximately 6m euros annually to the local economy. Plans to expand the facilities are being closely considered but protection was required from the restless sea. The realisation of these plans, however, is fundamentally dependent on the provision of adequate protection from coastal erosion, the statement read. Since 2002, an estimated 15m to 20m of dune face has been eroded from the beach front and the golf course. All efforts at soft management of the coastline have failed. All efforts to readjust the course have also been exhausted. In a statement, the group announced plans for a reduced version of the wall, that would extend to 900 metres in two sections and would see metal sheet piles inserted into the ground on the golf course with limestone boulders placed around them. Some campaigners believe that the international attention on Donald Trump's pledge to build a wall on the southern border of the US, did not assist the plans for Doonbeg. You could tell that they were upset, because there were already analogies being drawn with the Mexican wall, said Tony Lowes from Friends of the Irish environment who met with the Trump camp. You could tell that they did not like that because they could sense that this could develop into something more than a small planning battle in Ireland. Around 100,000 people from across the world signed a petition compiled by surfing group, Save the Waves, to oppose the original plans. Campaigners believe that the criticism that the President-elect has faced regarding his perceived antipathy towards the environment and climate change, did not play much of a role in fuelling the opposition. In this case I think the absurdity of the proposal, the outrage at what was about to be imposed was so great, that no one could examine the proposal without being shocked, said Tony Lowes. I have very rarely witnessed an environmental case that appeared so absolutely horrific. It is expected that the new proposal will be submitted before Christmas and could be determined by March next year. Analysts will be examining the new documents to see if there are any further references to climate change and the impact of rising seas. Follow Matt on Twitter and on Facebook

text: A new loan scheme is to be offered to Scottish farmers to prevent a repeat of the problems caused by delays to Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) payments. Rural Affairs Secretary Fergus Ewing announced the scheme, acknowledging that the IT system primarily responsible for the delays was not there yet. Mr Ewing stated that next year's payments were consequently not-risk free. However, he indicated that farmers and crofters would be permitted to apply for a loan valued at 80% of their complete entitlement. Agricultural union NFU Scotland endorsed the new scheme, stating it would provide clarity and certainty to farmers. However, opposition parties argued the scheme constituted an acknowledgement that difficulties with the CAP payment system might not yet have been resolved. Scotland's CAP Futures programme was intended to render the rural payment process more efficient. However, difficulties with a new Scottish government IT system resulted in delays to numerous farmers receiving the funds. In May, public spending watchdog Audit Scotland stated the prolonged delays had a significant impact on farmers - many of whom were already experiencing financial difficulties caused by low milk prices and severe flooding. Mr Ewing informed MSPs at Holyrood that 17,744 out of 18,479 eligible businesses had now received their 2015 payments, with the majority of outstanding cases anticipated to be paid by the 15 October deadline. He also stated he expected that the subsequent round of payments for 2016 would be substantially completed by the deadline at the end of June next year. However, Mr Ewing stated the new loan scheme would provide certainty for farmers and crofters over the winter, and would seek to inject up to £300m into the rural economy, safeguarding jobs and local agricultural businesses. He informed MSPs: Having learned lessons from the 2015 round of CAP payments, I am determined to provide as much certainty as we can, not just for farmers and crofters, but for the wider economy in our rural communities. I am therefore announcing today that farmers will not have to wait until 2017 to receive payment of their CAP entitlement. Letters will be issued before the end of the month to farmers inviting them to apply. Everyone who applies by the deadline of 12 October will receive a loan of 80% of their entitlement in November. Responding to the announcement, NFU Scotland president Allan Bowie stated it would have a positive impact on the entire rural economy. Mr Bowie added: Knowing that up to 80% of your support package will be delivered in early November gives clarity and certainty to farm businesses. The bitter legacy of the flawed 2015 payment run continues and the cabinet secretary again apologised for the problems, some of which still remain. On behalf of our members, we will continue to maintain pressure on the Scottish government until all outstanding payments for 2015 have been delivered. However, Peter Chapman, the Scottish Conservative rural affairs spokesman, stated the loan scheme was effectively an admission by Mr Ewing that problems with the computer system had still not been resolved. Mr Chapman added: He cannot deliver 100% payments in December as we should expect - instead he has to offer an 80% loan for November. These loans are an admission of failure. This is not good enough and it certainly will not win the trust of the farming community which has long run out of patience with the SNP on this issue. Mr Ewing should finally agree that we need a parliamentary inquiry into this issue. Mike Rumbles of the Scottish Liberal Democrats stated Mr Ewing's claim that the loan scheme was injecting £300m into the rural economy was complete nonsense because farmers should already be receiving full payment anyway if the new system was working properly. He added: The statement today was a dreadful admission of the failure of the Scottish government. His 80% loan plan will be offered to all applicants but this still means that the average farm business will be over £6,000 out of pocket goodness knows how long.

Mr Ewing said that next year’s payments would therefore not be risk-free. However, he said that farmers and crofters would be allowed to apply for a loan worth 80% of their total entitlement. Scotland's CAP Futures programme was intended to make the rural payment system more efficient. The agricultural union NFU Scotland praised the new system, saying it would give clarity and security to farmers. But the opposition parties argued that it was a tacit acknowledgement that the problems of the CAP payment system had not yet been solved. Mr Ewing told MSPs that 17,744 of the 18,479 eligible farmers had now received their 2015 payments, with most of the remaining payments expected to be made by the 15th of October. However, the new IT system of the Scottish government had caused many farmers to be late in receiving their payments. In May, Audit Scotland reported that the delay had been of serious importance to many farmers, who were already in financial difficulty after low milk prices and severe flooding. But Mr Ewing said that the new loan scheme would ensure certainty for farmers and crofters over the winter and would seek to inject up to £300m into the rural economy, safeguarding jobs and local agricultural businesses. He also said that he expected that the following round of payments for 2016 would be substantially completed by the deadline at the end of June next year. I therefore announce to you today that the farmer shall not have to wait until 2017 to receive his share of the CAP. All who apply by the deadline of 12 October will receive a loan of 80% of their CAP in November. A letter will be sent before the end of the month to the farmer inviting him to apply. The bitter legacy of the flawed 2015 payment run continued, and the cabinet secretary again apologised for the problems, some of which are still continuing. NFU Scotland president Allan Bowie said it would have a positive impact on the entire rural economy. Mr Bowie added: “Knowing that up to 80% of your support package will be delivered in early November will give clarity and certainty to farm businesses. However, Peter Chapman, Scottish Conservative rural affairs spokesman, said the loan scheme was an admission by Mr Ewing that the problems with the new IT system had not been resolved. “Instead of paying in full for December, as we expect, he has to offer a loan of 80% for November. On behalf of our members, we will continue to maintain pressure on the Scottish Government until all the outstanding payments for 2015 have been paid.” Mr Ewing should finally agree that we need a parliamentary inquiry into this issue. These loans are an admission of failure. They will not restore the trust of the farming community, which has long since lost patience with the SNP on this issue. This 80% loan scheme will be offered to all applicants, but it still means that the average farm will be over £6,000 out of pocket for goodness knows how long. Mike Rumbles of the Scottish Liberal Democrats claimed that Mr Ewing’s claim that the loan scheme was injecting £300m into the rural economy was nonsense, as the farmers should have been paid in full if the new system was working properly. He added that the statement was a dreadful admission of the failure of the Scottish government.
