text: European banking stocks have fallen sharply despite the victory of the pro-bailout New Democracy party in Greece's elections on Sunday. Whilst the outcome generated optimism that Greece would adhere to austerity policies and remain within the euro, analysts stated that considerable uncertainty persisted. The decline in banking shares was observed throughout Europe, with Germany's Commerzbank and France's BNP Paribas both falling 4.4%. Spanish bond yields remained unstable, climbing above the 7% perilous threshold. Broader share indices were varied. France's Cac 40 finished down 0.7%, whilst Germany's Dax was 0.3% higher. Both had previously risen 1%. London's FTSE 100 finished up 0.3% after declining in early dealings, whilst in New York, the Dow Jones finished down 0.2%. Amongst other banking shares, Deutsche Bank fell 1.1%, whilst Credit Agricole dropped 3.4%. In the UK, Royal Bank of Scotland dropped 5.0% and Lloyds Banking Group fell 3.6%, making them the largest fallers on the FTSE 100. The interest rate on the government bonds of Spain - the eurozone nation reported to be most at risk of requiring a complete international bailout in future - reached another fresh high. The yield on Spain's 10-year bonds had initially dropped as low as 6.767%, before climbing to 7.144%. Italy's 10-year bond yield also climbed, reaching 6.08%, after earlier dropping to 5.85%. The principal share indices of Spain and Italy also declined. By Robert Peston Business editor Read Robert's blog in full Spain's Ibex finished down 3.0%, whilst Italy's FTSE MIB lost 2.9%. In the currency markets, the euro was marginally lower against the dollar, at $1.2579 from $1.2637 late on Friday. Asian shares had earlier recorded strong gains, with Japan's Nikkei 225 index and South Korea's Kospi both finishing up 1.8%, whilst Australia's ASX 200 added 1.9%. Antonis Samaras, the leader of the New Democracy party, stated on Sunday that the Greek people voted today to remain on the European path and stay in the eurozone. There will be no further adventures. Greece's position in Europe will not be questioned. Adrian Slack, head of equities at Bastion Capital, stated the initial response to the Greek election outcome was excessively euphoric. He added: Fundamentally, the difficulties [in Greece and the eurozone] have not altered. Peter Schiff, of the brokerage Euro Pacific Capital, added: How long will it take for people to worry about Spain again? Spain's borrowing costs have been reaching euro-era record highs, suggesting that lenders were worried about Madrid's capacity to repay its debts. Last week, the ratings agency Moody's reduced Spain's credit rating to one level above junk. Yet other analysts were more positive. Masayuki Doshida, a senior market analyst at Rakuten Securities, stated the victory of Greece's New Democracy party had eased eurozone concerns for now. There will be a definite sense of relief spreading around today, stated Masayuki Doshida. Fellow analyst, David Lennox of Fat Prophets, told the BBC that the worst of the Greek crisis could now be finished. We believe that early punters are already taking the view that a floor has been established under the crisis for now, he stated. The elections in Greece were being monitored closely, not just by eurozone leaders but also investors across the globe. Greece, which is experiencing a sovereign debt crisis, has received two bailouts in the past two years. It was provided an initial package worth 110bn euros (£89bn; $138bn) in 2010, followed by another agreed last year worth 130bn euros. However, the EU and IMF have imposed tough austerity measures, including state spending reductions, as pre-conditions to those packages. There have been various protests against these cuts in Greece and the Syriza party had stated that it would renegotiate the conditions if it gained power. It had led to concerns that if eurozone leaders and Athens did not agree on the existing terms, Greece might be compelled to leave the eurozone. There were worries that such a move might spread contagion to other eurozone nations and result in turmoil in the global economy. However, the BBC's business editor, Robert Peston, stated the new Greek government still faced an uphill challenge. He stated that bankers had told him Greece required eurozone governments and the European Central Bank to write off a substantial portion of what they are owed.

text: France's prime minister says he will pay €2,500 (£1,825) for taking his children on a controversial trip to the Champions League final in Berlin. Manuel Valls faced criticism following his use of a government Falcon aircraft to transport two sons to the fixture on Saturday. He maintains he was conducting an official journey to discuss the Euro 2016 tournament, which France is staging. However Mr Valls stated he was mindful of public response and consented to cover the expenses for his children. Speaking during a visit to the French territory of Reunion in the Indian Ocean, the PM declared the journey was nothing extraordinary and emphasised that his sons' attendance contributed nothing to the expense. Nevertheless he stated France had no requirement for a needless controversy and to eliminate any uncertainty, I chose to bear the expense of the journey for my two children. The total expense of the trip is reported to have been approximately €20,000. Associates close to Mr Valls stated the €2,500 payment was calculated on the standard price of taking a commercial flight for the return journey from Poitiers to Berlin. Nevertheless some analysts stated the expense of chartering the Falcon aircraft, together with the security arrangements required, would be considerably more. The prime minister states he travelled to the Champions League final to meet Uefa President Michel Platini to discuss matters such as Euro 2016 and the Fifa corruption affair. However the utilisation of a government aircraft to transport him and his sons to witness Barcelona defeat Juventus 3-1 prompted incredulity. Born in Barcelona, Mr Valls is a supporter of the European champions. Earlier this week opposition MPs demanded Mr Valls repay the expense of the flight, and he encountered a series of taunts in the National Assembly. The affair sparked a storm of response on social media, with the hashtag #Vallsgate trending in France on Wednesday. Correspondents state the dispute has threatened to overshadow significant reforms designed to relax labour laws for small and medium-sized enterprises and adding tens of thousands of positions to the labour market. Under the Small Business Act, enterprises with no employees would be granted €4,000 (£2,920; $4,500) for providing their first worker a year-long contract. Unemployment in France stands at 10% and Mr Valls also proposed that employers should be permitted to extend temporary contracts up to a maximum of 18 months.

text: A collection of bitcoins worth about £8m, which had been confiscated by police in Australia, will be auctioned off in June. The 24,518 bitcoins shall be sold predominantly in batches of 2,000 - each possessing a value of approximately £680,000. Ernst & Young, the company organising the sale, stated the bitcoins had been seized as criminal proceeds but declined to provide further details regarding the case. One specialist said the authorities had selected a secure period to sell. Australian publications have previously reported that 24,500 bitcoins were confiscated by police in Victoria state in 2013, following a man's arrest for trading illicit drugs online. In 2015, Victoria's Asset Confiscation Operations department acknowledged it had recently acquired possession of 24,500 coins and would attempt to maximise their value, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. This represents a substantial quantity of Bitcoin, Dr Garrick Hileman, economic historian at the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, informed the BBC. It equals approximately one week's worth of new Bitcoin entering the market through mining. Presently around 4,000 new bitcoins are created daily as compensation for miners who provide their computing power to process Bitcoin transactions. The general consensus is that whenever 10,000 bitcoins are sold, the market price can be influenced substantially. The bitcoin price climbed to $530 (£362) on Friday, its peak level since August 2014. Dr Hileman stated the Australian authorities had selected a secure period to sell because uncertainty exists regarding Bitcoin's value in July. The Bitcoin protocol is structured to decrease the quantity of new bitcoins miners receive as compensation for processing transactions every four years. The compensation shall be halved on 14 July, therefore prices might rise due to the diminished supply of new bitcoins. However, questions remain whether security might deteriorate, if miner rewards are reduced substantially. Therefore it represents a secure time to sell, as no certainty exists about July's developments. The Australian Bitcoin sale, which shall be accessible to global bidders, marks the first such auction beyond the US. In 2014, the US Marshals Service commenced auctioning a collection of approximately 175,000 bitcoins that had been seized from the Silk Road internet marketplace founder. The final auction of those bitcoins drew 11 bidders, potentially due to each block's substantial cost. Dr Hileman stated the Bitcoin sale by Australian authorities represented recognition that the cryptocurrency was not unlawful. Whenever a government sells Bitcoin, it acknowledges this constitutes a different asset to drugs, for instance, which would not be auctioned, he informed the BBC. That constituted one of the significant conclusions from the US Marshal Service auction - they established a precedent that Bitcoin was not unlawful. Australia has been conducting its own regulatory process - and this establishes a position that Bitcoin is lawful to use in Australia.

text: Researchers attempting to learn why people snack are to study the health and habits of more than 100 Scots. These are external links and will open in a new window It forms part of a Scottish government initiative to address the obesity issue. The team at Aberdeen's Rowett Institute of Nutrition and Health hope to recruit 120 volunteers who will be monitored during a week-long period. Researchers will track their heart rates, activity levels and snacking patterns using heart sensors, GPS equipment and an electronic diary. The scientists hope to establish a connection between so-called executive functions in the brain and snacking behaviour. Dr David McMinn, from the institute, who is leading the research, said: We inhabit an environment where snack foods are easily accessible, and where office jobs and labour-saving devices mean that we are less active than previous generations. Since our environment facilitates consuming high-calorie snack foods and spending extended periods inactive, eating healthily and remaining active demands considerable self-regulation. It demands that we make an effort, such as choosing not to snack in order to maintain a healthy weight. He added: We are particularly interested in how food choices and physical activity behaviours are connected to psychological processes in the brain termed the 'executive functions'. We employ executive functions to accomplish goals, for example, planning actions beforehand, solving problems, ignoring distractions and resisting temptations. The executive functions can become depleted if used intensively, or owing to particularly stressful circumstances. text: The head of MI5, Sir Jonathan Evans, is to step down from the post next month, Home Secretary Theresa May has said. These are external links and will open in a new window In the Commons, Mrs May paid tribute to Sir Jonathan's 33 years of service with the security organisation. He succeeded Lady Manningham-Buller to become director general of MI5 in April 2007, and shall depart at the conclusion of his contract. I thank him for his invaluable contribution to public safety and national security, Mrs May stated. Speaking during Home Office questions, Mrs May said his work had encompassed investigating counter espionage, developing and implementing key security policies and most recently countering the threat of international terrorism. By Gordon Corera Security correspondent, BBC News Running MI5 is a position which could give you sleepless nights. There is the threat of terrorism - not long before Jonathan Evans assumed control, Britain had been struck by the 7 July attacks and MI5 faced questions of whether it could have prevented them. And it is not merely the al-Qaeda threat - the threat from Northern Ireland's security situation has risen up the agenda. There are also the issues that emerged from the post-9/11 years, such as allegations of security service complicity in mistreatment of former detainees like Binyam Mohammed. And most recently there were the Olympics to worry about. Jonathan Evans will be able to depart breathing a sigh of relief that he took MI5 through without any major disasters. New issues are present for his successor though, including how to address the growing threat of cyber espionage against Britain and how to manage in a new environment amid possibly questions about funding and priorities. He has witnessed the service evolving over the years and as director general has led the service through particularly challenging times of change and unrest, including the aftermath of the 7/7 bombings, she stated. His tireless work helped ensure the delivery of a safe and successful Olympic and Paralympic Games last year. Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper said: We also give thanks for the work Sir Jonathan Evans has undertaken over many years for the security of this country. At MI5, Sir Jonathan, who is in his mid-50s, initially concentrated on Irish-related terrorism in the 1980s and 1990s, before moving on to international counter-terrorism investigations in 1999. He was appointed director of international counter-terrorism just 10 days before the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon in 2001. Last year, in a rare public address just one month before the Olympic Games commenced in London, he said Britain had experienced a credible terrorist attack plot about once a year since 9/11. He warned: In back rooms and in cars and on the streets of this country, there is no shortage of individuals talking about wanting to mount terrorist attacks here. He was appointed Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath (KCB) in the 2013 New Year's Honours List.

text: Every year charitable trusts are set up in memory of people who have met violent or tragic deaths. Several develop into substantial charities - the Stephen Lawrence Charitable Trust, founded following the racially motivated killing of the young man, is marking its 20th anniversary. Others prosper temporarily before closing. However, how does establishing a charity or trust assist the families central to the tragedy? The Williams family, from Wellington, Shropshire, lost their teenage daughter in May. The 17-year-old's body was discovered off the Nant-y-Garth pass, near Wrexham, days after she had disappeared from home. Jamie Reynolds, 22, of Avondale Road, Wellington, Shropshire, has appeared before court charged with her murder. Following Georgia's death, friends rapidly raised sufficient funds for a memorial bench, but so many individuals had pledged money that the Georgia Williams Trust was established to create an enduring legacy. It has been truly heartening to witness people becoming involved, organising events and reading all their supportive messages, said her father Steve Williams. [The family] have been able to derive considerable comfort from what people have expressed and how they remember her. He continued: The trust will ultimately be utilised to enable young people of Telford and Wrekin to access enrichment activities - whether that be canoeing, rock climbing, tennis, flying or something else and also to encourage young people to volunteer. Richard Langton, chairman of the trust, acknowledges how it has assisted the family and remains determined to maintain close connections with them. The Charity Commission stated when people establish a new charity - particularly in response to a tragedy - they are frequently overwhelmed by others' generosity. With time donations naturally diminish and many small charities struggle to secure sufficient funding for their cause. The commission strongly advises people to question themselves whether they can ensure that when they establish a charity it remains sustainable, otherwise they risk disappointing beneficiaries. The Charity Commission We hope that the charity can provide a positive focus for the family during this extraordinarily difficult time for them and give them some comfort to know that there exists a positive legacy, that Georgia's name will continue, the West Mercia Police inspector stated. We shall continue to work closely with the family - we have a trustee in Scarlet Williams, Georgia's sister, who will be working with us to ensure we remain on track to deliver from the charity what the family desired. Mr Langton said the challenge was to establish a charity that can survive beyond these few incredibly painful months. The trust already has 5,200 followers on Facebook and 500 followers on Twitter, and Mr Langton is now appealing for those people to make contact and become involved. Ann Oakes-Odger understands first-hand the desperate emotion that parents endure when they lose a child, and also how having something positive to focus upon after the tragedy can assist. Her son, Westley, died after being stabbed in the neck whilst standing at a cash machine in Colchester, Essex, in September 2005. Two brothers were convicted in 2006 of his manslaughter and murder. She successfully campaigned to secure a new starting sentence for courts considering the minimum term for murderers who used a knife and proceeded to establish knifecrimes.org and Victims' Advocate, which assist people experiencing the same circumstances she endured. It has assisted after losing Westley, she said regarding establishing the two organisations. I felt certain that once the trial concluded there would be a substantial void to fall into if there was not something else to grasp onto and to take forward in memory of Westley. It has been many years since that occurred to Westley, but I still experience days when the shock still strikes, she added. It was a collection at her son's funeral which led Shropshire mother Karen Prior to raise tens of thousands of pounds for charity. It was not that we [as parents] desired to be in any publicity, she added. text: An online petition has been launched by residents of the town of Benson in the US state of Arizona against a radio station which broadcast advice late at night on how to hide child pornography. These are external links and will open in a new window Broadcasts transmitted by the station over a two-year period provided guidance on how to conceal viewing such images. The petition charges the station with transmitting a sickening message. Cave 97.7 FM proprietor Paul Lotsof has publicly declared he opposes Arizona's legislation on child pornography. He informed KVOA News 4 Tucson that he had provided a public service by transmitting the guidance, which has recently been removed from air. Mr Lotsof contends that possession of child pornography should not constitute a crime and that penalties for it are harsh. In numerous instances the punishments for pictures are more severe than the punishment for murder, he can be heard stating on a clip uploaded on YouTube by opponents of his outrageous opinions. Mr Lotsof asserts there is a distinction between viewing paedophile images and perpetrating paedophile acts. The difference is [that in] one instance, you're molesting children and abusing them, forcing children to do things that are not natural for children to do, and [in] the other instance, they're simply possessing pictures, he informed News 4 Tucson. Cave 97.7 describes itself as south-east Arizona's most powerful radio station. Listener figures are not available on its website. The petition on Change.org charges Cave with transmitting a sickening message about a huge issue that afflicts this country. There is no justification for this and [the station] needs to be shut down, it declares. We can keep this rubbish out of our community. The guidance was transmitted under the format of a Public Service Announcement (PSA) - a method by which messages in the public interest are distributed via the media. Federal Communication Commission officials informed News 4 Tucson that there were no regulations which clearly specified what could or could not be transmitted in relation to PSAs. The US has a long tradition of maintaining the principle of freedom of speech. But police in Benson state they are investigating whether the station's PSAs are in violation of the law, and that the children in pictures are victims of a crime. Freedom of speech does not include instructing people to commit crimes and continuing to disseminate this information could lead to judicial action being taken, a police statement declared. We are now seeking legal counsel on actions that can be taken for the content that has already been released and to ensure this kind of information is not released again. Arizona has some of the strictest laws in the US on child abuse and exploitation. In 2003 a secondary school teacher was sentenced to 200 years in prison after he was caught with thousands of images of child abuse on his computer.

text: Fidel Castro, who has died aged 90, was a huge figure in our lives, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has said. Mr Corbyn commended the former Cuban president's revolutionary heroism, his presence upon the global stage and Cuba's healthcare and educational systems. Mr Castro's demise was announced by his younger brother Raul Castro, his successor as Cuba's president. Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson stated Fidel Castro had been a historic, if controversial figure. Mr Johnson conveyed the UK's condolences to Cuba's government and people, and declared Mr Castro's demise marked the conclusion of an era for Cuba and the beginning of a new one for Cuba's people. He added: The UK shall continue to collaborate with Cuba's government on a broad range of foreign policy priorities, including regarding human rights. Live updates Obituary: Fidel Castro Fidel Castro: A life in pictures Fidel: The world icon Former Labour London mayor Ken Livingstone termed Mr Castro an absolute giant of the 20th Century. Former Labour MP George Galloway tweeted a photograph of himself with Mr Castro, writing: You were the greatest man I ever encountered Comandante Fidel. You were the man of the century. However, other senior Labour figures have been more critical. Mr Corbyn, a long-standing supporter of the Cuba Solidarity Campaign - which campaigns against the embargo on, and foreign intervention in, Cuba - characterised Mr Castro as a huge figure of modern history, national independence and 20th Century socialism. text: There is one sentence in the press release announcing Nicholas Serota's departure from Tate that stands out. It constitutes a direct quotation from the gentleman himself and states: I leave an institution that has the potential to reach broad audiences across the UK and abroad, through its own programmes, partnerships and online. It is that term potential which stands out. What does he signify by potential? He is discussing an institution that has evolved - under his stewardship - from a well-regarded but modestly attended gallery in Pimlico to an international art megabrand claiming the most visited museum of modern art globally (Tate Modern), two enormously popular regional galleries, a nationwide network of partnerships and a lending programme that sees Tate's collection of British art displayed in major museums from Beijing to Boston. By most individuals' assessment, Nicholas Serota has already fulfilled Tate's potential. However clearly, he does not perceive it in that manner, which represents the measure of the gentleman and an insight into why he has achieved such success during his tenure at Tate. He does not practise complacency. His remark regarding potential reflects three elements of his character: an inclination not to trumpet his own achievements, a relentless determination, and a challenging disposition. He does not wish the next incumbent to believe he or she faces an easy task: there remains work to be accomplished. He may be departing, but he is establishing the agenda before his exit. And who might that individual be to arrive and realise Tate's potential? The frontrunner I believe is Maria Balshaw, who has performed an excellent job as the director of the Whitworth in Manchester, a position she has combined with leading the city's cultural programme. Then there is Iwona Blazwick, the long-serving director of the Whitechapel Gallery in east London, who assisted in shaping Tate Modern's curatorial philosophy whilst she was employed by the gallery in the late 1990s. She has long been suggested as Serota's successor, and the route from Whitechapel to Tate is the one he followed. Of the internal candidates, the most apparent is Frances Morris, but she has only recently assumed the position as director of Tate Modern. The recently departed Jessica Morgan could also be a candidate, but again, she has scarcely settled into her role as the director at the DIA Art Foundation. The search committee is certain to look further abroad. Klaus Biesenbach from MoMA PS1 might receive a call, as could super-curator Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, and quite possibly Michael Govan of the LA County Museum. Finally, Tim Marlow from the Royal Academy and Matthew Slotover, the co-founder of Frieze, are both notable figures who could contribute something fresh to the proceedings.

A security researcher described the situation as alarming but commended the transparency of certain companies. The IT worker, who requested anonymity, stated: We have been awaiting [Nuance Communications'] iChart [product] since they were initially struck by the ransomware and are still awaiting its return. We shall likely need to transfer to another product or even another vendor to obtain the same type of benefit. A spokesperson for Nuance Communications refused to comment on the issue, but referred the BBC to an update from 5 July. Maersk had reinstated all of its major systems and customer interfaces, a spokesperson informed the BBC. However, he noted: There are certain delays on some processes owing to manual workarounds or backlogs that required clearing. In certain instances our response time to customers may be longer than normal, but we are nonetheless delivering them with the services they expect from us. There have been financial consequences, too. On one hand, it is alarming to observe large multinational corporations still experiencing the impact and attempting to restore systems, stated security researcher Kevin Beaumont. text: Levels of unconscious racist and sexist bias have been reduced by manipulating the way the brain learns during sleep. A team at Northwestern University in Chicago played sounds whilst people slept to activate and reinforce memories of an exercise conducted earlier that day. The trial involving 40 participants, published in the journal Science, demonstrated the changes persisted for at least one week. Experts stated the findings possessed potential across numerous situations, but also raised ethical concerns. Sexual and racial prejudice are widespread but may frequently be unintentional, according to the Northwestern team. They reference studies in computer games where people selected to shoot black characters more frequently than white ones or men being preferred over women despite possessing identical job applications. Participants' prejudices were evaluated using a series of publicly available tests at the study's commencement. They subsequently received counter-bias training. Throughout the session, photographs of faces were matched with words that contradicted widely-held stereotypes. Therefore female faces were matched with words such as maths or black faces with positive words such as sunshine. Distinctive sounds were played throughout the counter-bias training and were replayed at low volume during a 90-minute afternoon sleep. The outcome was a reduction in sexual and racial bias scores, which continued for at least one week. Therefore could this genuinely make someone less sexist or racist? Professor Ken Paller, the director of the cognitive neuroscience programme at Northwestern University, informed the BBC News website: We did not have people interact with or make decisions regarding other people, so that type of experiment is required to understand the complete effects of the methods we employed. However we suggest that modifying unconscious social bias is likely to influence the degree to which decisions are influenced by racist or sexist attitudes. He contends the technique may possess potential in addressing addiction or unhealthy eating. In a commentary, Gordon Feld and Jan Born from the University of Tubingen commended the study stating: This is the first to demonstrate that this method can be employed to break long-lived, highly pervasive response habits deeply embedded in memory. However they warned that sleep was a vulnerable state in which people did not possess wilful consciousness. They continued: Nevertheless, Aldous Huxley's description of a dystopian 'brave new world' where young children are conditioned to certain values during sleep reminds us that this research also requires guidance by ethical considerations. Professor Paller stated there were similarities to subliminal advertising and that there was an ethical discussion to be conducted. Nevertheless, he continued: More significantly, perhaps, is the question of whether people in positions of authority in society, such as judges and police officers, and perhaps people who make hiring decisions, should have their unconscious bias assessed and perhaps trained to some standard.

text: A firm has been handed a record fine for nuisance calls after making more than six million automated calls in a solar panel marketing campaign. Glasgow-based Home Energy & Lifestyle Management Ltd has been penalised £200,000 by the Information Commissioner. Complainants described feeling helpless against calls or discovering that calls were saturating answer machines. The firm blamed another company it employed to make calls and stated it was appealing against the decision. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said that the firm conducted an extensive automated call marketing campaign offering complimentary solar panels. One complainant informed the ICO that they had been awaiting news of a terminally ill family member and could not disregard the telephone. The fundamental point is companies attempting to sell a product must adhere to the regulations. Nuisance telephone calls are a contemporary plague, said the Information Commissioner Christopher Graham. People anticipate the Information Commissioner and other agencies to shut this down and we're now closing down on these telephone pests. The ICO said an organisation should possess people's consent, which specifically identifies the company involved, in order to make automated calls, but the company acknowledged it did not understand what the regulations were. To provide that consent, consumers must tick a box stating they are interested in a specific product from a specific company. This company's ignorance of the law is extraordinary. It did not even attempt to discover what the regulations were and its poorly conceived marketing campaign made people's lives miserable, said Steve Eckersley, head of enforcement at the ICO. The firm is also required to provide a method for consumers to cease receiving such calls, but in some instances it failed to do so. The Telephone Preference Service, which allows people to opt out of unsolicited calls, only applies when there is an actual person on the end of the telephone. In this instance Home Energy & Lifestyle Management (Helms) used specialist software to send automated messages, which can be repeated regularly. The company - part of the government's Green Deal scheme - was also misleading people in the calls as the solar panels were not complimentary, the ICO said. However, Helms responded, claiming that the campaign had ceased before the ICO investigation began and blaming another company for the issues raised. Helms had considerable difficulty in fully co-operating with the ICO, owing to the failure of the third party company to provide any information to verify and explain the scope of the calls made, the company said in a statement from its solicitor. It said the ICO had apparently disregarded its representations and pledged to appeal, as well as taking action against the other company.

text: Almost a third of dogs checked at random across the UK were found to be carrying a tick, researchers say. The finding emerges from the largest survey of ticks in dogs. Researchers also discovered that the risk of an animal acquiring a tick is as great in urban areas as in rural ones. Ticks can transmit a range of diseases including Lyme disease, and also a parasite discovered in the UK for the first time earlier this year that is potentially fatal to dogs. Lyme disease has the potential to cause serious health problems, such as meningitis and heart failure. In the most serious cases, it can prove fatal. Nearly 15,000 dogs from across the UK were examined in the study, which was conducted by Bristol University last year. Just under a third (31%) of these dogs checked at random during a visit to the vet were discovered to be carrying a tick. The researchers discovered that the arachnids are present right across the UK, with the highest risk areas being Scotland, East Anglia and the South West. There can be just as many in urban areas as in rural areas. Launched in April 2015, the project asked participating vets to examine dogs in their practice each week and complete a questionnaire relating to the clinical history of each dog. The species, life-cycle stage, sex and location of origin and whether it was carrying any pathogens were recorded. Prof Richard Wall, who led the Big Tick Project team at the University of Bristol, said: The work that we have undertaken shows that ticks are extremely widely dispersed. The records that we have obtained appear to show that we have had an increase in tick numbers right across the country. What we are primarily concerned about are the diseases that ticks carry. In the UK, we have relatively low rates of the prevalence of these pathogens at the moment and, in contrast, in continental Europe they have much higher rates of disease. As there appears to be a rise in tick numbers, we need to be concerned and be aware of the potential for increasing problems. Prof Wall said pet owners should be aware of the risk in woodland or areas of long grass, but urban areas were also affected. Responding to the new data, conservationist Chris Packham said the good solid hard data which was a tremendously significant project had revealed some very shocking and surprising things about the distribution, the population and potential that ticks have to give diseases to our pets and ourselves. It was surprising ticks were not just found in isolated parts of the UK, but all over the UK, he said. Ticks do not jump or fly, they climb on to clothes if a person brushes against something that the tick is holding on to. Typically they can be found in woods, urban parks, heathland and fields. They can also be found in gardens. Lyme disease is transmitted by the bite of a tick infected with Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria. The tick acts as a vector. In the same way that a mosquito transmits malaria when it sucks blood from a person, the tick does the same to an animal or a person. According to Public Health England, it is estimated that there are 2,000 to 3,000 new confirmed cases of Lyme disease in England and Wales each year, although not all cases are confirmed by laboratory testing. About 15% of cases are in people who have returned from abroad. One initial symptom can be a red circular rash around the bite - called a bullseye rash. But this is not always present and so cannot be relied upon as a warning signal. Victims can develop flu-like symptoms along with muscle and joint pain. Lyme disease can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated it can seriously damage a person's health, including affecting the nervous system, causing meningitis or heart failure. The threat of Lyme disease (Lyme borreliosis) in the UK is still thought to be small compared with other countries - some 3% of ticks carry the bacteria. However, given the results of this study showing the high numbers of ticks across the country and with the serious potential consequences of Lyme disease, scientists are urging people to be aware of the risks and do their best to avoid being bitten. The Big Tick Project has launched an online tool that people can access to discover where ticks are most prevalent. Sarah Bignell was a very fit and active vet before she went on a walking holiday in Aberfeldy in Scotland in 2011. There was a small note in the cabin saying this was a Lyme disease hotspot but I did not think anything of it. I had no idea, she says. Six weeks later, she started suffering pain in her bones, joints and nerves. Doctors attributed her symptoms to other conditions, including multiple sclerosis or a brain tumour. However, Sarah's background meant that she knew to push for a Lyme disease test. She had been bitten by a tick - and she had been completely unaware of it. She also had no bullseye rash. It became agony virtually overnight for Sarah to deal with sound or light. She could not swallow, and when she could, it was agony. She had developed encephalitis. I spent eight-and-a-half months locked in a room, she explains. She needed constant care and could no longer look after her dog and cat. Over the next four-and-a-half years, Sarah had many close calls. I was in danger of dying. I am very lucky, she says. The pain used to be so severe and my quality of life so awful, at that point I was living hour to hour. If I had been well enough I would have ended up in Switzerland and I would not be here now - I am a vet and I am used to ending suffering. With extremely strong treatment, Sarah says she now only has one or two really bad days a month. I still get bouts of extreme fatigue. Days when I think - having a shower or putting the washing out - which one should I do today? Again I am lucky, there are loads of people not having the same treatment. So what does she think should be done about Lyme disease? It is not particularly about investment or research, Sarah says. It is a very cunning and specialised bacteria. It is so complicated and mimics so many other diseases and each effect needs individual treatment. It is about being aware and not getting bitten, she explains. I am not saying avoid the outdoors. text: The violence and murder of a protester in Charlottesville, Virginia, over the weekend has been attributed to far-right elements that descended on the city to demonstrate against the proposed removal of a statue of Confederate war hero Robert E Lee. These are external links and will open in a new window President Donald Trump attracted widespread condemnation on Saturday when he stated that there was violence on many sides in Charlottesville and initially failed to explicitly condemn the white supremacists who organised the demonstration. On Monday, he yielded to pressure to denounce the KKK, white supremacists and neo-Nazis. However, many conservatives contend blame should be shared by Antifa, a loosely affiliated group of far-left demonstrators. Critics contend the media tends to excuse violence by Antifa militants simply because they are confronting white supremacists and their repugnant ideology. What precisely is Antifa? The social causes of Antifa (short for anti-fascist or Anti-Fascist action) are readily identifiable as left-leaning. Most members oppose all forms of racism and sexism, and strongly oppose what they regard as the nationalist, anti-immigration and anti-Muslim policies that Mr Trump has implemented. Nevertheless, as their name suggests, Antifa focuses more on combating far-right ideology than promoting pro-left policy. Unlike the mainstream left, they do not seek to gain power through conventional channels - winning elections and passing legislation into law. Antifa is anti-government and anti-capitalist, and their methodologies are often regarded as more closely aligned with anarchists than the mainstream left. Antifa does not shy away from militant protest methods, including the destruction of property and sometimes physical violence. They were present at the 2017 Berkeley protests of far-right speaker Milo Yiannopoulos and at violent demonstrations against Donald Trump's inauguration; they were also present at Charlottesville. Much like the far-right, Antifa members around the world comprise a patchwork of groups, though the most active appear to be based in the US, the UK (under the name Anti-Fascist Action) and Germany (Antifaschistische Aktion). The German movement was established in 1932 to provide a militant far-left group to counter the rapidly rising Nazi party. They were disbanded in 1933 after Hitler took control of parliament and resurrected in the 1980s as a response to neo-Nazism after the fall of the Berlin Wall. President Trump's election appears to have been something of a touchstone for the Antifa movement, which has links with the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement and various anarchist groups. According to James Anderson, one of a group of people who run the popular anti-fascist and anarchist news site, It's Going Down, interest has surged since Mr Trump's election. The It's Going Down website, which received around 300 hits daily in 2015, now attracts between 10-20,000 hits a day. Since the events in Charlottesville on Saturday, the It's Going Down Twitter handle has gained 2,000 new followers. Whilst interest may have surged since Mr Trump's election, it is all but impossible to quantify how many people are active members of Antifa. Much like the far-right, chapters of Antifa are loosely connected and highly secretive, and organise mostly on message boards such as Reddit and over social networks like Twitter and Facebook. Antifa has become a popular topic for right-leaning websites and amongst conservative pundits. Fox News commentator and conservative speaker Erick Erickson states in The Resurgent, a conservative blog, that Antifa and the white supremacists are two sides of a common coin. The people dead in Charlottesville died because of one neo-Nazi, but there were dozen [sic] of people left bleeding in the streets because of Antifa. Meanwhile, a change.org petition lobbying Mr Trump to declare Antifa a domestic terror organisation has attracted nearly 100,000 supporters. Whilst Antifa has gained relatively little attention in the mainstream media, that may soon change. According to Mr Anderson, the events in Charlottesville over the weekend represent a sea change in how Antifa is perceived. This is a huge turning point and vindication for our movement, he said. We are working with Black Lives Matter, local clergy, this is not a movement that wants to be a lone group of militants, he said. This is about popular power. Sometimes that looks controversial - but this is a broad movement, and we are looking to engage a wide variety of people.

text: A 15-year-old Austrian synchronised swimmer suffered severe injuries when she and two other teenagers were in a collision with a bus in the athletes' village at the European Games in Baku. Vanessa Sahinovic suffered multiple fractures and a head injury - though she is not in a life-threatening condition. Luna Pajer, 15, received injuries to her arms and has also returned to Vienna for specialist treatment. The Austrian Olympic Committee (AOC) stated the team would still compete. It's a very, very sad day, said Dr Karl Stoss, AOC president. It's a tough day for the team. Sporting motives and goals are not important at this moment. Event organisers stated the matter was now being investigated by police. Team doctor Dr Robert Kandelhard accompanied Sahinovic and Pajer back to Vienna. The private aircraft belonging to Azerbaijan president Ilham Aliyev was used to transport the injured athletes back to their homeland. They have already landed and can receive the best care there, added Stoss. I'm not a medical expert but the treatment has been really good so far. It's a real shock for us and tough to motivate the team to focus on sport. The AOC stated the collision occurred at 08:30 local time on Thursday, when the athletes were walking on the pavement in the Olympic village. Verena Breit, 15, was also injured in the incident and she spent an hour in hospital in Baku with a thigh injury, but has now returned to the athletes' village. A Baku 2015 spokesperson stated: This is a terrible accident, and at this time our thoughts and concerns are for the athletes involved, their families and the remainder of the Austrian delegation. The inaugural European Games feature 20 sports, 16 of which will be included in next year's Olympics, and commence on 12 June. text: British artist Benedict Drew is aiming to challenge a culture of unhealthy body image through pieces of art work being unveiled across digital screens in the London Underground today. The works have been commissioned by Art on the Underground, an initiative established by London Underground in 2000, intended to champion contemporary art in London. The video work, entitled de-re-touch, draws inspiration from London's distinctive underground environment and manipulates the language of advertising. At eight seconds in duration, the video functions as a disruption to the images and advertisements presented to commuters on the Underground. De-re-touch features a close-up shot of an ear, a pulsating fist and flashing text - alluding to the mass of bodies people encounter both as tube passengers and in advertising. To complement the video, the artist has produced an electronic and experimental audio piece available for download, which is intended to be heard whilst travelling. Drew has been working across video, sculpture and experimental music since his time at art school in the 1990s. Can you tell me a bit about your background? How did you begin creating art? I was extremely privileged with my mother operating a gallery in Canterbury, so I was raised around exceptional art, it was like a family profession. I was very fortunate in that regard. I attended Middlesex Arts school in the 90s which was a remarkable time, some truly excellent people had emerged from that art school, people like Hayley Newman - she was completely inspiring. I then returned to complete an MA at the Slade School of Fine Art approximately 5 years ago, it was extraordinary. What drew you to this project? It's truly marvellous to be invited to work with Art on the Underground, it's an organisation that's very public and so I've been conscious of their works for considerable time. Being requested to create something about this sight of the underground and within that type of space was genuinely challenging. It was rather pleasant to engage with something I'm so familiar with. The underground is such an intense environment. What do you find distinctive about London's underground environment? It's a very communal space and you're very close to people you don't know and that's rather unusual, in a city where we are all attempting to mark our own territory. It's quite archaic at times as well and the underground can be extremely confusing. I think it's quite remarkable how well people conduct themselves towards each other on the tube, given the cramped nature of it all - people surrender their seats for the elderly, people will stand on the right side of the escalator. What is it about advertisements that frustrate you? We're confronted with distorted images of bodies, particularly female bodies. I view [advertisements] this, as a form of oppression. - We're confronted with photographs that aren't even genuine, they are digital drawings. Creating the video work that sits amongst actual advertisements was important to me and when given this project, I felt it was impossible not to address this matter. I acknowledge that I'm a white, male artist and I'm privileged in that respect and that perhaps I'm not the best person to be discussing this, however it's all of our problem. The misrepresentation of bodies through a male gaze is a destructive thing and it's harmful and distorts our perception - enough is enough. That's why the work is called de-re-touch, it's a call to cease re-touching photographs. The video is rather messy and scrawling and fast moving which is very different to the adverts it will be positioned amongst. I suppose it's a small protest against a world of image making that remains very dominant in advertising today - Why will this unrealistic, imagined idea of a perfect body sell me an item of clothing or a gym membership? It's so disturbed and it seems so obvious to state it. You appear to feel very strongly about body image and negative, self-perceptions - is this a theme you will explore further in the future concerning your work? I don't know. I often consider my work as songs, like this piece is gestural. What do you hope for people to take away from your work? I want people to cease accepting these distorted images of bodies, I'd like everyone to simply say it's unacceptable because, it is - it's oppression. When you see television programmes from the 60s and seventies and you just see obvious racism or homophobia, now you think Goodness, that's so unacceptable, like that wouldn't occur now which is good, we've progressed. I think there will be a time where we simply look back and think oh my goodness, what were people thinking? Is your artwork planned or instinctual? It's complicated. It's emergent and comes out of a set of things I indulge in the things I see, music I listen to, or books I've read - it's rather like constructing a cultural universe and then out of that emerges a voice and forms the way you think, my work is excreted out of that. Do you ever have artist's block? And if so, how do you break out of it? Deadlines help! [laughs] It's tough but I'm quite productive and I work extensively. What I like about art, as an arena, is that anything can be permitted into it - if you wish to make shoes, you could do it and that is artwork. I make drawings, prints, sculptures, videos and music; so when I'm blocked with one medium, I can jump onto another, which I find quite useful. How do you know when a piece is finished? How do you know when to stop? Generally the day before the exhibition opens [laughs]. There's a sense that you can tinker with things forever but it's quite good to maintain hold of immediacy, like if you overwork something you can lose the energy within it. I think that's the case across all forms of work. What's next for you? I'm currently in the British Art Show which opened in Leeds a few weeks ago and that travels around the country, so the next place it goes to is Edinburgh so I need to begin thinking of how the space will handle the installation. I'm also teaching at the Slade Fine School of Art. I want to attempt to make some more music too, perhaps make a record? Benedict Drew's new pieces can be seen across a wide range of underground stations across London.

text: There are few areas of life in which comic and actor Lenny Henry has not made an impact - working in theatre, television, film and charity. The performer declared he was extremely pleased regarding his knighthood, which was initially disclosed in newspapers last weekend. Throughout his five-decade career, he has weathered periodic criticism whilst retaining the devotion of the British public. Born to Jamaican parents on 29 August 1958 in the West Midlands town of Dudley, Lenworth George Henry rose to prominence in 1975 aged merely 17 following his appearance on the television talent programme New Faces. His triumphant performance resulted in the comedy series The Fosters and the anarchic children's programme Tiswas, where he began to develop his own energetic and spontaneous comedic style. Nevertheless, his subsequent career decision would trouble him for numerous years. He joined the Black and White Minstrel Show, in which blacked up white performers sang songs from the American South - a concept which has subsequently been extensively ridiculed and condemned. The comedian spent five years touring with the programme, which he has since described as a grotesque parody of black people. I rather wish it had never occurred, but I do not regret that I participated, he informed The Telegraph last year. Whilst it was a strange, reprehensible situation to occupy, I was performing in enormous venues and discovering how to engage an audience. His departure route was the BBC sketch series Three of a Kind, which also featured Tracey Ullman and David Copperfield. Initially broadcast in 1981, it employed cutting-edge video effects and Ceefax-style graphics to present a rapid-paced, joke-laden programme - though many of its peculiarities appear outdated today. Simultaneously, the alternative comedy movement was intensifying, and through television producer Paul Jackson, Henry encountered the pioneering comedians of the Comic Strip collective - one of whom was Dawn French. Initially, French was disapproving of the comedian's approach and the stand-up material he continued to employ for earning a living, which had developed in northern working men's clubs. text: More than 100 primary school janitors in Glasgow are due to begin another three-day strike over a pay dispute. Members of the Unison trade union seek additional remuneration for duties which they describe as dirty, unpleasant, involve regularly working outside or heavy lifting. They commenced boycotting certain responsibilities in January and conducted a walkout in March. The caretakers are employed by Cordia, an arm of Glasgow City Council, which stated it was endeavouring to ensure schools operated normally but could not exclude some disruption. A council spokesperson said: This dispute exists between the employers, Cordia, and the section of caretakers who are members of the trade union, Unison. Contrary to the impression conveyed in sections of the media it does not encompass every school caretaker and is incorrect to state that there have been no discussions to attempt to resolve the dispute. The council will continue to collaborate with Cordia to ensure that our schools and nurseries will remain open for business as usual. The spokesperson added: Our expectation is that all Breakfast Clubs will function normally during the three-day industrial action. However, parents and carers must be aware that this remains subject to alteration at short notice depending upon local arrangements and circumstances. A spokesperson for Cordia said the employer had exhausted all stages of its formal grievance procedure with the caretaking staff. He said: The organisation is collaborating closely with Glasgow City Council Education Services to ensure there is minimal disruption at affected schools. Parents should be assured that any playground matters will be addressed by suitably-trained personnel and that office staff remain on-site for school entry procedures. It must also be noted that whilst pupil welfare remains of paramount importance to Cordia employees based in schools, any safety-related issues such as fire precautions are always the responsibility of the head teacher and their staff who will continue to conduct full risk assessments throughout the duration of strike action. Unison said caretakers were entitled to a Working Context and Demands Payment which ranges from approximately £500 to more than £1,000. The union said that since members commenced boycotting certain duties, schools and playgrounds were not being cleaned as swiftly and thoroughly as previously. The union said: Unison has apologised to parents and carers for any inconvenience caused during the dispute. The union has also advised parents and carers that during the industrial action certain practices have emerged that could be considered as potentially detrimental for pupils and staff. The union has advised parents and carers to verify that hazards are not occurring in their school. Unison said possible hazards included glass, excrement, drug paraphernalia and warned of the dangers of sickness not being cleared within schools immediately or without proper protection.

text: Iran has confirmed some of its computer systems were infected with the Duqu trojan, but said it has found a way to control the malware. Security organisations had previously identified Iran as one of at least eight nations targeted by the malicious code. The spyware is thought to have been designed to steal information to help launch additional cyber attacks. The sender has not been identified, but researchers have discovered a reference to an American television programme in Duqu's code. The Iranian news agency, IRNA, reported that the nation's cyber defence unit was taking measures to combat the infection. The software to control the virus has been developed and made available to organisations and corporations, Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, head of Iran's civil defence body, is quoted as stating. All the organisations and centres that could be susceptible to being contaminated are being monitored. Mr Jalali said a final report into which organisations had been targeted was still being prepared. Last year the Iranian government accused the West of attempting to disrupt its nuclear facilities using the Stuxnet worm computer attack. Then in April 2011 officials said the country's facilities had been targeted by a second piece of malware called Stars. Officials now describe the Duqu attack as the third virus to strike Iran. The computer security specialist Kaspersky Lab said it believed that Stars was a keylogging programme that may have been part of the same attack that installed Duqu. Keylogging programmes are able to collect information about a computer system, take screenshots, search for files and capture passwords. The firm also provided additional detail about how Duqu worked based on its analysis of other targets. It said another unidentified company received an email from an individual identifying himself as Mr B Jason who requested a joint business venture. The firm believed this was a reference to the Jason Bourne books and spy films. The recipient was asked to open a Microsoft Word attachment that referenced the targeted company's name in its title, and thus did not appear to be spam. It said that for every victim a separate set of attack files was created using a different control server. The firm said this occurred at least 12 times. When the addressee opened the file the malware became active through a Truetype font exploit, but did nothing until it detected that there had been no keyboard or mouse activity for ten minutes. Kaspersky Lab said the font was called Dexter Regular and its creators were identified as Showtime Inc. This is another prank pulled by the Duqu authors, since Showtime Inc is the cable broadcasting company behind the television series Dexter, about a CSI doctor who happens also to be a serial killer, the report stated. The firm said the exploit then loaded a driver onto the system. Analysis of the driver suggested it was compiled as long ago as August 2007. If this information is correct, then the authors of Duqu must have been working on this project for over four years, the report stated. The firm said the driver then began a process that led to the Duqu trojan being installed allowing the attackers to introduce new modules, infect other networked computers, and collect information. The company said efforts to identify the attackers have been complicated by the fact that the suspects appear to have deactivated several of the control servers thought to have been involved in the attacks.

text: More than 150 beavers living in Tayside waterways have adapted well to life in Scotland, studies have found. The Scottish government is examining whether to permanently reintroduce the creatures to the wild, with an experimental programme ongoing in Knapdale, Argyll. Research determined that the Tayside beavers, which stemmed from escapes or unlawful releases, had adapted well to the local habitat. Plans to trap or kill the unauthorised beavers became contentious. The Scottish government consented to observe the circumstances for three years when the issue was previously discussed in 2012, confronted with the alternative choices of relocating the creatures or acknowledging their existence. The results from the Tayside Beaver Study Group will assist in informing a governmental determination on the future of the creatures in Scotland, together with an experimental reintroduction of the animals at Knapdale in Argyll. There had been concerns that the beavers might harm ecosystems or transmit diseases, but the study group established by Scottish Natural Heritage indicates they have adapted effectively, despite certain land management difficulties. The beavers, which belong to the Eurasian species formerly indigenous to Britain, have been discovered in rivers and lochs extending from Kinloch Rannoch, Kenmore and Crieff in the west to Forfar, Perth and Bridge of Earn in the east. It is probable they are of Bavarian or German origin. They are successfully breeding offspring and continue expanding throughout the Tayside region, and are clear of diseases concerning humans, domestic creatures and other wildlife. The most substantial impact beavers might have is upon agricultural land, for instance by constructing dams on the River Isla or the Tay and creating flooding on cultivated land nearby. Several methods of safeguarding trees from being gnawed and felled have proven successful, preventing flooding, but the effect of the animals through burrowing into flood banks and damming drainage channels has proven more challenging to manage. The study group stated this would require addressing if the beavers are to remain in position, as 70% of reported adverse impacts from beaver activity cited a financial cost as a result. David Bale, chairman of the study group and SNH's area manager for Tayside and Grampian, described the findings as extremely useful. He stated: The findings demonstrate there is no apparent risk of diseases being transmitted from the Tayside beavers to other animals, or indeed to humans. The genetic tests inform us that they would be appropriate for permanent reintroduction to Scotland, because they are Eurasian rather than North American beavers. They are also sufficiently varied genetically to constitute a reasonable first step towards a complete reintroduction if that was the decision of the Scottish Government. Our work documenting the impacts of beavers on land management interests has demonstrated that in many circumstances, beavers are likely to cause few concerns. But if they were to be permanently reintroduced, efficient, effective and affordable methods of managing and reducing potentially substantial impacts on intensively cultivated land and other interests would have to be discovered. The reports from the study group will be presented to the government, alongside other beaver studies, in May. A spokesman for Scottish Land and Estates stated: We have been an active participant in the Tayside Beaver Study Group and are eager that as much information as possible is available to the government before the decision on the future of the beaver in Scotland. We are not opposed to beaver ever being reintroduced to Scotland; we simply wish to ensure that any reintroduction, whatever the species, is only advanced following a thorough assessment and justification process which ensures a competent decision in which impacts on land management have been fully recognised and accommodated. Scottish Land and Estates was pleased to host the environment minister on a visit to some Tayside farmers recently to discuss beaver impacts on land management and we are pleased that the report acknowledges that the Tayside population does have an impact and that if they were to be permanently reintroduced, efficient, effective and affordable methods of managing and reducing potentially substantial impacts on intensively cultivated land and other interests would have to be discovered.

text: Babies born by Caesarean are at higher risk of becoming obese, especially compared with siblings born by vaginal delivery, a large study suggests. Publishing in JAMA Pediatrics, the researchers stated this could be attributed to infants delivered vaginally being exposed to beneficial intestinal bacteria which serve a crucial function in dietary regulation. The research tracked over 22,000 infants through to adulthood. However, specialists indicated there were probably numerous different elements involved. These encompass the mother's nutrition, whether she experienced diabetes whilst pregnant and whether the infant received breast milk. Infants delivered through Caesarean section are less prone to receive breastfeeding, and this has been demonstrated to result in a heightened obesity risk. Children's nutrition also influences their subsequent weight. Rates have been increasing consistently over recent years, according to the Royal College of Midwives. In households where children were delivered through different approaches, those delivered through Caesarean section were 64% more prone to obesity than their siblings delivered through vaginal birth. However, the scientists could not establish that Caesareans caused obesity or clarify the processes underlying the connection. Their most probable explanation was that variations in gastrointestinal microbiota, or beneficial intestinal bacteria, between infants delivered through different approaches could influence outcomes. Microbiota refers to the microorganisms that inhabit our bodies and which differ between individuals. Nevertheless, this connection is neither completely established nor comprehended. Most frequently Caesarean deliveries result from medical requirement, rather than choice, and consequently this risk would supersede any concerns mothers ought to have regarding the potential for future weight problems. Professor Neena Modi, President of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health stated additional research was required to determine whether Caesarean delivery caused obesity. Caesarean section may be life-preserving for women and their infants. Nevertheless many women are currently contemplating Caesarean section where no medical indication exists. It is crucial that they are informed about the potential for increased obesity risk in their children, to assist them in making an informed delivery decision. She continued: It is equally crucial for parents to concentrate on elements they can control which certainly affect their infant's health. This includes maintaining healthy weight at conception, and during pregnancy.

In general, studies on the subject suggest that there is some relationship between caesarean section and obesity. However, this relationship is not fully defined or understood. It can be transferred from mother to child, for example, through a procedure known as vaginal seeding, when the child is born by caesarean section, but the doctors say that it can lead to infection. text: Ian Bell has stepped down as captain of Warwickshire in all formats of the game to focus on batting. The 35-year-old captained the Bears to One-Day Cup triumph in September 2016, but fewer than 12 months later the county sit bottom of the Division One Championship table. Bell, who last represented England in November 2015, was recently omitted from the Bears' T20 team. This is the correct time for me to step down, Bell stated. As a senior player, I shall support the team in every way possible and I believe that our squad has extremely exciting times ahead. It has been an absolute honour to captain my home county over the past 18 months and my decision to step down is something that I have considered long and hard about over a period of weeks. Bell is to be succeeded by former England batsman Jonathan Trott as captain of Warwickshire's Championship team. The county's sports director Ashley Giles stated Bell made a courageous decision to concentrate on batting. Having him focused entirely on scoring runs for Warwickshire and Birmingham Bears is a tremendous asset to the club, Giles stated. Warwickshire, who secured limited-overs silverware in Bell's first season as captain, are in Division One relegation difficulty, having lost five of their nine matches - four of them by an innings. Bell, the most capped international in Warwickshire history, having played 118 Tests, 161 one-day internationals and eight T20 matches, has scored 345 runs from 14 innings, at an average of 24.64. He has not made a Championship century since April 2016. In the T20 Blast, he has struck 251 runs in 12 matches at a strike rate of 117.29, but he was dropped down the order after a sequence of poor scores at opener. Having not batted at all in the Bears' penultimate match, he was omitted altogether for the final group match on Friday, which the Bears won against Lancashire at Old Trafford to secure a place in the quarter-finals. New Zealand international Grant Elliott captained the side and will be expected to do so again for this Friday's last-eight tie against Surrey at The Oval. Bell, who was part of the Birmingham Bears T20 Blast title-winning side in 2014, also won the Big Bash in Australia last winter with Perth Scorchers.

text: Heinz has been taken to court in Australia after a watchdog said it falsely marketed a children's food as healthy. These are external links and will open in a new window The legal action concerns Shredz, a snack manufactured from fruit juice concentrate and pastes. Heinz, which rejects the allegations, states the bars possess a similar nutrition profile to sultanas. However, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) contends they should be classified as confectionery. It alleges the snack, targeted at toddlers, comprises more than 60% sugar. The product is no longer available, but was sold in three varieties - peach apple and veg, berries apple and veg, and strawberry and apple with chia seeds. The packaging declared it was 99% fruit and veg and displayed a selection of fruits prominently on the front. The ACCC's barrister, Tom Duggan, informed the Federal Court in Adelaide that the berries, apple and veg Shredz contained up to 68.7 grams of sugar per 100 grams. Nutritionist Rosemary Stanton, who assisted in drafting Australia's dietary guidelines, stated the bars were more similar to sweets than fruit or vegetables. Confectionery with added vitamins remains confectionery, she stated. She noted that whilst the product did contain some dietary fibre as well as various vitamins, the same applies to many unhealthy foods. Certainly, there are some positive nutrients present, just as there are positive nutrients in a Big Mac, she stated. The nutritionist recommended that Shredz, in her view, should be classified as an occasional treat. The food company firmly rejects the allegations of misleading marketing. In a statement, Heinz dismissed the ACCC's claims regarding the bars' packaging. The Shredz products were snack foods sold in small individually-packaged portions suitable for children aged one to three, it stated. The Shredz products possessed a similar nutrition profile to dried apple or sultanas. Heinz supports the Shredz products and their packaging. The legal proceedings were initiated in June 2016 following a complaint regarding toddlers' foodstuffs by campaign group the Obesity Policy Coalition. The ACCC is pursuing financial penalties, corrective notices and costs from Heinz.

text: High street stores had a disappointing October, according to figures from the Scottish Retail Consortium (SRC). Whilst overall sales throughout the United Kingdom increased by 0.9% compared with the preceding year, statistics for Scotland demonstrated a decline of 2.4%. Like-for-like sales, which exclude factors including new store launches, were 2.8% lower, according to the SRC/KPMG Scottish Retail Sales Monitor. Temperate autumn conditions may have suppressed clothing sales, whilst electrical goods consumers may be awaiting sales events. David McCorquodale, head of retail at KPMG, stated the statistics were a sobering reminder of the fragility of the economic recovery. He continued: There is no question the falls in Scottish retail sales in October, when measured against a relatively poor month last year, are disappointing for retailers when considered alongside predominantly dry conditions and temperatures only slightly warmer than average. Mr McCorquodale stated the weather was not cold enough for sales of coats or boots to perform well, noting that with consumers perhaps awaiting heavy promotions, retailers were left promoting themed products for Halloween. He stated the forthcoming weeks would be crucial for retailers with the strategies surrounding Black Friday and the approach to Christmas beginning to emerge. Overall food sales declined by 3.2% when compared with October 2014, with shops unable to fully capitalise on the Rugby World Cup after Scotland exited the tournament. With Halloween occurring on a Saturday this year, some Scots chose guising rather than shopping, the SRC indicated. Whilst Scotland experienced the driest and sunniest October since 2003, sales of autumn and winter garments were hindered, although Halloween fancy dress outfits were reported to have performed well. Consumers also refrained from purchasing electrical products in expectation of reductions in the Black Friday sales at the month's end and total non-food sales for October declined by 1.8% on last year. SRC director David Lonsdale stated: This rather lacklustre set of results presents a disappointing October overall for Scotland's retailers, with total retail sales declining again once falling shop prices are considered. It could be that consumers are simply waiting for even superior deals in the approach to Christmas, perhaps with consideration towards potential online discounting at the month's end, despite the reality that shop prices are already at record lows. With the focus on the Autumn Statement and the Scottish Budget over the forthcoming weeks, retailers will be hoping for measures which place money in people's pockets and which encourage them to invest and expand.

text: A BBC sitcom has been criticised as Islamophobic during a Commons debate about whether the BBC's programmes and staff reflect UK diversity. Labour's Rupa Huq criticised Citizen Khan's portrayal of a quite backward Muslim family. The programme was accused of stereotyping Muslims when it commenced in 2012 and its creator, Adil Ray, has informed the Radio Times he had received death threats. The BBC stated the award-winning programme had received considerable positive feedback. However Ms Huq, MP for Ealing Central and Acton, whose sister Konnie is a former Blue Peter presenter, said: I feel as though I didn't know what the year is ... you would think it's an everyday tale of a Birmingham Muslim family but they're really quite backward. Again, the Islamophobic point [Labour MP Chuka Umunna] made, it's a beardy weirdy chap and they're not quite cutting off people's hands but I can imagine that being in a future episode. Citizen Khan prompted complaints when it launched in 2012 and Mr Ray has previously stated he had received abuse from people who believed it was mocking Islam or stereotyping Muslims. However the programme has won various awards at the Royal Television Society and Asian Media Awards. A BBC spokesman said: The fact that Citizen Khan returns for its fifth series this year is a sign of its popularity with all audiences - indeed the programme has won several awards, including Best TV character at the Asian Media Awards. We've also had positive comments from members of the Muslim community for the programme and for creator Adil Ray who, like the family portrayed, is a British Pakistani Muslim. As with all sitcoms the characters are comic creations and not meant to be representative of the community as a whole. Ms Huq made her comments during a backbench debate called by former culture minister David Lammy. Mr Lammy accused the BBC of hiring the same old faces from the same old schools to the same old jobs and said he had been contacted by black and Asian BBC staff who said that they cannot speak up because they do not want to be labelled a troublemaker. He also said the Chinese community was totally invisible on the broadcaster and said the BBC's new charter must address the lack of progress in boosting ethnic minority representation. He said although the BBC ran 29 schemes aimed at ethnic minorities between 1999 and 2014, the situation was not improving and the proportion of ethnic minority staff had dropped from 13.1% in 2015 to 12.2% now. The Labour MP for Tottenham praised the diversity of children's television, BBC Three and documentaries but questioned whether there was sufficient diversity in management. He said: We all go into Broadcasting House and see the security, see black staff at the junior ends, but walk into that newsroom, think about the editorial decisions that are being made, and ask yourself, is that really representative of our country as a whole? Conservative MP Helen Grant suggested the BBC could voluntarily disclose data on the recruitment, retention, promotion and pay of staff from ethnic minorities. Labour Sunderland Central MP Julie Elliott said the BBC should reflect every region in the UK, adding that Salford - where MediaCity UK is a major BBC base - was not where the North ends. Earlier, Mr Umunna attacked the representation of our Muslim communities on television. He said rising Islamophobia could partly be blamed on broadcasters' use of community leaders who purport to speak for that community but have no mandate whatsoever to do so. The BBC said it was making good progress on becoming more diverse but said it would continue to develop new and innovative ideas to do even better and would soon be setting out its new diversity strategy. Almost half of our workforce is made up of women and the proportion of our workforce who are black, Asian and other ethnic minority is at an all-time high, the spokesman added.
