text: Two Welsh councils are facing legal action over claims they continue to uphold motions alleged to be racist. Jewish Human Rights Watch, an organisation established to tackle a purported increase in anti-Semitism within the United Kingdom, has secured the right to a judicial review hearing concerning motions adopted by Swansea and Gwynedd councils. The legal battle is thought likely to cost both local authorities tens of thousands of pounds. Both councils have rejected the allegations. In 2010, Swansea council was attempting to engage in contracts with Veolia, a firm which was also part of a consortium seeking to construct a railway system connecting Israel to settlements in occupied East Jerusalem. The motion presented to the council declared the project not only contravenes UN demands but is in contravention of international law. It additionally stated the United Nations has demanded that Israeli settlement activities and occupation should not be supported. Several councillors urged the council leader at the time and its chief executive to support the position of the UN in regards to the Israeli settlements in East Jerusalem, so long as to do so would not be in breach of any relevant legislation. They additionally urged the council not to conduct business with any company in breach of international law or UN obligations or demands, so long as to do so would not be in breach of any relevant legislation. The motion was passed in June 2010, though it remains non-binding. In 2014, Gwynedd council adopted a motion which demanded a trade embargo with Israel, condemning the attacks by the Israeli state on the territory of the Palestinians living in the Gaza Strip. It additionally stated: It must be made clear that the proposal condemned the Israeli state and not the Jewish religion. However, a solicitor representing Jewish Human Rights Watch, Robert Festenstein, stated: We would like to see the motions quashed. I don't understand why they would pass it in the first place. I mean, they wouldn't pass a motion saying something derogatory about women, so why would they do that about Jews? Why would they pass a motion which has a detrimental impact upon the relationship with Jewish people in Swansea, particularly in Wales generally? It has absolutely nothing to do with Swansea. In a statement, a Swansea council spokesman declared: On 10 March 2016, full council decided not to rescind the notice of motion that was passed on 17 June, 2010. The council has never boycotted Israeli goods and has no intention of doing so. For legal reasons, it would be inappropriate to comment further. A spokesman for Gwynedd council stated: It would not be appropriate for us to comment regarding this matter due to ongoing legal proceedings which the council is defending. JHRW will also be pursuing action against Leicester council. The judicial review hearing will commence on Wednesday and is anticipated to last for two days.

text: Roger Ailes revolutionised cable news in the US, creating the hyper-partisan, opinion-based environment that currently dominates the American media landscape. These are external links and will open in a new window It is probably appropriate, then, that the reactions to the death of the man who established conservative media giant Fox News have been sharply split along partisan lines. He was a monster who poisoned American society and made people more stupid and angrier. Or he was a great American patriot and a media genius. Given, aged 36, stands as the most-capped player in Republic history having represented his nation 125 times. The Aston Villa goalkeeper stated that his decision to retire from international football had been exceptionally difficult. I have devoted 16 years of my life to my nation and I possess tremendous affinity with Giovanni Trapattoni's squad, he continued. I would like to thank Giovanni, Marco (Tardelli) and Alan Kelly for their support throughout my period with the team. Shay Given: 125 caps from 1996-2012 Robbie Keane: 120 caps from 1998 to the present day Kevin Kilbane: 110 caps from 1997 to the present day Steve Staunton: 102 caps from 1988-2005 Damien Duff: 100 caps from 1998 to the present day I shall continue to be Ireland's greatest supporter and wish the lads well as they commence their new campaign. Given earned his international debut at 19 in the 2-0 friendly loss to Russia, and swiftly established himself as the long-term successor to Paddy Bonner. Following continued excellence for club and country, he played every minute at the 2002 World Cup but could not prevent Ireland exiting in the second round on penalties against Spain. Another decade would pass before he played tournament football again, with the conclusion of the wait proving bittersweet as both he and his country suffered a difficult period at Euro 2012 as Ireland departed at the group stage after losing all three matches and conceding nine goals. Whilst he did confirm his international retirement, a Football Association of Ireland statement noted that Given had indicated he would be prepared to make himself available for any emergencies in future. The FAI statement noted that Trapattoni had spoken at length with Given on Monday afternoon before the retirement was confirmed. Trapattoni commended Given for his outstanding contributions to Ireland throughout his 16-year international career. I understand the difficult decision that Shay was required to make and appreciate all of his efforts during his international career, stated the Republic manager. He is a strong player with excellent character and his passion for representing his country always shone through. It has been a pleasure to work with him during my time with the team. I wish him the very best in his future.

text: A 15-year-old girl who was sentenced to 100 lashes for engaging in premarital sex has had her punishment overturned by a Maldives court. The High Court determined on Wednesday that the girl, whose stepfather faces trial for raping her, had been incorrectly convicted by a juvenile court of engaging in premarital sex with another man. Premarital sex remains illegal in the Maldives, a popular tourist destination. The case sparked outrage amongst rights groups who welcomed the recent ruling. We are relieved that the girl will be spared this inhumane 'punishment' based on an outrageous conviction, which we hope has also been overturned, stated Polly Truscott, Amnesty International's deputy Asia-Pacific director. No-one should ever be prosecuted for sex outside marriage in the first place. Ms Truscott stated that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. She urged the Maldives government to annul all outstanding flogging sentences. In its judgement the court stated the sentence of the lower court was based on a confession that the girl made whilst she was suffering post-traumatic stress disorder. It stated that she had been unfit for trial after the alleged rape. The Maldivian government appealed on behalf of the teenager following international outrage in February to punish her with 100 lashes when she reached the age of 18. The girl - who cannot be named for legal reasons - was only charged after police investigating the rape allegations discovered that she had been having consensual sex with another man. President Mohamed Waheed stated that he was overjoyed with the ruling, his spokesman Masood Imad told the AFP news agency on Thursday. Mr Imad stated: It is the government's policy to protect victims, but we had to do it within the framework of the law. The case was sent for prosecution after police were called to investigate a dead baby buried on the island of Feydhoo in Shaviyani Atoll, in the north of the country. Her stepfather was accused of raping her and impregnating her, then killing the baby. The legal system of the Maldives, an Islamic archipelago with a population of some 400,000, incorporates elements of Islamic law (Sharia) as well as English common law.

text: The European Space Agency (Esa) has turned off one of its most successful ever missions. These are external links and will open in a new window LISA Pathfinder was launched into orbit in 2015 to demonstrate crucial technologies that might be employed on some future project to detect gravitational waves - the ripples that disturb space-time when black holes collide. The satellite spectacularly exceeded the objectives established for it. And that success led directly to the selection in June of the LISA mission. This billion-euro enterprise, which is conceived as a trio of satellites, is anticipated to launch between 2030 and 2034. It will incorporate many of Pathfinder's systems, including its all-important laser interferometer instrumentation that we now know possesses the means necessary to capture gravitational waves (GW) in space. LISA Pathfinder has demonstrated that LISA is feasible at full sensitivity, more than we could hope for, said principal investigator Stefano Vitale. I believe it has been a stepping stone for GW astronomy, and an incredibly rewarding experience for all the team involved. Thank you, and stay tuned on LISA! he told BBC News. Professor Vitale was invited to send the final kill commands to Pathfinder, which has been conducting its measurement demonstration 1.5 million kilometres from Earth in the sunward direction. The commands, dispatched from Esa's mission control centre in Darmstadt, Germany, tricked Pathfinder to reboot itself onto software that had already been corrupted. It meant the gravity probe was locked down, unable to run its subsystems including its transmitter. The only way you could recover the spacecraft would be to go up there and attach an umbilical and restart from another computer, explained Pathfinder's spacecraft operations manager, Ian Harrison. The kill procedure, more properly known as passivating the satellite, ensures there is no hazard to future missions through a collision or interference of radio communications. The Darmstadt team in April had already fired the thrusters on Pathfinder to move it away from its station - a popular location for many Sun-studying missions. It should now drift harmlessly around our star. There's a very, very small chance it could return to the Earth-Moon system; it's so remote but you cannot actually say it's zero, said Ian Harrison. The mission analysis actually examined the planetary positions 500 years into the future. Gravitational waves - Ripples in the fabric of space-time Gravitational waves are the big thing in science right now. Ground-based laboratories in the US have recently begun detecting them from coalescing objects that are 20-30 times the mass of our Sun. But by sending an observatory into space, scientists would expect to discover sources that are millions of times bigger still, and to sense their activity all the way out to the edge of the observable Universe. It should significantly advance our understanding of gravity and how it works; and perhaps even highlight some chinks in Einstein's so-far flawless equations. LISA will detect gravitational waves by bouncing laser light between three spacecraft flying in a triangle formation, where the sides of the triangle are 2.5 million kilometres long. The light beams will be measuring the precise positions of small, free-floating blocks inside the satellites. When gravitational waves pass through the triangle, the distance between blocks of the different spacecraft should change by tiny amounts - just fractions of the width of an atom. Laser science: Lisa Pathfinder's technology demonstration LISA Pathfinder's laser and gold-block monitoring system was shrunk down to fit inside a single satellite. As such, it could not itself detect gravitational waves, but the exquisite sensitivity of the instrumentation demonstrated that the metrology principles were sound. LISA Pathfinder did more than we ever asked for, said Paul McNamara, Esa's Pathfinder project scientist. It met its requirements on day one, the day we switched on its science. But we then met and surpassed the requirements of LISA. So, it's been a phenomenal mission. It's sad to turn Pathfinder off but at some point we have to look to the future, he told BBC News. text: UK scientists have successfully germinated seeds from the critically endangered Japanese Birch, a species that has just 21 known trees remaining. The seeds were gathered last year during an expedition to a remote location in mountains near Tokyo. Specialists suggest that the remaining wild population of Betula chichibuensis is too small to sustain itself without assistance. The young trees will be distributed to other arboretums in an effort to help preserve the threatened species. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) predicts a bleak outlook for the tree species in the wild. In its Red List of Threatened Species, it notes: The small population and restricted distribution... make it vulnerable to natural disaster or disease. The species is also self-incompatible, requiring two individuals to be close enough to cross-pollinate one another, making seed production uncertain in small subpopulations. It adds that there was also evidence of deforestation and habitat degradation in the area where the remaining trees are found, presenting a threat to the survival of this species. Growing hope During 2014, a team led by researchers from the University of Oxford Botanic Gardens, in conjunction with the University of Tokyo, embarked upon an expedition to collect seed samples from the threatened birch trees. Part of the team was Dan Luscombe, a dendrologist from the Forestry Commission's Bedgebury National Pinetum and Forest. He told BBC News: I suppose we got rather lucky in terms of being there at the right time. It is found in a very, very remote location and it is not an easy place to reach. It has got very, very low viability so we were very fortunate that we were able to collect numerous seeds... as birch seeds shatter and shed everywhere, so once it has done that you will never find it. Mr Luscombe estimated that the team were able to collect approximately 1,000 seeds, from which the team at Bedgebury Pinetum were able to produce roughly 100 seedlings. Ideally, we always cultivate trees that have been sourced from the wild so we are conserving the gene (resource), he explained. At the end of the day, we have got these extremely rare trees and their habitats are highly threatened. If you want to put them back or want to put them somewhere else then you need to know how to grow them. The long-term aim of the project is also to plant Japanese birch saplings in arboretums throughout the country, as well as working closely with their Japanese colleagues to protect the survival of the threatened species in the wild. We will share the love so then other arboretums can try cultivating this species in different climates and soils etc, Mr Luscombe added. He also explained that planting specimens of the trees in various parts around the UK would reduce the risk of the species being lost to storm damage or disease. There are also plans to plant a grove of the trees, known as a seed orchard, to provide an ongoing supply of seeds.

text: Almost 1,500 secondary pupils across Aberdeen have been given anti-weapons lessons in the wake of the killing of schoolboy Bailey Gwynne. Bailey, aged 16, was stabbed during an altercation with a fellow student at Cults Academy. The pupil's killer is serving nine years for culpable homicide. An independent review into Bailey's death in October last year determined his death was potentially avoidable had teachers been aware his attacker was carrying a knife. The sessions will be introduced next year to P7 students in Aberdeen. Critics have questioned whether students would inform on their friends. PC Seb Cook, from Police Scotland, addressed one S1 class at Aberdeen's Hazlehead Academy: You will have heard about the tragic incident that occurred a year ago in Aberdeen. We never, ever want anything like that to occur again. You pupils will never need to bring anything sharp or dangerous into school. Hazlehead head teacher Jim Purdie stated: It is not simply about carrying weapons or blades, it is about the legal aspect of that, and then the consequences for the students, for their families, for their friends. There is an expression we frequently use, which is if we do not know things are occurring we cannot do anything about them. We are constantly reminding our children to accept responsibility. If there is something that is troubling them, they know whom to tell. One student, asked what they would do if they knew someone possessed a weapon, told BBC Scotland: I would probably just approach a teacher, perhaps even approach the person and simply say 'why are you doing that, consider the consequences'. Another stated: People say do not grass up a mate, but if it is serious I think you should. Police Scotland was asked about incidents involving weapons in schools. Supt Andy McKay, from Police Scotland Safer Communities, stated: Police Scotland relies on local authorities to report all incidents of weapon possession so that accurate figures can be compiled. Following the report into Bailey Gwynne's death, Aberdeen City have been working closely with Police Scotland to ensure each and every incident of weapon possession is reported, however it will be for other local authorities to consider this recommendation moving forward. As a result, the figures compiled to date may not provide a true reflection of the national picture regarding possession of weapons in schools due to inconsistent reporting and recording methods. Figures represent a snapshot in time, and may not accurately reflect a divisional or national perspective. A strategy designed to prevent knives and weapons entering Aberdeen schools was approved last month. Staff will be provided with clarity regarding the recording of incidents in schools, student searches and when and how to confiscate weapons, including knives. Other actions approved by the council include providing professional learning opportunities to teachers so that they can deliver anti-weapon and knife crime lessons. A review, conducted by child welfare professional Andrew Lowe, made 21 recommendations.

text: When Wes Metcalfe bought a cucumber from a Tesco shop in Dinnington, South Yorkshire, he did not expect it to come with a dead worm. He was so repulsed by the creature trapped within the packaging that he turned to Facebook to inform Tesco why it would be some time before he enjoyed another cucumber sandwich. Tesco's humorous response and Mr Metcalfe's reply to it have become viral. It began on Saturday, when he posted: Dear Tesco, yesterday I bought one of your excellent cucumbers to prepare my favourite meal - a cucumber sandwich. Upon unwrapping my cucumber, I found a worm within the packaging. I thought - finally, at last Tesco have developed something to surpass Aldi's complimentary-spider-with-bananas promotion. I enthusiastically called the children downstairs to come and meet our new companion. We chose to call him William. Our new companion appeared to be quite unresponsive, we simply attributed it to him being drowsy and decided to allow him some time to recover. Twenty-four hours later and William still has not moved - upon closer examination he appears rather flat (again, see photograph) and I believe he may be deceased. Well... I am no veterinarian, but I think the tight shrink wrapping on the cucumber may have compressed and killed William. I know Aldi's banana spiders were lethal, but at least they possessed some vitality in them. I now have three very distressed children, a worm funeral to organise and to crown it all I have completely lost my appetite for cucumber sandwiches, which as everyone knows are a staple at any wake. So come on Tesco, wriggle your way out of this predicament. Tesco's equally playful response commenced: I shall be heading to a muddy festival shortly, trudging through the fields of damp grass and soil much like William would have during his happier days. This means I will not be able to attend on the day unfortunately, though I have decided to compose a poem, which I hope you can recite on the day. Would that be acceptable? Here it is: 'An ode to William. Although life takes peculiar turns, we can all learn from William the worm. Let us assemble, light a candle to burn, and commemorate the life of William the worm. Lights shine bright, let us eat sponge cake through the night! Because there are many lessons to learn. He wriggles many miles; he brought us many smiles, so we stand confident and firm... William will return, very much like Arnie, though now we shall all check before we make a sarnie!' #PoemsforWilliam. Wishing you well, Rob - customer care. So touched was Mr Metcalfe by Tesco's tribute, he shared a photograph of William the worm's grave, with the post: Funeral update: well what can I say? It has been an emotional day, but the funeral proceeded without incident. Tesco Rob, we read out your poem, and there was not a dry eye among us. Continuing with the poem theme, here is another, which I think summarises today quite nicely. #RIPWilliam #justiceforwilliam #poemsforwilliam. As we assemble here today for William the worm, It is time to reflect on the lessons we can learn. Now, this poor worm's life was terminated far too early, After he was crushed to death in a cucumber I purchased. Tesco, please do not let this occur again. Do not let William's life be lost in vain. But let us not focus on who is to blame. Tesco have apologised acknowledging their shame. As we return William's body into the soil, Please do not shed a tear. Instead, think of the good, For William's death has brought us all here, Sharing jokes and spreading cheer. Before his death, William was entirely unknown, Spending his days in the mud alone. But now his name has travelled wide and far, William the worm - the viral superstar! The exchange did not conclude there. Tesco responded with their interpretation of Wonderwall by Oasis, and Mr Metcalfe replied with a version of Blur's Parklife, which he renamed Worm life. The Facebook exchange has been shared more than 30,000 times and has received more than 10,000 comments since being posted on Saturday. Mr Metcalfe, a trainee electrician from Sheffield, told BBC News: I enjoy making people laugh, but you simply cannot predict what will become viral. I think it became popular because Tesco's responses were so excellent. If they had not replied in such an entertaining manner, then it probably would not have become so significant on the internet. I have received a mostly positive response, but one lady did not understand the joke and reprimanded me for making a fuss about the worm. Mr Metcalfe said Tesco had offered him a £10 gift voucher to cover the cost of William the worm's funeral. I think Tesco have more than compensated for it, he said. If people can laugh about it all, then that is wonderful. There is sufficient seriousness in the world. Mr Metcalfe also confirmed he would resume eating cucumber sandwiches again.

text: Mark Wigglesworth has resigned as musical director of the English National Opera. In an electronic message, he stated he was departing because the ENO was evolving now into something I do not recognise. The organisation, which has endured a period of upheaval, announced he would leave at the end of the current season. He will continue to fulfil his contractual obligations as a conductor and looks forward to continuing to work with the wonderful musicians of ENO. Wigglesworth was declared as the organisation's new musical director in 2014. He stated at the time he regarded his appointment a huge privilege. He subsequently stated the organisation would continue to take risks and undertake adventurous work despite funding reductions. In the electronic message, which he dispatched to colleagues, the 51-year-old stated the ENO's plan for the future is one that the board and chief executive have always known I cannot support. As hard as I have attempted to argue to maintain what I believe to be the fundamental pillars of our identity, I have failed to persuade others of this necessity, he stated. I believe in efficiencies that increase our value for money and do not lose the opportunity of performing the highest quality opera to the largest number of people. Wigglesworth has been a regular at the Proms since 1991, conducting works by composers including Olivier Messiaen and Richard Wagner. His departure follows a series of difficulties at the English National Opera. In February last year, the Arts Council of England reduced the ENO's core funding to the organisation by £5m as it removed the organisation from its national portfolio of organisations for 2015-18. Two months subsequently, the ENO announced it was reducing ticket prices in an attempt to secure its financial future. Earlier this year, the organisation asked members of the chorus to transfer from a 12-month to a nine-month contract. The proposal resulted in the ENO chorus voting to strike over the changes, which they stated amounted to a reduction in pay. The chorus stated it would not appear in part of a performance of Akhnaten at the London Coliseum as part of the strike action. The ENO argued at the time that it faced bankruptcy if the proposed changes were not implemented. The pay dispute was subsequently resolved and the strike action called off.

text: When Avi Yaron was 26 years old he had a motorbike accident - a day he describes as the luckiest of his life. As physicians scanned his head to examine for damage, they discovered a tumour deep within his brain which might otherwise have remained undetected. And in 1993 the electronic engineering student from Israel was informed the mass they had just found was situated close to regions of the brain vital for movement and thought. He now confronted a choice - to undergo complex, invasive surgery that carried a risk of paralysis, or to discover another way. After a year of searching, Mr Yaron encountered a surgeon in New York who removed part of the tumour successfully, and samples revealed it was benign. The engineer was then advised to wait until technology had advanced sufficiently for the next operation to be less risky. But for Mr Yaron this was not an option. The possibility remained it could exert pressure on parts of the brain as it grew. He said: I was young and thinking of starting a family. I could not be passive about this sword hanging over my head. After five years of seeking out key surgeons and experts in technology, Mr Yaron had the remainder of the tumour removed during a conventional operation - with good results. But this epic search for better surgical options continued to weigh on his mind. He kept thinking of and experimenting with ways to perform brain surgery in a less invasive way. And over the last few years he perfected a method to perform surgery on the brain - in 3D. In the last 25 years minimally invasive surgery has become commonplace for the relatively easy-to-reach areas of the body, such as keyhole surgery on the abdomen and womb. And more recently surgeons have been able to use scopes (tube-like instruments) in brain surgery too. During these procedures a thin scope is inserted via a surgically-made or naturally-occurring port in the skin. A camera attached to the end of the scope transmits images to a screen for the surgeon to see. And surgical instruments are passed down the scopes to take samples of tissues or remove masses. Early versions allowed surgeons to examine 2D images in standard definition, evolving over the last decade into more high definition systems. Surgeons constantly translate these 2D images into 3D as they operate, much as we do when watching 2D television screens. More recently 3D technology has become available for certain types of operation. But 3D brain surgery has been a much harder feat to achieve. In neurosurgery the scopes need to be very small in diameter so they can pass through narrow ports such as the nose. But most 3D scopes rely on two optical channels - each containing a single sensor. Each sensor collects two separate images that are then combined together to give the appearance of three dimensions as a user looks at the screen - mirroring the way human eyes see. It has so far proved difficult to make an instrument small enough that is able to produce the high-quality images neurosurgeons require. But Mr Yaron says his team have solved this puzzle by thinking laterally. Rather than copying human anatomy, their scope mimics the compound eye of a bee. The scope contains a miniature sensor with hundreds of thousands of micron-sized elements, each looking in slightly different directions and mapping the surgical field from many different points. Using software this is translated into images for the left and right eye. Using this single sensor system, Mr Yaron's company, Visionsense, have produced a scope small enough to operate on the brain. Shahzada Ahmed from the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham who carried out one of the first 3D endoscopic neurosurgical procedures in the UK says: A bit like going to the cinema, Avatar is a great film in HD but it is an even better one in 3D. When I use the scope there is a better appreciation of depth and the pictures feel more real to me. It also allows him to see his instruments in 3D, which he feels gives him a better understanding of where they are in relation to key parts of anatomy. A number of studies are now being conducted to see if the 3D approach is better than commonly used 2D high definition systems. Hani Marcus, a neurosurgeon at the Hamlyn Centre, Imperial College London recently compared the scope to conventional tools, using a model brain and surgeons who are novices to this endoscopic approach. The study suggests the 3D aspect is beneficial - leading to a faster operation and subjective improvements in depth perception. But Mr Marcus says it would be a mistake to automatically assume 3D is definitely better than 2D, and believes further studies are needed. There are a number of potential problems - surgeons who are already accustomed to seeing 2D may find this approach hard to get used to. And just as some people don't enjoy watching 3D films and feel slightly nauseous, the same may hold for some surgeons. But for Mr Yaron, whose scope is now being used in the US and across Europe, this invention is the bright side of an issue that has been weighing on his mind for many years. He says: If I hadn't had this accident I wouldn't have been able to offer this solution. And I really know how it feels to need options.

text: Sony's film The Interview has been pulled after hackers threatened a 9/11 style attack on any cinemas which screened the comedy. The film, which features Seth Rogen and James Franco, depicts a fictional scheme to assassinate Kim Jong-un. A leaked sequence from the picture showed the dictator's head consumed in a slow-motion explosion. Cyber-attackers, identifying themselves as the Guardians of Peace, threatened a bitter fate for audiences of the dreadful production. There has been conjecture that North Korea orchestrated the cyber-assault, which exposed scripts from forthcoming films alongside stars' wages and staff members' private correspondence. Whilst North Korea denies participation, they have declared the picture an act of terrorism and pledged merciless revenge if it were distributed. Most recently they characterised the cyber-attack as a righteous deed and suggested it may have been executed by its supporters and sympathisers. Nevertheless, perhaps North Korea has greater concerns than a film described by one reviewer as muddled muck. It might wish to begin by examining these very genuine problems its population confronts. WARNING: this report contains information some may find distressing. More than one quarter of all North Korean youngsters have experienced stunted development from malnutrition. Two-thirds of the populace, roughly 16 million individuals, remain uncertain about their next meal's source, according to the UN. This food shortage means that North Korean males are, typically, between 3 - 8cm (1.2 - 3.1in) shorter than males in South Korea. North Korea has expanded its military stockpile and atomic programme rather than assisting to nourish its populace, another United Nations study discovered. The circumstances have worsened as households' mobility is severely restricted by the regime, making it difficult for them to obtain food. Earlier this year, Michael Kirby, who headed a UN Commission of Inquiry into North Korean human rights breaches, informed BBC World Service that households were being compelled to utilise their relatives' ashes as fertiliser owing to shortage of alternative resources. Meanwhile substantial amounts of state funds are expended on the Supreme Leader and the promotion of his personality cult. Kim Jong-Il, Kim Jong-un's deceased father, allegedly spent £700,000 annually on Hennessy cognac. The appalling circumstances in North Korean labour camps or detention facilities exceed what even the most sadistically inclined scriptwriter could conceive. Within these facilities, detainees are compelled to perform gruelling labour, tortured if they fail to follow regulations, abandoned to perish when wounded and intentionally starved to death. Former prisoner Jeong Kwang-il, who escaped North Korea in 2003, informed a UN committee he lost one third of his body mass in three months at a detention facility. Then they suspend you so you cannot stand or sit, he stated. If you are suspended like that for three days, four days, you urinate, you defecate, you are completely dehydrated… [it] was so agonising that I felt it was preferable to die. Detainees are compelled to inter the remains of those who perished. Except during winter they cannot because the earth is frozen solid, so they are kept in a storehouse until March. Jeong Kwang-il wrote in The Guardian: When we entered the storehouse to remove the corpses, it was truly horrific since the bodies were decomposed and consumed by rats. We interred corpses as if they were rubbish. No one knows or recalls who they were. Parents, grandparents and offspring are all penalised for the transgressions of one family member. Shin Dong-hyuk, 30, is thought to be the first individual born in a detention camp who succeeded in escaping. Shin believes that he and his household were incarcerated because two of his uncles fled to South Korea during the Korean War. He witnessed his own mother's execution. Despite numerous reports condemning North Korea for how it treats its population, the nation dismisses these as misconceptions. Earlier in September North Korea published a 50,000-word document stating its population enjoy authentic human rights and there had simply been serious misconceptions. On Tuesday North Korea's UN representative, Ja Song-nam stated that the so-called 'human rights issue' in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is politically manufactured and instead requested the United Nations Security council to examine reports of CIA torture. text: Six young voters from Wales who took part in an election debate geared around young people have described it as brilliant to a lot of hot air. More than 100 individuals aged 18-24 confronted five politicians in the debate organised by BBC's Newsbeat. Trust emerged as the principal issue but tuition fees, gender equality and the voting age also prevailed. Voters were accompanied by politicians from five major parties at Leeds City Museum on Tuesday evening. Sam Gyimah, representing the Conservatives, Sadiq Khan from Labour, Sal Brinton representing the Liberal Democrats, Mhairi Black from the SNP and Rhun ap Iorwerth, representing Plaid Cymru were all under scrutiny. BBC Wales tracked six Welsh audience members to capture their perspectives on the debate. Guto Gwilym, 21, Lampeter It was excellent to have that one hour which was entirely concentrated on young people and the issues we face. It was very much an evening where politicians listened to what we have to say and I very much hope that they have been making notes. For me - one matter we do need to address urgently now is diversity amongst MPs. Aled Illtud, 20, Aberystwyth It was pleasant to witness a different type of debate - it was much more dynamic. I did feel like there were more questions than there were responses but that perhaps reflects how passionate the audience members were. We appeared to have a barrage of questions directed at the politicians. It was wonderful to witness but I would have preferred more responses from the politicians. Peter Gillibrand, 18, Carmarthen I believe the debate focused too heavily on tuition fees. I would have preferred to hear more about what politicians would do for disabled people like my brother. He is severely autistic but the funding for many of the services he utilises has been reduced. I am a Plaid Cymru voter but I believe the real people who prevailed in this debate were the SNP and Lib Dems. The SNP lady was truly inspirational and the lady from the Lib Dems presented herself well too. She said 'look we made an error on tuition fees' but you felt she did genuinely care about young people. Robyn Holley, 21, Cwmbran It was everything I anticipated it to be - people shouting, numerous opinions swirling around and politicians simply being politicians. I was not impressed by what they had to say - it was simply a lot of empty rhetoric. I have contemplated not voting but I believe I will probably participate if only to attempt to change things. Gwion Dafydd, 20, Pembrokeshire I believe a couple of politicians said the correct things. I appreciated that Labour, Plaid Cymru and the Lib Dems all supported reducing the voting age for 16 and 17 year olds. It demonstrates they care about what young people have to say. I have greater respect for some of the parties now. Rhys Taylor, 21, Bangor I stood up and made a remark during the discussion on tuition fees. I believe it is important that politicians acknowledge when they have made an error and apologise if they cannot follow through with their promises. It is not often that we hear politicians apologising but the more we can get them to admit to their mistakes the more we will be able to trust them.

text: When BBC Alba was launched in 2008, as a collaboration between the BBC and the Gaelic TV body MG Alba, it was a huge achievement for supporters of the Gaelic language. They had long contended a dedicated channel would deliver superior service for Gaelic speakers than individual Gaelic programmes on the principal channels. They also contended that a dedicated Gaelic channel could fulfil a major role in helping to protect the future of the language itself. Uniquely for a BBC service within the UK, it constitutes a joint venture. Some of the programmes are funded by the BBC - others are the responsibility of MG Alba, financed by government money. However, there was disappointment once it became apparent that the channel would only be transmitted on satellite television - watched in 43% of Scottish homes - although programmes can also be accessed online through the BBC iPlayer. Supporters contended it was essential that the channel should also be transmitted on Freeview, like all the other public service channels. BBC management developed a plan which would make this feasible. The disadvantage was that it would mean that the BBC's radio stations would have to come off Freeview whenever BBC Alba was on the air. The BBC Trust postponed a decision earlier this year as it was also due to carry out a broader review on how all BBC services should be transmitted. It has now endorsed the scheme after extensive research, although no date has been established for BBC Alba's appearance on Freeview. Some are optimistic it will appear on Freeview by the time the digital switchover takes place in central Scotland next May and June. In practice, BBC Alba will be accessible in almost every home in Scotland and the challenge for the station will be to demonstrate that it can offer value to as many people as possible and appeal to viewers who cannot speak Gaelic. Some newspaper commentators have claimed it is challenging for Alba to show it is achieving this, as normal viewing figures are not available for the station. Instead, other forms of research have been employed. It is understood one reason for this is that the sample used to compile normal ratings does not include viewers in the islands of Scotland. Although the BBC's radio stations will no longer be transmitted on Freeview once this occurs, it is possible that they may return in the future as a result of technological improvements. Despite this, the main radio stations will still be transmitted on FM and medium wave as usual whilst the digital stations - such as 1 Extra and BBC7 - will still be available on satellite, cable, through digital radios and online. Deciding between the merits of BBC Alba and the radio stations was a challenging decision. However, the alternative to this could have involved the BBC purchasing capacity on another part of the Freeview system at commercial rates - capacity which might not have been able to reach viewers served by relay transmitters. The BBC Trust has also ruled that Gaelic programmes should remain on BBC Two Scotland, although it will no longer be specified as the BBC's key channel for Gaelic. However, the way Gaelic is scheduled on BBC Two Scotland is changing. Gaelic programmes were transmitted in a two-hour block on Thursday evenings until recently. Individual programmes are now appearing in a variety of slots across the schedule although the overall amount of Gaelic in peak viewing hours should remain the same.

Judge John Burgess said Khatkar, who declined to attend sentencing at Derby Crown Court, was a highly manipulative man who appears to have no feeling for others. text: Official figures released today by the Forestry Commission show that the government is falling far short of its own tree-planting targets. The Woodland Trust states that the drastic decline in new woodland planting is appalling and could result in serious environmental consequences. It has accused the government of missing its target in England by 86 per cent. The environment department, Defra, stated it remained committed to expanding woodland cover. Data released today by the Forestry Commission, the government body responsible for expanding Britain's woodlands, reveals that 700 hectares (seven km2) of woodland was planted in England last year. The target was to plant 5,000 (50 km2). Austin Brady from the Woodland Trust stated: These figures are all the more shocking against the backdrop of the growing evidence of the importance of trees and woods in tackling air pollution, improving water quality and offering scope to deliver natural flood management. Something is drastically wrong with the way woodland planting is being supported across the various government departments that share responsibility for trees and woods. The government has pledged to plant 11 million trees between 2015 and 2020. Environment Minister Elizabeth Truss has spoken of their importance in helping to prevent flooding. Speaking in the House of Commons in December 2015 she stated she wanted to examine the environment on a catchment level, making sure that we put in place tree-planting programmes that can both reduce flood risk and improve the environment. However, Mr Brady stated: There have been lots of really interesting and well-informed conversations - all the signals are positive, but the system of delivering the grants and getting things moving on the ground is not matching up with the fine words. It is not fit for purpose. The UK is one of the least wooded nations in Europe. Only 10 per cent of England is covered in trees. Average woodland cover in the EU is 37 per cent. Government funding has been made available but grant schemes for planting trees changed last year. There have been delays in processing contracts and payments. Under the Countryside Stewardship Scheme there are rigid rules determining the amount of land that needs to be planted and at what density to qualify for a grant. There is also confusion around whether planting trees disqualifies farmers from part of their EU farm subsidy payments. This leads many farmers and landowners to avoid new planting altogether. A Defra spokesperson stated: Woodland cover in England is at its highest level since the 14th Century and we are committed to growing it even further. The Countryside Stewardship scheme is an important opportunity to help expand our nation's woodlands, which is why the Forestry Commission is supporting landowners to make applications through a series of workshops and online support. The Woodland Trust states that more flexible schemes are needed to allow landowners with more limited space to be able to qualify for funding. There also needs to be more clarity. Currently the government departments involved in tree management include: Defra, the Forestry Commission, Natural England and the Environment Agency. text: An NHS trust has apologised unreservedly after a misdiagnosis resulted in a three-year-old boy having his legs and seven fingers amputated. Lou Harvey-Smith brought son Reuben to Ipswich Hospital in July 2015 following a burn injury. Two days subsequently she returned with him, presenting with fever, and received a diagnosis of tonsillitis. He subsequently received a diagnosis of toxic shock syndrome and underwent amputations. The trust acknowledged full liability and settlement discussions are proceeding. Following treatment at the hospital for the accidental burn, Reuben developed fever and throat pain. Ms Harvey-Smith returned with him and received antibiotics for tonsillitis. The subsequent day the child became critically unwell. His mother contacted the burns unit at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital seeking a second opinion. Medical staff suspected toxic shock, a life-threatening infection that would have resulted from bacteria entering the wound and releasing toxic substances into Reuben's bloodstream. The boy was transported urgently back to Ipswich Hospital then moved to St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, London, where medical staff performed the amputations. Ms Harvey-Smith, 41, from Chelmondiston, near Ipswich, stated: [Reuben] examined his amputated legs and declared 'poorly feet gone, get new ones.' He simply accepts the situation and continues forward. Nevertheless, she pursued legal proceedings against Ipswich Hospital NHS Trust which acknowledged toxic shock represented a significant possibility given the child's symptoms at that time, and amputation might have been prevented through earlier diagnosis and treatment. Ms Harvey-Smith's legal representative, Tim Deeling, stated: It proves extremely troubling they understood the connection between burns and toxic shock, yet failed to consider this possibility for Reuben's situation. The trust has provided an interim payment of £50,000. Additional training has been delivered to staff regarding recognition of septic shock syndrome warning indicators, he stated. The trust remained committed to ensuring that Reuben receives appropriate compensation enabling him to access the care, prosthetics and equipment required throughout his lifetime, he added.

Ronny Gal of Bernstein Research said, “We expect Mylan to face continued criticism over the price increases, and we anticipate increased pressure on the Food and Drug Administration to allow competition to enter the market.” Mylan’s chief executive, Heather Bresch, said that the company had spent hundreds of millions of dollars improving the product since buying it from Merck in 2007. The decision to launch a generic version of the EpiPen is a commercial decision, she said. The case is unusual because the brand-name product is still protected by a patent, and the competing therapies have failed to receive regulatory approval. In her view, the American health system was to blame for the price rise, as was the fact that Mylan only received $274 out of the $600 price for the medicine, the rest being shared by health insurance companies, pharmacists and other parties. The product generated $1 billion in turnover for Mylan last year. After the controversy over the price of EpiPen, Mylan shares fell about 12% last week. How much people pay for EpiPen, may depend on insurance coverage. The actress Sarah Jessica Parker, who had endorsed EpiPen, announced last week that she was ending her relationship with Mylan. In an earlier post, she had spoken about the importance of the drug for her family because of her son's peanut allergy. In the afternoon the shares were unchanged at 43.04 on the New York Stock Exchange. Other pharmaceutical companies such as Valeant, Turing and Pfizer have also been under fire in recent months for sharp increases in their prices.

text: Former England captain David Beckham is being cast away for the 75th birthday celebrations of BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs next weekend. More than 3,000 guests have appeared on the programme since its initial transmission on 29 January 1942. Presenter Kirsty Young stated that having Beckham selecting his favourite tracks for the anniversary programme was the perfect gift. Beckham, 41, declared music has been a huge element of his family's existence. He is wed to former Spice Girl vocalist turned fashion designer Victoria Beckham and the couple's youngest son Cruz, 11, issued a Christmas-themed single last month. It remains unknown whether he has selected any of his wife's hits with the pop group, or any of her solo projects. What is Desert Island Discs? Beckham declared: I'm delighted to join Desert Island Discs for its 75th anniversary celebrations. Music has been a huge part of my - and my family's - life and it is a real pleasure to highlight that on such an iconic programme. Young commented of her guest: His sporting legacy is of course extraordinary. And along with his charisma, cultural impact and humanitarian work, he is a modern man of many parts. He'll be a fascinating guest to welcome on to my little interview island. Desert Island Discs' anniversary will be commemorated with a three-hour programme on BBC Radio 4 Extra on 28 January, presented by Young, featuring some of the guests from previous programmes. They include Cilla Black, discussing her early career performing with The Beatles, and Richard Dimbleby, recounting taking a cutlery set from Hitler's bunker after being amongst the first correspondents to visit it following the dictator's death. Extracts from recently rediscovered episodes that are being incorporated into the programme's online archive will also feature. The programme featuring Beckham will restore the sound of the sea to the opening and closing of the show for the first time since the 1960s. BBC Radio 4 and Radio 4 Extra controller Gwyneth Williams stated: A sure way to uncover an elusive British national identity is to listen to this programme week after week. The broad range of guests is a measure of contemporary talent and achievement, and the music opens up different eras and prompts emotional memory in all of us. text: Derbyshire were denied a chance of a first Championship win for two years as bad light and rain saw their match with Nottinghamshire end in a draw. Rain delayed play until 13:45 BST and Nottinghamshire, who resumed on 313-6, added merely 36 runs before being dismissed for 349 as Tom Taylor (4-67) claimed three swift wickets. Pursuing 216 for victory, Wayne Madsen struck 61 and compiled 67 alongside Shiv Thakor (25). Derbyshire stood at 190-5, requiring 26 from 7.5 overs, when rain drove the players from the field for the final occasion. The outcome proved cruel on Derbyshire who had appeared positioned for their first Championship victory over Nottinghamshire since 2002. Following the visitors' decline to 36-2, Madsen and Thakor struck at above five per over to shift the match in their direction. With the winning target within reach, the players initially departed for poor light which left Derbyshire with nine overs to achieve the 36 runs needed for triumph. The resumption lasted seven deliveries and during that period Alex Hughes (24) was caught lbw by Luke Fletcher (2-46), but torrential rain forced the players from the pitch once more with Derbyshire tantalizingly near to a memorable victory. Nottinghamshire advance 13 points ahead of second-placed Kent who did not compete this week, whilst Derbyshire sit eighth with 36 points from five fixtures. Nottinghamshire head coach Peter Moores stated: I believe we must acknowledge them. Derbyshire occupied an excellent position to secure the match. The timing of the weather proved unfortunate for them, but recognition goes to their performance. Currently with all the weather applications available we receive numerous forecasts, but at the day's beginning we understood we would have an opportunity for some cricket. We prepared as though we intended to play but we sought to establish a lead of 250-270. They bowled effectively against us and it constituted a fine run chase from them. They applied pressure upon us. Derbyshire captain Billy Godleman commented: Clearly we feel disappointed that we could not complete the match and secure the victory. We have discussed internally about delivering quality first-class cricket throughout four days, not merely a session or a day, so I feel genuinely pleased the group managed to produce good consistent cricket across all four days. I believe everyone has fulfilled their role. It has represented a genuine team effort and everyone has contributed. We simply feel disappointed that the weather and light interfered and prevented us from a certain victory.

text: Terry Flanagan has accused fellow Mancunian and lightweight world champion Anthony Crolla of ducking him. Flanagan, aged 27, defends his WBO title against Mzonke Fana of South Africa at Manchester Arena on 9 July. Crolla, aged 29, defends his WBA title against Jorge Linares of Venezuela at the same venue on 24 September. We offered Crolla the bout and he declined it. If he desires the bout, he should approach his trainer and promoter and state he desires it, said Flanagan. It is probably the individuals surrounding him who are concerned about the bout, but it remains Crolla's decision ultimately. It is a straightforward bout to arrange. Frank [Warren, Flanagan's promoter] is not making it difficult for them. If anything, he is bending over backwards to make it occur. He is yielding to their demands. He has stated they can have it on Sky Sports [with whom Crolla's promoter Eddie Hearn has an exclusive agreement], but still they decline it. If we both continue winning, it might occur eventually, but I am not confident it shall. He knows my style will cause him problems and I do not think his team believe he can defeat me. It is disappointing because Anthony is a great fighter and he has appeared really good in his last three bouts. Let us just make proper bouts and have the best fight the best. Do not be afraid to lose. Flanagan, who remains unbeaten in 30 professional bouts, is making the third defence of his title against the 42-year-old Fana, a former super-featherweight world champion who made his professional debut in 1994. People say: 'Why are you fighting this old man [Fana]?' said Flanagan, whose most recent defence was a points victory over Derry Mathews of Liverpool in March. We desire the big bouts that the fans wish to see. All we can do is keep pushing for them and hopefully one of them will materialise. Warren states he made Crolla an offer of £500,000 to fight Flanagan and that Crolla chose to fight mandatory challenger Ismael Barroso instead. In the first defence of his title last month, Crolla stopped the previously unbeaten Venezuelan, improving his record to 31 victories from 38 professional bouts. Both Barroso and former WBC champion Linares stopped Kevin Mitchell of Britain last year.

text: The Swiss government has defended its law requiring asylum seekers to hand over assets in excess of $1,000 (£700; €900) following international criticism of similar proposals in Denmark. These are external links and will open in a new window. Authorities reportedly confiscated assets in just over 100 instances in Switzerland last year from nearly 30,000 asylum applications. The Swiss Refugee Council has denounced the practice as undignified. However, the government states the policy represents the wishes of Swiss electors. The UN refugee agency and human rights organisations have condemned Danish proposals to confiscate migrants' money and other personal possessions valued at more than 10,000 kroner (£1,000; €1,340, $1,450) to fund their accommodation. Danish parliamentarians discussed the proposals on Wednesday and the legislation is anticipated to be voted upon later this month. Asylum seekers in Switzerland must declare their possessions upon arrival, and anything exceeding $1,000 may be confiscated. The authorities collected a total of 210,000 Swiss francs ($210,000; €200,000) from 112 individuals in 2015 under the regulation, public broadcaster SRF reported on Thursday (in German). Government spokesperson Lea Wertheimer told Swiss television: Swiss law stipulates that asylum-seeking refugees who possess money must contribute to the expenses that they generate whilst remaining here. And that is why we confiscate their valuables once they arrive in Switzerland. However, Stefan Frey, from the Swiss Refugee Council, characterised the practice as daylight robbery. This is undignified he was quoted as stating. This must change. A Syrian man told Swiss television that he had been compelled to sell his house to pay people smugglers to help his family escape the conflict in their country, but the remaining money was confiscated when he arrived in Switzerland. In Zurich we were searched by the police. They confiscated all our money, he said, explaining that he possessed approximately £2,000 at the time. It appears that it is their right to confiscate it. They provided us with a receipt. The officers promised that the money would be returned, but until now this has not occurred. On Wednesday, the UNHCR condemned the proposals being considered in Denmark, stating it was difficult to believe that the country wished to seize the few possessions that asylum seekers had managed to preserve. However, Integration Minister Inger Stojberg said the measures simply placed migrants on equal terms with unemployed Danes, who must sell assets above a certain threshold to claim benefits. Wedding rings and other items of sentimental significance will not be included in the proposals. Unlike Denmark, Switzerland is not a member of the EU - but it is part of the Schengen Agreement, which is intended to enable passport-free travel between countries. Some countries have reintroduced border controls amid concerns regarding the arrival of more than a million migrants in Europe last year.

text: In the Mansion House speech that was abandoned last week due to the murder of Jo Cox MP, George Osborne was due to warn on the impact on financial services if Britain leaves the European Union. Numerous prominent banks, including JP Morgan and HSBC, have stated that employment could be eliminated in the capital. Today, one of France's most distinguished economists supports that assertion. Mathilde Lemoine is a former adviser to the French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin, and currently serves on that nation's equivalent of the Office for Budget Responsibility, the economic watchdog. She informed the BBC that should Brexit occur, transactions for companies across the EU in euro-denominated assets - a substantial and crucial component of the City's operations - would transfer to the eurozone. It is already the European Central Bank's position that euro-denominated business worth hundreds of billions of euros would be better executed - or cleared - on the continent. The Treasury disagreed, and considered it so vital to the wellbeing of the City it pursued an ultimately successful legal case through the European Court of Justice to prevent the ECB's proposals. Mrs Lemoine, who is currently chief economist at Edmond de Rothschild private bank, stated that judgement would collapse if Britain departed the EU. Should the United Kingdom exit the European Union this clearing house handling euro transactions will relocate to the eurozone and consequently numerous foreign banks, European banks and also non-European banks will relocate to the eurozone, she stated. London is amongst the finest financial centres globally due to the personnel, so the personnel can relocate. [The] expertise will transfer from London to the European Union and the eurozone, and consequently they can enhance the financial sector of the eurozone. How commerce and the UK's economy are influenced by membership of the EU. It represents a form of abnormality that the clearing houses handling euro transactions are situated in the City and not within the eurozone, because it signifies that the ECB cannot oversee the clearing houses and clearing houses are institutions which enable financial transactions and consequently there exists a systemic risk. Should the United Kingdom choose to exit the European Union the eurozone member states can demand immediately the relocation of the clearing houses handling euro transactions to the eurozone. She states the market could be valued between €600bn and €1tn. Therefore, it is certainly substantial and could signify thousands of positions relocating, although Mrs Lemoine stated the total figure was challenging to forecast. Those who advocate Britain exiting the EU argue that, whilst the UK might forfeit some services, liberated from EU regulation on matters like remuneration, London would prosper. And certainly one chief executive of a prominent bank informed me that London was the sole globally important financial centre in Europe and was destined to remain so because of its profound, liquid markets, professional services and sheer scale (Paris and Frankfurt, for instance, have considerably smaller financial centres). Gerard Lyons, the former economic adviser to Boris Johnson and chief economist at Standard Chartered, stated that the remainder of the EU would still require London. However one examines it, I believe London and the City will remain the principal financial centre of Europe, regardless of what occurs in the Referendum. And I believe the longer term perspective is to position London, not merely against the EU but against future competition from Hong Kong, Singapore and New York, he stated. And I believe we possess a tremendous capacity to achieve that outside the EU. Another concern for markets is that there could be an economic decline following Brexit. However Mrs Lemoine stated that the negative impact might not be as severe as numerous economists suggest. Numerous models forecast a catastrophe for the UK should Brexit occur, she stated. I can comprehend why the models forecast such a catastrophe, but that is not my assessment. Firstly, because their forecast does not account for any other measures being implemented. It is not feasible that the Prime Minister, the government and the Governor of the Bank of England would do nothing to enhance the situation. Naturally, they would act and they will implement various measures which will restrict the decline in GDP. Additionally, exporters can respond very rapidly to change in trade policies. Naturally, all situations are unique but recall when the United Kingdom departed the European monetary system in 1992? UK exporters shifted from the European Union to the remainder of the world, she stated. The UK exports towards the European Union declined sharply, but those towards countries outside the European Union accelerated sharply. As a consequence - against all expectations - UK exports accelerated by 5% overall.

text: India's Supreme Court has struck down a controversial law which allowed police to arrest people for comments on social networks and other internet sites. The court determined that the contentious Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was unconstitutional. In recent years, numerous individuals have been detained for their remarks on Facebook or Twitter, provoking indignation. The government had supported the legislation, stating it was intended to discourage people from posting offensive content. Tuesday's judgement was delivered by a two-judge panel of the Supreme Court on petitions submitted by civil liberties organisations and a law student who contended that Section 66A infringed people's fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 66A is unconstitutional and we have no hesitation in striking it down, news agency AFP quoted Justice RF Nariman as stating in court. The public's right to know is directly affected by section 66A, he added. Section 66A was extensive in its authority - it could imprison a person for three years for transmitting an email or other electronic message that causes annoyance or inconvenience. The legislation was first contested by a law student after two young women were detained in November 2012 in Mumbai for remarks on Facebook following the death of politician Bal Thackeray. Shaheen Dhada was arrested for condemning Mumbai's closure after Thackeray's death. Renu Srinivasan, who liked the comment, was also detained. The two were subsequently released on bail. The detentions prompted outrage in India with many demanding the law be abolished. text: The issue of foreign prisoners in England's jails has long been a contentious one. The revelation in 2006 that more than 1,000 foreign prisoners who ought to have been deported had not been cost Charles Clarke his position as home secretary. The matter has also been the focus of numerous select committee investigations. The issue continues to trouble the Conservative MP for Kettering, Philip Hollobone. During his tenure as an MP he has consistently raised concerns regarding the number of foreigners in British prisons and the failure to return them to their home countries to complete their sentences. A government minister has now not only commended him for his campaign, but acknowledged that he also shares Mr Hollobone's exasperation. Mike Penning, minister for policing and criminal justice, informed Parliament that whilst receiving briefings from officials he was very surprised... about some of the matters that are being undertaken and found it mind bogglingly difficult to understand why, in numerous cases, things do not occur. He was responding to a debate initiated by Mr Hollobone who had produced fresh statistics regarding the scale of the problem. There are, he informed MPs, 10,837 foreign national offenders in British prisons which constitute 13% of the prison population. The largest number of offenders (938) originate from Poland, followed by Ireland (779) and Jamaica (737). The expense of maintaining them, he stated was north of £300m annually. Such individuals need to complete their sentences in secure custody in prisons within their own country, he stated. At a time of severe restrictions on public spending, that represents far too substantial a bill to expect British taxpayers to meet. Mr Hollobone is particularly incensed that numerous of these countries lack prisoner transfer agreements with the UK. A mandatory agreement with Jamaica remains pending ratification by the Jamaican government, there exists only a voluntary agreement with Pakistan and India and no agreement with Somalia or Bangladesh or several EU countries including Poland. Poland, which tops the list with almost 1,000 of its nationals in British prisons, has a specific exemption from accepting prisoner transfers under that EU agreement until the end of December 2016, stated Mr Hollobone. That constitutes an absolute scandal. Poland should be securing those individuals in secure custody back in Poland, at the cost of Polish taxpayers. He is also urging the British government to utilise the substantial and growing international aid budget to construct suitable prisons in countries that supply us with a large number of prisoners. He has established that in 2012 Britain provided £973m in aid to Jamaica, Pakistan, Nigeria, Somalia, India and Bangladesh who have a combined total of 2,900 of their citizens in British gaols. It costs this nation more than £100m annually to imprison these individuals in our gaols. It would be sensible to spend some of that £973m on constructing prisons in those six countries, he contended. Mr Penning acknowledged that he had been briefed by his officials to ensure that I adhered to the line and read the speech, which I shall not do. He proceeded to acknowledge that he agreed with nearly everything Mr Hollobone had stated: The frustration that he can detect in my voice was in his voice. I share his frustration. The minister stated he would wish to see as many foreign nationals as possible complete their sentences in their country of origin and he added that it was crucial that our friends in Europe fulfil their obligations. I agree that we must work considerably harder because this matter has been neglected for too many years, he stated. Eight years indeed since Charles Clarke was compelled to resign and it appears it could be the same duration again before any resolution is discovered.

text: A petition calling for Nathan Gill to be removed as UKIP Wales leader has been sent to the party's ruling body. This follows allegations that party leaders wish to impose candidates from outside Wales for the assembly election. Six general election candidates endorsed the petition which alleges there exists no coherent plan to contest the campaign and no effective leadership in Wales. UKIP has challenged the credibility of the petition and its Wales chairman stated disgruntled members endorsed it. Numerous Welsh activists have voiced objections to former Conservative MPs Mark Reckless and Neil Hamilton being considered for selection, charging the party with parachuting them in. Earlier in February, Mr Gill declared that local members would determine the rankings of candidates for regional list seats, not the party's national executive committee. Nevertheless, some Welsh members remain dissatisfied with the manner the matter has been managed, with UKIP Vale of Glamorgan councillor Kevin Mahoney departing the party. It is recognised by all that UKIP in Wales is conducted on the basis of mutual respect and understanding, the petition declares. In view of the extraordinary circumstances prevailing and indeed, as a final resort, to prevent further damage and discord within 'the party' it is essential to censure and remove those responsible immediately. The petition charged Mr Gill with demonstrating a lack of leadership in all aspects relating to this matter. It stated through his inactivity or reluctance to resolve the prevailing circumstances, [he] has worsened the situation to the point where members no longer possess faith in his ability to lead UKIP in Wales in any effective manner. UKIP general election candidates supporting the petition were Joe Smyth (Islwyn), Darran Thomas (Brecon and Radnorshire), Ken Beswick (Torfaen), Blair Smillie (Alyn and Deeside), Nigel Williams (Delyn), and Paul Davies Cooke (Vale of Clwyd). Mr Williams, one of the petition organisers, stated it was better late than never to voice their concerns with the assembly election so near. He requested a leadership election, stating UKIP Wales could select any one from ten great people but Wales chairman David Rowlands declared it adds nothing to the debate. Gethin James, a UKIP councillor and assembly election candidate for Ceredigion, informed BBC Radio Cymru: It's not a favourable situation, but I'm 100% behind Nathan Gill. People don't understand how much work he's accomplished. The problem lies with the national executive, not with Nathan Gill. On Tuesday, Mr Gill informed BBC Wales he had no intention of resigning, stating claims that he had failed to support rank-and-file members in Wales were nonsense. A UKIP Wales spokesman declared: Despite efforts of one or two individuals telephoning around the party membership in Wales their petty 26 person petition included someone from England, six people who were not even members and a growing number who denied ever signing it.

text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and what is now known as the World Bank, were set up to manage the post-World War II global economy. These are external links and will open in a new window They were established in 1944 at a conference in Bretton Woods, in the American state of New Hampshire. Through promoting economic cooperation and assisting countries with balance of payments difficulties the founders hoped to prevent a recurrence of the 1930s Great Depression. The IMF seeks to maintain economic stability and to address - or preferably prevent - financial crises. Over time, its emphasis has shifted to the developing world. The World Bank's forerunner - the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development - was established to drive post-war recovery. Today, it is the world's premier development organisation, working for growth and poverty alleviation. Owned by the governments of its 187 member states, the Bank provides loans and grants and advises low and middle-income countries. The IMF is financed by a levy - termed a quota - paid by member nations. The quota is based on a country's wealth and it determines voting power within the organisation; those making larger contributions have greater voting rights. The IMF serves as a lender of last resort, disbursing its foreign exchange reserves for short periods to any member in difficulties. Since they were established, the IMF has been led by a European and the World Bank by an American national. The IMF and the Bank have served as a focal point for disparate causes - from environmentalists to anarchists - and meetings have occasionally been accompanied by violent street protests. Protesters and critics cite the exploitation of the poor and the environment and contend that freer trade threatens the livelihoods of millions of people. The IMF has acknowledged that compelling developing countries to open their markets to foreign investors can increase the risk of financial crises. Its former managing director Horst Koehler said in 2002 that the benefits of globalisation had not been equally shared. But he added that the objective should not be less globalisation but more and better globalisation. Established: Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA Date: 1944 Headquarters: Washington DC IMF-World Bank membership: 187 countries World Bank staff: 10,000 IMF staff: 2,500 IMF managing director: Christine Lagarde Christine Lagarde is the first woman to lead the IMF in the 65 years of the organisation's history. She trained as a lawyer and for more than two decades worked for a Chicago-based international law firm, where she specialised in major labour and anti-trust cases. She served as French trade minister from 2005 to 2007, when she was appointed finance minister, becoming the first woman to hold such a post in any of the G8 major industrial countries. Ms Lagarde assumed control of the IMF in July 2011 at a time when the organisation was facing some extremely tough challenges, with the eurozone in a state of deep crisis and fears looming that countries such as Greece could default on their loans. Never afraid of speaking her mind, she has blamed the 2008 worldwide financial crisis partly on the male-dominated, testosterone-fuelled culture at global banks. She is regarded with high esteem in the international arena and in 2009 was named best finance minister in Europe by the Financial Times. She has pledged to improve diversity at the IMF and to push ahead with reforms to give emerging economies more influence in the organisation. She took over after the previous head, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who had to resign over charges of sexual assault. He has subsequently been cleared. World Bank president: Jim Yong Kim Jim Yong Kim was selected as the new president of the World Bank in April 2012. The Korean-American health expert was president of Dartmouth College in the American state of New Hampshire. He faced a strong challenge for the post, which has traditionally gone to an American, from Nigerian Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala. Dr Kim succeeded Robert Zoellick and is serving a five-year term. Jim Yong Kim is a doctor praised for his pioneering role in treating HIV/Aids and reducing the impact of tuberculosis in the developing world. The IMF and World Bank attempt to assist countries or regions in economic turmoil - and often act as a lender of last resort for nation-states. Past interventions by the IMF have included providing funds for countries caught up in the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and loans to help South American countries such as Argentina and Brazil stave off debt default crises. In October 2008, the IMF activated an emergency funding scheme for countries facing economic distress resulting from the global financial crisis. As of August 2010, it had committed around $200bn in lending to a number of economies affected by the crisis. The biggest borrowers then were Hungary, Romania and Ukraine. The recent eurozone crisis also triggered extensive IMF intervention, including substantial bailouts for countries such as Greece, Portugal and Ireland in tandem with the European Union. It is currently contributing to the second international bailout of Greece, and discussing further loans to Hungary. The IMF can also grant emergency loans following natural disasters; these have included the 2004 Asian tsunami. Developing countries have voiced dissatisfaction with what they say is their lack of influence in the IMF and World Bank. This includes the so-called Bric countries - Brazil, Russia, India and China - whose economic power has grown significantly. They have called for changes to the quota system in which votes in the IMF are weighted in line with member nations' financial contributions. Under this system, the United States has 17% of the vote in the IMF, whereas India, with more than three times the population of the United States, has less than one third. And because constitutional changes in the IMF require 85% of the vote, the United States has a veto.
