text: The landlocked mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh is the subject of an unresolved dispute between Azerbaijan, in which it lies, and its ethnic Armenian majority, backed by neighbouring Armenia. In 1988, approaching the conclusion of Soviet governance, Azerbaijani forces and Armenian separatists commenced a violent conflict which resulted in the de facto autonomous state falling under ethnic Armenian control when a ceasefire was concluded in 1994. Discussions have thus far failed to yield a lasting peace settlement, and the disagreement remains amongst post-Soviet Europe's frozen conflicts. The conflict possesses origins extending back considerably over a century into rivalry between Christian Armenian and Muslim Turkic and Persian influences. Inhabited for centuries by Christian Armenian and Turkic Azeris, Karabakh became part of the Russian empire during the 19th century. Profile compiled by BBC Monitoring The two communities lived in comparative peace, though acts of violence on both sides during the early 20th century persist in the collective memory. Following the conclusion of World War I and the Bolshevik revolution in Russia, the new Soviet authorities, as part of their divide-and-rule strategy in the region, created the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Region, with an ethnic Armenian majority, within the Soviet Socialist Republic of Azerbaijan during the early 1920s. As Soviet authority weakened approaching the conclusion of the 1980s, simmering Armenian-Azeri tensions erupted into violence when the region's parliament voted to unite with Armenia. Throughout the combat, in which between 20,000 and 30,000 individuals are estimated to have perished, the ethnic Armenians secured control of the region. They also advanced to occupy Azerbaijani territory beyond Karabakh, establishing a buffer zone connecting Karabakh and Armenia. With the dissolution of the Soviet Union, in late 1991, Karabakh proclaimed itself an independent republic, further intensifying the conflict into a comprehensive war. That de facto status has not been acknowledged elsewhere. Whilst Armenia itself has never formally recognised the region's independence, it has become its principal financial and military supporter. A Russian-mediated ceasefire was concluded in 1994, leaving Karabakh as well as extensive areas of Azeri territory surrounding the enclave under Armenian control. Throughout the combat, in which more than one million abandoned their homes, the ethnic Azeri population - approximately 25% of the total before the war - fled Karabakh and Armenia whilst ethnic Armenians fled the remainder of Azerbaijan. Neither population group has been able to return home since the conclusion of the war. Karabakh is the Russian interpretation of an Azeri term meaning 'black garden', whilst Nagorno is a Russian term meaning mountainous. The ethnic Armenians prefer to call the region Artsakh, an ancient Armenian designation for the area. Both sides have had soldiers killed in sporadic violations of the ceasefire. The closure of borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan has caused landlocked Armenia severe economic difficulties. Since the truce, a simmering deadlock has prevailed. Azeris resent the loss of territory they regard as rightfully theirs, whilst the Armenians show no indication of willingness to return it. Russia, France and the US co-chair the OSCE's Minsk Group, which has been attempting to negotiate an end to the disagreement. In a December 2006 referendum, declared illegitimate by Azerbaijan, the region approved a new constitution. Nevertheless, there have since been indications of activity in the peace process, with occasional meetings between the Armenian and Azeri presidents. Substantial progress was reported at discussions between the leaders in May and November 2009, but progress stalled, and since then there have been numerous serious ceasefire violations. The most serious thus far occurred in April 2016, when dozens of soldiers on both sides perished in a fresh outbreak of hostilities.

text: Pupils at a County Antrim school have developed a new tool to target cyberbullying. The new reporting system, termed 'Step Up', is operational at Ballyclare High School and may be accessed from home, within school premises or via smartphone. The school considers it to be the first system of this nature in Northern Ireland. It enables pupils to raise concerns directly with the relevant teacher through the school website. Fourteen-year-old Emma Blacoe, who assisted in developing it, stated that teachers could receive substantial information regarding alleged incidents. text: Colombia's President Juan Manuel Santos has met 30 rebels of the ELN, the country's second largest armed group, who laid down their arms. Mr Santos described the development as a great step towards peace. The ELN, or National Liberation Army, is not participating in the peace negotiations with Colombia's largest rebel group, the Farc, but its leaders have indicated interest in joining the discussions. The government has demanded that the ELN must first free its hostages. The left-wing organisation has approximately 1,500 members, officials state. The 30-member group laid down their weapons in the south-eastern region of Cauca. Speaking in Cali, Mr Santos personally welcomed the rebels, including three expectant women, who surrendered their weapons and equipment. This is what the [peace] process represents. So every member of the ELN and the Farc follows their path fighting for their ideals, but without violence and without weapons, he stated. This represents the largest single ELN contingent to surrender, Mr Santos declared. On Monday, Farc's chief peace negotiator stated the armed conflict that has continued nearly five decades was approaching its conclusion. Ivan Marquez, who is participating in discussions with the Colombian government in Cuba, urged left-wing parties and unions to join the effort to secure peace. The government seeks to sign a peace agreement by November. However, Mr Marquez cautioned against hastening into a settlement. It is possible [to reach an agreement by November]. But to secure peace you require time. A poor peace deal is worse than war, he stated in an interview with Colombian network RCN. The first direct discussions between Colombia's largest rebel group and the government commenced in November last year. Thus far, however, the ELN has been excluded from the discussions. Last month, in what was viewed as an attempt to encourage the rival rebels to join the discussions, the Farc issued a statement saying the two groups were discussing unification. Q&A: Colombia peace discussions However, the government maintains that the rebels must first lay down their weapons and surrender all hostages. The group recently freed a Colombian soldier but is believed to be detaining other hostages. Chief government negotiator Humberto de la Calle stated the objective of the Cuban peace discussions was to persuade the rebels to abandon their armed struggle and join the political process. Agreement has already been reached on land reform, but the negotiations are continuing on five other items on the agenda. The Farc negotiator stated recently that a Constitutional Assembly should be convened to endorse the agreements reached in Cuba. The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) are believed to have some 8,000 fighters, down from approximately 16,000 in 2001. This represents the fourth attempt at a negotiated peace deal since the beginning of the conflict in the 1960s.

text: Nottingham Forest have made an approach to Burton Albion to speak with former player Nigel Clough in relation to their managerial vacancy. Forest dismissed former manager Philippe Montanier on 14 January. Burton sit three positions beneath Forest, who occupy 19th place and remain five points clear of the relegation zone, in the Championship. Forest declined to provide comment when approached by BBC Radio Nottingham, as did Burton when requested for a response by BBC Radio Derby. It represents an obvious connection and a sensible one from numerous perspectives, Clough informed BBC Radio Derby on Wednesday. All these types of loyalties you possess and everything, indeed they remain powerful, but in football individuals join rivals constantly. text: ScottishPower customers will soon be able to buy gas and electricity in bundles of days rather than signing up to standard or fixed-price deals. The system is founded upon the manner in which individuals refuel their vehicles with petrol or purchase data packages for mobile telephones. The firm states it represents an effort to streamline energy billing. ScottishPower chief executive Keith Anderson declared: We are telling customers to purchase it daily, rather than by kilowatts or a complex tariff they cannot comprehend. Consumers will utilise an application featuring a meter that monitors usage. The organisation will customise each consumer's day according to a personalised projection of their typical energy consumption. This will also fluctuate depending upon the season. Consumers will have the ability to purchase gas and electricity packages in quantities ranging from one day to one month, and up to 180 days in advance. The company has been testing the programme and states it could revolutionise how consumers purchase energy. Mr Anderson explained they returned to fundamentals and examined how individuals bought petrol for their vehicles. You visit the petrol station and put £50 into your vehicle. Instinctively you understand that will sustain you for two to three weeks. We considered why we should not apply the same principle to energy. A fuel meter provided within the application will subsequently inform customers of their energy consumption and remaining supply. Under the programme, termed PowerUp, consumers will not be required to pay a standing charge. Scottish Power stated its tariffs for the programme would feature some of the company's most competitive rates. It will be introduced to existing customers initially, and the organisation will subsequently consider whether to extend it to the broader market. A two-year inquiry into the energy sector by competition authorities discovered that numerous consumers were not engaged with the energy market and failed to switch to the most economical deals. The novel approach to purchasing energy has been endorsed by the industry regulator. In a statement, Ofgem declared: We seek greater competition to enhance choice and reduce prices for consumers. We encourage suppliers to provide new innovative tariffs to assist people in engaging with the market and discovering the optimal deal that suits them. Innovative tariffs can be adapted to individual consumer requirements and provide people with greater control over their energy bill and payment methods. Claire Osborne, energy specialist for Uswitch.com stated: Energy bills are notoriously challenging to comprehend and therefore this approach, similar to purchasing petrol, should assist consumers in using less, wasting less and paying less for their gas and electricity. The fact that the arrangement has no standing charge will appeal to many customers - particularly those with second properties which remain unoccupied for portions of the year - as there is nothing to pay on days when no energy is consumed.

text: The Dalai Lama has called on his fellow Nobel Peace Laureate, Aung San Suu Kyi, to do more to help persecuted Rohingya Muslims in her country, Myanmar. The Tibetan spiritual leader informed The Australian that he hoped Ms Suu Kyi might take action regarding the matter. The Dalai Lama stated that he was particularly disturbed by the predicament of thousands of Rohingyas stranded at sea. Ms Suu Kyi has encountered international condemnation for declining to speak publicly about the Rohingya matter. The Rohingya are not acknowledged as citizens of Myanmar (Burma) by the government there and remain effectively stateless. In his discussion with The Australian, the Dalai Lama urged all of Myanmar's Buddhists to remember the face of the Buddha when addressing the Rohingya minority. He revealed that he had pressed Ms Suu Kyi to take action on the matter twice since 2012, when an outbreak of interfaith violence occurred in Myanmar's Rakhine state. It's very tragic. In the Burmese situation I hope Aung San Suu Kyi, as a Nobel laureate, can take action, he informed the newspaper. I encountered her twice, initially in London and subsequently in the Czech Republic. text: Thousands of Yemenis have taken to the streets of the capital, Sanaa, to protest after an air strike killed more than 140 people at a wake on Saturday. Protesters assembled outside the United Nations headquarters calling for an international inquiry into the attack, attributed to the Saudi-led coalition. Saudi Arabia has not admitted any involvement but promised to investigate. It entered Yemen's civil conflict last year supporting the internationally recognised government. Influential former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, who has aligned himself with the Houthi insurgents controlling Sanaa, has urged people to assault troops on the Saudi frontier in retaliation. Over 500 individuals were injured in Saturday's bombardment, which struck the funeral of the father of Houthi-appointed Interior Minister Gawal al-Rawishan. Numerous Houthi officials were present and Mr Rawishan sustained serious injuries in the attack. Its consequences were characterised as a lake of blood by one rescue worker. The assault has been denounced by the United Nations, European Union and the United States. United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon stated that any intentional attack against civilians is completely unacceptable and demanded those responsible be held accountable. The Saudi-led coalition has promised to immediately investigate this matter alongside the Joint Incidents Assessment Team in Yemen and specialists from the United States who participated in earlier investigations. It referenced reports concerning the regrettable and tragic bombing in Sanaa, before stating: The coalition confirms that its forces have explicit instructions not to target populated areas and to avoid civilians. The United States announced it had initiated an immediate review of its already-diminished support for the coalition. White House National Security Council spokesman Ned Price stated US cooperation with Saudi Arabia was not a blank cheque. Houthi leader Abdul-Malek al-Houthi declared in a televised speech that the attack had occurred with a green light from Washington and utilising US weapons. The rebels' spokesman termed it an act of genocide. Yemen faces a dire humanitarian crisis with four out of every five of its 28-million population requiring assistance, according to the UN's humanitarian office. Nearly three million people have been displaced since the conflict commenced in 2014. The Houthis seized the capital then, compelling the government of President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi to flee. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted thousands of air strikes against the insurgents, of the Zaidi Shia sect, which it suspects are Iranian proxies. A recent United Nations report calculated that 3,799 civilians have been killed since the Saudi-led air campaign commenced in March last year, with coalition strikes accounting for 60% of civilian deaths over a yearlong period.

text: The Pope's plea to tackle climate change is likely to get a cool reception from some key energy politicians in the US. Republican Marsha Blackburn, the second-highest ranking member on the House energy committee, states the jury remains out on global warming. Pope Francis is to address the subject in a speech to Congress on Thursday. He informed a White House audience on Wednesday the issue could no longer be left to a future generation. Speaking earlier this year as part of a forthcoming Radio 4 documentary series Climate Change - Are we Feeling Lucky?, she claimed that the earth had cooled in the past 13 years by 1F. And she stated no evidence would convince her of man-made warming. She also dismissed the theory of evolution. Scientists describe her views as complete nonsense. The jury remains out saying man is the cause for global warming, after the earth began to cool 13 years ago, she states. When challenged that the earth's surface temperature had not increased substantially in 13 years - but had certainly not cooled, she stated: I think we've cooled almost 1 degree (F). The earth's scientific authorities - including the US space agency Nasa - state the earth continues warming, with ice melting, sea level rising and oceans warming. Ms Blackburn - who represents Tennessee, a major user of coal - refused to name the sources of her scepticism about mainstream science. We have met with different researchers, she states. We had had numerous committee meetings in which we've had individuals come to present and from all of that and what we have been able to read you come to an opinion. There are some that feel like human activity is the cause for carbon emissions and because of that we need to revert to where we were in the 1870s for carbon emissions. I just choose to disagree with that. Asked what scientific evidence would convince her that climate change was a threat, she replied: I don't think you will see me being persuaded. Asked whether she accepted the theory of evolution she stated: No, I do not. Ms Blackburn's views matter because Republicans in Congress are attempting to roll back President Obama's attempts to cut greenhouse gas emissions. Professor Brian Hoskins, a leading climate scientist at the Royal Society stated her remarks were absolutely staggering. It is nonsense to say the world has cooled, Hoskins stated. If no evidence will persuade Ms Blackburn of climate change, that shows how well-founded her views are. Correction 25 September 2015: An earlier version of this report implied that Marsha Blackburn's comments were made in relation to the Pope's address. They were actually given in an earlier interview and the headline and text have been amended to make this clear. Follow Roger on Twitter @rharrabin

text: A police force criticised for not doing more to stop a porn-obsessed murderer is being investigated over its handling of another man who went on to kill. West Mercia Police acknowledged failures regarding its earlier interactions with Jamie Reynolds, who subsequently received a prison sentence for the hanging of 17-year-old Georgia Williams. The constabulary contacted the police watchdog following allegations that Jason Conroy throttled a teacher in March 2013. He subsequently received a prison sentence for strangling 18-year-old Melissa Mathieson in Bristol. A spokesperson for the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) stated: We received a referral from West Mercia Police in January 2015. It related to the police handling of allegations made against Jason Conroy regarding an incident in Shropshire in March 2013. The IPCC investigation was suspended owing to the criminal prosecution of Mr Conroy but has now recommenced following his convictions. Reynolds, characterised in court as possessing morbid sexual fantasies, attempted to strangle a girl in 2008, before proceeding to hang Georgia five years subsequently. The constabulary and social services faced criticism in a serious case review last week after it emerged they were aware of the earlier attack. A following investigation led to misconduct meetings for four officers and one member of police staff. Reynolds is currently serving a rare whole-life sentence in prison after a judge stated he possessed the potential to become a serial killer. Conroy allegedly throttled a teacher at a Shropshire school in March 2013, but it was not reported to police at that time. A West Mercia Police spokesperson stated: Police became aware of the incident several months subsequently as an officer attended the address regarding a separate matter. It is understood the officer informed the victim no action could be pursued as a time limit had elapsed. Conroy, 18, strangled Melissa Mathieson last year at the Bristol centre where they both resided and received a prison sentence for a minimum of 19 years. His trial at Bristol Crown Court heard he had expressed as a child his desire to have sex with a deceased woman and he was characterised as possessing an abnormal sexual drive.

text: BBC Ouch wants your funny, confusing or embarrassing stories about those awkward situations which occurred because you're disabled or have mental health difficulties. These are external links and will open in a new window Relive those distinctive moments at Tales of the Misunderstood - a live storytelling event this summer. Perhaps the amusing story you recounted about losing your leg in a shark attack backfired, when your employer - having believed it to be factual - repeated it at a conference. The occasion when the waiter provided you with a children's menu at a restaurant because you are a person with restricted growth. Or how friends and colleagues awkwardly remove words like mad or crazy because they know you visit a therapist. We know your story is likely to be more captivating than our examples here and we are looking forward to hearing them. Whatever the tale, we are interested. All we ask is that the story is genuine, you are disabled or have a mental health condition, and that your story incorporates this. If selected, you will get to work with a leading comedy script producer and perform it before an audience at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival this August. Want to attempt it? Write up your story and send it to us - by 9 July - along with some information about yourself. If you just want to provide a summary for now, that is acceptable, but the people who succeeded last time mostly submitted lengthy stories in their first email. Email ouch@bbc.co.uk or direct message us on Facebook. If you have an excellent story, but need some access to tell it, we will work with you to improve and communicate it. The final story will need to last approximately seven minutes. It could be humorous like stand-up or an engaging insight into something the audience may not have considered. As well as performing it to a friendly crowd, we will also be filming it for the BBC. This is the second time we have put on a storytelling event, the first was in March 2017. Have a look at two of the acts from the first show in London - where many of those participating had never performed on stage before. Remember the deadline for your stories is 9 July. If we like yours we will be in touch to let you know the next step. Accommodation is available if you are coming a long way, and travel funding is available if you are based in the UK. We will endeavour to assist with all access requirements. And we can answer any questions via the aforementioned email address too. Please share this on social media - especially with those you know who can tell a good story. Bookmark this page and keep across Facebook for updates about being an Ouch storyteller and how to get free tickets. What Ouch's storytelling team said about being part of our first live event: Performing for the all-embracing BBC Ouch! audience has encouraged me to be courageous and creative in response to my difficulties, opening up a whole world of opportunities. The experience has taught me that sharing stories about our disabilities is something we owe not just to ourselves, but to each other. (John Servante) Disabled people are uniquely positioned to tell stories about people, kindnesses and weirdness ... but often these stories remain within disability circles and do not get out there for everyone to wonder at. (Damon Rose, Ouch editor)

text: Two people have been killed and two others injured in a stabbing in a house in Canterbury. A man believed to have been acquainted with the victims was detained at the property in Dickens Avenue shortly after 19:30 BST on Tuesday. Kent Police stated that two individuals had sustained fatal injuries and two others were transported to hospital. text: Welsh exiles Taulupe Faletau, George North, Jamie Roberts and Rhys Priestland will have to rely on being picked as wildcards for future Wales selection. The Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) senior player selection policy (SPSP) permits only three players who compete outside Wales to be chosen. Dominic Day, Nicky Thomas and Rhodri Williams are the other individuals impacted. Bath lock Luke Charteris is excluded from the regulation and available for selection. This marks the first occasion the WRU has disclosed its seven-man list, from which three wildcard selections are accessible for each Wales campaign, commencing from the 2016-17 season. The Six Nations, summer tour and autumn internationals constitute separate campaigns, and the wildcard selections may vary for each. Also termed 'Gatland's Law' in reference to Wales head coach Warren Gatland, the policy aims to ensure more players compete in their domestic rugby within Wales. In August 2014, the WRU and Wales' four professional regions signed a £60m, six-year agreement that resolved a protracted dispute regarding the sport's future. That agreement incorporated regulations that mean players based outside Wales could be disregarded in favour of home-based talent. The policy determined no player based overseas should represent Wales, though they may make exceptions. The SPSP does not impact players who signed contracts with clubs outside Wales before the policy was implemented, such as Toulon's Leigh Halfpenny and Exeter's Tomas Francis. Robert Howley will stand in for Gatland, who will assume responsibility for the 2017 British and Irish Lions tour to New Zealand. Wales host Australia, Argentina, Japan and South Africa at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in November. The squad for those Test matches will be announced on Tuesday, 18 October. Players have been aware that there would arrive a point, if they departed or signed new contracts outside Wales, that the policy would affect selection, said WRU chief executive Martyn Phillips. We are conscious that supporters may be worried that we will not be selecting from a complete list of players, but the alternative where players increasingly compete outside Wales is not sustainable for the long-term success of our game whether that be professional or community rugby. Clearly the player ultimately possesses the choice but we will do everything we can to ensure that playing in Wales provides the player the finest professional rugby experience possible.

Following Percival's opening penalty, Lewis Tierney touched down for Wigan, though tries from Percival and Morgan Knowles established a 16-4 half-time advantage for Saints. Anthony McCallen, aged 65, served as chaplain at the former St William's Children's Home in East Yorkshire, whilst James Carragher, aged 75, held the position of head. Both men contested a combined total of 87 sexual offences against children at the institution during the period spanning the 1970s to 1990s. Leeds Crown Court was told that Carragher, a previously convicted sexual offender from Merseyside, conducted late-night swimming sessions with boys who were unclothed. The jury was informed that both defendants targeted boys ranging in age from 10 to 16 years. A total of 18 men provided testimony detailing how they had been indecently assaulted. One complainant left the courtroom abruptly after informing the jury that the defendants had approached him whilst he slept and committed sexual assault. A further witness described how boys were taken swimming following lights-out at the establishment and instructed not to wear swimming attire. After the verdict was delivered, Judge Jeffrey Marson QC commended the jury members for their conduct throughout proceedings. He stated: Never before in my extensive career have I presided over a case where a jury was required to consider such numerous charges, which far exceeds normal parameters, and these represent some of the most challenging charges to adjudicate. Carragher, who received seven years' imprisonment in 1993 and 14 years in 2004 for sexual offences, entered not guilty pleas to 50 counts of indecent assault and 12 additional serious sexual offences. McCallen, also from Merseyside, who was previously convicted of abusing two boys during the 1990s, contested 18 indecent assault charges and seven other serious sexual offences. Following a 10-week trial and 11 days of jury deliberation, Carragher was found guilty of 21 indecent assault charges and three serious sexual offences, whilst being acquitted of 30 additional charges. McCallen was convicted on 11 charges in total, including one serious sexual offence, and was cleared of eight other charges. However, the jury could not reach decisions on 13 charges and was dismissed by the judge. Both defendants are scheduled for sentencing on 4th January. St William's in Market Weighton, which ceased operations in 1992, was under the ownership of the Diocese of Middlesbrough and operated by De La Salle Brotherhood members. text: Shares in the UK's biggest estate agent, Countrywide, have plummeted following the publication of its gloomy report on the property market. text: The flagship Conservative election pledge to open a further 500 free schools in England is being put into practice, with applications invited for new schools. The Government seeks to establish 270,000 additional places in free schools during the forthcoming five years. Education Secretary Nicky Morgan characterised them as contemporary engines of social justice. Labour's Tristram Hunt declared it an irresponsible utilisation of public funds. The commencement of the application process on Friday signals the launch of the starting gun for the subsequent wave of free schools. Amongst the proposals to be submitted shall be New Croydon Academy, emphasising science and technology, and Gipsy Hill Secondary Academy, where a consortium of primary schools in south London seeks to establish a secondary school. Free schools, with over 250 already operational and more than 150 approved, are new state schools which possess the same independence as academies, functioning outside the local authority and with enhanced flexibility regarding the curriculum and staffing. Throughout the election campaign, Prime Minister David Cameron stated these start-up schools were elevating standards and restoring discipline. They were introduced under the coalition Government, with the objective of bringing additional choice and innovation and permitting local parents and community groups to establish their own schools if they believed there was an absence of good quality local schools. However, the tendency has been towards free schools being established by existing professional school groups. An analysis published by the Policy Exchange think tank demonstrated that in the most recent waves of free schools, more than two-thirds were established by academies or academy chains. Fewer than one-fifth were established by parents and community groups. They have encountered opposition from Labour and the teachers' unions, who have accused the free-school project of failing to provide additional school places where they are most required. However, the Department for Education states that almost three-quarters of the 125,000 free school places created were in areas with a shortage. And it states half are in the most deprived communities in the country. Free schools are at the centre of the Government's commitment to deliver genuine social justice by ensuring all pupils have access to a world-class education, stated Mrs Morgan. This is at the core of our commitment to govern as one nation - creating a country where everyone, regardless of their background, can achieve their high aspirations. Free schools provided a fresh opportunity for families to break the cycle of disadvantage by providing a quality of schooling never before seen in many communities, stated the education secretary. Sarah Pearson, interim director of the New Schools Network, which supports the establishment of free schools, states they have been working with approximately 30 groups wanting to establish schools. These groups had been investing the hours in the last few months to finalise their applications, she stated. The New Schools Network provided examples of those expected to submit applications: Sir Craig Tunstall, executive head teacher of the federation leading the Gipsy Hill bid, stated they wanted to address the problem of bright pupils in primary school falling behind when they transfer to secondary school. In our area there is a shortage of outstanding secondary places and too often the first year is spent treading water academically because teachers and pupils are taking time getting to know each from scratch. However, Tristram Hunt, shadow education secretary, stated: When there is a shortage of school places, rising class sizes, widespread teacher shortages and schools face significant real-terms budget cuts, parents will find it peculiar that David Cameron continues to channel hundreds of millions of pounds into constructing new schools in areas where there is already a surplus of places. Christine Blower, leader of the National Union of Teachers, stated: As the Government knows, free schools and academies do not raise standards in any more effective manner than maintained schools. She stated it was far more about privatisation and ideology than social justice and equality. Chris Keates, leader of the NASUWT teachers' union, stated: Local authorities should be permitted to manage place provision and to determine the type of school provision that would best meet the needs of local communities.

text: Wrexham's appointment of Dean Keates as manager is not the first time the Welsh club have turned to a familiar face to lead them. Keates, who accumulated more than 150 league appearances and led the club to FA Trophy victory in 2013, has been given his inaugural managerial position as Gary Mills' replacement. Arfon Griffiths, Brian Flynn and most recently Andy Morrell were all former players granted their initial management opportunity by the north Wales club. Each of the three left their distinctive impression on a club which is presently in its eighth campaign outside the Football League. Wrexham have not staged a genuine play-off challenge since Morrell's tenure, who had Keates serving as club captain. Morrell, currently manager of National League North side Tamworth, was amongst the first to send Keates congratulatory messages regarding his appointment. He's ideal for it, Morrell informed BBC Radio Wales Sport. He's someone who is driven, passionate and has got Wrexham in his heart. He battled relentlessly when he was a player for them and risked his body and he'll do precisely the same thing in the managerial position as well. It's an excellent opportunity for him because these don't arise very frequently. Morrell, like Keates, originally assumed control on an interim basis in September 2011 when Dean Saunders departed for Doncaster Rovers and was subsequently made permanent. Nevertheless, Morrell inherited a side that was second in the Conference whilst Keates' Wrexham are presently 14th and eight points from the play-off positions. I was in a superior position because we had secured seven out of the 10 matches, Morrell recollects. All I needed to do was continue doing what we were doing and the players were excellent. Dean must somehow alter the mind-set of the players. They must transform that mentality into one that's a victorious one and he can achieve it. He'll lead from the front and he'll inform them precisely what he requires. The appointment has also prompted comparisons with another diminutive midfielder turned Wrexham manager Flynn. Despite being 5ft 5ins, Keates jested at his press conference: I'm slightly taller than Flynnie though. Flynn, the former Wales international, made the transition from player to manager at Wrexham as Dixie McNeil's successor in November 1989. He transformed a side which finished bottom of the Football League to FA Cup giant killers, with notable victories over Arsenal and West Ham United during his 12-year tenure. It's a very comparable situation to when Brian Flynn arrived and observe the success he achieved at the football club, said Peter Jones, chairman of Wrexham Supporters' Trust. We felt the opportunity for Dean was the appropriate time. He understands the club, he knows everyone here. text: The growing buy-to-let property market in the UK could post a threat to wider financial stability, a Bank of England committee has said. Buy-to-let mortgage lending possessed the capacity to amplify a housing boom and bust, the Bank's Financial Stability Committee (FPC) determined. Lending within this sector has increased by 40% since 2008, the FPC stated. It refrained from proposing any intervention by government or regulators at this juncture. The FPC remains alert to the rapid expansion of the market and potential developments in underwriting standards, the committee stated. As the market continues to expand, particularly if driven by relaxation of underwriting standards, the sector could present risks to broader financial stability, both through credit risk to banks and the amplification of movements in the housing market. The 40% rise in the outstanding stock of buy-to-let mortgage lending since 2008 contrasts with an increase of merely 2% in owner-occupier mortgage lending. The proportion of buy-to-let in the stock of outstanding mortgage lending has increased to 16% from 12% in 2008. The Bank stated that buy-to-let landlords were considerably more likely to sell if there was a substantial drop in house prices, causing property values to plummet further. A comparable amplified effect could arise should prices rise sharply. Any increase in buy-to-let activity in an upswing could add additional pressure to house prices. This could encourage owner-occupier buyers to take on even larger loans, thereby increasing overall risks to financial stability, the FPC stated. Throughout the Bank of England's three centuries of existence it has had to wrestle time and again with the problem of boom and bust. The doorman standing outside the Bank of England, as I entered today, was a reminder of this enduring struggle. He was dressed in the customary pink tails: the colour is Houblon pink, named after the first governor, Sir John Houblon, who assumed office in 1694. Could the rise of buy-to-let be placing us in danger again? The Bank's Financial Policy Committee states it has the potential to amplify the housing and credit cycles. It is cautious not to classify either the rush for buy-to-let or recent house price increases as a boom. However it is evident that bank officials view investors' enthusiasm for bricks and mortar as a problem which requires monitoring. Buy-to-let investors drive prices up more rapidly. Because they are more inclined to sell if the market encounters difficulties, they make prices fall more sharply. Reductions to the amount of tax relief that can be claimed on mortgage interest payments by buy-to-let landlords were announced by Chancellor George Osborne in his Budget in July. The amount that landlords will be permitted to claim will be set at the basic rate of tax, which is presently 20%. The change will be implemented over four years from April 2017. Mr Osborne suggested this would assist in creating a level playing field between homeowners and investors. The FPC stated that no intervention was required in the Help to Buy scheme - which sees the government guarantee part of a low-deposit home loan - as it presented no risks to financial stability in its current form.

text: Rakesh Shukla is a software engineer who's found his life's calling in looking after dogs that no-one wants, writes the BBC's Geeta Pandey in Bangalore. These are external links and will open in a new window The vehicle drew up outside a dusty farmhouse near the capital of the southern Indian state of Karnataka and suddenly dogs were everywhere, yelping and barking, leaping with joy. Within moments, they were all over Rakesh Shukla, nuzzling him and licking him, and Mr Shukla was equally delighted to see them. He spoke to them, patted some, scratched one behind the ears, and lifted another onto his shoulder. Then he provided me with a tour of his three and a half acre farm. At last count, Mr Shukla had 735 dogs. There are Labradors on the farm, there are Golden Retrievers, Great Danes, Beagles, Dachshunds, Rottweilers, Saint Bernards and even a pug. There are hundreds of mongrels as well. Most of the dogs are strays, the others have been abandoned by their owners. The latest arrivals were a group of 22 pedigreed dogs whose owner, a city businessman, was shot dead recently by criminals. Geeta Pandey recently spent 10 days working on a series of stories in Bangalore. This is her fourth report. You can find the other reports here: Why is Bangalore stuck in traffic jams? Women from Mars? The restaurant that has a city eating out of its hands I'm the final stop for these dogs. They are no longer cute and cuddly. Many are sick and no longer wanted, said Mr Shukla, 45. Affectionately known as the Dog Father, he calls the dogs his babies and himself their papa. Mr Shukla, who founded a software company along with his wife 10 years ago, spends three to four days every week on the farm, caring for his canines. I had worked in Delhi, in the United States and then established my own company in Bangalore, he said. Life was all about purchasing big cars and expensive watches and living a fancy life. I had travelled and seen the world many times over, but then I was not happy. Then Kavya entered his life: a beautiful 45-day-old Golden Retriever that he fell hopelessly in love with. It was in June 2009, and Mr Shukla remembers clearly the day he brought her home. When we arrived home, she went and hid in a corner. I got down to her level on the floor and I was calling out to her. She was looking at me, she was scared, but I could see she wanted to trust me, he said. And that's when the moment occurred - it was a physical feeling, my hair was tingling, I could feel a warm glow. And I've never needed to ask myself that question - 'why am I here?' - again after that. Mr Shukla's second dog, Lucky, came to him three months later when he rescued her from the streets. It had been raining for 12-13 days, she was wet and miserable, so I brought her home too, he said. Over the following days and weeks, whenever he encountered a stray or abandoned dog, he brought it home. Initially he kept them there but when his wife protested, he moved some of them to the office, where the top floor was converted into a home for dogs. In 2012, as the pack grew, Mr Shukla purchased land in Doddballapur town and established the farm - a sanctuary for dogs that are old, ailing or simply unwanted. The farm is designed for its canine residents, with lots of open spaces for them to run around and ponds to swim in, and there's double fencing to keep them secure. Every time we entered an enclosure, a cacophony of barks greeted us. The farm employs about 10 people, including trained veterinary assistants, to look after the dogs, cook for them and feed them. The dogs are fed 200kg of chicken and another 200kg of rice daily and many of the sick ones require regular medicines and attention. The daily cost of running the centre is 45,000 to 50,000 rupees ($663; £532 to $737; £592), according to Mr Shukla, who said he provided 93% of the funds. In the past year though, he has encountered problems with some animal activists, who have demanded that they be allowed onto the farm. He has also faced complaints that he is creating public unrest by keeping so many dogs. There have also been demands that he shut down the farm. He has refused to concede. I've made a pact with my dogs, he said. We will part only when one of us kicks the bucket.

text: JPeg pictures could soon have built-in restrictions making them harder to copy, if recommendations by the body overseeing the format are implemented. The Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) committee has requested controls regarding how image data within .jpg files is accessed. It is believed this would protect copyright and safeguard the privacy of individuals in images. Nevertheless, rights groups have stated the features could harm creativity. In an online summary of the proposals, the JPEG committee said photographs were frequently redistributed without relevant rights information attached, so they could easily be copied or published again without permission. And in certain cases, the privacy of the photographer could be compromised if metadata embedded in the images, which could include the geo-location of wherever the photograph was taken, was accessible. Currently, these concerns are not well addressed and [are] an inhibiting factor in the further proliferation of digital content distribution, the JPEG committee briefing stated. The JPEG committee has no concrete plans to change the JPEG format yet, but hopes to seek technological solutions once the specifics of the new proposals have been decided, according to convener of the committee Touradj Ebrahimi. Speaking to the BBC, Dr Ebrahimi said whatever changes might be made, JPEG files would still be freely shareable if their authors wanted them to be. One thing that's important to note is that this is not something we're imposing, he stated. We are just saying, 'Let people have a choice.' Those who are perfectly happy with today's situation and want to have security-free image sharing [will still be able to]. Currently, when someone wants to protect an image from being viewed by certain people, it is possible to publish it on websites with their own privacy protecting software, such as Facebook. However, if the photograph is taken from that site by someone who has access to it and sent elsewhere, it could then be distributed to anyone. Dr Ebrahimi suggested that it might be better to have access controls actually built into the file. It would be best if you have one image that is protected in such a way that if you have the rights, you see it clear; if you don't have the rights, you don't see it, he stated. The idea has caused some concern amongst rights groups such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). In a blog, the EFF warned against putting tight restrictions on JPEG files and suggested the move could stifle creativity - hampering an artist from using a photograph in a new work, for example. It might also be difficult to secure the restrictions from those who wanted to crack them, said Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group. He compared the situation to digital rights management (DRM) software, which is found on products such as DVDs and prevents copying of the content. DRM tends to be easily broken, he told the BBC. People who want to break the rules would still do that. Mr Killock also expressed concerns that companies might charge steep fees for allowing certain levels of access to restricted images. You're going to want to edit pictures, crop them, alter them, all of these sorts of things that DRM potentially restricts, so I guess the other major beneficiary would end up being software publishers, he stated. The JPEG format is the most widely used image format on the internet, and according to the JPEG committee, several billion JPEG images are produced every day.

text: How can busy working mums and dads keep tabs on their toddlers and stay connected to them during the working day? An increasing number of technology entrepreneurs believe they possess a solution. However, does employing additional technology provide time-pressed parents valuable new methods to engage with their children or merely render them more anxious? Molawa Adesuyi serves as co-founder and chief executive of Mytoddlr, an application that provides updates on what your young child is doing at nursery or crèche. He harbours no uncertainty about the utility of such technology. Most working parents deliver their children to day nurseries as early as 8 or 9am, and cannot collect them until 5 or 6pm, he states. And during this period, they possess absolutely no means of maintaining contact or remaining informed of their children's wellbeing throughout the entire day. This represents a major, major difficulty. Through the Mytoddlr application and website, nurseries enter information about the child's routine and behaviour during the day - from toilet breaks to sleeps - and parents receive these updates in real time on their telephones or computers. The nursery remains content, parents remain content, it constitutes a win-win for everyone truly, states Mr Adesuyi. However, is this not an additional administrative burden for nursery personnel? Mr Adesuyi maintains not, as it can actually diminish paperwork and provide an easier, quicker method of communicating with parents, he states. There exist such excellent applications available now for parents... solutions to genuine problems parents face. It remains simply pleasant to witness technology transform parenting, he concludes. Launched in 2015, Mytoddlr is being utilised by 2,000 parents in Lagos, Nigeria, and is presently being tested by some nurseries in London. Harsh Songra, 19-year-old founder and chief executive of smartphone application My Child, was motivated to launch his child development monitoring application after experiencing dyspraxia whilst growing up. This developmental disorder affecting coordination and movement can prove difficult to diagnose if parents do not know what to observe. I have understood the struggle of a family where the child possesses a disorder, he states. It required my parents over nine years to determine the specific difficulty, and I still experience some health problems, states Mr Songra. The My Child application assists parents in monitoring the development of a child up to 24 months old, posing questions, aggregating relevant content, and identifying local specialists. Launched in early 2015, the application has been downloaded more than 11,000 times in over 140 countries, and proves particularly popular in the US, India, Singapore and the UK. Mr Songra believes technology constitutes a useful parenting tool, but acknowledges that it may sometimes interfere with the work of professionals. At times it does influence their relationships with doctors, because parents become anxious about their child because of what they searched on Google, he states. The difficulty is that we tend to believe the content of one link over 100 others, and then take actions based on that knowledge. But we believe all this will certainly change with time, as there will be more awareness about these issues in the future. Parenting applications - from webcam baby monitors to location-tracking services, interactive games to health checkers - are certainly on the increase, as busy parents integrate the latest technology into their lives. One woman in Australia even utilised Siri, Apple's voice-activated iPhone assistant, to telephone an ambulance when her toddler daughter ceased breathing. However, for New Jersey-based entrepreneur Amit Murumkar, the motivation for creating an application was purely practical. My daughter was three... and would bring a piece of artwork back daily from her Montessori school, but there exists only so much you can place on a refrigerator door, he states. I also was a skilled artist as a child, and when I became a parent I thought, 'If only I could show the artwork I created to my own children.' So he constructed a smartphone application called Canvsly, that permits parents to capture these works of art on the application, organise them into albums, and invite grandparents or other family members to view and comment on them. The artwork can also be printed through the application and used to create gifts. As long as you trust the application's cloud storage provider, you could then discard the originals. Parents can proceed guilt-free and clutter-free, Mr Murumkar states, adding that the application has been downloaded in more than 100 countries. Anesu Charamba, a technology analyst at research consultancy Frost & Sullivan, believes such applications are helping parents raise and interact with their children in new and exciting ways. And as smartphones and cheaper, more reliable internet access spreads beyond developed economies to the rest of the world, early adopters will be joined by the majority, he believes. text: In our series of letters from African journalists, filmmaker and columnist Farai Sevenzo considers the role of cameras in conflict. An intriguing moment occurred at the recent Cannes Film Festival when the Mauritania-born film director Abderrahmane Sissako was responding to questions following the screening of his film Timbuktu - The Silence of Fear. Timbuktu film receives acclaim at Cannes The film presents a fictional account of those turbulent months when jihadists seized control of this historic town in Mali and enforced numerous regulations including prohibiting music and football, whilst introducing floggings and stoning. Sissako, amongst Africa's most reliable storytellers, became emotional at his press conference and stated that he was weeping for all those Malians who had endured what his film depicted. The genuine bravery, he remarked, was to be discovered amongst those who experienced this daily. Timbuktu was ultimately liberated but the authentic freedom belonged to those individuals who mentally sang these songs and this music that had been prohibited. The dramatists amongst us direct the camera towards such recent African incidents to provide us with moments of contemplation. However, in our 24-hour news environment the camera is omnipresent, initially in the possession of news correspondents - and in the possession of the jihadists as well. At the century's beginning the late Osama bin Laden continued delivering footage to news channels, which consequently became entangled in a twisted competition regarding who amongst them would obtain the subsequent tirade from the man who resided in the mountains. Who are Nigeria's Boko Haram Islamists? A decade and a half subsequently we possess YouTube, and militants from Syria to Somalia have embraced the camera as a soldier embraces the weapon. The fighters on our own continent have commenced providing us with footage with growing frequency. During this past month the escalating death toll of the deceased and missing in north-eastern Nigeria has brought two matters into clear focus - the leadership of President Goodluck Jonathan and the visage of Abubakar Shekau, the Islamist militant responsible for the abduction of more than 200 schoolgirls in Chibok. The Boko Haram leader has begun appearing before the camera with theatrical enthusiasm, declaring: I kidnapped your girls; I shall sell them in the marketplace. Since 14 April 2014 we have been compelled to await his every utterance in fresh videos, hoping that the anguish of Chibok's parents will shortly be diminished. From Shekau's diatribes, some individuals might deduce that this was a performer in a Nollywood film portraying the typical antagonist, that at any moment he would inform the camera something shocking - for example that he had already sold his own mother, aunts and sisters, and that these schoolgirls would follow the same path. Negotiations of a kind may be ongoing and the Nigerian military, possibly stung by persistent rumours of their notable absence from remote Nigerian villages under assault, now claim they know where the girls are located and are assessing the situation. It represents one of the paradoxes of our era that in our world saturated with cameras and recording devices, where the earth's atmosphere is filled with satellites - we cannot locate an aircraft or several hundred missing children who are not at sea but on solid ground within heartbreaking proximity of their yearning parents. When the dust settles on such incidents, the artists, novelists and filmmakers can provide us something the television bulletins cannot - the chance to reflect and to extract meaning from the propaganda of the combatants. Who are these individuals and what do they seek? How do the villagers respond to them? Is it fear or faith that is stirred? Where do the imams position themselves? Can the tension be resolved in a more traditional African manner with the elders rather than the soldiers? However, the artists and their cameras possess the privilege of time, which those on the frontline of this new conflict do not. And whilst answers to these enormous questions have remained elusive, the quest to discover them must not cease. Whether or not Nigeria's militants provide us another video, the seismic collision of ideologies in Nigeria's north as exemplified by Boko Haram's presence is amongst us and poses a very real and immediate threat which is spreading terror. Such terror exists in other African cities - Nairobi, Mogadishu and recently Djibouti. The silence of fear is no more desirable than the fear of the silence that met Chibok's parents when their daughters initially vanished all those weeks ago - before celebrities raised the hashtag placards. Nevertheless, in this era of instant footage and digital imagery, the most moving pictures remain those of mothers and fathers displaying aged photographs of teenage daughters they may never witness again. text: Zayn Malik has revealed that, in leaving One Direction, he has let the fans down. He announced his departure from the band on Wednesday. In an interview with The Sun he stated: I cannot do this anymore. The star acknowledged his decision was crazy and wild and a bit mad. However, I have never felt more in control in my life. I feel like I am doing what is right, right by myself and right by the boys. Zayn provided his interview just hours after announcing his departure from the world's biggest band. He rejected claims there were any rifts between the band members, saying those assertions could not be more wrong. However, he acknowledged he had wanted out of the band for some time. He stated: You know, I did attempt to do something that I was not happy doing for a while, for the sake of perhaps other people. Essentially, I am only upset [because] I feel like I may have let them down. It is not that I have turned my back on them [the fans] or anything, it is just that I simply cannot do that anymore because it is not real to me. He also rejected rumours it was the beginning of the end for the band, who were assembled on The X Factor in 2010. He declined to comment on speculation he could return in the future. Zayn departed the globally-successful pop group a week after withdrawing from their world tour due to stress. It followed after the singer was photographed with his arm around a blonde girl in Thailand, prompting speculation he had been unfaithful to his fiancée, Little Mix singer Perrie Edwards. Immediately following the announcement he flew back to the UK, and posted on Twitter: I am 22 years old... I love a girl named Perrie Edwards. And there are a lot of jealous [people] in this world. I am sorry for what it looks like. Announcing his departure from One Direction permanently on Wednesday, Zayn stated: After five years, I feel like it is now the right time for me to leave the band. Asked about his relationship by The Sun, Zayn said his two-year engagement had not been terminated. He described Perrie as a good girl who was supportive of his decision. Meanwhile, Zayn has reportedly visited a west London recording studio to work on solo material with Naughty Boy, who helped launch the careers of Emeli Sandé and Sam Smith. text: England women began their World Twenty20 campaign with a routine 36-run victory over Bangladesh in Bangalore. England, champions in 2009 and runners-up in the previous two tournaments, reached their total of 153-7 through 60 from captain Charlotte Edwards. Bangladesh, who have secured victory in merely five of the 29 T20 matches they have contested, never threatened the target. Katherine Brunt conceded 17 runs from her four overs whilst Anya Shrubsole claimed 2-27 as Bangladesh finished on 117-6. Sterner examinations await England, commencing with hosts India in Dharamsala on Tuesday. Here, spearheaded by Edwards, the leading runscorer in T20 internationals - men or women - they professionally handled modest opposition. The captain combined accumulation with powerfully dispatching the poor delivery, steering England through a potentially troublesome period when they lost Sarah Taylor and Heather Knight for the addition of merely one run. At 71-3, she was accompanied by Nat Sciver, who contributed 27 from a partnership of 47, whilst Danni Wyatt and Brunt provided late impetus as England accumulated 35 from the final three overs. The pursuit was always likely to prove excessive for Bangladesh, a side who had never previously exceeded 115 in a T20 international. Opener Sharmin Akhter was dismissed by the impressive Brunt in the opening over of the response and, thereafter, England maintained control throughout. Nigar Sultana and Salma Khatun did establish a Bangladesh record 64 for the fifth wicket, yet the match was already concluded as a contest. England coach Mark Robinson informed Sky Sports: I believed we regressed today. We were cautious and we do not wish to be cautious. We lost our direction in the middle with the bat and made poor decisions with the ball. Perhaps that is beneficial, because it reserves something in the tank. We were not poor. Six out of 10. We are progressing in the correct direction, but today we did not quite reach the heights. That is not how we stated we are going to play. In the middle of the innings, you cannot settle for six an over. We are superior to that. England captain Charlotte Edwards: It is always pleasant to commence with runs, but the victory was the most significant thing. It was a solid total, there is some work we can undertake on our bowling and fielding but we are quite satisfied. Bangladesh performed really well towards the conclusion, and we have a significant match next against India. The new coaches have challenged us to express ourselves, there is still much to emerge from us as a team. Former England batter Ebony Rainford-Brent on BBC Test Match Special: I would have liked to witness more from the middle order, where there was a slight flutter of wickets. That will be punished by Australia or India. We have discussed the dependence on Edwards and Taylor, and I would like to observe a substantial score emerging from Heather Knight as this tournament progresses, because she represents the next generation.

text: Eastern Ukraine has become a testing ground for Russia's new military capabilities. When Russia previously engaged in warfare, in Georgia during 2008, it appeared to be a straightforward triumph. However, Russia's military commanders were profoundly troubled by how poorly their forces executed in certain crucial aspects of contemporary warfare. Russia has devoted the seven years following that conflict to rearming, re-equipping, and retraining, with the aim of addressing those shortcomings, and attempting to narrow the capability divide with modern Western military forces. The outcomes are now visible in eastern Ukraine, where pro-Russian separatists have secured territory against Ukrainian government forces. Ukraine's military has not undergone the same rigorous modernisation programme, and is experiencing the consequences, confronting the advanced weaponry and systems provided by Russia. Two principal illustrations are the deployment of UAVs (drones) for reconnaissance and targeting, and the employment of electronic warfare. Both technologies were recognised as weakness areas within the Russian forces during 2008, and both have been extensively developed subsequently. Currently, they are in widespread deployment in eastern Ukraine, positioning Ukrainian government forces at a considerable disadvantage. Ukrainian forces lack adequate secure communications systems. The consequence is that their communications are both vulnerable to jamming, and frequently also reveal their position to Russian direction-finding apparatus. This can result in being rapidly targeted by Russian artillery, including Grad and other, more potent, rocket systems. As component of the non-lethal assistance supplied by the US, Ukraine has obtained specialised radar to attempt to identify the source of incoming mortar fire. However, their utilisation is constrained by the challenge in communicating the findings to other forces. Furthermore, for the present time, Ukraine has not obtained the more advanced systems that would identify the source of fire from longer-range artillery systems. Ukrainian forces are also surpassed by the tanks arriving from Russia. Not only are these more contemporary than Ukrainian variants, but Ukraine is also lacking in effective anti-armour weaponry in operational condition. All of these systems, plus medical assistance and field hospital equipment, are on the inventory of Ukrainian requests for support, to enhance the survivability of their forces when confronting new Russian military equipment. Casualties of Ukrainian aircraft over the conflict area demonstrate how well-equipped the Russian-backed separatists are for air defence. This encompasses not merely the Buk missile system - attributed with downing Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 - but also others such as Strela for deployment at lower altitudes and shorter ranges, and an extensive array of lighter, shoulder-launched missiles. Independent specialists, as well as Nato, Western leaders and the Kiev government, state there is clear evidence of direct Russian military participation, despite Russian denials. As component of its military transformation programme, Russia has been preparing for conflict with an intensive schedule of exercises and manoeuvres, involving tens of thousands of servicemen throughout the country. These exercises have been expanding in scale and complexity, and frequently have a narrative which is directly antagonistic to the West. Currently, in addition, Russia has the advantage of a live testing ground in eastern Ukraine, where it can trial its new weapons, systems and tactics. The outcomes - particularly if all of these are tested against any potential new US defensive systems supplied to Ukraine - will assist Russia in evaluating how its forces would perform in a direct confrontation with Nato. Keir Giles is an analyst with the Conflict Studies Research Centre in Oxford, and an Associate Fellow with the Russia and Eurasia Programme at Chatham House in London.

text: A smartphone app is as effective at testing eyesight as an optician's clinic, a trial suggests. The research team, based at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, anticipates it could revolutionise eye care for millions of individuals in isolated regions across the globe. Over 285 million individuals worldwide suffer from blindness or visual impairment. Treatment is frequently straightforward, requiring something as basic as spectacles or cataract surgery. The London-based research team, working alongside Scottish colleagues, adapted a smartphone to create a range of eye tests requiring minimal training and offering easy portability. The Portable Eye Examination Kit (Peek) employs the device's camera to examine the eye's lens for cataracts. The Acuity App utilises a diminishing letter displayed on screen, serving as a fundamental vision assessment. The system uses the camera's flash to illuminate the eye's posterior to detect disease. Initial clinical data from Kenyan trials demonstrate the vision assessment produces identical results to the letter rows displayed on opticians' walls. Participants' eyes underwent examination both at their residences and at an eye clinic. Additional results concerning retinal scanning await publication and are characterised as 'compelling'. text: Organisers of this summer's music festivals have been asked by the government to warn about legal highs. Crime Prevention Minister James Brokenshire dispatched correspondence to festival organisers requesting they caution attendees about the potential dangers of such substances. He additionally stated that narcotics legislation would be amended to permit temporary prohibitions on emerging substances whilst scientific guidance is obtained. Correspondence was similarly forwarded to local authorities and constabularies in festival regions. Mr Brokenshire stated: Throughout the festival period we recognise that individuals may be enticed to experiment with potentially hazardous new narcotics, especially when they are marketed as 'legal' or 'herbal'. This is why we are requesting festival organisers and police to collaborate with us in conveying the message that these substances may not be secure and could contain prohibited drugs. We intend to modify our narcotics legislation so we can react swiftly to emerging substances by implementing a temporary prohibition whilst we obtain comprehensive scientific guidance. Certain drugs formerly marketed as legal highs have subsequently been prohibited, including mephedrone, now a Class B narcotic. The Home Office stated that the drug naphyrone is marketed as NRG1 and distributed as plant food or bath salts, but may contain one or more prohibited drugs. The Government declared it will not permanently prohibit a substance without receiving comprehensive guidance from the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs. In the correspondence dispatched to festival organisers, Mr Brokenshire stated: As part of your preparations for this year's event I request you to examine the measures you have implemented to ensure that your festival provides as secure an environment as possible, to help safeguard the public, particularly young people from the potential dangers and risks of all drugs. The Government's guidance has been endorsed by Melvin Benn, managing director of Festival Republic, which organises the Latitude, Big Chill and Reading and Leeds Festivals. He stated: I can confirm that we do not permit legal high vendors to operate at any Festival Republic festival and completely endorse the minister's position.

text: You may not have heard of Judith Hill, but you've almost certainly heard her voice. The Californian vocalist has delivered backing vocals for Stevie Wonder, Elton John, Josh Groban, Carole King, Robbie Williams and Rod Stewart throughout her distinguished career. Most notably, she was scheduled to be a featured performer on Michael Jackson's ill-fated This Is It tour in 2009 - and can be observed performing a spine-chilling duet with the star in the posthumous film of the rehearsals. She subsequently appeared on the American version of The Voice - where her surprising elimination prompted judge Adam Levine to declare: I hate this country. Hill's attempts to establish a solo career were then chronicled in the Oscar-winning film 20 Feet From Stardom - which focused the spotlight on the (predominantly African-American) backing singers who have supported rock's biggest stars. However, the catalyst for her solo career proved to be Prince - who read about the star in a newspaper, and invited her to record an album at his Paisley Park Studios in Minneapolis. Hill discusses with the BBC their collaboration, her experiences as a backing singer, and the day that Michael Jackson died. What's the first song you recall hearing? Walk With Me by Vanessa Bell Armstrong Who was the first person who informed you you could sing? My mother was the first person to inform me I could sing. She recounts the story of how I was singing in the back car seat as a little girl, and she recognised that I had talent. We composed our first song together when I was four. How did you secure a position on Michael Jackson's This Is It tour? I performed a small gig in Los Angeles and became friends with some musicians there. One of them knew Michael's musical director and he invited me to audition. I undertook a small audition at the vocal director's house and a couple of weeks later I was employed. I remember them informing me, Michael is on your Myspace page. Change the picture! At the time, I was also employed to work at a clothing shop, so I resigned from that job and joined the This Is It tour. He was a master of stagecraft - what advice did he give you? Michael was fascinating to observe. Working with him taught me the importance of seizing every moment on stage. He painted pictures with every lyric and movement in his body. What do you recall of the day he died? I was sitting at a restaurant when my phone started ringing constantly. There were rumours of his death but I did not believe it. It was not until later that day when this nightmare became a reality as I arrived at the Staples Center for rehearsal. It was a very tragic day. They had already begun to dismantle the stage and pack up the equipment. Just the night before we were rehearsing... It was surreal. What was it like to perform at the memorial service? It was an overwhelming experience. I mean, that was the same stage we rehearsed with him [on] two weeks prior. But it was a beautiful service. You were eliminated from the American version of The Voice - what did that experience teach you? When I was on The Voice, I made discoveries about my vocal style. No matter what the song was, I always managed to transform it into a soul song whether I wanted to or not. I learnt that at the heart of it, I'm a soul singer. My roots run deep, starting from the early days of jamming with my parents on Sly and the Family Stone and Curtis Mayfield songs. What difference did 20 Feet From Stardom make to your career? 20 Feet From Stardom was a special project that resonated with so many people. We were honoured with an Oscar and Grammy and many wonderful opportunities have come my way because of it. People were inspired by the stories in the film and they continue to follow my story to see what happens next. How much of a struggle was it to make the transition to solo artist? It's a very difficult road - that 20 feet from being a backing singer to an artist is a long 20 feet! But what keeps me going is a passion for music. No matter what, it makes me happy to do it. What's the biggest difference between working as a backing vocalist and fronting your own material? Working as a backing singer is being part of a group effort to give the artist what they need. It's a fun community to be part of. Being a solo artist is a totally different experience. There is more responsibility and pressure, yet it is very rewarding. I love sitting in the driver's seat, directing everybody to achieve the sound I'm looking for. There's nothing more fulfilling than making the sounds you hear in your head become a reality. Who's the most demanding artist you've sung for? The most demanding was Natalie Cole. It was a short show, but she was very particular about how she wanted the vocals. I have much respect for her. She kept the singers on their toes! How did you end up working with Prince? I did an interview and was asked who is my dream collaborator. I said Prince! He saw the interview and personally reached out to me. I remember receiving the unknown call on my mobile phone and panicking whilst I was talking to him. I officially met him at his album listening party in Los Angeles. Shortly after, he invited me to Paisley Park and that was beginning of the collaboration. He's got a wicked sense of humour... Has he ever caught you out with a prank? He once called me and I did not recognise his voice because he pretended to be someone else. He can do great impersonations. What did he contribute to your album? He's a fantastic producer and arranger. He played many instruments, sang, arranged, and even wrote. He was very involved in the process, yet it was a great collaboration between his ideas and my ideas. Most of the songs were already written and he helped me come up with great grooves and effective edits. Why did you call it Back In Time? I wanted people to feel like they have travelled back into a golden era of funk/soul music. For me, personally, this record celebrates my childhood and upbringing in a musical family. Many of the lyrics are autobiographical - describing where I came from, my old stomping grounds, and the amazing musical community that inspired me along the way. The whole record feels like a dusty jam session in the basement of my parents' house. What song means the most to you? Angel In The Dark. I think about the many times I felt like I was trapped in a dark tunnel, yet God has always managed to rescue me at the right time. He is that Angel in the dark. Judith Hill's debut album Back In Time is out now on NPG Records.
