text: Egyptians go to the polls on 26 and 27 May to elect a new president. Results are anticipated on 5 June, and there exist few uncertainties that former defence minister Abdul Fattah al-Sisi shall triumph decisively. The sole remaining candidate is seasoned left-wing politician and previous presidential aspirant Hamdeen Sabahi. Why is the election being conducted early? The military removed Islamist President Mohammed Morsi following widespread demonstrations last July, and subsequently established a roadmap towards democracy which allowed for presidential elections two years before their scheduled date. A parliamentary ballot was intended to occur initially, but the transitional government reversed this sequence in January. Parliament shall be elected later this year, after the president is securely established in office. The new constitution of January 2014 restricts the president to two successive four-year terms. Mohammed Morsi is presently facing trial charged with inciting the killing of anti-government demonstrators, murdering prison guards during a 2011 jailbreak, espionage and conspiracy to perpetrate terrorist activities. What are the candidates' manifestos and support bases? Mr Sisi has presented an ambitious programme to advance agriculture, housing, education, impoverished regions and employment. He remains unclear regarding how the substantial funding required would be secured, beyond appealing for dedication from all and reduced profit margins for state and private enterprises. He campaigns beneath the motto Long live Egypt! and states his victory would signify the Muslim Brotherhood is finished as a political entity. Mr Sisi possesses the backing of numerous prominent businessmen, alongside a wide spectrum of political parties from the Islamist right to the moderate left. Hamdeen Sabahi, a prominent left-wing figure since the 1970s, provides an alternative to young electors who prefer a civilian candidate over a military one. Under the motto We shall pursue our dream, he pledges to fight corruption and incompetence whilst advancing civil rights. Like Mr Sisi, nevertheless, he states he will not re-legalise Mr Morsi's Muslim Brotherhood, which was prohibited as a terrorist organisation. The parties and movements supporting Mr Sabahi are predominantly left-wing. Abdul Fattah al-Sisi: New face of Egypt's old guard Who is Abdul Fattah al-Sisi? Who is Hamdeen Sabahi? Egyptian election: Voters' views Is the ballot likely to be free and fair? Two elements operate against this. Firstly, the election occurs amidst security and political upheaval. The Muslim Brotherhood continues to demonstrate against the removal of President Morsi, and the authorities have responded with a violent suppression of the Brotherhood and its supporters. Hundreds have perished in confrontations with security forces since last summer and hundreds of others face imprisonment or even death sentences, prompting additional protests. Secondly is the overwhelming backing Mr Sisi receives from the mainstream media, which are already depicting him as the next occupant of the presidential palace. Furthermore, the Muslim Brotherhood's own media within Egypt have been prohibited, so this significant opposition voice is confined to online television and news portals hosted overseas. These do not possess anything approaching the reach of the mainstream media. Who is monitoring the polls? Major Western monitoring organisations are not observing the vote. The US Carter Centre states it will not participate, though the European Union declares it will monitor the ballot across the nation. The Arab League will dispatch 100 monitors, and the African Union will also send a mission despite having suspended Egypt from membership last year. Who is calling for a boycott? Several but not all Islamist parties have declared that they will boycott the vote, though some have endorsed Mr Sisi. The Muslim Brotherhood considers Mr Morsi as the legitimate president and refuses to acknowledge the new election. The pro-Morsi National Alliance to Support Legitimacy describes the vote as a farce, and the Salafist Front has termed it illegitimate. The political wing of the Gamaa Islamiya (Islamic Group), the Building and Development Party, states most of its members also favour a boycott. The secular 6 April Youth Movement - prominent in the uprising against Hosni Mubarak - has also called for a boycott, stating the elections were merely a method of enthroning Mr Sisi. What problems will the new president face? Domestically, the new president will need to address severe political, economic, security and social problems. The public expects the president to handle unemployment, inequality and corruption, but restoring security may be his single greatest challenge. Internationally, the new leader will seek to maintain cordial relations with the US and the West, whilst attempting to improve relations with those nations that supported Mr Morsi - Turkey and Qatar and, to some degree, Iran. text: The centuries-old tradition of church bell-ringing is under threat because of a shortage of new recruits. A BBC local radio survey indicates it is becoming increasingly difficult to persuade newcomers to adopt the practice. Three-quarters of delegates at the annual conference of the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers stated it had become harder over the past decade to attract new members. Approximately eight out of ten delegates reported it was challenging to recruit individuals under 21. Tower captain at St James Garlickhythe in London, Dickon Love, stated that bell-ringing tends to be categorised alongside Morris dancing as an activity for elderly bearded men, but this was misleading. Bell-ringing is stimulating for the mind, he stated. It represents the finest form of heavy metal; it produces a loud, powerful sound, maintains physical fitness, and includes a competitive aspect as well. Moreover, it constitutes a highly social activity - following each practice session without exception, one can locate us at the local public house. They have succeeded in attracting some new recruits and possess a new set of eight bells, fitted four years previously, and a recently-recruited group of ringers, including an astrophysics professor and the art director of a prominent magazine. Pete McCoy, the tower captain at St Mary's Church in Walkley, Sheffield - who encountered his wife Judith through bell-ringing - stated that today's teenagers face more distractions than during his youth. He stated: There were not as many activities available for a teenager or young person as exist today. And is bell-ringing considered fashionable? I believe it is. However, do others share this view? Although nearly 40,000 ringers exist in the UK, just over half of the 180 delegates surveyed at the May conference in Portsmouth believed that declining church attendance has complicated recruitment efforts. 54% Agree 43% Disagree Kate Flavell, of the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers, states the 66 affiliated societies must do more to promote their pastime. They have partnered with the Heritage Open Days initiative to ring bells for the public at 500 locations including St Peter Mancroft in Norwich, where the first full peal was performed in May 1715.

text: UK Chancellor George Osborne is to embark on a week-long visit to China to boost commercial and political ties with the country. Mr Osborne, who shall be accompanied by business leaders and ministers, seeks to foster a new era in UK-China relations, the Treasury stated. His visit, commencing on Sunday, takes him to Beijing, Shanghai and Chengdu. China is the world's second largest economy, but there is mounting evidence that it is losing momentum. Speaking before the seven-day trip, the chancellor said the delegation was about exploring new opportunities to open up new markets. It comes before a state visit to the UK by Chinese President Xi Jinping in October - the first by a Chinese leader for 10 years. Mr Osborne met China's Vice Premier Liu Yandong in Downing Street on Friday, in preparation for the trip. The senior Chinese minister also held talks with Prime Minister David Cameron and Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond, on promoting closer ties between the UK and China. Mr Osborne said: I want us to forge closer economic and cultural links with China. Our partnership for growth, reform and innovation is helping to deliver record levels of investment and trade in both directions, but there is much more we can do. This trip is all about exploring new opportunities to open up new markets to benefit both economies. The centrepiece of Mr Osborne's visit shall be the UK-China Economic and Financial Dialogue in Beijing. Accompanying him shall be Treasury minister Lord O'Neill, Business Secretary Sajid Javid and Energy Secretary Amber Rudd. Mr Osborne is also going to promote his plans for a Northern Powerhouse in England, taking with him a delegation of senior business and local government figures, including Liverpool Mayor Joe Anderson and Manchester City Council leader Sir Richard Leese. The trip signifies a further warming in UK-Chinese relations after a dispute over Prime Minister David Cameron's decision to meet the Dalai Lama in 2012. Both Mr Cameron and Mr Osborne visited China last year, when the PM urged the country to invest in UK infrastructure, including nuclear power stations and high-speed rail. And earlier this year the UK became a member of the Chinese-backed Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. China recently revised down its 2014 growth figures from 7.4% to 7.3% - its weakest performance in nearly 25 years. For this year, the government is targeting annual economic growth of approximately 7%. Mounting evidence that the world's economic powerhouse is slowing down has caused major investment market falls.

text: David Cameron has visited a Lebanese refugee camp amid the crisis triggered by war in neighbouring Syria. Mr Cameron, who is conducting his inaugural visit to Lebanon as prime minister, encountered a family at a camp in the Bekaa Valley who are scheduled to be transported to the UK. He stated: I wished to come here to observe for myself and to listen for myself to accounts of refugees. The UK will receive up to 20,000 Syrian refugees during the next five years, Mr Cameron informed MPs earlier this month. He has designated Richard Harrington as minister for Syrian refugees to ensure the arrivals receive a warm welcome in the UK. The prime minister's visit occurs as European Union interior ministers are convening in Brussels to discuss proposals to distribute 160,000 asylum seekers across 23 EU states through compulsory quotas. Home Secretary Theresa May is anticipated to attend and resist proposals for an EU-wide quota system for refugees. Under EU law the UK, Ireland and Denmark are excluded from the quota proposal. James Landale, BBC deputy political editor It is David Cameron's inaugural visit to Lebanon and he is present with a clear objective: to address the criticism that Britain is not doing sufficient to tackle Europe's refugee crisis. So he toured a refugee camp in the Bekaa valley just one mile from the Syrian border to encounter just some of the families benefiting from British aid. He also visited a school at the heart of Beirut supported by British funding where Syrian and Lebanese pupils study together. The PM's contention is that this is the assistance Syrian refugees require rather than any encouragement to risk the perilous journey to Europe. So to a nation now accustomed to television images of Syrian refugees fleeing across Europe, Mr Cameron wishes to remind people of where the vast majority are located, namely in Lebanon, Turkey, Jordan and Syria itself. Mr Cameron asserts British aid is deterring hundreds of thousands of refugees from travelling to Europe. Aid agencies on the ground suggest poverty and an inability to pay the traffickers is a more significant factor. And whilst welcoming British aid, they also suggest it is nowhere near sufficient. So today is about the PM attempting to reframe a debate that has continued for many weeks, a debate that has not always proceeded his way. Migrant crisis: Why is it erupting now? EU migration: Crisis in graphics Mr Cameron stated: I wish to focus on how we assist Syrian refugees here in Lebanon, in Jordan, how we ensure we discourage people from making this dangerous journey to Europe but instead we take people from these camps and we make them welcome in the United Kingdom, in our country. Following a meeting with Lebanon's prime minister Tammam Salam, Mr Cameron stated the UK was determined to do all we can to strengthen the security of Lebanon. He stated training had already been provided to more than 5,000 Lebanese soldiers and the UK had assisted to build a series of watchtowers on the border with Syria. The UK will also train, equip and mentor the Lebanese armed forces, he stated. Lebanon is to receive £29m of the additional £100m in UK aid for Syria and surrounding countries announced by the prime minister earlier this month. This will fund food packages for thousands of refugees, as well as clean water, blankets, stoves, mattresses, counselling support and play areas for children. There are 1.1 million Syrian refugees registered in Lebanon, which is more than a quarter of Lebanon's population. The camp visited by the prime minister is operated by the UN's refugee agency and is one of 1,500 in the Bekaa Valley, which is less than a mile from the Syrian border. Mr Cameron also observed the enrolment of pupils on the first day of the academic year at the Sed el Bouchrieh school in Beirut. At the school Syrian children are joining classes alongside Lebanese children as part of a drive, part-funded by UK aid, to integrate refugees into the wider society. The former Labour foreign secretary David Miliband criticised the UK government for only agreeing to resettle 20,000 refugees during the next five years. Mr Miliband, who leads the aid agency International Rescue Committee (IRC), stated it was inadequate to take just 4,000 refugees from Syria per year and stated it was the equivalent of the number arriving on the beaches of Greek island Lesbos every day. Each country needs to shoulder the burden and agree to both relocate refugees who have reached the continent and resettle the most vulnerable from the Middle East, he stated.

text: More than a third of the workforce at a wind energy firm in Argyll and Bute have been told their jobs are under threat. CS Wind notified employees that as many as 60 positions could be eliminated at the Machrihanish facility owing to insufficient orders. The South Korean firm assumed control of the location on the former RAF airbase fewer than 12 months previously. It remained uncertain whether the difficulties would impact proposals to construct a new facility for offshore wind equipment. CS Wind could not be reached immediately for comment. The corporation purchased the turbine infrastructure company Wind Towers Scotland (WTS) last April, and pledged to generate new employment at the rural location near Campbeltown. It presently employs approximately 150 personnel. Local councillor Rory Colville stated he believed proposals for a new facility to manufacture offshore wind power equipment would continue to proceed, with construction scheduled to commence in July. He stated: There exists no indication that has been postponed. The company is requesting assurances from the administrations at Holyrood and Westminster that they remain committed to wind energy. It proves extremely important for the local economy that we maintain CS Wind's operations. Mr Colville stated investment had been undertaken in deep-water facilities to enhance the wind energy sector, but he additionally requested the former airbase be granted Enterprise Zone status. The location was purchased by a community-led consortium for £1 in 2012 and represents one of six locations competing to become the UK's inaugural space port. Scottish Energy Minister Paul Wheelhouse stated market conditions proved challenging for onshore wind energy companies but he additionally criticised UK ministers for their failure to deliver a viable 'route to market' for new projects. He stated: The announcement represents disappointing news for the workforce at Machrihanish and the broader Campbeltown community and will prove an extremely difficult period for those affected and their families. I understand from my personal discussions with management that this forms part of CS Wind UK's effort to enhance the long-term sustainability of the Machrihanish facility whilst confronting challenging market conditions. Argyll and Bute MSP Michael Russell stated he had discussed with both the company and the energy minister regarding the employment threat. He stated: I have been requesting assurances concerning the future of the staff who have been given notice regarding possible redundancies.

text: Russia will not compete at next month’s Paralympics in Rio after losing an appeal against a ban imposed for state-sponsored doping. Media playback is not supported on this device The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld the International Paralympic Committee's (IPC) prohibition on all Russian competitors. The IPC reached the decision following the McLaren report which outlined a Russian state-sponsored doping programme. Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev characterised the decision as cynical. Medvedev stated certain leaders of the Paralympic movement sought to squeeze out strong competitors, and he proceeded to describe the decision as a blow to all people with disabilities, not just Russians. The CAS panel, which intends to publish the complete grounds for its decision later, stated the IPC's decision to prohibit the entire Russian team was proportionate in the circumstances. It noted that the Russian Paralympic Committee did not submit any evidence contradicting the facts presented by the IPC. The Paralympics commence on 7 September. The IPC's decision contrasts with that of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which opted not to impose a blanket ban on Russia from the Olympic Games. The IOC faced widespread criticism for disregarding the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) recommendation to ban Russia. Instead, each individual sporting federation received the authority to determine if Russian competitors were permitted to compete. A three-person IOC panel then held the final say. Ultimately, more than 270 Russian athletes received clearance to compete at the Olympics, with Russia securing 56 medals in total and finishing fourth in the medal table. Russia had been scheduled to send 267 competitors across 18 sports to the Paralympics. The CAS statement noted that it had not examined the natural justice rights or personality rights of individual Russian athletes in reaching its decision. Russia's Paralympic team's solicitor, Alexei Karpenko, confirmed the decision was final, stating they would attempt to file an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, but it would require between one and two years for the court to consider the case. So I fear Russian Paralympians will not be attending the Games in any case, Karpenko added. IPC president Sir Philip Craven, who has characterised Russia's anti-doping system as broken, corrupted and entirely compromised, and claimed it placed medals over morals, stated he was greatly encouraged by the CAS decision. He said it was not a day for celebration, adding: We have enormous sympathy for the Russian athletes who will now miss out. It is a sad day for the Paralympic movement, said Craven. But we hope also a new beginning. We hope this decision serves as a catalyst for change in Russia and we can welcome the Russian Paralympic Committee back as a member safe in the knowledge that it is fulfilling its obligations to ensure fair competition for all. Russian sports minister Vitaly Mutko described the ban as political and not within legal framework, whilst solicitor Karpenko termed it a black day for the sports judiciary. He stated: I can only express huge disappointment at the ruling. The rights of Russian Paralympians have been blatantly violated. Regardless of whether the Russian Paralympics Committee is guilty of the charges, punishing innocent athletes and not permitting them to defend themselves - which was an opportunity afforded to the Russian Olympics athletes - this is a flagrant violation of human rights. Meanwhile, Dmitry Svishchev, the head of Russia's parliamentary sports committee, characterised the CAS decision as an inhumane act. Speaking to the state-owned TASS news agency, he added: [CAS has shown] an unprecedented impudence and lack of principle. How is it possible to bar the people who with their courage have earned the right to a proper life from the Games? Whatever this court is called, it is an inhumane court. One can punish officials, coaches, but by no means should athletes be punished: when observing what they do in spite of hardships and strain, one wants to remove their hat. text: You would think securing promotion to the top flight of a national league would mean a lucrative bonus for any footballer. However, Cardiff Metropolitan University football team's players have not earned a single penny despite achieving promotion to the Welsh Premier League. Indeed, the students, champions of Welsh League Division One, must pay for the privilege of participating. They must actually pay us £150 subscription each season and that is what funds our football budget for the year, director of football and former Wales international Dr Christian Edwards stated. First and foremost they are at the university to study and they must be good students in order to obtain their degrees and then it is their football life and their social life. They truly do sacrifice a great deal and many of these players are in their fifth, sixth year with us. Charlie Corsby is a PhD student and we have got a few Masters students. These players are not only developing as football players but developing as academics. Cardiff Metropolitan University, then known as UWIC, merged with League of Wales founder members Inter Cardiff in 2000. The students had failed to achieve promotion to the Welsh Premier the previous season when they lost out to Haverfordwest County on the final day of the campaign. Edwards stated the disappointment of missing out spurred the team on to go one better this season and they secured their place with a 3-0 victory at Taffs Well. We planted the seed in pre-season discussing about the one goal and we carried that throughout the season, Edwards told BBC Wales Sport. Barry Town pushed us very hard, Goytre pushed us very hard. We are glad we came out on top. Success on the pitch alone could not have secured promotion to the Welsh Premier League with the University investing in infrastructure and facilities to secure the required FAW domestic licence. Edwards recognises how difficult a task his side face in Welsh football's top flight next season but added they were not daunted by the prospect. We have played a couple of Welsh Premier League teams in the past few seasons in the Welsh Cup and in large parts of those games we have accounted ourselves very well, he stated. We do not think we are going to be ripping up any trees but we certainly think we can compete. The journey that we started some six years ago is one that is progressive and we always believe we are arriving somewhere rather than arrived. Caerphilly-born Edwards, who began his career at Swansea City, won one cap for Wales against Switzerland in 1996 when he came on as a substitute for current national team boss Chris Coleman. Edwards also played for, amongst others, Nottingham Forest and Bristol Rovers before retiring from professional football at the age of 30. Media playback is not supported on this device The central defender spent four seasons with Welsh Premier League side Aberystwyth Town, including a spell as caretaker manager in 2009. A member of the teaching staff of Cardiff Metropolitan University's School of Sport since 2010, he combined his roles as lecturer and director of football with his own academic studies. It was a natural step when I retired in 2006 to return to academia, Edwards stated. My wife said I could never retire and become somebody who did DIY. I was never going to obtain a job like that so the next thing for me was to study. I always enjoyed studying even when I played. When I was at Swansea as a youngster I did my A Levels and if I had not been fortunate to be a professional football player I think I would have been a PE teacher. Promotion to the Welsh Premier League has not been the only highlight for Edwards this year as in January he was awarded a doctorate by the University. The intention was a three-year degree and a PGCE and move on but the pathway allowed me to do a Masters degree and then I was fortunate to undertake a PhD, Edwards stated. Another door opened and a job came with it and it has been fantastic. I never set out to gain a Doctorate. My thesis was based around the culture of the football club so I owe a great deal to the football team, the players and the coaching staff in helping me gain my doctorate.

text: Generally speaking, England will be very happy to have won the Test series against Sri Lanka without really breaking sweat. Although they failed to complete the task quite as swiftly as they managed in the opening Test, their nine-wicket victory in the second Test at Chester-le-Street remained thoroughly comprehensive, with Sri Lanka never truly competitive throughout the match. England coach Trevor Bayliss assessed their display at eight out of 10. I would award them seven - they remain not entirely functioning at full capacity and, as captain Alastair Cook acknowledged, there were periods when they eased their intensity. However, that is perhaps being overly critical. It remains consistently difficult to properly evaluate a side when their opposition are weak, as Sri Lanka have been throughout most of this series. Yet one aspect is evident: James Anderson is bowling exceptionally well. Even facing world-class batsmen, he would continue making the ball behave identically. He stands at the peak of his form and his rise to the summit of the Test bowling rankings is thoroughly merited. Fast bowling represents such an unpredictable discipline, with so much dependent upon rhythm - that elusive element which proves so difficult to describe or measure. Anderson lacked rhythm in South Africa, yet suddenly he approaches his run-up contentedly again, 'kissing' the surface and claiming numerous wickets. One might contend that superior batsmen would handle him more effectively, but in these circumstances, moving the ball in both directions, Anderson presents a threatening challenge for anyone globally. One cannot undervalue the significance of the overs he delivered for Lancashire previously this season, claiming 12 wickets at an average of 20.75 across three fixtures. Regardless of identity and Test cricket experience, rhythm cannot be recovered in practice sessions. What a difference with Steven Finn. Finn was possibly the outstanding bowler of the series in South Africa, where Anderson faltered, yet now his rhythm appears to have abandoned him once more. He commits no errors - I understand well from my own playing career that occasionally one can charge in with identical effort and believe the ball is being released just as rapidly as usual, yet it simply fails to emerge with the same sharpness. My concern is that he possesses no chance to rediscover his rhythm before the final Test at Lord's commences on 9 June - there exists only one T20 Blast fixture for Middlesex in which he could potentially participate. Finn must feature at Lord's. There has been some discussion that England might wish to examine Jake Ball, who has remained in the squad for the initial two Tests, yet he can await his opportunity. Finn understands Lord's thoroughly and this could represent his chance to regain some form. Even whilst winning, one must seek to advance the team, and there exist several areas that will be causing the England management some anxiety presently. Jonny Bairstow has been outstanding with the bat this summer yet his wicketkeeping remains developing. He does commit errors: he drops catches and misses stumpings. It represents an extremely demanding role, and slow-motion replays can prove very harsh on keepers because one thinks 'how has he missed that?' Yet it occurs in an absolute instant. However, I do not believe his position behind the stumps faces threat. Unfortunately, those misses can occasionally prove expensive and, should he make too many, his place as keeper will face examination. The other concern is Nick Compton's form at number three. Whilst he will feel enormously relieved to have scored 22 not out in the second innings as England pursued 79 to win in Durham, his difficulty is that he has not accumulated substantial runs all summer - for England or Middlesex. Lord's represents a ground he knows intimately and he will be eager to perform well. It will offer a flatter surface than we have witnessed thus far this summer and the conditions should prove more favourable for batting. Should England win the toss and bat first, he will possess an excellent opportunity to secure that position - that represents how he will view it. I do not believe his England place necessarily depends upon his performance in the third Test - there exists quite a substantial interval between that match and the opening Test against Pakistan on 14 July and he could depart and score numerous runs for Middlesex. Yet should he fail to achieve a score, people will scrutinise him even more closely. One man whose place certainly faces no scrutiny is Cook. What a remarkable achievement for him to become the first Englishman to reach 10,000 Test runs. He has accomplished it in the most challenging manner possible - opening the batting, largely with the responsibility of captaincy, and with uncertainty regarding his partner at the opposite end. Those represent three elements with which most individuals would find extraordinarily difficult to succeed. One must possess complete admiration for him. He is not a stylist and he does not have spectators rushing to observe him, yet that represents Test cricket. One requires players like Cook to neutralise attacks and establish the foundation of an innings for the team. He has fulfilled that function absolutely superbly, and he will continue. For a period, he was as stubborn with his captaincy as he was with his batting and, as a leader, one does not truly desire that. Yet he has certainly opened up during the past year and his confidence has grown tremendously. Still he can venture out to bat, dismiss everything else and concentrate on what he must accomplish with a bat in his hands - and that represents a great tribute to him. That concentration has been in some respects Cook's defining characteristic as a Test batsman, and it was evident from the very start. I recall him arriving in Nagpur following that lengthy journey from the West Indies, merely two days before making his debut, and he scored 60 and a century. One thought, 'this fellow's rather special', because he can focus entirely on batting. Long may he persist. Jonathan Agnew was speaking to BBC Sport's James Gheerbrant.

text: After months of secrecy, the sequel to the late Stieg Larsson's best-selling Millennium series has been published. These are external links and will open in a new window The Girl in the Spider's Web, by David Lagercrantz, continues the narrative of punk super-hacker Lisbeth Salander which commenced in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo. However, as Lagercrantz explains, writing the new instalment brought with it the pressure of remaining faithful to Larsson's characters and criticism from Larsson's long-term partner. There has been so much secrecy surrounding this book, so I am longing to see what people think, says Swedish writer David Lagercrantz, speaking to the BBC just a few days before The Girl in the Spider's Web reached bookshelves around the world. With more than 80 million copies of Stieg Larsson's Millennium Trilogy already sold, Lagercrantz can be forgiven a few pre-publication nerves. I have felt pressure from the beginning, he admits. I am absolutely terrified. But I think the pressure actually made me a better writer. It would be a disgrace if I did not live up to [Stieg Larsson's] books or at least try my best. Larsson, who died of a heart attack aged 50 in 2004, did not live to see his novels - The Girl With Dragon Tattoo, The Girl Who Played with Fire and The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest - become a publishing sensation. The books were all adapted for the screen - three Swedish films and an American remake of Dragon Tattoo starring Rooney Mara and Daniel Craig. Despite being with him for 32 years, Larsson's partner Eva Gabrielsson was not entitled to anything from his estate under Swedish law, as they were not married and there was no valid will. She has been locked in a legal battle for a number of years with his father and brother, who inherited Larsson's estate. In December 2013, the estate and Swedish publisher Norstedts commissioned Lagercrantz to take on the characters of hacker and social misfit Lisbeth Salander and journalist Mikael Blomkvist. In the run-up to publication, Gabrielsson has described Lagercrantz as a totally idiotic choice and told The Sunday Times that the sequel was a money-making stunt that would have appalled Larsson. How has he dealt with the criticism? It was tough, he responds without hesitation. All I wanted to do was to follow my passion and tell a good story. This has been the thrill of my life. The only thing that troubles me and makes me sad is that Eva Gabrielsson and the family have not reached a settlement about the book. She could call me anything, I just have the deepest sympathy for her. I know this is good for Stieg's authorship. We are reading him again, he is becoming even more iconic. He saw what was coming - back in Stieg Larsson's day the extreme right and the racists were a small group of lunatics. Now they are everywhere. Has there been any contact with Eva? No. She is very angry and I accept that. I am daydreaming that we will one day have a good conversation about it. She called me an idiotic choice - well, the readers have to decide. She said I am not like Stieg Larsson, and I accept that. But if you want a copycat the circle would be so narrow. Born in 1962, Lagercrantz - the son of Swedish author and literary critic Olof Lagercrantz - was a journalist for the national newspaper Expressen before making his debut as an author in 1997 with Ultimate High, the story of Swedish adventurer Goran Kropp, who climbed Mount Everest without oxygen tanks or sherpas. His other books include Fall of Man in Wilmslow, a novel about British codebreaker Alan Turing, and I am Zlatan Ibrahimovic, the autobiography of the Swedish football star on which he was ghost-writer. Lagercrantz points out that he has always been interested in characters with a streak of genius who refuse to follow convention. That is what drew him to Lisbeth Salander, to the extent that she began to inhabit his dreams whilst he was writing the new book. I was absolutely obsessed. I was quite terrible to live with. My wife and children were very kind. I was scared I would do her an injustice. In the beginning I thought it would be easy to write her. She is such an extreme character. Many people are scared of Lisbeth Salander and so was I. I asked myself all the time: am I worthy? Such was the secrecy surrounding the project, Lagercrantz wrote on a computer without an internet connection. Nothing was sent digitally. Even the final proofs were hand-delivered to foreign publishers with individual couriers. We used code-words and we did not email anything, he recalls. We met in the cellars and things like that. The plot was influenced by the National Security Agency and the [Edward] Snowden affair. I was living in the same reality I was writing about. We were quite paranoid all the time. I am a talkative guy so it was hard, but I kept the secrets. There were no leaks, it was extraordinary. In Sweden the title of the book is Det som inte dodar oss (What Does Not Kill Us). Does he plan to write another Millennium novel? That we will see. The only thing I know is that I found myself as a writer. He says offers have been coming in from all over the world which he is discussing with his agent. One thing is for certain - I will not be Stieg Larsson for the whole of my life. I want to write new books. It is good to be insecure. The Girl in the Spider's Web (published in the UK by Quercus) is out now.

text: David Cameron's hurried visit to Paris on Monday night is yet another significant sign that his EU reforms - dismissed as weak by critics in the UK - are seen by some in the EU as going too far. France remains concerned by the Prime Minister's campaign to safeguard non-euro nations from eurozone regulations. One might argue that this appears wholly sensible. The majority of EU member states utilise the euro. Why should they be permitted to unite to the detriment of non-euro nations such as Britain? However, France believes David Cameron and George Osborne, the UK Chancellor, are employing duplicitous tactics. It suspects they are utilising this argument to secure an unjust advantage for the City of London and an indirect veto over eurozone and broader EU financial legislation. The French economy remains stagnant, to express it diplomatically, and the French president is preparing to commence the political campaign for re-election. He cannot appear to facilitate Britain's enhanced financial performance whilst his eurozone options remain constrained. A fortnight ago on the evening before the publication in Brussels of David Cameron's draft reform proposals, we were informed by a senior source familiar with the negotiations that the French postponed them for hours, expressing concern about the language regarding protections for non-eurozone nations. All leaders must endorse the reforms this Thursday for their approval at the EU summit. The French might once more object, dispute and potentially destroy the Prime Minister's prospects of an agreement. Should they choose to do so. A genuine possibility, nevertheless, is that following hours of private negotiations, the summit will conclude with the type of EU compromise so criticised by the bloc's detractors. Nevertheless in characteristic EU fashion, all parties wish to depart claiming they have secured something. The French will probably boast that the British failed to obtain a veto over eurozone legislation (despite David Cameron never requesting one). The nations of central and eastern Europe received Britain's commitment to assist in strengthening NATO in eastern Europe as a pre-summit incentive. They also aspire to limit reductions in EU migrant in-work and child benefits to the UK exclusively. The European Commission and council performed crucial functions as facilitator and mediator respectively and, consequently, received some respectful media coverage in Europe - something which, during these times of eurozone and migration crisis, they rarely experience. And David Cameron should secure his agreement in time for him to announce the referendum at the earliest opportunity - which is believed to be 23 June. He understands completely that, regardless of any deal's substance, his critics will condemn it. Therefore he appears to prefer ticking sufficient boxes, particularly the one that seems to address migration - the primary concern of many of his voters. He recognises that convincing the British public to support any agreement before the referendum represents a far greater challenge than securing support from 27 quarrelsome and preoccupied EU leaders. The Prime Minister wishes to leave his EU counterparts to return to arguably the most difficult issue on their agenda: refugees, boats and migrant quotas. On Monday, European Council President Donald Tusk urged EU leaders to assist David Cameron in achieving his reforms. It is high time we began listening to each other's arguments, the risk of dissolution is genuine. What is damaged cannot be repaired, he stated. If those represent Mr Tusk's remarks on Brexit (the concept of Britain departing the EU), what might he say regarding the refugee and migration crisis, combined with the gradual erosion of European unity? 'Audacious demand': UK's wish list seriously taken by EU leaders Guide: All you need to know about the referendum Referendum timeline: What will happen when? Q&A: What does Britain want from Europe? text: I have been working now for more than two decades and I've not seen a measles epidemic of this severity, says Doctor Raza Hasan, as he shows me around the measles isolation ward of the Lahore Children's Hospital. The ward is so overcrowded with infants and young children that they are sharing beds. At one point, as many as 70 new patients were arriving at the hospital daily. They are covered in rashes and burning with high fevers, some battling for their lives. In one corner, a boy lies motionless on his back, his eyes rolled back as flies crawl across his face. At least 40 children have perished in this hospital since the epidemic spread from southern Pakistan to Lahore and other areas of Punjab province at the start of the year. The burden of managing the epidemic weighs heavily on Dr Hasan, who recounts stories of families attacking medical staff at the hospital after discovering their children had perished. Whilst measles itself is seldom fatal, it can lead to life-threatening complications such as meningitis and pneumonia, particularly in developing nations where malnutrition leaves many children with compromised immunity. Some of them are arriving very late at the hospital, states Dr Hasan. After developing complications at home, their parents do not take them to doctors, they do not receive any treatment and so when they arrive here... there is not much we can do. Some are in the final stage of life or already deceased with meningitis or pneumonia, he continues. However whilst this may be accurate, it is not the complete story. It does not explain why so many children in Pakistan are contracting measles in the first place. The epidemic has spread rapidly with thousands of cases nationwide and 239 deaths between January and April 2013, according to Pakistan's national measles coordinator. One reason is the low vaccination coverage of the population, states Dr Tanvir Ahmed, the director-general of health services for Punjab province. In the districts there are even pockets where there is no vaccination coverage. The average [coverage] for Punjab is 58 per cent. Through an entrance off a narrow street in Lahore, we climb the stairs to the home of Nasara and Mohammed Ashfaq. The walls are bare and despite daytime temperatures exceeding 40C, there are no fans. Mohammed is cradling his daughter Yasmeen, who will be two this summer. She is covered in the measles rash and has had an alarmingly high fever. Just a few days ago, her brother Ehsan died at the Lahore Children's hospital from complications arising from measles. He was nine months old. Now the family is frightened to take Yasmeen to hospital and hope she will recover at home. Yasmeen, like her brother, had not been properly vaccinated against measles. I did not get him vaccinated because I was on my own at home with so many children, states Nasara. And we had to go out to get the vaccinations, so it was difficult because they were small. Whilst doctors here state families need to take more responsibility for ensuring their children are vaccinated, they accept the official vaccination programmes have often been poorly managed, leading to people missing out. We have removed nine district managers on the basis of poor performance of the programmes, states Dr Tanvir Ahmed, head of health services in Punjab. And we have improved our monitoring and supervision. There has also been an emergency measles vaccination campaign in recent weeks covering 2.6 million children in Lahore. In June another 11 million children are due to be inoculated in other parts of Punjab. Health experts hope this will bring the epidemic in the province under control by mid-July. They state they have the large stocks of vaccine necessary to achieve this in the province. However they state this is not the case in the southern province of Sindh, where the outbreak began. It is believed mass vaccination programmes will not commence in Sindh until the autumn. So in this area, which has already had by far the highest number of cases in the country, the epidemic could worsen in the coming months.

text: Labour remains committed to renewing the Trident nuclear weapons system, new shadow defence secretary Nia Griffith has said. She informed Forces TV that she had previously held serious doubts regarding it, though Labour policy remained supportive and this was unlikely to alter. Ms Griffith succeeded Clive Lewis following Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn's shadow cabinet reshuffle earlier this month. Mr Lewis's conference address on Trident underwent last-minute modifications. He was understood to have been stopped from making an unequivocal commitment to Labour renewing Britain's nuclear weapons system by the leader's office. Labour's formal policy supports renewing the Trident system, though leader Jeremy Corbyn - a long-standing CND campaigner - seeks to alter the party's stance and initiated a defence review to consider the matter. During her interview, Ms Griffith stated that Labour delegates at the party conference in September had endorsed the weapons system and that represents a commitment we shall maintain. She declared Labour cannot be shilly-shallying about regarding Trident, whilst adding that Britain must advocate for multilateral disarmament. What we must do now, and there exists a very strong sentiment for this, both within the Labour Party and amongst the wider public, is genuinely advance multilateral nuclear disarmament, the multilateral approach of uniting people across the globe to attempt making our world safer, she stated. Renewing Trident would require manufacturing four replacement submarines at a present estimated cost of £31bn. The contentious nuclear arms matter created division within Labour when MPs voted favourably for renewal in July, with 140 Labour MPs supporting renewal, 47 opposing and the remainder abstaining. CND, which seeks a global prohibition on nuclear weapons, voiced disappointment regarding Ms Griffith's remarks, stating the issue seemed to be getting sidelined. Labour has not debated Trident for 20 years yet it persists in maintaining its old policy despite the fact that most Labour members oppose Trident and the party leader has been elected twice with a strong anti-Trident stance, declared its general secretary Kate Hudson. We encourage Labour Party members to ensure the defence review gets published, alongside a full democratic debate within the party and at its next conference. Meanwhile, Mr Corbyn has announced the appointment of seven additional shadow ministers, bringing his team to 68 frontbenchers. Those taking shadow ministerial roles are Paula Sherriff (women and equalities), Richard Burden (transport), Wayne David (defence), Khalid Mahmood (foreign office), Rupa Huq (home affairs), Lyn Brown (home affairs) and Gill Furniss (business). Additionally, the former chief whip, Dame Rosie Winterton, has been appointed the party's envoy with responsibility for relations with Labour's international sister parties within the Party of European Socialists. Her removal as chief whip, as part of a reshuffle following Mr Corbyn's re-election, had angered numerous Labour MPs.

text: China's Communist Party and its more than two-million-man army aren't supposed to like video games. Home-video consoles, which had been gaining popularity throughout the 1990s, were formally prohibited in 2000 amid concerns they were corrupting Chinese youth. It represented a form of King Canute communism - an effort to stem the rising tide of capitalism and the influx of Western cultural products. Naturally, it ultimately failed and the strident warnings about electronic heroin were overwhelmed by consumer demand. Consoles remained obtainable through the grey market and the gaming industry simply shifted online. Today it constitutes an industry worth more than 50bn Chinese RMB ($7.9bn; £5.2bn) annually and the Communist Party and its military are now firmly involved in the enterprise. Since its public launch several months ago, Glorious Mission, a video game originally developed for and by the Chinese military, has been downloaded over one million times. It may appear like merely another shoot-'em-up blood-fest but it is, actually, China's newest propaganda instrument. It was developed as a training tool for Chinese soldiers and state-run television has broadcast images of ranks of them cheerfully gaming, controlling virtual People's Liberation Army troops in various battlefield scenarios. Notably, the virtual enemy they are confronting appears occasionally to bear at least some resemblance to the US and its allies, prompting questions about precisely what real-life scenarios they are training for. However, regardless of the effect on soldiers, the decision to make the game accessible to the broader public was made to instil patriotic values, the core values of the military, according to army sources. Gu Kai, vice-president of the software developers behind the game, Giant Network Technology, states that he believes the game will help generate new army recruits. I would hope that somebody will play the game and fulfil their dream, he states. Most young boys, from the bottom of their hearts, want to be a soldier. They like to fight, they like to win, and if this video game can make that dream come true, I won't be surprised. The propaganda appears, in places, rather unsubtle. One of the game's stages recreates the fiery atmosphere of camp life, according to one news report. In one Shanghai internet café, almost every one of the 100 or so terminals is occupied with someone engaged in intense online combat with a wide variety of foes; goblin, alien or human. One young man states he spends more than 10 hours weekly in here, and he agrees that online games might be a powerful tool for influencing thoughts and ideas. It's possible, he states. Most of the players here are young. A military video game could make you feel familiar with and then develop an affinity for the army. Glorious Mission, therefore, represents a swift about-turn for the Chinese military as well as a sign that China isn't merely censoring the internet, banning search terms and deleting posts which it does routinely, but also now attempting to harness its power. The country already possesses an army of Communist Party bloggers posting comments in support of the government. The seemingly rehabilitated gaming industry is simply the latest weapon. This year, reports in state media suggest that the authorities might be about to formally abandon their moral scruples about the gaming industry altogether, with the consoles ban apparently coming up for review. Gu Kai from Giant Network Technology tells me that he thinks China is now well and truly over it. I've met some of the officials, he states. They stopped worrying about video games years ago. Most of them are promoting gaming as a new, hopeful and fast growing industry. At least here in Shanghai all the officials are very open and supportive. China isn't the first to design a video game for military training purposes - Glorious Mission bears some resemblance to a game made 10 years ago, as a tool for the US military and also as a lure for army recruitment. But influencing the thoughts of the wider public and attempting to mould and foster nationalist sentiment and loyalty is a more ambitious battle, and in China's virtual world, it's a battle that's likely to intensify.

text: Christian Eriksen scored twice as Tottenham proved far too strong for spirited Hull City at White Hart Lane. The Denmark international found the net in both halves as Tottenham strengthened their hold on fifth position in the Premier League with their eighth victory of the campaign. Danny Rose served up Eriksen's opener on a platter within 15 minutes following excellent work down the left flank, and Kyle Walker performed similarly from the right to extinguish any prospect of a Hull fightback after the interval. Eriksen was extremely unfortunate not to secure the match ball after witnessing a brilliant free-kick pushed onto the post by Hull keeper David Marshall, permitting Victor Wanyama to clear up the rebound from several yards out. Hull cannot lodge any grievances regarding the loss but the comprehensive final scoreline was somewhat harsh on the Tigers after they competed with their opponents for extended periods. Nevertheless, 35 goals shipped in 16 matches represents a damning statistic for the club second-from-bottom of the table - as does the reality they have now suffered six consecutive away defeats, matching their top-flight record. Tottenham controlled possession and opportunities - registering 27 attempts in total - but clear-cut chances were at a premium. Wing-backs Rose and Walker posed a constant threat, nevertheless, and it was through them that Tottenham enjoyed the greatest success. After 14 minutes Rose raced down the flank to collect Jan Vertonghen's long pass, progressed and cut inside his marker before setting up Eriksen to drive the ball high into the net. With Tottenham deploying Eric Dier alongside Vertonghen and Toby Alderweireld in a three-man defence, Tottenham's wing-backs enjoyed greater freedom to advance and their second goal shared similarities with the first. This time it was Dier with a pass over the top for Walker to gather and progress into the box, and when he delivered low across the face of goal it was a simple task for Eriksen to slot home his second at the far post - his fifth goal in his previous four Premier League matches. Rose subsequently earned the free-kick from which Tottenham scored their third, crowning an excellent display by the England full-back. Despite the chasm between the teams in terms of league standing and resources, Hull delivered a performance that was, for a period, equal to their opponents. They managed 10 attempts on target away from home against a top-five team - something they have failed to achieve at home against inferior opposition this season - and with slightly more composure might have drawn Tottenham level at 1-1. Jake Livermore was the standout amongst Hull's players against his former side and it was he who nearly drew them level. His first opportunity came during a sustained period of Hull pressure after falling behind, but Hugo Lloris dropped well to deny his stabbed effort. The Tigers' second promising chance came as the Tottenham supporters were beginning to voice displeasure at their team's failure to assert themselves on the visitors at the beginning of the second half. Tottenham had multiple penalty claims rejected by referee Andre Marriner, and it was following one of those - after Eriksen was knocked over by Andrew Robertson - that Hull almost equalised. The counter-attack concluded with Livermore being released on the right of the box, but his initial attempt was blocked and his follow-up cleared away by the left boot of Lloris. Three minutes later Eriksen was converting his second goal of the evening and the match was finished for the Tigers. Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino: I believe it was a match we controlled. I believe the most significant thing is the three points, to be close to the top four. In certain parts the team performed well, which is difficult against a team fighting for survival. On Christian Eriksen: He was extremely close to a hat-trick. It was an excellent performance for him - he played exceptionally well. On Eric Dier: I know there are numerous rumours, but he's 100% our player. He's extremely important for us. He signed a contract following the Euros and demonstrated his commitment to the club. There's no question his future is at White Hart Lane. Hull manager Mike Phelan: We arrived here with a tremendous attitude. They've come here and played the ball, controlled it, limited their attempts, but at a certain point in the match we were more than value for money. I thought they performed excellently but we're on the receiving end of a 3-0 defeat - but we must remain positive. Every match is crucial, it's all on the next match and we can only look ahead. I'm remaining positive for these players and hopefully we can add to the squad in January. If we can continue creating opportunities and doing the correct things, I'm hoping we can convert positive performance into results. We're examining improving the squad. We certainly need to be adding that extra to give the club and supporters and players a boost. text: The Football League season is poised for another dramatic climax as six teams aim to be promoted by winning their respective play-off finals at Wembley. Saturday's Championship showpiece between Hull City and Sheffield Wednesday is valued at an estimated £170m for the victors. Barnsley and Millwall shall contest the League One final on Sunday, with AFC Wimbledon and Plymouth Argyle concluding the 2015-16 campaign in League Two on Monday. Saturday 28 May, 17:00 BST Hull manager Steve Bruce is a promotion veteran, having supervised Birmingham City's ascent to the Premier League in 2002 and 2007 and guiding the Tigers there in 2013. Saturday, however, shall be his first journey to Wembley for a play-off final - and it has not been a straightforward path for Bruce and his squad. Inconsistency plagued their season and then they nearly squandered a 3-0 first-leg advantage in their play-off semi-final against Derby County. You can simply detect there's a significant match around the corner, Bruce told BBC Radio Humberside. The players are tackling each other and champing at the bit. You simply have to put them on a slight leash at times because we need to release them on Saturday. Hull were last at Wembley in 2014 for their FA Cup final defeat by Arsenal, and the experience gained during Bruce's 18-year managerial career could prove vital as they attempt to return to the top flight at the first attempt. Media playback is not supported on this device At the opposite end of the spectrum, the closest Sheffield Wednesday head coach Carlos Carvalhal has come to Wembley is watching English league football on television as a child in Portugal. Carvalhal had a modest career managing in his homeland and in Turkey before joining Wednesday in June 2015. His side have marched steadily up the table throughout the season and their performances in the play-offs were clinical, as they defeated Brighton over two legs to secure their place at Wembley. The South Yorkshire side have not visited the national stadium since appearing in both domestic cup finals in 1993, and have only finished in the top half of the Championship table twice since they were relegated from the top division in 2000. Hull City are a strong team with a very spirited coach - they are a premier team and it shall be very tough, Carvalhal told BBC Radio Sheffield. My players know precisely what they need to do and we shall prepare for this match like any of the others. We expect a very good response from the players to the plan we shall put into place. Sunday 29 May, 15:00 BST In November 2015, Barnsley were bottom of the League One table having won just five of their 20 league matches. Six months on, they have won the Johnstone's Paint Trophy, secured the last third-tier play-off spot and ruthlessly beaten Walsall 6-1 on aggregate in their semi-final tie. Caretaker manager Paul Heckingbottom built upon the work started by Lee Johnson, leading Barnsley through a run of 12 wins in 15 league matches between December and March. Everything is bigger about the play-offs, Heckingbottom, who was part of the Barnsley squad promoted via the play-offs in 2006, told BBC Radio Sheffield. It's not just the prize at the end, but the bigger opposition, better-quality football and away matches at bigger stadiums that come in the Championship. It's a cup final after 46 rounds and a two-legged semi-final and that brings its own unique tension, adrenaline and excitement for everyone. That's what makes a victory that much more sweeter. Millwall are eyeing an immediate return to the Championship, after seeing their five-year stay in the second tier end last season. Club legend Neil Harris has masterminded their promotion push, having overseen a clear-out of players following relegation. We have come a long way as a group. We have a terrific bunch of lads and they have great spirit, the 38-year-old told BBC Radio London. Whatever happens on Sunday, the pride is back in the club and we have foundations to build upon. Harris, Millwall's record goalscorer, was part of the Lions side which won the League One play-off final in 2010, beating Swindon 1-0 at Wembley. Barnsley played there this year but they did not play against Millwall or in front of our fans there, he said. The noise at The Den in the second leg against Bradford was something special. That is what we shall have at Wembley, with 35,000 passionate fans going to back their team. Every time we have had that, the players have performed. You have to have the link between the terraces and the pitch at this club. text: Sharks have patrolled the oceans for at least 400 million years and evolved into a huge range of remarkable species. These are external links and will open in a new window. There are deep-sea lantern sharks that glow in the dark, wobbegong sharks that grow shaggy beards, and majestic, plankton-filtering whale sharks - the largest fish in the ocean. However, when many people think of these creatures, one thing comes to mind: shark attacks. As a beachgoer, diver or surfer your chances of encountering a shark, let alone being killed by one, are in fact extraordinarily slim; lightning strikes, bee stings and car accidents all pose far greater threats than sharks. In reality, people kill millions more sharks than sharks kill people. A quarter of all shark species, and their relatives the rays, are threatened with extinction, according to a recent report from the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The primary threat to sharks is overfishing and in greatest peril are the largest species. However, a controversial cull of sharks was recently ordered in Western Australia following a series of attacks. Scientists are now examining other approaches to deal with the shark attack issue. Professor Shaun Collin is leading a University of Western Australia (UWA) team of neurobiologists who are learning to think like sharks. We're trying to tread this very fine line of protecting both humans and sharks at the same time, Professor Collin told the BBC World Service programme Discovery. By studying shark brains and shark senses, the team is developing and testing various non-lethal repellents. The aim is to manipulate the sharks' finely-tuned senses in ways that discourage them from approaching and attacking people. One of these is a shark-proof wetsuit designed to make people look like poisonous, black and white banded sea snakes, something that many sharks tend to avoid. The striped wetsuit was first conceived years ago by marine biologist Walter Starck. Now a detailed understanding of shark vision is helping the UWA team to bring this idea up to date. Nathan Hart, assistant professor at UWA, explained to me that sharks do not see as well as humans. We've made sure that the size of the bands can be detected by a shark from a certain distance, he says. Tests of the new wetsuit design are currently underway. This involves wrapping the fabric around a barrel filled with dead fish and watching how sharks respond to it in the wild. It is still early days, but so far, Nathan told me, the results have been encouraging. Based on what we know about the sensory systems of sharks, they should reduce your risk to some extent, he says. Just like a seatbelt in a car, it does not reduce your risk to zero; it is a matter of reducing your risk by a certain amount and by as much as possible, he adds. As well as trying to protect individual swimmers, another tactic is to make certain areas out of bounds to sharks. We can try and define areas on the beaches where people are confident they can go and swim, says Dr Hart. Bubble curtains could be deployed to keep sharks away from popular beaches. The idea is to lay perforated hosepipes across the seabed and pump air through them and create a plume of bubbles that sharks may decide not to swim through. Sharks can see and hear the bubbles and also feel them with their lateral line, a system of sense organs many fish have. It is a system of what is known as 'distant touch'; it detects vibrations and very low-frequency sound in the water, Nathan explained. Early tests showed that tiger sharks eventually pluck up the courage to cross a barrier of bubbles, suggesting they have the ability to learn. Eugenie Clark, a veteran marine biologist at the Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida, pioneered studies of shark learning back in the 1950s. Nicknamed The Shark Lady, Dr Clark trained captive sharks to press targets with their snouts and ring bells for a food reward. She showed for the first time that sharks can learn and remember things. Eugenie told me about the time she took a trained baby nurse shark as a gift for the Crown Prince of Japan who shared her fascination with fish. The airline gave me an extra seat for the shark. Most people did not know, he was such a tiny thing he was less than two feet long. But he never made a mistake, says Eugenie. Recently, I witnessed for myself the capacity sharks have to learn and in particular that they can learn not to attack people. I went diving off the Pacific island of Fiji and saw my first bull sharks, notorious as one of the most aggressive shark species. Locals from Beqa Adventure Divers have trained a population of around 100 bull sharks to approach a diver, one-by-one, and gently take a chunk of fish offered to them by hand. The sharks have learnt how to behave if they want food. They know us very well, Fijian divemaster Papa told me before I jumped in the water. That is the good thing, they know what is going on. Preparing for the dive, I was not exactly sure how I would react to seeing these giant predators. But as soon as I got down beneath the waves my nerves evaporated and I saw just how graceful and calm bull sharks can be. There was no safety cage or any sort of repellent and I never felt in any kind of danger. As well as helping to shift the sharks' bad reputation as insatiable killers, the Fijian divers are showing that a live shark in the water is worth far more than a dead one. In Fiji and elsewhere around the world, sharks are under immense pressure from the demand in Asia for shark fin soup. Back in Western Australia, the shark cull continues amid beachside protests. The problem has been an abnormally high number of shark attacks, with seven fatalities over the last three years compared with 20 in the last century. The response of the Western Australia government has been to lay baited hooks offshore from popular beaches. Any great white, tiger and bull sharks that are caught and are larger than 3m long are shot and dumped at sea. One opponent of the cull is shark attack survivor Rodney Fox. Fifty years ago he suffered a horrific attack from a great white in South Australia but since then has become a dedicated shark advocate. We just have to learn how to live with the sharks and not just kill them from fear, he told me. He thinks killing sharks deliberately is an unscientific and irrational strategy to try to reduce the attack rate. But Western Australia's government says the cull is in place to protect swimmers and surfers. Premier Colin Barnett has said: The West Australian government is absolutely confident that the policy in place is the right policy and we intend to continue it. An open letter from more than 100 scientists has urged Mr Barnett to reconsider the cull, highlighting its environmental impact and the low chance of catching the individual sharks responsible for the attacks. Every scientist that I have heard of and talked to all agree that it is not the thing to do, says Mr Fox.

text: Poland's Prime Minister Beata Szydlo has vowed to press on with judicial reforms, saying the government would not yield to pressure from the street and from abroad. These are external links and will open in a new window On Monday, President Andrzej Duda vetoed a contentious law to substitute Supreme Court judges with government appointees. This followed thousands taking to the streets throughout Poland in demonstration. Mr Duda stated he reached his decision after consulting legal experts and judges. The European Commission had threatened to impose sanctions this week if the changes were not abandoned. European Council President Donald Tusk, a former Polish prime minister, had warned of a black scenario that could ultimately lead to the marginalisation of Poland in Europe. In a televised address, Ms Szydlo maintained that the Law and Justice (PiS) government would not retreat. We all wish to live in a just Poland, this is why the reform of the courts is required... text: Returning to Cold Feet after more than a decade since it was last seen on TV felt like putting on an old jumper, Fay Ripley has said. The actress stated she was thrilled to resurrect the character of Jenny, likening it to encountering an old friend. Co-star John Thomson declared the timing was appropriate to return to the programme as there existed presently a tremendous need for nostalgia. Eight fresh episodes of the comedy drama, which concluded in 2003 following five series, shall be transmitted this autumn. Chronicling the highs and lows of three couples in their thirties, over 10 million viewers watched the final episode, which depicted the funeral of central character Rachel, portrayed by Helen Baxendale. The fresh series shall reveal how life has affected friends Jenny and Pete, Karen and David and widower Adam in the subsequent years, as they encounter middle age and existence as parents of adolescent children. Ripley believed it might prove difficult returning to character, but found: Within a minute, it remained the same. It felt like returning to the past. We possess a shorthand when we collaborate together, all of us, which proves incredibly useful. She jested that meant they did not need to engage in any of the courteous behaviour when they reunited on set. You can simply enter and declare, 'I have a terrible headache, my menopause is causing me trouble', she remarked. Thomson stated the timing could not be superior to resurrect something so uplifting as Cold Feet. The world is not in an excellent state presently, and there exists a tremendous need for nostalgia, to reflect upon the days when circumstances seemed acceptable, he declared. Hermione Norris concurred it was reassuring to observe the former characters reunited again, but confessed she had been initially hesitant about reprising the character of Karen. It is that matter in life - you believe 'Do not return, simply progress forward', she stated. It was so characteristic of its era and it was so cherished, I believed perhaps it should remain untouched as I did not wish to undertake anything that would have undermined that. She stated the programme's creator, Mike Bullen, had convinced her it was not a remake, but instead a matter of returning to these characters in this phase of their existence - and disclosed Karen utilises dating application Tinder in the fresh series, demonstrating how technology and dating has progressed. Norris stated she did not re-examine any former episodes before filming commenced, declaring: It was remarkable how much I had forgotten - I could not recall how many children David and I possessed. She also stated she felt peculiar not to have Baxendale present, adding: I missed Helen enormously - because Rachel was Karen's closest friend. I genuinely felt her absence. It resembles how it would be in actual life, if you have lost a truly good friend. Ripley jested there would be no shower scene for Rachel - referencing the sequence in American soap opera Dallas when character Bobby Ewing returned, with his death the preceding year explained away as a dream. She added Baxendale was pleased with the programme continuing without her, stating: She is comfortable with it. Norris also stated she adored working with people her own age on the programme: I genuinely appreciate being with my own generation. As an actor, and as Karen. I discover as a woman, I adore being older. The burden of experience - you simply do not possess that as a 30-year-old. Robert Bathurst stated of his decision to return as David: It is entirely dependent upon the script. I would not have undertaken it for the sake of it. He stated the secret of the programme's success was that it has never been about anything - it concerns ordinariness, adding: It concerns people and how they interact together. Bathurst also hopes the fresh series will stand independently and attract a new generation of admirers. Amongst the new cast members is BBC Radio 1 presenter Cel Spellman, who portrays Adam and Rachel's teenage son Matthew - last observed as an infant in the final episodes of the previous series. He admitted it was intimidating to join the successful programme - and that he binge-watched the box set to prepare for the character. I began to understand why the programme was so successful, he stated, adding that his mother was a tremendous fan who pestered his head for details of the fresh storylines. But Mrs Spellman and Cold Feet admirers - shall have to wait somewhat longer to discover what awaits the characters, with programme executives keen to prevent any spoilers before it commences. text: An electrical fire in a tunnel under a pavement in central London is still burning as firefighters have reported difficulty tackling the blaze. The London Fire Brigade (LFB) stated that firefighters would be operating most of the night on Thursday. The service said the blaze, which has been alight for more than 24 hours, had been confined within the tunnel. Approximately 5,000 individuals were evacuated from Holborn on Wednesday after smoke was observed emerging from an inspection cover. Over 100 enterprises have been impacted. The LFB said the cordon on Kingsway had been reduced, though the road remained shut. Assistant Commissioner Dany Cotton stated: This represents a technically challenging and uncommon incident to address as it is subterranean. Combating fires in tunnels was extremely dangerous, she stated, and precautions had to be implemented to prevent the risk of a gas explosion. Firefighters have, nevertheless, been deploying water through access points throughout the night, to restrict the fire's spread, she continued. She requested people to avoid the immediate vicinity if feasible. A total of 35 firefighters and six fire engines remain at the blaze on Kingsway. Local road closures continue in effect. The fire's cause remains unknown, though it is thought the flames began amongst subterranean cables. Speaking to BBC London 94.9, Metropolitan Police Inspector Neil Johnson stated: I expect this road will remain closed long after this concludes because of damage the heat inflicts on the road. It must remain shut until a structural engineer inspects it thoroughly and either he or she determines what work must be undertaken and that work is completed - this is not an overnight task. On Wednesday, witnesses reported difficulty breathing and pandemonium in and around Holborn. UK Power Networks stated the number of customers presently affected by the power failures stood at approximately 1,000 and it had restored electricity to about 2,000. It is anticipated power will be restored to everyone affected by Thursday's end. Apologising to customers, Matt Rudling, from the company, stated: The gas continues burning beneath there and until we can gain access to that specific area we will not understand what has caused it and what we can do. He added that emergency generators were being utilised to supply electricity to the area and engineers were also attempting to connect some of the damaged cables to unaffected ones. Several West End theatres were compelled to cancel performances on Wednesday evening including Beautiful - The Carole King Musical, Charlie And The Chocolate Factory, Disney's The Lion King, Gypsy, Mamma Mia! The Play That Goes Wrong and The Woman In Black. Thursday's matinee performances at the Novello and Aldwych theatres were also cancelled. Councillor Richard Beddoe, from Westminster City Council, stated: We are relieved to learn that there were no serious casualties but the losses to major businesses in the West End, due to inadequate infrastructure, is simply not acceptable. We want to see action. The National Grid stated it was working with emergency services to isolate the gas supply. In a statement, the company, which operates gas transmission infrastructure in the UK, said the fire had affected one of its pipes. This represents a challenging operation due to the fire's location, access to our gas pipe and other utilities in close proximity. We cannot simply turn a valve and switch off the gas because of safety reasons and [the] impact on the gas network, the statement said.
