text: US illustrator Norman Bridwell, creator of the Clifford the Big Red Dog books, has died at the age of 86 following a fall at his home in Massachusetts. His endearing character initially appeared in 1963 and subsequently featured in over 40 tales, achieving sales of 120 million copies globally. Clifford's likeness has subsequently appeared on products and within American buildings, including the White House. Bridwell had finished two additional books which are scheduled for publication next year. Dick Robinson, president of the writer's longstanding publisher Scholastic stated: We are profoundly saddened by the passing of our devoted and gifted friend whose illustrations and tales have inspired all of us and generations of children and their parents. His spouse of 56 years, Norma, remarked: Many people were Clifford enthusiasts and that makes them Norman enthusiasts too. She was responsible for christening the character Clifford after her imaginary childhood companion. Throughout the decades, the bright red canine appeared in numerous tales, including Clifford Goes To Hollywood and Clifford and The Grouchy Neighbours, which became popular bedtime stories for children throughout the US and beyond. The dog frequently encountered difficulties before redeeming himself through a daring rescue or performing a good deed. Bridwell's spouse stated there were similarities between the writer and his creation. He has never been able to recognise that. Clifford attempts to do the right thing, Norman attempts to do the right thing, and he creates a mess of it. But he is the most lovable grown-up man. He is simply a nice fellow. Before he achieved fame with Clifford, Bridwell worked as a commercial artist during the 1950s. He made countless attempts to enter children's publishing, until a New York book editor suggested he develop a story around an illustration he had submitted of a child and her oversized dog. Additional rejections followed, until publishers Scholastic recognised his creation's potential - a decision which resulted in enduring success for the company. text: Residents of a mid Wales village have voted on proposals to install a new train station in the area. The Welsh Government requested Carno Station Action Group and the community council to consult with residents regarding two potential locations. One of the sites is the original station which closed in 1963 as part of the Beeching cuts to Britain's railways. The former station subsequently became part of the Laura Ashley site in Carno. The village is situated on the Cambrian line between Aberystwyth and Shrewsbury. A campaign to reopen Carno station commenced in 2002. In 2011 Mid Wales Transportation, a group collaborating with the Welsh Government, stated there was a strong case for future investment in the station following an appraisal. The site could be developed into a tourist information centre and a Laura Ashley museum if plans receive approval. Action Group chairman Jeremy Barnes stated the week-long consultation concluded on 22 March and the results would be processed before being forwarded to the Welsh Government. He added: We have discussed with the Welsh Government the possibility of the new station incorporating a tourist information centre, café, an office for the community council's clerk and a small museum dedicated to Laura Ashley should the existing site be selected. Carno is an expanding village with a population of approximately 750 and this proposed development will generate employment and provide residents affordable access to work further away. It is situated on the longest stretch of railway without an intermediate station in the whole of Wales, the 22 miles between Caersws and Machynlleth. There is strong consensus that the capital asset of the railway line passing through the village is being squandered whilst the trains pass through without stopping. The consultation followed a meeting between the action group and Transport Minister Edwina Hart last October. Fashion designer Laura Ashley maintained strong connections with Carno for nearly a quarter of a century before her death in 1985. Carno was the original Welsh headquarters of the Laura Ashley company when she relocated with her husband Bernard from Kent in 1961. She is interred in a churchyard in the village. Laura Ashley's former headquarters in Carno, where many of her products were manufactured, closed in 2004.

text: A US Senate report has condemned the CIA's use of enhanced interrogation on al-Qaeda suspects after the 9/11 attacks. The 480-page summary outlines the treatment administered to several of the organisation's senior figures. Particulars of the interrogation of three of the most notorious have now been disclosed publicly. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, Abu Zubaydah and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri were apprehended following 9/11 and remain in American custody at Guantanamo Bay. Previously characterised by US intelligence as one of history's most notorious terrorists, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is the self-admitted architect of the 9/11 attacks. He asserts to have personally decapitated the captured American journalist, Daniel Pearl. Born in Kuwait to Pakistani parents, he obtained his degree at an American university, before journeying to Afghanistan to combat the Soviets. There he is thought to have initially encountered Osama Bin Laden. He has been connected to, or admitted involvement in, numerous conspiracies, including a plot to destroy US aircraft over the Pacific in 1995. Following his apprehension in Pakistan in 2003, he was transported to detention facilities reportedly located in Europe. According to the Senate report, he was subjected to waterboarding no fewer than 183 times. A CIA operative characterised the procedure as a sequence of near drownings. However, the report stated some of the intelligence provided by Mohammed was fabricated. He remains in custody at Guantanamo Bay following a failed attempt to prosecute him in a New York court amid extensive opposition. Abu Zubaydah is considered to have been al-Qaeda's principal recruiter during the 1990s, and subsequently became a crucial organiser, connecting Osama Bin Laden to other al-Qaeda units. Whilst he is not thought to be directly connected to the 9/11 attacks, he is believed to have operated several camps in Afghanistan, where some of the attackers received training. Born in Saudi Arabia, he employed more than 30 false identities and earned a reputation as a master of disguise. He was apprehended in Pakistan in 2002 and transported to a detention facility reportedly situated in Thailand. At that time, US intelligence officers stated he was planning a terrorist attack in Israel. He was subjected to so-called enhanced interrogation methods for days continuously and waterboarded more than 80 times. On one instance, the treatment rendered him completely unresponsive with bubbles rising through his open full mouth. Records in the Senate report describe how Zubaydah spent 266 hours in a tiny, confined space scarcely larger than a coffin, and 29 hours in an even smaller container just 21 inches (53cm) wide and 2.5ft (76cm) deep and tall. In obtaining authorisation to employ harsh treatment on Zubaydah, US Justice Department lawyers relied on inaccurate CIA representations regarding him, the report determined. He is presently being detained at Guantanamo Bay prison facility. Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri gained prominence as the suspected coordinator of the terrorist assault on the USS Cole, a destroyer targeted by suicide bombers whilst it was moored in the port of Aden, Yemen. According to US intelligence, the Saudi-born Islamist was the commander of al-Qaeda's operations in the Gulf region. Besides the USS Cole assault, which killed 17 sailors, US intelligence chiefs believed the 49-year-old was implicated in conspiracies against various Western targets in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the Straits of Gibraltar, Morocco and Qatar. He purportedly fought alongside the Taliban in Afghanistan and was involved in earlier Chechen and Tajik insurgencies. After being detained in Dubai in 2002 he was confined for four years in several secret CIA installations worldwide, including in Poland and Thailand. During this period he endured water-boarding and mock executions, according to the report. In 2006 he was transferred to the Guantanamo Bay detention facility, where he has been confined ever since.

text: France rounded off their Euro 2016 preparations with a classy and comprehensive victory over Scotland. Didier Deschamps' team rampaged to emphasise their pre-tournament status as tournament favourites. Olivier Giroud silenced some of his detractors with the first two strikes and his Arsenal colleague Laurent Koscielny nodded a third before half-time. Substitutions mercifully disrupted the second-half tempo, permitting the Scots to depart with their dignity preserved. The truth is that this display and outcome provide no guidance in helping to resolve that question, but the tournament hosts certainly seem to possess the quality to achieve so. Their midfield choices are tantalising - the triumvirate of N'Golo Kante, Paul Pogba and Blaise Matuidi appear masterful, exuding power and athleticism. Giroud has been jeered by French fans and condemned by local press in the lead-up to the Euros, but a clever back-heel and an alert close-range follow-up secured him a standing ovation from the Metz crowd. Kingsley Coman, Dimitri Payet, Antoine Griezmann and Anthony Martial were also afforded playing time as Deschamps assessed his choices before Friday's competitive debut against Romania in Paris. Queries have been raised about the strength of their defence, but Scotland provided no examination of that. Gordon Strachan bemoaned his team's failure to pass and control the ball in Sunday's 1-0 loss to Italy and there was little to be satisfied about on this occasion either. They were granted more possession than against the Italians, but seldom utilised it purposefully and once more failed to produce a shot on target. Goalkeeper David Marshall, as he did six days previously, kept the damage to a minimum with a series of splendid saves and will be challenging to displace when the World Cup qualifiers commence in September. Another small morsel of comfort for the Scotland manager will be an assured performance from young Swansea full-back Stephen Kingsley when he entered in the second half, with Rangers winger Barrie McKay also making his senior international debut from the substitutes' bench. Pogba controlled the proceedings in imperious style and twice came within inches of adding a fourth goal, first hitting the post with a fierce free-kick before curling another onto the roof of the net. text: The body set up to probe deaths during the Troubles in Northern Ireland investigated cases where the state was involved with less rigour than others, a police watchdog has found. These are external links and will open in a new window Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary stated it appeared the Historical Enquiries Team's (HET) policy was founded upon a misrepresentation of the law. It stated their approach was inconsistent and contained serious shortcomings. HET was established in 2005 to re-examine 3,260 murders. The report also determined the HET's approach to cases involving the state was inconsistent with the European Convention on Human Rights. When questioned if HET had acted outside of the law, Her Majesty's inspector of constabulary, Stephen Otter stated: We believe it was acting unlawfully regarding state cases because it treats them differently in policy terms and in the manner that then acts out in practice. So state cases were less effective as a result and effectiveness is a key test of whether it's Article 2 compliant. HMIC stated the Historical Enquiries Team risked undermining the confidence of the families of those who perished during the Troubles in its effectiveness and impartiality. Northern Ireland's chief constable Matt Baggott agreed to a policing board request to commission the review by the HMIC following criticism of HET in a University of Ulster report. The report, by Dr Patricia Lundy, alleged the HET gave former soldiers preferential treatment and did not properly investigate deaths caused by the military. The HET rejected the allegations in her report. Responding to the HMIC report, Dr Lundy stated: I believe the HET as an organisation itself is irretrievable at this point. I believe it has implications for numerous different cases, not just the army cases, because we've heard the structural problems, there's no oversight, there's no complaints procedure and really it seemed to me that it was a bit of a law unto itself. Mr Otter stated Dr Lundy had presented a report that at the time was made out to be untrue. I do believe she deserves an apology from the chief constable on behalf of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), he stated. What is indefensible is that she did make these findings in 2009, so for four years nothing was being done to address those findings and I do find that that is very difficult to believe. Chief Constable Matt Baggott stated that all military cases investigated by HET will now be re-examined, and he accepted that HET put in place a policy that was wrong. A differential approach to military cases is wrong and I assure you this has ended, he stated. He also accepted the recommendations of the HMIC report in full and would work to implement them. The HET is reviewing more than 150 killings by soldiers between 1970 and September 1973. The HMIC inspection focused on whether the HET's approach to reviewing military cases conformed to current policing standards and policy. It examined material relating to 31 cases that the HET had reviewed. HET treats cases involving military differently as a matter of policy HET not conforming to current policing standards in a significant number of important areas A lack of explicit systems and processes Different teams adopting different working practices No clearly defined complaints process No independent review of the HET's processes (until now) HMIC examined if the HET adopted a consistent approach to both military and paramilitary cases. It also considered if the HET's review process met requirements to ensure it was compliant with human rights legislation. The report found the HET treats cases involving military differently as a matter of policy and this appeared to be founded upon a misinterpretation of the law. It also found that the HET did not always seek verification where a potential interviewee in a state involvement case claimed to be unfit for interview due to illness. HMIC stated this was entirely wrong and had led to military cases being reviewed with less rigour in some areas than cases not involving military. The inspection found that none of the 39 cases referred back to the PSNI for investigation since 2010 had involved state involvement. It is striking that not one state involvement case relating to the British Army has to date been referred to the PSNI for further investigation or prosecution, the report stated. Mr Otter stated: HMIC is concerned that the inconsistencies we found in our review may seriously undermine the capability of the HET's processes to determine whether the force used in killings during the Troubles was justified in state involvement cases, therefore potentially preventing the identification and punishment of those responsible. Our recommendations set out fundamental improvements that the PSNI and the HET need to make in order to ensure the team is effective in delivering its objectives in a manner that is consistent with the requirements of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights; and commands the confidence of the public of Northern Ireland, and in particular, of the families of the victims of the Troubles. Mr Otter stated the HET was created and continued to operate within an extraordinarily complex social and political context which presented those who established it with challenges unparalleled in UK terms. This context makes it even more important for the HET to operate to the highest standards of effectiveness and impartiality, so that the people of Northern Ireland, and the families of the victims whose cases are being reviewed, can have confidence in it, he added. HMIC interviewed more than 180 people from a range of organisations, including HET, criminal justice agencies, and non-governmental bodies. It also spoke to the families of 13 of the victims, some in Belfast and others in Londonderry. HMIC stated although many people it had spoken to would have preferred the HET to be independent from the PSNI, they also expressed an almost universal desire for it to be retained so long as improvements were made to the manner it operates. The HET is a special investigative unit attached to the PSNI to re-examine the deaths of thousands of people in Northern Ireland between 1968 and 1998. It is an independent unit which is directly accountable to Northern Ireland's chief constable.

text: Progressive music, the oft-maligned genre that had its heyday in the 1970s, is to be endorsed by the Official Charts Company (OCC). The coming week witnesses the publication of the inaugural monthly Official Progressive Albums Chart Top 30. The chart will showcase classic progressive bands including Pink Floyd, though the premier position belongs to 21st Century rock group Tame Impala. We believed it constituted an omission not to have established this considerably earlier, stated OCC chief Martin Talbot. Progressive music remains as vibrant and dynamic as it has ever been. It represents more a mindset than a musical category. The chart's announcement coincides with the annual Progressive Music Awards at Shakespeare's Globe Theatre in London on Thursday evening. Amongst those receiving recognition is Genesis founding member Tony Banks, who shall receive the 2015 Prog God Award. Rick Wakeman, who obtained the identical honour in 2012, informed the BBC that a chart devoted to the progressive genre was considerably overdue. It arrives merely 45 years behind schedule, though better delayed than absent, remarked the former Yes keyboard player. Progressive rock enjoys the most robust health it has ever experienced... the musical proficiency of contemporary bands is generally far superior to the standard that existed during the 1970s. The inaugural official progressive album chart, scheduled for publication in Prog Magazine next week, positions Tame Impala's album Currents at number one, preceding Muse's Drones. Official Progressive Albums Chart - Top 10 © Official Charts Company 2015 It demonstrates that magnificent broad range that progressive rock possesses, stated Wakeman. It no longer constitutes something to be mocked and dismissed. With numerous bands incorporating elements from it, it enjoys widespread acceptance as a legitimate contributor to the contemporary music landscape. Progressive rock, which emerged from 1960s psychedelia, was initially linked with bands including Pink Floyd, Rush, Genesis, Yes and King Crimson. It experienced renewed prosperity during the 1980s with groups like Marillion, whilst Muse, The Mars Volta and Porcupine Tree rank amongst the most recognised progressive acts of the 21st Century. Jerry Ewing, editor of Prog Magazine, stated: Progressive artists have consistently challenged the limits of musical tradition, and through doing so, many have become some of the highest-selling and most influential artists of all time, but progressive music did not cease in the 1970s, there are numerous people who appreciate progressive artists and simply appear unaware of it. You examine some of the highest-selling and celebrated artists of the modern period, such as Muse, Radiohead, Mogwai, Tame Impala, their work is extraordinary, they are challenging themselves, their listeners and inspiring a fresh generation, and the Official Progressive Albums Chart provides the platform through which this shall be acknowledged. The most recent new chart established by the Official Chart Company was the vinyl chart, during spring 2015. The new progressive chart joins other musical categories including dance, urban, jazz and blues and country. The monthly Top 30 will present the highest-selling titles ranked on physical and digital sales and audio streaming information. There exist some artists who welcome the term 'progressive', and there might be numerous others who reject it because it remains a stigmatised word, said the OCC's Martin Talbot. The punk conflicts were waged to eliminate progressive music. Part of our message is that progressive and disco emerged victorious from the punk conflicts - perhaps more than punk itself achieved. text: Doctors who carry out cosmetic procedures should give patients time to think before agreeing to go ahead, new guidance says. The General Medical Council has issued guidance to enhance the safety of surgical and non-surgical procedures, including facelifts, breast implants, dermal fillers and Botox treatments. The council will now seek consultation from doctors and the public regarding the guidance. Plastic surgeons stated they were already implementing a two-week cooling-off period. In 2013, a report from NHS England's medical director emphasised the risks linked to the cosmetic sector. This occurred following safety concerns after approximately 50,000 women in the UK received PIP breast implants. The French implants contained unauthorised silicone filler and demonstrated twice the rupture rate of alternative implants. In January, the Royal College of Surgeons issued a consultation on proposals to enhance standards in cosmetic surgery. The GMC establishes the standards expected of all UK doctors performing cosmetic procedures. It also seeks to assist patients in understanding what to expect from their doctor. Several key points in the new guidance state that doctors should: Professor Terence Stephenson, the chairman of the General Medical Council, stated that some patients in this field were vulnerable and required protection. We are clear that doctors must not pressurise patients to make hasty decisions they may subsequently regret and they must provide them with sufficient information so they can make an informed choice. Rajiv Grover, consultant plastic surgeon and former President of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (Baaps), endorsed the GMC's guidance because he stated some patients were psychologically unsuitable for cosmetic surgery. Cosmetic surgery has for too long been regarded as a commodity but regrettably once an operation is completed - it cannot be returned to the shop. He stated Baaps had required a two-week cooling-off period for many years and also promoted a second consultation with a surgeon before a decision was reached. The association is examining the development of a screening tool to assist in identifying patients who should not undergo surgery. The final GMC guidance is anticipated to be published in early 2016.

text: UKIP group leader Neil Hamilton has sparked a row after describing two senior female AMs as political concubines in Carwyn Jones' harem. The former Conservative MP made the reference to Liberal Democrat AM Kirsty Williams and Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood in his inaugural Senedd address. However, Ms Williams accused Mr Hamilton of employing blatant sexist language. Presiding officer Elin Jones urged AMs to demonstrate respect. Ms Wood and Ms Williams supported Mr Jones in his reinstatement as first minister, which received confirmation during the session. Throughout Mr Hamilton's address the UKIP AM stated he regretted the role Plaid Cymru had undertaken and added Ms Williams had succeeded in propping up this tottering administration. He continued: So I fear that these two ladies have simply made themselves political concubines in Carwyn's harem. What a gruesome prospect that must be. He enquired what the two had received in reward for the sacrifice of their political virtue. Mr Hamilton subsequently, reflecting upon the agreement between Labour and Plaid, also accused Ms Wood of being a very cheap date indeed. He also accused the first minister of being wholly impotent regarding the steel industry due to his commitment to the EU, which I suppose the members of his harem may be rather satisfied with. Speaking following the debate, he stated he did not regret making the comments. He informed BBC Wales: Je ne regrette rien. However, Ms Wood stated: This sexist language has no place in the National Assembly for Wales, or in society, and we shall not tolerate sexism, homophobia or racism. Following the remarks Elin Jones, presiding officer, has cautioned that members must respect each other during Senedd debates. She stated: In the interests of effective scrutiny and debate, there requires to be proper opportunity for all members to express themselves robustly and to be heard. Nevertheless, they must do so in a manner that demonstrates respect for others. Our exchanges are at their finest when members achieve that balance. That shall be my expectation of all members throughout the fifth assembly. I shall review the record of today's proceedings and make a ruling if I determine it is appropriate to do so.

text: Careers services for young people in England need to be urgently improved, says a report from an advisory body set up by the government. The National Careers Council, which has been examining the present condition of careers provision, emphasises an absence of consistency and accessibility. It cautions that too many young people fail to receive the guidance they require regarding employment. Deirdre Hughes, who led the council, stated that a cultural transformation in careers provision was urgently required. The report from the National Careers Council states there are enormous variations in the guidance available, depending upon where young people reside. It states that in one region there exist 134 careers advisory services, whilst in another there exists only one. There are also concerns that the National Careers Service has been organised to concentrate primarily on the requirements of adults, creating a gap in school-age guidance services. The service delivers over one million face-to-face guidance sessions for adults, yet there exists no provision for such individual guidance for young people. Instead, young people are provided with telephone advice lines and online information. The council states that it has been disappointed by the slow progress in enhancing careers services for young people. It demands the establishment of an employer-led advisory body to oversee creating an improved careers advice system. Furthermore, it demands that the government provide all schools with free or subsidised access to independent and impartial career development. It proposes there should be a fund to invest in successful models of careers advice so that they may be distributed more widely across other schools and regions. There have been a series of critical reports regarding the quality of careers provision and doubts concerning the decision to transfer responsibility for careers advice to individual schools. It is concerning that the new arrangements are failing to deliver good guidance, stated Ofsted chief Sir Michael Wilshaw last year, when the education watchdog warned that too few schools possessed the skills to deliver good quality advice. The Education Select Committee also reported last year that careers services were demonstrating a concerning deterioration. Neil Carberry, of the CBI, stated: The transfer of responsibility for careers advice to schools has been a failure. Schools, government and businesses all have a role to play in addressing the problem, it cannot be borne by schools alone. Brian Lightman, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, stated schools had been working diligently to deliver careers advice, but many are finding it extremely challenging. A stark postcode lottery is placing many young people at a genuine disadvantage, stated the head teachers' leader. Far too many young people are being required to make vital and extremely important decisions regarding their futures without access to sound and reliable information, stated Nick Chambers, director of the Education and Employers Taskforce charity. Deirdre Hughes, who led the group that produced the report, stated: Some progress has been achieved in the past 12 months, but this has been far too slow. Meanwhile, our education and labour markets remain complex and confusing for young people, parents and teachers, and there are substantial costs associated with this. We urge government and others to take action across England to halt the rapid decline in careers services for young people. Labour's shadow education secretary, Tristram Hunt, stated of the careers service: There is surely no other policy agenda where the government has so dismally failed our young people. He stated he would reverse the decision to make work experience placements optional and would want every school to have a governor responsible for developing links with local businesses to help provide careers advice and experience of the world of work.

text: The way alcohol is sold in airports is to be examined after a number of recent incidents involving drunk passengers, the new aviation minister has said. These are external links and will open in a new window Lord Ahmad stated he did not wish to kill merriment, but that he would examine the times alcohol was sold, and passenger screening. Statistics reveal 442 individuals were detained on suspicion of being intoxicated at an airport or on an aircraft in the past two years. The Government stated there were no plans to specifically tackle the issue. In one recent incident a female passenger struck an EasyJet pilot in the face after being instructed to leave an aircraft before departure from Manchester. In February, six men on a stag party were detained by German police after a mid-air altercation caused a Ryanair flight from Luton to Bratislava, Slovakia, to divert to Berlin. Lord Ahmad stated: If you're a young family travelling on an aircraft you want to go from point A to B, you don't want to be disrupted. I don't think we want to kill merriment altogether, but I think it's important that passengers who board aircraft are also responsible and have a responsibility to other passengers, and that certainly should be the factor which we bear in mind. He continued: In terms of specific regulations of timings of outlets [which sell alcohol] and how they operate, clearly I want to have a look at that. He also emphasised the value of screening travellers before they boarded aircraft. Glasgow and Manchester airports have trialled a scheme with shops selling alcohol in sealed bags in a bid to reduce problems on flights. Police statistics obtained by the Press Association through Freedom of Information requests showed at least 442 people were detained on suspicion of being intoxicated on an aircraft or at an airport in the UK between March 2014 and March 2016. Trade bodies representing UK airlines and airports said such incidents were a very rare occurrence, but warned they could lead to serious consequences. They pointed out that disruption on board an aircraft was an illegal offence which could carry a heavy penalty - including a travel ban, fine, or prison sentence. According to the Civil Aviation Authority's most recent passenger survey, some 238 million passengers passed through UK airports in 2014. Earlier this week budget carrier Jet2.com published a code of practice on disruptive passengers following collaboration between airlines, airports, the police and retailers. The zero tolerance approach includes airport shops advising passengers not to drink alcohol they have purchased before or during their flight, and training staff in bars and restaurants to limit or stop the sale of alcohol to prevent or manage disruptive behaviour. A Department for Transport spokeswoman said: Airport security is always under review, however there are no plans to specifically address the issue of alcohol at airports.

text: The fact that a record-equalling 10 Wales players have been selected to start the British and Irish Lions' crucial final Test against Australia is a source of great national pride. Head coach Warren Gatland has chosen to remain with the players he knows most thoroughly from managing Wales. They secured the Grand Slam in 2012, defeated England in the final match to claim this year's Six Nations and reached the 2011 World Cup semi-final. Gatland understands what they can achieve, but his choice does place some pressure upon him. If they triumph he becomes a hero. If they fail, everybody will be criticising him for selecting so many Welsh players. His choice also places additional pressure on the Welsh players to deliver. All selections represent a gamble in numerous ways, but it remains somewhat surprising that five alterations were made for the second Test and another six for the Sydney Test. It remains unusual to have so many alterations as successful teams do not do that - they remain settled. Gatland's front-row selection appears solid, although I believe England lock Geoff Parling remains quite fortunate to retain his place in the second row. And in the back row I would have included yet another Welsh player - flanker Justin Tipuric - in the starting line-up! The Welsh players will also possess the additional motivation of the nation's poor recent record - they have lost eight consecutively - against Australia. Wales have been truly unfortunate against the Wallabies recently though, and they could easily have won two of their three most recent matches. With those defeats in mind, they will be eager for revenge. I remain surprised that Ireland centre Brian O'Driscoll has been omitted as he would have been the perfect captain. But Wales lock Alun Wyn Jones is performing very well, and he will certainly lead by example. Provided Wales centre Jamie Roberts remains fully fit when he returns at the weekend, he possesses the ability to cross the gain line. An inability to do so represented a real problem last Saturday, when the Lions made no breaks whatsoever. To defeat the Australians, we must have somebody who can put us on the front foot. Whilst our regional teams have been very poor in recent years, fortunately the national team has been very consistent. Recalling the 1971 and 1974 Lions teams, of which I was a member, we also possessed a strong Welsh influence. You can truly take the positivity from the national team to the Lions - that certainly occurred in 1971 when we were series winners in New Zealand, and in 1974 when we finished unbeaten in South Africa. Let us hope the same thing occurs again for the Lions on Saturday. The last two matches have been decided by two-point and one-point margins, and it could go down to the final minute again. It will be very tight, and I think Australia will start as slight favourites. JPR Williams was speaking to BBC Sport's Matt Monaghan

text: Hospital beds in England may fill up with the elderly and vulnerable because of cuts to local authority social care funding, a top NHS figure has warned. The assertion originated from the NHS Confederation's chief executive, Nigel Edwards, in correspondence to the Daily Telegraph. Mr Edwards stated that individuals requiring medical treatment might be refused hospital accommodation as a consequence of the reductions. The Department of Health replied that an additional £2bn was being assigned to safeguard social care. Healthcare expenditure was protected in Chancellor George Osborne's Spending Review. Nevertheless, local authorities in England are confronting a 27% reduction in central government funding during the forthcoming four years. Mr Edwards, whose body represents health service organisations in England, described the £2bn temporary solution to social care funding announced in the Spending Review as providing welcome relief to many. However, he stated the financial constraints could still produce a knock-on effect upon the health service. In his correspondence to the Telegraph, Mr Edwards wrote: Reduced support from council services will rapidly result in heightened pressure on emergency services and hospitals. Hospital beds will be occupied by those who desperately require care because the support services the elderly need following discharge will not be accessible. • £81bn reduction from public expenditure across four years • 19% average departmental reductions - below the anticipated 25% • £7bn additional welfare reductions, encompassing modifications to incapacity, housing benefit and tax credits • £1.8bn rise in public sector pension employee contributions by 2014 • Increase in state pension age accelerated • 7% reduction for local councils from April next year • Permanent bank levy • Rail fares to increase 3% above inflation from 2012 He continued: Regarding the care of the most vulnerable in our society, it truly is vital that the NHS and local authorities are united in this endeavour. The Department of Health acknowledged that social care can influence NHS demands. A spokesperson stated: That is why we are reinforcing programmes such as re-ablement and the 30-day re-admission tariff, which will integrate hospital care with community care. We have assigned an additional £2bn by 2014-15 - this extra enhancement, alongside an ambitious efficiency programme, will ensure sufficient funding is available both to protect people's access to services and deliver new approaches to improve quality and outcomes. We anticipate local health and social care professionals will collaborate to ensure the funding is expended on joint health and social care priorities and improve outcomes for everyone. Councillor David Rogers, from the Local Government Association, stated the additional £2bn would not extend very far. Naturally that is most welcome, but as part of what councils communicated to the government before the Spending Review, there is likely to be a shortfall over that same period of approximately £6bn. Therefore, there will still be difficulties. However, I believe the crucial matter is to ensure that both councils and the NHS locally work increasingly closely together to provide the finest service to our residents. On Thursday, critics voiced concerns regarding whether the £2bn designated for social care, half of which is to derive from a direct grant to local government, would reach its intended destination. Jennifer Dixon, chief executive of the Nuffield Trust think tank, stated: The reality is that local authority budgets will be strained and funds for social care are not ring-fenced, therefore the extra £1bn per year is by no means guaranteed.

text: Antrim lost 2-06 to 0-09 to Limerick in their All-Ireland Qualifier Round 1B game at Corrigan Park on Saturday. Limerick had not secured a competitive victory throughout the year but early strikes from Ian Ryan and Sean McSweeney, a penalty, established their path to triumph. The home team held a 2-2 to 0-6 advantage at half-time and pressed forward to victory through scores from McSweeney, Ryan and Stephen Cahill. Goalkeeper Donal O'Sullivan produced three vital outstanding saves for Limerick. Antrim's championship run concluded in disappointing manner as the Saffrons failed to build upon their promotion to Division Three of the Football League. Antrim utilised the wind to their benefit in the first half and a free from Ryan Murphy following 40 seconds and a Kevin Niblock score from the right put the away side into a 0-2 to 0-0 advantage. The home side received a significant lift when Seanie Buckley found Ryan at the edge of the square and the St Senan's player struck the net with a low effort past Chris Kerr following five minutes. Antrim surrendered a second goal merely three minutes afterwards from McSweeney's penalty strike. Midfielder Darragh Treacy was brought down when he succeeded in getting behind the Antrim defence. McSweeney maintained his composure to fire the ball into the bottom right corner of the net to propel Limerick into a 2-01 to 0-02 lead. Those strikes provided Limerick with considerable confidence but Antrim replied effectively. Matthew Fitzpatrick became the first Antrim player to find his target with a fine score from the right in the 13th minute - perhaps he might have attempted goal - and four minutes subsequently Patrick McBride struck his team's fourth point to reduce the deficit to three points. Tommy Childs was a late replacement for injured Limerick captain Iain Corbett, and he excelled around the centre and created an excellent score from the right for Ryan following 18 minutes. Ryan possessed an outstanding opportunity for his second goal nine minutes from the conclusion when he rose ahead of substitute Martin Johnson, only for Kerr to thwart him with an excellent save using his feet. And Antrim subsequently concluded the half impressively and McBride and Sean Burke scored to establish a two-point lead at the interval. Equipped with a two-point advantage and a strengthening wind behind them, Limerick appeared lively from the start in the second period and following some solid defensive work, it was corner-back Cahill who extended their lead to three in the 44th minute. Following scoring merely six points in 50 minutes Antrim would always require a goal to mount a recovery and that opportunity arrived to Martin Johnson as he advanced from the right, but Donal O'Sullivan executed a superb save to preserve his goal intact. The introduction of Tomas McCann provided Antrim with a much-needed injection of pace in attack and he followed a free from Ryan Murray with one of his own to reduce the Limerick advantage to two points with nine minutes remaining. Ryan extended that to a goal with a free but Antrim twice came close to finding the net in the final stages but O'Sullivan delivered excellent saves to deny Ryan Murray and Martin Johnson and secure their place in the subsequent round. Limerick: D O'Sullivan; P Browne, S Cahill (0-1), S O'Dea; B Fanning, J McCarthy, P Ranahan; D Treacy, S Buckley; G Noonan, P Nash, T Childs; S McSweeney (1-3, 1-0 pen, 0-3f), I Ryan (1-2), H Bourke. Subs: E Hogan for Bourke (50 mins), P Hannon for Nash (63 mins), I Corbett for Childs (66 mins). Antrim: C Kerr; K O'Boyle, J Crozier, R Johnson; P McBride (0-2), P Gallagher, M Sweeney; S McVeigh, M McCann; J Laverty, M Fitzpatrick (0-1), K Niblock (0-2, 1f)); R Murray (0-2f), N McKeever, S Burke (0-1). text: Saturday's FA Cup final between Arsenal and Aston Villa at Wembley will be watched by half a billion viewers in more than 120 countries. Nearly 90,000 supporters will attend Wembley for the 134th final of the world's oldest cup competition as two sides of elite, millionaire athletes compete for glory. However, what precisely was the scene at the original final back in 1872? An estimated crowd of 2,000 witnessed 22 amateurs play on a cricket ground, without nets, as Wanderers defeated Royal Engineers 1-0 through a goal from Morton Betts. BBC Sport, with assistance from Matthew Taylor, professor of history at De Montfort University, examines the first final 143 years ago... Before the 1872 FA Cup, no regular competitive matches were being played in England. Football Association secretary Charles Alcock devised plans for the first FA Cup which saw 15 sides enter the first round of November 1871. Enter Barnes, Civil Service, Hitchin, Crystal Palace (confusingly not the current Palace but their predecessors who were dissolved in 1876), Maidenhead, Marlow, Queen's Park, Donington School, Upton Park, Clapham Rovers, Royal Engineers, Reigate Priory, Wanderers, Harrow Chequers and Hampstead Heathens, who received a bye. Early difficulties and the logistical challenges of scheduling football fixtures across Britain in the steam era meant that Scottish club Queen's Park progressed to the semi-finals without actually playing a match. The semi-finals - both scoreless draws - were played at Kennington Oval. Royal Engineers secured their place in the final with a 3-0 replay victory over Crystal Palace, whilst Wanderers progressed when Queen's Park decided they could not afford another expensive trip to London for the replay and withdrew. The historian's view: The general consensus is that the FA Cup was based on the knockout competitions between 'Houses' at major public schools such as Harrow. However, Alcock may also have drawn inspiration from existing competitions in the provinces, such as Sheffield's Youdon Cup, launched in 1867. Certainly football was equally, if not more, established and popular in Sheffield as it was in London at this time, and the elite ex-public schoolboys based in the capital knew and played against teams from Sheffield, Nottingham and elsewhere. Alcock - the mastermind behind the entire concept - played in defence for Wanderers. Established in 1859 as Forest Football Club, the side mainly comprised former Harrow public schoolboys and adopted the name 'Wanderers' because they played their fixtures at different venues. However, by 1869 the club was based at Kennington Oval, where Alcock also happened to be the secretary of Surrey cricket club. Royal Engineers were founded in 1863 by Major Francis Marindin - an extraordinary individual. Having served in the Crimean war, he would go on to play in the 1872 final, become president of the FA in 1874 and then referee eight further FA Cup finals. The 1872 final was held at Kennington Oval, also the venue for the first international football match between England and Scotland in 1870. The Oval would go on to host 20 of the subsequent 21 FA Cup finals, with the 1873 final played at Lillie Bridge - close to Chelsea's modern home at Stamford Bridge. The historian's view: Many football clubs played on cricket grounds in the late 19th century. Football clubs often emerged from existing cricket clubs, as a method of the players keeping fit in the winter. Purpose-built football grounds did not emerge in significant numbers until the 1880s and 1890s. Whilst supporters at this year's final will have to navigate through the crowds at Wembley, it was a more sedate affair in 1872. Football had yet to catch on and around 2,000 are said to have been at the Oval. Much has changed beyond recognition in football but the cost of attending remains an issue... The historian's view: Attendances for football matches were not large in the early 1870s, with one reason for the relatively low attendance the price of tickets, which at one shilling (five pence in today's money) was higher than for most matches at the time. The Oval crowd was said to be 'very fashionable', so presumably comprised of the well-to-do and the upper middle-class, as well as those connected with the 'old boys' public school network that ran the Football Association at this time. Royal Engineers could lay claim to being the Barcelona of their day, with their revolutionary tactic of 'passing' the ball to a team-mate at odds with the usual approach of chasing the ball into space. The only goal of the final came after 15 minutes when Betts, playing under the pseudonym A H Chequer, derived from his membership of the Harrow Chequers club, collected the ball after a long dribble from Walpole Vidal and struck home. Goalkeeper was not yet a specialist position, with keepers regularly playing outfield. The historian's view: It was not unusual for teams to line up with six or seven forwards in the early 1870s. Most teams at this time still relied primarily on individual dribbling, with team-mates supporting the dribbler in an effort to move the ball towards the opponents' goal. Some authorities have claimed that Royal Engineers were the first team to develop a passing game, and were doing so at around the time of the first FA Cup final. It is fair to say that the footballers of Oscar Wilde's age were a different breed to today's sporting stars. The Wanderers' band of ex-public schoolboys and the aristocratic elite produced some notable sportsmen. As well as the pioneering Alcock the team contained several men who played first-class cricket, a goalkeeper who was capped by England as a defender and a forward who was capped by England in goal. Forward Edward Bowen was noted for walking the 90 miles between Cambridge and Oxford in 26 hours in between his football and playing cricket for Hampshire; full-back Edgar Lubbock went on to become the deputy governor of the Bank of England and wing-wizard Walpole Vidal - known as the prince of dribblers - would later become a vicar. As one would expect, the Royal Engineers side had all seen military service from across the world, with experiences spanning from India to the Crimea, Bermuda, Gibraltar and the Zulu war. Forward Henry Waugh Renny-Tailyour played football and rugby union for Scotland as well as cricket for Kent and would still find time to become a managing director of Guinness, whilst half-back Alfred Goodwyn would suffer the unfortunate fate of being the first international footballer to be killed in a riding accident in India two years after the final. The historian's view: Most of the players in the first final had learnt the game in elite public schools and at university. The Wanderers was open only to those who had attended leading public schools and Oxbridge. Three of the Cup final line-up had attended Eton and four had gone to Harrow. The early rules were very different. In a nod to cricket, players had to appeal for a goal and changed ends after each goal, not at half-time. This once allowed Walpole Vidal to score three times without the opposition touching the ball. The historian's view: Modern supporters would be surprised by some of the features of football in 1872. Rather than a crossbar, a tape was pitched between two posts eight feet above the ground. Throw-ins were not determined by the team whose player had kicked the ball off the pitch but by the first player to reach the ball. However, these rules were not consistent across the country. Variations existed in different areas and it was not until 10 years later, in 1882, that a uniform set of rules was established by the FA. The 2015 final will be refereed by Jon Moss, who can expect some criticism from the stands. It was a different story for civil servant Alfred Stair, the referee chosen for the first three FA Cup finals. Stair was the head of the Inland Revenue - presumably seen as a trustworthy gentleman of his day - and also played football for Upton Park. The historian's view: In the earliest days of football, referees were literally peripheral figures. They stood outside the playing area and were only called upon to adjudicate if the umpires (who were appointed by each club and stood in either half of the pitch) could not reach agreement. For winners Wanderers it was the start of a golden - if brief - era of success. They retained the trophy in 1873 by defeating Oxford University 2-0 and added three more trophies before the end of the decade. Their haul of five FA Cups has only been bettered by Blackburn Rovers, Newcastle, Aston Villa, Chelsea, Liverpool, Tottenham, Manchester United and Arsenal. However, by 1881 Wanderers could not field a side as players left to play for some of the newer clubs springing up across the country and the team folded in 1887. A reformed side was founded in 2009 and the club currently play in the Surrey South Eastern Combination. In fact they are seeking a new manager to get the club back in the FA Cup by 2022. The Engineers reached four finals and won the Cup in 1875. They continue to play on and are currently managed by Capt Simon Mayers, who has a 25-man squad to select from around 8,000 men based around the world. The historian's view: Football became increasingly popular over the next decade or so, as it became embedded in British working-class culture. Its popularity was helped by entrepreneurs who realised the opportunities that existed in enclosing playing fields and charging the public for entry. The next step from this, as teams began to act as representatives of their localities, was for ambitious club committees to 'poach' the best players and pay for them to play for their teams. Within less than a decade of the first FA Cup final, professional football had emerged in England, though it was not legalised by the FA until 1885.

text: A gay man has won a landmark ruling which will give his husband the same pension rights as a wife would receive. These are external links and will open in a new window The Supreme Court ruled unanimously that should John Walker, 66, pass away, his husband shall be entitled to a spouse's pension, assuming they remain wed. The former cavalry officer stated it would drag the government into the 21st century, whilst human rights organisation Liberty declared thousands could benefit. A government spokesman confirmed it would examine the implications of the judgment. BBC legal affairs correspondent Clive Coleman stated the decision will have a dramatic effect on the entitlement of thousands of civil partners and spouses in same sex marriages. They will now enjoy identical pension rights and entitlements as those in heterosexual marriages, our correspondent added. The judgment means Mr Walker's husband - who is in his fifties - will now be entitled to a spousal pension of approximately £45,000 annually, rather than around £1,000 per year. Mr Walker declared it was to our government's great shame that it has taken so many years, huge amounts of taxpayers' money and the UK's highest court to drag them into the 21st Century. He continued: Finally this absurd injustice has been consigned to the history books and my husband and I can now get on with enjoying the rest of our lives together. Mr Walker pursued legal action as he wished to ensure that, should he die first, his husband would receive an adequate pension. Most occupational pension schemes provide 50% of a pension's value to a spouse for the remainder of their lives after their husband or wife dies - without considering the marriage date. However, the Equality Act 2010 contains an exemption for employers, permitting them to exclude civil partners from spousal benefits paid before December 2005. The Supreme Court has now determined the exemption under the 2010 act is incompatible with EU law and must be disapplied. Emma Norton, a solicitor from Liberty, which represented Mr Walker, urged the government to guarantee Brexit would not threaten the judgment. This ruling was made under EU law and is a direct consequence of the rights protection the EU gives us, she stated. We now risk losing that protection. The government must promise that there will be no rollback on LGBT rights after Brexit. A government spokesperson said the rights of same sex couples had been transformed for the better since 2010. During the hearing, it stated the cost of applying the ruling retrospectively would be £100m for private sector schemes and a further £20m for the public sector.

text: At one of the shops serving the troops in Camp Bastion there are plenty of reminders that this war is nearly over, at least for those who have travelled from Britain and America. Fewer goods remain available for purchase. Several items still in stock are being offered at reduced prices. The souvenirs on display continue at full price, yet they also indicate that the conclusion is now approaching. Drinking glasses bear the message Been there; Done that, whilst a mug displays Happiness is Helmand in the rear view mirror. Bastion was formerly a thriving military metropolis, comparable in sheer scale to Reading. However, it is now gradually becoming more of a ghost town. Compounds that were previously filled with tents or military vehicles now lie vacant. Fewer men and women in uniform walk about, and the constant chopping of air by helicopter blades has become more sporadic. Whilst Bastion is progressively shrinking, most other British bases in Helmand have already vanished. During the height of the conflict, approximately 10,000 British military personnel occupied 137 bases throughout the province in southern Afghanistan. Today there are roughly 4,000 UK personnel occupying merely two: the main operating base at Bastion and an observation post called Sterga 2, which provides a valuable vantage point over the Helmand valley. In forthcoming months Sterga will be transferred to Nato command with the British-led Task Force Helmand absorbed into Regional Command South West with a US Marine Corps brigadier general in overall command. Lashkar Gah, a main operating base and the former British headquarters, has been transferred to the Afghans. The buildings that until recently accommodated a British provincial reconstruction team are to become a health centre. Not that there will be any UK presence to observe the transformation when it occurs. Make no mistake: this represents a complete withdrawal by the British from one of the most violent regions of Afghanistan. Camp Price was formerly home to 2,000 troops. During recent weeks it has been demolished. Chainsaws and diggers are the new weapons for British soldiers. The saws are employed to tear down the Hesco walls that formerly protected them, whilst the diggers level the ground. From dust to dust. Even the concrete barriers which became improvised memorials, with graffiti honouring fallen comrades, have been removed. Captain David Goodman observes as the final shipping containers are lifted onto lorries. A total of 600 containers have departed Price since October. He states: I am now dreaming of ISO containers. We have been dispatching 20 or 30 daily and it is a nightmare, waking up thinking 'did this container depart?' Scarcely anything has been left behind. This raises questions about what will be the enduring legacy of British forces after eight years in Helmand and 448 British military deaths. It is certainly not peace. As the final containers are loaded onto lorries at Camp Price you can still hear gunfire in the distance. Lieutenant Colonel Mike Caldicott of the Royal Logistic Corps led the final military convoy out of Price and it was probably one of the last logistic patrols in Helmand. He is convinced they have made a difference. I only wish that people at home could observe the changes I have witnessed through my eyes, he states. I think they would feel considerably better about the investment we have made. That view contrasts with some of the soldiers we interviewed who appear more eager to dwell on going home than on what they leave behind. One puts it simply: Job done, get home. Another remarks: I will miss the sun, that is probably about it. Most of the soldiers we speak to believe they have made a difference. However, you will not find many in uniform repeating the claim made by David Cameron last year that it is already mission accomplished. The most senior British general in Afghanistan, Lieutenant General John Lorimer, states extraordinary things have been achieved across the country. However, when I ask him if it is mission accomplished he carefully avoids repeating the phrase. Instead he states: There is still much to be done. One senior British officer tells me that if Iraq was the A-level examination, Afghanistan is the PhD. Back home, the assessment is probably more stark. The current reticence over military intervention reflects the public's weariness of war. Margaret Evison lost her only son, Mark, in Helmand in 2009. She states she has had time to adjust to her loss but adds: There is nothing in my mind that would justify my son's death. On the broader question of what has been achieved she states she is not sure the British withdrawal comes at a time when Afghanistan is more stable. As for David Cameron's assertion that it is mission accomplished, her response is Well he has to say that! Brigadier James Woodham will be the final commander of Task Force Helmand. He too states there is still much work to do. He believes there has been progress but admits that ultimately history will be the judge of what has been achieved. What seems strange is that after investing so much here for the past eight years there will soon be no British military presence at all to help write the final chapter.

He says, “I dream of the containers now; we are shipping twenty or thirty a day and it’s a nightmare, when you wake up and wonder if this one was among them.” The question remains, what will be the legacy of the British after eight years and 448 British soldiers killed? Lieutenant Colonel Mike Caldicott of the Royal Logistic Corps led the last convoy from Camp Price, and it will probably be the last. He believes they have made a difference. Not peace, though. Most of the soldiers we talked to believe they've made a difference. This opinion differs from that of certain soldiers we've talked to, who seem more eager to think of their return than of what they are leaving behind; one simply says: “Operation completed, home.” I think they would have a much better view of the investment we have made. I asked if this is a mission accomplished, he avoided the expression. But there are not many who repeat the words of last year's David Cam-eron, that the mission has been accomplished. One said: I'll miss the sun, that's all. The most senior British general in Afghanistan, Lieutenant General John Lorimer, speaks of the astonishing achievements that have been made throughout the country. But he says: “There is still much to be done.” At home, the judgment may be more severe; the present unwillingness to intervene militarily is probably due more to public weariness of war than to any lack of results. Margaret Evison lost her only son Mark in Helmand Province in 2009. She says she has had time to come to terms with the loss, but adds, “There is nothing in my mind that can justify the death of my son.” Brigadier James Woodham will be the last commander of the Helmand operation, and he too says that there is still much to be done. A senior British officer said to me: If Iraq is the “A” level, then Afghanistan is the doctorate. He thinks there has been progress, but he admits that history will be the last judge. As for the British government's claim that the mission has been accomplished, she answers: "But he would say that!" It is strange that after having spent so much during the past eight years, there will be no British military presence to write the last chapter.

text: Basketball's biggest star LeBron James has announced his return to the Cleveland Cavaliers - the team where he began his NBA career 11 years ago. The 29-year-old made the declaration in an interview with Sports Illustrated on Friday. James has remained a free agent since 1st July after opting out of the final two years of his Miami Heat contract. I always believed I would return to Cleveland and finish my career there, James stated. James, named the NBA's most valuable player on four occasions, terminated his contract in Miami last month. He would have earned $42.7m (£25.1m) in the two years remaining on his deal. His decision triggered a scramble for the player, but he revealed a return to his home state of Ohio was always in his thoughts. After last season, free agency was not even a thought, said James, who originates from Akron, 40 miles from Cleveland. But I have two boys and my wife, Savannah, is pregnant with a girl. I began thinking about what it would be like to raise my family in my home town. I examined other teams, but I was not going to leave Miami for anywhere except Cleveland. The more time passed, the more it felt right. This is what makes me happy. After joining the Cavaliers as the first draft pick in 2003, James rose to superstardom over the next seven years before he was tempted to Miami in 2010, where he formed a devastating partnership with Chris Bosh and Dwyane Wade. His announcement on leaving for Miami was made during a staged ESPN television programme called The Decision. It led to a backlash from Cleveland fans who burnt James jerseys in anger. James, who would have earned $20m (£11.7m) next season, won NBA titles with Heat in 2012 and 2013. He also led Miami to the NBA Finals in 2011, when they lost to Dallas, and 2014, when they were heavily beaten by San Antonio. Speaking of his time in Miami, James said: The hardest thing to leave is what I built with those guys. I have talked to some of them and will talk to others. Nothing will ever change what we accomplished. We are brothers for life. News of James's departure was announced over the loudspeaker at Cleveland airport and Cavaliers ticket phone lines crashed, reported ESPN. In 2010, Cavaliers owner Dan Gilbert wrote an open letter criticising James and describing his departure as a shocking act of disloyalty and a shameful display of selfishness and betrayal. But on Friday he tweeted: My eight-year-old: 'Daddy, does this mean I can finally wear my LeBron jersey, again?' Yes it does, son. Yes it does! In Miami, a mural featuring James was defaced - according to South Florida news station WPLG Local 10. Heat owner Micky Arison tweeted: I am shocked and disappointed in today's news. However I will never forget what LeBron brought us for four years. Thanks for the memories. The situation could yet become significantly worse for the Heat. Wade and Bosh both joined James in opting for free agency this summer and may now follow their former team-mate's lead by confirming moves away from Miami. In addition to the Sports Illustrated interview, James posted a photograph of himself in a Cavaliers uniform on Instagram with the phrase I'm coming home. He told Cleveland fans not to expect instant success, however. When I left Cleveland, I was on a mission, James said. I was seeking championships, and we won two. But Miami already knew that feeling. Our city has not had that feeling in a long, long, long time. I am not promising a championship. I know how hard that is to deliver, James said. We are not ready right now. No way. Of course, I want to win next year, but I am realistic. It will be a long process, much longer than it was in 2010. My patience will get tested. I know that.

text: The jobs market has seen a substantial decline in people starting full-time jobs since the start of the year, according to a regular survey of recruiters. The hiring index is compiled by the Markit data company, alongside recruitment consultants REC. It showed a steep fall in both permanent placements and individuals available for such positions. There was, nevertheless, an increase in demand for permanent and temporary personnel during January. The sector which has continually demonstrated the greatest level of demand for recruits is nursing, medicine and care, followed by engineering and construction. A projection by the Construction Industry Training Board (CITB), also released on Wednesday, estimates there will be 12,000 recruits required in the next five years, as workers depart the sector or leave the country. It anticipates the total number of construction workers will decline, as major infrastructure contracts, including the Queensferry Crossing, reduce from very high levels. Growth in the house-building and repair market is set to be between only 1% and 2%. Ian Hughes, a director at CITB, stated: Whilst we have incorporated Brexit into this projection, there remain many unknowns to life after departing the EU. We will be working with our industry to understand what it means for our migrant workforce and what we must do to attract and develop more of our own. The REC/Markit recruitment survey revealed starting salaries rising, but not as rapidly as a parallel survey indicated for the rest of Britain. Overall, the picture appeared weaker than the figures across the rest of Britain, where other recent survey evidence has demonstrated the jobs market to be notably stronger. Recruitment consultants reported that there has been an increase in employment of temporary staff, at the fastest rate for more than a year. Hourly rates of pay for temporary staff rose, but the pace of wage inflation slowed. Kevin Green, chief executive of REC, observed: The jobs market in Scotland continued to worsen in January, with recruiters reporting a decline in permanent placements for the fourth consecutive month. Scotland's economy is not as robust as the rest of the UK. The energy sector has weakened, and continuing political uncertainty is affecting business confidence. Vacancies in Scotland remain in growth, so demand for staff is strong, despite employers showing hesitancy when it comes to investment decisions. This suggests the market could recover if confidence is restored. The survey encompasses around 100 recruitment and employment consultants in Scotland.

text: The families of victims of a loyalist gun attack have accepted a police apology after the weapon used in the murders was discovered in a museum. Five Catholics perished when the Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) discharged firearms in Sean Graham's betting shop on Ormeau Road during February 1992. Chief Constable George Hamilton encountered the families to apologise on behalf of the Police Service of Northern Ireland. The families commended his apology, which they characterised as heartfelt. They stated he clarified that it did not occur during his tenure as PSNI chief constable, but pledged to collaborate with additional investigations into their case. Police officers had previously informed the relatives that the murder weapon had been officially disposed of but last month, the BBC Panorama programme disclosed that it had appeared as an exhibit in the Imperial War Museum in London. The programme stated that investigators assigned the responsibility of re-examining paramilitary murders in Northern Ireland had discovered the gun on display in an exhibit on the Troubles. The assault rifle was employed in seven unsolved murders, five of them in the betting shop attack. The weapon has now been withdrawn from display and is undergoing additional tests. The victims of the Ormeau Road shooting included a 15-year-old boy, James Kennedy. Following the meeting with the Chief Constable, Billy McManus, whose father was also killed in the attack, said: It was a heartfelt apology. He did say in the meeting, he is a human being. He added that firstly, Mr Hamilton acknowledged the hurt inflicted upon the families by the manner in which they discovered the gun exhibit. He did provide us a full commitment that he will support the Police Ombudsman and the third one was that, if you've violated the law in any part of collusion, the full force of the law is going to come down on you, Mr McManus added. The meeting with the PSNI chief was facilitated by Relatives for Justice (RFJ). RFJ spokesman Mark Thompson said Mr Hamilton delivered a fulsome apology and promised that the PSNI would collaborate fully with the ombudsman's investigation into the case.

text: Ex-captain Michael Vaughan has backed Kevin Pietersen's claims that England's bowlers were an intimidating clique, adding they could be disrespectful. Pietersen, who was dismissed in February, alleges there existed a bullying culture, whereby players were compelled to apologise if they committed errors in the field. Vaughan stated the bowlers' cabal has been a problem for several years. The likes of Graeme Swann and Stuart Broad have been disrespectful to fielders, he wrote in the Telegraph. Vaughan, 39, who led Pietersen in England's 2005 Ashes-winning side, added: No one drops a catch deliberately. How would they feel if every time they delivered a poor ball everyone turned to them and said: 'What the hell are you doing?' Vaughan said he had experienced a similar situation in his early years at Yorkshire, where he would hate fielding because he was frightened of making an error. The irony is that James Anderson has spoken about how difficult it was for him when he first played for England, Vaughan added. Media playback is not supported on this device. So I hope these bowlers understand what they are doing to the guys around them, particularly the inexperienced ones. Nottinghamshire fast bowler Ajmal Shahzad, who played one Test and 11 one-day internationals for England, concurred with Pietersen's assessment of cliques in the dressing room. I wish I could have socialised with my peers somewhat more and been accepted slightly more, Shahzad told BBC Radio 5 live. Off the pitch you would go off and socialise with your friends in the team, and there were perhaps two or three cliques who would stick together. I suppose these cliques are not a healthy thing to develop. Pietersen, whose new book is published on Thursday, also accused wicketkeeper Matt Prior of being a disruptive influence on the team. Former England spinner Swann described Pietersen's claims as codswallop. He added that the book was the biggest work of fiction since Jules Verne. Pietersen had his England central contract terminated following the 5-0 Ashes defeat in Australia, as the England and Wales Cricket Board set out to create a new team ethic. Speaking to the Telegraph on Monday, he claimed he had been marginalised and demonised by England and that former coach Andy Flower ruled by fear. Former England batsman Geoffrey Boycott said Flower had failed to man-manage Pietersen. Boycott told BBC Radio 5 live: I have played in numerous teams. The best captains I played with could be forthright when they wanted to be but understood the different needs of the members of the team. The real leaders can handle different types of people. It has been quite obvious for some time that the England set-up has not been able to handle KP. KP perhaps has part of the blame but if you are someone like Andy Flower, you're not out there scoring runs, so your job is to pull all the players together. Media playback is not supported on this device. Former England captain Mike Gatting said: Think of bullying KP, I'm not sure that's quite right. He's a larger than life character, he is his own person at times and he gets on and does things, he told 5 live. Perhaps he didn't like what was being done, but he was captain remember, for a brief time. Sadly that didn't last long. So he had a chance to actually mould something in that team and he didn't take it. Former England batsman Allan Lamb told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: It's quite sad to hear but I think it's something that's gone on.
