text: Pakistan's Supreme Court is considering corruption allegations against Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, amid mounting pressure over his family's wealth. These are external links and will open in a new window. The action follows after investigators stated his family had failed to explain the source of its financial assets. The investigation commenced when the Panama Papers disclosures connected his children to offshore entities used to purchase London properties. This heightened suspicion the entities were employed to launder illegally obtained wealth, allegations Mr Sharif vigorously denies. He maintains the properties in London were obtained legitimately and that he personally does not possess them. However, the matter is becoming a significant challenge to him. Opposition parties accuse his family of exploiting their political influence to accumulate wealth through unlawful methods and are demanding he resign. Thus far Mr Sharif has declined, describing the investigators' report as a compilation of allegations and assumptions. His choice to remain in office was supported by the federal cabinet last week. Hundreds of security officers have been positioned around the Supreme Court, sections of which have also been enclosed with barbed wire. The Joint Investigation Team (JIT), established in April, states it has discovered significant gaps/disparity among the known and declared sources of income and the wealth amassed by Mr Sharif and his family. It charges Mr Sharif with hiding assets, exaggerating the wealth of his father with the purpose of justifying his family's wealth, and of not reflecting in his wealth declaration an exorbitant increase in his family's wealth during his first decade in office (1985-93). It charges his heir-apparent, daughter Maryam Sharif, of being the beneficial owner of offshore companies through which the London properties were obtained, and of falsifying documents to demonstrate she was a trustee for her brother, the actual owner. This accusation is founded on a copy of a trust document which she signed in February 2006. The JIT states the document was printed in Calibri typeface, which was not commercially accessible until January 2007. The presence of the properties and the offshore companies connected to them was revealed in the leak of 11 million documents possessed by the Panama-based law firm Mossack Fonseca. The family stated that the funds for the properties, as well as the family's enterprises in the UK and the Gulf region, originated from the sale of their UAE-based Gulf Steel Mills. The mill was established by PM Sharif's father, the late Mian Mohammad Sharif, in the early 1970s, and he subsequently invested the proceeds from its sale in a Qatar-based enterprise. The Sharif family have presented a letter from former Qatari Prime Minister Prince Hammad bin Jassim al-Thani explaining the money trail. He was not available to be questioned by the JIT. However, the JIT states it discovered no evidence of a money trail leading from Pakistan through Dubai and Qatar to the London properties. The JIT report has split the nation - something very evident in media coverage. Audiences following any of the pro-government television channels would conclude that the JIT report was a collection of falsehoods, but debates on pro-opposition channels leave no uncertainty in the minds of their viewers that they believe Mr Sharif and his family are linked with corruption. The report addresses complex matters of international finance, involving a maze of financial regulations from numerous states and regulatory authorities. Therefore, whilst much of what it claims may be founded in reality, experts have identified instances where the JIT appears to have either concealed its lack of access or understanding, or has included opinions that do not possess a sound foundation. Questions have also been posed over the Supreme Court's decision that the two military intelligence agencies, the MI and the ISI, would provide one representative each to the six-member JIT, which should ideally comprise financial experts only. Additionally, the Supreme Court's decision to allow the ISI exclusively to arrange secretarial services to the JIT has not been received well by those who believe this service has been actively engaged in political management of Pakistan's ruling superstructure since the 1980s. Many suspect the ISI is interfering ahead of elections due in 2018 so it can maintain its influence over the political establishment. There are three possibilities: A disqualification would mean that Mr Sharif would be excluded from politics for life, as required under the honest and sagacious provision of the constitution. His daughter and political heir would face the same prospect. It is not clear how the situation will be managed by the Supreme Court, which is itself under enormous pressure. Establishing the JIT to examine the prime minister's wealth was an unprecedented action. The JIT is not a creation of the constitution or the executive, but a creation of the Supreme Court. As such, few consider it probable that the court would dismiss the JIT's report entirely. If disqualified, the prime minister is likely to announce a successor - possibly his brother Shahbaz, who is chief minister of Punjab - and allow the government to complete its term. In any other circumstance, analysts expect him to remain and, if he must, to go down fighting.

text: A recovering alcoholic has been jailed for four months for stealing £11,000 from a faulty Ulster Bank cash machine. A judge informed Peter Anthony Young, 58, of Hunter's Way, Ardglass, that he had deliberately exploited the significant fault in the bank's system nearly four years previously. This allowed customers to withdraw money from cash machines without impacting their account balance. After conducting a review, the bank identified that the funds had been withdrawn by Young. A prosecution barrister informed Downpatrick Crown Court that on 22 June 2012, Ulster Bank had suffered a computer failure in its system. After conducting a review, Ulster Bank identified that Young, who was amongst its customers, had £11,000 withdrawn from his account on that date, stated Ms Ivers. The judge was informed there had been 22 individual withdrawals of £500 on the date in question. The prosecution barrister stated the bank made numerous attempts to contact Young unsuccessfully before ultimately reporting the matter to police as fraudulent. The PSNI commenced an investigation and Young voluntarily attended a police station and confessed to making the withdrawals, informing police he had spent the money on alcohol. The prosecution barrister stated the defendant, who was a customer of Ulster Bank, had made no attempt to repay the funds and the outstanding balance he owed now totalled £10,908.40. A defence barrister described it as an exceptional case and stated that when Young was questioned by police in September 2014 he made candid admissions to his offences. Reading between the lines from the court documents, it appears Mr Young was in the company of other individuals drinking with them that date and when he was withdrawing money it became clear to him and the others that there was a defect with this machine, he informed the court. This was always going to catch up with him. He is not in any way blaming others. The defence barrister stated that Young's life had entered a downward spiral following the death of his mother in 1991 and stated that by the age of 34 he was an alcoholic, homeless and living on the streets of Belfast. The barrister added that the father-of-five was now a recovering alcoholic, who was attending Alcoholics Anonymous sessions, was part of a church group and was also attending a rehabilitation programme. The defence barrister stated Young could be made the subject of a community order which would leave something suspended over his head that would remind him not to deviate from the straight and narrow again. I would encourage the court to give him an opportunity to continue to better himself, the barrister added. The judge stated Young had gone to the machine on one occasion to withdraw £500 on the date in question. He chose to return to this machine a further 21 times to withdraw the money when he knew he did not possess the funds in his account, he stated. He knew perfectly well what he was doing and he deliberately exploited the faulty cash machine. The judge stated Young, who is surviving on social security benefits, had not repaid any money he had stolen from Ulster Bank. I do not believe I could deal with this case by way of a suspended sentence. The minimum sentence I can impose is one of four months in custody.

text: Schools in Beijing are closed and outdoor construction halted as the Chinese capital's first ever pollution red alert came into effect. These are external links and will open in a new window The alert, the highest possible warning level, was issued late Monday and will remain in effect until midday on Thursday. Restrictions have been imposed on car usage and some factories have been ordered to cease operations. This occurs as China, the world's largest polluter, participates in discussions on carbon emissions in Paris. This marks the first occasion China has declared a red alert under the four-tier alert system, which was implemented slightly over two years ago, although pollution levels were far from the city's worst. At 07:00 local time on Tuesday (23:00 GMT on Monday), when the alert became effective, the US Embassy's air pollution monitor in Beijing reported that the concentration of the tiny particles known as PM 2.5 was at 291 micrograms per cubic metre. By 11:00 it had decreased very slightly to 250 - still a level it described as very unhealthy. Concentrations of the poisonous particles in the suburbs were reported at several times that figure. The World Health Organisation recommends 25 micrograms per cubic metre as the maximum safe level. As I cycled into the office this morning, smog mask secured firmly in place, the traffic was certainly lighter. Beijing's first red alert means half of all cars must remain off the roads; odd numbered licence plates today, even numbered ones tomorrow. However, although the air is indeed an unpleasant, filthy grey, the pollution index is actually considerably lower than it was this time last week, when the quantity of dangerous particulate matter (PM 2.5) surged to around 40 times the World Health Organisation's maximum guideline. Today, it is merely 10 times that limit. So why red now? Well, the absence of any previous red alerts has been met with increasingly loud howls of derision. Perhaps it is the growing public pressure that has finally made the difference this time around. Coal-powered industries and heating systems, as well as vehicle emissions and dust from construction sites, all contribute to the smog which has been exacerbated by humidity and an absence of wind. The order will last until 12:00 on Thursday, when a cold front is expected to arrive and clear the smog. As well as restrictions on construction and schools - which were advised to close if they did not have good air filtration systems - cars are only permitted to drive on alternate days, with the day depending on whether a car's number plate ends in an odd or even number. Its negotiators here point to their continued investment in renewable sources of energy, in an effort to reduce coal consumption, particularly in urban areas. These efforts to go green may not be having an immediate effect on the air in Beijing but they have had an impact on global output of carbon dioxide. A strong agreement here in Paris will not immediately solve China's air woes, but if it ultimately pushes down the price of renewables even further, it could play a part in solving the issue long term. text: An elderly woman was beheaded by a man who went on a rampage in north London, the Old Bailey has heard. Palmira Silva, 82, was in her garden when Nicholas Salvador attacked her with a knife and decapitated her, prosecutors stated. The court was told he was armed with a wooden pole and machete and was detained following a violent confrontation in which he was tasered six times. The 25-year-old from Enfield denies murder on grounds of insanity. Prosecutor Jonathan Rees QC informed the jury the killing occurred three days after Mr Salvador had lost his employment, and there was no dispute he killed her. He stated at the time of the killing, on the afternoon of 4 September last year, the defendant was residing three doors away from Mrs Silva in Nightingale Road. On the day of the assault the defendant armed himself and decapitated two of his hosts' cats, because he believed they were demons, the court was told. He then proceeded through several back gardens, forced his way into a house and then attacked a vehicle containing two members of the family he was residing with. Mr Salvador then jumped over a wall into Mrs Silva's garden where she was repeatedly stabbed before being decapitated, the court was told. It was stated Mr Salvador believed he was killing a supernatural entity in the form of Hitler returned from the dead, or a demon who had assumed the form of a little old lady, Mr Rees stated. The prosecutor informed the jury the defendant fled and was detained in the front room of another house following a violent and chaotic confrontation with police in which he was tasered repeatedly and kicked and punched, but to little effect. He had displayed signs of mental illness, repeating phrases such as red is the colour and I am the king. One witness had described how, before the assault, he appeared like a headless chicken and seemed to be searching for more cats to kill, the court was told. In the weeks before the assault, Mr Salvador had displayed signs of odd behaviour and developed an interest in shapeshifters - supernatural entities that can transform into another being or form. After being charged the 25-year-old was remanded in custody at Belmarsh prison before being transferred to high-security Broadmoor Hospital due to his mental illness. Mr Rees stated that psychiatrists would give evidence that he was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. Mrs Silva came to Britain from Italy in 1953 and operated a cafe with her husband. She had two children, six grandchildren and one great grandchild. Mr Salvador also denies a charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm on grounds of insanity and assaulting a police officer after Pc Bernard Hamilton received a leg injury which required hospital treatment. The case continues.

text: Ahead of the general election on 7 May, BBC Radio Merseyside is holding three special debates in front of a live audience. Three principal constituencies - Wavertree, Southport and Wirral West - have been selected and you shall receive the opportunity to interrogate the candidates aspiring to secure the honour of representing you at Westminster for the forthcoming five years. Roger Phillips shall be presenting the first of the hour-long debates in Wavertree - one of Liverpool's so-called secure Labour seats - from 12:00 BST. Located to the east of the city centre, the constituency remains predominantly residential. It accommodates a substantial technology park, which maintains close connections to the university, and possesses a considerable student population which enhances the local economy. Electors shall hope that they do not encounter a repetition of the 2010 debacle in which the polling station on Dunbabin Road exhausted ballot papers precisely as the polls were preparing to close. Liverpool City Council states the difficulties last time at a small number of polling stations were caused by a number of people arriving at the close of polls and not all of the polling stations possessed a complete allocation of ballot papers. We are ensuring that all stations possess a complete allocation and additional training has been delivered for staff. Also anyone in the queue by 22:00 BST shall be afforded the opportunity to vote. So who shall be competing for those votes? Luciana Berger, the shadow health minister, comfortably retained the seat for Labour five years ago with a majority exceeding 7,000. She succeeded Jane Kennedy - the constituency's MP since it was established in 1997 - who was elected Merseyside's Police Commissioner in 2012. At one point it appeared that former Labour Councillor Jake Morrison would contest against Ms Berger. He was merely 18 when he was elected in 2011 but his relationship with the party deteriorated last year when he announced his retirement at the considerable age of 22. If re-elected, Ms Berger states she would take practical action to support people who are seeking employment, for example by holding another jobs fair to bring together employers and local people. I shall promote apprenticeships and opportunities for young people and support our excellent small businesses. She continued: I shall continue to campaign for changes to law around dangerous dogs to make our neighbourhoods safer, and I shall build upon my strong record of standing up for the people of Liverpool Wavertree to ensure their concerns are heard where it matters and that genuine change is delivered for our community. The Liberal Democrats targeted this seat in 2010 without success. Their hopes this time rest with 20-year-old student Leo Evans. He is pledging to protect green spaces like Calderstones Park, increase the NHS budget by £8bn annually with considerable emphasis on mental health, work to ensure Liverpool benefits from any devolved power - particularly ensuring connection to HS2 and HS3 - and continue the largest expansion of apprenticeships since the 1950s. James Pearson represents the Conservative candidate. The former Trafford councillor unsuccessfully contested the Church ward in last year's Liverpool City Council elections, and this constitutes his first parliamentary contest. Mr Pearson possesses three principal priorities for Wavertree: He wishes to support business and investment, safeguard the NHS and defend the armed services and their families. He feels particularly passionate about the last of these objectives since he serves as an officer in the Army reserves and has served in Afghanistan and Cyprus. His party secured merely 7.5% of the vote in 2010, however, and it would constitute a tremendous shock were they to triumph this time. Adam Heatherington represents UKIP, and he shall be hoping to secure votes from disaffected traditional Conservatives and Labour supporters alike. A former candidate for Liverpool Mayor, the supply teacher states more needs to be accomplished to enhance the Wavertree economy which, he states, is performing beneath the national average. He wishes to witness more investment in Wavertree Technology Park where there exists considerable vacant offices and retail spaces… business rates remain excessively high. We possess a brain drain in this city - too many students are departing to work in Manchester, Leeds and London. We require more focus on vocational qualifications and bring them up to equal standing with academic qualifications and we require more investment in our young people, he stated. The Green party is also hoping to achieve some impact in Wavertree. Peter Cranie, the party's former election co-ordinator, failed to secure a place in the European Parliament when he contested last year. He remains realistic about his chances next month, acknowledging that the party is concentrating much of their efforts on nearby Liverpool Riverside where Martin Dobson is standing. But he does believe he is providing everyone in Wavertree the opportunity to express their support for the more radical policies against austerity. We consider it obscene that the five wealthiest families in Britain own the same wealth as the 13 million least well-off, he stated. That is why the Greens shall commit to ending austerity and genuine redistribution of wealth for a fairer and better society. The Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition are also contesting this seat. Council worker Dave Walsh represents their candidate. He states he wishes to get those who have been disenfranchised and disengaged in politics re-engaged as well as defending local services including libraries and Sure Start Centres. The party is fielding more candidates than ever before - 130 across the country - vowing to push for an increase in the minimum hourly wage to £10 and renationalise the railways. Finally, Leo Evans is standing as an independent after acquiring a taste for politics participating in Until They Kick Us Out - a theatre production from Liverpool's Young Everyman Playhouse, which addresses themes of young people and democracy. The 18-year-old student from Edge Hill wishes to support school leavers, push for a higher minimum wage, introduce rent caps for students and low income families, and improve social housing. He insists his campaign constitutes more than merely a protest vote. With seven candidates standing, Wavertree represents one of the most fiercely contested constituencies on Merseyside. To hear the candidates respond to questions from our listeners, please tune in to BBC Radio Merseyside from 12:00 until 14:00.

text: Italian Prime Minister Mario Monti claimed Europe had one week to save the euro ahead of yet another crunch EU summit on Thursday and Friday. The French president has called for a growth pact, Tony Blair has urged a grand bargain, the markets demand a big bazooka, whilst in Germany there are murmurings about federalism. Yet the economic and financial solutions to the eurozone crisis are actually surprisingly straightforward. How so? Simple. Just ask how the exact same problems have been resolved by the members of that other large (and much better functioning) single currency area - the United States of America. Europe's real problem is that almost all of the solutions are far from politically acceptable. The eurozone's fundamental problem is that the southern European economies have become fundamentally uncompetitive - their wages rose too rapidly during the boom years, which led them to import far more than they exported, and borrow the difference. The southern economies' excessive debts, persistent uncompetitiveness and resulting need to continue borrowing - along with Germany's reluctance to provide them the money - is what has driven the financial panic that has made it much harder for southern European governments and banks to borrow from markets. What's more, the seizing up of European financial markets - not to mention the collective determination of Europe's governments to cut spending, and the European Central Bank's focus on price stability - is threatening to push the entire continent into a long and deep recession, something that would merely compound the debt problems. So, if the eurozone were to look at the US model for inspiration in its hour of need, what sorts of changes - economic, financial and, ultimately, political - might need to be considered? Europe's most immediate task is to restore confidence in its banks. All the bad loans made by eurozone banks (loans to mortgage borrowers, property speculators and even governments that may not be fully repaid) may need to be cleaned up (by injecting money into the banks), with the potential losses borne by the eurozone as a whole - because many national governments probably cannot afford it. In the case of Spain's banks, the current bailout deal leaves Spain's government sitting on all the losses. Deposits at all eurozone banks may need to be guaranteed in euros by the eurozone as a whole, in order to stop panicky investors from moving their money from banks in southern European countries at risk of exiting the euro, to Germany (and increasingly to Switzerland and Denmark). All of Europe's banks may need to be placed under a common regime of regulation and supervision, with troubled banks given equal access to rescue loans, and being wound up by a central authority when they go bust. Europe's biggest long-term conundrum is how to stop governments like Spain or Italy going bust - and restore confidence in their commitment to stay within the euro - whilst ensuring that all governments are more responsible with their finances in future. The biggest sticking point is eurobonds. A large chunk of eurozone government debt may need to be amalgamated - with governments standing behind each other's finances - in order to reinforce the commitment of governments to staying in the euro: In the long-run, a US-style federal budget may be needed to cover the cost of recessions, so that individual governments don't risk going bust when their national economies get into trouble. For example, the cost of a minimum level of social security - especially unemployment benefits - could be permanently shared across the eurozone, paid for by a common income tax. The new French President Francois Hollande was elected on a platform demanding a growth pact in Europe - a set of reforms designed to boost European economies and mitigate the pain being inflicted by government spending cuts across the continent. The European Central Bank may need to have its mandate changed so that it has an explicit dual target to support employment as well as price stability, just like its American counterpart, the US Federal Reserve does, as proposed by Mr Hollande. The eurozone may need to pay for large-scale investment in infrastructure, particularly in southern Europe, much in the way that West Germany invested in rebuilding East German after reunification in 1990. Proposals on the table include increasing the European Investment Bank's ability to lend, and creating common project bonds to finance major construction. All Europeans (and especially southerners) are having to implement structural reforms that will increase their long-term growth and strengthen government finances (although at the risk of hurting growth in the short-term). These include removing restrictions on market competition, raising the retirement age, laying off (over many years) a lot of state employees, and making it much easier to hire and fire employees. Mr Hollande has resisted many of these reforms in France. Rebalancing means solving the big underlying competitiveness problem faced by southern Europeans that led to their economies racking up so much debt in the first place. The ECB and German government may need to stimulate high wage inflation in Germany for several years in order to eliminate the country's current massive competitive trade advantage over southern Europe - something that is already beginning to happen. In the same way that Washington helps out struggling US states, the southern European governments may need to be given money (given, not lent) by the rest of the eurozone via direct fiscal transfers, so that they can afford to prop up their economies until they have regained their competitiveness. These transfers could end up taking the form of bailout loans that are never repaid. Structural reforms - particularly labour market reforms - also play a key role in rebalancing, by ensuring that wages in southern Europe do not rise too quickly, as they did in the past decade. To make a full banking, fiscal and monetary union work, the eurozone governments would need to hand power to a central authority (the European Commission) that can pay for and supervise all of the above, whilst national governments accept that in future they have to keep their own spending strictly within their limited means. As most of the above reforms involve Germany sharing its wealth with the rest of Europe (and all European nations handing power to Brussels), Berlin is insisting on the principle of no taxation without representation - in other words a move towards full federalism, with spending and regulation controlled by a directly elected presidency of the European Commission.

The financial and economic solutions to the crisis of the eurozone are surprisingly simple. Not to mention that the seizing of the European financial markets, the shared determination of the governments to reduce their budgets and the European Central Bank's emphasis on price stability, is threatening to throw the whole continent into a long, deep crisis, which would aggravate the debt crisis. It may be necessary to clear all bad loans made by European banks to mortgagees, property speculators and even governments (and perhaps even to governments themselves) by injecting money into banks and absorbing the risk of the resulting losses into the common eurozone budget, because national budgets may be unable to afford it. All the banks of Europe may be placed under a common supervision and control, with equal access to rescue loans, and with equal responsibility for a common bankruptcy. In the case of Spain's banks, the current agreement leaves the losses to the Spanish government. It may be necessary to guarantee the deposits of all banks in the eurozone in the currency, so as to prevent panicked investors from fleeing the banks in southern European countries at risk of leaving the UE, to Germany (and increasingly to Switzerland and Denmark) in the hope of escaping the drachma. The mandate of the European Central Bank must be enlarged to include a dual target of employment and price stability, like its American counterpart, the US Federal Reserve, which has been proposed by Francois Hollande. For example, the costs of minimum social security - and especially unemployment insurance - would be shared permanently across the entire currency area, with a common tax on income. Among the proposals is an increase in the European Investment Bank’s power to lend and the creation of a common bond fund for large-scale construction. Rebalancing means solving the fundamental problem of competitiveness in southern Europe, which is what led to the excessive accumulation of debt in the first place. These include lifting the restrictions on competition in the market, raising the retirement age, laying off many employees over several years and making it much easier to recruit and dismiss employees. text: And so it begins. The campaign for the assembly's fifth election finally commences, though politics in Cardiff Bay has possessed a pre-election atmosphere for some time now. Much of the campaigning style and events will sound familiar, but this time there shall be fundamental differences. Initially, all parties will be struggling to make their voices heard against a cacophonous background of the EU referendum campaign. Then there exists the UKIP factor - the party possesses a realistic opportunity of securing numerous seats for the first time and, in doing so, altering the political dynamic at the assembly. All parties face problems to surmount. Labour confronts the triple blow of criticism regarding their NHS management, appearing refreshed after 17 years in government and the uncertain influence of their UK leader Jeremy Corbyn in marginal constituencies where they face the Conservatives. Regarding disappointing elections, the Liberal Democrats must attempt to recover from their devastating result last year. The Conservatives face the task of ensuring EU referendum divisions do not undermine efforts to sustain the party's Welsh momentum, following some notable general election victories. Plaid Cymru must generate some form of electoral momentum following several disappointing election outcomes. UKIP clearly possesses a significant opportunity to return several AMs, which would provide them with a power base they have lacked in any UK political institution thus far, though they have been plagued by severe internal divisions. An incoming Welsh Government shall, eventually, possess greater powers than any previous administration, but expect the campaign to be dominated by the NHS, which has been devolved since 1999. The policy-makers must all grapple with assisting a health service under tremendous financial pressure, whilst simultaneously maintaining support in areas such as education and the economy. There exist numerous policies where broad consensus exists amongst the parties, such as the requirement for apprentices and business rate relief for small companies, but there are several highly divisive issues, including proposals for an M4 relief road and council reorganisation, where voters face genuine choices. The jury remains out on what shall happen to turnout, which previously was 42%. The risk is that assembly politics will be overshadowed by the EU referendum, but simultaneously media interest surrounding the NHS, particularly over the past five years, will also have heightened devolution's profile in the public consciousness.

text: Mfon Udoh scored a hat-trick as Nigeria's Enyimba beat visitors Etoile du Sahel of Tunisia 3-0 in the first leg of their last 16 African Champions League tie on Sunday. Earlier on Sunday the Democratic Republic of Congo's AS Vita Club defeated visiting Mamelodi Sundowns of South Africa 1-0. The aggregate victors of the fixture shall advance to the group phases. Whilst the defeated side will receive a second opportunity in the Confederation Cup. Udoh netted his opening goal following nine minutes and subsequently added a second for Enyimba after the interval and completed his treble with a powerful strike just prior to the match's conclusion. This means Udoh is presently the tournament's leading scorer with seven goals thus far. Etoile contested the final 19 minutes of the fixture with ten men following Ghazi Abderazek receiving a second yellow card for dissent and being dismissed. The fixture represents a repeat of the 2004 final which Enyimba ultimately won on penalties after both legs had concluded 2-1 to the home side. Ugandan goalkeeper Dennis Onyango had maintained Sundowns in the contest in Kinshasa with several excellent saves as Vita Club's Ghanaian star Bernard Morrison proved troublesome. The sole goal of the encounter was netted in stoppage time at the game's end as Morrison was again afforded excessive time and whilst his effort was well saved by Onyango his deflection fell to Kule Mbombo, who scored. Vita's countrymen TP Mazembe face a difficult challenge if they are to retain their crown following a 2-0 defeat on Saturday at Morocco's Wydad Casablanca. Abdellatif Noussir scored his opening goal of the campaign just prior to half-time for Wydad and Reda Hajhouj converted a spot-kick midway through the second period in Marrakech. Managed by twice Real Madrid coach John Toshack, Wydad are seeking to claim the competition a second time, having previously triumphed in 1992. Mazembe are pursuing a sixth crown, which would render them the second most accomplished club after eight-time champions Al Ahly of Egypt. Also on Saturday record eight-time title-holders Al Ahly secured a 1-1 draw in Tanzania with Young Africans. Led by former Tottenham manager Martin Jol, the Cairo Red Devils established an early advantage when Amr Gamal headed home after 11 minutes to provide Ahly an away goal. The home team responded eight minutes subsequently, forcing an equaliser from an Ahmed Hegazi own-goal. Ahly's great adversaries Zamalek, directed by another former English Premier League manager, Alex McLeish, defeated debutants Mouloudia Bejaia of Algeria 2-0 in Cairo. Mahmoud 'Kahraba' Abdel Moneim placed Zamalek ahead just prior to the hour and they doubled the advantage eight minutes from time through Ahmed Hamoudi. Asec Mimosas of Ivory Coast capitalised on home advantage to defeat Al Ahly Tripoli of Libya 2-0. Dao Youssouf placed the Ivorians ahead following 59 minutes, with Aka Serge adding a second ten minutes from time. Al Merreikh of Sudan and Entente Setif of Algeria drew 2-2 as they met for the second consecutive season. On Saturday, Merreikh fell behind to a Eude Dagoulou strike following 15 minutes. Raji Abdalati levelled for the hosts following 20 minutes, only for Abdelmoumene Djabou to restore Setif's lead just three minutes subsequently. However Abdalati ensured the first leg would conclude in a draw with his second of the encounter to make it 2-2. Stade Malien had aspirations of becoming the first qualifiers from Mali virtually extinguished following a shock 3-1 home defeat to Zesco United of Zambia. The encounter commenced promisingly for the hosts as Moussakoye Diallo scored, but Mwape Mwelwa equalised before half-time and Idris Ilunga secured a late brace.

text: The HS2 link between Birmingham and Crewe marks a sad day for Stoke-on-Trent, Tristram Hunt has said. City MP Mr Hunt stated the line from London to Manchester could have been delivered more swiftly and economically with a route through the Potteries. The HS2 line from Birmingham to Crewe is scheduled to open in 2027. Transport Secretary Patrick McLoughlin has proposed a junction be constructed in South Staffordshire to serve Stoke-on-Trent. Under the revised plans, a 43-mile HS2 section between Birmingham and Crewe will be opened six years earlier than originally planned. Further updates on this story and others on Stoke and Staffordshire. The HS2 project seeks to enhance transport links with the north of England. The government anticipates the London to Birmingham route will be completed by 2026. Crewe has been selected above Stoke-on-Trent as the next key staging post on the route to Manchester. Stoke-on-Trent previously submitted a bid for an HS2 railway station in its city centre. Responding to the selection of Crewe over the city, Labour MP Mr Hunt stated: With Crewe rather than Stoke benefiting from this substantial investment, plans for a northern gateway partnership between Stoke-on-Trent and east Cheshire become more significant. Mark Winnington, Staffordshire County Council member for the economy, environment and transport, stated the current route will cut through miles of countryside and be a big blow to communities. Mr Winnington stated: HS2 will cut through 45 miles of Staffordshire countryside and from the outset we have been concerned about the impact a project of this scale will have not only on the environment but also on residents living close to the proposed route. For six years Crewe will be the only place in the North West with an HS2 connection - in theory that means Cheshire can live up to the title it has given itself as gateway to the Northern Powerhouse. In reality it is no big surprise, given the government-owned company responsible for HS2 has recommended Crewe should receive a stop all along. But it is clearly a blow for Stoke-on-Trent, which mounted a rival bid to host a hub, and even threatened legal action if it failed. Now the government and Cheshire officials state they are committed to ensuring North Staffordshire feels the benefits of high speed rail. Michael Jones, leader of Cheshire East Council, stated the HS2 Birmingham to Crewe link would be a game-changer for Crewe and its surrounding regions. It is a real once-in-a-generation opportunity, the like of which Cheshire East has not seen before, he stated. Conservative MP for Lichfield, Michael Fabricant, described the announced route as environmentally damaging to beautiful parts of Staffordshire. Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, Robert Flello stated: Crewe might look on a map [as if it is] next door to Stoke-on-Trent but the reality is it is a good hour by car from my constituents. Conservative MP for Stafford, Jeremy Lefroy, called on Mr McLoughlin to look again at the proposed route.

text: An own goal from goalkeeper Ryan Clarke in the 95th minute denied Neal Ardley's AFC Wimbledon their first win of the season as Rochdale earned a share of the spoils at the Crown Oil Arena. Andy Barcham's first-half header appeared as if it would prove sufficient for the Dons to elevate themselves from the bottom four, but Clarke deflected Jamie Allen's corner into his own goal to leave the away side at the foot of League One. The Dons took the lead 12 minutes into the match, the goal originating from a Rochdale offensive move. Donal McDermott's corner was unintentionally returned to the set-piece deliverer by Matt Lund and when McDermott tried to overcome Chris Whelpdale he was stripped of possession deep in Wimbledon's half. Whelpdale sprinted the full length of the pitch down the right flank before delivering a cross into the box for Barcham to nod beyond Conrad Logan. Dale pressed vigorously for a leveller after the interval with Jamie Allen striking a shot against the crossbar and Clarke thwarting Calvin Andrew on two separate occasions. The hosts' challenge became more arduous when Callum Camps received his marching orders for a second cautionable offence, but Clarke's fine work was negated when he deflected Allen's corner deep into stoppage time into his own goal. text: A schoolgirl has become the first child in Wales to be given an official hearing dog. Poppy represents one of more than 45,000 children across the United Kingdom for whom deafness forms part of daily existence. The 14-year-old, who suffers profound deafness, states the yellow Labrador has boosted her confidence and assists her sleeping during the night. She represents one of 27 children throughout the UK to have received a hearing dog from the charity Hearing Dogs for Deaf People. It was not until Poppy reached nine years of age that civil engineer Richard and housewife Rebecca observed minor alterations in their daughter's behaviour which alarmed them. She was increasing the volume on the television, stated Rebecca. When she sat in the car she would not hear me when I spoke to her, despite her brothers and sister being able to hear from the rear. Worried, they had Poppy, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, referred to an audiologist who was astonished to discover the schoolgirl suffered profound deafness and could scarcely hear anything, yet had been concealing this through lip-reading. Despite her severe deafness there was no impact upon her academic work so the early indicators had not been detected. Rebecca stated: What we discovered when she received her diagnosis was that she had become rather skilled at lip reading, which was how she had managed to navigate her way through school. Nobody had noticed as there was no alteration in her academic work. She received a diagnosis of the rare condition Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1. Although she received hearing aids to wear in both ears, she became reclusive and lost confidence both in socialising and performing minor tasks such as visiting shops. She experienced difficulty falling asleep at night as she could not wear hearing aids, which meant she could not hear anything whatsoever and remained constantly anxious about someone entering her room. Poppy endured three years feeling increasingly isolated until her mother discovered hearing dogs, who assist deaf people in a comparable manner to guide dogs. There are 850 deaf people, predominantly adults, partnered with dogs throughout the UK. Due to her profound deafness, Poppy became the first child to be partnered with a hearing dog in Wales. The dog received the name Tanni after Baroness Tanni Grey Thompson and was one of merely 12 distributed that year. Source: Hearing Dogs for Deaf People One year later and Poppy states Tanni has transformed her life. Having her has increased my confidence, stated Poppy. She provides me with greater independence. Previously when my mother went out I would remain at home, now I can accompany her and enter shops. Previously I was extremely reluctant to enter a shop and pay independently. I was concerned as they would not know I was deaf, but now they can observe from Tanni that they must speak clearly as she wears a special harness when we venture out. Another positive aspect is that people ask questions about Tanni and I feel pleased discussing her. It has made me more confident answering questions generally. I have acquired a best friend. Tanni accompanies Poppy everywhere, except school. She has received training to alert Poppy if there is a fire alarm or if her mother requires her. Poppy stated: She wakes me in the morning, if my mother wishes to inform me we are going out or it is teatime she will write a note and place it in a purse which Tanni then brings in her mouth to me. So she will approach to fetch me and then nudges me. As I mature and become more independent we could train her to respond to the doorbell, telephone and text messages. And Poppy has finally achieved the good night's sleep she had desired. She stated: I used to sleep with the door open as I did not know who was entering the room, I had the bed positioned so I could see directly down the landing with the door open. Now Tanni wakes me if someone enters, so I can sleep with the door closed. Andrew James, National Client Services Manager for Hearing Dogs for Deaf People, stated: We have now placed 27 hearing dogs with deaf children across the UK, and we are delighted that Poppy and Tanni represent the first child partnership in Wales. The Hearing Dogs for Deaf Children project has proved a tremendous success since its launch in 2012 and we have witnessed growing interest each year, so the charity intends to expand our work with children over the forthcoming years. Hearing dogs exert an important influence upon a deaf child's life, and we could not be more pleased with the positive difference that Tanni has made to Poppy and her family. There are presently 29 deaf people with hearing dogs in Wales.

text: Six years ago Yingluck Shinawatra, a novice who had only been in politics for two months, led the Pheu Thai party, founded and funded by her older brother Thaksin, to a resounding election victory. These are external links and will open in a new window It was a remarkable outcome for a party which had witnessed two former administrations toppled by a coup and a disputed court ruling, and whose supporters had just the previous year been engaged in an occupation of Bangkok, which concluded in violence. A crucial element of Ms Yingluck's victorious manifesto was a generous pledge to rice farmers. That lies at the centre of the legal proceedings against her. Under the new programme the government was intended to purchase the entire rice harvest, and pay 15,000 baht (£350; $450) per tonne, well above the 11,000 baht guaranteed by the former government. It was enormously popular with farmers. However economists and agricultural specialists immediately questioned its feasibility. The price of 15,000 baht was considerably higher than the global rice price, and Thailand exports more of its harvest than any other nation - it was the world's leading rice exporter at the time. Its main competitors India and Vietnam, it was forecast, would simply increase their exports at Thailand's expense, offering a price much lower than the Thai government could, unless it was prepared to incur enormous losses. And there were numerous warnings that the programme was susceptible to corruption. Six years later Ms Yingluck faces a potential 10-year prison sentence on charges of malfeasance, or dereliction of duty, over the rice programme. She has not been charged with corruption, but with failing to prevent it, in her capacity as prime minister and as chair of the National Rice Policy Committee. If found guilty she could be permanently barred from politics - she has already been banned for five years after being impeached in 2015. Predictably Ms Yingluck and her party have cried foul. After all her government was toppled, in 2014, by the same army officers who now govern Thailand. They justified their coup by the need to restore order, but had conspicuously failed to offer her support as she faced sustained protests in Bangkok, which had paralysed her administration. The military is not regarded as impartial, and it wields authoritarian powers, even extending to judicial proceedings. The rice programme was extraordinarily expensive and wasteful. The precise cost, of rice that rotted in storage, that was stolen or improperly sold, is still disputed. But the government estimates it cost the state at least $8bn - some estimates reach as high as $20bn, although these include the overall cost of the subsidy, not just losses through corruption and mismanagement. The programme did raise farmers' living standards, but was almost certainly unsustainable. There is substantial anecdotal evidence of corruption, although few cases have yet reached court. The best-known case, in which a former commerce minister and 27 other defendants are accused of an allegedly fraudulent government-to-government deal to sell rice to China, will conclude on the same day Ms Yingluck hears her verdict. Ms Yingluck argued in court that she was not responsible for day-to-day operation of the programme, and that as a key policy platform when she was elected she could not order it to be cancelled. She pointed to what she believes are multiple procedural flaws in the case. Whatever the merits of the case against her, few observers doubt that the military government wants to see Thaksin Shinawatra's political movement weakened before it permits the restoration of some form of democracy. Ms Yingluck is extremely popular, and an effective vote-winner. With Mr Thaksin entering his 10th year of exile, his party is struggling to find a replacement leader. But her fate presents Thailand's current rulers with some dilemmas. If she is acquitted Mr Thaksin, who is protective of his younger sister, might be emboldened to push for a greater share of power in a post-election Thailand than the military is prepared to accept. An acquittal would outrage hard-line conservatives, and those who led the protests against the Yingluck government. If she is sent to prison, hard-line opponents of the Shinawatra clan would be satisfied, and she would be completely removed from politics. Convicting her would also help the generals to justify their coup, as part of a fight against corruption. But it risks making the telegenic Ms Yingluck into a symbol of resistance for the so-called red-shirt mass movement that supports her. Red-shirt leaders acknowledge that mobilising large-scale protests against a conviction would be difficult under a military government. They have ruled out any repeat of the occupation of central Bangkok that ended so badly seven years ago. But they say they would view a conviction as the first shot in a re-ignited conflict with the military, as an end to any pretence of reconciliation. And they do not rule out localised demonstrations of anger by Ms Yingluck's supporters. text: The number of people who think you must speak English to be considered truly British has increased over the past 10 years, a survey suggests. It also found 61% believed EU immigrants should be required to wait three years before being eligible to claim benefits. Nearly a quarter said the primary reason immigrants came to the UK was benefits. NatCen Social Research has been conducting the report for 31 years. Its survey evaluates changing social attitudes in Britain. The report's authors say a key finding of their latest work is that the threshold to being considered British has risen over time. The proportion of people who agreed it was important a person should have resided in Britain for most of their life to be considered British is now 77%, rising from 69% in 2003. Some 74% agreed it was important to have been born in Britain to be considered British - falling from 76% in 2003. And 85% agreed respecting institutions/laws was very or fairly important to be considered British - rising from 82% in 2003. On immigration, 77% of people wanted immigration reduced substantially or slightly - a figure that is sharply higher than 1995 but largely unchanged since 2008. The report's authors said the British view that current immigration was too high was well established and stable. Half believed the primary reason immigrants came to Britain was for work, but 24% said the main reason was to claim benefits. The proportion of people who believe immigrants increase crime rates in Britain rose from 37% in 2003 to 43% in 2013. London divide The authors said the survey also reflected the divide on attitudes to immigration between London and the rest of Britain mirrored in the performance of the anti-EU party, UKIP, in recent elections. The survey suggested 54% of Londoners believed immigration was good for the economy, but this figure fell to 28% outside the capital. Referring to the 61% who believed EU immigrants should be required to wait at least three years before being eligible to claim benefits, the report's authors said this contrasted with rules that came into force this year requiring EU migrants to demonstrate they are earning at least £149 a week for three months before being eligible to access a range of benefits. This, the report said, demonstrated a considerable gap between public opinion and reality. Other findings include: Penny Young, chief executive of NatCen Social Research, said: In an increasingly diverse, multi-cultural country, we might expect people to be more relaxed about what it means to be British, yet the trend is moving in the opposite direction. It is now more difficult to be considered British than in the past and one message comes through loud and clear; if you want to be British, you must speak English. She added that the public want stricter rules on benefits and many are unaware of the policies that are in place to control immigration. Rules on immigrants claiming benefits vary depending on which benefit they wish to claim. The government has been imposing new restrictions in recent months, including one which came into force in January under which migrant jobseekers must be in the UK for three months before they can claim Jobseeker's Allowance. The survey interviews were conducted from June to November 2013 - before the so-called Trojan Horse attempt by Islamists to take control of schools in Birmingham became public knowledge. Education Secretary Michael Gove responded to the Trojan Horse issue by saying schools should promote British values.

text: The Church of England's ruling body has decided that women bishops should be allowed, but there are further steps to take before they can be ordained. The General Synod has granted minimal concessions to traditionalist Anglicans who opposed the proposal. They had requested to be under the care of a male alternative bishop on terms acceptable to them. However, the synod determined that women bishops should be able to decide the identity and functions of any such bishop. The BBC's religious affairs correspondent Robert Pigott stated that women bishops would only need to consult a code of practice guiding them in their dealings with traditionalists. He stated that the decision made during a synod meeting at York University had left considerable division in its wake. Synod members determined there was no requirement for further delay to the progress of a draft law permitting women to be made bishops. The law must now receive approval from a majority of the Church's 44 diocesan synods, before returning to the General Synod. It must then receive a two-thirds majority at the General Synod before receiving parliamentary approval and the Royal Assent. Our correspondent stated it had been an extraordinary weekend of intense emotion and whilst supporters were celebrating a breakthrough, some traditionalists had departed the synod chamber in tears. Proposals to establish a class of male-only bishops to oversee traditionalist parishes were rejected on Saturday. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Rowan Williams, and Archbishop of York, John Sentamu, had placed their personal prestige behind the compromise plan, which would have permitted parishes unwilling to serve under a woman bishop to call upon the oversight of a male alternative. It would also have granted that alternative bishop considerable legally-backed independence and autonomy as part of a joint jurisdiction over those parishes. Although the proposal gained a majority of votes in the synod as a whole, it failed because clergy - who vote separately from lay people and bishops - defeated it by just five votes. Our correspondent stated that Dr Williams had placed his reputation on the line with the compromise plan and would now be in a difficult position as he attempted to deal with discontent traditionalists who would probably remain in the church. The proposals will now go out to dioceses and return to the synod in a year's time when there will be a final vote. Campaigner Christina Rees, a member of the General Synod and chairwoman of Women in the Church, told the Press Association the synod's decision on Monday was a wonderful outcome. She stated: This is wonderful news. It is entirely consistent with what synod indicated it wanted two years ago. In one sense I am not surprised but I am delighted, it is very, very good news. However, traditionalists have warned that the decision could result in many of them leaving the Church of England. The Reverend Prebendary David Houlding, a leading member of the Catholic Group on the General Synod, stated he was concerned and he felt as if traditionalists were running out of options. He told PA: There are several people who will be making hard decisions about their future. I am remaining in the Church of England for the time being until I am driven out. I am not going willingly, I will only go if forced. The more this continues in this manner, the more it seems as if the door is shutting. The scope for remaining in the Church of England is getting more and more narrow and the options are rapidly closing.

text: Chris Evans and Nick Grimshaw both lost listeners over the last three months, according to the latest industry figures from Rajar. Evans's breakfast programme on BBC Radio 2 fell by 414,000 listeners compared with the preceding quarter to 9.06 million. However, the show remained the most popular radio programme in Britain. Grimshaw drew 5.25 million weekly listeners between July and September, falling 184,000 on the previous quarter. The declines are likely attributed to fewer people tuning into breakfast programmes during the summer period. However, digital station BBC Radio 6 Music achieved a new record audience of 2.34 million listeners. This marks the fifth successive quarter that the digital station has recorded record ratings. Helen Boaden, Director of BBC Radio, stated she was delighted that more and more people are discovering the station's irresistible combination of outstanding alternative music and witty presenters. Whilst Grimshaw's numbers declined, Radio 1 overall increased, from 9.46 million last quarter to 9.87 million weekly listeners between July and September. The number rose further to 10.9 million when listeners aged 10 to 14 were incorporated in the data. The station is presently attempting to attract a younger demographic. Ben Cooper, controller of Radio 1, stated the numbers should be viewed alongside the increase to 1.5 million views a day on our YouTube channel and our 8.5 million users on social media. BBC Radio 4 recorded a weekly reach of 11.2 million, its second highest audience on record. The network's flagship Today programme lost 250,000 listeners to 7.1 million but its sister programme The World At One achieved an all-time high of 3.75 million. In commercial radio, LBC, Heart and Capital all expanded their number of weekly listeners compared with the preceding quarter - whilst Absolute Radio gained more than half a million. The breakfast programmes on Classic FM and talkSPORT expanded their reach nationally, but several commercial breakfast shows lost listeners. Kiss's Rickie, Melvin and Charlie fell from 2.13 million national listeners in the previous quarter to 1.83 million between July and September. The Chris Moyles breakfast programme on Radio X shed 36,000 listeners in London but expanded the overall number of listeners across Britain - reaching 703,000. However, Capital's breakfast programme, presented by Dave Berry, George Shelley and Lilah Parsons, declined slightly, but remained the most popular commercial breakfast show in Britain. Overall, Rajar - the official body responsible for measuring radio audiences in Britain - stated 89% of British people - or 48.2 million adults - listened to the radio at least once weekly over the quarter, an increase of 320,000 on the previous year. text: Governor Scott Walker's campaign for president is premised on more than just his conservative achievements in Wisconsin, of which there are many. The candidate also routinely, almost ceaselessly, proclaims what he has had to surmount - and whom he has managed to vanquish - to implement them. Conservative audiences throughout the US appear to adore him for it. For the previous five years Democratic adversaries in a state that possesses a lengthy tradition of progressive policies have battled the governor over every inch of political ground. Now many are questioning whether they are, in part, accountable for his emergence as a presidential contender. Is Candidate Walker a monster of their own creation? I consider Walker as one of the most destructive forces in American politics today, states Dave Obey, a retired Democratic congressman from Wisconsin. But Mr Walker's ascent, he continues, would not have been feasible without the misguided recall efforts that occurred in the state. The recall campaign was a 2012 initiative to conduct a special election to remove Mr Walker from office during the middle of his first term as governor. It followed months of protests by more than 100,000 demonstrators in Madison, the state capital, in an unsuccessful attempt to prevent passage of a law drastically reducing the collective bargaining power of the state's public employees unions, including teachers. I don't fault the unions for believing that they ought to vote for the recall because he literally was putting them out of business economically as well as politically, Mr Obey adds. But sometimes it is beneficial if you don't think with your spleen. The unsuccessful recall efforts, Mr Obey states, made Mr Walker a hero amongst grass-roots conservatives, permitted him to establish a national fundraising network and provided him a unique talking point in the crowded Republican field. Including his 2014 re-election, he has won three elections in five years - in a state that has not voted for a Republican president in more than 30 years. Another Wisconsin Democratic insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, was more blunt regarding the recall effort. It was something you simply couldn't politically be against, because the activists were so incensed, he states. I just wanted this to go the [expletive] away. I was praying they wouldn't obtain the signatures, but I couldn't stand up in public and say that. He states that the protests, although well-intentioned, were destined for failure thanks to Republican control of the state legislature. And the recall election was a disaster because the Wisconsin public was not sold on the legitimacy of the effort. At its core was a sort of purity and innocence and stuff that would almost make you believe in American democracy - but it was just so tragically flawed, he states. It was not going to work, it was just a children's crusade. During his presidential announcement event on Monday, Mr Walker's political war record emerged again and again. There was discussion of agitators being transported in from out of state during the Madison protests and death threats made against Mr Walker and his family. Do you remember what it was like to witness your governor persecuted for simply putting you back in charge? Wisconsin Lieutenant Governor Rebecca Kleefisch asked the audience of around 300. Like a David to Goliath, Governor Scott Walker had your back. And America, he will again. text: Los Angeles, known as the homeless capital of the US, has passed a $1.87bn (£1.29bn) plan to help get an estimated 40,000 people off the streets. Municipal authorities aspire to expand homeless accommodation facilities and construct quality housing throughout the forthcoming decade. It represents the most grave humanitarian crisis facing our county presently, municipal official Sachi Hamai stated. Los Angeles proclaimed a state of public emergency the previous year as homeless population numbers surged by 12.4% across two years. Citizens and officials attribute a combination of joblessness, narcotics and escalating rental costs and property values to the expanding crisis. Up to 40,000 homeless individuals are forecast to reside throughout Los Angeles county, with two-thirds dwelling on streets, in temporary shelters or within vehicles. Initiatives to be implemented within a decade-long strategy encompass investment in temporary and permanent accommodation, permitting overnight vehicle parking for those residing in automobiles, and establishing a municipal network of mobile washing and sanitation facilities. Officials shall allocate $150m throughout the subsequent two years, designated specifically for homeless housing provision. Several legislators question the funding source, though the city's mayor has suggested it might derive from fresh revenue and reallocated existing resources. It might encompass matters relating to revenue expansion or priority restructuring of finances. We lack 100 million surplus dollars available where we might declare, 'Right, we intended to distribute this amongst other programmes, let us dedicate everything to homelessness.' It shall demand challenging choices, Mayor Eric Garcetti stated. The proposals require municipal adoption, with budget voting scheduled for April. Los Angeles currently expends approximately $1bn annually on medical, psychiatric and social welfare expenditure for its homeless population. The City of Angels possesses an alternative designation: America's homeless capital. This capital's centre lies in shadows, beneath gleaming tower blocks, along Skid Row in central Los Angeles. Within this realm of glamour and spectacle, forgotten individuals have established encampments. Street upon street, homeless persons and their meagre possessions - tarpaulins, shelters and trolleys - lie dispersed across pavements under scorching sunshine. The majority of faces are African-American.

text: Quentin Tarantino's first western, 2013's Django Unchained, was his highest grossing film in the USA - and now the 52-year-old director's latest movie, The Hateful Eight, is also set in the wild west, fulfilling his desire to breathe life into obsolete or dormant genres and make them my own, or even remake them. Located in Wyoming following the American Civil War, The Hateful Eight brings together a cast of Tarantino regulars including Samuel L Jackson, Kurt Russell and Reservoir Dogs stars Tim Roth and Michael Madsen. The film also features Single White Female actress Jennifer Jason Leigh as the sole woman amongst the eight, whilst Tarantino quips that Channing Tatum interns for an initial role in one of his pictures. Just as Django Unchained drew criticism, accusing the director of demonstrating insensitivity regarding slavery, The Hateful Eight is reported to have generated discomfort at early screenings in Hollywood concerning its race-related dialogue, alongside the violence directed at Leigh. Nevertheless, Harvey Weinstein, the film's executive producer, has described accusations of misogyny against Tarantino as fishing for stupidity, and both Tarantino and Leigh have received Golden Globe nominations for screenplay and actress, which Tarantino states he finds thrilling. Leigh portrays Daisy Domergue, a captured criminal en route to execution by hanging. Russell, who spent the four-and-a-half-month filming period chained in handcuffs to Leigh for the storyline, explains that they had worked out carefully the violence we were expected to inflict upon each other. When such matters are involved, you must trust that actor, because without trust you cannot perform your scenes properly. I wished to make it appear effortless and it was crucial that she remained safe in my care, enabling her to perform the role as required. Tarantino himself defends his screenplay: The violence is intended to send shockwaves through the audience, to generate sympathy for Daisy, but I have also confined all my characters within a cabin during a blizzard. It creates a pressure cooker regarding storyline and you understand my approach; that any piece of shocking violence may occur. So you suggest I may cross all boundaries with seven characters, but the eighth I must safeguard? It contradicts the entire narrative. Regarding the racial issues within the film, however, with Jackson portraying a former Union soldier carrying a letter from Abraham Lincoln, Tarantino acknowledges that during the past 18 months, numerous themes we addressed in the film, we witnessed on our television screens - referring particularly to the riots following the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown in 2014 by a white police officer in Missouri. The director's initial draft of The Hateful Eight was leaked online in January 2014, following which Tarantino initially abandoned the project. Now he states he feels grateful that the first draft emerged after all, because it remains on record that I was not writing a screenplay in response to these events occurring. He does consider his scripts possess deeper significance, stating: I enjoy concealing what I wish to express beneath a story. I believe historically, no other genre addresses modern America more effectively than the western. The westerns of the 1970s following Vietnam and Watergate were extremely cynical, for instance. Django Unchained performed exceptionally well and I hope it somewhat reinvented the genre, so presently we have two major westerns arriving in cinemas - The Revenant featuring Leo DiCaprio and this one. I have always maintained that to be recognised as a western director you must create three of them, so I suppose I may need to produce one more. However, cowboy programmes such as the 1960s television series Bonanza also provided inspiration for creating The Hateful Eight; and the film maintains a retrospective atmosphere throughout, with a three-hour duration, a musical overture from composer Ennio Morricone and a 12-minute intermission for audiences. The picture itself was filmed on 70mm stock, utilising the identical lenses employed to shoot the Ben Hur chariot sequence in 1959. (However numerous cinemas will screen a shorter non-70mm version of the film as few venues possess the specialised equipment required.) Last year Tarantino announced he might retire following the completion of 10 films - The Hateful Eight represents his eighth, if Kill Bill is counted as one picture. Russell, who appeared for Tarantino in 2007's B-movie tribute Deathproof, considers that it would be tragic if he did, describing the director as in a class of his own. You simply recognise within several frames of this film's opening who is directing it. text: A motorised wheelchair user has been convicted of ramming a policeman during a loyalist protest in north Belfast. Samuel Baxter pinned the officer's leg against a police vehicle after he was prevented from passing through security cordons on Twaddell Avenue, Belfast Magistrates Court was told. The 53-year-old was also convicted of disorderly conduct during one of the nightly demonstrations in the locality. Baxter, of Canmore Close, will receive his sentence next month. Police witnesses informed the court that one constable sustained a bruised shin in the incident after Baxter repeatedly manoeuvred his wheelchair weighing up to 28 stone towards them. Baxter stated he was only in the vicinity for family matters and had no participation in the protests concerning a disputed Orange Order parade. He maintained that he was attempting to pass through the police barrier to get his friend who had a blood clot to hospital. text: The group representing many of Scotland's councils has urged them to reject the Scottish government's funding settlement offer. Council leaders within the Convention of Scottish Local Authorities voted 21 to 7 to reject the unacceptable agreement. The motion stated the Scottish Government's approach was wholly misguided and threatens grievous injury to communities and citizens. Finance Secretary John Swinney described the offer as a deal worth taking. Councils have until 9th February to respond to the settlement offer. All councils within the Cosla grouping not governed by the SNP united against the agreement, with some examining the possibility of a legal challenge. Scotland's four remaining councils not part of Cosla also convened, and are exploring whether the terms of the agreement being offered are lawful. The funding package offered prioritises maintaining the council tax freeze, which has been in place since 2007, with any councils breaking it facing a loss of Scottish Government funding. Nevertheless, some councils are considering raising taxes regardless in the face of budget pressures. Discussions have been taking place between Mr Swinney and council leaders, with the deadline for the agreement to be accepted repeatedly deferred. Following a meeting of Cosla in Edinburgh, President David O'Neill announced the grouping had rejected the funding package as totally unacceptable and an attack on our democratic mandate. He stated: The Scottish Government is essentially forcing individual councils into having to accept the agreement. Regrettably, I fully accept that individual councils, due to the horrendous sanctions they would face, will find that they have no other option but to give in to central direction on this occasion. In imposing the agreement on individual councils, the most vulnerable in our communities will be left to pick up the pieces. Today's vote at Cosla is largely symbolic but demonstrates precisely how angry some councils are over the budget offer. Twenty-one of 28 councils supported a motion condemning the funding offer. Only SNP councils voted against. The move makes it difficult for local government to present a united front. Some councils are genuinely angry - even allowing for the politically-charged atmosphere as the Holyrood election approaches. Initially they feared they would have to make larger cuts and savings than they anticipated. Then their concern deepened when it emerged the agreement on offer made it even more difficult than before to contemplate raising council tax to help compensate. One council, Moray, had proposed an 18 per cent rise in its council tax rates but the calculations which led to this figure are now redundant. Meanwhile SNP councils, whilst not disputing that the funding offer is a challenge, believe the offer is, on balance, the best they can expect. The Government made a manifesto commitment to freeze the council tax for the whole of this parliamentary term - it believes this has been a popular policy which has been a help to family budgets. It also argues it has protected councils from the worst of what it calls Westminster spending cuts. The move by the four councils not in Cosla - which include Glasgow and Aberdeen - to explore whether the offer is lawful rests on a very specific point. But the fact they are examining this option demonstrates the depth of their concern. And, indeed, shows how many trump cards the Scottish Government holds. Realistically councils have little choice but to accept the Government's funding offer. This raises longer term questions about the whole system of council funding. A recent report - commissioned jointly by the Government and Cosla - set out several possible alternatives to the council tax in detail. There is also a debate over whether councils should be less dependent on the Government and have more ways of raising cash locally. The parties are all likely to set out their proposals ahead of May's Holyrood election. The motion accepted by Cosla stated the agreement would see council budgets slashed by £350m, and would be undeliverable without an unacceptable level of cuts to services and staffing. Trade union GMB Scotland has claimed 8,785 local authority jobs are under threat due to budget cuts, and is planning a rally outside the Scottish Parliament next week. Jenny Laing, leader of Aberdeen City Council, which is not part of Cosla, said the relationship between the Scottish Government and councils was broken. Speaking after the Scottish Local Government Partnership (SLGP) met in Glasgow, she stated: This is the most significant grant cut ever applied to local government. And when we have carried out our civic duty to question the settlement on behalf of our residents, we have been held to ransom by the Scottish Government's attempt to control decisions which should be made by democratically-elected representatives. She said the group was seeking legal advice on the matter. Scottish Labour and the Liberal Democrats said it was now time for Mr Swinney to re-think the agreement on the table. Responding to the Cosla and SLGP votes, John Swinney said: This is an agreement worth taking. Our funding proposals deliver a strong but challenging financial settlement for local government, despite cuts to the central budget by the UK Government. It is an agreement that will see an additional £250m invested in social care, it will help councils deliver the Living Wage giving 40,000 people a pay rise, it will freeze council tax for a ninth consecutive year, and it protects the pupil-teacher ratio, helping improve attainment. Overall, as a percentage of total revenue expenditure, the reduction in local authority budgets is around just 2 per cent. So whilst I recognise this will not be easy for councils to accommodate, some of the language used to describe the agreement has been unnecessary. I hope and expect cooler heads will come to realise this is an agreement councils can and should accept.
