text: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has condemned Turkey's shooting down of a Russian warplane on its border with Syria on 24 November. These are external links and will open in a new window This marks the first occasion a Russian aircraft has crashed in Syria since Moscow commenced air strikes against opponents of President Bashar al-Assad in September. Both Russia and Turkey state the Russian Su-24, an all-weather attack aircraft, was shot down by Turkish F-16s in the Turkey-Syria border region on 24 November. President Putin stated the aircraft, which carried two crew members, was flying at an altitude of 6,000m (19,685ft) when it was struck by an air-to-air missile. The aircraft crashed in the mountainous Jabal Turkmen region of the Syrian province of Latakia, which is disputed by Syrian government and rebel forces. The pilot and a marine dispatched on a rescue mission by helicopter were killed. In a letter to the UN Security Council, Turkey's permanent representative Halit Cevik stated that two aircraft of unknown nationality had approached Turkish airspace near the town of Yayladagi in Hatay province. The aircraft were warned 10 times over the course of five minutes via an emergency channel and requested to change direction, he stated. Both aircraft ignored the warnings and subsequently flew 2.19km (1.36 miles) and 1.85km (1.15 miles) into Turkey for 17 seconds from 09:24:05 (07:24:05 GMT), according to Mr Cevik. Following the violation, aircraft 1 departed Turkish national airspace. Aircraft 2 was engaged whilst in Turkish national airspace by Turkish F-16s conducting air combat patrolling in the region. Aircraft 2 crashed onto the Syria side of the Turkish-Syrian border. The Turkish military also released what it claimed was the radar image of the path the Russian aircraft took, demonstrating it briefly flew across Turkey's southernmost tip. However, Mr Putin stated the Su-24 was over Syrian territory, 1km (0.6 miles) from Syria's border with Turkey, when it was struck. It crashed 4km from the border, he stated. The Russian defence ministry maintained that the aircraft remained within Syria's borders throughout its mission, did not violate Turkish airspace and received no warnings. It released a video demonstrating what it claimed was the Su-24's flight path. The pilot who survived the crash, Capt Konstantin Murakhtin, told Russian television he had not received a warning before being shot down. Subsequently, Mr Putin stated that the US military, which leads the coalition that Turkey belongs to, knew about the location and time of our aircraft' flights, and we were struck exactly there and at that time. The US state department rejected that, maintaining that Russia had not notified the US in advance about the flight. US military officials stated there were indications the downed aircraft entered Turkish airspace for a matter of seconds, and that it had been warned to stay out. Further details were provided on 27 November by Russian air force commander Gen Viktor Bondarev. He stated Russian and Syrian radar data pointed towards an ambush by the two Turkish F-16s. The F-16s spent one hour and 15 minutes flying in the region where the incident occurred, he stated, and the one that fired the missile penetrated 2km inside Syria, spending 40 seconds in Syrian airspace. The timings demonstrated that they could not have taken off from their Diyarbakir airbase for the interception - they were positioned to attack, he stated. The two Su-24s had just bombed two groups of rebels and one was shot down just after completing another bombing run, 5.5km south of Turkey, he stated. Was jet downing an overreaction? Video footage released by Turkish media demonstrated that the Su-24's two crew - the pilot and the navigator - ejected as their burning aircraft plummeted to the ground. Rebels from Syria's ethnic Turkmen community, whose villages Turkey stated had been bombed by Russian aircraft in recent weeks, opened fire at the crew as they attempted to parachute into government-held territory. One of them was dead when he landed on the ground, the rebels stated. A video was also posted online showing gunmen standing around a man in a flight suit who was motionless on the ground. The following day, Russia confirmed the pilot, Lt Col Oleg Peshkov, had been killed. However, it stated the navigator, Capt Murakhtin, had been rescued and taken to Russia's Hmeimim airbase in Latakia by Syrian government forces. A Russian marine, Aleksandr Pozynich, was also killed during an attempted rescue mission, when an Mi-8 helicopter he was travelling in came under fire. Who are the Turkmen in Syria? Russia is one of several countries directly involved in the conflict in Syria, which has left more than 250,000 people dead since March 2011. Moscow is an ally of President Assad and is conducting air strikes to support his government. It states it is targeting only terrorists - above all jihadist militants from Islamic State (IS). However, Western analysts state Russia's strikes have mainly hit Western-backed rebels fighting President Assad's troops. The Su-24 bombers attacked by Turkey on 24 November were targeting terrorists from Russia's North Caucasus, the Russian government states. Syrian rebels have meanwhile received substantial support from Turkey, an opponent of Mr Assad. Ankara also permits the US-led multinational coalition against IS to use its airbases to conduct strikes on the jihadist group in Syria. What is Russia's endgame in Syria? Syria crisis: Where key countries stand Russia immediately deployed S-400 anti-aircraft missiles at the Hmeimim airbase in Syria - a significant demonstration of force in the troubled region. The S-400 can strike targets up to 400km (248 miles) away, so at Hmeimim the missiles cover the airspace of Syria, Lebanon, Cyprus, half of Israel and a large portion of Turkey, the Russian state-controlled news channel RT reports. It can strike any existing aircraft or missile travelling at speeds of up to 4.8km (three miles) per second, RT states. Targets at heights of up to 30km are within range. Russia is also suspending the reciprocal visa-free regime with Turkey from 1 January. Russia has banned charter flights to and from Turkey, and Russian travel firms have been instructed to stop selling Turkish holidays. That move and warnings to Russians not to travel to Turkey, are expected to impact Turkey's tourist industry, as it is a top destination for Russian tourists. A decree signed by President Putin on 28 November calls for the banning or limitation of imports from Turkey, the work of Turkish companies in Russia and any Turkish nationals working for Russian companies. The government is drawing up a list of the sectors affected. The government states fruit and vegetables will be the main food imports to be restricted, starting in a few weeks' time. Russia has already tightened inspections of Turkish food. It is an important market for Turkish exporters. And President Putin has refused to speak to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, despite the latter's telephone calls, a Kremlin aide stated. The reason: Mr Putin is waiting for Turkey to apologise. However, Turkish PM Ahmet Davutoglu has made clear that no Turkish prime minister or president will apologise ... because of doing our duty. Mr Putin maintained that the downed Su-24 had posed no threat. He stated it had been carrying out preventative attacks against IS in Latakia, and also that Russia had established large quantities of oil were entering Turkey from IS-held areas, providing the jihadist group with significant funding. This was a stab in the back by the accomplices of terrorists, Mr Putin declared. Although Turkey's policy of allowing Syrian rebel fighters and arms shipments to pass through its territory has been exploited by IS, officials have denied supporting the group. Activists state IS has little or no presence near the crash site. The last occasion a Nato state shot down a Russian or Soviet aircraft was in the 1950s. After an extraordinary meeting of the alliance's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg declared: We stand in solidarity with Turkey and support the territorial integrity of our Nato ally. President Erdogan warned that everyone should respect the right of Turkey to defend its borders. He also noted that Turkey's actions were fully in line with the new rules of engagement adopted after Syria shot down a Turkish jet in 2012. The rules state that all elements approaching from Syria are considered an enemy threat. Profile: North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato)

text: Reports of child rape to police in England and Wales have risen by 37% over the last five years, figures show. Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary (HMIC) reported 5,674 recorded instances of child rape in 2009/10 and 7,775 instances in 2013/14. However, fewer than one-third of child rape instances result in suspects being charged or summonsed, the statistics indicate. Recorded adult rapes increased 38% from 9,383 in 2009/10 to 12,952 in 2013/14 the report stated. Approximately one-fifth of adult instances result in suspects being charged or summonsed. The Metropolitan Police recorded the greatest number of adult rapes per 100,000 population in 2013/14 with 3,056, whilst Dyfed-Powys recorded the fewest with 62. The North Wales constabulary recorded the greatest number of child rape instances per 100,000 population with 144 in 2013/14 whilst Hertfordshire recorded the fewest with 73. Essex, Kent and Suffolk constabularies ranked lowest in the table for charges or summonses for child rape instances, with 21% of instances resulting in action. Northumbria ranked highest in the same table with 47% of instances resulting in charges or summonses. Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper stated: These statistics are extremely concerning and a shocking condemnation of the expanding justice gap established by this government. During the past four years, there has been a terrible pattern of recorded rape incidents increasing, whilst prosecutions and convictions decrease. Rape and the sexual abuse of children are amongst the most repugnant and heinous offences. Victims deserve justice. Crime prevention minister Lynne Featherstone stated rape sentencing durations had increased and the overall number of rape prosecutions in England and Wales had risen, from 3,819 in 2009/10 to 3,891 in 2013/14. The coalition government maintains that every rape report must be treated seriously, every victim must be handled with dignity and every investigation must be pursued thoroughly and professionally, she stated. The rise in rape reports to police is encouraging as it demonstrates more victims are finding courage to come forward. Paul Ford, secretary of the Police Federation National Detectives' Forum, stated: Policing faces considerable pressure through budget reductions and this affects the standard of service that policing can deliver to victims. Devon and Cornwall records amongst the highest rates of adult and child rape. Nevertheless, only 15% of adult rape instances and 27% of child rape instances lead to charges or summonses the statistics show. The constabulary's Police and Crime Commissioner Tony Hogg stated police performance regarding rape remained under regular review. Fee Scott of Devon Rape Crisis stated: We shall achieve far better results if we trusted people and we do not judge them on their clothing, activities, words or alcohol consumption. All of this prevents women from coming forward because they fear the response they shall receive from authorities. This report presents a most depressing picture of the potential outcome.

text: England need to work on how they play spin bowling after their tour of India ended in a crushing Twenty20 defeat, says head coach Trevor Bayliss. England surrendered eight wickets for eight runs across 19 deliveries to suffer defeat by 75 runs in Bangalore, with spinner Yuzvendra Chahal claiming 6-25 from his four overs. The defeat confirmed a 2-1 T20 series loss for England, who had also lost the Test and one-day series throughout the tour. We are certainly not world-class players of spin, acknowledged Bayliss. We are playing against players who are very good players of spin, and they possess very good spinners themselves. When you do not grow up on it, as players here do, it proves difficult. It represents a learning process. England lost 86 wickets to spin across all formats during their tour of India, having also struggled against it on their previous tour in Bangladesh. Pursuing 203 to win on Wednesday, they remained in the game at the halfway stage of their reply, but after Chahal dismissed both captain Eoin Morgan and vice-captain Joe Root, the tourists collapsed. It proves a little bit disappointing the way we concluded our series, said Bayliss. It does not reflect the type of cricket we have played over here. But it represents what can happen in a T20 match when you are chasing a big total. Morgan said: Everybody feels gutted. Today represented a big game for us. There was a series on the line and we wanted to produce a good performance but in fact we have produced one of our worst in a long time. If we can take anything from it, it represents the first time it has happened in two and a half years. England won only three of their 13 matches throughout the tour - one ODI, one T20 and a tour match against India A. However, they produced their best cricket in the limited-overs series, scoring more than 300 in each of the ODIs and producing some improved bowling displays in the T20s. The results have not gone the way we would have liked, said Bayliss. We have played some pretty good cricket here at times. We have still got a lot of work to do - the boys have been very honest about where they stand. We have got to put together a batting and a bowling performance in one game - we seem to bat well in some games, and bowl well in others. Morgan added: There has not been a lot between the sides, particularly in the one-day series. There were 15-20 runs between the winning and losing of the series. The improvements we have shown since then have been considerable in our bowling department. When you are going well you have to take advantage of it. But we are really strong at the moment. Home advantage proves huge, around the world. We have pushed India right to the cusp in both [limited-overs] series. Following the 4-0 Test series defeat in India, Alastair Cook said he had questions about his role as England captain, admitting Root was ready to be his successor. Australian Bayliss said he had not spoken to Cook since he departed the tour but said he would contact him in due course. I am heading home to Australia for a little while in the next day or so, added Bayliss. I shall put the feet up for a little bit and I am sure I shall speak to him at some stage. I shall give it a couple of days - I am sure we shall exchange a text message or something. As I said to him when he left, and there was a lot of speculation, it remains totally up to him. He will know if it represents time to step down. I am happy either way, whether he stays or goes. There remains plenty of time.

text: Nigeria's central bank governor Lamido Sanusi has been suspended by the president for financial recklessness and misconduct. Mr Sanusi is widely regarded following his implementation of banking sector reforms since his appointment in 2009. He was designated central bank governor of the year for 2010 by Banker magazine. The controversy emerges at a time when elections approach and some of the president's senior officials face very awkward questions. Mr Sanusi's critics speculate about his own political aspirations and question whether he is exploiting his position to damage President Jonathan's prospects in 2015. However, to many Nigerians it will seem that the president has chosen to suspend the whistleblower rather than concentrate on preventing fraud. Attempts to combat corruption seldom succeed in Nigeria. In 2007 Nuhu Ribadu was suspended as head of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission. Foreign exchange, bond and money markets have ceased trading due to uncertainty created by the action, Reuters news agency reports. text: Rail passengers have been speaking of their frustration after overrunning engineering works saw services thrown into chaos. No trains have been running between Paddington in west London and Reading for the majority of the day, disrupting routes to the west country and Wales. At King's Cross in London, which serves northern and eastern England and Scotland, all services were suspended. Lengthy queues formed at Finsbury Park station as passengers awaited trains to Peterborough and destinations further north. The 12:15 service from Peterborough to Edinburgh departed Peterborough at 13:05 and was completely full. An elderly German couple expressed disbelief. No possibility of reaching the buffet car and when we eventually could access it, it had been shut since Newcastle. Seats only became available from Doncaster and York though passengers remained standing in the doorways. We could have boarded alternative less crowded services from Peterborough but these arrived and departed without information from staff who appeared to lack leadership. There seemed to be no management presence today. Perhaps still on their holidays. It was bitterly cold waiting an hour on Peterborough station platform. There are insufficient waiting facilities. Soon be home but no festive spirit on Network Rail. Service nearly an hour delayed at Edinburgh. Passengers were standing in the corridors and vestibules between carriages. Despite being extremely busy, people were generally simply grateful to be aboard a train. The mood was very cordial with passengers conversing and assisting each other with luggage and offering seats to those who required them more. I had boarded the service at Finsbury Park but passengers who joined at Peterborough said they had been informed the train was empty so there would be ample seating. Clearly not accurate. Most of us had been waiting on platforms for over an hour without sufficient information. The additional point to make is that there were insufficient staff to provide information. I arrived at Finsbury Park at 09.50 and was informed there would be no service until 11:00 and there were no East Coast personnel available to tell us where trains were bound. Website not current so more people continued arriving. Eventually departed without knowing its destination at approximately 11.20. I was intending to visit my friend in Bradford and her family for the first time before travelling onwards to Liverpool to see friends I had not seen for over a year. Finsbury Park was extremely busy and passengers were required to carry baggage and small children up a steep spiral staircase to travel from the Underground platform and up towards the train platforms. Once you reached the top of the spiral staircase you were met with a tunnel packed wall-to-wall with passengers - elderly passengers, young children and babies crying, pushchairs, baggage and you were unable to reach any of the platforms. There was nobody available to advise you what to do or where to proceed. We were all trapped in this tunnel and it was becoming increasingly busy as passengers were still arriving and I began to feel slightly worried as I could observe a genuine crowd control problem beginning to develop. Several railway staff forced their way through the tunnel of passengers but they were all rather discourteous and unhelpful when questioned. Some of the staff members were truly behaving in an unprofessional manner and they did not appear to understand how to manage the situation. I was standing in the freezing cold attempting to determine if any of the destination options would transport me close to Leeds or Bradford. I overheard I could board a service to Peterborough and change there and there was a Peterborough service on the display but then that never appeared. By this stage I was extremely tired and cold... I decided then that I had endured enough and would make my way back to Reading. I had to leave the platform and return down into the tunnel full of people. Upon exit from Finsbury Park there was an enormous crowd of several hundred people standing outside. I had to make my way through and around to the underground entrance and make my way back across the city to Waterloo so I could return to Reading. I cannot believe I have had to completely abandon my plans that I had been anticipating. I am utterly exhausted and too concerned to risk travelling again tomorrow.

There was no possibility of getting into the restaurant car, and when we finally did it had been closed since Newcastle. The train from Peterborough was a long one, but it arrived and departed without notice, and a lack of leadership on the part of the staff. Seats became available on the Doncaster and York lines, although the passengers were still standing at the doors. Management seemed to have withdrawn. It was still holiday season, perhaps. There are not enough waiting-rooms. We stood for an hour on the platform of the Peterborough station. It was freezing cold. The service was no longer festive. The train was nearly an hour late in leaving for home. The passengers were standing in the corridors and vestibules between the compartments. In spite of the overcrowded condition of the train, everyone was happy. There was a good atmosphere among the passengers, who conversed, helped each other with their luggage, offered their seat to those who needed it more. I got on at Finsbury Park, but passengers who had got on at Peterborough said they had been told that there was plenty of room in the train. Obviously not. Most of us had been waiting for more than an hour on the platform without adequate information. And then there were not enough employees to give information. The site was not kept up to date, so people kept on coming. At the station, at ten minutes to nine, I was informed that there would be no service until eleven, and that there were no people from the north who could tell me where the trains were going. I finally got on board at about eleven-twenty without knowing where I was going. I was going to see my friend’s family for the first time in Bradford and then travel on to Liverpool to see friends I had not seen for a year. Finsbury Park Station was very crowded and it was necessary to take your luggage and small children up a steep spiral staircase to reach the platforms above. Once there, you found yourself in a tunnel of people, old and young, young children crying, push-chairs and cases, with no possibility of getting out on to the platform. No one was there to tell us what to do or where to go. Here we were, all together in the tunnel, and as more and more people arrived I began to feel a little uneasy because I could see that a crowd was beginning to form. Some railroad employees pushed their way through the throng of passengers, but they all turned out to be rather unfriendly and brusque when asked for directions. I stood in the cold and tried to figure out which of the available options would take me somewhere near Leeds or Bradford. There were some very unprofessionally acting employees who seemed to know nothing about how to handle the situation. I heard a suggestion that I could take the train to Peterborough and change there, and I saw a Peterborough connection on the monitor, but it disappeared. I thought I had endured enough and that I would go back to Reading. I was by then very tired and cold. I had to leave the platform and go down the crowded tunnel. At the exit from Finsbury Park there was an enormous crowd of several hundred people outside. I had to fight my way through it, find the steps down to the metro, cross town and go back to the library. I cannot imagine that I had to abandon completely my plans as they had been. The next day I was too tired and too worried to risk travelling.

These are external links and will open in a new window MP Makhosi Khoza has consistently demanded Mr Zuma's resignation. Last week, she declared he was a disgrace. She has received death threats cautioning her to cease advocating for a secret ballot when MPs vote on Mr Zuma next month. Parliament and the police chose to provide security for her. Last week, the ANC stated she had overstepped the mark and must face disciplinary action for criticising the president. The ANC in her home province of KwaZulu-Natal termed her remarks a blatant betrayal of the core values of the party. Ms Khoza, 47, has also been a critic of corruption within the ANC. Mr Zuma has faced numerous corruption allegations, all of which he denies. The National Assembly is expected to vote on a motion of no-confidence in him on 8 August. Milton Nkosi, BBC News, Johannesburg The decision to charge Makhosi Khoza with ill-discipline is the finest example of how the ANC is shooting itself in the foot. Following its catastrophic performance in last year's local government elections, the party pledged to self-correct. But what the South African electorate is witnessing is the ANC inflicting wounds on itself that might not heal in time for the next general election due in 2019. Ms Khoza is a PhD MP and one of its most popular out of the over 200 in the National Assembly. She is being punished for speaking truth to power. This is precisely what Nelson Mandela warned South Africans about his party's impunity when he said: If the ANC does to you what the apartheid government did to you, then you must do to the ANC what we did to the apartheid government. The ANC appears like an unstoppable train rattling downhill at breakneck speed. If there was ever an example of when the 105-year-old party needed to apply the brakes it is here. But the people are likely to punish these leaders in two years' time. Last week Ms Khoza received a death threat stating she had 21 days left to live. She termed Mr Zuma a disgrace at a ceremony to mark Nelson Mandela's birthday on 18 July. She was addressing civil society groups, unions and business leaders pressing for Mr Zuma's removal in next month's no-confidence vote. There is no suggestion that he is connected to the death threats. Jacob Zuma has survived several previous votes of no-confidence. The constitutional court ruled in June that parliament had the right to conduct a secret ballot, but the speaker has yet to announce a decision on the issue. Mr Zuma is due to stand down as ANC president in December and whoever takes over would lead the party into the 2019 elections.

text: A rugby fan was nearly six times over the drink-drive limit after downing a bottle of vodka in the NekNominate craze, a Cardiff inquest has heard. Stephen Brookes, aged 29, from Rumney, perished after a companion recorded him consuming three-quarters of a 75cl bottle during an internet drinking challenge. He had been nominated by an acquaintance to consume the beverage for Facebook. The coroner delivered a verdict of death by acute alcohol poisoning and cocaine consumption. The inquest heard Mr Brookes had been consuming alcohol earlier on Sunday 9 February following Wales versus Ireland in the Six Nations. However, he was challenged by companions to consume the vodka rapidly. The inquest heard labourer Mr Brookes declared he would be fine moments before executing the feat. Yet within minutes he had fallen and lost consciousness. Companions transported him home but he was subsequently discovered deceased. His cousin Jodie Cummings informed South Wales Police: Stephen had been viewing a rugby match with companions at a residence. He had obtained a 75cl bottle of vodka. Several weeks previously he had been NekNominated. This involves someone nominating an acquaintance to consume something such as a bottle or pint. Past midnight whilst I was in the lavatory, Stephen consumed the bottle of vodka. It was recorded and I observed it on a companion's telephone. I witnessed him consume the bottle of vodka rapidly. He simply raised the bottle aloft. Subsequently he appeared cheerful and remarked, 'you know me'. He was moving about. However 10 minutes later his equilibrium had deteriorated. He was speaking incoherently - everything occurred so rapidly. Companions informed police how individuals were urging him to consume the vodka around 01:30, the day following his viewing of Wales versus Ireland in the Six Nations rugby. Another companion Shaun Chivers stated the vodka disappeared within seconds as he was filmed at the gathering near his residence. I observed Stephen had three quarters of the bottle remaining and I knew he would consume it rapidly, he stated and advised his companion to cease fooling about. He continued: The following moment he consumed the bottle and it vanished in seconds. Shortly afterwards he was staggering everywhere. Mr Brookes expired within an hour of the NekNominate stunt and was subsequently found to contain 458 millilitres of alcohol in his blood - the drink-driving limit stands at 80. He also contained a substantial level of cocaine in his blood and had consumed between 10 and 20 lines of cocaine. Pathologist Thomas Hockey stated he was clearly well above the fatal threshold for alcohol.

text: After months of sotto voce claims that some businesses were simply too scared to put their head above the independence parapet, tonight comes the most significant move by anti-independence members of the UK business community ahead of the September vote. A letter endorsed by 133 enterprises with global interests asserts that the uncertainty surrounding a Yes vote represents poor prospects for business. The signatories span various sectors - banking, mining, engineering, food, whisky, technology and several SMEs. Some have previously expressed anti-independence views. Many are newcomers. The letter bears the signatures of - amongst others - Douglas Flint, HSBC's chairman; Andrew Mackenzie, chief executive of mining conglomerate BHP Billiton; and Sir John Grant, executive vice president of policy at energy firm BG Group (and previously the UK government's Brussels representative). Audrey Baxter, executive chairman of Baxters Food Group; Simon Thomson, Cairn Energy's chief executive; and Ian Curle, chief executive of Edrington, which possesses the whisky brands The Macallan and The Famous Grouse, also provide their endorsement. It shall be published in Wednesday's Scotsman newspaper. The letter was coordinated by Keith Cochrane, chief executive of engineering company Weir Group, who has previously cautioned of substantial risks should Scotland vote for independence. Its supporters state that no political organisations have participated in compiling the list. One source indicated that it emerged from frustration regarding what is viewed as insufficient cohesiveness concerning the business and independence debate. The signatories represent approximately 50,000 Scottish jobs, I have been informed, from major employers such as Babcock shipbuilding to small engineering companies in Glasgow's east end. Advocates of an independent Scotland can indicate their own array of supporters from business and economics, naturally. The former chairman of The Royal Bank of Scotland, Sir George Mathewson, has stated that Scotland's crucial financial services sector - for instance - would prosper should Scotland vote yes. There is nothing to indicate that being part of a smaller nation impedes a financial services industry. Switzerland, for instance, has - in Geneva and Zurich - not one, but two of the world's Top 10 financial centres. Singapore, with 5 million inhabitants, is ranked 4th, he has stated. Investment is an increasingly global enterprise, where success depends considerably more on people than on boundaries. The economist and former head of Scottish Enterprise, Sir Donald MacKay, has contended that an independent Scotland would be in superior fiscal condition than the UK is presently. An independent Scotland should utilise that financial advantage to invest in re-engineering our economy towards industrial, manufacturing and tradeable services development, he has contended. Jim McColl, one of Scotland's wealthiest men and head of engineering investment enterprise Clyde Blowers Capital, has disclosed that he is so enthusiastic about independence he would contemplate relocating to Scotland in the event of a Yes vote. For the present, at least, Mr McColl resides in Monaco. Willie Walsh, chief executive of IAG, owner of British Airways, also states that independence could indeed be beneficial for Scotland. I would not be surprised should additional names be disclosed this week. Both sides of the debate have made the evident point that it is for the voters to determine. With this letter voters will certainly possess a clearer understanding of the issues that are troubling those businesses concerned about a potential yes vote. Those centre around five key subjects - the currency, an independent Scotland's relationship with the European Union, the tax and regulation changes that may be introduced post-independence, pensions and how exports may be affected (an issue connected to the EU debate). The letter states that much is at stake: Our economic connections within the United Kingdom are very close and support more than a million Scottish jobs. As job creators we have examined carefully the arguments made by both sides of the debate. Our conclusion is that the business case for independence has not been established. I am informed that this is not the beginning of a new campaign by businesses against independence - but is a single occurrence. It does, however, come before a CBI dinner in Glasgow on Thursday evening at which Sir Mike Rake, the CBI's president and chairman of BT Group, is likely to make similar arguments against independence. Business for Scotland responded tonight, issuing this statement: Business for Scotland has 2,500 members who operate businesses in Scotland, employ people across the country in a range of industries, and all believe that Scottish independence is in the best interests of Scotland and Scottish business. It's a position reached after examining the facts and figures and realising that, from a simple balance sheet perspective as well as other considerations, our best interests lie in becoming an independent country. It shall be for the Scottish voters to determine how much weight they accord either side in this debate.

text: A tipper truck which killed four people when its brakes failed had clocked up almost 450,000 miles (724,000km), the driver's trial has heard. Four-year-old Mitzi Steady, Robert Parker, 59, Philip Allen, 52, and Stephen Vaughan, 34, perished in the collision in Bath during February 2015. Bristol Crown Court was told the lorry represented an accident waiting to happen. Motorist Phillip Potter, 20, refutes causing the fatalities through dangerous and careless driving. His employer Matthew Gordon similarly refutes 14 charges whilst the haulage firm's mechanic Peter Wood refutes four allegations. Mr Potter and Mr Gordon were operating two lorries transporting 30-tonne loads from a Wiltshire quarry on 9 February, the court was told. Mr Gordon, who was travelling ahead of Mr Potter, halted his lorry on Lansdown Lane in Weston village but Mr Potter's brakes failed and he was forced to swerve to prevent a collision, the court was told. The lorry struck several pedestrians including Mitzi and her grandmother Margaret Rogers and a vehicle containing Mr Allen and Mr Vaughan, both from Swansea, and Mr Parker, from Cwmbran, south Wales. Prosecutor Adam Vaitilingam QC stated: (Mr Potter's) lorry proceeded to hurtle down Lansdown Lane without control. It inflicted absolute devastation. By the time it eventually came to rest, four people had sustained fatal injuries - a four-year-old girl who had been crossing the road with her grandmother and three men who had been travelling together in the same vehicle. Mr Vaitilingam described Mr Potter as an inexperienced driver who had only been with the company for a matter of days. He stated Mr Gordon's business, Grittenham Haulage Limited, was established in December 2013 and was a shambles from start to finish with no transport manager in position at the time of the collision. The business did not conduct the recommended brake efficiency tests on the vehicle, which was an accident waiting to happen, he stated. Mechanic Peter Wood was engaged to conduct inspections on the lorries. The final safety examination on the vehicle occurred in January 2015, weeks before the collision, when he considered it safe to operate, the court was told. Mr Vaitilingam stated: If Mr Wood did conduct a safety inspection that day it was wholly inadequate. On the date of the collision the lorry had serious and longstanding defects with its braking system, meaning that it was and had been for some time in a dangerous condition. This sort of catastrophic brake failure does not simply occur through misfortune. Mr Potter, of Dauntsey, Wiltshire, is additionally charged with causing serious injuries to Karla Brennan and Margaret Rogers - Mitzi's grandmother - through dangerous driving. He refutes a total of 10 charges against him. Mr Gordon, 30, also of Dauntsey, refutes 14 charges against him. Mr Wood, 55, from Brinkworth, Wiltshire refutes the four charges against him. The trial proceeds.

text: Great Britain will have a team of 264 athletes competing at the Rio Paralympics in 19 sports. The British squad has never concluded beyond the top five in the medal standings. At London 2012, they secured 120 medals, comprising 34 golds, to place third behind China and Russia - and expectations are elevated they can exceed that in Brazil. Here you shall discover the names of every athlete chosen by the British Paralympic Association. London medals: Two (one gold, one silver) Competition dates: 10-17 September Venue: Sambodromo Former gold medallists John Cavanagh and John Stubbs lead the GB archery team for Rio. Cavanagh, who shall be participating in his fifth Games, secured gold in Athens whilst Stubbs prevailed on his Games debut in Beijing four years subsequently. Amongst the newcomers are London 2012 Games Maker Jo Frith, who has secured European and world medals since transferring from swimming to archery, 16-year-old Jess Stretton and Invictus Games veteran Mikey Hall. London medals: 29 (11 gold, 7 silver, 11 bronze) Competition dates: 8-18 September Venue: Olympic Stadium London 2012 gold medallists David Weir, Richard Whitehead, Aled Davies and Hannah Cockroft are amongst the 13 track and field athletes nominated in the first round of selections for the Rio Paralympics. All of those chosen secured gold or silver medals at last year's IPC Athletics World Championships in Doha and demonstrated form in 2016. The team also comprises Libby Clegg, who shattered the 200m world record at the Anniversary Games in her new T11 class, and Jonnie Peacock, who shall be seeking to defend his T44 100m title, plus numerous debutants. London medals: Two (one silver, one bronze) Competitions dates: 10-16 September Venue: Carioca Arena 2 David Smith, Stephen McGuire and Nigel Murray have all been nominated in the 10-strong GB boccia team. McGuire is world individual champion in the BC4 classification, whilst Smith secured team gold alongside double Paralympic gold medallist Murray at Beijing 2008. London medals: None (sport making its debut) Competition dates: 14-15 September Venue: Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas Canoeing shall make its Paralympic debut in Rio and Great Britain will be one of only two nations, alongside Australia, to possess a full quota of six boats in action. All of the team possess experience at World and European Championships, with Anne Dickins and Emma Wiggs current world champions in their respective categories. Wiggs represented Great Britain in sitting volleyball at London 2012 and Nick Beighton competed in rowing, whilst Jeanette Chippington shall be participating at her sixth Games after a successful swimming career. London medals: 22 (Eight gold, nine silver, five bronze) Competition dates: 8-11 September (track) 14-17 September (road) Venues: Rio Olympic Velodrome (track), Pontal (road) The British Para-cycling squad has enjoyed tremendous success on the track and the road in recent times, topping the medal table four years ago. Dame Sarah Storey, who secured four golds at London 2012, has been chosen for her seventh Games, having made her debut as a swimmer in Barcelona 1992. London 2012 medal winners Neil Fachie, Karen Darke, Jody Cundy, Helen Scott and Jon-Allan Butterworth also feature in the squad alongside Kadeena Cox, who shall be competing in both cycling and athletics in Rio. London medals: 11 (five gold, five silver, one bronze) Competition dates: 11-16 September Venue: Olympic Equestrian Centre The five riders chosen for the Paralympic equestrian squad in Rio possess 13 Games' worth of experience between them and a shared haul of 30 Paralympic medals. Lee Pearson shall be aiming to add to his 10-gold-medal haul whilst Sophie Christiansen shall be defending the three titles (two individual and one team) she secured at London 2012. Sophie Wells, who secured team gold with Pearson and Christiansen four years ago, returns alongside double individual gold medallist Natasha Baker. The squad is completed by 67-year-old five-time gold medallist Anne Dunham, who shall be competing in her fifth Games. London medals: None Competition dates: 8-16 September Venue: Deodoro Stadium All but two of the football team shall be making their Paralympic debut with former Everton FC Academy player Michael Barker and Scottish veteran Jonathan Paterson competing in their third Games. The squad, which shall be captained by former Birmingham City player Jack Rutter, has representatives from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland - many of whom competed internationally for their home nations at recent World and European Championships. London medals: Two (one silver, one bronze) Competition dates: 8-10 September Venue: Carioca Arena 3 The judo team became the first complete GB squad to be nominated for the Rio Paralympics. London 2012 silver medallist Sam Ingram shall be competing in his third consecutive Games and he is joined by a trio of newcomers in Jonathan Drane, Chris Skelley and Jack Hodgson. London medals: One (bronze) Competition dates: 8-14 September Venue: Riocentro Pavilion 2 World and European champion Ali Jawad leads the GB powerlifting squad, eager to compensate for the disappointment of missing out on a medal at London 2012. Natalie Blake shall be competing at her fifth Games, Zoe Newson secured bronze four years ago and there is a debut for Micky Yule, a former staff sergeant in the Royal Engineers, who lost both of his legs in an explosion whilst serving in Afghanistan in 2010. London medals: one (gold) Competition dates: 9-11 September Venue: Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas Gold medallists Tom Aggar and Pam Relph lead the GB rowing squad for Rio. Aggar secured men's single sculls gold when the sport made its debut in 2008 whilst Relph was part of the victorious mixed coxed four in London but has four new crewmates this time around in Dan Brown, Grace Clough, James Fox and cox Oliver James. Former gold medal-winning handcyclist Rachel Morris shall be making her rowing debut whilst Laurence Whiteley and Lauren Rowles shall be making their first appearances at a Games. London medals: Two (one gold, one bronze) Competition dates: 12-17 September Venue: Marina da Gloria, Guanabara Bay Defending Paralympic champion Helena Lucas was the first athlete to be nominated for either Rio Games when she was chosen in April 2015. Lucas shall compete in the 2.4mR category and shall be joined by London bronze medallists Alexandra Rickham and Niki Birrell and the Sonar crew of John Robertson, Hannah Stodel and Stephen Thomas, who shall be competing in their fourth Games. London medals: three (one silver, two bronze) Competition dates: 8-14 September Venue: Olympic Shooting Centre Three-time Paralympic medallist Matt Skelhon has been nominated as part of the GB shooting team, aiming to add to his medal haul. Skelhon secured gold in Beijing in 2008 and followed that up with silver and bronze in London. He is one of six athletes with previous Games experience whilst Issy Bailey, Owen Burke, Lorraine Lambert and Stewart Nangle shall be making their debuts in Rio. London medals: 39 (Seven gold, 16 silver, 16 bronze) Competition dates: 8-17 September Venue: Olympic Aquatics Centre A 30-strong squad shall represent GB in swimming at the Rio Paralympics. Six swimmers - Ellie Simmonds, Ollie Hynd, Josef Craig, Jessica-Jane Applegate, Jon Fox and Bethany Firth - secured gold at London 2012 and 20 of the team bring previous Games experience. Abby Kane, who turns 13 in August, shall make her debut whilst veteran Sascha Kindred, 38, shall be participating in his sixth Games. London medals: Four (one silver, three bronze) Competition dates: 8-17 September Venue: Riocentro Pavilion 3 World number ones Will Bayley and Rob Davies lead the 12-strong GB table tennis squad for the Rio Paralympics. The squad possesses a wealth of experience, with Sue Gilroy competing in her fifth Games. Liverpool's Jack Hunter-Spivey is the only member who has yet to compete at a Paralympics. London medals: None (sport is making its debut) Competition dates: 10-11 September Venue: Fort Copacabana Great Britain shall take 11 athletes and two guides to the inaugural Paralympic triathlon event at Rio - the most of any country. Reigning world champion Lauren Steadman is included, as are Andy Lewis and Alison Patrick, who secured European gold in Lisbon in May. London medals: None Competition dates: 8-16 September (women), 8-17 September (men) Venues: Rio Olympic Arena and Carioca Arena 1 Both the GB men's and women's squads shall be represented in Rio. The men's squad go in as three-time European champions after completing the hat-trick in Worcester last September and shall be hoping to improve on their fourth-placed finish four years ago. All but one player was part of the European-winning team with 19-year-old Gregg Warburton the only newcomer for Rio, whilst Simon Munn shall be competing in his seventh Paralympics and Terry Bywater in his fifth Games. Women's coach Myles Thompson has chosen a youthful team with an average age of 22.5, all of whom represented GB at last year's Europeans where they secured a fifth consecutive bronze medal. Clare Griffiths (nee Strange) shall be participating in her fifth Games whilst there are seven debutants, comprising teenagers Katie Morrow (16), Charlotte Moore (17), Joy Haizelden (17) and Leah Evans (19). Great Britain has nominated Dimitri Coutya and Piers Gilliver as their fencing squad for this summer's Paralympic Games in Rio. The pair, who secured silver medals at the 2015 World Championships, shall be making their Paralympic debuts. London medals: None Competition dates: 12-16 September Venue: Youth Arena London medals: None Competition dates: 14-17 September Venue: Carioca Arena 1 Alan Ash, who shall be competing at his fifth Games, and Coral Batey, the sole female, have both been included in the 12-strong Great Britain wheelchair rugby team for Rio as they bid to secure a first medal in the sport. Ash first competed for GB at the 1996 Games in Atlanta but failed to make the squad for London 2012. Jonathan Coggan, Bulbul Hussain, Mike Kerr and Mandip Sehmi all possess previous Games experience. London medals: two (one silver, one bronze) Competition dates: 9-16 September Venue: Olympic Tennis Centre London 2012 medallists Jordanne Whiley, Lucy Shuker and Andy Lapthorne have all been nominated on the 10-strong Great Britain wheelchair tennis squad for the Rio Paralympics. Whiley and Shuker secured women's doubles bronze four years ago whilst Lapthorne claimed quad doubles silver with the now-retired Peter Norfolk. Jamie Burdekin secured bronze with Norfolk in Beijing. Teenager Alfie Hewett and quad player Antony Cotterill shall be making their debuts.

text: California regulators have accepted an offer from farmers to reduce their water usage by 25% in an effort to combat the record four-year drought. Several hundred farmers agreed to concessions following threats from state officials to curtail their water rights. California has previously mandated a 25% reduction for cities and towns. However, critics argue that state Governor Jerry Brown has failed to sufficiently reduce consumption by the farming industry's influential water rights holders. The agreement between California's Water Resources Control Board and the farmers - who have previously resisted pressure to commit to reductions - indicates the deteriorating effects of California's drought. text: Jacob Boehme remembers when he knew something was seriously wrong. It was 1998 and Boehme had endured a persistent cold for months. An Aboriginal elder positioned me between her legs and began to chant over me, he recollects. Conducting a healing ritual, she wiped the perspiration from his underarms and spread it across his head and neck. Finally, she murmured: Ahh, you must visit a Western physician. Everything appears red. I cannot assist you. Boehme received an HIV diagnosis. In a period when antiretroviral therapies were in their early stages, it was the first such news his physician had conveyed. He was overcome and nearly weeping, Boehme states. I was required to comfort him. Now aged 43, Boehme is not merely still living, he has transformed his experiences as a gay, indigenous, HIV-positive man into a solo performance. Blood on the Dance Floor, which recently appeared at the Sydney Festival, examines what our comprehension of blood signifies, from ancestry to wellness. Merging narrative and movement, the production features a sketch about being a theatrical gay elder in costume, examination of prejudice surrounding HIV within the gay community (especially when seeking a partner), and sequences where Boehme is positioned, dancing, against flowing blood, with bubbling crimson cells displayed upon the wall. Most crucially, he states, is transforming the discourse on what being HIV-positive represents. Everything depicted in the media or entertainment has always constituted some form of commemoration of the AIDS crisis from the 1980s. Everyone perishes, he explains. That bears no relevance to me and to numerous other men and women I know living with HIV. There exists no representation of a healthy functioning individual with employment and future prospects - you never observe that portrayed anywhere. Another vital measure, he states, is expanding our comprehension of who contracts the virus. According to the University of New South Wales, notification rates (the reporting of newly-diagnosed cases) of indigenous men with HIV increased twofold in the previous five years from 6.2 per 100,000 to 12.4 per 100,000. By comparison, non-indigenous notification rates decreased by 12%, stated the report by the university's Kirby Institute. Despite this, education campaigns predominantly remain targeted towards white men, states Boehme. Recall the last occasion you observed an HIV education campaign featuring someone from the Aboriginal, Asian or African community on those advertisements? You only observe gay white men in their undergarments, he notes. It renders quite numerous people feeling entirely disregarded and it encompasses not only the gay male community - it includes heterosexual males living with HIV, children living with HIV as well. It has never constituted a gay white man's illness. Born in Melbourne to a non-indigenous mother and father from the Narungga and Kaurna peoples of South Australia, Boehme recognised he was gay from age four. The performer - who serves as the incoming creative director of the Melbourne Indigenous Arts Festival - has consistently received his family's support. Others frequently prove less fortunate. In certain Aboriginal communities, prejudice towards homosexuality persists, maintains Boehme. When you enter communities that continue strongly upholding the principles of the former mission era, that creates difficulties, through those Christian and distinctly Victorian concepts of sex, gender and sexuality, he states. Blood on the Dance Floor was conceived following rehearsals in a warehouse. Boehme was preoccupied with my blood, with the purity of my blood. After cutting his heel on a protruding nail, I returned to my seat and realised I had left a trail of blood across the dance floor. And [my friend] declared 'ah, there's your title'. Blood constitutes a life force that connects us, it can serve to define us and can serve to discriminate, to divide, or to actually unify, Boehme states. When composing the show, the artist maintained a small crystal vessel of his own blood upon his desk. Suddenly I was linked to my father, then my grandmother, then an entire lineage of our forebears that I never encountered and through that, those voices began to speak through me. In that blood, in those genetic codes, there exist thousands of generations residing in that small vessel. Boehme states blood connects him to his heritage and, most importantly, to his condition. But it also liberates him. Irrespective of what characteristics or skin tone we possess, truly our blood constitutes the element that binds us together, he states. A particularly intense moment in Blood on the Dance Floor addresses the suicide of Boehme's friend in 1996 after learning he was HIV-positive. It was a period when there remained this phantom hovering about as though it constituted a death sentence. There existed considerably more shame surrounding HIV and he simply could not manage. Boehme still recalls when he discovered. His friend's partner, intoxicated, declared at a dinner gathering that his companion was positive. I gazed at him. And he stated, 'I reject that expression. I reject anyone's sympathy. Do not dare present me with that expression.' Merely two years subsequently - as antiretroviral medications were being distributed to the broader population - Boehme received his own diagnosis. In Australia during the 1990s approximately 1,000 people died annually from AIDS. Today, deaths remain so minimal they are not documented. That precisely explains why I insisted we honour him, Boehme states regarding his friend. He did not receive an opportunity. In Australia, you can locate similar information at Lifeline and Beyond Blue.

text: On 15 November 37 police and crime commissioners will be elected in England, along with four in Wales. The PCCs, as they shall be known, will be charged with scrutinising their force and holding it accountable. They will also be empowered to hire and dismiss the chief constable and establish the force's budget. The commissioners will receive payment and are intended to enable local people to have a voice on how crime is addressed in their area. Nominations for candidates in South Yorkshire have now formally closed. BBC News has examined each of the police forces in advance of the elections. The county comprises a mixture of urban sprawl alongside areas where there was extensive mining, steelworks and engineering. By James VincentBBC Yorkshire Political Reporter As police forces contract and begin sharing services, the major challenge for South Yorkshire's police commissioner will be ensuring the public feel secure. We are consistently told that crime is declining here, but so is the number of police officers we possess. A council tax increase to fund one hundred additional officers is cushioning the impact of losing 400 in the past couple of years, but there are genuine concerns South Yorkshire is being asset-stripped. Divers, mounted officers and firearms teams could all shortly be shared across Yorkshire, and the challenge will be maintaining a good service whilst attempting to save money; a common theme throughout the public sector. The force chose to retain its own police helicopter and join the new National Police Air Service that should begin serving South Yorkshire in April 2013. The popularity of the helicopter is not in question, but the long-term viability of paying for two services may be an early decision for the person who is elected at the top of the police. Officers at South Yorkshire Police cover an area of 600 square miles (1,554 sq km), with some centres of population, including the city of Sheffield, and other areas of open countryside. Priorities identified by the force include improving confidence and satisfaction, alongside enhancing community safety. Senior officers have identified the tackling of serious and organised crime, terrorism and extremism as priorities throughout the county. Currently the force is headed by Chief Constable David Crompton who has a deputy and two assistant chief constables, a director of finance and an assistant chief officer responsible for human resources. South Yorkshire Police states it works closely with the county's police authority and rank and file officers' union, the Police Federation. The force is also part of the Regional Chief Constables' Group (RCCG) and the Joint Police Authorities Committee (JPAC). Together they outline the principles to guide policing delivered locally by individual forces, to communities within Yorkshire and the Humber. South Yorkshire Police Authority has established a budget of £251m for 2012/2013. The figure is based upon an increase on the police authority council tax precept of 3.95%. Based on the average Band D property, this was an increase of £5.22 from the previous year. The budget would enable the authority to defer a reduction of 110 police officers in 2012/13 and fund a further 22 police and community support officers (PCSOs) for the next three years, it claimed. The authority had also made a commitment to offset some other planned reductions in police resources in 2013 and 2014. By increasing the council tax precept the county's police authority said it hoped to secure approximately £2m annually which would balance the need for further cuts in policing from 2013 onwards. South Yorkshire Police said a snapshot of the year 2010/11 showed that total crime had fallen by 9% - burglaries had been reduced by 5%; criminal damage was down by 17%; vehicle crime had dropped by 17% and incidents of robbery were down by 14%.

text: We arrive at the Ebola Treatment Centre in the forested town of Gueckedou in South East Guinea to a grim scene. These are external links and will open in a new window A small bundle lies wrapped in white plastic sheeting, whilst grim-faced men load yellow disinfectant containers into a pick-up vehicle. We are invited to witness the heartbreaking duty they are about to undertake. We travel for several minutes into the woodland. Upon arrival, a small pit has already been dug. This represents the final resting place of Ebola's latest victim: a four-month-old infant boy named Faya. He contracted the virus from his mother, who perished several weeks previously. His becomes the 20th unmarked grave in this dark and isolated clearing. I was present with him moments before his death, states Adele Millimouno, a Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) nurse recruited from a neighbouring village. I had been giving him milk. I departed briefly for a short rest, but was then summoned back and he had died. I felt completely devastated. This represents merely another day on the front line of the current Ebola outbreak. Gueckedou was where the disease's first case was documented in March. Medical charities addressing what has become the worst Ebola outbreak in history state they anticipate the crisis will persist until at least year's end. Over 670 individuals have perished from Ebola in West Africa. Last week Nigeria became the fourth nation to confirm a fatality from the lethal virus. Médecins Sans Frontières and the International Federation of the Red Cross, which collectively deploy almost 400 international personnel combating the outbreak, state the situation across West Africa remains uncontrolled. A treatment facility in Gueckedou, operated by MSF, had - until 22 July - treated 152 Ebola patients, of whom 111 have perished. It is the survivors that Adele states provide her the strength to continue this distressing work. I summon the courage to come and labour here to help rescue my community. I feel extremely proud of our work. We have managed to save approximately 40 people. The following morning we travel in a convoy with health officials to a village 12km distant called Kollobengou. The previous time health workers attempted to enter this village they were assaulted and instructed not to return. Numerous people died before me. It was an extremely difficult period for me particularly when the young children perished. Sometimes I went outside and wept. Some people before they die, we grasp their hands, we touch their heads, we sit beside them briefly. Ebola voices: Combating the deadly virus in Guinea Many believed medics were actually introducing the virus into communities, and harvesting organs from the deceased. Others who did believe the virus existed were too frightened to seek assistance. Now, following negotiations with community leaders - and another death in the village overnight - they have consented to permit medics entry. As we enter, the fear is tangible. Residents gradually emerge from their dwellings and gather in the village centre. The local ministry of health official responsible for coordinating the battle against the virus stands and urges people not to fear and to permit health workers to question them and assess individuals who might be ill. They also distribute soap and chlorine. The virus is eliminated easily if people maintain proper personal hygiene. But as one resident observed: How can we wash constantly if we lack clean water for washing? Eventually, two families present two extremely ill relatives. They are swiftly transported to the treatment facility. Health workers were already aware of four Ebola deaths in the village. It emerges that three additional deaths have occurred. A total of 48 others have had close contact with Ebola victims. They must now be monitored daily for the three-week incubation period to ensure they do not develop the illness. Two villages in Gueckedou still refuse to admit health workers. This represents a substantial improvement from several months ago when 28 villages were resisting assistance - but remains a significant concern. Tarik Jasarevic, from the World Health Organisation, states unclear messages from health workers regarding the virus at the outbreak's beginning is partially responsible for villages closing their doors. People heard there exists no vaccine or treatment for Ebola so many thought 'why would we attend a treatment centre if no treatment exists?' Then people who eventually went, some perished. So there existed a perception that if you are removed from your village it means certain death. We did not place sufficient emphasis on the fact survivors exist and the sooner you attend the treatment centre the better chance you possess of surviving, and you are not endangering your family's health. text: More black, Asian and ethnic minority lives will be saved under an opt-out organ donation system, a charity says. Roy Thomas, the chairman of Kidney Wales Foundation (KWF), stated these groups are three times more likely to require a transplant compared to the remainder of the population. However, he stated fewer than 2% have registered with the NHS Organ Donation Register. This comes as a donor expert accused the Welsh government of misleading the assembly regarding its organ donation bill. John Fabre, professor of clinical sciences at King's College London, stated the policy was misinterpreted based upon information from Spain's system. Prof Fabre, the author of numerous papers on international systems of organ donation, claimed Spain's high donation rate resulted from the available facilities and coordination in the Spanish health service, not from the legislation. The Human Transplantation Bill, which could become law by 2015, would mean adults residing in Wales would have to opt-out of the organ donation system if they did not wish to donate after death. Presently, people must actively opt-in to become a donor. However, KWF used the example of Belgium, where only 2% of the population opted-out of a presumed consent system and stated it proved a great success with donor rates increasing by 55% in the first five years. In evidence to the assembly's health and social care committee, Mr Thomas stated a change in the law was a key component to a change in organ donation. He added: It is, however, key that the proposed legislation is implemented with the goodwill of the people of Wales. A transplant law provides only a legal environment which can influence the extent to which potential donors can be utilised. The law in proper practice will be essential. Mr Thomas told the committee: We have been campaigning for the change in the law over many years and we have a determination to see the successful implementation of the law because of the clear effect it will have in changing the cultural approach in Wales and the UK regarding organ donation. A Welsh government spokesman stated the Spanish government's website points to the adoption of appropriate legislation as one element of the success of their model for organ donation.

text: One million people who work in crowded places in the UK are to be trained over the next 12 months in how to deal with a possible terrorist attack. The scheme, to be unveiled by the National Police Chiefs Council, will witness personnel deliver police counter-terrorism training and guidance to fellow workers. The programme will expand an existing initiative, which presently witnesses police train approximately 100,000 employees annually. Police stated they require everyone to play a part in keeping the public alert. Detective Chief Superintendent Scott Wilson, the national counter-terrorism coordinator, will unveil an expansion to Project Griffin to permit existing trainers at firms to deliver police training and guidance to fellow workers. Public limited companies situated in bustling city centres - alongside those in the entertainment, sports and retail industries - will be targeted. We require everyone to play a part in keeping the public alert, not alarmed, Detective Chief Superintendent Wilson stated. Project Griffin was originally established by the City of London and Metropolitan police forces in 2004 to advise and train managers and security personnel of large organisations on how to address security and counter-terrorism matters - it has subsequently been extended to other forces throughout the UK. Police can assist in explaining what the threats and risks to different industries are, but companies are better positioned to explain to personnel precisely what action they can take to improve their security and how to respond if the worst occurs, Detective Chief Superintendent Wilson stated. He stated: Individual organisations possess vital protective security information such as building layouts, security equipment and safety procedures. They possess the local knowledge that could be crucial to keeping personnel and the public safe. BBC security correspondent Frank Gardner stated the matter of preparing for a potential terror attack had been troubling the police and intelligence agencies ever since the marauding terrorist attacks in Mumbai in 2008. And following the recent attacks in Brussels and Paris, efforts to prepare workers in busy areas will now be massively stepped up to brief one million personnel in the next 12 months, our correspondent stated. Terror attacks in Mumbai in 2008 killed 174 people, whilst attacks by gunmen and suicide bombers left 130 people dead in Paris in November last year. Last month, bomb attacks at Brussels airport and a metro station killed 32 people. The move comes amid an increase in the number of trained police firearms officers to address the possibility that criminals inspired by the so-called Islamic State could open fire in a public place using automatic weapons smuggled in from mainland Europe, our correspondent added.

text: A mother who took her toddler son to Syria has been jailed for six years for joining the so-called Islamic State. Tareena Shakil, aged 26, becomes the first British woman to return from the self-proclaimed caliphate and receive conviction for the offence. During sentencing, Mr Justice Inman stated she had demonstrated no remorse and had understood her son's destiny would ultimately be as an IS fighter. He addressed Shakil: You permitted him to be photographed beside an AK47. Shakil, of Birmingham, previously from Burton-upon-Trent in Staffordshire, acknowledged travelling to Syria whilst denying IS membership and encouraging terrorist acts through Twitter messages. Delivering sentence at Birmingham Crown Court, the judge stated: Most disturbingly you transported your toddler son to Syria understanding how he would be utilised. You accepted your function in supplying future fighters. Shakil positioned the boy, then 14 months old, for photographs wearing an IS-branded balaclava, which the judge characterised as amongst the most repugnant aspects of the case. Mr Justice Inman informed Shakil she had embraced Isis, transmitting messages upon her Syrian arrival declaring she would not return to Britain, informing her family that killing murtadeen (apostates) formed part of her faith and expressing her desire to die as a martyr. He stated it was evident she had been radicalised through online communications with prominent terrorist group members. Shakil, convicted on Friday, insisted she brought her son to Syria in October 2014 to escape an unhappy family life. Shakil departed from East Midlands Airport to Turkey, informing friends she was embarking on a family beach holiday, before crossing into Syria. However, once in the war-ravaged nation, she claimed to have become unhappy there also and chose to return voluntarily after recognising her error. She stated she boarded a bus and bribed a taxi driver for partial transportation before re-crossing into Turkey in January 2015. Sentencing her to four years for IS membership and two years consecutively for encouraging terrorist acts, Mr Justice Inman stated she would qualify for licence release after serving half her sentence. As she received imprisonment, Shakil's family members declared the proceedings a farce. Following the sentencing hearing, children's charity NSPCC commented: This represents a profoundly troubling case which could have resulted in tragedy for the toddler concerned.

text: Worcester chief executive Jim O'Toole says giving head coach Carl Hogg sole charge of the first team was necessary because players weren't getting the dual-management structure. Following former director of rugby Dean Ryan's departure on 30 June, Hogg and high performance director Nick Johnston initially divided responsibilities. However, Warriors have chosen to alter arrangements following a sequence of disappointing results. Granting Carl complete leadership is now appropriate for us, O'Toole informed BBC Sport. It all returns to Dean Ryan's exit during the summer. When he departed, beyond his substantial experience and rugby knowledge, what we effectively lost at brief notice just prior to the season's commencement was his management level. Carl, as head coach beneath Dean, was accountable for the first team. Nick was accountable for the athletes and their preparation. We made a decision then to pioneer a dual-management system, which I've heard (England boss) Eddie Jones discuss as being how the southern hemisphere operates it. He's a strong supporter of that type of structure. Following six months, we assessed it. My opinion, shared with my fellow directors, was that the players weren't understanding it. Nick remains in his position, but streamlining the management by granting Carl complete leadership is the correct action to take. Ultimately, the players must be clear regarding what they're here to accomplish. Injury-affected Warriors have secured just two victories in 14 matches this season, achieving only one win and two draws in the Premiership. After Sunday's 26-12 home loss to Wasps, they sit 11th in the table, six points above bottom club Bristol, where they will visit on Boxing Day. Having previously endured relegation twice since first achieving Premiership status in 2004, their present troubles, whilst intensified by an extensive injury list, have prompted criticism from disappointed supporters. O'Toole has responded to that by organising a meeting with 40 of the club's more frequent critics, and regards managing dissatisfied customers as a significant aspect of his role. Contemporary communication channels are accessible to everyone, he stated. I maintain daily communication with supporters on Twitter, on club forums, on email, telephone and text messaging. I've even received messages sent to me on Facebook Messenger from individuals who I'm not friends with, who insist on conveying their message and like to inform me how matters can be enhanced. I didn't arrive to manage a rugby club to socialise with the players. text: Afghanistan's two presidential election candidates have agreed to an audit in an attempt to resolve a dispute over the result of last month's vote, US Secretary of State John Kerry has said. Both candidates, Abdullah Abdullah and Ashraf Ghani, have consented to accept the outcome. The examination of all 8m ballot papers would commence within 24 hours, Mr Kerry stated. Provisional results indicate Mr Ghani has prevailed, but both candidates accuse each other of electoral fraud. Results declared by Afghanistan's electoral officials grant Mr Ghani 56.44% of votes in the 14 June run-off, with Mr Abdullah securing 43.45%. The results were notably different from those obtained in the initial round of voting, conducted in April, when Mr Ghani finished a distant second. Afghanistan's present President Hamid Karzai, who assumed office following the US-led removal of the Taliban, is departing after more than 10 years. He has endorsed the audit and consented to postpone his successor's inauguration to permit time for the examination, which is anticipated to require several weeks. At a press conference with the two candidates, Mr Kerry declared that every single ballot would be audited. This represents the strongest possible indication by both candidates of a wish to restore legitimacy to the process and to Afghan democracy, he stated. Ballots in Kabul would be examined first, and the International Security and Assistance Force (Isaf) would transport the remainder from the provinces, he added. The agreement was forged in two days of intensive negotiations and extends much further than many Afghans had anticipated, the BBC's Karen Allen in Kabul reports. It demonstrates how much international political, military and financial commitment depends on ensuring Afghanistan does not regress into violence, our correspondent notes. At the press conference, Mr Ghani characterised the move as the most comprehensive audit in the history of elections... such a process would eliminate any uncertainty about the result. Meanwhile, Mr Abdullah stated the two sides had achieved a technical and political agreement. I trust this serves the benefit of Afghan people, he added. Vote counting is to commence early on Sunday morning, with the ballot boxes being transported under strict security to counting venues. The votes will remain under constant protection until new results are revealed. The structure for a unity government may be taking shape, but the particulars about the potential division of power remain unclear. Mr Kerry arrived on Friday for a hastily organised visit, amid concerns over reports that Mr Abdullah was considering a parallel government. Speaking on Saturday as the audit was announced, Mr Kerry cautioned of a challenging road ahead due to important obligations required and difficult decisions to be made. He added: We trust that the promise of the coming weeks will deliver the authenticity and credibility that the people of Afghanistan deserve. Analysts suggest Mr Ghani and Mr Abdullah both possess strong support and any division in the government or armed forces could compromise the country's stability.
