text: The number of hours that ambulances spent waiting at A&Es in the North West of England has more than doubled in the past two years, the BBC has found. Freedom of Information data reveals an increase from 17,413 hours in 2013-14 to 46,160 in 2015-16 exceeding the standard 15-minute handover period. Every trust in the region except one has experienced increases with waiting times rising six-fold at the Royal Liverpool Hospital. North West Ambulance Service stated that demand for emergency care is increasing. The Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals' Trust stated it had recently recruited several hospital-trained paramedics in its emergency department to assist in the safe handover of patients to return ambulances to the road. At national level, merely one of the UK's 13 ambulance services is presently achieving its target to reach seriously ill and injured patients, the investigation discovered. Delays have also been attributed to a crisis in social care provision resulting in bed-blocking caused by delays in the discharge of elderly patients. During the period covered by the FoI, the number of hours spent by ambulance crews waiting to hand over patients at North West A&E units increased by 167% with numerous hospitals experiencing even greater increases: Aintree Hospital in Merseyside, where last week 20 ambulance staff were photographed waiting to hand over patients owing to a surge in 999 calls, recorded a 234% increase. One paramedic at Aintree stated they spent more than half of their shift standing in corridors. The sole hospital where handover times actually decreased was Wythenshawe in Manchester where the number of hours has fallen by 9%. We have all witnessed stories of lengthy waits at A&E - detrimental for patients but detrimental for ambulance crews too. Put simply if they are trapped in a hospital, they are not out on the road addressing other emergencies. Simply to clarify these totals, ambulance services permit 15 minutes to hand patients over. These figures represent the number of additional hours they have been required to spend waiting to accomplish that. For the previous financial year, that totalled 46,160 hours for the North West - a substantial increase on two years earlier when it was just under 17,500. So why are the figures increasing so dramatically? Well, the number of people attending A&E is steadily increasing as the population ages. But several hospital trusts are also highlighting the gaps in social care provision, particularly for the elderly. One trust informed me they currently had the equivalent of three wards being occupied by people who should not be in hospital at all, simply because there was not anywhere suitable for them to go. And if those beds are occupied, that means there are fewer for the patients arriving at A&E. Overall, handover delays at hospitals across England, Wales and Northern Ireland have demonstrated a 52% increase in the previous two years. Lisa Grant, chief nurse at the Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals, stated: Hospitals across the area are collaborating with partners in community and social care to help to safely discharge patients who no longer require hospital care, providing beds for those in the emergency department who need to be admitted to a ward. A statement from the North West Ambulance Service stated: We are witnessing more and more people in need of our services, especially for Red incidents for patients with serious and life-threatening conditions. This contributes to additional activity at hospital emergency departments. During busy periods this can regrettably result in ambulance crews having to wait longer to hand over patients into the care of hospital staff before they can be clear to respond to other emergencies.

text: A chronology of key events: 9th century - The County of Barcelona was established alongside several other counties as a consequence of Charlemagne's endeavours to create a buffer zone between his Frankish Empire and Muslim-controlled Spain. 1023-76 - Under Ramon Berenguer I, the county of Barcelona obtains a dominant position within the region. 12th cent - Initial reference to the term Catalonia appears. 1131-1162 - Reign of Ramon Berenguer IV, whose marriage to Queen Petronilla of Aragon leads to the county's dynastic union with the Kingdom of Aragon. Despite forming part of the Crown of Aragon, Catalonia retains its own traditional rights and parliament, the Corts catalanes. 14th-15th cents - Aragon obtains the kingdoms of Sardinia, Sicily and Naples, becoming a major Mediterranean maritime empire consequently. 1469 - Ferdinand I of Aragon and Queen Isabella of Castile wed, establishing a dynastic union of their kingdoms and laying the foundations of the Kingdom of Spain. 1492 - Christopher Columbus's discovery of the Americas initiates the creation of Spain's overseas empire, the shift of commercial activity from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic and the decline of Catalonia's economic and political significance. 1640-52 - The Reapers' War - Catalonia rebels against Philip IV of Spain's taxation policies, is briefly declared a republic under French protection before being reoccupied by Spanish forces. 1705-14 - War of the Spanish Succession. Catalonia's support for rival claimant to the Spanish throne, Archduke Charles of Austria, of the House of Habsburg, against King Philip V, from the House of Bourbon, leads to the suppression of its parliament and traditional liberties upon the latter's victory. 1716 - The Nueva Planta decree dismantles the separate Catalan legal system, brings Catalonia under direct rule from Madrid and abolishes the administrative use of the Catalan language. 1812-13 - Napoleon briefly annexes Catalonia to France, before French forces withdraw from Barcelona under an armistice signed with the Duke of Wellington. 1808-33 - Catalonia becomes the scene of some of the most intense fighting of the First Carlist War between the liberal supporters of Queen Isabella II and the absolutist supporters of her uncle and rival, the Infante Carlos. 19th cent - Catalonia stands at the forefront of industrialisation in Spain and experiences a cultural renaissance; beginning of a movement to revive Catalan culture and language, leading to the rise of Catalan nationalism. 1901 - Establishment of the Catalan nationalist Regionalist League. The legacy of Gen Franco's dictatorial rule still looms over relations between Catalonia and Madrid Buried unpleasant truths? 1913 - The four provinces of Catalonia are granted limited joint self-government in the Commonwealth of Catalonia under the leadership of Enric Prat de la Riba. 1925 - The Commonwealth is suppressed during the dictatorship of Spanish Prime Minister Miguel Primo de Rivera. 1931 - Spain becomes a republic; an autonomous Catalan regional government, the Generalitat, is established under the leadership of the Revolutionary Left of Catalonia. 1936 - Insurrection of Spanish nationalist troops led by Gen Francisco Franco triggers the Spanish Civil War. Catalonia remains loyal to the Republic, with both the Generalitat's regular forces and popular militias fighting on its side. 1938 - English author George Orwell publishes Homage to Catalonia, a memoir of his time fighting with left-wing Republican forces in the region. 1938-9 - Franco's forces overrun Catalonia, paving the way for the collapse of Republican resistance elsewhere in Spain. 1939-75 - Franco dictatorship; suppression of political opposition as well as Catalan autonomy, language and culture. Thousands of Catalan activists are executed or go into exile. 1960s - Catalonia benefits from the beginning of mass tourism in coastal Spain and increasing industrialisation. Barcelona attracts large numbers of migrants from other Spanish regions. 1975 - Death of Franco sets in motion a process of democratisation under the new king, Juan Carlos. 1977 - Restoration of a provisional regional government, again named the Generalitat, under the leadership of Josep Tarradellas. 1978 - New democratic Spanish Constitution recognises existence of distinct national communities within Spain, beginning of the process of regionalisation. 1979 - Catalonia granted a statute of autonomy and recognised as a nationality. Catalan becomes the joint official language of Catalonia with Spanish. 1980 - Centre-right moderate nationalist Convergence and Union wins first elections to the new regional parliament. Its leader, Jordi Pujol, becomes the first president of the new regional government. 1992 July-August - Summer Olympic Games in Barcelona. 2003 - Jordi Pujol retires as president of the regional government, after 23 years in the post. 2003 November - Despite winning the largest number of seats in regional elections, Convergence and Union is ousted for the first time in 23 years by a coalition of Socialists, the Revolutionary Left and Greens. Socialist Pasqual Maragall becomes regional president. 2006 June - Pasqual Maragall stands down, is replaced by fellow Socialist Jose Montilla. 2006 August - Reformed version of Catalonia's autonomy statute comes into force, granting the regional government greater powers and financial autonomy. Its preamble also uses the word nation to describe Catalonia. 2009 December - Between December 2009 and April 2011, Catalan nationalists hold a series of informal, non-binding votes on independence in regional towns and cities, including the capital Barcelona. 2010 July - Constitutional Court in Madrid strikes down part of the 2006 autonomy statute, ruling that there is no legal basis for recognising Catalonia as a nation within Spain and that Catalan should not take precedence over Castilian in the region. The decision is criticised by the regional government. Regional parliament votes to ban bullfighting, making Catalonia the first region of mainland Spain to do so. 2010 November - The centre-right nationalists Convergence and Union - led by Artur Mas returns to power after regional elections. 2011 September - Ban on bullfighting comes into force in Catalonia. 2012 August - Catalonia asks the Spanish government for a 5bn-euro bailout. 2012 September - Some 1.5m people take part in Catalonia's annual independence rally in Barcelona, amid growing Catalan anger at financial transfer from the region to the rest of Spain. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy rebuffs a call by regional leader Artur Mas for greater fiscal independence. 2012 November - Snap elections held to provide support for a referendum on independence see the governing Convergence and Union losing ground to the left-wing Republican Left (ERC) party. Both support independence but the ERC opposes the Catalan government's spending cuts. Pro-independence moves 2012 December - Regional head Artur Mas is re-elected after his Convergence and Union signs a governing pact with the left-wing ERC. Both parties support holding a referendum on secession from Spain in 2014. 2013 January - Catalonia's regional parliament approves a declaration of sovereignty aimed at paving the way for a referendum on independence from Spain in 2014. 2014 March - Spain's constitutional court rules that a planned referendum in November on Catalonia's independence is unconstitutional. 2014 April - Spanish parliament rejects proposal by Catalonia's regional assembly to hold a referendum on independence in November. 2014 September - Regional President Artur Mas signs a decree calling for a non-binding referendum on independence to take place in November. Spain's constitutional court suspends the plans, saying it needs time to consider the vote's constitutionality. 2014 October - Regional President Artur Mas insists a non-binding referendum on independence for the region in November will proceed, but under a different legal framework, after the original plan was ruled unconstitutional. 2014 November - More than 80% of those taking part in a non-binding informal vote on separation from Spain opt for independence. About two million out of 5.4 million eligible voters cast ballots. 2015 January - Regional President Artur Mas calls new regional elections for 27 September to gauge support for a possible declaration of independence.

If England is to win in India they need to make the best use they can of the man who may not be the most popular in the world, but who can be shown to be committed to English cricket. Joe Root, Alex Hales, and Nick Compton are among those who can vie for the place of Cook's partner. I think it will be easier to find a replacement at the top than at the bottom. One solution would be to promote Jonathan Trott to the number one position in the batting order, leaving Bell at No. 3. However, it is clear that Cook has an enormous task ahead of him, and it will not be easy. He will need all the help and support that his senior players can give him. It is easier to bring a new young opening batsman into the team than to ask a middle-order batsman to open.

text: As Westminster does from time to time, there is a frothing row this morning over where a memo - which purports to reveal the government's private Brexit woes and is splashed on the front of The Times - actually comes from. To suggest that Downing Street is cross would be an understatement. They are incandescent at the story emerging, not merely because the allegations within it are embarrassing and criticise the prime minister's approach, but because they maintain the document was not authored by anyone with genuine comprehension of what is occurring, but by a consultant, believed to be from the company Deloitte, whose assessment formed part of a proposal for work. The Times refutes that, stating that senior civil servants were indeed also engaged. However whoever is correct, the document does signify because it emphasises what we have reported and others have documented about repeatedly. Five months following the referendum, the cabinet is battling to agree a shared position on what Brexit means Brexit actually signifies. There exists a spectrum of opinion around the table, and an enormous amount of work has been commissioned across government to assist in settling upon a view. The Department that is working on the plan, DEXEU, (or Dexit as it is simpler to call it if we can manage it to catch on) has commissioned 51 separate studies of different sectors of the economy to 'assist'. However as a senior source indicated this week they simply do not know what they are going to do - the entire thing is a dreadful mess. Information is accumulating, decisions are not. And with a very narrow majority in the Commons, ministers are concerned about losing the arguments and attempting to avoid major confrontations. The prime minister's holding position of Brexit means Brexit is coming under genuine pressure now. Downing Street was always conscious that it could not last. Until that changes they will remain vulnerable to the accusations set out in the memo, whoever its author, and the accusations of chaos from the opposition.

text: More than 150 people in Wales have been reported to police for meeting children following sexual grooming over the last five years, new figures show. Dyfed-Powys Police recorded the highest number of complaints with 60, whilst North Wales registered the lowest with 26. Nearly 60 per cent of the offences reported between 2011 and 2015 involved online grooming. NSPCC Cymru seeks mandatory online safety education to be incorporated into the curriculum. Data secured by the charity through the Freedom of Information Act revealed 155 complaints were lodged against adults charged with meeting a child under 16 years following sexual grooming. South Wales Police recorded 35 reports whilst Gwent Police received 34. Dyfed-Powys Police recorded the highest number of offences involving online grooming with 37, followed by Gwent Police with 22, North Wales Police with 17 and South Wales Police with 16. NSPCC Cymru has demanded compulsory online safety education in schools from September to instruct pupils about the risks of social media and online grooming. NSPCC chief executive Peter Wanless stated: Education is the key to teaching children how to use the internet safely so they do not find themselves at risk of serious harm. Online safety is a 21st century child-protection challenge and it is something that we must tackle head on. The Welsh Government stated it maintained an extensive e-safety education programme, which incorporated online resources and classroom materials to help pupils think critically, behave safely, and participate responsibly online. We have also established an online one-stop shop, Hwb, providing assistance for children and young people to stay safe on the web, a spokesman stated. South Wales Police, Dyfed-Powys and Gwent Police stated they collaborated with schools to educate pupils on issues including grooming, sexual exploitation, the taking and sharing of inappropriate images and staying safe online. Gwent Police Superintendent Leanne Brustad stated the force delivered 1,874 lessons to nearly 50,000 pupils in 2014/15, whilst South Wales Assistant Chief Constable Jon Drake stated it collaborated with agencies to ensure those working with young people understood the signs of such abuse. Dyfed-Powys Police stated it had allocated additional resources to addressing the issue and it maintained a team of digital detectives, forensic computer and mobile phone investigators. North Wales Police has been approached for comment.

text: A US appeals court has overturned the money laundering conviction of a once-powerful former Republican congressman, citing insufficient evidence. Tom DeLay was found guilty in 2010 of unlawfully channelling corporate funds to Republican political candidates in Texas. By a 2-1 majority, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the jury's verdict, determining that prosecutors had failed to demonstrate the money was tainted. Mr DeLay, initially elected to Congress in 1984, ascended to majority leader in 2003. Dubbed the hammer, Mr DeLay was celebrated for his capacity to maintain the Republican caucus strictly aligned with party policy during tight votes. The Texan congressman and former pest control entrepreneur stepped down in June 2006 after his indictment on money laundering charges and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Federal prosecutors stated that during the 2002 mid-term election campaign, Mr DeLay's assistants accepted £121,935 ($190,000) contributed by corporate lobbyists to a campaign committee under his control and transferred it to a division of the Republican National Committee. That organisation subsequently allocated the money to seven state legislative candidates. Six of these candidates prevailed, granting the Republican Party dominance of the Texas House of Representatives, which subsequently enacted a redistricting scheme that delivered additional Republicans to Washington in 2004, strengthening Mr DeLay's grip on authority. Mr DeLay maintained the exchange was lawful and that no corporate funds were provided to state-level candidates. He condemned the prosecution as a political vendetta. A Texas jury found him guilty in November 2010. The subsequent January he received a three-year prison sentence but was permitted to remain at liberty pending appeal. On Thursday, the appeals court determined that the prosecution had failed in its obligation to demonstrate that the funds delivered to the seven candidates were ever tainted. Mr DeLay's solicitor, Brian Wice, informed the Associated Press that Mr DeLay felt vindicated. He's elated. He's satisfied. He's simply somewhat stunned, he stated. I'm hoping that with today's triumph, he shall be able to resume his life as he previously knew it.

text: A Taser gun was used three times in less than 30 seconds as police tried to apprehend a man who had killed a woman, an inquest has heard. These are external links and will open in a new window Matthew Williams was discovered assaulting Cerys Yemm, 22, at the Sirhowy Arms Hotel, Argoed, on 6 November 2014. Williams, 34, was subjected to a Taser by police who detained him and he subsequently died. Gwent Coroner's Court in Newport also heard there were bite marks on Miss Yemm's body and lacerations that could have been inflicted by a broken ceramic cereal bowl. Michael Rees, a South Wales Police armourer, examined Tasers employed by all officers involved in attempting to arrest Williams. He told the inquest only one had been utilised, it was partially covered in blood and had been activated four times during the incident. It was deployed at 01:37:11 and then at 01:44:14, 01:44:28 and 01:44:41. Forensic scientist Gillian O'Boyle examined the scene and said it contained 15 pieces of broken crockery that fitted together to form an almost complete cereal bowl. Most of these had blood on them, with DNA analysis showing it belonged to Miss Yemm and Williams. She concluded: The pattern of the blood was as if the bowl had been employed to strike an individual and had broken as part of this, but said she could not say who had been holding it. There were also cuts in Miss Yemm's clothing, that could have been inflicted by a sharp-edged item, such as a ceramic piece, Ms O'Boyle added. Forensic dentist Romina Carabott concluded that three bite marks on Miss Yemm's abdomen and another on her wrist were probably all inflicted by Williams. Williams, released from prison two weeks before the incident, was found to have 12.2 grams of class B mephedrone, 9.9 grams of mephedrone mixed with monosodium glutamate and 1.02 grams of amphetamine sulphate mixed with caffeine. Forensic pathologist Dr Richard Jones, who conducted Miss Yemm's post mortem examination, told the inquest he found 24 areas of injury across her body with at least 89 separate injuries. Half of the injuries were to her head, and Dr Jones said the cause of death was given as sharp force trauma to the face and neck. He added that bite marks had no bearing on her death, nor did traces of amphetamines and cannabis in her body. The inquest continues.

text: All photographs by Olivia Acland These are external links and will open in a new window Throughout its 11-year civil war, Sierra Leone gained notoriety for blood diamonds. Rebel and government forces battled savagely over diamond-rich territories in the country's north and financed themselves through selling the gems to international purchasers. Fourteen years following the conflict's conclusion, diamond extraction operations continue in the northern district of Kono. A South African firm, Koidu Holdings, operates a substantial mine employing advanced machinery to blast through kimberlite and locate diamond-rich zones in the deep earth. Adjacent to this, artisanal miners occupy river banks, equipped with sieves, spades and buckets. One such miner, Philo, has laboured in Kono for the previous 23 years, but was forced out during the conflict and resided in Guinea as a refugee. When the war subsided in December 2000, he returned home and resumed diamond mining again one year later. Numerous artisanal miners will acknowledge that they have not discovered a diamond in months and remain desperately impoverished. Nevertheless in a nation where 70% youth unemployment exists, mining at least offers some form of livelihood. Most men mine in a team of three. Philo collaborates with two companions. One dives to collect a bucket of mud and grit from the riverbed, whilst another man secures him so he does not drift with the current. The third gathers the bucket and empties it into a pile. Once sufficient material exists, the sifting commences. The three men exchange roles regularly, to prevent becoming too cold. Philo complains of chills when he emerges from the water and consumes a packet of cheap rum to warm himself, stating: This work is tough and physically demanding - if I possessed the qualifications or opportunity to pursue another job then I would immediately. The marshy area surrounding the river has been excavated by artisanal miners, who are scattered throughout, urgently collecting mud and sifting through it. Finally, after three hours of sifting, Philo is delighted to have discovered a tiny diamond. Some miners can invest in what is termed a rocker. They employ a power hose to spray water through a layer of mud piled onto fine mesh. Once the mud is cleared they are more likely to identify a glinting diamond. However, Philo lacks this luxury. We cannot afford this type of machinery, we must manage with merely a bucket, spade and shaker [sieve], he states. In the local market each shaker costs 25,000 Leones (approximately £3.50). Shortly after Philo has found a diamond, he packs up early and travels into town with his team. He is content, stating: This was a very good day, we had not seen a diamond for nearly a month. On the route to his house, he encounters his elder brother outside a shop. They greet each other before the rocky kimberlite mountain that has been formed by Koidu Holdings' blasts. Philo states that he envies their machinery and wealth, particularly as diamonds in shallow ground are becoming depleted. Back home, Philo relaxes in his room with his uncle. During the conflict his mother was shot and killed by rebels, just outside the room in which he now sits. His entire house was burnt down and required rebuilding. The following day Philo travels into Koidu town to sell his diamond in an office just off the high street. The current rate is $3,200 (£2,520) for a carat that is 40% pure, and considerably less for gems of lower purity. Philo receives only $35 (approximately £28) for his discovery, but he is satisfied as it exceeds his expectations.

On the way, he meets his older brother outside a store. At the local market each diamond costs twenty-five thousand leones, or about a pound and a half. At home, Philo is resting in his uncle’s room; they meet outside in front of the mass of rock blasted by Koidu Holdings, and Philo says he envies them their machines and their wealth, especially as the d’Argentiers’ shallow diggings are nearly exhausted. He is satisfied, and says, “It was a good day; we haven’t had a diamond in nearly a month.” In the war, his mother had been killed by a band of rebels, just outside the room where he now sat. The house was burned down, and had to be rebuilt. The next day Philo set out for Koidu to sell his diamond in a shop on the outskirts of town. The current price is 3,200 francs per pound of gold of forty per cent, and much less for the impure ones. Phileas had only been able to obtain thirty-five francs, or about twenty-eight pounds, for his find, but he was well satisfied, for the amount exceeded his expectations.

text: This morning on the Today programme, Ed Miliband prayed in aid Sir Nick Macpherson when repeating his view that the big economic mistake of the last Labour government was a failure to regulate the banks properly, rather than to spend too much. Sir Nick serves as the Treasury's permanent secretary, the second most influential civil servant in Britain and the individual upon whom George Osborne as chancellor depends most heavily for fiscal advice and policy implementation. In a review of a book on austerity by Bill Keegan, the leading figure among Keynesian economic commentators, Sir Nick wrote: The 2008 crisis was a banking crisis pure and simple. Excessive risk had accumulated in the system; the regulators failed to recognise the magnitude of that risk or to tackle it. It was 'a failure of the Group of Seven economic policymaking establishment', myself included. Inevitably, nations with larger banking sectors, notably the UK, suffered greater damage. Or to express it differently, Sir Nick is raising his hands and acknowledging that he and the remainder of the economic decision-making elite in the wealthy developed nations were blind to the reckless risks being assumed by banks in their quest for profits and bonuses. He is acknowledging that the UK Treasury depended far too heavily on revenues produced by the swollen financial services sector: corporation taxes paid by banks on their inflated profits proved to be unsustainable; equally transient was capital gains tax and stamp duty generated by bubbles in the property market and in financial securities, both of which were inflated by banks' irresponsible provision of finance. This serves to explain why when the Conservatives say that Labour overspent and Ed Miliband maintains the UK's economic difficulties were entirely the result of a global banking crisis, they are contradicting each other far less than may seem the case. As I stated on Friday, Gordon Brown and his economic advisers - who included Nick Macpherson from the impartial civil service, together with Ed Balls and Ed Miliband from his party - felt confident increasing spending by four percentage points of GDP from 2000 to 2007, partly because of their confidence that the expansion of the City and of tax revenues linked with that expansion would not prove a brief windfall for the Treasury. Brown was mistaken, as were Macpherson, Balls and Miliband. That mistake has been granted official recognition, as it were: with the advantage of hindsight, both the IMF and the OECD have determined that the UK's cyclically adjusted deficit - the portion of the gap between spending and revenues that normal growth will not eliminate - was larger in the UK than in other major wealthy countries. Therefore according to the IMF, in 2007 the cyclically adjusted deficit was 5.3% in the UK, compared with 3.5% in the US and 3.7% in France. And one significant reason for the UK's larger so-called structural deficit was that financial services constitutes a vastly bigger proportion of the UK economy than of the US economy and that of any other of our principal competitors. None of which serves to absolve the Labour government of Brown, Miliband and Balls. They must be held accountable for making substantial and significant long-term public spending commitments on the foundation of money produced by a swollen banking sector that could not be depended upon. That said, it is worth observing that only days before Northern Rock collapsed, and City euphoria disappeared, George Osborne as shadow chancellor was promising to match the Labour government's pledges to continue raising public expenditure. In other words, Osborne was effectively part of Sir Nick Macpherson's blinkered economic establishment. Even so, it does not make Brown, Miliband and Balls less blameworthy that Osborne also failed to recognise that the government was living beyond its means. They were in office, he was not. Which is why many voters appear to be saying that if Miliband and Balls wish to pursue their argument that Cameron and Osborne have failed to restore living standards for millions, they need to make a better attempt at accepting responsibility for the initial damage to those living standards.

text: Pressure is increasing on world powers and Iran to sew up a deal on Iran's nuclear programme after many months of negotiations. Should an accord be reached, debilitating sanctions that have impacted daily existence in Iran shall be removed. BBC Persian received accounts from ordinary Iranians regarding their expectations for the discussions. The atomic negotiations influence every Iranian citizen's existence. The cause is inflation resulting from sanctions. Numerous households can no longer manage to exist as they previously did. Should they fail to secure an accord presently whilst President Rouhani remains in power, both parties shall encounter considerable difficulties ahead. Iran's economy has been devastated since the most recent sanctions upon the petroleum and financial sectors. I possess three manufacturing plants. Eight years previously they operated at maximum capacity, presently all three have closed. Approximately 400 labourers, technicians and engineers have become unemployed. There exist many individuals like myself who previously owned small production enterprises in manufacturing towns. Currently our graveyards are expanding more rapidly and performing better than our manufacturing towns. I monitored every moment of the previous negotiation round. Should you recall, one could genuinely observe the tension upon John Kerry's countenance. It demonstrates Mr Obama requires finding a method to settle this issue. Regardless of how powerful the lobbying groups are on the opposing side, I consider the American president is resolved to secure an agreement and he can accomplish that. I remain pessimistic. As our leader states we do not trust America, Britain or the West generally. Presently we observe that certain individuals in Iran have placed their confidence in them and believe they can advance matters through negotiation, and the [Supreme] leader has consented to that. It is occurring but personally, I consider the process shall fail. It is merely a matter of timing. I do not believe an agreement is achievable. There exist numerous entrenched factions in Iran such as the Basij [volunteer paramilitary organisation] and most significantly those connected to the Supreme Leader's office. These factions shall not permit it to occur and citizens will continue experiencing the burden. I am a farmer yet I cannot market the rice I cultivate. It is unjust to our citizens. I am an educator. I am monitoring negotiations with anticipation. Yet occasionally it seems as though it continues indefinitely. Regardless I do not believe we shall observe any substantial changes immediately. Transformation will require time to accomplish. It shall not occur the day following an agreement.

text: Almost half (45%) of young people are checking their mobile phones after they have gone to bed, a poll suggests. These are external links and will open in a new window A survey of 2,750 pupils aged 11 to 18 revealed one in 10 acknowledged examining their mobile telephones for notifications at least 10 times nightly. The research was conducted by Digital Awareness UK and the Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference. The organisations caution that nocturnal mobile usage results in students arriving at school exhausted and incapable of concentrating. They suggest implementing a digital detox and removing mobile devices for 90 minutes before bedtime or maintaining them outside the bedroom. Of the 45 per cent of survey participants who examine their telephones when they ought to be sleeping, nearly all (94 per cent) are using social media - with one-tenth stating they would experience anxiety about missing out if they failed to check their device before sleeping. Within this group, 75 per cent are listening to music and more than half (57 per cent) are viewing films. One-third (32 per cent) of these young people state their parents remain unaware that they check their mobile device after retiring to bed. The results also demonstrate: Charlotte Robertson, DAUK co-founder, stated: One of the most significant topics currently is excessive social media consumption and how it affects our physical and emotional wellbeing. Many of them [children] are awakening sometimes with more than 100 notifications from conversations that occurred overnight. They wish to be that individual who responds at 01:00, and appears quite fashionable, to ensure they catch the joke - it constitutes a major driver, that anxiety of wanting to know what has occurred. HMC chairman Mike Buchanan stated: The data indicates those who check their telephones are primarily motivated by not wanting to miss out. Evidently there are occasions when children are not concentrating because they are tired, and that produces an obvious impact on their capacity to keep pace with what is happening - there exists a desire to remain within the group. It is not that this [technology] is entirely dreadful and terrible and that we should all be wringing our hands. It is rather a matter that here is the reality, let us utilise it and attempt to influence the use of technology in a positive manner.

text: So Eddie Jones has gone from South Africa's Stormers to England's strugglers, from Cape of Good Hope to capable of good, it is to be hoped. The agreement has been reached swiftly but it remains no less significant for that. Never previously has the England rugby union side been guided by a foreign coach. That they shall be presently owes much to Jones' substantial coaching credentials and something to his availability compared with that of the other preferred candidates. It is also attributable to the flip-flop - not the rubber-soled footwear favoured upon the beaches of Jones' native Australia, but the tendency of those responsible for such appointments in English sport to select the polar opposite of whoever was considered to have last failed in the position. This is a strategy perfected by the Football Association and adopted by others since. One can trace the reversals back through the years: economical and understated Roy Hodgson replacing the costly and authoritarian Fabio Capello, a vastly experienced foreign name to succeed the inexperienced and overwhelmed Englishman Steve McClaren, himself the vociferous antithesis of detached Sven Goran Eriksson, who secured the position initially because he was regarded as a composed tactical genius compared with the passionate yet naive Kevin Keegan. Keegan, man of the people, succeeded the eccentric and isolated Glenn Hoddle. Born-again Christian Hoddle followed Terry Venables - who had resigned to clear his reputation in connection with off-field business matters. Venables' international experience and attractive playing style contrasted with the direct British fundamentals of Graham Taylor. And so forth, and so into other sports. England cricket exchanged taciturn foreigner Duncan Fletcher for the ebullient and homegrown Peter Moores. When Moores proved lacking in international experience and authority, he was succeeded by steely Zimbabwean Andy Flower, former world number one-ranked batsman. Then, when Flower was considered too stern, the cheerful Moores was recalled, quickly to be dismissed again when the same shortcomings became evident - and succeeded this time by a wise old Australian in Trevor Bayliss. Media playback is not supported on this device The RFU has long followed the same pattern, ever since Sir Clive Woodward departed the Twickenham hot-seat. Andy Robinson too stern? Introduce the attacking philosophy of Brian Ashton. Ashton lacking authority? Summon the dark charisma of Martin Johnson. Johnson exposed in the first coaching position he had ever undertaken? Time for Stuart Lancaster, a grassroots coach with minimal public recognition. Which brings us to Jones. Lancaster possessed one season of Premiership experience before he was appointed to the England position, a season which concluded with a financially-strapped Leeds side being relegated back to the Championship. He had never previously attended a rugby match at the Millennium Stadium or the Stade de France. Jones? Jones has coached everywhere - at two different Super Rugby teams in Australia, as an assistant to Jake White for the South African national team, in England with Saracens and with Japan in the three years preceding the last World Cup. He has guided the Wallabies to one World Cup final and assisted the Springboks in winning the next in 2007. Whether he is the correct man for England remains less certain. No other union possesses the financial or playing resources enjoyed by the RFU. It is one of the reasons why, unlike Wales, Scotland and Ireland, it has always reached into its vast hinterland for the man to lead its national team. Even now the logic can be challenged. RFU chief executive Ian Ritchie insisted that Lancaster's successor must possess international experience. That makes sense if Lancaster's shortcomings were the sole benchmark - but not on other criteria. Lancaster failed for various reasons. Not all of them are present in every other English coach, simply because they share the same nationality. text: Mexico's Congress has approved sweeping changes to the country's energy industry which will see private oil contracts awarded in the country for the first time since 1938. Fresh legislation approved on Wednesday will open the marketplace to international petroleum companies. Consequently, state-controlled energy corporation Pemex will forfeit the monopoly it has maintained since nationalisation. President Enrique Pena Nieto has positioned energy reform as the centrepiece of his government. He anticipates the modifications will restore production to 2004 levels by 2025. Deteriorating infrastructure, bureaucracy and corruption have reduced Mexican production from 3.6 million barrels daily in 2004 to merely 2.5 million. The termination of Pemex's monopoly necessitated constitutional amendments, enacted into law last year. The reforms are anticipated to draw billions of dollars of investment into the nation, the world's ninth-largest petroleum producer. They additionally authorise private electricity generation. President Pena Nieto tweeted: A more competitive and prosperous Mexico. They have established the foundation for a new era of development and prosperity for Mexican families. Pemex, officially known as Petroleos Mexicanos, will be required to compete with international giants such as Chevron, Exxon Mobile and BP. Bidders are anticipated to begin signing fresh contracts with the Mexican state from 2015 to explore, produce and refine petroleum. Previously, they were permitted only to hold service contracts with Pemex. The dismantling of the oil industry represents the culmination of years of attempts to liberalise the Mexican economy that commenced in the early 1980s. In July, fresh legislation compelled the break-up of billionaire Carlos Slim's America Movil empire, Latin America's largest telecommunications company. The most contentious element of the energy reforms is a provision to transfer approximately one-third of the state oil company's pension debts to the federal government's balance sheet. Critics of the bill stated taxpayers would be required to bear the cost of years of mismanagement of the pension fund. To emphasise their point, they carried a life-size photograph of the late President Lazaro Cardenas, who nationalised the industry in 1938, onto the floor of the Senate.

text: The fastest animal on land rarely uses its top speed to capture prey, according to a new analysis. A study of cheetahs has revealed that instead, the creature employs extraordinary acceleration and swift changes in velocity whilst hunting. The creatures achieve this acceleration by generating nearly five times more power than that of renowned sprinter Usain Bolt during his record-setting 100m race. The results are published in the journal Nature. The findings astonished the scientist who conducted the research, Prof Alan Wilson of the Royal Veterinary College in Hatfield, UK. They are exceptional athletes - not merely in terms of their velocity, but also with their capacity to accelerate and manoeuvre in capturing the prey, he told BBC News. The maximum speed for a cheetah is frequently cited as 65mph (105km/h) - a result measured in 1965 and published in the Journal of Zoology three decades later by a scientist in Kenya. He was timing the run of a semi-domesticated cheetah running in a straight line on a firm dirt track. However, a well-fed zoo cheetah is not accustomed to running very fast - it does not need to. Consequently, few measurements of zoo cheetahs found speeds greater than that of a greyhound, approximately 40mph (64km/h). Therefore for years, researchers wondered whether cheetahs might run much faster than 65mph in the wild in order to capture prey. Prof Wilson and his team at the college's Structure and Motion Laboratory decided to find out by following five animals in the wild for a year using tracking collars fitted with movement detectors and GPS systems. They discovered that the cheetahs did indeed run very fast at times - close to 60mph - but only occasionally. On most hunts they attained approximately 30 to 35 mph but they were accelerating and changing direction much more rapidly than has been observed in any other land animal. They discovered that cheetahs could increase their speed by nearly 7mph (10km/h) in a single stride. They've arranged to have a low gear so they can accelerate very rapidly up to their top speed, said Prof Wilson. Brief bursts of speed can be quantified in power per kilogramme of the animal's weight. Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt exerted 25 W/kg during his record-breaking run in 2009. A horse used in a polo match exerts slightly more power per kg, around 30 W/kg, and a greyhound's is double that at 60 W/kg. However, a cheetah can reach 120 W/kg. The researchers also discovered that cheetahs also have a very strong grip, so much so that they rip up the ground as they run. They found it was the use of the animals' claws that enabled them to turn very sharply and to accelerate and decelerate very quickly. The measurements have only been made possible because of the collars that have been developed by Prof Wilson specifically for the experiment. It is very difficult for GPS to work on an animal that is ducking and diving, so the collar is an innovation in its own right, he said. We've been working on GPS for 12 years and the collars are the result of those labours. They are not your typical GPS tracking system that you get in the car or phone. The GPS is far more accurate we are getting positions and speeds five times a second. We combine those with readings from other instruments and we finish up with something that is very much more accurate both in terms of speed and position and very much more robust, Prof Wilson explained. The team are currently using the collars to track lions and African wild dogs to obtain comparative measurements. Follow Pallab on Twitter

They discovered that the cheetah could double his speed in a single step. In most of their hunts they only reached a maximum speed of 35 miles per hour, but they could accelerate and change direction faster than any animal on the ground. The momentary speed of an animal can be measured by the amount of power it uses per kilogram of its weight. A polo horse gives about 30 watts per kilogram, a greyhound double that, at 60 watts per kilogram. At the time of the world record, Usain Bolt achieved 25 watts per kilogram. However, a cheetah can reach 120 watts per kilogram. Scientists discovered that cheetahs also have very strong claws, to the point that they rip up the ground as they run. They also found that it was thanks to this claw that these animals could turn very quickly, accelerate and stop quickly. “We’ve been working on GPS for 12 years now, and these collars are the result. It’s not easy to apply it to an animal that squats and dives, so the collar is an invention in its own right,” Professor Wilson said. Professor Wilson explained that they did not use a simple GPS, as one gets in a car or a cell phone. “The GPS is much more accurate, and we can receive our position and speed five times a second. We combine this with measurements from other instruments, and what we have in the end is something much more accurate, both as regards position and speed, and much more reliable,” he said. The collars are being used to track lions and African wild dogs to make comparative measurements. Follow Pallab on twitter.

text: There may be one positive that comes out of the negative number issued on Wednesday morning by the Scottish government. These are external links and will open in a new window With a decline of 0.2%, October-to-December output from the Scottish economy certainly captures attention - because if there is another quarter of contraction, it is termed recession. Recessions are not the end of the world as we understand it. Indeed, an absence of recessions would break with the world as we understand it. The economic cycle is precisely that - a cycle that tends to deliver slowdowns. Australia is the only major country in modern times to have avoided recession for decades. But they are more difficult to explain where one's close neighbours are not facing the same downturn. So that gap with the UK numbers is difficult to explain away, or to ignore. There is nothing that can be done to prevent recession for Scotland now, because the quarter in question - January to March - has just ended. We can only know we are in recession long after it has started, and usually after it has ended. Confirmation of recession, or not, is scheduled for 3 July. The figures give us a bit more understanding of what has been occurring in the economy, but often raise more questions than leave clear answers. They show services flat in the final quarter of the year, and that constitutes three-quarters of the economy. Over the year, these figures point to stagnant public sector services. It is hard to count the output of health and education, but on this count, they hardly shifted. The strongest performers were financial services and, even more so, firms classified as technical, scientific and administrative support services. Construction has fallen from an elevated high in its measure of output over the past three years - a factor that has kept Scotland out of recession in past quarters. Within the production sector, there are some particularly steep falls. Manufacturing is down 8% in two years, textiles by more. Metals and machinery is down 24% in two years. It plays a big role in the supply chain for the oil and gas sector. The category including computer equipment has fallen 6% since 2013, and 44% since the start of the century. That was roughly when we stopped talking about Silicon Glen. Even food and drink - held up as the big hope for production and exports - saw output fall slightly from 2015 to 2016. Overall, if you compare the end of 2016 with the final three months of 2015, the economy is producing the same amount. It has stalled, while the UK economy is reckoned to have grown 1.9%. If you add up the four quarters of 2015 and compare them with the four quarters of 2016, you get to the anaemic growth rate of 0.4%, while the UK economy is up 1.8%. How does that compare with other economies? While Scottish output stalled, the US was up 2% between December 2015 and December 2016, the Eurozone up 1.7%. Developing economies grow faster. India was up 7% and China by nearly as much. Closer comparators to Scotland include Ireland, bouncing back from the depths with 7.2%, and Iceland doing likewise, with a bumper 11.3% growth. Norway saw 1.8% growth, not helped by the oil and gas downturn either. Sweden and Denmark saw 2.3% growth. Down in the doldrums with Scotland was Russia on 0.3% growth. Those over-dependent on oil revenues, as well as those afflicted by war, dominate the list of those with contracting economies: Brazil continued a nightmare contraction with 2.5% less output last year, and Venezuela has gone hideously wrong, down 18%. The numbers for the final quarter of 2016 make it hard to argue that the downturn has been all about the oil and gas slump, because the stalled, becalmed and contracting bits of the economy are much more widely spread. A boost from the weakening of the pound after the June referendum is not clear. Export sectors have not performed as might have been expected. And the service sector - representing three-quarters of the economy - has been flat. So what has changed that might explain this? The Scottish government looks to Brexit uncertainty. Its newly-commissioned measure of consumer sentiment tanked after the referendum - less for individual household expectations than for expectations for the economy as a whole. I asked finance secretary Derek Mackay - he was on a life science business visit just after the results came out - why Scotland is feeling the Brexit effect any differently from the rest of the UK. Perhaps Scots are better informed about what Brexit entails, he suggested. Perhaps it is because they are more pro-Europe, and therefore feel the loss of that trading relationship more keenly. Perhaps so, but something more than that has to be occurring. What else could that be? The distinctive parts of the story in Scotland include the low business start-up and growth rates, the lack of corporate headquarters in the country, and relatively poor research and development spending by businesses. Some blame over-dependence on the public sector. With a squeeze on spending, there could be a proportionately bigger effect for a country with a bigger public spend. There are issues of being at the periphery of Europe, though that does not seem to be holding back Ireland or Iceland. A more subdued (and sensible?) property market releases less equity to homeowners on which they can borrow to spend and invest more. Plus, yes, there is politics. If Brexit is pinpointed as the key source of uncertainty which has hit consumer confidence and thus hit economic growth, I asked the finance secretary if the prospect of another independence referendum is a help or a hindrance to the economy. The answer: independence can be good for the economy. Even the debate about independence can, he says, be a positive. Meanwhile, release of the latest Gross Domestic Product figures brings to mind the debate about how much statistics can be trusted, when they are based on survey evidence, on what economists can infer and impute, on educated guesses, and seasonal adjustment to smooth out volatility. There is a lively debate (some well-informed, some not) on whether the Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (GERS) figures can be trusted. In 2013 and 2014, they were trusted as the basis for the economic case made in the Scottish government's independence white paper. With less oil and gas revenue changing fiscal circumstances, they are a lot less helpful to the cause now. So what does the finance minister think, given that it is his part of the Scottish government that compiles them? GERS is a range of estimates, he tells me. A number of the statistics are based on estimates. I do not believe GERS is the starting position of an independent Scotland. It is a reflection of where we are now. So I will take those statistics at face value. But that is separate to the argument we can have about what you could do with the economic levers of an independent nation, where we could make different choices. I accept the estimates as they are, but I think we could do so much better. So if they are a reflection of where we are, are they an accurate reflection? In terms of the statistics available between the UK government statistics, the ONS (Office for National Statistics) and what the Scottish government produces, yes, they are accurate, says Mr Mackay. But they are an accurate assessment of estimates of where we are right now - not the starting position of an independent Scotland. The next set of GERS figures, covering the financial year which ends within a few hours of me writing this, is due for publication around August.

text: First-time buyers are being warned they could pay tens of thousands of pounds more interest if they sign up for 40-year mortgages. Sales of extended-term mortgages have achieved record heights, with most young purchasers opting to borrow for periods exceeding the conventional 25 years. The monthly instalments are reduced, enabling them to secure larger loans to purchase their ideal properties. However, one of Britain's largest mortgage brokers states the interest costs can soar, as purchasers must continue making payments for such extended periods. Fifteen years previously, virtually every first-time purchaser held a 25-year mortgage, yet elevated prices have compelled people to seek alternative methods to overcome the market. Currently 60% borrow for extended periods. The standard term is 30 years, though many are selecting terms of 35 or 40 years enabling them to take larger steps onto the property ladder. The immediate benefit was more advantageous than the future burden, states Chris Pearson, who has recently purchased a property with his partner Katie Baynes in Cheadle, Manchester. We had spent considerable time saving for a deposit and required a property that was sufficiently large. They hold a 40-year mortgage from Nationwide and succeeded in borrowing £300,000. I believe I shall be 72 when we have finally settled it, Chris acknowledges. The appeal is evident. One pays £948 monthly for a standard 25-year mortgage, yet only £716 when extending the term to 40 years. One achieves savings of considerably more than £200 monthly. What occurs is that the interest paid monthly remains constant whilst the capital repayments, which constitute part of the monthly charge, are distributed across a longer duration. That represents the positive aspect. The difficulty is that one must pay interest for an additional 15 years. In this instance one would pay an extra £60,000. Interest across 25 years totals approximately £84,000, whilst the sum across 40 years is £144,000, a substantial charge for borrowers. It constitutes a genuine hazard, cautions David Hollingworth from London & Country Mortgages, who computed the calculations. They must comprehend that they will pay thousands more in interest throughout the mortgage's duration. Katie and Chris state they are depending upon house prices continuing to increase, to strengthen their finances. We are trapped in a cycle really, Katie states. We are undertaking an enormous risk. Mortgage regulation has been strengthened, with stricter controls regarding what people can afford with their regular earnings. Yet there exist no regulations limiting mortgage term lengths or preventing families who are already struggling from committing themselves for four decades. In effect, these borrowers are postponing the moment of reckoning and depleting their future prosperity. David Hollingworth recommends they maintain their mortgages under review and reduce the repayment period once they can afford to make higher payments. Such an approach, he states, will save them a fortune. Yet what if interest rates increase, making mortgages more costly, or if the family income remains static? Homeowners like Katie and Chris in Cheadle might discover that the 40-year arrangement is all they can ever afford and their mortgage becomes a burden in later years.

text: Walsall interim head coach Jon Whitney is not certain of his future role at Bescot, despite coming so close to leading the club to promotion. The Saddlers suffered a 6-1 aggregate defeat to Barnsley in their League One play-off semi-final. However, Whitney's two-month tenure proved their most productive period as they narrowly missed automatic promotion by just one point. I have intended to remain part of it. What position that might be we shall discover, he stated. Whitney informed BBC WM: I must reflect, step back, draw breath and observe where it leads me. The mid-season exit of manager Dean Smith to Brentford, combined with their relatively disappointing form under his successor Sean O'Driscoll, ultimately proved damaging for the Saddlers. When former Liverpool assistant manager O'Driscoll secured his opening victory at the Banks's Stadium in December, with Walsall positioned second in League One, he informed BBC Sport: They are performing above their level. I believe the second half of the campaign will prove somewhat more challenging. However, that did not entirely materialise once O'Driscoll had left following a home league loss to Barnsley in March. Indeed, had the success rate of 2.08 points per match Walsall achieved after O'Driscoll's departure been sustained across a complete season, the Saddlers would have claimed League One convincingly. Whitney continued: This has represented an extraordinary transformation for me since Dean departed, and particularly since Sean left. However, I must follow where my instincts guide me and I shall need to do that during the coming days when all the feelings have calmed. I must examine myself and assess my personnel and determine whether I could have acted differently. However, the players have acquired the appetite for it now. We remain a progressing club, who have exceeded expectations this campaign, but we must create several more opportunities like that. This experience can only have proved beneficial. We shall attempt to maintain the squad intact if possible, though it may prove a considerable challenge. We can only assess when we understand the players we are retaining and the players we are recruiting. text: Technology developed by a professor at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh could help millions of people exposed to high levels of arsenic in their water supplies. These are external links and will open in a new window The world's first solar-powered, completely autonomous treatment facility has recently opened in Bangladesh. It has already dramatically reduced levels of the toxic chemical. In Western nations we typically take water for granted. However, in numerous parts of the world water carries a lethal payload. At Heriot-Watt, Professor Bhaskar Sen Gupta points to data indicating more than 137 million people from 70 countries are exposed daily to arsenic in their drinking water. If the same water is utilised for irrigation it means arsenic can accumulate in their crops as well. We have the golden era of British crime fiction to thank for arsenic's reputation as a deadly poison. It is not typically immediately fatal in drinking water. Rather, it is linked to a variety of debilitating diseases: cancers, disfiguring skin conditions, even type 2 diabetes. Professor Sen Gupta is a water technologist whose current area of interest lies in Bangladesh. There the arsenic in the water supply occurs naturally. It is transported as silt in the rivers that flow down from the Himalayas, as it has for millions of years. Until just a few decades ago, it remained harmless and inert in the banks of rivers and streams. But now it is dissolving, colourless and tasteless, into the shallow aquifers from which people draw their water. It may be from a natural source but human activity caused the problem. In a classic example of the law of unintended consequences, the introduction of new, improved varieties of rice has thrown nature out of balance. The new, high-yielding varieties of rice require considerably more water and fertiliser, Professor Sen Gupta says. Fertiliser-rich water from the rice fields reaches the sub-surface, but due to lack of oxygen the arsenic bearing minerals become by default a kind of participant in the reaction and break up, producing a very toxic type of arsenic. Professor Sen Gupta's solution involves, in effect, playing a trick on nature. Water is pumped out of a well, gradually oxygenated in the air, and then sent back down the well again. The oxygenated water meets bacteria that normally live in an oxygen-free environment. That is why the rise in oxygen level must be gradual. To do it suddenly would cause the bacteria to die. The oxygen encourages them to change the arsenic from a liquid to an inert solid which is absorbed onto the surface of grains of sand in the aquifer. All this takes place out of sight down the well. At no point does the arsenic come to the surface. The technique - it is called subterranean arsenic removal or SAR - uses no chemicals and produces no waste. Professor Sen Gupta and his colleagues have been working on SAR for almost a decade. What is new is that it now runs on solar energy and is an autonomous system. Once the delicately balanced process is established, the equipment can be operated remotely. The first plant is now operational in the Comilla district of Bangladesh. It was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, with the support of the Bangladesh Green Energy Foundation. The project serves 200 schoolchildren and - because the process eventually spreads through the aquifer - it will be able to serve 1,000 people. The World Health Organisation's safe guideline for arsenic in water is 10 micrograms per litre. The level in the well was 239 micrograms per litre. After just seven weeks the process brought that figure down to just two. And - almost inevitably in this connected world - Professor Sen Gupta says there is an app to run it all: We can operate the plant from anywhere in the world as long as you have the wifi connection. The NGO who are operating it, the Bangladesh Green Energy Foundation, are actually operating it from Dhaka more than 300km [186 miles] away. Professor Sen Gupta wants to transfer his knowledge from Heriot-Watt to the world. He says: We as a global university would like to be responsible for global problems and global issues - and be part of the solution. He is hoping to establish a charity to take the work further. It will have a simple selling point: with £5,000, you can improve a thousand lives.

Her daughter Yelena, 29, was treated for her injuries in hospital and her condition is said to be stable. Other victims include Dilbara Alieva, 20, from Azerbaijan, who was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries. text: Bradford City's three-match winning run came to an end as they were held to a draw by Oldham Athletic at Valley Parade despite dominating the game. Oldham took the lead in the fifth minute when Marc Klok delivered a free-kick from the right to the far post, where unmarked defender Peter Clarke found the net with a downward header. Bradford controlled the remainder of the first half as the away side's defence survived a succession of close calls. Goalkeeper Connor Ripley produced an excellent one-handed save to thwart winger Mark Marshall, Timothee Dieng and Josh Cullen both saw efforts deflected for corners, and Billy Clarke squandered a fine opportunity when he directed James Meredith's cross wide. Oldham managed to preserve their advantage until the interval, but Bradford justifiably drew level after 57 minutes when Ousmane Fane brought down Cullen and Clarke converted from the penalty spot. Bradford maintained their dominance, but failed to convert possession into goals as Oldham's defence remained resolute. Report provided by the Press Association. text: The ever-expanding emissions crisis at VW is having a direct effect on sales. I am informed that the initial evidence demonstrating customers are abandoning VW shall be disclosed in the new car registration statistics to be released by the Society of Motor Manufacturers & Traders (SMMT) on Thursday morning. VW sales in the UK have fallen by more than 8% compared with the equivalent period last year, I am given to understand. Two additional VW marques - Seat and Skoda - are likewise experiencing sales reductions. However, I understand that Audi sales are maintaining their position. Naturally, these represent merely one month's statistics and follow years of increasing - and record-breaking - numbers. And other manufacturers have evidently also witnessed sharp declines, even though they are not involved in the emissions scandal. Yet my industry sources are stating that VW is attributing the sales reduction to the events of the past six weeks. With its share price now one-third lower than at the commencement of the crisis, it is evident that VW is bearing a substantial commercial cost for the expanding emissions scandal. The BBC has been informed that Patrick McLoughlin, the transport secretary, has spoken to Herbert Diess, a senior VW official in Germany, today and demanded compensation for any reduced resale value of cars embroiled in the crisis. Whitehall sources inform me that VW has acknowledged that payments may have to be made. Louise Ellman, chair of the Transport Select Committee, has also informed the BBC that the committee is likely to expand its inquiry into VW and the testing of all motor vehicles. She has written to the German manufacturer demanding additional details on how defeat devices came to be employed. The committee will examine the responses we receive, but I anticipate the committee will wish to undertake further work on this very significant issue, she informed the BBC. It concerns the scandal of Volkswagen, but it also concerns the wider policy of testing, where there are major questions regarding the testing of all vehicles. The credit rating agency, Moody's, has also downgraded the German manufacturer, which could mean that VW must pay more to borrow money. Today's downgrade reflects mounting risks to Volkswagen's reputation and future earnings following its announcement on 3 November concerning irregularities in CO2 and fuel consumption levels for certain Volkswagen group vehicles, stated Yasmina Serghini-Douvin, a Moody's senior credit officer and lead analyst on Volkswagen. She stated Moody's was also considering fresh allegations [which VW denies] from the US on 2 November that defeat devices were also installed in certain Audi, Porsche and Volkswagen models in the US. With sales declining and the value of the company share price reduced by one-third, VW's relentless pursuit of the truth is proving to be a costly and damaging process.

text: Chinese central bank governor Zhou Xiaochuan has accused speculative forces of targeting the country's currency, the yuan. He stated there was no justification for the yuan to continue depreciating in value and that China would not permit international speculators to control market sentiment. Mr Zhou's comments emerge as Chinese markets prepare to reopen on Monday following a week-long New Year holiday. Attempts to defend the yuan have diminished China's foreign currency reserves. At $3.23tn (2.84tn euros; £2.2tn), China still possesses the world's largest reserve of foreign currency holdings. However, that has fallen by $420bn over six months and remains at the lowest level since May 2012. In January alone, the reserves dropped by $99.5bn as the People's Bank of China sold dollars in an attempt to support the value of the yuan. Mr Zhou's observations came in an interview published in the Caixin financial magazine. International speculative forces have recently concentrated on shorting China, the People's Bank of China governor informed the magazine, without providing further details. He rejected concerns that China's currency reserves were declining too rapidly, stating: It is normal for foreign reserves to rise and fall as long as the fundamentals face no problems. The Chinese economy recorded growth of 6.9% in 2015, its slowest rate since 1990. Concerns of an economic slowdown have prompted some investors to relocate their money out of China in pursuit of better returns elsewhere. Nevertheless, Mr Zhou said China would not tighten its capital controls as a consequence. Capital outflow and capital flight are two different concepts, he added. The Chinese authorities fear a rapid devaluation of their currency, as it could destabilise the economy. Many Chinese businesses hold debt in dollars and managing those debts with a severely weakened yuan could create problems and cause some companies to fail. Therefore China has been attempting to engineer an ordered devaluation of the yuan, but that is proving difficult to deliver. Investors have been attempting to withdraw funds from investments priced in yuan and speculators have been wagering on further falls in the currency. To stabilise the situation, China has been selling dollars and purchasing yuan. And it has been employing other tactics, including restricting currency speculation and instructing offshore banks to retain their reserves of yuan.

text: Championship side Oldham Roughyeds stunned last season's Challenge Cup finalists Hull KR to reach the last 16. The Roughyeds, positioned fourth from the bottom of the second tier, held a 24-6 advantage at half-time following tries from Will Hope, Richard Lepori, Steve Roper and Adam Clay. Shaun Lunt, Dane Tilse, Maurice Blair and Joe Wardill scored after the interval to provide the Super League team with hope. However, missed conversions proved expensive as Gary Middlehurst and Lepori's second try ensured victory for Oldham. Hull KR manager James Webster characterised his team's display as an utter embarrassment. Media playback is not supported on this device. Rovers, who suffered a 50-0 defeat to Leeds in last year's Wembley final, have secured victory just twice in Super League this season and lost 40-0 to Catalans Dragons in their previous fixture. They remained expected to defeat part-time Oldham, who are competing in their inaugural Championship season following promotion from League 1. Nevertheless, Oldham outscored them six tries to five, whilst Lewis Palfrey's six conversions against Ben Cockayne's one provided the second-tier team with an ultimately comfortable winning margin against the hosts, who concluded with 12 players after Cockayne was dispatched to the sin-bin moments before Lepori's try with the match's final play. Meanwhile, last season's Championship champions and Challenge Cup giant-killers Leigh, who eliminated Super League teams Wakefield and Salford, are eliminated following a 10-8 defeat at League 1 team Toulouse. Batley Bulldogs have also progressed to the sixth round following a 28-10 triumph over fellow Championship team Featherstone Rovers. Oldham Roughyeds manager Scott Naylor: This is arguably the most significant victory since the club reformed [in 1997]. We discussed reaching 20 minutes, then 30 minutes and observing developments. We did not anticipate the half-time score would be 24-6 and we understood they would emerge in the second half and mount a challenge after receiving considerable criticism. For the club, this represents something we shall treasure. It constitutes a momentous day for Oldham and it could prove a momentous evening for the players. I shall return home and enjoy several beers with my family. Hull KR manager James Webster: It represented the greatest embarrassment of my career since before I departed school. What we delivered was utter embarrassment. I have protected these players since my arrival here, but I must apologise to everyone connected with this club. That does not meet the standard required to justify the wages they receive. Supporters sacrifice cars, holidays to support this club because I interact with these individuals daily. I comprehend what people believe and it is entirely accurate. Congratulations to Oldham because I considered they performed excellently. text: Japanese carmaker Toyota has regained its slot as the world's biggest vehicle maker, capping a year of a dramatic turnaround in its fortunes. Toyota announced it sold 9.75 million vehicles in 2012, representing an increase of more than 22% from the previous year. General Motors, which held the position of largest vehicle manufacturer in 2011, sold 9.29 million vehicles in 2012. Toyota's sales in 2011 were damaged by natural disasters in Japan and Thailand which disrupted production at its manufacturing facilities. Nevertheless, Toyota, along with other Japanese manufacturers that were impacted, has witnessed a consistent recovery since that time and has been reclaiming market share in crucial markets including the United States. The past two years have proved extremely challenging for Toyota, Vivek Vaidya, an automotive analyst with Frost & Sullivan, informed the BBC. The recapture of the leading position would certainly be encouraging for the company and represents positive news for its investors and shareholders, he stated. Toyota's competitors also announced record figures in vehicle sales for 2012. Nissan Motor reported it sold 4.94 million vehicles worldwide, rising nearly 6% from the preceding year, whilst Honda Motor stated it experienced an increase of 19% from the previous year, selling 3.82 million vehicles. Alongside the natural disasters, Japanese manufacturers have also been affected by a robust yen. A strong currency not only renders Japanese products more costly to international purchasers but also impacts companies' profits when they convert their overseas earnings back to Japan. This particularly affects firms - including Toyota - which depend significantly on international sales. Nevertheless, Japanese manufacturers have gained support in recent weeks as the yen has declined against the US dollar. The Japanese currency has fallen approximately 15% against the US dollar since November last year. It was trading near 90.8 yen against the US dollar in Asian trading on Monday. Analysts stated the decline was expected to generate a beneficial effect on Toyota's expansion. The weakening of the yen provides welcome assistance for Toyota, remarked Frost & Sullivan's Mr Vaidya. We are expected to witness profit margins increase, providing it with additional available funds and the capacity to invest in developing new technologies, which should support its growth trajectory moving forward. The Japanese manufacturer increased its annual profit projection in November. It has forecast a net profit of 780bn yen ($8.6bn; £5.4bn) for the financial year ending 31 March 2013, rising from its previous forecast of 760bn yen. Nevertheless, the manufacturer does encounter some potential obstacles, particularly from the ongoing territorial dispute between Japan and China. China represents the world's largest automotive market and is regarded as essential to future expansion of companies such as Toyota. Nevertheless, the dispute concerning a group of islands in the East China Sea, which intensified late last year, has damaged relations between the two nations and witnessed Japan's exports to China decrease. The dispute remains unresolved and some worry that it may escalate again in the forthcoming months and further damage trade relations between the two nations. The concern is that any such development may witness anti-Japan sentiment increase and damage sales of Japanese brands in China. Analysts stated that any such decline was expected to generate a detrimental effect on Toyota's expansion.
