text: History, they say, is written by the victors. Beneath the shadow of a towering windmill at what was formerly one of the most productive sugar plantations in the West Indies, it is not difficult to envisage the legion of imperious Englishmen at its command. Yet whilst an abundance of documentation meticulously records the details of the industry which helped construct the British Empire, precious little is known about the lives of the African slaves upon whom it depended. Researchers investigating an 18th-century slave village during a major excavation project at Betty's Hope plantation in Antigua hope to alter that. One of merely a handful ever uncovered in the Caribbean, the discovery of the site and recent artefacts is poised to illuminate a grim past. Dr Georgia Fox, leading the project, describes the initial discovery of the village in 2013, which had evaded archaeologists for decades, as a eureka moment. Combining high-tech electronic surveying equipment with maps dating back to 1710 enabled one of her team of students from California State University, Chico, to identify its location. It felt like a miracle, she told the BBC. We had seen all these dots on the maps and we now realised they signified the slave village. It was an extraordinary discovery. Subsequent excavation works have revealed a wealth of fascinating relics which, for the first time, provide a glimpse into the daily lives and culture of the plantation's 400 slaves. First we discovered what appeared to be a very specific type of rough pottery, called Afro-Antiguan ware, made by slaves. Pots were fashioned by coiling pieces of local clay and would have been used for cooking stews, Dr Fox explains. Recently we were able to go really deep into the heart of the village and we discovered some remarkable things like cowrie shells from East Africa which were used as currency, for games or good luck charms. This in itself raises interesting questions as slaves in Antigua tended to be from West rather than East Africa. Then we discovered Dutch delftware which was probably bartered for, traded or given to the slaves as hand-offs, followed by two corners of a beautifully made limestone wall which was tantalising as most slave homes were standard wattle and daub, Dr Fox continues. Excavation by Dr Fox's team commenced in 2007 at the plantation's Great House, followed by the Still House where rum, then sugar's most important by-product, was produced. The once 700-acre site dates back to around 1650 and comprised a largely self-sustainable living complex accommodating everyone from field workers, servants and overseers to tradesmen, a blacksmith and a doctor. At its peak, each of the plantation's twin windmills could have produced 12 tonnes of sugar crystals a day. Less than 5% of the sprawling site has been investigated thus far. Items uncovered at the Great House include children's toys, musket balls, buttons, cutlery, a door knocker, clay tobacco pipes and a cod liver oil bottle. The organic materials used to construct slave houses, such as palm fronds, sticks and mud, made the adjacent village's identification difficult. Local historian and Unesco representative Reg Murphy, who oversees all of Antigua's archaeology projects, said the work was vital to piece together a complete history of the island where most of the population are slave descendants. Everything we learn is about the glory of sugar and the industrial colonial legacy, he says. You never hear about the day-to-day lives of the workers, the other side of the coin. This is a way of learning about their daily routine, what they ate, how they lived, seeing it from their perspective. There were over 400 slaves at Betty's Hope at one time - their stories have never been told. For Dr Fox, the significance extends further still. There were sugar plantations throughout the world but the Caribbean was the gateway to the New World and had a tremendous impact on the development of America. This was the beginning of capitalism and it all started in the Caribbean. It is important to remember how the New World was created - this is everybody's history. Although slavery was abolished in 1834, Antigua's sugar production remained an economic mainstay until the 1960s when it was replaced by tourism. Dr Fox adds: Sugar changed the world. Every time you bite into a chocolate bar or add sugar to your tea or coffee, you are taking part in a long history and reaching into the past.

text: Ulster secured a home quarter-final and condemned Leicester to an away tie as they ended the Tigers' unbeaten home run of 25 matches in the Heineken Cup. The interval score stood at 9-9 following hat-tricks of penalties from Leicester fly-half Toby Flood and visiting scrum-half Ruan Pienaar. A Flood penalty and Niall Morris's converted try established a 19-9 advantage for Tigers. However, a Pienaar penalty and his converted try restored parity before his fifth penalty secured Ulster a dramatic victory. With Leicester holding a 10-point lead and thirty minutes remaining, it appeared they would not merely end the sole unbeaten record in this season's competition but also secure a home quarter-final berth. Yet the Ulster players launched themselves at the hosts in every tackle and at each breakdown to unsettle them and allow South African scrum-half Pienaar to steer the Irish province to victory at Welford Road, ensuring qualification as top seeds. The 1999 champions and 2012 beaten finalists are presently redeveloping their Ravenhill ground to accommodate 18,000 supporters. They pledge it shall be prepared for the quarter-finals on the weekend of 4-6 April and given their supporters' passion it is unlikely to be anything but a sell-out when they host Saracens, who become the eighth and final qualifiers after Leicester's losing bonus point meant Tigers finished as the best runners-up in the group stages. Leicester dominated initially in a fierce encounter with their scrum functioning well and full-back Mathew Tait, who would subsequently limp off injured, appearing lively. Second row Graham Kitchener nearly supplemented his excellent line-out work with a try as he was brought down just short following a 40m charge, but despite failing to cross the line Flood's boot guided Tigers to a 9-3 lead. Nevertheless, Ulster combine Irish defiance with a mixture of power and rugby intelligence from South Africa and with Pienaar, the architect of their operation, orchestrating proceedings and landing his penalties they drew level at the interval. Once more the hosts commenced better following the restart and when Ulster open-side flanker Chris Henry broke early from a scrum Flood restored Tigers' lead, which they shortly extended to 10 points. Tom Youngs charged forward from a high Flood kick and when Tigers recycled possession the fly-half threaded through a precise grubber kick and winger Morris won the race to touch down. Flood converted to establish a 19-9 scoreline and surely Leicester were progressing, but Ulster were in no disposition to accept defeat and responded five minutes later when hooker Youngs went off his feet at a ruck and Pienaar found the target with the penalty. Then arrived the decisive moment of the match as Pienaar charged down Flood's kick and won the race to touch down, before converting his own score from wide out to make it 19-19. Media playback is not supported on this device. The match was open and Leicester went close after Flood's superb penalty to the corner earned them an attacking line-out, only for the fly-half to drop a pass five metres from the line as Tigers pressed forward. Ulster once again battled their way back into Leicester territory and Pienaar confirmed his quality with a long-range penalty to put the visitors ahead. Leicester had a late scrum in the Ulster half but the visitors won the ball against the head and with it went Tigers' hopes as the Irish province achieved six victories from six and arranged what promises to be a spirited house-warming celebration at Ravenhill. Ulster captain Johann Muller: It appears as though it's occurring every week, when Ruan scores all the points - he was outstanding. We arrived here to secure a home quarter-final. Sarries completely outplayed us last season - they are an excellent side and don't mind travelling away to achieve a result. It's two months away and at this point we shall simply enjoy the moment. We have not accomplished anything yet and there's a tremendous amount of work remaining if we are to accomplish something. Leicester boss Richard Cockerill: We're disappointed with the result, but it was an excellent match. Ten points ahead we needed to control the game better but we did not manage the back field as effectively as we would have preferred and they exposed us. At the moment it's probably Toulon [away in the last eight], tomorrow it may be Clermont who have an impressive home record - what is it, 73 matches unbeaten? We are in the quarter-finals and we have endured considerable adversity [through injuries], so that's not an inadequate effort from us. The conversion gave the Tigers a 19–9 lead, but Ulster were not to be denied and five minutes later Youngs was caught offside at a ruck, and Pienaar’s penalty put the score level. The Tigers had come to Ravenhill for a home quarter-final. We were utterly outplayed by Saracens last year; they are an excellent team and are happy to win away. The Tigers had a late scrum in the Ulster half, but the visitors took the ball against the head and the hopes of the Tigers went with it. The Irish province celebrated a sixth victory out of six and set the tone for a raucous celebration at Ravenhill. The director of the Leicester team, Richard Cockerill, said: “We were disappointed with the result, but it was a good game. Ruan seems to score the goals every week, he was superb. The league is two months away, and we are just going to enjoy the moment. “Today it is Toulon that is the favorite, tomorrow it might be Clermont, who has a pretty record at home, what is it, 73 games unbeaten? We are in the quarterfinals, we have suffered a lot, we are not making insufficient efforts. We have not yet achieved anything, and there is still a great deal of work to do if we are to achieve anything. Not used: Stankovich, Balmain, Williams. But we did not manage our defence as well as we should have done, and they made us pay for it. Ulster: Payne, Trimble, Cave, Marshall, Gilroy, Pienaar, Black, Best, Afoa, Muller, Tuohy, Henry, Williams. Not used: Herring, Lutton, M’Ilwaine, P. Marshall, M. Allen. Ulster Subs: Hamilton for Tait, Mele for B. Youngs, Hawkins for T. Youngs, Deacon for B. Youngs, Mafi for K. Youngs, Williams for Smith. The spectators: ten. text: Auditors have warned MSPs about severe problems faced by three health boards. An Audit Scotland report discovered that a new IT system at NHS24 has cost 50 per cent more and taken two years longer to implement than originally planned. The watchdog also cautioned that NHS Tayside failed to achieve break-even for the third consecutive year, depending on a £14m loan from the Scottish Government. Concerns were also highlighted regarding finances at NHS Highland, which auditors stated needs to depend less on one-off savings. In a report to MSPs, Audit Scotland stated delays in implementing the new computer systems at NHS24 had brought substantial additional costs and risks, with the timetable for completion extending from June 2013 to October 2015. The estimated cost of the system is now £117.4m, 55 per cent higher than the original estimate of £75.8m. Auditors discovered overspends on staffing, holiday pay and primary care prescribing left NHS Tayside depending on loans for the third consecutive year. The health board required £14.2m from the Scottish government simply to break even in 2014/15. As well as repaying the loan, auditors cautioned the board would need to make savings of £27m in 2015/16. NHS Highland was given a critical report on its 2013/14 accounts, and auditors stated improvements had been made. However, they stated more needed to be done to develop longer-term financial planning and reduce dependence on one-off savings. Responding to the report, NHS24 chief executive Ian Crichton stated the report outlines a series of weaknesses dating back to 2011. He stated: Delays in this major IT programme have led to a significant increase in costs. During the last 16 months an expert team has been working hard to bring the project back on track. The new system will be in place by the end of October. NHS Tayside chief executive Lesley McLay stated the board was facing challenges due to increasing demands on services. She stated: NHS Tayside's board has been building a programme of improvement and transformation since the beginning of this financial year. This medium-term programme, led by clinical staff who are partnered with managers, prioritises the delivery of service improvement and benefits for patients and also supports the delivery of sustainable financial balance for NHS Tayside. NHS Highland chairman Garry Coutts welcomed the report, stating it reflected the robust measures taken to improve following the 2013/14 audit. He stated: It is heartening to read in this latest report that the auditor has concluded that we have strengthened our financial management arrangements, transparency and scrutiny of our financial performance. This latest report makes the point that it is important for the board to build on these improvements given the challenges ahead. That is something we are determined to do.

text: The Beast's beastliness falls well short of savage these days, and generates only faux outrage in the stilted setting of green benches. Veteran Labour MP Dennis Skinner, long dubbed the Beast of Bolsover, has been ejected from the chamber for calling the prime minister Dodgy Dave. Whilst Mr Skinner's anger is undoubtedly genuine, he has become the establishment's licensed fool, the undignified element of the constitution. His barbs are as nothing compared with the grievances of some right-wing Labour MPs about the manner they have been treated by activists. And they scarcely raise the temperature in the same fashion as tweets praising Hitler. Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, a man who wishes to become president is calling his critics, particularly if they are women, ugly, dogs, dummies and clowns, though not always simultaneously. Far more elegant, and I would suggest far more distressing to the target, are Petronella Wyatt's observations on the Chancellor George Osborne, a man she says she admires: His complexion is Eastern, with the fish-belly pallor of Vlad the Impaler. His eyes have a Mongolian slant and his voice the twang of a Gypsy's zither. Despite Jeremy Corbyn's appeal for a new politics, has it actually become coarser and ruder than ever before? Perhaps not. Churchill called Ramsey MacDonald the boneless wonder and Stanley Baldwin that great turnip. According to a book I'm reading at present, James II was insulted to his face by one discontented subject, who said he was an ugly lean-jawed, hatchet faced, Popish dog. His successor William of Orange fared little better - one gentleman of Holborn was fined for observing the new king was a rogue and a son of a whore. But politicians and public figures must do better than mere abuse. Whilst I have only the vaguest notion what the 18th Century Prime Minister Lord North looked like, Horace Walpole's description makes me chuckle. Two large prominent eyes that rolled about to no purpose (for he was utterly short-sighted) a wide mouth, thick lips and inflated visage, gave him the air of a blind trumpeter, Walpole said. A deep untunable voice which, instead of modulating, he enforced with unnecessary pomp, a total neglect of his person, and ignorance of every civil attention, disgusted all who judge by appearance. Of course, the insults that endure well are those that combine venom with wit, and, better still, insight. The poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge's observations on Pitt the Younger may fall short of poetry but strike to the heart of that remote, odd and brilliant man. Coleridge said: He has patronised no science, he has raised no man of genius from obscurity; he counts no prime work of God among his friends. He has no attachment to female society, no fondness of children, no perception of beauty in natural scenery; but he is fond of convivial indulgences, of that stimulation which, keeping up the glow of self-importance and the sense of internal power, gives feelings without the mediation of ideas. Perhaps, pithy is superior. Told by Lord Sandwich he would die either on the gallows or of the pox, radical MP John Wilkes replied: That depends, my Lord, whether I embrace your mistress or your principles. Not only clever but short enough to fit on Twitter. But there lies a pointer to what may have altered. I am constitutionally against hand-wringing over changes wrought by technology, or accusations the world these days is going to hell in a handbasket, but social media has made an impact on the public mood. First, the restrictions on Twitter make it ideal for recommending and linking to longer articles and blogs. But they do not encourage reasoned debate, and instead summon the mood of the mob. A passing thought is entombed in text, the bad-tempered growl over a news item transmogrified into a hail of arrows shot into a victim. Serious harassment has become so commonplace, it has given rise to a new lexicon of offence, from flaming to trolling. Much less seriously, I cannot be the only journalist who feels a bit disgruntled tweets attacking my work for bias or stupidity never delve in to identify the particular cause of offence. Abuse has become the point, rather than simply the flashy thunderhead of an argument. If you reply, it gets worse. Twitter exchanges, through their very brevity, get more heated. Email correspondence (or the even more old-fashioned sort) tends to lower the temperature and even lead to greater understanding. Social media also encourages the herding together of like-minded people, who reinforce each other's values, refusing to listen to the other side. The less they listen, the less they understand, the greater the reason to credit their opposition with base motives. There is no point wondering if their values might be valid or their views worth considering - they are simply sons of whores or hatchet-faced dogs. The mobs move through the virtual city, and all that can be clearly heard through the tumult are curses and imprecations. Social media can be a friend of the instinctively clenched fist. Reaction is instant - swifter than thought - with no time to mull, reflect and debate, and with no need to put a human face to a hated meme. Such reactions stay largely in the virtual realm - but they are the enemy of the sort of politics that seeks resolutions and solutions to often complex problems.

text: The cost of a basket of shopping at the same shop in Jersey and the UK can cost up to 10% more. BBC Radio Jersey's business correspondent, Chris Rayner, has been investigating the expense of a shopping basket at three supermarkets in Jersey and in Hampshire. He compiled a basic shopping list using products recommended by Jersey's Consumer Council. The list comprised a litre of milk, a kilogram of white potatoes, cat litter, soap, toothpaste and ketchup. The research discovered products such as coffee at the identical store in the UK cost £1.32 more in Jersey. Mr Rayner stated: Whilst the quality of life here may be superior, many believe we pay more for the privilege, whether through higher rents, more costly food and travel expenses. The BBC examined three supermarkets in Jersey, the Co-op in Charing Cross, Waitrose at Rue des Pres and Marks & Spencer in King Street; and three in Petersfield in Hampshire: Tesco, Waitrose and Marks & Spencer. He stated he discovered that conducting business in Jersey was not inexpensive either. The Channel Islands Co-op is amongst the supermarkets that imports tonnes of food and other products from the UK every week which costs the company £60,000 monthly. Colin Mcleod, the Co-op's chief executive, stated: We have high land costs, we have high construction costs, we have high labour costs. However, we are doing our utmost in that environment for our members. A spokesperson for Waitrose in Jersey stated: We continuously monitor our prices to ensure we remain as competitive as possible, and due to this shoppers may discover that many of our products now cost less than when we initially opened our stores on the island. We must reflect the additional costs of transporting products to the Channel Islands in our prices but we pass on the savings of UK VAT to our customers in Jersey and have hundreds of relevant and meaningful promotions across our stores each week. Tony O'Neill, the chief executive of Sandpiper CI, stated over half their products in Marks & Spencer are sold on promotion. The Citizens Advice Bureau and the Community Savings Bank informed the BBC they were seeing more clients. Brian Curtis, executive chairman of the Community Savings Bank, stated it was not merely those who find themselves unemployed. He stated: I know some individuals on middle incomes who have not received any increase [in wages] for three years. They still have employment, so that is satisfactory in itself, but adapting to a different scenario is not straightforward for some of these individuals.

text: Charles Green has confirmed that Rangers will apply for Scottish Football League membership. Media playback is not supported on this device At a Hampden meeting on Wednesday, Scottish Premier League clubs voted overwhelmingly to reject the application from Green's Rangers newco. Green stated that he was deeply disappointed by the 'no' vote. He continued: If our application were to be accepted, Rangers will play in whichever division the SFL sees fit and we will move forward from there. Rangers entered administration in February owing up to £134m to unsecured creditors. The club will eventually be liquidated and its registrations with the Scottish FA and SPL were terminated. We regret that our club and our supporters were given false hope The majority of SPL clubs had indicated they were against the newco application prior to the vote but Green complained that he had been given false hope of success. We are deeply disappointed that our application to rejoin the SPL has been rejected overwhelmingly by the member clubs, stated Green. This time last week, all of us at Rangers were resigned to the fact that we would not be admitted, due mainly to the public declarations of clubs indicating they would not support our application. At the weekend, we were approached by representatives from the SPL suggesting our application still stood a chance of success and we should discuss this further with clubs. This we did in good faith but with the knowledge of the hurdles that lay ahead of us. Media playback is not supported on this device We had asked the SPL whether it would be more appropriate for us to withdraw our application but were advised against this. We made a presentation to the SPL clubs this morning, detailing our proposals in support of our application and this included what we believed to be penalties and sanctions that would have dealt fairly with the difficulties caused by events at Rangers prior to our acquisition of the club on 14 June. Sadly, this was rejected by the other clubs and we regret that our club and our supporters were given false hope by this initiative. We will now proceed as we had planned from late June to apply for membership of the SFL. It is entirely a matter for them whether our application will be accepted or rejected and we will make no representation to any member club prior to that application being considered. We also recognise that the SPL has been placed in a difficult position because of the way events have unfolded. SFL clubs met on Tuesday to discuss an SFA proposal that would see Rangers enter Division One and are expected to put the matter to a vote on 12 July. A simple majority is required in that ballot, with 12 of the 30 clubs already publicly opposed, whilst Cowdenbeath, whose chairman Donald Findlay QC is a former Rangers vice chairman, said they would support Rangers' application to join the SFL, but only if the Ibrox club entered the Third Division.

text: The world's highest paid YouTube star, PewDiePie, has defended himself over allegations of anti-Semitism in a new YouTube video. The Swedish content creator described the accusations - which led to Disney severing relations with him - as insane and unfair. He stated any offensive remarks he had made were taken out of context and that he had been blatantly misrepresented. Several of his videos from recent months were discovered to include Nazi references or anti-Semitic imagery. PewDiePie, whose actual name is Felix Kjellberg, stated in his YouTube video: I am sorry for the words I used as I know they offended people. I do strongly believe that you can joke about anything, but I also believe that there is a right way and not the best way to joke about things, he stated. He said that as a rookie comedian he could take jokes too far. He maintained that he did not support right-wing groups that advocated hatred and that recent articles highlighting his alleged anti-Semitism by newspapers including the Wall Street Journal were personal attacks and attempts to discredit him. The Swede is reported to have earned $15m through YouTube in 2016. He has been linked with Disney via Maker Studios, a company with a network of YouTube stars. The YouTuber has attracted several billions of views per month and generated vast amounts of revenue from advertising. Disney announced on Tuesday that whilst Mr Kjellberg had a reputation for being provocative and irreverent, some of the videos he produced were inappropriate. In one of the controversial videos, Mr Kjellberg paid two Indians through a crowd-sourcing website to hold up a sign which read Death to all Jews. In his response to the criticism, he said he was attempting to demonstrate how people would say anything for $5. In other videos he also displayed swastikas drawn by a fan, played the Nazi Party anthem and performed a brief Hitler salute - all of which he says was done as a joke and taken out of context. Mr Kjellberg said that he had been accused of normalising hatred in the jokes, whereas in fact it was his media critics who were doing this by their unfair attacks on him. YouTube itself said earlier that it had cancelled the release of Mr Kjellberg's new series Scare PewDiePie 2, and had removed him from its Google Preferred scheme, which highlights advertiser-friendly content creators. In 2016, PewDiePie was temporarily suspended from Twitter after making jokes about so-called Islamic State.

text: The Easter Rising was one of the most important, fundamental events in the history of Ireland. The six-day insurrection in Dublin witnessed republican rebels attempting to overthrow British authority. More than 450 individuals perished, thousands sustained injuries and square miles of Dublin's city centre were reduced to rubble beneath a bombardment of artillery fire. For Ireland's press, it represented the story of the century - save that it was a story scarcely anyone could publish. The turmoil and disorder in the capital, an absence of dependable eyewitness accounts and the constraints imposed by a British government on a war footing meant Ireland's principal newspapers were prevented from printing comprehensive coverage of the conflict. Ultimately, it fell to a small, weekly newspaper in County Fermanagh to surpass the larger dailies in covering the story. The Impartial Reporter, situated in Enniskillen, is believed to be the first newspaper in Ireland to publish a first-hand, eyewitness report of the Rising. In 1916, the newspaper was owned by William Copeland Trimble, whose son - William Egbert - chanced to be in Dublin when the Rising commenced on Monday 24 April. Due to William Egbert's presence in the city, the Impartial Reporter was able to provide the first ground-level reports of the fighting in Dublin, published on Thursday, 27 April. The outbreak of rebellion in Dublin has astonished the country! its report declared. Like a lightning flash the carefully-developed plans of the Sinn Feiners were executed on a religious festival and holiday. It proceeded to report armed Sinn Fein volunteers capturing government buildings and strategic positions, and effectively maintaining control of the principal portions of the city. Dr Éamon Phoenix, head of history at Stranmillis College, Belfast, stated that William Egbert's position on the ground provided the Impartial Reporter an invaluable exclusive. He was able to very rapidly locate people from Fermanagh who were caught up in the fighting, such as British troops, he stated. He was able to obtain reports of British soldiers who were killed, or regarding troops being deployed from barracks. He was the sole trained reporter on the ground who was able to transmit reliable reports, so the Impartial Reporter secured a first. Sarah Saunderson, current editor of the Impartial Reporter, stated William Egbert - or Bertie - possessed strong connections with Dublin that assisted him in obtaining the Rising story. He studied law at Trinity College, Dublin, until his legal career was terminated when he was home for holiday in 1901 and found himself battling a fire on the paper's premises. Bertie Trimble never returned to Trinity as he was required at home to assist with the family business. However, Trinity's loss was the Impartial's benefit. With Bertie's Dublin connections, he was in the correct place at the correct time to deliver an impressive exclusive for the Impartial Reporter. Whilst the small County Fermanagh weekly newspaper was able to publish the first verified accounts of violence, other newspapers were struggling to print anything. In Dublin, stated Dr Phoenix, the Irish Times was unable to distribute and the Irish Independent offices were damaged in the fighting. Meanwhile, newspapers in Belfast knew of a serious state of affairs in Dublin but could not publish details due to a lack of first-hand accounts and the Defence of the Realm Act. This wartime legislation prevented newspapers from spreading reports likely to cause disaffection or alarm amongst Her Majesty's forces or amongst the civilian population. Dublin isolated reported the Belfast Telegraph headline for Tuesday, 25 April, the day following the Rising's commencement, but added that we are prevented from publishing details. The News Letter was similarly restricted, reporting that the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland had been compelled to cancel a planned journey to Belfast in order to remain in Dublin. Shortly before six o'clock certain very alarming rumours began to be whispered about in the city of serious trouble in Dublin, it reported. It added Up until the time of going to press no reports of the happenings in Dublin have come to hand. Under these circumstances we refrain from publishing the facts which we have in our possession. The first people in Belfast would have heard about the Rising would have been when the viceroy did not appear on Easter Monday, stated Dr Phoenix. A group waited all afternoon at the railway station and, when he failed to come, they telephoned Dublin. What they heard back was that the viceroy would not be able to come as he was 'attending to an emergency'. On Thursday, it can finally report what it knows - albeit without the benefit of a first-hand account, like the Impartial Reporter, and with the caveat: We hope these reports are accurate but it is proper to remember the difficulty in maintaining communications. On the same day, the Belfast Telegraph was able to attribute its story, headlined 'Stamping Out Rebellion', to the many Belfast people who had winged their way back to the north after being in Dublin. It also included a scathing condemnation of the Rising and those who supported it: It is a sad reflection on the Irish race that a very substantial body of ostensibly sane men could be misled by a parcel of frothy ranters whose history is the very negation of commonsense conduct. Public opinion would shift in the days following the Rising, particularly with the execution of 16 of the Rising's leaders. By then, newspapers were able to freely print stories on Ireland's ongoing political strife. But, for one history-making week in April, it was one small paper that gained the advantage over its rivals.

The News Letter was also prevented from publishing details. While the small Fermanagh paper was able to print the first verified accounts of the riots, other papers had great difficulty in getting out any news at all. Dr. Phoenix reported from Dublin that the Irish Times could not be distributed, and the offices of the Irish Independent had been damaged by the fighting. - Until the moment of this writing, no news of the events in Dublin has reached us. A few minutes before six o'clock, some very alarming rumors of serious trouble in Dublin were whispered in the city. The paper announced that the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland was forced to abandon his trip to Belfast and stay in Dublin. Dr. Phoenix said that the first rumor of the Uprising in Belfast was that the Viceroy had not appeared at the station on Easter Monday. A group of people had waited for him all afternoon and when he did not appear, they telephoned Dublin, which told them that the Viceroy could not come because he was attending an emergency. Under these circumstances we refrain from publishing the facts we have in our possession. For a momentous week in April it was a small newspaper that took the lead. On the same day the Belfast Telegraph, under the title “Drum-Beating Rebellion”, attributed its news to the many Belfast people who had flown back from Dublin, and criticized the rising and the men who had supported it: “It is a sad reflection on the Irish race that a very large group of men who appear to be sane have been so misled by a group of ravers whose history is the very opposite of common sense. We hope these reports are accurate, but it is useful to remember the difficulties of maintaining communication.” The newspapers had been forbidden to report on the events of Ireland until the days following the rising, when the execution of the leaders and the other executions of insurgents changed public opinion.

text: Some doctors in England are being offered thousands of pounds to cut the number of patients being sent to hospital, an investigation has found. General practitioner surgeries are receiving payments to assist local NHS organisations in restricting patient referral numbers and reducing expenditure, the medical publication Pulse discovered. Affected appointments encompass scans and specialist consultations - including those for cancer sufferers. The British Medical Association declared such incentives were misguided. No fewer than nine clinical commissioning groups (CCGs) were providing GP surgeries with payments for achieving targets, according to Pulse's investigation. In one instance, Birmingham South Central CCG was providing surgeries with more than £11,000 to decrease new outpatient attendances, follow-ups, A&E attendances and emergency admissions by 1%, compared with 2014/15. It stated the programmes, which exclude cancer referrals, were designed to incentivise best quality practice and drive improvements in the quality of primary medical care. Our priority is to ensure that patients have access to services that they require, when they require them, stated a spokesperson for Birmingham South Central CCG. Another CCG informed Pulse it had considered the full impact of the incentive programme and was confident that there is no conflict of interest. Pulse reported that one programme had already been examined by the General Medical Council, the organisation which regulates medical standards in the UK, after local GP leaders expressed their concern. The publication highlighted that initial hospital referrals for cancer sufferers should occur within two weeks of a GP first suspecting the condition. Dr Chand Nagpaul, chairman of the GPs committee of the doctors' trade union the British Medical Association, informed BBC Radio 4's Today programme that such programmes were a financial contaminant to patient-doctor trust. He stated: It's short-sighted and misguided of CCGs to introduce such mechanisms, because they do lead to the potential for patients questioning the motives of GP referrals. We believe it is far more appropriate for CCGs to introduce clinical pathways that ensure patients are referred appropriately rather than these crude, salesman-like bonuses which pay GPs simply to make reduction to referrals in numerical terms. Dr Peter Melton is local GP and clinical chief officer for North East Lincolnshire CCG, which provides the equivalent of more than £6,000 to surgeries that reduce outpatient referrals to the same level as the 25% with the lowest referral rates (which include two-week urgent cancer referrals) in 2014/15. He stated the CCG was already amongst the finest in England for referring suspected cancer sufferers to a consultant within two weeks and the programme was not about avoiding sending people to hospital. It is not focussing on referral reduction per se but on better clinical and quality standards for the patient, he explained. The expectation is surgeries will be encouraged to investigate more locally and monitor the patient in the first instance rather than automatically refer in to a secondary care service. Analysis by the BBC's Helen Briggs The NHS is under pressure to make savings, with a target of carving out £22bn of efficiency savings by 2020. NHS leaders wish to reduce patient referrals that are deemed inappropriate, particularly when patients could be cared for locally. Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) are groups of GPs that work together to plan and design local health services. There are more than 200 CCGs across England and, according to Pulse, at least nine are providing payments for keeping within targets for outpatient referrals and follow ups. It is not clear how extensive the practice is elsewhere. Some have questioned the wisdom of the move, stating patients could miss out on vital care. But CCGs have defended their stance, stating it is about good practice, not about keeping people who require treatment out of hospital. In November the NHS advisory board stated GPs in England should nearly double the number of patients referred to hospital for cancer tests. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence stated delays in spotting symptoms could be costing thousands of lives each year. NHS England stated: We explicitly wish to increase not deter appropriate referrals for cancer checks. Dr Rosie Loftus of the charity Macmillan Cancer Support described the findings outlined in Pulse as very worrying. This is yet another sign of an NHS which is seriously over stretched and not giving GPs the resources and support they require, she stated. NHS Lambeth Clinical Commissioning Group, which provides payments for surgeries moving towards the average referral rate, stated, like all CCGs, it wished to reduce the number of patients being sent to hospitals unnecessarily. The part of the payment relating to the rate of referrals is a small part of the funding and is not designed to stop GPs referring patients who have a clinical need for hospital treatment such as cancer patients, stated a spokesperson.

text: A villain-turned-leading man of Bollywood, a bohemian at the feet of a hippy guru, a successful politician: Vinod Khanna was a man who lived many lives, writes Sudha G Tilak. These are external links and will open in a new window Vinod Khanna, who has passed away aged 70, belonged to the second generation of Punjabi stars who dominated Bollywood - termed Partition Punjabis. His family originated from Peshawar in Pakistan and had relocated to India in 1947 when the nation was partitioned. The screen heroes of that era were all dashing protagonists renowned for their robust good looks, refined on-screen mannerisms and distinctive styles. He epitomised all of this but also brought all the flair of 1970s cinema to his performances. Khanna completed his studies at college in Mumbai but had been captivated by films since school and soon began focusing on acting full-time. He made his cinema debut in 1968 with Man ka Meet. Film critic Jai Arjun Singh observes that Khanna's Bollywood journey was unconventional for his era. He was the first contemporary Bollywood star who commenced by portraying antagonistic roles. Khanna's villainy was striking as it merged his handsome appearance with a sharp dangerous threat that made him compelling on screen. He excelled at playing villain roles more than the traditional Bollywood protagonist, states Singh. If Dharmendra was the original beefcake of Bollywood in the 1970s, the 1980s was controlled by the persona of Amitabh Bachchan's angry young man. However Mr Singh states there was a period when Bollywood observers forecast that Khanna posed a threat to superstar Bachchan's fame. The pair appeared in numerous films together. In Amar Akbar Anthony, one of Bollywood's greatest successes ever, a sequence shows Khanna thrashing Bachchan thoroughly and carrying him across his shoulders. It left numerous admirers of the superstar bewildered. It was unthinkable for me to envisage my hero being defeated. Even by his elder brother in the picture, writes Diptakirti Chaudhuri, in a volume on Bollywood. Khanna was a heartthrob with captivating eyes and the blend of his physique and attractive features helped him surge to the summit. He performed in action films, thrillers, and romantic dramas and, for a period, commanded the marquee in Bollywood. His significant films include Mera Gaon Mera Desh, Gaddar, Imtihaan, Muqaddar ka Sikander, Inkaar, Amar Akbar, Antony, Qurbani, Kudrat, Dayavan amongst others. However in the 1980s, Khanna, by then a family man and leading star, abandoned acting in cinema to withdraw to an ashram operated by Rajneesh, a unconventional spiritual teacher, favoured by westerners, in the western Indian city of Pune. The tabloids dubbed him Sexy Sanyasi, referring to an ascetic devotee of Hinduism. I am, I suppose, a human being who does what seems right to him at the moment, does what he truly wishes to do, he once told a journalist who enquired whether he was a star or a sanyasi. Certainly, it is simple to cling to one thing, to be and do that all your existence - but within you is a voice stating there must be something more to existence. I search for that something more. Following his return from the ashram, his marriage concluded and he disappeared from public consciousness. However he proceeded to remarry and gradually returned to acting at his own rhythm. Much later, in 1997, he entered politics - subsequently being elected to parliament four times. He was once appointed a junior foreign minister. Khanna is survived by his wife, daughters and sons. He will be eternally remembered as an actor who composed his own unconventional narrative.

text: Fighting has eased in parts of Syria where a Russian-led initiative to halt the country's six-year war took effect from midnight, activists say. These are external links and will open in a new window The agreement announced by Russia on Thursday to establish four de-escalation zones receives support from Turkey and Iran. However, the principal Syrian opposition group states it has minimal confidence in the agreement. In other areas of Syria, campaigners report government warplanes have struck central Hama province, whilst there are accounts of bombardment and gunfire in additional regions. The opposition High Negotiations Committee (HNC) declared on Friday the safe zones proposal lacked safeguards and compliance mechanisms. It additionally stated it would not accept Iran as a guarantor of the agreement. The UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, informed the BBC the accord was significant because it was being executed by three nations who could ensure its success. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) reported Syrian fighter aircraft on Saturday struck rebel positions in Hama. A rebel commander verified that combat had commenced after midnight, Reuters reports. The Syrian military has thus far not remarked on the matter. The so-called memorandum on the creation of de-escalation areas was revealed by the Russian military following discussions in Kazakhstan's capital Astana. Russia's foreign ministry released the complete text of the accord on Saturday. The aim is to cease attacks by all parties and to provide the conditions for the safe and voluntary return of refugees alongside the rapid provision of relief supplies and medical assistance. The four zones shall remain in position for six months, though their boundaries must be determined by Russia, Iran and Turkey by 4 June. According to the proposal, the four zones shall be established in: Russian Deputy Defence Minister Alexander Fomin stated on Friday that there had been no bombing operations by Russian aviation in the four zones since 1 May. However, he emphasised that Russia's air force would continue targeting militants from the Islamic State (IS) group elsewhere in Syria. The US has voiced concern regarding Iran, stating the nation had only contributed to the violence, not stopped it. The Syrian government of President Bashar al-Assad is not a signatory, though its state news agency has declared it endorses the proposal. The Astana discussions were intended to reinforce an oft-violated ceasefire which was initially agreed in December. A partial cessation of hostilities was announced at the end of last year, yet violence has persisted on multiple fronts. Syria's conflict has claimed more than 300,000 lives since it began in 2011.

text: The people who have been closely involved with the Kevin Pietersen story recognised it was always destined to finish in a dramatic parting of the ways. It has invariably concluded in this manner, regardless of his location. Media playback is not supported on this device However, if England have failed in their efforts to handle him, then so has everybody else. At minimum the decision not to select him again was unanimous and taken by those at the England and Wales Cricket Board who understand what truly transpired. It has been taken by individuals within the dressing room, not by journalists or supporters. Players have stated various matters off the record regarding Pietersen and his conduct, but when a camera or dictaphone is placed before them they will inform you what a splendid fellow he is. On the field of play, he may have been England's top run scorer in the 5-0 Ashes whitewash in Australia, but he dug deep and battled only once, when he scored 71 and 49 at Melbourne. If he had averaged 40 and been caught behind every occasion, then he may have survived. Nevertheless, the manner he got out in the first three Tests in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth will have played a significant part in the decision taken by the ECB. Pietersen has invariably batted however he feels on a specific day, but if he could not get his head down and play for the team when they were up against it, could he ever do so? His international career could easily have concluded 18 months ago when he sent text messages to the South Africa dressing room, undermining then captain Andrew Strauss. That was disgraceful - and Pietersen knew it. The ECB did everything it could to bring him back on board, but when you have been so completely and utterly dismantled, as England have been this winter, you must draw a line. Nov 2004: Makes England one-day debut, scoring 27 not out against Zimbabwe Jan/Feb 2005: Scores three hundreds in one-day series in South Africa July 2005: Makes Test debut in opening Ashes Test, scoring 57 & 64 not out Sept 2005: Scores 158 on the final day of the Ashes series as England win urn for first time in 18 years Aug 2008: Named England Test and one-day captain Jan 2009: Resigns as England captain following a rift with coach Peter Moores, who is sacked May 2010: Scores 248 runs and is named player of the tournament as England win the World T20 in West Indies Jan 2011: Part of England team that wins a Test series in Australia for first time since 1987 May 2012: Announces retirement from international limited-overs cricket Aug 2012: Reverses his retirement decision Aug 2012: Dropped for third Test against South Africa for sending provocative texts to opposition players, days after scoring a brilliant century at Headingley Oct 2012: Agrees to be reintegrated into England team after signing new ECB contract. Recalled for India tour and scores 186 in Mumbai in 2-1 series win Sept 2013: Helps England to 3-0 Ashes series victory over Australia Jan 2014: Part of England team that suffers 5-0 whitewash in Australia Feb 2014: Told he is no longer in the ECB's plans England's new managing director, Paul Downton, states he wants to rebuild not only the team, but also the team ethic and philosophy. And he is precisely right. Teams sometimes become too settled, get stuck in their ways and lose sight of what they are there to do. text: Being in a wheelchair doesn't mean that I can't do it or anyone else can't do it - we're just as capable as any other models. Wednesday marked a milestone moment for Gemma Flanagan as she navigated her first catwalk appearance in a wheelchair at a London fashion event.It was so amazing to do it and not fall off. My biggest worry was I'd roll off the end or the side, she said.Her modeling career began years earlier when she balanced work as an air hostess with part-time runway appearances, before illness changed her mobility forever.The 32-year-old, who celebrates her birthday this week, discovered unexpected confidence during her debut wheelchair performance. I surprisingly felt just as confident as I have done in the past which, considering it was the first one in my chair, I wasn't sure how I'd cope with, she explained.Traditional runway work had allowed her certain freedoms that initially concerned her. When you're walking you can kind of have a little strut and do your thing. That's what I was worried about - not being able to show the clothes off as well, she noted.However, the designer's response proved her fears unfounded. The designer's just so pleased with how I showcased their items and at the end of the day that's what modelling's about.Models of Diversity organized the fashion show, which took place at London's Olympia during the Ideal Home Show. The group actively campaigns for greater representation across fashion and beauty industries.Gemma envisions a future where disabled models become standard rather than exceptional. The more people that are open to using models with disabilities then the more people will see it as normal, she advocates.Current industry practices frustrate her, particularly the tokenistic approach many companies adopt. We've all been in campaigns that have been a one-off for companies and a lot of them aren't paid either, she reveals.Her vision extends beyond charity cases or diversity checkboxes. It would be good to use models with disabilities just as models, not as one-offs - we're better than that, she says.Looking ahead, Gemma has secured several upcoming projects. I've got a hair show in May and a couple of shoots lined up with local photographers, she announced.Her wheelchair has evolved from obstacle to opportunity in her professional mindset. I want to do a lot more using my chair. I'm in it near enough all of the time now. Part of me doing this show was to embrace myself and embrace the fact that the chair isn't the enemy anymore.The transformation involves shifting public perception entirely. It's basically seeing past the metal and the wheels and just saying, 'that's a gorgeous model' rather than 'a girl in a chair'.Guillain-Barré Syndrome, diagnosed in 2011, dramatically altered Gemma's life trajectory. The serious nervous system condition required extensive rehabilitation spanning seven months as she relearned fundamental skills including speaking, writing, and walking.Initial medical optimism has given way to realistic acceptance. When I got ill they were hoping I'd make a full recovery, she said. Recent developments have made walking with crutches increasingly difficult, leading to greater wheelchair dependence.Her consultant's assessment suggests current limitations may be permanent. But I've started getting worse again and the consultant thinks this may be the best I'm ever going to be, she acknowledged.Despite emotional challenges, Gemma maintains positive momentum. I've been a bit up and down, but now I feel OK mostly.Her broader mission transcends personal achievement. I want to show other people they don't need to be defined by their disabilities.Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube

text: Michael Bostwick's second-half strike secured a comfortable win for Peterborough over MK Dons. Peterborough United climbed above their opponents in the League One standings following a commanding 2-0 victory, with both Andrew Hughes and Michael Bostwick finding the net for their maiden strikes of the campaign.The away side wasted no time establishing their dominance, breaking the deadlock within barely sixty seconds. Marcus Maddison's expertly delivered free-kick located Hughes completely unmarked at the near post, allowing the ex-Newport defender to expertly volley home from close range inside the six-yard area.Karl Robinson's MK Dons struggled to create meaningful opportunities, waiting nearly half an hour before registering their first genuine threat. The chance materialized when Nicky Maynard broke through the defensive line and squared the ball to Daniel Powell, but the 25-year-old winger's effort was brilliantly thwarted by experienced Peterborough goalkeeper Mark Tyler.Despite a brief resurgence from the home team during the second period, Grant McCann's visitors secured their victory with a second goal in the 71st minute. Once again, Maddison proved instrumental from a set-piece situation, his free-kick delivery finding the towering Bostwick, who powered a header beyond Dons keeper David Martin.The match concluded with MK Dons 0, Peterborough United 2, as the second half drew to a close.Throughout the latter stages, both teams created several opportunities. Dean Bowditch's right-footed attempt from distance sailed wide of the target, while Chris Forrester's shot from the left was comfortably gathered by the goalkeeper. Marcus Maddison nearly extended Peterborough's advantage, but his left-footed strike from the right flank was saved low to the keeper's left.The Dons continued pressing for a consolation goal, with Ben Reeves coming close on multiple occasions. His right-footed effort from the left side of the penalty area narrowly missed the top corner, while another attempt from outside the box was saved in the bottom right corner.Several substitutions punctuated the second half's action. Peterborough introduced Jermaine Anderson for Gwion Edwards, followed by Shaquile Coulthirst replacing Tom Nichols, and Callum Chettle coming on for Paul Taylor. MK Dons responded by bringing Kabongo Tshimanga on for Nicky Maynard.The match featured its share of disciplinary action, with George Baldock receiving a yellow card for a poor challenge, while Paul Taylor and Darren Potter were also cautioned for similar infractions. A brief delay occurred when Marcus Maddison required treatment for an injury, but play resumed without further incident.Bostwick's decisive header from Maddison's free-kick proved to be the match-winner, finding the top left corner to seal all three points for the visitors and complete a satisfying afternoon's work for McCann's side.Report supplied by the Press Association.

text: Labour MP Simon Danczuk has been suspended by the party after newspaper allegations about his private life. Labour MP Simon Danczuk has been suspended from the party following allegations in The Sun that he exchanged explicit messages with a 17-year-old girl.The Rochdale representative acknowledged on Twitter that while the story was not entirely accurate, it reflected an extremely low point in his life. Offering an unreserved apology for his inappropriate behaviour, Danczuk admitted: I was stupid [and] there's no fool like an old fool.Labour's general secretary moved swiftly to suspend Danczuk's party membership pending a full investigation. A party spokesman confirmed: The general secretary of the Labour Party has today suspended Simon Danczuk's membership of the party, pending an investigation into allegations published in the media today. A full investigation will now take place under the authority of the National Executive Committee, which will be responsible for determining any further action.The suspension means Danczuk, who has represented Rochdale since 2010 and separated from his wife earlier this year, has lost the Labour whip and will now sit as an independent MP.Known as an outspoken backbencher, the 49-year-old has frequently clashed with Labour leadership. He has been particularly critical of current leader Jeremy Corbyn while describing former leader Ed Miliband as one of the worst Labour Party leaders in history.Danczuk gained prominence through his high-profile campaign exposing historical child abuse. He co-authored a book detailing alleged abuse by former Rochdale MP Cyril Smith and pushed for action regarding a missing 1980s dossier about alleged Westminster paedophiles.However, in July, Danczuk announced he was stepping back from his child abuse campaigning to seek help for depression, acknowledging it had damaged his marriage. He stated he was in no doubt the work had taken its toll.The timing of these allegations proves particularly damaging given Danczuk's reputation as a child protection campaigner. BBC political correspondent Chris Mason noted the embarrassment factor for an MP who had dedicated recent years to child protection issues, despite the girl being above the age of consent.In his Twitter statement, Danczuk expressed regret that the episode might overshadow the important work we're doing to help Rochdale [and] that's where my focus lies.Both Jeremy Corbyn and shadow chancellor John McDonnell emphasized the National Executive Committee investigation's independence when questioned about the matter.NEC member and Corbyn ally Ken Livingstone urged caution against premature judgments based solely on the suspension. We won't be rushing to any judgement, he told the BBC, while acknowledging the party's obligation to investigate.Livingstone added: The simple fact is that it might not be illegal but a lot of people are going to disapprove of that sort of age gap and that sort of texting, particularly given this is an MP who made the exposure of child abuse a key part of his political career.

text: Manchester City earned their first Premier League home win in almost three months as they battled past Watford at Etihad Stadium. Manchester City secured a crucial 2-0 victory over Watford at the Etihad Stadium, with Pablo Zabaleta and David Silva finding the net to end their troubling home form drought.The Blues, sitting fourth in the table and desperate to halt a potential third consecutive top-flight loss, struck first through an unmarked Zabaleta. The Argentine defender calmly converted Kevin de Bruyne's deep cross with a composed side-footed finish.Following the interval, Raheem Sterling nearly doubled the advantage but saw his effort clip the Watford crossbar. The visitors' most promising opportunity fell to Odion Ighalo, who disappointingly poked his chance over the bar.Watford's failure to capitalize proved costly when Silva sealed the victory with a late second goal. The Spaniard tucked home during a swift City counter-attack, marking his 200th league appearance in style. However, the triumph was overshadowed by a serious knee injury to Germany midfielder Ilkay Gundogan, which manager Pep Guardiola confirmed will sideline him for several months.The victory provides much-needed relief for Guardiola's struggling side. Cast your mind back to late September when City had achieved a perfect start under their new Spanish manager - 10 consecutive victories, including six Premier League wins that established a four-point lead at the summit.Fast forward to mid-December, and the landscape appears dramatically different. Since that initial purple patch, City have tumbled from first place, managing just four wins from their previous 15 matches before hosting Watford. This alarming decline has prompted questions about Guardiola's methods, which delivered unprecedented success at Barcelona and Bayern Munich.Most tellingly, the Blues hadn't secured a home league victory since that tenth consecutive triumph - a comprehensive 4-0 demolition of Bournemouth on September 17. While Saturday's performance lacked the fluency and intensity of those early Guardiola days, City will undoubtedly welcome a gritty display that maintains their fourth-place standing.It has been a long time without a win playing at home, it has been strange, reflected Zabaleta.The result leaves City seven points adrift of leaders Chelsea, trailing Liverpool and Arsenal by a single point each. The Gunners visit the Etihad on Sunday, presenting another crucial test.City's recent struggles stem clearly from defensive frailties. The Blues had managed just one clean sheet across their previous 17 matches, and following Saturday's humiliating 4-2 defeat at champions Leicester City, Guardiola overhauled both personnel and formation.England centre-back John Stones notably paid the price, relegated to the bench as Guardiola abandoned his three-centre-back system for a traditional four-man defense. The tactical switch yielded immediate dividends, with City appearing more organized and resolute than at any point during the past two months.It was not the prettiest game tonight but we had determination to win the game. We had the clean sheet we've been talking about and were solid defensively, added Zabaleta.Nevertheless, City nearly suffered punishment when Ighalo escaped Zabaleta's attention, only to guide Norden Amrabat's right-wing delivery over the crossbar. Goalkeeper Claudio Bravo, who has faced criticism from City supporters, also produced a crucial save from Hornets midfielder Etienne Capoue.It is not easy to come to a new club and a new country, Guardiola said of the Chile international, who arrived from Barcelona during the summer. I know what people say about him, but he has good experience. When moments arrive he has to be brave. Today he was excellent.Under Italian manager Walter Mazzarri, Watford have displayed contrasting personalities - capable of defeating Manchester United and Everton to reach seventh place, yet equally prone to capitulating in Liverpool's 6-1 demolition and losing three from four before last weekend's victory over the Toffees.This performance fell somewhere between those extremes. The Hornets showed admirable resilience in preventing City from carving them open, though attacking opportunities remained scarce.Despite netting three against Everton recently, Mazzarri's team have struggled for goals throughout the campaign. Captain Troy Deeney hasn't scored since October 1, enduring an eight-match barren spell that ultimately cost him his starting position at the Etihad.Instead, Mazzarri deployed a fresh strike partnership featuring last season's leading scorer Ighalo alongside 20-year-old former Liverpool forward Jerome Sinclair. Sinclair, making his full debut following a £4m summer transfer, remained largely peripheral, while Ighalo worked tirelessly but squandered his clearest scoring opportunity in the closing stages.The defeat, combined with positive results for West Brom and Southampton, saw Watford slip to 11th position.Watford manager Walter Mazzarri reflected: We were unlucky because of the chance for Ighalo. If he had scored we would have drawn the game and in my opinion that would have been the fair result. Ighalo played a great game and he deserved to score. But my whole team played well and they deserved something more. I'm very happy with them.Regarding midfielder Roberto Pererya's injury: He has a knee problem. We need to understand what it is. We will know in the next days. We have not been lucky with injuries. I am not happy with this one. I don't know how bad it is. I also asked during the game if he felt a twist. He said it was a knock. I am not sure.On Deeney's omission: We wanted to get Deeney ready for Sunderland. We have three games in a week and he is on four yellow cards.Former England defender Phil Neville on Match of the Day commented: It was not about the performance tonight, it was about getting the result. They did not play at their fluent best but they did score a couple of really good goals. It wasn't convincing, it was a bit of a nervous atmosphere at the Etihad today but it was an important three points. It's pathetic that Pep Guardiola has been getting criticism so soon into a season. We wanted Pep to come to England and now we are trying to destroy him, I don't get it.Looking ahead, Manchester City face another Premier League home fixture against title rivals Arsenal, with the Gunners visiting the Etihad on Sunday (16:30 GMT). The Hornets return to road duties, traveling north to face bottom-placed Sunderland on Saturday (15:00).

text: A Carmarthen school at the centre of a police investigation into claims of historical abuse has been criticised by care inspectors in a new report. The residential facility at Rhydygors school in Carmarthen has been found lacking in meeting fundamental standards, according to Care and Social Services Inspectorate Wales. This follows additional criticism from Estyn school inspectors in September.Located in Johnstown, Rhydygors School serves pupils with social, emotional and behavioural difficulties through specialized education programs. The institution's governors have stated they are working to build upon existing improvements that address issues highlighted in the Estyn evaluation.Recent developments have intensified scrutiny of the school. This month, Dyfed Powys Police confirmed the arrest of six former employees under Operation Almond, which examines abuse allegations spanning from 1976 to 1986 at the facility.The CSSIW assessment delivered a stark conclusion: Overall, we found that young people and their representatives cannot be confident that due care and attention has been paid to the national minimum standards for residential special schools in the period since our last inspection, as the service has not fully met these standards.Monthly monitoring visits from Carmarthenshire council have been implemented to oversee the quality of student care. The report identified several deficiencies, including insufficient awareness of national minimum standards among acting head teacher Margaret Davies and the governing body.Staff qualification requirements present another challenge. While regulations mandate that 80% of care staff possess relevant qualifications, the residential unit has fallen short of this benchmark. Additionally, the service neglected to conduct the mandatory annual review of welfare provisions for boarding students.Estyn's separate evaluation characterized the school's performance as adequate while deeming improvement prospects unsatisfactory. The inspectors noted: The school's arrangements for safeguarding pupils generally meet requirements but a few areas give a cause for concern.Matthew Harries, the school's chair of governors, acknowledged the challenges while emphasizing progress. Rhydygors was inspected by Estyn in September 2014 and, as the new chair of governors, I will be looking to build on the progress that has been made to address the recommendations of the report, Harries stated. Indeed, we are pleased that progress has been made in many of these areas as noted in the more recent CSSIW report.Despite the identified shortcomings, a CSSIW spokesperson clarified their position: We do not have any significant concerns about Rhydygors School.Operation Almond's investigation extends beyond Rhydygors, encompassing abuse allegations at Cartref-y-Gelli children's home in Carmarthen between 1986 and 1990.

text: The spacecraft which made a spectacular landing on a comet last year has discovered a rich array of carbon compounds. A leading scientist's description of the discovered chemicals as a frozen primordial soup underscores findings that could revolutionize our understanding of life's origins on Earth.The breakthrough emerged from data collected when the Philae lander made its historic touchdown on comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko 67P last November. Released from the European Space Agency's Rosetta mothership during the culmination of a decade-long mission, the lander's seven instruments have now yielded extraordinary results published in a special Science journal collection.Among the most striking discoveries, the COSAC device detected 16 organic compounds - four previously unknown to exist on comets. These findings bolster theories suggesting comets delivered life's essential ingredients to early Earth.I see this cometary material that we're analysing as frozen primordial soup. It's the kind of stuff that if you had it, and warmed it up somehow, and put it in the right environment, with the right conditions, you may eventually get life forming out of it, explained Prof Ian Wright of the Open University, who leads the Ptolemy instrument.Wright emphasized the profound implications: What we may be looking at here is our abiological ancestral material - this is stuff that went into the mix to produce life. In many ways it's quite a humbling thing to be working on, because this is life before life happened.Ptolemy's analysis revealed polyoxymethylene, a polymer formed from formaldehyde chains. The simplest unit of this polymer is a single carbon, two hydrogens and a single oxygen, and this then repeats itself. That same ratio of elements occur in carbohydrates and sugars so it's very interesting and implicated in the biological cycle we have on Earth, Prof Wright noted.Fred Goesmann and colleagues detailed COSAC's 16 compound discoveries in separate research, highlighting their biological significance. Hydroxyethanal functions as an efficient initiator in the prebiotic formation of sugars, while methanenitrile represents a key molecule in the prebiotic synthesis of amino acids and nucleobases and even offers an elegant pathway to sugars.The researchers concluded that the comet's chemical complexity and nitrogen-containing organics imply that early solar system chemistry fosters the formation of prebiotic material in noticeable concentrations. However, no papers reported more sophisticated compounds like amino acids, though further analysis might reveal their presence.Professor Charles Cockell, director of the UK Astrobiology Centre, praised the mission's significance despite not participating directly. Finding simple organic compounds on a comet out there in space, showing us that they could have been delivered to the early Earth, early in the history of our planet, is tremendously exciting, he told the BBC.It gives us better ideas about how those building blocks of life may have formed and where they may have come from. It confirms there is organic chemistry throughout the universe, that carbon-containing compounds, some of which are very complex, could be being formed on comets in our solar system.Prof Mark McCaughrean, the European Space Agency's senior science advisor, offered an illuminating analogy: Imagine you want to build a house and you go to a forest, where there are trees, mud and rocks. You could make a house out of that, but it would be hard work. Well, we've now discovered the comet is more like a hardware shop - lots of pre-made building blocks, like door frames, bricks etc. It gives you a head start.McCaughrean acknowledged a crucial unanswered question: One of the big questions, though, is this material made on the comet? Or is it made first in space and then incorporated into the comet? We don't know the answer to that yet.The published data originated from Philae's turbulent landing sequence. Ptolemy activated ten minutes post-touchdown as planned. The idea was we'd just have time for a sniff of the air - there was no great reason to do it, it was to check the instrument had survived landing, an insurance policy to get some data as soon as possible, Prof Wright explained.Philae's failure to anchor at its intended landing site created an unexpected opportunity. The lander bounced upward, allowing Ptolemy to sample airborne material during flight. We've just got a snapshot of some dust that was flying around as we landed but we've got some very significant data, Prof Wright said.Following months of silence, Philae reestablished contact last month, though communications remain sporadic and the spacecraft's condition uncertain. Scientists theorize the lander may have shifted position due to gas jets from underlying rocks or suffered damage from cliff debris as surface temperatures rise.Gas jet intensity increases as the comet nears the Sun, with perihelion - its closest solar approach - scheduled for August 13. Mission teams maintain optimism about Philae's survival and potential for renewed contact.Regardless of future communications, substantial data collected during Philae's initial 60 hours on the comet awaits analysis and publication, promising additional revelations about these cosmic building blocks of life.

text: Nigeria's main opposition party has condemned a weekend raid of its Lagos offices by state security agents. The State Security Service defended its weekend raid on an All Progressive Congress office, claiming it was investigating allegations of voter card cloning ahead of February's elections, while the opposition party demanded an independent inquiry into what it called government oppression.According to the SSS, agents seized a server, three hard drives and 31 bags of documents during Saturday's operation after placing the building under surveillance. The service said it received a petition alleging that individuals were cloning Inec [Independent Electoral Commission] permanent voters cards, with the intention of hacking into [the] Inec database, corrupting it and replacing them with their own data.Based on this information, the Service placed the building under surveillance and having been convinced that some unwholesome activities were going on in the building, it undertook a raid of the premises, the SSS stated.However, APC deputy chairman Lawal Shuaibu disputed the government's account, telling the BBC that more than a dozen computers had been destroyed, a server had been vandalised and 28 people arrested during the raid.We call for an independent commission of inquiry to ascertain the reasons why armed officers raided our office, Shuaibu said, describing the incident as another one in the string of attacks and illegal actions of the administration.The opposition party maintained that the office functioned as a data centre for processing party membership registrations and constituted a legitimate operation. APC spokesman Lai Mohammed drew parallels to America's most infamous political scandal, comparing the raid to the Watergate scandal in the United States, which led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974.Just like the Watergate scandal in the USA, the state-sponsored security operatives apparently acting at the behest of the ruling PDP [People's Democratic Party] government turned the office upside down, and pulled out and vandalised everything in sight, Mohammed told the AFP news agency.Speaking to the BBC Hausa service, Shuaibu expressed broader concerns about government tactics. Nigerians have been witnessing the way and manner the government have been using force in oppressing us, he said. This is to be condemned and we have been restraining ourselves from taking actions based on the provocations by the government and the security personnel.The confrontation comes as Nigeria prepares for what analysts warn could be a particularly contentious election cycle. The APC, formed through a 2013 merger of four opposition parties, has positioned itself as the primary challenger to President Goodluck Jonathan's PDP, which has maintained power since military rule ended in 1999.Adding to concerns about electoral stability, the International Crisis Group recently issued warnings about February's upcoming vote. If this violent trend continues, and particularly if the vote is close, marred or followed by widespread violence, it would deepen Nigeria's already grave security and governance crises, the think tank cautioned.The organization emphasized the stakes involved, stating that the government, its agencies and all other national figures must work urgently to ensure that the vote is not conducted in an explosive situation as this could further destabilise the country. Their assessment characterized the election as potentially volatile and vicious.

text: Writer and humourist Shovon Chowdhury gives his perspective on a recent advert featuring lesbians in India, arguing that we shouldn't be surprised, given India's ancient liberal tradition, which accepted all forms of sexuality and sexual expression. A friend exclaimed, They did an ad about lesbians!Initially mishearing librarians, I felt confused but optimistic. Reading habits in this country often concern me, so this seemed positive. Then he revealed the truth.The advertisement, promoting a women's clothing brand, depicts two women in love. Well-directed and expertly acted, it proved annoyingly difficult to ridicule. Did this represent a monumental leap forward?It appeared so, until Parveen Babi came to mind.This celebrated actress illuminated our youth and brought national pride by gracing Time magazine's cover. The lesbian narrative isn't as revolutionary as current discourse suggests.In 1983's Razia Sultan, Parveen Babi and Hema Malini reclined together on an opulent boat in carefree intimacy. Hema Malini dozed while Parveen Babi gazed intensely, crooning a lullaby. When Hema Malini awakened, they kissed—though feathers concealed the moment. Such concealment was standard then; feathers, flowers, and dupattas routinely masked romantic scenes.This television commercial offers a contemporary setting with fewer feathers, making the scenario more accessible. Viewers think, That could be my cousin or my best friend's sister.Cinema, however, pioneered this territory. Generally, Indian cinema has driven significant social transformation.Post-independence filmmakers, feeling freedom's warmth, boldly embedded positive social messages into their work as part of nation-building efforts.Until the 1990s brought a television revelation: home viewing eliminated the need to venture out. This discovery diminished cinema's significance.Increased television consumption meant expanded advertising, introducing economic factors.Television serial producers are notoriously frugal, resulting in glacially-paced dialogue and arrows taking multiple episodes to reach their targets. While TV writers receive meager compensation, advertising professionals earn substantially more.Consequently, advertisements often surpass programs in quality.
