text: There has been a 65% increase in children recorded as home educated in the UK over six years. Freedom of Information requests submitted to 190 local authorities revealed that 36,609 children are currently receiving home education, representing an increase of at least 10,399 pupils in a school population of approximately 9.5 million.The actual number of home-educated children may be significantly higher than reported. While children withdrawn from traditional schools are documented as home-educated, those who never enter the formal school system might not appear in official statistics.Data from 178 councils covering the past three years demonstrates a 26% surge in home education numbers. Among 133 local authorities with records spanning from 2009-10 to 2014-15, the figures show an almost two-thirds increase.Parents cite various motivations for choosing home education over traditional schooling. These include lifestyle preferences, dissatisfaction or conflicts with local schools, addressing special needs, combating bullying, and religious considerations.Graham Stuart, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Home Education, suggests that improved record-keeping by councils might partially explain the apparent increase, though he maintains that any figures likely underestimate the true numbers.Local authorities have created groups to share best practice, and we're seeing what I hope is an increasing trend to stop treating home education as a problem to be regulated, and instead see it as an opportunity to be facilitated and supported, said the Conservative MP and former chairman of the education select committee.While parents aren't legally required to explain their decision to withdraw children from school, 41 council areas have collected information about motivations, offering insights into the diverse reasons behind home education choices.Philosophical or lifestyle differences top the list at 13.4% of cases. In Gloucestershire, this category accounts for 235 of the 641 home-educated children. Dissatisfaction with local schools or conflicts follows at 9.3%, with Hertfordshire recording 240 out of 724 parents citing this reason.Religious or cultural factors motivate 6.2% of families, while bullying concerns affect 4.8% and special needs or medical issues influence 4.3%. Rising school enrollment pressures have led 3.4% of parents to choose home education after failing to secure places at preferred schools.Dr Helen Lees of Newman University Birmingham, who has extensively researched alternative education, believes some parents reject the structured assessment and testing prevalent in traditional schools.She says parents find online accounts of the success of home education and are saying: If they can do it why can't we do it. They're hearing from groups on Facebook or Yahoo that it's working well, the children are happy.The documentation of parental motivations remains inconsistent, partly because parents have no obligation to provide explanations, resulting in incomplete comprehensive data.Limited demographic information about home-educating families follows similar patterns. Among the few local authorities collecting religious data, approximately 31% of home educators belong to faith groups, though this may not necessarily drive their educational choice. Half of these families identify as Christian, while one-third are Muslim.Geographic variations in home education growth suggest multiple contributing factors. Counties with grammar school systems show relatively high numbers, with Kent recording 1,429 and Essex reaching 1,191 home-educated children.Rhondda Cynon Taf demonstrates dramatic growth, expanding from five home-educated children in 2009-10 to 65 currently.Recent concerns have emerged from Ofsted regarding potential misuse of home education rights. A small number of individuals may be exploiting these provisions to place children in unregistered and potentially illegal educational settings.Education Secretary Nicky Morgan has echoed these concerns, requesting Chief Inspector of Schools Sir Michael Wilshaw to gather evidence for possible prosecutions.Current government consultations address greater regulation of part-time educational settings providing more than six to eight hours weekly of instruction. However, officials have emphasized their commitment to preserving parental educational choice rights.Parents have no legal obligation to send children to traditional schools, though they must ensure provision of suitable education at home.The government continues to respect the rights of parents to home educate their children, whether at home or in a combination of other settings, provided a suitable full-time education is being arranged.

After his meeting on Monday with Hassan Rouhani, the Prime Minister emphasized the importance of convincing Russia and Iran that a new Syria under a different leader would serve their interests and help in the fight against the so-called ISIS. - Yes. During the later meeting of the counter-terrorism conference, presided over by President Barack Obama, the Prime Minister presented the extent of British participation and stressed the importance of winning the propaganda war and the battle for hearts and minds. "It does not mean that you seek a phony solution, that you think you can work with Assad against Daesh, because that would be self-defeating. " He also admitted that the western powers had failed to support the moderate Syrian opposition, admitting that the efforts made in this direction were not sufficient. He defended the recent British airstrike in Syria that killed three British fighters, saying that it had stopped the terrorists who were about to strike against the United States and Great Britain. It is necessary to follow the right path, no matter how long it takes, and to persuade others.

text: General Motors chief executive Mary Barra has apologised for an ignition switch fault in some cars linked to at least a dozen deaths in road crashes. During Tuesday's US congressional hearing, General Motors CEO Mary Barra expressed being disturbed by her company's earlier statements regarding the expensive nature of replacing faulty components.The automotive giant has recalled 2.6 million vehicles due to the defective parts, though critics argue the company's response came far too late. Initial reports of ignition switch problems in GM vehicles, including the Chevrolet Cobalt and Saturn Ion models, surfaced over a decade ago. However, recalls only commenced this February—just one month following Ms Barra's appointment as chief executive.Appearing before a US House of Representatives panel examining the matter, Ms Barra testified: I cannot tell you why it took years for a safety defect to be announced... but I can tell you that we will find out.She continued: As soon as l learned about the problem, we acted without hesitation. We told the world we had a problem that needed to be fixed. We did so because whatever mistakes were made in the past, we will not shirk from our responsibilities now and in the future. Today's GM will do the right thing.Her testimony included a heartfelt apology: That begins with my sincere apologies to everyone who has been affected by this recall, especially to the families and friends of those who lost their lives or were injured. I am deeply sorry.Ms Barra characterized as disturbing the possibility that financial concerns might have delayed immediate replacement of the defective switches.Republican Fred Upton, chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, addressed Ms Barra directly: With a two-tonne piece of high-velocity machinery, there is zero margin for error; product safety is a life or death issue. But sadly, vehicle safety has fallen short.The recall initially encompassed 1.6 million pre-2007 vehicles, with GM expanding coverage last week to include over 800,000 additional cars manufactured between 2008-11.The central problem involves a manufacturing defect in ignition switches that allows keys to spontaneously move from run to accessory or off position while vehicles operate at full speed.GM has initiated an internal probe into the issue and established a new senior position dedicated to overseeing vehicle safety and recalls last month.In the first indication that victims might receive compensation, Ms Barra announced GM's decision to engage consultant Kenneth Feinberg to assist in planning for those who suffered the most from this tragedy. Mr Feinberg previously managed compensation matters for the 11 September 2001 attacks, the BP Gulf of Mexico oil spill, and last year's Boston Marathon bombing.Monday brought news of another GM recall affecting more than 1.3 million vehicles due to electronic power steering issues that the company stated could increase the risk of a crash.

text: A law has come into force in France which makes it an offence for a Muslim woman to conceal her face behind a veil when in public. France has become Europe's pioneering nation in publicly prohibiting a garment that certain Muslims consider a religious obligation.Readers of the BBC News website across France have shared their perspectives on this development. Below are selected responses from their submissions.In my opinion, the law appears to be against individual liberties. I am a Muslim but I don't wear a head scarf as I think it's not faithful to my principles. However, this ban will certainly stigmatise Islam. This practice concerns a small number of Muslim women in France and in that way it appears extreme and unfair, because these women will tend to be confined at home most of the time. The consequences will be socially disastrous. Through this law you can see that Islam in France is perceived as a threat to French values and society. Sabrina, Lille, FranceA Paris-based Muslim expressed support for the legislation. As a Muslim living in Paris, I'm so glad that this new law is here, for there has been a growing problem for some time now in Paris, with the radicalisation of young Muslims. Some of the more extreme Muslims have begun to use dress as a symbol or statement against French society. I feel that the extreme example of the Muslim faith works against all that Muslims in France stand for. That is, that we can live in harmony side by side with other religions and faiths. Jean Paul Baptiste, Paris, FranceFrom Aix en Provence came praise for the measure's protective intent. At last a law that protects the dignity and the human rights of women. This is not a racist law, it is a brave and progressive law that aims to put an end to the scandalous persecution of women in the Muslim community. I am not Sarkozy's biggest fan and I wish someone else was leading my country, but I support this law 100% as the plight of women having to wear this garment around the world really saddens me. Rachel Sword, Aix en Provence, FranceAnother supporter cited social concerns. I agree with this law. The women who walk around in public in the burqa, cause feelings of both fear, and pity. I have often heard that these women complain of being totally ignored by those around them - hardly surprising, really. Hiding your identity causes others to become wary and suspicious. Fiona Ricard, Gailhan, FranceA human rights lawyer from Strasbourg offered nuanced views. Despite being a human rights lawyer, I have mixed feelings about the law. Freedom of religion dictates that people should be able to manifest their faith how they wish, though it can be restricted by the state if there are strong reasons and it is proportionate. I think it should not be banned outright and that it is excessive, but it should perhaps be restricted in the case of employment or other areas of society. Whilst the state has to respect the diverse values of its population, immigrants also have to respect the values of the society they have chosen to live in - and France is a secular state. Andy, Strasbourg, FranceWarning against potential backlash, one reader argued the approach could prove counterproductive. Enacting a law to ban face covering veils in France is taking an approach that will polarise and entrench opinions. Very few Muslim women want to wear face veils, but telling them they can't will make them want to do so to protect what they see as an attack on their identity. Why take a line that will push Muslims (the majority of whom are not conservative) into a more polarised stance (unless of course it's to win a few votes)? Naveen Webber, Gex, FranceA British expatriate offered cultural perspective on the debate's significance. I have been living in France for about six months now and the relative lack of political correctness is a refreshing change from UK. The veil ban is not a big issue here, more like a gentle re-assertion of French equality values. It definitely has nothing to do with a personal crusade by Sarkozy to win votes. Robin Marshall, Avignon, France

text: The museum at Cuba's most famous beach, the Bay of Pigs, is under renovation. Workers busily install new multi-media exhibits inside while builders outside lay concrete patio work and apply fresh paint to the museum entrance.April's grand reopening will coincide with the 55th anniversary of the Bay of Pigs invasion, when hundreds of CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at Playa Giron in their doomed mission to topple Fidel Castro's socialist revolution.This failed assault represented a nadir in US-Cuba relations - exceeded only by the missile crisis that followed twelve months later - and continues serving as a symbol of Washington's covert Latin American interventions.Though many original Cuban defenders, including militia members and regular army soldiers, survive today, only a handful remain in Playa Giron itself, with several in declining health.Dolores Vic Hernandez, now 83, didn't engage the invading forces directly but vividly remembers fleeing from them. She escaped her coastal home for the surrounding hills alongside her sister-in-law and their children.We only had the clothes we were wearing and the babies were in nappies. We collected our friend who had six children and whose husband was in Havana and we took her with us to the mountains.Though Dolores moves less freely now and her vision deteriorates, one can easily envision the determination she possessed as a young mother protecting her family amid escalating conflict.I'm a person who's never been afraid of anything, she declares defiantly, describing how she entered an abandoned house to gather a little coffee and sugar, some biscuits for the children for their mountain journey.Castro ultimately assumed command of revolutionary forces at Giron, orchestrating a famous victory that would embarrass Washington for decades.Following the announcement of US-Cuba normalization, elder statesman Fidel Castro has offered only brief commentary on the new relationship:I don't trust in the United States' policy nor have I exchanged a word with them, he wrote in Granma, the state newspaper, just over a year ago.His distrust seems unsurprising given the numerous CIA assassination attempts he survived during his presidency.Castro added that President Raul, his brother, was taking the pertinent steps in accordance with his prerogatives and the faculties bestowed on him by the National Assembly and the Cuban Communist Party.Some interpreted this as less than enthusiastic endorsement.Cuban academic Esteban Morales disagrees: That didn't mean to say he doesn't support the process, argues Dr. Morales, who has written extensively about Cuba-US relations.I think Fidel is someone who's wise enough to know that this is the only possible path. What is the alternative? Stand against the US canons firing across the bow like we did in the past? No. That's why Fidel intellectually understands that this is a moment to advance.Dr. Morales believes Castro was instead alerting Cubans to Washington's true intentions: Fidel knows perfectly well that international relations is a wide battlefield.We don't expect the United States to turn into our best friends or allies overnight, not by a long way. But perhaps in time they might become trusted neighbours.Fidel isn't alone in harboring doubts.There are Cubans who are nervous about (the opening), observes Jon Lee Anderson of the New Yorker, author of the definitive Che Guevara biography.They seem to be people who were already of a certain age when the revolution came along and this has been their life, the true believers in Fidel Castro's long project of socialism.Their Cuban concerns encompass social and cultural dimensions alongside economic and political ones, Anderson argues.They worry about what will happen to their way of life. They worry about 'will the Miami Cubans come and buy everything and shut them out?' And they worry about the influence of capitalism in eroding their values.However, they may be too late: Most people in Cuba are aware that in the 25 years since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the changes that already began in Cuba, that erosion began some time ago.While rapid US relationship progress might seem improbable to Fidel's generation, Cuba's youth majority grows impatient for accelerated change.No better symbol exists than President Obama strolling Old Havana streets with his family.Obama plans to meet private business owners, engage dissidents, and deliver a major address emphasizing young people's role in shaping Cuba's future.Earlier this month, tens of thousands of young Havanans gathered on the Malecon for Major Lazer's concert - promoting 'Musicabana', a landmark electronic music festival scheduled for later this year.This is the first international music band to come to Cuba at the top of their game, explains Fabien Pisani, concert organizer and 'Musicabana' director.What is interesting here is that this is the music that every kid who is 12 through to 17 is listening to right now.So you can see the degree of excitement here, to be able to touch that and dance and sing together.The performance occurred mere meters from the US embassy in the 'Anti-Imperialist Plaza' - previously synonymous with government-organized anti-US demonstrations.This time, an estimated 150,000-200,000 people filled the square not to protest, but to dance in late afternoon sunshine.In Playa Giron, Dolores Vic would proudly identify as a true believer in Fidel Castro's socialist vision, five-and-a-half decades after the Bay of Pigs disaster.Fidel is like a god to me, she says from her Playa Giron home, recounting how she once prepared traditional Cuban rice, beans, and chicken fricassee when he visited the region.Dolores somewhat shares his wariness about renewed US relations.I have a few doubts as there are always a few bad people over there who'd want to harm us. But there are a lot of good ones too, she concedes.Nevertheless, she cannot contain her excitement about Obama's approaching visit.I never dreamt I'd see this, she says, eyes gleaming.I never thought that in my lifetime a US president would come to Cuba.

text: A teachers' union is warning that schools are increasingly likely to use unqualified teaching staff. The NASUWT teachers' union will present alarming findings at its Cardiff annual conference, revealing widespread concerns about unqualified staff in classrooms across the nation.Chris Keates, NASUWT leader, warns that Parents no longer have the certainty when they send their child to school that they will be taught by qualified teachers. Shadow education secretary Tristram Hunt goes further, declaring this is nothing less than a scandal.However, Conservative representatives counter these claims, insisting fewer teachers lack qualified status now compared to 2010 levels.Survey results from 4,600 union members paint a troubling picture: 61% report working alongside unqualified staff, while 66% describe the situation as deteriorating due to funding constraints. Ms Keates condemns this trend as jeopardising the educational progress of children and denounces unqualified staffing as a crude cost-cutting measure.Teachers' survey responses reveal deep frustrations: They lack any training in classroom management and discipline and I feel that parents are being misled by the quality of teaching within the school.This controversy has emerged as a key general election battleground. Labour campaigns against academies and free schools hiring teachers without qualified status or those still in training.The rising number of unqualified teachers in our schools shows yet again that the Tory plan is threatening standards and failing children and working families, Hunt argues. He claims David Cameron eliminated qualification requirements, resulting in over 400,000 children are now being taught by unqualified teachers without receiving training in skills vital to the profession such as classroom discipline, safeguarding and how to deliver effective teaching for all children.Liberal Democrats similarly advocate mandatory qualified status for all teachers.Both Liberal Democrats and Conservatives maintain that unqualified teacher numbers exceeded current levels during Labour's tenure, disputing claims of increasing unqualified staff usage.Conservative party representatives emphasize declining numbers since 2010: The number of teachers without qualified status has gone down since 2010. And we need to keep this in perspective - only 3.7% of teachers are 'unqualified'.They defend headteacher autonomy: But most importantly, we've given head teachers more freedom over the teachers they employ because we trust them to know what is best for their schools.Conservatives highlight exceptional unqualified educators: There are some brilliant teachers who have not got qualified teacher status - nuns, great linguists, computer scientists, engineers and other specialists that inspire their pupils. They may have worked in the independent sector or have experience in the outside world.Liberal Democrat spokespeople promise to change the law to guarantee a qualified teacher in every classroom, emphasizing that Teaching must be recognised as the vitally important and high status profession that it is, able to attract and retain the very best people.While acknowledging improvements, they maintain every student deserves qualified instruction: It is good news that there are now fewer unqualified teachers working in schools than under the previous Labour government. However, every child deserves to be taught by a qualified teacher, regardless of what type of school they attend.Department for Education statistics from 2013 show unqualified teacher numbers increased from 14,800 to 17,100 compared to the previous year, though remaining below 2010's figure of 17,800 teachers without qualified status.Academy schools present a different trajectory: unqualified teacher proportions have climbed annually since 2010, rising from 2,200 to 7,900.

text: Shaun Johnson scored a winning drop-goal as New Zealand beat England in a tense and physical Four Nations match at a sell-out Huddersfield. Media playback is not supported on this deviceThe Kiwis secured a crucial 17-16 victory that propels them significantly closer to the 20 November final, with man of the match Johnson - who famously scored a decisive try against England in the 2013 World Cup semi-final - striking the winning blow with 14 minutes remaining.New Zealand's triumph came after they successfully defended their slender lead in the closing stages, earning precious points in this tournament format.England's early dominance saw Gareth Widdop convert two penalties while the hosts repeatedly menaced the New Zealand try line during the opening 20 minutes. However, the momentum shifted dramatically as David Kidwell's squad seized control through Jordan Kahu's penalty and Jordan Rapana's corner try, establishing a 6-4 halftime advantage despite England's territorial supremacy.The second half began with New Zealand doubling their lead when Johnson intercepted a Widdop pass, racing 80 yards for a converted try courtesy of Kahu's boot. England's response came through Huddersfield Giants winger Jermaine McGillvary, who crossed in the corner to narrow the deficit to two points.Rapana's second try - set up by a spectacular Manu Ma'u offload - appeared decisive until Ryan Hall answered with a corner touchdown, created by Widdop's sublime flicked pass. text: George the Poet, a spoken word performer and rapper who wants to use his voice as a force for change in society, has come fifth on the BBC Sound Of 2015 list, which showcases emerging artists for the coming 12 months. Growing up on north west London's Stonebridge Park estate, George Mpanga witnessed injustices that would shape his artistic mission. The 23-year-old, who studied politics, psychology and sociology at Cambridge University while conducting poetry workshops for London children, now stands on the brink of major releases: a debut album with Island Records and his inaugural poetry collection.I want people to be aware of their power, Mpanga declares, expressing his desire to inspire others toward greater achievements.As the first artist revealed from the BBC Sound Of 2015 top five, Mpanga joins a prestigious list. The rankings emerged from polling 139 DJs, critics and broadcasters about their preferred emerging acts. Each day this week unveils another top-five selection, culminating in Friday's winner announcement.**The Evolution from Rap to Poetry**When asked whether he identifies primarily as poet or rapper, Mpanga explains: Chronologically I was a rapper first, but at this point in time I'm primarily a poet.His discovery of language's power traces back to maternal influence. I was always into music and my mum used to talk me through a lot of lyrics. I remember her sitting me down and talking to me about the Bob Marley song Buffalo Soldier. 'Dreadlock Rasta/Taken from Africa/Brought to America/Fighting on arrival/Fighting for survival.' It made a big impression.Church experiences reinforced this linguistic awakening. I grew up in church and again my mum used to read the Bible with me. And then I saw the pastor commanding an audience, and thought, I want to do that. I remember watching the film of Malcolm X and seeing what he did with words and thinking, I really want to do that.Mpanga views his artistic transition as natural progression rather than departure. I believe rap to be a specialist form of poetry - specialist only in that it is very strict on time metre, which you can find in traditional forms of poetry. In William Blake's poem London, you find a lot of very regimented thought.He continues: I would argue that I did start off writing in a traditional poetry form but the extension of that was I was performing them. But if you took the music away, the essence was exactly the same as what William Blake was offering.**Inner City Influences**Mpanga's urban upbringing profoundly shaped his worldview. It made a profound impact on me. I was exposed to quite a range of life. I saw people lose loved ones, I saw people make a lot of money, make a lot of change.A particularly disturbing childhood memory crystallized his mission. When I was in year six - I must have been 10, 11 - I took a shine to these kids who were in my primary school. They were lovely kids. Sunshine every time they opened their mouths. I remember them flippantly mentioning that the night before, their dad was beating up their mum and their big sister had to fight him off with a baseball bat. They didn't understand the gravity of what they were saying. But this disturbed me.This experience sparked an initial desire for universal intervention. I remember trying to fight everything, trying to save everyone from every calamity. At some point I realised that I'm not going to be able to save everyone, but that when I do have the platform I will do everything to enact structural change...Current frustrations stem from systemic barriers. A lot of my frustrations stem from the fact that I can't share my blessings with my family and friends, my community. There are structural things that keep them in place, whether that's the disintegration of their family or their inability to organise themselves financially and sustain their communities financially, or the lack of political influence on the things that affect them.These obstacles create professional isolation. All of these things make it harder for me to move forward professionally with everyone I grew up with. That needs to change.**Creating Change Through Example**Mpanga's approach combines personal demonstration with artistic content. I need to be an example of what I think needs to happen. So for example I'm self-employed. I have an enterprising mind. I demonstrate these things and I think it will be beneficial if everyone has a degree of enterprise.His EP The Chicken and the Egg addresses premature parenthood through dual strategy. I need to be an example, but at the same time there's the content. My EP, The Chicken and the Egg, is about premature parenthood. Discussing that helps. For one thing, you're giving visibility to the issue. Secondly, you're providing some sort of catharsis for anyone who can relate.Though drawing from observation rather than personal experience regarding premature parenthood, Mpanga explains: I draw partially from personal experience and I also draw from observation. When pressed about the EP's subject matter, he clarifies: No. It didn't happen to me. It happened all around me.**Entertainment Over Politics**Mpanga deliberately chose artistic expression over political channels. Because the political space is too regulated. And it's already exclusive. Entertainment isn't as exclusive. If I'm known for making sounds that people want to hear, it's much harder to justify stymieing that process.He maintains confidence in entertainment's transformative potential. Yeah. Apart from the fact that anything's possible, it's very obvious. I speak. You listen. You come to my gig. All we need to do is make decisions. That's it. Job done.**Future Vision**Looking ahead five years, Mpanga envisions comprehensive realization of his current advocacy. I see the manifestation of everything I'm talking about now.His ultimate goal involves creating infrastructure for community empowerment. I see myself providing the structures for people to enact and demonstrate of all the things I'm talking about - autonomy, taking control, owning the entertainment space.For skeptics, Mpanga offers practical proof over rhetoric. If what I'm saying sounds too lofty for you, demonstration's the highest form of argument. First I'm going to show you how to do it, then I'm going to invite you to do it.

text: Chelsea underlined their title credentials with a superb come-from-behind victory over Manchester City at the start of an engrossing weekend of Premier League action. West Ham faced an impressive Arsenal side in defeat, while Bournemouth delivered a stunning seven-goal thriller against Liverpool.Tottenham, Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Stoke and West Brom all secured victories, with Manchester United and Everton settling for a draw at Goodison Park.My team of the week appears above.Do you agree with my team of the week? Or would you go for a different team? Why not pick your very own Team of the Week from the shortlist selected by BBC Sport journalists and share it with your friends?Pick your XI from our list and share with your friends.**THIBAUT COURTOIS (CHELSEA)**During the early exchanges, Sergio Aguero's tip over the bar was made to look effortless by Courtois. His subsequent save from Kevin de Bruyne proved slightly more crucial, but his most spectacular intervention came from Aguero's second attempt - by which point the striker must have considered the Belgian unbeatable.An excellent finish was required to beat the Belgium international goalkeeper initially, yet Courtois quickly demonstrated he had no intention of conceding again. Manchester City's mounting frustration stemmed from missing numerous chances while finding Courtois equal to everything they delivered.What I adore about Courtois is his lack of theatrics - he consistently appears for crucial matches. Making saves is his sole focus. He doesn't conduct himself like a star demanding perfect grooming or immaculate positioning. His rather ungainly appearance, complete with preppy hairstyle, matters little. He's proving himself one hell of a goalkeeper.**DAVID LUIZ (CHELSEA)**Aguero's tackle on the Brazil international Luiz carried animosity from previous encounters. Neither player would retreat from their confrontation, though this wasn't Luiz's first victory over the Argentine. The rivalry between these magnificent football nations is legendary, but the Premier League title chase only intensified the flames.I've previously noted Luiz's glorious current form - he niggled, pushed and pulled Aguero throughout, hoping the striker would break. And break he did. Neither Luiz nor Chelsea could have anticipated Aguero's extreme reaction, resulting in his dismissal and suspension.Luiz executed his role perfectly. His immense performance left Manchester City reconsidering their title strategy without Aguero for several games.**MARC MUNIESA (STOKE)**Against an indifferent Watford, I witnessed Muniesa perform brilliantly for a successful Stoke side. He seemed worth monitoring closely then, but his display against a completely outclassed Burnley was so remarkable it demanded recognition.His composure on the ball clearly reflected his Barcelona youth development. His goal, however, belonged in Gerard Pique's playbook.Watching a central defender initiate a move from his own half, follow play into the opposition penalty area, demand the ball from a goalscorer, receive it, then finish like Lionel Messi was utterly unexpected.Pure class from start to finish - quintessentially Barcelona.**GARETH MCAULEY (WEST BROM)**West Brom in the top six? They occupied that position Saturday night. This must be a dream. Tony Pulis's achievements at The Hawthorns remain unclear, but he's simultaneously inspired playing and belief.Their defenders currently shine brightest, with McAuley proving once again to be a massive asset. McAuley consistently contributes goals, typically from set-pieces, rarely misses matches and demonstrates total commitment.His block preventing Troy Deeney from scoring his 100th goal represented an intervention of monumental significance.Pulis performs admirably - he simply needs to prevent James McClean from behaving recklessly. McClean possesses considerable footballing ability, yet engaging in unnecessary confrontations won't enhance his reputation or West Brom's winning prospects.**KYLE WALKER (TOTTENHAM)**Walker's cross for Harry Kane's early header declared Tottenham's intentions. Swansea couldn't complain about what followed - they'd been warned about Spurs' mood, particularly Walker's.We've witnessed Spurs' devastating potential when motivated. However, I'd have preferred last week's draw against Chelsea and a comfortable 2-0 victory over this swashbuckling Swansea win. My reasoning: I'm exhausted by Tottenham's false title optimism - they demolish lesser teams yet suffer stage fright against bigger clubs.Walker doesn't typically falter on grand stages, but this 5-0 Swansea victory merely conceals deeper issues. Last week's Chelsea defeat exceeded a simple blip - it clearly indicated more work remains at White Hart Lane before serious title consideration.Destroying teams like Swansea is admirable, but they won't compete for Premier League titles soon.**JAMES MCARTHUR (CRYSTAL PALACE)**McArthur delivered an excellent performance when Palace desperately needed three points. The Scot appeared commanding throughout, with manager Alan Pardew requiring this more than anyone. Defeat wasn't acceptable.I'm a Pardew supporter, but despite their recent harrowing results, Palace are overachieving. They've simply lost direction temporarily. The Southampton result impressed, and with players like McArthur performing correctly in proper positions, they should recover.Last week's decision to assign Christian Benteke marking duties against Swansea resembled comic book tactics. Defenders defend, attackers attack - why complicate matters?**RYAN FRASER (BOURNEMOUTH)**I hoped someone would emerge from Sunday's fixtures - Fraser did exactly that. He burst onto the scene ten minutes into the second half when Liverpool were cruising.Liverpool's defensive frailties, which I've consistently highlighted, couldn't have been better exposed than against the Cherries. Fraser's determination and enthusiasm dragged Bournemouth back into contention. He won the penalty, scored the equaliser and electrified fans with expectancy about possibilities.Criticising Liverpool's defence would be too simple, so I won't. Manager Jurgen Klopp must address this obvious problem quickly (and I remain unconvinced by his goalkeeper).**NACHO MONREAL (ARSENAL)**The scene resembled Game of Thrones. Hostilities barely commenced before West Ham appeared besieged in their own fortress. Arsenal had breached their walls, and these uncompromising attackers intended no mercy.Most alarmingly, before the Hammers could breathe, Monreal delivered two crosses that scrambling West Ham defenders desperately cleared - and so it continued.Monreal defended with identical intensity to his attacks, neutralising dangerous Manuel Lanzini early.I've never been completely convinced by Monreal's overall Arsenal performances, but against West Ham he appeared determined to prove himself. Take note, Kieran Gibbs.**MATT PHILLIPS (WEST BROM)**At QPR during their Premier League survival battle, I considered Phillips a player possessing all puzzle pieces - they simply weren't properly arranged.Now, under Tony Pulis at West Brom, those pieces are falling into place nicely. He appears transformed under Pulis' guidance, making Gordon Strachan's refusal to select Phillips for international duty mysterious.Scotland must possess exceptional players if they can afford excluding Phillips given his current form.**ALEXIS SANCHEZ (ARSENAL)**You won't witness many superior hat-tricks. Neither will you see a striker equally eager to assist teammates as score personally. That's Sanchez - a complete professional.I found myself laughing hysterically watching Match of the Day as Gary Lineker predictably challenged Alan Shearer about his world-class striker definition. 'Links' absolutely demolished Alan, continuing to bait him over his statement that only Aguero qualified as world-class in the Premier League. I support 'Links' completely.Sanchez easily joins that category - I struggle understanding what he lacks for inclusion. I've previously stated in this column that when more people agree than disagree about a player's world-class status, those agreeing are typically correct.**DIEGO COSTA (CHELSEA)**Costa improves with every performance. Most revealing about Aguero's tackle on Luiz and the subsequent fracas was Costa's complete absence from involvement. What has Antonio Conte told him?I've long maintained (unlike most pundits) that Costa needn't get involved. Quality players never did - only those lacking ability were more likely to cause trouble. Did you observe Costa spinning Nicolas Otamendi, leaving the defender stranded before unselfishly providing a glorious pass for Willian's goal? Simply sensational.How ironic that City's golden boy Aguero should adopt the same behaviour we once criticised Costa for. More concerning was Pep Guardiola's reluctance to condemn the incident when Guy Mowbray interviewed the City manager after the game. Nobody has praised Aguero more than me, but Pep must understand the fine line between endorsing team commitment and blatant thuggery.

text: Welsh cyclist Elinor Barker believes there is less pressure on GB's women's Olympic pursuit team in Rio because they are not clear favourites to win. Following their golden triumph at London 2012, Team GB experienced a significant downturn, sliding to third place at the 2016 World Championships. Now, the British squad—comprising Barker, Laura Trott, Ciara Horne and Joanna Rowsell Shand—faces formidable competition from USA and Canada.The competitive landscape has shifted dramatically, according to 21-year-old Barker. There's maybe less pressure now because it's not necessarily ours to lose, she explained. It's still ours to win, but there's not a dominant force in women's team pursuit now which there had been for many, many years.This transformation has created an unprecedented level of uncertainty and excitement. I think it makes it much more exciting but it also means no one is watching any one team, Barker noted. We're all watching each other, we're all interested in what everyone is going to do and there's probably about five teams who could quite easily win it if it goes well for them on the day which makes it pretty exciting.Four years ago, Barker was merely a 17-year-old spectator, glued to her television as the GB team of Trott, Rowsell Shand and Danielle King defeated USA in the pursuit final at the 2012 Games. The prospect of competing at Rio still feels surreal to her.Probably a combination of luck and very hard work has got me here, Barker reflected. I wouldn't be here if I hadn't worked very hard and been very specific in my training but I've also been very lucky in the opportunities I've been given.The Cardiff native was part of the squad that secured bronze at this year's World Championships, though their medal hopes were nearly derailed by a disappointing early-round performance that prevented them from reaching the final.That bronze medal came after years of British dominance in the event, and the team's struggles drew considerable criticism. However, Barker views the setback as a valuable learning experience for the GB team.It just goes to show people make mistakes all the time but it doesn't mean that we're not a good team, she emphasized. text: An adventurer is to spend Christmas Day alone in the Antarctic as he bids to become the first Scot to undertake a solo, unassisted and unsupported expedition to the South Pole. The physical demands are equally punishing, with the explorer burning over 10,000 calories daily as he pushes toward his goal.Robertson's motivation stems from personal adversity he has overcome. Just one year ago, he underwent surgery to remove what doctors suspected was a brain tumour, though it proved to be a large and rare cyst. At 48, this political heavyweight - a label he firmly disputes - carved his reputation through ministerial service in Labour's government and a period as the party's deputy chairman.The West Bromwich East MP has built his profile as a determined campaigner, tackling issues from historical child abuse to mounting recent legal challenges against government surveillance legislation. However, his phone hacking crusade brought him greatest recognition.During the 2011 Commons culture select committee hearings, he played a starring role in grilling Rupert and James Murdoch. His relentless investigation earned widespread praise, leading to co-authoring Dial M for Murdoch - an account of his hacking adventure - while establishing himself as a regular presence on rolling news channels.Since then, he has consistently pushed for stricter press regulation and full implementation of Leveson Inquiry recommendations.Following his select committee success in confronting the Murdochs, Ed Miliband recruited him into Labour's top team, tasking him with organizing forces to secure an overall majority in the next general election.His campaign leadership record proved patchy - while Labour famously lost the safe Bradford West seat to a resurgent George Galloway, the party secured other by-election victories during his tenure.His downfall stemmed from controversy surrounding trade union influence over Labour candidate selection processes.After Labour's general election defeat, he launched his deputy leadership bid, promising to rebuild the party across the UK.A former trade union official who once flatshared with Unite leader Len McCluskey, Mr Watson entered Parliament in 2001 representing West Bromwich.Following initial service in the whips' office, he moved to the Ministry of Defence, where he helped secure pardons for soldiers executed for cowardice during World War One.However, in 2006, he resigned his defence minister position, demanding Tony Blair's resignation for the Labour Party's and country's benefit - a move that accelerated the then prime minister's eventual departure.Accusations emerged of conspiring against Mr Blair with Gordon Brown after revelations that he had visited the then chancellor at his North Queensferry, Fife home shortly before stepping down.While both men denied any plotting, many within and beyond Labour remained skeptical of their denials.When Gordon Brown assumed leadership and the premiership in 2007, Mr Watson returned to government as a whip, before his 2008 appointment as minister for digital engagement.This role suited him perfectly.Recognized as an early social media adopter, he became the first MP to maintain a blog and describes himself as an apprentice nerd due to his technological enthusiasm.During this period, however, accusations surfaced linking Mr Watson to the scandal involving Gordon Brown's spin doctor Damian McBride's plot to spread smears about senior Conservatives.The Mail on Sunday accused him of encouraging Mr McBride, while the Sun published a cartoon depicting him under the headline Mad dog was trained to maul.Mr Watson subsequently secured substantial libel damages from both publications through the High Court, which ruled the stories connecting him to the plot were false.He stepped down from his ministerial role following the McBride controversy, insisting family reasons motivated his decision - he wanted to retreat from front-line politics and focus on his wife and children.Seeking what he termed a productive life as a backbencher, he joined the culture select committee to pursue interests in sport and the arts.Just two days after joining, however, the Guardian newspaper revived the phone hacking story, prompting the committee to investigate - once again propelling Mr Watson into the spotlight.The first thing News International did was try to have me removed from the committee, he claimed in 2011.I realised then that these people were never going away. Something had clearly gone wrong with newspapers and somebody had to get to the truth.There weren't many MPs who were prepared to do that for fear of being targeted, so I decided I had to do it.People then started coming to me - whistleblowers and victims - and I felt I had a responsibility towards them. I couldn't walk away.A prolific Twitter user discussing politics alongside his latest music, film and video game discoveries, he even managed to reference little-known blues-rock band Drenge in his 2013 resignation letter from the general election co-ordinator position.In that letter, Mr Watson - son of a union official and social worker, who has two children with estranged wife Siobhan - stated his departure would benefit Labour's future unity.His resignation followed controversy over the Falkirk seat being vacated by Labour's Eric Joyce - Unite union faced accusations of hijacking the candidate selection process, with Mr Watson's office manager being the union's preferred choice.Writing to Mr Miliband, Mr Watson said he wasn't quitting due to unattributed shadow cabinet briefings around the mess in Falkirk... though they don't help.He acknowledged that some party members hadn't forgiven his 2006 defence minister resignation, adding: I fully accept the consequences of that decision and genuinely hope my departure allows the party to move on.Now serving as deputy leader, he stands at the forefront of the party's latest attempt to move forward - this time from general election defeat.

text: Police are too sensitive about asking victims of crime if they are disabled, an inspection has found. A joint inspectorate examination of police, probation services, and the Crown Prosecution Service across England and Wales has revealed that disability hate crime remains overlooked and under-reported within the criminal justice system.The comprehensive review calls for establishing a new common definition of such crimes to guarantee swift and effective handling. Senior police officials acknowledged they have worked hard to improve its handling of these cases.Police forces in England and Wales documented over 1,700 disability hate crimes during 2011-12. The tragic case of Fiona Pilkington sparked this joint review - she took her own life along with her disabled daughter Francecca Hardwick in 2007 following repeated unsuccessful complaints to police about youth harassment.Without urgent reforms, inspectors cautioned that similar tragedies could occur again. Their investigation encompassed staff interviews across six police forces and corresponding CPS and probation trust offices in Cleveland, Cumbria, Derbyshire, Hertfordshire, Greater Manchester and West Midlands. Additionally, they observed seven court proceedings and consulted with disabled victims, witness care unit representatives, witness service staff, victim support personnel, and various independent disability advocates.Disabled individuals informed inspectors that officers and control-room operators had grown too sensitive about causing offence, resulting in reluctance to inquire whether victims had disabilities.Steve Ashley, programme director to HM Inspectorate Constabulary (HMIC), explained: There's a lack of willingness by police officers and police staff in control rooms to ask the right of questions to establish whether it's a crime, whether its anti-social behaviour and what effect disability is having on that person in terms of the effect on the crime.Confusion surrounding disability hate crime definitions compounds the problem, according to Mr Ashley. It's not as easy as identifying a religiously-motivated attack or a racially-motivated attack. Police officers don't like to say to people 'Are you disabled?', he said.When questioned whether another Pilkington-type case could occur given the review's discoveries, Mr Ashley confirmed: Yes, it could.Mencap, a disability charity, cited internal research indicating nine out of ten people with learning disabilities have experienced hate crimes. Emma Harrison, the charity's assistant director, stated the review demonstrated that victims of disability hate crime continue to be let down at every stage of the criminal justice system.Harrison praised the review's recommendation requiring police, probation services, and CPS collaboration to address these serious and continued failings.The review's key recommendations include establishing a single, clear and uncomplicated disability hate crime definition to eliminate confusion. It suggests the three agencies examine how front-line personnel participate in disability hate crime training programs.Police should actively encourage crime victims to report incidents, preventing under-reporting from remaining a significant concern, the review stated. Inspectors also recommended that the Law Commission - the legal reform body - consider creating standalone disability hate crime offenses.CPS chief inspector Michael Fuller, representing all three agencies, acknowledged: This report finds that in many ways disability hate crime is the hate crime that has been overlooked. The criminal justice system must therefore change to provide an improved service for those with disabilities.Victim Support chief executive Javed Khan emphasized that police must deliver improved services to disabled hate crime victims.The Association of Chief Police Officers defended their efforts, stating the police service had worked hard to improve its handling of disability hate crime through consultations with disabled communities to understand harassment patterns and reporting barriers, then collaborating with communities and agencies to eliminate those obstacles.A Home Office spokeswoman concluded: The Home Office has improved the way police forces collect and record data on hate crimes, including those against disabled people, and we will keep working with disability groups to ensure victims have the confidence to come forward.

text: England's Sarah Taylor says she is still not the finished article after returning from a break to deal with anxiety problems, but is back and ready for the summer's home World Cup. The 28-year-old Taylor made the difficult decision to step back from cricket in May last year, citing what she termed a mental injury.In her first public comments since that pivotal moment, Taylor revealed: I still have anxiety day to day. But I'm in a much better position than I was, including in my cricket.Considered among the world's most gifted female cricketers, the wicketkeeper-batter made history as Australia's first woman to compete in first-grade men's cricket. Her impressive international record spans 101 one-day matches, accumulating 4,072 runs with an average of 39.76.After returning to international competition against Ireland in Dubai this April, Taylor earned her spot in England's World Cup squad, announced Monday.During an ECB interview, she reflected on her journey: I've learned that the person I became over the last three or four years wasn't me, I wasn't being honest with myself. That was the biggest step for me, to actually come out and admit it.The breakthrough came through seeking professional support. I was able to get the help that I needed. Anyone who is struggling, I would suggest talking about it because the more people who understand the better, Taylor emphasized.Her current approach focuses on practical management: It's now just a case of putting a lot of strategies in place to cope with day-to-day tasks and cricket. Hopefully I can use them and push them towards performances and playing well for my country.England's World Cup journey begins against India in Derby on 24 June, following warm-up encounters with Sri Lanka and New Zealand.Describing her recent experiences, Taylor acknowledged ongoing challenges: If you have a look at my last 12 months it's been a rollercoaster of anxiety from day to day stuff to my return to cricket. It's been very graduated. The ECB have been brilliant in terms of not rushing me back in.She candidly assessed her current state: I'm not the finished article. New places are still a struggle for me and I still have to push through those on a day-to-day basis. Where I'm most comfortable is out in the middle. Those small tasks, they will come. I've made great strides to be able to be in the position I am now.

text: A dog owner whose pet was the latest victim to die from from Alabama Rot says more needs to be done to inform owners of the risks. A Hampshire dog owner whose beloved pet succumbed to the mysterious Alabama Rot disease is calling for expanded warning measures across the New Forest, following his three-year-old Labrador-collie cross's tragic death.Bodhi fell ill after exploring the Whitefield Moor area of the New Forest with owner Steve Kirwan from Lyndhurst. Within two weeks of developing symptoms in February, the dog died from kidney failure - becoming another victim of the deadly condition that has claimed 24 canine lives across the UK since 2012.The enigmatic disease, officially termed cutaneous and renal glomerular vasculopathy (CRGV), was first documented in the United States during the 1980s. While its exact trigger remains elusive, the condition typically begins with lesions or wounds appearing on dogs' legs, paws, and faces - though these initial signs don't always manifest. Within two to seven days, affected animals develop kidney failure symptoms including vomiting, decreased appetite, and lethargy.Recent data from the Forestry Commission reveals a concerning pattern. From November 2012 through March of the previous year, authorities recorded 12 confirmed cases and two unconfirmed instances - with five occurring within the New Forest boundaries. Since December, an additional 12 cases have emerged, half of which were concentrated in the same Hampshire woodland area. Veterinary specialists continue examining 22 more suspected cases.Beyond Hampshire's borders, the disease has struck dogs in Northamptonshire, Yorkshire, Monmouthshire, Dorset, Shropshire, Surrey, Cornwall, Worcestershire, and County Durham. Importantly, research indicates the condition doesn't spread between dogs.In response to the outbreak, the Forestry Commission has deployed warning posters across 29 New Forest car parks, urging dog owners to remain vigilant. However, Kirwan argues these measures fall short of what's needed.I don't think it's enough, he stated. There's a number of car parks in the New Forest, far more than 29. I think the coverage needs to be right across the forest, because there is a real concentration in the New Forest as [part of the] national picture.Bodhi's case proved particularly puzzling - the dog never developed the characteristic lesions but began dragging his hind legs. Despite veterinary suspicions of Alabama Rot and subsequent treatment attempts, the pet failed to respond and ultimately required euthanization.The investigation into Alabama Rot's precise cause involves a collaborative effort between Anderson Moores Veterinary Specialists in Hursley near Winchester, the Forestry Commission, Environment Agency, Suffolk's Animal Health Trust, and local veterinary practices.David Walker from Anderson Moores acknowledged the research challenges ahead: There's huge amounts of research ongoing, multiple different avenues, but at this stage we are no closer to knowing what the trigger is. Research is going to continue but there is the prospect that we could research this disease for five, ten years and not find the underlying cause. But that doesn't mean we're not going to keep looking.

text: A £5 note engraved with a tiny portrait of Jane Austen and said to be worth up to £50,000 has been found in a Christmas card. A second special £5 note featuring microscopic artwork by Birmingham-based engraver Graham Short has surfaced in Scotland on Thursday, following the discovery of the first note in change from a Welsh café earlier this month.Two additional banknotes remain circulating throughout England and Northern Ireland, each bearing unique serial numbers AM32 885552 and AM32 885554.The Tony Huggins-Haig Gallery in Kelso, Scottish Borders, which spearheaded this innovative project, advises anyone discovering these notes to make contact immediately.According to Mr Huggins-Haig, who spoke with BBC WM, the latest recipient chose to remain anonymous after checking the note on the off chance. He revealed an unexpected twist in the discovery: When somebody opened their Christmas card from a loved one, it was contained in that Christmas card. The person who put it in didn't necessarily know what they were doing.With half the notes now found, Huggins-Haig encourages continued vigilance: That's two down and there's still two out there. Keep checking your change.Short's concept emerged from his desire to commemorate the 200th anniversary of Jane Austen's death next year. The specialist micro-engraver created 5mm portraits of the beloved author on the transparent sections of the new plastic Bank of England £5 notes. Each banknote features distinct quotes, ensuring individual uniqueness.Interestingly, both recipients have expressed intentions to retain their discoveries rather than sell them. Short shared mixed feelings about this decision: I don't know whether I'm disappointed that they haven't wanted to sell them because I wanted them to have some money for Christmas, but the fact that they are so happy to keep them, that's nice as well.The artist himself has developed an amusing habit of scrutinizing his own change, admitting he feels terrified of finding one of his creations. When someone gives me a £5 note in my change now I always check. Wouldn't it be awful if it came back to me? People would say it was a fix.See more stories from across Birmingham and the Black Country here

text: The family of a 20-year-old woman from Glasgow who has travelled to Syria and married an Islamic State (IS) fighter have said that she has betrayed them. The parents of a young woman who joined ISIS in Syria have issued a heartbreaking public appeal, expressing their devastation while condemning their daughter's actions.Muzaffar Mahmood and Khalida Mahmood revealed their horror upon discovering that their daughter Aqsa had become radicalized. Their anguish became public following Twitter posts attributed to Aqsa that urged people in Britain to replicate terrorist attacks like those witnessed in Woolwich and the United States.Despite their profound disappointment, the couple emphasized their enduring love for their daughter and their desperate desire for her return.We still love you, Aqsa, but we now have to put your family, your brother and sisters first as you have betrayed us, our community and the people of Scotland when you took this step, the couple declared in their statement. You have torn the heart out of our family and changed our lives forever. Please come home.The parents issued a stark warning to other families: If our daughter, who had all the chances and freedom in life, could become a bedroom radical, then it is possible for this to happen to any family.Reports indicate that privately-educated Aqsa used a Twitter account operating under the name Umm Layth to promote terrorist activities. The account has subsequently been removed from the platform.Last November, Aqsa traveled via Turkey to reach Aleppo in Syria, prompting her family to report her disappearance to authorities.Her parents described how she had previously attended Craigholme School before proceeding to university, noting that she was well integrated into society and raised with love and affection in a happy home.During a Glasgow news conference, solicitor Aamer Anwar read the family's statement while Mrs Mahmood fought back tears. The parents themselves remained silent throughout the proceedings.She may believe that the jihadists of Isis are her new family but they are not and are simply using her, they stated.The couple painted a picture of their daughter's earlier life: Aqsa was always a very sweet, peaceful, intelligent child and inquisitive about everything. We had high hopes for her and would have loved for her to be a doctor and to save lives. We dreamed that one day we would see her married with children but sadly that no longer looks likely.Their statement continued: As parents we would have liked for her to listen to us but we gave her everything possible in terms of love, freedom and education and she chose the path which we could never approve of.The parents expressed their complex emotions: All parents want to be proud of their children but sadly we now feel nothing but sorrow and shame for Aqsa. We are not in denial and do not make any excuses for her and absolutely condemn her involvement in Isis and recent comments. But she is our daughter and we still love her, fear for her life and would urge her to return home whilst she still can.Communication between Aqsa and her family continued after her arrival in Syria through social media platforms until Tuesday, when media outlets reported her ISIS involvement.Mr Anwar explained: Because of yesterday, all contact appears to have terminated with their daughter. So, they are hoping that this plea will go out to their daughter and that she will think again and return home. They want her to come home while she still can. They are telling her that she is wrong, that she is deluded if she thinks she is helping people in Syria.According to the solicitor, Aqsa, who holds British nationality, had grown concerned and upset after viewing media coverage and online content about killings in Syria, telling her parents she wished to provide assistance.Working alongside Police Scotland, her parents stated: IS are killing in the name of religion and claiming to defend the weak, but by joining with them our daughter is brainwashed and deluded and helping those engaged in genocide.They emphasized that no single factor could be blamed for her transformation: There is no smoking gun, no family member, no fundamentalist preacher that can be blamed for her radicalisation. Aqsa, like many young people in our community, was naturally angry and frustrated at the loss of innocent life in the Middle East but this is not the way to help.The parents expressed broader concerns about societal implications: We are concerned that a growing climate of fear in this country means that children will not discuss how they feel with their family and friends, and this will only spell disaster for society.Their statement concluded with profound grief: We know that in the days and months ahead we will be scouring social media for clues of whether our daughter is still alive. As we try to hold back the tears today, we feel we have lost our child.

text: Home Secretary Theresa May's internet monitoring plans need significant work, a committee has ruled. Britain's intelligence agencies will gain sweeping new surveillance powers under the draft Investigatory Powers Bill, which mandates that internet service providers retain all web activity records for twelve months.The proposed legislation would also grant authority for bulk personal data collection and permit smartphone hacking operations by British spies. According to ministers, these changes represent necessary updates to existing laws, enabling authorities to combat terrorism and organized crime by adapting to modern criminal technology.However, civil liberties advocates argue the bill constitutes mass surveillance of British citizens. Following a parliamentary committee's critical report, campaigners insist the home secretary must return to the drawing board.This report shows just how much homework the government has to do on this landmark legislation, said Shami Chakrabarti, director of Liberty.Andy Burnham, Labour's shadow home secretary, has contacted Mrs May expressing his party's support for the bill's overarching objective - providing police and security services with necessary powers. Nevertheless, he urged the government to reconsider its proposals to achieve the right balance for our security and privacy.Mrs May responded that the government would carefully consider findings from three committees examining the Bill before finalizing proposals.This is vital legislation, and we are absolutely determined to get it right, she stated. Our draft Bill followed three independent reports on investigatory powers, whose authors were unanimous a new law was necessary. We are clear we need to introduce legislation which responds to the threats we face in the digital age, protects both the privacy and security of the public, and provides world-leading oversight and safeguards.While consensus exists regarding the need for new surveillance legislation, parliamentary reports have highlighted significant concerns about implementation details. The current law suffers from complexity and opacity, yet emerging evidence suggests the proposed replacement hasn't fully addressed these fundamental issues.The critical question remains whether the Home Office will incorporate suggested reforms, particularly given the tight timeline - final legislation must be introduced imminently to allow parliamentary debate and passage before year's end.In their 194-page assessment, the Joint Committee on the Draft Investigatory Powers Bill concluded that Internet Connection Records' value to law enforcement agencies could outweigh the intrusiveness involved in collecting and using them.The committee acknowledged technology companies' concerns about privacy protection feasibility, specifically regarding Mrs May's promise to collect only website names rather than individual page data. While witnesses suggested this might prove technically impossible, the Home Office continues collaborating with industry partners seeking solutions.Parliamentary members also demanded ministers clarify encryption policies, ensuring tech companies won't be forced to create back door access for intelligence services.Additionally, the Home Office must better justify bulk data collection practices, including email and internet traffic interception revealed by US whistleblower Edward Snowden, along with other extensive surveillance operations.Committee chairman Lord Murphy of Torfaen emphasized that the Home Office faces a significant amount of further work to do before Parliament can be confident that the provisions have been fully thought through.Former Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg, who previously blocked Mrs May's surveillance legislation attempt - critics dubbed it the snooper's charter - condemned the current bill as a dragnet approach and disproportionate.Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the Liberal Democrat MP criticized the Home Office's desire to collect everything on everyone while searching for terrorist or criminal intelligence.Implying that everyone may be guilty when millions of innocent people are just going about their everyday business free of any wrongdoing at all is... something which is not in keeping with long-standing British traditions, Mr Clegg argued.He questioned whether retaining comprehensive data - everything from the music you download on Spotify, to the app that you open, to the supermarket website that you visit - represents proportionate action in a liberal democracy to go after the bad guys.Clegg advocated for a narrower approach to data retention, noting other nations focus collection efforts on individuals who flicker on the radar screen of security services in the first place.The extensive bill primarily addresses British intelligence agency operations, establishing clear legal frameworks following Edward Snowden's disclosures.Proposed equipment interference warrants would authorize intelligence operatives to hack suspects' smartphones and computers, extracting data both domestically and internationally.Additional warrants would cover bulk database downloads containing personal information, potentially including medical records, plus internet traffic interception for future GCHQ analysis.Many techniques remained unknown publicly until recently, previously governed by scattered, outdated legislation predating internet technology.

text: Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said the inconclusive election result means no party can govern alone. Following 13 years of uninterrupted dominance, Erdogan's AKP faces the unprecedented challenge of coalition negotiations after securing just 41% of the vote—a dramatic decline from their 2011 performance that has stripped them of their parliamentary majority.The election results mark a potentially transformative moment in Turkish politics. While the AKP emerged as the largest party with a vote share that would be enviable in most democracies, their grip on absolute power has suffered what many describe as a significant blow.I believe the results, which do not give the opportunity to any party to form a single-party government, will be assessed healthily and realistically by every party, Mr Erdogan said, urging all political forces to preserve the atmosphere of stability in Turkey.In Ankara, Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu has begun crucial discussions with AKP cabinet members and officials to evaluate their options. Once official results are declared, he will have 45 days to establish a functioning government—a task complicated by the apparent reluctance of opposition parties to enter coalition talks with the AKP.Deputy Prime Minister Numan Kurtulmus has warned that no government can be formed without AKP participation, though he acknowledged that fresh elections remain a possibility if coalition efforts fail.The electoral outcome has effectively derailed Erdogan's ambitious constitutional reform agenda. His quest for a two-thirds majority that would have transformed Turkey into a presidential republic now lies in ruins, dealing a severe setback to his plans for expanded executive powers.A historic breakthrough came from the pro-Kurdish HDP, which successfully crossed the critical 10% threshold to secure parliamentary representation for the first time. HDP leader Selahattin Demirtas declared victory over authoritarian tendencies, stating: The discussion of executive presidency and dictatorship have come to an end in Turkey with these elections.Financial markets responded nervously to the political uncertainty. The Turkish lira plummeted to near-record lows against the dollar on Monday morning, while the Istanbul stock exchange witnessed an immediate drop of over 8%. The central bank moved swiftly to stabilize the currency by reducing interest rates on foreign currency deposits.This election represents the end of what critics have characterized as a one-man political show that has dominated and polarized Turkish society for over a decade. Despite retaining substantial support among religious and conservative voters who credit the party with their political liberation, the AKP's era of unchallenged supremacy appears to have concluded.Opposition parties now face their own strategic calculations—whether to attempt forming an anti-AKP coalition or force the ruling party into an unstable minority government arrangement.Are you in Turkey? text: Overall crime in England and Wales fell by 15% in 2013, official figures show. Crime levels across England and Wales plummeted to their lowest point since records began over three decades ago, according to the latest Crime Survey for England and Wales, which documented 7.5 million offences against households and adults in 2013.The Office for National Statistics (ONS) published the CSEW report, which estimates crime levels by surveying victims directly about their experiences. Results showed a dramatic 15% decline in crimes against households and adults for the year ending December 2013 compared to the previous year.This represents the steepest percentage drop since the survey's inception 33 years ago in 1981.Police-recorded crime statistics painted a similar picture, falling 2% in 2013 to 3.7 million recorded offences. However, certain categories bucked the downward trend, with fraud surging 25% and reported sexual offences climbing 17% in the aftermath of the Jimmy Savile scandal.Danny Shaw, BBC Home Affairs correspondent, noted that while declining crime rates have been consistent since the mid-1990s, what is unexpected, however, is the size of the reduction. He emphasized that the 15% fall is the biggest percentage decline since the survey began 33 years ago.Shaw added: The 22% drop in violence is also substantially more than in other years - reinforcing recent findings from Cardiff University's study of people treated for crime-related injuries.The ONS attributed the overall crime reduction primarily to significant decreases in household theft, which dropped 25%, and violence, which fell 22%. Vandalism reports also declined by 15% throughout the year.Among younger victims, crimes experienced by children aged 10-15 totaled 762,000 in 2013, representing a 13% decrease from 2012 levels.Police-recorded statistics showed reductions across most major crime categories, though some areas experienced increases. Shoplifting incidents rose 6%, while violence against persons climbed 1% - a rise officials attributed to improved recording practices and increased public reporting.The fraud increase followed centralized recording procedures for such crimes. Meanwhile, allegations involving high-profile figures, particularly those connected to the late DJ Savile, contributed to the spike in recorded sexual offences.Crime Prevention Minister Norman Baker celebrated the results, stating: Under this coalition government, overall crime is down by more than 10% according to both the independent crime survey and police-recorded crime. Today's statistics are more good news and the evidence is clear: police reform is working and crime is falling.However, Adam Pemberton, assistant chief executive at Victim Support, offered a measured response while welcoming the decline: It is important to remember that for many of the victims of 7.5 million crimes committed last year, the impact will have been severe and long-lasting.Chief Constable Jeff Farrar, who oversees crime statistics for the Association of Chief Police Officers, said the data confirmed the influence of high-profile operations targeting sexual abuse and fraud.Shaw cautioned that police-compiled statistics should be treated with an abundance of caution - not just because of concerns the figures have been fiddled but also because they hinge on whether victims report crimes to police or not.The statistics exclude Scotland and Northern Ireland. Scottish government data from June showed a 13% drop in recorded crime for the year ending March 2013, while Northern Ireland experienced a 2.9% crime reduction in 2012/13 compared to the previous year.Ministers characterized the findings as demonstrating that government reforms were proving effective in reducing criminal activity nationwide.

text: About one-third of workers in Clackmannanshire and Dumfries and Galloway will benefit from the national living wage, according to research. Analysis from the Resolution Foundation reveals that Scotland will experience uneven effects from the upcoming national living wage implementation.Starting in April, workers aged 25 and above will receive a minimum of £7.20 per hour under the new national living wage. The UK government has stated that millions of people will enjoy a pay rise.According to the study, approximately 500,000 Scottish employees will see their wages affected by this change. However, the impact varies dramatically by location. Clackmannanshire and Dumfries and Galloway will see one-third of their workforce benefit, while Aberdeen workers face a much smaller impact at just 16%. Similarly modest effects are expected in Edinburgh (17%), Dundee (18%) and Glasgow (19%).The Foundation expresses strong support for the new wage floor but warns that lower-paying regions will face greater implementation challenges. They urge collaboration between the Scottish government, the Fair Work Convention, local leaders and businesses nationwide to prevent job losses and avoid trapping large numbers of workers at the legal minimum wage.Employers should prioritize productivity improvements in retail, hospitality, cleaning and care sectors to make the national living wage financially viable, the Foundation recommends. The organization argues that the UK government's pay structure doesn't constitute a true living wage and advocates for expanding the voluntary living wage of £8.25 throughout the country.Conor D'Arcy, policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation, said: The welcome new national living wage will have a huge impact on low pay, particularly towards 2020 as it approaches £9 an hour.
