text: Prosecutors in Austria say former Kazakh ambassador Rakhat Aliyev, found dead in a Vienna prison on Tuesday, appears to have killed himself. Vienna prosecutors have dismissed claims of foul play in the prison death of Rakhat Aliyev, the former Kazakh diplomat and vocal critic of his country's leadership.Authorities pointed to post-mortem findings on Aliyev's body, discovered hanging in his cell while he awaited trial on charges of murdering two bankers in Kazakhstan. His legal team is demanding a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death.The deceased had previously been married to Dariga Nazarbayeva, the eldest daughter of Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev. Kazakhstan had convicted Aliyev in absentia for attempting to overthrow the government, though Austria consistently rejected extradition requests.Aliyev's dismissal as Kazakhstan's ambassador to Vienna occurred in 2007, marking the beginning of his transformation into an outspoken opponent of President Nazarbayev's regime.The timing of his death proved particularly significant - he was scheduled that same day to provide testimony against two former cellmates facing blackmail charges. These individuals allegedly threatened to arrange his murder in a manner designed to appear as suicide.Vienna's deputy chief prosecutor Gerhard Jarosch emphasized that forensic analysis revealed no evidence of external involvement in Aliyev's death. An experienced forensic expert conducted the examination, Jarosch confirmed.Neither the examination of his body along with the prison cell in which it was found nor the prison's CCTV footage showed any signs of violence or other third-party involvement in his death, he said.Routine toxicological testing results were expected within days, which would determine whether Aliyev's blood contained substances beyond his prescribed heart medication at the time of death.Following public disclosure of the alleged threats against him, prison officials had transferred Aliyev to solitary confinement, though he was not placed under suicide watch protocols.Klaus Ainedter, one of Aliyev's attorneys, expressed serious reservations about the official explanation to Austrian press agency APA. I have significant doubts, Ainedter stated. I visited him only [on Monday]. There was absolutely no indication of a danger of suicide.The murder charges against Aliyev dated back to 2007, with Austrian authorities twice refusing Kazakhstan's extradition demands, citing concerns about fair trial prospects in his home country. He had been detained since June after voluntarily surrendering once Austria agreed to conduct the trial domestically.Aliyev maintained his innocence throughout, characterizing the murder accusations as politically motivated persecution.As a businessman with extensive connections throughout Kazakhstan's elite circles, Aliyev became increasingly vocal in his opposition to President Nazarbayev following his ambassadorial dismissal.President Nazarbayev has maintained virtually unchallenged control over Kazakhstan since the nation gained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. His administration has prioritized economic reforms while steadfastly resisting political democratization efforts.The high-profile nature of Aliyev's case in Austria attracted prominent legal representation and generated allegations that Kazakhstan's secret service attempted to manipulate the judicial proceedings.

text: Apple has just turned 40 years old - a timely reason to track down a man who helped start the firm and then walked away. An hour's drive from Las Vegas into Nevada's desert leads to what seems like civilization's edge. Keep going. That's where Pahrump awaits.In this remote outpost lives the co-founder of Earth's most valuable, arguably most powerful corporation.At 81, Ronald G Wayne carries a unique distinction. Four decades ago, at age 41, he worked for Atari, where he encountered an impressionable young Steve Jobs who consistently sought Wayne's counsel on various matters.Should he venture into slot machine manufacturing? Wayne advised against it.Was a spiritual journey to India worthwhile? Wayne responded: if you must, just exercise caution.Then came the history-altering question: Could you help me talk some sense into Steve Wozniak?Wayne's response was simple: Bring him over to the house. We'll sit down, and we'll chat.The beloved, charismatic Wozniak - known as Woz - had been collaborating with Jobs on transforming business computers into personal devices. Both men regularly attended the legendary Homebrew Computer Club, where enthusiasts dissected circuitry and reconstructed it with the enthusiasm of imaginative children playing with Lego blocks.Wozniak excelled above all others. His circuit board design became the foundation for the Apple 1, the company's inaugural computer that commanded $365,000 (£254,300) at a 2015 auction.Jobs coveted Wozniak's genius exclusively for Apple. Wozniak resisted.The resolution came at Wayne's Mountain View, California apartment during a crucial meeting.Wayne recalls: Jobs thought that I was somewhat more diplomatic than he was.He very anxious to proceed with Steve Wozniak to get this into production. But Wozniak, being the whimsical character that he was, everything he did was for the pure fun of it. Woz had no concept of business, or the rules of the game.Within approximately 45 minutes, Wayne achieved a breakthrough.He bought into it. He understood, Wayne explains.It was at that moment Steve Jobs said: 'We're going to start a company. It will be the Apple Computer Company.'Using an IBM typewriter, Wayne immediately drafted the incorporation documents, amazing Wozniak with his ability to produce four pages of legal language from memory.The ownership structure was straightforward: Jobs and Wozniak each received 45%, while Wayne claimed 10% and responsibility for mediating disputes.Twelve days later, Wayne withdrew from the partnership.For very excellent reasons that are still sound to me today, he maintains, four decades and $600 billion in market capitalization later.Jobs, the masterful salesman, had secured Apple's first major contract. The Byte Shop, a small computer retailer, ordered 50 machines. Fulfilling this required borrowing $15,000.However, Wayne had learned - from a source he can't recall - that the Byte Shop had questionable payment practices.Wayne explained his concern: If the company goes poof, we are individually liable for the debts.Jobs and Wozniak didn't have two nickels to rub together. I had a house, and a bank account, and a car… I was reachable!Wayne informed the Steves he would assist informally but could no longer maintain official company involvement.His enduring contribution included designing Apple's original logo - an ink drawing depicting Newton beneath a tree with an apple suspended overhead. Though Wayne signed the artwork, Jobs noticed.Wayne remembers Jobs demanding: Take that out! He complied.Months after formally severing Apple ties, Wayne received correspondence.The letter says all you gotta do is sign away every possible interest you could have in the Apple Computer Company, and the cheque is yours, he recounts.The compensation: $1,500.As far as I was concerned, it was 'found money'. So I went ahead and I signed.Today, Pahrump sits 500 miles (800km) and an entire universe from Apple's Cupertino headquarters.Wayne's modest, cherished home showcases artifacts from his life as an inquisitive engineer and collector. An antique silver slot machine guards the entrance. A functioning 1930s radio, encased in beautiful mahogany, stands against one wall.He describes creating a detailed Nautilus replica - both interior and exterior - from the film 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea. Without blueprints, he studied freeze-frames for reference. Upon completion, he donated it to a museum.Currently, a 10% Apple stake would be worth nearly $60 billion. If Wayne harbors regrets, he conceals them masterfully.I would've wound up heading a very large documentation department at the back of the building, shuffling papers for the next 20 years of my life. That was not the future that I saw for myself.If money was the only thing that I wanted, there are many ways I could've done that. But it was much more important to do what appealed to me.My advice to young people is always this - find something you enjoy doing so much that you'd be willing to do it for nothing… and you'll never work a day in your life.A small study corner box contains Wayne's fan mail - autograph requests, advice seekers, and admirers' messages.One letter from Jason jokes about whether the notoriously self-assured, combative Steve Jobs could ever accept Wayne's constructive criticism.Wayne reflects: He was a fascinating man.Who made Apple what it is? Obviously, Jobs.Was Jobs a nice guy? In many ways, no. But that doesn't matter.Wayne viewed himself as adult supervision for Jobs's ambitions, even providing early encouragement.Jobs says: 'You know, I'm having second thoughts about this. There are other things I want to do'.I said: 'Steve, whatever it is that you want to do, you can do it a lot more easily with money in your pocket. Go ahead and make the money, and do whatever you want to do. Just don't forget what you wanted the money for'.He forgot. I think he became so involved in the mechanics of running Apple that it was more like he was caught up to such an extent that nothing else mattered.Though Wayne feels no remorse about abandoning his Apple role, one regret persists: selling his original signed contract copy for $500.That identical document brought $1.6 million at a 2011 auction - another what if for the collection.Surveying Wayne's home reveals no Apple products. He prefers building and customizing his own technology - it's more enjoyable, he explains.In 2011, someone gifted him an iPad 2. Like much else in his life, Wayne gave it away.Follow Dave Lee on Twitter @DaveLeeBBC and on Facebook.

text: Katie Archibald admitted to being surprised at the margin of victory as she helped Great Britain win Olympic gold in the women's team pursuit. America come out harder than us. In all the previous rides we've not been up until the last kilo.While the British quartet dominated the final stretch, their American counterparts crossed the finish line at four minutes 12.454 seconds, falling short of matching the relentless pace set by the victorious team.Speaking moments after their triumph, the Milngavie cyclist near Glasgow described the exhilarating finale: I had a sneaky look at the end to see if we were there and once you get that champing-on-the-bit sensation, we felt like super heroes, I suppose.The magnitude of the achievement wasn't lost on Archibald. It's pretty special. I've not won a team pursuit since the Europeans this year. It's all the cliches at the moment; it's overwhelming, it's a dream come true, because nobody really expects that they'll make that gold medal. Every athlete goes through their injuries and trials and tribulations and whatnot. It will kick in in about 10 minutes, no doubt, and the legs will start hurting.What makes Archibald's golden performance even more extraordinary is her remarkable recovery from devastating injuries sustained in a motorbike accident last December. The crash left her with a ruptured posterior cruciate knee ligament and fractured elbow, forcing her absence from March's World Championships.This Team GB triumph has elevated the Rio Games to become Scotland's most successful Olympics on foreign soil, with 10 medals claimed thus far - surpassing the previous record of eight from Sydney 2000. Two additional medals await on Sunday, with tennis champion Andy Murray and cyclist Callum Skinner poised to add to the tally.Looking ahead to future competitions, Archibald expressed her enthusiasm: That feels pretty special, pretty exciting for the Gold Coast in 2018, referencing the upcoming Commonwealth Games where Scotland competes independently.The cyclist marveled at the recent surge in Scottish cycling excellence: It's pretty mad, with Callum [Skinner, also a gold medal winner] getting in the track cycling scene, that progression over the last few years. text: Hourly pay rates for Tesco store staff will rise by 10.5% over the next two years, the supermarket has said. Tesco has unveiled plans to boost hourly wages from the current £7.62 to £8.42 by November 2018, marking what the company describes as its largest store pay investment in a decade.The supermarket giant will implement the increases across three phases: wages will climb to £8.02 this November, advance to £8.18 by July 2018, and reach the final £8.42 target by November 2018. This progression will position Tesco workers above the anticipated £7.90 National Living Wage threshold expected for 2018.Currently set at £7.50 for adults aged 25 and over, the National Living Wage serves as the effective minimum wage for this age group, while younger workers receive lower minimum wage rates. Government budgets indicate statutory minimum pay rates will continue climbing through at least 2020, prompting companies to prepare for these changes while maintaining competitiveness in staff recruitment and retention.However, the wage improvements come with trade-offs. Sunday and Bank Holiday overtime premiums will decrease from time-and-a-half to time-and-a-quarter after July 2018, though maternity pay terms have been enhanced.Despite these increases, Tesco's new rates still trail behind competitors Aldi and Lidl. Aldi recently announced hourly pay of £8.53, while Lidl's website indicates store staff earn £8.45 per hour.This reward package sees our biggest investment in store pay for a decade, and gives colleagues a sustainable pay deal that rewards them for everything they do, while allowing us to also attract new talent, said Tesco UK chief executive, Matt Davies.The move reflects broader economic pressures as UK wage growth has remained sluggish in recent years while inflation has risen, prompting other supermarkets to increase their pay scales.Retail analyst Steve Dresser noted the strategic necessity behind such changes: This is designed to meet the government legislative requirement around the minimum wage. A Tesco announcement that it will raise hourly pay from £7.62 to £8.42 by November 2018 represents the company's biggest investment in pay in a decade. This increase will take Tesco's pay rate above the £7.90 expected in next year's National Living Wage, which is the real minimum for employees over the age of 25, while those under 25 are on a lower rate. The budgets of the government, which have announced that the minimum wage will continue to rise until at least 2020, have made employers rethink about how they can protect the competitiveness of pay and still keep costs low. “This package of reward is our biggest investment in store pay for a decade and gives our colleagues a sustainable pay deal that rewards them for everything they do, while allowing us to attract new talent,” said Tesco UK chief executive Matt Davies. It is a matter of meeting the government's legislative requirement, as it is well known that most companies which have had to face the rise have had to reduce bonuses and other perks to employees, in order to meet the core wage rise. The overtime rate for Sundays and bank holidays will be reduced from a half to a quarter, from July on, but maternity pay terms have been improved.

text: With the #OscarsSoWhite controversy and calls for the Brit Awards to be more truly representative, there has never been more discussion about diversity in the arts. While recent high-profile Shakespeare productions like Hamlet and King Lear have showcased predominantly BAME casts, industry insiders argue that genuine diversity remains elusive. As one critic puts it, you can walk onto a building site and see more diversity than in the average theatre.Paapa Essiedu, currently starring as Hamlet for the Royal Shakespeare Company, describes theatre as being caught between two worlds at the moment. Despite positive rhetoric about the present and future, he explains: I still don't see or feel that impact. What is required is for people to be more bold and more adventurous in what they back.The casting of veteran actor Don Warrington as King Lear at Manchester's Royal Exchange exemplifies this tension. Warrington argues such casting should not be in any way startling, yet numerous reviews highlighted his race - something he considers an indictment of where we are. Though conditions have improved during his nearly five-decade career, the very fact that his casting generates discussion reveals an ongoing problem.There's a higher visibility, but the question is about the quality of that visibility and the quality of the parts, Warrington notes. I don't think that is where it should be.Hamida Ali, Equity's equalities and diversity organiser, echoes these concerns. One of the things we remain concerned about is how surprised we might be when we see a black actor in a lead role, not just in Shakespeare, but in general. It says something in itself that that remains something of note.While consensus exists around the problem, Ali observes that what the cause is, who is responsible and what the solutions are is perhaps more in debate.The King Lear production partnered with Talawa, a company established in the 1980s in direct response to the lack of creative opportunities for actors from minority ethnic backgrounds. Three decades later, artistic director Michael Buffong maintains there's still a rapid need for change.What we need is different people to reflect different aspects of the same world, otherwise we have this very narrow viewpoint, Buffong explains.Essiedu advocates for theatre to become more diverse about the stories we're telling and the people that are telling them. This approach, he argues, would naturally create more opportunity for a more diverse group of actors. He emphasizes their responsibility: We're in 2016 in an international, multicultural, integrated society and we've got a responsibility as artists to reflect that in the work that we create.Matthew Xia, associate artistic director at the Royal Exchange, suggests the situation has actually deteriorated, claiming theatre has gone backwards in so many ways. The problem extends beyond artistic choices to organizational structures, he argues.In the majority of organisations, the moment you get to the leadership, it drops right down with regards to proportionate representation of the cities that they are working in, Xia observes. It's beyond me, because you can walk onto a building site and see more diversity than you can see in what is meant to be the liberal end of the work spectrum.This systemic issue requires fundamental change, according to Buffong: change the gatekeepers, because that's where the power is. He distinguishes between superficial representation and authentic storytelling: You can cast two black actors in a play and go 'wow, we've got two black actors' but that's not really the same as having a story from a particular point of view. Just because there is a black actor on the stage doesn't necessarily mean it's your story.Dawn Walton, founder of Sheffield's Eclipse theatre company, which uses the Black British experience to create new work that will enrich the canon of British theatre, shares this perspective. She criticizes the industry's focus on cross-casting as a solution: There is a belief in theatre that what is on stage is what needs to be diverse, so cross-casting is always where people go - casting a black whatever - but if that solved it, we'd have beaten this in the 1970s.The real issue lies with theatre boards, Walton argues, because they're very much into doing the same thing over and over again... but the country has shifted. Consequently, the institution is becoming less and less relevant because it doesn't represent what goes on right outside its doors.Xia highlights how actors of colour remain marginalized, noting theatre is still at a place where actors of colour are expected to play peripheral characters unless the play is explicitly dealing with race, which is ridiculous. He's encountered troubling attitudes from directors that reveal a lack of understanding about roles and who can play what.The human experience is so much broader than that, Xia emphasizes. Ultimately, people are always going to represent their world on stage, so if their world has been monocultural, it's highly likely that's how the work will be rendered.Neil Darlison, Arts Council England's director of theatre, acknowledges that diversity of theatre generally is an issue. He believes theatres recognize this challenge because ultimately it's going to affect their business. However, he identifies encouraging developments, particularly in metropolitan centres, where the diversity of people working in organisations and running them is better than it was. These organizations are beginning to reflect the stories of the inhabitants of the city.Regarding solutions, Warrington advocates for deliberate intervention: We have to wake up our consciences and we can do that by having a deliberate policy, so that it becomes part of everyday life. It has to become something we do.Buffong supports immediate action: I'm in favour of anything that gets an instant result. Targets, quotas, ringfencing money - I'm in favour of making it happen now. The idea of more initiatives and training is so over. There's a wealth of people who just need the opportunity to work.However, legal frameworks may complicate progress, according to Ali. While the law in some ways supports equality, it contains problematic exemptions: There are exemptions from the duty not to discriminate where appropriate and casting is one of those. If you are casting for realism purposes or because of the way a character is written, that is permitted, so you could argue that exemption has worked against progress.She acknowledges the complexity: I understand that we're talking about an artistic process, but we must recognise it is an industrial one, and decisions made have an impact disproportionately on working opportunities. It's a difficult and thorny question because there are pros and cons on both sides.For Essiedu, the solution may be straightforward: representation breeds inspiration. We mimic what we see, so we need to put that in front of people to get that machine started, he explains. His own experience illustrates this principle: I'd never seen a black actor performing the lead in a Shakespeare play until I was 18 and I saw Chiwetel Ejiofor doing Othello in the Donmar Warehouse. Because I hadn't seen it, I didn't think it was possible and I didn't explore that avenue.This visibility creates a ripple effect: People from whatever background are only going to be inspired to write or perform if they see it. If you've got an artistic director who is willing to try and fail, then you're going to get a wider palette of works. Some of it will probably be terrible, but some of it will be unbelievably brilliant.Hamlet is in cinemas from 8 June and at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon 13 August.

The need, according to him, is for more diversity in the story-telling, the characters, and the people who tell it. What is needed, he says, is for different people to show different aspects of the same world, otherwise you have this very narrow view. The problem goes beyond artistic choices, he argues: In most organizations, Xia remarks, when you reach the management, the representation of the cities in which they operate falls drastically, which is completely beyond me, because you can go to a construction site and see more diversity than in the liberal side of work. It is a question of systemic change, says Buffong: Change the gatekeepers, because that is where the power lies. Xia, on the other hand, is emphatic that the human experience is much wider, and that inevitably people will be represented on stage according to their worldview. He has met directors who have a disturbing lack of understanding of roles and who can play what. The fact is, Darlison, the theatre director of the British Council, recognizes the problem of diversity in the theatre in general. Theatres, he believes, are aware of this challenge, because they are aware of the business. It has to be something we do.” Buffon argues for immediate action. “I support anything that gives immediate results,” he says. For her the law may promote equality in one sense, but it is not without its own problem: It is possible to cast for the purpose of realism, or because of the way a character is written, and you can argue that this exception has worked against progress. The law is complicated, because it includes some exemptions from the duty not to discriminate: Casting is one of them. text: Sinn Féin has dismissed a proposal to stand independent anti-Brexit candidates as part of a general election pact in Northern Ireland. Parties that backed remaining in the European Union during last year's referendum were urged by the SDLP to forge an electoral pact for the 8 June Westminster election, though the proposal has now collapsed.Colum Eastwood, the SDLP leader, had floated the possibility of fielding agreed candidates without party labels as one potential approach. However, Sinn Féin's John O'Dowd dismissed this as not a credible offer.Various anti-Brexit parties have engaged in discussions about establishing what Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill termed a progressive alliance across certain constituencies. The strategy aimed to capture seats currently held by parties supporting Britain's EU departure.Meanwhile, pro-Brexit parties have pursued similar unity talks. Both the Democratic Unionist Party and Ulster Unionists, who voted in Parliament to activate the Brexit process, have explored the possibility of fielding single unionist candidates in selected areas.Eastwood's independent anti-Brexit candidate proposal reportedly targeted three specific constituencies: East Londonderry, Fermanagh and South Tyrone, and North Belfast.The Upper Bann MLA O'Dowd rejected the plan, insisting any alliance must center on political party representation. He argued: We don't believe that's an acceptable way forward. It is political parties that will drive forward change in this society.O'Dowd characterized Eastwood's proposal as an attempt to stymie Sinn Féin and bolster the SDLP - that's not what progressive political alliances should be about. Despite this rejection, he indicated Sinn Féin remained open to discussions with other parties about potential arrangements.Following Sinn Féin's opposition, Eastwood conceded defeat. If Sinn Féin have ruled that out, I think it's very, very difficult, he acknowledged, admitting there is probably no chance now for his proposal's success.The SDLP leader emphasized his party's broader vision: We have always said that we would not do a pact with Sinn Féin alone. We wanted this to be broad; we wanted this to be non-nationalist; we wanted to go right across the political spectrum.Additional complications emerged Tuesday when the Green Party announced it would not align with parties lacking its vision for a progressive society. Green Party leader Steven Agnew cited the SDLP's selection of sitting MP Alasdair McDonnell as its South Belfast candidate for the snap election as ending any prospect of constituency-level cooperation.

text: Police Scotland has said that it does not collate or hold specific figures on child sexual exploitation. BBC Scotland's Freedom of Information requests seeking data on child exploitation cases, concerns and complaints over the past four years have revealed a troubling gap in record-keeping. Police Scotland responded that such figures are not held on a single system, a revelation Scotland's Children's Commissioner has branded disturbing.The disclosure coincides with the launch of a new police unit designed to address what authorities acknowledge as Scotland's complex web of child abuse and neglect. This specialized unit will equip local teams with enhanced expertise to conduct thorough investigations into child sexual exploitation, online offences and various forms of abuse.Police Scotland's FOI response explained: Child exploitation covers a broad range of criminal activity and doesn't correlate to a specific offence, but rather can involve a range of differing offences...The level of data you have requested is not held on a single system.The data gap emerges against the backdrop of last summer's Jay report, which exposed how more than 1,400 children suffered horrific sexual abuse in Rotherham, South Yorkshire. Meanwhile, Glasgow City Council identified 97 children as victims or potential victims of sexual exploitation last year.While the Association of Chief Police Officers reports that most English and Welsh forces now flag such offences in their records, senior Scottish officers maintain this approach presents significant challenges.Children's Commissioner Tam Baillie expressed alarm at the situation: I am disturbed that we do not yet collect police figures on children who are the subject of sexual exploitation. This was a recommendation of the Scottish Parliament and features in the Scottish government action plan on child sexual exploitation. The reason this is so important is that unless we know the scope of the problem we are trying to deal with, then we won't have the appropriate or proportionate response.Assistant Chief Constable Malcolm Graham of Police Scotland emphasized the inherent difficulties in addressing child sexual exploitation, noting that victims rarely come forward voluntarily. Our priority is to be focussing on identifying as many victims as we can and identifying perpetrators who have the intent to commit these devastating crimes so we can prevent the abuse from happening, he stated.Graham positioned Scotland as a leader in tackling child sexual exploitation, explaining: Sexual exploitation is a form of abuse and it is not a specific crime type recorded as such. Children and young people may be victim of repeated rapes, physical assaults or grooming offences and we categorise all of these in crime recording. But what is most important here is our focus on identifying who these victims are. Our focus is always on where there are child protection issues, and on keeping children safe.Martin Crewe, director of Barnardo's Scotland, acknowledged the impact of recent revelations: Rotherham was a real wake-up call and led to the Scottish government's national action plan last year but we could and should be doing more. Our concern is that we don't know the full extent of the problem. We welcome the work of the police. Since the publication of the Barnardo's Scotland petition in 2011 we have been pushing for a better understanding of child sexual exploitation in Scotland.Despite ministerial commitments dating back to January 2013, when Aileen Campbell, Minister for Children and Young People, promised action to improve the way child sexual exploitation is identified by Scotland's new single police force to make this form of abuse more visible, sexual exploitation remains neither recorded nor centrally collated as a distinct category.The Scottish government maintains that broader child abuse statistics are available. A spokeswoman emphasized: The safety of our children is a key priority for the government and an issue we take extremely seriously. The launch of the National Child Abuse Investigation Unit will help to target and bring to justice those who seek to harm our young people. The unit has been set up to tackle all forms of child abuse, and child sexual exploitation is one aspect of this. We have robust legislation in place to cover a wide range of these offences, including online abuse and are working to strengthen the law even further.She acknowledged the inherent challenges in quantifying the problem: The extent of the problem is often difficult to assess because abuse by its very nature is concealed. That's why prevention and swift action to safeguard children are a big part of our strategy to tackle these terrible crimes. This includes robust National Child Protection guidance, action to tackle emerging forms of child abuse including child sexual exploitation, a national public awareness campaign and guidance for night-time workers such as taxi drivers and hotel staff who may come into contact with those at risk.

text: The range and quality of research at Scotland's universities has been praised in a new UK-wide survey. Scotland's universities have largely strengthened their positions in the latest research excellence rankings, with Edinburgh University securing 4th place and Glasgow University claiming 13th position in the national standings.The comprehensive assessment revealed that over 85% of Scottish university research delivers outstanding or highly significant impact across society and the economy - a performance exceeding the UK-wide average. These findings emerged from Research Fortnight's analysis of the 2014 Research Excellence Framework (REF 2014) results.REF 2014 represented a massive evaluation exercise examining research quality across various disciplines at UK universities. Expert panels assessed work from more than 52,000 academics spanning 154 institutions throughout the United Kingdom.Both Edinburgh and Glasgow universities climbed one position compared to the previous 2008 assessment. The top 50 also featured St Andrews, Strathclyde, Aberdeen, Dundee, Heriot-Watt and Stirling universities. Notably, Strathclyde's physics department earned recognition as Britain's finest - surpassing Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial College.While Aberdeen and Dundee experienced slight declines in overall rankings, other Scottish institutions advanced their positions. The data broadly indicates that Scottish universities have sustained or enhanced their research standings since tuition fees for Scottish students were eliminated.International assessments similarly suggest Scottish universities are maintaining their global positions. All 18 of Scotland's higher education institutions conduct research deemed world-leading quality, while Scotland outperforms the UK average regarding research impact assessment.REF 2014 introduced a novel element by evaluating research impact on economy, society, public policy, culture and quality of life for the first time.Laurence Howells, chief executive of the Scottish Funding Council, said: Today we have had confirmation that our universities' research is world-leading and impacts on almost every aspect of daily life, from the way we treat patients in hospital, to the way we communicate with smartphones.He added: By making the most of our investments in research, Scotland's universities are rightly on the podium with the best in the world. It is particularly satisfying that Scotland's pioneering approach to collaboration through research pooling has helped to bring this success in the REF.Edinburgh University achieved remarkable breadth of excellence, with each of its three colleges securing at least one UK-leading research area. The university's research in Sociology, Earth Systems and Environmental Sciences, and Computer Science and Informatics topped UK rankings based on research breadth and quality.Principal Prof Sir Timothy O'Shea said: Research at the University of Edinburgh is constantly expanding the depth of human knowledge and making an impact on the wider world - whether it be improving the effectiveness of youth justice policy and practice, or shaping the technologies used to manage the world's data.He continued: Our outstanding researchers enable us to forge links with charities, businesses, policy makers and other universities, so that together we can tackle long-standing challenges at home and overseas.Glasgow University highlighted diverse achievements including groundbreaking medical research developing new drugs and treatments, revolutionary software transforming electric motor design, innovative animal disease control methods for TB in cattle and rabies, positive influence on knife crime policy, and contributions to transforming Stirling Castle into a premier UK heritage destination.Principal and vice-chancellor Prof Anton Muscatelli said: It is particularly pleasing that, in line with the aspirations of the university set out in the university's 2020 Global Vision, 31% of our output was judged to be of 'world-leading' quality. This success lies at the very heart of our contribution to the UK's economy and, in particular, Scotland's economy.Education Secretary Angela Constance welcomed the findings, emphasizing Scotland's global recognition for pioneering research, with four universities ranking among the world's top 200 institutions.This achievement represents more universities per capita than any nation except Switzerland, she noted.Ms Constance added: The 2014 Research Excellence Framework has now shown that all of our institutions are producing world-class research in a variety of areas.She emphasized research's economic importance: Research is also key to our economic growth and prosperity. Figures published earlier this year showed that our £124m investment in eight innovation centres has the potential to generate up to £1.5bn and around 5,000 jobs for the economy, through sectors such as energy, aquaculture and construction.However, the University and College Union raised concerns about employment conditions, warning that world-leading research frequently relies on zero-hours contract workers. The union cautioned institutions against using perceived low scores to justify staff reductions.Additionally, the union stressed that significant research excluded from or receiving lower REF ratings still contributes immensely to knowledge advancement.UCU Scotland official Mary Senior said: Our universities must be free to continue pushing the boundaries in their cutting-edge work. We must also recognise that a lot of research not included or rated highly in the REF is still incredibly important.She continued: Too often our world-leading research is being conducted by people with little or no job security. Universities must avoid any knee-jerk reactions to the results or use perceived low scores to try and make unnecessary cuts.Senior concluded: We are not alone in criticising what we see as a flawed process when it comes to the REF and have outlined the need for a fundamental overhaul of the research system. We want to see better funding that expands our research base, covering more institutions and more diverse areas of research.

text: The mother of an RAF airman who went missing more than three weeks ago has said she absolutely believes her son is still alive. A 23-year-old RAF gunner stationed at Honington in Suffolk disappeared following an evening out in Bury St Edmunds during the early hours of September 24.Corrie Mckeague's mother, Nicola Urquhart, spoke to the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme, stating: Nobody can just disappear.Originally from Dunfermline in Fife, Mr Mckeague was captured on CCTV at 03:20 BST walking alone through Bury St Edmunds while consuming takeaway food - his final confirmed sighting.Mobile phone tracking data revealed the device remained in Bury St Edmunds early on September 24 before relocating to the Barton Mills area. According to Ms Urquhart, this journey required 28 minutes, which is how long it would take to drive [between the two places].While authorities cannot confirm whether Mr Mckeague possessed his phone during this movement, his mother indicated that accepting rides from strangers would be typical behavior for him. She described her son as someone who, if he saw someone walking down the road and he was in a car, he would stop and give that complete stranger a lift. Ms Urquhart emphasized that entering a stranger's vehicle was genuinely something Corrie would do.Neither the missing airman nor his mobile device have been located by police.Regarding the phone's disappeared signal, Ms Urquhart suggested many possibilities existed - from battery depletion to physical damage.The ongoing police investigation continues searching for the missing serviceman, though Ms Urquhart revealed they have got so much CCTV they've still not been able to watch it all.They've widened the parameter to look further out. They've got [access to] private CCTV. But not a single [new] image of Corrie [has been discovered], she added.Despite believing somebody does know something about her son's disappearance, Ms Urquhart acknowledged the public's eagerness to assist. However, she expressed frustration: But nothing, not one person [has been able to] give us anything - and that just doesn't make sense.Anyone possessing relevant information should contact Suffolk Police's incident room at 01473 782019.For more updates on this story, visit BBC Suffolk LiveThe Victoria Derbyshire programme airs weekdays from 09:00 to 11:00 on BBC Two and the BBC News Channel.

text: UN human rights chief Zeid Raad Al Hussein has described the Syrian city of Aleppo as a slaughterhouse. During an emergency session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on Friday, Mr Zeid delivered stark warnings about the ongoing devastation in Syria's former commercial capital. The siege and bombardment targeting Aleppo's rebel-controlled eastern districts represent crimes of historic proportions unfolding across the war-torn nation, he declared.The assault on eastern Aleppo, launched by government forces with Russian air support one month prior, has exacted a devastating toll. Nearly 500 deaths and 2,000 injuries have resulted from the offensive, transforming what was once Syria's largest city into a battlefield of unprecedented destruction.Syrian government officials have defended their military operations, claiming civilian casualties stem from the presence of terrorists in the area. This justification comes as the ancient metropolis—historically a center of commerce and industry—remains carved into two hostile zones since fighting erupted in 2012. Western sectors fall under President Bashar al-Assad's control, while rebels maintain their grip on the east.The humanitarian crisis deepened dramatically at September's onset when government troops and Iranian-backed militiamen successfully cut off the rebels' final supply route into eastern territories. This strategic maneuver trapped approximately 275,000 residents under siege conditions.Following the breakdown of a US-Russia brokered nationwide ceasefire two weeks later, Assad's forces initiated a comprehensive ground offensive. The campaign to seize complete control of Aleppo has been accompanied by aerial bombardments of extraordinary scale and ferocity.Mr Zeid painted a harrowing picture of the current situation during his Geneva address: The ancient city of Aleppo, a place of millennial civility and beauty, is today a slaughterhouse - a gruesome locus of pain and fear, where the lifeless bodies of small children are trapped under streets of rubble and pregnant women deliberately bombed.His office has compiled extensive documentation revealing violations of international humanitarian law by multiple parties involved in the Aleppo conflict. While armed opposition groups persist in launching mortar attacks and projectiles into civilian areas of western Aleppo, the commissioner emphasized that government forces and their allies bear responsibility for the vast majority of civilian casualties through indiscriminate air strikes across eastern districts.These violations constitute war crimes. And if knowingly committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against civilians, they constitute crimes against humanity, Mr Zeid stated unequivocally.The international community's inability to halt the bloodshed—particularly the UN Security Council's failure to protect civilians—represents a moral failing that should haunt everyone of us, the commissioner added.Syria's permanent UN representative, Hussam al-Din Ala, responded with visible anger, maintaining that his government was conducting legitimate counter-terrorism operations.Humanitarian efforts have faced significant obstacles. The UN announced that security concerns forced postponement of planned medical evacuations scheduled for Friday's second 11-hour humanitarian pause—a unilateral declaration by the Syrian government and Russia.Russia has committed to suspending air strikes between 08:00 and 19:00 local time (05:00-16:00 GMT) on Saturday, creating windows for civilian and rebel departures through designated safe corridors. However, these evacuation opportunities have attracted minimal participation, with rebel factions denouncing the initiative as tantamount to forced displacement and capitulation.Meanwhile, Save the Children has issued alarming reports about the escalating use of internationally banned cluster munitions. Aid workers and medical personnel in eastern Aleppo have documented widespread deployment of these weapons, according to the charity's latest warnings.The Violations Documentation Centre, operated by activists, recorded 137 cluster-bomb attacks in Aleppo between 10 September and 10 October—representing a staggering 791% increase compared to the average frequency during the preceding eight months.

text: All living flowers ultimately derive from a single ancestor that lived about 140 million years ago, a study suggests. Scientists have achieved a groundbreaking reconstruction of the world's first flower by merging evolutionary models with the most comprehensive dataset of living flower characteristics ever compiled.The research team analyzed features from 792 living species to infer what the ancestral flower looked like. Their findings reveal a complex bloom featuring multiple concentric cycles of petal-like organs arranged in sets of three within distinct whorls, possessing both male and female reproductive parts.There is no living flower that looks exactly like the ancestral one - and why should there be? This is a flower that existed at least 140 million years ago and has had considerable time to evolve into the incredible diversity of flowers that exist today, explained Hervé Sauquet from Université Paris-Sud, France, co-author of the study published this week in Nature Communications.The mystery surrounding flower origins has persisted largely due to the absence of fossil evidence from the era when flowering plants' common ancestor is believed to have flourished. Today's flowers - reproductive structures found in approximately 90% of terrestrial plant species - showcase remarkable beauty, yet their evolutionary beginnings remained elusive.Dr Jason Hilton from the University of Birmingham, UK, who wasn't part of the research team, noted the challenge: The structure and organisation of the ancestral flower has remained enigmatic. text: A petition calling for jousting to be made an Olympic sport has been launched by English Heritage. However, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) stated it remains unaware of any official recognition request.Olympic inclusion requires sports to meet stringent criteria: governance by an international federation, widespread global practice, and approval from the IOC's executive board. English Heritage has initiated preliminary discussions with both the IOC and the Federation Equestre Internationale (FEI), which oversees Olympic equestrian disciplines.Recognition from the FEI would be essential before the IOC could consider jousting as an Olympic sport, English Heritage explained. The charity acknowledged this represents a long road but cited encouraging signs in the sport's development.Sewell, who competes professionally, draws parallels to established Olympic disciplines: Just like the Olympic British equestrian team, we ride beautiful horses to an exceptional level. The former factory furniture assembler emphasized jousting's demanding nature, requiring huge amount of skill and a daily training regime alongside mental fortitude to sit fearlessly in your saddle, face your rival, and offer yourself as a target.His journey began through historical re-enactments, but Sewell stressed his athletic focus during a BBC Radio 4's Today programme interview: I'm a sportsman, I'm not an actor. He recalled the transformative moment: As soon as I got on a horse everything changed and I thought: this is what I want to do, I want to be good at this. For Sewell, jousting has evolved from being a hobby to being a sport and a career.International interest continues expanding, with tournaments flourishing in Belgium, Brazil, and New Zealand. Maryland has recognized jousting as its official state sport since 1962, and American competitors have initiated their own Olympic campaign.Modern jousting maintains safety standards while preserving its competitive essence, according to Sewell. The rules are essentially that you are in a single combat situation, in a designated area, in a pitch - or 'tilt-yard' - and in that yard is a tilt rail. Competitors thunder toward each other along the rail, with scoring based on hit style and strength.Athletes don 20-kilogram armor suits while wielding 12-foot lances single-handedly, controlling their horses' reins with the other hand during full gallops reaching 30mph. text: Two 15-year-olds have been given life sentences with 20-year minimum terms for the murder of a mother and daughter in Lincolnshire in April. At Nottingham Crown Court, two teenagers received sentences for the brutal killings of dinner lady Elizabeth Edwards, 49, and her 13-year-old daughter Katie, who were smothered and stabbed as they slept in their Spalding home.Mr Justice Haddon-Cave described the crime as having few parallels in modern criminal history during sentencing. The perpetrators, aged just 14 at the time of the murders, appear to be Britain's youngest double-murderers.This case has defining and particularly chilling features, the judge declared, branding the killers' behavior as grotesque. The court learned disturbing details about the aftermath: following the murders on April 13 in Dawson Avenue, Spalding, the pair shared a bath, engaged in sexual activity, and watched four Twilight vampire films.The judge addressed the teenagers directly: There is a clear intention to kill both victims - both defendants admitted wanting to murder them. There was remarkable premeditation and planning - it was, on any view, substantial, meticulous and repeated.He emphasized the brutality of the attacks: The killings were brutal in the form of executions, and both victims, particularly Elizabeth Edwards, must have suffered terribly in the last minutes of their lives.The couple, characterized in court as having a Bonnie and Clyde-style relationship, repeatedly stabbed both victims. Mrs Edwards endured eight stab wounds, including two to her throat - a calculated move to prevent her screams from alerting Katie. The daughter suffered two severe neck wounds before being smothered with a pillow by the boy.Both teenagers were equally responsible for the murders and had revelled in what you achieved, the judge stated during his remarks. I see no reason to distinguish between you in any way. Had you been adults you may have been facing the whole of your lives in prison for this double murder.Karen Thompson, deputy chief crown prosecutor for the East Midlands, spoke outside court: This is one of the most distressing and disturbing cases that I have ever encountered. text: Steven Wilson is often dubbed the hardest working musician in the world of progressive rock. At this month's Progressive Music Awards in London, the multi-talented musician claimed three victories, with Hand. Cannot. Erase. earning album of the year honors. The Guardian awarded the work five stars, describing it as a smart, soulful and immersive work of art.Wilson has served as the creative engine behind numerous musical ventures since the 1980s, most notably the rock band Porcupine Tree. With two sold-out Royal Albert Hall performances approaching, he's preparing to release Transience, a vinyl-exclusive double LP designed to highlight the more accessible elements of his solo catalog.In conversation with the BBC, Wilson discusses his vinyl passion, demanding schedule, and reveals how comic actor Matt Berry became his opening act.**Regarding vinyl's significance to him:**I grew up at the very tail end of the vinyl era, and at the time, I remember, we couldn't wait for CD to come along because vinyl was so frustrating. You would buy the record, take it home, and it would have a scratch, and you would have to take it back again.While Wilson appreciates CDs and acknowledges their superiority for certain genres like classical music, he finds digital formats lacking in emotional connection. But the problem with the CD and digital downloads is that there's nothing you can really cherish or treasure.He compares vinyl ownership to displaying artwork: Owning vinyl is like having a beautiful painting hanging in your living room. It's something you can hold, pore over the lyrics and immerse yourself in the art work.The appeal extends beyond nostalgia, Wilson observes: I thought it was just a nostalgic thing, but it can't be if kids too young to remember vinyl are enjoying that kind of experience.**On treasured vinyl pieces:**Wilson admits to a complete collection purge: The truth is I got rid of 100% of my vinyl in the 90s. All the vinyl I have is re-bought. I started off from the perspective that I wanted to recreate the collection I had when I was 15, but it's gone beyond that.His first parental purchase request was Electric Light Orchestra's Out of the Blue. If I still had my original copy, it would have sentimental value, but, alas, it's in a charity shop somewhere.**The Transience compilation concept:**Originally intended for Record Store Day, the project evolved when we missed the boat on that. Wilson's record company proposed gathering his shorter, more accessible material. I got a bit obsessed by the idea to make something like 'an introduction to Steven Wilson', and I was committed to it being a vinyl-only release. Anyone who buys the vinyl does also get a high-res[olution] download.Wilson dismisses concerns about misrepresentation: No - because although I do focus on more long-form pieces of music, there is one thing I have always valued above everything else: melody.He distinguishes his approach from technical-focused progressive rock: There is a lot of progressive rock which focuses on the technical complexity of the track rather than the melodic side. Pink Floyd, the most successful progressive rock band of all time, have stood the test of time because the emphasis was always on melody and atmosphere.**Albert Hall performances preview:**Wilson promises distinct experiences: I don't want to give away too much. The repertoire will be completely different each night.The opening show will present a version of the Hand. Cannot. Erase. show I've been doing this year - but on steroids - with a couple of guests. The second evening offers more of a trip into my history, which is more aimed at the fans have been following me for years.**Matt Berry's involvement:**The collaboration emerged from tour bus entertainment: Myself and everyone on the tour bus are massive fans of [Channel 4 comedy series] Toast of London to the point that we are quoting it endlessly.Wilson investigated Berry's musical work, discovering Music for Insomniacs. I chatted with him about our love of Mike Oldfield and asked him to play at the Royal Albert Hall. He confesses: I'm going to be incredibly star struck by my opening act.**Remix work influence:**Wilson has tackled albums by XTC, Tears for Fears, and Yes, acknowledging subtle creative impact: I don't consciously draw from that, but, inevitably, if you are deconstructing these classic albums they really get into your head.His previous album, The Raven That Refused to Sing, reflected this influence: was without doubt the most old-school progressive album I've ever done. I don't think it was coincidence that I had been remixing King Crimson, Jethro Tull and Yes almost exclusively for the previous year.Hand. Cannot. Erase. showed different influences: opened up a lot more because I'd been working on Tears for Fears and XTC.**Work ethic and industry challenges:**Wilson embraces his reputation with qualification: You can remove the word progressive. I think I am probably one of the most work-obsessed people in the music business today, and I don't say that with any sense of pride because believe me it's a curse.He traces this drive to family influence: I think I get it from my father, who also had an incredibly strong work ethic. If I don't do anything for a whole day, I start to feel this creeping guilt. That's why the remix work has been such a gift to me because it means I don't have to be doing my own music all the time.Wilson offers sobering industry perspective: The music industry is a hard place to make a living for yourself. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone as a profession now. I work every day, and I'm not rich, but I make a good living. I love what I do, it's a privilege, but if I was lazy about it, I don't think I'd be able to survive.Transience arrives in the UK on 25 September. Steven Wilson's Royal Albert Hall performances on 28 and 29 September form part of his 2015-16 European tour.

text: Food bank use in Scotland has increased to record levels, with more than 60,000 referrals over a six-month period, according to a charity. Food banks across Scotland distributed 60,458 three-day emergency food parcels between April and September, marking a 17% surge compared to the previous year, according to new figures from the Trussell Trust.With an average of 1.7 referrals per person, the charity estimates approximately 35,000 individuals sought assistance during this six-month period. Benefit payment delays remained the primary driver of food bank usage, accounting for 28% of referrals—unchanged from last year's proportion.However, the data reveals shifting patterns in financial hardship. While benefit changes as a referral cause declined from 18% to 16%, low income cases climbed from 18% to 21%—a trend that concerns Scotland network manager Ewan Gurr.Difficulties related to welfare benefits are still driving the majority of people to our Scottish food banks but now one in five of those referred is on a low income, Gurr explained. Among that number is a growing body of people in low paid employment who are simply unable to make the pay cheque stretch far enough when crisis hits.Economic instability compounds the problem, Gurr noted. The increasing instability of the oil, gas and steel industries has already led to significant numbers of people being made redundant and figures revealed in the last week also show that unemployment has risen in Scotland while decreasing in the rest of the UK.The charity anticipates challenges ahead, particularly recalling last December when low income referrals spiked as heating costs strained household budgets further.SNP MSP Kevin Stewart branded the statistics alarming, emphasizing that UK government benefit changes and delays continue to be the most common reason for people seeking emergency food aid.Stewart criticized Conservative policies while highlighting Scottish government efforts: While Tory ministers have their head in the sand on the issue, the Scottish government recognises this link and is spending almost £300m over three years to mitigate Tory social security cuts.He condemned planned austerity measures: That any government would consider further cuts to the incomes of the poorest families in our society in the face of such clear evidence of rising poverty is appalling - yet George Osborne is set to plough ahead with £12bn more social security cuts.A UK government spokesman defended current policies, stating: Our reforms have secured record employment, a near record number of job vacancies and a growing economy. We maintain a strong social safety net and continue to spend around £80bn on working age benefits.The spokesman disputed welfare reform criticism: We know that the reasons for food bank use are complex and overlapping and it is spurious to claim that it is driven by changes to welfare. Work remains the best route out of poverty and thanks to this government's long term economic plan thousands of people are experiencing the dignity of a job, the security of a wage and the peace of mind that comes from supporting your family, many for the first time.Food donation statistics positioned Scotland second nationally behind England's northwest region. Population-adjusted data suggested Scotland experiences disproportionately high food bank referral rates compared to other UK regions, the trust reported.Scottish Labour's equality spokesman Neil Findlay expressed dismay at the figures: In a country as wealthy as Scotland it is unacceptable that more than 60,000 people had to rely on food banks over the last six months. As winter approaches, the need for extra support is only going to increase.Findlay called for governmental action: These figures should act as a wake-up call to both of Scotland's governments. After eight years of the SNP in office, and more than five years of the Tories, the gap between the richest and the rest in Scotland remains unacceptably high.The Trussell Trust operates as a charity motivated by Christian values, managing 50 Scottish food banks within its 425-strong UK network. All recipients receive professional referrals from social workers, health visitors, or schools liaison officers before accessing services.

text: Skier Dave Ryding matched Britain's best ever alpine World Cup result when he finished second in the Kitzbuhel slalom in Austria. After commanding the first run, the 30-year-old ultimately surrendered his lead to Austria's Marcel Hirscher, securing a historic second-place finish that marked his maiden World Cup podium appearance.This achievement represents Britain's finest alpine skiing performance in more than three and a half decades, dating back to Konrad Bartelski's runner-up position in an Italian downhill race in 1981.Having already notched sixth and seventh-place finishes earlier this season, Ryding's breakthrough moment came on one of skiing's most prestigious stages.The first run was just insane, he told BBC Sport. I knew I had skied it clean, but couldn't believe it when I crossed the finish line.Managing the pressure between runs proved crucial for the Lancashire native. In between runs I tried not to get the heart rate up or get stressed. I was trying to tell myself I wasn't the last one to go but it was tough. It was a mental battle with myself but I won the mental battle.Despite losing to the Austrian star, Ryding found satisfaction in his performance. Hirscher skied so well, so coming second almost felt like a victory. It's crazy. I'm just really proud of what I've achieved.The British skier's journey has been particularly challenging since UK Sport withdrew funding from the alpine programme in 2010, though he continues to receive alternative sponsorship. Learning his craft on Pendle Ski Club's dry slope, Ryding joined Britain's ski team in 2006 and has competed in two Winter Olympics - 2010 and 2014 - with a best finish of 17th place.Entering the decisive second run, Ryding held a commanding 0.29-second advantage over Italy's Stefano Gross, while Hirscher trailed by 1.02 seconds from seventh position. However, the three-time overall slalom champion and 2013 Kitzbuhel winner delivered a spectacular final run, vaulting from seventh to claim victory and leaving Ryding 0.76 seconds behind.The atmosphere proved electrifying for the more than 60,000 spectators in attendance. Kitzbuhel is like the FA Cup final in England, Ryding observed. The downhill race is the number one but the slalom is also massive. The fans are incredible. The noise, he added, was deafening.Since the World Cup's 1967 inception, British men's podium appearances remain extraordinarily rare. Across five decades of competition, only Ryding and Bartelski have achieved top-three finishes, while women's circuit success came through Gina Hathorn (1967) and Divina Galica (1968).Bartelski's Val Gardena triumph prompted a French commentator's incredulous reaction: This is not possible, he is English!Historical precedent exists from the pre-World Cup era, when Britain's Gordon Cleaver captured the combined race on Kitzbuhel's legendary Hahnenkamm course in 1931.While alpine skiing no longer receives UK Sport backing, the Great British freestyle ski and snowboard programme thrives with substantial investment. Following Jenny Jones' groundbreaking slopestyle bronze in Sochi, the team secured £4.9 million funding for the four-year cycle culminating in the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics.World Cup victories have followed across multiple disciplines: Katie Ormerod became the first British snowboarder to win big air, while cousin Jamie Nicholls triumphed in slopestyle. Halfpipe success came through Lesley McKenna and Rowan Cheshire, with Zoe Gillings-Brier conquering snowboardcross. Skier James Woods has claimed three World Cup slopestyle victories.In related developments, cross-country skier Andrew Musgrave achieved his career-best World Cup result on Saturday, finishing sixth in a 15-kilometer race in Sweden.

text: An archive of sketchbooks, drawings and letters belonging to artist Lucian Freud has been acquired by the nation through the acceptance in lieu scheme. A remarkable archive of Lucian Freud's private sketchbooks and correspondence has been designated for the National Portrait Gallery, settling an inheritance tax bill of £2,940,000 through the inheritance in lieu scheme. The institution, which broke attendance records with its 2012 Lucian Freud Portraits exhibition, will receive this unprecedented collection from the artist's estate.Spanning from the mid-1940s until Freud's death in 2011, the 47 sketchbooks contain previously unseen material that chronicles the development of one of Britain's most celebrated painters. Many items have never been published or exhibited, with plans underway to display selections next summer.Culture Minister Ed Vaizey emphasized the significance of this acquisition: This rare collection of Lucian Freud drawings and letters provides a fascinating glimpse into the work of one of our most pioneering artists. Bringing these never seen before treasures into public collections means that everyone can enjoy and see the early beginnings that shaped his most celebrated work.Among the archive's most poignant elements are 162 childhood drawings depicting family life, created while Freud lived in Germany before his family's 1933 flight to England as Hitler rose to power. His mother carefully preserved and dated these early works, offering intimate documentation of the artist's formative years.The collection includes preparatory studies for major works, with several sketchbook drawings revealing Freud's portrait development process. These show how he began with features like the nose and eyes before expanding outward, including early studies for his 1985 charcoal drawing of Lord Goodman.Beyond fine art, the archive encompasses Freud's commercial design work, featuring book cover concepts including one for his daughter Esther Freud's 1992 novel Hideous Kinky and Nigel Dennis's Cards of Identity from 1955.According to the National Portrait Gallery, this material will give added context to their existing Freud holdings: a self-portrait in oils and the Lord Goodman charcoal drawing from 1985.Dr Nicholas Cullinan, director of the National Portrait Gallery in London, described the archive as a very important, extensive and generous gift to the nation that would serve as a vital source of reference.Sir Peter Bazalgette, chair of Arts Council England, noted that the collection provided a real insight into the life of one of Britain's most compelling and influential artists.

text: Three years ago thousands of Tunisians protested on the streets, demanding, among other things, more economic opportunity. The departure of Tunisia's former President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali resulted from widespread protests that ignited the broader Arab Spring movement throughout North Africa and the Middle East.Since Ben Ali's removal in 2011, Tunisia's economic reforms have remained stagnant amid persistent political turmoil that continued through the previous year's end. Nevertheless, the appointment of a moderate interim government comprising independent officials in December, coupled with January's constitutional agreement, has generated fresh hope for pro-business transformations that could enable small enterprises and entrepreneurship to thrive.This growing confidence received a significant boost from World Bank support, which granted Tunisia $1.2bn (£719m) in loans last month to accelerate economic and political reforms. According to the World Bank, this funding encompasses $750m in support of government reforms to level the economic playing field and promote growth and job creation, plus $100m designated for expanding lending to small and medium-sized enterprises.Tunisian entrepreneurs eagerly await reforms that would simplify their operations. Ramzi el Fekih, 46, identifies an improved judicial system as crucial for helping new businesses launch and expand in Tunisia.As chief executive of Viamobile, a mobile banking and payments application, Mr el Fekih established his company in Tunisia during 2009 after returning home following 25 years abroad, including two decades in California's mobile technology sector.The biggest difference between working here and in California is the lack of trust, Mr el Fekih explains. People try to protect themselves, because they have been had before, but it becomes very constraining.He emphasizes the need for systemic change: There is so much control, that we can't move, but what we need is a judicial system that punishes people who don't follow the law.Mr el Fekih also advocates for dramatically reduced regulation and bureaucracy, citing his frustration with the two-year approval process required by Tunisia's central bank for Viamobile. Despite these challenges, he expresses no regret about returning to his homeland.I really believe that there is a huge potential in Tunisia and Tunisian entrepreneurs, he states.With the new constitution now established, Mr el Fekih hopes Tunisian authorities will rapidly implement reforms. Drawing from mobile technology terminology, he offers this analogy: What politicians can do is design an easy and accessible operating system, so entrepreneurs can follow and create applications. Now is the time.Zied Jallouli, 29, another entrepreneur, identifies securing financial backing as the primary obstacle facing Tunisian start-ups.Raising funds here for a big idea is really, really tough, Mr Jallouli says, shaking his head.Together with his business partner, he developed Disrupt CK, a smartphone application that allegedly helps consumers purchase clothing or other goods similar to items featured in films or television programs. Users simply point their smartphone at the television and press the app button to receive a list of suggested products, according to Mr Jallouli.Unable to secure backing from Tunisian banks or wealthy local investors, Mr Jallouli eventually obtained funding from Thomas Adner, a Swedish expatriate and former Tetra Pak executive who had worked in North Africa for eight years.Mr Adner was so impressed with Mr Jallouli's innovation that he joined the company as chief marketing officer.There are some great business opportunities in Tunisia, Mr Adner observes, highlighting the affordable cost of hiring skilled web developers and programmers. You can run quite a few miles with the cash that you have.However, Mr Adner identifies multiple barriers to conducting business in Tunisia that require elimination.Back home [in Sweden] it takes about 30 minutes to register a new business, and in two days all the paperwork is done, he notes. Tunisian authorities make it not only very difficult to start a company, it takes months if not longer. There is so much red tape here, for anyone who wants to start a business. The government really needs to make it easier to start a company.Laurent Gonnet, the World Bank's financial sector specialist in Tunisia, concurs that substantial work remains necessary to support businesses throughout the country. He characterizes Tunisia's commercial banks as extremely cautious and risk averse, particularly regarding technology companies.Gonnet adds that Tunisia is also one of the last countries that lack a private credit rating system, further complicating entrepreneurs' efforts to persuade banks to provide business financing.Fortunately, the nation's political leaders appear genuinely committed to pro-business reform, likely motivated by World Bank pressure and challenging economic conditions, including 16% unemployment.This commitment hopefully will survive general elections scheduled for year's end.We are reviewing the investment code in order to reduce red tape, states Dhamir Mannai, an assembly member from current President Moncef Marzouki's CPR party.Moncef Cheikhrouhou, representing the opposition Democratic Alliance and serving as deputy chairman of parliament's finance, planning and development committee, declares that entrepreneurship is most needed to create wealth.We are treating this as an urgent matter, and are looking for input from entrepreneurs as well, he concludes.

text: A former Labour chief whip has urged Jeremy Corbyn to reflect on Tony Blair's approach when party leader by ruling out the de-selection of MPs. During a BBC Radio 4's The Westminster Hour interview, Baroness Hilary Armstrong revealed that Jeremy Corbyn had been the greatest rebel ever while serving as a backbencher, yet Tony Blair chose not to discipline him because he believed Labour should remain a broad church.The baroness emphasized that Mr Corbyn must now demonstrate his own tolerance as concerns mount over potential forced departures of his opponents from the party.While expressing satisfaction that Labour party chairman Ian Lavery had rejected de-selection as a viable path forward, Baroness Armstrong highlighted troubling patterns of behavior targeting certain MPs.I know MPs where basically there is a process of harassment, where at every meeting they are criticised, they are challenged, they are told that they don't represent the people in the room, she explained. And all this is meant to do is grind them down, is wear them down, and get them to believe they shouldn't be in the Labour party any more.According to Baroness Armstrong, sectarianism has begun ruling in certain areas of the party.The summer period and upcoming party conference present a crucial opportunity for the Labour leader, she argued. Jeremy has the opportunity over the summer and at party conference to make it absolutely clear that he is not going to lead a narrow sectarian faction, he's going to lead a broad church that is tolerant, Baroness Armstrong stated.She posed a direct challenge: And the real test for Jeremy is, is he up to it?Baroness Armstrong recalled how Mr Corbyn's own voting record had created tensions, noting he voted against his own government more than 500 times. This pattern had generated discontent among party members in his Islington North constituency.I had a couple of folk from Jeremy's constituency come to see me and say 'People are a bit upset with Jeremy always being against the Labour government, what if we try to de-select him?' she recounted.At the time, she had advised these constituents that party leadership would not support such efforts.Reflecting on Blair's approach, Baroness Armstrong said: The prime minister was very clear about that when Jeremy was a backbench MP. And he was right, we shouldn't have worked to de-select him.She concluded with a pointed message for the current leader: But I hope that Jeremy will now reflect on that and I hope that he will be absolutely determined to make sure it doesn't happen under his watch.

text: Brighton kept the pressure on their Championship automatic promotion rivals with victory at Birmingham, whose hopes of a play-off place all but ended. A debut strike from on-loan Northern Ireland forward Kyle Lafferty put Birmingham in front, though Connor Goldson's glancing header soon restored parity for Brighton.The visitors then seized control when in-form centre-back Lewis Dunk climbed highest from a corner delivery to head Brighton into the lead shortly after the interval.Brighton comfortably managed the remainder of the contest and maintain their position just one point adrift of the automatic promotion places.While Birmingham stay in ninth position, they now trail the play-off spots by 11 points following victories for both Sheffield Wednesday and Derby County.Gary Rowett's Birmingham have managed only two wins from their last 10 fixtures, contrasting sharply with Brighton's impressive eight-match unbeaten streak.Jiri Skalak's precise set-piece deliveries proved decisive for the Seagulls, as both Goldson and Dunk outmuscled their respective markers to convert excellent crosses into goals.The second period saw Birmingham fail to manufacture clear-cut opportunities as Brighton maintained control with relative ease. Substitute James Wilson spurned a golden chance to extend the lead further during the dying moments.Birmingham manager Gary Rowett commented:I've warned the players if they think they can take their foot off the gas then they'll be coming in on Sundays and their days off.I think I'd look a bit stupid if I said we could still get into the play-offs now, the gap's 11 points.I was really pleased with Kyle Lafferty, when I took him off a fan was screaming he was our only chance of a goal, but he hasn't played a lot of football and needs to be fitter.Brighton assistant manager Colin Calderwood reflected:If you really want to go for it you have to chase the three points and get them. Winning tonight helps us but it won't take us up.We weren't aware of Middlesbrough being 2-0 up at half-time, but whether Middlesbrough win or lose, if we win every game we'll have a chance. Well, we won't have a chance, we'll be up.Everyone has experienced highs and lows on the final day and we hope to be involved in some of the action towards the end.
