text: Formula 1 is the most technologically advanced sport on the planet, and the latest radical rule changes have imposed a whole new set of challenges on the teams. **Special Report: The Technology of Business** Hey you, get on to my cloud Domain shift sends cyber world dotty How to cash in with off-the-peg apps Taj Mahal comes to your living room Sochi 2014: Hi-tech Winter GamesAt the Lotus F1 Team headquarters in Enstone, Oxfordshire, preparations for the 2014 racing season are in full swing ahead of the Melbourne, Australia opener on 16 March. The BBC visited to witness how technology serves as a crucial lifeline for a team facing significant challenges.Operating with a budget roughly half that of Formula 1's elite teams, Lotus confronts multiple obstacles that make technological innovation essential for survival. The organization recently weathered the departure of team principal Eric Boullier to McLaren, while new leadership grapples with a £140m financial shortfall from the previous year that prompted star driver Kimi Raikkonen's defection to Ferrari.Matthew Carter, the chief executive brought in by owners Genii Capital to stabilize operations, emphasizes how technological optimization can translate into tens of millions of dollars in annual revenue differences. In F1, where every tenth of a second matters, this impact becomes critical.We are operating on half the budget of some of the big boys, so we have to think of different ways of making that work and being competitive, he says.This reality demands maximizing technology's potential across all business operations.The sport's latest regulatory overhaul has created unprecedented complexity. New rules mandate smaller turbo-charged engines paired with more powerful electric batteries and energy recovery systems, while narrower front wings and lower chassis designs reduce downforce. These changes have generated thousands of new drawings, components, and testing requirements.Nick Chester, chief technical director for Lotus F1 Team, describes the magnitude: They're the biggest rule changes I've seen in 20 years of working in the sport. We had to start developing this car two and a half years ago.To enhance operational efficiency, the team abandoned its fragmented software approach—where different packages handled separate functions—and committed to a £4m, four-year contract with Microsoft's Dynamics enterprise resource planning (ERP) software for organization-wide implementation, Chester explains.The Microsoft partnership, while not exclusive to Lotus, enables software customization to meet specific team requirements and provides access to the technology giant's research and development team in Redmond, Washington, he notes.This ERP system orchestrates the intricate process transforming computer-aided designs, guided by computational fluid dynamics, into wind-tunnel-refined carbon-fibre racing machines that ultimately speed around tracks.It helped us cope with an increase from 12,000 to 14,000 drawings that the new car required, he says. It also enables us to run parallel design programmes and allocate resources accordingly.Throughout a racing season, vehicles typically receive 200 to 250 aerodynamic and mechanical upgrades, generating an additional 6,000 drawings that must be planned, resourced, and delivered to tracks punctually, Chester explains.Laser 3D printing technology has significantly reduced development expenses by converting designs into prototype components with unprecedented speed and cost-effectiveness compared to previous methods.According to IT director Michael Taylor, enhanced technology minimizes time lost on routine administrative tasks through process automation.If you can free up an aerodynamicist's time by just one minute a day, over the course of the year that's a significant amount of time. And if you can extend the design lifecycle, in theory, you create a better design, he says.When component failures occur, teams must pinpoint exact causes and identify weakness origins throughout the entire timeline—from initial material purchase orders through the moment of breakdown.We need a single source of truth, says Mr Taylor.Data management represents a massive aspect of the sport. On-board computers and numerous sensors that communicate wirelessly with teams generate up to 50 gigabytes of information per race, all requiring immediate analysis.While cars race at speeds reaching 200mph in locations like Abu Dhabi, the Enstone-based team monitors real-time data streams remotely through VMware's virtual desktop technology.All commercially sensitive information resides in two concrete bunkers at the Oxfordshire facility. External cloud storage services haven't earned sufficient trust yet, though Taylor anticipates such transitions in the future.Highly confidential files are securely shared with partners like engine provider Renault using EMC's Syncplicity software. It's like a commercial version of Dropbox, he says.IT enables everything inside this business. And the be-all and end-all of our IT strategy is to give us a competitive edge, says Mr Taylor.The sport's governing body, the FIA, has imposed restrictions on in-season testing across tracks, wind tunnels, and simulators to reduce costs and help smaller teams remain viable.While boss Matthew Carter considers these limitations absolutely essential, they place greater emphasis on IT systems to bridge the gap.The lack of testing in F1 means we have to do an awful lot of work back here, making sure there's a real good correlation between the information we get from the simulator and wind-tunnel testing and what happens on the track, so that we can continue punching above our weight, he says.If you stop investing in technology and stand still, others overtake you very rapidly in this sport.

text: A financial scam was committed once every 15 seconds in the first half of the year, prompting a new campaign to highlight the risks. Financial fraud cases surged dramatically in the first half of this year, with over one million incidents involving cards, cheques, phones, or online platforms documented by Financial Fraud Action (FFA), according to new data.The figures represent a staggering 53% increase compared to the same six-month period in the previous year, highlighting the escalating threat posed by modern fraudsters.FFA, which receives funding from banks and payment card companies, is intensifying efforts to educate the public about fraud prevention. While banks frequently reimburse victims for their losses, this protection isn't universal. Additionally, many fraud victims remain silent about their experiences due to embarrassment.The Take Five initiative has emerged as a key weapon in this fight, garnering support from police forces, banking institutions, and consumer advocacy groups. The campaign specifically targets individuals whose hectic lifestyles may leave them vulnerable to sophisticated scams.Katy Worobec, FFA's director, emphasized the campaign's core message: We are asking people to take five - to take that moment - to pause and think before they respond to any financial requests and share any personal or financial details.Home Office Security Minister Ben Wallace highlighted the severe consequences facing fraud victims, noting how criminals employ increasingly cunning and convincing tactics. He explained that fraudsters prey on people who are trying to get on with their lives but in a moment where they are busy or distracted become vulnerable.Wallace also outlined government initiatives, stating: At the same time, the government is working closely with law enforcement and the banking sector through the Joint Fraud Taskforce to take action to stop the organised criminals behind financial fraud.Despite banking industry claims of preventing £7 out of every £10 in potential fraud losses, substantial sums continue flowing to criminals. Financial fraud losses totaled £755 million last year alone - marking a 26% year-on-year increase. Experts believe unreported cases add significantly to these already substantial figures.Contemporary bank robbers have abandoned traditional methods, instead wielding email deception, phone scams, and text-based fraud as their primary tools. This shift is reflected in official crime statistics, which now incorporate fraud data as a standard category.According to the British Crime Survey, fraud and cyber crime now constitute nearly half of all recorded offences, underscoring the magnitude of this growing threat.Police specialists acknowledge that while consumers generally understand the risks of sharing personal information, they remain susceptible to sophisticated manipulation tactics.FFA's research revealed telling patterns about victim vulnerability. The survey found that victims most commonly fell prey to scams because they believed callers were legitimate. Nearly four in ten respondents reported feeling pressured during fraudulent interactions, while a similar proportion admitted their guard dropped during busy periods.Additional research commissioned by a comparison website painted an even starker picture, suggesting that more than four in ten individuals required credit or debit card cancellations following fraud incidents within the past year.Jody Baker, head of money at comparethemarket.com, contextualized these findings within modern spending habits: Most of the transactions we make now are digital and our research suggests that over a quarter of people carry as little as £10 in cash.Baker continued: With so many of us shopping and banking on the internet, combined with a rise in contactless payments, it is more important than ever to be vigilant when managing your money.The Met Police has also contributed to public education efforts through their Little Book of Big Scams, providing additional resources for fraud prevention.

text: Families of football fans who died in the Hillsborough disaster are pursuing High Court misconduct action against the South Yorkshire and West Midlands police forces, lawyers have said. Following a 27-year battle by bereaved families, legal representatives have announced civil action against two police forces over the Hillsborough disaster, citing systematic misconduct and cover-up attempts.Saunders Law Solicitors confirmed that families have filed misfeasance in public office claims against both South Yorkshire Police and West Midlands Police. The legal proceedings, initially launched in 2015, had been suspended awaiting the inquest conclusions delivered this week.Tuesday's jury verdict found that 96 fans were unlawfully killed at the FA Cup semi-final on 15 April 1989, with police failings contributing to the tragedy. The inquests determined that match commander Ch Supt David Duckenfield bore responsibility for manslaughter by gross negligence through breaching his duty of care. Jurors concluded that police errors exacerbated dangerous conditions at the stadium.The civil action targets both the disaster itself and its aftermath, with families seeking accountability through the courts. Misfeasance in public office represents a civil claim alleging that public officials misused or abused their authority.South Yorkshire Police held responsibility for planning and operational management on the disaster day, while West Midlands Police conducted the initial investigation into officer conduct. However, legal representatives assert evidence reveals the systematic cover-up intended to transfer the blame for what happened from South Yorkshire Police to the innocent, by spreading lies, doctoring evidence, pressurising witnesses and suppressing the truth.The evidence indicates abuse on an industrial scale by both forces, transcending any one bad apple explanation, according to the legal team's statement. They argue this demonstrates institutional misfeasance directed against supporters.Current South Yorkshire Police chief constable David Crompton faced suspension Wednesday due to the force's approach during the inquest process. In 2012, Mr Crompton acknowledged grave errors occurred during the Hillsborough disaster and issued a profound apology. Following Tuesday's verdict, he described the match policing as catastrophically wrong and unequivocally accepted the findings.Controversy emerged when retired South Yorkshire police officers received messages encouraging pride in their service despite the inquest conclusions. A website for former force members praised their dedicated and courageous careers, prompting anger from Hillsborough families.The bereaved families continue demanding criminal prosecutions following the hearings. The Crown Prosecution Service stated it would formally consider whether any criminal charges should be brought against any individual or corporate body based upon all the available evidence.Two ongoing investigations into the disaster and subsequent events may conclude by year's end. Operation Resolve, a police inquiry, examines circumstances leading to the fatal crush, while a separate IPCC investigation probes alleged cover-up activities.Both police forces have been approached for comment regarding the civil action.

text: Taking Northern Ireland out of the EU would be an act of profound legal and constitutional, as well as political, significance the High Court has heard. During the third day of judicial review proceedings challenging EU withdrawal, a barrister representing cross-party assembly members opposed to Brexit delivered pointed criticism of the government's approach.The legal team for this cross-party group contends that parliamentary scrutiny should govern the Brexit process, not royal prerogative alone. Their barrister emphasized a critical oversight: Secretary of State James Brokenshire has failed to provide guidance on broader implications, despite his responsibility to champion Northern Ireland's interests.The Northern Ireland Office must take a position on whether Brexit is good or bad for Northern Ireland and make that position known to the British government, he added.Meanwhile, a parallel legal challenge emerges from victims campaigner Raymond McCord, whose son Raymond Jnr was murdered in 1997. McCord's legal representatives argue that the Good Friday Agreement renders Northern Ireland's EU departure unlawful. His barrister went further, suggesting Northern Ireland could effectively veto Brexit for the entire UK.Following Belfast's concluded hearings, McCord declared: I believe that enough has been done for us to stop Brexit and for Northern Ireland not to exit out of Europe.However, legal counsel for both the secretary of state and Northern Ireland Executive mounted comprehensive rebuttals. They maintain the Good Friday Agreement presents no legal obstacle to EU withdrawal. The secretary of state's barrister noted nothing prevents the Northern Ireland Executive from initiating parliamentary debate and conveying positions to Westminster.Wednesday afternoon brought testimony from Attorney General John Larkin, QC for the NI Executive, who dismissed claims that the Good Friday Agreement blocks EU departure. Larkin posed a crucial question: could the Belfast Agreement function if participants weren't EU members?The answer is inevitably yes, he said. We already have that.His evidence included the Isle of Man, Jersey and Guernsey—territories outside both UK and EU membership.After three days of submissions at Belfast High Court, Mr Justice Maguire announced he will give immediate consideration to the case. The court may reconvene depending on similar Brexit challenges scheduled for London next week.Following Belfast's concluded hearings, McCord declared: I believe that enough has been done for us to stop Brexit and for Northern Ireland not to exit out of Europe.

text: Developing post-Brexit trade with the Gulf region will be the focus of a two-day trip to Bahrain by Theresa May. Making history as the first UK prime minister and female politician to participate in the six-nation Gulf Co-operation Council, Mrs May acknowledges the contentious nature of her diplomatic mission. Critics will undoubtedly question Britain's pursuit of stronger relationships with these states, given their problematic human rights track records, she admits.But we don't uphold our values and human rights by turning our back on this issue, she insisted, defending her approach.Tuesday evening will see the prime minister dining alongside leaders from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman, followed by her address to the plenary session Wednesday morning. Key announcements include a space technology partnership with Abu Dhabi and the introduction of a new multiple five-year visa entry system designed to facilitate UK businesses operating in Saudi Arabia.The potential for collaboration extends far beyond these initial agreements, Mrs May emphasized. There is so much we can do together - whether it is helping one another to prevent terrorist attacks, Gulf investment regenerating cities across the UK or British businesses helping Gulf countries to achieve their long-term vision of reform, she explained.So I hope my visit will herald the start of a new chapter in relations between the United Kingdom and the Gulf.Bilateral discussions are expected to cover the volatile situations in Syria and Yemen, alongside the complex relationship with Iran, according to Downing Street officials. These conversations come as Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson revealed Sunday that he has consistently raised concerns with his Saudi Arabian counterpart regarding the kingdom's role in Yemen's civil war, particularly amid accusations of civilian casualties during bombing campaigns targeting Houthi rebels opposing the government.Despite these concerns, Johnson maintained that no threshold has been crossed that would necessitate suspending British arms sales to Saudi Arabia.Mrs May's itinerary includes meeting with young people in Bahrain to assess political and social reform progress since the 2011 widespread unrest that triggered a heavily criticized governmental crackdown in the Gulf nation.Addressing anticipated domestic criticism, she stated: No doubt there will be some people in the UK who say we shouldn't seek stronger trade and security ties with these countries because of their record on human rights.[But] we achieve far more by stepping up, engaging with these countries and working with them to encourage and support their plans for reform, she continued. That is how Britain can be a force for good in the world as well as helping to keep our people safe and create new opportunities for business.Government analysis has identified £30bn worth of high-value opportunities for British enterprises across 15 different sectors throughout the region over the coming five years, officials report.

text: Up to 21 inquests into controversial killings in Northern Ireland are to proceed after a suspension was lifted. A legal challenge brought by bereaved families has formally concluded at Belfast's High Court on Monday, ending their dispute over suspended inquests that were originally commissioned by Attorney General John Larkin.The controversial hearings had been brought to a standstill when senior coroner John Leckey raised doubts about whether his authority extended to conducting the proceedings. This decision sparked fierce criticism from relatives whose loved ones' deaths were scheduled for examination.Following Monday's court ruling, several families expressed complete loss of confidence in Mr Leckey's handling of their cases.The inquests had reached only preliminary stages before being suspended last November, creating widespread uncertainty about the attorney general's jurisdiction to authorize such proceedings. Mr Leckey, who has served as the Stormont Executive's chief legal adviser since his 2010 appointment, had referenced concerns over potential national security implications.Central to the legal dispute was whether these cases should have fallen under the purview of the advocate general for Northern Ireland instead.The coroner's suspension decision triggered intense anger among families seeking answers about their relatives' deaths. Legal representatives for multiple families responded by launching court challenges, arguing that the suspension was both unlawful and procedurally unjust.Among the cases scheduled for scrutiny was the death of Francis Rowntree, an 11-year-old child struck by a rubber bullet fired by a soldier in west Belfast during 1972.The inquests also covered Gerard Slane's case - a 27-year-old father of three who was fatally shot by the Ulster Defence Association at his residence in 1988. His murder generated allegations of collusion between loyalist paramilitaries and security forces.Additional proceedings involved relatives of Gerard Casey, killed by the Ulster Freedom Fighters in Rasharkin, County Antrim in 1989. The suspended inquests also encompassed the deaths of Danny Doherty and William Fleming, both shot dead by the SAS in Londonderry in 1984, and Francis Bradley, killed by the SAS near Castledawson, County Londonderry in 1986.The families' comprehensive judicial review challenge had been scheduled for full hearing next week.Speaking outside the courthouse, solicitor Paul Pierce, who represents Mr Slane's widow Teresa, welcomed developments: We welcome the decision by the coroner to lift the suspension in relation to these inquests.John Teggart, whose father was killed during the 1970s Ballymurphy incident, emphasized the continuing need for accountability, stating that questions need answered.

text: There is a new class of planet out there that astronomers are calling the mega-Earth. A celestial giant with Earth-like rocky composition has astronomers scrambling to create new planetary categories.Scientists at an American Astronomical Society meeting in Boston revealed details about Kepler-10c, a world that weighs 17 times more than Earth yet maintains a solid surface. Located approximately 560 light-years from our solar system, this massive planet has forced researchers to reconsider fundamental theories about planetary formation.The proper way to call it is something bigger than a 'super-Earth, so how about 'mega-Earth, Prof Dimitar Sasselov, of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA), told reporters. He also used the phrase, the Godzilla of Earths!.The discovery challenges long-held scientific assumptions. Previously, theorists believed any planet of such enormous size would inevitably accumulate vast amounts of hydrogen gas, transforming it into a Neptune or Jupiter-like world rather than maintaining rocky characteristics.They confess it is something of a head-scratcher.NASA's Kepler telescope initially identified the planet using its signature method of detecting minute brightness variations as worlds transit their host stars. This technique revealed Kepler-10c's diameter of 29,000km—slightly more than double Earth's width—but mass calculations required additional investigation.Astronomers subsequently employed the Harps-North instrument at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo in the Canary Islands to determine the planet's gravitational influence on its parent star. These measurements, combined with diameter data, confirmed that Kepler-10c possesses incredibly dense material rather than gaseous composition.It's 17 - in fact, it's more than 17 - Earth masses, and that brings the density to 7.5 grams per cubic centimetre, which is a lot more than what we know of rock here on Earth (5.5g/cm3), said Prof Sasselov.The extraordinary density results primarily from compression rather than exotic materials, according to researchers. But remember, this is a very massive planet, which means those same minerals are highly compressed, Prof Sasselov explained.So, what you see in the density is mostly due to compression rather than different composition. The composition comes out as being a combination of rocks and some volatiles, probably 5-15% at most of water.Perhaps most intriguingly, Kepler-10c orbits an ancient star approximately 11 billion years old—formed during the universe's early epochs when successive stellar explosions had limited time to forge the heavy elements essential for rocky planet construction.This timing suggests that solid worlds may have emerged much earlier in cosmic history than previously imagined, potentially expanding the timeframe for life's development throughout the universe.The discovery broadens our comprehension of planetary diversity while providing new insights into the transition points between rocky and gaseous world formation. Additionally, it indicates that ancient stellar systems shouldn't be overlooked in humanity's quest to find extraterrestrial life.It is [on] solid planets that is the place, as far as we know - and we very little about the origins of life - where we think the chemistry is capable of building those molecules that lead to the emergence of life from geochemistry, says Prof Sasselov.Follow Jonathan on Twitter.

text: Terror attacks can be difficult for adults to understand - so how should we talk to children about terrorism? An NSPCC report from last year disclosed that children are experiencing mounting anxiety over global events, with many reaching out to Childline counselors about concerns ranging from the EU referendum and US presidential election to Middle Eastern conflicts.The question emerges: how can parents navigate distressing news discussions with their children while avoiding additional stress?BBC Radio Scotland featured insights from psychologist Emma Kenny and First News editor Nicky Cox on this pressing concern.Children cannot escape troubling news stories even when parents attempt to shelter them at home - playground conversations and social media exposure remain inevitable. According to Cox, well-intentioned parental protection may actually harm children's understanding.If you think as a parent you've done a really good job in shielding your child, you're doing them a disservice because they're going to go into school, they're going to be talking about in the playground, in the lunch hall, and they're going to be getting information second, third and fourth hand, Cox explained.Parents must recognize their limited control over children's information access, she emphasized. They need to be sure that they make sure that children get accurate information and they are empowered to know the truth when they are talking to their friends.Cox, serving as First News editor-in-chief, described her team's careful approach to fact presentation for young readers. Teaching children to distinguish reliable sources from fake news represents a crucial educational priority.We tell the truth, she stated. I think there's absolutely no reason not to tell them the truth because they are going to hear all sorts of misinformation if they're on the internet or they're just talking at school.The abundance of false information online and in casual conversations makes proper source identification essential. There is so much fake news out there, there is so much misinformation out there and it is important that they are educated to recognise where to go to get proper information, Cox added. text: London Underground office staff have voted for industrial action in a row over ticket office closures. Transport Salaried Staffs' Association members delivered a decisive mandate for industrial action, with nearly 68% supporting strikes despite a modest 44% turnout.Since ticket offices shuttered across the network, union representatives report their members have endured unprecedented abuse levels. Research commissioned by the TSSA reveals most personnel feel significantly less secure after transitioning from protected office environments to open station concourses.Tom Edwards, BBC London Transport Correspondent, notes these closures represented one of the underground system's most dramatic transformations in decades.The strategic shift toward automated payment systems—including Oyster cards and contactless technology—aimed to relocate staff from behind protective glass barriers directly onto ticket gate areas. However, unions consistently resisted this restructuring, arguing the redeployment created increased isolation for workers and exacerbated staffing deficits.Tomorrow will likely see the TSSA, representing station personnel, announce its chosen form of industrial action. While strikes remain possible, an overtime prohibition could alternatively be implemented.Members backed other industrial measures by an overwhelming nine-to-one margin.According to union officials, staff increasingly face hostility from passengers when ticket machinery malfunctions.Manuel Cortes, TSSA general secretary, characterized the ballot as members' willingness to take part in a strike to let the world know that the Tube they are using is not fit for safe purpose.Our customer service assistants are overwhelmingly trying to warn the public that the Tube they use is not safe. We no longer have enough staff, he said.London Underground's chief operating officer Steve Griffiths responded: We urge the TSSA leadership to work with us constructively on the issues they have raised rather than threaten to disrupt our customers with strikes.The office closures formed part of former London mayor Boris Johnson's Fit for the Future programme. Current mayor Sadiq Khan has commissioned a comprehensive review of this initiative.Meanwhile, tube drivers plan 24-hour strikes on 6 and 7 December, timing that coincides with Southern Rail guards' walkout.

text: The new Harry Potter play in London has removed the use of live owls from the production. An incident during Tuesday's opening preview performance prompted the removal of live owls from Harry Potter and the Cursed Child after one bird escaped into the Palace Theatre auditorium and refused to return to its handler following a brief flight sequence.By Thursday evening's part two performance, audiences discovered a notice posted at the venue stating no real birds would appear in the production. This marked a swift policy change for the highly anticipated two-part theatrical adaptation.The production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is currently in its preview stage, with the process designed to allow the creative team time to rehearse changes or explore specific scenes further before the play's official opening, producers explained in an official statement.As part of this process earlier this week the decision was made not to feature live owls in any aspect of the production moving forward.The statement emphasized that welfare standards had been maintained throughout: The owls that were associated with the production were expertly cared for by a team of certified trainers and an on-site specialist veterinary surgeon (Steve Smith, MRCVS) who ensured the owls' welfare and enrichment needs were safeguarded at all times. This was of utmost importance to the production.Animal rights organization Peta (People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals) praised the decision. Director Mimi Bekhechi declared: Peta commends the production team for coming to its senses and recognising that treating owls like props goes against every message of respect and kindness that JK Rowling's wonderful books taught us.Bekhechi added: Harry Potter can now join the ranks of innovative stage productions like War Horse, The Lion King and Running Wild which prove that animals need not be exploited for the theatre - and that the possibilities of prop design are limited only by our own creativity.Thursday's performance generated additional excitement when JK Rowling appeared in a stage-right box just before the second act commenced. Her presence triggered audience screams and hundreds of theatregoers straining to glimpse the beloved author.The theatrical production, which won't officially open until 30 July, represents a collaboration between Rowling, writer Jack Thorne and director John Tiffany. Set nineteen years beyond the events of the seventh and final book, the Deathly Hallows, the story follows an adult Harry (Jamie Parker) working at the Ministry of Magic while his youngest son Albus (Sam Clemmett) grapples with the heavy burden of the Potter family legacy.Preview performances for the West End production, scheduled to run through May 2017, launched this week.

text: Liam Neeson and Graham Norton have called for the introduction of same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland ahead of a planned protest in Belfast. Northern Ireland remains the sole region across the UK and Ireland where same-sex marriage continues to face prohibition, a situation that has thrust several prominent figures into advocating for change.Among those lending their support to the campaign are Snow Patrol's Gary Lightbody and The Fall actress Bronagh Waugh, who have joined a growing chorus of celebrity voices calling for marriage equality.The marriage equality debate has emerged as a critical obstacle in the stalled negotiations aimed at restoring Stormont's power-sharing arrangement. Recent media coverage has intensified following the Democratic Unionist Party's partnership agreement with UK Prime Minister Theresa May, struck after her failure to secure a Westminster majority in the general election. With the spotlight on Northern Ireland at the minute, now is our chance to really step up our campaigning a gear and give Northern Ireland what it so clearly wants and deserves, finally - equal marriage, she declared.

text: Chinese internet giant Tencent insists its profits won't take a hit from a decision to limit the time children can play one of its most popular games. Children under 12 now face daily one-hour restrictions when playing Honour of Kings, while those aged 12 to 18 can access the game for just two hours per day.The gaming giant Tencent implemented these time constraints following harsh criticism from the state-run People's Daily, which branded the popular mobile game as poison and demanded stricter online gaming regulations.Known alternatively as Kings of Glory, this fantasy role-playing multiplayer online battle arena game bears striking similarities to League of Legends, another Tencent title that dominates the global PC gaming market. However, Honour of Kings distinguishes itself through its foundation in Chinese historical characters and its mobile-first design philosophy.The mobile platform focus explains much of its success in China, where countless gamers lack home access to gaming consoles or personal computers. Players download the app without charge but purchase character upgrades and costume enhancements to progress through levels. Monthly spending per player ranges from approximately $1.50 to $6, according to various estimates.Though individual expenditures appear modest, the collective revenue proves substantial given the game's massive user base exceeding 50 million monthly active players.Educational professionals and parents express mounting concerns about children developing gaming addictions. While gaming-related anxieties aren't unprecedented, Honour of Kings has attracted exceptional condemnation from People's Daily, which characterized it as a harmful drug damaging teenagers and advocated for enhanced regulatory oversight of online gaming platforms.Tencent's business model fundamentally relies on encouraging existing players to invest more time in their gaming products. The company's most recent annual report explicitly outlines strategies for converting casual players into midcore or hardcore gaming enthusiasts.Gaming revenues dominated Tencent's financial performance in the first quarter, generating $3.9 billion of the company's total $7.2 billion quarterly earnings—representing more than half of all income. Two flagship titles anchor this success: League of Legends maintains global leadership, while Honour of Kings serves as China's top-grossing mobile game.According to Chinese gaming industry database CNG, Honour of Kings produced approximately $810.5 million during the first quarter alone, accounting for roughly 11% of Tencent's total revenue.Beyond gaming, Tencent operates across diverse sectors including payment services, social media platforms, and messaging applications—most notably the extraordinarily successful WeChat. However, the company's overwhelming dependence on the Chinese market creates significant vulnerability to domestic regulatory shifts.This regulatory sensitivity materialized immediately following the time restriction announcement, when Tencent shares plummeted 4%, erasing $12 billion from the company's market capitalization. Stock prices have since recovered partially.Despite short-term volatility, Tencent has experienced remarkable growth exceeding 40% over the past year. Company officials maintain that the new restrictions will minimally impact financial performance, citing the relatively small proportion of under-12 users within their overall customer base.

text: I'm not a tech person. Chad Mureta's perspective challenges typical expectations of tech millionaires—a stance made more surprising given his archetypal status in Silicon Valley's elite circles.Through app development, Mureta amassed his wealth. Downloads exceeding fifty million have made his creations household names: the Emoji app, which expanded users' visual messaging options with entertaining graphics, and Fingerprint Scanner Pro, a mobile security application. Annual revenues between $3m and $5m (£1.9m to £3.3m) flow into his company, App Empire.Yet Mureta diverges sharply from conventional tech entrepreneurs. A near-fatal encounter redirected his entire trajectory.The year 2009 found him returning from a basketball game, his life spiraling downward. Previous ventures—eBay sales, timeshare marketing, nightclub management—had failed. Real estate work left him profoundly dissatisfied, his future unclear and purposeless.A deer suddenly appeared on the motorway ahead. Swerving to avoid collision, Mureta's vehicle struck the central barrier with devastating force. Four complete rolls followed before the car finally stopped.His left arm sustained catastrophic damage. Hospital physicians nearly performed an amputation.Six grueling months of hospitalization awaited, followed by another half-year in rehabilitation. A $100,000 medical debt loomed—American healthcare demands patient payment, and insurance coverage proved inadequate.I was at such a low place, he says. Very depressed, couldn't sleep, tonnes of medication - and actually very suicidal. I was in so much pain I didn't think I could go on any more.Hollywood screenwriters might reject what followed as implausible—yet Mureta maintains its authenticity.His smartphone miraculously survived the wreckage. Brand new that morning, the device emerged relatively intact despite his shredded clothing, retaining 12% battery power.Hospital observations sparked inspiration. Watching doctors casually browse his phone, Mureta envisioned enhanced mobile security features. Strong medications initially scattered his thoughts.Then a friend's magazine article about app development crystallized everything. Individual programmers were revolutionizing technology from basement workshops during those pioneering days.I just had this 'A-ha' moment, where I said, 'holy cow, I'm going to do this', says Mr Mureta. I was sitting there, on all these IV drips, morphine, and I looked around and I finally saw the picture. I entertained a different destiny.I'll never forget that emotion - I can't describe it in words. It was this transparent moment: here's your answer, and you're foolish if you look at anything else.Implementation proved challenging. App development resources remained scarce compared to today's accessibility, and Mureta lacked coding expertise.Recovery time, however, provided invaluable opportunity.I just sat there, looking at all these apps, he says. I was asking: 'Why? Why does the customer like this app?' That gave me the competitive advantage to make this happen.Fortune smiled when a doctor mentioned his Indian cousin's entry into app development. Mureta borrowed $1,800 from his stepfather, navigating language barriers and technical complexities to shape his inaugural product.Fingerprint Security Pro launched two months later.The application offered no genuine security—merely a novelty that simulated fingerprint scanning while denying phone access, featuring a concealed unlock button. Users embraced it enthusiastically. First-month earnings reached $12,000, launching Mureta's empire.Since the accident, the now-34-year-old entrepreneur has established and sold three app companies while developing over fifty applications.App Empire generates revenue by educating others in app development and distribution through personalized instruction and published guides. Success stems from Mureta's strategic focus on his strengths while delegating other responsibilities. His lean, agile operation combines freelance talent with a compact full-time core.Personal involvement remains minimal.I work probably one or two hours a day on App Empire, he says. I just make sure things are running smoothly.This approach explains Mureta's self-assessment as a non-tech person, despite his technological fascination. While unable to personally code applications, he excels at guiding their creation and successful launches.Discussing his traumatic accident comes easily to Mureta, partly because his recovery journey has motivated others facing similar challenges.Though never fully restored, his arm was preserved. I have titanium all the way up from my elbow, he says. It was ground breaking and unbelievable surgery. Because I still have feeling in my arm, I can use it for the most part, and most people wouldn't even know - aside from the crazy, bear-like scar I have on there!.

text: If this secret left-wing plan to take over the Labour Party comes to pass, our electoral existence is in peril. When Tom Watson spoke to me Monday morning, his words carried unmistakable sharpness.The question remains: was Labour's deputy leader genuinely worried about his party's trajectory, or was his primary concern the fate of Unite - the union whose name now seems ironically inappropriate? These two concerns have become impossibly intertwined.Watson once shared a flat with Unite's general secretary Len McCluskey, forging a personal bond that has since crumbled. Their relationship soured last summer when Watson couldn't persuade McCluskey to convince Jeremy Corbyn to set a departure date as party leader, despite eight out of 10 MPs declaring no confidence in him.Personal grievances now fuel political warfare.McCluskey faces re-election at month's end, and Watson's allies recognize a golden opportunity to undermine both the union boss and the current party leadership. Gerard Coyne, the West Midlands organiser challenging McCluskey from the political right, has earned Watson's backing.Watson's support stems partly from Unite's generous funding of Corbyn's two leadership campaigns under McCluskey's stewardship. A leadership change might block future financial support for any left-wing successor.Initially, Coyne pitched his campaign around McCluskey's excessive Westminster focus at members' expense. However, Corbyn's Westminster critics argued this message lacked the punch needed for media attention. They pushed to reframe the contest as a proxy war for Labour's soul.This weekend delivered Watson the perfect ammunition for his shock and awe campaign to jolt party and union members into action.Jon Lansman created Momentum to preserve the energy from Corbyn's first leadership campaign, channeling newcomers who joined Labour to transform both party and country. Yet recordings of his Richmond remarks, obtained by the Observer, revealed his greater interest in changing Labour than changing government. He discussed how an early election would disrupt our plans while emphasizing what we need to do next is a number of things to change the nature of the Labour Party.Watson found even more ammunition in suggestions of strengthening ties between McCluskey and Momentum. Lansman speculated that assuming Len McCluskey wins the general secretaryship...Unite will affiliate to Momentum and will fully participate in Momentum.Watson argues McCluskey prioritizes funding left-wing Labour factions over the party itself. He hopes this revelation will motivate moderate Unite members to vote for leadership change.Acting Unite leader Gail Cartmail denied any Momentum affiliation plans, criticizing Watson for failing to verify his story before publication.Regardless of union funding, what constitutes the hard-left plot Watson believes threatens Labour's survival?Momentum's primary goal involves changing Labour's leadership rules. Currently, leadership candidates need 15% support from MPs and MEPs before the broader, left-leaning membership votes. Corbyn only made the 2015 ballot because right-wing MPs 'lent' support to broaden debate - a mistake they won't repeat.Lansman emphasized reducing this crucial 15% threshold should Corbyn step down. September's Labour conference will almost certainly offer delegates the chance to lower the barrier from 15% to just 5% - making it far easier for left-wing candidates.Lansman stressed we really need to win that vote and we have to work to get delegates to that conference. Meanwhile, internal groups like Labour First and Progress - representing Brownites, Blairites, and former modernisers - collaborate across constituencies to select sympathetic delegates.Like Watson, they believe replacing Corbyn with someone sharing his politics would waste Labour's opportunity to appeal to voters who consider the party too left-wing. Preventing these changes requires securing more anti-Corbyn delegates than leadership supporters at autumn conference.Watson's apocalyptic warnings partly serve as a rallying cry for demoralized moderate members. Conversely, Lansman's candor about Momentum's intentions might encourage newer left-wing members to attend tedious party meetings that nominate conference delegates, rather than simply joining demonstrations.Watson's second concern involves Momentum's alleged plans to remove MPs and councillors deemed hostile or right-wing. Momentum maintains its right to express views while leaving selection decisions to local members. Far from secret plotting, Lansman spoke at a public meeting.McCluskey could still win the union contest while Momentum fails to secure desired leadership changes, potentially perpetuating the armed standoff between Corbyn supporters and opponents - likely to Labour's electoral disadvantage.Leadership sources already warn that Watson's intervention means we are really worried about our local election prospects this spring by highlighting divisions. They were going to be tough enough to begin with but this stuff from Watson put the elections in real jeopardy, they say.Poor results would provide anti-Corbyn forces with fresh evidence of leadership failure. However, leadership supporters are preemptively shifting blame toward the deputy leader.Following Monday afternoon's shadow cabinet away day, Corbyn and Watson issued a joint statement describing robust and constructive discussions. Yet there may have been considerably more robustness than construction in their exchange.

He discussed how an early election would disrupt our plans and said the priority should be a series of actions to change the nature of the Labour Party. The union, which is now the most powerful in the Labour Party, has a general secretary in Len McCluskey, who he believes is more interested in funding left-wing parties than in putting the party first, and who, in his opinion, is a threat to the party. A bad result in the local elections would give the anti-Corbyn forces more evidence of the failure of the leadership, which leadership supporters are already blaming on the deputy leader. text: The daily commute to work is something to be put up with rather than enjoyed, yet how we get there and how long it takes has an impact on how we feel. When Britain's average worker dedicates 54 minutes daily to commuting, the psychological toll becomes inevitable.This substantial portion of working life extracts costs beyond mere financial burden. Office for National Statistics research reveals a troubling pattern: personal wellbeing deteriorates with each additional minute spent traveling to work. Happiness, life satisfaction, and sense of purpose all diminish as commute duration extends.The ONS study, examining over 60,000 employed individuals between 2012 and 2013, identified commutes lasting one to one-and-a-half hours as particularly damaging to wellbeing. Bus journeys exceeding 30 minutes emerged as the most mood-dampening transport option.One commuter's experience illustrates the extreme end of this spectrum: I live in Porthcawl, Wales, and travel a minimum of five days a week to Watford. My alarm goes off at 03:30 each day and my journey takes two-and-a-half to three hours. My day can last as long as 12 hours. I then travel home when there is a lot more traffic than there is in the mornings, with average of three to three-and-a-half hours being the norm for this single journey.Transportation patterns from the 2011 census show 59% of workers drive or receive lifts in cars or vans, while 7.2% use buses or coaches, 5% take trains, and 3.8% rely on underground or tram systems.Theoretically, commuting shouldn't harm psychological health since people voluntarily relocate for better housing, green space, and improved living standards. However, reality proves different.University of Sheffield Professor Jenny Roberts conducted longitudinal research tracking 14,000 individuals over 13 years, contrasting with the ONS's single-survey approach. Her Journal of Health Economics publication revealed gender disparities: women suffered adverse effects from commuting despite generally shorter commutes and working hours, while men remained unaffected even after controlling for income, job satisfaction, and housing quality.The only reason we could come up with was trip-chaining, Prof Roberts explains. Women tend to make more interim stops on their journey, via the nursery or the school or the shops, so they have less flexibility and do more multiple activities. This adds stress to commuting.The wellbeing-commuting connection stems from established stress-mental health links. Unpredictable elements—delayed trains, traffic congestion, adverse weather—create feelings of powerlessness. Research additionally identifies boredom and social isolation as contributors to commuter unhappiness.Nevertheless, some travelers discover benefits in daily journeys, utilizing time for work, reading, or decompression.Paradoxically, 'extreme commuting' of three hours or more often produces greater satisfaction than shorter trips. These marathon journeys typically represent deliberate lifestyle choices by higher-income individuals who can maximize travel time productivity.Cyclists and pedestrians benefit from physical activity's wellbeing advantages, though the ONS notes cycling can prove stressful, particularly when chosen from necessity rather than preference or involving heavy traffic routes.Prof Rogers emphasizes the broader significance: Do people really make that calculation when moving out to a suburban house of how much time, how much income it's going to cost and how it's going to affect their mental health?Since commuting affects everyone, understanding its psychological impact becomes crucial, yet people rarely analyze their transportation choices comprehensively.

text: In a football match, it is not usual to start 3-0 down. As the government prepares for the Autumn Statement at month's end, it finds itself in an economically precarious position.George Osborne, the former Chancellor, had established three fiscal rules designed to demonstrate to a skeptical public the government's commitment to reducing the country's deficit—the gap between public service expenditure and tax revenue—while maintaining strict control over debt accumulation, which represents the total amount the government owes.These three commitments have all either been violated or discarded entirely: the welfare spending ceiling, the commitment to decrease debt relative to national income, and the 2020 pledge to achieve balanced books and eliminate the deficit.Following the referendum outcome, the final target was abandoned amid a series of economic downgrades for Britain's economy. Should these projections materialize, government revenue will decline, making deficit elimination increasingly challenging without implementing additional tax increases and public sector reductions.This fragmented landscape presents current Chancellor Philip Hammond with significant challenges as he prepares for his inaugural major economic presentation—the Autumn Statement scheduled for two weeks hence.The Institute for Fiscal Studies' report released today illuminates the obstacles lying ahead.Given the anticipated economic deceleration, the IFS suggests the chancellor faces a public finance outlook deteriorated by £25bn compared to March's Budget predictions.Assuming no policy modifications—a substantial assumption considering Mr Hammond represents (a) a new chancellor and (b) has already discussed a fiscal reset—the IFS projects tax revenues declining by £31bn.According to the IFS, this shortfall will receive partial compensation through the £6bn the government might recover by terminating EU budget contributions.However, this too constitutes a significant assumption.Numerous government sources indicate that facilitating a smooth transition toward an EU free trade agreement—particularly without freedom of movement arrangements—may require continued budget payments.Brexit's public finance implications aren't entirely negative, naturally.The Bank of England's interest rate reduction to 0.25% decreases government debt servicing costs.Sterling's depreciation, while increasing import prices, simultaneously reduces Britain's trade deficit by enhancing export competitiveness.Additionally, increased dollar earnings and profits from UK-based global companies will benefit government tax collections.Nevertheless, these factors remain relatively marginal compared to the predicted economic slowdown's overall adverse impact.Some observers believe these pessimistic forecasts may prove overly negative—similar to this year's recession predictions that failed to materialize.Should this prove accurate, public finance estimates will require complete revision once again.Such represents the challenging and unpredictable nature of economic forecasting.With the Autumn Statement approaching, the Office for Budget Responsibility—the official economic oversight body—will provide weekly Treasury updates regarding public finance projections.The OBR will likely reduce UK economic growth forecasts, following the Bank of England's lead.Consequently, government revenue projections will be lowered.The government's response options include further spending cuts (politically unpalatable), tax increases (equally unpalatable), or relaxing deficit reduction targets (most probable).Should economic growth indeed decelerate, Mr Hammond's flexibility to recover those abandoned objectives will remain severely constrained.

text: Canada's Denis Shapovalov said he was incredibly ashamed and embarrassed after he was defaulted for hitting the umpire with a ball - handing Great Britain Davis Cup victory in Ottawa. Canada's Davis Cup hopes crumbled in devastating fashion when 17-year-old Denis Shapovalov was defaulted for striking umpire Arnaud Gabas in the eye with a ball hit in frustration.The incident occurred during the decisive fifth rubber against Great Britain, with Shapovalov trailing Kyle Edmund 6-3 6-4 2-1 after dropping serve. In a moment of anger, the Wimbledon junior champion smashed the ball out of court, where it struck the French official directly in the eye.Luckily he was OK but obviously it's unacceptable behaviour from me, said Shapovalov following the automatic default. I just feel awful for letting my team down, for letting my country down, for acting in a way that I would never want to act.The young Canadian's remorse was evident as he continued: I can promise that's the last time I will do anything like that. I'm going to learn from this and try to move past it.What made the incident particularly crushing for Canada was the timing. Vasek Pospisil had just defeated Dan Evans to level the World Group first-round tie at 2-2, setting up what should have been a thrilling decider. Instead, Shapovalov's moment of lost control handed Britain victory and ended his nation's Davis Cup campaign.Following the default, Shapovalov sought out Gabas in the referee's office to apologize personally. The umpire was subsequently taken to Ottawa General Hospital as a precautionary measure due to bruising and swelling around his left eye.The International Tennis Federation acknowledged in their statement that it was clear that Mr Shapovalov did not intend to hit Mr Gabas. However, the consequences remain severe. Referee Brian Earley possesses authority to impose fines up to $12,000 (£9,600), though the ITF may substantially increase penalties and potentially suspend Shapovalov from future Davis Cup participation.GB captain Leon Smith expressed sympathy while emphasizing the gravity of the situation: Unfortunately for the young lad this is going to get an awful lot of attention. This will be looked at closely and it should be as it is dangerous. Whether it's an umpire or a young kid who's at the side of the court, that really could be a serious injury, so I'm sure it will be dealt with swiftly and pretty firmly.Britain's victory sets up an away tie against France from 7-9 April, recreating the 2015 quarter-final matchup in London that Britain won en route to reclaiming the Davis Cup title after 79 years.Former Great Britain Davis Cup captain John Lloyd offered perspective on the incident's implications: We don't know yet how the umpire's eye is but we could see it was already closing. You don't know about permanent damage until he sees the doctor.Lloyd continued his assessment of Shapovalov's situation: It's devastating for Shapovalov. He let himself down, he let his country down. He could have caused serious damage to the umpire. He will realise that he can't do that sort of thing again and he's going to get a lot of trouble in the press for this, quite rightly so because he deserves it, but he will rebound.Despite the severity of the incident, Lloyd identified potential for redemption: If you look to the brighter side we've seen some undoubted talent in him, if he can just control it a little bit. There's nothing wrong with getting emotional - we've seen great champions like John McEnroe get emotional - but you can't go to that extent and he'll have to curb it a little bit.

text: Motorists trying to access a new system for hiring a car have been experiencing problems with the DVLA website. Starting Monday 8 June, significant changes to Britain's driving licence system have sparked widespread confusion and technical difficulties, though Northern Ireland drivers remain unaffected by the new arrangements.The DVLA's digital transformation eliminates paper counterparts entirely, moving all driving endorsements and convictions to an online-only system. While the agency reports that over 20,000 drivers successfully accessed the new platform without problems, numerous complaints emerged about malfunctioning services and overwhelming demand.Technical chaos unfolded across the country as the system launched. Richard Stock from U-drive in Bristol described the morning's frustrations: The DVLA system has fallen over a dozen times this morning. Another operator nearby had a queue of customers out of the door. His company faced queues of 20 customers as staff battled to access driver details online.The DVLA acknowledged exceptionally high demand on its website and confirmed urgent investigations into the technical issues were underway.Under the new rules, motorists seeking car rentals must generate special temporary codes as proof of their driving record. However, these codes expire after just three days, potentially forcing holidaymakers to seek internet access during their travels to obtain fresh verification.Industry criticism has been swift and pointed. The project's being rushed through. It's not brilliant, declared Gerry Keaney, chief executive of the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA). The organization argues that rental companies should have direct access to an online system for checking convictions themselves, rather than relying on customer-generated codes.Public awareness remains alarmingly low. The RAC previously highlighted widespread ignorance of the new requirements, while a recent money.co.uk survey revealed that 73% of drivers were unaware they needed to produce codes when hiring vehicles. The AA has even advised motorists to carry their now-invalid paper counterparts as backup.DVLA chief executive Oliver Morley dismissed complexity concerns, stating: It's very easy to view and share your driving record. Just go to gov.uk and search for 'view driving licence'. He noted that drivers can save their records as PDF files on mobile devices, and the agency has created step-by-step guidance for users.For those who forget their codes, a telephone service operates weekdays from 8am to 7pm and Saturdays from 8am to 2pm. However, many rental transactions don't require conviction evidence, prompting advice for travelers to contact hire companies beforehand to clarify documentation requirements.International complications loom large, as smaller overseas rental firms may remain unaware of Britain's system changes. The DVLA has been developing these modifications for months, yet implementation appears to have caught many stakeholders off-guard.Eight million existing paper licences bearing endorsements will continue operating, though courts will no longer add new penalties to these documents.Government officials defend the overhaul as a cost-saving measure that reduces bureaucracy. Last year alone, the DVLA replaced 445,000 lost paper counterparts, charging motorists £20 each for replacements.The BVRLA has issued its own guidance for drivers navigating the transition, while emphasizing that superior solutions exist. The association maintains that direct industry access to conviction databases would eliminate customer inconvenience entirely.These arrangements apply exclusively to Britain, as Northern Ireland operates under separate licensing schemes unaffected by the digital transition.

text: The number of people playing golf is falling and Rory McIlroy believes speeding the game up at grassroots level could reverse that trend. Sport England data reveals a dramatic decline in young golfers, with participation among 16 to 25-year-olds nearly dropping by half from 2009-10 to 2012-13. This concerning trend has sparked widespread discussion about potential solutions to broaden golf's appeal.The primary barrier remains financial accessibility. Many suggest that golf's expensive nature deters younger players from entering the sport.How about some of the mega millions earned at the top end of golf being used to subsidise struggling clubs and younger players? proposes bigted, highlighting the sport's wealth disparity.The transition from junior to full membership presents another significant hurdle. Peter shares his experience: My son was a junior member at a prestigious London club until he was 18. Once he had been to university and returned home he would have to become a full member which he can't afford. Clubs should do more to provide a bridge from junior membership to full membership.Joining fees compound the problem. AndyL explains: Joining fees are the issue, to join a decent course near me I'd have to find £3,000 on top of membership. If I relocated again in a year's time that's a sunk cost. Not too appealing when trying to save for a house. Meanwhile, those most settled in life, the retiree who can play seven times a week, doesn't have these concerns - clubs will pay the ultimate price for pricing a generation out of the game in 20 years.Dave Harrison emphasizes broader cost concerns: Make it cheaper. Green fees, lessons, gear, balls, all too expensive. Golf clubs and manufacturers at fault.However, Chrisf offers a counterpoint: Most clubs offer payment plans and there has never been so much used golf equipment available as now. There's no need to buy new kit and many would benefit from using a half set in a lightweight bag rather than the mobile homes on wheels that trundle round our courses making such a mess in the winter months.Gary R reinforces the cost argument: Slow play has nothing to do with the falling number of younger players playing golf. The primary reason is COST - to play one round; to be a member; to buy golf clubs et al.Beyond financial barriers, suggestions focus on structural changes to make golf more accessible and enjoyable. Christian Porter advocates comprehensive reform: Clubs need to widen the gap between groups on the time sheet, offer nine, 12, 14 and 18-hole competitions and subsequently offer specific memberships to match the competitions and the members' needs. Also clubs should look at the concept of zone golf, pin positions ranging from easy, to medium and hard. The game needs to be 1. more affordable; 2. less stressful; 3. enjoyable.Cultural changes also feature prominently in proposed solutions. Sam Hatton suggests: To attract young golfers we need to show the fun side of golf and get rid of stupid dress codes to make it more accessible.Time constraints present another obstacle. Ray Bundell reflects: Time stopped me playing golf at 11. Went to tennis. A game of nine holes got me back: Family fun.Several contributors propose pace-of-play improvements. Christian recommends: How about a timer. Players should have a set time to take their shot. This would add urgency and pressure.Electric Kid suggests social elements: Have specific blocked out times for junior fourballs so three or four groups can play together and then speak about the game after.Course design modifications feature in many suggestions. Nozzie advocates: Shorter courses where more sensible club selection and ball accuracy with a difficult layout is the way.Lyle Hill proposes etiquette changes: The player who is deemed first to putt on the green should putt out completely, saving oodles of time - marking the ball, cleaning the ball, lining up the ball etc.Alan presents innovative scheduling ideas: Design or adapt courses to have three six-hole loops. So time-restricted people can play the first six, or the first twelve. text: The makers of the Raspberry Pi computer have created a version of its graphical front end that can run on ordinary desktop computers. The Raspberry Pi Foundation has announced a significant expansion of its Pixel desktop environment, making it available for standard PCs and Apple Mac computers for the first time.This cross-platform release ensures users experience identical software whether working on a Raspberry Pi or conventional machines. The Foundation views this development as crucial to delivering what it calls the best desktop computing experience possible.Eben Upton, co-creator of the Raspberry Pi, explained how this unified approach addresses a common educational challenge. Students frequently begin projects on the credit-card sized Pi devices in classrooms, then must transition to PCs or Macs to continue their work at home.There is no learning curve, and no need to tweak... schoolwork to run on two subtly different operating systems, Upton stated. Both versions employ exactly the same productivity software and programming tools, in exactly the same desktop environment.The cross-platform strategy serves an additional purpose for the organization itself. Upton noted that creating this broader version keeps the Raspberry Pi foundation honest by forcing developers to identify which user interface elements require improvement.Since Pixel's core software relies on relatively dated computer architecture, Upton believes it should function effectively on vintage machines. However, he cautioned that the software remains experimental, potentially containing bugs or minor issues that could cause performance problems on certain systems.Originally launched in September, Pixel represented a complete overhaul of the main graphical interface that Pi owners interact with during operation. The system builds upon Debian, an open source Linux distribution.Two notable omissions exist in the desktop version: Minecraft and Mathematica are unavailable because the Pi organization hasn't secured licensing rights for these applications beyond its own hardware platform.The Raspberry Pi achieved a historic milestone in April of last year, officially becoming Britain's best-selling computer ever manufactured. Sales have now exceeded 10 million units since the device's 2012 debut, establishing it as a widely adopted educational programming tool.

text: Doctor Who's Peter Capaldi has passed on his sonic screwdriver to Jodie Whittaker who becomes the 13th doctor and first woman to take on the role of television's famous Time Lord. The announcement marks a historic moment, as Jodie Whittaker becomes the 13th Doctor and breaks new ground as the first woman to embody the iconic Time Lord. Her Christmas debut will witness Peter Capaldi's regeneration, continuing a legacy that began six decades ago.The Doctor Who lineage commenced in 1963 with William Hartnell, whose portrayal launched the beloved BBC series. Hartnell's previous credits included The Army Game and the inaugural Carry On film, Carry On Sergeant, from 1958. Health complications forced his departure in 1966, leading to the show's first regeneration.Patrick Troughton inherited the role, bringing his memorably disheveled and quirky interpretation to screens from 1966 to 1969. His scruffy demeanor and eccentric personality defined three years of time-traveling adventures.The transition to Jon Pertwee in 1970 introduced audiences to the first color Doctor. Pertwee's raffish portrayal ran until 1974, during which the Time Lord faced exile on Earth while collaborating with Unit - the United Nations Intelligence Taskforce. This era also pioneered the beloved multi-Doctor format.The Three Doctors, broadcast across December 1972 and January 1973, united Pertwee with both Troughton and Hartnell in what became Hartnell's final performance before his death in 1975.Tom Baker's arrival in 1974 established the longest-serving Doctor tenure to date. His distinctive deep voice, wild curls, and impossibly long scarf became synonymous with the character across seven years. Baker's popularity endured, delighting fans with his surprise appearance in 2013's 50th anniversary special.Peter Davison's youthful energy replaced Baker in 1981, marking the Fifth Doctor's three-year journey through the show's 21st series. His era coincided with Doctor Who's 20th anniversary celebration, featuring a special that reunited him with Pertwee and Troughton. Richard Hurndall stepped in to represent the deceased Hartnell, while Baker's absence was cleverly masked using footage from an unbroadcast adventure.A 1983 promotional photo shoot required additional creativity, employing an unconvincing Baker mannequin alongside Hurndall, Davison, Pertwee, and Troughton.Colin Baker (unrelated to Tom) assumed control of the Tardis in 1984 but faced challenges including an 18-month production hiatus that limited his tenure to under three years. Despite the constraints, he shared screen time with Troughton's final return in 1985's The Two Doctors. Troughton's sons, David and Michael, would later contribute their own Doctor Who appearances.Sylvester McCoy's Scottish Doctor emerged in 1987, continuing until the show's cancellation in 1989. BBC One controller Michael Grade's disdain for the increasingly budget-constrained production contributed to its demise, though some argue this period deserves reevaluation.A 1996 revival attempt produced a television film featuring McCoy's regeneration into Paul McGann on American television. The hoped-for series never materialized, making McGann's stint the briefest of all Doctors.Christopher Eccleston spearheaded Doctor Who's triumphant 2005 return as a well-funded, ambitious production. However, the Salford-born actor's single-series commitment disappointed fans, with his departure announced mere days after his debut aired.David Tennant's Christmas Day 2005 debut in The Christmas Invasion launched his popular interpretation. His amiable approach and infectious enthusiasm captivated audiences until his New Year's Day 2010 farewell.Matt Smith continued the youth trend, becoming the youngest Doctor at 27 when he debuted as the 11th incarnation. His four-year tenure encompassed Doctor Who's 50th anniversary, maintaining and strengthening the show's renewed success.The milestone anniversary produced The Day of the Doctor, uniting Smith with Tennant while introducing Sir John Hurt as the previously unknown War Doctor.Peter Capaldi brought extensive Doctor Who universe experience to his 2013 casting. The lifelong fan had previously appeared in a 2008 episode and Torchwood spin-off. His hawkish features introduced fresh intensity and maturity from his August 2014 debut.Capaldi's recent adventure featured David Bradley portraying the original Doctor, with Bradley set to return in this year's Christmas special. Bradley's casting particularly pleased fans following his portrayal of William Hartnell in An Adventure in Space and Time, the 2013 dramatization of the show's origins.Now Whittaker prepares to make history this Christmas, joining this distinguished theatrical lineage that spans from 1963 to the present day.Follow us on Facebook, on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, or on Instagram at bbcnewsents. If you have a story suggestion email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

text: Celtic reached an important milestone by beating Aberdeen in the League Cup final, says manager Brendan Rodgers. Celtic claimed their historic 100th major trophy with a commanding 3-0 victory, marking manager Brendan Rodgers' inaugural silverware at the helm. Goals from Tom Rogic, James Forrest and Moussa Dembele secured the triumph for the Northern Irishman's side.Following the milestone achievement, Rodgers emphasized that his really impressive players must use this success as a foundation for future accomplishments.It's a winning club, that's what the history of this club has been based on, declared the former Liverpool manager. It marks a milestone, the century of trophies and we've got to start off the next century of trophies. That will be important for us and the club.The domestically unbeaten Celtic dominated proceedings throughout most of the encounter. Rogic and Forrest found the net during the opening 45 minutes, establishing a comfortable two-goal cushion before the break.Aberdeen mounted a brief resurgence after halftime, but their hopes were extinguished when Anthony O'Connor's penalty concession allowed Dembele to seal the victory from the spot.It's a great night for the Celtic supporters to celebrate and we push for the next one, Rodgers reflected. It's six months and a week since I came in and we talked about what we wanted to achieve and how we wanted to do it and we're well on our way to that.The manager outlined his broader vision for the club's development. We're trying to improve standards on and off the field. We're shaping up the team to play in a certain style and that's going very well.Despite the celebratory atmosphere, Rodgers maintained his analytical approach. There are things we'll analyse, what can we do better, how can we improve. Ultimately, the goal was to win the cup and thankfully we've won it.Rather than savoring personal glory, Rodgers redirected attention to his squad's collective effort, particularly highlighting Scott Brown's midfield mastery.I've a huge job to do here in terms of building on it and sustaining it, he acknowledged. It's a great achievement. For the players, it's something to show for the great work they've been doing. It's great for the confidence and it sets us up for the rest of the season.Regarding his captain's contribution, Rodgers added: If I'm to say anything on getting my own first trophy as Celtic manager, having Scott as the captain is a huge honour. He really dominated the game and collectively he pulls the team together on the field.Meanwhile, Aberdeen manager Derek McInnes encouraged his disappointed squad to channel their frustration into motivation for potential future cup final appearances this season.McInnes acknowledged that several players failed to reach their peak performance levels, while maintaining that Celtic remain vulnerable in knockout scenarios despite their growing strength.There's a lot of pain and not feeling good about ourselves, McInnes admitted. We were beaten by a better team. The difference is that, when we take them on in a cup final, we need everyone to be at their maximum.The Aberdeen boss stressed the importance of resilience moving forward. It's important we try to pick ourselves up. We're a team that can get to another final this season. This isn't an end-of-season defeat. There's so much more to come this season. We expect more of ourselves and people maybe expect more of us.McInnes concluded with characteristic defiance: It's important that we stick together and recognise there's plenty to play for. I don't mind putting ourselves up there to be shot down. We were huge underdogs, but I still expected us to win and I still thought we would win the game.

text: A team of UK scientists hopes to shed light on the mysteries of bleeding canker, a disease that is threatening the nation's horse chestnut trees. Scientists have decoded the genetic blueprint of a bacterial strain responsible for a devastating infection that threatens Britain's horse chestnut population.Published in the journal PLoS One, the research reveals crucial insights into bleeding canker disease, which had already infected nearly half of England's two million horse chestnuts by 2007, according to survey data showing the pathogen's alarming spread rate.The disease manifests through distinctive bark lesions that weep resin onto tree trunks and branches. When these cankers encircle the entire trunk, they sever the tree's nutrient pathways, ultimately killing the horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum).Researchers analyzed the complete genome of Pseudomonas syringae pathovar aesuli (Pae) using three specimens gathered from various UK locations. These British samples were then compared against the sole other documented case - material collected from an Indian horse chestnut during the 1960s.Co-author Dr David Studholme, now at the University of Exeter but formerly with The Sainsbury Laboratory in Norwich during the study period, made a striking discovery. What we found was that the three British samples were all identical, he explained to BBC News.
