text: Double Olympic champion Alistair Brownlee says he may not return to triathlon for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. While the World Triathlon Series launches Friday in Abu Dhabi, defending champion Alistair Brownlee won't be competing as he transitions toward half-Ironman distances.The 28-year-old Yorkshire athlete secured triathlon gold in Rio 2016, successfully defending his London 2012 Olympic title. However, his Olympic future remains uncertain.There's a chance I could never be at an Olympic Games again but to say I'll never do it is impossible, Brownlee explained. The Olympic Games are just fantastic and I'd definitely love to be there but the course in Tokyo is going to play a big part in terms of whether I feel I can go there and win.His decision timeline is clear: It's going to be a case of sitting down at the end of 2018 and weighing it up - am I enjoying the long distance stuff? Am I still able to be competitive enough to win a medal in Tokyo?This season, Brownlee has confirmed only one World Series appearance - defending his title in Leeds on 11 June. Meanwhile, his brother Jonny, the Rio silver medallist, will launch his campaign at the Gold Coast on 8 April.Brownlee's 2017 strategy involves mixing standard Olympic distances (1.5km swim, 40km bike, 10km run) with half Ironman competitions, known as Ironman 70.3 for their total 70.3-mile distance.The Ironman 70.3 World Championship in September represents an obvious target as he progresses toward full Ironman distance - something that's remained on his bucket list.Ironman has got to be one of those things you always want to do - it's like the London or Boston marathon of triathlon, he noted.Reflecting on Rio 2016, the two-time Olympic champion acknowledged his victory felt incomplete without longtime rival Javier Gomez, who missed the Games after breaking his elbow in a cycling accident.It definitely took a bit away from my gold in Rio that Gomez wasn't there, Brownlee admitted. You want to be there in your best shape and race the best athletes in their best shape - we were fortunate to have that in London and it would have been fantastic to have had that in Rio as well but what happened happened.Despite this regret, confidence remains: But on that day, on that course, I'm fairly confident I'd have had him anyway.With the 33-year-old Gomez recovered from injury, Brownlee anticipates strong World Series competition from the Spaniard and current champion Mario Mola, 27. He believes brother Jonny, 26, could complete the podium and potentially claim the title with a bit of luck and a fair wind behind him.Brownlee admits he might have grown bored with World Series racing after experiencing the same kind of racing against basically the same people for the last 10 years. His new objectives, however, provide fresh motivation and could extend to 10,000m running and marathon competitions.I now have an opportunity to try these other things without hurting my chances if I do decide I want to compete in four years in Tokyo, he said.Post-Rio considerations have been extensive: I thought about a lot of things after Rio. I definitely want to run a marathon and that might be in the not too distant future.While professional cycling presents another possibility, Brownlee remains realistic about his prospects: The other obvious thing is cycling and trying to make a wholehearted jump into being a professional cyclist but although that's possible, I'm very aware that in that arena and in running, I can be good and get to a level where I could be professional, but never to a level where I can win stuff.His competitive drive ultimately shapes these choices: I still feel like I want to be the best at what I'm doing so that's why I'm choosing things I feel like I can win.

text: Donald Trump made a string of promises during his long campaign to be the 45th president of the United States. As Donald Trump's presidency nears the 100-day milestone, a clear pattern emerges: the commander-in-chief has dramatically altered his position on numerous cornerstone campaign promises that once dominated headlines - from his proposed Muslim ban to the ambitious Mexican border wall.**Climate Change and Paris Agreement** During his campaign, Trump dismissed climate change as a Chinese-manufactured hoax and condemned Paris regulations as obstacles to American economic expansion. However, after months of internal White House deliberations at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, the president ultimately chose to withdraw from the agreement. While exiting the Paris deal - endorsed by nearly 200 nations - requires several years, this decision represents an unambiguous fulfillment of his campaign commitment.**Healthcare Reform** Trump's signature rally promise involved dismantling and replacing Obamacare, his predecessor's initiative to provide coverage for approximately 15% of uninsured Americans. Republicans have consistently opposed the Affordable Care Act, labeling it a job killer that burdens businesses with excessive costs and represents government overreach into private sector operations.Yet within 48 hours of his electoral victory, Trump moderated his stance, expressing desire to preserve the law's strongest assets. When House Republicans advanced their replacement plan with full presidential support, it faced fierce opposition from medical professionals, hospitals, and healthcare industry stakeholders. The Congressional Budget Office projected millions would lose insurance coverage, causing public approval to plummet. Despite Democratic opposition and Republican party divisions, the House passed the legislation, though the Senate announced plans for complete revision.**Border Wall Construction** Trump's pledge to construct a US-Mexican border barrier ranked among his most contentious campaign commitments, with his insistence that Mexico would finance the project. Mexico categorically refuses payment responsibility, and even Trump acknowledges America must provide upfront funding before seeking reimbursement through alternative methods.Congressional Republicans are examining financing mechanisms for the wall, though many balk at costs potentially reaching $21.5bn (£17.2bn) according to Department of Homeland Security internal assessments - significantly exceeding Trump's $12bn (£9.6bn) estimate. Additional obstacles include landowner resistance to government land grab tactics and environmental group litigation filed in April.We're building the wall, he declared in February. In fact it's going to start very soon.**Trade Agreements** Trump initially characterized Nafta as a disaster and warned the TPP is going to be worse, so we will stop it. He fulfilled his Trans Pacific Partnership withdrawal pledge within days of taking office. Regarding the North American Free Trade Association, after threatening complete withdrawal, the White House announced US-Canada agreement to commence renegotiation discussions.**Immigration and Travel Restrictions** Trump's original proposal called for a total and complete Muslim entry ban until authorities could figure out what's going on, later shifting to extreme vetting during his candidacy. As president, he implemented two travel bans, both facing legal challenges. The modified second version still prohibited entry from six predominantly Muslim nations, prompting a Hawaii judge to rule it violated constitutional religious discrimination protections. A Maryland judge referenced Trump campaign statements as supporting evidence.Trump has criticized judicial overreach and suggested Supreme Court appeal possibilities, though he remained largely silent on the issue during recent media interviews.**Deportation Policy** Trump initially promised supporters that all 11.3 million undocumented immigrants have to go. As election day approached, his position softened, then post-election he reduced the target to two to three million deportations of people who 'are criminal and have criminal records, gang members, drug dealers.'The Migration Policy Institute estimates 890,000 illegal immigrants possess criminal records, including border crossing violations. Deportation numbers peaked in 2012 and have declined since, with insufficient data to determine increases following Trump's inauguration.**NATO Alliance** Trump repeatedly questioned NATO's relevance, calling it obsolete while criticizing members for inadequately paying their bills. In a July 2016 New York Times interview, he suggested America might not defend members facing Russian invasion.However, during NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg's April White House visit, Trump acknowledged terrorism threats had highlighted the alliance's importance. I said it [Nato] was obsolete, Trump stated. It's no longer obsolete.**ISIS Strategy** In November 2015, Trump vowed to obliterate Islamic State using profanity-laden threats. As president, he authorized deployment of America's largest non-nuclear weapon against an ISIS stronghold in Afghanistan.**China Relations** Trump promised to designate Beijing a currency manipulator immediately upon taking office, previously accusing China of raping America by suppressing the yuan to boost export competitiveness. In April, he told the Wall Street Journal that China hadn't been currency manipulators recently and was actually preventing further yuan devaluation.**Supreme Court Appointments** I am looking for judges and have actually picked 20 of them. They'll respect the Second Amendment and what it stands for and what it represents. Trump successfully appointed conservative justice Neil Gorsuch, requiring Senate procedural rule changes but achieving victory nonetheless.**Torture Policies** Trump initially endorsed waterboarding immediately and promised to make it also much worse, insisting torture works. Post-inauguration, he deferred to opposing views from Defence Secretary James Mattis and CIA director Mike Pompeo. During confirmation hearings, Pompeo stated he would absolutely not reinstate such methods.**Hillary Clinton Investigation** Lock her up became a primary Trump supporter rallying cry, demanding Hillary Clinton's imprisonment over private email server usage during her State Department tenure. Trump supported calls for renewed investigation, telling Clinton during debates: If I win, I am going to instruct my attorney general to get a special prosecutor to look into your situation.His tone shifted immediately after victory, describing his former opponent - previously called such a nasty woman - as someone deserving a debt of gratitude. He later claimed he hadn't given [the prosecution] a lot of thought and had other priorities. On November 22, Trump's spokeswoman announced he wouldn't pursue further investigation to help Clinton heal.**Infrastructure Investment** Trump's victory speech promised the country's infrastructure will become, by the way, second to none, and we will put millions of our people back to work as we rebuild it. While he continues pledging substantial investment in roads, rail, and airports, concrete action remains absent.**Embassy Relocation** Trump campaigned on relocating the US embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem - a divided city claimed by both Israelis and Palestinians. He approved a waiver maintaining the current location while suggesting eventual relocation. The question is not if that move happens, but only when, the White House stated, explaining the decision aimed to maximize the chances of successfully negotiating a deal between Israel and the Palestinians.

text: A Venezuelan teenager taking part in an anti-government protest has been killed in Caracas, the chief prosecutor's office has confirmed. The protests routinely devolve into violent confrontations, with demonstrators hurling petrol bombs and stones while police respond with tear gas.Since April 1, protest-related violence has claimed more than 70 lives, according to official figures from the chief prosecutor's office. However, information ministry data suggests higher casualty numbers, indicating that most victims were participating in anti-government demonstrations.The death toll encompasses not only protesters and security personnel but also civilians caught in crossfire and a group of men electrocuted during bakery looting.Monday's opposition demonstration specifically targeted government proposals to establish a citizens' assembly for drafting a new constitution. Opposition leaders denounce the constituent assembly as President Nicolás Maduro's strategy to consolidate power while circumventing the opposition-controlled National Assembly.Maduro defends the constitutional rewrite as necessary protection for social programs established under his socialist administration and that of predecessor Hugo Chávez.While anti-government forces battled security personnel in Altamira, pro-government supporters staged an anti-imperialist march in support of the constituent assembly downtown. Their demonstration aimed to message Organization of American States (OAS) members convening in Mexico against interfering in Venezuelan internal affairs.OAS foreign ministers again addressed Venezuela's political and economic crisis but failed to reach consensus on a resolution condemning the Venezuelan government. The draft resolution urging President Maduro to abandon constitutional assembly plans secured support from 20 countries, faced opposition from five, and saw eight abstentions.Adoption required twenty-three votes, leaving the measure short of passage.

text: On 2 May 2011, Barack Obama announced that al-Qaeda leader Osama Bin Laden had been killed by US forces in Pakistan. Near Pakistan's capital Islamabad, a deadly shooting at a compound thrust the nation back into international headlines for troubling reasons.Pakistan had grown accustomed to negative coverage spanning both political turmoil and economic struggles. South Asia's perceived basket case economy suffered from dwindling foreign reserves, a weakening currency, and minimal foreign direct investment. Foreign investors would hardly consider it an attractive destination for their capital.Mattias Martinsson thought differently. The soft-spoken Swede launched Pakistan's inaugural foreign equity fund in October 2011, six months after that fateful incident. Initially unable to secure backing, he and his partners invested $1 million of their personal funds. That investment has since grown to $100 million.It was a tough sell at the time, Martinsson chuckles during a phone conversation from Stockholm.His understatement barely captures the challenges. Following Bin Laden's death, enraged investors hurled stones at the exchange as share prices plummeted. Then the US military bombed a Pakistani military base, and Pakistan initiated a blockade of the routes for Nato supplies. The market went down 10%, Martinsson recalls.Despite these setbacks, he maintained his position. By 2012, circumstances began improving when the government introduced a tax amnesty encouraging Pakistani expatriates to repatriate funds. The market went up and we raised $50m in three months, he remembers. This marked the first time in decades that capital inflows exceeded outflows.Nearly ten years later, Martinsson's persistence appears justified.Pakistan's inclusion in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index on June 1, 2017, signals a significant turnaround, attracting increasing investor interest. This index encompasses 23 high-growth economies, including powerhouses like India, China, and Brazil.The KSE 100, Pakistan's primary index, has consistently surpassed the broader index's performance. A $100 investment in the KSE from January of the previous year would be worth $164 today, compared to just $137 in the MSCI—a compelling case for inclusion.Emerging Markets Index membership provides reputational validation regarding a country's growth potential and corporate transparency. Pakistan previously held this status but was relegated to frontier market classification after the exchange's four-month closure in late 2008 following dramatic price drops, trapping foreign investors' capital.Nadeem Naqvi, managing director of the Karachi Stock Exchange, explains from Karachi: We were kicked out in 2008 after the financial crisis because of measures Pakistan took at the time to stop foreign funds from fleeing the country. Obviously foreign investors got a rude shock.Extensive lobbying and reforms facilitated re-inclusion. We did a lot of lobbying and reforms to get re-included again into this index, Naqvi states, assuring investors of the KSE's liquidity. Parliament's 2012 Pakistan Stock Exchanges Act enhanced corporate governance and implemented safeguards against repeating 2008's mistakes.Pakistan's GDP has surged recently, driven largely by middle-class expansion fueled by Chinese investment through Beijing's One Belt One Road initiative. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) involves $46 billion in Chinese spending on Pakistani infrastructure—roads, ports, and highways.It's just starting, Naqvi observes. You'll see the real impact in the next 12 to 24 months. That'll be an added impetus to the growth rate. Chinese investors now control 40% of the Pakistan Stock Exchange.All of this is going to add to the confidence of the middle class to spend more, and add to domestic demand, Naqvi predicts. In five to six years the growth rate should average out to above 6%.However, recent security incidents along CPEC routes raise questions about the project's long-term sustainability.Mark Mobius, executive chairman at Templeton Emerging Markets Group, acknowledges both opportunities and risks. Having invested in Pakistan for 15 years, he remains generally optimistic.It's great for Pakistan's ego... they love the idea that [they] are no longer in the frontier market index, Mobius notes. [But] there's a real problem of government change, tension with India is very critical, he cautions.Even major disruptions—including Osama Bin Laden's killing and former PM Benazir Bhutto's assassination—haven't derailed the KSE's upward trajectory. This year's performance has outpaced other regional indices, establishing it among Asia's top performers.The KSE 100 Index's 20-year chart tells a remarkable story.Martinsson reflects: There is a general impression that the last 20 years have been a disaster in Pakistan. But this is one of the best equity markets in the world. This was always a good investment story. You just have to be brave and take the risk.

text: Five disabled social housing tenants have lost their Court of Appeal bid to have benefit cuts for those deemed to have spare bedrooms ruled unlawful. The Court of Appeal has rejected legal challenges to two of the government's most contentious welfare reforms, including the housing benefit changes critics label the bedroom tax.Lord Dyson, Master of the Rolls, acknowledged these were among the government's most controversial measures but ruled the court could only intervene if policies were manifestly without reasonable foundation - a stringent test he determined was not met.Legal representatives for disabled claimants had contended that regulations across England, Wales and Scotland inadequately addressed the accommodation requirements of people with disabilities. However, the court ruled it could not interfere with the government's controversial housing benefit modifications.The judgment also dismissed claims from two single parents who argued the government's overall benefit cap breached human rights legislation and common law due to its effects on vulnerable families.Ugo Hayter, representing two challengers, expressed bewilderment at the Court of Appeal's decision and indicated plans to pursue the matter at the Supreme Court level.The court recognised that our clients and thousands of disabled people across the UK had a need for accommodation not provided for by the new housing benefit rules, however the court decided that disabled tenants should not have their housing needs met on an equivalent basis to their able-bodied counterparts, just because they are disabled, Hayter stated.Instead disabled tenants are being forced to rely on short-term and discretionary payments.Jayson Carmichael, an appellant from Southport, Merseyside, described feeling devastated by the outcome and vowed to continue the legal battle.I hope we can appeal it in the Supreme Court. It must be the worst High Court decision that's ever been made, I'm very angry about it, Carmichael said.We're going to continue to fight for justice, because we haven't really got a spare bedroom because of my wife's severe disabilities and to say that disabled people are justifiably discriminated against can't be right for Britain in 2014.As a full-time carer for his wife Charlotte, who has spina bifida and cannot share a bedroom with him, Carmichael explained the additional pressures the case has created.We have to fight loads of medical issues; I'm a 24/7 carer and I do overnight care for her and everything, and on top of the fight in this case it's just put me in a state of exhaustion, he said.We have had some help with some discretionary housing payments but we've been promised no more for this year, so we might fall behind with our rent like other disabled tenants now.The couple's cramped two-bedroom housing association flat leaves little space once medical equipment is accommodated, Carmichael noted.We're hoping to stay. We haven't got much room as it is; with medical equipment there's not really a lot of space in a two-bedroom housing association flat.Anne McMurdie, whose legal firm represents three appellants, emphasized that disabled tenants seek equality rather than additional funding.Disabled tenants are not asking for extra funds - they are asking for housing benefit to be paid at a level which meets their needs - for the same right as others. Discretionary payments are not the answer, McMurdie said.Carmichael also criticized the ruling's broader implications: It's ludicrous because human rights laws have been implemented by tribunal judges up and down the country. I think we're just being made an example of because of our high profile in this group case.Disability organizations expressed strong disappointment with the decision. Richard Kramer, deputy chief executive of Sense, a national deaf-blind charity, said the organization was extremely disappointed with the outcome.Although this decision concerns the cases of five individuals, the impact of this policy has been devastating for many disabled people, Kramer stated.Richard Hawkes, chief executive of Scope disability charity, characterized the ruling as a setback for the campaigners and a major blow for the 400,000 disabled people who are feeling the impact of this policy.Kevin Williamson, head of policy at the National Housing Federation, said the court action demonstrated how desperate people had become, adding: Disabled people across the country are being forced to cut back on food and heating to pay the bedroom tax.The legal challenge originally encompassed 10 families, though five cases involving disabled children are no longer active after becoming subject to exemptions from the benefit reduction. Among remaining challengers is wheelchair user Richard Rourke, 46, from Bakestone Moor, Derbyshire, who requires additional space for mobility equipment storage.Under the policy implemented since April last year, tenants with one deemed spare bedroom face 14% housing benefit reductions, while those with two or more spare bedrooms see 25% cuts.The Department for Work and Pensions, defendant in both cases, welcomed the rulings. A spokesman stated: Reform of housing benefit in the social sector is essential to ensure the long-term sustainability of the benefit. But we have ensured extra discretionary housing support is available for vulnerable people.Regarding the benefit cap, the spokesman added: We are pleased that the courts have ruled again that the benefit cap complies with the European Convention on Human Rights. The benefit cap sets a fair limit to what people can expect to get from the welfare system - so that claimants cannot receive more than £500 a week, the average household earnings.Despite the setback, campaigners indicated their determination to continue challenging these policies through higher courts.

Late Tuesday evening in New York, negotiations between Mr Kicillof and hold-out investors collapsed without reaching an accord. These creditors are insisting on complete repayment of $1.3bn (£766m) for their bond holdings.A US judge's ruling mandates that hold-outs receive payment by Wednesday night unless a deal materializes. President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner brands them vultures, alleging they exploit Argentina's financial distress for substantial profits.The situation becomes more precarious because successful hold-out demands could prompt other bondholders - who previously accepted cuts reaching 70% of their original investments - to seek full compensation as well.Street interviews reveal that while most Argentines find the debt crisis's complexities bewildering, two Spanish words resonate universally: fondos buitres - vulture funds.Despite governmental defiance, resignation permeates public sentiment. Argentina has defaulted previously and appears destined to repeat this pattern.Carina Etchegaray, mother to teenagers aged 14 and 16, experienced devastating losses during Argentina's 2001 default. Her family's house-buying dreams evaporated when the government implemented the corralito - literally meaning small enclosure in Spanish - which partially froze bank accounts and restricted withdrawals.When we finally had the money, because of devaluation, we could only buy a car for the same quantity of money we had for a house, she says.Nevertheless, she maintains pragmatism: We live with this shadow of crisis. You have to adapt - in this country, it's the way of life.Entrepreneur Federico Dumas embodies this adaptation, though not as Argentina would prefer. His software company faces constrained investment due to uncertainty.I'm afraid of everything and my customers are not willing to invest, so that will affect my business, he says, expressing hope for reasonable resolution. But if the country goes into default, I'm very afraid of what's going to happen to my business and my employees.Guillermo Nielsen, who spearheaded Argentina's 2005 debt restructuring negotiations, describes current circumstances as unprecedented, regardless of default outcomes.I never imagined this - not in my wildest dreams, he says. People, although they were unsatisfied and they were very tough negotiations, they knew that Argentina was not able to pay, so that's a very big difference. Today, Argentina has the money - back then, we didn't have the money. In my own perception, I think the incoming negotiations are going to be much tougher than the ones we had to go through.Nielsen's primary concern involves potential acceleration clause triggers following default, forcing Argentina to repay bonds within drastically compressed timeframes - a genuinely alarming prospect.However, speculation dominates with mere hours remaining before the deadline. No concrete decisions have emerged, leaving only continued discussions.Negotiation details remain opaque. As locals observe, Argentina's characteristic approach ensures talks will persist until the final moment.Until then, the vultures maintain their circling pattern.

text: William Hague is standing down as an MP after an illustrious 25 year career in the House of Commons. In a reflective BBC interview with Norman Smith, former foreign secretary and Conservative Party leader William Hague acknowledged minimal regrets from his political career, save for the 2001 general election defeat.I'm not one for having a lot of regrets but I do regret that we didn't get things back together again faster in the Conservative Party, he added.Hague joins a substantial exodus from Westminster's green benches following the 7 May general election. text: A County Down couple, who foster five boys including two sets of siblings with a range of complex needs, have been named Northern Ireland's Foster Carers of the Year. After dedicating 15 years to fostering, Glen and Regina Mahon received recognition for their steadfastness, generosity and big-heartedness, leaving the couple stunned by their victory.We were gobsmacked - I couldn't believe it when they said our names. When we heard the other personal stories, we both said so many other carers deserved to win, Regina shared with the BBC, describing their reaction as ecstatic.Their Ballykinler home houses five boys ranging from seven to 17 years old, yet maintains an atmosphere of tranquility. Football boots and kits scattered throughout corners of the kitchen—the home's central hub—tell the story of an active household kept organized through structured routines.The boys all have chores. One brings the bin out in the morning, the other sets the table - we have chores, Regina explained. That's what makes us work.Each child arrived vulnerable and seeking love and support, bringing complex health challenges including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and epilepsy. The youngest lives with a hypoplastic heart condition. Though initially strangers from three separate families, strong bonds formed not only between the children and their foster parents but among the siblings themselves.Speaking from their kitchen following weekend celebrations, Regina reflected on their journey with gratitude. Every one of them is a character. There is no doubt about it, she said. These are children who are traumatised for one reason or another and they are looking for reassurance and compassion and patience, someone to listen to them.While acknowledging the difficulties, she emphasized their commitment: Each one does have complex needs - it is tough. But, you wouldn't be without them.One extraordinary act of dedication distinguished the Mahons from other finalists. During a child's 16-week stay in Birmingham for major heart surgery, Glen took extended leave to remain at the hospital bedside.Why did I do it? How could I not, he said. If it was one of your own you'd be over there with them. I didn't mind at all.Glen described the demanding schedule: I had to be at his bedside 24 hours a day, that was before his op and then he was in intensive care. All in all, 16 weeks. It was harder on him as he took longer to mend.Their motivation stems from a simple philosophy about children's fundamental needs. You do it because these children need love and care. They need a family, said Glen. They arrive and they are cowering at the door. Then they come round and feel part of the natural environment.The emotional rewards are profound: They call you mum and dad. It brings a lump to your throat. It feels good.Across Northern Ireland, more than 2,150 children currently live with over 2,000 foster families. Despite these numbers, the Fostering Network calculates that at least 170 additional foster families are required annually to meet growing demand. Particular shortages exist for carers willing to support teenagers, disabled children, and sibling groups.Kathleen Toner, director of the Fostering Network, emphasized the lasting impact potential carers can make: Foster carers can provide children with a home for as long as they need it. The survey results clearly indicate that children and young people want and need stability.She issued a direct appeal: If you have room in your heart, and in your home, then 2016 could be the year that you start to make a positive difference to a child - a positive difference that can last a lifetime.The past four years have witnessed a 14% surge in young people requiring foster care. Toner attributes this increase to multiple factors: People are more aware of child protection issues. Also, people in Northern Ireland are more aware of the challenges that children in families are facing where there are problems and they are bringing those issues to the attention of social services.The organization actively works to debunk common misconceptions about fostering, including the false belief that single individuals cannot become foster carers. No official upper-age limit exists for potential carers, and previous parenting experience is not mandatory.For the Mahons, receiving the award represents a humbling milestone. However, their greatest joy comes from inspiring the next generation—their son and daughter-in-law have registered as foster carers, continuing the family's tradition of opening their hearts and home to children in need.

According to McIntyre, failing to consider this option would have been remiss given Rangers' precarious position.Craig Whyte, 46, faces accusations of fraudulently acquiring Rangers and denies both charges - one involving fraud and another under the Companies Act related to the purchase.During his second day of testimony from the witness box, McIntyre detailed the mounting financial pressures confronting Rangers in the months before Whyte's May 2011 takeover of the club.Rangers confronted a looming HMRC bill of approximately £50m, known as the Big Tax Case, McIntyre explained. Defence QC Donald Findlay characterized this debt as a nuclear missile aimed directly at Rangers, describing it as like an exocet, nothing could be done to stop it.While Rangers board members maintained hope they could challenge the sum owed - with legal counsel suggesting strong prospects for success - Findlay pressed the witness on whether this tax bill represented a potentially terminal event for the club.When asked about the board's first discussions regarding possible administration for Rangers, McIntyre couldn't pinpoint a specific date but acknowledged the subject would have cropped up during 2010.The court learned of a March 2011 directors' meeting where Rangers officials examined the HMRC debt and its potential consequences for the club. Findlay questioned McIntyre: Rangers could not contemplate paying up that size of debt? McIntyre confirmed this assessment.The jury later heard that Rangers eventually entered administration much later, though this was nothing to do with the Big Tax Case.Testimony revealed that Rangers' former owner Sir David Murray, who acquired the club in 1988, allegedly called Whyte's offer the only show in town. Findlay asked McIntyre: Did it become abundantly clear that Murray would do virtually anything to secure the deal with Mr Whyte?McIntyre disagreed with this characterization, responding: I would not put it like that. I don't think a deal would have been done under any circumstance.The defence advocate countered: A deal was done under any circumstance...Rangers was bought for a pound. McIntyre clarified: With commitments and obligations.Prosecutors allege Whyte deceived Sir David Murray and others by claiming funds were available to complete all necessary payments for acquiring a controlling and majority stake in the club. These required payments encompassed clearing the £18m bank debt, £2.8m for the small tax case liability, a £1.7m health-and-safety liability and £5m for the playing squad.The Crown contends Whyte possessed only £4m from two sources but secured a £24m loan from Ticketus which was held subject to an agreement or agreements being entered into between the club and Ticketus after said acquisition.The second charge under the Companies Act focuses on the £18m transaction between Whyte's Wavetower company and Rangers to eliminate bank debt.The trial continues before eight men and seven women.

text: A 14-year-old boy who stabbed a supply teacher before bragging about the racially-motivated attack on Facebook has been handed an 11-year sentence. A teenage boy received an 11-year extended sentence for the racially motivated stabbing of teacher Vincent Uzomah, 50, at Dixons Kings Academy in Bradford on 11 June.Bradford Crown Court heard clear evidence that the attack was racially motivated. The sentence comprises six years' detention and five years on licence, with the possibility of serving half the custodial term.While admitting causing grievous bodily harm with intent, the boy denied attempted murder. The court learned he racially abused Mr Uzomah before plunging a kitchen knife into his stomach - a weapon he had deliberately brought to school.Prosecutor Jonathan Sharp revealed the boy had pre-planned the assault, discussing it with a friend beforehand. More disturbingly, he later made sick boasts about his actions on Facebook.Six hours passed before his arrest, during which time - just 20 minutes after the stabbing - he posted a status update containing the line I stick a blade straight in his tummy. The post garnered 69 likes, which Judge Durham Hall QC called an appalling reflection of a small microcosm of our society.The attack stemmed from the boy's hostility toward Mr Uzomah during the teacher's seven-week tenure at the school. Mr Sharp told the court: The defendant disliked him, claiming he couldn't teach, and freely referred to him by the epithet beginning with the letter n, including saying it in anger just before he attacked him.A dispute over the teenager's mobile phone triggered the violence. Witnesses described him as getting angry, red in the face, Mr Sharp said. He approached Mr Uzomah and reached into his pocket, but at that point he took out the knife and stabbed Mr Uzomah in the stomach. Mr Uzomah thought he was going to die.Judge Durham Hall QC characterized the boy, who cannot be named due to his age, as out of control and a bully who could not tolerate being told off during sentencing.Despite his ordeal, Mr Uzomah demonstrated remarkable grace outside court: As a Christian, I have forgiven this boy who has inflicted this trauma and pain on to me and my family. It was, however, important for the law to run its course and for a strong message to be sent out, especially to kids of similar tendencies, that violence is never acceptable. Our prayer for him is that he will make use of the opportunities and support that will be provided to him, to become a changed person who will make a positive contribution to society.Det Supt Simon Atkinson from West Yorkshire Police condemned the assault: This was a shocking and very serious attack on a man doing a job he loved, and he was lucky that the consequences were not more serious. His attacker showed no concern by fleeing the scene...he worryingly showed a further lack of remorse towards his victim by boasting about it on social media.Mr Sharp described Mr Uzomah's forgiveness as truly remarkable when speaking outside court. He explained: The victim has suffered serious physical and psychological injuries, has had to put his career plans on hold and is uncertain when, or if, he will feel able to return to teaching - a profession he loved. It was also profoundly distressing to Mr Uzomah - and shocking - that the youth posted a Facebook update boasting of what he had done. This subsequently received 69 'likes' from his circle of acquaintances. In the circumstances it is remarkable that Mr Uzomah has expressed his desire to forgive the attacker, whilst wishing to see justice done as a deterrent to others.Dixons Kings Academy issued a statement on their website: This was a very shocking crime, and today a young man has had to face the consequences of his actions. We are pleased that Mr Uzomah is making a good recovery, and our school community will continue to do what we can to support Vincent and his family.

text: Listening to new music is rewarding for the brain, a study suggests. A groundbreaking study utilizing MRI technology has revealed how the brain's reward system responds to unfamiliar music, with Canadian researchers discovering that specific neural regions activate when individuals encounter songs for the first time.Published in the journal Science, the research demonstrates that stronger neural connections form in the nucleus accumbens—a key reward center—when listeners experience greater enjoyment from new musical pieces.Dr Valorie Salimpoor from Toronto's Rotman Research Institute explained the significance to the BBC's Science in Action programme: We know that the nucleus accumbens is involved with reward. But music is abstract: It's not like you are really hungry and you are about to get a piece of food and you are really excited about it because you are going to eat it - or the same thing applies to sex or money - that's when you would normally see activity in the nucleus accumbens. But what's cool is that you're anticipating and getting excited over something entirely abstract - and that's the next sound that is coming up.The experimental design, conducted at McGill University's Montreal Neurological Institute, involved 19 volunteers who listened to 60 carefully selected musical excerpts tailored to their individual preferences. During the study, participants experienced 30-second tracks while positioned inside MRI machines, simultaneously having access to a simulated online music store where they could purchase songs they enjoyed.Brain scan analysis revealed the nucleus accumbens lighting up during music exposure, with activity levels serving as reliable predictors of purchasing behavior. This neural response allowed researchers to determine participants' musical appreciation before any verbal feedback was provided.As they are listening to this music, we can look at their brain activity and figure out how they are appreciating or enjoying this music before they even tell us anything, Dr Salimpoor noted. And that's part of this new direction that neuroscience is going in - trying to understand what people are thinking, and inferring their thoughts and motivations and eventually their behaviour through their brain activity.The investigation uncovered an additional layer of complexity: the nucleus accumbens communicates with the auditory cortical stores, a brain region responsible for archiving sound information from previously encountered music.According to Dr Salimpoor, this brain area varies significantly between individuals: This part of the brain will be unique for each individual, because we've all heard different music in the past.Future research directions will explore how these neural mechanisms shape musical preferences and whether brain activity patterns can explain individual attractions to specific musical genres.Additional coverage of this research is available through the BBC World Service programme Science in Action, with broadcast schedules accessible online, along with podcast downloads and on-demand listening options.

text: Engineers have produced an alloy that springs back into shape even after it is bent more than 10 million times. Revolutionary memory shape alloys hold tremendous potential across numerous applications, yet current versions suffer from durability limitations that cause premature failure.Scientists have now developed a groundbreaking material composed of nickel, titanium and copper that demolishes existing performance benchmarks. This exceptionally durable alloy demonstrates such remarkable resilience that it opens doors to applications in artificial heart valves, aerospace components, and next-generation solid-state cooling systems.The breakthrough research has been published in Science Magazine.While memory alloys already find use in certain applications, particularly medical procedures, their adoption has remained limited. Medical stents exemplify current usage - these devices can be compressed into compact forms before expanding to their intended configuration to support blood vessel walls.However, these materials have consistently fallen short of their full potential, particularly in demanding high cycle fatigue scenarios where repeated use is essential.Prof Manfred Wuttig, a senior author of the study from the University of Maryland in the US, explained the fundamental limitation: Usually shape memory alloys - like in minimally invasive surgery - they regain their shape once, or a few times, but not multiple times.This is highly unusual. It's kind of a leap forward, he told the BBC.Working alongside researchers at the University of Kiel in Germany, Prof Wuttig's team engineered this revolutionary alloy through precise crystallization control. The arrangement of nickel, titanium and copper atoms enables seamless switching between dual configurations - a process that can repeat indefinitely.This critical phase transition mechanism drives the alloy's ability to return to its original form after deformation. The transformation can be activated through heat application or, in alternative alloy variants, occurs automatically upon tension release.The research team identified that microscopic impurity particles - specifically a titanium-copper compound called Ti2Cu - serve as the crucial element facilitating smooth transitions between states.This particular precipitate is fully compatible with both crystal structures, so it sort of assures that they fully transform from A to B and back again, Prof Wuttig said.Testing involved creating small 1cm-square specimens less than 1mm in thickness, which underwent rigorous evaluation using both thermal and mechanical stress protocols.Achieving the remarkable 10 million cycle milestone demanded considerable time and sophisticated automation, according to Prof Wuttig.With stress it's not so difficult. You can buy [or build] little stress-strain machines... So you can automate that and then it's not so difficult. But it takes in the order of weeks to generate the number of cycles.Temperature cycling presented greater challenges.It's much more difficult with temperature.The team employed specialized furnace systems capable of rapidly heating and cooling samples through 10 million complete thermal cycles.Again, it took a few weeks to conduct the experiment, Prof Wuttig said.Advanced microscopy and X-ray analysis revealed structural changes within the alloy during testing.We did experiments in a synchrotron, where the X-rays would tell us exactly what the crystal structures are, Prof Wuttig explained.Prof Richard James from the University of Minnesota, who contributed to previous memory alloy development achieving 16,000 cycles, described the 10 million cycle achievement as breathtaking in his journal commentary.Prof John Huber, a materials engineer at the University of Oxford, praised the research significance.It's a significant find, he told BBC News.Normal shape memory alloys show quite significant changes in their properties, over quite a small number of cycles. The properties decay away.He emphasized the practical implications: [Ten million] is what you start to need for cyclic applications - it gets you into the high cycle fatigue regime. That opens up potentially quite a lot of applications.According to Prof Huber, potential applications include aircraft wing flaps and control surfaces, spacecraft solar panel deployment mechanisms, and artificial heart valves.Refrigeration technology particularly excites Prof Wuttig and his research team.Your refrigerator has a compressor. It compresses and expands a liquid that goes through phase transition, Prof Wuttig explained. So instead of that liquid, you could use this alloy.The alloy's unprecedented durability makes refrigeration applications viable for the first time.That alloy needs to be stressed and recover millions of times. Refrigerators have to last 20 years, right? That's the expectation.Follow Jonathan on Twitter

text: Former soap-actress Tracy Brabin has been selected as Labour's candidate for the Batley and Spen by-election prompted by the killing of Jo Cox. Following a hustings event on Friday, Tracy Brabin emerged victorious over fellow nominee Jane Thomas to become the Labour Party's candidate for the Batley and Spen constituency.The by-election, scheduled for 20 October, follows the tragic death of Jo Cox, the constituency's former MP. Mrs Cox was fatally shot and stabbed in Birstall, West Yorkshire, on 16 June.A Batley native, Ms Brabin previously collaborated with Mrs Cox on efforts to preserve the town's library. Her television career spans multiple popular British soaps - she portrayed Tricia Armstrong in Coronation Street during the 1990s, later appearing as Roxy Drake in EastEnders and Carole in Emmerdale. Beyond acting, she has contributed as a writer to various productions including Family Affairs, Tracy Beaker and Hollyoaks.Expressing her emotions following the selection, Ms Brabin declared herself humbled and privileged by the opportunity to follow in Mrs Cox's footsteps.Jo was my inspiration. I intend to do her proud, she said. Obviously no-one wanted this, but I'm the only person on the ballot paper that can stand up for everyone in Batley and Spen. I'm hoping people will put party politics to one side and we can work together.In related developments, Brendan Cox, Mrs Cox's widower, recently met with US President Barack Obama at the White House in Washington DC. Accompanied by his two children, Mr Cox shared on Twitter that their conversation centered on Jo and fighting extremism. He commended President Obama for being excellent with the kids, noting that the kids gave him their best drawings.Yorks&Humber Labour celebrated the announcement via Twitter: Many congratulations to @Tracy4MP who has been selected as Labour's candidate for Batley and Spen. She'll be a strong voice for everyone.Ms Thomas, who challenged Ms Brabin for the nomination, previously sought parliamentary office as Labour's candidate in the 2010 general election, finishing second to Conservative opponents in Keighley, West Yorkshire.As a gesture of respect, the Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and UKIP have announced they will not field candidates in the upcoming by-election. However, the ballot will proceed as the English Democrats confirmed their deputy chairman, Therese Hirst, will contest the seat, while Jack Buckby represents Liberty GB.In the 2015 general election, Jo Cox secured Batley and Spen with a majority of 6,057 votes, with the Conservatives placing second and UKIP finishing third.

text: Parents who restrict their children to a vegan diet could face a jail term if a controversial bill is passed by the Italian parliament. A draft bill targeting parents who feed their children vegan diets has emerged in Italy, with proponents arguing such dietary choices deprive minors of essential elements for [children's] healthy and balanced growth.The legislation comes from Elvira Savino of the centre-right Forza Italia party, following several prominent Italian incidents involving malnourished children removed from their families. Over the past 18 months, four separate cases saw children hospitalized in Italy after receiving vegan diets.Medical professionals suspect that in some instances, the guardians of these hospitalized children lacked proper understanding of how to supplement vegan diets safely for young people. The American Dietetic Association and other nutrition experts maintain that vegan diets can work for children, though they emphasize careful attention to ensuring complete nutrient intake—particularly vitamin B12.Vegan diets exclude all animal-derived products entirely.According to Reuters, Ms Savino's proposed legislation will undergo parliamentary committee review before reaching the chamber floor for debate, likely occurring later this year. Simultaneously, three competing bills seek to expand vegan and vegetarian meal availability in Italian cafeterias.In her bill's preamble, Ms Savino acknowledges Italy's growing acceptance of substantial health benefits associated with vegetarian or vegan eating patterns. There is no objection if the person making this choice is an informed adult. The problem arises when children are involved... The vegetarian or vegan diet is, in fact, deficient in zinc, iron, vitamin D, vitamin B12 and omega-3.The proposed legislation seeks to stigmatise the reckless and dangerous eating behaviour imposed by parents who enforce vegan diets to the detriment of minors.Penalties would include up to one year imprisonment, escalating to four years maximum when children develop illness or permanent injury, and six years if death occurs.Critics among nutrition specialists question the bill's scientific foundation, while other observers warn its vague language could potentially criminalize parents beyond the vegan and vegetarian communities—including those with obese children. Many advocates suggest comprehensive public health education would prove more effective than punitive approaches for enhancing children's nutritional outcomes.

text: The plays of William Shakespeare have endured for centuries, and so have many of the names he created for his characters. To commemorate the anniversary of the Bard's passing, we reached out to individuals bearing Shakespearean names - a Hero, a Lysander, a Macbeth, and a William Shakespeare - discovering how these literary monikers have shaped their experiences.**William Shakespeare, London**While my parents never explicitly explained their choice to name me William, I suspect my father influenced their decision. He too was called William, though he was the first in our family line that I know of. Breaking with tradition, I named my children Peter and Susan.Growing up during the War, I don't recall anyone remarking on my name - people had more pressing concerns then. The connection to the other William Shakespeare has always intrigued me. Our family tree research suggests a possible link, though its legitimacy remains uncertain.Though I've studied the playwright's works extensively, my connections to him are limited. During a visit to Stratford upon Avon, I jokingly offered to sign books for tourists at a local bookshop - the owner didn't appreciate the humor.**Shuna Macbeth Blankenhaus, Sweden**Regardless of where my multicultural experiences take me, one constant remains: everyone remembers my Shakespearean middle name. My lecturers and fellow literature students particularly enjoy it, as if I were destined for this academic path.Beginning my bachelor's degree in England, studying English and German literature felt inevitable - I'm now pursuing my master's in Sweden. My collection of Shakespeare works spans various editions in both languages, reflecting my fascination with translation and reissue processes.Shakespeare permeates my studies since his works constantly appear in contemporary post-colonial and world literature discussions. I cherish my name deeply, loving the amusing reactions and the fact that introductions rarely require repetition.The only negative associations involve superstitions about bad luck. My two sisters and I all share the middle name Macbeth, earning us the family nickname three little witches. Friends call me Lady Macbeth when I'm angry or make snobbish remarks about food. Despite being lighthearted, my Shakespearean identity has been a constant companion.**Ariel Ophelia Meadows, New Zealand**Shakespeare clearly captivated my parents. My father favored Ariel, fascinated by the shape-shifting sprite's quest for freedom, while Ophelia honored my great grandmother. My mother, a university theatre major, appreciated the Shakespearean connection.The name serves as an excellent icebreaker. I immediately recognize Shakespeare enthusiasts when they ask, Ariel, as in The Tempest? rather than referencing The Little Mermaid. People delight in discovering my Shakespearean middle name too, and it certainly impressed English teachers and literature professors throughout my education.This early Shakespeare connection sparked lifelong interest in his works. At age five, my parents took me to Shakespeare in the Park in Savannah, Georgia. A Midsummer Night's Dream captivated me so completely that we attended multiple performances. The fairies, mischievous Puck, and humor created magical memories that remain among my fondest from childhood.Later, I performed Ophelia's monologue from Hamlet in high school English class. I still enjoy occasional plays and favorite film adaptations.Reflecting on these characters reveals shared restrictions: Ariel enslaved, Ophelia constrained by nobleman's society. While life overwhelmed the latter - though she remained beloved and revered in death - Ariel's determination ultimately won freedom. Both taught me about strength and kindness.**Lysander Fockaert, Belgium**After watching A Midsummer Night's Dream, my mother declared she wanted to name her next child Lysander. My father agreed without discussion - they both loved it.Occasionally, people meeting me only through written correspondence assume I'm female, mistaking Lysander for Lisanne, a common Belgian name. Fortunately, this confusion is rare.New introductions often require multiple repetitions before people realize they haven't encountered the name before. Though from one of Shakespeare's better-known plays, average Belgians remain unfamiliar with it. However, after explaining its Shakespearean origins, they express admiration and call it wonderful.Such distinctive names make excellent conversation starters, and I believe mine sparked my interest in Shakespeare, literature, and cultural activities generally.**Hero Selwood, Cornwall**My parents drew inspiration from both Much Ado About Nothing's character and the Greek myth of Hero and Leander. My mother adored Shakespeare.Childhood teasing proved unpleasant - classmates would ask, Why aren't you called Heroine since you're a girl? I disliked my name then but appreciate it now.My name invariably sparks conversation during first meetings and sticks in people's memories, which embarrasses me since I'm terrible with names myself.Hero is becoming increasingly popular. During my childhood in the mid-50s, it was extremely rare. Now Myleene Klass has a daughter named Hero, newspaper writers mention naming daughters Hero, my niece bears the name, and my brother's friend's daughter too.My work involves extensive customer email correspondence, and phone conversations often surprise them when they discover I'm a woman - disconcerting yet amusing.**Puck Creemer, Holland**Childhood brought name-related bullying from classmates who found Puck strange - typically a dog's name. I assumed my parents had named me after someone's pet.Learning later about my Shakespearean namesake improved things until I discovered Puck was a mean male goblin from A Midsummer Night's Dream. While I lack particular Shakespeare interest, my parents certainly do.My name has affected life both negatively and positively. Peers bullied me, but older people consistently praised it as wonderful.Despite early dislike, I've grown to love my name. I now appreciate my Shakespeare connection and feel honored bearing this unique yet famous moniker.**Portia Miller, Berkshire**My name attracts considerable attention but frequent mispronunciation. Named after The Merchant of Venice's heroine, most people don't recognize this connection and ask about meaning. They assume I'm named after the car brand initially.Reading my name proves difficult for many, resulting in Pour-tia pronunciations. My parents discovered the name through Ellen DeGeneres, whose wife is actress Portia de Rossi, later finding it classy upon learning more.I know Shakespeare's story and admire Portia's character - she stands firm in her beliefs. I consider it unique.**Lynsey Richards (mother of Arden), Northern Ireland**My husband hails from Stratford upon Avon, and we live in Belfast. We previously lived together in Stratford on Arden Street downtown.Expecting a daughter, we wanted something meaningful yet unique. Our love for Forest of Arden visits and all things Shakespearean made Arden perfect for our little girl.Fortunately, she suited the name upon arrival and still does. Everyone comments on its beauty, and we love how it reminds us of Stratford.*Compiled by Andree Massiah*

text: Children's mental health services are in a state of emergency and must be prioritised, a leading doctor has said. A £1.4bn government pledge to revolutionize mental health services for young people faces scrutiny as medical professionals demand concrete action over promises.This is an emergency. We've talked about it for too long, we haven't done enough to resolve the situation and the longer we leave it, the worse the problem gets, declared Dr Richard Vautrey, a Leeds GP and deputy chair of the British Medical Association (BMA). The government, he insisted, needs to turn rhetoric into reality.Current statistics reveal that one in 50 children under 18 maintain contact with specialist mental health services across England. NHS Digital began tracking under-19s accessing mental health services in January, recording 235,189 cases by June.However, significant regional disparities plague treatment accessibility. BBC analysis uncovered that 40% of areas providing data showed average treatment delays exceeding one month. The Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust recorded the nation's longest average waiting period, with typical patients enduring 18-week delays before beginning treatment.Oxford Health challenges NHS Digital's calculations, asserting their median waiting time measured 34 days in June. NHS Digital maintains that mental healthcare providers bear complete responsibility for data accuracy in their submissions.Bradford patients face nearly two-month treatment delays, according to Catherine Wright from the local trust, who attributes this to surging service demand. Our local target is to see all patients within 11 weeks and we are seeing 100% of all urgent cases within a week. But because we have seen a large increase in referrals, this is having an impact on waiting times, Wright explained.The data collection process itself presents challenges. Only 65% of mental health care providers have submitted quality data since NHS Digital initiated specific tracking for children and young people in January. This incomplete information complicates strategic mental health care planning decisions.NHS England establishes clear treatment timelines: 50% of children and young people diagnosed with psychosis should receive treatment within two weeks of referral. Those with eating disorders require care within four weeks of referral, or one week for urgent cases.The government announced its £1.4bn investment commitment in February. Mental health minister Alistair Burt stated we are investing more than ever before in mental health and will make sure the NHS delivers on this plan.Despite these financial commitments, the limited nature of available data compounds the challenge of addressing children and young people's mental health care needs effectively.

text: A court in Egypt has sentenced one of the country's most prominent pro-democracy activists, Alaa Abdul Fattah, to 15 years in jail for illegal protest and attacking a police officer. The verdict against Mr Abdul Fattah was delivered while he remained barred from entering the courtroom, according to his family. A pivotal figure in the 2011 uprising that toppled Hosni Mubarak, Mr Abdul Fattah received this sentence just three days following Abdul Fattah al-Sisi's inauguration as Egypt's new president.Since the military's removal of former President Mohammed Morsi in July 2013, Egyptian authorities have launched severe crackdowns targeting both Islamist groups and secular opposition figures. This widespread suppression has resulted in hundreds of deaths and thousands of arrests across the country.Following his participation in protests demanding the abolition of legislation that prohibited unauthorized demonstrations, Mr Abdul Fattah was taken into custody in November. His arrest came as part of the broader governmental offensive against dissent.Speaking to the BBC on Wednesday, Mr Abdul Fattah's mother, Laila Soueif, confirmed that court officials denied her son access to hear his verdict. Alaa and his lawyers were outside the court. They were refused entry, she explained.She criticized the judicial proceedings, stating: There was not justification for the judge to issue this verdict in absentia... we expected a court hearing with the prosecution and witnesses speaking. I believe that the judicial system in Egypt has nothing to do whatsoever with law and justice.The family intends to appeal the ruling, Soueif announced.This marks another detention for the activist, who previously faced imprisonment under Mubarak's administration and underwent questioning regarding his involvement in 2013 demonstrations opposing the Muslim Brotherhood.According to BBC correspondent Orla Guerin reporting from Cairo, this severe sentencing intensifies worries about Egypt's commitment to democratic principles and freedom of expression. During a recent BBC interview, Mr Abdul Fattah predicted that authorities planned extended imprisonment for him, describing the current government as more oppressive than Mubarak's regime.President Sisi secured 96.9% of votes in May's presidential election, though voter participation fell short of 50%. The low turnout reflected successful boycott campaigns led by Morsi's Muslim Brotherhood alongside various liberal and secular opposition groups.Sisi's electoral triumph occurred nearly one year after his military coup removed Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president, amid massive public demonstrations against Morsi's governance. Morsi had succeeded Hosni Mubarak, who resigned in 2011 after nearly thirty years of authoritarian rule, succumbing to widespread anti-government protests.

text: Scunthorpe gave their League One play-off prospects a boost with victory over second-placed Bolton. A crucial 11th-minute strike proved decisive as Scunthorpe United secured victory over Bolton Wanderers. Josh Morris delivered a curled free-kick toward the back post, where defender David Mirfin rose to nod the ball home.Despite facing late pressure from the visitors, the Iron thoroughly deserved their triumph. text: A dog which went missing on a mountain, sparking a social media campaign by more than 6,000 people to find him, has been rescued. When Border Collie Jasper disappeared during a routine hike up Scafell Pike in the Lake District with owner Adam Nolan, what followed became an extraordinary community effort that captured hearts across social media.The four-year search mission began after Jasper vanished around 14:00 on Sunday near Cam Spout Crag, situated below Scafell Pike. For Mr Nolan, from Cleator Moor, this wasn't an unusual outing - Jasper regularly accompanied him on fell walks and runs throughout the rugged terrain.Devastated by his companion's disappearance, Mr Nolan launched an appeal on social media platforms. The #FindJasper campaign rapidly gained momentum, spreading far beyond the local area as dog lovers, mountain rescue teams, helicopter crews, and police joined the intensive search operation.By Wednesday, following a potential sighting in Seascale, a determined Mr Nolan declared his unwavering commitment: he wouldn't cease searching until Jasper was home and in front of the fire.The breakthrough came in Thursday's early hours when Wasdale Mountain Rescue successfully located the missing dog. Geoff Horky from the rescue team had climbed Scafell Pike responding to intelligence about a sighting near the summit.I'm over the moon to announce the safe return of my best friend Jasper, Mr Nolan posted on Facebook. This morning Geoff Horky [from the rescue team] ascended Scafell Pike in response to the information received yesterday regarding the sighting of Jasper Near the Scafell Pike summit.Geoff found Jasper at 2.00am in very good condition. The Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team were then alerted and began the rescue operation. Upon hearing the news I followed the Wasdale Mountain Rescue team to Lingmell Col were I was united with Jasper.Naturally, there are numerous individuals who I would like to thank, but at the moment I would say a huge thank you to Geoff and the Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team for their heroic efforts this morning.The remarkable rescue effort inspired significant public generosity. A JustGiving page established by Mr Nolan to support the rescue team had accumulated over £25,000 by 19:00 GMT, demonstrating the widespread impact of Jasper's story.Wasdale Mountain Rescue confirmed their involvement in the successful operation. A spokesman stated: The team are pleased to announce that we have been involved in the successful rescue of Jasper. The team responded and recovered Jasper back to the valley to meet Adam.

text: India's space agency has successfully launched its heaviest rocket. From a launching site in Sriharikota off the Bay of Bengal, the massive 640-tonne rocket thundered into the sky, marking what one website described as a big day for India.This launch represents a pivotal moment for the Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro), significantly reducing its dependence on European vehicles for deploying heavy satellites into orbit. The achievement has sparked euphoric and colorful media coverage across the nation, with websites drawing vivid comparisons - likening the rocket's weight to 200 elephants or five jumbo jets.Such striking analogies underscore the launch's critical significance for India, which is aggressively pursuing a larger slice of the global commercial satellite launch market. Until now, the country has depended on foreign nations to transport heavy satellites into space - an expensive arrangement that has strained Isro's budget.The GSLV Mark III boasts the capability to deliver payloads exceeding three tonnes into high-altitude orbits where spacecraft relay television signals, telephone calls, and broadband connections. However, it falls short of being the world's heaviest rocket - that distinction still belongs to Nasa's Saturn V, operational from 1967 to 1973, which had a total lift-off mass approximately four times greater than India's GSLV Mark III.According to the NDTV website, the rocket matches the weight of five Jumbo jets - a crucial factor since communication satellites are notably heavy. The enhanced capacity provides India with greater flexibility for launching various satellite types.Previously, we could send [satellites weighing] up to two tonnes. This represents a double quantum jump for India, explained Ajay Lele from the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses to the AFP news agency.Dubbed the monster by one newspaper, Isro anticipates this rocket will eventually transport an astronaut to space by 2024. India aspires to join the exclusive club of nations - currently comprising the US, China, and Russia - capable of sending humans into space.According to experts, this successful launch will energize India's indigenous space programme. The achievement builds upon Isro's recent accomplishments, including a Mars mission and the record-breaking launch of over 100 satellites in a single mission earlier this year.In pursuit of entertaining comparisons, BBC research revealed that the rocket's 43-meter (141-foot) height surpasses the Statue of Liberty, which stands at 33.83 meters excluding its pedestal foundation.Cartoons by the BBC's Kirtish Bhat

While you might assume Wimbledon's climactic moments are approaching with finals on the horizon, the tournament is actually just beginning its next chapter.SW19 is preparing to welcome the world's elite wheelchair tennis competitors, and British athletes arrive with championship titles to protect.Here's everything you need to know about this latest Wimbledon competition.**What exactly is wheelchair tennis?**This sport caters to men and women with disabilities below the waist who compete using wheelchairs in both singles and doubles championships.Court dimensions, balls, and rackets remain identical to traditional tennis, though players can allow the ball to bounce twice before returning it, and they use specially designed wheelchairs.Lucy Shuker, Britain's top-ranked player, explains: The wheels are cambered out at about 22 degrees, they have wheels at the front and back so it means, in theory, you shouldn't tip out backwards. I've got straps around my waist and knee guards which lock me in place.According to Geraint Richards, GB Wheelchair Tennis performance director, these athletes literally zoom around the court.Richards notes: Gustavo Fernandez, the reigning Australian Open champion, will actually fall out of his chair and still win that point. The audience will be amazed.**How do the pristine grass courts affect play?**Though it may appear unusual, wheelchairs do navigate Wimbledon's immaculately maintained surfaces.Shuker describes the challenge: It's hard work. The bounces aren't necessarily true and where you think you're going to take a ball at shoulder height it's probably going to bounce a lot lower.She continues: There's a definite drag on grass and you have to continually keep pushing otherwise the chair will stop.However, she notes that drop-shots become particularly effective since opponents often can't reach them in time.**Are British players competitive?**Absolutely. British athletes currently hold Paralympic titles, grand slam victories, world rankings leadership, and Wimbledon championships in both singles and doubles categories.Three key players to watch:**Gordon Reid** At 25, Reid defends both his Wimbledon singles and doubles titles. Rio Paralympics brought him singles gold and doubles silver alongside fellow Brit Alfie Hewitt.Reid made history in 2007 at age 15, becoming Britain's youngest men's Singles National Champion. His first grand slam singles victory came at the 2016 Australian Open, followed by his Wimbledon triumph.Coming from a tennis-oriented family, Reid contracted Transverse Myelitis at age six—a neurological condition causing spinal cord inflammation and nerve fiber damage.**Alfie Hewett** Hewett, 19, began playing in 2005 and dominated as world number one junior from 2013 to 2015.His Paralympic debut at Rio yielded doubles silver with Gordon Reid and singles silver after losing to Reid in an all-British final.**Lucy Shuker** Following a 2001 motorcycle accident that left her paralyzed from the chest down, Shuker discovered wheelchair tennis.She attempted the sport before even leaving the hospital. Previously a badminton player, she represented Great Britain at Beijing, London, and Rio Paralympics, becoming the first Brit to compete in all four major Grand Slams.Shuker recalls: when I first started everyone said I was too disabled but she concentrated on developing supportive chair technology.Partnering with Jordanne Whiley, Shuker secured Great Britain's inaugural women's wheelchair tennis medal at London 2012 in doubles. The duo successfully defended their bronze at Rio.She reflects: My Nana said to me that I'd lost my sparkle after my accident, but that I'd found it again with tennis and it definitely made my body better so dealing everyday with disability is a lot easier.Approaching this year's championship, she feels confident: I feel fit. I've been training hard and trying a style of play that will hopefully give me an advantage.**Does Wimbledon hold special significance?**Every British player responds with an emphatic yes.Shuker explains: As a British player, Wimbledon's the one you grew up watching and everyone all over the world knows about it.She adds: It's the hardest one because it's on grass, but it's an honour to play there. You've got the home support and it has that constant buzz like the Paralympics.The calendar includes other major events: Grand Slams encompass the Australian Open, Wimbledon, Roland Garros, and the US Open, plus the Paralympics and The Uniqlo Wheelchair Tennis Tour featuring 150 tournaments with $2m total prize money.**Is this a new sport?**Not at all—it's existed for four decades, though 2016 marked wheelchair singles' Wimbledon debut.The sport originated in 1976 when former acrobatic skier Brad Parks suffered an injury resulting in paraplegia. During rehabilitation, he met wheelchair athlete Jeff Minnenbraker, and together they explored this sporting possibility.Following demonstration at the 1988 Seoul Paralympics, it achieved full medal status at the 1992 Barcelona Games. London 2012 featured competitors from 31 nations.Wimbledon introduced its first wheelchair men's doubles tournament in 2005, with the singles championship premiering in 2016.**Can anyone participate?**Certainly! Currently, 333 venues nationwide offer training facilities, though contacting your local club, LTA, or Tennis Foundation representative beforehand is recommended.Richards advises: Most clubs are now accessible and a lot will have some chairs so that first experience can be good.He continues: You can play in your day-chair, it's not prohibitive. As you get better at the sport, the chairs get a lot more expensive, but that's where we come in.

He seemed very agitated, Mr Paxman testified, describing his carer as being in a bad temper, a foul mood.
