text: The debate over flying the Confederate flag has reignited in the US, but the American South isn't the only place in the world you'll see the emblem - it's also proudly displayed in the rural Brazilian town of Santa Barbara D'Oeste. In Brazil, an annual gathering brings together descendants of roughly 10,000 Confederates who escaped to South America following the American Civil War. This unique family reunion showcases a fascinating cultural phenomenon that might perplex many Americans.The celebration features quintessentially Southern traditions, according to Asher Levine, a Reuters correspondent based in São Paulo. They all take part in stereotypically southern things like square dances, eating fried chicken and biscuits, and listening to George Strait, Levine explains. And a lot of Confederate flags everywhere, all over the place.Six to seven generations have passed since their ancestors left the antebellum South, yet these Brazilian families maintain remarkable connections to Southern American culture. The Confederate banner remains a prominent symbol at their festivities, though its meaning has evolved significantly from its original context.For these descendants, Levine notes, the flag represents ethnic heritage rather than political ideology. They see themselves as ethnically American to some degree, he observes. At an Italian festival, you would see people waving an Italian flag. Or on Saint Patrick's Day you see people waving the Irish flag. They see it that way. They don't have any political affiliation to it whatsoever.Generations of intermarriage between Southern whites and Brazilians have created a diverse community that would likely astonish American observers. The visual contrast is striking: people of various skin tones, including those with African heritage, proudly display Confederate symbols.A lot of people who are descendants of these confederates have African blood as well, so you'll see at the party people with dark skin waving the Confederate flag, Levine reports.One particularly memorable scene involved an American visitor's amazement at witnessing a young girl performing Amazing Grace - a hymn commonly heard in African American churches throughout the United States - while standing atop a Confederate flag.The symbolism permeates every aspect of the celebration. Children brandish miniature flags while women don Confederate-themed dresses, creating a spectacle that would be unthinkable in the contemporary United States.You know, the symbolism is totally lost on them, but for us it's quite a contrast, Levine reflects.Brazil's perspective on American racial tensions also differs markedly from domestic viewpoints. Despite the country's own complex racial dynamics, Levine suggests that recent events like the Charleston shootings are interpreted primarily through the lens of gun violence rather than racial conflict.When they see an event like what happened in South Carolina last week, they wonder if it's really so much better in the United States, safety-wise, he explains.This story was originally broadcast on PRI's The World. text: Portsmouth made history in staging the The America's Cup World Series, the city council leader has said, despite criticism from some spectators. The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge found themselves among disappointed spectators as Sunday's racing was abandoned due to severe weather conditions, forcing organisers to evacuate public viewing areas.Team Origin Events announced that ticket holders for both the Fanzone Arena and Grandstand would receive full refunds following the cancellation. However, the decision sparked widespread criticism on social media regarding spectator facilities and refund policies.City council leader Donna Jones confirmed that a detailed analysis of the event would be conducted in response to the mounting complaints.Social media platforms, particularly the organisers' Facebook page, became flooded with spectator grievances covering everything from pricing to inadequate toilet facilities and poor catering services. Paul Dornan voiced concerns shared by many, calling the £45 Fanzone entry fee a lot for what you got.The event's impact extended beyond disappointed race fans, with local seafront businesses reporting significant losses. Blue Reef Aquarium manager Lindsay Holloway attributed declining trade to miscommunication and frankly poor management by event organisers.Mark Askey, who operates local boat tours, revealed that his takings were down 70% compared to the same period last year. It was a big deterrent for us and numerous other small businesses, he explained.Team Origin Events defended their arrangements, with a spokesman explaining that the Fanzone area provided direct views of the racing course and enabled access to the free waterfront festival arena and the specific kids area. The spokesman added: We have set out from the start to engage with the existing seafront attractions to ensure that everyone benefited from this event.Further controversy emerged on Friday when holders of tickets to a cancelled South Coast proms concert received refunds plus complimentary entry to Saturday's pop concert. This gesture angered those who had paid up to £48 for Saturday show tickets. Organisers described the free tickets as a gesture of goodwill.Record-breaking yachtsman Sir Robin Knox-Johnston acknowledged the weather-related cancellation as necessary but expressed broader concerns: It was the right decision to cancel racing - but the real tragedy is Portsmouth built up so hard, but it has lost out on this big event.Despite the setbacks, Ms Jones emphasized the historical significance of the occasion: We need to remember this is the first time since 1861 this cup has been back on British soil, so regardless of what happens in the future, we've created history this weekend.

text: The Labour Party has made legal checks to ensure its leadership contest is complying with the law and try to avoid challenges to the result. Under new regulations, the public can register as registered supporters for £3 to participate in voting, though the contest faces persistent concerns about members from rival parties attempting to sway results.Acting leader Harriet Harman's spokeswoman dismissed suggestions of any plans to halt or suspend the election process. The party's focus is on making sure that the 2014 rules are fully complied with, the spokeswoman stated. We have taken legal advice to make sure that the rules are being complied with and that all due diligence as possible was being done. But there were no plans to halt or suspend the contest. We keep a close eye on the process.Labour officials confirmed they barred a Conservative activist who paid £1 to join under the discounted military veterans rate, preventing his participation in the leadership vote. Alan Pearmain, serving as both parish councillor and deputy chairman of the South Ribble Conservative Association, admitted to the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme that his membership represented mischief-making.In a significant endorsement, Scotland's Daily Record threw its support behind left-wing candidate Jeremy Corbyn. This front-page backing came one week after the Daily Mirror, its sister publication, endorsed Andy Burnham.Responding to the endorsement, Mr Corbyn expressed satisfaction: I'm obviously pleased to have the backing of a paper that has such a long tradition of support for the Labour Party. I'm sure that, at least in part, this endorsement will have been made with Labour's future in Scotland in mind, which is important as Labour has a real need to reconnect with communities in Scotland if we are to succeed across the UK.Former Home Secretary David Blunkett, supporting Andy Burnham's candidacy, joined other senior Labour figures voicing concerns about a potential Corbyn victory. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he observed: Jeremy Corbyn has not only been good at opposition against the Tories, he's also been profoundly good at opposition against my party. He added: If you want to continue being in opposition, vote for somebody who is good at opposition.Blunkett emphasized his preference for somebody who can actually address the world of tomorrow rather than taking us back to Old Labour or, for that matter, New Labour in the 90s, because we are addressing an entirely different world.Sarah Brown, former Prime Minister Gordon Brown's wife, endorsed Yvette Cooper for leadership while selecting Andy Burnham as her second preference.Current polling indicates Ms Cooper remains locked in competition with Mr Burnham to become the primary challenger against Mr Corbyn, while Liz Kendall holds fourth position. Last year's special Labour conference overwhelmingly approved the transition from an electoral college system—which balanced MPs, party members, and trade unionists equally—to one member, one vote with £3 public registration options.However, critics including backbench Labour MPs Simon Danczuk and Graham Stringer argue the reformed system remains vulnerable to exploitation.The election results will be revealed at a special conference on September 12.• Everything you need to know about the four candidates hoping to become the next Labour leader.

text: Nearly 15 years ago, successful Nigerian businessman Anselm Okoukoni was one of the desperate African migrants prepared to do anything to get to Europe. Custom dictated that as his widowed farmer mother's eldest son, the burden of caring for his six siblings would fall squarely on his shoulders upon university graduation.Even before completing his statistics degree, he had resolved not to swell the ranks of his country's jobless university graduates. Yet embassy after embassy - Italy, Germany, Spain, Austria, France, Belgium, the UK, and the US - denied him visa applications.Fortune shifted when an acquaintance connected him with someone who claimed to arrange Greek visas for approximately 400,000 naira, then worth about $3,500 (£2,350).My uncle in America had already told me to let him know whenever I got a visa, Mr Okoukoni said.His uncle promptly wired $5,000 - not as a loan but as a gift toward his nephew's future - covering the visa, airfare, and travel expenses.In December 2002, the 24-year-old departed Nigeria for a country where he knew no one, quickly relocating to Italy where friends awaited.Anselm Okoukoni: I felt I was doing something professional. I was paying taxes. text: Planning permission for a controversial peace centre at Northern Ireland's former Maze prison has been granted. A peace-building and conflict resolution centre has received planning approval for the former Maze Prison site, ending years of heated political debate about the controversial location near Lisburn that held paramilitary prisoners throughout the Troubles from 1971 to 2000.The prison became synonymous with conflict when ten men perished during the 1981 republican hunger strikes. Unionist concerns centered on preventing the site from transforming into a republican shrine.Despite protests from some opponents of the new centre, planners reportedly received only one formal objection to the building application. World-renowned architect Daniel Libeskind, famous for his work on New York's Ground Zero redevelopment plan, designed the facility.The standalone structure will be positioned between two retained building complexes that preserve elements of the original prison, including a watch tower, prison hospital, compound and H Block. Additionally, a pair of World War II hangars from the former Long Kesh RAF airfield will remain on the site.Northern Ireland Environment Minister Alex Attwood announced the approval, stating: There is learning to be taken from the conflict here. The centre can contribute to sharing this learning and perhaps to help inform the resolution of conflict in other places.Attwood praised the architectural vision, saying: I believe that good planning needs good design. That is certainly the case in the design of the centre created by Daniel Libeskind, a world leader in architecture and a friend of Northern Ireland.An £18m European Union grant will cover most expenses for the peace-building and conflict resolution centre. The broader redevelopment of the 350-acre former prison site carries a £300m price tag, with a substantial portion allocated to the Royal Ulster Agricultural Society (RUAS).Since the jail's closure in 2000, continuous debate has surrounded the site's future use. Plans for a new national sports stadium were previously rejected following years of disagreement.Political momentum shifted in April when DUP MLA Edwin Poots announced his party had made a corporate decision to support the former Maze Prison site redevelopment. Speaking on BBC NI's The View, the Lagan Valley MLA emphasized that faster redevelopment would be beneficial and assured it would not become a republican shrine.Simultaneously, senior republican ex-prisoner Seanna Walsh advocated for inclusive storytelling at any new peace and reconciliation centre, insisting it must reflect experiences of all parties involved, including loyalists and the British Army.

text: Married couple Dilshad and Barinder Hothi are joint founders of the international training company, the Knowledge Academy, which they aim to turn into the Amazon of the education world. The question of who truly leads when spouses jointly operate a business becomes particularly intriguing with the Hothis, where determining the answer proves remarkably difficult.Their conversations reveal a dynamic partnership - they interrupt one another with shared passion, complete each other's thoughts, and display an infectious enthusiasm that makes their roles seem fluid rather than hierarchical.Barinder's excitement centers on their company's unique position within the saturated professional training marketplace. The future is about blending, she explains. Our online learning courses are traditional, computer-based courses, as you would expect, but we have what we call walk-in clinics. So if someone wants to chat through an issue, they can find a locally-based instructor, pop in, ask questions, get the human interaction.Meanwhile, Dilshad articulates their broader ambitions with characteristic expansiveness. From the company's inception, he explains, they recognized how the internet was revolutionizing consumer behavior across books, groceries, and clothing purchases, leading them to wonder: Why won't it do the same for training?His confidence in their trajectory is unwavering. I knew there was a phenomenal opportunity, he states. In the next 10 years we'll be a global household name, I firmly believe that - a bit like Google or Facebook - we will probably be as big, if not bigger.Such bold predictions might appear presumptuous, yet the Knowledge Academy's meteoric rise over six years supports Dilshad's optimism. The company now ranks among the world's largest training organizations, offering over 5,000 courses across an unprecedented geographical reach. By year's end, they project availability in 3,000 cities spanning 210 countries - from the United States to Australia, from Bhutan to Chile.Their curriculum spans dozens of professional disciplines, encompassing project management, IT, social media, aviation, and animation. High-profile clients including Rolls Royce, HSBC, PwC, and Disney have utilized their services.Despite their global operations, the Hothis' success stems from a distinctive cultural fusion combining Indian heritage with English influences.Barinder's background reflects the immigrant experience: her parents, Punjab natives who settled in Britain, operated a Harrow restaurant despite speaking no English. Neither of them spoke any English, she recalls, explaining how this circumstance drew her and her siblings into early business responsibilities, assisting with banking and customer relations.Education remained paramount in their household, as typical in many Asian immigrant families. I still can hear my mum now saying 'Study, because this is what is going to help you in life,' Barinder remembers.Dilshad's formative years present an inverse cultural experience. I was born and brought up in India itself, he notes. His air force father selected an education designed to replicate British public school traditions. They put me in Lawrence School, Sanawar, he says. It's the Eton equivalent of India.At this Himalayan foothills institution - a former colonial military school - Dilshad embraced British customs, becoming house captain and excelling at cricket while absorbing the competitive atmosphere. I think my school background was very important, being a house captain. We were very competitive and sports-driven. We had a cricket competition and field hockey and athletics and I used to build tactics and think how many medals I'd go after.Their paths converged when Dilshad arrived in the UK at 21, meeting Barinder through family connections. While he gained experience at a UK training company, she worked for Microsoft.The couple's entrepreneurial leap occurred during what many would consider terrible timing - launching in 2009 amid global economic collapse. However, Barinder views this decision positively: It was actually the best decision ever. Any other time would have been more challenging.The economic downturn created unexpected opportunities. Widespread redundancies generated a large pool of job-seekers lacking formal credentials to present to potential employers. There were so few positions that you needed to have more badges on your CV to get a job, Dilshad observes.Professional networking platforms like LinkedIn have since amplified this trend, making qualifications more visible and therefore increasingly crucial.One emerging challenge threatens their partnership: the risk of their business completely consuming their personal relationship. Though they spend barely 10 minutes together during 8am-6pm workdays, evening conversations around the kitchen table and weekend walks inevitably return to business matters.Their nine-year-old daughter has become so familiar with their office environment that she operates the franking machine competently and can name virtually every staff member.Quite often we have to tell each other to turn the iPads off, Barinder admits.They've established a rhythm of intensive work periods followed by luxury getaways - brief escapes to destinations like Dubai. Neither appears to resent the required dedication, though their approaches differ markedly.I'm more conservative, Barinder characterizes herself. Typically British.Asked about operating without Barinder's moderating influence, Dilshad grins: I'd try to do 10 things at once.Returning to the original question of leadership, Dilshad offers this division: Barinder's in charge of the people. I'm probably in charge of the strategy itself.When asked about disagreements, his response is diplomatic: Barinder has been very supportive.But if she's merely supportive, does this confirm his ultimate authority? Barinder's laughter suggests otherwise, though she refuses to concede any ground in this particular negotiation.

text: Great Britain's Bradley Wiggins strengthened his grip on the Tour de France's yellow jersey with a stunning win in the stage nine time trial. Bradley Wiggins delivered a masterful time trial performance, conquering the 41.5km course from Arc et Senans to Besancon in 51 minutes and 24 seconds. The British cyclist outpaced teammate Chris Froome by 35 seconds, securing his maiden Tour de France stage victory at age 32.The triple Olympic champion's triumph marked a historic moment for British cycling, creating an unprecedented one-two finish on the stage podium. Cadel Evans had a poor start and tried to chip away at the deficit but never looked like recovering it.Evans, the defending champion who started the day trailing by merely 10 seconds, now finds himself 1 minute and 53 seconds behind Wiggins in the overall standings. text: Pop stars have always been clothes horses for fashion designers - but more and more of them are turning to designing themselves. This year has witnessed Skepta launching his inaugural fashion collection, while Zayn Malik's Versace Versus line made its debut. These artists have joined an expanding roster of musicians-turned-designers that features established names such as Victoria Beckham, Kanye West and Rihanna.The question remains: how challenging is it for pop stars to achieve design success in an industry where traditionally, aspiring designers needed extensive apprenticeships before their creations reached runways?**Victoria Beckham's Fashion Evolution**Farewell to the artist once called Posh Spice - welcome Victoria Beckham, acclaimed British fashion designer. When the former Spice Girl debuted her fashion line in 2008, skepticism and mockery followed. However, her inaugural collection of merely 10 dresses stunned critics.Nicole Phelps observed in Vogue: The woman formerly known as Posh Spice has launched a dress collection, and, believe it or not, it's one of the hottest things going in New York this week.Mrs Beckham's trajectory has been consistently upward since then.Glamour's fashion director Natalie Hartley explains: With Victoria Beckham, everyone wanted to hate her and put her down and she learnt from the beginning how to do everything from scratch - now, she might not be able to pattern-cut but does that really matter?Beckham is getting respect because right at the beginning, she really put her neck on the line. I remember the early days when she would do her shows in New York, she would talk you through the collections herself and she became very friendly with the editors. It was a very clever move.People felt like they got to know her and she would remember you every season… she was actually very personable and I think that won them over.VB secured multiple prestigious honors, including two British Fashion Awards for best brand in 2011 and 2014. Beyond her signature collections, she partnered with Target, creating accessible clothing in extended sizes for consumers unable to afford designer pricing.She once declared: I want a woman to look and feel like the best version of herself.**Kanye West's Fashion Journey**Among numerous US musicians venturing into fashion - alongside Jay Z and Pharrell - Kanye stands prominent. Kim Kardashian's husband initially explored fashion through a 2009 Nike partnership, producing the Air Yeezys, followed by additional footwear collaborations with luxury brands including Luis Vuitton.Demonstrating serious fashion commitment, West completed a Fendi internship that same year. Original 2009 Air Yeezys currently command $1,349.99 (£1,055) on eBay.The rapper introduced DW Kanye West, his women's label, at 2011 Paris Fashion Week. Reception proved lukewarm among fashion insiders.The Daily Telegraph's Lisa Armstrong dismissed it as a stupendously vacuous enterprise. The New York Times' Suzy Menkes wrote: His collection of sexpot low-bodice dresses and skintight pants, decked out with heaps of ginger fur, did not inspire the fashion crowd to tell him to give up his day job.However, Style.com noted it was a work in progress. Undeterred, Kanye's 2012 second line received considerably better reviews. He subsequently produced five Yeezy clothing seasons plus an Adidas trainer collaboration.Natalie Hartley comments: I am actually a fan of Kanye's Yeezy collections. I love sportswear and think he has done a great job making simple, modern sportswear. He has also grafted to learn the ropes, he is passionate about fashion, and who can knock that?**Gwen Stefani's Design Empire**The No Doubt frontwoman entered fashion with L.A.M.B's 2004 launch - an acronym referencing her solo debut Love.Angel.Music.Baby. Regular New York Fashion Week presentations have garnered predominantly positive responses.L.A.M.B's Facebook description reads: a playful juxtaposition between classic Hollywood movie star glamour and more modern and casual street influences. L.A.M.B. is always a mixture of vintage inspiration mashed up with modern and futuristic elements.Commercial success has been substantial, generating millions annually and enabling expansion into Harajuku Lovers (Japanese street style-inspired) and Design With Purpose (her eco-friendly collaboration with Seven for all Mankind founder Michael Glasser).While Natalie Hartley admits being personally not hugely in to [Gwen's] style, she acknowledges Stefani's authentic approach: her fan base are up for dressing just like her.Stefani previously stepped back from New York Fashion Week, explaining: the only reason I haven't [been] lately is because it falls when my kids go back to school and I was like, 'Oh, I guess I will go to NYFW and miss my kid's first day of kindergarten.' No.Fashion enthusiasts can rejoice - Gwen has returned to runway presentations.**Rihanna's Authentic Approach**RiRi has become a designer's muse, appearing in Stella McCartney, Chanel, Prada and Giambattista Valli creations. Yet she transcends being merely a fashion model - she's designed across multiple brands for years.Her portfolio encompasses underwear, denim and T-shirts for Armani Jeans and Emporio Armani Underwear, plus River Island high street collections.Natalie emphasizes Rihanna's genuine fashion credentials: Rihanna does stuff that's true to her. She wouldn't put anything together she would never wear herself.Her 2014 appointment as Puma creative director, overseeing womenswear direction, marked a career milestone. Subsequent Puma trainer successes include creeper-style shoes and furry sliders.Recent partnerships feature an all-denim Manolo Blahnik collection (including thigh-high boots) and Dior sunglasses. Beyond clothing and footwear, RiRi markets multiple fragrances - Kiss and Crush included - plus Chopard jewelry.**Tinie Tempah's Sustainable Vision**The south London rapper began fashion exploration shortly after his 2010 debut single Pass Out reached number one. His Disturbing London label reflects his aesthetic - street style merged with high fashion.Consistently recognized among Britain's best-dressed men, Tinie introduced What We Wear this year.Natalie observes: Tinie Tempah's whole stance is sustainability and recycling materials. text: The UK is to spend £25m on building a prison in Jamaica so that foreign criminals in the UK can be sent home to serve sentences in the Caribbean. During his arrival in Jamaica, Prime Minister David Cameron unveiled a groundbreaking agreement designed to resolve longstanding negotiations regarding prisoner transfers between the nations.The announcement comes as more than 600 Jamaican nationals remain incarcerated in British facilities, unable to face deportation due to inadequate prison conditions in their home country. This foreign aid-financed initiative is projected to deliver annual savings of £10 million to taxpayers once transfers commence in 2020, according to government officials.Under the Jamaica prison scheme, over 300 current inmates are anticipated to be repatriated. The program targets individuals sentenced to minimum four-year terms with at least 18 months remaining in custody. Previously, such transfers proved impossible due to concerns that substandard Jamaican jail conditions would enable successful human rights law challenges.Jamaica ranks third among foreign nations whose citizens serve prison sentences in the UK. Nearly 70% of imprisoned Jamaicans face convictions for violence and drug-related crimes.Britain will fund approximately 40% of construction costs for the proposed 1,500-capacity facility. Cameron, fresh from United Nations discussions in New York regarding the Islamic State conflict, emphasized the deal's significance.It is absolutely right that foreign criminals who break our laws are properly punished but this shouldn't be at the expense of the hard-working British taxpayer, he said. That's why this agreement is so important. It will mean Jamaican criminals are sent back home to serve their sentences, saving the British guard of honourtaxpayer millions of pounds but still ensuring justice is done. And it will help Jamaica by helping to provide a new prison, strengthening their criminal justice system.The Prime Minister, making the first British leader's visit to the island in 14 years, will additionally announce £300 million in aid funding for Caribbean infrastructure projects encompassing roads, bridges and ports.Cameron described the regional infrastructure fund, delivered through Caribbean Development Bank collaboration, as crucial for supporting Caribbean economic growth.Upon arriving at Kingston Airport, Cameron received an honour guard welcome with national anthems before visiting RFA Lyme Bay, the British vessel currently conducting anti-drug smuggling and emergency relief operations throughout the Caribbean.His itinerary concludes with discussions alongside Jamaican Prime Minister Portia Simpson-Miller and a formal reception.BBC political correspondent Carole Walker notes that the PM has expressed intentions to revitalize what he considers a neglected UK-Jamaica relationship.

text: Australian politician Bob Katter has defended a video that depicts him killing his electoral rivals. A 71-year-old independent politician from north Queensland has sparked controversy with a satirical campaign advertisement featuring toy gun violence, drawing sharp criticism from Australia's Prime Minister and fellow politicians.The contentious video shows Mr Katter, who heads Katter's Australia Party and represents the Kennedy electorate, blowing smoke from a toy gun after apparently shooting two faceless men representing the major political parties, whose bodies lie motionless in the dirt.Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull demanded Mr Katter withdraw the advertisements, condemning them as being in the worst of taste. However, the veteran politician defended his campaign material, describing the ads as brilliant and screamingly funny.Created in collaboration with satirical website Betoota Advocate, the advertisement opens with Labor Party and Liberal-National coalition members installing a sign reading Australia for sale. Mr Katter throws the sign down, and when it's replaced, he uses a black marker to change it to Australia not for sale before the scene transitions to the gunplay sequence.I think most people will enjoy the humour. I thought it was very funny, I must admit, Mr Katter told the ABC. What's not funny is the selling off of this country. We hate it and we're tenaciously opposed to it.The timing of the advertisement's release drew particular scrutiny, coming shortly after a gunman killed 49 people at Orlando's Pulse nightclub in Florida. During an appearance on the Sunrise breakfast television program, presenter David Koch challenged Mr Katter about this timing.Mr Katter claimed he was unaware of the Orlando shooting and argued that similar advertisements had not generated controversy previously.Political reactions were swift and critical. Queensland Senator Barry O'Sullivan labeled the ad abhorrent, while Finance Minister Mathias Cormann called it unfortunate.The controversy raises questions about Australia's political discourse and humor boundaries. If this represents the peak of political scandal during the campaign, it suggests Australia may be experiencing one of the world's most mundane election cycles.Mr Katter's advertisement reflects Australia's larrikin humor tradition - politically incorrect, jarring, and perhaps not as amusing as intended. Yet whether it truly qualifies as abhorrent or represents the worst of taste remains debatable, particularly regarding its release following the Orlando tragedy.Regional Australian audiences, geographically and culturally distant from Florida, may well appreciate Mr Katter's irreverent humor style. While humor can be crude or poorly timed, and sometimes misses its mark entirely, voters retain the ultimate judgment through the ballot box on July 2.Betoota Advocate editor Clancy Overell, who portrayed one of the shot characters, acknowledged the video might wind people up but questioned whether Mr Katter fully grasped this potential. Defending the timing, Mr Overell told the BBC that American shootings occur daily, arguing that Australians can't be prevented from making jokes and about cowboys and western-style gunplay.This isn't Mr Katter's first venture into unconventional campaign advertising. A 2012 Queensland state election video featured him line dancing with young people and apparently spinning on his head, though a body double likely performed the acrobatic stunt.

text: Oldham Athletic are hoping to complete the signing of convicted rapist Ched Evans on Thursday. A controversial signing appears imminent as Oldham Athletic moves closer to finalizing a deal with 26-year-old Welsh striker Ched Evans, despite fierce opposition that has generated a petition with 60,000 signatures.The agreement with Evans has been reached in principle, though remaining legal complications could potentially delay completion of the transfer. A board member revealed to the BBC that the club was minded to sign Evans, crediting the Professional Footballers' Association as instrumental in facilitating the move.Club owner Simon Corney stated Wednesday that the League One side, currently sitting 14th in the table, had an 80% probability of securing the striker's signature.Evans, formerly of Manchester City and Sheffield United, received a five-year prison sentence in April 2012 for rape and was released in October after completing half his term.The proposed signing has sparked intense debate among football commentators and former players speaking on BBC Radio 5 live.Guardian sports writer David Conn expressed strong reservations about Evans' readiness for a return: There's been no decency shown to her after the event. You can still say 'I maintain my innocence of the crime, while apologising for what I did which I don't dispute,' and show some decency and empathy for this woman.Conn continued: When I saw that Evans' supporters' website, and understood the way the victim has continued to be treated, that was a tipping point for me to make me feel that he has not done enough to show himself as someone who should have that second chance. I don't think he's ready yet.Former England international Danny Mills offered insight into the unique dynamics of professional football environments: The dressing room is unlike any other place on the planet. Rightly, or wrongly, morally right or morally wrong, the dressing room is a sanctum of protection. Things will be said. There might be press cuttings quite possibly put on his locker, or where he gets changed.Mills also highlighted football's pragmatic nature: Trouble is with football, it becomes very, very selfish at times and if Ched Evans goes into that dressing room and starts to play good football and starts to score the odd goal then, rightly or wrongly, whatever you think should happen, those players will forget about everything off the pitch if he's doing the business on the pitch.BBC commentator Guy Mowbray questioned the message such a signing would send to existing squad members: What does it do to members of the squad who think, 'If you're that desperate to get that sort of player in, with everything that it brings, then thanks very much. You can't rate me very highly can you?'.Former Sunderland striker Kevin Phillips focused on the practical implications for the struggling club: The interesting thing for me is that Oldham are struggling, they need a centre forward, and it'll be quite interesting to see how the supporters react when he scores his first goal.Phillips added: I'm pretty sure there's going to be many in that crowd saying they won't turn up, but I'm sure they will at some point, and it'll be interesting to see whether they celebrate if he scores a goal.He emphasized the compartmentalized nature of on-field performance: It's quite unique being on that football pitch because you put everything to the back of your mind. If he scores a goal, I'm pretty sure the players at that time will celebrate. They need a goalscorer.The rehabilitation debate featured prominently in discussions. Mills presented the argument for second chances: To play devil's advocate for a moment, he's committed a crime, he's served his sentence in prison - supposedly - therefore he should have been rehabilitated, therefore he comes back into it. Should he not be allowed to do his job of work?However, Conn countered with employment realities: You have the right to work in theory, but you don't have a right to walk back into your chosen profession. No employer, no football club has a duty to employ him.Daily Mirror chief sports writer Oliver Holt offered a nuanced perspective on criminal rehabilitation: The last thing I want to be is to be seen as some sort of champion of Ched Evans... but I believe in a society where once criminals have served their sentence they deserve the chance to rehabilitate.Holt warned against selective justice: I just think we're on dangerous ground when we start making slightly random judgements about which criminals we allow back to work, and which criminals we don't.Mowbray expressed bewilderment at Oldham's decision-making: I am very, very surprised that they're going down this route. With everything that's gone before it, I can't believe that they're that desperate that they would take this signing with all the baggage and the problems that will come with it.He outlined potential consequences: There are financial implications, with sponsorship deals being lost, there might even be implications with policing costs, with the extra security needed.Mowbray concluded pessimistically: I struggle to see it really ending positively for the club, or indeed the player, because if they're going to all this trouble, there's immense pressure on him as well.

text: A man who was sexually assaulted by a Church of England priest has criticised police accusing them of failing to investigate his complaint. A Devon man who reported clergyman Vickery House's sexual abuse to police in 2001 claims his allegations were ignored for over a decade before authorities finally launched an investigation.House received a six-and-a-half-year prison sentence last year following his conviction for sex offences targeting boys and young men. The abuse spanned decades, with his youngest victim - a 14-year-old boy - assaulted in Devon in 1970.With encouragement from his wife, the Devon victim contacted police in 2001 to report his ordeal. However, Sussex Police didn't begin the investigation that ultimately secured House's conviction until May 2012 - eleven years later.The psychological toll proved devastating for the victim. I reached a point when I couldn't function properly as a human being, he explained to the BBC. If it had been dealt with properly at that time I could have dealt with all the issues around that and moved on with my life ten or 15 years ago.Beyond personal consequences, he believes earlier action could have prevented additional suffering. It would have made a huge difference to my children. I also may have saved some other people from being abused, he said. I'm disappointed that that there is no hint of an apology for their lack of action.Devon and Cornwall Police acknowledge having no records of any local investigation concerning the victim, though they don't question his account. We do not doubt he spoke to a police officer, a spokesperson confirmed.The force attributed the delayed response to outdated procedures. Back in 2001 the way in which police dealt with complaints of historic sexual abuse was very different and not at all reflective of today's policing, their representative explained.Legal action now looms as the victim has enlisted a lawyer to file a complaint with the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC).House's criminal network extended beyond individual offending. He maintained close ties with former Bishop of Gloucester Peter Ball, who received a 32-month sentence last year after admitting to molesting young men between 1977 and 1992. Three victims suffered abuse from both men through their involvement with Give a Year For Christ, a Church of England program operating in Litlington, East Sussex.BBC-obtained documents reveal how institutional interference may have delayed justice. text: Eye doctors are warning about bird-scaring explosives, called bangers, being modified and used as fireworks. Medical professionals fear this hazardous behavior could proliferate nationwide.In a letter published in the British Medical Journal (BMJ), concerned physicians detailed their worries about the misuse of these farming implements. Originally designed to protect crops from wildlife, deer scarers—alternatively called bangers or rookies—feature slow-burning rope fuses that detonate multiple explosives sequentially along their length. When modified by cutting the fuse, these devices become dangerous projectiles that can be ignited and thrown.Edward Pringle, a retinal fellow at Sussex Eye Hospital and co-author of the BMJ correspondence, described the horrific nature of these injuries: These banger fireworks are easy to throw into a crowd, people look at them and debris shoots into the eye. It's like a hand grenade going off - a flash in front of the eye, and then the feeling of a blunt injury.The medical professional drew stark comparisons to battlefield conditions: Doctors normally see these types of injuries in a war zone. We were seeing them in a small market town - those throwing them and the people turning up to public events don't realise how dangerous they can be.The November 5, 2011 incident at Lewes proved catastrophic. Eight patients required emergency treatment at Sussex Eye Hospital following the celebration, which drew over 60,000 attendees. Among the victims, two lost their sight permanently, while three others now face lifelong glaucoma risks.Safety organizations have condemned this reckless behavior. Since just over half of all firework injuries occur during public events, they recommend that organizers actively engage their audience in the safer use of fireworks and encourage eye protection.National statistics reveal the broader scope of firework-related eye trauma. Should these methods fail, seek immediate medical assistance.

text: More than half of overseas students in the UK say they have felt less welcome because of policies on migration, a survey suggests. Research spanning 105 institutions and involving over 500 international students reveals that 52% hold negative views regarding efforts to reduce migration figures. Nearly half of North American students studying in the UK express similar concerns.The debate over immigration policy has prompted universities to advocate for excluding students from headline migration statistics. Business Secretary Vince Cable recently cautioned that the UK's torrid immigration discourse threatens to undermine the economically significant recruitment of international students. Cable highlighted concerns about public panic surrounding migrant numbers and its potential negative impact on overseas students.Regent's University in London commissioned the survey examining international student attitudes in the UK, which presents a nuanced picture. Despite feeling less welcomed due to migration targets, students report positive experiences overall in the UK.Approximately 80% of respondents endorsed the quality of their courses and instruction, while nearly 90% would recommend UK study to others. A clear divide emerges between public migration reduction campaigns and students' personal interactions with UK residents—almost 90% report feeling welcomed by individuals they encounter.However, integration challenges persist within university settings. One-quarter of international students feel disconnected from the university community. The survey reveals that 40% of overseas students primarily socialize with compatriots, and roughly 20% acknowledge experiencing isolation.Nearly one-third of international students endorsed the statement that my university is only interested in the fees I pay.Despite concerns that anti-immigration negative rhetoric might deter prospective students, this year's application data contradicts such fears. While some individual countries show declining numbers, overall figures from Ucas admissions service, released last month, demonstrate increased international student applications compared to the previous year.Aldwyn Cooper, vice-chancellor of Regent's University—a private institution that achieved university status this year—commented: These findings show that UK higher education is unmatched in its global reputation. Our universities are second only to the USA as the favoured destination for international students, and to maintain this strong appeal around the globe the government is developing an industrial strategy to ensure our universities stay ahead in the global race.

text: Chairman Daniel Levy has defended Tottenham's lack of transfer activity this summer and claimed the spending by other Premier League clubs is unsustainable. Premier League clubs have already splashed out over £850m during the current transfer window, set to close on 31 August, yet Tottenham remain conspicuously absent from the spending spree despite receiving £45m from Manchester City for Kyle Walker's transfer this month.Chairman Daniel Levy defended the club's restrained approach during a Nasdaq Q&A session in New York, emphasizing fiscal responsibility. Now everybody pays big money for good players.Levy expressed concern about the financial implications of unchecked spending. An academy player has that affinity with the club and that's what the fans want to see.

text: An Olympic marathon runner from Ethiopia staged a daring protest against his home government when he crossed the line in Rio on Sunday. During his silver medal victory, marathon runner Feyisa Lilesa raised crossed arms overhead—a symbolic gesture representing the Oromo people, who face severe police brutality and government oppression.Lilesa hails from Oromia, the regional homeland where most of Ethiopia's 35 million Oromo population resides. At a subsequent press conference, he repeated this defiant display while declaring that returning to Ethiopia would endanger his life.According to human rights organizations, Ethiopian security forces have murdered hundreds of civilians in recent weeks while suppressing anti-government demonstrations.The Ethiopian government are killing the Oromo people and taking their land and resources so the Oromo people are protesting and I support the protest as I am Oromo, Lilesa explained his actions. The Ethiopian government is killing my people so I stand with all protests anywhere as Oromo is my tribe. My relatives are in prison and if they talk about democratic rights they are killed. I raised my hands to support with the Oromo protest.The athlete warned that returning home could prove fatal. If not kill me, they will put me in prison, he stated. I have not decided yet, but maybe I will move to another country.When questioned about potential International Olympic Committee (IOC) sanctions, Lilesa responded: I cannot do anything about that. This was my feeling. I have a big problem in my country, it is very dangerous to make protest in my country.Olympic Rule 50 prohibits political demonstrations and protests, with IOC officials currently investigating the incident. The 1968 Summer Games saw American athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos famously expelled after displaying the black power salute during their medal ceremony.Ethiopia has experienced widespread unrest in recent months, stemming from multiple grievances including government attempts to redistribute Oromia land. Amhara region residents have similarly protested over land disputes.Following Oromo demonstrations that began in November—with this ethnic group comprising roughly one-third of Ethiopia's population—authorities abandoned plans to expand Addis Ababa's boundaries.However, these protests have revealed deeper concerns about the community's political marginalization and exclusion from economic progress.New York-based Human Rights Watch reports over 400 deaths during security force confrontations in Oromia, though the government challenges these figures.Correction 22 August 2016: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated that US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos were stripped of their medals.

text: History is useful when trying to make sense of present tensions between Russia and the West. Near Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, within the Defence Academy's walls, sits a warehouse housing an exceptional military collection on library shelves. This treasure trove, accumulated methodically across five decades to understand adversaries better, contains countless volumes in Russian and languages from former Soviet territories.The Russian Military Studies Archive, as it's now known, serves as an invaluable record chronicling the USSR's trajectory, Cold War dynamics, and ongoing East-West tensions. Maintaining such archives has grown increasingly challenging since the Warsaw Pact's dissolution and the digital age's arrival. Budget-conscious administrators often view physical book libraries as unaffordable luxuries.Fortunately, this military repository escaped the landfill's fate. Russia's renewed status as a security concern has revitalized interest in recent years. Understanding recent history becomes crucial when attempting to decipher Moscow's current actions and future intentions.Certain memorabilia evokes one of my career's most remarkable episodes: those three August 1991 days in Moscow when defense officials, KGB operatives, and Communist leaders attempted overthrowing the government. They sought to stop and reverse Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika reforms, believing these changes would destroy their nation.That moment remains unforgettable. History balanced on a razor's edge, with the world's future hanging in uncertainty. Venturing from our BBC Moscow office, I discovered tanks lined along the inner ring road, bewildered young soldiers emerging from turrets, unsure of their location.While the tanks appeared threatening, the young occupants did not. Masha, our cleaning lady in her customary headscarf and apron, limped forward to scold them with a wagging finger.What do you think you are doing here? Your mothers would be ashamed of you, she scolded. Take yourselves back to the barracks where you belong.The coup collapsed because Russia's new President, Boris Yeltsin, declared their actions illegal, urged military disobedience, and appealed to Muscovites for support in forcing the plotters' retreat.The public response proved both amazing and humbling. Soviet citizens, who years earlier feared public dissent, now flooded the streets to challenge the Kremlin. Young mothers with pushchairs, briefcase-carrying civil servants, and musicians clutching guitars and violins converged on the Russian parliament, demonstrating through sheer numbers their refusal to be intimidated or allow regression.The collection includes leaflets from that period—some still bearing mud from being trampled—hastily printed and distributed throughout Moscow by Yeltsin's supporters to counter coup leaders' state media broadcasts. I recall them plastered across metro stations.Their words carry power and urgency. Over Russia storm clouds are gathering, clouds of dictatorship and terror… Soldiers! I believe at this tragic hour that you will make the right choice, declares one appeal. Another, addressed from Yeltsin to Moscow's citizens, states: my heartfelt thanks to you all for your courage.Recently, 1991 occupies my thoughts frequently. I wonder whether many Russians might again flood the streets if economic decline worsened and desperation emerged. Alternatively, would they maintain low profiles, focusing grimly on survival? Do they feel differently about their country and leader today—more supportive and less willing to risk upheaval?Russian opposition leaders must constantly contemplate these questions. Vladimir Putin and his inner circle undoubtedly do the same.Notably, 1991's political climate differed dramatically from today's environment. Russians then felt entitled to protest, having received permission from above—through Yeltsin's encouragement and because Mikhail Gorbachev, the Communist Party's General Secretary, had spent six years telling them that speaking out was their right.This top-down empowerment arguably influenced 2011's events, when middle-class Muscovites again demonstrated en masse against electoral fraud. They possibly responded to the relaxed atmosphere prevailing during Dmitry Medvedev's presidency, before Mr Putin's return.Today's mood differs significantly. Public discourse space has contracted. Rather than encouragement, grassroots movements often face suspicion as threats. New legislation and prominent opposition leaders' murders combine to convince critics they should remain silent or emigrate.Patriotism's surge following Russia's 2014 Crimean takeover has strengthened the leadership's message: Russia faces external threats from NATO and jihadists while confronting domestic difficulties. Now more than ever, the narrative continues, the country requires strong leadership to maintain unity, eliminate the fifth column of enemies, and ensure Russia's safety.Historical lessons point to events nearly a century ago, when Bolshevik revolution devastated the nation. President Putin's supporters argue that revolution and bloodshed represent the last things Russia needs.However, reflecting on my personal Russian experience across three or four decades, I consistently observe that the giant surprises by awakening precisely when it appears to slumber. I cannot forget those Moscow citizens, young and old, who crowded the city center in 1991 to prevent Communist restoration.Nobody, probably not even the demonstrators themselves, anticipated such street rebellion. Who can predict Russia's destiny?History provides numerous parallels from which we extract different lessons. Perhaps a new twist, catching everyone off-guard, represents the most probable outcome.

text: More than 60% of Australia's major organised crime figures now deal in crystal meth, a new report has found. A devastating assessment from the Australian Crime Commission (ACC) has identified crystal methylamphetamine - commonly called ice - as the most dangerous illegal substance threatening Australian communities today.The comprehensive report revealed alarming trends in both drug purity and availability. Over recent years, ice has become significantly more potent, amplifying its destructive potential across the nation.While methylamphetamine appears in various forms, the crystalline ice variant dominates Australia's illicit drug landscape. The report highlighted that Australia commands some of the world's steepest crystal meth prices, creating lucrative opportunities that increasingly attract organized criminal enterprises to this trade.Criminal syndicates have adopted particularly sinister tactics, deliberately adulterating crystal meth with additional illegal substances specifically designed to heighten addiction potential, according to the findings.Border security faces mounting pressure as the ACC documented a considerable increase in the number and weight of detections at the Australian border while domestic production shows no signs of declining. International criminal networks are expanding their reach, with Mexican cartels forging stronger partnerships with Australian distribution channels.The report traced supply chains back to their origins, finding that domestic manufacturers increasingly source precursor chemicals from India and China to cook the drug locally.ACC chief executive Chris Dawson emphasized how the drug's availability and addictive nature has created new demand in urban, rural and disadvantaged communities.Ice is a devastating, insidious drug. It affects everyone from users, their families, and their communities, and the authorities who deal with the users, he said.Recent seizures underscore the scale of the problem. Last November, New South Wales police intercepted over 800 kilograms of methylamphetamine alongside two tonnes of MDMA, with combined street value estimates reaching A$1.5bn (£800m; $1.2m). This month brought another significant bust when authorities uncovered 230 kilograms of liquid methylamphetamine concealed within 20,000 bottles of flavoured water bound for a Sydney warehouse.The ACC's response calls for unified action. The report advocates for a collective national response to combat the drug's expanding influence.Everyone plays a role in the fight against illicit drugs - including governments, law enforcement, health, education, industry, non-government organisations and the community, Mr Dawson said.

text: Former Chancellor George Osborne is to become editor of the London Evening Standard newspaper, in a surprise move that has angered opposition MPs. Jeremy Corbyn has branded George Osborne's appointment as Evening Standard editor a joke, demanding an immediate by-election in the former chancellor's Tatton constituency.The Labour leader's criticism came as the Tory MP expressed his delight at succeeding Sarah Sands, who departs to edit the BBC's Today programme. While Osborne plans to maintain his role as MP for Tatton in Cheshire, editing the paper four days weekly, he faces mounting pressure to abandon politics entirely.It takes multitasking to a new level and is an insult to the electors he is supposed to serve, Corbyn declared. The appointment makes a mockery of the independence of the media.Tatton, which Osborne has represented since 2001, faces abolition at the next election.Standard proprietor Evgeny Lebedev defended the choice, describing Osborne as London through and through and expressing confidence he's the right person to build on the fantastic legacy of Sarah Sands.I am proud to have an editor of such substance, who reinforces The Standard's standing and influence in London and whose political viewpoint - socially liberal and economically pragmatic - closely matches that of many of our readers, Lebedev tweeted.The newspaper outlined how Osborne's average of four days a week schedule would accommodate his parliamentary duties, allowing him to vote and contribute in Parliament in the afternoon after the paper has gone to print, and be in his constituency.Addressing Standard journalists in the newsroom, the 45-year-old called his appointment a great honour to lead one of Britain's most influential newspapers. He sought to allay neutrality concerns, promising to be independent and fearless in championing Londoners' interests.Growing up as a Londoner, I've always known that the Evening Standard is an institution that plays a huge part in the life of the city and its people, he said.Despite his Conservative allegiance, Osborne pledged editorial independence: I am proud to be a Conservative MP, but as editor and leader of a team of dedicated and independent journalists, our only interest will be to give a voice to all Londoners.He outlined his editorial philosophy: We will judge what the government, London's politicians and the political parties do against this simple test: is it good for our readers and good for London? If it is, we'll support them; if it isn't we'll be quick to say so.Acknowledging his inexperience, Osborne told journalists: I've got to learn from you because I may have run the country but I haven't actually run a newspaper. I know there's a lot for me to learn.BBC media editor Amol Rajan, formerly of The Independent, explained the logistics: with the afternoon paper printing at 11:00 GMT, Osborne will work from 05:00 GMT until midday before balancing other commitments.Rajan noted that most newspaper editors spend years crafting headlines, sub-editing copy, designing pages, planning stories, and above all reporting. Osborne lacks this experience and will need to grasp some basic skills very quickly if he is to keep Standard staff on-side.Support came from Patti Goddard, president of the Tatton Conservative Association, who backed the former chancellor's exciting career move, insisting it wouldn't affect his reputation as a hard-working constituency MP.London Mayor Sadiq Khan congratulated Osborne on covering the world's greatest city.However, criticism mounted from multiple quarters. Labour's John Mann said Osborne was already invisible in Parliament, with the new job devaluing democracy. Fellow Labour MP Paul Flynn condemned the revolving door between government and private sector.Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas demanded parliamentary assurances that Conservatives wouldn't exert undue influence over the newspaper, calling for Osborne's removal from the Privy Council to prevent access to confidential government briefings.Robert Barrington of Transparency International called it an astonishing conflict of interest damaging democracy that smacks of greed and the accumulation of power.Former Tatton MP Martin Bell's initial reaction was that it sounds like fake news to me, telling BBC Radio 5 Live the politician would need to be superman to juggle various roles.Political figures responded with humor: former Labour leader Ed Miliband joked on Twitter he would shortly be announced as editor of Heat magazine, while Lib Dem leader Tim Farron suggested his next role would be editing adult comic Viz.Since leaving frontline politics, the former six-year chancellor has become a US university visiting fellow and BlackRock adviser, earning £650,000 for four monthly days' work.Osborne harbored journalistic ambitions in his youth, failing to secure a Times trainee position after Oxford University, where he edited Isis magazine. He briefly freelanced for the Daily Telegraph's diary column.Defending his appointment, he told BBC News: there are plenty of examples of MPs who've edited newspapers and magazines over the years.Conservative colleague Boris Johnson edited The Spectator while an MP but resigned as a condition of joining David Cameron's front bench in 2005. The foreign secretary, endorsed by the Standard during his successful 2008 and 2012 mayoral campaigns, called Osborne's appointment brilliant and good for the city.However, most MP-journalist examples, including Labour's Michael Foot (Evening Standard editor) and Conservative Bill Deedes (Daily Telegraph editor), didn't hold both positions simultaneously.The National Union of Journalists criticized the appointment as blatantly cynical amid staff pay cuts and reduced hours, though it welcomed receiving Osborne's membership application.

In a message to the journalists of the Evening Standard in the newsroom, the 45-year-old expressed delight at being appointed to replace Sarah Sands, who is leaving to become editor of the Today programme. Despite Osborne’s intention to keep his Tatton constituency as he edits the paper four days a week, he will be under intense pressure to give up politics altogether. ‘It is time for us to move to a multi-tasked world and it is a slap in the face for the voters he is meant to serve,’ Corbyn said, ‘and the appointment is a mockery of the independence of the media.’ The new editor also sought to allay any fears about the Evening Standard’s impartiality. ‘Growing up as a Londoner, I’ve always known that the Evening Standard is an institution that plays a huge part in the life of this city and its people,’ he said. Despite his Conservative allegiance, Osborne pledged editorial independence: ‘I am proud to be a Conservative MP, but as editor and leader of a team of dedicated and independent journalists, our only interest will be to give a voice to all Londoners. He outlined his editorial policy, saying: ‘We will judge everything the government, its ministers and its politicians do against this simple test: is it good for our readers and good for London? If it is, we’ll support them, if it isn’t, we’ll be quick to say so.’ Osborne has no experience in this field, and will have to learn some of the basic skills of the job very quickly, if he is to be kept on side by the staff. He had a journalistic ambition in his youth, but failed to become a Times trainee. Since leaving frontline politics, the former chancellor, who had been Chancellor for six years, has become a visiting fellow at a university in the United States and a consultant for BlackRock, earning £650,000 a year for four monthly days of work. But the criticisms came from many sides: the labour member John Mann, who said the new role devalued the Parliament; his fellow labour member Paul Flynn said that the new job was degrading to democracy; the Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas called it an astonishing conflict of interest that depletes democracy, and called for Osborne to be removed from the Privy Council to prevent his access to confidential government briefings. The former Tatton MP Martin Bell said his first thought was that it sounded like fake news, and former Lib Dem leader Tim Farron said that he was going to be announced as editor of the adult comic Viz. The Foreign Secretary, who had the Evening Standard’s backing in both his successful mayoral elections, said his appointment was brilliant and good for the city. The Conservative Boris Johnson had been editor of The Spectator while an MP but resigned as a condition of joining the front bench of the government in 2005. In defending his appointment, Osborne said on BBC News, ‘There are plenty of examples of MPs who have been editors of newspapers and magazines over the years.’ The Lib Dem, who had briefly written for the Daily Telegraph’s diary column, defended his appointment, saying there were plenty of examples of MPs who had been editors of newspapers or magazines. Most of the examples of MPs turning to journalism – including Labour’s Michael Foot (editor of the Evening Standard) and Conservative (editor of the Daily Telegraph) – did not hold both posts at the same time.

text: Video sites such as YouTube will be forced to pay more to musicians and record companies under plans to reform European copyright laws. European Commission Proposes Sweeping Copyright Reforms to Ensure Fair Artist CompensationThe European Commission has unveiled ambitious new copyright legislation that would fundamentally reshape how digital platforms compensate creators and publishers across the continent.Under the proposed directive, news publishers will gain recognition as rights holders for the first time in European law. This groundbreaking change means platforms like Google News must pay licensing fees when displaying excerpts or snippets from news articles.Carlo Perrone, head of the European Newspaper Publishers' Association, hailed the creation of copyright protections for news publishers as a significant and historic step for European media.The music industry, which has persistently criticized YouTube for inadequate compensation, stands to benefit significantly from these reforms. More than 1,000 artists, including Lady Gaga and Coldplay, previously signed a letter urging the Commission to address what they termed the value gap - arguing that platforms like YouTube were unfairly siphoning value away from the music community and its artists and songwriters.European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker emphasized the directive's core mission: I want journalists, publishers and authors to be paid fairly for their work, whether it is made in studios or living rooms, whether it is disseminated offline or online, whether it is published via a copying machine or hyperlinked on the web.The proposed legislation will mandate that publishers and producers disclose to performers and authors the profits generated by their creative works. However, the Commission has yet to specify enforcement mechanisms for compelling platforms like YouTube to increase artist payments.YouTube's current revenue model involves selling advertising space and distributing profits among rights holders, contrasting sharply with subscription-based streaming services like Spotify and Apple Music, which pay record companies per-play royalties.Industry representatives have welcomed the Commission's intervention. Geoff Taylor, BPI chief executive, argued it was inequitable that platforms such as YouTube are building huge businesses using music and other content while paying only a fraction of the royalties paid to artists and labels by services such as Spotify and Apple Music.Robert Ashcroft, chief executive of PRS for Music, which represents nearly 120,000 UK songwriters, composers and music publishers, praised the move to require searchable platforms like YouTube to obtain licenses from rights holders. The European Commission's proposed new copyright directive provides the framework for this essential legal clarity, Ashcroft stated.IFPI, representing the global recording industry, characterized the proposals as a positive initial step toward improved European content licensing. Chief executive Frances Moore noted: Importantly, it confirms that user uploaded content services such as YouTube, which are the largest source of on-demand music, should not be able to operate outside normal licensing rules. However, there is a lot more to do to make this a workable proposal.UK Music maintained this week that YouTube continues underpaying artists, stating the Google-owned platform was yet to deliver fair financial returns for rights owners and creators, artists, composers, songwriters and publishers. The band Two Door Cinema Club echoed these concerns: I don't think things at the minute are fair. YouTube don't pay a fair royalty.Google counters that it has distributed over $3bn (£2.3bn) to the music industry since 2007. A Google spokesperson responded to the proposals by saying: We believe there's a better way. text: Back in the heady days of May 2010, when the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats united in government, they set out a detailed set of policy proposals called the Coalition Agreement. Following the cash-for-honours scandal, disagreement between parties gave way to what seemed like encouraging developments. One paragraph declared: We will... pursue a detailed agreement on limiting donations and reforming party funding in order to remove big money from politics.The independent Committee on Standards in Public Life deemed the matter significant enough to launch an investigation weeks later. Chairman Sir Christopher Kelly acknowledged that significant difficulties remain, yet felt encouraged enough to state that there is sufficient will to reform the system to give us some hope that it ought to be possible to find a solution.In Whitehall's diplomatic language, such words represent boldly optimistic territory. Sir Christopher's outlook wasn't merely positive—it overflowed with hope.Following months of delays, Sir Christopher's recommendations have finally emerged. His proposal centers on capping individual political party donations at £10,000.Additionally, he suggests requiring union members to make individual decisions about contributing money to the Labour Party. The current system forces members to opt out if they prefer keeping their funds away from Ed Miliband's coffers.These two reforms would dramatically slash income for the three major parties. In exchange, Sir Christopher recommends public financing—taxpayers would fund political parties directly.Parties holding MPs or seats in Scottish Parliament, Welsh, and Northern Ireland assemblies would receive approximately £3 per vote received.Around 30 million people voted in the previous general election. The proposal would theoretically generate £90m for party distribution across a five-year parliamentary term—substantial funding indeed. Tax-free large donations to parties would also become possible for the public.However, universal disagreement has emerged. Conservative committee member Oliver Heald authored a dissenting opinion opposing the £10,000 cap. Tories favor £50,000 limits and want union members able to direct fees toward parties beyond Labour.Labour's Margaret Beckett outlined her resistance to union reforms. Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg—whose party would benefit from state funding—has rejected immediate taxpayer support increases.Just last week, he informed MPs: It would not be right to ask our hard-pressed taxpayers to pay more to political parties at a time when they are having to deal with so many cuts and savings elsewhere.Numerous government officials share this sentiment.Sir Christopher Kelly contends that public concern about party funding runs deep, suspicion toward major donors persists, and all three largest parties made manifesto reform commitments.Conservatives, Labour, and Liberal Democrats unanimously agree that consensus represents the sole path forward.Ironically, that remains their only point of agreement. While the coalition agreement promised pursuing reform, it stopped short of guaranteeing achievement.

text: New rules for moving livestock will be disastrous for small agricultural shows, the Farmers Union of Wales said. Welsh farmers are voicing strong opposition to new livestock movement regulations they describe as overly restrictive and costly, as the Welsh Government's quarantine unit system takes effect from 10 June.Under the revised framework, agricultural producers must register quarantine units (QUs) on their properties to facilitate livestock transfers while circumventing traditional six-day standstill requirements. The Welsh Government maintains these measures emerged through collaborative industry partnerships.The existing protocol mandates a six-day farm-wide lockdown whenever new animals arrive, preventing any livestock departures during this period. Seasonal agricultural shows currently enjoy exemptions from these restrictions.Previously, farmers could utilize approved isolation units - designated fields or sheds separated from other animals - to bypass standstill rules. However, these isolation facilities become obsolete after 10 June, requiring producers to transition to the fee-based quarantine system.The new framework encompasses 61 specific requirements, mandating installations such as double gates and double fencing, plus specialized protective clothing. Registration costs £172.80 for a single QU, rising to £244.80 for two units.Gwilym Jones from Blaenau Ffestiniog expressed frustration: It makes no sense to show, it's not worth it. The rules are going backwards instead of forwards.Geraint Jones of Ystrad Meurig adopted a more defiant stance: I will break the law, and if they want to put me in jail, they can - I've got nothing to lose. If they want to kill the countryside, they're doing the right thing.Texel sheep exhibitor Sian Davies, who participates in shows nationwide, criticized the modifications as measures that cost money, they're a nuisance and they increase paperwork. She alleged government offices lack adequate knowledge, stating: I called the office in Aberystwyth and they didn't know what I was referring to.Geraint Jones reported similar communication difficulties with Cardiff and Carmarthen offices, though the Welsh Government hasn't acknowledged any registration process delays.Farmers Union of Wales vice-president Brian Walters warned of severe consequences: This is disastrous for smaller agricultural shows. We don't feel there is enough evidence to indicate that diseases are passed between livestock at agricultural shows to justify such draconian measures.England has postponed similar regulatory changes until autumn, successfully avoiding disruption to the show season.The Welsh Government defended its approach in an official statement: The new QU system was designed to simplify the standstill regime and provide extra flexibility whilst maintaining disease movement curbs. It was developed in partnership with the farming industry.Officials emphasized the system's broader application beyond agricultural shows: Although QUs can be used to manage movements to and from shows it is important to note they are intended to be used for all types of animal movement, not just for shows.The government stressed the collaborative development process: The alternative arrangements to the six-day standstill were developed at the request of the industry (through the Working Smarter review) and in close collaboration with the industry through the LIDAG (Livestock Identification Advisory Group) over the past few years - not rushed, worked through systematically, and collaboratively, with the support of Independent Veterinary Risk Assessments.According to officials, recommendations were published in January 2012, with comprehensive industry communication occurring through letters in April and May 2017, supplemented by an extensive outreach campaign.

text: Supermarkets and other big businesses could face higher business rates under a Welsh Conservative government, with a tax cut for smaller companies. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has unveiled plans to overhaul business rates calculations, positioning small enterprises at the heart of the Welsh government should his party secure victory in May's assembly election.The proposed reforms would establish separate rate structures for large and small businesses, ensuring bigger companies contribute more while extending existing rate relief to additional small firms. Currently, Wales operates under a single rate system, unlike England and Scotland which already maintain differentiated approaches.Wales is a nation of shopkeepers, and those small firms are the lifeblood of the Welsh economy; which is why they need support to develop and grow, Mr Davies declared, emphasizing that small businesses were vital to Wales and required assistance to develop and grow.Under the Conservative blueprint, a dedicated team of Welsh government officials would focus exclusively on small business needs, remaining accountable to the assembly. The package includes previously announced measures such as eliminating age restrictions on job creation schemes and streamlining business lending processes through the Welsh government.Business rates, currently paid to local councils based on property valuations, already feature Welsh government discounts known as rate relief. Properties valued up to £6,000 currently face no rate obligations, a threshold the Conservatives pledge to expand.However, retailers have expressed caution about the proposals. The Welsh Retail Consortium, representing shop owners, advocated for fundamental reform of business rates for all, whether that be small, medium sized or larger businesses while warning against creating winners or losers or more complexity.A consortium spokeswoman acknowledged the welcome acknowledgement of the need to keep down costs but raised concerns that many high street retailers wouldn't benefit. She warned against the new rate structure for medium and larger commercial premises potentially opening the door to even higher taxes, as has been proposed in Scotland.
