text: An error with the Global Positioning System (GPS) network has been blamed for causing problems with digital radio broadcasts last week. A software malfunction triggered by the US Air Force's decommissioning of a GPS satellite disrupted BBC digital radio reception across parts of Britain, the broadcaster has confirmed.The disruption began on January 26 when satellite SVN23 was taken out of service, creating unexpected ripple effects throughout the GPS network that lasted several hours. Multiple satellites experienced problems as a result of the decommissioning process.The outages were caused by a rogue GPS satellite (SVN23), which was taken out of service in the evening of 26 January, the BBC stated in response to listener complaints about poor reception.Digital radio listeners noticed the problems immediately. I live on the Worksop side of Sheffield and for the past two days the reception of the BBC National Ensemble [BBC radio stations] has been virtually non-existent indoors, Darcy72 posted on Digital Spy's online forums last week.The technical explanation reveals how interconnected modern broadcasting systems have become. DAB transmitters require precise frequency synchronization, achieved by locking onto GPS satellite signals that broadcast time data accurate to within nanoseconds. When SVN23 was decommissioned after 25 years of operation—far exceeding its original seven-and-a-half-year design lifespan—the timing network experienced significant disruption.While the core navigation systems were working normally, the co-ordinated universal time timing signal was off by 13 microseconds which exceeded the design specifications, the US Air Force explained. The issue was resolved at 06:10 MST, however global users may have experienced GPS timing issues for several hours.The timing error was substantial enough to throw GPS positioning off by nearly 4km in some cases. Finland's Metsahovi Radio Observatory detected the time discrepancy, though it remains unclear whether other global systems, including navigation tools, suffered similar disruptions.Prof Danielle George, a radio engineer at the University of Manchester, questioned the preparedness for such an event. They knew they were decommissioning it so shouldn't they have been aware this would happen? she asked. It was decommissioned after 25 years - actually it should have just had a seven-and-a-half-year lifespan so it lasted a lot longer than it should have done.George noted that DAB transmitters typically wouldn't struggle with a single satellite failure. They shouldn't have seen an issue with that because as far as I understand the way they work is they need two frequencies to lock and there are a number of GPS [signals] to look at, she told the BBC.The incident has prompted warnings about society's growing dependence on GPS technology. Martyn Thomas, a fellow at the Royal Academy of Engineering who has long criticized technological reliance on GPS, called the disruption a cautionary tale.This should be treated as a warning of what could go wrong, Thomas said. The world is dependent on GPS for a vast range of critical applications from navigation to financial trading, and precision docking of oil tankers to high tech farming.Looking ahead, Thomas emphasized that backup systems are crucial. In the future, he said, it was essential that there was back-up.The BBC continues seeking additional information from the US Air Force regarding the incident's full scope and impact.

text: Councils have warned they may be charging more for services despite some already increasing such revenue by more than 100% in three years. Local councils across England generated over £11 billion through fees, charges and sales during the 2014/2015 financial year, according to government statistics.Since 2012/2013, income from fees and charges has grown by 3% overall. The Local Government Association acknowledged that councils must navigate a challenging balancing act when determining fee structures.These charges encompass diverse services ranging from car parking and adult social care to planning applications and country parks. Revenue patterns vary dramatically between authorities - while some councils have boosted income from these sources by tens of millions, others have experienced declining fees, charges and sales revenue.Six English councils achieved remarkable growth exceeding 100% over three years: Breckland, Devon, Hinckley and Bosworth, South Northamptonshire and Sedgmoor. Meanwhile, Derbyshire, Westminster, Bristol and Shropshire emerged as the largest gainers in absolute terms, each collecting tens of millions more annually.Derbyshire's fees, charges and sales income surged by £33m between 2013/2014 and 2015. A council spokeswoman explained: Like all councils we are looking to increase our income where we can as we need to find savings of £157m between 2013 and 2018.There are also many areas where we are charging more for our services than we were.These include increasing co-funding contributions for adult social care, charging for home to school transport for pupils who attend faith schools and charging for parking at some of our countryside sites.Sharon Taylor, acting leader of the Local Government Association, warned: There is a law of diminishing returns with council charges. If you increase prices it can result in a reduction in the use of services. It has to be a reasonable increase; it is a balancing act.Councils of whatever political persuasion are aware that family budgets are tight and they don't want to put costs up.At the end of the day, fees and charges have to be balanced against council tax rises.At Cambridge City Council, where fees and charges revenue climbed from £20.5m to £23.1m across three financial years, departments must justify any fee increases above inflation rates before implementation.Lewis Herbert, leader at the Labour-led council, said: We are trying to strike a balance between the costs of running services and not hitting our residents.We are not trying to cry wolf and are not in as bad a position as some councils, but it really is touch and go for many of us because we have to see what is in the detail of the government's plans for local government.We are more business-like than some councils so may build a cafe at the crematorium or selling flowers or renting out more space in the Guildhall building - so stretching income by selling more rather than increasing charges.The Department for Communities and Local Government declined to provide comment when contacted.

text: Brazil's President Michel Temer has nominated his justice minister to the Supreme Court as it prepares to rule on one the biggest corruption scandals in the country's history. Alexandre de Moraes, among Mr Temer's most trusted allies, has been selected as the new minister to fill the Supreme Court vacancy left by Judge Teori Zavascki's death in last month's plane crash.The 49-year-old lawyer from the PSDB party, which forms part of Mr Temer's governing coalition, joined the cabinet in May following Mr Temer's replacement of President Dilma Rousseff amid impeachment proceedings. Mr Temer defended his choice, citing Mr Moraes's solid academic credentials.Critics have demanded a less politically charged appointment, given that numerous senior politicians face charges in the ongoing corruption scandal. This year, Mr Moraes confronted his gravest challenge as minister when prison riots resulted in over 100 inmates being killed by fellow prisoners. In response, he unveiled plans to establish police intelligence units and enhance cooperation with neighboring nations to diminish gang control over Brazilian prisons.The Senate must ratify Mr Moraes's nomination, prompting him to request a 30-day leave of absence for preparation. However, analysts believe rejection is unlikely, as the government commands a substantial Senate majority.The Supreme Court will soon begin examining extensive evidence compiled during the Petrobras corruption investigation. Judge Zavascki had overseen this probe, dubbed Operation Car Wash, and compiled a list identifying dozens of politicians who allegedly accepted bribes from Brazilian construction giant Odebrecht to secure lucrative Petrobras contracts. Odebrecht has acknowledged paying $1bn (£800m) in bribes across 12 countries to obtain contracts.According to the BBC's Daniel Gallas, Judge Zavascki was highly respected, and his appointment to oversee the Car Wash investigation significantly enhanced its credibility within the Supreme Court. On January 19, his aircraft crashed into the sea during heavy rain near Paraty. Opposition figures suspected foul play and demanded comprehensive investigation.Following Judge Zavascki's death, the Supreme Court has functioned with ten judges. Last week, Judge Edson Fachin assumed responsibility for overseeing the corruption investigation after being randomly selected from five Supreme Court judges on a shortlist.

text: Arkansas will become the first US state in 17 years to hold two executions on the same day, if two inmates are put to death as planned on Monday evening. Defense attorneys for Jack Jones and Marcel Williams are pursuing execution stays based on their clients' deteriorating health conditions.Arkansas had originally scheduled eight death row inmates for execution across 11 days, rushing to use lethal injection drugs before their expiration date. The state carried out its first execution since 2005 on Thursday when Ledell Lee was put to death.Kenneth Williams faces execution Thursday, despite his legal team's claims of intellectual disability. Court orders have suspended the remaining four planned executions from the original eight-inmate schedule.Arkansas's chief prosecutor has pledged to fight through legal barriers and return the condemned prisoners to the execution chamber. The last time any U.S. state executed two inmates on a single day occurred in Texas during 2000.Both men scheduled for Monday's executions have confessed their guilt. In 1996, Jones received his death sentence for raping and strangling Mary Phillips while attempting to kill her 11-year-old daughter. text: Saudi King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz has died, royal officials have announced, weeks after he was admitted to hospital. The death of King Abdullah, who had governed the oil-rich kingdom since 2005 and was approximately 90 years old, occurred following complications from a lung infection. His half-brother Salman, aged 79, has now assumed the throne.King Salman moved quickly to reassure the nation about continuity, declaring his commitment to established policies within hours of becoming monarch. We will continue adhering to the correct policies which Saudi Arabia has followed since its establishment, he announced during a televised address on state television.The late king's health had deteriorated significantly in recent years, with King Salman gradually assuming more of Abdullah's royal duties as his condition worsened. Saudi television's transition to broadcasting Koranic verses—a traditional signal of senior royal deaths—preceded the official announcement. According to the statement, Abdullah passed away at 01:00 local time (22:00 GMT Thursday).In Jeddah, Saudi Arabia's second-largest city, a somber atmosphere prevailed as residents gathered for Friday prayers. The quiet streets reflected the subdued mourning across the kingdom. Local residents expressed their grief, with one Jedawi describing the shock of awakening to news of the king's death despite knowing of his illness. Another compared the loss to losing a family member. The adjustment to this significant loss will begin only after the king's burial.The succession arrangements were swiftly announced. Muqrin, another half-brother in his late 60s, has been designated as the new crown prince. All three men—Abdullah, Salman, and Muqrin—are sons of modern Saudi Arabia's founder, King Abdulaziz (known as Ibn Saud), who died in 1953.King Salman requested the royal family's Allegiance Council to formally recognize Muqrin as heir. He also made strategic appointments: Interior Minister Prince Mohammed bin Nayef became deputy crown prince, securing second position in succession, while the king's son, Mohammed bin Salman, was named defense minister. State television confirmed that other key ministers—including those overseeing foreign affairs, oil, and finance—retained their positions.The new monarch updated his official Twitter profile, writing: I ask God to help me succeed in my service of the dear [Saudi] people.Following Wahhabi traditions—the ultra-conservative Sunni Islamic practice observed in the kingdom—King Abdullah will be interred in an unmarked grave immediately following Friday prayers. This religious establishment views all life and death as submission to divine will, requiring no official mourning period. Government operations continue normally, and flags remain at full height.Multiple challenges confront Saudi Arabia under King Salman's leadership. Ensuring smooth succession without internal family power struggles represents the primary concern. Additionally, jihadist threats persist both domestically and regionally.The kingdom now finds itself positioned between the aggressive Islamic State to the north and al-Qaeda's presence in Yemen to the south. While Saudi warplanes participate in US-led coalition strikes against IS, this involvement generates significant domestic opposition.The government struggles to address reform demands while misusing anti-terrorism legislation to suppress reformers and critics. text: A doctor who misled other medics about Pauline Cafferkey - a nurse who developed the Ebola virus - has been suspended from practising for a month. Both were keen to reach home for the Christmas holiday period, the tribunal learned.While queuing for Public Health England clearance at Heathrow, Dr Ryan and Ms Cafferkey assisted PHE staff by taking their own temperatures. When Dr Ryan measured Ms Cafferkey's temperature, the thermometer showed 38.2C - above normal levels and a key warning sign of the deadly virus.However, the pair agreed to record a lower reading of 37.2C on the screening form. This deception allowed Ms Cafferkey to board her connecting flight to Glasgow, unknowingly carrying Ebola and placing others at unwarranted risk, according to tribunal findings.Ms Cafferkey became ill the following day and endured a prolonged battle with Ebola and its severe complications before eventually recovering.The tribunal heard that Dr Ryan's misconduct extended beyond the airport incident. Five days later, when a consultant called to investigate the screening process, Dr Ryan provided a dishonest response about her role in the temperature recording.Dr Ryan defended her actions, explaining she was experiencing disbelief, fear and panic at the time. She told the hearing: Pauline Cafferkey was my friend and someone I cared about and was really worried she might die.While acknowledging extenuating circumstances surrounding her airport behavior, the tribunal condemned her subsequent dishonesty as deeply deplorable.Dr Bernard Herdan, the tribunal chairman, delivered the verdict: Since the tribunal is satisfied the risk of repetition of your misconduct is low, and there is no risk to patient safety, it has concluded that a one-month suspension will be sufficient to mark the seriousness of your misconduct and to send a message to the profession that dishonesty by a doctor cannot be tolerated under any circumstances.The case forms part of a broader pattern of misconduct related to the airport screening. In September 2016, the Nursing and Midwifery Council cleared Ms Cafferkey of misconduct charges, with the panel determining that her illness had impaired her judgment regarding hiding her infection.Additionally, senior nurse Donna Wood received a two-month suspension from the NMC in November after the panel found she had suggested recording the lower temperature on Ms Cafferkey's screening form to expedite their passage through passport control.

text: St Johnstone extended their unbeaten streak against Hearts to six games as they held the hosts to a draw at Tynecastle. We were ahead, then we let them score a bad goal, and then they scored an offside goal, and went ahead. Hearts had a golden opportunity when Bjrn Johnsen was through on goal, but Steven Anderson made a crucial block to preserve the score-line, and five minutes from the end the substitute Chris Kane appeared to have won for the visitors, converting Wotherspoon’s cross with a cool finish that sparked a furious outcry from the home support. Their persistence was rewarded in the closing seconds when Callum Paterson rose to meet a Cowie corner and head home a goal which kept them in third place, above Rangers on goal-difference. The Saints' manager Tommy Wright said: "It may have lacked quality in places, but I thought it was a thrilling and entertaining game, and I think we got a very good point. We are disappointed not to have won, but the way we fought back was very encouraging. But we fought back and showed our quality and equalized. The match showed the lack of consistency in both sides. I’ve seen the first goal Hearts scored, and I can say that the assistant referee’s view is a clear one, a very good one. Brian Easton doesn’t think it was over, but the angle of the film doesn’t show anything clearer. In his fifth season, Paterson salvaged a draw with his fifth goal. Hearts had lost five goals in their last two games without a win, and St Pats had won only once in their last four. The goal which was disallowed, the assistant referee seemed to think Joe Shaughnessy was a couple of yards offside, but when I saw the game again, it looked level to me, so maybe we got the short straw. In the last five matches against Robbie Neilson’s men the home team had won three and drawn twice. Recent history favoured the home team.

text: A woman has told the Surjit Singh Chhokar murder trial she did not tell police who attacked her partner because she was distraught. During her testimony on the murder trial's second day, Elizabeth Bryce, 56, revealed she has now identified all three men she alleges attacked her partner. Initially, she had provided police with only one name - Andrew Coulter - but has since named the remaining two suspects as Ronnie Coulter and David Montgomery.The 48-year-old Ronnie Coulter faces murder charges in connection with Mr Chhokar's death in Gowkthrapple, North Lanarkshire, though he denies the allegations and points blame toward his co-accused.Under cross-examination by defence counsel Donald Findlay QC, Ms Bryce explained her initial reluctance to fully cooperate with investigators. I was distraught. At the time I wasn't thinking. I was distraught at my man lying dead at my feet, she testified when asked why she hadn't immediately identified all those responsible.Though Ms Bryce acknowledged knowing all three suspects, she explained that anger motivated her to single out Andrew Coulter first. This stemmed from her earlier confrontation with him regarding a missing giro cheque that her 32-year-old partner had mentioned. Following her inquiries, she learned the cheque had allegedly been cashed at the post office by Andrew Coulter.The defence challenged Ms Bryce's credibility, with Mr Findlay accusing her of tailoring her evidence. A significant discrepancy emerged regarding her partner's final words. Her police statement, recorded the day after Mr Chhokar's death, quoted his last words as I've been stabbed. However, during court proceedings, she testified he actually said they stabbed me.Ms Bryce firmly rejected allegations that she had modified her testimony. When pressed by Mr Findlay, she conceded having probably told a few lies but not in the case of what happened to Chhokar. She also acknowledged a conviction for £13,000 benefit fraud, though dismissed its relevance to the current proceedings.The defence questioned her account of witnessing both Coulters and David Montgomery pass her window twice on the day of the incident. According to Wednesday's testimony, Ms Bryce described grabbing a garden spade and rushing from her Garrion Street home in Wishaw to confront the three men, whom she claimed were dragging her partner across the street. She testified that blood just flew out of Mr Chhokar before he collapsed and died.Beyond the murder charge, Ronnie Coulter faces additional allegations including forging Mr Chhokar's signature on a £100 giro cheque. He also denies charges of breaking into Mr Chhokar's residence at Caplaw Tower, Gowkthrapple, stealing a cooker, and attempting to pervert justice by destroying or disposing of a knife and clothing.The trial continues before Lord Matthews.

The party also sought powers for councils to address clusters of betting shops opening simultaneously.Shadow culture minister Clive Efford argued the regulatory landscape had transformed since initial licensing, with online gambling now generating over £2bn annually. These machines are an example of Cameron's Britain - one rule for constituents and another for big business which operate the betting shops, he declared.Fellow Labour MP Brian Donohue compared fixed-odds betting terminals to cocaine, describing them as absolutely and totally addictive.While acknowledging the machines' concerning growth, Ms Grant maintained existing powers allow councils to reject new gambling premises applications and review current licenses. She expects voluntary industry protection measures - including play suspensions and automatic stake alerts - by March.The government awaits research findings on machine usage patterns and player impact before determining additional interventions. There is no green light for these machines. Their future is unresolved pending the research we have started, Grant told parliamentarians.Grant accused Labour of rank hypocrisy, total cynicism and outright opportunism, stating: Labour bought these machines into being and they have the audacity to bring forward a motion blaming the government for any harm caused.The Association of British Bookmakers rejected targeting allegations, emphasizing their High Street presence serves millions of working class people throughout Britain while maintaining they seek to reach the widest audience possible.The industry body acknowledged machine concerns and expressed openness to constructive dialogue with politicians about the appropriate powers for local authorities. However, it disputed widespread problem gambling claims, asserting the industry continues to develop its approach to harm mitigation for the small number of gamblers who do experience problems.Parliament previously rejected Labour calls to slash maximum stakes from £100 to £2 and reduce top prizes from the current £500 limit.

text: A top NFL official has acknowledged a link between head trauma in American football and the brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). For the first time, a league executive has acknowledged this critical connection.When United States politicians questioned Jeff Miller, the NFL's vice president of health and safety, about CTE, his response marked a historic moment. Asked whether there was a link between the game and neurodegenerative diseases like CTE, Miller replied: The answer to that question is certainly yes.This admission stands in stark contrast to earlier statements from the league. During the lead-up to Super Bowl 50 earlier this year, neurosurgeon Mitch Berger, who heads the NFL's subcommittee on long-term brain injury, maintained that no connection between American football and CTE had been proven.Illinois representative Jan Schakowsky sharply criticized Berger's position, accusing the league of peddling a false sense of security by minimizing head trauma risks.Football is a high-risk sport because of the routine hits, not just diagnosable concussions, said Schakowsky. What the American public needs now is honesty about the health risks and clearly more research.While the NFL has previously recognized that head trauma, especially concussion, threatens players' long-term health, neither NFL commissioner Roger Goodell nor other senior officials have made such definitive public declarations.Miller's testimony drew upon research by Boston University neuropathologist Ann McKee. Speaking to committee members, she expressed absolute certainty about the disease's connection to football—a condition detectable only posthumously.I unequivocally think there's a link between playing football and CTE, said McKee. We've seen it in 90 out of 94 NFL players whose brains we've examined. We've found it in 45 out of 55 college players and six out of 26 high school players.The stakes remain enormous, with approximately 5,000 former players pursuing legal action against the NFL, alleging the organization concealed the dangers of repeated head trauma.CTE manifests through symptoms including memory loss, depression and progressive dementia. Researchers have discovered the disease in dozens of former American football players' brains, though diagnosis remains possible only after death.

text: Stoke held Southampton to a goalless draw despite having Marko Arnautovic sent off in Mark Hughes' 400th match as a Premier League manager. Southampton squandered a golden opportunity to claim victory against ten-man Stoke City, settling for a frustrating 0-0 draw that left Claude Puel's side ruing missed chances at St. Mary's.The turning point arrived in the 23rd minute when Marko Arnautovic received his marching orders for a dangerous studs-up challenge, leaving Stoke to battle with a numerical disadvantage for over an hour. Despite controlling possession throughout, Southampton failed to capitalize on their man advantage in what proved to be a lackluster encounter.The most glaring miss came from substitute Jay Rodriguez, who inexplicably failed to connect with Sofiane Boufal's inviting second-half cross when presented with the game's clearest opening. The 27-year-old forward appeared caught between decisions, unable to determine which foot to use as the ball rolled across the six-yard box.James Ward-Prowse came closest to breaking the deadlock late on, but his close-range effort following Glen Johnson's defensive error was deflected wide of the target. Ryan Bertrand had earlier tested Stoke goalkeeper Lee Grant with a fierce drive from distance, representing one of Southampton's few direct approaches.Mark Hughes' Stoke offered minimal attacking threat after Joe Allen's early effort was turned behind by Fraser Forster within the opening six minutes. Xherdan Shaqiri endured a particularly disappointing evening, his frustration evident when he struck a dugout seat with his fist after being substituted for Mame Biram Diouf in the second half.The red card incident sparked controversy, with home supporters voicing their disapproval as Arnautovic's studs made contact high on Boufal's thigh. While the challenge appeared late and reckless, Hughes defended his player post-match.It's unfortunate because he obviously caught him high on the thigh but the ball was bouncing around and it wasn't a violent movement to take the player out, Hughes explained. The ref wasn't great on the night, he missed a number of decisions and clearly missed an elbow from Shane Long on Bruno Martins Indi - that needs looking at again.Hughes added: Overall the ref put us in a situation and we had to show real work ethic and understanding of what was required. Given the circumstances, the point we gained was magnificent.Southampton manager Claude Puel expressed his disappointment with his team's inability to convert their numerical superiority into goals.We're disappointed. Eleven against 10 you have to do better. In the first half we were too nervous, in the second half we were better and created a few possibilities, but it was not enough, Puel said. There were good crosses and good combinations, but our play was too slow and not effective in the final third. It was two points lost and it's a shame.Regarding Arnautovic's dismissal, Puel was unequivocal: I think it's a important foul, it was very dangerous, he does not play the ball.The result sees Southampton climb to ninth position in the table, while Hughes' Stoke remain in 12th place. For Hughes, this landmark 400th match managing in England's top flight will hardly be remembered fondly - a milestone that highlighted his 36% win percentage, matching Alan Pardew but trailing behind Harry Redknapp (37%) and David Moyes (41%).Stoke's defensive resilience ultimately proved decisive, though their point owed more to Southampton's profligacy than their own organizational excellence. Johnson's heavy touch in his own penalty area should have been punished more severely, while Allen's hesitancy contributed to Southampton's best chance of the evening.Despite dominating possession after the dismissal, Southampton's approach play, while aesthetically pleasing, consistently broke down in the final third. As players, we play alongside each other and all we're asking for is the same opportunity.However, Latapy emphasized his desire for merit-based selection: Since John Barnes, there hasn't been another black manager, but I have to say this: I don't want a job because of the colour of my skin. text: Oxfordshire could be voting for its first elected mayor by 2018, according to a council leader. He believes shared priorities - including A34 road improvements and addressing the county's housing crisis - would unite local leadership.The six councils examining devolution possibilities include Oxfordshire County Council, Oxford City Council, and the district councils of Cherwell, West Oxfordshire, South Oxfordshire, and Vale of White Horse. Their potential government lobbying efforts could incorporate an elected mayor within a broader devolution proposal.An Oxfordshire County Council spokesperson, representing the authority overseeing transport infrastructure, social care, and children's and adult services, stated: We cannot pass up the chance to secure infrastructure investment from the government, so we will work closely with the district and city councils on a devolution bid - which is likely to include an elected mayor and combined authority. OxLEP will continue to work closely with all local authorities, universities, business and other partner organisations to create the conditions that will best enable the county's already thriving economy to flourish and grow in future.**Analysis: Bethan Phillips, BBC Oxford political reporter:**Oxfordshire's absence of elected mayoral leadership reportedly contributed to the county's recent failure to secure hundreds of millions in government project funding.Council leaders and the Local Enterprise Partnership assembled a £382m funding request covering railway station upgrades, new A34 junctions, and road construction projects. text: Sinn Féin and the SDLP have criticised the government's plan for Brexit, but a White Paper published on Thursday has been welcomed by unionists. Brexit Secretary David Davis presented the government's comprehensive plan to the House of Commons, outlining 12 key principles that Prime Minister Theresa May had previously articulated during a significant London address.The blueprint encompasses multiple critical areas, spanning trade arrangements, immigration policy, devolution matters, and the complex issue of the Irish border. These themes form the backbone of the UK's approach to European Union withdrawal.DUP Deputy Leader Nigel Dodds characterized the plan's central stress as leveraging Britain's EU departure to strengthen the union. He emphasized this rationale underpinned his party's Brexit support, declaring: This is why the DUP supported Brexit, and this is precisely what Brexit lets the UK do.Dodds expressed satisfaction that officials had took the time to restate the obvious - that Brexit would have no impact on the Common Travel Area, or the unique relationship between British and Irish citizens. He noted this arrangement long predated EU membership and will happily outlast it.Conversely, the White Paper triggered sharp criticism from Sinn Féin, which had advocated for continued EU membership. Michelle O'Neill, the party's northern leader, accused the government of acting in its own self-interest. She argued: It's clear the only credible approach is for the north to be designated a special status within, rather than outside of, the EU.SDLP's Mark Durkan delivered equally harsh assessment, dismissing the document as padded out with platitudes lacking solid content. The Foyle MP criticized the government's direction, claiming they had charted a Brexit course with no sat-nav, map or compass.While both Sinn Féin and the SDLP advocate for Northern Ireland's special post-Brexit status, Northern Ireland Secretary James Brokenshire has rejected this approach as fundamentally flawed.Ulster Unionist MP Danny Kinahan offered a more positive response, welcoming the White Paper's publication and emphasizing that clarity represents what constituents and businesses deserve in order to best plan for the future. He pledged: Now that we know the government's intentions, we will work tirelessly to hold them to their commitment to ensure a frictionless border, protect the rights of UK citizens in EU member states and secure the best trade deal possible for Northern Ireland and the rest of the UK.Following two days of parliamentary debate, MPs endorsed the European Union Bill on Wednesday evening by a decisive margin of 498 votes to 114. The DUP and Ulster Unionists backed the legislation, while the SDLP and independent unionist Lady Sylvia Hermon opposed it.Next week's committee stage will see detailed parliamentary scrutiny of the bill, with the Labour Party promising to introduce amendments during the process.

text: A study confirming a link between atmospheric pollution and heart-attack risk strengthens the EU case for tougher clean-air targets, experts say. A comprehensive BMJ study examining long-term health data from 100,000 individuals across five European nations has uncovered evidence of cardiovascular harm from air pollution, even when exposure levels remain within legally permitted limits.The collaborative research, conducted by European universities and institutes, represents the most extensive investigation ever undertaken into pollution's impact on European populations. Its findings reveal that prolonged exposure to airborne contaminants - such as residing alongside heavily trafficked urban thoroughfares - exacts a measurable health cost over time.According to the study's results, each 5 µg/m3 annual increase in fine-particulate pollution (PM 2.5) - considered the most hazardous variety due to its ability to penetrate deeply into human tissue - correlates with a 13% relative rise in heart attack incidence. This association persists even after researchers accounted for additional risk factors including smoking habits.The investigation also established connections between elevated levels of larger-particulate pollution (PM 10) and increased cardiac event risk. Crucially, these correlations remained statistically significant when pollution concentrations fell below existing European regulatory thresholds.While experts acknowledged the documented risks, they emphasized that individual danger levels remain comparatively modest. Factors such as tobacco use and hypertension contribute more substantially to personal heart attack probability than industrial and vehicular emissions, according to medical professionals.However, some researchers questioned the study's definitiveness, arguing that the analysis failed to account for participants' historical exposure to previously higher pollution concentrations.Prof David Coggon from the University of Southampton's Department of Occupational and Environmental Medicine expressed measured skepticism: This study adds to the evidence that particulate air pollution is a cause of heart disease, but it does not establish that there are important health risks from levels of exposure below current exposure limits. This is because the differences in risk that were observed may have been a long-term effect of exposures in the past when levels of pollution were higher.Conversely, Jon Ayres, professor of environmental and respiratory medicine at the University of Birmingham, advocated for policy reform: There is no doubt that further reduction of PM levels would result in improvements in cardiac health in Europe. One can only hope that our European politicians will be persuaded of the importance of these findings and reassess their position on air pollution in Europe.The research authors argue their findings strengthen the case for tightening EU particulate matter pollution standards. Present European Union regulations establish annual PM 2.5 limits at double the World Health Organization's recommended levels.Current UK statistics indicate approximately 30,000 premature deaths annually result directly from air pollution exposure, which medical research has connected to asthma, various pulmonary diseases including cancer, and cardiovascular complications.A recent Defra analysis suggests no safe exposure threshold exists for PM 2.5 pollution, with this form of artificial contamination reducing average UK life expectancy by seven to eight months.A Defra spokeswoman responded: Air quality has improved significantly in recent decades and the UK currently meets the EU limits for this type of pollution. We want to keep improving air quality and reduce the impact it can have on human health and the environment.

text: Restoration work has started on a World War I cemetery in Surrey built for Muslim soldiers killed in combat. The Horsell Common Preservation Society has set an ambitious deadline to restore a deteriorating Grade II listed war memorial, targeting completion by August 4 next year to coincide with the centennial of World War I's outbreak.Located in Woking, the historic structure has suffered years of deterioration and vandalism. The preservation society expects to finish the first restoration phase by November, with partial funding secured from English Heritage. Plans also include establishing a memorial garden at the location.Its architectural interest and unique status as a site of memory for Muslims who died fighting for Britain in two world wars is recognised in its national designation as a Grade II listed structure, explained Paul Stamper, English Heritage's senior designation adviser.Woking council leader John Kingsbury emphasized the heritage site's significance for local residents and descendants of war casualties. Meanwhile, David Robbins, chairman of Horsell Common Preservation Society, expressed hopes that the community would take pride in this unique war memorial upon completion.The memorial's history traces back to World War I, when over one million troops from pre-independence India served Great Britain. Wounded soldiers received treatment at South East hospitals, with Hindu and Sikh personnel taken to crematoriums. However, Muslim soldiers lacked proper burial facilities until 1915, when Woking's site began development and reached completion in 1917.Records from the preservation society indicate that 17 burials occurred at the site in 1917, each marked with distinctive round arched headstones oriented westward following Islamic tradition. The burial ground later accommodated a Sandhurst military academy cadet in 1920, before the War Graves Commission assumed maintenance responsibilities in 1921.World War II brought eight additional Muslim soldier interments, including three members of the Free French forces. However, following extensive vandalism in 1968, all remains were relocated to Brookwood cemetery and the ground lost its consecrated status.Despite these changes, the structure maintains its designation as a Registered War Memorial.

text: Coach Vern Cotter insisted Scotland can still secure a top-half finish in this year's Six Nations despite a record points defeat by England. Scotland's aspirations for their first Twickenham victory since 1983 crumbled spectacularly as they surrendered a record points haul in a crushing 61-21 defeat - matching the devastating 40-point margin from their 43-3 humiliation in 2001.The injury toll proved catastrophic, with Stuart Hogg, Mark Bennett, Tommy Seymour and Ryan Wilson all departing with injuries, three suffering head knocks that decimated Scotland's tactical plans.We have had two away games and eight concussions, Cotter told BBC Scotland, highlighting a concerning pattern that extends beyond this single match.The cascade of forced substitutions left Scotland scrambling to reorganize their formation. It isn't the only reason but we certainly had to make early replacements. We finished with (scrum-half) Ali [Price] on the wing and (replacement fly-half) Duncy [Weir] at full-back so there were a few changes, Cotter explained.Despite the heavy defeat, Cotter maintained perspective while acknowledging England's superiority. We take it on the chin. Credit to England. I thought they played well. We didn't play particularly well, although we scored three tries. We would have liked to have scored four so we could have come away with something [a losing bonus point].The coach's immediate concern shifted to damage assessment ahead of their upcoming fixture. My priority at the moment is to check out the casualties and see how many we have got to prepare for Italy at home next week.Scotland's self-inflicted wounds began early when Fraser Brown received a yellow card after merely two minutes, immediately handicapping the visitors against their formidable hosts.We wanted to start well, against a good team, but we did everything to help them in a lot of ways, Cotter admitted, recognizing how his team facilitated England's dominance.The coach identified specific areas requiring urgent attention. There are some things there we need to deal with if we want to put on a better performance next week. We will sit down and have a good look at those.Scotland's attacking moments showed promise when they maintained possession, but consistency remained elusive. We scored three tries when we had possession but we just couldn't get fast possession in that first half. As soon as we got good tempo and speed we managed to get over the advantage line.However, their inability to sustain momentum proved costly. But we couldn't string things together. Our defence from set-pieces, especially from line-outs, wasn't good. There is a lot to work on and improve. We will analyse it and work hard to get a couple of good training sessions in.Looking ahead, Cotter remained optimistic about Scotland's tournament prospects despite the setback. We can still finish in the top end of the table and that will be our objective. If our feet weren't on the ground, they definitely are now. We will work hard to put on a good performance next week.Currently fifth in the standings, Scotland shares points with Wales while trailing Ireland and France by a single point. Next Saturday's schedule features Scotland hosting Italy in the early kickoff, followed by France welcoming Wales in the afternoon, and England traveling to face Ireland in the evening fixture.Scotland's scoring came through Gordon Reid's try, complemented by a double from Huw Jones, with Finn Russell converting all three attempts.Captain John Barclay, leading the team in Greig Laidlaw's continued absence, offered a frank assessment of the performance. It certainly wasn't a good day.The skipper refused to question his team's effort while acknowledging their shortcomings. It wasn't through lack of trying, just too much error. We didn't play well. Credit to England. They played well, they executed plays under pressure - maybe not under enough pressure.

text: The first new design of an electricity pylon in almost 90 years has been erected at a site in Nottinghamshire. Following nearly a century of faithful service, Britain's iconic steel lattice pylon has undergone a revolutionary redesign.Standing at approximately 120ft (36m), the innovative T-pylon represents a significant reduction from the towering 165ft (50m) height of its traditional predecessors. National Grid officials explain that this modernized infrastructure will address the growing demand to capture energy from an expanding array of lower-carbon power sources.The breakthrough engineering allows the compact tower to maintain full 400,000-volt operational capacity despite its reduced stature, achieved through an ingenious cable-holding mechanism. Rather than the conventional three-arm attachment system, engineers have implemented a diamond configuration that consolidates cable management into a single arm within a dramatically compressed footprint.Supporting 60 tonnes per arm, the streamlined design features merely eight primary structural elements plus bolts, dramatically simplifying construction processes. Installation time has plummeted from a full week to just one day.National Grid representatives emphasize that these advanced pylons address the fundamental shift from coal dependency toward alternative generation methods including wind, solar and nuclear power. Unlike the traditional ring of coal-fired plants concentrated in central England, these emerging low-carbon energy sources originate from diverse geographical locations across the country.The inaugural test line will remain isolated from the broader grid network, serving exclusively as a training facility for staff and contractors. Personnel will particularly utilize the installation to master stringing conductors (wires) onto the pylons, as the innovative design demands entirely different technical approaches.Danish company Bystrup's T-Pylon concept emerged victorious from National Grid's 2011 international design competition. Beyond their reduced height, these structures promise decreased visual impact through their ability to follow the contours of the land, according to officials.Project manager Alan Large highlights enhanced maintenance accessibility, noting that operators will no longer need to scale the towers themselves, instead working from elevated platforms positioned adjacent to the structures. The pylons' smooth, impenetrable surfaces will additionally provide superior vandalism resistance.The new design won't displace the 88,000 existing lattice pylons currently spanning UK countryside. Instead, T-pylons will primarily serve new power line construction projects throughout England and Wales.National Grid has submitted applications to deploy these structures for connecting the forthcoming Hinkley Point C nuclear facility to Britain's electricity transmission infrastructure.The UK's electrical transmission network originated with the construction of the inaugural pylon near Edinburgh in 1928.Follow Claire on Twitter.While some view them as landscape eyesores, others appreciate their skeletal aesthetic appeal.However, for a dedicated community of pylon enthusiasts, these towering structures represent a source of enduring fascination.Read more: Pylon passion

text: The final of this year's Britain's Got Talent drew the lowest audience in the show's 10-year history, according to overnight figures. The Britain's Got Talent finale drew its lowest audience in the show's decade-long history, with 8 million viewers watching the live broadcast and another 500,000 tuning into ITV+1.Viewership climbed to 9.7 million when Army bandsman and magician Richard Jones was crowned champion. This marks a significant decline from the previous record low of 10.7 million in 2014, when vocal group Collabro claimed victory.Jones, a 25-year-old lance corporal with The Household Cavalry, captivated both judges and audiences with his military-inspired magical performance. I can't believe it, thank you so much to everyone that voted - it's been an incredible experience, it means the world to me, he expressed after his historic win.As the talent competition's first-ever magician winner, Jones secures the £250,000 prize along with a coveted spot at the Royal Variety Performance.The live broadcast captured 39.7% of total television viewing, though complete consolidated numbers including on-demand and catch-up services won't be available for another week. ITV representatives reported peak audiences reached 10.5 million when combining both channels.Competition for viewers came from the simultaneous Uefa Champions League Final between Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, available on BT Sport's subscription service and free via YouTube.Last year's finale attracted an average 11.7 million viewers with a 46.6% audience share. The show's peak remains 2009, when over 17 million watched Diversity's memorable victory over Susan Boyle.While the finale typically ranks among the year's most-watched programs, this year's numbers likely exclude it from the top 10.**'Brilliantly British'**Dressed in his Household Cavalry uniform, Jones performed a card trick narrating the story of Britain's oldest living magician, 97-year-old Fergus Anckorn, and how magic sustained him as a Singapore prisoner of war. The act's climax brought Anckorn himself onto the stage.Judge Alesha Dixon praised the standing-ovation performance as poignant, noble and brilliantly British.On Britain's Got More Talent, head judge Simon Cowell explained Jones's victory extended beyond magical ability. I think people rooted for him as a person, Cowell observed. His presentation, his whole performance was immaculate - it was very patriotic and heart-warming and he deserved to win.Amanda Holden added her enthusiasm: I'm absolutely delighted because when magic first started on Britain's Got Talent it was rubbish and after 10 years he has done such a great job.The Army celebrated with congratulatory tweets and shared images of The Band of the Household Cavalry marking Jones's triumph.Swing performer Wayne Woodward, who emerged as bookmakers' Saturday afternoon favorite, secured runner-up position with his interpretation of Nina Simone's Feeling Good.Third place went to Boogie Storm, the disco-dancing Star Wars stormtroopers collective.The 12-finalist lineup included sword swallower Alex Magala, whose dangerous act required pre-recording for safety. His performance involved sliding upside-down down a pole while handcuffed, stopping mere centimeters from a running chainsaw.Additional finalists featured young singers Jasmine Elcock and Beau Dermott, mother-son pair Mel and Jaime, 100 Voices of Gospel, dance acts Shannon and Peter plus Balance Unity, impersonator Craig Ball, and dancing dog Trip Hazard.Marking the show's 10th anniversary, previous winners and memorable contestants delivered a special performance. Ashley Banjo of Diversity choreographed the segment, featuring six champion acts: 2008's George Sampson, 2010's Spelbound, 2012's dancing dog Pudsey, and 2013 winners Attraction.Last year's runner-up Jamie Raven participated, though 2015 champions Jules Dwyer and dog Matisse were notably missing.Dwyer faced controversy when revelations emerged that a stunt double replaced Matisse during the final performance. Ofcom determined the public was misled but concluded ITV had no intention to deceive viewers.

text: Nicola Sturgeon has claimed Labour's leader in Scotland told her she would not oppose a second independence referendum after the Brexit vote. During a heated live television debate, Scotland's political leaders engaged in fierce exchanges ahead of Thursday's general election, with the most explosive moment coming when Nicola Sturgeon accused Kezia Dugdale of privately abandoning Labour's opposition to Scottish independence.The STV debate brought together the leaders of Scotland's four major parties for their final confrontation before voters head to the polls. Independence, Brexit, healthcare, education, benefit cuts, and policing dominated the discussions, while a studio audience posed questions about terrorism and security concerns.The evening's most contentious moment erupted when Ms Sturgeon claimed the Scottish Labour leader had confided in her during a private conversation nearly a year ago. According to the First Minister, Ms Dugdale suggested that Brexit had fundamentally altered Labour's stance on independence.When Ruth Davidson pressed the SNP leader for clarification, asking: Did you just tell people you had a private conversation with Kezia last June in which she had said she was going to drop Labour's opposition to independence? Ms Sturgeon responded: She said she thought Brexit changed everything and the Labour party could no longer go on opposing a second independence referendum.Ms Dugdale vehemently rejected this characterization, declaring: The idea that I would do anything other than protect the United Kingdom and fight to remain in the UK is an absolute nonsense. She later took to Twitter, stating: Any suggestion that I ever said to Sturgeon that I'd change Labour's position on #indyref2 is a categoric lie + shows how desperate she is.Undeterred, Ms Sturgeon maintained her position: Look, I know what was said, I'm not having a go at you Kezia - you are entitled to change your mind. What you are not entitled to do though is to be always having a go at me just for wanting to give the people of Scotland a choice.Liberal Democrat leader Willie Rennie launched a scathing attack on Ms Sturgeon's decade-long governmental record, particularly targeting healthcare and education failures. He declared the First Minister should be ashamed of mental health service waiting times affecting young people.Mr Rennie accused Ms Sturgeon of prioritizing independence above all else: For the last year, almost week in, week out, Nicola Sturgeon has taken the opportunity to put independence first - every single time. This time it happened to be Brexit was the excuse. And it's quite noticeable when, in this election campaign, she doesn't talk about it any more because she knows that people are sick, fed up of it, people want to turn their back on another divisive independence referendum.He called on Ms Sturgeon to cancel another referendum, arguing that Scots were sick and fed up of the issue.Ms Sturgeon countered by highlighting what she called the ridiculous contradiction in Mr Rennie's stance - opposing a second independence referendum while supporting another EU referendum.Ruth Davidson faced intense scrutiny over Conservative policies, particularly the controversial rape clause and proposed changes to social care funding. The policy requires women to provide evidence of rape to claim tax credits for more than two children, while the dementia tax would force elderly people in England to sell homes to fund care if their assets exceed £100,000.Ms Sturgeon expressed outrage at the welfare changes, noting that many people had been 'appalled' by the policy, which she said would save £300m from the benefits bill at the same time as the Conservatives spend £380m on a tax cut for the richest 15%.You could use that money that is going to the richest to get rid of that two-child tax cap and the rape clause, Ms Sturgeon said. Why don't you ask your bosses in Westminster to make that choice and remove the rape clause once and for all?Ms Dugdale joined the attack, dramatically brandishing the form women must complete while challenging the Scottish Tory leader: Your Tory party is just as callous and heartless as it has always been, is it not?Ms Davidson defended the policy, arguing: This is about ensuring that people who have had children in the very worst of circumstances get extra help. According to the response, 49% of Radio 1's playlist features artists without a top 10 single, while Capital FM includes just 12%. Similarly, BBC One dedicates 27% of its primetime schedule to factual programming, compared to ITV's 12%.This defense comes as the government concludes its public consultation on the BBC's charter renewal, which has attracted more than 80,000 responses, according to culture secretary John Whittingdale's announcement at the Conservative Party Conference this week.When launching the green paper in July, Mr Whittingdale indicated that hard questions would be posed regarding the BBC's scale and ambitions, questioning whether the corporation should attempt to do all things or adopt a more precise approach.The BBC's response acknowledges that the Government consultation is right to insist that the BBC should be distinctive. Seven party leaders clashed in Thursday evening's televised debate, the sole occasion Prime Minister David Cameron and Labour's Ed Miliband would share a platform before the 7 May general election.Scotland's public funding sparked heated exchanges when UKIP's Nigel Farage declared English taxpayers were cheesed off with money flowing north of the border. However, SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon countered that Scots had paid more tax per head of population in every single year for the last 34 years.Cameron promoted Conservative economic policies, stating: Let's not go back to square one, Britain can do so much better than that. Meanwhile, Miliband outlined his prime ministerial agenda, repeatedly using the phrase if I am prime minister while promising minimum wage increases, zero-hours contract bans, and NHS rescue efforts.Liberal Democrat Nick Clegg joined the debate alongside Plaid Cymru's Leanne Wood and Green Party leader Natalie Bennett, creating an unprecedented seven-way political showdown.Post-debate polling revealed mixed results across different surveys. YouGov's 1,100-person poll crowned Sturgeon the clear winner with 28%, followed by Farage at 20%, Cameron at 18%, Miliband at 15%, Clegg at 10%, Bennett at 5%, and Wood at 4%. However, ComRes polling for ITV showed a four-way tie between Cameron, Miliband, Farage, and Sturgeon, though Cameron led on leadership capability questions.ICM's Guardian poll favored Miliband with 25% support, narrowly ahead of Cameron's 24%, while Farage secured 19% and Sturgeon 17%, with Clegg trailing at 9%. The Daily Mirror's Survation poll placed both Tory and Labour leaders tied at 25%, Farage close behind at 24%, Sturgeon at 15%, Clegg at 6%, Bennett at 3%, and Wood at 2%.YouGov's Times scoring system awarded Sturgeon 6.7 out of 10, while Miliband and Cameron each received 5.9, with Clegg and Farage both scoring 5.5.Opening the debate, Sturgeon positioned the SNP—polling suggests record Westminster representation—as Scotland's champion while extending friendship to England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, promising to help to bring about change for you too.Farage challenged Scotland's financial arrangements, claiming canny Scots had secured advantageous terms under the Barnett formula. He argued: This all has to be rebalanced because frankly English taxpayers are a bit cheesed off with so much of their money going over Hadrian's wall, giving people no prescription charges and no university tuition.The debate highlighted Britain's transformed political landscape. Where two parties once dominated, and three-party politics seemed permanent just five years ago, seven politicians—including three women—now commanded the stage.Sturgeon, dressed boldly in red, attacked the old boys' network in SW1, while the female participants appeared coordinated in their early assault on Westminster austerity policies.Cameron framed the election choice starkly: The choice at this election is sticking with a plan that is working or going back to the debt, taxes, borrowing and spending that got us in this mess in the first place. I say let's not go back to square one. Britain can do so much better than that.He added: The problem - and the real choice - is with Ed Miliband, who still thinks the last government didn't tax too much and borrow too much.Miliband fired back, accusing Cameron of dwelling on the past rather than addressing the future: Some people will tell you that this is as good as it gets for Britain. I say Britain can do so much better than it has done over the last five years.European Union membership emerged as another flashpoint, with Miliband criticizing Cameron's European marginalization: I don't think our place lies outside the EU. I think that would be a disaster for jobs, a disaster for families and business.Miliband also attacked Clegg for betraying young people over tuition fees, prompting the Liberal Democrat leader to challenge Miliband's pious stance and demand an apology for crashing the economy.Clegg confronted Cameron over deficit reduction strategies, questioning his refusal to ask the wealthy to contribute more while imposing ideologically-driven cuts. Responding to Cameron's competence and chaos election framing, Clegg urged him to imagine the chaos in people's lives caused by health, education, and childcare spending cuts.The SNP reported gaining 1,200 new members during the two-hour broadcast. Deputy leader Stewart Hosie MP claimed victory based on averaged polling data, highlighting Sturgeon's strong and persuasive performance.Scottish Labour's Jim Murphy emphasized the debate's clarity regarding Scottish electoral choices: In the debate there were seven passionate speakers but only two potential prime ministers. There are lots of ways to protest against David Cameron but only one way to replace him.UKIP's Scottish MEP David Coburn defended Farage's comments on Radio Scotland's Good Morning Scotland programme: I think most reasonable Scots believe in the fair allocation of money. I think the SNP may make a big fuss about this but I think fair minded Scots like myself and everyone else believe we should give the English a reasonable deal too.

text: Restrictions put on terror suspects by the home secretary may be withering on the vine, a group of MPs and peers has warned. A parliamentary committee has declared that the incoming government following the 2015 election must urgently address the effectiveness and role of Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPims), warning that the counter-terrorism tool appears to be losing its practical utility.The Joint Committee on Human Rights issued a report emphasizing the inherent danger of subjects disappearing while under TPim supervision. However, the Home Office defended the measures as representing the most robust protections that judicial authorities would permit.Under TPim arrangements, individuals face multiple constraints: mandatory overnight residence at designated addresses, electronic GPS monitoring, regular reporting obligations, and severe limitations on travel, movement, personal associations, communications, financial activities, employment, and educational pursuits.**Analysis by Dominic Casciani, Home Affairs Correspondent, BBC News**The TPim system faces a dramatic reduction in scope - by month's end, six suspects will gain their freedom, leaving just one individual under monitoring conditions. The secretive nature of these arrangements makes it impossible to confirm whether additional unknown subjects exist.Control orders, TPims' more restrictive predecessor, faced widespread criticism for imposing house-arrest conditions deemed unjust and oppressive. TPims not only inherited these detractors but attracted additional opposition, including security professionals who argued the revised system had become insufficiently stringent.Currently showing promise is an earlier intervention strategy involving charges for terrorism preparation offenses. This approach may encompass suspects who previously would have faced TPim consideration due to police concerns about substantial intelligence lacking concrete courtroom evidence.**System Overview and Concerns**December 2011 marked TPims' introduction, replacing the stricter control order framework to prevent suspected terrorist activities. The committee's report revealed eight active TPim notices as of November, all targeting British nationals.However, seven of these arrangements will terminate by month's end, according to the findings. The committee advocated for TPim examination within broader counter-terrorism power reviews.Government officials were urged to engage more transparently and substantively with terrorism legislation reviewer recommendations. The report concluded: We are left with the impression that in practice TPims may be withering on the vine as a counter-terrorism tool of practical utility.Committee members determined the measures lacked genuine investigative qualities, suggesting alternative terminology like Terrorism Prevention Orders. They endorsed the independent reviewer's assessment that TPims inherently carries an inherent risk of the subject absconding.**High-Profile Disappearances**Two notable cases highlighted these escape risks. Mohammed Ahmed Mohamed, connected to Somali militant organization al-Shabab, vanished in November after donning a burka during a west London mosque visit. His disappearance followed Ibrahim Magag's December 2012 escape via black taxi after removing his electronic monitoring device.Committee Chairman Hywel Francis stated: There is no evidence that they serve any investigative function and even as preventive measures they seem to be going out of favour with the agencies. Very few TPims are in operation and almost all of these are due shortly to lapse after their two-year duration.Francis emphasized insufficient available information about affected individuals prevents proper assessment of whether imposing such powers remains necessary. The next government will need to look again at these measures within the context of counter-terrorism powers more generally, he added.**Expert Perspectives**David Anderson, terrorism legislation's independent reviewer, described TPims as a necessary evil during BBC Radio 4's Today programme. One thing it shows is that police and prosecutors are doing their job, he observed. We've had a lot of convictions over the last couple of years, a lot of guilty pleas and a lot of heavy sentences.Anderson noted TPims don't present a long-term solution.Home Secretary Theresa May claimed TPims would assist authorities in gathering prosecution-supporting evidence. Nevertheless, the committee reported it failed to find any evidence linking the measures to increased suspect charges.Seven suspects face lifted or soon-to-expire TPim restrictions, including individuals allegedly involved in terrorist attack planning. These two-year measures cannot undergo renewal.A Home Office spokesperson responded: TPims were introduced because control orders were not working and their powers were being struck down by the courts. They now provide some of the strongest possible protections that the courts will allow.

text: The idea that party leaders are decisively important in the winning or losing of general elections is implicit in much political journalism and it is a belief that some political leaders themselves - Tony Blair, in particular - have been eager to propagate. The conventional wisdom proves false in most cases.Only when elections hang by the thinnest of margins can a leader's personal appeal and the gap between their popularity and that of their main rival truly tip the scales from defeat to victory. Indeed, it's quite common for the less popular leader's party to emerge victorious on election day.Consider the oft-cited Margaret Thatcher's rout of James Callaghan - yet the Labour leader enjoyed a commanding 20-point lead over Mrs Thatcher right before the Conservative triumph in 1979. The victory belonged not to Thatcher personally, but to the Conservative Party over Labour.Post-World War Two UK electoral analysis reveals that Harold Wilson stands alone as the only leader whose personal influence could have determined whether his party governed or sat in opposition - and this occurred just twice, in October 1964 and February 1974. These razor-thin contests saw Wilson commanding vastly superior popularity compared to his Conservative opponents: Sir Alec Douglas-Home in 1964 and Edward Heath in 1974. Notably, the Conservatives still captured the 1970 election despite Wilson's continued popularity advantage over Heath.Given that May 2015's election appears destined for cliff-hanger status, with no single party likely achieving overall majority, might journalists' obsessive leader-focus finally prove warranted? Almost certainly not.Both major parties should strategically allocate substantial interview opportunities to other front-bench figures rather than overexposing David Cameron and Ed Miliband throughout what promises to be Britain's longest campaign in memory - a full four months, thanks to the fixed election date. Nick Clegg might wisely share whatever diminished spotlight the Liberal Democrats can secure, particularly with Vince Cable initially.Mr Clegg faces slim odds of replicating his 2010 campaign success, when he dominated as the standout performer among the three party leaders, especially during televised debates. Even then, despite unprecedented media exposure and rampant Cleggmania, the party's national vote climbed merely 1%, leaving the Lib Dems with five fewer MPs than in 2005.Nigel Farage will undoubtedly maintain his dominance over UKIP coverage, though the defection and subsequent election of two Conservative MPs under the UKIP banner makes him appear less of a solo act than previously. However, UKIP's ascendancy stems not from exceptional leadership ability - Farage possesses oratorical gifts, but his ministerial potential remains unknown and perhaps unknowable. Instead, their by-election victories and polling success primarily reflect the party's role as immigration sentiment's respectable voice.While major parties avoided the immigration debate, UKIP gave voice to widespread public concerns about high immigration levels. Their European Union membership challenge resonates less with most voters, except where it connects to immigration issues. The EU itself and sovereignty questions certainly matter deeply to many Conservative and UKIP activists alike.UKIP likely won't capture more than a handful of general election seats, yet they could significantly influence outcomes by drawing more Conservative than Labour votes. The crucial question remains: how stark will the difference be between Conservative and Labour defections to UKIP - potentially very substantial, favoring Labour electorally if the party can convince core supporters it hasn't abandoned them or its roots.The Green Party may or may not expand beyond its single House of Commons seat, but possesses potential to affect numerous constituency outcomes. Media leader-fixation may prevent the Greens from receiving attention their support levels merit, particularly among young voters. How many street-stopped citizens could identify the current Green party leader? Not Caroline Lucas - Natalie Bennett.The Greens' collective leadership approach may have cost them media coverage, yet hasn't prevented them from surpassing Liberal Democrat support - 7% nationally versus the Lib Dems' 6% in the final pre-Christmas YouGov poll. The Greens will certainly erode Lib Dem votes in May's election while threatening Labour in some marginal constituencies.Among all non-Conservative, non-Labour parties - including Northern Ireland's significant parties - the Scottish National Party uniquely may hold the electoral key for this UK general election. By objective measures, they represent a more serious political force than UKIP and will likely secure far more seats.Unlike UKIP, with whom they're sometimes misleadingly compared, the SNP has proven governmental competence and effectiveness. After governing as Scotland's minority administration from 2007 to 2011, they achieved outright majority in 2011 despite a highly proportional electoral system specifically designed to prevent any single party - especially the SNP - from monopolizing government positions.Historically, Scots have voted differently for Westminster versus Edinburgh parliaments. Labour not only won 41 of 59 Scottish seats in 2010's general election but increased its Scottish vote share by 2.5% while dropping 6.5% UK-wide.Labour's House of Commons majority prospects after May 7 depend heavily on retaining most Scottish seats. Currently, this appears unlikely. A December 2014 ICM general election poll showed the SNP leading Labour by 17 points, with other parties trailing distantly.Without regaining credibility north of the border, Labour faces the prospect of Scottish House of Commons seats falling to nationalist control. The SNP's two-decade rise has frequently been credited to Alex Salmond's exceptional leadership abilities. While his political talent is undeniable, this again exemplifies overattributing success to individual leaders.Following Nicola Sturgeon's seamless leadership transition - herself a formidable politician - party support has continued growing. The SNP categorically refuses to support any Conservative government but might, for a price, sustain a Labour administration.Such arrangements carry profound implications. The predictable English backlash would fuel the separatist party's agenda while spelling long-term trouble for Labour - and for the British state's continued existence within current boundaries.
