But the EU itself and the question of sovereignty are of course of great importance to both Conservatives and UKIP activists. While the big parties avoided the discussion of the high level of migration, UKIP gave a good voice to the general concern about high migration. The crucial question is the difference between the number of Conservative and Labour defectors to UKIP - a very big difference which would be extremely beneficial for Labour, if it could convince its core voters that it had not abandoned them and its roots. The Green Party may or may not get more than one seat in the House of Commons, but it has the potential to influence many districts. How many people you stop in the street, who know who the current leader of the Green Party is? Not Caroline Luca but Natalie Bennet. Of all the non-Conservative, non-Liberal parties of the United Kingdom, and that includes the parties of the Republic of Ireland, the Scottish National Party is the one which, in the end, may hold the electoral key to this British general election. It is a more serious political force than UKIP and is certain to win more seats. The Scottish people have always voted differently in the two parliaments. The Greens' collective leadership policy may have lost them some media coverage, but it has not prevented them from beating the Liberals in the last YouGov poll, by 7 to 6, at the end of December. The Greens will certainly take Liberal votes in May and may even threaten the Labour Party in some of the marginal seats. On the prospect of a majority in the House of Commons after the 7th of May, depends in large measure on the preservation of the majority of Scottish seats. Not only did the Labour party win 41 of the 59 Scottish seats in the last general election, but it also increased its vote in Scotland by two thousand five hundred, whereas it lost six thousand votes in the United Kingdom. After governing Scotland from 2007 to 2011, it attained in 2011 a clear majority, despite a highly proportional system, specially designed to prevent any party, especially the SNP, from monopolizing power. The rise of the SNP over the last two decades has been credited to the exceptional leadership of Alex Salmond. It’s no use denying that he was an extremely talented politician, but this tendency to over-credit success to a single individual is a problem again. The party’s rise under Nicola Sturgeon’s leadership is equally impressive. Such a combination would have profound consequences. The Scottish National Party refuses to support any Conservative government, but for a price it would support a Labour government. And without a resurgence of its popularity in Scotland, the Labour party faces the possibility of losing Scottish seats in the House of Commons to the nationalists. English reaction would provide a field for the nationalists and would cause long-term trouble for the Labour Party and for the continuation of the British State within its present boundaries.

text: Swedish journalists Johan Persson and Martin Schibbye have been speaking to the BBC about their time in prison in Ethiopia. After spending more than 400 days behind bars serving an 11-year sentence, the pair has now been released. Martin Schibbye and Johan Persson faced convictions for illegal entry into the country and providing support to the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), a rebel organization.The case thrust Ethiopia's treatment of journalists into the international spotlight due to their harsh sentences. In June 2011, both men were captured alongside ONLF rebels while working in the region.The journalists consistently argued they were simply performing their professional duties. Amnesty International, the human rights organization, declared that the pair had been prosecuted for conducting legitimate work. However, Ethiopian government spokesman Bereket Simon had previously justified the imprisonment, claiming the journalists were caught red handed collaborating with terrorist organisations.Reports indicate that former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi pardoned the journalists prior to his death in August, which led to their eventual freedom.Speaking to the BBC World Service programme Newsday, Johan Persson described the appalling prison conditions they endured. It was 200% overcrowded. It was very hot. There was a lack of water. It was dusty. There were rats, fleas and many people were sick with HIV or tuberculosis, he said.More concerning than the physical conditions, according to Persson, was the prison's population composition: What's interesting is who they put in there: journalists and the political opposition.While both men acknowledge entering Ethiopia illegally, they maintain their trial lacked fairness. The trial was a joke, said Mr Persson. Meles Zenawi was saying on national television, three or four weeks before the trial started, that we were guilty.The terrorism support charge that resulted in their conviction, they argue, represents a broader pattern of abuse against Ethiopian journalists. For the last few years Ethiopia has been using its anti-terror legislation to crack down on the media and to crack down on journalism, Mr Schibbye told Newsday.The freelance reporters had spent four days in the Ogaden—an ethnic Somali region in eastern Ethiopia—before their arrest occurred. Martin Schibbye recounted their capture: The Ethiopian army spotted us. Then they followed in our footsteps for three to four days. Then they ambushed us.We were attacked by about 150 Ethiopian army soldiers who opened fire on us. We got hit quite quickly. I got hit in the shoulder and Johan got hit in the arm. Somebody shouted, 'media, media, international press,' and we were arrested, said Martin Schibbye.Following their detention, the journalists claim they were forced at gunpoint to participate in filming that would later document their alleged relationship with the Ogaden National Liberation Front. Two civilians, who we'd never seen before, were dressed up as rebels. The soldiers gave them guns and stood them in front of us, and they testified against us and said that we came with them from Somalia, says Mr Schibbye.According to the journalists, senior Ethiopian civilian officials orchestrated the filming. This was not being done by some crazy militia: the director was the vice president in the region, and in the evening the regional president called us and said, 'We are not satisfied by your performances in the film,' said Mr Schibbye. This fabricated footage was subsequently presented as evidence during their court proceedings.Local ethnic Somalis have maintained an insurgency in Ethiopia's eastern Ogaden region, creating a volatile environment. We were walking through villages where there had been people living till recently, but now they had fled, forced out by the conflict. There was heavy fighting and that was one of the reasons why we were detected and followed and ambushed by the Ethiopian army, Mr Persson said.Despite their year-long imprisonment ordeal, both journalists express no remorse about their Ethiopian assignment. Martin Schibbye views risk-taking as an essential aspect of foreign correspondence, believing journalists must reject the notion of no-go zones.His colleague shares this conviction: As long as governments make laws to protect themselves against journalists, our job is to break those laws. I would do the same again today.

text: Belfast bantamweight Michael Conlan earned a morale boosting win for the Ireland boxing team at the Olympics as he clinched a quarter-finals place. Avagyan's most notable career accomplishment remains his European Championship bronze medal from three years prior.While the Armenian fighter improved his output during the latter portion of round one, Conlan had already secured sufficient advantage to claim a 10-9 verdict across all three judges' scorecards.Early in the second round, the 2012 flyweight bronze medallist found himself momentarily vulnerable when caught by a significant left hook while pressed against the ropes. Nevertheless, Conlan responded effectively with multiple quality shots, again capturing the round 10-9 unanimously.Entering the final round trailing on points, Avagyan adopted a more aggressive approach out of necessity. text: A year into power, if there is one thing that becomes clearer about the Xi Jinping leadership of the Communist Party of China, it is that it understands the value of political symbolism. When Mr Xi assumed the role of party secretary last November, among his earliest destinations was Shenzhen—sacred ground of the Reform and Opening up Process that began in 1978 and home to one of China's most vibrant Special Economic Zones.The pivotal December 1978 gathering at Beijing's Jingxi Hotel witnessed ideological breakthroughs that enabled China to embrace foreign investment and market mechanisms. More than three and a half decades later, approximately 400 party elites reconvened at this identical venue—a symbolic choice that sparked anticipation of momentous developments.However, the communique released on 12 November following the three-day Third Plenum of the 18th Party Congress should dispel any expectations that this leadership intends to orchestrate the same dramatic transformation achieved in 1978.The context has fundamentally shifted. Unlike the exhausted nation emerging from late Maoism that desperately needed radical economic revitalization, today's China operates as a global economic powerhouse with immense potential for the coming decades. Any misstep now carries far greater consequences than in that earlier era. The current challenge, as Premier Li Keqiang articulates, involves unlocking internal growth sources rather than changing course entirely.The plenum's most significant message centers on enhancing and perfecting market mechanisms while liberalizing sectors that could generate new growth. No fundamental departure from the established trajectory appears necessary at present.Challenging the core tenets of the Reform and Opening Up period was never a realistic possibility. The plenum report affirms the party's primacy with unmistakable clarity, maintaining its paramount societal role. Internal unity and collective leadership remain as treasured as during the Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao administration.Through Deng Xiaoping theory and Socialism with Chinese characteristics, the goal remains achieving the primary state of socialism—a process the communique acknowledges will require many years.The document contains more explicit references to establishing a national security coordination body. This appears to represent the previous leadership's pro-stability obsession in new form, attempting to finally coordinate and streamline security decision-making. This becomes particularly relevant since the current Politburo Standing Committee lacks a member with specific security responsibilities, unlike its predecessor.Q&A: China's Third Plenum Third Plenum: Key issuesThis leadership continues prioritizing stability highly. The early November car explosion in Tiananmen, coupled with the simultaneous homemade bomb attack in Taiyuan, will only reinforce their conviction that relaxing vigilance isn't viable.Before the plenum, Politburo member Yu Zhengsheng referenced impending deeper reforms. These clearly involve implementing more flexible systems allowing rural residents to relocate to urban areas, secure employment, establish residence, access social welfare, and—perhaps most crucially—educate their children there.Recent months have seen heavy government emphasis on accelerating urbanization. Creating frameworks to enfranchise rural dwellers and provide relocation incentives becomes essential. Yet implementation remains critical—while the stated intentions appear robust, the challenge lies in convincing provincial governments they can absorb costs associated with new citizen waves requiring social services.Whether provinces will receive expanded tax-raising powers remains unspecified, though this would seem a logical consequence of residential influxes.Regarding economic reform, developing financial markets emerges as the strongest theme. Here we observe Li Keqiang's intellectual influence—he's most closely associated with October's Shanghai Free Trade Zone establishment, where China might liberalize its capital account and accelerate yuan trading.Finance represents a critical sector for this leadership, serving as a key mechanism for delivering high service economy components and creating high value-added economic structures.This plenum provides a framework confirming themes already emerging from current leadership: no rapid ideological or political transformation, continued emphasis on material well-being, sustained growth pursuit, with urbanization achievement before 2020 as the primary driver.The plan's boldest feature stakes nearly everything on urban China resolving current growth challenges, sustainability issues, and inequality problems. This represents an enormous gamble, as China's planned urbanization rate exceeds any society's previous attempts.Vast questions remain about achieving social cohesion and determining what social and political structures might ultimately emerge to create the harmonious society the previous leadership frequently championed.Kerry Brown is professor of Chinese politics at the University of Sydney, team leader of the Europe China Research and Advice Network (ECRAN) funded by the European Union, and an Associate Fellow of the Asia Programme at Chatham House.

text: Spain and Germany sought to reassure investors that Spain would not need a full international bailout, after its borrowing costs hit a record high. A joint statement from German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble and Spanish counterpart Luis de Guindos challenged market sentiment, arguing that Tuesday's record-breaking 7.6% yield on Spain's 10-year government bonds failed to accurately represent the nation's economic fundamentals - essentially dismissing the market's assessment of the country's implied borrowing costs.Wednesday will see Mr Guindos meeting with French Finance Minister Laurent Fabius as Spain's deteriorating financial position continues alarming investors. Rising borrowing costs compound concerns, while the Catalonia region has announced its need for government funding assistance.Spain asserted Tuesday that both Italy and France support immediate implementation of measures agreed during last month's negotiations. The proposed aid would target Spanish banks directly without burdening national debt levels. According to Spain, there has been a worrying delay in executing agreements hammered out during the 29 June eurozone leaders summit.Central to these provisions is enabling the future European bailout fund - the ESM - to inject capital directly into struggling banks, particularly those in Spain, while bypassing national governments entirely. However, constitutional challenges in Germany have stalled the fund's creation, preventing Berlin from ratifying the agreement until 12 September.Speed is an essential condition for the success of any European action, declared the Spanish foreign ministry's statement.France's European Affairs Minister Bernard Cazeneuve, however, flatly denied any agreement with Italy and Spain regarding immediate implementation. It makes no sense to say that. We are following the decisions taken at the European summit and are working on them, Mr Cazeneuve stated.The Italian government similarly issued a categorical denial of participation in any joint initiative alongside Spain.Market tensions over Spain's financial strain are reflected in the record-high yield on the government's benchmark 10-year bond. Rating agency Moody's has warned that Spain faces increased likelihood of requiring a full bailout, which would pressure the eurozone's strongest economies, particularly Germany.By Andrew Walker BBC World Service Economics correspondentThe difference between problematic and ultimately unsustainable debt situations often hinges on higher borrowing costs. However, the impact on interest bills develops slowly - explaining why bond yield spikes don't immediately devastate Spanish government finances. The process resembles turning an oil tanker.Government borrowing typically involves selling bonds - promises to repay - with effective interest rates fixed for each bond batch's lifetime. Every time Spain seeks new market funding, the prevailing interest rate becomes part of total borrowing costs. The upward trend means the tanker gradually turns toward the rocks. The eurozone must decide whether to seize control, providing new bailout assistance to prevent further borrowing cost increases.Consequently, the agency shifted Germany's AAA credit rating outlook to negative - the initial step toward potential downgrade within two years.Monday saw Spain's market regulator attempting to restrict investment selling through widespread short-selling bans. This market technique allows traders to sell stock before delivery, expecting price drops that enable cheaper purchases to fulfill orders.Additional developments include:Spain has secured a 100bn euro ($125bn; £80bn) loan package for bank use - different support from bailouts provided to Greece, Ireland and Portugal. However, several of the country's 17 autonomous regions face deep debt and are queuing to access a new 18bn-euro public fund.By Gavin Hewitt Europe editorCatalonia's assistance request, the second-largest region, follows Valencia's similar call for help. text: In January 1842, Charles Dickens arrived on American shores for the first time. These are external links and will open in a new windowWhen Charles Dickens arrived in Boston, Massachusetts, crowds welcomed him with rock star enthusiasm. Yet behind the celebrity treatment lay a serious mission: the renowned novelist was determined to stop the flood of cheap, poorly-made pirated editions of his books circulating throughout America.Such unauthorized copies spread freely because United States law offered no copyright protection to foreign authors. Dickens expressed his outrage in a scathing letter to a friend, using a vivid metaphor to describe his predicament. He likened the situation to being robbed and then forced to parade publicly in absurd clothing.Is it tolerable that besides being robbed and rifled, Dickens wrote, an author should be forced to appear in any form - in any vulgar dress - in any atrocious company?While Dickens's metaphor was both powerful and theatrical, the argument for what he demanded - legal protection preventing the free copying and adaptation of creative ideas - has never been straightforward.50 Things That Made the Modern Economy highlights the inventions, ideas and innovations that helped create the economic world. It is broadcast on the BBC World Service. You can find more information about the programme's sources and listen online or subscribe to the programme podcast.Copyright and patents create monopolies by design. Dickens's British publishers would have extracted maximum profits from Bleak House copies, leaving cash-poor literary enthusiasts empty-handed. However, these substantial potential profits serve as powerful incentives for innovation.Writing Bleak House required considerable time and effort from Dickens. Had other British publishers been able to copy his work as freely as American publishers did, he might never have undertaken the project at all.Intellectual property therefore represents an economic balancing act - a fundamental trade-off. Overly generous protection for creators means beneficial ideas spread too slowly through copying and adaptation. Insufficient protection might discourage the creation of valuable ideas entirely.Politics has always influenced this delicate balance. During the 1800s, Britain's legal framework provided robust protection for British authors and inventors because the UK dominated global culture and innovation - much as it does today.However, American literature and technological innovation remained underdeveloped during Dickens's era. The US economy operated in aggressive copying mode, seeking the cheapest possible access to Europe's finest intellectual offerings.American newspapers brazenly filled their pages with copied content while simultaneously publishing attacks on the meddlesome Mr. Dickens.Several decades later, as American authors and inventors gained prominence, US lawmakers developed increasing appreciation for intellectual property concepts. Newspapers that once opposed copyright protection now depend upon it for survival.Developing nations today follow similar patterns: the transition from copying others' ideas to creating original content correlates directly with stronger intellectual property protections. Recent developments illustrate this trend - China established its first copyright system only in 1991.Modern intellectual property concepts originated in 15th Century Venice, alongside many other innovations. Venetian patents explicitly aimed to encourage innovation through systematic protection.Inventors automatically received patents for useful inventions. Though temporary, these patents could be sold, transferred, or inherited during their validity period. Patents were forfeited if unused and invalidated if the invention closely resembled previous ideas.These remarkably modern concepts quickly generated equally modern complications.During Britain's industrial revolution, engineer James Watt developed superior steam engine designs. After spending months creating a prototype, he invested even greater effort in securing patent protection. His influential business partner Matthew Boulton successfully lobbied Parliament for patent extensions.Boulton and Watt leveraged their patent to extract licensing fees and destroy competitors - including Jonathan Hornblower, whose superior steam engine design led to his financial ruin and imprisonment.Despite the unsavory details, surely Watt's celebrated invention justified such measures? Perhaps not, according to economists Michele Boldrin and David Levine, who argue that steam-powered industry truly flourished only after the patent expired in 1800, when rival inventors finally revealed ideas they had suppressed for years.What happened to Boulton and Watt after losing their ability to sue competitors? They thrived regardless. Rather than pursuing litigation, they focused on manufacturing the world's finest steam engines. Their prices remained high while order books expanded dramatically.Rather than incentivizing steam engine improvements, the patent actually delayed technological progress.Yet intellectual property protection has become increasingly expansive since Boulton and Watt's time, not more restrictive.Copyright terms continue extending. Originally lasting 14 years with one renewal option in the US, they now persist for 70 years beyond the author's death - typically exceeding a century.Patents have broadened considerably, with grants issued for vague concepts. Amazon's one-click US patent protects the hardly revolutionary notion of purchasing internet products through single-button clicks.Through inclusion in so-called trade agreements, US intellectual property systems now exert global influence. Meanwhile, intellectual property scope continues expanding to encompass plants, buildings, and software.What makes gambling wrong but insurance right? TV Dinner: The hidden cost of the processed food revolution Geeks v government: The battle over public key cryptography How the world's first accountants counted on cuneiformThese expansions prove difficult to justify yet easy to explain: intellectual property generates enormous value for owners, justifying expensive legal and lobbying investments. Meanwhile, restriction costs spread widely among barely-aware consumers.Figures like Matthew Boulton and Charles Dickens possess strong incentives for aggressive lobbying toward more severe intellectual property laws, while steam engine purchasers and Bleak House readers rarely organize politically to object.Economists Boldrin and Levine propose a radical solution: eliminate intellectual property entirely.Alternative rewards for innovation exist - first-mover advantages over competitors, strong brand establishment, or superior product understanding. In 2014, Tesla opened its patent archive to expand the entire electric car industry, calculating overall company benefits.Most economists consider complete intellectual property elimination excessive, citing crucial cases like new medicines where invention costs are enormous while copying costs remain trivial.However, even intellectual property defenders generally argue that current protections provide more than adequate incentives for new idea creation.Dickens himself eventually discovered financial advantages in weak copyright protection. Twenty-five years after his initial US visit, he returned seeking profit opportunities. He calculated that widespread readership of cheap unauthorized copies had created sufficient fame to support a lucrative lecture tour.His calculation proved correct: leveraging pirated work distribution, Charles Dickens earned millions in today's currency through public speaking engagements.Perhaps intellectual property proved more valuable when freely distributed.Tim Harford writes the Financial Times's Undercover Economist column. 50 Things That Made the Modern Economy is broadcast on the BBC World Service. You can find more information about the programme's sources and listen online or subscribe to the programme podcast.

text: The gap between male and female life expectancy is closing and men could catch up by 2030, according to an adviser for the Office for National Statistics. Research by Prof Les Mayhew reveals that the life expectancy gap between men and women, which reached its peak of nearly six years during the 1970s, is steadily narrowing as male longevity rates climb more rapidly than female rates.The dramatic decline in male smoking habits appears to be the primary driver behind this convergence. Prof Mayhew, who holds a statistics professorship at Cass Business School, conducted his analysis using life expectancy data from England and Wales, specifically examining survival prospects for 30-year-olds.While men have trailed significantly behind women for decades, his research demonstrates they are now catching up. Should present patterns persist, Prof Mayhew forecasts that both genders could achieve an average lifespan of 87 years by 2030.What's interesting at the moment is that in the last 20 years or so, male life expectancy at 30 has jumped by about six years and if it jumps by the same amount in the next 20 years it will converge with female life expectancy, he said.Healthier male lifestyles appear to be the underlying cause. One of the main reasons, I think, is the trend in the prevalence of smoking. Smoking took off after 1920 in the male population and at its high about 80% of males smoked, Prof Mayhew explained.This was reflected in more divergence in the life expectancy, so by the time you get to about 1970 it was at its peak - the difference in life expectancy was about 5.7 years.Additional contributing factors include the shift toward safer, office-based employment. Previously, millions of men labored in dangerous industries like coal mining. Medical advances have also extended male lifespans, particularly benefiting those with heart disease—a condition that disproportionately affects men—allowing them to live considerably longer than previous generations.Women, conversely, adopted smoking habits later than men, though female smoking rates are now declining rapidly while male rates plummet even faster.Despite these trends, gender disparities in life expectancy persist from birth. The study focused exclusively on individuals who had survived to age 30, but boys face higher mortality risks during their first year and are more prone to engaging in dangerous activities or experiencing fatal accidents throughout their lives.This suggests women may maintain their longevity advantage for the foreseeable future.Prof David Leon from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine noted: In virtually all countries in the world, women do have a slight advantage.Nevertheless, he acknowledged that this gap is definitively shrinking in certain nations.Countries with lower overall life expectancy, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, exhibit minimal gender differences. This occurs because infectious diseases are not picky about men and women, Prof Leon explained.Conversely, nations that have largely conquered infectious diseases, such as those in Eastern Europe, display much larger disparities mostly dominated by lifestyle factors.Russia exemplified this extreme during the 1990s, when the life expectancy gap reached 13 years—an absolutely massive difference in what Prof Leon characterized as a very gendered society.The UK represents his third category of countries where life expectancy gaps are beginning to contract.Men are getting a bit better behaved and women are adopting male life expectancies, he said.

text: How often do we really look into someone's eyes? Strangers exchange fleeting glances on busy streets, while we gaze affectionately at loved ones - yet rarely do we maintain eye contact beyond mere seconds.This happens far too infrequently, according to Nuala McKeever, who describes herself as a happiness teacher. The 40-year-old believes sustained eye contact offers a pathway to powerful, spiritual reconnection between people, and her understanding of the human spirit runs deep.Following her departure from a high-pressure financial services career, Nuala embarked on a transformative journey that ultimately led her to become a 'laughter-yoga' instructor. Though originally from Londonderry, she has made Belfast her home and collaborates with friend Michelle Major to operate the Sunshine Project.Their mission centers on spreading peace and love, which brought the duo to an area near Victoria Square, Belfast, on Thursday. There, they organized an event inviting passersby to experience 60 seconds of unbroken eye contact with volunteers.Curious about this intimate encounter with a stranger, I decided to participate.The team established their setup at Belfast's Corn Market during the lunch hour. Volunteer gazers took positions within hula hoops, seated on cushions or chairs, with empty spaces positioned directly in front of them. Public participants were invited to sit or stand facing these volunteers and engage in wordless, sustained eye contact for exactly one minute.Nuala became my partner for the exercise. She instructed that we should each focus on the other's left eye - a technique designed to prevent the natural tendency to break contact by shifting our gaze between eyes.Discomfort immediately set in as our 60-second session commenced. Meanwhile, Nuala appeared completely serene, her head tilted gently to one side. The urge to examine her facial features or look away intensified as time passed, but our eyes remained locked together.Gradually accepting this constraint and allowing myself to relax, I began experiencing the practice's beneficial effects. A profound calm washed over me while everything in my peripheral vision blurred into insignificance. Momentarily, we seemed to be the sole occupants of the bustling city center.The session's conclusion brought Nuala's arms around me in an embrace - a gesture that would have felt far stranger without our preceding minute of intense eye contact. She confided that I had stirred emotions in her, though she couldn't identify the reason.I often see myself when I stare into someone's eyes, she said. Eye contact is how we connect as human beings and it is different every time, but it always reminds me that I am part of something much bigger than myself. When we look into each other's eyes we see beyond our difference, I can't think of anywhere where this is more important than in Belfast.Participant Marcela Vojacova, 44, shared her motivation for joining the project. I wanted to see what could be achieved by staring into another person's eyes and what I might see, she said. When I take part I feel a sense of fulfilment, love and happiness - I hope the other people do too.Mark Graham approached the event seeking stress relief and found himself pleasantly surprised by the outcome. I have a job interview coming up and sharing 60 seconds with Marcela really helped me to relax, he said. For the time we were sharing the experience it was like no one else was around. I think a lot of people would laugh at the idea of taking part in something like this but it could be really helpful for some.

text: Free movement of workers in the EU has made life tougher for low paid workers in the UK, Andy Burnham has said. In his inaugural major address as shadow home secretary, Andy Burnham launched an appeal aimed at reclaiming Labour supporters who had defected to UKIP.During his speech, Burnham challenged Labour's previous stance, declaring it was not true that free movement had benefited everybody as the party had historically maintained.UKIP responded by calling Burnham's remarks a welcome recognition of the blindingly obvious, though they argued that if he genuinely wanted to address the issue, he should advocate for Britain's EU departure.Meanwhile, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn—who decisively defeated Burnham in the leadership contest—has continued emphasizing the valuable contributions made by EU migrants to Britain.People that have migrated to this country over many years have made an enormous contribution to our society, helped our economic growth, helped our health service and helped our social services and our education services, so don't look upon immigration as necessarily a problem, it's often a very great opportunity, Corbyn stated during an interview on BBC Radio 4's Today programme.Corbyn acknowledged that Burnham had highlighted during the leadership campaign the government's need to focus more intensively on addressing shortages in doctors' surgeries, school places, and housing challenges in specific regions.However, Burnham argued in his Brighton address that Labour had failed to acknowledge certain consequences of EU migration, leaving the party appearing disconnected from public concerns.To win back the voters we lost to UKIP, I want to reframe the debate about immigration and the way Labour approaches it, he declared to the assembled delegates.For too long, we have argued that free movement across Europe benefits everyone and affects all areas equally. That's just not true.In places, a free market in labour benefits private companies more than people and communities. Labour hasn't faced up to that and that's why we look out of touch.Burnham positioned David Cameron's upcoming EU renegotiation—preceding the planned in/out referendum—as a crucial opportunity for worker protection.The truth is that free movement on the current rules is widening inequality. It has built the economic power of the big cities and that is good. But it has made life harder for people in our poorest communities, where wages have been undercut and job security lost.The coming referendum presents a chance to change that. Let's seize it as an opportunity to put Labour back on the front foot and back in touch.Let's put forward a new vision for a social Europe. A Europe that puts people before profits and multinationals; a floor beneath all workers. The Tories and UKIP want to take those protections away.Let's have the strength to take on their scapegoating rhetoric which won't pay anybody's bills, feed anybody's kids or protect anybody's job.We welcome people here to work, as we always have. But let's make it work for everyone with new EU rules to stop undercutting, protecting the going rate for skilled workers.UKIP employment spokeswoman and MEP Jane Collins dismissed Burnham's statements as the desperate attempts of a man who has ignored the plight of the working classes due to mass immigration for years.

text: Justin Timberlake has said he'll be performing at this year's Eurovision Song contest in Stockholm, Sweden. Eurovision will witness an unprecedented moment when Justin Timberlake takes the stage during Saturday's grand final interval, marking the first occasion in the competition's history that a globally renowned artist has performed independently at the event.The 35-year-old superstar will deliver a non-competitive performance, as clarified by Eurovision officials. His appearance represents a historic departure from traditional Eurovision programming.This is a fantastic opportunity, we are very happy and excited that Justin Timberlake will perform his new song together with his band in our show, stated Sven Stojanovic, one of the show's producers. It makes it extra special that the Swedish songwriters Max Martin and Shellback have co-written and co-produced the song together with Justin Timberlake.The nine-time Grammy award-winner will showcase Can't Stop the Feeling, his latest single created for the Dreamworks animation Trolls. This performance coincides with his promotional tour for the track.Broadcasting arrangements remain consistent with previous years, as Graham Norton returns to provide commentary for BBC One's live final coverage from the Globe Arena. Meanwhile, BBC Radio 1's Scott Mills will team up with The Great British Bake Off's Mel Giedroyc to co-host BBC Four's live semi-final broadcasts on 10 and 12 May.Timberlake's Eurovision announcement follows his recent appearance at this year's Bafta TV awards, where he joined actress Anna Kendrick to present the best drama series trophy to BBC Two's Wolf Hall.Recent Eurovision developments include Romania's expulsion from the competition due to unpaid fees. text: Pupils have been so violent or disruptive that on eight occasions last year teachers held ballots to refuse to teach them in their classes. NASUWT teachers' union members have conducted refusal to teach ballots in cases involving pupil assaults on staff, with students subsequently facing expulsion or relocation as a result.Schools minister Nick Gibb stated teachers had been given the backing they need to tackle poor behaviour following these union actions.According to NASUWT leader Chris Keates, this trend demonstrates deteriorating behavioral issues in schools. The frequency of such ballots across the UK has climbed for three consecutive years - from three instances in 2012 and four in 2013, reaching eight in 2014.During the union's annual Cardiff conference, officials revealed additional cases where ballot threats led to alternative arrangements for disruptive students without formal voting procedures.Several incidents prompted these ballots. In western England, a 16-year-old had attacked students, teachers, the head teacher, and responding police officers. Following the teachers' ballot, this pupil received off-site education. A north Wales secondary school teenager with a disruptive history threatened to slit the throat of another student, resulting in expulsion after teachers voted. At an English midlands secondary school, a student who the union claims had assaulted and threatened staff and pupils remained enrolled but was prohibited from NASUWT member-taught classes.Another ballot emerged from disagreement over teacher intervention with a student known for attacking others. When allegations surfaced that teachers had assaulted this pupil, a refusal to teach ballot followed, leading to the student's school removal.Ms Keates characterizes schools as facing a widespread and increasing problem of pupil indiscipline.The union surveyed members about behavioral experiences, collecting approximately 3,500 online responses. Nearly three-quarters claimed a widespread behaviour problem in schools today exists - exceeding last year's similar survey proportion.While not representing a comprehensive sample, 82% of respondents reported pupil verbal abuse and 38% faced parental abuse within the past year. Additionally, 23% experienced physical threats from students and 16% suffered assault.Respondents identified an excessive focus on data-driven targets as the primary factor in declining behavior, cited by almost two-thirds of teachers.Ms Keates attributed problems to expanding class sizes and the lack of support for children with special needs in mainstream schools.Saturday's conference will address pupil indiscipline, examining claims that behavioral standards suffer from a blame culture in schools that seeks to hold individual teachers responsible for poor pupil behaviour, whilst overlooking the critical role that school leaders should play.The motion will additionally critique inconsistent rule application regarding behavior policies.School reform minister Nick Gibb declared: The Conservative party is committed to giving schools the backing they need to tackle poor behaviour. That's why we've made it easier to search pupils, brought back same-day detentions and clarified teachers' power to use reasonable force.We've also made sure that a head teacher's ability to exclude pupils isn't undermined by external bodies. As a result, three quarters of teachers now rate behaviour in their school as good or better.A Liberal Democrat spokesman commented: It is vital that teachers have the resources they need to manage behaviour and support those children who need extra help.This is exactly why, in government, Liberal Democrats protected school budgets and introduced the pupil premium - extra money to support the children most likely to struggle in class.

text: Is banning a person from contesting for public office if he or she does not have a toilet at home a good idea? Gujarat's western state in India has taken a bold stance on sanitation by implementing unprecedented electoral requirements. This week, state legislators approved legislation mandating that candidates possess home toilets to qualify for municipal and village council elections. Current office holders face a six-month deadline to declare toilet ownership or risk disqualification.The initiative aligns with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's anti-open defecation campaign, a cornerstone priority since his May ascension to Delhi's leadership following his decade-long Gujarat governance. While the objective merits praise, critics argue the individual-focused approach fails to address manual scavenging's systemic horrors. Modi's BJP legislators in Gujarat have zealously embraced their leader's sanitation crusade.Open defecation undeniably devastates millions of Indian lives, creating persistent health crises. Nearly half the population continues this practice. Gujarat, despite ranking among India's wealthiest states, struggles with toilet infrastructure. Chief Minister Anandi Patel ambitiously targets open defecation free status within two years. Recent findings revealed over 70,000 Ahmedabad residents defecating outdoors in the state's primary city. Economic prosperity doesn't guarantee sanitation success.However, connecting democratic participation to private utility ownership raises troubling questions.Gujarat houses 40% of its population across 159 municipalities and eight municipal corporations, marking it among India's most urbanized regions. Over 18,500 villages contain approximately 13,500 councils. These electoral bodies prove vital for Gujarat's democratic health and developmental progress. Citizens possess inalienable rights to seek office in their communities.Economist Hemant Shah condemns the legislation as undemocratic and discriminatory, warranting court challenges.Gujarat's crowded cities contain thousands residing in sprawling chawls—cramped structures housing dozens of families sharing single toilets. Would chawl dwellers face electoral exclusion lacking private facilities? What becomes of shantytown residents whose entire living quarters match non-existent toilet dimensions?The government should first provide space and money to build toilets for the poor. The poor are most affected by urban planning because it has always excluded them. Now they can't dream from standing for public office just because they don't have the space or money to build their own toilets? asks Professor Shah. The question demands serious consideration.

text: Scientists have discovered another eight pieces of genetic code linked to osteoarthritis, bringing the total number to 11. Scientists have identified genetic factors responsible for at least half of an individual's susceptibility to osteoarthritis, a widespread joint condition, potentially paving the way for innovative treatment approaches.Published in *The Lancet*, the groundbreaking study analyzed DNA samples from 7,400 UK patients diagnosed with osteoarthritis alongside 11,000 healthy control subjects. This comparison enabled researchers to identify the most significant genetic code regions warranting detailed investigation.To validate their findings, the team conducted a follow-up analysis involving an additional 7,500 osteoarthritis patients and approximately 43,000 unaffected individuals from Iceland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and the UK.The expanded research not only confirmed three gene variants previously linked to the condition but also uncovered eight additional genetic associations with osteoarthritis development.Among the newly identified variants, the most impactful was located near the GNL3 gene region. This gene produces a crucial protein involved in cellular maintenance processes. Three additional variants were discovered in DNA sequences that regulate cartilage formation, bone development, and body weight control.However, researchers emphasize that additional investigation is essential to identify the precise DNA modifications within these genetic regions and determine their exact mechanisms in triggering osteoarthritis.John Loughlin, professor of musculoskeletal research at Newcastle University and one of the study's principal investigators, explained the significance of the findings: We know that osteoarthritis runs in families and that this is due to the genes that people pass on, rather than their shared environment. In this study we were able to say with a high degree of confidence which genetic regions are the major risk factors for developing osteoarthritis: the first time that this has been possible for this common yet complex disease. It's an important first step.Prof Alan Silman, medical director of Arthritis Research UK, the charity that funded the work, emphasized the breakthrough's importance: Until we understand the cause of this complex disease, we cannot hope to find a cure. This is a major breakthrough in our understanding of osteoarthritis, which we hope will help us to unlock the genetic basis of the disease.The research represents a crucial advancement in comprehending the hereditary components underlying this prevalent joint disorder, with experts believing inherited elements contribute to at least half of any person's risk of developing the condition.

text: The number of young men using steroids in London is rising on a regular basis a drugs charity has warned. The South Westminster Drug and Alcohol Service has reported a surge in young male clients seeking help for anabolic steroid abuse, marking a troubling shift in the demographic profile of users.While Home Office statistics indicate 60,000 people used steroids across the UK in 2014, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence warns this represents merely the tip of the iceberg. In response, NICE has recommended that gyms provide sharps bins for needle disposal.Roy Jones from the South Westminster service has witnessed this transformation firsthand. Our numbers are increasing on a regular basis, he explained. I've been working with steroid users for 16 years and when I first started, the guys taking them were body builders in their 30s. Now the average age I see is 23.This demographic shift concerns Professor Gillian Leng, deputy chief executive of NICE, who identifies a disturbing pattern among young professionals. It's fair to say it is becoming a much more normal thing to do among some groups of young men who are concerned about the way they look...injecting steroids has become a solution, she stated.The true scale of steroid use likely far exceeds official figures, according to professional bodies. Government statistics only capture individuals who end up in police custody, creating significant underreporting. Professor Leng elaborated: I think it is inevitable that the number is a lot higher. From the epidemiology (the data) we have about the kind of people who use steroids - it's a group that's not all going to appear in custody so that figure is bound to be the tip of the iceberg - it might be three times that number.**What are anabolic steroids?**A 25-year-old City of London worker, speaking anonymously to BBC London, exemplifies this trend. After two years of steroid use, he described purchasing drugs from a dealer at his local gym—a practice he says is common among his peers.I started taking them because I felt I couldn't get any bigger training naturally, he revealed. It was the next step for me. There's immense pressure to look good - it's part of the culture we live in, we all want that big figure.Major gym chains have begun responding to this crisis. Easygym has installed sharps bins across all locations, while Fitness First, Virgin Active and David Lloyd have implemented them in select clubs. These gyms maintain zero tolerance policies toward steroids, positioning the bins as health and safety measures for diabetic members and razor disposal.The Department of Health has delegated responsibility to local authorities, stating it had given local areas the power and the funding to tackle public health issues like this.However, the consequences can be fatal. Matthew Dear, 17, from Southend, died following an adverse reaction to steroids. His mother Tina established the Matthew Dear Foundation to educate people about steroid dangers.When we lost Matthew six years ago, people thought it was a problem that wasn't going to boil over, Tina said. We are now at that point where it is boiling over and somebody needs to take ownership.Natural bodybuilder Rolandas Malinauskas from east London, a former British Champion who strictly avoids steroids, believes many young men ignore the risks. In the long term, you do not win with steroids - they create a mirage, he warned. You can build muscle naturally but it takes time and dedication. Its all about precision, training and diet.

text: England seem set to end the series in South Africa with a defeat after a horrible start to their second innings. England's collapse to 18-3 from an overnight position of 52-3 suggests that only something extraordinary can prevent a comprehensive defeat, with the victory target of 382 now appearing entirely theoretical.While South Africa's pace bowling exposed England's well-documented vulnerabilities, it also demonstrated just how treacherous the Centurion surface becomes, particularly when facing the new ball. The familiar challenges were all present: mounting pressure, poor light conditions, England batting purely for survival rather than victory.Though one might expect England to have performed better, the new ball's behavior on this pitch creates immense difficulties. The unpredictability proves especially troublesome for batsmen when deliveries landing in identical spots produce completely contrasting reactions.Captain Alastair Cook experienced this firsthand - receiving one delivery that rolled along the ground followed by another that nearly struck his armpit. With barely half a second to react while mentally calculating the pitch's potential response, such uncertainty becomes inevitable.Elite batsmen must navigate these scenarios, yet executing this proves far more challenging than discussing it.Alex Hales fell to a delivery that stayed low, marking another disappointing failure. Across four matches, he has accumulated just 136 runs. My assessment remains unchanged: any opening bowler would consider Hales a more vulnerable target than an opening batsman should present.England may persist with him, having previously dropped Adam Lyth after seven matches. Their options are dwindling, having tested eight opening batsmen since Andrew Strauss's 2012 retirement.Nick Compton could move up the order, though he has failed to excel either opening or batting at number three, playing a careless shot that made him the third England wicket lost within the first 10 overs.Serious consideration is required, but resolving the opening position remains essential.During early summer conditions when England faces three Tests against Sri Lanka, Hales might accumulate runs, potentially launching his Test career with a single significant score. However, his technical deficiencies continue generating repeated discussion.Beyond one 60-run innings, his other attempts have stalled, with the manner of dismissals proving most disappointing.Pressure creates unusual reactions, and Hales, Compton, and James Taylor all recognize their positions face scrutiny. Discarded players like Gary Ballance and Ian Bell will consider that strong domestic season starts could force their return.These players will participate in county cricket with several early-season opportunities. They must compete and fight to earn selection.This competitive environment benefits the team - demanding tough selection battles - though none will rest easily before selection for the first Sri Lankan Test at Headingley on 19 May.Bell's return seems unlikely, as England appears to have moved forward following his involvement in the 2-0 UAE defeat against Pakistan last year.Ballance, with four centuries and six fifties across 15 Tests, remains someone they want reintegrated, but he must earn his recall.Having lost the series, South Africa ironically now enjoys excellent individual form, creating substantial future optimism.Hashim Amla delivered another beautiful performance, displaying courage after multiple thumb strikes. His failure to secure a second match century proved unfortunate.Diminutive Temba Bavuma, following his magnificent Cape Town century, continues impressing everyone. His excellent attitude, superior footwork, and sound technique have made him a revelation, alongside young fast bowler Kagiso Rabada, who claimed two more wickets while dismantling England's top order during that brief pre-close session.Both arrived with promise but have demonstrated potential for highly successful Test careers.Tuesday presents a significant opportunity for Rabada, who needs one wicket to become South Africa's youngest bowler to claim 10 in a Test match.Despite bowling 29 overs while taking seven wickets in his first-innings haul of 7-112, his movement appeared unimpaired. text: Syrian forces are continuing their crackdown on protesters in the port city of Latakia for a third day, reportedly using tanks and gunboats. Saturday marked the beginning of this assault, occurring just one day after massive anti-government demonstrations swept through the city.By Jim MuirBBC News, BeirutWhen the revolt erupted in mid-March, Latakia quickly became one of the affected cities. text: A Spanish MP has provoked criticism by taking her baby into parliament and breastfeeding him during its first session since an inconclusive general election last month. Carolina Bescansa commanded widespread attention as she pursued her candidacy for parliamentary speaker, drawing focus from across the political spectrum.Among those photographed embracing the infant was Pablo Iglesias, the leader of the anti-austerity Podemos party.Following the 20 December election, political leaders continue their struggle to forge a government coalition. Socialist MP Patxi Lopez secured the vote, becoming the first speaker in history from a party that hadn't won the most seats in an election.Previously, Ms Bescansa has brought her son to parliament for ceremonial occasions, including her MP swearing-in ceremony.In 2012, Iolanda Pineda of the Socialists' Party of Catalonia (PSC) similarly brought her infant into Spain's upper parliamentary house.Italian politician Licia Ronziulli first appeared with her baby in the European parliament during September 2010, when her child was six weeks old. Subsequently, photographs of the MEP with her daughter have chronicled the girl's development over time.A group of UK MPs campaigned last year to overturn restrictions preventing new mothers from breastfeeding babies in the House of Commons chamber.Wednesday marked Spanish MPs' first parliamentary session, yet governmental formation remains deadlocked.Mariano Rajoy's Popular Party advocates for a coalition including the Socialists (PSOE) and centre-right Ciudadanos (Citizens) party, which placed fourth in the election.Conversely, the Socialists pursue an alliance with Citizens and Podemos. Podemos maintains its insistence on a Catalonian independence referendum—a demand the other two parties categorically reject.Should major parties fail to reach consensus, King Felipe VI will designate a party leader to attempt government formation, with MPs subsequently voting on the nomination.Fresh elections may become necessary if agreements cannot be reached.

text: Newcastle Falcons survive a second-half fightback from Bristol at Kingston Park to earn their third win of the season. Newcastle secured a hard-fought 19-14 victory over Bristol, though the Falcons were left frustrated after nearly surrendering a commanding first-half advantage.The hosts dominated early proceedings through tries from Juan Pablo Socino, Will Welch and Joel Hodgson, establishing a commanding 19-point cushion. However, Bristol mounted a spirited fightback in the second period, with John Fisher and Mitch Eadie crossing the whitewash to reduce the gap to just five points.Despite their late surge, the visitors - still winless since their Premiership return - couldn't complete what would have been a remarkable comeback. The defeat leaves Bristol rooted to the bottom of the table with six losses from six matches, though they did secure their second losing bonus point of the campaign to double their points tally.The match's closing stages proved tense as both sides were reduced to 14 men, with Newcastle's Alex Rogers and Bristol's Gaston Cortez receiving yellow cards. Bristol pushed desperately for the winning score but fell just short of their first victory since promotion.Newcastle's grip on the contest could have been stronger had Joel Hodgson and Mike Delany converted second-half penalty opportunities that would have provided crucial breathing space. Instead, the Falcons had to rely on their impressive opening 40 minutes, with Hodgson's slick try just before the interval ultimately proving the difference.Newcastle director of rugby Dean Richards expressed mixed emotions despite the victory: If you'd asked me 15 minutes before kick off would I take a 19-14 win the answer would have been yes, but I'm sitting here now slightly frustrated and so is the team.We're in the top half of the Premiership with three wins and a couple of losing bonus points but we do have a lot of injuries to key players and were a little frustrated rather than happy.We played so well in the first half and could have scored two or three more tries and we could have done with those in the second half because we took our foot off the gas.They had two chances and took them both and our kicking went off a little and that was probably the root cause of the problem. I never thought we would ever lose but we could well have thrown it away.Bristol's Andy Robinson found positives in his side's second-half revival despite another defeat: I thought we started reasonably well but we lost our discipline and it was a bit of an own goal when Newcastle scored their first try and that gave them the momentum.In the second half, we started to get up off the line, made our tackles and gained momentum. We scored two really good tries but unfortunately just could not keep that momentum going.That second half was pleasing in that it proved we do have the talent to succeed in the Premiership.We did some good things here today and in the opening game of the season, but we wanted at least one win from the first six games of the season and we're frustrated we haven't done that.Newcastle: Hammersley; Tait, Waldouck, Socino, Sinoti; Delany, Young; Vickers, Lawson, D Wilson, Green, Olmstead, M Wilson, Welch (capt), Hogg.Replacements: Sowrey, Rogers, Welsh, Witty, Temm, Takulua, Hodgson, Agulla.Bristol: J Williams; Edwards, Tovey, Hurrell, Lemi; Pisi, Cliff; Traynor, McMillan, Perenise, Glynn, Sorenson, Eadie, Lam (capt), Crane.Replacements: Crumpton, Bevington, Cortes, Phillips, Fisher, Williams, Jarvis, Wallace.For the latest rugby union news follow @bbcrugbyunion on Twitter.

text: On a warm Saturday afternoon in March a group of campaigners heads to the Golden Lane estate in central London. With local council elections approaching within days, a group of volunteers isn't campaigning for any particular candidates. Instead, members of We Can Win are working to educate residents about their local authority's distinctive electoral process—one they firmly oppose.The City of London Corporation governs the Square Mile, London's financial hub, operating separately from the Greater London Authority that oversees the entire capital. While fewer than 8,000 people call the City home, approximately 450,000 individuals work there daily. The Corporation grants voting rights to a portion of these workers, expanding the electorate to nearly 19,000.Campaign director Dan Firth expresses his concerns: I was under the impression, in its simplest form, democracy was about one person one vote. But in the City of London Corporation elections, businesses have almost double the votes of ordinary people and to me that feels like an injustice.We Can Win pursues two primary objectives: challenging what they view as corporate voting privileges and encouraging maximum residential voter participation.Residents cluster primarily in four of the City's 25 wards: Portsoken, Queenhithe, Aldersgate and Cripplegate, which encompasses Golden Lane. Common Councillors and an alderman represent each ward. While Common Councillor elections occur every four years—with the next scheduled for 23 March—aldermen face election at least every six years as their terms conclude.Campaigner Georgia O'Brien shares her experience: Some residents I spoke to were already aware of how the voting system worked. But those who didn't know were shocked. When I explained that workers had almost double the number of votes as residents, they just looked utterly defeated.Beverley Bytheway, a Golden Lane resident active in the residents' association, remained unaware that workers receive voting rights alongside residents. Living on a road that borders the London Borough of Islington, she assumed both councils operated under identical electoral systems.Her view of the Corporation is critical: If they could offload the residents, they would... they're really not interested.The City of London Corporation maintains transparency about its electoral system, with detailed voter registration information available on its website for both residents and workers.The City is a democratic institution, a spokesman insisted. All of its councillors are elected.Residents follow the traditional one-person, one-vote principle, but business voting allocations depend on employee numbers. Sole traders and companies with up to nine employees receive one vote. Organizations employing up to 50 staff can appoint one voter per five employees. Companies exceeding 50 employees can designate 10 voters, then one additional voter per 50 employees thereafter.The City's spokesman explained: As the local authority we provide public services to both 7,400 residents and 450,000 City workers. Therefore to reflect the needs of the workers who come to the City each day, businesses located in the City can appoint people to vote in our local elections.The votes allocated to a business are proportional to their number of employees - the first 50 staff entitles a business to appoint 10 voters, but every additional 50 members of staff only entitle it to appoint an extra one voter, so the largest firms do not dominate the list of voters as they could do if it was a simple proportional representation of their workforce size.Corporate guidance emphasizes diversity in voter selection: It is important that people nominated to vote reflect the make-up of the organisation as a whole - from chief executive to entry-level employees and even regular contractors - so that the City Corporation represents the full range of the City's workforce. text: All it takes to officially run for the Republican presidential nomination is a one-page form sent to the Federal Election Commission, the US government entity in charge of overseeing campaign laws. The simple act of declaring presidential ambitions represents just the beginning. This year alone, 213 hopeful commander-in-chiefs have taken that initial step.Everything following that announcement proves far more challenging.While filing candidacy paperwork with federal authorities is straightforward, it guarantees placement on zero state-level primary or caucus ballots - the crucial pathway to accumulating delegates needed for securing the Republican National Convention nomination in July.Ballot qualification becomes a grueling, state-by-state marathon. Each jurisdiction maintains distinct rules and regulations, demanding substantial time and financial resources. Only campaigns with exceptional organization and professional management can navigate this complex process successfully.New Hampshire exemplifies these challenges with its $1,000 (£600) ballot access fee - a modest sum for the early-voting state that has historically shaped or shattered presidential ambitions.However, South Carolina presents a far steeper barrier. As the third state in the nomination sequence and a critical battleground for Republicans seeking Southern momentum, candidates faced a Wednesday deadline requiring a $40,000 (£26,500) payment to the state's Republican Party. Half covers administrative costs passed to state government; the remaining $20,000 flows directly into party coffers.It's extortion, declares Richard Winger, editor of Ballot Access News, questioning the practice's legality.The 1972 Supreme Court ruling provides relevant precedent. Justices unanimously declared unconstitutional a fee reaching $8,900 for local Democratic Party primary participation.Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote: Many potential office seekers lacking both personal wealth and affluent backers are, in every practical sense, precluded from seeking the nomination of their chosen party, no matter how qualified they might be and no matter how broad or enthusiastic their popular support.Winger argues this precedent directly applies to South Carolina's fee structure. I think it's unconstitutional. If all these states started doing this, pretty soon it'd be up to a million dollars.Beyond South Carolina and New Hampshire, eight additional states impose primary filing fees, typically around $1,000. Arkansas demands $25,000 for its 1 March primary, with payment due by 9 November. Kansas and Kentucky caucus participation costs $15,000 each.Campaign finance regulations further complicate matters. Filing fees must originate directly from candidates or their campaign funds - subject to contribution limits and reporting requirements - rather than from friends, relatives, or independent Super PACs that can accept unlimited donations from wealthy supporters.South Carolina's prohibitive cost reportedly influenced former Texas Governor Rick Perry's decision to abandon his financially struggling presidential bid in mid-September. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker paid the fee but withdrew the following month, with his campaign carrying over $750,000 in debt.Despite these substantial barriers, no legal challenges have emerged against the fees. All 15 remaining Republican candidates paid South Carolina's requirement. Some, including New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, former New York Governor George Pataki, and long-shot former Virginia Governor Jim Gilmore, filed within days or hours of the afternoon deadline. Candidates appear willing to pay rather than challenge the political establishment.Democratic candidates face fees too, though generally lower amounts. In South Carolina, candidates like Hillary Clinton must pay $2,500 to the state party, which then covers the remaining $20,000 in state election administration costs from its own resources.Financial barriers represent only one obstacle. Many states require candidates to collect up to 5,000 signatures from registered in-state voters - demanding robust national organizations with motivated volunteers or funds for professional signature-gathering services.Virginia's 2012 requirements proved particularly challenging. Ballot seekers needed petitions containing at least 10,000 names, with only eventual winner Mitt Romney and libertarian Ron Paul qualifying. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and former Senator Rick Santorum - both previous primary winners - failed to meet requirements.For 2016's 1 March balloting, Virginia reduced signature requirements to 5,000, due by 10 December, but mandates at least 200 names from each of the state's 11 congressional districts. Many states maintain similar district-by-district requirements, where insufficient signatures in any single district eliminates ballot access.Some states offer alternatives. Texas's delegate-rich 1 March primary allows presidential candidates to either pay a $5,000 filing fee or submit signatures from 300 registered voters across at least 15 of the state's 36 congressional districts.Florida presents unique options. Candidates can pay $25,000, gather at least 3,375 volunteer-obtained signatures statewide, or commit to attending the Sunshine Summit - a November presidential forum hosted by the state Republican Party in Orlando.The summit could generate substantial party revenue, with organizers expecting to sell 2,500 tickets. Two-day passes cost $200, while premium reserve seating commands $1,000 (all major credit cards accepted).First-in-the-nation Iowa operates differently, requiring no petitions, filing fees, or formal ballots. Caucus voters can support any candidate, and sufficient turnout translates to delegate victories.Yet Iowa's caucus system creates distinct challenges. Motivating Iowans to attend cold February weekday evening gatherings and advocate for their preferred politician demands logistical efforts that can make South Carolina's $40,000 admission price appear insignificant.

text: Venezuela has donated $500,000 to US President Donald Trump's inauguration, newly released records show. Federal Election Commission documents reveal that Citgo Petroleum, the US subsidiary of Venezuela's state-owned oil company, contributed to Donald Trump's inauguration fund amid the country's devastating economic collapse.The disclosure emerges while Venezuela grapples with severe food shortages, rampant violent crime, and crushing inflation. Wednesday's street demonstrations, where tens of thousands demanded fresh elections, turned deadly with three fatalities during the protests.Major corporations also appear in the filing documents, including Pepsi's $250,000 donation and Walmart's $150,000 contribution. NFL team owners and their affiliated companies collectively donated over $5 million, while casino magnate and billionaire Sheldon Adelson contributed $5 million.The oil-rich nation currently faces a severe economic crisis that threatens to spiral into hyperinflation. At least two people were fatally shot during Wednesday's street protests calling for President Nicolas Maduro's resignation.Given this turbulent backdrop, Venezuelan media's limited coverage of their government's $500,000 inauguration contribution through the state-owned oil company appears less surprising.However, Venezuelan analysts are voicing outrage over the revelation.Jose Manuel Puente, a public policy professor at IESA university in Caracas, expressed his anger to the BBC: We have been experiencing four consecutive years of recession, we have the highest inflation in the world and are facing scarcity in many basic goods. It is scandalous that Venezuela, facing such a crisis, would make those donations to the inauguration of a US president, who at least in theory, is ideologically confronted with the revolution.PDVSA's US subsidiary Citgo reportedly facilitated the payment. This marks another instance of Citgo's involvement in politically charged US activities. Under Maduro's predecessor Hugo Chavez, the company previously distributed subsidized fuel to low-income residents across several major American cities.Critics at the time characterized Chavez's initiative as propaganda designed to irritate his ideological opponents in Washington.The current Maduro administration, however, appears to have adopted a less confrontational stance toward the US government. Recent quotes from the Venezuelan president describe Trump as the victim of a brutal hate campaign, adding that he won't be worse than Obama.Puente explains to the BBC: The (Bolivarian) revolution is pragmatic. text: Neil Gaiman's The Ocean at the End of the Lane has been voted 2013's Book of the Year, winning the public vote by a considerable margin. Neil Gaiman's fantasy masterpiece triumphed over distinguished National Book Award recipients Kate Atkinson and David Walliams in a remarkable public victory.Readers crowned the story of a man's return to his childhood home for a funeral as their ultimate choice, selecting it from among this year's 10 National Book Award winners through popular vote.I'm amazed and thrilled, declared the graphic novelist upon learning of his win.Gaiman revealed the deeply personal nature of his work: I've never written a book before that was so close to my own heart - a story about memory and magic and the fear and danger of being a child. I wasn't sure that anyone else would like it.The author's astonishment was palpable as he continued: I'm amazed and thrilled that so many other people have read it, loved it, and made their friends read it too. Winning a National Book Award was thrilling; discovering that the public have made The Ocean at the End of the Lane their Book of the Year is somewhere out beyond wonderful. Thank you to everyone who voted.The Ocean at the End of the Lane had previously claimed victory in the Audiobook of the Year category, demonstrating its cross-format appeal.Public voters selected Gaiman's work over formidable competition, including Gillian Flynn's bestselling Gone Girl, David Jason's autobiography My Life, and schoolgirl Malala Yousafzai's powerful memoir I Am Malala for the coveted Book of the Year distinction.The online voting process, which determines the sole reader-chosen book award, concluded on 19 December.Previous winners of this prestigious public honor include EL James' controversial sensation Fifty Shades of Grey, Caitlin Moran's feminist manifesto How To Be A Woman, and David Nicholls' beloved romance One Day.Dame Mary Perkins, whose company Specsavers sponsors the awards, praised Gaiman's achievement as this fantastic award.The competition was tough but to be chosen by members of the public as well as your industry peers truly is a tribute to hard work, dedication and creativity, she said.Gaiman established his reputation through acclaimed graphic novels, notably The Sandman series and Coraline. His recent television work includes two Doctor Who episodes starring Matt Smith, while he currently develops a Sandman prequel. Additionally, his novel American Gods is being adapted for television.

text: South Korea says its third attempt at launching a rocket to put a satellite in space has been a success. At 16:00 local time (07:00 GMT), the Korea Space Launch Vehicle-1 (KSLV-1) successfully lifted off from the Naro Space Center, marking a pivotal moment for South Korea's space ambitions.Science Minister Lee Ju-ho confirmed that the satellite, designed to collect climate data, had achieved its proper orbit. This triumph arrives just weeks after North Korea deployed its own three-stage rocket to position a satellite in orbit—a move that drew widespread international condemnation.The 140-tonne Naro rocket represented a collaborative effort between South Korea and Russia, with Moscow having committed to supporting Seoul through three launch attempts. However, the path to success proved challenging, as previous missions in 2009 and 2010 ended in failure, while this latest attempt faced two technical postponements.Wednesday's launch from the facility located 480km (298 miles) south of Seoul proceeded according to plan, with officials confirming the rocket achieved its target altitude and successfully deployed its payload.After analysing various data, the Naro rocket successfully put the science satellite into designated orbit, Mr Lee announced to reporters, noting that satellite separation occurred 540 seconds post-launch.We now have leapt up a step to become a space-power nation, he declared, emphasizing that South Korea would harness this overwhelming moment as a strong, dynamic force to propel an independent space programme forward.The payload, designated Science and Technology Satellite-2C, carries instruments for climate data collection. According to Yonhap news, ground station contact was anticipated at 05:00 Thursday, when operators would make their final assessment of the mission's success.While South Korea maintains satellites in orbit, these were previously launched from foreign territories. The nation's inaugural domestic launch attempt in 2009 saw the satellite fail to separate from the rocket while in orbit. The 2010 effort ended catastrophically when the rocket exploded moments after takeoff.Success became increasingly critical following North Korea's December 12 rocket launch, which successfully placed a satellite in orbit. Pyongyang subsequently announced intentions for a high-level nuclear test and additional long-range rocket launches.The United Nations condemned the North Korean launch as a prohibited missile technology test, subsequently voting to expand sanctions against Pyongyang. International pressure continues mounting for North Korea to abandon its nuclear test plans.
