text: Italy produced a passionate and tactically superior display to end Spain's quest for a third consecutive European Championship title and secure a mouth-watering quarter-final tie against world champions Germany. Spain's reign as European champions came to a crushing end as Italy delivered a masterclass in tactical discipline and counter-attacking football, securing a 2-0 victory that sent La Roja home from their first knockout defeat at a major tournament since the 2006 World Cup.The Azzurri's triumph was built on the foundation of their wing-back system, with Mattia de Sciglio and Alessandro Florenzi providing devastating width in attack before Italy retreated to protect their advantage in the closing stages. Their approach proved far more threatening than Spain's possession-based game until the final whistle.Giorgio Chiellini broke the deadlock in the first half, scrambling home from close range after David de Gea could only parry Eder's free-kick in challenging, greasy conditions. The Juventus defender's opportunistic finish set the tone for what would become a comprehensive Italian victory.Southampton's Graziano Pelle delivered the knockout blow in injury time, converting from eight yards when substitute Matteo Darmian's cross deflected invitingly into his path. The striker's clinical volley capped a devastating counter-attack against Spain's increasingly desperate and tired legs.Only De Gea's heroics prevented a more embarrassing scoreline for Spain. The Manchester United goalkeeper produced a string of spectacular saves, making three crucial stops in the opening 45 minutes before denying Eder one-on-one in the second half following Pelle's sublime through-ball.Italy's performance radiated the intensity and fierce determination of a team seeking revenge for their humiliating 4-0 defeat in the 2012 final. They controlled proceedings for most of the match, only facing sustained pressure in the latter stages when Sergio Ramos headed wide and Gianluigi Buffon was forced into action by long-range efforts from Andres Iniesta and Gerard Pique.With full-time approaching, Buffon produced a brilliant diving save to deny Pique from close range before Italy broke clear to seal their decisive second goal.Spanish newspaper Marca's headline 'The End' following Spain's early World Cup exit in Brazil 2014 seemed premature then, but appears prophetic now. La Roja's European championship reign has been terminated by opponents who swarmed all over them with a hunger and desire that Spain's aging stars could no longer match.Vicente del Bosque's contract situation adds uncertainty to Spain's future. The coach who memorably guided the team since replacing Luis Aragones after the 2008 European Championship now oversees a side desperately needing fresh impetus. The introduction of 35-year-old Aritz Aduriz at halftime - a striker with just one previous international goal - perhaps symbolized a team requiring new direction.Former Spain international Xavi's pre-match prediction of a troublesome match proved accurate. Spain resembled a boxer with too many rounds in their legs, with only the imperious Iniesta offering attacking drive and creativity. Sergio Busquets failed to influence proceedings while David Silva remained peripheral on a night when Italy rarely allowed their opponents time on the ball.Without De Gea's brilliance, the tie would have been settled by halftime. His three sensational first-half saves included denying a Pelle header, tipping Emanuele Giaccherini's acrobatic overhead kick onto the post, and a full-stretch one-handed stop to thwart the same player after he cut inside from the left.Chiellini, part of an all-Juventus back three alongside Leonardo Bonucci and Andrea Barzagli, had predicted the match would be decided by small details. His team played like they left nothing to chance, from their passionate national anthem rendition to their immediate intensity as rain began falling at kickoff.Antonio Conte's touchline presence was electrifying throughout. The coach, who issues countless positional instructions during matches, will bring this same electric energy to Chelsea's dugout next season. His 3-5-2 system's rapid transitions from defense to attack, maximizing wide areas, proved impossible for Spain to handle.Spain couldn't pass through Italy's superbly organized structure and lacked the pace to exploit the flanks. When Pelle scored with seconds remaining, Conte leaped onto his team's dugout in celebration.Despite talking down his team's pre-tournament chances and calling Spain big favourites before Monday's match, Conte's body language and drive suggest he believes this side can progress far in the competition.Italy goalscorer Giorgio Chiellini said: We deserved this win. We could have killed the game off earlier. After years of Spain dominating, we have been able to get some revenge. This is just the beginning, we will enjoy this victory but there is still a long way to go until the end. The best is to come.Spain coach Vicente del Bosque said: They were probably better. They don't play great football but they are strong in the air, very physical and they were dangerous. We came out in the second half with a chance and the players tried to do the best they could. We tried everything but we couldn't score.Italy now advance to face Germany in Saturday's quarter-final in Bordeaux. The Azzurri have never lost to the Germans at a major finals, though they'll be without suspended Thiago Motta.Match ends, Italy 2, Spain 0. Second Half ends, Italy 2, Spain 0. text: Derby County climbed into the Championship play-off zone for the first time under new boss Paul Clement as they proved too good for Wolves. Derby County stretched their impressive form with a commanding 4-2 victory over Wolverhampton Wanderers, with Chris Martin delivering a masterclass performance that included two first-half goals.The striker's opening salvo featured a spectacular 20-yard curler followed by a commanding header, sandwiching Benik Afobe's well-struck response for the visitors. Despite Martin missing a penalty saved by Emiliano Martinez, Bradley Johnson's gentle effort extended Derby's advantage to 3-1 before the interval.Johnny Russell added a fourth goal after the break, though Adam Le Fondre pulled one back for Wolves with a looping volley from Sheyi Ojo's knockdown that crept past home goalkeeper Scott Carson's fingertips.Le Fondre's strike provided some consolation for a penalty appeal Wolves felt they deserved before halftime, when his goalbound effort struck former Wolves defender Jason Shackell's elbow. Additionally, Derby's second goal carried controversy as Martin appeared to use Kortney Hause's shoulders for leverage while heading home.Johnson's third goal came fortuitously, the ball deflecting off his outstretched boot after Wolves failed to clear Russell's corner - which had resulted from Martinez's penalty save following Danny Batth's foul on Tom Ince.Kenny Jackett's side did produce one moment of training ground brilliance for their opener, with Afobe lashing home James Henry's corner to neutralize Martin's early strike.However, the visitors remained largely outplayed throughout, particularly during sustained Derby pressure that culminated in Russell's close-range finish for the hosts' fourth goal.While Le Fondre's late goal provided a more respectable scoreline, few could dispute Derby's deserved victory as they extended their remarkable run to 16 points from 18 available, climbing to sixth position.Wolves, who had secured consecutive 3-0 victories before the international break, dropped to 11th place and now sit five points behind the playoff positions.Derby head coach Paul Clement told BBC Sport: Our best performance of the season. We've had some good first halves and some good second halves, but this time we were solid throughout and were deserved victors.Chris Martin put in the best performance I've seen from a Championship centre forward from the games I've seen this season. A great finish for the first, a brave header for the second and he led the line well.It was a shame he didn't finish off the penalty for what would have been a first-half hat-trick. But he was a well-deserved man of the match.Against a good side, it was also a great response from the team to come back and score the way we did following the penalty miss. We could have gone in at half-time on a low. But to make it 3-1 was a big moment.Wolves head coach Kenny Jackett told BBC Sport: Derby were strong and take some stopping, but our defending was poor. We didn't work hard enough to put in enough blocks and cut down things at source.There were too many key moments when we didn't defend well enough. They had too many shots and far too many of them we gifted them.Their penalty was the right decision. I also thought we should have had one for the handball, but it would be hard to get those sort of decisions here.Our keeper's held his hand up for the second goal. He should have left it to Kortney Hause to deal with, but he's a good keeper and he'll learn from that.Match ends, Derby County 4, Wolverhampton Wanderers 2.Second Half ends, Derby County 4, Wolverhampton Wanderers 2.Foul by Richard Keogh (Derby County).Conor Coady (Wolverhampton Wanderers) wins a free kick in the attacking half.Corner, Derby County. text: A fund to raise money for the families of the five Birmingham wall collapse victims has passed £20,000. A devastating workplace accident at Hawkeswood Metal in Nechells claimed five lives Thursday when workers were crushed beneath a massive 15-foot concrete and scrap metal wall that collapsed during their shift.The Birmingham Mail launched a fundraising campaign that has generated an overwhelming response from donors nationwide, according to the newspaper's editor. The victims - all Spanish nationals with Gambian roots - have been identified locally as Bangaly Dukureh, Ousman Jabbie, Alimamo Jammeh, Mohammed Jangana and Saibo Sillah. Each man leaves behind a wife and children.By Friday, rescue teams had successfully extracted all five bodies from the debris. Authorities have scheduled post-mortem examinations for Monday while keeping the facility shuttered during the ongoing investigation.Mr Reeves, the Mail's editor, explained the fundraising initiative's purpose: No money can ever fill the void left by a loved one, especially in a tragedy of this sort. But at least if the families are freed from the concerns of paying for funerals, travel for family members, and all the other immediate financial worries that get in the way of grieving, then it is worthwhile to raise some money to help.The community support extends beyond financial assistance, Reeves emphasized: The response is overwhelming, and as well as the financial support, we hope this sends a message to the families that Birmingham cares about them and feels their pain.Family members are urgently requesting the swift return of their loved ones' remains for burial ceremonies that comply with Islamic traditions. A sixth worker, also a Spanish citizen of Gambian descent, survived the incident with a fractured leg.Police investigators report having a reasonable idea about the circumstances surrounding the fatal collapse.The tragedy strikes a company with a troubled safety record. Hawkeswood Metal Recycling Ltd, operating for over four decades with approximately 50 employees, processes more than 500,000 tonnes of scrap metal annually at its Nechells location. In 2012, the firm faced a £50,000 penalty after a worker's arm became caught in machinery, leading to a guilty plea for health and safety violations at Birmingham Crown Court.Earlier this year, the same facility experienced a significant blaze when 700 tonnes of scrap metal ignited in February.

text: Women who wore pantsuits in support of Hillary Clinton on US election day are now being urged to donate them to poor and homeless women. Meena Harris, a software company policy manager, has launched the Pantsuit Drive with backing from the invitation-only Facebook group Pantsuit Nation and its 3.7 million subscribers.Harris conceived the initiative after dropping off dry cleaning near her San Francisco home, reflecting on what an obvious privilege it is to even own a pantsuit, let alone to buy a new one for a special occasion. The former Facebook employee, who studied at Stanford and Harvard, detailed her inspiration in an article for feminist newsletter Lenny Letter.In 2016, too many women still struggle to raise their families. They are disproportionately minimum-wage workers who juggle multiple jobs to make ends meet, and they still don't earn equal pay. The pay gap for women of colour isn't just a gap, it's a canyon, Harris wrote, explaining her motivation to address workplace inequality faced by women of colour.Pantsuit Nation founder Libby Chamberlain is encouraging members to donate to the cause. The Facebook page takes its name from Mrs Clinton's trademark trouser suits, which became iconic throughout her presidential campaign. On polling day, Harris posted a photograph of herself wearing a blue pantsuit alongside her mother and young baby, paying tribute to the Democratic candidate's signature style.The campaign, which Harris has dubbed Pantsuits for Progress, aims to donate professional clothing to organizations supporting poor and homeless women with job-interview preparation and employment opportunities. Harris described it as a way of honouring Hillary's public service - while recognising the roads we still must travel.Chamberlain highlighted the initiative's importance by sharing the story of Tanene Allison, a Pantsuit Nation member who is now a Harvard Kennedy School graduate and communications and strategy consultant. Allison had been homeless at age 20 when she was offered a job interview but lacked both bus fare and appropriate clothing.Job interviews can be hard enough, but they're outright terrifying when you're afraid you'll walk in looking like you live in a homeless shelter, Allison was quoted as saying. A woman at her youth shelter helped assemble an interview outfit from donated clothes, ultimately helping Allison secure the position.

text: Hosts France advanced to the Euro 2016 final with their first victory over Germany in a major tournament since 1958 on a night of high emotion in Marseille. In a pulsating semi-final at Marseille's Stade Velodrome, Antoine Griezmann delivered two crucial strikes to propel France into Sunday's Euro 2016 final against Portugal at the Stade de France. The tournament's leading marksman proved decisive in both halves, sealing a memorable victory for the hosts.The breakthrough arrived precisely at half-time when Italian referee Nicola Rizzoli penalized Germany's Bastian Schweinsteiger for handball during an aerial duel with Patrice Evra. Griezmann stepped up confidently to convert the penalty, giving France a vital advantage heading into the interval.Despite sustained German pressure throughout the second period, France's resolve held firm. With 18 minutes remaining, Griezmann struck again, capitalizing on Manuel Neuer's inability to fully clear Paul Pogba's dangerous cross by turning the ball home from close range.Germany's late surge nearly yielded dividends when Joshua Kimmich rattled the woodwork, while Hugo Lloris produced a spectacular save to deny another Kimmich header. However, the World Cup holders couldn't find the equalizer they desperately sought.Didier Deschamps' France had endured a sluggish tournament start, but inside the cavernous Stade Velodrome, there was palpable sense that national emotion was carrying the team toward Sunday's climax in Paris. The significance wasn't lost on anyone – fourteen players who featured in the November friendly between these nations at the Stade de France, when the first explosions of the Paris attacks were heard during a night that claimed 130 lives and wounded hundreds more, were again in the starting lineups.Following a day of scorching temperatures, the Velodrome's atmosphere crackled with electricity. The bond between France's players and supporters crystallized in one stirring second-half moment when, as Germany pressed for an equalizer, the entire stadium erupted into a thunderous rendition of La Marseillaise to inspire their heroes forward.Now, one final challenge awaits against Portugal on Sunday – and an entire nation expects.The 25-year-old Atletico Madrid forward entered Euro 2016 carrying France's hopes, viewed as both their primary threat and most potent weapon. Griezmann has magnificently fulfilled those expectations, transforming pressure into performance while emerging as both talisman and match-winner. His tournament tally now stands at six goals – matching Thierry Henry's European Championship record, though Henry's came across three separate tournaments.While Griezmann may not yet belong in the elite tier occupied by Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo and Luis Suarez, each tournament performance edges him closer to that exclusive bracket.His impact proved decisive when France trailed the Republic of Ireland in the last 16, scoring twice to wrest control from Martin O'Neill's side. On this grander stage, he again emerged as the game-changer.Early in the match, Griezmann had already tested Neuer with a precise low drive following slick interplay with Blaise Matuidi. Even during Germany's first-half dominance, he ensured the World Cup holders could never settle. His penalty conversion displayed composure under pressure, while his second goal showcased sharp reactions when Neuer failed to handle Pogba's delivery.Griezmann possesses an exquisite first touch, links play with genuine quality, functions as a complete team player, and delivers crucial goals. He represents the total package.With Olivier Giroud continuing to struggle amid growing supporter criticism, Griezmann often carries France's attacking burden alone. Yet his presence provides constant hope, and he'll again be their inspiration in Paris on Sunday.Germany's quest to join France and Spain in achieving the European Championship-World Cup double has ended in disappointment. Joachim Low's side has historically tormented host nations, eliminating six at major tournament semi-finals, including England at Euro 96 and most memorably demolishing Brazil 7-1 at the 2014 World Cup.This time, France successfully broke that curse.Low's team impressed for extended periods but either lacked the killer instinct or found themselves thwarted by resolute French defending and outstanding goalkeeping from Hugo Lloris.Germany's tendency toward needless penalty concessions continued, with Schweinsteiger's raised arm inviting punishment while his team dominated – mirroring Jerome Boateng's quarter-final gift to Italy.The evidence suggests Germany remains a European football superpower, yet France expertly exploited every weakness before an euphoric home crowd.Former France striker Thierry Henry on BBC One: A sign of a great team is that you take advantage of mistakes. You punish a team. France did that. They were like an Italian or German side of old times. Two opportunities. Two goals.I am actually so emotional at the moment. It's nice to see that togetherness in the team, and with the fans. At the back they were great, Evra, Sagna, Umtiti. Everybody.The main man Griezmann, we all knew that he had to play this type of game. We again have a hero, a striker who can make us win tournaments. Hopefully. What a player.It will be a tricky game against Portugal but let's enjoy it. Final of the Champions League: Ronaldo v Griezmann. Final of the Euros: Ronaldo v Griezmann.Germany manager Joachim Low: In 2012 or 2010 when we went out, the other sides were better than us. Today that wasn't the case. We were better than the French.We were the better team. We had good body language. We were good in the one-on-one. It was unfortunate that we conceded the goal.The side did everything I told them. We had a lot of courage. There's nothing to blame them for.We had our chances. Regretfully we didn't score. We didn't have the luck we needed.France manager Didier Deschamps: I'm delighted for the players. It was a tough game against a team that made us suffer but we suffered together.We haven't only had easy games. Germany were and are still the best side. We did what we needed to do. We were clinical, and Lloris was great when we needed him to be.We are in a final. We have our chance and Portugal have their chance too. It's not as if just because we're hosts and have knocked out Germany that gives us extra power. Portugal believe in themselves, and we believe in ourselves. It's still very open.France forward Antoine Griezmann: I'm very pleased. We knew it would be very tough and we held firm defensively, our keeper played very well.We have to rest up well and already start thinking about the final. We will start training for it tomorrow.Against Portugal, it's 50-50, anything can happen in a final, it's a one-off game.Match ends, Germany 0, France 2. Second Half ends, Germany 0, France 2. text: Another City shareholder has called on Sky's independent directors to explain why they have backed a takeover by Rupert Murdoch's 21st Century Fox. A growing chorus of shareholders is challenging Sky's board to justify their provisional acceptance of 21st Century Fox's £10.75-per-share takeover bid, with critics demanding greater transparency about the decision-making process.The US media conglomerate announced its offer last Friday, targeting the 61% of Sky shares it doesn't already control. While independent directors from both companies have reached preliminary agreement on the proposed price, investor skepticism is mounting.Richard Marwood from Royal London Asset Management has called for full disclosure of the advisory information used by Sky's independent directors. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he argued: Those independent directors have taken advice, and we think that they should share that with shareholders, to actually allow the rest of us to see [if] £10.75 is the right price, so we are all acting from the same information.Sky's position as a FTSE 100 company means its shares are distributed among numerous City investment firms. Trading at 982p on Wednesday, the stock has attracted attention as government officials face mounting pressure to refer any potential deal to media regulator Ofcom for review.Though Royal London ranks as Sky's 68th largest investor with merely 2.4 million shares—representing 0.14% of total ownership—Marwood's concerns echo broader shareholder sentiment calling for Sky's leadership to justify their stance and potentially seek better terms.The independence of Sky's board has come under particular scrutiny from major investors including Standard Life and Jupiter Asset Management. Their criticism centers on the dual role of James Murdoch, Rupert Murdoch's son, who serves simultaneously as Sky's chairman and Fox's chief executive.Additional governance concerns arise from other board connections: Chase Carey, previously Fox Television's chief executive and co-chief operating officer of Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation, sits on Sky's board. Meanwhile, Sky non-executive director John Nallen also holds the position of chief financial officer at 21st Century Fox.Marwood highlighted these question marks surrounding Sky's corporate governance structure. We had concerns when he [James Murdoch] was appointed to be the chairman of Sky, just for this situation, he explained. We felt if there were ever to be a bid, there would be a conflict, and our fears have been realised with what's happened.While acknowledging Sky's efforts to address investor concerns through independent director oversight, Marwood emphasized the need for additional clarity. To some extent, Sky have tried to allay the fears of investors by having these independent directors opining on the bid. But I think more transparency to give us some confidence that there is some independence there would be very good, he added.

text: Hungary has passed a law that critics say could undermine the independence of its central bank. In parliament's final session of the year, Hungary's ruling Fidesz party leveraged its two-thirds majority to push through controversial constitutional amendments targeting the central bank.The legislative move has triggered a cascade of international consequences. Standard & Poor's relegated Hungary's debt to junk status last week, with the proposed constitutional changes serving as a key factor in the downgrade decision. Meanwhile, both EU and IMF officials abruptly terminated aid negotiations with Hungary due to concerns over the new law.The financial fallout intensified Thursday when Hungary was forced to abandon portions of a planned bond auction after investors demanded significantly higher interest rates on the country's proposed debt issuance. This development underscores the growing market skepticism surrounding Hungary's fiscal stability.Hungary had been pursuing a standby credit facility worth 15-20 billion euros ($19.5bn, £12.6bn) as insurance against potential difficulties in issuing new debt. However, both the International Monetary Fund and European Commission have expressed serious reservations about providing assistance given the controversial legislation.Central bank governor Andras Simor has characterized the bill as nothing short of a takeover of the central bank. The European Central Bank has similarly criticized the law, stating it raises concern as to whether [it] could be used to influence the decision-making process, to the detriment of central bank independence.The government's desire to maintain low interest rates to stimulate economic growth conflicts with recent monetary policy decisions. Last week, Hungary's central bank raised rates for the second consecutive month, increasing them to 7% from 6.5%. This tightening comes as consumer price inflation runs at 4.25%, significantly exceeding the official 3% target.According to BBC Eastern Europe reporter Nick Thorpe, Some amendments have been made since the original draft was presented before the Christmas holiday, but concerns remain that the essence of the law has not changed. The reform of the bank would introduce deputy governors and allow the government greater potential influence over key aspects of monetary policy, such as the level of interest rates.The current crisis echoes Hungary's previous financial difficulties. In 2008, the country received a 20-billion-euro standby loan from the IMF to prevent debt default. However, newly-elected Prime Minister Viktor Orban chose not to renew the standby facility last year.Standard & Poor's has pointed to heightened risks to the country's ability to repay its debts due to the weakening domestic and global economic outlook. The agency stated: In our view, the predictability of Hungary's policy framework continues to weaken, harming Hungary's medium-term growth prospects.The downgrade trend began last month when Moody's also reduced Hungary to junk status, citing the economy's substantial debt burden and dim growth prospects.

text: The OFT has made a move to try to help people access discounts when booking online, after closing an investigation into competition practice between three companies. The Office of Fair Trading has concluded its investigation into major online booking platforms Booking.com, Expedia, and hotel chain InterContinental Hotels (IHG), implementing new conditions that allow discounted room rates under specific circumstances.Originally launched in 2010, the probe examined allegations of agreements and coordinated practices that could establish fixed or minimum resale prices. Initial concerns centered on whether these arrangements violated competition law by restricting price competition between platforms.Following extensive review, the OFT has now permitted such arrangements while imposing particular requirements. The new framework enables online travel agents to offer hotel room discounts - a practice previously prohibited - but only after customers meet certain criteria.To access discounted rates, consumers must first enroll in a membership program with either a hotel, one of the booking agents, or another online platform. Additionally, customers must have previously purchased at least one room at full price from the online agent or hotel before becoming eligible for future price reductions, according to the OFT's stipulations.Both Booking.com and Expedia rank among Britain's dominant online travel booking services.The decision's potential impact on market competition and consumer pricing remains contentious among industry observers.Gaucho Rasmussen, the OFT's enforcement director, defended the ruling after examining the conditions very, very carefully. Consumer research conducted by his office revealed that a significant amount of people would shop around and use smaller websites and new starters, he explained.Following two rounds of public consultation, Mr Rasmussen characterized the outcome as optimal, suggesting that evolving market conditions would enable smaller platforms to innovate and maintain competitive advantages.However, industry critics question whether these measures will genuinely enhance competition or reduce consumer costs.Dorian Harris, who founded discount booking platform Skoosh, expressed strong skepticism about the decision's effectiveness. I am baffled by the outcome, he stated, arguing that the changes would fail to open markets or drive down pricing.According to Mr Harris, smaller companies like Skoosh lack the financial resources to restructure their marketing approaches and hotel partnerships to comply with the OFT's requirements, making it difficult to provide competitive discounts.The conditions create additional barriers for newcomers, Mr Harris contends, as consumers will hesitate to purchase full-rate accommodations from unfamiliar websites like Skoosh to qualify for future discounts. Instead, customers will likely gravitate toward established platforms such as Expedia, where they have probably already made premium-rate purchases that would qualify them for reduced rates.The OFT have not understood the market. It is a huge failure in assessment, Mr Harris declared, arguing that the conditions would strengthen rather than challenge the market position of Booking.com and Expedia. text: A diamond ring bought at a car boot sale for £10 has been sold for £656,750 at auction in London. A remarkable diamond ring purchased for a nominal sum at a West London hospital charity shop has shattered auction expectations, selling for nearly double its estimated value at Sotheby's Wednesday sale.The 26-carat cushion-shaped white diamond, believed to date from the 19th Century, commanded an impressive final price despite initial estimates of £350,000. For over three decades, its owner wore the exceptionally-sized stone as everyday jewelry, completely unaware of its true worth.The extraordinary discovery began in the 1980s when the anonymous owner acquired what she assumed was costume jewelry from West Middlesex Hospital in Isleworth. The diamond's filthy mount and lack of typical sparkle convinced her it held no genuine value.The owner would wear it out shopping, wear it day-to-day. It's a good looking ring, explained Jessica Wyndham, head of Sotheby's London jewellery department. No-one had any idea it had any intrinsic value at all. They enjoyed it all this time.Only after thirty years of daily wear did the owners seek professional evaluation at Sotheby's, where experts confirmed the stone's authenticity and exceptional quality.This discovery echoes another remarkable find involving a Hampshire resident who purchased a floral vase for £10 at a car boot sale. Initially planning to resell the item on eBay, the owner withdrew it when bidding unexpectedly reached £10,000.Professional assessment revealed the excellent investment was actually a rare enamel two quails vase from Beijing's Imperial Palace. John Axford, Asian art expert at Woolley & Wallis auctioneers, identified the four-character mark of Qianlong, the sixth Qing dynasty emperor, dating the piece between 1736 and 1795.The imperial vase ultimately sold in Salisbury during November 2016 for £61,000 including buyer's premium—double its £30,000 guide price.Wednesday's Sotheby's auction featured another historically significant piece: a Cartier diamond brooch once belonging to Margaret Thatcher. The geometric chevron-designed piece, worn on the day she tendered her resignation as Prime Minister to the Queen, exceeded expectations by selling for £81,250 against estimates of up to £35,000. Proceeds will benefit charity.It was a thrill to bring the hammer down on two objects which have been the subject of so much interest and attention over the last few weeks and to see that attention translate into such strong bidding competition, Wyndham reflected on the successful sale.

text: Supporters and opponents of Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych are to hold rival protests in Kiev, amid fears of possible clashes. Opposition parties and activists anticipate that hundreds of thousands will participate in Sunday's Dignity Day demonstration at central Independence Square, while supporters of Mr Yanukovych plan to assemble at the adjacent Mariinskyi Park.The current wave of protests erupted last month following the president's abrupt decision to withdraw from a pivotal agreement with the EU. Mr Yanukovych has expressed concerns that the association and trade agreement could jeopardize numerous enterprises reliant on Russian trade relationships.Though the president maintains his eventual intention to sign the deal, he has acknowledged facing intense pressure from Moscow, which prefers Kiev's participation in a Russian-led customs union. Several thousand pro-EU demonstrators spent the night in Independence Square before their rally, scheduled to commence at 12:00 local time (10:00 GMT) on Sunday.Following special police attempts to dismantle them earlier this week, barricades surrounding the main protest camp in the capital's center have been reinforced. Opposition leaders have called for continued vigilance among protesters, expressing concern that provocateurs might instigate confrontations between opposing demonstrators.Authorities face accusations from the opposition of transporting people to Kiev for the pro-government rally while providing financial compensation and meals. Though officials formally deny these claims, several rally participants have confirmed being compelled to attend.Saturday saw both rival factions conducting demonstrations in close proximity, with no reported incidents of violence.In related developments, Mr Yanukovych has suspended his deputy security chief and Kiev's mayor following police violence against pro-EU protesters on 30 November. Prosecutors are examining potential abuse of office charges against Volodymyr Syvkovych and Olexander Popov, along with two additional senior officials, regarding the crackdown.This action has galvanized pro-EU protesters, who demand the dismissal and punishment of all crackdown participants. They also seek the government's resignation.While pro-EU demonstrations have captured the capital and other western and central Ukrainian cities, President Yanukovych maintains support in eastern and southern regions. Correspondents note this backing may be eroding, with pro-EU rallies already occurring in the south-east.Although protesters cite Mr Yanukovych's EU deal reversal as the catalyst for mass demonstrations, they now seek complete reload of what they characterize as a corrupt governance system. They contend that signing the EU agreement would eliminate corruption and enhance Ukraine's economic openness and transparency, pointing to western neighbors who achieved EU membership as examples.Conversely, the government and its supporters worry that economic liberalization would damage the country's economy, particularly the industrial south-east dependent on Russian trade. Moscow has already applied economic pressure through customs delays and Ukrainian chocolate bans, raising concerns about potential escalation should Kiev move closer to Brussels.

text: Swiss pilot Andre Borschberg has begun his bid to cross the Pacific, from China to Hawaii, in the zero-fuel Solar Impulse aeroplane. At 02:39 local time (18:39 GMT), an extraordinary aircraft departed from Nanjing, beginning what promises to be one of aviation's most challenging journeys. Despite possessing a wingspan that exceeds that of a jumbo jet, this experimental plane weighs no more than a large automobile.The pilot, Mr Borschberg, faces a grueling five to six days of continuous flight as he attempts to reach his central Pacific destination. Throughout this marathon journey, he plans to remain awake for extended periods, relying only on brief catnaps for rest.From a control room situated in Monaco, his entire progress will be under constant surveillance. Flight strategists and meteorologists will provide continuous updates, guiding him along the optimal route as conditions change.This marks the seventh segment of the single-seat, propeller-driven aircraft's ambitious mission to circle the globe powered solely by solar energy. While the project maintained steady momentum after its March departure from Abu Dhabi, weather delays on China's eastern seaboard forced a standstill lasting more than a month.Solar Impulse requires a precise combination of meteorological conditions: favorable winds for forward momentum and clear skies to maximize the efficiency of its 17,000 wing-mounted photovoltaic cells. By dusk, these cells must ensure the aircraft's lithium-ion batteries reach full capacity to sustain flight until the following dawn.Though Mr Borschberg brings extensive piloting experience and engineering expertise to understand the plane's complex systems, he acknowledges the mission's formidable nature.It's more in the end about myself; it's going to be an inner-voyage, he told the BBC before departure. It's going to be a discovery about how I feel and how I sustain myself during these five or six days in the air.Bertrand Piccard, who has piloted Solar Impulse during other voyage segments, explained to the BBC: There's one pilot at a time, so the pilot needs to do everything on his own. And it's a very large aeroplane, big wingspans, sensitive to turbulence, flying quite slow. So sometimes it's difficult to handle when the air moves. But we have an auto-pilot, we have toilets on board, we have food for days, water reserves and everything, and we are well trained.The journey spans more than 8,000km (5,000 miles) to Kalaeloa airport on Hawaii's O'ahu island. Should adverse weather or significant technical difficulties arise early in the flight, Mr Borschberg retains the option to return to China or Japan. However, once he passes a critical point, this safety net disappears.Both Mr Borschberg and his support team have developed contingency plans for a potential Pacific ditching should serious problems emerge. In such a scenario, the pilot would not remain with the aircraft due to electrocution risks in water. Instead, he would evacuate with a dinghy and await rescue by ship.Successfully reaching Kalaeloa airport would establish multiple aviation records, including the longest-duration flight for a single-seater aircraft.Rather than previewing aviation's future, the Solar Impulse project primarily aims to demonstrate clean technology's broader potential.The journey's previous segments include:LEG 1: 9 March. Abu Dhabi (UAE) to Muscat (Oman) - 441km; in 13 hours and 1 minute LEG 2: 10 March. Muscat (Oman) to Ahmedabad (India) - 1,468km; in 15 hours and 20 minutes LEG 3: 18 March. Ahmedabad (India) to Varanasi (India) - 1,215km; in 13 hours and 15 minutes LEG 4: 19 March. Varanasi (India) to Mandalay (Myanmar) - 1,398km; in 13 hours and 29 minutes LEG 5: 29 March. Mandalay (Myanmar) to Chongqing (China) - 1,459km; in 20 hours and 29 minutes LEG 6: 21 April. Chongqing (China) to Nanjing China - 1,241km; in 17 hours and 22 minutes

text: There is no obvious link between tough laws and levels of illegal drug use, a government report has found. The Home Office report examining international drug policies should put an end to mindless rhetoric surrounding the issue, according to Liberal Democrat minister Norman Baker. Baker, who holds the Home Office portfolio, leveled accusations at the Conservatives for suppressing these findings over several months.However, Prime Minister David Cameron dismissed the research as lacking specific conclusions and firmly stated his opposition to drug decriminalization. I don't believe in decriminalising drugs, Cameron declared.Earlier parliamentary debates saw Green MP Caroline Lucas pressing the government to reassess what she termed failing drugs laws. Current legislation permits sentences of up to seven years imprisonment for Class A drug possession, with life sentences possible for production or supply offenses.The comprehensive Home Office study analyzed the UK's drug misuse strategies against those employed by 13 other nations, revealing diverse approaches:- Nine countries have authorized drug consumption rooms, including Canada, Denmark and Switzerland - Eight nations are testing pure heroin treatment for addicts instead of methadone, including Switzerland, the Netherlands and the UK - Four operate specialized drug courts where guilty pleas to drug offenses can lead to treatment rather than incarceration, including the US - One country, Portugal, established dissuasion commissionsExamining approaches ranging from zero-tolerance to decriminalisation, researchers concluded that drug use stems from factors more complex and nuanced than legislation and enforcement alone.Portugal's experience proved particularly noteworthy. Since reclassifying drug possession as a health rather than criminal matter in 2001, the country witnessed considerable improvements in drug user health outcomes. The Home Office cautioned, however, that these results couldn't be solely attributed to decriminalisation.Baker advocates treating drug use as a health issue, rather than presuming locking people up is the answer.Alex, a recovering heroin and crack addict from London, shared his perspective:The majority of my family either suffer from addiction or have died as a consequence of it. I have buried two friends this year.Addiction is a progressive illness. I started smoking cannabis when I was 18 or 19 at university.I was abstinent in the army, but used alcohol in cross-addiction for about six years. I served in Iraq and was blown up in Basra. Post-Iraq, I worked in contract security and would use when I got back to the UK.I'm 38. I got clean at 30 and go to 12-step fellowship meetings nearly every day.I don't believe for one moment that the current laws deter any addict from using, to assume they do makes the assumption that addicts have control and choice.The views of the Home Office are out of touch and most probably based in ignorance of what addiction is. No-one I know chose to become an addict.The fact the Home Office is responsible for drug policy, including treatment, is alarming and probably why the UK is blighted with addiction.Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg criticized Conservative attitudes as representing a totally misplaced, outdated, backward-looking view.Baker elaborated: We've had what I would call mindless rhetoric over the last 40 years which has tended to say there is only one solution and anyone who offers any alternative must by definition be 'soft on drugs'.Conservative suppression of the report occurred due to its inconvenient truths, Baker claimed.Tory MP Michael Ellis, serving on the Home Affairs Committee, accused the Liberal Democrats of hijacking the report for political purposes. Their frankly pro-drugs policy is dangerous and irresponsible, Ellis stated.Cameron defended government policy, noting declining drug use under current leadership. Under this government drug use is falling and I think that's because we have followed an evidence-based approach, he said.We have been focusing on education and prevention and treatment - that is the right approach to take.While calling the report interesting, Cameron emphasized its limitations: It doesn't draw specific conclusions. I don't think anyone can read that report and say it definitely justifies this approach or that approach.BBC home affairs correspondent Danny Shaw observed the stark coalition divisions:The divisions within the coalition could not be more sharply exposed.The official Home Office position is that its drug strategy is working.Norman Baker, the Liberal Democrat minister with responsibility for drugs, says 'radical' change is needed.Mr Baker's claims have been fuelled by his department's own report, which finds no link between how tough a country is on drugs and how many people use them.It's an important finding, but the study also makes clear that drug policy is highly complex - approaches which may work abroad can't necessarily be implanted into the UK.The report acknowledged the inappropriateness of direct policy comparisons between countries due to varying data collection methods and other factors. Nevertheless, researchers noted it remained not clear whether decriminalisation impacts drug use levels.Looking across different countries, there is no apparent correlation between the 'toughness' of a country's approach and the prevalence of adult drug use, the study concluded.Action on Addiction's Nick Barton welcomed the findings: Today's report once again highlights the need for addiction to be treated as a health condition, rather than a criminal justice one. He emphasized that imprisoning drug users was rarely a solution.Transform founder Danny Kushlick, whose organization has campaigned for legal drug regulation for nearly two decades, hailed the report's significance. For the first time in over 40 years the Home Office has admitted that enforcing tough drug laws doesn't necessarily reduce levels of drug use, Kushlick observed.BBC Europe correspondent Matthew Price provided context on Portugal's transformation:Back in the 1990s Portugal was struggling with a heroin epidemic of almost epic proportions. text: Vital health services in England including stop smoking, obesity and sexual health clinics are at risk, experts are warning. In January, Chancellor George Osborne announced his intention to slash £200m from the £2.8bn public health budget - a move that has sparked fierce opposition from medical professionals across the country.Since councils control these funds rather than central government, the cuts fall outside the administration's pledge to safeguard NHS spending. However, healthcare leaders argue this funding proves essential for easing strain on the broader health system.An unprecedented coalition of 11 major healthcare organizations has now mobilized against the proposals. The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Royal College of Nursing, NHS Confederation, and Faculty of Public Health are among those demanding Osborne reverse course in a strongly-worded letter.Their correspondence warns that depleting these resources will inevitably generate increased illness and widen health disparities throughout the population. The letter emphasizes how NHS England's chief executive Simon Stevens built his pre-election funding case around health improvements - requesting an additional £8bn annually while promising £22bn in efficiency gains by 2020.We urge you to consider very seriously the position we have outlined, to reverse these cuts in your forthcoming spending review and give a clear commitment that no further cuts will be made to public health budgets in future years, the letter states.November will see the Chancellor outline his parliamentary spending framework, making the timing of this intervention crucial.Prof John Ashton from the Faculty of Public Health delivered a stark assessment of the potential consequences: The legacy of a decision to cut the public health grant will be major further burdens on the health service within the foreseeable future.Avoidable ill health, heart disease, sexual health problems, unplanned pregnancies - these are the kind of things which are being affected by this irrational cut to funding.NHS Confederation chief executive Rob Webster echoed these concerns, highlighting the remarkable unity among healthcare professionals: There is an unprecedented consensus that we can only address the problems facing the NHS if we invest in the future of our nation's health by helping people to stay well.Open any report from any director of public health in any part of the country and you can see health inequalities and poor health putting pressure on NHS services and blighting people's lives.We need the upcoming spending review to protect public health budgets.Government officials maintain that NHS investment remains a top priority, with additional funding set to be revealed during the spending review. Nevertheless, a spokesman acknowledged the challenging fiscal landscape: Difficult decisions need to be made across government to reduce the deficit and ensure the sustainability of our public services.

text: The RMT union is staging a day of protests in support of safer Scottish railways. Railway workers across Scotland staged protests at stations nationwide as the RMT union demanded the Scottish government establish an urgent timeline for removing Abellio from its ScotRail franchise operation.The union insists that only through public ownership can Scotland's rail network achieve enhanced safety standards, arguing that profit-driven motives undermine essential improvements. Meanwhile, ScotRail defended its record, highlighting substantial investments totaling hundreds of millions in new rolling stock and advanced technology systems.According to RMT claims, Dutch operator Abellio extracts £1 million monthly in profits that could otherwise fund critical railway infrastructure needs. However, a Scottish government spokesperson dismissed these allegations, stating: Any notion excessive profits are siphoned off is quite simply a fallacy.The franchise agreement, secured by Abellio in 2015 for a decade-long term, includes provisions allowing contract termination after five years should punctuality rates drop below 84.3%. ScotRail maintains that union criticisms lack foundation, acknowledging performance declines while emphasizing current levels remain approximately 90%.Public pressure has intensified with nearly 20,000 signatures on a petition urging Transport Minister Humza Yousaf to make ScotRail bosses improve Scotland's trains or strip them of their contract. Recent regulatory action saw ScotRail penalized £483,000 for substandard train and station performance.First Minister Nicola Sturgeon signaled last week that franchise removal remained a viable option should performance standards continue deteriorating.RMT General Secretary Mick Cash declared: RMT is campaigning to make Scotland's trains safer, more secure and accessible. This can only be done with a publicly-owned service where profit isn't the main motive of the operator.Cash further stated: RMT calls on the Scottish government to set out a timetable for bringing ScotRail under public ownership, and with the current level of anger that's reinforced in the petition there can be no excuse for the dragging of heels. The union is available for talks with ministers to take the issues of safe staffing, investment and public ownership forwards.ScotRail responded firmly, with a spokesman saying: These comments bear no scrutiny whatsoever. Performance has dipped by around 1% - but is still tracking around the 90% mark - and we have a robust performance improvement plan to rectify that. At the same time, we are investing hundreds of millions of pounds on new trains, refurbishing our existing fleet and introducing queue-busting smart technology to keep people moving.Government officials emphasized existing profit controls, with a spokesman explaining: This government has ensured profits are capped, that this cap is tighter than any previous franchise and that at least 50% of revenue above that cap is reinvested into our railways. A manifesto commitment was made to facilitate a public sector bid for our railways and ministers remain firmly committed to this.Current performance metrics show 89 of every 100 trains arriving within five minutes of schedule, falling short of the contractual requirement of 91. Consequently, authorities mandated ScotRail implement comprehensive improvement measures addressing service quality and congestion while reducing 'skip stopping' practices pending new fleet arrivals.The government spokesman concluded: We fully expect ScotRail to hit their anticipated targets to lift performance. This contract will deliver very real improvements across the term - new and better trains, improvements at stations, initiatives on fares and a revolution in the end-to-end journey experience.

text: In just a few years, Wonga has become one of the country's biggest, and certainly fastest growing, money lenders. Errol Damelin, Wonga's founder, remains remarkably unperturbed by critics who have branded his company little more than a digital loan-shark exploiting vulnerable borrowers. Since launching in autumn 2007, the firm has issued four million small, short-term loans totaling over a billion pounds.At a journalist briefing this week, Damelin appeared confident and upbeat about his business prospects and the legitimacy of short-term lending. Wonga is a platform for the future of financial services, the digital revolution has not yet begun in financial services, he declared, positioning his company as the financial world's equivalent of iTunes.Drawing comparisons to tech giants like Google, Amazon, PayPal and Netflix, Damelin emphasized that leveraging technology and customer data would drive success. Wonga is on a multi-year and multi-decade journey to build the future of financial services, using data and technology to make objective and unprejudiced decisions, said Mr Damelin.The company's recent business loan service launch has generated fresh attention, adding to ongoing controversies. January saw criticism over advertisements encouraging working students to borrow for overseas trips, while March brought calls from football fans demanding removal of Wonga's adverts from club websites.Wonga's online platform delivers swift lending decisions, transferring money to bank accounts within 15 minutes of application approval. Over 100 staff members focus solely on developing technology and maintaining website functionality.The system's cornerstone combines information about potential customers through an extensive in-house credit scoring operation. Damelin explained that his computers employ artificial-intelligence software to collect and analyze up to 8,000 different data points about applicants when determining loan eligibility.We have built the world's first, completely straight-through processing system for credit, so when somebody comes to Wonga as an individual, or as a business-owner, and applies for a cash advance, the whole process is completely automated, he said.This eliminates traditional scenarios of dressing formally and pleading with bank managers for loans or overdraft extensions, particularly for short-term cashflow issues.Currently, Wonga's technology rejects approximately 66% of applicants deemed too risky, requiring regular income, bank accounts, functioning debit cards, mobile phones and good credit records. This filtering results in only about 7% of Wonga borrowers failing to repay - below the 10% bad debt rate plaguing credit card lending that has cost banks billions in recent years.Beyond basic questioning, the credit scoring process incorporates sophisticated analysis of website usage patterns, offering valuable customer insights. The firm monitors how potential borrowers manipulate online sliders determining loan amounts and duration. Those immediately maximizing the slider to £400 for 30 days (the current first-time personal loan limit) show higher default likelihood than others.The great thing about that is that our decisions are always objective, we are not subject to the same kind of imperfections that traditional lenders have, where different bank managers have different preferences and often prejudices which affect how people get access to credit, Damelin argued.Regarding costs, Wonga openly acknowledges charging an APR of 4,214% annually - a figure prominently displayed on their front page. Borrowers receive clear information about repayment amounts and deadlines.However, Damelin maintains that price isn't the primary concern for his target audience. Instead, he sells speed, convenience and transparency alongside cash. We have dared to ask some hard questions, like how can we make loans instant, how can we get money to people 24 hours a day, seven days a week, how can we be totally transparent? he said.So what we have built is a solution around speed and convenience, and helping people by dealing with them when they want to deal with us.Wonga counters business criticism by highlighting customer satisfaction. Using the net-promoter score measurement, the company claims a rating exceeding 90%, meaning most customers would recommend services to friends and family. This contrasts sharply with most banks' negative scores, while even highly-rated institutions like First Direct score below 50%.Despite this, the regulated money lending industry faces poor public perception and increased scrutiny. February saw the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) announce renewed examination of payday lending practices. Two years earlier, the OFT concluded that payday lenders and other high-cost credit businesses - including home-credit lenders and pawn brokers - shouldn't face interest rate caps.Current concerns focus on questionable selling practices, including targeting financially unsuitable borrowers and allowing debt rollovers that increase obligations.Wonga distances itself from the payday lending business's less reputable elements. For Errol Damelin, expansion now targets small companies facing sudden cash shortages.Financial services is a challenging place to innovate in, so we are responding where we can deliver a better service, he says. Businesses have been crying out for a solution that is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to solve relatively small, relatively short-term cashflow problems.

text: A senior Labour MP has called for its leadership contest to be paused over fears it has been infiltrated by supporters of other parties. Labour faces mounting pressure over allegations that supporters from rival political parties are infiltrating its leadership contest to back Jeremy Corbyn, though the party firmly denies these hard left and Conservative infiltration claims.Barry Sheerman revealed that registration applications have come from members spanning the political spectrum - including the Socialist Workers Party, Green Party, Conservatives, and UKIP. However, Labour's spokeswoman dismissed demands to halt the leadership race entirely.The party maintains a very robust verification system designed to block fraudulent and malicious applications, with additional screening measures now in place to ensure rule compliance. According to BBC sources, approximately 1,000 applications have already been rejected, while an exclusion list targets individuals who previously stood against Labour or assisted opposition campaigns.Diane Abbott, a Corbyn supporter, branded Sheerman's concerns ridiculous, arguing they stem from people who think their side will lose. She emphasized that This election is being fought under rules that were agreed by the whole party last year.The controversial system, implemented under former leader Ed Miliband's reforms, allows anyone to become a registered supporter for £3 and participate in the leadership vote. Applicants must simply confirm they support the aims and values of the Labour Party.Corbyn's surging popularity has prompted warnings from rival candidates Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, and Liz Kendall about the party's potential leftward shift. Sheerman's criticism echoes similar calls from backbench MPs Graham Stringer and John Mann, who have demanded the contest be suspended.The Huddersfield MP, a former select committee chairman first elected in 1979, told the BBC that massive numbers of new members joining to vote carried malign motivations. He claimed Labour MPs were dumbfounded by the contest's structure and warned the process faced real trouble.Acting leader Harriet Harman has distributed emails to Labour MPs listing new constituency members, requesting they identify suspicious names. Sheerman acknowledged he might spot some usual suspects but warned many infiltrators would remain undetected.Despite supporting Liz Kendall, Sheerman denied his concerns were politically motivated, citing his previous battles against entryism and his belief that the current system contains fundamental flaws.Labour emphasizes that verification continues and ballot papers remain unsent. text: Chelsea moved six points clear at the top of the Premier League as Cesc Fabregas' first-half goal beat a stubborn Sunderland at the Stadium of Light. Chelsea secured their tenth consecutive Premier League triumph with Fabregas finding the net from the box's edge, guiding his shot into the far corner against Sunderland.Jordan Pickford, Sunderland's goalkeeper, produced crucial saves to deny former teammate Marcos Alonso and Willian, preventing the Blues from extending their winning margin. The Black Cats, who had organized defensively to counter Chelsea's attacking prowess, created limited opportunities but nearly salvaged a point when Patrick van Aanholt's injury-time effort was brilliantly stopped by Thibaut Courtois.Following Arsenal's midweek stumble against Everton, this hard-earned victory ensures Antonio Conte's squad will sit atop the Premier League table come Christmas Day.Consistency has underpinned Chelsea's remarkable winning streak, with Conte fielding unchanged lineups in eight of nine matches leading up to their Sunderland encounter. text: Montpellier defender Mathieu Deplagne appealed for help after losing a tooth on the pitch during his side's victory over Marseille. Steve Mounie's decisive goal secured Montpellier a 3-1 victory over Marseille in Friday's Ligue 1 encounter, but the match will be remembered for an unusual post-game search mission involving defender Mathieu Deplagne's missing tooth.The 25-year-old Deplagne suffered the dental injury during the closing stages of the contest and required substitution. Following the final whistle, Montpellier's backroom staff joined the defender in scouring the pitch for his lost tooth, though their hunt proved unsuccessful.Mathieu lost a tooth and we went to look for it, but we couldn't find it, confirmed Montpellier manager Frederic Hantz.Algeria's Ryad Boudebouz dominated the first half with a brace that established Montpellier's commanding 2-0 advantage at the interval. Marseille managed to narrow the gap through an unfortunate own goal by goalkeeper Laurent Pionnier, but Mounie's strike ultimately sealed the three points for the home side.The victory propelled Montpellier to 12th position in the league standings, drawing level on points with 10th-placed Marseille. The visitors' struggles continued as they managed just one victory in their last five Ligue 1 outings.Marseille fielded Newcastle United loanee Florian Thauvin on the wing alongside Tottenham's on-loan forward Clinton N'Jie in their attacking lineup.The second half saw numerous attempts from both sides, with Marseille pushing for an equalizer. Andre Zambo Anguissa's header missed the target, while Romain Alessandrini and Hiroki Sakai both failed to convert their chances. Montpellier's Morgan Sanson also came close with a right-footed effort from distance.Deplagne's injury occurred late in the match, causing a brief delay before Anthony Vanden Borre replaced him. The defender had earlier received a yellow card for a foul on Thauvin.Thauvin managed to pull one back for Marseille with a header from close range, assisted by Alessandrini's cross, but Mounie's response from the center of the box ensured Montpellier claimed all three points.The match concluded with Montpellier making tactical substitutions, bringing on Joris Marveaux for Boudebouz and Paul Lasne for Souleymane Camara, while Marseille introduced Antoine Rabillard in place of N'Jie.

text: On Saturday, Scotland's Paul Craig will complete a remarkable journey from the Hearts youth team to the Ultimate Fighting Championship. A mixed martial arts fighter from Craigneuk is preparing to step into the octagon at Sacramento's Golden 1 Center, where he'll face Brazilian Luis Henrique Da Silva before an 18,000-strong crowd. The bout marks a historic moment as he becomes only the fourth Scottish fighter to reach the UFC.At 29, he has inked a four-fight contract with what he describes as the Champions League of MMA - a remarkable journey from his former days at Tynecastle. This pinnacle of combat sports seemed an impossible dream until he witnessed opponents breaking down in tears after their defeats.Reflecting on his football aspirations, Craig admitted: The truth was I wasn't good enough. I knew that myself so I went into the role of coaching football.While coaching provided some satisfaction, the competitive fire still burned within him. I was OK, it was enjoyable, but I really missed the competitive side, I missed having some sort of competition. I started messing about with martial arts and found that I was really good at it, he explained.His UFC ambitions weren't part of any grand plan. It was never a case of 'I'm going to be in the UFC one day'. I was driving up and down the length and breadth of Britain fighting in various competitions in regards to jiu-jitsu. My coach said to me 'there's an opportunity, do you fancy it?' and it was down on a show in Sunderland.That pivotal moment came against Gary Sivills, a highly regarded fighter with championship aspirations. I always remember the guy I fought was Gary Sivills, and he was the top guy down that way. He had a really good record, he then wanted to fight for a British title, and he was using me as some cannon fodder, a stepping stone. He was expected just to walk through me. I had no pressure at all, I was going in as underdog.The underdog role suited Craig perfectly. I took four or five friends down with me, and I beat him in like a minute and 37 seconds. I went to speak to him afterwards and he was sobbing his eyes out and I couldn't work out why.A similar scene unfolded in his professional debut with BAMMA (British Association of Mixed Martial Arts) against Karl Moore. It wasn't until I then beat a guy called Karl Moore as a pro in my first fight in BAMMA. He was touted as being the next big thing, and it went two rounds. I remember the same thing, him crying.These emotional encounters provided Craig with profound insight into the sport's psychological toll. I thought about all the guys I've fought and they'd all been trying to get to this one point. All these guys are trying to make it to the UFC, and I've stopped them. I understand the pressure they were under.Outside the cage, Craig dedicates himself to education through Skillforce, a charity focused on helping students maximize their potential and reconnect with learning.His perfect professional record - eight victories in eight fights, all finishing before the final bell - has captured UFC attention. He now stands ready to compete on the same platform that transformed Conor McGregor from Irish fighter into global phenomenon.Da Silva presents a formidable challenge with his kickboxing expertise, but Craig's preparation alongside Scottish boxers Stephen Simmons and Jay McFarlane has bolstered his confidence ahead of attempting to halt the Brazilian's impressive 12-fight winning streak.Speaking to BBC Scotland, Craig emphasized the significance of reaching the sport's apex: The UFC is the pinnacle, everyone wants to fight there. It's going to be a good, tough opponent and I wanted that. I wanted to show people that I deserve to be in the UFC and I deserve to fight a top 20 opponent.His boxing training has transformed initial skepticism into mutual respect. As you can imagine, me as an MMA fighter going into a boxing gym, I'm always going in as an underdog, but I'm holding my own. I'm sparring with the best pro guys in Scotland. It's moving me beyond because the stand up was where I had the holes and I do believe the stand up is where I'm strong now, the strongest part of my game.Craig's confidence extends to predicting a swift conclusion to the contest. I believe I can knock him out in the first round. If not the first round, definitely I'm going to put him down in the second round and it's going to be over.Despite his reputation for ground-based victories, Craig sees this fight as an opportunity to showcase his evolved striking abilities. I'm always tipped as the submission fighter, but this is the time I get to show my stand up, and because he's a stand up guy it's going to be a good fight.

text: The UN special envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, says he is appalled and shocked that rebels in Aleppo are targeting civilians in the city. Scores of civilians have perished in western Aleppo during the last 48 hours due to relentless and indiscriminate rocket attacks, according to Mr de Mistura, who warned that such assaults could constitute war crimes.The violence erupted Friday when rebel forces launched an offensive designed to shatter the government's siege of eastern Aleppo, where approximately 275,000 residents have endured months of encirclement.Since September, Russian and Syrian government aircraft have conducted sustained bombing campaigns against Aleppo. The bombardment has reportedly resulted in more than 2,700 casualties—both killed and wounded—during this period.While Russia paused its aerial operations on 18 October to facilitate evacuations of sick and wounded civilians, the initiative has seen minimal response from residents reluctant to abandon their homes.Syrian state media reported Sunday that rebel forces had deployed chemical weapons against government-controlled neighborhoods in Aleppo. However, a spokesman for one rebel faction rejected these allegations, stating that rebel groups lack access to such armaments, according to the Associated Press news agency.The Sana news agency claimed that 35 individuals in the Dahiyet al-Assad and Hamdaniya districts experienced breathing difficulties and numbness symptoms.Since rebel attacks commenced, activists report that over 40 civilians have lost their lives in western Aleppo. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights documented that 16 of these victims were children, while also recording 55 military deaths and 64 rebel casualties. These figures remain unverified.External rebel forces are reportedly spearheading the current offensive, with Hamdaniya—currently under Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's forces—serving as a primary target. The attacking coalition includes Jabhat Fateh al-Sham, the rebranded former al-Qaeda affiliate previously known as Nusra Front, alongside fellow Islamist group Ahrar al-Sham.This marks the rebels' second major attempt to break Aleppo's siege. Their previous effort in August succeeded in temporarily establishing a corridor linking the city's eastern and western sectors, following the government's complete encirclement in July for the first time.The metropolis, once Syria's commercial center, has remained split between opposing forces since 2012.

text: Undercover journalist Mazher Mahmood plotted to change a witness statement in a case against pop singer Tulisa Contostavlos, the Old Bailey has heard. Two men accused of conspiring to pervert justice have denied the charges in a case stemming from the collapsed prosecution of singer Tulisa Contostavlos.The defendants - undercover reporter Mazher Mahmood, dubbed the Fake Sheikh, and his driver Alan Smith - allegedly worked together to alter crucial evidence that could have helped Miss Contostavlos's defense in her 2014 drug supply case.Miss Contostavlos faced accusations of supplying cocaine, but prosecutors ultimately dropped the case against the former N-Dubz star and X Factor judge. The court was told that Mr Mahmood held a vested interest in securing her conviction.According to the prosecution, the self-proclaimed king of the sting had targeted Miss Contostavlos by masquerading as a powerful Hollywood film producer interested in casting her in a major blockbuster. The singer allegedly facilitated the sale of half an ounce of cocaine to Mr Mahmood through one of her contacts for £800, leading to her arrest and charges for involvement in supplying a class A drug after Mr Mahmood provided evidence to authorities.The current charges center on allegations that Mr Mahmood, 53, from Purley, south London, and Mr Smith, 67, from Dereham, Norfolk, conspired to modify a police statement that Mr Smith had given because it supported Miss Contostavlos's case.Sarah Forshaw QC, opening the prosecution case, explained to jurors how a June 2014 hearing had essentially placed Mr Mahmood's journalistic methods under scrutiny. He liked to call himself the king of sting, he boasted in a book he had written of the number of convictions that he personally was responsible for, she stated.The prosecutor emphasized Mr Mahmood's awareness that any evidence of improper conduct as an agent provocateur - potentially inducing Miss Contostavlos to commit acts she wouldn't normally consider - could devastate both his reputation and the prosecution's chances of success.The critical alteration involved Miss Contostavlos's expressed opposition to hard drugs, which she had shared with Mr Smith during their conversation. Miss Contostavlos had expressed her disapproval of hard drugs to his own driver, that was the bit of the statement that was altered, Miss Forshaw told the court.Originally, Mr Smith had informed a police officer that he recalled Miss Contostavlos discussing a family member's cocaine dependency during their car journey, describing her as really negative about cocaine. However, within 24 hours, he contacted police requesting to retract that portion of his statement.The prosecution alleges that during this crucial day, Mr Smith forwarded his interview transcript to Mr Mahmood, followed by multiple text messages and phone calls between the pair.At a pre-trial hearing in Southwark Crown Court during June 2014, Mr Mahmood testified under oath that he hadn't discussed Miss Contostavlos's anti-drug comments with Mr Smith. He deliberately misled the court - not only had he discussed it but he had been sent a copy of the statement, Miss Forshaw declared.The case took a dramatic turn when Mr Mahmood later admitted to the jury that he had indeed reviewed Mr Smith's statement, causing Miss Contostavlos's trial to collapse immediately afterward.Miss Forshaw emphasized the significance of Mr Smith's statement modification: There is no doubt that Smith did change his statement... The change would undoubtedly have disadvantaged Miss Contostavlos's case. It would have deprived her of supporting evidence from Mahmood's own right-hand man that she made an anti-drugs comment at a time when untainted by any influence or pressure.Describing the evidence as overwhelming, the prosecutor concluded: Mr Mahmood may be the master of subterfuge and deception. But on this occasion it is he, together with his employee, who are exposed.The jury heard Miss Contostavlos's account of how Mr Mahmood deceived her following their May 2013 meeting at London's Metropolitan Hotel in Park Lane. In her statement to the court, she acknowledged limited recollection of events due to being drunk at the time.Miss Contostavlos confirmed that Mr Smith had driven her home afterward, during which she discussed an unnamed family member struggling with a hard drug problem.The formal charges accuse Mr Mahmood and Mr Smith of conspiring between June 22 and July 22, 2014, to have Mr Smith alter his draft police statement with intent to pervert the course of justice.Both defendants maintain their innocence as the trial continues.
