text: Nurses and midwives who complete their training in hospitals outside Europe will now face shorter tests to check they are fit to work in the UK. The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) is implementing sweeping changes to how overseas-trained healthcare professionals qualify to work in Britain, introducing computer-based examinations and simulated clinical scenario tests to replace the current minimum three-month supervised practice requirement.These new assessment methods will launch this autumn, targeting the approximately 1,000 nurses who annually migrate to the UK from countries outside the European Economic Area. The majority of these healthcare workers originate from Australia, India, and the Philippines, contributing to a workforce where overseas-trained professionals represent roughly 10% of all registered nurses and midwives.The regulatory overhaul addresses significant bottlenecks in the current system. According to the NMC, existing supervised placements—which can extend from three months to a full year—create delays that fail to meet urgent staffing demands. The regulator characterizes the present framework as insufficiently agile enough for employers who need to recruit quickly.Additionally, experts have identified severe shortages in available placement programs, creating substantial barriers for applicants seeking to complete their qualifications. The proposed two-part testing system aims to eliminate these obstacles while maintaining rigorous standards.This will ensure the hundreds of nurses and midwives who trained overseas and wish to practise in the UK are assessed in a a proportionate and robust way, in order to protect the public, the NMC states. The regulator emphasizes that similar evaluation methods have already gained acceptance among other healthcare regulatory bodies.Jackie Smith, the NMC chief executive, clarified the scope of these changes: The new system will not replace the need for employers to ensure that the staff they recruit display the behaviours, skills and knowledge necessary for the specific role to which they are recruited, and provide further support and development as required.However, nursing leadership has expressed cautious optimism tempered by calls for additional transparency. Janet Davies, executive director of nursing at the Royal College of Nursing, acknowledged the potential benefits while demanding more comprehensive information.Health care in the UK relies on the hard work and dedication of many nurses who trained overseas, Davies said. These proposals may well form part of a more robust and consistent mechanism for ensuring that nurses who work in the UK are equipped to practise in the UK.Nevertheless, Davies emphasized the need for detailed evaluation criteria: However, we need to know more about how nurses will be evaluated as part of this system before we can judge whether or not the system is adequate.The nursing executive also highlighted broader concerns about recruitment practices and workplace support systems. Whether nurses come from the EU or the rest of the world, it is vital that employers are recruiting them for the right reasons and supporting them when they get there, she stated. Too often, nurses are recruited from overseas to fill short term gaps and given inadequate support to care for patients well.Current statistics reveal the substantial scale of international recruitment in UK healthcare. Official figures indicate that approximately 67,000 nurses and midwives who completed their training outside Europe currently maintain NMC registration. This population supplements the existing workforce of more than 600,000 nursing and midwifery professionals who trained within Europe and secured registration with the UK regulator.The regulatory changes represent a significant shift in how Britain evaluates and integrates international healthcare talent, potentially accelerating the qualification process while maintaining patient safety standards.

text: Norwich City had to come from behind to beat League Two side Swindon Town in the opening round of the EFL Cup. Norwich City overcame a spirited Swindon Town comeback to secure a 3-2 victory at Carrow Road, though the visitors made them work hard for their progression.The match began with Swindon creating the first opportunity when James Brophy tested Angus Gunn early on. However, it was the visitors who struck first blood through Oliver Lancashire, who directed a free-kick delivery into the net to give Swindon an unexpected lead.Norwich's response proved swift and decisive. Cameron Jerome restored parity before Wes Hoolahan combined brilliantly with James Maddison in a neat one-two exchange, allowing Hoolahan to complete the turnaround and put the Canaries ahead. Maddison then extended the advantage further, netting the third goal to seemingly put the result beyond doubt.The home side made tactical adjustments from their weekend draw at Fulham, introducing Hoolahan, Ivo Pinto and Josh Murphy to the starting eleven. Maddison emerged as the orchestrator of Norwich's attacking movements throughout the first period, while also demonstrating his defensive awareness by clearing Harry Smith's effort off the goal line.Despite trailing by two goals at the interval, Swindon refused to surrender. Paul Mullin reduced the deficit after the restart, converting a header from Chris Hussey's set-piece delivery to reignite hopes of an unlikely comeback.The visitors pressed forward relentlessly in search of an equalizer that would force extra-time. Gunn was called into action to produce an outstanding save, denying Mullin a second goal. The Norwich goalkeeper also had to repel late attempts from Ellis Iandolo and James Dunne as Swindon threw everything forward in their desperate pursuit of parity.The closing stages saw several booking incidents, with Mario Vrancic, Conor Thomas, Lawrence Vigouroux and Ellis Iandolo all receiving yellow cards as tensions rose. Norwich made three substitutions, bringing on Marley Watkins for Hoolahan, Alexander Tettey for Harrison Reed, and Russell Martin for Ivo Pinto.Josh Murphy came close to adding a fourth for Norwich with efforts from the left side of the box, while Swindon continued to threaten through headers and long-range attempts. text: Plans to help nearly 100,000 small businesses due to be hit by changes to rates next month are being considered by Communities Secretary Sajid Javid. Approximately 25,000 businesses are confronting a dramatic cliff edge as new business rates revaluations take effect, ratings agency CVS has warned.During Wednesday discussions with Mr Javid, CVS presented multiple proposals aimed at addressing the crisis. The Treasury now scrambles to devise additional support measures for smaller enterprises following widespread business community backlash.While ministers maintain that the revaluation—the first implemented since 2010—will result in three-quarters of companies experiencing either unchanged or reduced rates, significant pressure mounts on both Mr Javid and Chancellor Philip Hammond. The duo faces demands for intervention to assist businesses confronting substantial increases in regions where rental values have surged dramatically.The current situation draws criticism for allegedly benefiting large retailers and online companies at the expense of traditional high street establishments.Wednesday's discussions between CVS and Mr Javid resulted in the firm proposing a comprehensive package potentially worth £150m. Government action to soften the revaluation's impact is anticipated in next week's Budget announcement.The Secretary of State was clearly in listening mode and it was evident to me that he was acutely aware of the potential impact that the revaluation will bring to some communities and the anger felt by small businesses, particularly the retail and leisure sectors, stated CVS chief Mark Rigby.Rigby continued: He was clear in his determination to find a meaningful, targeted solution to ease the financial burden for those most in need ahead of the April tax changes.At Wednesday's Prime Minister's Questions, Theresa May signaled that Mr Hammond would tackle the issue during the Budget. May explained that both Mr Hammond and Mr Javid had received instructions to make sure that the support that is provided is appropriate and is in place for the hardest cases. She added her expectation that the Chancellor to say more about this next week in the Budget.The government previously established transitional relief systems valued at £3.6bn, designed to gradually implement increases across five years.Additional mitigation strategies under consideration include introducing packages resembling the retail relief scheme—which provided £1,500 to qualifying firms before ending last April—alongside potentially raising thresholds for tapered relief eligibility.

text: The publisher of GQ magazine has been found guilty of contempt of court over its coverage of the News of the World (NoW) phone-hacking trial. The High Court determined that GQ magazine had generated a substantial risk of seriously impeding or prejudicing the trial involving Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson and other defendants.According to the court's findings, an article published by Conde Naste Publications Ltd in GQ potentially implied to jury members that News of the World's proprietors either directed phone hacking activities or possessed knowledge of such operations.While Mrs Brooks received acquittals on all charges, Mr Coulson faced conviction for conspiracy to hack phones, resulting in an 18-month prison sentence.Lord Thomas, serving as Lord Chief Justice, indicated that a subsequent hearing would determine Conde Naste's penalty.Michael Wolff authored the controversial GQ piece, which appeared in the men's publication during April 2014 - more than three months after the Old Bailey proceedings had commenced.The Attorney General initiated legal action against Conde Naste, with Andrew Caldecott QC providing representation.During a July hearing, Mr Caldecott explained to the court: The thrust of the piece was that [Rupert] Murdoch, proprietor of News International, was, or probably was, implicated in voicemail interception and that he should have been prosecuted and in his absence the trial had an air of unreality about it.Caldecott emphasized that prosecution arguments in court had never advanced such theories. Additionally, he noted the article suggested defense attorneys maintained a hidden agenda focused on safeguarding Mr Murdoch's interests while concealing his potential involvement.Defending Conde Naste, Adrienne Page QC characterized the publication as a highly subjective, personal and impressionistic sketch based upon the experience of visiting the trial courtroom.However, Lord Thomas, presiding alongside Mrs Justice Nicola Davies, concluded the article constituted seriously prejudicial material.Following the court's decision, Attorney General Jeremy Wright QC stated: While it is rare to bring proceedings against publishers, the GQ article went against the most fundamental principle of our criminal justice system; namely that everyone is entitled to a fair trial and it is not for the press to decide who is deserving of this protection.

text: A major children's musical drama is being made in Northern Ireland by the Disney Channel. Disney Channel's ambitious 10-episode series The Lodge will debut this September, marking a significant milestone for Northern Ireland's entertainment industry. The production represents the channel's largest-scale venture into the region, employing nearly 100 cast and crew members across multiple County Down locations.So far Northern Ireland's been mostly known for swords and dragons - Disney Channel is bringing songs and dancing, declared David Levine, Disney Channel's UK and Ireland head. This marks the first time the network has undertaken a production of such magnitude in Northern Ireland.Levine emphasized the substantial investment involved: We're investing quite a bit, and you have production, post-production, builders, sets and filming in multiple locations here.Primary filming occurs at Montalto Lodge near Ballynahinch, while additional scenes capture the scenic beauty of Castlewellan and Tollymore Forest close to Newcastle. The production boasts impressive local involvement, with 46 of the 67 crew members hailing from Northern Ireland, including local producer Raymond Lau. The complete cast numbers 22 performers.At the heart of The Lodge lies 15-year-old Skye's compelling journey. When she and her father abandon city life to manage their family's countryside lodge, Skye discovers her father's secret plan to sell the beloved business. Racing against time, she has one summer to persuade him otherwise.Sophie Simnett, known for her recent work in BBC's Dickensian, brings Skye to life. The role demanded extensive preparation beyond traditional acting skills.There are a lot of sub-plots, all of which involve a lot of activity, Simnett explained. So as well as the singing and dancing, I had to learn to rock climb as there is one scene where I go on a date and go rock-climbing. We also had to learn how to kayak as there is a scene where the whole group go kayaking.Thomas Doherty, whose credits include TV's Dracula and the film Hercules, portrays Sean, Skye's love interest. He is fun-loving, he's very sporty, and he has a love interest in Skye, Doherty described his character.Drawing on his musical theatre background, Doherty found the role particularly rewarding: I originally trained to do musical theatre, so it was amazing to get this. We've had choreography, we've had singing coaches, so we've had the best training and it's good fun.Production will wrap before summer's end, with The Lodge premiering first on Disney Channel throughout the UK and Republic of Ireland. European audiences can expect the series to follow on the channel across the continent.

text: On a small yet busy lane in central Bangalore is a three-storey white house with a bright orange gate. Tucked away behind an unassuming orange gate and white facade lies a breeding ground for India's next generation of business innovators, though passersby might never suspect what's happening inside.Bangalore, southern India's bustling metropolis, has established itself as the nation's entrepreneurial epicenter. The city magnetizes ambitious entrepreneurs from every corner of India and beyond, all drawn to this computer industry hub in search of breakthrough concepts, financial backing, and workspace solutions.Yet these driven individuals face a fundamental challenge: where to live. When entrepreneurship consumes every waking moment, retreating to a sterile hotel room or mundane dormitory hardly inspires continued innovation.Enter the Construkt Start-up Hostel—a 20-bed sanctuary that opened its doors this past May, proudly claiming the distinction of being India's inaugural start-up hostel. This home-away-from-home concept allows budding business minds to cohabitate with peers who share their passion, facilitating round-the-clock idea exchange and collaboration.During my visit, over half the bunk beds were occupied. Beyond standard amenities like kitchen facilities and laundry services, the hostel prioritizes what matters most to aspiring entrepreneurs: reliable wi-fi and an ever-ready coffee maker.A striking feature dominates the ground floor—an entire wall transformed into a massive blackboard. Chalk-drawn calendar grids map out the month's upcoming start-up and technology events throughout the city. Listed activities range from investor pitch boot camps to data analysis conferences, exemplifying how Construkt's founders actively connect residents with Bangalore's broader entrepreneurial ecosystem.The hostel attracts two primary demographics: individuals still crystallizing their business concepts and those with defined ideas seeking market validation in Bangalore.Krishna Elakara, a 42-year-old Construkt resident of Indian heritage who has spent his entire life abroad—most recently in Australia—is developing a fitness training product. From the hostel's first-floor mini-library, a cheerful space doubling as a reading room, he explains his Bangalore pilgrimage.All the elements you need to put together a start-up, they're here, he says. I'm staying at this hostel because I want to build my network in the city. Other hostels or hotels usually have tourists, whereas here you meet people with a similar mind-set.The hostel's semi-circular living room regularly hosts open hack sessions, where residents gather to dissect and refine business proposals. Krishna takes the spotlight as the first presenter during my visit.Questions fly: What's unique about your idea? and Who would you partner with?Shashikiran Rao, 36, one of Construkt's founders, grins as he describes the process: We take the idea and tear it apart, and let everyone jump in and poke holes into it. We're very good at it. The idea is to help entrepreneurs develop their plans.Next up is Aashna Kaur, a 24-year-old business administration graduate who has spent over a year consulting with start-ups. Now pursuing her own venture, she's weighing two concepts: technology supporting solo female travelers or products encouraging greater female workforce participation in India.After more than a week at Construkt, Aashna pays approximately $14 (£10.70) nightly or $220 monthly. When I inquire whether cost drives her choice, she clarifies that comparable hotel rates exist—possibly cheaper—but the networking potential makes Construkt irresistible.Currently, the hostel attracts not only aspiring entrepreneurs but also individuals exploring career directions. Prerna Gautam, still pursuing her university studies, relocated from Mumbai to Bangalore for a summer internship at Microsoft Accelerator, the tech giant's program helping entrepreneurs bridge the idea-to-execution gap.Though uncertain about post-graduation plans, Prerna credits her Bangalore experience with sparking interest in start-up culture.As Construkt eyes a second Bangalore location, PricewaterhouseCoopers consultant Sudhir Singh acknowledges the concept addresses market demand while questioning its scalability.There is definitely a space for something like this, but I don't know if it'll catch on like wildfire, he says. It's where I'm sure a lot of aspiring entrepreneurs would choose to stay to network, but I'm not sure a well established entrepreneur would live there unless there are some innovative programmes they're creating to attract such people to the place.Back at Construkt, the atmosphere buzzes with contentment. Music drifts through the space as residents share food and drinks. Some focus intently on laptops while others engage in animated discussions spanning business, technology, and politics.The cultural shift is remarkable. Previously, launching one's own company was considered foolhardy—too risky and impractical for Indian sensibilities. Today, I'm told, graduating without a start-up concept might actually invite social judgment.This entrepreneurial path brings inevitable challenges: securing funding, recruiting talent, managing payroll. Yet none of these obstacles seem to deter India's ambitious youth from pursuing their business dreams.

text: Scottish rugby suffered two body blows this week and, rather like boxer Ricky Burns who drew with his opponent after getting one heck of a hiding from opponent Raymundo Beltran, it's a little battered, a little broken and in need of time off the canvas. The first positive steroids test in Scottish rugby history delivered a shocking blow, though perhaps no more surprising than the ongoing debate about Scottish, Welsh and Irish teams qualifying for the Heineken Cup from a league without relegation. Today, however, let's focus on the pressure young players face to bulk up for rugby success, saving the Heineken Cup discussion for another time.Sam Chalmers - son of Craig, one of Scotland's finest players - issued a public statement expressing regret and claiming he purchased the substances online. This explanation carries echoes of the convenient lone wolf narrative. Critical questions remain: Was he truly the only player involved? Did he discuss these substances with teammates?Age-group rugby coaches report an increasingly common pairing of weight training with supplement use. The pressure for players to increase both size and weight is undeniable - I accept this reality completely. Over 150 years, rugby pitches haven't changed dimensions while human physiques have evolved dramatically. Modern rugby emphasizes powering through opponents rather than maneuvering around them.However, I reject the notion that players face pressure to purchase steroids. The moment someone buys these substances, they're cheating - knowingly violating rules while hoping drug testers won't catch them. Players who've considered steroids but resisted deserve recognition. Those lacking sufficient size should pursue different careers, as rugby no longer accommodates all body types.Young players increasingly view supplements as essential training companions - consuming them before gym sessions, during workouts, and immediately afterward. This culture may indoctrinate athletes into believing natural nutrition alone cannot achieve their goals. Perhaps this mindset creates a slippery slope toward artificial enhancement, with illegal steroids representing the ultimate forbidden aid.Can adequate size be achieved through food alone? This question demands serious consideration.The IRB's website reveals telling statistics: 1,542 tests conducted in 2012 across all tournaments and events - including the HSBC Sevens World Series, Rugby World Cup 2015 qualifiers, and various international matches - yielded 21 anti-doping violations, representing 1.36% of the entire program.These figures suggest approximately 1.4% of elite players attempt drug-assisted cheating. Website records show several athletes caught using stanozolol - the same steroid favored by both Sam Chalmers and disgraced Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson.Global rugby testing in 2011, according to World Anti-Doping Agency figures on the IRB website, involved 5,553 tests with 61 violations - just over 1%. Lower league players or those desperately trying to break into the system likely represent higher risk categories, though concrete evidence remains elusive.During my 1995 Rugby World Cup coverage in South Africa, I documented a disturbing trend that bears repeating: Cape Town GPs reported unprecedented requests from schoolboys seeking steroid prescriptions, often accompanied by supportive parents. Could similar scenarios unfold here?Sam Chalmers belongs to the most vulnerable demographic - young men aspiring to professional or elite-level rugby careers. His situation will prove challenging, but life rarely offers easy paths. Players and coaches involved in Bloodgate, eye-gouging allegations, and the 60-plus rugby athletes caught by IRB drug testing faced similar difficulties.This represents a crucial test. Chalmers must serve his punishment before returning to the game.One final consideration: I strongly suspect he wasn't acting alone. Younger players than Sam Chalmers likely remain undetected.What are your thoughts? Do players face genuine pressure to use steroids?You can follow John Beattie on Twitter @bbcjohnbeattie

text: Donald Trump's plan to erect a huge sea wall at his Irish golf course has been withdrawn in the light of stiff opposition. Environmental groups have successfully forced the withdrawal of controversial plans for a massive coastal wall at Donald Trump's Irish golf resort, though a scaled-back version is now in the works.The Trump International hotel and golf links at Doonbeg, situated on County Clare's west coast and purchased in 2014, had proposed constructing a two-mile limestone barrier following severe storm damage that year. The original €10m structure would have stood 4m high and 20m wide, requiring 200,000 tonnes of rock for its construction.Climate change featured prominently in the initial application, with documents stating that the rising sea levels and increased storm frequency and wave energy associated with global warming can increase the rate of erosion. The protective barrier was presented as essential defense against the wasting impacts of the seas while also benefiting the broader community through coastal protection works.However, environmental campaigners mounted fierce opposition, particularly over threats to the tiny, EU-protected whorl snail, Vertigo angustior. The proposed wall raised concerns about its impact on the Carrowmore dunes special area of conservation.Six months ago, Clare County Council requested additional information from the Trump organization regarding the structure's environmental impact, but no response was provided. Yesterday, council officials received notification that the application was being withdrawn.We got notification from the applicant yesterday that they were withdrawing their application, a council spokesman told BBC News.The Trump group cited excessive planning delays as their reason for withdrawal. In their statement, they emphasized the resort's €6m annual contribution to the local economy and indicated that expansion plans were under close consideration, though adequate coastal protection remained essential.The realisation of these plans, however, is fundamentally dependent on the provision of adequate protection from coastal erosion, the statement read. Since 2002, an estimated 15m to 20m of dune face has been eroded from the beach front and the golf course. All efforts at soft management of the coastline have failed. All efforts to readjust the course have also been expended.The organization has announced a dramatically reduced alternative: a 900-meter wall constructed in two sections, featuring metal sheet piles driven into the golf course ground with limestone boulders positioned around them.Tony Lowes from Friends of the Irish environment, who met with Trump representatives, suggested that international attention surrounding Donald Trump's promised US-Mexico border wall complicated the Irish proposal.You could tell that they were upset, because there were already analogies being made with the Mexican wall, said Lowes. You could tell that they didn't like that because they could sense that this could turn into something more than a little planning battle in Ireland.The opposition gained global momentum when surfing organization Save the Waves collected approximately 100,000 signatures from worldwide supporters opposing the original plans.Campaigners dismiss suggestions that criticism of the President-elect's environmental stance significantly influenced the opposition movement.In this case I think the absurdity of the proposal, the outrage at what was about to be inflicted was so great, that no one could look at the proposal without being shocked, said Lowes. I have very rarely seen an environmental case that looked so absolutely horrific.While local residents and businesses largely supported the wall, environmental groups maintained strong resistance throughout the process.The revised proposal is expected for submission before Christmas, with a potential decision by March next year. Analysts anticipate scrutinizing the new documents for any continued references to climate change and rising sea level impacts.Follow Matt on Twitter and on Facebook

text: Researchers attempting to learn why people snack are to study the health and habits of more than 100 Scots. Scientists at Aberdeen's Rowett Institute of Nutrition and Health are launching an innovative study to examine the psychological triggers behind unhealthy snacking behaviors, as part of Scotland's broader initiative to combat rising obesity rates.The research team aims to enlist 120 volunteers for comprehensive week-long monitoring that will track multiple aspects of their daily lives. Participants will wear heart sensors and GPS devices while maintaining electronic diaries to record their cardiovascular responses, movement patterns, and snacking behaviors.Central to this investigation is exploring how executive functions - key cognitive processes in the brain - influence people's food choices and eating patterns.Because our environment makes it easy to consume high-calorie snack foods and spend long periods of time inactive, eating well and being active requires considerable self-regulation, explained Dr David McMinn, the study's lead researcher from the institute. It requires us to make an effort, such as deciding not to snack in order to maintain a healthy weight.Dr McMinn emphasized the challenging nature of modern living conditions. We live in an environment where snack foods are readily available, and where desk jobs and labour-saving devices mean that we are less active than in previous generations, he said.The research focuses specifically on understanding how psychological brain processes called 'executive functions' correlate with dietary and activity choices. We use executive functions to achieve goals, for example, planning actions in advance, solving problems, ignoring distractions and resisting temptations, Dr McMinn noted.These crucial cognitive abilities can become compromised under certain conditions. The executive functions can be depleted if used intensively, or due to particularly stressful situations. We are interested to know if reductions in executive functions are associated with behaviours such as snacking on unhealthy foods or sedentary behaviour, he added.We are particularly interested in the way food choices and physical activity behaviours are linked to psychological processes in the brain called the 'executive functions', Dr McMinn said.The study seeks volunteers over 18 years old who aren't currently taking beta-blockers and can visit the university's health sciences building on the Foresterhill campus for preliminary psychological assessments before beginning their seven-day monitoring phase.Dr McMinn outlined the comprehensive data collection approach: Information from the different monitoring devices will be used to identify where periods of snacking, activity, sedentary behaviour, and stress occur.The ultimate goal extends beyond mere data collection. The aim is to try to understand why people snack, because we all know that sticking to a healthy diet is easier said than done, Dr McMinn concluded.

For the study, 120 volunteers will be followed for a week and will be asked to wear a heart-rate monitor and to carry a smart phone that will record their movements. We use our executive functions to achieve our goals, for example by planning in advance, solving problems, ignoring distractions and avoiding temptations. But in certain conditions, these crucial functions of the brain can be weakened. The study focuses specifically on the brain's executive functions in relation to food and exercise choices. They can be depleted by overuse or by stress. The study seeks volunteers over eighteen who are not taking beta-blockers and who are able to go to the university’s health science building on Forester Hill for a preliminary psychological assessment before their seven-day observation. We live in an environment where snacks are always available and sedentary work and labor-saving devices make us less active than previous generations. Dr. McMinn explained the complex system of data collection: "We are particularly interested in the relationship between food choices and physical activity behavior and the psychological processes in the brain known as executive functions. We are interested to know if a reduction in executive functions is associated with the behaviors of snacking on unhealthy foods and sedentary behavior."

text: The head of MI5, Sir Jonathan Evans, is to step down from the post next month, Home Secretary Theresa May has said. During Home Office questions in the Commons, Mrs May honored Sir Jonathan's remarkable three-decade tenure with the security service, spanning 33 years of dedicated service.Following his appointment as MI5's director general in April 2007 - succeeding Lady Manningham-Buller - Sir Jonathan will step down upon his contract's completion.I thank him for his invaluable contribution to public safety and national security, Mrs May declared.Mrs May outlined his extensive portfolio, which encompassed counter espionage investigations, the development and implementation of crucial security policies, and most recently, combating international terrorism threats.**Analysis: The Challenges of Leading MI5***By Gordon Corera, Security correspondent, BBC News*Leading MI5 presents challenges that could easily cause sleepless nights for any director general.The terrorism threat loomed large - shortly before Jonathan Evans assumed leadership, Britain endured the devastating 7 July attacks, prompting scrutiny over whether MI5 might have prevented the tragedy. Beyond al-Qaeda concerns, Northern Ireland's deteriorating security situation has increasingly demanded attention.Post-9/11 complications also emerged, particularly allegations regarding security service involvement in the mistreatment of former detainees such as Binyam Mohammed. Most recently, the Olympics presented another significant security challenge.Jonathan Evans can depart with considerable relief, having successfully guided MI5 through his tenure without major catastrophes.However, his successor faces fresh challenges: addressing Britain's growing cyber espionage threat and navigating a transformed operational environment amid potential questions regarding funding and strategic priorities.Mrs May praised his adaptability, noting: He has experienced the service evolving over the years and as director general has led the service through particularly challenging times of change and unrest, including the aftermath of the 7/7 bombings.She emphasized his Olympic contribution: His tireless work helped ensure the delivery of a safe and successful Olympic and Paralympic Games last year.Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper added her recognition: We also give thanks for the work Sir Jonathan Evans has done over many years for the security of this country.**Career Trajectory**Sir Jonathan, now in his mid-50s, began his MI5 career addressing Irish-related terrorism throughout the 1980s and 1990s before transitioning to international counter-terrorism investigations in 1999.His appointment as director of international counter-terrorism came just 10 days before the September 11 attacks struck the World Trade Center and Pentagon in 2001.In a rare public address last year - delivered merely one month before London's Olympic Games commenced - he revealed that Britain had faced a credible terrorist attack plot about once a year since 9/11.His stark warning emphasized the persistent threat: In back rooms and in cars and on the streets of this country, there is no shortage of individuals talking about wanting to mount terrorist attacks here.The 2013 New Year's Honours List recognized his service with appointment as Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath (KCB).

text: Every year charitable trusts are set up in memory of people who have met violent or tragic deaths. Charitable organizations emerge from tragedy in vastly different ways - while the Stephen Lawrence Charitable Trust marks two decades since its founding following the teenager's racially motivated killing, countless others experience brief periods of activity before dissolving.Yet what role do these trusts and charities play in supporting grieving families during their darkest moments?In Wellington, Shropshire, the Williams family endured devastating loss this past May when their teenage daughter's life was cut short. Days after 17-year-old Georgia went missing from home, her body was discovered near the Nant-y-Garth pass, close to Wrexham. Jamie Reynolds, 22, from Avondale Road in Wellington, Shropshire, has since faced court proceedings on murder charges.Following Georgia's tragic death, friends initially mobilized to fund a memorial bench. However, the overwhelming response from donors led to something much larger - the establishment of the Georgia Williams Trust to ensure her memory would endure.Steve Williams, Georgia's father, expressed his gratitude for the community's response. It has been really heartwarming to see people getting involved, organising events and reading all their supportive comments, he said. [The family] have been able to take a lot of comfort from what people have said and how they remember her.The trust's mission extends beyond remembrance. The trust will ultimately be used to enable young people of Telford and Wrekin to access enrichment activities - whether that be canoeing, rock climbing, tennis, flying or something else and also to encourage young people to volunteer, Williams explained.Trust chair Richard Langton understands the organization's therapeutic value for the family while maintaining his commitment to preserving their involvement. A West Mercia Police inspector emphasized the charity's potential impact: We hope that the charity can provide a positive focus for the family at this incredibly hard time for them and give them some comfort to know that there is a positive legacy, that Georgia's name will live on.The trust maintains strong family connections through Georgia's sister Scarlet Williams, who serves as a trustee. We will continue to work closely with the family - we have a trustee in Scarlet Williams, Georgia's sister, who'll be working with us to make sure we stay on track to deliver from the charity what the family wanted, Langton noted.Building sustainable momentum presents ongoing challenges. Despite attracting 5,200 Facebook followers and 500 Twitter supporters, Langton recognizes the need to develop an organization capable of surviving beyond these few incredibly painful months. He's actively encouraging social media followers to get in touch and get involved.The Charity Commission acknowledges that tragedy-born charities often face overwhelming initial generosity, followed by declining donations over time. Many smaller organizations struggle to maintain adequate funding, leading the commission to strongly recommend that founders carefully consider long-term sustainability to avoid risk letting beneficiaries down.Ann Oakes-Odger intimately understands both the desperate emotion parents face after losing children and how positive action can provide healing. Her son Westley was fatally stabbed at a Colchester, Essex cash machine in September 2005. Two brothers received convictions for manslaughter and murder in 2006.Oakes-Odger channeled her grief into successful advocacy for enhanced minimum sentencing guidelines for knife-wielding murderers, subsequently founding knifecrimes.org and Victims' Advocate to assist others facing similar ordeals.It has helped after losing Westley, she reflected on establishing both organizations. I felt sure that once the trial was over there would be a big void to drop into if there wasn't something else to grab onto and to take forward in memory of Westley.Even years later, the pain persists. It's been many years on since that happened to Westley, but I still have days when the shock still does hit, she added.Funeral collections sometimes spark charitable endeavors, as Shropshire mother Karen Prior discovered when mourners' generosity inspired her family's philanthropic journey. Two-year-old Lewis died while awaiting heart transplantation due to left heart syndrome, diagnosed just five days after his 2001 birth.The funeral's generous donations prompted Karen and husband Colin to establish a memorial foundation. Their fundraising efforts supported the Royal Shrewsbury Hospital's Rainbow Ward, where Lewis had spent considerable time, along with Hope House hospice.After recently dissolving The Lewis Prior Foundation, which generated between £15,000 and £17,000, the Priors experienced firsthand how charitable support diminishes over time.It just seemed to be the right time to stop, Mrs Prior explained. We were a small charity - at the start we got lots of support and did lots of charity events, but as time went on support tailed off.Despite the foundation's closure, Prior harbors no regrets about the decade-long endeavor. It helped us get through 10 years - it made us stronger.The family's approach prioritized awareness over personal recognition. It wasn't that we [as parents] wanted to be in any publicity, she clarified. We used our other son Tom to present cheques - it was mainly to keep the condition in people's minds and to keep his name alive.

text: An online petition has been launched by residents of the town of Benson in the US state of Arizona against a radio station which broadcast advice late at night on how to hide child pornography. A Change.org petition demanding the shutdown of Cave 97.7 FM has emerged after the Arizona radio station broadcast guidance on concealing child pornography viewing over two years.Paul Lotsof, who owns Cave 97.7 FM, has openly challenged Arizona's child pornography legislation. Speaking to KVOA News 4 Tucson, he defended the controversial broadcasts as a public service, though the content has since been removed from air.According to Lotsof, child pornography possession shouldn't constitute a criminal offense, describing current penalties as excessive. A YouTube clip posted by his critics captures him stating: In many cases the penalties for pictures is worse than the penalty for murder.The station owner draws a clear line between viewing illicit images and physical abuse. The difference is [that in] one case, you're molesting children and abusing them, causing children to do things that are not natural for children to do, and [in] the other case, they're just possessing pictures, he explained to News 4 Tucson.Cave 97.7 bills itself as south-east Arizona's most powerful radio station, though audience statistics aren't publicly available on their website.The online petition condemns Cave for transmitting a sickening message about a huge issue that plagues this country. Petitioners declare: There is no excuse for this and [the station] needs to be shut down. We can keep this garbage out of our community.These controversial messages were packaged as Public Service Announcements (PSAs) - traditionally used by media outlets to share information benefiting the public interest.Federal Communication Commission representatives informed News 4 Tucson that no specific regulations clearly define acceptable PSA content boundaries.While America maintains strong free speech protections, Benson police are examining whether the station's PSAs violated legal statutes. Law enforcement emphasizes that children depicted in such imagery are crime victims.Freedom of speech does not include telling people to commit crimes and continuing to pass on this information could lead to judicial action being taken, police stated. We are now seeking legal advice on actions that can be taken for the content that has already been released and to ensure this kind of information is not released again.Arizona enforces among America's strictest child abuse and exploitation laws. A 2003 case saw a high school teacher receive a 200-year prison sentence after authorities discovered thousands of child abuse images on his computer.

text: Fidel Castro, who has died aged 90, was a huge figure in our lives, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has said. The death of Fidel Castro has prompted a spectrum of reactions from British political figures, with Jeremy Corbyn leading tributes while others voiced sharp criticism of the former Cuban leader's human rights record.Raul Castro, the younger brother who succeeded Fidel as Cuba's president, announced the revolutionary leader's passing, marking what Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson called the end of an era for Cuba and the start of a new one for Cuba's people.Johnson, describing Castro as a historic, if controversial figure, extended the UK's condolences to Cuba's government and people. He emphasized that Britain will continue to work with the government of Cuba on a wide range of foreign policy priorities, including on human rights.Corbyn, who has long supported the Cuba Solidarity Campaign against foreign intervention and blockades targeting the island nation, hailed Castro as a huge figure of modern history, national independence and 20th Century socialism. The Labour leader praised Castro's revolutionary heroism, his global presence, and Cuba's achievements in health and education.From building a world-class health and education system, to Cuba's record of international solidarity abroad, Castro's achievements were many, Corbyn stated. For all his flaws, Castro's support for Angola played a crucial role in bringing an end to apartheid in South Africa and he will be remembered both as an internationalist and a champion of social justice.While acknowledging that there were problems and there are problems of excesses by all regimes, Corbyn argued that we have to look at the thing in its totality and noted that Castro had seen off a lot of US presidents.This perspective drew sharp rebuke from former Labour home secretary Jacqui Smith, who countered that Castro 'saw off' so many US presidents is because they're democratically elected. Labour MP Mike Gapes, formerly chairman of the Commons Foreign Affairs Select Committee, pointed to Human Rights Watch findings of much worse than just some 'problems and excesses' in Cuba.Other Labour figures offered mixed assessments. Former London mayor Ken Livingstone called Castro an absolute giant of the 20th Century, while former MP George Galloway tweeted alongside a photo with Castro: You were the greatest man I ever met Comandante Fidel. You were the man of the century.However, criticism emerged from within Labour ranks as well. Former cabinet minister Peter Hain praised Cuban forces' 1988 defeat of South African troops in Angola as a vital turning point in the struggle against apartheid, but added that Castro was criticised, rightly, for his attacks on human rights and curbs on free speech and his attitude towards gay Cubans which were indefensible.Liberal Democrat leader Tim Farron acknowledged Castro as undoubtedly a significant leader but insisted we must not overlook the appalling human rights abuses including brutal summary executions for which he was responsible.Even supporters acknowledged flaws. Livingstone admitted on Radio 4's Today programme: Of course Fidel did things that were wrong. Initially he wasn't very good on lesbian and gay rights. Despite praising health, education, and wealth distribution achievements under Castro, Livingstone predicted Cuba would eventually evolve toward something like a traditional west European democracy.In London, coincidentally hosting the Latin America Conference—Britain's largest annual Latin American solidarity event—delegates marked proceedings with a minute's silence followed by applause honoring Castro's life. The Cuba Solidarity Campaign described him as demonstrating that another world is possible, economically and politically.Cuban ambassador to the UK Teresita Vicente Sotolongo, visibly emotional when discussing her two meetings with Castro, described the former president as a very warm person. She reflected: I don't think we were ever prepared to think that he's not here in person, not with us. But I am confident his legacy we will go on.Rob Miller from the Cuba Solidarity Campaign, who met Castro as a teenager, remembered him as charming and very interested in our lives. Miller observed: Fidel embodies that David and Goliath spirit that has seen Cuba develop its own ways and its own politics, its own destiny.Paul Webster, UK ambassador to Cuba from 2001-2004 and now a Boston University international relations lecturer, characterized Castro as a good reader of human nature which helped him consolidate power. However, he cautioned about future uncertainty: For many Cubans its almost impossible to conceive of a world, a Cuba, without Fidel. So change will have to be carefully managed.Conference delegates expressed genuine sadness at Castro's passing, viewing him as an iconic figure who challenged American dominance. When confronted with human rights criticisms, supporters dismissed these as US-perpetrated myths, preferring to focus on Castro's achievements.A book of condolence will be opened at London's Cuban embassy as the nation mourns the loss of its revolutionary leader.

text: There is one sentence in the press release announcing Nicholas Serota's departure from Tate that stands out. The man's own words reveal everything: I leave an institution that has the potential to reach broad audiences across the UK and abroad, through its own programmes, partnerships and online.That single word - potential - demands scrutiny. What exactly does he mean?Under Nicholas Serota's leadership, this institution has transformed dramatically. What began as a respected yet modestly attended Pimlico gallery has evolved into a global art powerhouse. Tate Modern now claims the title of world's most visited modern art museum, while two thriving regional galleries complement a nationwide partnership network. The lending programme showcases Tate's British art collection in prestigious venues spanning from Beijing to Boston.Most observers would argue Serota has already fulfilled Tate's potential. Yet his perspective differs entirely - a telling insight into both his character and the secret behind his remarkable tenure. Complacency simply isn't in his vocabulary.This potential reference reveals three defining traits: his reluctance to self-promote, an unrelenting ambition, and his confrontational approach to challenges.His message to whoever follows is clear: don't expect smooth sailing. Work remains unfinished. Though departing, he's deliberately establishing the roadmap ahead.So who might step forward to unlock this remaining potential?Maria Balshaw emerges as the likely frontrunner. Her exceptional leadership at Manchester's Whitworth, combined with her role directing the city's cultural initiatives, positions her strongly.Iwona Blazwick presents another compelling option. The veteran Whitechapel Gallery director helped establish Tate Modern's curatorial approach during her late-'90s stint there. Long considered Serota's heir apparent, she would follow his exact career trajectory from Whitechapel to Tate.Among internal possibilities, Frances Morris stands out most prominently, though she recently assumed the Tate Modern directorship. Jessica Morgan, despite her recent departure to lead the DIA Art Foundation, might also warrant consideration, although she's barely begun settling into that position.International searches seem inevitable. Klaus Biesenbach from MoMA PS1 could receive consideration, alongside super-curator Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev and potentially Michael Govan from LA County Museum.Two additional noteworthy candidates emerge: Tim Marlow from the Royal Academy and Matthew Slotover, Frieze's co-founder - both distinguished figures capable of introducing fresh perspectives.

What began as a respected, but modestly attended, Pimlico gallery has turned into a major international art institution. This is what he says himself: ‘I leave an institution that has the potential to reach a wide audience across the UK and abroad, through its own activities, through collaborations, and through its online presence.’ Serota would be considered, by most, to have fully developed the potentialities of the Tate. The Tate Modern now boasts the title of the world's most visited museum of modern art, and two thriving regional galleries complement a nationwide network of affiliates. The loan program enables British art to be seen in prestigious venues from Beijing to Boston. His message to his successor is clear: do not expect the smooth sailing. There is unfinished business. Although leaving, he deliberately leaves the map on the table. And who will take advantage of this untapped potential? The candidate, perhaps the most obvious, is Maria Balshaw. Iwona Blazwick, a former director of the Whitechapel Gallery, who helped establish the curatorial direction of Tate Modern during her late-1990s stint there, is another interesting possibility. She is considered the long-standing heir to Serota, and she would be following the exact same career path from Whitechapel to Tate. Among the internal candidates, Frances Morris is the most prominent, though she is the director of Tate Modern. Her excellent work as director of the Whitworth in Manchester, combined with her role as Director of Culture in the city, places her well. The international search is inevitable: the names of Klaus Biesenbach from MoMA PS 1 could be considered, the super-curator Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, and perhaps also the director of the Los Angeles County Museum, Michael Govan. Two more remarkable candidates come to mind: Tim Marlow, director of the Royal Academy, and Matthew Slotover, co-founder of Frieze – two distinguished figures, both capable of introducing fresh perspectives. Despite her recent resignation, Jessie Morgan, who has just led the DIA Art Foundation, could be considered, although she has only just begun to settle into her post.

text: Gatwick Airport has been given approval to run six narrower flight paths to allow planes to fly in less airspace. Following a comprehensive review of airspace modifications implemented in 2013, the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has granted approval for more concentrated aircraft departure routes from Gatwick Airport. The decision leverages cutting-edge satellite navigation technology to reshape how planes navigate after takeoff.The CAA's rationale centers on environmental benefits, with officials arguing that concentrated flight paths will reduce the overall number of people exposed to aircraft noise. This approach represents a significant shift from traditional aviation patterns that relied on ground-based navigation beacons.We absolutely understand that aircraft noise disturbs many people and we have taken the required amount of time to fully assess the considerable amount of feedback we have received from across the local communities, explained Phil Roberts, the CAA's head of airspace, air traffic management and aerodromes. As we have done throughout this review, we will continue to consider the environmental impact of all our airspace decisions.Modern satellite navigation systems enable aircraft to fly in tighter formations and utilize reduced airspace, eliminating the need to navigate via ground-based beacons. This technological advancement allows planes to operate closer together while maintaining safety standards. New European legislation mandates that the UK maximize utilization of this technology, prompting Gatwick's implementation of concentrated flight paths as compliance with these requirements.However, the changes have sparked fierce opposition from local communities and campaigners. Sally Pavey, representing the Gatwick Area Conservation Campaign, criticized the plan as creating a superhighway of planes. Critics argue that Gatwick's operations are causing significant disruption across southeastern England.Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat, representing Tonbridge and Malling, voiced strong concerns about the impact on his constituents. There are communities as far over as Hildenborough and Tonbridge, running through Leigh and Penshurst, Chiddingstone, Edenbridge and even over my own home, just south of Edenbridge, who are very badly affected by the noise and it is absolutely unbearable, he stated. Tugendhat indicated he would examine the changes more thoroughly while calling on Gatwick to become a better neighbour.Gatwick Airport operates approximately 350 daily flights from its single runway. Airport representatives have indicated that the narrowed flight paths will eventually enable them to rotate routes on and off, potentially offering relief periods for communities experiencing concentrated over-flight.The approval represents a balancing act between technological efficiency, environmental considerations, and community concerns, as aviation authorities navigate the complex challenge of modernizing air traffic while addressing local opposition to increased noise concentration.

text: After two days of talks, Labour and Plaid Cymru have got a deal. Following Plaid's withdrawal of Leanne Wood as a candidate, Carwyn Jones secured reinstatement as first minister on Wednesday.The agreement's specifics reveal convergence across multiple policy areas where both parties find common ground, though strategic omissions in contentious territories could spark future disputes.Both Labour and Plaid have pledged to focus efforts on initiatives that enjoy support from across much of the assembly, targeting areas where their respective manifestos already demonstrated consensus.Key priorities include establishing a National Infrastructure Commission alongside a Welsh development bank. Additionally, three joint committees will oversee financial, legislative and constitutional collaboration.The election revealed substantial cross-party agreement on various issues, with Plaid and Labour manifestos showing particular alignment in areas now incorporated into their deal.**Apprenticeships and Skills** While both parties committed to expanding apprenticeship opportunities, their numerical targets differed significantly. Plaid proposed creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships, whereas Labour's more ambitious plan called for 100,000 all-age apprenticeships.**Healthcare Workforce** Healthcare staffing emerged as another shared priority. Plaid's flagship proposal involved recruiting 1,000 additional doctors and 5,000 nurses, while Labour focused specifically on attracting more GPs to Wales.Treatment funding also featured prominently in both manifestos. Plaid advocated for a £50m New Medicines and Treatments Fund for Wales, while Labour proposed an £80m equivalent fund.**Childcare Provision** Most parties addressed childcare in their platforms. Labour promised 30 hours of free weekly childcare for working parents with three and four-year-olds. Plaid's approach involved providing full-time early education of 30 hours weekly by 2021.**Economic Development** Banking solutions for Welsh businesses appeared in both manifestos, though with different approaches. Plaid favored establishing a national bank of Wales, while Labour preferred a Welsh development bank concept.Business rates reform represented another area of convergence. Labour pledged cuts for all small firms, while Plaid similarly planned to reduce business rates to support smaller enterprises.**Child Protection** Both parties addressed potential smacking bans, though Labour attached significant conditions to its commitment. Plaid proposed legislation removing the reasonable chastisement defense, while Labour said it would seek cross party support for identical measures.**Plaid's Perspective** The party claims success on five of its nine primary manifesto commitments. Party representatives highlight the National Infrastructure Commission—an independent body taking a strategic infrastructure approach with access to new financial resources—as a major victory absent from Labour's original manifesto.For overlapping areas like apprenticeships and childcare, Plaid emphasizes ensuring Labour treats these issues as genuine priorities.**Labour's Position** Labour successfully re-elected its first minister while maintaining, according to party claims, all governmental commitments without compromise.**Notable Exclusions** Two significant issues from the previous Welsh Government remain unaddressed due to lack of consensus.The M4 Relief Road represents a major divide. Labour supports constructing a black route six-lane motorway south of Newport, while Plaid advocates upgrading existing roads following Professor Stuart Cole's proposed blue route.Local government reform approaches also differ substantially. Labour has proposed consolidating Wales' 22 councils into eight or nine entities, whereas Plaid suggests maintaining current council structures while adding regional coordinating authorities.Labour's 2016 manifesto deliberately avoided specifying M4 route details or final council numbers, despite previous commitments on both issues.Plaid's long-standing demand for single transferable vote elections received no consideration in the agreement.Speaking to the chamber Wednesday, Ms Wood explained insufficient time existed to consider and negotiate on the most difficult issues including the M4, detailed steel industry rescue measures, fair voting or student finance.She indicated Plaid would revisit these matters through the budget and the other vehicles that are available to us.

text: Malaga have been banned from European competition for at least one season because of unpaid bills. UEFA has imposed a four-season European competition ban on Malaga, marking the first major decision by the governing body's club financial control body regarding significant overdue payables.The Spanish club, currently sitting fourth in La Liga and preparing to face Porto in the Champions League last 16, will not be affected this campaign. However, should they qualify for any European competition over the next four seasons, the suspension will take effect.Uefa's club financial control body has taken its first decision due to the presence of significant overdue payables, stated UEFA. Malaga is excluded from participating in the next Uefa club competition for which it would otherwise qualify for in the next four seasons.This punishment represents UEFA's commitment to enforcing Financial Fair Play regulations, designed to prevent clubs from excessive spending beyond their financial capabilities.Malaga has responded with fierce opposition to the ruling. Malaga wishes to express its total disagreement at the decision issued today by Uefa, and considers the intended actions against the club to be completely unjustified, the club declared. The club believes they are being made a 'scapegoat' and an 'example of' by Uefa by this unfair treatment.Beyond the competition ban, UEFA has also imposed a 300,000 euros (£244,000) fine on the Martiricos club. An additional season's suspension looms unless Malaga can demonstrate by March's end that they have resolved outstanding payments to other teams, staff members, and tax authorities.The club's recent trajectory had appeared promising following Sheikh Abdullah Al-Thani of the Qatari Royal Family's acquisition of ownership in June 2010. Under manager Manuel Pellegrini's guidance over the past two years, Malaga secured their historic first Champions League qualification while bringing in notable players including Argentine defender Martin Demichelis, Brazil's Julio Baptista, Frenchman Jeremy Toulalan and Chile's Manuel Iturra.However, financial pressures forced the sale of key assets last summer, with Santi Cazorla departing for Arsenal and Joris Mathijsen joining Feyenoord. Internal discord emerged when former Manchester United striker Ruud van Nistelrooy and Cazorla were among several players threatening legal action over unpaid wages last season.The Liga de Futbol Profesional (LFP) had already imposed a transfer ban in January after Malaga failed to make a required payment to Osasuna for Spain full-back Nacho Monreal.Five additional clubs face comparable one-year bans across the next three seasons unless they satisfy UEFA that specified debts have been cleared: Croatia's Hadjuk Split and Osijek, Romania's Rapid Bucharest and Dinamo Bucharest, and Serbia's Partizan Belgrade.

text: German Chancellor Angela Merkel has warned the UK that countries at the bargaining table negotiate better deals than those outside the room. During a Berlin news conference alongside NATO General Secretary Jens Stoltenberg, German Chancellor Angela Merkel expressed her hope that Britain would remain within the European Union ahead of the June 23 referendum, though she emphasized the decision ultimately rests with British citizens.Obviously, it is up to the citizens of the UK themselves how they wish to vote on the upcoming referendum, Merkel stated. I've said repeatedly before that I personally would hope and wish for the UK to stay part and parcel of the EU.The Chancellor described Britain's EU membership as being of benefit to all of us, positioning the UK as part and parcel of the union. Yet concerns about how British voters might interpret her comments have made her cautious about speaking out. Her intervention today, while relatively measured, carried an underlying warning delivered in her characteristically guarded manner.The EU, Merkel cautioned, would never offer the same compromises to an outsider that it extends to member states. We work well together with the UK particularly when we talk about new rules for the EU, she explained. We have to develop those together with the UK and whenever we negotiate that, you can much better have an influence on the debate when you sit at the bargaining table and you can give input to those negotiations and the result will then invariably be better rather than being outside of the room.Emphasizing the single market's importance—a free trade area encompassing the movement of goods, people, and capital—Merkel warned that countries outside the EU will never get a really good result in negotiations.It would be not only be in our interest but it could also be in the interest of Britain when it can bring its whole political weight to the negotiating table as part and parcel of the EU, she added.The timing of Merkel's comments appears coordinated with statements from other European leaders who have made clear they wouldn't rush to help the UK renegotiate rights and access following a potential Brexit. Her intervention reflects growing unease in Berlin that Brexit has become a realistic possibility.Labour MP and Leave campaigner Kate Hoey dismissed Merkel's intervention, telling the BBC the German leader would be well advised to stay out of what is a very, very important vote for British democracy.I really don't think that Angela Merkel telling the British people how they should vote in a democratic referendum in three weeks time will affect anyone's vote, Hoey said. text: Levels of unconscious racist and sexist bias have been reduced by manipulating the way the brain learns during sleep. Northwestern University researchers in Chicago have developed a groundbreaking technique that uses sound cues during sleep to reduce unconscious bias, with effects lasting at least one week according to findings published in Science journal.The study involved 40 participants who underwent what researchers termed counter-bias training - a process where facial images were deliberately paired with words contradicting common stereotypes. Female faces appeared alongside terms like maths, while black faces were matched with positive words such as sunshine. Throughout this training, distinctive audio cues played in the background.During subsequent 90-minute afternoon naps, these same sounds were replayed at low volumes. The intervention successfully reduced both sexual and racial bias scores, with improvements persisting for a minimum of seven days.According to the Northwestern team, sexual and racial prejudice remains widespread yet frequently unintentional. They reference computer game studies revealing players' tendency to shoot black characters more frequently than white ones, and research showing men receiving preference over women despite identical job qualifications.Initial bias assessment utilized publicly available testing protocols before participants received the specialized training intervention.Prof Ken Paller, who directs Northwestern University's cognitive neuroscience programme, acknowledged limitations when speaking to BBC News: We didn't have people interact with or make decisions about other people, so that sort of experiment is needed to know the full effects of the methods we used.Nevertheless, Paller suggested the approach shows promise: We suggest that modifying unconscious social bias is likely to influence the extent to which decisions are influenced by racist or sexist attitudes. He envisions potential applications for addressing addiction and unhealthy eating behaviors.University of Tubingen researchers Gordon Feld and Jan Born offered praise in their commentary, calling this the first to demonstrate that this method can be used to break long-lived, highly pervasive response habits deeply rooted in memory.However, they raised concerns about sleep's vulnerable state, noting people lack wilful consciousness during rest. Their commentary warned: However, Aldous Huxley's description of a dystopian 'brave new world' where young children are conditioned to certain values during sleep reminds us that this research also needs to be guided by ethical considerations.Paller acknowledged ethical parallels to subliminal advertising while posing broader questions: More importantly, perhaps, is the question of whether people in positions of authority in society, such as judges and police officers, and perhaps people who make hiring decisions, should have their unconscious bias evaluated and perhaps trained to some standard.The research opens new possibilities for addressing deeply ingrained social biases while simultaneously raising important questions about consent and ethical boundaries in unconscious mind modification.

The Information Commissioner has imposed a £200,000 penalty on Glasgow-based Home Energy & Lifestyle Management Ltd following complaints about relentless automated calls.Victims reported feeling helpless against the barrage of calls, with some finding their answering machines completely overwhelmed by messages. The firm has pointed fingers at a third-party company it contracted for the calling campaign and announced plans to challenge the decision.According to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), the company orchestrated an extensive automated marketing blitz promoting supposedly free solar panels. The impact on recipients was severe - one complainant explained to the ICO that they couldn't ignore their phone while anxiously awaiting updates about a terminally ill relative.Information Commissioner Christopher Graham emphasized the broader issue: The bottom line is companies trying to sell a product have got to stick to the rules. Nuisance phone calls are a modern pest. He added that People expect the Information Commissioner and other agencies to close this down and we're now closing down on these phone pests.The ICO's investigation revealed that organizations must obtain explicit consent - specifically naming the company involved - before launching automated calling campaigns. However, the company acknowledged it was unaware of these legal requirements. Proper consent requires consumers to actively check a box indicating interest in specific products from the particular company.Steve Eckersley, the ICO's head of enforcement, expressed disbelief at the company's approach: This company's ignorance of the law is beyond belief. It did not even bother to find out what the rules were and its badly thought out marketing campaign made people's lives a misery.Beyond the consent violations, the firm also failed to provide adequate opt-out mechanisms for consumers in certain instances. While the Telephone Preference Service allows people to avoid unsolicited calls, this protection only covers live-person interactions. Home Energy & Lifestyle Management (Helms) deployed specialized software for automated messaging, enabling frequent repetition of calls.The company's marketing claims were also deceptive, according to the ICO. Despite being part of the government's Green Deal initiative, Helms misled recipients by advertising solar panels as free when they actually carried costs.Helms has mounted a defense, asserting that their campaign had already concluded before the ICO's investigation began. The company's legal representative issued a statement shifting responsibility: Helms had significant difficulty in fully co-operating with the ICO, owing to the failure of the third party company to give any information to verify and explain the extent of the calls made.The firm claims the ICO seemingly disregarded its explanations and has committed to both appealing the fine and pursuing legal action against the contracted calling company.

text: This week three senior figures were appointed to oversee investigations into claims that a small group of hard-line Muslims had tried to take over schools in Birmingham. A self-described concerned citizen accompanied the papers with an urgent letter to council leader Sir Albert Bore, claiming discovery of the materials in a school administrator's office. Purportedly authored in Birmingham for Bradford recipients, it outlines a systematic five-step strategy for school takeovers under the Operation Trojan Horse banner.The document's authenticity faces widespread skepticism. Critics argue genuine conspiracies rarely provide such convenient written evidence. text: Female workers continue to face a rapid rise in pay inequality when they get into their 30s and 40s, according to the Resolution Foundation. A striking 9% pay disparity awaits women born between 1981 and 2000 once they celebrate their 30th birthday, according to new research. This represents a dramatic increase from the modest 5% wage difference these same women experience during their twenties.The findings reveal that motherhood imposes a sharp and long-lasting financial penalty on women's earnings. Over an entire career, this penalty can cost women hundreds of thousands of pounds in lost income, the think-tank determined.Laura Gardiner, senior policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation, explained the paradox facing today's young women: Young women today face relatively little disadvantage in terms of their pay packets compared to what their parents' and grandparents' generation faced. But while many millennial women haven't experienced much of a pay gap yet, most probably will once they reach their 30s, when they start having children. What's more this pay penalty is big and long-lasting, and remains for younger generations despite the progress in early careers.Despite decades of workplace advancement, the research demonstrates that the gender pay gap affecting women in their thirties has remained virtually unchanged across generations.These conclusions align with previous findings from the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), which published comparable research last year. The IFS study revealed that while men typically experience wage growth throughout their thirties, women's salaries generally stagnate during this crucial decade.Jo Swinson, a former member of the coalition government and now director of Equal Power Consulting, attributes part of the problem to persistent workplace bias. There is some occupational segregation, with more men going into science and engineering-type roles, but we also know there is discrimination at work, she told the BBC.Alternative explanations focus on employment patterns rather than discrimination. Critics argue that the wage gap reflects women's greater likelihood to pursue part-time employment during childbearing years. Since part-time positions typically offer lower hourly wages than full-time roles, this career choice naturally impacts overall earnings.The Resolution Foundation advocates for coordinated action between policymakers and businesses to completely eliminate pay disparities.However, Jill Kirby, a former director of the Centre for Policy Studies think tank, cautions against imposing unwanted changes on women's career choices. Women who are highly-qualified will choose to take less demanding jobs - more nine to five, and less nine to nine-type jobs - when they have a family, because they actually feel there are better things in life than spending all their time at the office, she told the BBC.Beginning in April 2018, organizations employing more than 250 people must publicly report comprehensive data about internal pay gaps between male and female employees.A government spokesperson acknowledged ongoing challenges while highlighting recent progress: The gender pay gap is at a record low, but we have to push further to eliminate it completely. Shining a light on organisations' pay gaps means employers can take action to tackle the causes and drive change.
