text: Almost a third of dogs checked at random across the UK were found to be carrying a tick, researchers say. A comprehensive study examining nearly 15,000 dogs across the UK has revealed that one in three pets carries ticks, with urban environments posing equal risks to rural settings. The research, conducted by Bristol University last year, represents the most extensive tick survey ever undertaken on canines.Scotland, East Anglia and the South West emerged as the highest-risk regions, though the arachnids were discovered throughout the entire country. Contrary to common assumptions, city areas proved just as tick-infested as countryside locations.These blood-sucking parasites pose significant health threats, transmitting diseases including Lyme disease and a recently identified parasite that can prove fatal to dogs. Lyme disease itself can trigger severe complications such as meningitis and heart failure, with potentially deadly outcomes in extreme cases.The Big Tick Project, initiated in April 2015, enlisted veterinarians nationwide to examine dogs weekly and document clinical histories. Each tick's species, development stage, gender, origin location and pathogen status was meticulously recorded during routine veterinary visits.Prof Richard Wall, who spearheaded the Bristol University research team, emphasized the widespread distribution of ticks. The work that we have carried out shows that ticks are extremely widely dispersed. The records that we have got appear to show that we have had an increase in tick numbers right across the country, he stated.The professor highlighted disease transmission as the primary concern. What we are primarily concerned about is the diseases that ticks carry. In the UK, we have relatively low rates of the prevalence of these pathogens at the moment and, in contrast, in continental Europe they have much higher rates of disease. As there seems to be a rise in tick numbers, we need to be concerned and be aware of the potential for increasing problems.While woodland and long grass areas remain traditional risk zones, Prof Wall stressed that urban environments also harbor these parasites.Television naturalist Chris Packham praised the research as providing good solid hard data from a tremendously significant project that revealed some very shocking and surprising things about the distribution, the population and potential that ticks have to give diseases to our pets and ourselves. He expressed surprise at finding ticks distributed nationwide rather than confined to isolated regions.Unlike flying insects, ticks cannot jump or take flight. Instead, they attach themselves to clothing when people brush against vegetation where the parasites cling. Common habitats include woodlands, urban parks, heathland, fields and gardens.Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria causes Lyme disease transmission through infected tick bites. Similar to mosquitoes spreading malaria through blood consumption, ticks function as disease vectors when feeding on humans or animals.Public Health England estimates 2,000 to 3,000 new confirmed Lyme disease cases occur annually in England and Wales, though laboratory testing doesn't verify all instances. Approximately 15% of cases involve individuals who contracted the disease abroad.The characteristic bullseye rash - a red circular mark surrounding the bite site - serves as one initial symptom, though its absence cannot rule out infection. Flu-like symptoms often develop alongside muscle and joint pain.Antibiotic treatment can cure Lyme disease effectively. However, untreated cases may cause severe health deterioration, including nervous system damage, meningitis or heart failure.Currently, only 3% of UK ticks carry the bacteria, making the Lyme disease threat relatively small compared to other nations. Nevertheless, given this study's findings regarding high tick populations nationwide and the serious potential consequences, scientists urge public awareness and bite prevention measures.The Big Tick Project has created an online resource allowing people to identify areas with highest tick prevalence.Sarah Bignell's experience illustrates the disease's devastating impact. The formerly active veterinarian contracted Lyme disease during a 2011 walking holiday in Aberfeldy, Scotland, despite a cabin warning about the local hotspot.There was a small note in the cabin saying this was a Lyme disease hotspot but I didn't think anything of it. I had no idea, she recalls.Six weeks later, bone, joint and nerve pain began. Medical professionals initially suspected multiple sclerosis or brain tumors, but Sarah's veterinary background prompted her to request Lyme disease testing. She had been unknowingly bitten by a tick and never developed the telltale bullseye rash.Sound and light sensitivity became agonizing virtually overnight. Swallowing difficulties and encephalitis followed. I spent eight-and-a-half months locked in a room, she explains, requiring constant care and unable to tend her pets.Over four-and-a-half years, Sarah faced multiple life-threatening episodes. I was in danger of dying. I am very lucky, she says. The pain used to be so severe and my quality of life so awful, at that point I was living hour to hour. These critics maintain that media outlets frequently overlook Antifa's violent tactics simply because the group opposes white supremacists and their reprehensible beliefs.What exactly is Antifa?Anti-fascist or Anti-Fascist action - abbreviated as Antifa - champions distinctly left-wing social causes. The majority of participants reject racism and sexism in all manifestations while vehemently opposing what they perceive as Trump's nationalist, anti-immigration and anti-Muslim agenda.Their primary focus, as the name suggests, centers on combating far-right ideology rather than promoting progressive legislation. This distinguishes them from mainstream leftist movements that pursue power through conventional democratic processes - electoral victories and legislative achievements.Antifa's anti-government and anti-capitalist stance aligns their methods more closely with anarchist movements than traditional left-wing politics. The group embraces militant protest tactics, including property destruction and occasional physical confrontations.Their presence was notable during the 2017 Berkeley demonstrations against far-right speaker Milo Yiannopoulos, the violent protests surrounding Donald Trump's inauguration, and the Charlottesville incident.Similar to far-right organizations, Antifa operates as a global network of loosely affiliated groups. The most prominent chapters appear concentrated in the US, the UK (operating as Anti-Fascist Action) and Germany (known as Antifaschistische Aktion).Germany's movement originated in 1932 as a militant far-left response to the rapidly ascending Nazi party. The website's daily traffic surged from approximately 300 hits in 2015 to between 10-20,000 hits currently. Saturday's Charlottesville events alone generated 2,000 new Twitter followers for the It's Going Down account.Despite heightened interest since Trump's presidency began, determining Antifa's actual membership remains virtually impossible. Anderson believes the weekend's Charlottesville events mark a sea change in public perception of Antifa.This is a huge turning point and vindication for our movement, he said.We are working with Black Lives Matter, local clergy, this is not a movement that wants to be a lone group of militants, he said.This is about popular power. Sometimes that looks controversial - but this is a broad movement, and we are looking to engage a wide variety of people.

text: Kenya's Julius Yego, who refined his javelin technique watching YouTube videos, says his World Championship gold medal was really unbelievable. Despite standing at just 5ft 9ins, the 26-year-old athlete delivered a Commonwealth record throw of 92.72m, securing victory by nearly four metres in a sport where his relatively small stature typically presents challenges.Very few athletes have done what I have done, he declared, reflecting on his journey after overcoming a serious injury that nearly prevented his Beijing competition. I had a serious injury and thought I won't compete in Beijing.The 85kg Commonwealth champion originally aspired to join Kenya's renowned running tradition but transformed his technique through studying YouTube videos of Olympic and world champions Jan Zelezny of the Czech Republic and Norwegian Andreas Thorkildsen.His unconventional training method led to remarkable success, though he believes such self-taught excellence won't be replicated. There will not be another YouTube athlete coming through, he stated. I want to go back and watch my throw, it was almost perfect.The triumph came amid controversy as team-mates Joyce Zakary and Koki Manunga tested positive for doping at the championships, adding to thirteen Kenyan athletes currently suspended for doping violations.Addressing the scandal, Yego maintained his stance on clean competition: I can't dwell on that, it's a shame. I always believe you can win clean. In sport you win clean.Born fourth in a family of seven from Nandi South County, according to his IAAF profile, Yego's athletic journey began when police recruiters near Nairobi spotted his potential. National force head coach Nicholas Kilisio recognized his talent early, explaining: We saw the talent in him and decided to take him. He had a small frame but we have bulked him up.Following national junior title victories, Yego earned selection for Kenya's 2010 African Championships team, claiming bronze in his debut international competition.His career trajectory changed dramatically upon meeting Finnish javelin coach Petteri Piironen, who also trains world silver medallist Ihab El Sayed of Egypt. An IAAF scholarship brought Yego to Finland for two weeks during winter 2011-12, where temperatures plummeted to -30C.Piironen recalled his first impression in 2013: He had been throwing 78m, so I knew if he could throw that without a coach he must be talented. He was quite explosive, had a good upper body, but he was quite weak in the legs and I had to change some technical things.As Kenya's sole field athlete among 44 team members at London 2012, Yego finished 12th while establishing a national record of 81.81m.Progress continued at the 2013 World Championships in Moscow, where his 85.40m throw narrowly missed bronze medal position.His breakthrough arrived in 2014 when he captured Commonwealth gold in Glasgow with an 83.87m throw, becoming the first Kenyan to claim a field event title at the Games.BBC Radio 5 live's Allison Curbishley observed: Julius Yego is on billboards everywhere in Kenya. If he was a legend already in Kenya he's now elevated himself to a global icon. He will enjoy every moment of this. Another medal for Kenya - they are taking over the world.BBC Sport's Denise Lewis praised the performance: This was fantastic for his country. It's quality when you see so much power go through a singular point in the javelin. It's a great story of determination and eagerness to learn.Kenya leads the medal standings with six golds among 11 total medals, with other champions including: Hyvin Kiyeng Jepkemoi - women's 3,000m steeplechase David Rudisha - men's 800m Nicholas Bett - men's 400m Ezekiel Kemboi - men's 3,000m steeplechase Vivian Jepkemoi Cheruiyot - women's 10,000m

text: More than one body has been discovered during a search for one of the Disappeared in the Republic of Ireland. The Independent Commission for the Location of Victims' Remains (ICLVR) initially believed it had discovered the remains of Joe Lynskey during excavations at a County Meath bog. However, following Thursday's discovery, investigators found additional human remains at the site.Joe Lynskey, abducted from west Belfast in 1972, was among those murdered and secretly buried by the IRA. The term the Disappeared encompasses victims who suffered this fate during the Troubles - murdered by republicans and buried in unmarked graves.What began as a search for a single body has evolved into something far more complex. Senior investigator Jon Hill explained that identification remains in preliminary stages, warning of a challenging recovery ahead.There are most certainly two bodies - we're at quite an early stage but there may be more, Hill stated. We were looking for Joe Lynskey, expecting it to be a single grave, and quite clearly that isn't the case.The discovery location sits within close proximity to where two other victims of the Disappeared are thought to rest. Hill noted that Seamus Wright and Kevin McKee's bodies were believed to be buried within a couple of hundred yards of the current search area.Both Wright and McKee were IRA members who met the same tragic end as Lynskey in 1972 - abducted and killed by their own organization. Hill confirmed that their families have been notified of the developments.Lynskey's background adds another layer to this tragic story. A former Cistercian monk from west Belfast's Beechmount area, he later joined the IRA before his abduction near his home in August 1972.Thursday's breakthrough came through contractors working under forensic archaeological supervision. The recovery operation will resume Friday, after which the state pathologist will perform post-mortem examinations to begin formal identification procedures.The Coghalstown bog excavations commenced in March, with forensic teams initially focusing their efforts on approximately 15 acres of bogland. Last month brought a poignant moment when Maria Lynskey, Joe's niece, visited the site to appeal for assistance in locating her uncle's remains.She described her family's endurance of years of pain following his disappearance. In Thursday's brief statement, Ms. Lynskey expressed gratitude to the ICLVR and those who have engaged with the commission in the search for Joe.Our thoughts are with the other families whose loved ones remain disappeared, she added.Sinn Féin president Gerry Adams acknowledged the emotional toll on affected families, stating that uncertainty surrounding the recovered bodies must be hugely traumatic for the families involved.I thank everyone who has helped in the search of the remains of those who were killed and secretly buried by the IRA, Adams said. Republicans have co-operated fully with the commission and we now need to continue to do our utmost to bring closure for the remaining families.Established through a 1999 treaty between British and Irish governments, the ICLVR operates with a specific mandate: gathering confidential information to locate missing victims' bodies. Crucially, this information cannot be utilized in criminal proceedings.Throughout its 16-year existence, the commission has pursued cases involving 16 individuals officially designated as the Disappeared. Their efforts have yielded significant results - 10 victims' remains have been successfully recovered and formally identified to date.

text: A 15-year-old Austrian synchronised swimmer suffered severe injuries when she and two other teenagers were in a collision with a bus in the athletes' village at the European Games in Baku. Two Austrian athletes suffered serious injuries when struck by a vehicle in Baku's Olympic village, though both are expected to recover, officials confirmed Thursday.Vanessa Sahinovic endured multiple fractures and a head injury but remains in stable, non-life-threatening condition. Her teammate Luna Pajer, 15, sustained arm injuries requiring specialized medical attention. Both athletes have been transported back to Vienna for treatment.The collision occurred at 08:30 local time Thursday morning as the athletes walked along a pavement within the Olympic village compound. A third team member, 15-year-old Verena Breit, also suffered injuries in the incident but was released after spending one hour at a Baku hospital for treatment of a thigh injury. She has since returned to the athletes' village.Austrian Olympic Committee president Dr Karl Stoss expressed the delegation's shock over the incident. It's a very, very sad day, said Dr Karl Stoss, AOC president. It's a tough day for the team. Sporting motives and goals are not important at this moment.Despite the traumatic circumstances, the Austrian Olympic Committee confirmed their remaining team members will continue participating in the inaugural European Games. However, Stoss acknowledged the emotional toll on the delegation. It's a real shock for us and tough to motivate the team to focus on sport.Team physician Dr Robert Kandelhard escorted both seriously injured athletes during their medical evacuation to Austria. The transportation was facilitated using a private aircraft belonging to Azerbaijan president Ilham Aliyev.They have already landed and can get the best care there, added Stoss. I'm not a medical expert but the treatment has been really good so far.Event organizers have launched an official investigation into the circumstances surrounding the accident. A Baku 2015 spokesperson issued a statement addressing the incident: This is a terrible accident, and at this time our thoughts and concerns are for the athletes involved, their families and the remainder of the Austrian delegation.The spokesperson emphasized that authorities are treating the matter seriously. The incident is now a matter of a police investigation and until that process is complete we will be making no further statement.The European Games, featuring 20 sports with 16 Olympic disciplines represented, are scheduled to commence on 12 June in what marks the competition's debut edition.In a separate development, British newspaper the Guardian claims it has been banned from entering Azerbaijan to cover the event. It says the decision appears to be linked to its report on the country's preparations for the event, which contained criticism of the government's clampdown on freedom of speech and any political opposition.

text: British artist Benedict Drew is aiming to challenge a culture of unhealthy body image through pieces of art work being unveiled across digital screens in the London Underground today. London Underground's Art on the Underground initiative, established in 2000 to champion contemporary art in London, has commissioned new works that challenge conventional advertising imagery in the capital's transit system.Benedict Drew's video installation, de-re-touch, draws inspiration from London's distinctive subterranean landscape while deliberately disrupting advertising conventions. The eight-second piece functions as a visual interruption amid the constant stream of commercial imagery that bombards daily commuters.Featuring close-up shots of an ear, a pulsating fist, and rapidly flashing text, de-re-touch confronts viewers with references to the masses of bodies encountered both as passengers and within advertising spaces. Drew has also produced a complementary experimental electronic audio piece, available for download and intended for listening during underground journeys.Drew's artistic practice spans video, sculpture, and experimental music, roots that trace back to his art school years in the 1990s.Discussing his artistic origins, Drew explains: I was very privileged with my mother running a gallery in Canterbury, so was I brought up around amazing art, it was like a family trade. I was very lucky in that respect. I went to Middlesex Arts school in the 90s which was an amazing time, some really good people had come out of that art school, people like Hayley Newman - she was totally inspiring. I then went back to doing an MA at the Slade School of Fine Art about 5 years ago, it was amazing.The underground commission particularly appealed to Drew because of Art on the Underground's public visibility and his longtime familiarity with their programming. Being asked to make something about this sight of the underground and within that kind of space was really challenging. It was quite nice to engage with something I'm so familiar with. The underground is such an intense place, he notes.London's underground environment fascinates Drew for its paradoxical nature as shared public space. It's a very shared space and you're very close to people you don't know and that's kind of unusual, in a city where we are all trying to mark our own territory. It's quite archaic as times as well and the underground can be super confusing. I think it's quite remarkable how well people behave towards each other on the tube, given the crampness of it all - people give up their seats for the elderly, people will stand on the right side of the escalator.Drew's frustration with advertising centers on its distorted representation of human bodies, particularly female forms. We're confronted with distorted images of bodies, especially female bodies. I see [advertisements] this, as a kind of oppression. - We're confronted with photos that aren't even real, they are digital drawings. Making the video work that sits amongst real advertisements was important to me and when given this project, I felt it was impossible not to address this issue.Acknowledging his position, Drew states: I acknowledge that I'm a white, male artist and I'm privileged in that respect and that maybe I'm not the best person to be talking about this, however it's all of our problem. The misrepresentation of bodies through a male gaze is a destructive thing and it's harmful and warps our perception - enough is enough.The work's title directly addresses photo manipulation practices. That's why the work is called de-re-touch, it's a call to stop re-touching photos. The video is kind of messy and scrawling and fast moving which is very different to the adverts it will be sitting amongst. I guess it's a small protest against a world of image making that is still very dominant in advertising today - Why will this unrealistic, imagined idea of a perfect body sell me an item of clothing or a gym membership? It's so messed up and it seems so obvious to say it.When asked about future exploration of body image themes, Drew remains uncertain: I don't know. I often think of my work as songs, like this piece is gestural.His hopes for audience reception are clear: I want people to stop accepting these distorted images of bodies, I'd like everyone to just say it's unacceptable because, it is - it's oppression. When you see television programmes from the 60s and seventies and you just see obvious racism or homophobia, now you think 'Gosh, that's so unacceptable', like that wouldn't happen now which is good, we've moved on. I think there will be a time where we just look back and think 'oh my gosh, what were people thinking?'Drew's creative process emerges organically from cultural consumption. It's complicated. It's emergent and comes out of a set of things I indulge in the things I see, music I listen to, or books I've read - it's kind of like constructing a cultural universe and then out of that emerges a voice and forms the way you think, my work is excreted out of that.Regarding creative blocks, Drew finds practical solutions: Deadlines help! [laughs] It's tough but I'm quite productive and I work a lot. What I like about art, as an arena, is that anything can be allowed into it - if you wish to make shoes, you could do it and that is artwork. I make drawings, prints, sculptures, videos and music; so when I'm blocked with one medium, I can jump onto another, which I find quite useful.Completion timing often depends on external pressures: Generally the day before the exhibition opens [laughs]. There's a sense that you can tinker with things forever but it's quite good to keep hold of immediacy, like if you overwork something you can lose the energy within it. I think that's the case across all forms or work.Drew's upcoming projects include participation in the British Art Show, which recently opened in Leeds before traveling to Edinburgh, requiring spatial adaptation considerations. He also continues teaching at the Slade Fine School of Art while contemplating musical ventures: I want to try to make so more music too, maybe make a record?Benedict Drew's new pieces are now visible across numerous underground stations throughout London.

text: There are few areas of life in which comic and actor Lenny Henry has not made an impact - working in theatre, television, film and charity. Lenworth George Henry expressed being very chuffed about receiving his knighthood, news that broke in the press last weekend.Throughout his five-decade journey in entertainment, Henry has weathered periodic criticism while maintaining his beloved status among the British public.The future Sir Lenny entered the world on 29 August 1958 in Dudley, West Midlands, born to Jamaican parents. Fame arrived swiftly in 1975 when the 17-year-old appeared on TV talent show New Faces, launching a career that would span generations.His triumphant New Faces performance opened doors to comedy series The Fosters and the chaotic children's program Tiswas, platforms where Henry began developing his distinctive energetic and impromptu comedic approach.Yet his subsequent career decision would shadow him for decades. Henry joined the Black and White Minstrel Show, a production featuring blacked up white performers singing American Southern songs - a format now widely condemned and mocked.The comedian toured with this show for five years, later describing it as a grotesque parody of black people.I sort of wish it had never happened, but I don't regret that I did it, Henry revealed to The Telegraph last year. Although it was a weird, reprehensible position to be in, I was working in huge venues and learning how to work a crowd.Liberation came through BBC sketch series Three of a Kind, featuring Tracey Ullman and David Copperfield alongside Henry. Debuting in 1981, the program utilized cutting-edge video effects and Ceefax-style graphics for rapid-fire, joke-packed entertainment - though many elements appear antiquated now.Simultaneously, the alternative comedy movement was gaining momentum. Through TV producer Paul Jackson, Henry encountered the innovative Comic Strip comedians, including Dawn French.Initially, French criticized Henry's style and the stand-up material he performed for survival in northern working men's clubs. His routine included wiping forehead sweat and claiming it tasted like chocolate, or threatening to relocate next to hecklers who wouldn't quiet down.Despite rocky beginnings, the pair developed mutual affection, marrying in 1984 at St Paul's Church in London's Covent Garden.Henry's political consciousness evolved concurrently. In 1984, he declined to judge a Miss Blackpool beauty contest, denouncing it as degrading to women.Television success accelerated with BBC One's The Lenny Henry Show, followed by The Delbert Wilkins Show.As a philanthropist, Henry co-founded Comic Relief in 1985, an organization that has generated over £1bn across three decades.BBC One's Chef! proved another triumph in 1993, while Henry simultaneously nurtured emerging black comedy talent, helping establish BBC Two's The Real McCoy sketch show.Serious dramatic roles beckoned next. Hope and Glory featured Henry as a struggling head teacher when it premiered on BBC One in 1999, joining projects like White Goods, Alive And Kicking and The Man.Henry also co-created and produced the 1996 BBC drama serial Neverwhere with Neil Gaiman.Theatre called in 2009 when Henry tackled the title role in Northern Broadsides' Othello production at West Yorkshire Playhouse in Leeds. The London transfer earned Sir Lenny best newcomer recognition at the London Evening Standard theatre awards.Personal tragedy struck in 2010 as Henry's 25-year marriage dissolved in divorce. Subsequently, his older brother Hylton lost his wife and two children to cancer and TB.Sir Lenny described these cataclysmic deaths as perspective-shifting events that reinforced his family devotion.Work became his refuge. In 2011, Henry made his Royal National Theatre debut in London, portraying Antipholus of Ephesus in Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors, building on his Othello success.His dramatic credentials solidified in 2014 when he claimed best actor honors at the Critics' Circle Theatre Awards for his leading performance in Fences.Recently, Sir Lenny has emerged as a vocal advocate against British television's ethnic diversity deficit.I'm used to being the only black person wherever I go, he observed. There was never a black or Asian director when I went to the BBC. Eventually I thought 'where are they all?' I spent a lot of time on my own.Things have changed a bit, but rarely at the BBC do I meet anyone of colour in a position of power.During his March 2014 Bafta speech, Henry condemned the minority shortage as appalling, continuing to champion this cause publicly.Reflecting on his knighthood, the star noted his mum would have absolutely been chuffed while confessing his own amazement.It was lovely, it was a lovely feeling, it was like being filled with lemonade for 10 or 15 minutes, he shared with BBC Radio 2.

text: Iran has confirmed some of its computer systems were infected with the Duqu trojan, but said it has found a way to control the malware. Iran has become the latest victim of the sophisticated Duqu spyware, marking what officials describe as the third virus to strike the country following previous cyber assaults.Security researchers had already pinpointed Iran among at least eight nations in Duqu's crosshairs. The malicious software appears engineered specifically for data theft, creating a foundation for subsequent cyber operations.While the perpetrators remain unidentified, investigators have uncovered curious cultural references embedded within Duqu's programming code that point to American television content.Iran's state news agency IRNA confirmed that the nation's cyber defense forces have mobilized against the infection. Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, who leads Iran's civil defence body, announced progress in containment efforts.The software to control the virus has been developed and made available to organisations and corporations, Jalali stated. All the organisations and centres that could be susceptible to being contaminated are being controlled.According to Jalali, investigators continue working on a final report documenting which organizations fell victim to the attack.This latest cyber incident follows a pattern of digital warfare targeting Iran. In 2010, Iranian authorities blamed Western nations for deploying the Stuxnet worm against nuclear installations. Subsequently, in April 2011, officials reported discovering Stars, a second malware variant targeting national infrastructure.Kaspersky Lab's security experts believe Stars functioned as keylogging software, potentially operating as part of the broader Duqu campaign. Such programs possess extensive surveillance capabilities, including system information gathering, screenshot capture, file searches, and password harvesting.The cybersecurity firm's detailed analysis revealed Duqu's sophisticated delivery mechanism. In one documented case, an unidentified company received correspondence from someone calling himself Mr B Jason, proposing a business partnership. Researchers suspect this alias references the Jason Bourne fictional spy franchise.Recipients received Microsoft Word attachments bearing company-specific titles, cleverly disguising the malicious payload as legitimate correspondence rather than obvious spam.Duqu's creators employed unique attack strategies for each target, generating separate file sets and utilizing different command servers. Kaspersky documented at least twelve such customized attacks.The malware activated through a Truetype font vulnerability once victims opened infected documents, but remained dormant until detecting ten minutes of user inactivity—a clever evasion technique.Particularly intriguing was the font's designation as Dexter Regular, credited to Showtime Inc. Kaspersky researchers noted this represented another prank pulled by the Duqu authors, since Showtime Inc is the cable broadcasting company behind the TV series Dexter, about a CSI doctor who happens also to be a serial killer.Following activation, the exploit installed system drivers that analysis suggests were compiled as early as August 2007. If this information is correct, then the authors of Duqu must have been working on this project for over four years, Kaspersky's report concluded.These drivers initiated processes culminating in full Duqu trojan deployment, enabling attackers to introduce additional modules, compromise networked systems, and extract sensitive information.Investigation efforts face significant obstacles as suspected perpetrators have apparently shut down multiple command servers believed central to the attack infrastructure, effectively covering their digital tracks.

text: Parents should have lessons provided by the government on how to raise their children, Britain's leading public health expert has said. The Faculty of Public Health (FPH) has unveiled a comprehensive report demanding urgent mental health improvements, with outgoing president Professor John Ashton delivering a stark warning about widespread neglect of children by schools and parents alike.According to the report's findings, mental, emotional, and psychological problems now account for more disability than all physical health problems put together. This alarming statistic underscores the scale of a crisis that Professor Ashton believes requires immediate state intervention to prevent children from being crippled by conditions such as anxiety, anorexia and obesity.The research reveals that one in 10 children between ages five and 16 currently suffer from mental health issues severe enough to warrant professional support and treatment. Central to these problems, the report emphasizes, is the quality of the parent-child relationship and parenting more broadly, which played a primary role in determining outcomes.Professor Ashton painted a troubling picture of modern child development, explaining: We've done well in terms of producing live, healthy babies over the last 60, 70 years, but, by the time children are leaving school, between 10% and 15% of them are in trouble emotionally or mentally, and suffer from things like obesity, eating disorders, anxiety and stress. His assessment was blunt: Having produced healthy babies we then set about neglecting them.The report's author, Professor Sarah Stewart-Brown, highlighted the critical nature of early intervention, noting that the first 1,001 days of a child's life are particularly important and that over three-quarters of all mental health problems emerge in childhood and adolescence. While acknowledging that diet and activity played a role in mental health, she emphasized that supporting parenting is key.Despite the grim statistics, both professors expressed optimism about prevention possibilities. The report states: Although we cannot say yet exactly how much of the burden of mental illness could be prevented, we know prevention is possible.Professor Ashton outlined practical solutions, suggesting that parenting advice and support could be provided by investing in existing networks - such as health visitors and schools. His recommendations extend to modern communication methods, including using social media to reach parents and setting up 24/7 helplines - for example for people raising adolescents.Professor Stewart-Brown advocated for a multi-faceted approach, proposing that programmes based in schools, workplaces, doctors' surgeries, and in the community could help.Given what Professor Ashton described as the huge financial and human cost of mental health problems, he argued that addressing root causes should become a priority. The Faculty of Public Health, which represents 3,300 professionals and establishes standards for public health specialists across the UK, is positioning this report as a call to action for systematic change in how society approaches children's mental wellbeing.

text: Germany's second-biggest lender, Commerzbank, is planning to cut 9,600 jobs over the next four years and end dividend payments for the first time. Germany's second-largest lender, Commerzbank, announced Thursday a sweeping restructuring plan that will eliminate nearly 10,000 positions while simultaneously creating 2,300 new roles in expanding business segments.The €1.1bn (£948m) overhaul aims to achieve sustainably increased profitability by the end of 2020, according to the bank's statement. Friday's board meeting will determine the final details of this strategic transformation.With approximately 51,300 employees as of last year, Commerzbank plans to focus on its core businesses serving private and small business customers alongside corporate clients while advancing digital processes. The restructuring will merge the bank's Mittelstandsbank division, which serves medium-sized German companies, with its corporates and markets unit.This consolidation may force Commerzbank to write off roughly €700m during the third quarter. Additionally, the bank intends to scale back its investment banking operations, a move designed to reduce earnings volatility and regulatory risk and will free up capital to be invest in core client businesses.The announcement coincides with Deutsche Bank's denial of reports suggesting Germany's government was preparing a rescue package for the nation's largest lender. Deutsche Bank currently faces a massive $14bn (£10.8bn; €12.5bn) US fine for mis-selling mortgage-backed securities prior to the 2008 financial crisis.Employee representatives will soon enter discussions regarding the job reductions, which translate to 7,300 net full-time position losses after accounting for new role creation in growth areas. The restructuring is projected to generate billions in annual savings while enabling investment in emerging business sectors.The German government maintains a 15% stake in Commerzbank, acquired during the 2008 financial crisis intervention. Critics argue that German banks have responded too slowly to credit crunch aftermath, facing shared challenges including intensified competition, costly regulatory compliance, and profit-eroding ultra-low interest rates.Despite anticipated write-offs and increased loan loss provisions due to shipping market weakness, Commerzbank expects to achieve a modest net profit for 2016.Market reaction was mixed Thursday. Commerzbank shares dropped 3% in Frankfurt trading, while Deutsche Bank stock gained 1% following Wednesday's 2% increase, though the shares remain near 30-year lows reached earlier this week.However, Deutsche Bank faces mounting pressure from short-sellers. Investors continue betting against the stock, anticipating potential share issuance that would dilute existing holdings' value, allowing them to profit by repurchasing at reduced prices.

text: More than 150 beavers living in Tayside waterways have adapted well to life in Scotland, studies have found. A comprehensive study examining beavers that have established themselves across the Tayside region reveals the animals have successfully adapted to their Scottish environment, though agricultural concerns remain unresolved.The Tayside Beaver Study Group's findings will influence the Scottish government's upcoming decision on whether to grant permanent status to these populations, which emerged from escapes or unauthorized releases. This decision comes as officials simultaneously evaluate a separate trial reintroduction program currently running in Knapdale, Argyll.When authorities last addressed the beaver situation in 2012, they committed to three years of monitoring rather than pursuing the contentious alternatives of trapping or culling the animals. The current study, commissioned by Scottish Natural Heritage, addresses earlier concerns about potential ecosystem damage and disease transmission.The Eurasian beavers—a species historically native to Britain—now inhabit waterways spanning from Kinloch Rannoch, Kenmore and Crieff westward to Forfar, Perth and Bridge of Earn eastward. Genetic analysis suggests Bavarian or German origins for these populations.According to the study group's assessment, the animals demonstrate successful reproduction while continuing territorial expansion throughout Tayside. Disease testing revealed no threats to humans, domestic animals, or native wildlife species.However, agricultural impacts present the most significant challenge. Dam construction on major waterways like the River Isla or Tay could trigger flooding across nearby farmland. While tree protection methods have proven effective against beaver gnawing and felling, managing the animals' burrowing activities in flood banks and drainage ditch damming remains problematic.The study group emphasized that 70% of reported negative impacts carried financial consequences, making impact management crucial for any permanent reintroduction decision.David Bale, who chairs the study group and serves as SNH's area manager for Tayside and Grampian, described the research as very useful.The findings show there is no evident risk of diseases being transmitted from the Tayside beavers to other animals, or indeed to humans, Bale stated.The genetic tests tell us that they would be suitable for permanent reintroduction to Scotland, because they are Eurasian rather than North American beavers. text: Babies born by Caesarean are at higher risk of becoming obese, especially compared with siblings born by vaginal delivery, a large study suggests. A comprehensive study tracking over 22,000 individuals from birth to adulthood has revealed a potential connection between Caesarean delivery and increased obesity risk later in life, according to findings published in JAMA Pediatrics.The research, conducted by American scientists from Harvard Medical School and partner institutions, discovered that children delivered via Caesarean section showed a 15% higher likelihood of developing obesity after researchers controlled for various factors including maternal weight and age. Even more striking was the comparison within families: when siblings were born through different delivery methods, those delivered by Caesarean faced a 64% greater obesity risk compared to their vaginally-born brothers and sisters.However, the study's authors acknowledge they cannot definitively establish Caesarean delivery as the direct cause of obesity or fully explain the underlying mechanisms. Their hypothesis centers on differences in gastrointestinal microbiota—the beneficial gut bacteria that naturally colonize our bodies and vary between individuals.The researchers suggest that vaginally-born babies gain exposure to healthy gut bacteria that may play a crucial role in dietary regulation. These microorganisms, collectively termed microbiota, have been linked to various diseases but also show promise in treating conditions and promoting overall health.Currently, about 26% of UK births occur via Caesarean section—a surgical procedure involving incisions in the abdomen and uterus to deliver the baby. The Royal College of Midwives reports that these rates have climbed consistently in recent years.Multiple factors beyond delivery method influence childhood obesity risk, experts emphasize. Maternal diet, gestational diabetes, and breastfeeding practices all contribute significantly. Caesarean-delivered babies face reduced breastfeeding rates, which research has already connected to heightened obesity risk. Children's own dietary patterns also substantially impact their future weight trajectories.Medical professionals have developed vaginal seeding, a technique transferring maternal vaginal fluid containing beneficial bacteria to Caesarean-born infants. However, doctors caution about potential infection risks associated with this procedure.Dr Simon Cork, research associate in Imperial College London's investigative medicine department, stressed the complexity of childhood obesity factors extending far beyond birth delivery methods.Overall, the literature surrounding this area suggests that there may be a link between Caesarean section and obesity. However, this link is neither fully proven nor understood, Cork explained.Most often Caesarean births are as a result of medical necessity, rather than elective, and as such this risk would outweigh any concerns mothers should have regarding the possibility of future weight issues.Prof Neena Modi, President of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, called for additional research to determine whether Caesarean delivery directly causes obesity.Caesarean section can be life saving for women and their babies. However many women are now considering Caesarean section where there is no medical indication, Modi noted.It is important that they are told about the possibility of increased risk of obesity in their children, to help them make an informed birth choice.She emphasized controllable factors that definitively impact infant health: It is also important for parents to focus on factors that they can influence which definitely impact on their infant's health. This includes maintaining a healthy weight at the time of conception, and throughout pregnancy.

text: Ian Bell has stepped down as captain of Warwickshire in all formats of the game to focus on batting. However, the county now finds itself languishing at the foot of Division One's Championship table, barely a year after that success.The 35-year-old, whose last England appearance came in November 2015, recently found himself excluded from the Bears' T20 lineup entirely.This is the right time for me to stand down, Bell said. As a senior player, I will support the team in all ways possible and I believe that our squad has very exciting times ahead. It's been an absolute honour to lead my home county over the last 18 months and my decision to stand down is something that I have thought long and hard about over a period of weeks.Ashley Giles, the county's sports director, praised Bell's brave choice to concentrate purely on his batting responsibilities. This season, he has managed 345 runs across 14 innings at an average of 24.64, failing to register a Championship century since April 2016.His T20 Blast campaign yielded 251 runs in 12 matches with a strike rate of 117.29, though he was demoted in the batting order following a sequence of disappointing scores as opener. After failing to bat in the Bears' penultimate group fixture, he was omitted completely from Friday's final group match against Lancashire at Old Trafford - a victory that secured the Bears' quarter-final berth.New Zealand international Grant Elliott took over captaincy duties for that match and is anticipated to continue leading the side in Friday's last-eight encounter against Surrey at The Oval.Bell previously celebrated T20 Blast success with Birmingham Bears in 2014 and added to his trophy collection by winning the Big Bash with Perth Scorchers in Australia last winter.

text: Heinz has been taken to court in Australia after a watchdog said it falsely marketed a children's food as healthy. A legal battle has erupted over Heinz's discontinued Shredz snacks, with Australia's consumer watchdog challenging the food giant's marketing claims about products targeted at young children.The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has taken Heinz to Federal Court, arguing that Shredz - manufactured from fruit juice concentrate and pastes - should be classified as confectionery rather than healthy snacks. The regulator contends these toddler-focused products contained more than 60% sugar content.During Federal Court proceedings in Adelaide, ACCC lawyer Tom Duggan revealed that the berries, apple and veg variety of Shredz contained up to 68.7 grams of sugar per 100 grams. The discontinued snacks were available in three varieties: peach apple and veg, berries apple and veg, and strawberry and apple with chia seeds.Marketing materials for the products prominently displayed fresh fruits on packaging while claiming the contents were 99% fruit and veg. However, nutrition expert Rosemary Stanton, who contributed to Australia's dietary guidelines, disputes these health claims.Confectionery with added vitamins is still confectionery, she said. Stanton compared the nutritional value to other processed foods, noting: Sure, there are some positive nutrients in there, just as there are positive nutrients in a Big Mac.While acknowledging that Shredz contained dietary fibre and various vitamins, Stanton emphasized that many unhealthy foods share similar characteristics. She recommended treating Shredz as an occasional treat rather than a regular snack.Heinz has mounted a vigorous defense against the allegations, categorically denying any misleading marketing practices. The company maintains its products were appropriate snack foods designed for children aged one to three years.The Shredz products had a similar nutrition profile to dried apple or sultanas, Heinz stated, rejecting the ACCC's packaging claims. Heinz stands behind the Shredz products and their packaging.The company emphasized that Shredz were sold in small, individually-packaged portions suitable for the target age group.This legal challenge originated from a June 2016 complaint filed by the Obesity Policy Coalition, a campaign group focused on children's food products. The ACCC is pursuing financial penalties, corrective notices and legal costs from Heinz as part of its enforcement action.The case highlights ongoing tensions between food manufacturers and health advocates over marketing practices for children's products, particularly regarding sugar content and nutritional claims.

text: Former US Open champions Roger Federer and Maria Sharapova enjoyed straight sets wins at Flushing Meadows on a day that brought some notable exits. Australia's Sam Groth fell to Swiss second seed Roger Federer in straight sets, 6-4 6-4 6-4, as the five-time US Open champion advanced to the third round. Meanwhile, Russia's fifth seed Maria Sharapova secured her spot in the fourth round by defeating Germany's Sabine Lisicki 6-2 6-4.The tournament witnessed major upsets as both two-time champion Venus Williams and second seed Simona Halep crashed out in their third-round encounters. Williams, playing before her home crowd, suffered a dramatic 6-0 0-6 7-6 (7-5) defeat to Italy's Sara Errani. The match saw Williams twice recover from being down a break in the decisive third set and even had the opportunity to serve out the victory, yet Errani's fighting spirit forced a tie-break. Williams' downfall came through excessive unforced errors, totaling 52 throughout the match.Errani, who had previously never won more than three games in a set against Williams across three prior meetings, will face Croatia's Mirjana Lucic-Baroni in the next round. The 32-year-old Croatian qualifier stunned Romania's Halep 7-6 (8-6) 6-2, marking her first Grand Slam fourth-round appearance since reaching Wimbledon's semi-finals in 1999. Off-court difficulties had derailed Lucic-Baroni's career, but she returned to Grand Slam competition in 2010 following an eight-year absence.Germany's sixth seed Angelique Kerber also exited early, falling 6-1 7-5 to Switzerland's Belinda Bencic. It was unbelievably good. I will remember forever that moment. I don't know why I did that. I was not angry. The conditions were tough again, said Berdych, 28, who avoided becoming the first top-10 seed to go out of the men's tournament. You go from day till early evening. I was happy I was able to break her.Other notable results: Shuai Peng (Chn) beat Roberta Vinci (Ita) (28) 6-4 6-3; Grigor Dimitrov (Bul) (7) beat Dudi Sela (Isr) 6-1 6-1 6-2; Lucie Safarova (Cze) (14) beat Alize Cornet (Fra) (22) 6-3 6-7 (3-7) 6-4; Gael Monfils (Fra) (20) beat Alejandro Gonzalez (Col) 7-5 6-3 6-2.Mirjana Lucic-Baroni (Cro) beat Simona Halep (Rom) (2) 7-6 (8-6) 6-2After so many years, to be here again, it's incredible, said Lucic-Baroni, who contested only two professional matches between 2004 and 2006. text: High street stores had a disappointing October, according to figures from the Scottish Retail Consortium (SRC). Scotland's retail sector faced a challenging October as sales declined 2.4% compared to the previous year, contrasting sharply with the UK's overall 0.9% growth, according to the SRC/KPMG Scottish Retail Sales Monitor.The disappointing performance became more pronounced when examining like-for-like sales, which exclude variables such as new store launches. These figures revealed a steeper 2.8% decline, painting a concerning picture for Scottish retailers.Unusually mild autumn conditions appear to have significantly impacted consumer behavior, particularly dampening demand for seasonal clothing. Meanwhile, shoppers showed reluctance to purchase electrical goods, seemingly anticipating better deals during upcoming promotional periods.There is no doubt the declines in Scottish retail sales in October, when measured against a relatively weak month last year, are disappointing for retailers when set against mainly dry weather and temperatures only marginally warmer than average, explained David McCorquodale, head of retail at KPMG. He characterized the results as a sobering reminder of the frailty of the economic recovery.The weather conditions proved particularly problematic for retailers hoping to capitalize on seasonal merchandise. McCorquodale noted the temperatures wasn't cold enough for strong sales of coats or boots, forcing retailers to focus on pushing themed products for Halloween while shoppers remained cautious, perhaps waiting for heavy promotions.Food retailers experienced their own struggles, with total food sales dropping 3.2% compared to October 2014. The Rugby World Cup failed to provide the expected boost after Scotland's early tournament exit prevented stores from fully capitalizing on the sporting event.An unusual factor emerged with Halloween falling on a Saturday this year - the SRC suggested some Scots chose traditional guising activities over shopping trips, further impacting retail footfall.Despite Scotland experiencing its driest and sunniest October since 2003, the pleasant weather paradoxically hurt autumn and winter clothing sales. However, Halloween fancy dress costumes bucked the trend, reportedly performing well.Consumer caution extended to electrical products, with shoppers deliberately postponing purchases in anticipation of Black Friday discounts later in the month. This strategic waiting resulted in total non-food sales falling 1.8% compared to the previous year.McCorquodale emphasized the critical nature of the coming weeks for retailers, noting that the tactics around Black Friday and the run-up to Christmas beginning to unfold would prove vital for recovery.SRC director David Lonsdale delivered a stark assessment: This rather pallid set of results paints a disappointing October overall for Scotland's retailers, with total retail sales edging down again once falling shop prices are taken into account.Lonsdale suggested consumer behavior might reflect strategic patience rather than reduced spending power. It could be that shoppers are simply holding out for even better deals in the run-up to Christmas, perhaps with an eye towards potential online discounting at the end of this month, despite the fact that shop prices are already at record lows.Looking ahead, retailers are pinning hopes on upcoming political developments. With the spotlight on the Autumn Statement and the Scottish Budget over the next few weeks, retailers will be hoping for measures which put money in peoples' pockets and which encourage them to invest and grow, Lonsdale concluded.

text: The singers of global hit Despacito have lashed out against the Venezuelan president, accusing him of using their song for political gains. During his weekly television broadcast Sunday, President Nicolas Maduro unveiled a politically charged remix of the global hit Despacito, transforming the chart-topping song into propaganda for his contentious constitutional assembly election.The reworked version promotes Maduro's plans for a new citizen's assembly set to convene Sunday with authority to rewrite Venezuela's constitution. As the altered tune played, the president clapped enthusiastically while his audience swayed to the beat.Our call to the 'Constituent Assembly' only seeks to unite the country ... Despacito! the modified lyrics declare.The original artists reacted with fury. Luis Fonsi unleashed his anger across social media platforms: At no point was I asked, nor did I authorise, the use or the change in lyrics of Despacito for political means, and much less so in the middle of the deplorable situation experienced by Venezuela, a country I love so much.He continued: My music is for all those who want to listen to it and enjoy it, not to be used as propaganda that tries to manipulate the will of a people who are crying out for their freedom.Daddy Yankee's response proved equally scathing. On Instagram, he shared Maduro's image marked with a bold red cross. That you illegally appropriate a song [Despacito] does not compare with the crimes you commit and have committed in Venezuela, he declared. Your dictatorial regime is a joke, not only for my Venezuelan brothers, but for the entire world.While Despacito literally means slowly and originally referenced seductive romance, Venezuela's sanitized adaptation strips away sexual content entirely. The reimagined chorus urges: Slowly, take your vote rather than weapons, and express your ideas. Always in peace and calm.When presenting the remix to his supporters, Maduro explained that a creative team had produced the version. What do you think, eh? the grinning president asked his crowd, seeking approval for the musical makeover.Venezuela continues experiencing turbulent months marked by frequently violent demonstrations. Last week's general strike drew millions of participants, while approximately 100 people have perished amid ongoing unrest that compounds the nation's economic collapse—a crisis leaving citizens without adequate food and medical supplies.Maduro's proposed constituent assembly would possess constitutional rewriting powers and could circumvent the opposition-dominated legislature. While critics argue he seeks to establish permanent dictatorship, Maduro maintains this represents the sole path toward restoring peace to his fractured country.The Puerto Rican original has achieved unprecedented worldwide success. A collaboration featuring Canadian pop sensation Justin Bieber recently claimed the record as history's most-streamed song.Diosdado Cabello, another prominent Socialist Party figure, recently exploited Despacito for political messaging as well. As the song says, step by step, slowly and suavely, they [the critics] want to create a coup, he stated to local media outlets.Opposition forces have responded with viral social media parodies, including Madurito. Another version, Bien Flaquito (Very Skinny), satirizes the country's severe food shortages.

text: A BBC sitcom has been criticised as Islamophobic during a Commons debate about whether the BBC's programmes and staff reflect UK diversity. Death threats and accusations of promoting harmful stereotypes have shadowed the BBC's award-winning sitcom Citizen Khan, as parliamentary criticism intensifies over the broadcaster's diversity record.Creator Adil Ray revealed to Radio Times that he has faced death threats over the comedy, which launched in 2012 amid complaints about its portrayal of Muslim families. The show continues to draw fire from within Labour ranks, with Ealing Central and Acton MP Rupa Huq delivering scathing criticism during a recent parliamentary debate.I feel as if I didn't know what the year is ... you would think it's an everyday tale of a Birmingham family of Muslims but they're really quite backward, Ms Huq stated. The MP, whose sister Konnie previously presented Blue Peter, escalated her attack by referencing concerns raised by colleague Chuka Umunna: Again, the Islamophobic point [Labour MP Chuka Umunna] made, it's a beardy weirdy chap and they're not quite cutting off people's hands but I can imagine that being in a future episode.Despite the controversy, Citizen Khan has secured recognition at both the Royal Television Society and Asian Media Awards, with the BBC defending its fifth series as evidence of broad audience appeal.The fact that Citizen Khan returns for its fifth series this year is a sign of its popularity with all audiences - indeed the show has won several awards, including Best TV character at the Asian Media Awards, a BBC spokesman responded. The broadcaster emphasized that creator Ray shares the same British Pakistani Muslim background as his fictional family, adding: As with all sitcoms the characters are comic creations and not meant to be representative of the community as a whole.The criticism emerged during a broader parliamentary assault on BBC diversity practices, led by former culture minister David Lammy. The Tottenham MP launched a comprehensive attack on the corporation's recruitment patterns, alleging it continues hiring the same old faces from the same old schools to the same old jobs.Lammy revealed he had been contacted by black and Asian BBC employees who cannot speak up because they do not want to be labelled a troublemaker. His concerns extended beyond individual shows to systemic representation issues, particularly highlighting the Chinese community as totally invisible on the broadcaster.Statistical evidence supports Lammy's concerns, with ethnic minority staff representation declining from 13.1% in 2015 to 12.2% currently, despite 29 diversity schemes operating between 1999 and 2014. The MP questioned whether genuine diversity exists in management positions, observing: We all go into Broadcasting House and see the security, see black staff at the junior ends, but walk into that newsroom, think about the editorial decisions that are being made, and ask yourself, is that really representative of our country as a whole?While praising diversity achievements in children's television, BBC Three and documentaries, Lammy insisted the new BBC charter must address persistent representation failures.Conservative MP Helen Grant proposed voluntary disclosure of recruitment, retention, promotion and pay data for ethnic minority staff, while Labour's Julie Elliott from Sunderland Central argued the BBC should reflect every UK region, noting that Salford's MediaCity UK location represents only part of northern England.Earlier in the debate, Umunna had targeted television's broader treatment of Muslim communities, linking rising Islamophobia to broadcasters' reliance on self-appointed community leaders who purport to speak for that community but have no mandate whatsoever to do so.The BBC responded by claiming good progress on diversity while promising to develop new and innovative ideas to do even better through an upcoming diversity strategy. Almost half of our workforce is made up of women and the proportion of our workforce who are black, Asian and other ethnic minority is at an all-time high, the spokesman concluded.The parliamentary criticism reflects ongoing tensions between creative freedom and responsible representation, as the BBC navigates complaints about both its programming content and internal diversity record.

text: Two Welsh councils are facing legal action over claims they continue to uphold motions alleged to be racist. An organization established to combat what it describes as rising anti-Semitism across the UK has secured judicial review proceedings against two Welsh councils over controversial motions they adopted.Jewish Human Rights Watch will challenge resolutions passed by both Swansea and Gwynedd councils, in legal action that could burden the local authorities with costs reaching tens of thousands of pounds. Both councils have rejected the allegations against them.The judicial review hearing commences Wednesday and is anticipated to continue for two days. JHRW plans similar action against Leicester council.Back in 2010, Swansea council was considering contractual involvement with Veolia, a company that belonged to a consortium developing a railway system connecting Israel to settlements in occupied East Jerusalem. The motion presented to councillors declared this project not only contravenes UN demands but is in contravention of international law. It further stated that the United Nations has demanded that Israeli settlement activities and occupation should not be supported.Several councillors urged both the council leader and chief executive at that time to support the position of the UN in regards to the Israeli settlements in East Jerusalem, so long as to do so would not be in breach of any relevant legislation. They additionally requested the council avoid conducting business with any company in breach of international law or UN obligations or demands, so long as to do so would not be in breach of any relevant legislation.Though approved in June 2010, this motion carries no binding force.Four years later, Gwynedd council adopted its own motion advocating for a trade embargo against Israel, denouncing the attacks by the Israeli state on the territory of the Palestinians living in the Gaza Strip. The resolution emphasized: It must be made clear that the proposal condemned the Israeli state and not the Jewish religion.Robert Festenstein, the solicitor representing Jewish Human Rights Watch, expressed his position clearly: We would like to see the motions quashed. I don't understand why they would pass it in the first place. I mean, they wouldn't pass a motion saying something derogatory about women, so why would they do that about Jews? Why would they pass a motion which has a detrimental impact upon the relationship with Jewish people in Swansea, particularly in Wales generally? It has absolutely nothing to do with Swansea.Responding to the legal challenge, a Swansea council spokesman issued a statement: On 10 March 2016, full council decided not to rescind the notice of motion that was passed on 17 June, 2010. The council has never boycotted Israeli goods and has no intention of doing so. For legal reasons, it would be inappropriate to comment further.Meanwhile, a Gwynedd council spokesman declined detailed comment: It would not be appropriate for us to comment regarding this matter due to ongoing legal proceedings which the council is defending.

text: The European Space Agency (Esa) has turned off one of its most successful ever missions. The LISA Pathfinder satellite, launched in 2015 to validate crucial technologies for future gravitational wave detection missions, has officially concluded its operations after dramatically exceeding all performance expectations.Gravitational waves represent ripples that traverse space-time when black holes merge, and Pathfinder's remarkable achievements directly enabled the June selection of the LISA mission - a billion-euro endeavor featuring three satellites scheduled for launch between 2030 and 2034.LISA Pathfinder has shown that LISA is feasible at full sensitivity, more than we could hope for, said principal investigator Stefano Vitale. I think it has been a stepping stone for GW astronomy, and an incredibly rewarding experience for all the team involved. Thank you, and stay tuned on LISA! he told BBC News.The future LISA mission will integrate numerous Pathfinder systems, particularly the critical laser interferometer instrumentation now proven capable of detecting gravitational waves (GW) in space.Prof Vitale personally transmitted the final termination commands to Pathfinder from Esa's Darmstadt, Germany mission control center. The satellite had been operating 1.5 million km from Earth in a sunward position, conducting measurement demonstrations.These commands forced Pathfinder to reboot using pre-corrupted software, effectively disabling the gravity probe and preventing operation of subsystems including its transmitter. The only way you could recover the spacecraft would be to go up there and attach an umbilical and restart from another computer, explained spacecraft operations manager Ian Harrison.This passivating procedure eliminates potential hazards to future missions from collisions or radio interference. In April, the Darmstadt team had already used Pathfinder's thrusters to relocate it from its station - a coveted position for solar observation missions.The satellite should now drift safely around our star, though Harrison noted: There's a very, very small chance it could return to the Earth-Moon system; it's so remote but you can't actually say it's zero. The mission analysis actually looked at the planetary positions 500 years into the future.Currently, gravitational waves represent science's most significant breakthrough. Ground-based US laboratories have recently begun detecting these phenomena from merging objects measuring 20-30 times our Sun's mass. However, space-based observatories could potentially discover sources millions of times larger and detect activity extending to the observable Universe's edge.Such capabilities should substantially enhance our gravity comprehension and potentially reveal flaws in Einstein's previously flawless equations.LISA will identify gravitational waves by reflecting laser light between three spacecraft arranged in triangular formation with 2.5 million km sides. These light beams will monitor precise positions of small, free-floating blocks within the satellites.When gravitational waves traverse the triangle, distances between blocks in different spacecraft should alter by minuscule amounts - mere atomic width fractions.Pathfinder's laser and gold-block monitoring system was miniaturized for single-satellite operation. While incapable of detecting gravitational waves itself, the instrumentation's exceptional sensitivity validated the metrology principles.LISA Pathfinder did more than we ever asked for, said Paul McNamara, Esa's Pathfinder project scientist. It met its requirements on day one, the day we switched on its science. But we then met and surpassed the requirements of LISA. So, it's been a phenomenal mission. text: UK scientists have successfully germinated seeds from the critically endangered Japanese Birch, a species that has just 21 known trees remaining. During an expedition to mountainous terrain near Tokyo last year, researchers gathered crucial seeds that may represent the final hope for a critically endangered tree species.The Betula chichibuensis faces an uncertain future, with experts warning that its remaining wild population lacks the numbers needed for natural survival. According to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the species confronts a dire prognosis in its natural habitat.The IUCN's Red List of Threatened Species highlights the precarious situation: The small population and restricted distribution... make it susceptible to natural disaster or disease. Additionally, the organization notes a critical biological challenge: The species is also self-incompatible, requiring two individuals to be close enough to cross-pollinate one another, making seed production uncertain in small subpopulations.Environmental pressures compound these natural vulnerabilities. Evidence points to ongoing deforestation and habitat degradation within the tree's remaining territory, presenting a threat to the survival of this species, the IUCN reports.**A Race Against Time**In 2014, a collaborative team from the University of Oxford Botanic Gardens and the University of Tokyo launched a critical conservation mission. Among the expedition members was Dan Luscombe, a dendrologist representing the Forestry Commission's Bedgebury National Pinetum and Forest.Reflecting on the challenging collection process, Luscombe shared with BBC News: I guess we got little lucky in terms of being there at the right time. The remote location presented significant obstacles. It is found in a very, very remote location and it is not an easy place to get to. It has got very, very low viability so we were very lucky that we were able to collect a lot of seeds... as birch seeds shatter and shed everywhere, so once it has done that you will never find it.The expedition yielded approximately 1,000 seeds, which researchers at Bedgebury Pinetum successfully cultivated into roughly 100 seedlings. This achievement represents a significant conservation milestone for the threatened birch species.**Conservation Through Cultivation**The project's philosophy centers on preserving genetic diversity through wild-sourced specimens. text: Almost 1,500 secondary pupils across Aberdeen have been given anti-weapons lessons in the wake of the killing of schoolboy Bailey Gwynne. A year after 16-year-old Bailey's fatal stabbing at Cults Academy during a confrontation with another student, police officers are delivering knife crime prevention sessions to Aberdeen schoolchildren. The attacker, now serving a nine-year sentence for culpable homicide, had carried the weapon undetected by staff.Next year will see these educational sessions extended to P7 pupils across Aberdeen, following an independent review that concluded Bailey's death was potentially avoidable had teachers been aware his killer possessed a knife.At Aberdeen's Hazlehead Academy, PC Seb Cook addressed an S1 class directly: You'll have heard about the tragic incident that happened a year ago in Aberdeen. We never, ever want anything like that to happen again. You guys will never need to take anything sharp or dangerous into school.However, critics question whether students would actually report friends carrying weapons. When BBC Scotland asked pupils about their response to discovering someone with a weapon, responses varied. I would probably just go up to a teacher, maybe even up to the person and just say 'why are you doing that, think of the consequences', one student explained.Another demonstrated conflicted loyalty: People say don't grass up a mate, but if it's serious I think you should.Hazlehead head teacher Jim Purdie emphasized the broader implications: It's not just about carrying weapons or blades, it's about the legal aspect of that, and then the consequences for the pupils, for their families, for their friends. There's an expression we often use, which is if we don't know things are happening we can't do anything about them. We are constantly reminding our children to take responsibility. If there's something that is upsetting them, they know who to tell.Police Scotland faces challenges in tracking school weapon incidents accurately. Supt Andy McKay of Police Scotland Safer Communities explained: Police Scotland relies on local authorities to report all incidents of weapon possession so that accurate figures can be collated. Following the report into Bailey Gwynne's death, Aberdeen City have been working closely with Police Scotland to ensure each and every incident of weapon possession is reported, however it will be up to other local authorities to consider this recommendation moving forward.McKay acknowledged data limitations: As a result, the figures collated to date may not offer a true reflection of the national picture in relation to possession of weapons in schools due to inconsistent reporting and recording methods. Figures represent a snapshot in time, and may not accurately portray a divisional or national perspective.Last month saw approval of a comprehensive strategy targeting weapon prevention in Aberdeen schools. The initiative will provide staff with clear guidance on incident recording, pupil searches, and weapon confiscation procedures, including knives. Additionally, the council approved professional development opportunities enabling teachers to deliver anti-weapon and knife crime education.Child welfare professional Andrew Lowe conducted the review that generated 21 recommendations following Bailey's death in October last year.
