text: When Wes Metcalfe bought a cucumber from a Tesco shop in Dinnington, South Yorkshire, he did not expect it to come with a dead worm. A Sheffield man's discovery of a deceased worm in his Tesco cucumber has sparked a viral social media exchange that has captivated thousands online.The saga began Saturday when trainee electrician Mr Metcalfe took to Facebook with a humorous complaint that would eventually garner over 30,000 shares and 10,000 comments.Dear Tesco, yesterday I purchased one of your fine cucumbers to make my favourite dish - a cucumber sandwich, his post began. Upon opening my cucumber, I discovered a worm inside the wrapping. I thought - at last, finally Tesco have come up with something to beat Aldi's free-spider-with-bananas offer.The customer's witty narrative continued as he described introducing his children to their new pet, whom they christened William. However, their excitement was short-lived.Our new pet appeared to be very unresponsive, we just put it down to him being sleepy and decided to give him some time to come round. Twenty-four hours later and William still hasn't moved - on closer inspection he seems quite flat (again, see picture) and I think he may be dead, Mr Metcalfe wrote.His complaint took an increasingly theatrical turn: Well... I'm no vet, but I think the tight shrink wrap on the cucumber may have squashed and killed William. I know Aldi's banana spiders were deadly, but at least they had some life in them.The post concluded with mock despair over planning a worm funeral and losing his appetite for cucumber sandwiches - which as everyone knows are a favourite at any wake - before challenging Tesco to wiggle your way out of this one.Tesco's response proved equally creative and tongue-in-cheek. Customer care representative Rob crafted a poetic tribute, explaining his upcoming festival plans would prevent attendance at William's funeral.I'll be heading to a muddy festival shortly, trawling through the fields of damp grass and dirt much like William would've during his happier times. This means I wont be able to make it on the day unfortunately, though I've decided to compose a poem, which I hope you can read out on the day, Rob wrote.His poem, titled An ode to William, included the lines: Although life takes funny turns, we can all learn from William the worm. Let us gather, light a candle to burn, and celebrate the life of William the worm. Lights shine bright, let's eat sponge cake through the night! Because there's many a lesson to learn. He wriggles many miles; he gave us many smiles, so we stand confident and firm... William will be back, very much like Arnie, though now we will all check before we make a sarnie!Mr Metcalfe was deeply moved by this gesture, sharing an image of William's grave alongside another poem. Funeral update: well what can I say? It's been an emotional day, but the funeral went without a hitch. Tesco Rob, we read out your poem, and there wasn't a dry eye amongst us, he posted.His eulogy verse reflected on the tragedy while maintaining the humorous tone: As we gather here today for William the worm, It's time to reflect on the lessons we can learn. Now, this poor worm's life was cut far too short, After he was crushed to death in a cucumber I bought. Tesco, please don't let this happen again. Don't let William's life be lost in vain.The exchange escalated further with musical parodies. Tesco responded with their version of Oasis's Wonderwall, prompting Mr Metcalfe to counter with a Blur's Parklife adaptation he dubbed Worm life.Speaking to BBC News, Mr Metcalfe reflected on the unexpected viral success. I enjoy making people laugh, but you just can't tell what will go viral. I think it went crazy because Tesco's responses were so good. If they hadn't replied in such a fun way, then it probably wouldn't have gone so big on the internet.While reactions were largely positive, not everyone appreciated the humor. I've had a mostly positive response, but one lady didn't get the joke and told me off for making a fuss about the worm, he noted.Tesco offered a £10 gift voucher to cover William's funeral expenses, which Mr Metcalfe deemed more than adequate compensation. I think Tesco have more than made up for it. If people can laugh about it all, then that is great. There is enough seriousness in the world.The Sheffield resident also confirmed his willingness to resume consuming cucumber sandwiches, suggesting William's legacy won't permanently impact his dietary preferences.

text: Mark Wigglesworth has resigned as musical director of the English National Opera. The English National Opera faces another significant blow as Musical Director Mark Wigglesworth announces his departure, citing irreconcilable differences with the company's future direction.Wigglesworth, 51, revealed his decision through an email to colleagues, stating the ENO was evolving now into something I do not recognise. His exit will occur at the end of the current season, according to company officials.The conductor's relationship with ENO began in 2014 when he assumed the musical director role, describing his appointment then as a huge privilege. Despite subsequent funding cuts, he had previously expressed commitment to maintaining the company's reputation for risk-taking and adventurous programming.However, his recent correspondence reveals deep frustration with organizational changes. The ENO's plan for the future is one that the board and chief executive have always known I cannot support, Wigglesworth wrote. As hard as I have tried to argue to maintain what I believe to be the fundamental pillars of our identity, I have failed to persuade others of this necessity.The company confirmed that he will continue to honour his contractual commitments as a conductor and looks forward to continuing to work with the wonderful musicians of ENO.Wigglesworth emphasized his philosophy regarding operational improvements: I believe in efficiencies that increase our value for money and do not lose the opportunity of performing the highest quality opera to the largest number of people.A seasoned conductor who has appeared regularly at the Proms since 1991, performing works by composers including Olivier Messiaen and Richard Wagner, Wigglesworth's departure represents the latest crisis for the troubled opera company.ENO's recent history has been marked by severe financial pressures. The Arts Council of England delivered a devastating blow in February last year, slashing the company's core funding by £5m while removing it from the national portfolio of organizations for 2015-18.Responding to the funding crisis, ENO implemented ticket price reductions two months later, hoping to stabilize its financial position. Additional cost-cutting measures followed this year when management proposed reducing chorus members' contracts from 12 months to nine months.The contractual changes sparked fierce resistance from performers, who viewed the proposal as a pay reduction. ENO chorus members voted to strike, threatening not to appear in portions of the London Coliseum performance of Akhnaten.Management defended the controversial measures, arguing the company faced bankruptcy without implementation of the proposed changes. The labor dispute was eventually resolved, leading to the cancellation of strike action.Despite these resolutions, Wigglesworth's departure signals ongoing institutional instability at one of Britain's premier opera companies during this period of unprecedented turmoil.

Towards the end of the year, further cost-cutting measures were put into effect, the management proposed a reduction of the contract for the chorus from twelve months to nine months. This step was resented by the chorus, which saw it as a reduction in salary, and the chorus threatened to strike and to boycott part of the performance of Ahnaten at the London Coliseum. text: When Avi Yaron was 26 years old he had a motorbike accident - a day he describes as the luckiest of his life. During a routine head scan to assess potential injury damage, doctors made an unexpected discovery that would alter one man's life trajectory forever. Deep within his brain, they detected a tumor that might have gone unnoticed indefinitely without the accident that brought him to medical attention.The year was 1993 when the Israeli electronic engineering student received devastating news: the newly found mass was positioned perilously close to brain regions essential for both movement and cognitive function. Confronting this diagnosis, he faced an agonizing decision between undergoing complex, high-risk surgery that threatened paralysis or pursuing alternative solutions.Following twelve months of intensive research, Mr Yaron located a New York-based surgeon who successfully extracted a portion of the tumor. Laboratory analysis revealed the mass was benign, offering some relief. Medical professionals then recommended a waiting approach, suggesting he postpone further intervention until technological advances could reduce surgical risks.However, this passive strategy proved unacceptable to Mr Yaron. The remaining tumor posed an ongoing threat, potentially exerting dangerous pressure on critical brain tissue as it expanded.I was young and thinking of starting a family. I could not be passive about this sword hanging over my head, he explained.Following five years of consulting leading surgeons and technology specialists, Mr Yaron underwent conventional surgery to remove the tumor's remainder, achieving positive outcomes. Yet his extensive quest for superior surgical alternatives continued haunting his thoughts, driving him to explore and test methods for less invasive brain procedures.Through years of development, he ultimately perfected a revolutionary approach: three-dimensional brain surgery.Over the past quarter-century, minimally invasive techniques have transformed surgery for easily accessible body regions, including abdominal and uterine keyhole procedures. Recently, surgeons have successfully adapted scope technology for brain operations as well.These procedures involve inserting thin scopes through surgically created or natural skin openings. Cameras mounted on scope ends transmit visual data to monitors, allowing surgeons to observe their work while passing instruments through the scopes to collect tissue samples or remove masses.Initial versions provided surgeons with standard-definition 2D imagery, which has evolved into high-definition systems over the past decade. Throughout operations, surgeons continuously convert these flat images into three-dimensional understanding, similar to how we interpret 2D television screens.While 3D technology has recently emerged for specific surgical procedures, achieving three-dimensional brain surgery presented far greater challenges. Neurosurgical scopes require extremely narrow diameters to navigate tight passages like nasal cavities.Traditional 3D scopes depend on dual optical channels, each housing individual sensors that capture separate images. These images combine to create three-dimensional appearance on screens, replicating human vision. However, creating sufficiently compact instruments capable of producing the high-quality imagery neurosurgeons require has proven exceptionally difficult.Mr Yaron's team solved this challenge through innovative thinking. Instead of mimicking human anatomy, their scope replicates bee compound eyes. The device incorporates a miniature sensor containing hundreds of thousands of microscopic elements, each oriented in slightly different directions to map surgical areas from multiple perspectives.Software processes this data into left and right eye images. Through this single-sensor approach, Mr Yaron's company, Visionsense, developed a scope compact enough for brain surgery applications.Shahzada Ahmed from Birmingham's Queen Elizabeth Hospital, who performed among the UK's first 3D endoscopic neurosurgical procedures, offered this comparison: A bit like going to the movies, Avatar is a great movie in HD but it is an even better one in 3D.When I use the scope there is a better appreciation of depth and the pictures feel more real to me, Ahmed noted.The technology also enables three-dimensional instrument visualization, enhancing his spatial understanding of tool positioning relative to crucial anatomical structures.Multiple studies are currently investigating whether 3D approaches surpass commonly used 2D high-definition systems. Hani Marcus, a neurosurgeon at Imperial College London's Hamlyn Centre, recently tested the scope against conventional tools using model brains and surgeons inexperienced with endoscopic techniques.His research indicates 3D benefits, demonstrating faster operations and subjective depth perception improvements. Nevertheless, Mr Marcus cautions against automatically assuming 3D superiority over 2D systems, emphasizing the need for additional research.Several potential complications exist: surgeons accustomed to 2D visualization may struggle adapting to this new approach. Additionally, just as some individuals experience nausea watching 3D films, similar effects might affect certain surgeons.For Mr Yaron, whose scope now operates across the United States and Europe, this innovation represents the positive outcome of years of personal struggle.If I hadn't had this accident I wouldn't have been able to offer this solution. And I really know how it feels to need options, he reflects.

text: The number of people seeking to buy guns in Colorado has soared since last week's mass shooting in the US state's town of Aurora, say law officials. Following the cinema massacre, gun purchase applications surged dramatically as Colorado residents sought background checks required for legal firearm acquisition. The three-day period immediately after the tragedy witnessed a striking 43% increase compared to the preceding week's figures.The Aurora theater shooting during a midnight screening of The Dark Knight Rises claimed 12 lives and wounded 58 moviegoers, with 20 victims still hospitalized. On Monday, suspected shooter James Holmes, 24, made his initial court appearance facing charges related to the rampage.Authorities allege Holmes deployed two gas canisters into the packed auditorium before unleashing random gunfire on the audience. According to prosecutors, the defendant had legally purchased his arsenal and accumulated thousands of ammunition rounds in his booby-trapped apartment, which contained explosive devices.Colorado Bureau of Investigations data reveals the stark contrast in background check applications. While 880 people sought state-approved screenings on Friday, July 13—days before the attack—the numbers jumped to 1,216 on July 20, the shooting day, and climbed further to 1,243 on Saturday. Weekend totals reached 2,887 approved applications, marking a 43.5% spike from the previous weekend.Though bureau statistics don't track actual firearm purchases, gun retailers confirmed increased sales activity. Dick Rutan, proprietor of Gunners Den in Arvada, Colorado, described business as off the hook.What they're saying is, 'they want to have a chance,' Rutan explained to the Denver Post. They want to have the ability to protect themselves and their families if they are in a situation like what happened in the movie theatre.At another establishment, employee Jake Meyers discovered up to 20 customers waiting outside his workplace the morning after the shooting. A lot of it is people saying, 'I didn't think I needed a gun, but now I do,' the Denver Post quoted him. When it happens in your backyard, people start reassessing, 'Hey, I go to the movies'.Brandon Baker, owner of Rocky Mountain Guns & Ammo in Parker—merely 15 miles from Aurora—reported elevated sales alongside increased requests for firearms training courses.The phenomenon extended beyond Colorado's borders. Associated Press reporting indicated similar trends nationwide, with Florida recording a 14% weekly increase and Oregon showing 11% growth from June to July. Florida's background checks rose 10% in the post-shooting days compared to the same July period.Law enforcement officials noted this pattern following previous significant incidents, including President Barack Obama's election and the January 2011 Arizona shooting that killed six people and wounded Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords.Such spikes typically stem from concerns that mass violence events might trigger government reconsideration of Second Amendment rights guaranteeing citizens' firearm ownership.Tuesday saw a small contingent of Democratic lawmakers in Washington renew calls for high-capacity magazine bans. However, minimal expectations exist for gun control legislation during the presidential election campaign period leading to November.Holmes faces formal charges next week. The presiding judge prohibited cameras from the hearing, responding to victim families' media requests to avoid using the suspect's name and photographs.His Monday court appearance, marked by apparent disorientation, sparked speculation regarding his mental condition. As of Tuesday, twenty shooting victims remained hospitalized, including six in critical condition.

Then Sunderland, with a right-foot shot from the outskirts of the penalty area, failed to hit the target. Bury made a substitution, with Wahbi Khazri replacing Stephen Dawson in an injury crisis. Then came their first corner of the game after Harry Bunn’s shot on the turn was blocked outside the penalty area and George Honeyman fired one back which Sunderland managed to block. At the other end, Sunderland won another corner, which was cleared again by Jason Steele. And the half ended with a shot by Aiden McGeady, a shot from the left of the penalty area which the goalkeeper saved, with the Sunderland player, Jason Steele, in the position of the assistant.

text: After leaders of the billion-euro Human Brain Project hit back at critics, six top neuroscientists have expressed dismay at their public response. A controversy surrounding the Human Brain Project (HBP) has intensified following last week's open letter signed by over 600 researchers declaring the initiative not on course and demanding an independent review.The HBP leadership's response, expressing that members were saddened by the protest, has drawn criticism from six prominent neuroscientists writing in Nature. Project chair Prof Henry Markram has characterized the opposition as a personal crusade, further inflaming tensions.Instead of acknowledging that there is a problem and genuinely seeking to address scientists' concerns, the project leaders seem to be of the opinion that the letter's 580 signatories [now over 600] are misguided, wrote Prof Richard Morris, a distinguished neuroscientist from the University of Edinburgh, alongside five colleagues in their Nature correspondence.The six authors, who describe themselves as neuroscientists in Europe who care about the success of research projects large and small in our field, did not sign the original protest but express disappointment with the HBP leadership's publicly reported stance. They advocate for a more open-minded attitude in their letter.Prof Richard Frackowiak, co-executive director of the HBP, disputed suggestions that project leaders were dismissive when speaking to the BBC. We've taken this extremely seriously, he stated, strongly objecting to such characterizations.The European Commission announced the HBP in January 2013 as one of two flagship technology projects, with graphene research being the other. Last week's open message to the EC voiced concerns about the project's narrow scientific focus and closed management approach, with hundreds of neuroscientists pledging to boycott HBP-related funding unless their demands were met.While the HBP team issued a diplomatic response acknowledging important concerns, Prof Henry Markram from Switzerland's EPFL (Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne) later questioned the letter's motivation in a BBC email. He suggested Dr Zachary Mainen, Director of the Champalimaud Neuroscience Programme in Portugal, was the primary driving force behind the protest.Prof Markram noted that Dr Mainen belonged to a group of cognitive scientists who were repositioned outside the project's core. We have issued a formal response to explain the project better, but we will no longer be taking his Open Letter seriously, he wrote.This characterization faces strong opposition from signatories and observers alike. Dr Alexandre Pouget from the University of Geneva, who assisted Dr Mainen in organizing the open message, rejected the one man crusade narrative. You don't get the support of 600 people if it's a one man crusade, he argued.Dr Pouget, who participated in the HBP before flagship funding but withdrew with several colleagues in 2012, explained his concerns: It was originally supposed to have a big theory component, but many of us were worried about the increasing focus on simulations.Prof Frackowiak acknowledged that internal communication could have been more proactive while defending the leadership against autocracy accusations. We remain a project that is totally open and is building infrastructures for the use of the whole community, he maintained.He outlined upcoming structural changes, explaining that our governance procedures are evolving. A new chair will soon be appointed with a role separate from Prof Markram, who will transition to CEO.Support for the project has emerged from an unexpected quarter. US Congressman Chaka Fattah, a supporter of the HBP's American counterpart the BRAIN Initiative, defended the project in the Huffington Post: The Human Brain Project is large and ambitious, and as a result has the potential to be a disruptive force in a field that for far too long has been narrowly focused on an incremental approach.The European Commission has acknowledged the open message, thanking authors for their feedback and highlighting a rigorous annual review scheduled for January 2015. When asked about the review's transparency and independence—key demands from signatories—an EC spokesperson indicated it would take into account the requests contained in the open letter... while respecting the existing rules which are related to data protection.Dr Pouget reported a very positive meeting with the head of the EC's FET (Future and Emerging Technologies) Flagships Unit, which funds both the HBP and Graphene Flagship. I'm still waiting to see what happens next. We certainly hope that the European Commission will take this crisis seriously, he said, adding: What happened last week is very unusual.Prof Frackowiak rejects the crisis characterization, viewing recent events more optimistically. I think this has been good, because it's raised the issue in the public eye, he commented. Our next scientific review will be in January and we're looking forward to it.

text: Six young voters from Wales who took part in an election debate geared around young people have described it as brilliant to a lot of hot air. At Leeds City Museum on Tuesday evening, over 100 young people aged 18-24 confronted five politicians in a BBC Newsbeat-organized debate that put trust at the center of discussion, alongside tuition fees, gender equality, and voting age reforms.The political lineup facing the youthful audience included Sam Gyimah from the Conservatives, Labour's Sadiq Khan, Liberal Democrat Sal Brinton, the SNP's Mhairi Black, and Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth. Representatives from five major parties found themselves under intense scrutiny from voters who didn't hold back their concerns.BBC Wales tracked six Welsh audience members to capture their perspectives on the evening's proceedings.From Lampeter, 21-year-old Guto Gwilym expressed enthusiasm about the format: It was brilliant to have that one hour that was purely focused on young people and the issues we have. It was very much a night where politicians heard what we have to say and I very much hope that they've been taking notes. For me - one thing we do need to tackle urgently now is diversity among MPs.Aled Illtud, 20, from Aberystwyth, appreciated the debate's energy while noting its limitations: It was nice to see a different kind of debate - it was much more energetic. I did feel like there were more questions than there were answers but that maybe reflects how passionate the audience members were. We seemed to have a battalion of questions thrown at the politicians. It was beautiful to see but I would have liked more answers from the politicians.The focus on tuition fees frustrated Peter Gillibrand, an 18-year-old from Carmarthen, who wanted broader policy discussions: I think the debate concentrated too much on tuition fees. I would have liked to hear more about what politicians would do for disabled people like my brother. He's severely autistic but the funding for lots of the services he uses has been cut. I'm a Plaid Cymru voter but I think the real people who won this debate were the SNP and Lib Dems. The SNP lady was really inspirational and the lady from the Lib Dems came across well too. She said 'look we made a mistake on tuition fees' but you felt she did really care about young people.Cynicism marked the response from Cwmbran's Robyn Holley, 21: It was everything I expected it to be - people shouting, lots of opinions whirling around and politicians just being politicians. I wasn't impressed by what they had to say - it was just a lot of hot air. I have considered not voting but I think I will probably turn out if only to try and change things.More optimistic was Gwion Dafydd, 20, from Pembrokeshire: I think a couple of politicians said the right things. I liked that Labour, Plaid Cymru and the Lib Dems all supported lowering the voting age for 16 and 17 year olds. It shows they care about what young people have to say. I have more respect for some of the parties now.Rhys Taylor, 21, from Bangor, who actively participated in the debate, emphasized the importance of political accountability: I stood up and made a comment during the discussion on tuition fees. I think it's important that politicians admit when they've made a mistake and apologise if they can't carry through with their promises. It's not often that we hear politicians apologising but the more we can get them to own up to their mistakes the more we will be able to trust them.

text: When BBC Alba was launched in 2008, as a collaboration between the BBC and the Gaelic TV body MG Alba, it was a huge achievement for supporters of the Gaelic language. Advocates had consistently maintained that establishing a specialized channel would deliver superior programming for Gaelic speakers compared to scattered Gaelic content across mainstream networks.A dedicated Gaelic service, they contended, could serve as a crucial instrument in preserving the language's future viability.BBC Alba represents an unprecedented collaboration within UK broadcasting - a unique joint venture arrangement. While the BBC finances certain programming, MG Alba shoulders responsibility for other content through government funding.Initial disappointment emerged when the channel launched exclusively on satellite television, reaching only 43% of Scottish households, though viewers could access content via BBC iPlayer online. Advocates insisted the service required Freeview availability alongside other public broadcasting channels.BBC management developed a proposal enabling this expansion, albeit with significant trade-offs. Radio stations would cease Freeview transmission during BBC Alba's broadcast hours - a compromise that sparked considerable debate.Earlier this year, the BBC Trust postponed its decision while conducting a comprehensive review of broadcasting distribution across all BBC services. Following extensive research, the Trust has now endorsed the plan, though no launch date for Freeview availability has been announced.Optimists anticipate BBC Alba's Freeview debut could coincide with central Scotland's digital switchover scheduled for May and June.Once implemented, BBC Alba will reach virtually every Scottish household. The station faces the challenge of demonstrating broad appeal and value, particularly among non-Gaelic speakers.Media critics have questioned Alba's ability to prove its worth, citing the absence of conventional viewing statistics. Alternative research methods have been employed instead, partly because standard ratings samples exclude Scotland's island communities.While BBC radio stations will lose Freeview access during this transition, future technological advances may restore their availability. Meanwhile, flagship radio services will continue broadcasting on FM and medium wave, with digital stations like 1 Extra and BBC7 remaining accessible through satellite, cable, digital radios, and online platforms.The Trust acknowledged the difficulty of choosing between BBC Alba and radio services. The alternative - purchasing commercial Freeview capacity - might have excluded viewers dependent on relay transmitters and proved financially prohibitive.Additionally, the BBC Trust has determined that Gaelic programming will persist on BBC Two Scotland, though it will no longer serve as the corporation's primary Gaelic outlet.BBC Two Scotland's Gaelic scheduling approach is evolving significantly. The previous format featured concentrated two-hour Thursday evening blocks, but individual programs now appear throughout various time slots while maintaining equivalent peak-hour Gaelic content overall.

text: Pirelli will be told to produce a tyre drivers can push to the limit in 2017 as Formula 1 bosses seek to make the sport more exciting. Formula One's governing body will direct Pirelli to create tyres that enable drivers to maintain aggressive racing for extended periods, the BBC has discovered.Currently, rapid degradation forces drivers to manage their tyres rather than race at maximum capacity. The 2017 season promises cars that will be four to five seconds per lap quicker than today's machines.While Pirelli has expressed readiness to manufacture more competitive tyres for next year, the Italian company emphasizes the need for additional track testing to complete its development work. Twelve testing days have been allocated for 2016 to serve this purpose.During a recent meeting where teams and drivers voiced frustration with existing tyres, Pirelli chairman Marco Tronchetti Provera assured attendees that the company could produce whatever the F1 wanted as long as it had clear commission.The tyre manufacturer has received preliminary data about expected 2017 car performance to begin design work. By March's end, the FIA will deliver comprehensive specifications outlining desired tyre characteristics along with all necessary technical information.Since joining Formula One in 2011, Pirelli was tasked with ensuring multiple pit stops per race. This objective was achieved through tyres susceptible to thermal degradation - components that lose performance permanently once exceeding specific temperatures.This design philosophy means drivers frequently operate below their limits during races to preserve tyre life and optimize overall race times. The temperature ceiling sometimes prevents drivers from pushing maximally even during qualifying sessions.Driver dissatisfaction, long-standing but manageable, reached crisis levels last season after two high-speed tyre failures at Belgium's Grand Prix, occurring at approximately 200mph.Drivers want tyres fit for maximum-attack racing, Alexander Wurz, chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, recently informed BBC Sport.For 2016, Pirelli modified tyre characteristics hoping to make grip loss less predictable, theoretically allowing harder driving. However, world champion Lewis Hamilton expressed disappointment after testing the new compounds in Barcelona this week.It's definitely not better, that's for sure, Hamilton stated. It just feels like a harder tyre and it's not giving me any more grip. I think I prefer last year's.The 2017 acceleration plans faced temporary disruption when Pirelli indicated its tyres would require abnormally elevated pressures to handle projected cornering force increases. Teams and the FIA initially pursued reduced modifications, but analysis revealed these wouldn't achieve performance objectives.This week's newly agreed regulations represent a compromise based on McLaren's proposal. The strategy emphasizes generating more aerodynamic downforce from underbody components while increasing mechanical grip proportionally.Both wheel track width and bodywork dimensions will expand, accompanied by larger tyres. These combined changes target the four-to-five second per lap improvement expected for 2017.

text: A rapist who was found guilty of attacking six women in one night has been jailed for life. text: First Minister Carwyn Jones has launched Welsh Labour's general election campaign - making no reference to UK party leader Jeremy Corbyn in a speech to activists in Cardiff. Welsh Labour launched its general election campaign Monday with First Minister Carwyn Jones presenting five key pledges while deliberately avoiding mention of UK party leader Jeremy Corbyn.Speaking to activists, Jones emphasized that the upcoming vote should focus on seven years of Tory failure rather than Brexit. The pledges span NHS improvements, housing initiatives, educational reforms, and enhanced policing measures.We are in Welsh Labour together, councillors, MPs and AMs, we are united, Jones declared. Labour's achievement knows no bounds when it stands united.The Welsh Labour leader highlighted the party's success in repelling Conservative advances during last Thursday's local elections, particularly in target areas including Flintshire, Newport and Swansea. While acknowledging some reversals, Jones said the party would learn from that.Jones called for voters to return a battalion of Welsh Labour MPs, expressing pride in the party's local campaigning approach and its record governing Wales. The party makes no apology for these achievements, he stated.Three of Labour's five Welsh pledges address devolved responsibilities in health, education and housing sectors.Regarding Brexit, Jones insisted: This is not the Brexit election. That was the referendum last year - a result I respect. I was a Remainer - so was Theresa May. He criticized Prime Minister Theresa May for having no plan for EU departure, claiming she was merely posturing.We produced a plan, where's their plan? Jones challenged.The first minister's omission of Corbyn contrasts sharply with the UK leader's Cardiff visit in April, when he addressed approximately 700 supporters on Whitchurch Common shortly after the election announcement. At that rally, with Jones present, Corbyn urged the crowd to join a journey of hope and excitement while praising Labour's Welsh governance record.When questioned by BBC Wales about Corbyn's absence from Monday's launch, Jones explained: It is Welsh Labour's campaign launch which he was fronting personally. He dismissed suggestions that Corbyn represented an electoral liability, stating: It's pretty clear to people who would be prime minister if we got a majority.Jones emphasized devolution's importance: We live in an age of devolution. That's why it's hugely important that parties put forward their Welsh pledges.This strategy represents a clear attempt by Jones' Welsh Labour to distinguish itself from Corbyn's UK Labour party. The Welsh-focused approach reportedly helped the party retain several councils last week and successfully challenged Conservative advances in marginal Assembly seats during last year's campaign.However, the approach raises questions about general election dynamics, where Corbyn, not Jones, would enter Downing Street following a Labour victory. This Welsh Labour strategy contrasts markedly with Conservative messaging, which frequently emphasizes Theresa May's leadership role.Jones maintained that austerity showed no signs of ending under Conservative governance, reinforcing his message that this election has to be about seven years of Tory failure.

text: Official figures released today by the Forestry Commission show that the government is falling far short of its own tree-planting targets. Government woodland planting efforts in England have fallen catastrophically short of targets, with environmental groups condemning the appalling failure that threatens serious ecological consequences.New data from the Forestry Commission reveals a staggering shortfall: just 700 hectares (seven km2) of woodland was established in England last year, representing merely 14% of the ambitious 5,000-hectare (50 km2) target. The Woodland Trust branded this an 86% miss rate as drastic decline in forest expansion.Austin Brady from the Woodland Trust expressed alarm at the figures, stating: These figures are all the more shocking against the backdrop of the growing evidence of the importance of trees and woods in tackling air pollution, improving water quality and offering scope to deliver natural flood management.Brady continued his criticism: Something is drastically wrong with the way woodland planting is being supported across the various government departments that share responsibility for trees and woods.The disappointing results come despite government commitments to establish 11 million trees between 2015 and 2020. Environment Minister Elizabeth Truss has previously emphasized their flood prevention potential, telling the House of Commons in December 2015 that she wanted to examine the environment on a catchment level, making sure that we put in place tree-planting programmes that can both reduce flood risk and improve the environment.However, implementation has failed to match rhetoric. There have been lots of really interesting and well-informed conversations - all the signals are positive, but the system of delivering the grants and getting things moving on the ground is not matching up with the fine words. It is not fit for purpose, Brady observed.England's woodland crisis is particularly acute given the nation's status among Europe's least forested countries. Tree coverage spans merely 10% of English territory, dramatically below the 37% EU average.Multiple bureaucratic obstacles hamper progress despite available government funding. Grant schemes underwent changes last year, creating processing delays for contracts and payments. The Countryside Stewardship Scheme imposes inflexible requirements regarding land area and planting density for grant qualification.Additional confusion surrounds potential conflicts between tree planting and EU farm subsidy eligibility, deterring many farmers and landowners from new forestry projects entirely.Defra defended its record through a spokesperson: Woodland cover in England is at its highest level since the 14th Century and we are committed to growing it even further. The Countryside Stewardship scheme is an important opportunity to help expand our nation's woodlands, which is why the Forestry Commission is supporting landowners to make applications through a series of workshops and online support.The Woodland Trust advocates for more adaptable programs accommodating landowners with limited space, plus clearer coordination among responsible departments: Defra, the Forestry Commission, Natural England, and the Environment Agency.Beyond environmental advantages, economic benefits are substantial. The government's Natural Capital Committee report, which assigns monetary values to natural resource ecosystem services, estimates that woodland planting of up to 250,000 additional hectares ... near towns and cities can generate net societal benefits in excess of £500 million per annum.Follow Claire on Twitter.

text: An NHS trust has apologised unreservedly after a misdiagnosis resulted in a three-year-old boy having his legs and seven fingers amputated. In July 2015, Lou Harvey-Smith brought her son Reuben to Ipswich Hospital following an accidental burn injury. When she returned two days later due to his developing fever, medical staff diagnosed tonsillitis and prescribed antibiotics.The situation deteriorated rapidly the next day as Reuben became critically ill. Seeking a second medical opinion, Ms Harvey-Smith contacted the burns unit at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital, where doctors immediately suspected toxic shock syndrome - a potentially fatal condition triggered by bacteria infiltrating wounds and releasing dangerous toxins into the bloodstream.Emergency transfer back to Ipswich Hospital preceded Reuben's urgent relocation to St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, London, where surgeons performed the necessary amputations. The young boy's response to his condition has been remarkably resilient, according to his 41-year-old mother from Chelmondiston, near Ipswich.[Reuben] looked at his amputated legs and said 'poorly feet gone, get new ones,' Ms Harvey-Smith recalled. He just accepts it and gets on with things.Despite her son's positive attitude, Ms Harvey-Smith pursued legal proceedings against Ipswich Hospital NHS Trust. The trust subsequently acknowledged that toxic shock represented a significant possibility given Reuben's presenting symptoms, and conceded that amputation might have been prevented through earlier recognition and intervention.Tim Deeling, representing Ms Harvey-Smith, expressed serious concerns about the hospital's response. It is extremely concerning they were aware of the link between burns and toxic shock, yet didn't consider this for Reuben's case, he stated.The trust has provided an interim compensation payment of £50,000 while settlement discussions continue. A hospital spokesman confirmed their position: In an ongoing legal case the trust has admitted full liability for shortcomings in the A&E care provided to Reuben in July 2015 and have offered an unreserved apology.Additional staff training focusing on septic shock syndrome recognition has been implemented, the spokesman noted. The trust remains committed to ensuring that Reuben is appropriately compensated so that he has the care, prostheses and equipment that he needs throughout his life, he added.

text: The maker of the EpiPen will start selling a generic version in the wake of criticism about steep price increases. In an extraordinary commercial move, Mylan announced plans to launch a generic version of its EpiPen auto-injector within several weeks, carrying a $300 list price that represents roughly half the cost of the current branded product.The generic alternative will be identical to the existing EpiPen, which currently costs $600 for a two-dose package and serves as a critical emergency treatment for severe food and insect allergies. Over the past decade, EpiPen prices in the United States have skyrocketed by 500%, generating widespread criticism from politicians, parents, and healthcare advocates.Our decision to launch a generic alternative to EpiPen is an extraordinary commercial response, stated Mylan chief executive Heather Bresch. We determined that bypassing the brand system in this case and offering an additional alternative was the best option.The announcement comes as the company faces intense scrutiny over its pricing strategy. Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton has denounced the price increases as outrageous and unjustified, while countless families struggle with the mounting costs of this life-saving medication.Allergy patients typically require multiple devices—keeping them at home, school, work, and in vehicles—with each unit expiring after 12 months. This necessity multiplies the financial burden on families managing severe allergies.Mylan's decision represents an unusual strategy since the branded EpiPen remains under patent protection and competing treatments have struggled to gain regulatory approval from the Food and Drug Administration. The product currently generates $1 billion in annual sales for the pharmaceutical company.Bresch defended the company's position by pointing to the complex U.S. healthcare system, explaining that Mylan receives only $274 of the $600 list price while insurers, pharmacies, and other intermediaries claim the remainder. Individual patients' out-of-pocket costs vary significantly based on their insurance coverage.Since acquiring the product from Merck in 2007, Mylan has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in product improvements, according to Bresch.The pricing controversy has taken a toll on Mylan's market performance, with shares dropping approximately 12% last week amid the public outcry. Stock prices remained flat at $43.04 during afternoon trading in New York.Celebrity endorser Sarah Jessica Parker severed ties with Mylan last week, ending her promotional relationship with the company. Parker had previously advocated for EpiPen access due to her son's peanut allergy.Bernstein analyst Ronny Gal predicted continued pressure on the company, noting: We suspect Mylan will continue to receive some heat for its price increases and there will be heightened pressure on FDA [regulator the Food and Drug Administration] to bring competition to the market.The EpiPen controversy reflects a broader pattern of pharmaceutical pricing disputes, with companies including Valeant, Turing, and Pfizer facing similar criticism for dramatic price increases in recent months.

text: Former England captain David Beckham is being cast away for the 75th birthday celebrations of BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs next weekend. Since its inaugural broadcast on 29 January 1942, Desert Island Discs has welcomed over 3,000 guests to its metaphorical shores.For the programme's milestone 75th anniversary, presenter Kirsty Young has secured what she describes as the perfect gift - football legend David Beckham selecting his cherished musical tracks.The 41-year-old former England captain revealed that music occupies a central place in his household. His marriage to Victoria Beckham - the former Spice Girl who transitioned into fashion design - creates a naturally musical environment. Their family's musical connections extend to the next generation, with 11-year-old son Cruz releasing a Christmas-themed single just last month.Whether Beckham's selections will include any tracks from his wife's pop group catalogue or her solo work remains undisclosed.I'm delighted to join Desert Island Discs for its 75th anniversary celebrations, Beckham stated. Music has been a huge part of my - and my family's - life and it is a real pleasure to highlight that on such an iconic programme.Young praised her upcoming guest's multifaceted appeal: His sporting legacy is of course extraordinary. And along with his charisma, cultural impact and humanitarian work, he is a modern man of many parts. He'll be a fascinating guest to welcome on to my little interview island.The anniversary celebration will unfold as a three-hour special on BBC Radio 4 Extra on 28 January, with Young presenting highlights from previous episodes. Featured segments include Cilla Black reminiscing about her early singing days alongside The Beatles, and Richard Dimbleby recounting his experience taking cutlery from Hitler's bunker as one of the first correspondents to visit after the dictator's demise.Additionally, extracts from recently rediscovered episodes will debut as they join the programme's expanding online archive.Beckham's episode marks a nostalgic return - the sound of ocean waves will bookend the programme for the first time since the 1960s.BBC Radio 4 and Radio 4 Extra controller Gwyneth Williams reflected on the show's cultural significance: A sure way to uncover an elusive British national identity is to listen to this programme week after week. The broad range of guests is a measure of contemporary talent and achievement, and the music opens up different eras and prompts emotional memory in all of us.Follow us on Facebook, on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, or on Instagram at bbcnewsents. If you have a story suggestion email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

text: Derbyshire were denied a chance of a first Championship win for two years as bad light and rain saw their match with Nottinghamshire end in a draw. text: Terry Flanagan has accused fellow Mancunian and lightweight world champion Anthony Crolla of ducking him. At Manchester Arena, two British lightweight champions will defend their world titles in separate bouts, though a unification clash between them remains elusive.Terry Flanagan, 27, puts his WBO crown on the line against South Africa's Mzonke Fana on 9 July. Meanwhile, Anthony Crolla, 29, will face Venezuela's Jorge Linares in defense of his WBA belt on 24 September at the same venue.The absence of a domestic showdown has sparked frustration from Flanagan, who claims his rival declined the opportunity.We offered Crolla the fight and he didn't want it. If he wants the fight, he should go to his coach and promoter and say he wants it, said Flanagan.According to Flanagan, external influences may be steering Crolla away from the bout. It's probably the people around him who are worried about the fight, but it's Crolla's decision at the end of the day.The unbeaten champion insists promotional complications aren't the issue. It's an easy fight to make. Frank [Warren, Flanagan's promoter] isn't making it hard for them. If anything, he's bending over backwards to make it happen.Warren has reportedly made significant concessions, including broadcast arrangements. He's giving in to their demands. He's said they can have it on Sky Sports [with whom Crolla's promoter Eddie Hearn has an exclusive deal], but still they don't want it.Despite potential future opportunities, Flanagan remains pessimistic about the matchup materializing. If we both keep winning, it might happen down the line, but I'm not confident it will. He knows my style will give him problems and I don't think his team believe he can beat me.The WBO champion expressed disappointment given Crolla's recent form. It's a shame because Anthony's a great fighter and he has looked really good in his last three fights. Let's just make proper fights and have the best fight the best. Don't be scared to lose.Flanagan's upcoming third title defense comes against 42-year-old Fana, a former super-featherweight world champion who turned professional in 1994. The challenger brings veteran experience to face Flanagan's perfect 30-fight record.Addressing critics of his opponent selection, Flanagan said: People say: 'Why are you fighting this old man [Fana]?' All we can do is keep pushing for them and hopefully one of them will come off.His last successful defense came via points victory over Liverpool's Derry Mathews in March.Warren disclosed that he offered Crolla £500,000 to face Flanagan, but the Manchester fighter opted to fulfill his mandatory obligation against Ismael Barroso instead.Crolla's first title defense last month saw him stop the previously unbeaten Venezuelan, extending his professional record to 31 victories from 38 contests.Both Barroso and Crolla's upcoming opponent Linares, a former WBC champion, previously defeated Britain's Kevin Mitchell by stoppage last year.

text: The Swiss government has defended its law requiring asylum seekers to hand over assets in excess of $1,000 (£700; €900) following international criticism of similar proposals in Denmark. Switzerland's authorities confiscated assets from asylum seekers in just over 100 instances during 2015, despite processing nearly 30,000 asylum applications that year. This practice has drawn sharp criticism from advocacy groups, though the government maintains it reflects Swiss public sentiment.Under Swiss regulations, asylum seekers must disclose their financial assets upon arrival, with authorities authorized to seize anything exceeding $1,000. According to public broadcaster SRF's Thursday report, officials collected 210,000 Swiss francs ($210,000; €200,000) from 112 individuals throughout 2015.Government spokeswoman Lea Wertheimer defended the policy on Swiss television, stating: Swiss law states that asylum-seeking refugees who have money have to contribute to the costs that they cause while being here. And that's why we take their valuables away once they arrive in Switzerland.The Swiss Refugee Council has mounted fierce opposition to these measures. Stefan Frey, representing the organization, condemned the practice as daylight robbery, adding: This is unworthy. This has to change.A Syrian refugee shared his experience with Swiss television, describing how authorities seized his remaining funds after he sold his home to pay smugglers for his family's escape from conflict. In Zurich we were controlled by the police. They took away all our money, he explained, noting he possessed approximately £2,000 at the time. It seems that it is their right to take it away. They gave us a receipt. The officers promised that the money would be returned, but until now this has not happened.Meanwhile, Denmark faces international condemnation for similar proposals currently under parliamentary consideration. Danish lawmakers debated legislation Wednesday that would authorize seizure of migrants' cash and personal items valued above 10,000 kroner (£1,000; €1,340, $1,450) to offset accommodation costs. The bill awaits a vote later this month.The UN refugee agency and human rights organizations have strongly criticized Denmark's proposed measures. On Wednesday, the UNHCR expressed disbelief that Denmark would consider confiscating asylum seekers' few remaining possessions.However, Integration Minister Inger Stojberg justified the proposals, arguing they create parity with unemployed Danish citizens who must liquidate assets above specified thresholds to qualify for benefits. The legislation would exempt wedding rings and other sentimental items from seizure.Switzerland operates outside the European Union framework but participates in the Schengen Agreement, designed to facilitate passport-free movement between member nations. The migration crisis, which brought over one million people to Europe last year, has prompted several countries to reinstate border controls despite these agreements.

text: In the Mansion House speech that was abandoned last week due to the murder of Jo Cox MP, George Osborne was due to warn on the impact on financial services if Britain leaves the European Union. A prominent French economist has endorsed warnings from major financial institutions like JP Morgan and HSBC about potential job losses in London's financial district following Brexit.Mathilde Lemoine, who previously advised French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin and currently serves on France's economic oversight body equivalent to the Office for Budget Responsibility, supports these concerns. Now chief economist at Edmond de Rothschild private bank, she explained to the BBC how Brexit could trigger a significant shift in financial operations.According to Lemoine, euro-denominated transactions for EU firms—representing a substantial portion of the City's business—would relocate to the eurozone if Britain exits the European Union. The European Central Bank has already advocated for moving hundreds of billions of euros worth of euro-denominated business to be cleared within continental Europe.The Treasury previously challenged this position, considering it vital to London's financial health. They successfully fought the ECB's proposals through the European Court of Justice. However, Lemoine warns this legal protection would disappear with Brexit.If the United Kingdom leaves the European Union this clearing house dealing with euro transactions will relocate to the eurozone and therefore many foreign banks, European banks and also non-European banks will relocate to the eurozone, she said.London is one of the best financial centres in the world due to the people, so the people can move. [The] skills will move from London to the European Union and the eurozone, and therefore they can improve the financial sector of the eurozone.Lemoine describes the current arrangement as problematic, noting: It's a sort of abnormality that the clearing houses dealing with euro transactions are based in the City and not within the eurozone, because it means that the ECB cannot supervise the clearing houses and clearing houses are institutions which facilitate financial transactions and therefore there's a systemic risk.She emphasizes that eurozone members could immediately demand the relocation of euro-transaction clearing houses upon Brexit. If the United Kingdom decides to leave the European Union the eurozone member states can request immediately the relocation of the clearing houses dealing with euro transactions to the eurozone.The market value ranges between €600bn and €1tn, according to Lemoine's estimates. While this could result in thousands of job relocations, she acknowledges the exact number remains unpredictable.Brexit supporters argue differently, suggesting that freedom from EU regulations—particularly regarding compensation—would allow London to thrive despite losing some services. A major bank chief executive emphasized to me that London remains Europe's sole globally significant financial center, destined to maintain this status due to its deep, liquid markets, professional services, and scale. By comparison, financial centers in Paris and Frankfurt are considerably smaller.Gerard Lyons, former economic advisor to Boris Johnson and ex-chief economist at Standard Chartered, believes the EU will continue requiring London's services.Whichever way one looks at it, I think London and the City will remain the major financial centre of Europe, no matter what happens in the Referendum, he said.And I think the longer term outlook is to position London, not just against the EU but against future competition from Hong Kong, Singapore and New York. And I think we have a great ability to do that outside the EU.Markets also worry about potential economic decline post-Brexit. However, Lemoine suggests the negative consequences might be less severe than many economists predict.Many models predict a disaster for the UK if Brexit happens, she said. I can understand why the models predict such a disaster, but that's not my evaluation.She explains that these predictions fail to account for responsive measures: Firstly, because their prediction doesn't account for any other measures being put in place. It's not possible that the Prime Minister, the government and the Governor of the Bank of England would do nothing to improve the situation.Of course, they would act and they will implement various measures which will limit the decline in GDP. In addition, exporters can react very quickly to change in trade policies.Lemoine draws parallels to Britain's 1992 exit from the European monetary system: Of course, all situations are unique but remember when the United Kingdom left the European monetary system in 1992? UK exporters moved from the European Union to the rest of the world.The UK exports toward the European Union slimmed sharply, but those towards countries outside the European Union accelerated sharply. As a result - against all expectations - UK exports accelerated by 5% overall.

text: India's Supreme Court has struck down a controversial law which allowed police to arrest people for comments on social networks and other internet sites. A two-judge Supreme Court bench delivered Tuesday's landmark ruling, declaring the contentious Section 66A of the Information Technology Act unconstitutional following petitions from civil rights organizations and a law student who contended the provision infringed upon fundamental rights to free speech and expression.Section 66A is unconstitutional and we have no hesitation in striking it down, Justice RF Nariman stated in court, according to news agency AFP. He further emphasized, The public's right to know is directly affected by section 66A.The sweeping legislation had empowered authorities to imprison individuals for up to three years for transmitting emails or electronic messages deemed to cause annoyance or inconvenience. This broad scope triggered widespread arrests in recent years, with numerous individuals detained for social media posts on Facebook and Twitter, generating significant public backlash.Despite government arguments that the law served as a necessary deterrent against offensive online content, the court sided with challengers who viewed it as a violation of constitutional freedoms.The legal challenge originated after a November 2012 incident in Mumbai involving two young women arrested for Facebook commentary following politician Bal Thackeray's death. Shaheen Dhada faced detention for criticizing Mumbai's shutdown following Thackeray's passing, while Renu Srinivasan was arrested merely for liking the comment. Both women were subsequently released on bail.This arrest sparked nationwide indignation, with many demanding the law's abolition. Multiple subsequent arrests under the provision led to widespread accusations of governmental overreach.The ruling generated immediate celebration across social media platforms. Within moments of the court's announcement, #Sec66A began trending on Twitter as Indians praised the decision.Delhi's ruling Aam Aadmi Party expressed approval of the order, while journalist Swati Vashishtha emphasized that citizens' right to dissent represented their most crucial freedom. text: The issue of foreign prisoners in England's jails has long been a contentious one. Back in 2006, the revelation that over 1,000 foreign prisoners who should have been deported remained in UK custody ended Charles Clarke's tenure as home secretary. Multiple select committee investigations have since examined this persistent issue.The problem continues to frustrate Philip Hollobone, Conservative MP for Kettering, who has consistently highlighted concerns throughout his parliamentary career about foreign nationals in British prisons and the failure to repatriate them to serve sentences in their home countries.Recently, a government minister not only commended Hollobone's campaign but confessed to sharing his exasperation. During a parliamentary debate initiated by the Kettering MP, Mike Penning, minister for policing and criminal justice, revealed his surprise at official briefings, describing himself as very surprised... about some of the things that are being done and finding it mind bogglingly difficult to work out why, in many cases, things do not happen.Hollobone presented fresh statistics demonstrating the scale of the challenge. Currently, 10,837 foreign national offenders occupy British prisons, representing 13% of the total prison population. Poland tops the list with 938 offenders, followed by Ireland with 779 and Jamaica with 737.The annual cost of housing these prisoners exceeds £300 million, according to Hollobone's calculations. Such people need to serve their sentences in secure detention in prisons in their own country, he argued. At a time of severe constraints on public expenditure, that is far too large a bill to ask British taxpayers to pay.Particularly galling to Hollobone is the absence of prisoner transfer agreements with many of these nations. While a compulsory agreement with Jamaica awaits ratification by the Jamaican government, only voluntary arrangements exist with Pakistan and India. No agreements whatsoever exist with Somalia, Bangladesh, or several EU countries, including Poland.Poland, which is top of the list with almost 1,000 of its nationals in our prisons, has a specific derogation from accepting prisoner transfers under that EU agreement until the end of December 2016, Hollobone stated. That is an absolute outrage. Poland should be securing those people in secure detention back in Poland, at the expense of Polish taxpayers.His solution involves leveraging Britain's expanding international aid budget to construct appropriate detention facilities in countries that contribute significant numbers of prisoners. Research revealed that in 2012, the UK provided £973 million in aid to Jamaica, Pakistan, Nigeria, Somalia, India and Bangladesh – nations whose citizens total 2,900 inmates in British facilities.It costs this country more than £100m a year to incarcerate these people in our jails, Hollobone calculated. It would be a good idea to spend some of that £973m on building prisons in those six countries.Minister Penning acknowledged that officials had briefed him to ensure that I stuck to the line and read the speech, which I will not do. Instead, he endorsed virtually all of Hollobone's arguments: The frustration that he can hear in my voice was in his voice. I share his frustration.Penning expressed his desire to see maximum numbers of foreign nationals serve sentences in their countries of origin, emphasizing the importance that our friends in Europe fulfil their commitments. He concluded: I agree that we have to work much harder because this matter has been ignored for too many years.Eight years have passed since Clarke's forced resignation, yet prospects for resolution appear equally distant.

text: A petition calling for Nathan Gill to be removed as UKIP Wales leader has been sent to the party's ruling body. A petition demanding the removal of UKIP Wales leader Nathan Gill has emerged amid mounting tensions over candidate selection for the upcoming assembly election.The controversy stems from allegations that party leadership seeks to impose external candidates on Welsh constituencies. Particular criticism has focused on former Conservative MPs Mark Reckless and Neil Hamilton being considered for selection, with Welsh activists condemning what they perceive as parachuting outsiders into the region.Six parliamentary election candidates have endorsed the petition, which alleges UKIP Wales lacks both coherent planning for the campaign and effective leadership. The signatories include Joe Smyth (Islwyn), Darran Thomas (Brecon and Radnorshire), Ken Beswick (Torfaen), Blair Smillie (Alyn and Deeside), Nigel Williams (Delyn), and Paul Davies Cooke (Vale of Clwyd).Williams, among the petition's organizers, acknowledged the timing concerns given the proximity of assembly elections but insisted it was better late than never to voice their grievances. He advocated for a leadership contest, suggesting Wales could select from any one from ten great people.The petition directly targets Gill's leadership capabilities, stating: Through his inactivity or unwillingness to resolve the prevailing circumstances, [he] has exacerbated the situation to the point where members no longer have faith in his ability to lead UKIP in Wales in any effective way.Earlier this February, Gill had announced that regional list candidate rankings would be determined by local membership rather than the national executive committee. Despite this concession, Welsh members remain dissatisfied with the handling of candidate selection, exemplified by UKIP Vale of Glamorgan councillor Kevin Mahoney's departure from the party.The petition emphasizes that UKIP in Wales is operated on the basis of mutual respect and understanding and calls for immediate action to prevent further harm and disharmony within 'the party.'However, the petition faces credibility challenges. Wales chairman David Rowlands dismissed it as contributing nothing meaningful to discussions, while UKIP has questioned both the petition's legitimacy and its supporters, labeling them disgruntled members.Gethin James, a UKIP councillor and Ceredigion assembly candidate, defended Gill during a BBC Radio Cymru interview: It's not a good situation, but I'm 100% behind Nathan Gill. People don't know how much work he's done. The problem is with the national executive, not with Nathan Gill.Gill himself rejected calls for his resignation Tuesday, telling BBC Wales he had no intention of stepping down and dismissing accusations of failing to support grassroots Welsh members as nonsense.A UKIP Wales spokesperson challenged the petition's validity, stating: Despite efforts of one or two individuals phoning around the party membership in Wales their petty 26 person petition included someone from England, six people who were not even members and a growing number who denied even ever signing it.

text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and what is now known as the World Bank, were set up to manage the post-World War II global economy. Born from a 1944 conference in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, these twin institutions emerged with ambitious goals: preventing another catastrophic economic collapse like the 1930s Great Depression through enhanced international cooperation and assistance to nations facing balance of payments difficulties.The International Monetary Fund focuses on maintaining global economic stability while confronting—or better yet, preventing—financial crises. Its attention has gradually shifted toward developing nations over the decades. Meanwhile, the World Bank evolved from its original incarnation as the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, initially designed to fuel post-war recovery efforts. Today, it stands as the globe's premier development organization, dedicated to fostering growth and alleviating poverty.Operating under the ownership of 187 member governments, the World Bank provides loans, grants, and advisory services to low and middle-income nations. The IMF operates through a quota system where member countries pay charges based on their economic strength—a structure that also determines voting influence within the organization, giving wealthier contributors greater decision-making power.As a financial safety net, the IMF functions as the ultimate lender, deploying foreign exchange reserves for brief periods to assist struggling members. A traditional leadership arrangement has persisted since inception: Europeans typically head the IMF while Americans lead the World Bank.**Leadership and Controversy**Christine Lagarde made history as the IMF's first female managing director in its 65-year existence. The former lawyer spent over twenty years with a Chicago-based international law firm, specializing in major labor and antitrust litigation. Her political career included serving as French trade minister (2005-2007) before becoming finance minister—the first woman to hold such a position among G8 nations.Lagarde assumed IMF leadership in July 2011 during turbulent times, with the eurozone crisis threatening countries like Greece with potential loan defaults. Known for her candid assessments, she has partially attributed the 2008 global financial crisis to testosterone-driven cultures within male-dominated banking institutions. The Financial Times recognized her as Europe's best finance minister in 2009.Her tenure began after Dominique Strauss-Kahn's resignation following sexual assault charges, from which he was later cleared. Lagarde has committed to enhancing organizational diversity and advancing reforms that would grant emerging economies greater institutional influence.Jim Yong Kim became World Bank president in April 2012, the Korean-American health expert having previously led Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Despite facing strong competition from Nigerian Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Kim secured the traditionally American-held position for a five-year term, succeeding Robert Zoellick. His medical background includes pioneering work in HIV/AIDS treatment and tuberculosis reduction across developing regions.**Operations and Interventions**Both institutions serve as economic lifelines for troubled countries and regions. The IMF's intervention history includes funding during the 1997 Asian financial crisis and providing crucial loans to South American nations like Argentina and Brazil to prevent debt defaults.Following the October 2008 global financial crisis, the IMF launched emergency funding mechanisms for economically distressed countries. By August 2010, approximately $200 billion had been committed to crisis-affected economies, with Hungary, Romania, and Ukraine representing the largest borrowers.The eurozone crisis prompted extensive IMF involvement, including substantial bailouts for Greece, Portugal, and Ireland in partnership with the European Union. Current activities include contributing to Greece's second international bailout and negotiating additional Hungarian loans. Emergency lending also extends to natural disaster responses, such as assistance following the 2004 Asian tsunami.**Criticism and Reform Pressures**These institutions have become focal points for diverse opposition groups—from environmental activists to anarchists—with meetings sometimes marred by violent street demonstrations. Critics argue that policies exploit impoverished populations and environments while threatening millions of livelihoods through aggressive free trade promotion.The IMF has acknowledged that pressuring developing nations to open markets to foreign investment can heighten financial crisis risks. Former managing director Horst Koehler stated in 2002 that globalization's benefits hadn't been equally distributed, though he advocated for more and better globalisation rather than retreat.Developing nations, particularly the BRIC countries (Brazil, Russia, India, and China), express frustration over their limited institutional influence despite growing economic power. They challenge the quota-based voting system where the United States commands 17% of IMF votes while India, with triple the U.S. population, holds less than one-third that proportion. The U.S. effectively maintains veto power since constitutional changes require 85% approval.The traditional European-American leadership division also faces scrutiny. Upon taking office, Lagarde appointed Zhu Min, former deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, to a newly established deputy managing director position, signaling potential shifts in institutional representation.**Key Facts:** - Conceived: Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA - Date: 1944 - Headquarters: Washington DC - IMF-World Bank membership: 187 countries - World Bank staff: 10,000 - IMF staff: 2,500 - IMF managing director: Christine Lagarde

text: The landlocked mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh is the subject of an unresolved dispute between Azerbaijan, in which it lies, and its ethnic Armenian majority, backed by neighbouring Armenia. A century-old rivalry between Christian Armenian and Muslim Turkic and Persian influences forms the foundation of this enduring conflict, with roots extending far beyond the Soviet era.The mountainous region of Karabakh - derived from an Azeri term meaning 'black garden,' with 'Nagorno' being Russian for mountainous - has housed both Christian Armenian and Turkic Azeri populations for centuries. Ethnic Armenians call this territory Artsakh, referencing its ancient Armenian designation. During the 19th century, the area became incorporated into the Russian empire, where these two communities coexisted in relative harmony despite occasional early 20th-century brutalities that continue to resonate in collective memory.Following World War I and Russia's Bolshevik revolution, Soviet authorities implemented their regional divide-and-rule strategy by creating the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Region in the early 1920s. This territory, despite having an ethnic Armenian majority, was placed within the Soviet Socialist Republic of Azerbaijan.As the 1980s drew to a close and Soviet authority weakened, long-simmering Armenian-Azeri tensions erupted when the region's parliament voted to unite with Armenia. This decision triggered the violent confrontation that began in 1988 between Azerbaijani forces and Armenian secessionists.The ensuing warfare proved devastating, claiming an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 lives. Ethnic Armenians secured control over the region while simultaneously occupying additional Azerbaijani territory beyond Karabakh's borders, establishing a buffer zone connecting Karabakh to Armenia. More than one million people abandoned their homes during this period - the ethnic Azeri population, comprising roughly 25% of the pre-war total, fled Karabakh and Armenia, while ethnic Armenians escaped other parts of Azerbaijan. Neither group has managed to return since the conflict's end.The Soviet Union's collapse in late 1991 prompted Karabakh to declare itself an independent republic, though this de facto status lacks international recognition. The declaration transformed the conflict into full-scale warfare. While Armenia has never formally acknowledged the region's independence, it serves as its primary financial and military supporter.A Russian-mediated ceasefire agreement in 1994 concluded the active fighting, leaving both Karabakh and extensive surrounding Azerbaijani territories under Armenian control. This truce established the current de facto independent state controlled by ethnic Armenians.The aftermath has created a persistent stalemate. Azerbaijanis harbor resentment over territories they consider rightfully theirs, while Armenians demonstrate no inclination to relinquish control. Armenia's landlocked position has resulted in severe economic difficulties due to closed borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan.Intermittent ceasefire violations have continued claiming soldiers' lives on both sides. The OSCE's Minsk Group, co-chaired by Russia, France, and the United States, has persistently worked to mediate a resolution to this dispute.December 2006 witnessed a referendum - deemed illegitimate by Azerbaijan - where the region endorsed a new constitution. Subsequently, the peace process showed occasional signs of revival through sporadic meetings between Armenian and Azerbaijani presidents.May and November 2009 talks between the leaders reportedly yielded significant progress, though momentum eventually stalled. Since then, numerous serious ceasefire breaches have occurred, with April 2016 marking the most severe escalation when dozens of soldiers perished on both sides during renewed hostilities.This conflict remains classified among post-Soviet Europe's frozen conflicts, with negotiations failing to achieve a permanent peace agreement. The dispute continues to defy resolution despite decades of diplomatic efforts.Profile compiled by BBC Monitoring
