text: JPeg pictures could soon have built-in restrictions making them harder to copy, if recommendations by the body overseeing the format are implemented. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) and other rights groups have raised concerns about new proposals from the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPeg) committee to implement access controls for .jpg file image data, warning the features could stifle creativity.According to several billion JPeg images produced daily, the JPeg format remains the internet's most prevalent image format. The committee argues that current practices allow photographs to be redistributed without proper rights information, enabling unauthorized copying and republication.Privacy concerns also drive the proposals, as photographer metadata embedded in images - including geo-location data from photo sites - can compromise personal security when accessible to unauthorized users.Currently, these concerns are not well addressed and [are] an inhibiting factor in the further proliferation of digital content distribution, the JPeg committee briefing said.Committee convener Touradj Ebrahimi emphasized to the BBC that any future changes wouldn't eliminate free sharing capabilities for willing authors. The committee lacks concrete plans for format modifications but seeks technological solutions once proposal specifics are finalized.One thing that's important to note is that this is not something we're imposing, he said. We are just saying, 'Let people have a choice.' Those who are perfectly happy with today's situation and want to have security-free image sharing [will still be able to].Existing protection methods rely on website-based privacy software like Facebook's systems. However, once authorized users extract and redistribute these images elsewhere, protection disappears entirely.Dr Ebrahimi advocates for file-embedded access controls instead. It would be best if you have one image that is protected in such a way that if you have the rights, you see it clear; if you don't have the rights, you don't see it, he said.The EFF has published blog warnings against restrictive JPeg limitations, suggesting such moves could hamper artistic creativity by preventing photographers' works from being incorporated into new artistic pieces.Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group, questioned the security effectiveness of proposed restrictions, drawing parallels to digital rights management (DRM) software used on DVDs to prevent content copying.DRM tends to be easily broken, he told the BBC. People who want to break the rules would still do that.Killock also warned about potential corporate exploitation, suggesting companies might impose expensive fees for various access levels to restricted images.You're going to want to edit pictures, crop them, alter them, all of these sorts of things that DRM potentially restricts, so I guess the other major beneficiary would end up being software publishers, he said.

text: Londoners are offering shelter and comfort to those affected by the terror attack on the capital by sharing the hashtag #SofaForLondon on social media. Across London's faiths, strangers opened their doors as taxi drivers ferried stranded residents away from police cordons that had sealed off London Bridge and Borough Market, leaving countless people unable to reach home.The city's response proved swift and generous. Pubs, hotels, businesses, and places of worship from multiple religions provided shelter and sustenance to those displaced by the evening's events. Social media became a lifeline, with strangers extending invitations for tea, conversation, or overnight accommodation.Twenty-two-year-old George Moss found himself among those helped by this spontaneous network of kindness. After losing his mobile phone and becoming trapped by police cordons between Borough Market and Elephant and Castle, friends Holly Robinson and Mary Lynch took him in. The pair had posted on Twitter, welcoming any strangers needing somewhere to stay at their Vauxhall home.Using a journalist's phone to reassure his parents of his safety, Moss discovered the #SofaForLondon hashtag on Twitter. After that I went towards Vauxhall and found Holly and Mary who very kindly gave me a place to stay, he said. I would have been in a pickle, I wouldn't have anywhere else to go.Lynch, 23 and originally from Nottingham, explained her motivation: If I had been in that situation I would want to know that people were going to open up their homes. Birmingham native Robinson added: You have to give whatever you can, whenever you can.The Royal Oak pub on Tabard Street in Southwark became an impromptu refuge for approximately 150 displaced people. Barman Radek Malis described the scene: There were people standing in the street who were evacuated from hotels nearby or who couldn't get back so we invited them in.Among those seeking shelter were families with children and foreign visitors, many unable to speak English. text: How can busy working mums and dads keep tabs on their toddlers and stay connected to them during the working day? Tech entrepreneurs increasingly claim they've discovered solutions for modern parenting challenges, but the question remains: do these digital tools genuinely enhance parent-child connections, or do they simply fuel parental anxiety?Molawa Adesuyi, who co-founded and leads Mytoddlr, champions his nursery monitoring app with unwavering confidence. The platform delivers real-time updates about children's daycare activities directly to parents' devices.Most working parents drop off their children in day nurseries as early as 8 or 9am, and can't pick them up till 5 or 6pm, he says. And in this time, they have absolutely no way of keeping in touch or staying abreast of their children's welfare all through the day. This is a major, major problem.Through Mytoddlr's app and website interface, childcare providers log detailed information about each child's daily routine and behavior patterns—everything from bathroom visits to afternoon rest periods. Parents then receive these comprehensive updates instantly via their smartphones or computers.According to Mr Adesuyi, the system creates mutual satisfaction: The nursery is happy, parents are happy, it's a win-win for everyone really.When questioned about potential administrative burdens on nursery staff, Mr Adesuyi dismisses these concerns. He argues the technology actually streamlines operations by reducing traditional paperwork while establishing more efficient parent communication channels.There are such great apps out there now for parents... solutions to real problems parents have. It's just nice to see technology change parenting, he concludes.Since its 2015 launch, Mytoddlr serves 2,000 parents across Lagos, Nigeria, while London nurseries currently participate in trial programs.Personal experience drove 19-year-old Harsh Songra to create My Child, a developmental monitoring smartphone application. His motivation stemmed from his own childhood struggle with dyspraxia, a coordination and movement disorder that often evades early detection without proper awareness.I have known the struggle of a family where the child has a disorder, he says. It took my parents over nine years to figure out the specific problem, and I still go through some health issues, says Mr Songra.My Child assists parents in tracking developmental milestones for children up to 24 months old through targeted questioning, curated content aggregation, and local specialist identification.Following its early 2015 debut, the application has accumulated over 11,000 downloads across more than 140 countries, with particularly strong adoption rates in the US, India, Singapore and the UK.While Mr Songra advocates for technology as a valuable parenting resource, he acknowledges potential interference with professional medical relationships.At times it does affect their relations with doctors, because parents become paranoid about their child because of what they searched on Google, he says. The problem is that we tend to believe the content of one link over 100 others, and then take actions based on that knowledge. But we believe all this will surely change with time, as there is going to be more awareness about these issues in the future.The parenting app ecosystem continues expanding rapidly—encompassing webcam baby monitors, location-tracking services, interactive games, and health assessment tools—as time-pressed parents increasingly incorporate cutting-edge technology into their daily routines. One Australian mother even utilized Siri, Apple's voice-activated iPhone assistant, to summon emergency services when her toddler daughter experienced breathing difficulties.For New Jersey entrepreneur Amit Murumkar, app development arose from purely practical considerations rather than technological ambition.My daughter was three... and would bring a piece of art back daily from her Montessori school, but there is only so much you can put on a refrigerator door, he says. I also was a good artist as a kid, and when I became a parent I thought, 'If only I could show the art I did to my own kids.'His solution, Canvsly, enables parents to digitally capture their children's artwork, organize pieces into themed albums, and share collections with grandparents and extended family members for viewing and commentary.The platform additionally offers printing services and gift creation options. Parents comfortable with cloud storage security can subsequently dispose of physical originals without guilt.Parents can go guilt-free and clutter-free, Mr Murumkar says, noting the app's distribution across more than 100 countries.Tech analyst Anesu Charamba from research consultancy Frost & Sullivan views these applications as empowering parents to nurture and engage with their children through new and exciting ways.As smartphone penetration and affordable, dependable internet connectivity expand beyond developed nations to emerging markets worldwide, he predicts early adopters will soon be joined by mainstream users.Follow Technology of Business editor @matthew_wall on Twitter Click here for more Technology of Business features

text: In our series of letters from African journalists, filmmaker and columnist Farai Sevenzo considers the role of cameras in conflict. At the recent Cannes Film Festival, a powerful moment unfolded when Mauritania-born director Abderrahmane Sissako fielded questions following the screening of his work Timbuktu - The Silence of Fear.The fictional narrative recreates those turbulent months during which jihadists seized control of Mali's ancient town, implementing harsh regulations that prohibited music and football while introducing brutal punishments like lashings and stoning.During his press conference, Sissako—recognized as one of Africa's most reliable storytellers—became emotional and wept openly, explaining that his tears were for all Malians who had endured the experiences depicted in his film.The real courage, he said, was to be found among those who lived this on a daily basis.Timbuktu was indeed eventually freed but the true liberation was for those people who in their heads sang these songs and this music that had been banned.While dramatists among us focus their cameras on recent African events to provide moments for contemplation, our 24-hour news environment ensures cameras are omnipresent—wielded by journalists and jihadists alike.During the early 2000s, the late Osama bin Laden regularly supplied footage to news networks, creating a twisted competition among broadcasters over who would receive the next tirade from the mountain-dwelling terrorist.Fast-forward fifteen years to the YouTube era, where fighters spanning from Syria to Somalia have embraced cameras with the same fervor soldiers show for weapons. Continental combatants increasingly present us with their own footage.This past month, the escalating death toll and disappearances in north-east Nigeria have brought two elements into stark relief: President Goodluck Jonathan's leadership and the visage of Abubakar Shekau, the Islamist militant responsible for abducting over 200 schoolgirls in Chibok.With theatrical enthusiasm, the Boko Haram leader has embraced camera appearances, declaring: I abducted your girls; I will sell them in the market.Since 14 April 2014, we've been compelled to scrutinize his every utterance in successive videos, hoping to alleviate the anguish of Chibok's parents.Observing Shekau's diatribes, some might mistake him for a Nollywood actor portraying the quintessential antagonist—someone who might momentarily confess to the camera something shocking, such as having already sold his own mother, aunts and sisters, with these schoolgirls destined for identical fate.Negotiations may be proceeding, and Nigeria's military—perhaps responding to persistent rumors about their notable absence from remote Nigerian villages under siege—now claims knowledge of the girls' location while reviewing the circumstances.Our era presents a striking paradox: despite living in a world saturated with cameras and recording devices, where satellites populate the earth's atmosphere, we remain unable to locate a missing aircraft or several hundred disappeared children situated not at sea but on solid ground within heartbreaking proximity to their grieving parents.Once such events conclude, artists, novelists and filmmakers can offer what television news cannot—opportunities for reflection and extracting meaning from combatants' propaganda.These creators can explore fundamental questions: Who are these individuals and what drives them? How do villagers perceive them? Does fear or faith motivate responses? What positions do imams take?Can traditional African methods involving elders rather than soldiers defuse tensions?However, artists and their cameras enjoy the luxury of time unavailable to those confronting this new struggle's frontlines.While solutions to these monumental challenges remain elusive, the quest for answers must persist.Regardless of whether Nigeria's militants release additional videos, the ideological earthquake in northern Nigeria represented by Boko Haram's presence continues spreading genuine fear and immediate danger.Similar fear permeates other African cities—Nairobi, Mogadishu and recently Djibouti.The silence of fear proves no more desirable than the fear of silence that initially greeted Chibok's parents when their daughters vanished weeks before celebrities raised hashtag signs.Nevertheless, in this era of instant footage and digital imagery, the most heartbreaking images remain those of mothers and fathers clutching aging photographs of teenage daughters they may never encounter again.If you would like to comment on Farai Sevenzo's column, please do so below.

text: Zayn Malik has revealed that, in leaving One Direction, he has let the fans down. Just hours after shocking the music world with his departure announcement on Wednesday, Zayn delivered a candid interview to The Sun, declaring: I can't do this anymore.The singer characterized his bombshell decision as crazy and wild and a bit mad. However, he emphasized a newfound sense of clarity: But I've never felt more in control in my life. I feel like I'm doing what's right, right by myself and right by the boys.Zayn's exit from the globally dominant pop group came exactly one week after he abandoned their world tour, citing stress as the primary factor. The departure followed controversial photographs showing the singer with his arm around an unidentified blonde woman in Thailand, sparking widespread speculation about infidelity regarding his relationship with fiancée Perrie Edwards of Little Mix.Upon returning to the UK immediately after the announcement, Zayn addressed the cheating rumors via Twitter: I'm 22 years old... I love a girl named Perrie Edwards. And there's a lot of jealous [people] in this world. I'm sorry for what it looks like.During his Sun interview, the star firmly dismissed suggestions of internal band conflicts, stating such claims couldn't be more wrong. Nevertheless, he acknowledged harboring exit desires for an extended period.You know, I did try to do something that I wasn't happy doing for a while, for the sake of maybe other people, he revealed. Basically, I'm only upset [because] I feel like I may have let them down.Zayn emphasized his continued respect for supporters: It's not that I've turned my back on them [the fans] or anything, it's just that I just can't do that anymore because it's not real to me.Addressing his formal departure statement, Zayn explained: After five years, I feel like it is now the right time for me to leave the band.The singer actively countered speculation about One Direction's future, dismissing rumors that his exit signaled the group's demise. The band, originally assembled on The X Factor in 2010, continues without him. Zayn declined to address potential return possibilities.Regarding his personal life, Zayn confirmed his two-year engagement to Perrie Edwards remains intact. He praised her as a good girl who was supportive of his decision.Reports suggest Zayn has already begun pursuing solo opportunities, allegedly visiting a west London recording studio to collaborate with Naughty Boy, the producer behind successful launches for artists including Emeli Sande and Sam Smith.Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube

text: England women began their World Twenty20 campaign with a routine 36-run victory over Bangladesh in Bangalore. Captain Charlotte Edwards' commanding 60 propelled England to 153-7 in their tournament opener, though the 2009 champions and recent two-time finalists faced little resistance from Bangladesh, who managed just 117-6 in reply.Bangladesh's struggles continued as they failed to threaten England's total, extending their poor T20 record to just five victories from 30 matches. Katherine Brunt's economical bowling figures of 4-0-17-1 and Anya Shrubsole's 2-27 helped restrict the opposition comfortably.Edwards, the leading run-scorer in T20 internationals across both men's and women's cricket, expertly navigated England through a precarious phase. When Sarah Taylor and Heather Knight departed for the addition of merely one run, leaving England at 71-3, the captain's blend of patient accumulation and aggressive stroke-play against loose deliveries proved crucial.Nat Sciver provided valuable support with 27 runs in a 47-run partnership alongside Edwards. The innings gained momentum in its closing stages as Danni Wyatt and Brunt contributed late fireworks, with England plundering 35 runs from the final three overs.Bangladesh's chase never gained traction against a team that had previously struggled to surpass 115 in T20 international cricket. Brunt struck immediately in the reply, bowling opener Sharmin Akhter in the first over, effectively ending any hopes of an upset.Though Nigar Sultana and Salma Khatun established a Bangladesh record fifth-wicket stand of 64 runs, the contest had already been decided. England maintained control throughout, setting up Tuesday's more challenging encounter against hosts India in Dharamsala.England coach Mark Robinson expressed mixed feelings about the performance, telling Sky Sports: I thought we went backwards today. We were safe and we don't want to be safe. We lost our way in the middle with the bat and made poor decisions with the ball. text: Eastern Ukraine has become a testing ground for Russia's new military capabilities. Russia's 2008 military campaign in Georgia appeared to deliver swift success, yet the conflict exposed critical weaknesses that deeply troubled Moscow's military leadership. The poor performance in several modern warfare domains prompted a comprehensive seven-year transformation program focused on rearming, re-equipping, and retraining forces to bridge the capability gap with contemporary Western militaries.The fruits of this modernization effort are now visible across eastern Ukraine, where pro-Russian separatists have steadily advanced against Ukrainian government forces. Unlike Russia, Ukraine's military has not undergone comparable intensive modernization, leaving it vulnerable to the advanced weapons and systems flowing from Russian sources.Two critical technologies exemplify this transformation: unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for surveillance and targeting, plus electronic warfare capabilities. Russian forces identified both as significant vulnerabilities during the 2008 Georgian conflict, subsequently investing heavily in their development. These systems now operate extensively throughout eastern Ukraine, creating substantial disadvantages for Ukrainian government troops.Secure communications represent a particular weakness for Ukrainian forces. Their vulnerable communication networks face constant jamming while simultaneously revealing unit positions to Russian direction-finding equipment. This exposure enables rapid targeting by Russian artillery, including Grad systems and other more powerful rocket platforms.Among the non-lethal assistance provided by the United States, Ukraine has received specialized radar designed to identify incoming mortar fire sources. However, communication difficulties limit the effectiveness of sharing this intelligence with other units. Ukraine has not yet received more sophisticated systems capable of pinpointing longer-range artillery positions.Russian tank deployments further outmatch Ukrainian capabilities. These modern armored vehicles surpass Ukrainian models in performance, while Ukraine simultaneously lacks sufficient functional anti-armor weaponry. Ukrainian support requests encompass all these systems, plus medical support and field hospital equipment, aimed at improving force survivability when confronting advanced Russian military hardware.Ukrainian aircraft losses over the conflict zone demonstrate the sophisticated air defense capabilities of Russian-backed separatists. Beyond the Buk missile system—blamed for destroying Malaysia Airlines flight MH17—separatist forces deploy Strela systems for lower-altitude, shorter-range targets, plus numerous lighter shoulder-launched missiles.Despite Russian denials, independent experts, NATO, Western leaders, and the Kiev government cite clear evidence of direct Russian military involvement. Russia's military transformation includes intensive exercise programs involving tens of thousands of personnel nationwide. These maneuvers have grown in scale and complexity, often featuring storylines directly antagonistic toward the West.Eastern Ukraine now provides Russia with a live testing environment for new weapons, systems, and tactics. The results—particularly if tested against potential new US defensive systems supplied to Ukraine—will help Moscow evaluate how its forces might perform in direct NATO confrontation.Keir Giles is an analyst with the Conflict Studies Research Centre in Oxford, and an Associate Fellow with the Russia and Eurasia Programme at Chatham House in London.

text: Canada and the European Union are to sign a long-delayed landmark trade deal at a summit in Brussels on Sunday. Wallonia's objections centered on demands for enhanced protections regarding labor standards, environmental safeguards, and consumer rights. The region also sought additional shields for local farmers who would encounter increased competition from Canadian agricultural imports.Belgian Prime Minister Charles Michel announced Thursday that negotiators had successfully crafted an addendum addressing these regional concerns after extensive discussions.Slovakia's Prime Minister Robert Fico, representing the country currently holding the EU presidency, hailed the final approval as a milestone in the EU's trade policy.The Ceta represents a modern and progressive deal, opening the door to new opportunities, while protecting important interests, he said. The top seed himself acknowledged his subpar performance, a factor that could work in Murray's favor.I think Andy has slimmed down a little bit; he seems to be a bit leaner, he's moving really well, still has all the power, improved his second serve, Navratilova added. text: Three men and a woman are trapped and four people have been taken to hospital after three explosions at a wood treatment works near Macclesfield. At 09:10 BST, a devastating explosion ripped through Wood Flour Mills on Tunstall Road in Bosley, causing a four-storey building to collapse and triggering massive fires, according to the fire service.The blast has created what fire officials describe as a scene of devastation, leaving 50 workers jobless, Cheshire East Council confirmed. Search and rescue teams are preparing to enter the site when daylight breaks.Emergency responders assessed 35 people who were on the premises during the incident. Cheshire Police reported that four individuals received treatment for breathing difficulties, while four others required hospitalization in Birmingham, Merseyside and Stoke.A 29-year-old woman suffered the most severe injuries. A 29-year-old woman has sustained serious burns and blast injuries to her head, face, arms and chest, West Midlands Ambulance Service stated. An air ambulance transported her to Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham.Four people remain missing in what has become a desperate search operation. Assistant Chief Constable Guy Hindle of Cheshire Police explained: Four people remain unaccounted for and urban search and rescue teams are assessing the scene to see whether it is safe to go into the property to locate them. We are working with the four families.The dangerous conditions have prevented immediate rescue attempts. Steve Barnes from Cheshire Fire and Rescue Service said: When we arrived it was a scene of devastation. The surrounding area is unsafe and hazardous to firefighters. Earlier warnings indicated firefighters could not rule out additional explosions.Crews are working to secure the area before attempting any rescue operations. Chief fire officer Paul Hancock stated: We are still dealing with four unaccounted people. We believe they are somewhere in the building. We will endeavour to deal with that issue in a few hours' time once we get the incident under full control.Although search teams plan to enter at first light Saturday, pockets of fire continue burning throughout the structure.The facility houses multiple hazardous materials, including heating oil, kerosene, acetylene and asbestos. Additionally, a silo contains highly flammable wood flour used in manufacturing wood laminate flooring.North West Ambulance Service deployed six ambulances and two rapid response vehicles to the scene, supplemented by an air ambulance. An NWAS spokesperson confirmed: Two patients have been taken to Royal Stoke University Hospital and one patient has been taken to Whiston Hospital in Merseyside.Authorities have not yet determined the cause of the explosion.Patrick Jones, a shift worker who had clocked out just over three hours before the blast, expressed his concern: I am still worried about my mates. There are four of them that are still missing. Police cordons prevented him from approaching the site.The explosion's impact extended far beyond the immediate area. Smoke drifted northeast, prompting authorities to advise residents 15 miles away in Wildboarclough to keep doors and windows closed.More than 40 students at Bosley St Mary's C of E Primary School, located approximately one mile from the explosion site, were confined indoors as a precautionary measure.Headteacher Raj Barard described the moment: We heard and we felt the explosion just after 09:00 BST. Police told us to keep the children indoors. It felt like an earthquake. We had our leavers service in the school instead of at the church over the road.BBC Radio Manchester reporter Jonathan Ali observed the ongoing situation six hours after the initial blast: Six hours later, the smoke plume is still hanging over this factory. At around 14:40 there was the brief sound of popping noises as things continued to explode. This was a four-storey factory which, in the words of the fire service, has now collapsed to one storey. Basically it has collapsed in on itself.Local residents described the terrifying experience. Sarah Nixon from Bosley Cloud, living less than half a mile away, said: I live less than half a mile from the wood flour mill and the explosion sounded as if a car had just crashed into the house with a very deep bang. The explosion shook the whole house rattling windows and doors, just like an earthquake. The black and grey smoke plummeted up along with flames and has engulfed the valley below.Angela Shuker, whose farm is adjacent to the wood treatment facility, recalled: Our doors in the house just banged. We could see the flames rising not far from us down the road from the mill.Eighteen-year-old Charli Alston witnessed the explosion while walking her dog: I was walking down my drive and there was just a huge bang. It sounded like a thunder cloud, we didn't know what it was. We looked over and there were massive plumes of flames. Almost as high as the hill next to it.Electricity North West temporarily cut power to 165 Bosley homes allow firefighters to carry out their work safely, though service has been restored to most residences.This marks the second major incident at the facility - a blaze occurred at the wood flour mill in 2012.

text: Organisers of this summer's music festivals have been asked by the government to warn about legal highs. Crime Prevention Minister James Brokenshire has reached out to festival organizers with a direct request: alert attendees about the potential dangers lurking in so-called legal substances. His initiative extends beyond festivals, encompassing letters dispatched to both councils and police forces operating in festival regions.The minister's correspondence comes alongside a significant policy announcement regarding drug legislation reform. Brokenshire revealed plans to modify existing drug laws, enabling authorities to impose temporary prohibitions on emerging substances while awaiting comprehensive scientific evaluation.During the festival season we know that people may be tempted to try potentially dangerous new drugs, particularly when they are advertised as 'legal' or 'herbal', Brokenshire explained. That is why we are asking festival organisers and police to work with us to send out the message that these substances may not be safe and could contain illegal drugs.The minister emphasized the urgency of legislative change: We are going to change our drug laws so we can respond quickly to emerging substances by introducing a temporary ban while we seek full scientific advice.This warning carries particular weight given recent developments in drug classification. Previously available legal highs have faced prohibition, with mephedrone now classified as a Class B substance serving as a prime example.According to Home Office findings, the drug naphyrone operates under the NRG1 brand name. Despite being marketed as innocuous plant food or bath salts, officials warn it may harbor one or multiple illegal substances.The government maintains its commitment to thorough evaluation, stating it will refrain from implementing permanent bans without complete guidance from the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs.Brokenshire's letter to festival organizers carried a specific call to action: As part of your preparations for this year's event I ask you to review the measures you have put in place to ensure that your festival is as safe an environment as possible, to help protect the public, especially young people from the potential harms and risks of all drugs.The governmental stance has garnered support from industry leaders. Melvin Benn, managing director of Festival Republic—the company behind Latitude, Big Chill, Reading and Leeds Festivals—expressed his endorsement.I can confirm that we do not allow legal high traders to trade at any Festival Republic festival and fully support the minister's view, Benn stated.

text: Lawyers representing cyclists injured on Edinburgh's tram tracks have warned the city council it must take action to prevent a fatality. A legal firm has revealed to BBC Scotland that it's currently handling nearly 100 compensation cases related to cyclist injuries, with lawyers at Thompsons Solicitors estimating the council faces a bill reaching hundreds of thousands of pounds. Meanwhile, allegations suggest the actual number of injured cyclists far exceeds what official reports indicate.The council has maintained its defense of safety protocols, though it cannot comment on pending court cases. Officials reportedly believe they possess a strong legal position.Patrick McGuire, a partner at the firm, described the severity of injuries: We've had people who've lost finger tips, we've had people who've had broken collar bones, we've had people who've had broken legs. To my mind, it's absolutely inevitable that unless something happens we will see a death on the streets of our capital city.City of Edinburgh Council transport convener Lesley Hinds emphasized existing safety measures: We have always encouraged cyclists to take care when travelling near the tram tracks, especially during wet weather when they can become slippery. The council advises that it's best to cross the tracks as close to a right angle as possible and to take extra care to avoid getting wheels caught in between the rail grooves. We have also installed signage which helps to guide cyclists along the safest possible routes.Cyclists identify Haymarket in the city's west end as the most perilous stretch of tram line. The tramline's crossing angle with the road creates what they describe as nearly impossible navigation conditions. Growing pressure mounts on the council to implement a coloured pathway system to guide riders through the intricate network of busy junctions.Local businessman Hamish Mitchell underwent surgery following his accident in the area. My wheel slipped on the surface of the tram line, he recounted. I landed on my knee, pulled my hip, damaged my shoulder, broke three teeth and took the end off my finger. All of that happened in milliseconds.David Steele sustained injuries after falling on the Haymarket track and expressed his frustration to BBC Scotland: I was really angry. Why has my simple commute into town to do a bit of shopping now become a life-threatening journey? My motivation is to get action to get it sorted. We've got to redesign the junction to make it safer for all road users.The council's handling of a freedom of information request regarding tram line accident details has come under examination. Despite reporting their incidents, cyclists have informed BBC Scotland that their cases don't appear in official records. This discrepancy fuels claims that the problem's true scale surpasses statistical representations.Legal representatives have championed cyclists' rights to pursue compensation while advocating for improved road layouts. Patrick McGuire of Thompsons Solicitors stated: Edinburgh city council have a statutory duty under the Road Traffic Act to ensure the safety of cyclists, to ensure the lessons from previous accidents are learned, and to make changes. They have utterly failed in that. Cyclists are doing absolutely the right thing in coming forward and demanding these changes.

text: The leader of Colombia's largest armed rebel group, the Farc, has said he ordered the organisation in September to stop buying guns and ammunition. The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia's leader, Rodrigo Londono Echeverri—better known as Timochenko—announced his organization's commitment to reducing hostilities with Colombian military forces through a key decision that underscores the Farc's dedication to peace.Nearly three years of negotiations between the leftist insurgency and Colombia's government have brought both parties to anticipate signing a comprehensive agreement by March. The conflict, which began when the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia initiated its armed rebellion in 1964, has claimed an estimated 220,000 lives.Havana became the venue for peace discussions in November 2012, with the primary objective of persuading rebels to abandon their military campaign and participate in legitimate political processes. Timochenko conveyed his announcement through a tweet directed at Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos.Four major agenda items have reached consensus: rebel political participation, land rights issues, drug trafficking concerns, and transitional justice—the latter being recently resolved. The question of how to handle punishment for crimes committed by rebels had represented one of the most challenging aspects of negotiations.Following the September 23 announcement of a transitional justice agreement, President Santos traveled to Cuba, where he and Timochenko shook hands for the first time. Santos established a six-month timeline ending March 23, 2016, for finalizing the peace accord, though rebels have expressed interest in signing even earlier.Work continues on various outstanding issues and implementation details. Any final agreement must receive approval from Colombian citizens through a referendum.Santos declared last month his willingness to participate in a bilateral ceasefire with the Farc beginning January 1, 2016, contingent on substantial negotiation progress. The rebels have already announced their own truce.As a goodwill gesture, Santos has also halted radio and television campaigns designed to encourage Farc defections—campaigns that would typically intensify during the pre-Christmas period.

text: You may not have heard of Judith Hill, but you've almost certainly heard her voice. A Californian vocalist who has lent her voice to legends including Stevie Wonder, Elton John, Josh Groban, Carole King, Robbie Williams and Rod Stewart throughout her distinguished career, Judith Hill's journey to solo stardom took an unexpected path.Her most notable opportunity came when she was selected as a featured performer for Michael Jackson's planned This Is It tour in 2009. Following Jackson's death, audiences witnessed her spine-tingling duet with the King of Pop in the posthumous rehearsal film. Hill later competed on the US version of The Voice, where her surprising elimination led judge Adam Levine to famously declare: I hate this country.The Oscar-winning documentary 20 Feet From Stardom chronicled Hill's quest for solo success while highlighting the predominantly African-American backup singers who have supported rock's biggest names. However, it was Prince who ultimately catalyzed her solo breakthrough after reading about her in a newspaper and extending an invitation to record at his Minneapolis-based Paisley Park Studios.In conversation with the BBC, Hill reflects on her collaboration with Prince, her backing vocalist experiences, and the tragic day Michael Jackson passed away.**What's the first song you remember hearing?** Walk With Me by Vanessa Bell Armstrong**Who was the first person who told you you could sing?** My mother was the first person to tell me I could sing. She tells the story of how I was singing in the back car seat as a little girl, and she saw that I had talent. We wrote our first song together when I was four.**How did you land a job on Michael Jackson's This Is It tour?** I did a small gig in Los Angeles and became friends with some musicians there. One of them knew Michael's musical director and he invited me to audition. I did a small audition at the vocal director's house and a couple weeks later I was hired. I remember them telling me, Michael is on your Myspace page. Change the picture! At the time, I was also hired to work at a clothing shop, so I quit that job and joined the This Is It tour.**He was a master of stagecraft - what tips did he give you?** Michael was fascinating to watch. Working with him taught me the importance of seizing every moment on stage. He painted pictures with every lyric and movement in his body.**What do you remember of the day he died?** I was sitting at a restaurant when my phone started blowing up. There were rumours of his death but I didn't believe it. It wasn't until later that day when this nightmare became a reality as I arrived at the Staples Center for rehearsal. It was a very tragic day. They had already begun to collapse the stage and pack up the gear. Just the night before we were rehearsing… It was surreal.**What was it like to sing at the memorial service?** It was an overwhelming experience. I mean, that was the same stage we rehearsed with him [on] two weeks prior. But it was a beautiful service.Hill's Voice experience proved educational despite its disappointing conclusion. When I was on The Voice, I made discoveries about my vocal style. No matter what the song was, I always managed to turn it into a soul song whether I wanted to or not. I learned that at the heart of it, I'm a soul singer. My roots run deep, starting from the early days of jamming with my parents on Sly and the Family Stone and Curtis Mayfield songs.The documentary 20 Feet From Stardom significantly impacted her trajectory. 20 Feet From Stardom was a special project that resonated with so many people. We were honoured with an Oscar and Grammy and many wonderful opportunities have come my way because of it. People were inspired by the stories in the film and they continue to follow my story to see what happens next.Transitioning from backup to lead presented considerable challenges. It's a very rough road - that 20 feet from being a backing singer to an artist is a long 20 feet! But what keeps me going is a passion for music. No matter what, it makes me happy to do it.The contrast between roles is stark, Hill explains. Working as a backing singer is being a part of a group effort to give the artist what they need. It's a fun community to be a part of. Being a solo artist is a totally different experience. There is more responsibility and pressure, yet it is very rewarding. I love sitting in the driver's seat, directing everybody to achieve the sound I'm looking for. There's nothing more fulfilling than making the sounds you hear in your head become a reality.Among the artists she's supported, Natalie Cole stands out. The most demanding was Natalie Cole. It was a short show, but she was very particular about how she wanted the vocals. I have much respect for her. She kept the singers on their toes!Her collaboration with Prince began serendipitously. I did an interview and was asked who is my dream collaborator. I said 'Prince!' He saw the interview and personally reached out to me. I remember receiving the unknown call on my cell phone and freaking out while I was talking to him. I officially met him at his album listening party in Los Angeles. Shortly after, he invited me to Paisley Park and that was beginning of the collaboration.Prince's playful nature occasionally surfaced. He once called me and I didn't recognize his voice because he pretended to be someone else. He can do great impersonations.His contribution to her album was substantial. He's a fantastic producer and arranger. He played many instruments, sang, arranged, and even wrote. He was very involved in the process, yet it was a great collaboration between his ideas and my ideas. Most of the songs were already written and he helped me come up with great grooves and effective edits.The album title Back In Time reflects her artistic vision. I wanted people to feel like they have travelled back into a golden era of funk/soul music. For me, personally, this record celebrates my childhood and upbringing in a musical family. Many of the lyrics are autobiographical - describing where I came from, my old stomping grounds, and the amazing musical community that inspired me along the way. The whole record feels like a dusty jam session in the basement of my parents' house.One track holds special significance. Angel In The Dark. I think about the many times I felt like I was trapped in a dark tunnel, yet God has always managed to rescue me at the right time. He is that Angel in the dark.Judith Hill's debut album Back In Time is out now on NPG Records.

text: Egyptians go to the polls on 26 and 27 May to elect a new president. Egypt prepares for presidential elections with results anticipated on 5 June, where former defence minister Abdul Fattah al-Sisi appears poised for a decisive victory. His sole opponent is Hamdeen Sabahi, a seasoned left-wing politician and previous presidential candidate.**Early Election Timeline**Following mass demonstrations last July, the military removed Islamist President Mohammed Morsi from power and subsequently established a democratic roadmap that accelerated presidential elections by two years. Originally, parliamentary elections were scheduled first, but the interim administration reversed this sequence in January. Parliamentary voting will occur later this year after the presidency is secured.Under the January 2014 constitution, presidential terms are restricted to two consecutive four-year periods. Meanwhile, Mohammed Morsi faces trial on charges including inciting protester murders, killing prison officers during a 2011 jailbreak, espionage, and terrorist conspiracy.**Campaign Platforms and Backing**Mr Sisi has unveiled sweeping development proposals targeting agriculture, housing, education, impoverished regions, and job creation. However, his funding strategy remains unclear beyond appeals for national dedication and reduced profit margins across state and private sectors. Running on Long live Egypt! he declares that his victory would render the Muslim Brotherhood finished politically.His coalition spans from Islamist right to moderate left parties, supported by prominent business figures. Hamdeen Sabahi, a leftist stalwart since the 1970s, appeals to younger voters preferring civilian over military leadership. His We will pursue our dream campaign emphasizes anti-corruption efforts and civil rights promotion.Both candidates oppose re-legalizing the Muslim Brotherhood, now designated a terrorist organization. Sabahi's support comes predominantly from left-wing parties and movements.**Electoral Integrity Concerns**Two primary factors threaten fair elections. Security and political instability persist as the Muslim Brotherhood continues protesting Morsi's removal, met with violent government suppression. Since summer, hundreds have died in security force clashes, with hundreds more facing imprisonment or death sentences, fueling additional demonstrations.Additionally, mainstream media overwhelmingly favors Mr Sisi, already depicting him as the presumptive president. The Brotherhood's domestic media face bans, limiting opposition voices to foreign-hosted online platforms lacking mainstream reach.**International Oversight**Major Western monitoring organizations will not observe voting. While the US Carter Centre declined participation, the European Union will conduct nationwide monitoring. The Arab League plans deploying 100 observers, and the African Union will send a mission despite suspending Egypt's membership last year.**Boycott Movements**Various Islamist parties announced boycotts, though some endorsed Mr Sisi. The Muslim Brotherhood, recognizing Morsi as legitimate president, rejects the election entirely. The pro-Morsi National Alliance to Support Legitimacy labels the vote a farce, while the Salafist Front calls it illegitimate.The Gamaa Islamiya's political wing, the Building and Development Party, reports majority member support for boycotting. The secular 6 April Youth Movement, instrumental in Hosni Mubarak's overthrow, also advocates boycotting, viewing elections as merely enthroning Mr Sisi.**Presidential Challenges Ahead**Domestically, the incoming president confronts severe political, economic, security, and social crises. Public expectations center on addressing unemployment, inequality, and corruption, though security restoration may prove the paramount challenge.Internationally, the new leader must balance maintaining Western and US relations while improving ties with former Morsi supporters including Turkey, Qatar, and Iran to some degree.

text: The centuries-old tradition of church bell-ringing is under threat because of a shortage of new recruits. Attracting fresh faces to the ancient art of bell-ringing has become increasingly challenging, according to findings from a BBC local radio survey presented at a recent gathering of enthusiasts.The annual conference of the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers revealed troubling recruitment trends, with three-quarters of attendees reporting greater difficulty in drawing new members over the past decade. The struggle proves even more pronounced when targeting younger demographics - approximately eight in ten delegates acknowledged the challenge of recruiting anyone under 21.Despite these obstacles, some tower captains remain optimistic about their craft's appeal. Dickon Love, who leads the team at St James Garlickhythe in London, believes misconceptions plague the activity. Bell-ringing often gets lumped together with Morris dancing as something suited only for old men with beards, Love explained, though such stereotyping misses the mark entirely.Bell-ringing is exciting for the mind, Love emphasized. It's the best of form of heavy metal; it's a big loud noise, it keeps you fit, there's a competitive element as well. And it's a very social thing to do - after each practice without fail you can find us down the local pub.Love's tower has managed to buck the recruitment trend, successfully attracting newcomers to work with their new set of eight bells, which were installed four years ago. Their newly-recruited band includes diverse professionals, from a professor of astrophysics to the art director of a well-known magazine.At St Mary's Church in Walkley, Sheffield, tower captain Pete McCoy - who found love through bell-ringing when he met his wife Judith - attributes recruitment difficulties to modern distractions. Today's teenagers face far more entertainment options than previous generations, McCoy observed.There weren't so many things for a teenager or young person to do as there are today, he noted. And is it cool to ring bells? I think it is. But does everyone else?The recruitment challenges extend beyond generational preferences. Among the 180 delegates surveyed during May's Portsmouth conference, just over half identified declining church attendance as an additional barrier to finding new ringers. This factor affects recruitment efforts despite the UK's substantial community of nearly 40,000 active bell-ringers.Conference polling revealed the split in opinion: 54% Agree [that declining church attendance hampers recruitment] 43% DisagreeKate Flavell, representing the Central Council of Church Bell Ringers, advocates for enhanced promotional efforts across the organization's 66 affiliated societies. The council has partnered with the Heritage Open Days initiative to showcase their craft, organizing public demonstrations at 500 locations nationwide.Among these venues stands St Peter Mancroft in Norwich, a site of particular historical significance where the first full peal was performed in May 1715, marking a milestone in bell-ringing tradition.

text: David Cameron has visited a Lebanese refugee camp amid the crisis triggered by war in neighbouring Syria. The Minister of Sport Vitaly Mutko called the ban political and outside the bounds of the law, while Karpenko called it a black day for the Court of Arbitration for Sport. Dmitry Svishchev, the head of the Parliamentary Commission on Physical Education, called the CAS decision inhuman. And he added: “Whatever this court is called, it is an inhuman court. How can you prevent people who by their courage have earned the right to a decent life from enjoying it? To punish innocent athletes and to refuse them the right to defend themselves, as was the case with the Olympic team, is an obvious violation of human rights.” Russian para-champions were shocked and outraged. Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren's report to Wada showed that, between 2011 and 2015, the Russian Ministry of Sport manipulated the urine samples of para-athletes in eight sports, including five summer sports governed by the IPC, and the Sochi Paralympics of 2014. This is why the IPC announced the retesting of all the samples of the Russian team at the Paralympics. Yesterday evening everyone was in a good mood, everyone thought that everything was going to be all right, that our fellows were going to be sent off. Many of them had already received their equipment and now this decision has come, which is really very disappointing. You can punish the officials, the coaches, but not the athletes: you look at what they do, in spite of all the hardships and adversities, and you just want to congratulate them. This is an inhumane treatment. Eight-time world champion Oksana Savchenko said: “We are all shocked, of course, and we are all sad. And it may be for that reason they didn’t let us go. We are the leading team, we are the ones who produce great results, we win most of the medals, and we always bring glory to our country.” The four-time Olympic and world champion Karen Pickering, Britain’s four-time world champion, said she backed the IPC’s decision: “Congratulations to the IPC for taking this very strong stand — and it was absolutely right of Crash to support it. Such a way of treating people with disabilities is... there are no words. The lads still don’t know — they’re still in training.” ‘In the meantime, the paralympics go ahead, despite the difficult financial situation. I find it a pity that the IOC did not follow suit, because there is a real appetite amongst the athletes that they do not want to see former drug cheats at the Olympic games. This is a complete humiliation... simply, they’ve trampled us underfoot.’ * The Rio 2016 Organizing Committee faces significant budget cuts as a result of Brazil's economic difficulties and low ticket sales, which affects venues, staff and transport. I think that Russia shouldn't have been in Rio, and there are many athletes who could say that I should have been on the podium. At long last, the delayed travel grants are reaching the athletes. But ten countries may miss the deadline for the Rio closing date.

text: You would think securing promotion to the top flight of a national league would mean a lucrative bonus for any footballer. Despite achieving promotion to the Welsh Premier League, Cardiff Metropolitan University's football squad hasn't received any financial compensation for their success. The students, who claimed the Welsh League Division One title, must actually pay to participate in the sport they excel at.They actually have to pay us £150 subscription each season and that's what funds our football budget for the year, explained Dr Christian Edwards, the director of football and former Wales international.Edwards emphasized the academic priorities of his players: First and foremost they're at the university to study and they have to be good students in order to get their degrees and then it's their football life and their social life.The commitment required from these student-athletes is substantial. They really do sacrifice a lot and a lot of these players are in their fifth, sixth year with us, Edwards noted. Among the dedicated players is Charlie Corsby, currently pursuing a PhD, alongside several Masters students. These players are not only developing as football players but developing as academics, Edwards added.The university's football program has deep roots, dating back to 2000 when Cardiff Metropolitan University (formerly UWIC) merged with Inter Cardiff, one of the founding members of the League of Wales.Last season brought heartbreak when the students narrowly missed promotion, losing to Haverfordwest County on the campaign's final day. However, this setback became motivation for the current season's triumph, which they sealed with a decisive 3-0 victory at Taffs Well.Edwards revealed their season-long strategy: We sowed the seed in pre-season discussing about the one goal and we carried that throughout the season. The path wasn't easy, as Barry Town pushed us very hard, Goytre pushed us very hard. We're glad we came out on top, he told BBC Wales Sport.Achieving on-field success alone wouldn't have guaranteed Welsh Premier League promotion. The University made significant investments in infrastructure and facilities to obtain the necessary FAW domestic licence.Looking ahead to next season's challenges in Welsh football's elite division, Edwards maintains realistic optimism. His team has faced Welsh Premier League opponents in recent Welsh Cup matches, where in large parts of those games we've accounted ourselves very well.We don't think we're going to be ripping up any trees but we certainly think we can compete, Edwards stated. He views their achievement as part of an ongoing process: The journey that we started some six years ago is one that is progressive and we always believe we are arriving somewhere rather than arrived.Edwards, born in Caerphilly and a former Swansea City player, earned his sole Wales cap in 1996 against Switzerland, entering as a substitute for current national team manager Chris Coleman. His playing career included stints at Nottingham Forest and Bristol Rovers before he retired from professional football at 30.Following retirement, the former central defender spent four seasons with Welsh Premier League club Aberystwyth Town, where he also served as caretaker manager in 2009.Since 2010, Edwards has been part of Cardiff Metropolitan University's School of Sport teaching staff, balancing his lecturer and director of football duties while pursuing his own academic goals.It was a natural step when I retired in 2006 to go back to academia, Edwards reflected. His wife's practical assessment played a role: My wife said I could never retire and become somebody who did DIY. He added, I was never going to get a job like that so the next thing for me was to study. I always enjoyed studying even when I played.Edwards' academic inclinations showed early: When I was at Swansea as a youngster I did my A Levels and If I hadn't been fortunate to be a professional football player I think I would have been a PE teacher.This year brought double celebration for Edwards, as January saw him awarded a doctorate by the University alongside the team's promotion success.His academic journey exceeded initial expectations: The intention was a three-year degree and a PGCE and move on but the pathway allowed me to do a Masters degree and then I was fortunate to undertake a PhD. The opportunities kept expanding: Another door opened and a job came with it and it's been fantastic. I never set out to gain a Doctorate.Edwards' doctoral research connected directly to his football role: My thesis was based around the culture of the football club so I owe a lot to the football team, the players and the coaching staff in helping me gain my doctorate.

text: Generally speaking, England will be very happy to have won the Test series against Sri Lanka without really breaking sweat. Despite not completing their victory with the same lightning pace as the opening Test, England's commanding nine-wicket triumph in the second Test at Chester-le-Street remained thoroughly dominant, leaving Sri Lanka essentially out of contention throughout.While England coach Trevor Bayliss awarded their display an eight out of 10, I would rate it a seven. The team hasn't quite reached peak performance levels, and captain Alastair Cook himself acknowledged periods where they eased off the accelerator. Perhaps that assessment borders on nitpicking.Evaluating any side becomes challenging when facing subpar opposition, which Sri Lanka has largely provided throughout this series.However, one aspect stands crystal clear: James Anderson's bowling has reached absolutely brilliant heights. Against even world-class batsmen, he would generate identical movement and threat with the ball.Currently operating at his peak, Anderson's ascent to number one in the Test bowling rankings represents thoroughly earned recognition.Fast bowling remains such a capricious discipline, with rhythm serving as that elusive element - impossible to adequately describe or measure. Anderson lacked any rhythm during the South Africa tour, yet suddenly he's charging in with renewed joy, 'kissing' the pitch and claiming wickets in abundance.While superior batsmen might handle him more effectively, in these conditions with the ball swinging both directions, Anderson poses a formidable challenge to any batsman worldwide.The significance of his Lancashire appearances earlier this season cannot be overstated - 12 wickets at 20.75 across three matches proved invaluable.Regardless of experience or Test matches played, rhythm cannot be rediscovered through net sessions alone.Steven Finn presents a stark contrast. Having arguably been South Africa's series standout while Anderson struggled, Finn now appears to have lost his rhythm once again.His technique shows no obvious flaws - from personal playing experience, I understand how you can charge in with identical effort, believing you're releasing the ball with usual pace, yet it emerges without that crucial snap.My concern centers on his lack of opportunities to regain rhythm before the final Test at Lord's commences on 9 June - only one potential T20 Blast appearance for Middlesex remains available.Finn must feature at Lord's. Despite speculation about England examining Jake Ball, who has remained with the squad for both Tests, Ball can afford to wait. Finn's Lord's familiarity might provide the perfect platform for rediscovering form.Even during winning periods, teams must continue evolving, and certain areas will concern England's management currently.Jonny Bairstow has excelled with the bat this summer, though his wicketkeeping remains developmental. Mistakes occur: dropped catches and missed stumpings happen.Wicketkeeping presents enormous challenges, and slow-motion replays can be merciless, prompting thoughts of 'how did he miss that?' Yet these moments unfold in absolute split-seconds.His position behind the stumps faces no immediate threat. Unfortunately, such errors can prove costly, and excessive mistakes would invite scrutiny of his keeping role.Nick Compton's form at number three poses another concern. While his 22 not out during England's 79-run chase in Durham's second innings brought relief, he hasn't accumulated substantial runs all summer - for either England or Middlesex.Lord's familiarity will fuel his desperation for success. The pitch should prove flatter than this summer's previous surfaces, offering more favorable batting conditions.Should England win the toss and bat first, he'll have an excellent opportunity to secure that position - his likely perspective on the situation.His England future doesn't necessarily depend on third Test performance - a substantial gap exists before the Pakistan series opener on 14 July, allowing potential run-scoring opportunities for Middlesex.However, failure to score will intensify scrutiny.Cook's position faces no such questioning. His achievement as the first Englishman reaching 10,000 Test runs represents incredible accomplishment.This milestone came through the most challenging route possible - opening the batting, largely bearing captaincy responsibilities, with constant uncertainty regarding his opening partner. These three factors would challenge most players immensely.He commands absolute admiration. Though not a stylist who draws crowds rushing to watch, that epitomizes Test cricket.Players like Cook are essential for blunting attacks and establishing innings foundations for teammates. He has fulfilled this role brilliantly and will continue doing so.Previously, his captaincy matched his batting's obduracy - undesirable qualities in a skipper. However, he has definitely become more expansive over the past year, with confidence growing enormously.Yet he retains the ability to compartmentalize everything while batting, focusing solely on his role with bat in hand - tremendous testament to his character.This focus has arguably defined Cook's Test batting career from the very beginning.I recall his arrival in Nagpur after that lengthy West Indies journey, just two days before his debut, where he scored 60 and a century.The immediate thought was 'this player's genuinely special' - his complete batting focus was evident. May that continue indefinitely.Jonathan Agnew was speaking to BBC Sport's James Gheerbrant.
dipper: Generally speaking, England will be very happy to have won the Test series against Sri Lanka without really breaking sweat. The England coach, Trevor Bayliss, gave their performance an eight out of 10, but I would give it a seven; the team has not quite reached peak performance and Captain Alastair Cook himself acknowledged that there were times when the team took its foot off the pedal. This may seem like nitpicking, but when you face such feeble opposition as Sri Lanka did in the series, it is hard to get a clear view of your opponents. One thing, however, that is crystal clear is that James Anderson's bowling has reached a fantastic level. In such conditions, the bowling is swinging in both directions and the ball is kissing the pitch. Against world-class batsmen, he will have equal success. Now operating at his peak, the emergence of James Anderson as the best of the fast bowlers is well deserved. In the last tour of South Africa, he lacked rhythm, but suddenly he was charging in with renewed joy and taking wickets in abundance. Whether you are inexperienced or have played many tests, rhythm cannot be found in a confined net. My concern is that Finn has only one opportunity to regain his rhythm before the final Test at Lord’s starts on 9 June – one more Twenty20 game for Middlesex. He must play at Lord’s. Even when a team is winning, it must always evolve, and the current England management will be concerned about certain areas. Jonny Bairstow has excelled with the bat this summer, but his wicketkeeping remains developmental. Mistakes happen: dropped catches, missed stumpings. Wicketkeeping presents immense challenges, and slow-motion replays can be brutal, leaving you thinking, “How did he miss that?” Despite speculation that England are evaluating the possibility of promoting Jake Ball, who has stayed in the squad for both tests, Ball can wait. Lord’s familiarity might be the perfect platform for him to find his feet. But those moments only last a split-second. Lord’s position behind the stumps is in no danger, although such mistakes can prove costly and invite scrutiny of his wicket-keeping role. There is also concern about the form of Compton at number three; his 22 not out during England’s 79-run second-innings chase at Durham was a welcome relief, but he has not made a substantial score this summer, either for England or for Middlesex. He commands absolute admiration. His position is unquestioned. His feat in becoming the first Englishman to score 10,000 Test runs is phenomenal. He did it in the most difficult circumstances – opening the batting, largely the captain and in constant doubt as to who his opening partner will be. Should England win the toss and bat first, he will have an excellent opportunity to strengthen his position – a situation from which he will almost certainly view it. His England future doesn’t depend on the third Test; there is a long gap before the Pakistan series starts on the 14th July, and he will have an opportunity to score runs for Middlesex. Earlier his captaincy matched his batting in obduracy—unskilled qualities in a captain—but he has become much more expansive in the past year and his self-confidence has grown enormously. Yet when he takes guard, he can still compartmentalize everything and focus on the task at hand, and that is a tribute to his character. Cook may not be a stylist who brings throngs of fans to the ground to watch him, but that is exactly the essence of Test cricket: players like him are essential to absorb attacks and lay the foundations of their side’s innings. Jonathan Agnew was talking to BBC Sport's James Gheerbrant. May it continue indefinitely.

text: Reading moved in to the second round of the EFL Cup thanks to Liam Kelly's well-taken brace against Gillingham. Reading secured a 2-0 victory over Gillingham, with 21-year-old Liam Kelly delivering both decisive strikes to break down stubborn visiting resistance.The deadlock remained intact until the 71st minute when Kelly unleashed a superb effort from the edge of the area, finding the top left corner with assistance from Pelle Clement. The young midfielder sealed the triumph late in the contest, hammering home from close quarters following excellent build-up play by former Swansea winger Modou Barrow.Gillingham's most promising opportunity fell to Tom Eaves, whose effort from the center of the box was expertly thwarted by Reading goalkeeper Anssi Jaakkola in what proved to be the visitors' clearest chance of the encounter.The match concluded Reading 2, Gillingham 0, with the second half producing all the decisive action.Late drama saw Stephen Quinn fire wide from the center of the box, while Josh Parker's long-range attempt sailed high and wide. Kelly's second goal came after Modou Barrow's assist, with the midfielder finding the bottom left corner from outside the area.Pelle Clement came close but missed narrowly from the right side of the box. Luke O'Neill required treatment for an injury, causing a brief delay. Conor Wilkinson fouled Sam Smith, who earned Reading a free kick in the attacking third.Gillingham made tactical changes, bringing Ben Chapman on for Jake Hessenthaler. Scott Wagstaff won another free kick in the attacking half following Omar Richards' challenge.Modou Barrow's left-footed attempt from distance sailed just over the crossbar. text: After months of secrecy, the sequel to the late Stieg Larsson's best-selling Millennium series has been published. These are external links and will open in a new windowDavid Lagercrantz's The Girl in the Spider's Web picks up where The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo left off, continuing the saga of punk super-hacker Lisbeth Salander. However, as Lagercrantz reveals, crafting this new chapter came with intense pressure to honor Larsson's legacy and harsh criticism from the original author's longtime partner.Just days before The Girl in the Spider's Web reached global bookstores, Swedish writer David Lagercrantz spoke with the BBC about his anticipation. There's been so much secrecy about this book, so I'm longing to see what people think, he said.Given that Stieg Larsson's Millennium Trilogy has already moved more than 80 million copies worldwide, Lagercrantz's pre-publication nerves are understandable.I've felt pressure from the start, he admits. I'm absolutely terrified. But I think the pressure actually made me a better writer. It would be a disgrace if I didn't live up to [Stieg Larsson's] books or at least try my best.Larsson never witnessed his novels become a publishing phenomenon. The author died of a heart attack in 2004 at age 50, before The Girl With Dragon Tattoo, The Girl Who Played with Fire and The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest achieved global success. However, France suspects the British duo of employing deceptive tactics.French officials believe Cameron and Osborne are exploiting this reasoning to secure unfair benefits for London's financial district while obtaining backdoor veto power over both eurozone and broader EU financial rules.With France's economy struggling and President François Hollande facing re-election battles, he cannot afford to appear as though he's enabling Britain's financial success while eurozone constraints limit his own options.Brussels sources revealed that French negotiators delayed publication of Cameron's draft reform proposals by several hours just two weeks ago, expressing anxiety over language concerning non-eurozone country protections. text: I have been working now for more than two decades and I've not seen a measles epidemic of this severity, says Doctor Raza Hasan, as he shows me around the measles isolation ward of the Lahore Children's Hospital. Babies and young children crowd the ward so densely that bed-sharing has become necessary. In one corner lies a motionless boy, his eyes rolled backward as flies traverse his face.Since the epidemic migrated from southern Pakistan to Lahore and additional Punjab province areas at year's beginning, this hospital alone has recorded at least 40 child fatalities.Dr Hasan carries the epidemic's emotional toll heavily, recounting incidents where grieving families have physically attacked hospital medical staff upon learning of their children's deaths.Though measles rarely proves fatal independently, it triggers life-threatening complications including meningitis and pneumonia—particularly dangerous in developing nations where malnutrition compromises children's immunity.Some of them are arriving very late at the hospital, says Dr Hasan.After developing complications at home, their parents don't take them to doctors, they don't get any treatment and so when they come here…. there is not much we can do.Some are in the final stage of life or already dead with meningitis or pneumonia, he goes on.However, this explanation remains incomplete. It fails to address the fundamental question: why are Pakistani children contracting measles at such alarming rates initially?The epidemic's rapid nationwide spread has generated thousands of cases and 239 fatalities between January and April 2013, according to Pakistan's national measles co-ordinator.One reason is the low vaccination coverage of the population, says Dr Tanvir Ahmed, the director-general of heath services for Punjab province.In the districts there are even pockets where there is no vaccination coverage. The average [coverage] for Punjab is 58%.Up narrow stairs from a Lahore street entrance, we reach Nasara and Mohammed Ashfaq's residence. Bare walls surround the family, and despite daytime temperatures exceeding 40C, no fans provide relief.Mohammed cradles two-year-old Yasmeen, whose body displays the characteristic measles rash alongside dangerously elevated temperatures. Days earlier, her nine-month-old brother Ehsan succumbed to measles complications at Lahore Children's hospital.Fear now prevents the family from seeking hospital treatment for Yasmeen, hoping instead for home recovery. Neither child received proper measles vaccination.I didn't get him vaccinated because I was on my own at home with so many children, says Nasara.And we had to go out to get the vaccinations, so it was difficult because they were small.Medical professionals acknowledge that while families must assume greater vaccination responsibility, official programmes have suffered from poor management, causing widespread missed opportunities.We have removed nine district managers on the basis of poor performance of the programmes, says Dr Tanvir Ahmed, head of health services in Punjab.And we have improved our monitoring and supervision.Recent weeks brought emergency measles vaccination campaigns reaching 2.6 million Lahore children. June plans include inoculating another 11 million children throughout Punjab's remaining areas.Health experts anticipate provincial epidemic control by mid-July, claiming adequate vaccine stockpiles exist for Punjab's needs.Sindh province presents a different challenge entirely. This southern region, where the outbreak originated, lacks similar vaccine availability. Mass vaccination programmes won't commence there until autumn.Consequently, Sindh—already recording the country's highest case numbers—may experience worsening conditions in upcoming months.

text: Labour remains committed to renewing the Trident nuclear weapons system, new shadow defence secretary Nia Griffith has said. Labour's new shadow defence secretary has declared the party will maintain its commitment to Trident renewal, despite acknowledging her own previous reservations about Britain's nuclear deterrent.Speaking to Forces TV, Ms Griffith admitted she once held serious doubts about the weapons system but emphasized that Labour policy remains unchanged and unlikely to shift. Her appointment followed Jeremy Corbyn's recent shadow cabinet reshuffle, which saw her replace Clive Lewis in the defence brief earlier this month.The leadership change came after Mr Lewis faced last-minute alterations to his conference speech on Trident. Sources suggested the leader's office prevented him from making an unequivocal commitment to renewing the UK's nuclear weapons programme.This tension reflects the broader divide within Labour over nuclear policy. While the party's official stance supports Trident renewal, leader Jeremy Corbyn—a veteran CND campaigner—seeks to reverse this position and has initiated a defence review to explore alternatives.Ms Griffith stressed that September's party conference delegates endorsed the weapons system, creating a commitment that we will stick to. She warned against indecision, stating Labour can't be shilly-shallying about on Trident while simultaneously advocating for international nuclear disarmament efforts.There is a very strong mood for this, both within the Labour Party and in the broader public, to really push forward on multilateral nuclear disarmament, she explained. We need a multilateral approach of bringing people together across the globe to try to make our world a safer place.The Trident replacement programme involves constructing four new submarines with current cost estimates reaching £31bn. This contentious issue previously fractured Labour when MPs voted on renewal in July—140 Labour members supported the programme, 47 opposed it, and others abstained.CND expressed frustration with Ms Griffith's position, with general secretary Kate Hudson criticizing the apparent sidelining of the debate. Labour hasn't debated Trident for 20 years but it insists on clinging to its old policy in spite of the fact that the majority of Labour members oppose Trident and the party leader has been elected twice with a strong anti-Trident position, Hudson stated.The organization urged party members to demand publication of the defence review alongside comprehensive democratic discussion at the next conference.Separately, Mr Corbyn expanded his frontbench team by appointing seven additional shadow ministers, bringing the total to 68 members.
