text: Brussels has been placed on its highest level of terror alert. A week following the devastating Paris attacks that claimed 130 lives, Belgium's capital finds itself under maximum security alert as Prime Minister Charles Michel warned of imminent threats.Several individuals with arms and explosives could launch an attack... perhaps even in several places, Michel declared, prompting unprecedented security measures across Brussels.The heightened alert has transformed the Belgian capital into what residents describe as a city under siege. Military personnel and police forces have established a visible presence throughout key areas, fundamentally altering daily life for Brussels' inhabitants.Kiran, a Brussels resident, observed the extensive security deployment firsthand. Army and police are on patrol in the Sainte Catherine area of Brussels, she reported. The city's primary commercial artery has been completely sealed off. Rue Neuve the main shopping street in Brussels is fully closed, Kiran noted, adding that major transportation routes now feature security checkpoints at regular intervals. On one main road running from north to south from the station I could see every 100m there were army trucks or police patrols. From my house earlier I could see a large police and army presence.Social media has become a platform for residents to express their anxieties about the current situation. @IdairaRobayna tweets what the feeling is like in Brussels, while @OphelinhaP tweets her concerns for the coming days.The security measures have particularly impacted young people's routines and activities. University student Marie-Emmanuelle André-Dumont described experiencing a day full of insecurities, with widespread cancellations affecting normal life.Everything has been cancelled, or almost. I feel like the city is in a state of war, André-Dumont explained. Her first encounter with the heightened security came during the early morning hours. I was actually out in the early hours on Saturday when I first saw lots of police and military vehicles on the streets suddenly.The ripple effects extend beyond entertainment and social activities. I planned to go to a concert and shopping which has now been cancelled. My little brother's soccer game has been cancelled too because there's no public transport, she continued. text: The number of people who think you must speak English to be considered truly British has increased over the past 10 years, a survey suggests. A comprehensive study tracking British social attitudes over three decades has revealed increasingly stringent views on what defines national identity, with language emerging as the paramount requirement for being considered truly British.NatCen Social Research's latest annual survey, encompassing 3,000 respondents, demonstrates that 95% now consider English proficiency essential to British identity - a significant jump from 86% recorded in 2003. This linguistic requirement has become the clearest marker of belonging in contemporary Britain.The research, spanning 31 years of social attitude monitoring, reveals what authors describe as a key finding: the threshold to being considered British has got higher over time. Multiple criteria for British identity have become more demanding, with 77% of respondents believing extended residence - living in Britain for most of one's life - is crucial, compared to 69% a decade earlier.Birth requirements have remained relatively stable, with 74% considering British birth important for national identity, down marginally from 76% in 2003. Meanwhile, respect for institutions and laws has gained importance, with 85% viewing this as essential compared to 82% previously.Immigration attitudes reflect this hardening stance. The survey found 77% favor reducing immigration a lot or a little - a proportion that has remained largely unchanged since 2008 despite being sharply up on 1995. Authors note this anti-immigration sentiment represents a well established and stable British viewpoint.Perceptions of immigrant motivations reveal mixed understanding. While half of respondents believe work drives immigration to Britain, nearly a quarter (24%) attribute it primarily to benefit-seeking. Additionally, 43% now associate immigration with increased crime rates, rising from 37% in 2003.Regarding EU migrants specifically, 61% support requiring three-year waiting periods before benefit eligibility. This preference contrasts sharply with current regulations implemented this year, which mandate EU migrants demonstrate weekly earnings of at least £149 for three months before accessing various benefits. Researchers identify this as a considerable gap between public opinion and reality.Geographic divisions mirror recent electoral patterns, particularly UKIP's varied performance across regions. London residents show markedly different attitudes, with 54% viewing immigration as economically beneficial, while this figure plummets to just 28% elsewhere in Britain. This metropolitan-provincial split reflects broader political divisions on European Union membership and immigration policy.Penny Young, NatCen Social Research's chief executive, highlighted the paradoxical nature of these findings: In an increasingly diverse, multi-cultural country, we might expect people to be more relaxed about what it means to be British, yet the trend is going in the opposite direction.Young emphasized the linguistic imperative: It is now harder to be considered British than in the past and one message comes through loud and clear; if you want to be British, you must speak English. She also noted public demands for tougher rules on benefits and many are unaware of the policies that are in place to control immigration.Current benefit regulations vary significantly depending on specific entitlements sought. Recent government restrictions include January's new rule requiring migrant jobseekers to remain in the UK for three months before claiming Jobseeker's Allowance.The survey data collection occurred between June and November 2013, preceding public revelation of the so-called Trojan Horse controversy involving alleged Islamist attempts to control Birmingham schools. Education Secretary Michael Gove subsequently responded by mandating schools promote British values.These findings illuminate Britain's evolving national identity amid increasing diversity, revealing growing emphasis on cultural assimilation rather than relaxed multicultural acceptance.

text: Chris Evans and Nick Grimshaw both lost listeners over the last three months, according to the latest industry figures from Rajar. BBC Radio 2's breakfast show, hosted by Evans, experienced a significant decline of 414,000 listeners during the latest quarter, bringing its audience down to 9.06 million. text: It sounds like the screenplay from a heist movie. The scene unfolds like something from a heist movie: criminals infiltrate a diamond-filled vault, methodically selecting treasures from hundreds of safe deposit boxes while the outside world remains oblivious to the unfolding theft.London's famed Hatton Garden jewellery quarter—a collection of modest shops and traders—has spawned countless mysterious tales over the years. Stories circulate about hidden underground tunnels connecting gold repositories and ultra-secure workshops where artisans painstakingly create precious pieces by hand.However, verifying these legends proves challenging given the insular nature of the family-run businesses that dominate this secretive network, rarely welcoming outsiders into their world.The district's diamond-trading prominence emerged in the late 1800s when De Beers established London as their distribution hub for South African gemstones. Today, Hatton Garden spans several Holborn streets centered around its namesake thoroughfare. Within this compact tenth-of-a-square-mile territory operate 300 establishments—dealers, suppliers, and craftspeople all concentrated in remarkable density.Joanna Hardy, who spent over two decades working as an independent jewellery expert in Hatton Garden, hesitates to validate the area's myths and speculation, explaining this reluctance stems from industry fundamentals.It's not so much a secret, it's that this is a trade that is built on trust, she explains.The community's closed nature, Hardy emphasizes, results from the extraordinary value of merchandise rather than deliberate secrecy. People think that it's all about top secret stuff but it's because of the high value of the goods that make it a very closed community. text: The gang behind a Halloween ride-out in Leeds which was likened to scenes from the film Mad Max has been jailed. A massive motorcycle gathering that brought chaos to Leeds city centre on Halloween has resulted in prison sentences for 13 individuals, with the ringleader receiving two years behind bars.David Armitage, 26, from Brookfield Road in Headingley, orchestrated the disruptive event through social media platforms despite not participating in the actual ride. Judge Geoffrey Marson QC emphasized the severity of the situation while sentencing Armitage to two years imprisonment.This is a case which calls for a deterrent sentence, Judge Marson declared. Behaviour of this sort, having serious effects on this city, cannot be tolerated.Video evidence captured Armitage instructing participants to shut down the city centre, despite his absence from the actual ride. His co-defendants, who had previously pleaded guilty to causing a public nuisance, received sentences ranging from 12 to 18 months.Ch Supt Paul Money condemned the reckless behavior, stating: The behaviour of these individuals and others that night put people's safety at risk, caused unnecessary fear to the public and created an image of lawlessness in the heart of the city that we simply could not allow to go unchallenged.The incident's aftermath saw Leeds City Council implement protective measures through a legal injunction. text: Governor Scott Walker's campaign for president is premised on more than just his conservative achievements in Wisconsin, of which there are many. Conservative audiences nationwide have embraced a candidate who relentlessly trumpets his political victories and the adversaries he's vanquished along the way. His boastful rhetoric resonates powerfully with Republican voters who admire his combative style.Wisconsin's Democratic establishment has spent half a decade battling their governor across every political battleground in a state historically known for progressive governance. Today, many Democrats question whether their fierce opposition inadvertently propelled his presidential ambitions. Did they create the very political monster now threatening national office?I regard Walker as one of the most destructive forces in American politics today, says Dave Obey, a retired Democratic congressman from Wisconsin. However, Mr Walker's ascent, he argues, would not have been possible without the misguided recall efforts that took place in the state.The 2012 recall campaign sought to oust Mr Walker mid-term through a special election. This effort emerged after massive demonstrations in Madison, where over 100,000 protesters flooded the state capital for months, desperately trying to prevent legislation that would gut public employee unions' collective bargaining rights, particularly affecting teachers.Mr Obey acknowledges the unions' motivation: I don't blame the unions for thinking that they ought to vote for the recall because he literally was putting them out of business economically as well as politically. Yet he cautions, But sometimes it is helpful if you don't think with your spleen.These failed recall attempts transformed Mr Walker into a conservative folk hero, according to Mr Obey. The efforts established his national fundraising apparatus and provided him with distinctive campaign ammunition in a crowded Republican presidential field. Remarkably, including his 2014 re-election victory, he's triumphed in three contests within five years—all in a state that hasn't supported a Republican presidential candidate for over three decades.A Wisconsin Democratic insider, requesting anonymity, offered harsher criticism of the recall strategy. It was something you just couldn't politically be against, because the activists were so pissed off, he explains. I just wanted this to go the [expletive] away. I was praying they wouldn't get the signatures, but I couldn't stand up in public and say that.The protests, despite noble intentions, were doomed given Republican legislative control, he argues. The recall election proved disastrous because Wisconsin voters questioned its legitimacy. At its core was a sort of purity and innocence and stuff that would almost make you believe in American democracy - but it was just so tragically flawed, he reflects. It was not going to work, it was just a children's crusade.Mr Walker's Monday presidential announcement repeatedly highlighted his political warfare credentials. Speakers referenced out-of-state agitators allegedly bused into Madison protests and death threats targeting Mr Walker's family.Wisconsin Lieutenant Governor Rebecca Kleefisch asked the roughly 300-person audience: Do you remember what it was like to see your governor persecuted for simply putting you back in charge? Like a David to Goliath, Governor Scott Walker had your back. According to Baxter's account, he was attempting to navigate through the police cordon to transport a friend suffering from a blood clot to medical care.Baxter testified that the officer he allegedly assaulted instructed him: Sit down, you're not getting through, OK. He contended that the constable's flak jacket became entangled with his wheelchair's gear stick, resulting in an unintentional forward movement of approximately one inch.However, a police inspector painted a different picture, describing Baxter as swearing and abusive during the confrontation. text: The group representing many of Scotland's councils has urged them to reject the Scottish government's funding settlement offer. Finance Secretary John Swinney's funding settlement faced overwhelming rejection from Scottish councils, with Convention of Scottish Local Authorities (Cosla) leaders voting 21 to 7 against what they branded an unacceptable package.The motion condemned the Scottish government's approach as wholly misguided and warned it threatens grievous injury to communities and citizens. Despite Swinney's assertion that this represents a deal worth taking, councils have until 9 February to formally respond to the settlement offer.A united front emerged among all non-SNP councils within Cosla, with several exploring potential legal challenges. Scotland's four remaining councils outside the Cosla framework also convened separately, investigating whether the proposed terms meet legal requirements.The contentious funding package maintains the council tax freeze implemented in 2007, threatening any councils that break it with loss of Scottish government funding. However, mounting budget pressures are pushing some councils to consider tax increases regardless of potential penalties.Negotiations between Swinney and council leaders have stretched on, with acceptance deadlines repeatedly extended. Following Edinburgh discussions, Cosla president David O'Neill declared the funding package totally unacceptable and an attack on our democratic mandate.The Scottish government is basically forcing individual councils into having to accept the deal, O'Neill stated. Sadly, I fully accept that individual councils, due to the horrendous sanctions they would face, will find that they have no other option but to give in to central direction on this occasion. In imposing the deal on individual councils, the most vulnerable in our communities will be left to pick up the pieces.While today's Cosla vote carries largely symbolic weight, it exposes deep council anger over the budget proposal. Of 28 councils, 21 supported the condemnation motion, with only SNP-controlled authorities dissenting. This division undermines local government's ability to present unified opposition.Genuine fury exists among councils, amplified by the politically-charged atmosphere preceding the Holyrood election. Initial fears about deeper cuts and savings than anticipated intensified when the deal's terms made council tax increases even more difficult to contemplate. Moray Council's proposed 18% council tax rise now faces obsolete calculations.SNP councils, while acknowledging funding challenges, view the offer as the best available option. The government maintains its manifesto pledge to freeze council tax throughout this parliamentary term, arguing the policy's popularity and family budget benefits. Officials also claim protection of councils from severe Westminster spending reductions.The four non-Cosla councils—including Glasgow and Aberdeen—are examining the offer's legality on specific grounds. Their pursuit of this avenue demonstrates both their profound concerns and the Scottish government's commanding position.Realistically, councils possess limited alternatives to accepting the government's funding proposal. This situation raises fundamental questions about council funding systems' long-term viability.A recent joint government-Cosla report detailed several council tax alternatives. Ongoing debates question whether councils should reduce government dependency and expand local revenue-raising capabilities. Political parties will likely present proposals before May's Holyrood election.Cosla's approved motion claimed the deal would slash council budgets by £350m, proving undeliverable without an unacceptable level of cuts to services and staffing. Trade union GMB Scotland warns 8,785 local authority positions face elimination due to budget cuts, planning a Scottish Parliament rally next week.Aberdeen City Council leader Jenny Laing, whose authority operates outside Cosla, declared the Scottish government-council relationship broken. And when we've carried out our civic duty to question the settlement on behalf of our residents, we've been held to ransom by the Scottish government's attempt to control decisions which should be made by democratically-elected representatives.The group is seeking legal advice on the matter, Laing confirmed.Scottish Labour and Liberal Democrats demanded Swinney re-think the proposed deal.Responding to both Cosla and SLGP votes, John Swinney maintained: This is a deal worth taking. text: Jane Haining was a quiet farmer's daughter from the south of Scotland who ended her life as a slave labourer in the most notorious extermination camp the world has ever known. Dr David Kaufman, director of the University of Edinburgh's centre for Modern Conflict studies, explains that Hungary's capital boasted a thriving middle-class Jewish community. The city earned the nickname 'Jewdapest' since Jewish professionals comprised 60% of doctors and half the lawyers.Despite the Church of Scotland mission school's overtly Christian character, Jewish families eagerly sought enrollment for their daughters. Rev Aaron Stevens, current minister at St Columba's Church of Scotland in Budapest, attributes this to the quality of the education the girls received and also with the way the girls were accepted.Jewish girls who came here were not seen as second class pupils. They were just as welcome, Rev Stevens explains.Jane assumed a maternal role for boarding students. Katalin Packard, a former pupil interviewed for the BBC Scotland documentary Jane Haining: The Scot who died in Auschwitz, remembered her as kind and welcoming and warm.For students, Jane represented the mission's core principles of fairness, tolerance and equality. Former pupil Dr Zsuzanna Pajzs recalls: We never felt we were not equal with each other or with the Christian pupils. We did not even notice who was Christian and who was Jewish.Hitler's 1933 election as German chancellor occurred less than twelve months after Jane's Budapest arrival, marking the beginning of Europe-wide persecution against Jews throughout the 1930s.The Hungarian political elite tended to gravitate towards Nazi Germany in the 1930s, Dr David Kaufman notes. The Hungarian Jewish population see themselves as different from the rest of the Jewish populations of Eastern Central Europe. They see themselves as successfully assimilated within Hungarian culture. But in social terms they are not really accepted because there is still a latent, casual anti-Semitism which pervades Hungarian society.Britain's 1939 war declaration following Nazi Poland's invasion coincided with Hungary's Nationalist government implementing anti-Semitic legislation to appease fascist sympathizers before aligning with Germany. Authorities began detaining long-term Budapest Jewish residents lacking citizenship.While Hungary's German alliance prevented invasion as Nazi territories expanded, the government continued protecting Hungarian Jewish lives despite stripping them of employment, social standing, civil rights and dignity. Former student Eve Haller, now a prominent American social activist, never forgot how the Scottish Mission school restored that lost respect.Growing Church of Scotland concerns for missionary safety prompted repeated letters urging Jane's return home. Her refusal came with this response: If these children needed me in days of sunshine, how much more do they need me in these days of darkness?Former pupil Annette Lantos reflects: She could not grasp the evil in which she was functioning. It was not part of her ability to understand what she was confronted with. She lived in a different world. A world that was civilised and reasonable and rational, where people did not kill each other for no reason.The situation deteriorated catastrophically when Hitler focused on Hungary and its Jewish population. Nazi troops marched into Budapest on a March 1944 Sunday afternoon.Jane reportedly wept while sewing yellow stars that branded her students as Jews. Her open sympathy placed her in mortal danger.A single incident triggered disaster. Within weeks of invasion, Jane reprimanded the cook's son-in-law for consuming food meant for students. His denunciation brought a Gestapo police car to the school the following morning.Arrested on espionage on behalf of England suspicions, she was initially held locally before transport to Poland's Auschwitz, where Jewish industrial slaughter reached its peak. Daily, approximately 12,000 Hungarian Jews were shipped to Auschwitz, most proceeding directly to gas chambers. Over one million people perished at Auschwitz.As a political prisoner, Jane entered labor camps where inmates endured screaming, beatings and dog attacks. She survived merely two months at age 47.Her death certificate lists cachexia following intestinal catarrh as the cause. text: Reports of child rape to police in England and Wales have risen by 37% over the last five years, figures show. Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary (HMIC) revealed alarming statistics showing child rape cases surged from 5,674 recorded incidents in 2009/10 to 7,775 in 2013/14. Meanwhile, adult rape cases experienced a dramatic 38% increase, climbing from 9,383 to 12,952 over the same period.The prosecution rates paint an even more troubling picture. Fewer than one-third of child rape cases result in suspects being charged or summonsed, while adult cases fare slightly worse with only about one-fifth leading to formal charges or summons.Regional disparities in recorded cases are stark. The Metropolitan Police topped adult rape statistics in 2013/14 with 3,056 cases per 100,000 people, contrasting sharply with Dyfed-Powys at the bottom with just 62. For child rape cases, North Wales recorded the highest rate at 144 per 100,000 people, while Hertfordshire registered the lowest at 73.When examining prosecution success rates, significant variations emerge across forces. Essex, Kent and Suffolk performed worst for child rape charges, with merely 21% of cases resulting in action. Conversely, Northumbria achieved the highest success rate at 47% of cases seeing charges or summons.Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper condemned the findings: These figures are extremely disturbing and a shocking indictment of the widening justice gap created by this government. Over the last four years, there has been a dire trend in recorded incidents of rape going up, but prosecutions and convictions going down. Rape and the sexual abuse of a child are some of the most abhorrent and heinous crimes. And victims deserve justice.Crime prevention minister Lynne Featherstone defended the government's record, noting increased rape sentencing lengths and rising prosecution numbers from 3,819 in 2009/10 to 3,891 in 2013/14. The coalition government is clear that every report of rape must be taken seriously, every victim must be treated with dignity and every investigation must be conducted thoroughly and professionally, she said. The increase in the number of rapes being reported to police is encouraging as it shows more victims are finding the courage to come forward.Paul Ford, secretary of the Police Federation National Detectives' Forum, highlighted resource constraints: Policing is under significant pressure through budget cuts and this is having an impact on the level of service that policing can provide to victims.Devon and Cornwall exemplifies the concerning trend, recording among the highest rates of both adult and child rape yet achieving poor prosecution outcomes. Only 15% of adult rape cases and 27% of child rape cases result in charges or summons. Police and Crime Commissioner Tony Hogg acknowledged that police performance on rape remains under regular review.Fee Scott of Devon Rape Crisis emphasized systemic issues affecting victims: We will get a lot better outcomes if we believed people and we don't judge them on what they were wearing, doing, saying or drinking. All of that stops women coming forward because they are fearful of the reaction they will get from the authorities. This report gives a very depressing picture of what the outcome might be.

text: Rock-bottom Aston Villa avoided defeat for a third successive Premier League match as they held neighbours West Brom in an uninspiring stalemate. Aston Villa's struggles in front of goal continued as they were held to another draw, this time managing a goalless stalemate against West Bromwich Albion at The Hawthorns.The visitors should have been handed a spot-kick during the opening period after Jordan Ayew went down under challenge from Albion's Jonas Olsson. However, referee decisions went against Remi Garde's side once more.While Villa dominated possession with over 60% of the ball and registered 15 attempts on goal, their familiar lack of clinical finishing proved costly. Ashley Westwood's low drive represented their most threatening moment, though home goalkeeper Ben Foster was seldom tested throughout the encounter.For the hosts, attacking opportunities proved even more scarce. Tony Pulis' men failed to register a single effort on target across the full 90 minutes - mirroring their disappointing display at Southampton the previous weekend. Craig Dawson's header sailed over the crossbar, while Stephane Sessegnon dragged an effort wide after the interval, but genuine scoring chances remained at a premium.The Midlanders entered this fixture having been dismissed as certain relegation candidates by numerous observers. Their position at the foot of the table appeared hopeless following a catastrophic opening half to their Premier League campaign, accumulating merely eight points from their initial 20 fixtures.Recent weeks, however, have provided Villa supporters with fragments of optimism. Their breakthrough victory over Crystal Palace at home - ending a drought stretching back to opening day - preceded consecutive stalemates at Leicester City and now Albion. Despite this modest improvement, a nine-point gap to safety with 15 matches remaining leaves their survival hopes hanging by a thread.Villa's goalscoring woes have defined their season, with just 18 strikes across all competitions making them the division's most toothless attack. This chronic shortage of cutting edge again undermined their efforts despite controlling large periods of the match.Albion arrived seeking to complete a Premier League double over their neighbors for the first time in 51 years, having secured a 1-0 triumph at Villa Park in September. England Under-21 forward Saido Berahino provided the decisive moment that afternoon, though his influence has diminished considerably amid ongoing speculation regarding his Albion future.Pulis introduced Berahino with approximately 30 minutes remaining, hoping to inject attacking urgency into his side's performance. The striker, however, joined his teammates in failing to seriously test Villa goalkeeper Mark Bunn throughout a forgettable encounter.The stalemate moved Pulis' 13th-placed team seven points clear of the relegation zone, providing valuable breathing space in their quest for top-flight survival.Aston Villa manager Remi Garde reflected: I'm a little bit disappointed because we wanted three points. In another situation we might be happy with a point but we need more points than that. We tried, we did our best, especially in the second half, but they defended well.If you see the team playing now, we look more like a team now than we used to. Players have the right attitude, but sometimes we miss talent or quality to score goals.Should Jordan Ayew have been awarded a first-half penalty? Maybe.I talked with the referee and he told me he didn't see it like that. Even without a penalty we created many chances and with more accuracy could have scored.West Bromwich Albion manager Tony Pulis commented: We had to grind it out, it was a typical derby game, very ferocious, with effort and commitment. We've had eight games in four weeks and although people might be disappointed, the effort and commitment put in was first class.We need every point to maintain our Premier League status - and that's what we've done.I don't think Villa should have been given a penalty. Jonas Olsson might have touched him, but the ball is rolling out and the lad's gone down too easily.Both sides will now turn their attention away from Premier League matters. FA Cup duties await next weekend, with Albion welcoming League One opponents Peterborough to The Hawthorns while Villa face the daunting prospect of hosting Manchester City at Villa Park.

text: The chief executive of tech support firm Zendesk has become the latest high-profile figure to have his Twitter account hacked. text: Nine landless farmers in Paraguay have been charged with murder after six police officers died during clashes in eastern Canindeyu province. text: England need to work on how they play spin bowling after their tour of India ended in a crushing Twenty20 defeat, says head coach Trevor Bayliss. We're certainly not world-class players of spin, admitted Bayliss. We're playing against players that are very good players of spin, and they've got very good spinners themselves. text: Nigeria's central bank governor Lamido Sanusi has been suspended by the president for financial recklessness and misconduct. Nigeria's President Goodluck Jonathan has suspended Central Bank Governor Lamido Sanusi, a move that has sent shockwaves through financial markets and raised questions about the government's commitment to fighting corruption.The suspension comes after Mr Sanusi made explosive allegations that $20bn (£12bn) in oil revenue had vanished from government coffers. Nigeria's state oil firm has vehemently denied the accusations, dismissing them as unsubstantiated.Foreign exchange, bond and money markets have ceased trading due to uncertainty triggered by the suspension, according to Reuters news agency reports.Mr Sanusi, who has earned widespread respect for banking sector reforms implemented since his 2009 appointment, was honored as central bank governor of the year for 2010 by Banker magazine. He has vowed to challenge his suspension to protect the central bank's independence.The timing proves particularly sensitive, with elections approaching and President Jonathan's governing party fractured over whether he should seek re-election. Earlier this month, Mr Sanusi testified before a senate committee that of $67bn in oil sales between January 2012 and July 2013, $20bn remained unaccounted for.The reality is anyone who challenges the oil sector is striking at the heart of the vested interests that control the Nigerian state and one should be ready for the consequences, Mr Sanusi told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.By Will Ross BBC News, LagosDescribing Lamido Sanusi as merely a fly in the ointment for President Goodluck Jonathan would vastly understate the situation.His explosive claims threaten to uncover high-level fraud within Nigeria's infamously opaque and corrupt oil industry. According to his calculations, over $1bn went missing monthly during a 19-month period.The scandal emerges as elections approach and senior presidential officials face increasingly uncomfortable inquiries.Critics question Mr Sanusi's political motivations, suggesting he may be exploiting his position to damage President Jonathan's 2015 electoral prospects. However, many Nigerians will likely perceive that the president chose to silence the whistleblower instead of addressing the alleged fraud.Anti-corruption efforts in Nigeria historically achieve little success. In 2007, Nuhu Ribadu faced suspension as head of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission. Nigerian pidgin speakers capture the challenge perfectly: To fight corruption. No be easy job o.The Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation responded to the allegations by claiming they demonstrated little understanding of the technicalities of the oil industry.Currently attending a high-level meeting in Niger, Mr Sanusi has departed the gathering. His deputy, Sarah Alade, who accompanies him, will assume interim responsibilities until a replacement governor receives appointment.Sources informed the BBC Hausa service that President Jonathan requested Mr Sanusi's resignation in December, but the governor refused. Constitutional limitations prevent the president from directly dismissing the central bank governor—only the National Assembly possesses this authority.Although Mr Sanusi's term was scheduled to conclude in June, correspondents emphasize the suspension's immediate timing carries profound significance.The presidential statement announcing the suspension cited investigations into breaches of enabling laws, due process and mandate of the Central Bank of Nigeria. It characterized his tenure has been characterised by various acts of financial recklessness and misconduct... [and] far-reaching irregularities.Nigeria ranks among the world's largest oil producers, making the allegations particularly damaging to the country's reputation and governance credibility.

In the bitter cold, they tried to find a way forward, they heard it was possible to go to Peterborough and change there for Leeds or Bradford, but the promised train never came. “At that point I was very tired and cold, and I decided to go back to Reading,” the passenger explained, and described the difficult return through the crowds of several hundred people gathered in Finsbury Park. “There were some who acted very unprofessionally and did not seem to know how to deal with the situation,” the passenger added. The day’s disorder completely prevented visits that had been long-awaited. "I am too tired and too worried to risk starting on a new journey tomorrow," said a defeated traveller, who was to have seen his friends at Bradford and Liverpool for the first time in a year. "I can't believe I've had to give up all the plans I had been so looking forward to."

text: An outspoken member of South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) party has been charged with ill-discipline for speaking out against President Jacob Zuma. Parliament and police have agreed to provide security protection for MP Makhosi Khoza following death threats she received for her vocal opposition to President Jacob Zuma.The 47-year-old legislator has become one of the most outspoken critics demanding Mr Zuma's resignation, recently declaring him a disgrace during a Nelson Mandela birthday ceremony on 18 July. At that event, she addressed civil society groups, unions and business leaders who are pushing for the president's removal in next month's no-confidence vote.Her persistent calls for Mr Zuma to step down have drawn severe backlash from her own party. The ANC announced last week that Ms Khoza had crossed the line and must face disciplinary action for her public criticism of the president. The party's KwaZulu-Natal branch, representing her home province, condemned her remarks as a blatant betrayal of the core values of the organization.The threats against Ms Khoza have escalated beyond political censure. Last week, she received a death threat warning she had only 21 days left to live. The menacing message specifically targeted her advocacy for a secret ballot when MPs vote on Mr Zuma next month. There is no indication that the president is connected to these threats.Ms Khoza has also emerged as a prominent voice against corruption within the ANC ranks. Mr Zuma himself has faced numerous corruption allegations throughout his tenure, though he denies all charges against him.The National Assembly is scheduled to vote on the motion of no-confidence against Mr Zuma on 8 August. While the constitutional court ruled in June that parliament has the authority to conduct a secret ballot, the speaker has not yet announced whether this option will be exercised. Mr Zuma has successfully weathered several previous no-confidence votes during his presidency.BBC correspondent Milton Nkosi, reporting from Johannesburg, views the decision to charge Ms Khoza with ill-discipline as emblematic of the ANC's self-destructive tendencies. Following devastating losses in last year's local government elections, the party pledged to self-correct, yet appears to be inflicting deeper wounds on itself ahead of the 2019 general election.The South African electorate is witnessing the ANC inflicting wounds on itself that might not heal in time for the next general election, Nkosi observed. He noted that Ms Khoza, a PhD holder, ranks among the most popular of the over 200 MPs in the National Assembly, making her punishment particularly counterproductive.Nkosi drew parallels to Nelson Mandela's warning about party impunity: If the ANC does to you what the apartheid government did to you, then you must do to the ANC what we did to the apartheid government. He characterized the 105-year-old party as resembling an unstoppable train rattling downhill at break-neck speed, suggesting that voters will likely hold these leaders accountable in two years' time.Mr Zuma is expected to step down as ANC president in December, with his successor positioned to lead the party into the 2019 elections.

text: A rugby fan was nearly six times over the drink-drive limit after downing a bottle of vodka in the NekNominate craze, a Cardiff inquest has heard. A 29-year-old man from Rumney fatally consumed three-quarters of a 75cl vodka bottle during a filmed social media drinking challenge, an inquest has heard.Stephen Brookes died from acute alcohol poisoning and cocaine use after accepting a NekNominate dare from friends on Facebook, with a coroner recording this as the official cause of death.The tragic incident unfolded in the early hours following Wales' Six Nations match against Ireland on Sunday 9 February. Mr Brookes had been drinking throughout the day while watching the rugby with friends.According to testimony from his cousin Jodie Cummings to South Wales Police, the fatal challenge occurred after midnight. Stephen had been watching a rugby match with friends at a house. He had taken a 75cl bottle of vodka, she explained.A few weeks ago he had been NekNominated. This is something where somebody nominates a friend to down something like a bottle or a pint.Ms Cummings witnessed the devastating moment: After midnight when I was in the bathroom, Stephen down the bottle of vodka. It was filmed and I saw it on a friend's phone. I saw him neck back the bottle of vodka. He just held the bottle in the air.Initially, the labourer appeared confident about the stunt, telling friends he would be OK before attempting it. Afterwards he was in good spirits and said, 'you know me'. He was dancing around. But 10 minutes later his balance had gone. He was slurring his words - it all happened so quickly, Ms Cummings recalled.The inquest revealed that around 01:30, friends were encouraging Mr Brookes to consume the vodka during the party near his home. Witness Shaun Chivers described how quickly events deteriorated.I saw Stephen had three quarters of the bottle left and I knew he was going to neck it, Mr Chivers testified, adding that he told his friend to stop messing around.The next thing he necked the bottle and it was gone in seconds. Soon after he was swaying all over the place.The vodka disappeared within seconds as Mr Brookes performed for the camera, according to Mr Chivers' account to police.Within minutes of completing the challenge, Mr Brookes collapsed and lost consciousness. Friends transported him home, but he was discovered dead shortly afterward.Post-mortem examination revealed catastrophic alcohol levels in his system. Mr Brookes had 458 millilitres of alcohol in his blood - nearly six times the legal drink-drive limit of 80. Additionally, toxicology results showed high cocaine levels, with evidence he had consumed between 10 and 20 lines of the drug.Pathologist Thomas Hockey confirmed that Mr Brookes was clearly well over the fatal alcohol range.The entire deadly sequence - from consuming the vodka to his death - occurred within approximately one hour, highlighting the rapid and devastating effects of extreme alcohol consumption combined with drug use.

text: After months of sotto voce claims that some businesses were simply too scared to put their head above the independence parapet, tonight comes the most significant move by anti-independence members of the UK business community ahead of the September vote. A coalition of 133 global businesses has published a letter declaring that the uncertainty surrounding a Yes vote represents bad for business conditions.Wednesday's Scotsman newspaper will feature the letter, which draws signatories from diverse sectors including banking, mining, engineering, food production, whisky manufacturing, technology, and various small-to-medium enterprises. While some signatories have previously expressed anti-independence views, many are voicing their concerns for the first time.Notable signatories include Douglas Flint, HSBC's chairman; BHP Billiton chief executive Andrew Mackenzie; and Sir John Grant, BG Group's executive vice president of policy and former UK government representative in Brussels. Additional support comes from Audrey Baxter, executive chairman of Baxters Food Group; Cairn Energy chief executive Simon Thomson; and Ian Curle, who leads Edrington, the company behind whisky brands The Macallan and The Famous Grouse.Weir Group chief executive Keith Cochrane orchestrated the letter, having previously warned of substantial risks should Scotland choose independence. According to organizers, no political organizations participated in compiling the signatory list. One source described the initiative as emerging from frustration over perceived incoherence in the business community's independence debate.The signatories represent approximately 50,000 Scottish jobs, spanning from major employers like Babcock shipbuilding to small engineering firms in Glasgow's east end.However, independence supporters can marshal their own impressive business backing. Former Royal Bank of Scotland chairman Sir George Mathewson argues Scotland's crucial financial services sector would thrive under independence.Being part of a smaller country doesn't hinder a financial services industry, Mathewson has stated. Switzerland boasts two of the world's Top 10 financial centres in Geneva and Zurich. Singapore, with just 5 million people, ranks 4th. Investment has become an increasingly global business where success depends more on people than borders.Sir Donald MacKay, economist and former Scottish Enterprise head, contends an independent Scotland would enjoy superior fiscal health compared to the current UK position. An independent Scotland should leverage that financial advantage to invest in re-engineering our economy toward industrial, manufacturing and tradeable services development, MacKay has argued.Jim McColl, among Scotland's wealthiest individuals and head of engineering investment firm Clyde Blowers Capital, has revealed such enthusiasm for independence that he would consider relocating from Monaco back to Scotland following a Yes vote.IAG chief executive Willie Walsh, whose company owns British Airways, also suggests independence could benefit Scotland.Additional names may emerge this week.While both debate sides acknowledge that voters must ultimately decide, this letter provides voters clearer insight into business concerns regarding potential independence.These concerns center on five critical areas: currency arrangements, an independent Scotland's European Union relationship, post-independence tax and regulatory changes, pensions, and export implications tied to EU membership questions.Much is at stake, the letter states. Our economic ties inside the United Kingdom are very close and support more than a million Scottish jobs. As job creators we have looked carefully at the arguments made by both sides of the debate. Our conclusion is that the business case for independence has not been made.Sources indicate this represents a one-off initiative rather than launching a sustained business campaign against independence. However, it precedes Thursday evening's CBI dinner in Glasgow, where CBI president and BT Group chairman Sir Mike Rake will likely present similar anti-independence arguments.Business for Scotland responded tonight with this statement: Business for Scotland has 2,500 members who run businesses in Scotland, employ people across the country in a range of industries, and all believe that Scottish independence is in the best interests of Scotland and Scottish business. It's a position reached after looking at the facts and figures and realising that, from a simple balance sheet point of view as well as other considerations, our best interests lie in becoming an independent country.Scottish voters will ultimately determine how much weight to assign either side in this debate.

text: A tipper truck which killed four people when its brakes failed had clocked up almost 450,000 miles (724,000km), the driver's trial has heard. A devastating crash in Bath during February 2015 claimed four lives: four-year-old Mitzi Steady, along with Robert Parker, 59, Philip Allen, 52, and Stephen Vaughan, 34.At Bristol Crown Court, prosecutors described the fatal truck as an accident waiting to happen. Three men now face serious charges in connection with the tragedy.Twenty-year-old driver Phillip Potter denies causing deaths through dangerous and careless driving. His employer Matthew Gordon faces 14 separate offences, while company mechanic Peter Wood contests four charges - all three have entered not guilty pleas.The court learned that on 9 February, Potter and Gordon were operating two trucks, each carrying 30-tonne loads from a Wiltshire quarry. Gordon's vehicle, traveling ahead of Potter's truck, came to a stop on Lansdown Lane in Weston village. When Potter's brakes failed, he attempted to swerve around Gordon's stationary truck to prevent a rear-end collision.The out-of-control vehicle struck multiple pedestrians, including young Mitzi and her grandmother Margaret Rogers. It also collided with a car carrying three men: Allen and Vaughan, both from Swansea, and Parker from Cwmbran in south Wales.Prosecutor Adam Vaitilingam QC told the court: (Mr Potter's) lorry continued to career down Lansdown Lane out of control. It caused absolute devastation. By the time it finally came to a stop, four people had suffered fatal injuries - a four-year-old girl who had been crossing the road with her grandmother and three men who had been travelling together in the same car.Vaitilingam characterized Potter as an inexperienced driver who had only been in the company for a matter of days.Gordon's business, Grittenham Haulage Limited, established in December 2013, operated as a shambles from start to finish without a transport manager during the crash period, according to the prosecution. The company failed to conduct mandatory brake efficiency testing on the vehicle.Wood, employed as the fleet's inspection mechanic, had conducted the truck's final safety assessment in January 2015 - mere weeks before the fatal incident - declaring it roadworthy.However, Vaitilingam argued: If Mr Wood did carry out a safety inspection that day it was wholly inadequate. On the date of the crash the lorry had serious and long standing defects with its braking system, meaning that it was and had been for some time in a dangerous condition. This sort of catastrophic brake failure doesn't just happen through bad luck.Potter, from Dauntsey, Wiltshire, additionally faces charges for causing serious injuries to Karla Brennan and Margaret Rogers - Mitzi's grandmother - through dangerous driving, bringing his total charges to 10.Gordon, 30, also from Dauntsey, contests all 14 charges. Wood, 55, of Brinkworth, Wiltshire, denies his four charges.The trial is ongoing.

text: Great Britain will have a team of 264 athletes competing at the Rio Paralympics in 19 sports. Never has the British team dropped below fifth place in the Paralympic medal standings. Their London 2012 performance yielded 120 medals - 34 of them gold - securing third position behind China and Russia. Expectations run high for surpassing that achievement in Brazil.Below are the athletes chosen by the British Paralympic Association across all sports.**ARCHERY** London medals: Two (one gold, one silver) Competition dates: 10-17 September Venue: SambodromoFormer gold medallists John Cavanagh and John Stubbs lead Great Britain's archery contingent for Rio. Cavanagh, competing in his fifth Games, claimed gold in Athens, while Stubbs secured victory on his debut in Beijing four years later.The newcomers include Jo Frith, a London 2012 Games Maker who transitioned from swimming to archery and has since captured European and world medals. Also debuting are 16-year-old Jess Stretton and Invictus Games veteran Mikey Hall.**ATHLETICS** London medals: 29 (11 gold, 7 silver, 11 bronze) Competition dates: 8-18 September Venue: Olympic StadiumAmong the 13 track and field athletes selected in the first round for Rio Paralympics are London 2012 gold medallists David Weir, Richard Whitehead, Aled Davies and Hannah Cockroft. Each athlete selected earned gold or silver at last year's IPC Athletics World Championships in Doha while maintaining strong 2016 form.The roster features Libby Clegg, who shattered the 200m world record at the Anniversary Games in her new T11 class, and Jonnie Peacock, defending his T44 100m title. Many debutants complete the squad.**BOCCIA** London medals: Two (one silver, one bronze) Competition dates: 10-16 September Venue: Carioca Arena 2David Smith, Stephen McGuire and Nigel Murray feature in the 10-member GB boccia team. text: California regulators have accepted an offer from farmers to reduce their water usage by 25% in an effort to combat the record four-year drought. Following threats from state officials to revoke their water rights, several hundred farmers have agreed to voluntary reductions in a unprecedented concession.While California has already mandated a 25% water usage cut for cities and towns, critics argue that state Governor Jerry Brown has failed to adequately address consumption by the farming industry's influential water rights holders.This agreement between California's Water Resources Control Board and farmers—who had previously resisted commitments to reduce usage—signals the deteriorating conditions of California's ongoing drought crisis.Thursday's US Drought Monitor report revealed that 94% of California faces severe drought conditions or worse. The farming sector consumes 80% of all water extracted from the state's land resources.Representing the first such agreement in over three decades, this deal encompasses farmers operating in the Sacramento and San Joaquin river delta region.Senior rights holders in this classification include not only farmers but also irrigation districts, hydropower utilities, and municipalities such as San Francisco.This year has already seen water restrictions imposed on thousands of junior water rights holders—those whose water claims extend back only to 1914. These restrictions primarily affect farmers receiving no federal irrigation deliveries.California's water rights system requires junior holders to cease drawing from rivers and streams, ensuring adequate flow remains for those holding older, more established claims.Thursday's meeting brought together approximately 350 farmers to explore strategies for avoiding more severe mandatory reductions to their water allocations.That doesn't necessarily mean they'll all participate in the voluntary 25% reduction, said Michael George, the state's water master for the delta. But he said he believed many would.Recent weeks have seen mounting criticism of the farming industry from residents forced to eliminate lawn sprinklers and limit shower times under threat of substantial penalties.The farmers now have until 1 June to submit detailed plans outlining their proposed reduction strategies under the new agreement.

text: Jacob Boehme remembers when he knew something was seriously wrong. In 1998, Boehme endured a persistent cold that had plagued him for months. During a healing ceremony, an Aboriginal elder positioned him between her legs and began singing. She wiped sweat from his armpits, spreading it across his head and neck. After the ritual, her verdict was stark: Ahh, you need to go to a Western doctor. Everything is red. I cannot help you.The subsequent HIV diagnosis arrived during antiretroviral treatment's early days. His doctor, delivering such news for the first time, became emotional. He was choked up and almost crying, Boehme recalls. I had to console him.At 43, Boehme has transformed his journey as a gay, indigenous, HIV-positive man into Blood on the Dance Floor, a solo performance that recently appeared at the Sydney Festival. The show examines blood's significance across heritage and health through storytelling and dance.The production features diverse elements: a comedic portrayal of a camp gay elder in drag, frank discussions about HIV stigma within gay dating culture, and striking visuals where Boehme moves against projected blood streams with bubbling red cells cascading across walls.Central to his mission is reshaping HIV-positive narratives. Anything shown in the media or entertainment, it's always been some kind of memorialisation of the Aids crisis back in the '80s. Everybody dies, he elaborates. That's not relevant to me and to many of the other men and women that I know living with HIV. There isn't an image of a healthy functioning person with employment and prospects - you don't see that portrayed anywhere.Equally crucial is expanding awareness of who contracts the virus. The University of New South Wales's Kirby Institute reports that indigenous men's HIV notification rates doubled over five years, rising from 6.2 per 100,000 to 12.4 per 100,000, while non-indigenous rates dropped 12%.Yet education campaigns predominantly target white men, Boehme observes. Tell me the last time you saw an HIV education campaign with someone from the Aboriginal, Asian or African identity on those posters? You just see gay white men in their underwear, he points out. It makes quite a lot of people feel completely dismissed and it's not just the gay male community - it's heterosexual males living with HIV, kids living with HIV too. It's never been a gay white man's disease.Melbourne-born to a non-indigenous mother and a father from South Australia's Narungga and Kaurna peoples, Boehme recognized his sexuality at age four. The incoming creative director of the Melbourne Indigenous Arts Festival has consistently enjoyed family support.However, others face different circumstances. Homosexuality stigma persists in certain Aboriginal communities, Boehme maintains. When you go into communities that are very much still holding up the values of the old mission days, that's when you get a problem, through those Christian and very Victorian ideas of sex, gender and sexuality, he says.The show's conception emerged during warehouse rehearsals, when Boehme became obsessed about my blood, about the cleanliness of my blood. After cutting his heel on an exposed nail, I sat back down and realised I left a trail of blood on the dance floor. And [my friend] went 'ah, there's your title'.Blood, it's a life force that connects us, it can be used to define us and can be used to discriminate, to separate, or to actually unite, Boehme says.While crafting the performance, he kept a small crystal decanter containing his own blood on his desk. Suddenly I was connected to my dad, then my grandmother, then a whole line of our ancestors that I never met and through that, those voices started to then speak through me. In that blood, in those codes, there are thousands of generations sitting in that little decanter.Blood links him to ancestry and illness alike, yet also liberates him. Regardless of what features or skin colour we have, really our blood is the thing that ties us together, he says.One particularly intense sequence addresses his friend's 1996 suicide following HIV diagnosis. During that period, there was still this spectre hanging around like it was a death sentence. text: On 15 November 37 police and crime commissioners will be elected in England, along with four in Wales. Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) will assume responsibility for overseeing their respective forces and ensuring accountability. These elected officials will possess the authority to appoint and remove chief constables while determining force budgets.The paid commissioners are designed to give local communities greater influence over crime prevention strategies in their neighborhoods. Candidate nominations for South Yorkshire have officially concluded.BBC News has examined each police force in preparation for the upcoming elections.South Yorkshire encompasses a diverse landscape combining urban areas with regions historically dominated by mining operations, steel production, and engineering industries.**By James Vincent, BBC Yorkshire Political Reporter**With police forces contracting and increasingly sharing resources, South Yorkshire's incoming police commissioner faces the critical challenge of maintaining public safety confidence. While crime statistics consistently show declining rates, the number of police officers continues to decrease.A council tax increase funding an additional hundred officers helps mitigate the loss of 400 personnel over recent years, though genuine concerns persist about South Yorkshire being systematically stripped of resources.Specialist units including divers, mounted police, and firearms teams may soon operate across Yorkshire on a shared basis. The challenge lies in preserving service quality while achieving necessary savings—a recurring theme throughout public sector operations.The force chose to maintain its police helicopter while joining the National Police Air Service, scheduled to begin serving South Yorkshire in April 2013. Though the helicopter's popularity remains unquestioned, the long-term financial sustainability of funding dual services may become an early decision for the newly elected commissioner.South Yorkshire Police officers patrol 600 square miles (1,554 sq km), encompassing populated centers like Sheffield alongside expansive rural areas.The force has prioritized improving public confidence and satisfaction while enhancing community safety measures.Senior leadership has identified combating serious organized crime, terrorism, and extremism as county-wide priorities.Chief Constable David Crompton currently leads the force, supported by a deputy, two assistant chief constables, a finance director, and an assistant chief officer overseeing human resources.South Yorkshire Police maintains close collaboration with the county's police authority and the Police Federation, representing rank-and-file officers.The force participates in the Regional Chief Constables' Group (RCCG) and Joint Police Authorities Committee (JPAC).These organizations collectively establish guiding principles for local policing delivery by individual forces serving Yorkshire and Humber communities.South Yorkshire Police Authority established a £251m budget for 2012/2013.This figure reflects a 3.95% increase in the police authority council tax precept. For average Band D properties, this represented a £5.22 annual increase.The budget enables the authority to postpone reducing 110 police officers in 2012/13 while funding 22 additional police and community support officers (PCSOs) for three years. The authority committed to offsetting other planned resource reductions in 2013 and 2014.Through the council tax precept increase, the county's police authority aimed to secure approximately £2m annually, balancing requirements for further policing cuts from 2013 onward.South Yorkshire Police reported that 2010/11 data revealed total crime decreased by 9%—burglaries fell 5%, criminal damage dropped 17%, vehicle crime declined 17%, and robbery incidents decreased 14%.

text: We arrive at the Ebola Treatment Centre in the forested town of Gueckedou in South East Guinea to a grim scene. Stone-faced men load yellow disinfectant cans into a pickup truck while a tiny bundle wrapped in white plastic sheeting awaits its final journey. We witness the heartbreaking ritual about to unfold.Minutes later, deep in the forest, a small hole has been prepared. This dark, lonely clearing will become the final resting place for Ebola's latest victim: four-month-old Faya, who contracted the virus from his mother after she died weeks earlier. His grave marks the 20th anonymous burial in this somber location.I had been feeding him milk, recalls Adele Millimouno, a Medicines Sans Frontieres (MSF) nurse from a nearby village. I was there with him just before he died. I stepped away, just for a short break, but then I was called back and he was dead. I was totally devastated.Such scenes define daily reality on the front lines of the latest Ebola outbreak. Gueckedou reported the disease's first case in March, and medical charities now battling history's worst Ebola outbreak predict the crisis will persist until year's end at minimum.West Africa has recorded more than 670 Ebola deaths. Nigeria recently became the fourth nation confirming a fatality from the deadly virus. The situation across West Africa remains uncontrolled, according to Medicines Sans Frontieres and the International Federation of the Red Cross, organizations deploying nearly 400 international staff to combat the outbreak.MSF's Gueckedou treatment center had, until July 22, treated 152 Ebola patients—111 died. Yet survivors provide Adele with strength to continue this harrowing work.I muster the courage to come and work here to help save my community, she explains. I feel very proud of our work. We have been able to save around 40 people.The following morning, our convoy accompanies health officials to Kollobengou village, 12 kilometers away. Health workers faced attacks during their last visit and were ordered never to return.Lots of people died in front of me. It was a very difficult time for me especially when the young children died. Sometimes I went outside and cried, one worker recounted. Some people before they die, we hold their hands, we touch their heads, we sit by them for a little while.Community suspicion ran deep. Many believed medics brought the virus while harvesting organs from the dead. Others, despite acknowledging the virus's existence, remained too frightened to seek help.After negotiations with community leaders—and another overnight death—villagers finally agreed to permit medical access. Fear permeates the air as residents emerge from huts, gathering in the village center.The local health ministry official coordinating the anti-virus campaign urges residents to overcome fear, allowing health workers to conduct assessments and question potentially ill individuals. Teams distribute soap and chlorine, since proper hygiene easily eliminates the virus.One resident raises a practical concern: How can we wash all the time if we have no clean water to wash with?Two families eventually present severely ill relatives, who are immediately transported to the treatment center. While health workers knew of four village Ebola deaths, three additional fatalities emerge. Forty-eight others had close contact with victims and require daily monitoring throughout the three-week incubation period.Two Gueckedou villages still refuse health worker access—a significant improvement from months earlier when 28 villages resisted assistance, yet still concerning.Tarik Jasarevic from the World Health Organization attributes village resistance partly to unclear initial messaging about the virus.People heard there is no vaccine or treatment for Ebola so many thought 'why would we go to a treatment centre if there is no treatment?' he explains. Then people who did eventually go, some of them died. So there was a perception that if you are taken from your village it means a certain death. We didn't put enough emphasis on the fact there are survivors and the sooner you go to the treatment centre the better chance you have of surviving, and you are not risking the health of your family. Because those taking care of sick people are exposed the most.Dr. Abdurahman Batchili, Ebola outbreak coordinator for Gueckedou's health ministry and surrounding forest region, reports improvement with fewer daily patient registrations.The population is starting to be aware of the dangers of this outbreak. We hope with this momentum that in one or two months at the latest, we will end this outbreak, he states. However at our borders, there is a critical situation in countries such as Sierra Leone so we have to remain vigilant along our borders.During three days ending July 23, Sierra Leone recorded 71 new cases and Liberia 25, compared to Guinea's 12. Weekly, thousands cross the hundreds of kilometers of border Guinea shares with Sierra Leone and Liberia, yet only 13 Ebola screening posts monitor the entire length.Medical charities dismiss hopes for swift outbreak resolution as unrealistic.We are very sceptical that the outbreak will be done by the end of the year, says Antoine Gauge, MSF emergency response head in Guinea. Ebola has no limits between borders. People here are travelling, they have family in Sierra Leone and Liberia. For sure in Guinea, we are at a more advanced stage of the response, but we can't say there will be no cases here soon.At the treatment center during visiting hours, 13-year-old Alfonz—an Ebola survivor after receiving early treatment—comes to see his little sister, Marian. He watches through an orange plastic barrier, unable to touch her. Instead, a health worker in full biohazard gear holds her.Initial tests bring good news: Marian tested negative. However, Ebola proves cruel and indiscriminate. The children's mother remains critically ill and may not survive.As this crisis continues, many more tragic stories like hers will sadly unfold.Follow @tulipmazumdar on Twitter.

text: More black, Asian and ethnic minority lives will be saved under an opt-out organ donation system, a charity says. The Welsh government faces accusations of misleading the assembly regarding its organ donation legislation, as debate intensifies over a proposed opt-out system that could take effect by 2015.Professor John Fabre of King's College London, an expert in donor systems and author of multiple papers on international organ donation frameworks, challenged the government's interpretation of Spain's successful model. According to Prof Fabre, Spain's impressive donation rates stem from superior healthcare facilities and coordination within their health service system, rather than from legislative changes as the Welsh government has suggested.Under the proposed Human Transplantation Bill, Welsh adults would automatically become organ donors unless they actively choose to opt-out of the system. This represents a fundamental shift from the current approach, where individuals must deliberately opt-in to become donors.Roy Thomas, chairman of Kidney Wales Foundation (KWF), strongly supports the legislative change, presenting evidence to the assembly's health and social care committee. Thomas highlighted the urgent need within ethnic minority communities, noting that these populations face three times higher likelihood of requiring transplants compared to the general population. However, fewer than 2% of these community members have registered with the NHS Organ Donation Register.It is, however, key that the proposed legislation is implemented with the goodwill of the people of Wales, Thomas emphasized during his committee testimony. A transplant law provides only a legal environment which can influence the extent to which potential donors can be used. The law in proper practice will be essential.KWF points to Belgium's presumed consent system as evidence supporting the opt-out approach. In Belgium, merely 2% of citizens opted out of the system, which KWF describes as a great success that generated a 55% increase in donor rates during its initial five years of implementation.Thomas described legal reform as a key component in transforming organ donation practices, emphasizing his organization's long-standing advocacy efforts. We have been campaigning for the change in the law over many years and we have a determination to see the successful implementation of the law because of the clear effect it will have in changing the cultural approach in Wales and the UK on organ donation, he stated.Defending their position, a Welsh government spokesman referenced the Spanish government's own website, which points to the adoption of appropriate legislation as one element of the success of their model for organ donation.The controversy underscores broader questions about how policy makers interpret international best practices when crafting domestic legislation, particularly in the sensitive area of organ donation where cultural attitudes and medical infrastructure both play crucial roles.

text: Worcester chief executive Jim O'Toole says giving head coach Carl Hogg sole charge of the first team was necessary because players weren't getting the dual-management structure. Warriors have restructured their leadership following a disappointing start to the season, with Carl Hogg now taking sole charge after sharing management responsibilities with high performance director Nick Johnston since Dean Ryan's departure as director of rugby on 30 June.The decision comes after Warriors managed just two victories from 14 matches this campaign, including only one win and two draws in the Premiership. Currently sitting 11th in the table with a six-point cushion above bottom-placed Bristol - their Boxing Day opponents - the club has endured familiar struggles despite significant injury problems.Giving Carl sole leadership is now right for us, O'Toole explained to BBC Sport, outlining the reasoning behind abandoning their experimental dual-management approach.The initial power-sharing arrangement emerged from necessity following Ryan's summer exit. It all goes back to Dean Ryan's departure in the summer. When he left, aside from his considerable experience and rugby intellect, what we in effect lost at short notice just before the start of the season was his level of management, O'Toole said.Under Ryan's tenure, responsibilities were clearly divided - Hogg handled first-team duties as head coach while Johnston managed athlete preparation. The club's attempt to maintain this structure through shared leadership drew inspiration from southern hemisphere rugby models.We took a decision at the time to pioneer a duo-management system, which I've heard (England boss) Eddie Jones talk about as being how the southern hemisphere does it. He's a big advocate of that type of structure, O'Toole noted.However, a six-month review revealed fundamental problems with player understanding. After six months, we reviewed it. My view, shared with my fellow directors, was that the players weren't getting it, O'Toole admitted.The change maintains Johnston in his existing role while consolidating authority under Hogg. Nick continues in his role, but streamlining the management by giving Carl sole leadership is the right thing to do. Ultimately, the players have to be clear about what they're here to do.Warriors' current predicament has intensified supporter frustration, particularly given the club's history of relegation battles since joining the Premiership in 2004. Sunday's 26-12 home loss to Wasps further highlighted their struggles this season.O'Toole has responded proactively to fan criticism by organizing meetings with the club's most vocal detractors, viewing supporter engagement as central to his role. He recently arranged a session with 40 regular critics to address concerns directly.Modern communication channels are open to everybody, he observed, describing his extensive interaction with supporters across multiple platforms. I have daily communication with supporters on Twitter, on club forums, on e-mail, telephone and text messaging. I've even had messages sent to me on Facebook Messenger from people who I'm not friends with, who insist on getting their message across and like to tell me how things can be improved.Rather than avoiding difficult conversations, O'Toole embraces the challenge of managing passionate supporters. I didn't come to run a rugby club to hang around with the players. For me, it's about the excitement and passion of dealing with a large number of committed supporters and the environment that creates.His approach emphasizes respectful dialogue while acknowledging the emotional investment driving fan criticism. People like to give their opinions and I'm here to receive them. If people come to me and communicate politely, I take it all on board. It's the old point about 'the customer is king'.They're not always right and some people get a bit carried away but people aren't unpleasant just for the sake of it. You know it's only because they care, O'Toole concluded.

This is the strongest possible signal by both candidates of a desire to restore legitimacy to the process and to Afghan democracy, he declared, confirming that every single ballot would undergo scrutiny.The audit process will prioritize Kabul ballots initially, with the International Security and Assistance Force (Isaf) transporting remaining votes from provincial areas. text: The number of hours that ambulances spent waiting at A&Es in the North West of England has more than doubled in the past two years, the BBC has found. Emergency ambulance crews across the North West are spending dramatically more time waiting to hand over patients at hospital emergency departments, with delays soaring from 17,413 hours in 2013-14 to 46,160 hours in 2015-16 - all beyond the standard 15-minute handover window, according to Freedom of Information data.The crisis has hit nearly every trust in the region, with the Royal Liverpool Hospital experiencing a staggering six-fold increase in wait times. At Aintree Hospital in Merseyside, delays have surged by 234%, prompting scenes last week where 20 ambulance staff were photographed queuing to hand over patients following a spike in 999 calls.One paramedic at Aintree said they spent more than half of their shift standing in corridors, highlighting the severity of the situation affecting emergency response capabilities.Only Wythenshawe Hospital in Manchester bucked the trend, achieving a 9% reduction in handover delays during the same period.The implications extend far beyond hospital walls. When ambulance crews remain trapped in emergency departments, they cannot respond to other life-threatening emergencies across their communities. These figures represent additional hours spent waiting beyond the allocated 15-minute handover period - meaning the North West's total of 46,160 extra hours in the most recent financial year represents a massive jump from the previous figure of just under 17,500 hours.Several factors drive this alarming escalation. An aging population continues pushing A&E attendance figures steadily upward. However, hospital trusts increasingly point to critical gaps in social care provision, particularly affecting elderly patients, as a major contributing factor.One trust revealed they currently have the equivalent of three wards being occupied by people who should not be in hospital at all, simply because there was not anywhere satisfactory for them to go. This bed-blocking phenomenon directly reduces capacity for incoming A&E patients requiring admission.The problem extends beyond the North West, with handover delays across England, Wales and Northern Ireland showing a 52% increase over the past two years. Nationally, the investigation revealed that only one of the UK's 13 ambulance services currently meets its target for reaching seriously ill and injured patients.Delays stem partly from what experts describe as a social care crisis, where discharge delays for elderly patients create bottlenecks throughout the hospital system.Lisa Grant, chief nurse at the Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals, explained: Hospitals across the area are working together with partners in community and social care to help to safely discharge patients who no longer require hospital care, providing beds for those in the emergency department who need to be admitted to a ward.To address the handover crisis, the Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals' Trust has recently recruited hospital-trained paramedics for its emergency department, aiming to facilitate safe handover of patients and return ambulances to active service more quickly.North West Ambulance Service acknowledged the mounting pressure in their statement: We are seeing more and more people in need of our services, especially for Red incidents for patients with serious and life-threatening conditions. This contributes to additional activity at hospital emergency departments. During busy periods this can unfortunately result in ambulance crews having to wait longer to hand over patients into the care of hospital staff before they can be clear to respond to other emergencies.The data paints a stark picture of an emergency care system under unprecedented strain, where rising demand collides with capacity constraints and social care shortfalls, ultimately compromising response times for the most vulnerable patients.
