text: A chronology of key events: The formation of the County of Barcelona in the 9th century marked the beginning of Catalonia's distinct political identity. Charlemagne established this county alongside several others as part of his strategy to create a protective buffer between the Frankish Empire and Muslim-controlled Spain.Ramon Berenguer I's reign from 1023-76 saw Barcelona's county emerge as the dominant force in the region. The 12th century brought the first recorded use of the term Catalonia, establishing the area's unique identity.A pivotal moment arrived during Ramon Berenguer IV's rule (1131-1162), when his marriage to Queen Petronilla of Aragon created a dynastic union with the Kingdom of Aragon. Despite joining the Crown of Aragon, Catalonia maintained its traditional rights and parliament, the Corts catalanes.The 14th and 15th centuries witnessed Aragon's expansion into a major Mediterranean maritime empire through the acquisition of Sardinia, Sicily, and Naples. However, the 1469 marriage between Ferdinand I of Aragon and Queen Isabella of Castile established a dynastic union that would lay the groundwork for the Kingdom of Spain.Christopher Columbus's 1492 discovery of the Americas initiated Spain's overseas empire, shifting commercial focus from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic and diminishing Catalonia's economic and political significance.**Periods of Conflict and Suppression**The Reapers' War (1640-52) erupted when Catalonia revolted against Philip IV of Spain's taxation policies. The region briefly became a republic under French protection before Spanish troops reoccupied it.During the War of the Spanish Succession (1705-14), Catalonia's support for Archduke Charles of Austria against King Philip V from the House of Bourbon proved costly. Philip V's victory resulted in the suppression of Catalonia's parliament and traditional liberties.The 1716 Nueva Planta decree delivered a devastating blow, dismantling Catalonia's separate legal system, imposing direct rule from Madrid, and abolishing administrative use of the Catalan language.Napoleon's brief annexation of Catalonia to France (1812-13) ended when French troops withdrew from Barcelona following an armistice with the Duke of Wellington. The First Carlist War (1808-33) brought fierce fighting to Catalonia between liberal supporters of Queen Isabella II and absolutist supporters of her rival, the Infante Carlos.**Industrial Renaissance and Cultural Revival**The 19th century positioned Catalonia at the forefront of Spanish industrialization while experiencing a cultural renaissance. This period marked the beginning of a movement to revive Catalan culture and language, fostering the rise of Catalan nationalism.The Catalan nationalist Regionalist League formed in 1901, followed by the creation of the Commonwealth of Catalonia in 1913, which gave the four provinces limited joint self-government under Enric Prat de la Riba's leadership. However, Spanish Prime Minister Miguel Primo de Rivera's dictatorship suppressed the Commonwealth in 1925.**Republic, Civil War, and Franco Era**Spain's transformation into a republic in 1931 enabled the creation of an autonomous Catalan regional government, the Generalitat, under the Revolutionary Left of Catalonia's leadership.Gen Francisco Franco's 1936 insurrection sparked the Spanish Civil War, with Catalonia remaining loyal to the Republic through both the Generalitat's regular forces and popular militias. George Orwell published Homage to Catalonia in 1938, documenting his experience fighting with left-wing Republican forces in the region.Franco's forces overran Catalonia in 1938-9, paving the way for Republican resistance to collapse elsewhere in Spain. The subsequent Franco dictatorship (1939-75) brought severe suppression of political opposition, Catalan autonomy, language, and culture. Thousands of Catalan activists faced execution or exile.The legacy of Gen Franco's dictatorial rule still looms over relations between Catalonia and Madrid*Buried unpleasant truths?*The 1960s brought benefits to Catalonia through mass coastal tourism and increased industrialization, with Barcelona attracting numerous migrants from other Spanish regions.**Democratic Transition and Autonomy**Franco's death in 1975 initiated democratization under new king Juan Carlos. The restoration of a provisional regional government, again called the Generalitat, occurred in 1977 under Josep Tarradellas's leadership.The 1978 democratic Spanish Constitution recognized distinct national communities within Spain, beginning the regionalization process. Catalonia received an autonomy statute in 1979, gaining recognition as a nationality with Catalan becoming the joint official language alongside Spanish.Centre-right moderate nationalist Convergence and Union won the first elections to the new regional parliament in 1980, with leader Jordi Pujol becoming the first president of the new regional government.Barcelona hosted the Summer Olympic Games in July-August 1992, showcasing the region internationally.**Modern Political Developments**After 23 years in office, Jordi Pujol retired as regional president in 2003. Despite winning the largest number of seats in November 2003 regional elections, Convergence and Union lost power for the first time in 23 years to a coalition of Socialists, Revolutionary Left, and Greens, with Socialist Pasqual Maragall becoming regional president.Jose Montilla replaced Pasqual Maragall as fellow Socialist president in June 2006. A reformed autonomy statute came into force in August 2006, granting greater powers and financial autonomy to the regional government, with its preamble describing Catalonia as a nation.Between December 2009 and April 2011, Catalan nationalists conducted informal, non-binding independence votes in regional towns and cities, including Barcelona.**Constitutional Challenges and Independence Movement**July 2010 brought a significant setback when Madrid's Constitutional Court struck down part of the 2006 autonomy statute, ruling no legal basis existed for recognizing Catalonia as a nation within Spain and that Catalan should not take precedence over Castilian. The regional government criticized this decision.The regional parliament also voted to ban bullfighting in 2010, making Catalonia mainland Spain's first region to do so, with the ban taking effect in September 2011.Convergence and Union, led by Artur Mas, returned to power following November 2010 regional elections.**Financial Crisis and Pro-Independence Moves**Catalonia requested a 5bn-euro bailout from the Spanish government in August 2012. September 2012 saw approximately 1.5 million people participate in Catalonia's annual independence rally in Barcelona, reflecting growing anger at financial transfers from the region to the rest of Spain.Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy rebuffed regional leader Artur Mas's call for greater fiscal independence. November 2012 snap elections, held to support an independence referendum, saw Convergence and Union lose ground to the left-wing Republican Left (ERC) party, though both supported independence while ERC opposed the Catalan government's spending cuts.Artur Mas secured re-election in December 2012 after Convergence and Union signed a governing pact with the left-wing ERC, with both parties supporting a 2014 secession referendum.Catalonia's regional parliament approved a declaration of sovereignty in January 2013, aimed at paving the way for a 2014 independence referendum.Spain's constitutional court ruled the planned November referendum unconstitutional in March 2014, with the Spanish parliament rejecting Catalonia's regional assembly proposal for an independence referendum in April 2014.Regional President Artur Mas signed a decree in September 2014 calling for a non-binding November independence referendum, but Spain's constitutional court suspended the plans pending constitutionality review.Despite legal challenges, Artur Mas insisted in October 2014 that a non-binding independence referendum would proceed under a different legal framework after the original plan was ruled unconstitutional.More than 80% of participants in the November 2014 non-binding informal vote on separation from Spain chose independence, with about two million out of 5.4 million eligible voters casting ballots.Regional President Artur Mas called new regional elections for 27 September in January 2015 to gauge support for a possible independence declaration.

In the wake of General Franco’s death, under the reign of the new King Juan Carlos, the Provisional Generalitat was restored in 1977, and in 1979 a statute of autonomy was granted to Catalonia, which was recognised as a nationality, and Catalan became a co-official language. Under the leadership of Josep Tarradellas, the Provisional Generalitat was restored in 1977. At the first elections of the Generalitat, in October of that year, Convergencia i Unió, led by Jordi Pujol, obtained a majority of the seats, and Jordi Pujol was elected the first president of the Generalitat. José Montilla, also a socialist, took his place as president in June of that year, and in August the new Statute of Autonomy came into force, with a greater fiscal and more power of the regional government, and in the preamble the declaration of Catalonia as a nation. text: More than 150 people in Wales have been reported to police for meeting children following sexual grooming over the last five years, new figures show. Online safety is a 21st century child-protection challenge and it is something that we need to tackle head on.The Welsh Government responded by highlighting its current extensive e-safety education programme, which encompasses online resources and classroom materials designed to help pupils think critically, behave safely, and participate responsibly online.We have also created an online one-stop shop, Hwb, providing help for children and young people to stay safe on the web, a government spokesman explained.Police forces across Wales have already established educational partnerships with schools. text: A US appeals court has overturned the money laundering conviction of a once-powerful former Republican congressman, citing insufficient evidence. The money allegedly flowed from DeLay's controlled campaign committee to the Republican National Committee, which then redistributed the funds to seven Texas legislative candidates.The strategy proved politically successful—six candidates secured victories, delivering Republican control of the Texas House of Representatives. This triumph enabled a redistricting effort that sent additional Republicans to Congress in 2004, further cementing DeLay's political dominance.First elected to Congress in 1984, the former pest control businessman ascended to majority leader in 2003. His nickname reflected his reputation for maintaining strict party discipline during crucial votes, keeping the Republican caucus unified through his formidable political skills.DeLay consistently maintained his innocence, arguing the financial arrangements were legal and insisting no corporate money directly reached state candidates. He characterized the prosecution as a politically motivated attack against him.Following his indictment on money laundering and conspiracy charges, DeLay resigned from Congress in June 2006. A Texas jury found him guilty in November 2010, resulting in a three-year prison sentence the following January. However, he remained free during the appeals process.Thursday's appellate decision focused on the prosecution's inability to prove the candidates received tainted funds, according to the court's ruling.DeLay's attorney, Brian Wice, described his client's emotional response to the Associated Press: He's ecstatic. He's gratified. He's just a little bit numb. Wice expressed optimism about DeLay's future, stating, I'm hoping with today's victory, he will be able to resume his life as he once knew it.

text: A Taser gun was used three times in less than 30 seconds as police tried to apprehend a man who had killed a woman, an inquest has heard. On November 6, 2014, at the Sirhowy Arms Hotel in Argoed, police discovered Matthew Williams, 34, attacking 22-year-old Cerys Yemm. Following his arrest via Taser deployment, Williams subsequently died, prompting an inquest at Gwent Coroner's Court in Newport.The court learned that Miss Yemm's body bore bite marks alongside cuts potentially inflicted by fragments of a shattered ceramic cereal bowl.South Wales Police armourer Michael Rees testified about examining all Tasers carried by officers during Williams' arrest. His investigation revealed only one device had been deployed, bearing partial blood traces and activated on four separate occasions throughout the incident. The timestamps showed usage at 01:37:11, followed by three additional deployments at 01:44:14, 01:44:28, and 01:44:41.Scene examination by forensic scientist Gillian O'Boyle uncovered 15 ceramic fragments that reconstructed into nearly a complete cereal bowl. Blood evidence on most pieces contained DNA from both Miss Yemm and Williams. O'Boyle concluded: The pattern of the blood was as if the bowl had been used to hit an individual and had broken as part of this, though she couldn't determine who wielded it.Additionally, Miss Yemm's clothing displayed cuts consistent with sharp ceramic fragments, O'Boyle noted.Forensic dentist Romina Carabott determined that Williams likely caused three bite marks on Miss Yemm's abdomen plus another on her wrist.Drug analysis revealed Williams possessed 12.2 grams of class B mephedrone, 9.9 grams of mephedrone combined with monosodium glutamate, and 1.02 grams of amphetamine sulphate mixed with caffeine. Williams had been released from prison just two weeks prior to the incident.Dr Richard Jones, the forensic pathologist conducting Miss Yemm's post-mortem examination, documented 24 injury areas encompassing at least 89 separate wounds across her body. Head injuries comprised half of these wounds, with Dr Jones attributing death to sharp force trauma to the face and neck.The pathologist clarified that neither the bite marks nor traces of amphetamines and cannabis found in her system contributed to her death.The inquest proceedings continue.

text: All photographs by Olivia Acland Sierra Leone's brutal 11-year civil war thrust the nation into international headlines due to blood diamonds. In the country's northern regions, rebel forces and government troops waged savage battles for control of diamond-rich territories, financing their operations through stone sales to global buyers.Fourteen years have passed since the conflict's conclusion, yet diamond extraction continues in Kono, the northern district that remains at the heart of the industry. Koidu Holdings, a South African corporation, operates an extensive mining facility equipped with advanced technology capable of blasting through kimberlite deposits and pinpointing diamond-concentrated zones deep underground.Along the riverbanks nearby, artisanal miners gather with their basic equipment: sieves, spades, and buckets. Among them is Philo, who has spent 23 years working Kono's diamond fields. The war forced him to flee, and he lived as a refugee in Guinea until December 2000, when hostilities began subsiding. He resumed mining operations a year after returning home.Most artisanal miners acknowledge going months without discovering diamonds, living in desperate poverty. However, in a nation where 70% of young people lack employment, mining offers at least minimal income opportunities.Typically, men work in three-person teams. Philo collaborates with two friends using a systematic approach: one diver descends to collect buckets of riverbed mud and grit, while a second holds him steady against the current. The third team member gathers the bucket and deposits its contents into a growing pile. Once sufficient material accumulates, the sifting process begins. The men rotate positions regularly to prevent excessive cold exposure.This work is tough and physically straining - if I had the qualifications or opportunity to do another job then I would at once, Philo explains, complaining of chills after emerging from the water. He consumes packets of cheap rum for warmth.The swampy terrain surrounding the river bears evidence of extensive artisanal excavation, with miners scattered throughout the area, frantically scooping and sifting mud. After three hours of painstaking work, Philo celebrates discovering a tiny diamond.Some miners can afford rockers - equipment utilizing power hoses to spray water through mud layers piled onto fine mesh. Once cleared, diamonds become more visible. This luxury remains beyond Philo's reach.We are not able to afford this kind of machinery, we have to manage with just a bucket, spade and shaker [sieve], he explains. Local markets sell each shaker for 25,000 Leones (approximately £3.50).Following his diamond discovery, Philo packs up early and heads to town with his team. This was a very good day, we hadn't seen a diamond for nearly a month, he says happily.En route home, he encounters his elder brother outside a shop. They exchange greetings before the rocky kimberlite mountain created by Koidu Holdings' explosive operations. Philo expresses envy toward their machinery and wealth, particularly as shallow-ground diamonds become increasingly scarce.At home, Philo unwinds in his room with his uncle. During the conflict, rebels shot and killed his mother just outside this same room. His entire house was destroyed and required rebuilding.The next day brings a trip to Koidu town, where Philo sells his diamond at an office near the high street. Current rates reach $3,200 (£2,520) for 40% pure carats, with lower-purity gems commanding significantly less. Philo receives only $35 (approximately £28) for his discovery, yet feels pleased since the amount exceeds his expectations.

text: A US judge in Seattle has issued a temporary nationwide block on President Donald Trump's ban on travellers from seven mainly Muslim nations. A federal judge in Seattle delivered a nationwide blow to President Trump's immigration restrictions Friday, with Judge James Robart rejecting government attorneys' arguments that US states lacked legal standing to contest the executive order.The controversial directive, implemented last week, sparked widespread demonstrations and created chaos across American airports. According to the State Department, approximately 60,000 visas have been revoked since the order took effect.Trump's executive action imposed a 120-day halt to the US Refugee Admissions Programme while establishing an indefinite prohibition on Syrian refugees. Citizens from seven nations—Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen—now face a 90-day suspension of visa privileges.Washington state initiated the legal challenge, later joined by Minnesota in the lawsuit targeting the president's ban. Bob Ferguson, Washington State Attorney General, has condemned the restriction as both illegal and unconstitutional, arguing it creates religious discrimination.The Seattle decision represents a significant setback for the Trump administration. As the BBC's David Willis reports from Washington DC, nationals from the affected countries can theoretically resume US visa applications, though the administration retains the right to appeal.Trump has defended his policy as essential for American security, promising visa processing would resume once the most secure policies were established. He has consistently denied characterizations of the measure as a Muslim ban.Multiple state attorney generals have declared the order unconstitutional. While several federal judges have temporarily prevented deportations of visa holders, the Seattle ruling marks the first with nationwide application.Legal challenges are proceeding in at least four additional states—Virginia, New York, Massachusetts and Michigan—with courts examining Trump's executive order.Earlier Friday, a Boston judge refused to extend temporary restrictions that had prevented detention or removal of foreigners legally authorized for US entry. That Massachusetts-specific ban expires February 5.

text: This morning on the Today programme, Ed Miliband prayed in aid Sir Nick Macpherson when repeating his view that the big economic mistake of the last Labour government was a failure to regulate the banks properly, rather than to spend too much. Excessive risk had built up in the system; the regulators failed to appreciate the scale of that risk or to address it.It was 'a failure of the Group of Seven economic policymaking establishment', myself included. Inevitably, countries with bigger banking sectors, notably the UK, were worse affected.This admission represents Sir Nick's frank acknowledgment that he, alongside the broader economic decision-making elite across wealthy developed nations, remained blind to the reckless risks banks pursued while chasing profits and bonuses.His concession extends to recognizing how the UK Exchequer became dangerously dependent on revenues from an inflated financial services sector. Corporation taxes from banks' excessive profits proved unsustainable, while capital gains tax and stamp duty from housing and financial securities bubbles—both inflated by banks' irresponsible lending—proved equally fleeting.This context explains why the apparent contradiction between Tory claims that Labour overspent and Ed Miliband's insistence that a global banking crisis caused the UK's economic troubles is less stark than it appears.From 2000 to 2007, Gordon Brown and his economic team—including the impartial civil service's Nick Macpherson, plus party colleagues Ed Balls and Ed Miliband—felt justified increasing spending by four GDP percentage points. Their confidence stemmed partly from optimism that City growth and associated tax revenues would prove more than a temporary Exchequer windfall, as I noted on Friday.Brown's judgment proved incorrect, as did that of Macpherson, Balls, and Miliband.This error has received official recognition: both the IMF and OECD have retrospectively calculated that the UK's cyclically adjusted deficit—the portion of the spending-revenue gap that normal growth cannot eliminate—exceeded that of other major wealthy nations.IMF figures show the UK's 2007 cyclically adjusted deficit at 5.3%, compared to 3.5% in the US and 3.7% in France. A significant factor in the UK's larger structural deficit was financial services' disproportionately massive share of the British economy compared to the US and other major competitors.However, this context doesn't absolve Brown, Miliband, and Balls' Labour government. They must answer for making substantial long-term public spending commitments based on revenues from an unsustainable, bloated banking sector.Nevertheless, it's noteworthy that mere days before Northern Rock's collapse ended City euphoria, shadow chancellor George Osborne pledged to match Labour's promises for continued public expenditure increases.Effectively, Osborne belonged to Sir Nick Macpherson's same blinkered economic establishment.Yet Osborne's failure to recognize the government's unsustainable spending doesn't diminish Brown, Miliband, and Balls' culpability.They wielded power; he didn't. text: Pressure is increasing on world powers and Iran to sew up a deal on Iran's nuclear programme after many months of negotiations. Ordinary Iranians shared their perspectives with BBC Persian on the ongoing nuclear negotiations, as the prospect of lifting crippling sanctions that have transformed daily life hangs in the balance.The nuclear talks touch every Iranian citizen's existence through sanctions-driven inflation that has forced countless families to abandon their previous lifestyles. Without an agreement during President Rouhani's tenure, significant challenges await both negotiating parties.Since the most recent sanctions targeted Iran's oil and banking sectors, the nation's economy has suffered devastating blows. One business owner explained the harsh reality: I own three factories. Eight years ago they were working at full capacity, now all three are shut. About 400 workers, technicians and engineers have lost their jobs. There are many people like me who used to have small manufacturing companies in industrial cities.The industrial decline has reached alarming proportions. These days our cemeteries are growing faster and doing better than our industrial cities, the factory owner observed.Regarding American commitment to negotiations, the same individual noted: I was following every single minute of the last round of negotiations. If you remember, you could really see the stress on John Kerry's face. It shows Mr Obama needs to find a way to resolve this matter. However strong the lobbies are on the other side, I believe the US president is determined to make a deal and he can achieve that.Skepticism runs deep among other Iranians, however. One citizen expressed fundamental distrust: I'm not optimistic. As our leader says we don't trust the US, the UK or the West in general. Now we see that some people in Iran have put their trust in them and think they can move things forward by negotiation, and the [Supreme] leader has agreed to that. It's happening but personally, I believe the process will fail. It is just a question of when.Internal opposition poses another significant obstacle. I don't think a deal is possible. There are a lot of entrenched groups in Iran like the Basij [volunteer paramilitary force] and most importantly those who are linked to the office of the Supreme Leader. These groups won't let it happen and people will keep feeling the pressure, another Iranian warned.The agricultural sector faces its own struggles. A farmer lamented: I'm a farmer but I can't sell the rice I produce. It's not fair on our people.Even those following negotiations closely maintain realistic expectations about immediate change. A teacher shared: I am a teacher. I'm following negotiations with excitement. But sometimes it feels like it's dragging on and on. Either way I don't think we will witness any major changes straight away. Change will take time to achieve. It won't happen the day after an agreement.

text: Almost half (45%) of young people are checking their mobile phones after they have gone to bed, a poll suggests. A comprehensive study involving 2,750 students aged 11 to 18 has revealed alarming patterns of nighttime mobile phone usage, with one in ten participants confessing to checking notifications at least ten times nightly.Conducted jointly by Digital Awareness UK and the Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference, the research highlights how after-hours device usage leaves students exhausted and struggling with concentration during school hours. Both organizations advocate for implementing a digital detox strategy, suggesting mobile devices be stored away 90 minutes before bedtime or kept entirely outside bedrooms.Among the 45% of respondents who admitted to phone checking during sleep hours, an overwhelming 94% engage with social media platforms. Remarkably, one-tenth expressed anxiety about potentially missing out if they failed to check their devices before sleep. Music listening proved popular among 75% of this group, while more than half (57%) watched films on their devices.Perhaps most concerning, a third (32%) of these young people reported that their parents remain unaware of their nighttime device usage.Charlotte Robertson, co-founder of DAUK, addressed the broader implications: One of the biggest topics around at the moment is excessive social media consumption and how it is affecting our physical and emotional wellbeing.She elaborated on the psychological pressure students face: A lot of them [children] are waking up sometimes with over 100 notifications from conversations that have happened overnight. They want to be that person that is responding at 01:00, and seen to be quite cool, to make sure they catch the joke - it's a huge driver, that anxiety of wanting to know what's happened.HMC chairman Mike Buchanan offered perspective on the underlying motivations: The data suggests those who do check their phones, they're mostly driven by not wishing to miss out. Clearly there are some times when children are not concentrating because they are tired, and that has an obvious impact on their ability to keep up with what's going on - there is a desire to stay within the group.However, Buchanan emphasized a balanced approach to technology: It's not that this [technology] is all horrible and terrible and that we should all be wringing our hands. It is more a case that here's the reality, let's use it and try to influence the use of technology in a positive way.

text: So Eddie Jones has gone from South Africa's Stormers to England's strugglers, from Cape of Good Hope to capable of good, it is to be hoped. The appointment unfolded with remarkable speed, yet its significance remains undiminished. For the first time in history, England's rugby union team will operate under foreign leadership. Jones' extensive coaching credentials and his immediate availability, compared to other coveted candidates, largely explain this groundbreaking decision.The selection also reflects a familiar pattern - though not the beach footwear synonymous with Jones' Australian homeland, but rather the tendency of English sporting authorities to choose the complete opposite of whoever previously failed in the role.The Football Association pioneered this approach, which other sports have subsequently adopted.This pattern of reversals spans decades: the modest, budget-conscious Roy Hodgson succeeded the costly, authoritarian Fabio Capello; the seasoned foreign appointment replaced the inexperienced, overwhelmed Englishman Steve McClaren; McClaren himself served as the passionate counterpoint to the detached Sven Goran Eriksson, who initially secured the position because his tactical acumen and composure contrasted sharply with Kevin Keegan's emotional yet unsophisticated approach.The populist Keegan had replaced the reclusive, unconventional Glenn Hoddle. The spiritually reborn Hoddle followed Terry Venables - who departed to address off-field business controversies. Venables' international expertise and appealing playing philosophy stood in stark contrast to Graham Taylor's direct, traditional British methods.This cycle extends beyond football into other disciplines. English cricket replaced the reserved foreign coach Duncan Fletcher with the animated, domestic choice Peter Moores. When Moores lacked international gravitas and influence, the steely Zimbabwean Andy Flower, a former world-leading batsman, took over.Subsequently, when Flower appeared too stern, the upbeat Moores returned, only to face swift dismissal as identical weaknesses emerged - ultimately succeeded by the experienced Australian Trevor Bayliss.The RFU has consistently followed this blueprint since Sir Clive Woodward's dramatic departure from Twickenham. Robinson too rigid? Enter Brian Ashton's attacking philosophy. Ashton lacking command? Summon Martin Johnson's compelling presence. Johnson exposed in his inaugural coaching role? Enter Stuart Lancaster, a grassroots developer with minimal public recognition.This progression leads to Jones. Lancaster possessed merely one Premiership season before receiving England's top job - a campaign that concluded with financially struggling Leeds relegated to the Championship. He had never previously attended matches at Cardiff's Millennium Stadium or Paris's Stade de France.Jones presents a different profile entirely. His coaching journey spans continents - two separate Super Rugby franchises in Australia, assistant roles with Jake White's South African national team, English experience with Saracens, and three years developing Japan before the recent World Cup.His resume includes guiding Australia to one World Cup final and contributing to South Africa's 2007 triumph. Whether he suits England's specific needs remains uncertain.No other rugby union possesses the RFU's financial strength or player depth. This advantage explains why England, unlike Wales, Scotland, and Ireland, traditionally selects from its extensive domestic talent pool for national leadership.Current logic deserves scrutiny. RFU chief executive Ian Ritchie demanded Lancaster's successor possess international credentials. While sensible given Lancaster's specific limitations, this criterion ignores other considerations.Lancaster's failures stemmed from multiple factors. These shortcomings don't automatically afflict every English coach simply due to shared nationality.Had Wales adopted Ritchie's philosophy, Warren Gatland wouldn't have secured appointment - the architect of two Grand Slams during England's struggles and a World Cup semi-final despite limited resources.Ireland would have overlooked Joe Schmidt, who delivered their Six Nations championship last spring. Scotland would have missed Vern Cotter's expertise, who nearly guided his adopted nation to World Cup semi-final glory but for questionable officiating.Michael Cheika, universally praised for Australia's recent resurgence? He lacked international coaching experience initially. Woodward, who elevated England to unprecedented heights? Also an international newcomer upon appointment.Jones boasts impressive achievements, particularly Japan's stunning World Cup upset - their historic 34-32 victory over South Africa two months ago.He merits recognition for both their extraordinary success and execution style. However, will identical methods translate to England's vastly different structure, where he'll exercise less player control and work with different personalities?His late-1990s Brumbies represented Super Rugby excellence. Yet this won't magically produce a breakdown specialist comparable to George Smith if Jones considers current captain Chris Robshaw inadequate for specialized requirements.His record includes setbacks too. Despite Japan's superior World Cup performance compared to England, Australia dismissed Jones in 2005 following eight defeats in nine matches. He resigned from Queensland Reds in 2007 after they finished last in Super 14.Coach selection represents the straightforward element. Transforming the operational system to develop more world-class players matching New Zealand's championship skill-set proves more crucial yet considerably more challenging.Like players, coaches require optimal environments for success - a fortuitous combination of human and financial resources, appropriate specialist support staff, and effective leadership above.Without these elements, the cycle repeats, and one revolution suffices for anyone.

In the case of Wales, if they had followed Ritchie's method, they would not have chosen to call in Warren Gatland, the man who brought two Grand Slams to Wales when England were in their worst period, and who had taken them to the semi-finals of the World Cup, although they had little money to pay him. Ireland would have had to pass over Joe Schmidt, who brought them their Six Nations crown last spring. Jones has a good record, with some setbacks. Clive Woodward, who brought England to unprecedented heights? Vern Cotter, who nearly led his adopted country to World Cup glory, if it weren't for some suspect officiating. The highlight is Japan’s stunning World Cup victory against South Africa, 34-32, in June. The ’90s Brumbies were SuperRugby powerhouses, but will that produce a specialist breakdown player like George Smith if he considers the present captain, Chris Robshaw, unsuitable for such specialist requirements? He deserves recognition for the Brumbies’ extraordinary success, and for their method in achieving it, but will the same method succeed in England, where he will have much less control of the players and must deal with quite different personalities? Japan had done better in the World Cup than England, but even with that, Eddie Jones was sacked from his job as coach of Australia in 2005 after losing eight of nine matches; in 2007, the year after he had left the Queensland Reds, they finished bottom of the Super 14. A coach is an easy matter, but transforming the system so that it can produce world-class players with the skills of a winner is more important and far more difficult. Just as the players themselves need a successful environment, a combination of human and financial resources, and the right support from the appropriate experts, above all leadership.

text: Mexico's Congress has approved sweeping changes to the country's energy industry which will see private oil contracts awarded in the country for the first time since 1938. Wednesday's legislative approval of groundbreaking energy laws marks the end of Pemex's decades-long monopoly, ushering in a new era where international oil companies can compete directly in Mexico's energy sector.The state-owned energy giant Petroleos Mexicanos, officially known as Pemex, will now face competition from global petroleum powerhouses including Chevron, Exxon Mobile and BP following the historic vote. This transformation stems from constitutional amendments that President Enrique Pena Nieto signed into law last year, making energy reform the defining achievement of his presidency.Mexico's oil production has declined dramatically over the past two decades, falling from 3.6 million barrels daily in 2004 to merely 2.5 million today. Deteriorating infrastructure, bureaucratic inefficiencies, and widespread corruption have contributed to this steep decline. Pena Nieto anticipates the reforms will reverse this trend, projecting production levels will return to 2004 peaks by 2025.A more competitive and prosperous Mexico. They have laid the foundation for a new era of development and prosperity for Mexican families, the President declared via Twitter.Starting in 2015, international bidders will begin negotiating contracts directly with the Mexican government for exploration, production, and refining operations. Previously, foreign companies could only secure service agreements with Pemex itself. The legislation also permits private electricity generation, further expanding market liberalization.These sweeping changes represent the culmination of Mexico's economic liberalization efforts that commenced in the early 1980s. The world's ninth-largest oil producer expects to attract billions in foreign investment through these reforms. Earlier this year, similar liberalization occurred when July legislation dismantled billionaire Carlos Slim's America Movil empire, Latin America's dominant telecommunications conglomerate.However, controversy surrounds one particular provision transferring approximately one-third of Pemex's pension obligations to federal government books. Critics argue this burdens taxpayers with costs from years of pension fund mismanagement.Opposition lawmakers dramatically illustrated their disapproval by bringing a life-sized portrait of former President Lazaro Cardenas onto the Senate floor, honoring the leader who nationalized Mexico's oil industry in 1938.

text: The fastest animal on land rarely uses its top speed to capture prey, according to a new analysis. Revolutionary research on cheetahs has revealed that these big cats rely on extraordinary acceleration and lightning-fast speed variations during hunts, rather than simply maintaining top velocity.These magnificent predators generate this explosive acceleration by producing nearly five times the power output of legendary sprinter Usain Bolt during his world-record 100-meter dash. The groundbreaking findings appear in the journal Nature.Prof Alan Wilson from the Royal Veterinary College in Hatfield, UK, who spearheaded the investigation, expressed his astonishment at the results. They are remarkable athletes - not just in terms of their speed, but also with their ability to accelerate and manoeuvre in capturing the prey, he told BBC News.Conventional wisdom has long held that cheetahs reach maximum speeds of 65mph (105km/h) - a figure established in 1965 by a Kenyan scientist who timed a semi-domesticated cheetah sprinting along a straight, firm dirt track. This measurement was later published in the Journal of Zoology three decades after the initial study.However, captive zoo cheetahs, well-nourished and comfortable, rarely need to unleash their full potential. Consequently, most zoo-based speed measurements barely exceeded those of greyhounds - approximately 40mph (64km/h). This discrepancy left researchers questioning whether wild cheetahs might actually surpass the 65mph benchmark when pursuing prey in their natural habitat.Determined to solve this puzzle, Prof Wilson and his colleagues at the college's Structure and Motion Laboratory embarked on a year-long field study. They monitored five wild cheetahs using sophisticated tracking collars equipped with movement sensors and GPS technology.Their discoveries were illuminating: while the cheetahs occasionally reached speeds approaching 60mph, such bursts were rare. During typical hunting scenarios, the cats maintained speeds of 30 to 35 mph. What truly distinguished them was their unprecedented ability to accelerate and change direction with remarkable agility - surpassing any other terrestrial animal previously studied.The research team documented that cheetahs can boost their velocity by nearly 7mph (10km/h) within a single stride. They've arranged to have a low gear so they can accelerate very rapidly up to their top speed, said Prof Wilson.Power output measurements, calculated per kilogram of body weight during brief speed bursts, reveal the cheetah's exceptional capabilities. Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt generated 25 W/kg during his 2009 record-breaking performance. Polo horses produce slightly higher outputs at approximately 30 W/kg, while greyhounds double that figure at 60 W/kg. Remarkably, cheetahs can achieve 120 W/kg.The investigation also uncovered the cheetahs' incredibly strong grip strength, so powerful that their claws literally tear up the ground during runs. This claw deployment proves crucial for executing sharp turns and rapid acceleration or deceleration maneuvers.These precise measurements became feasible only through Prof Wilson's specially designed tracking collars. It is very hard for GPS to work on an animal that is ducking and diving, so the collar is an innovation in its own right, he said.The development process spanned over a decade. We've been working on GPS for 12 years and the collars are the result of those labours. They are not your typical GPS tracking system that you get in the car or phone, Prof Wilson explained.The GPS is far more accurate we are getting positions and speeds five times a second. We combine those with readings from other instruments and we finish up with something that is very much more accurate both in terms of speed and position and very much more robust, Prof Wilson explained.Currently, the research team is deploying these advanced collars to study lions and African wild dogs, seeking comparative data across different predator species.Follow Pallab on Twitter

text: There may be one positive that comes out of the negative number issued on Wednesday morning by the Scottish government. Scotland's economy contracted by 0.2% during the October-December period, a figure that commands significant attention given that another quarter of decline would officially signal recession.While recessions aren't economic apocalypses, their absence would actually contradict historical patterns. Economic cycles naturally include slowdowns, with Australia standing alone among major nations in avoiding recession for decades. However, explaining Scotland's downturn becomes challenging when neighboring countries aren't experiencing similar contractions. The gap between Scottish and UK performance proves difficult to dismiss or rationalize.January-March has already concluded, meaning Scotland cannot now prevent recession for that quarter. Economic data reveals recessions only long after they begin, typically after they've ended. Official confirmation awaits July 3rd.Current figures provide economic insights while simultaneously raising new questions. Services remained flat during the year's final quarter, despite representing three-quarters of Scotland's economy. Annual data indicates stagnant public sector services, with health and education output barely registering movement despite measurement difficulties.Financial services emerged as strong performers, with technical, scientific and administrative support services showing even greater strength.Construction output has declined from previously elevated levels over three years - a sector that previously helped Scotland avoid recession in earlier quarters.Production sector declines prove particularly steep. Manufacturing dropped 8% across two years, with textiles falling further. Metals and machinery plummeted 24% over two years, significantly impacting oil and gas sector supply chains.Computer equipment categories fell 6% since 2013 and 44% since 2000 - roughly when Silicon Glen discussions ceased. Even food and drink production, championed as Scotland's production and export hope, experienced slight output decreases from 2015 to 2016.Comparing late 2016 with 2015's final quarter reveals economic stagnation, while UK economy growth reached 1.9%. Annual comparisons show Scotland's anemic 0.4% growth against the UK's 1.8%.International comparisons highlight Scotland's struggles. While Scottish output stalled, US growth reached 2% between December 2015 and 2016, with Eurozone growth at 1.7%. Developing economies typically grow faster - India achieved 7% growth, China nearly matching that figure.Scotland's closer comparators include Ireland, rebounding dramatically with 7.2% growth, and Iceland's remarkable 11.3% expansion. Norway managed 1.8% growth despite oil and gas sector challenges. Sweden and Denmark both achieved 2.3% growth.Scotland joined Russia's doldrums with 0.3% growth. Oil-revenue dependent nations and war-affected countries dominate contraction lists: Brazil continued nightmare decline with 2.5% output reduction, while Venezuela collapsed catastrophically by 18%.Fourth-quarter 2016 numbers challenge arguments that oil and gas slumps explain everything, as stagnation and contraction spread widely across sectors.Post-referendum pound weakening hasn't provided expected export sector boosts. Service sectors - representing three-quarters of the economy - remained flat.The Scottish government attributes struggles to Brexit uncertainty. Newly-commissioned consumer sentiment measures plummeted post-referendum, reflecting broader economic rather than individual household expectations.Finance Secretary Derek Mackay, speaking during a life science business visit following results release, addressed why Scotland feels Brexit effects differently than the UK.Perhaps Scots understand Brexit implications better, he suggested. Perhaps stronger pro-European sentiment makes trading relationship losses more acutely felt.Perhaps so, but something more than that has to be going on, additional factors must contribute. Scotland's distinctive challenges include low business start-up rates, limited corporate headquarters, and relatively poor business research and development spending.Some blame excessive public sector dependence. Spending squeezes could disproportionately affect countries with larger public expenditure.European periphery positioning creates issues, though Ireland and Iceland seem unaffected.More subdued property markets release less homeowner equity for borrowing, spending, and investment.Politics adds complexity. If Brexit uncertainty damages consumer confidence and economic growth, I questioned whether independence referendum prospects help or hinder the economy.Mackay's response: independence benefits the economy. Even independence debates can prove positive, he argues.Latest Gross Domestic Product releases prompt discussions about statistical reliability, given their foundation on survey evidence, economic inference, educated estimates, and seasonal volatility adjustments.Lively debates surround Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (GERS) figure trustworthiness - some well-informed, others less so.During 2013-2014, these figures supported the Scottish government's independence white paper economic arguments. Reduced oil and gas revenues have since changed fiscal circumstances, making them less supportive now.Given his government department compiles these statistics, what does the finance minister think?GERS is a range of estimates, he explains. A number of the statistics are based on estimates. I don't believe GERS is the starting position of an independent Scotland. It's a reflection of where we are now.So I'll take those statistics at face value. But that's separate to the argument we can have about what you could do with the economic levers of an independent nation, where we could make different choices. I accept the estimates as they are, but I think we could do so much better.Regarding accuracy as current reflections: In terms of the statistics available between the UK government statistics, the ONS (Office for National Statistics) and what the Scottish government produces, yes, they are accurate, says Mr Mackay. But they are an accurate assessment of estimates of where we are right now - not the starting position of an independent Scotland.The next GERS figures, covering the financial year ending within hours of this writing, await August publication.

text: Walsall interim head coach Jon Whitney is not certain of his future role at Bescot, despite coming so close to leading the club to promotion. Walsall's remarkable season ended in heartbreak as they suffered a crushing 6-1 aggregate defeat to Barnsley in their League One play-off semi-final. Despite this disappointment, Jon Whitney's brief two-month tenure as manager represented the club's most productive period, with the team falling just one point short of securing automatic promotion.Whitney's future at the club remains uncertain, though he expressed his desire to continue being involved. I've planned to be part of it. Which role that is then we'll see, he stated. Speaking to BBC WM, Whitney emphasized his need for reflection: I need to reflect, sit back, take a breath and see where it takes me.The Saddlers' campaign was significantly disrupted by managerial changes. Dean Smith's mid-season departure to Brentford, followed by the underwhelming performance under replacement Sean O'Driscoll, ultimately derailed their promotion ambitions. O'Driscoll's arrival in December initially coincided with Walsall sitting second in League One. After winning his first match at the Banks's Stadium, he cautioned BBC Sport: They are punching above their weight. I think the second half of the season is going to be a little bit more difficult.However, O'Driscoll's prediction proved inaccurate following his own departure after a home league loss to Barnsley in March. The statistics reveal a striking transformation under Whitney's leadership. His impressive win ratio of 2.08 points per game would have been sufficient to secure the League One title comfortably if maintained across an entire campaign.Reflecting on the turbulent period, Whitney acknowledged the challenges: This has been an incredible shift for me since Dean went, and especially since Sean went. I need to look at myself and look at my staff and see if I could do anything different. But the players have got the taste for it now, he explained. He characterized Walsall as a developing club, who have overachieved this season, while stressing the importance of creating similar opportunities in the future.The manager acknowledged that retaining the current squad presents significant challenges. We are going to try to keep the squad together if we can, but it might be a big ask. We will only be able to judge when we know the players we are keeping and the players we are bringing in, Whitney concluded.The season's managerial statistics tell the story of Walsall's rollercoaster campaign:Dean Smith (until 30 Nov): 19 games - 10 wins, six draws, three losses, 36 points, 1.89 points per gameJon Whitney/John Ward/Neil Cutler (30 Nov-18 Dec): One game - one win, three pointsSean O'Driscoll (18 Dec-6 Mar): 14 games - five wins, five draws, four losses, 20 points, 1.42 points per gameWhitney (6 Mar onwards, excluding play-offs): 12 games - eight wins, one draw, three losses, 25 points, 2.08 points per game

text: Technology developed by a professor at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh could help millions of people exposed to high levels of arsenic in their water supplies. Bangladesh has unveiled the world's first fully autonomous, solar-powered treatment plant designed to combat arsenic contamination—and early results show dramatic reductions in toxic chemical levels.While Western nations rarely question their water quality, millions worldwide face a deadly threat lurking in their daily supply. Prof Bhaskar Sen Gupta from Heriot-Watt University highlights alarming statistics: over 137 million people across 70 countries encounter arsenic exposure through their drinking water every day. When this contaminated water irrigates crops, arsenic accumulates in food sources as well.Though British crime fiction immortalized arsenic as a lethal poison, its real-world impact differs significantly. Rather than causing immediate death, arsenic exposure through drinking water triggers various debilitating conditions—cancers, severe skin disorders, and even type 2 diabetes.Bangladesh represents Prof Sen Gupta's primary focus as a water technologist. The country's arsenic contamination stems from natural sources, transported as sediment through rivers flowing from the Himalayas over millions of years. For decades, this arsenic remained safely trapped in riverbanks and stream beds. However, it now dissolves invisibly and without taste into shallow aquifers that supply local communities.Despite its natural origins, human intervention created this crisis. Modern agricultural practices demonstrate the law of unintended consequences perfectly. New rice varieties designed for higher yields disrupted nature's delicate balance.The new, high-yielding varieties of rice require a lot more water and fertiliser, Prof Sen Gupta explains. Fertiliser-rich water from the rice fields reaches the sub-surface, but due to lack of oxygen the arsenic bearing minerals become by default a kind of participant in the reaction and break up, producing a very toxic type of arsenic.Prof Sen Gupta's innovative approach essentially outsmarts nature itself. The system extracts water from wells, gradually introduces oxygen, then returns it underground. This oxygenated water encounters bacteria adapted to oxygen-depleted environments—requiring gradual oxygen introduction to prevent bacterial death.Increased oxygen levels prompt these bacteria to transform liquid arsenic into harmless solids that bind to sand particles within the aquifer. This entire process occurs underground, never bringing arsenic to the surface.The subterranean arsenic removal (SAR) technique operates without chemicals and generates zero waste. Prof Sen Gupta and his team have refined SAR over nearly ten years.The breakthrough lies in solar power integration and autonomous operation. Once calibrated, this delicately balanced system runs via remote control.Comilla district in Bangladesh now hosts the inaugural plant, supported by Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council funding and Bangladesh Green Energy Foundation assistance. The facility currently serves 200 schoolchildren, with capacity expanding to 1,000 people as the process spreads throughout the aquifer.Results prove remarkable. Initial arsenic levels measured 239 micrograms per litre—far exceeding the World Health Organisation's 10-microgram safety threshold. After merely seven weeks, levels plummeted to just two micrograms per litre.Modern connectivity enables global operation, as Prof Sen Gupta notes: We can run the plant from anywhere in the world as long as you have the wifi connection. The NGO who are running it, the Bangladesh Green Energy Foundation, are actually running it from Dhaka more than 300km [186 miles] away.Prof Sen Gupta envisions knowledge transfer from Heriot-Watt to worldwide applications. We as a global university would like to be responsible for global problems and global issues - and be part of the solution, he states.His planned charity will offer compelling value: £5,000 can transform a thousand lives.

text: The first victims of the St Petersburg metro explosion have been named, as investigators continue to piece together the identity of the attacker. A devastating explosion that ripped through St. Petersburg's metro system on Monday has claimed 14 lives and left nearly 50 people wounded, with investigators pointing to a suicide bombing carried out by Akbarzhon Jalilov, a man born in Kyrgyzstan.The attack, which occurred between two stations, has revealed heart-wrenching stories of heroism and tragedy. Among the victims was Irina Medyantseva, a 50-year-old doll-maker who, according to Russian reports, made the ultimate sacrifice attempting to protect her daughter from the blast. Medyantseva succumbed to her injuries while being transported in an ambulance, though her 29-year-old daughter Yelena survived with injuries and remains in stable condition at a local hospital.The victims spanned generations, from 18-year-old Ksenia Malyukova to 71-year-old Yuri Nalimov, Russia's investigative committee confirmed. Dilbara Alieva, a 20-year-old from Azerbaijan, initially survived the explosion but later died from her wounds after being hospitalized. Kazakhstan's foreign ministry reported that one of their citizens, 20-year-old student Maksim Aryshev, also perished in the attack. Social media initially and incorrectly identified Aryshev as the bomber on Monday.Kyrgyzstan's security service identified the suspected perpetrator as Akbarzhon Jalilov, born in the Kyrgyz city of Osh in 1995, who had acquired Russian citizenship. Russian investigators later corroborated this identification and revealed that Jalilov had also planted a second explosive device that failed to detonate. No terrorist organization has claimed responsibility for the bombing.St. Petersburg's metro system has resumed operations, yet the scars of Monday's violence remain visible. At Sennaya Ploshchad station, where the attack's aftermath is most keenly felt, passengers encounter a massive memorial of flowers. Throughout the morning, residents have continuously added to this shrine, leaving behind notes, stuffed animals, and lighting candles in remembrance.The city struggles to return to normalcy while grappling with profound shock. Emotional residents, some in tears, continue visiting the memorial site. I felt compelled to bring flowers because this attack was so terrible, said Irina, a local woman whose mother was horrified by the attack's random nature. Everyone I know is fine, but it could have been any one of us.Tuesday morning brought additional bomb scares to the metro system, forcing the closure and cordoning off of several stations as security teams conducted sweeps. These incidents underscore a city now living on edge.The explosion struck Monday afternoon after the train departed Sennaya Ploshchad station. Senior investigator Svetlana Petrenko informed Russian media that the train driver's crucial decision to proceed to Tekhnologichesky Institut station likely prevented additional casualties by enabling rapid rescue operations.Train driver Alexander Kaverin described his actions to reporters: I just followed the procedure. You will know that this isn't the first terrorist act that we've had, there've been explosions before, so smart people came up with smart procedures. And these procedures say that in this situation I had to take the train to the nearest station. This is what I did. The train kept moving. There was a bang and lots of dust, but the train kept on moving.The discovery of an unexploded device at Ploshchad Vosstaniya station on Monday further indicated a coordinated assault. Metro officials announced that both Kaverin and another employee who located the unexploded bomb would receive recognition for their actions.

text: Japanese carmaker Toyota has regained its slot as the world's biggest vehicle maker, capping a year of a dramatic turnaround in its fortunes. General Motors, the world's largest automaker in 2011, witnessed Toyota reclaim the global crown after the Japanese manufacturer reported selling 9.75 million vehicles throughout 2012 - representing a remarkable surge of more than 22% compared to the previous year. Meanwhile, GM's sales reached 9.29 million vehicles during the same period.The dramatic turnaround for Toyota comes after the company's 2011 performance suffered devastating setbacks from natural disasters that struck both Japan and Thailand, severely disrupting production capabilities across its manufacturing facilities. Since those challenging times, Toyota and fellow Japanese automakers have experienced a consistent rebound, successfully recapturing market share in crucial territories like the United States.Vivek Vaidya, an automotive analyst with Frost & Sullivan, explained to the BBC: The last two years have been very difficult for Toyota. He emphasized that the regaining of the top slot would definitely be heartening for the firm and is good news for its investors and share holders.Other Japanese manufacturers also achieved impressive milestones in 2012. Nissan Motor reported global sales of 4.94 million vehicles, marking nearly a 6% increase from the prior year, while Honda Motor experienced an even more substantial 19% jump, reaching 3.82 million vehicles sold.Beyond natural catastrophes, Japanese carmakers have grappled with the burden of a strengthened yen. When the currency appreciates, it not only inflates the cost of Japanese products for international consumers but also diminishes corporate profits as companies convert foreign revenues back to yen - a particular challenge for export-dependent firms like Toyota.Recent weeks have brought welcome relief as the yen has weakened considerably against the US dollar. Since November, the Japanese currency has plummeted nearly 15%, trading around 90.8 yen per dollar during Monday's Asian trading session.This currency shift promises positive implications for Toyota's expansion prospects. The decline in the yen is a welcome relief for Toyota, Frost & Sullivan's Mr Vaidya noted. We are likely to see profit margins rise, giving it more cash in hand and the ability to invest in developing new technologies, which should help in its growth momentum going forward.Reflecting this optimism, Toyota upgraded its annual profit projections in November, forecasting a net profit of 780bn yen ($8.6bn; £5.4bn) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2013 - an increase from the previously estimated 760bn yen.Nevertheless, significant challenges loom ahead, particularly the ongoing territorial tensions between Japan and China. As the world's largest automotive market, China represents a critical growth engine for companies like Toyota. The dispute over islands in the East China Sea, which intensified late last year, has strained bilateral relations and contributed to declining Japanese exports to China.With the territorial conflict remaining unresolved, concerns persist that renewed tensions could emerge in coming months, potentially damaging trade relationships further. Such developments risk fueling anti-Japanese sentiment among Chinese consumers, which could severely impact Japanese automotive brands' sales performance in this vital market.Industry analysts warn that any deterioration in China sales would likely create substantial headwinds for Toyota's continued growth trajectory.

text: History, they say, is written by the victors. Beneath the shadow of a massive windmill that once dominated one of the West Indies' most prolific sugar estates, visions of commanding British colonists easily come to mind.Yet despite meticulous records documenting the industry that fueled the British Empire's expansion, the experiences of enslaved Africans who made it all possible remain largely untold.An ambitious excavation at Betty's Hope plantation in Antigua aims to remedy this historical gap. Researchers are investigating an 18th-century slave settlement—among only a few ever discovered in the Caribbean—hoping recent archaeological finds will illuminate this dark chapter of history.The village's discovery in 2013 marked what Dr Georgia Fox, the project's leader, calls a eureka moment after the site had evaded archaeologists for decades.Her team from California State University, Chico, successfully located the settlement by combining cutting-edge electronic surveying technology with historical maps from 1710.It felt like a miracle, Dr Fox told the BBC. We'd seen all these dots on the maps and we now realised they signified the slave village. It was an amazing discovery.The excavations have since yielded remarkable artifacts that provide unprecedented insights into the daily existence and cultural practices of the plantation's 400 enslaved people.First we found what appeared to be a very specific type of rough pottery, called Afro-Antiguan ware, made by slaves. Pots were created by coiling pieces of local clay and would have been used for cooking stews, Dr Fox explains.More recent deep excavations into the village center revealed extraordinary discoveries. We found some remarkable things like cowrie shells from East Africa which were used as currency, for games or good luck charms, she notes.These shells raise intriguing questions, given that Antigua's enslaved population typically originated from West Africa rather than East Africa.Additional finds included Dutch delftware—likely obtained through bartering, trading, or as gifts to slaves—and two corners of a beautifully made limestone wall which was tantalising as most slave homes were standard wattle and daub, Dr Fox continues.Dr Fox's team initiated excavation work in 2007, beginning with the plantation's Great House before moving to the Still House, where rum—sugar's primary byproduct—was produced.The former 700-acre complex, established around 1650, functioned as a largely self-sufficient community housing field laborers, domestic servants, overseers, skilled tradesmen, a blacksmith, and a physician.During peak operations, the plantation's twin windmills could generate 12 tonnes of sugar crystals daily. Researchers have explored less than 5% of the extensive site thus far.Great House excavations have uncovered children's toys, musket balls, buttons, cutlery, a door knocker, clay tobacco pipes, and a cod liver oil bottle.The slave village proved challenging to locate due to the organic building materials—palm fronds, sticks, and mud—used in constructing the dwellings.Reg Murphy, a local historian and UNESCO representative who supervises Antigua's archaeological projects, emphasizes the research's crucial importance in reconstructing the island's complete history, particularly for a population largely descended from enslaved people.Everything we learn is about the glory of sugar and the industrial colonial legacy, he says.You never hear about the day-to-day lives of the workers, the other side of the coin.This is a way of learning about their daily routine, what they ate, how they lived, seeing it from their perspective. There were over 400 slaves at Betty's Hope at one time - their stories have never been told.Dr Fox sees even broader implications in the work. There were sugar plantations throughout the world but the Caribbean was the gateway to the New World and had a tremendous impact on the development of America.This was the beginning of capitalism and it all started in the Caribbean. It's important to remember how the New World was created - this is everybody's history.While slavery ended in 1834, sugar production continued as Antigua's economic foundation until tourism replaced it in the 1960s.Sugar changed the world. Every time you bite into a chocolate bar or add sugar to your tea or coffee, you are taking part in a long history and reaching into the past, Dr Fox adds.

text: Ulster secured a home quarter-final and condemned Leicester to an away tie as they ended the Tigers' unbeaten home run of 25 matches in the Heineken Cup. The interval arrived with scores locked at 9-9, as fly-half Toby Flood's hat-trick of penalties for Leicester matched scrum-half Ruan Pienaar's trio for the visitors.Leicester surged ahead after the break when Flood added another penalty before Niall Morris crossed for a converted try, establishing a 19-9 advantage. Ulster's response came through a Pienaar penalty followed by his converted try to draw level, before his fifth successful kick secured a dramatic victory.With Leicester holding a commanding 10-point cushion and thirty minutes remaining, the Tigers appeared destined not only to shatter Ulster's perfect record in this season's competition but also secure home advantage for the quarter-finals.The Irish province's players, however, launched themselves into every tackle and breakdown with ferocious intensity, forcing the hosts onto the defensive. South Africa scrum-half Pienaar orchestrated Ulster's remarkable comeback at Welford Road, a triumph that guarantees their qualification as top seeds.Ulster, the 1999 champions and 2012 runners-up, are currently reconstructing their Ravenhill stadium to accommodate 18,000 supporters. The venue promises completion for the quarter-finals scheduled for April 4-6, and given their passionate fanbase, a sell-out seems certain when they welcome Saracens. The London club secured the eighth and final qualifying spot after Leicester's losing bonus point confirmed the Tigers as the best group runners-up.Initially, Leicester dominated this brutal encounter. Their scrum functioned effectively while full-back Mathew Tait, who later departed with injury, displayed early promise. Second row Graham Kitchener nearly crowned his excellent line-out performance with a try, charging 40 meters before being hauled down inches short. Despite failing to cross, Flood's accurate kicking established a 9-3 Tigers lead.Ulster, however, combines Irish determination with South African physicality and rugby intelligence. With Pienaar orchestrating their game plan and converting his penalty opportunities, they reached parity at half-time.Leicester again started strongly after the restart. When Ulster open-side flanker Chris Henry broke prematurely from a scrum, Flood restored the Tigers' advantage, which they quickly extended to ten points.Tom Youngs powered forward from Flood's high kick, and when Leicester recycled possession, the fly-half delivered a precise grubber kick that winger Morris won in the race to touch down. Flood's conversion made it 19-9, seemingly putting Leicester in control.Ulster refused to surrender, striking back five minutes later when hooker Youngs transgressed at a ruck, allowing Pienaar to find his target. The game's decisive moment arrived when Pienaar charged down Flood's kick, won the race to the ball, and converted his own try from wide out to level at 19-19.With the match balanced on a knife-edge, Leicester threatened after Flood's excellent penalty to the corner earned an attacking line-out. The fly-half, however, spilled a pass five meters from the line as the Tigers pressed forward.Ulster fought their way back into Leicester territory, where Pienaar demonstrated his class with a long-range penalty to edge the visitors ahead.Leicester earned a late scrum in Ulster territory, but the visitors won possession against the head, extinguishing the Tigers' hopes as the Irish province completed six victories from six matches and arranged what promises to be an electric homecoming at Ravenhill.Ulster captain Johann Muller said: It seems like it's happening every week, when Ruan scores all the points - he was outstanding. We came here to get a home quarter-final. Sarries totally outplayed us last season - they are a great side and don't mind going away to get a result. It's two months away and at this stage we will just enjoy the moment. We have not achieved anything yet and there's a huge amount of work left if we are to achieve something.Leicester boss Richard Cockerill commented: We're disappointed with the result, but it was a good game. Ten points up we needed to control the game better but we did not manage the back field as well as we would have liked and they exposed us. At the moment it's probably Toulon [away in the last eight], tomorrow it may be Clermont who have an average home record - what is it, 73 games unbeaten? We are in the quarter-finals and we have suffered a lot of adversity [through injuries], so that's not a bad effort from us.Leicester: Tait; Morris, Smith, Allen, Goneva; Flood, B Youngs; Ayerza, T Youngs, Cole, Slater, Kitchener, Gibson, Salvi, Crane.Replacements: Hamilton for Tait (38), Mele for B Youngs (69), Hawkins for T Youngs (68), Deacon for Kitchener (46), Mafi for Crane (19), Williams for Smith (80).Not Used: Stankovich, Balmain, Williams.Ulster: Payne; Trimble, Cave, L Marshall, Gilroy; P Jackson, Pienaar; Black, Best, Afoa, Muller, Tuohy, Wilson, Henry, Williams.Replacements: Court for Black (55), Henderson for Tuohy (64), Diack for Williams (55).Not Used: Herring, Lutton, McIlwaine, P Marshall, Allen.Att: 24,000Ref: Nigel Owens (Wales).

After the Tigers had established a lineout, Flood put a penalty into the corner, a clever prank, which the Ulster flanker Tom Youngs tracked down, but which the Ulster winger Morris, beating the Tom Youngs chase, won the race to grab, and the kick went in, giving us a 19-point lead. The Tigers' inside-half dropped the ball five meters from the line as the forwards pressed. The Ulstermen then drove back into Leicester territory and Pienaar, in his elegant way, tipped the advantage to the visitors with a penalty kick from long range. We came here to win a home quarter-final, and last year it was Sarries who absolutely dominated us, they're a wonderful team and don't mind away. We are disappointed with the result, but we are happy with the game. We should have controlled the game better at ten points, but we didn't manage our backs as well as we wanted to and they took advantage. And when the Tigers had a late scrum in the Ulster half, the Ulstermen held the ball at the head of the scrum and thus put an end to their hopes, thereby securing a sixth victory in six games, and setting up an electric return home at Ravenhill. For a quarterfinal, and with the misfortune of the injuries, this is not bad. Now it's Toulon who'll be away in the semi-finals, but tomorrow it could be Clermont who are excellent at home: 73 matches without a loss, I think. Two months later, we will have to enjoy the moment, because we still have a lot to do if we want to get something out of it.

text: Auditors have warned MSPs about severe problems faced by three health boards. A watchdog investigation has revealed that NHS24's new computer system has exceeded its original budget by 55% and experienced a two-year delay in implementation, according to Audit Scotland findings.The report to MSPs disclosed that the IT project's completion date shifted dramatically from June 2013 to October 2015, while costs ballooned from an initial £75.8m estimate to £117.4m. Audit Scotland warned that these delays created substantial additional costs and risks for the health service.Meanwhile, NHS Tayside faces mounting financial pressures, requiring a £14.2m Scottish Government loan to achieve break-even status in 2014/15 - marking the third consecutive year the health board has needed emergency funding. Overspending on staffing costs, holiday pay, and primary care prescribing contributed to the shortfall.The financial challenges don't end there for NHS Tayside. Beyond repaying the existing loan, auditors cautioned that the board must identify £27m in savings for the 2015/16 period.NHS Highland also drew scrutiny, though auditors acknowledged improvements following critical findings in their 2013/14 accounts review. Despite progress, the watchdog emphasized the need for enhanced long-term financial planning and reduced dependency on temporary cost-cutting measures.Ian Crichton, NHS24's chief executive, acknowledged the report outlines a series of weaknesses dating back to 2011. He explained: Delays in this major IT programme have led to a significant increase in costs. During the last 16 months an expert team has been working hard to bring the project back on track. The new system will be in place by the end of October.NHS Tayside chief executive Lesley McLay attributed the difficulties to increasing demands on services, stating: NHS Tayside's board has been building a programme of improvement and transformation since the beginning of this financial year. This medium-term programme, led by clinical staff who are partnered with managers, prioritises the delivery of service improvement and benefits for patients and also supports the delivery of sustainable financial balance for NHS Tayside.Garry Coutts, NHS Highland's chairman, expressed satisfaction with the audit findings, describing them as recognition of robust measures implemented after the 2013/14 review. He commented: It is heartening to read in this latest report that the auditor has concluded that we have strengthened our financial management arrangements, transparency and scrutiny of our financial performance. This latest report makes the point that it is important for the board to build on these improvements given the challenges ahead. That is something we are determined to do.
